# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 39

Volume front matter

Series title page

## Patrology in Full

That is, a universal library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III: a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with numerous manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indices following each volume and each author of importance; arranged with chapters properly distributed within the text itself, and with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as by works possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in what places in their works, commented on the several texts of the several books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, and the low price; especially since this collection, single, methodical, and chronological, brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, gathered from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Complete Courses* in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Class IV: On Various Subjects

*(C, G)*

## Sermon 341

[Note: [Col. 1493] Corrected against two *cl.* manuscripts, against *c.s.r.v.*, and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1493] Elsewhere, *On Time*, sermon 40.]

### On the Three Ways in Which Christ Is Understood in Scripture; Preached Against the Arians

[Note: [Col. 1493] Bede and Florus frequently cite this sermon in connection with Paul’s Epistles.]

## Chapter One

### 1. Christ Is Named in Scripture in Three Ways

Our Lord Jesus Christ, brothers, insofar as we have been able to observe the sacred pages, is understood and named in three ways when he is preached—whether through the Law and the Prophets, through the apostolic Epistles, or through faith in the events that occurred, which we learn in the Gospel.

The first way is according to God and that divinity which is coequal and coeternal with the Father, before the assumption of flesh.

The second way is when, having assumed flesh, the same one is both God who is man and man who is God, according to a certain distinctive property of his excellence by which he is not made equal to other human beings, but is read and understood to be the mediator and head of the Church.

The third way is, in a certain sense, Christ in his entirety, in the fullness of the Church—that is, the head and the body—according to the fullness of a certain perfect man, in whom we individually are members. This is preached to believers and offered for recognition to the discerning.

Within so short a time we cannot either recall or explain all the many testimonies of Scripture by which we might establish all three of these categories. Nevertheless, we cannot leave everything unproved. By recalling certain testimonies, therefore, we shall enable you yourselves to observe and discover in the Scriptures the others that, because of the limits of time, we are not permitted to recall.

## Chapter Two

### 2. The First Way in Which Christ Is Preached as God: The Likeness of the Word

To the first way of making known our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior, the only Son of God, through whom all things were made, belongs that passage which is the noblest and most glorious in the Gospel according to John:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:1–5).

These words are marvelous and astonishing, and before they are understood they ought to be embraced. If food were placed before your mouths, one person would take one portion of the food and another person another portion. One food would reach everyone, though not the whole food would reach everyone.

So now, as it were, a kind of food and drink of words is placed before your ears; and yet the whole reaches everyone. Or perhaps, when I speak, one person takes one syllable for himself and another person another? Or one person takes one word and another another word? If that were so, I would say as many words as I see people, so that at least individual words might reach everyone. Indeed, I easily say more words than there are people here; yet everything reaches everyone.

Is a human word, then, not divided into syllables so that everyone may hear, while the Word of God is cut into fragments so that it may be everywhere? Do we imagine that these words, which sound and pass away, can in any respect be compared with that Word which remains unchangeable? Or, because I have said these things, have I compared them?

But in whatever way I could, I wished to make this clear to you: what God displays in bodily things may help you to believe what you do not yet see concerning spiritual words.

Let us now pass to better things. Words resound and depart. Think about justice in your spiritual thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 1494] These words—“in your spiritual thoughts”—seem to be superfluous.]

A person established in these western regions thinks about justice; a person established in the East thinks about justice. How is it that one thinks of the whole of justice and the other of the whole? How does one see the whole and the other the whole? For whoever sees justice, according to which he conducts some action, conducts it justly. He sees inwardly and acts outwardly.

From where does he see inwardly, if nothing is present to him? Since he himself is placed in one part, will another person’s thought not reach that same part? Yet when you, placed here, see in your mind the same thing that someone placed far away sees, and the whole shines for you while the whole appears to him—because divine and incorporeal things are wholly everywhere—believe that the whole Word is in the Father and the whole in the womb.

Believe this concerning the Word of God, who is God with God.

## Chapter Three

### 3. Another Way in Which Christ Is Commended as God and Man

But now hear another presentation, another way in which Scripture presents Christ. What I have said was said before the assumption of flesh.

Now hear what Scripture proclaims at this point: “The Word,” it says, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

For if the one who had said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” had remained silent about the humanity of the Word, he would have proclaimed the divinity of the Word to us in vain.

In order that I might see that reality, this reality is enacted here with me; in order that he might cleanse me for contemplating it, he himself comes to the aid of my weakness. By assuming human nature from human nature itself, he became man.

He came with the beast of his flesh to the one who lay wounded on the road (Luke 10:30–37), in order to shape and nourish our small faith through the mystery of his incarnation,

[Note: [Col. 1495] Some books read, “strengthen.”]

and to make the mind clear for seeing what he never lost through what he assumed.

He began to be man, yet did not cease to be God. This, therefore, is the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the fact that he is mediator, according to the fact that he is head of the Church: that God is man and man is God, as John says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

### 4. Christ Commended in Both Ways by the Apostle

Hear both realities now in that very well-known passage of the apostle Paul:

“Though he was in the form of God,” he says, “he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

This is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

How could the Apostle say, “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized,” if he is not equal to God? But if the Father is God and he is not God, how is he equal? Where John says, “The Word was God,” Paul says, “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.”

And where John says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” Paul says, “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

Pay attention: through the fact that he became man, through the fact that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, through this he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

What did he empty? Not that he might lose his divinity, but that he might put on humanity, appearing to human beings as what he had not been before he was man.

By appearing in this way he emptied himself—that is, preserving the dignity of his majesty and offering flesh as the garment of humanity.

Thus, through the fact that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant—not taking the form of God. When he spoke of the form of God, he did not say “he took it,” but “when he was established in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” But when he came to the form of a servant, he said, “taking the form of a servant”—through this, therefore, he is mediator and head of the Church, through whom we are reconciled to God by the mystery of humility

[Note: [Col. 1495] Some codices read, “humanity.”]

and of his passion, resurrection, ascension, and future judgment, so that those two future events may be heard when God has spoken only once.

Where are two events heard? Where it says that he “will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

## Chapter Four

### 5. Warning to Beware the Arian Heresy: Virginity of Mind, Integrity of Faith; the Serpent Seducing by a Promise of Knowledge

Holding fast to this, brothers, do not be astonished at the questions of human beings, which spread like cancer, as the Apostle said (2 Timothy 2:17). Rather, guard your ears and the virginity of your minds, like those betrothed by the friend of the bridegroom to present a chaste virgin to one man, Christ.

Your virginity is in the mind. Bodily virginity exists in a few members of the Church; virginity of mind must exist in all the faithful.

The serpent wishes to corrupt this virginity. Concerning him the same Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may also be corrupted and fall away from the chastity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

He says, “your minds”—that is, your thoughts. For this is more properly meant. The senses are understood also of this body: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. The Apostle feared that our minds might be corrupted, where the virginity of faith resides.

Go on now, soul,

[Note: [Col. 1496] Florus and the Cistercian book read, “Now therefore, soul.”]

preserve your virginity, to be made fruitful afterward in the embrace of your bridegroom.

Therefore, as it is written, “Hedge your ears with thorns” (Sirach 28:28).

The question of the Arians disturbed the weaker brothers of the Church, but through the Lord’s mercy the Catholic faith prevailed. He did not abandon his Church; and if he disturbed it for a time, he disturbed it for this reason: that it might always plead with him by whom it would be established upon a solid rock.

The serpent still mutters and does not keep silent. By a certain promise of knowledge he seeks to cast down from the paradise of the Church the one whom he will not permit to return to that paradise from which the first man was cast out.

## Chapter Five

### 6. The Serpent Now Does in the Church What He Once Did in Paradise; How the Father Is Greater Than the Son According to the Arians; the Son Equal to the Father in the Form of God and Less in the Form of a Servant

Pay attention, brothers. What happened in that paradise is happening in the Church. Let no one deceive us away from this paradise. It is enough that we fell from the other; let us be corrected by experience.

It is the same serpent who continually suggests wickedness and impiety. At times he promises impunity, just as he promised it there, saying, “Will you indeed die?” (Genesis 3:4). He suggests such things so that Christians may now live wickedly.

“Will God,” he says, “destroy everyone? Will God condemn everyone?” He says, “I will condemn”; and, “I will forgive those who change; let them change their deeds, and I will change my threats.”

He is the one who murmurs and mutters and says: “Look where it is written, ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John 14:28), “and you say that he is equal to the Father?”

I accept what you say—but I accept both, because I read both. Why do you accept one and refuse the other? For you read both with me.

“Look, ‘The Father is greater than I.’” I accept this, not from you but from the Gospel. And you accept from the Apostle that the Son is equal to God the Father. Join both together; let both agree, because the one who spoke through John in the Gospel himself spoke through Paul in the Epistle.

He cannot disagree with himself. But you do not wish to understand the harmony of the Scriptures because you yourself love to quarrel.

“But I prove it from the Gospel,” he says: “‘The Father is greater than I.’”

And I prove it from the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

How are both true? How does the Apostle teach us, “I and the Father are one”? “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.”

Hear, “The Father is greater than I”; but, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

Look, I show why he is greater; you show in what respect he is not equal. For we read both.

He is less than the Father insofar as he is the Son of Man; equal to the Father insofar as he is the Son of God, because “the Word was God.”

Mediator, God and man: God equal to the Father, man less than the Father. Therefore he is both equal and less: equal in the form of God, less in the form of a servant.

You, then, say: in what way is he equal and in what way less? Is he equal in one part and less in another? Apart from the assumption of flesh, show me one who is both equal and less. I want to see the basis on which you will demonstrate this.

## Chapter Six

### 7. Before the Incarnation the Son of God Was in No Way Less Than the Father

Consider the foolish impiety of savoring the flesh, as it is written: “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Romans 8:6).

Stop here. I am still setting aside the incarnation, and I am not yet speaking of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God. Rather, as though what has already happened had not yet happened, I consider with you: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God.”

I consider with you: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.”

Show me there both the greater and the lesser. What will you say? Will you divide God according to qualities—that is, according to certain bodily or animal affections in which we perceive one thing to be one way and another thing another?

I can indeed speak in this natural manner, but whether you understand it in this way, God knows.

Therefore, as I began to say, before the assumption of flesh, before the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, show me the lesser; show me the equal. Is God one thing and another, so that on one side the Son is less than him and on another side equal to him?

It would be as though we said: “There are certain bodies.” You could say to me, “It is equal in length but less in strength.” Often two such bodies present themselves that they are equal in height but one is weaker and the other stronger.

Are we therefore going to imagine God and his Son as bodies of this kind? Are we going to imagine the one who was wholly in Mary, wholly with the Father, wholly in the flesh, and wholly above the angels?

May God turn such thoughts away from the hearts of Christians.

Perhaps you will think in this way also, saying: “They are equal in strength and length but different in color.” Where is color except in bodily things? But there is the light of wisdom. Show me the color of justice.

If these things have no color, you would not say them of God if you possessed any sense of shame.

### 8. The Son Cannot Be Called Equal in One Respect and Less in Another; In God Power, Wisdom, and the Other Virtues Are Not Distinct

What, then, will you say? “They are equal in power, but the Son is less in wisdom”?

God is unjust if he gave equal power to lesser wisdom. If they are equal in wisdom but the Son is less in power, God is envious, since he gave lesser power to equal wisdom.

But in God everything that is said is the same thing. For in God power is not one thing and wisdom another, strength one thing and justice another, or chastity another.

Whatever of these you say about God is neither understood as one thing and another, nor said worthily; for these are qualities of souls, which that light somehow floods and affects according to their own qualities, just as this visible light affects bodies when it rises.

If it is removed, all bodies have one color—or rather, they must be said to have no color. But when it is brought in and illuminates bodies, although it is itself of one kind, it nevertheless covers them with different brilliance according to the different qualities of the bodies.

Thus these are affections of souls that are rightly affected by that light which itself is not affected, and formed by that which is not formed.

## Chapter Seven

### 9. Justice and Similar Terms Are Said of God Not Properly, but Because Nothing Better Can Be Said

Nevertheless, brothers, we say these things about God because we do not find anything better to say.

I call God just because in human words I find nothing better. For he is beyond justice. Scripture says, “The Lord is just, and he has loved justice” (Psalm 10:8).

But Scripture also says that God repents (Genesis 6:7), and that God does not know (Genesis 18:21). Who would not shudder? God does not know? God repents?

For this reason Scripture also descends beneficially to those expressions at which you shudder, lest you think that the things you consider great are spoken worthily.

And if you ask, “What, then, is said worthily of God?” someone might perhaps answer you and say, “That he is just.”

But another, understanding this more profoundly, might say that even this word is surpassed by his excellence, and that even this is unworthily said of him, although it is appropriately said according to human capacity.

Thus, when someone wishes to prove from Scripture that it is written, “The Lord is just,” he may rightly be answered that the same Scriptures also state that God repents. In this way, just as he does not accept the latter according to the custom of speakers, as human beings ordinarily repent, so he should understand that the term “just” does not correspond to God’s surpassing excellence—although Scripture properly uses it, so that by means of various words the mind may gradually be led toward what cannot be spoken.

You call God just; but understand something beyond the justice you usually imagine in a human being.

Yet Scripture has called him just; therefore it has also called him repentant and ignorant—things you no longer wish to say. As, then, you understand those expressions that now horrify you to have been spoken because of your weakness, so also understand those that you value highly to have been spoken on account of some greater strength.

[Note: [Col. 1498] The Colbertine manuscript reads, “weakness.”]

But whoever goes beyond even these things and begins to think worthily of God, insofar as this is granted to a human being, will discover silence to be praised by the ineffable voice of the heart.

## Chapter Eight

### 10. The Son of God Cannot Be Called Equal in One Respect and Unequal in Another

Therefore, brothers, since in the Lord power is the same as justice—whatever you say of him, you say this same thing, although you say nothing worthily—you cannot say that the Son is equal to the Father in justice but not equal in power, or equal in power but not equal in knowledge.

For if he is equal in one respect, he is equal in every respect, because everything you say there is the same and has the same force.

It is enough, then, that you cannot explain how the Son is unequal to the Father

[Note: [Col. 1499] Several manuscripts read, “equal.” Perhaps it should read, “equal and unequal.”]

unless you posit certain differences in the substance of God. Once you posit them, truth drives you outside, and you do not enter that sanctuary of God where he is seen with the greatest purity.

Since you cannot say that he is equal in one respect and unequal in another, because there are no parts in God; and since you cannot say that he is equal in one respect and less in another, because there are no qualities in God; according to God you cannot call him equal unless he is equal in every respect.

How, then, can you call him less, unless it is because he took the form of a servant?

Therefore, brothers, always pay attention to these matters. If you receive a certain rule in the Scriptures, the light itself will show you everything.

Whenever you find the Son called equal to the Father, understand this according to his divinity. But according to the form of a servant that he assumed, understand him as less, in accordance with what was said, “I am who I am,” and with what was said, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:14–15, 6).

In this way you will hold both what belongs to his nature and what belongs to his mercy.

I think enough has been said about that manner in which our Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, the head of the Church, having become mediator through whom we are reconciled to God, is presented in Scripture as God and man.

## Chapter Nine

### 11. Christ Is Understood in the Third Way as Head and Body

The third way is that in which Christ in his entirety is preached according to the Church—that is, the head and the body.

For the head and the body are one Christ—not because he is incomplete without the body, but because he has also deigned to be complete with us, although without us he is always complete, not only in that he is the Word, the only-begotten Son equal to the Father, but also in the very man whom he assumed and with whom he is at once God and man.

Nevertheless, brothers, how are we his body, and how are we one Christ with him?

[Note: [Col. 1499] The Regius book and Florus read: “How are we his body, if we are not also one Christ with him?”]

Where do we find that the head and body are one Christ—that is, the body together with its head?

The bride speaks, as it were, in the singular with her bridegroom in Isaiah. Certainly one and the same person speaks; and see what he says:

“He bound a turban upon me like a bridegroom, and he adorned me with an ornament like a bride” (Isaiah 61:10).

As bridegroom and bride: he calls the same person bridegroom according to the head and bride according to the body.

They appear to be two, yet they are one. Otherwise, how are we members of Christ? The Apostle states most clearly: “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

All of us together are Christ’s members and body—not only those who are here in this place, but throughout the whole earth; nor only those who exist at this time, but what shall I say? From righteous Abel to the end of the age, as long as human beings beget and are begotten, whoever of the righteous passes through this life, whatever exists now—that is, not merely in this place but in this life—and whatever is yet to come of those who will be born—all of this is one body of Christ, while individuals are members of Christ.

If, then, all are the body, individuals are members. There is certainly a head of which this is the body.

“He himself,” it says, “is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn, holding first place” (Colossians 1:18).

And because it is also said of him that he is always the head of every principality and power (Colossians 2:10), this Church, which is now on pilgrimage, is joined to that heavenly Church in which we have the angels as fellow citizens.

We would arrogantly claim that we will become their equals after the resurrection of our bodies, unless Truth had promised it, saying: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke 20:36). Thus one Church is formed, the city of the great King.

## Chapter Ten

### 12. Christ Is Proclaimed in Scripture in Three Ways; Christ and the Church Are One Christ

Thus, at times Christ is presented in Scripture so that you understand the Word to be equal to the Father.

At other times he is presented so that you understand the mediator: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14); the only-begotten one through whom all things were made “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

At other times he is presented so that you understand the head and the body. The Apostle himself explains most clearly what was said in Genesis concerning man and wife: “The two,” he says, “will become one flesh.”

Observe him explaining this himself, so that we may not appear to dare to say something on the basis of our own conjectures.

“The two,” he says, “will become one flesh.” And he added: “This mystery is great.”

And lest anyone should still think that this concerned man and woman according to the natural union of the two sexes and bodily intercourse, he says: “But I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31–32).

According to this, then, what was said—“The two will become one flesh”—is understood of Christ and the Church: “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:5–6).

And just as bridegroom and bride, so head and body, because “the husband is the head of the wife.”

Whether, then, I say “head and body” or “bridegroom and bride,” understand one and the same thing.

For this reason the same Apostle, when he was still Saul, heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), because the body is joined to the head.

And when, already a preacher of Christ, he suffered from others what he himself had done as a persecutor, he said: “I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Colossians 1:24), showing that what he suffered belonged to the afflictions of Christ.

This cannot be understood according to the head, which now suffers nothing of this kind in heaven, but according to the body, that is, the Church. This body, together with its head, is one Christ.

## Chapter Eleven

### 13. Let the Bride of Christ Act So as to Be Without Spot or Wrinkle

Present yourselves, therefore, as a body worthy of such a head, a bride worthy of such a bridegroom.

That head cannot have an unworthy body, nor can so great a man take an unworthy wife.

“He might present to himself,” it says, “a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Ephesians 5:27).

This is the bride of Christ, having neither spot nor wrinkle.

[Note: [Col. 1501] See *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 38.]

Do you not wish to have a spot? Do what is written: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove your wickednesses from your hearts” (Isaiah 1:16).

Do you not wish to have a wrinkle? Stretch yourself out upon the cross.

For it is not enough that you be washed; you must also be stretched out, so that you may be without spot or wrinkle.

Through washing, sins are removed; through being stretched out, desire for the future age is produced, for the sake of which Christ was crucified.

Hear Paul after being washed: “Not from works of righteousness that we ourselves have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5).

Hear the same man after being stretched out: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14).

# Sermon 342

[Note: [Col. 1501] First revised against Florus, *v.*, and Sirmond; and then, after the edition, corrected against *cl.*.]

[Note: [Col. 1501] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons, number 8.]

### On the Evening Sacrifice

[Note: [Col. 1501] Florus cites this sermon on Romans 11, 1 Corinthians 11, and Hebrews 9.]

In which the beginning of John’s Gospel is explained.

## 1. The Sign of the Cross; the Sacrifice of the Cross

A sermon must be delivered on the evening sacrifice.

For we prayed by singing, and by praying we sang:

“Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2).

In prayer we recognize the human being; in the stretching out of the hands we recognize the cross.

This, then, is the sign that we bear on our forehead, the sign by which we are saved. A sign mocked in order that it might be honored; despised in order that it might be glorified.

God appears as a human being so that the human being may plead; God is hidden so that the human being may die.

“For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

This sacrifice, in which the priest is himself the victim, redeemed us by the blood poured out by the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 1501] Sirmond reads, “not only.” Florus’s reading, “yet not,” is more suitable.]

Yet he did not create us with blood, but redeemed us with blood.

For he created us in the beginning—that is, the Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. We were created by him.

The continuation of the passage adds: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” This is by which we were created.

But by what were we redeemed? Hear:

“What was made,” he says, “in him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

He is still God; what is still being said is that which always remains unchangeable. What is still being said is that which hearts must be cleansed to behold.

But he does not yet say by what they are to be cleansed.

“The light,” he says, “shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

But so that they may not remain darkness and may be able to comprehend it—for sinners are darkness, and unbelievers are darkness—so that they may not remain darkness and may be able to comprehend it, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

See the Word; see the Word as flesh; the Word before flesh.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; all things were made through him.”

Where is the blood here? Look: he is already your creator, but not yet your price.

How, then, were you redeemed? Because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Source/review notes: The manuscript reading *batorum* is retained as uncertain or corrupt because the supplied source gives no secure gloss. Variorum-note boundaries and all supplied column anchors are preserved.

## 2. John Sent Before Christ as a Lamp Before the Light

Pay close attention to what was said a little earlier: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Since, therefore, the darkness did not comprehend the light, human beings needed a human testimony. They were unable to see the day; perhaps they could endure a lamp. Since they were less capable of seeing the day, they could nevertheless endure a lamp in some fashion: “There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light.”

Who was the one about whom it says here that he came to bear witness to the light? [Note: [Col. 1502] Codex cl. reads: “Who was he, about whom it says here that he came to bear witness to the light? Who was he, about whom? John concerning Christ, a lamp concerning the day. Who was he, about whom? John concerning Christ; therefore, a lamp concerning the day. We do not do John an injury; but if we cannot steadfastly gaze upon our day, let us at least praise it with honor. He came to bear witness to the light. He was not the light, but he came to bear witness to the light. How was he not, and so on.”]

How was he not the light, if he was at least a lamp? First observe that he was a lamp. Do you wish to hear of a lamp from the day, and of the day from a lamp? [Note: [Col. 1502] This should be read in accordance with the same codex cl.: “Do you wish to hear of a lamp, a lamp from the day into the day. From a lamp.”]

“You sent to John,” he says, “and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light: he was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:33, 35). What, then, did this John see, that he despised the lamp? “He was not the light, but he came to bear witness to the light.” To what light? “There was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” If every human being, then John as well. [Note: [Col. 1502] Thus the same codex cl., without repeating the word “John,” which remains in the printed editions: “If every human being, then John: John who did not yet …”] He who did not yet wish to reveal the day had himself kindled his own lamp as a witness. But it was such a lamp as could be lit by the day.

Hear John himself confessing: “We have all received from his fullness.” He was thought to be Christ, yet he confessed that he was a human being. He was thought to be the Lord, yet he confessed that he was a servant. You rightly recognize your humility, O lamp, lest the wind of pride extinguish you.

“For there was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world”—that is, every living creature capable of illumination, namely, every human being possessing mind and reason, by which he can become a participant in the Word.

## 3. The World Is Understood in Two Ways

What, then, was that true light, which enlightens every human being possessing a mind and coming into this world? Where was it? “It was in this world.” But the earth too was in this world, and the sun and moon were in this world. Hear about your day, O eye of the human mind: “It was in this world, and the world was made through it.”

It was here in such a way that, even before the world existed, it was not as though there were nowhere for it to be. For God contains by dwelling; he is not contained. Therefore, in a marvelous and ineffable manner, he was in this world.

“And the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” What is the world that was made through him? [Col. 1503] “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), because all things were made through him.

What is the world that did not know him? There is “world” and “world,” just as there is “house” and “house”: a house in construction, and a house in its inhabitants.

A house in construction: as when we say, “He made a great house; he built a most beautiful house.” A house in its inhabitants: as when we say, “A good house—may the Lord bless it; a bad house—may God spare it.”

Thus the world was made through him: both the dwelling and the inhabitants. And the world did not know him—the inhabitants did not know him.

## 4. How Christ Was Not Received by His Own; the Jews Cut Off Because of Pride, the Gentiles Grafted into the Olive Because of Humility; the Centurion’s Humility and Faith

“He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” Why, then, did he come, as though he did not know beforehand that his own would not receive him? Hear why he came. [Note: [Col. 1503] The same codex cl. reads: “Hear for whom he came.”]

“But as many as received him.” His own did not receive him, and his own did receive him. [Note: [Col. 1503] The words “and his own did receive him” are restored from the same codex cl. It reads: “His own did not receive him; the world did not believe.”] The world did not believe, and the whole world believed.

Just as we say, “The whole tree is full of leaves,” does that mean there is no room for fruit? Both can be said and understood: the tree is full of leaves, and the tree is full of fruit. It is one tree in both cases, but its leaves are scattered while its fruits are gathered.

Therefore, his faithful, his servants, [Note: [Col. 1503] The word “his” is here restored from the same codex cl.: “Therefore, his faithful, servants, his beloved.”] his beloved, whose glory, hope, and possession he is—when you hear, “His own did not receive him,” do not grieve, because by believing you belong to him.

“His own did not receive him.” Who are these? Perhaps the Jews, once called out of Egypt, freed by a mighty hand, led across the Red Sea, escaping by dry land while the pursuing enemies were deprived of passage; fed with manna, brought out of slavery, led to a kingdom, purchased by so many benefits.

Behold his own, who did not receive him. But by not receiving him they became alien. They were in the olive tree, but through pride they were broken off.

The wild olive was contemptible, rejected because of the bitterness of its berries. [Note: [Col. 1503] In the same codex cl.: “contemptible because of the bitterness of its berries”; where we had written *baccarum* (“berries”), the codex reads *batorum*, an uncertain or corrupt form for which the source supplies no meaning.] Throughout the whole world it existed; the whole world bristled with the wild olive. [Note: [Col. 1503] The words “with the wild olive” are added from the same codex cl. It reads: “The whole world bristled; yet nevertheless …”] Yet through humility it deserved to be grafted in where the olive tree was cut off through pride (Romans 11:17).

Hear the olive tree boasting and deserving to be broken: “We were not born from slavery; we have Abraham as our father.” The answer is: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.”

Against what they had said—“We were not born from slavery”—comes this: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free.” You boast that you are free? “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:33–39).

How much safer, then, for a human being to be the slave of a human being than of perverse desire?

Nevertheless, through pride they did not receive the humble one. See the wild olive worthy to be grafted in: that centurion, not from the Israelites but from the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 1503] The same codex cl. reads: “not from Israelites, but from Gentiles.”]

“Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” And the Lord: [Col. 1504] “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel.”

In the olive tree I did not find what I found in the wild olive. Therefore let the proud olive tree be cut off, and let the humble wild olive be grafted in.

See the one who grafts; see the one who cuts off: “Therefore I say to you, many will come from the east and the west”—many wild olives will come to be grafted into the olive tree—“and they will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

You have heard how the humble wild olive is grafted in; hear how the proud olive tree is cut off: “But the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:8–12).

Why? Because his own did not receive him. And why was the wild olive grafted in? Because “to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God.”

## 5. Power Given So That We May Become Children of God

Lift up your heart, human race; breathe in the air of life and of the most secure freedom. [Note: [Col. 1504] The same codex cl. reads: “breathe in the airs of life and of the most serene freedom.”]

What do you hear? What is promised to you? “He gave them power.”

What power? Perhaps the power by which human beings become inflated, judging human heads and pronouncing sentences concerning the innocent and the guilty?

“He gave them power to become children of God.” For they were not yet children, and they were becoming children. [Note: [Col. 1504] We use this reading from the same codex cl.: “For they were not yet children, and they become children.”]

For the one through whom they become children of God was already the Son of God, and became the son of man. Thus they were already children of human beings, and they became children of God.

He descended to what he was not, because he was something else. He raised you to what you were not, because you were something else. [Note: [Col. 1504] The words “He raised you to what you were not, because you were something else” are added from the same codex cl. It reads: “Because he was something else. Therefore, raise your hope.”]

Therefore raise your hope. Great is what has been promised to you, but it was promised by one who is great.

It seems great and incredible, [Note: [Col. 1504] The words “but it was promised by one who is great. It seems great” are added from the same codex cl. It reads: “Great is what has been promised to you, and it seems incredible.”] and it is considered almost impossible that children of human beings should become children of God.

But more has been done for them, because the Son of God became the son of man. Therefore raise your hope, O human being; drive unbelief from your heart.

Something more incredible has already been done for you than what was promised to you. Do you marvel that a human being should have eternal life? Do you marvel that a human being should reach eternal life? Marvel instead that God, for your sake, reached death.

Why do you doubt the promise, having received so great a pledge?

See, therefore, how he strengthens you, how he confirms God’s promise: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.”

By what generation? Not by the customary one, not by the old one, not by a transitory or carnal one. “They were born,” he says, “not of flesh, nor of blood, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

Do you marvel? Do you not believe? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–2, and so forth).

Behold from where the evening sacrifice was made. Let us cling to him; let him who was offered for us be offered with us. For in this way, through the evening sacrifice, the old life is put to death, and at dawn the new life rises.

# SERMON CCCXLIII

[Note: [Col. 1505] This sermon is not found complete in our manuscripts.]  
[Note: [Col. 1505] Otherwise, no. 2 among the published sermons from the manuscripts of the Great Chartreuse.]  
On Susanna and Joseph, with an exhortation to chastity. [Note: [Col. 1505] Possidius reviewed it in chapter 10 of the *Index*. The same sermon exists, though shortened by more than half, among the Latin homilies published under the name of John Chrysostom.]

[Col. 1505]

## 1. Susanna as an Example of Conjugal Chastity; Chastity as a Gift of God; Susanna Divinely Freed from False Witnesses

May the divine readings and the holy oracles of God, which have sounded in our ears, make a nest in our minds: may they not fly away and pass on, or sit briefly and depart, but may they produce something.

For if “the sparrow finds a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Psalm 83:4), how much more should the sparrow be the word of God and the turtledove the mercy of God?

We heard the reading about Susanna. Let conjugal chastity be built up, resting upon so firm a foundation and fortified by such a wall that it may repel those lying in wait and convict false witnesses.

The chaste woman would have remained a chaste woman about to die unless the one who saw what was hidden from the judges had been present. Her words were written down—words that she spoke in the garden, that is, in her own orchard. No human being heard those words except the two men who were plotting against the modesty of another man’s wife and, when she resisted, were devising a false testimony.

They alone heard what she said: “I am distressed on every side. For if I do this, death awaits me; but if I do not, I shall not escape your hands. Yet it is better for me not to escape your hands than to sin in the sight of God” (Daniel 13:22).

She despised what she heard because she feared the one whom she did not see, although she herself was visible to his divine eyes. For just as she did not see God, so she was not unseen by God.

God saw what she was building; he watched over his work; he dwelt in his temple. He himself was there and answered those lying in wait. For if the giver of chastity had abandoned her, chastity would have perished.

She said, therefore, “I am distressed on every side.” Yet she was also waiting for the one who would save her from faintheartedness and from the storm of false witnesses, like evil winds.

Amid those winds and waves, however, chastity did not suffer shipwreck, because the Lord was steering the vessel.

The cry was raised; they came; the proceedings began; the case reached judgment. Susanna’s household had believed the false elders against its mistress. Although her blameless and immaculate life seemed sufficient to offer credible testimony to her chastity, nevertheless those elders considered it irreligious not to believe them.

No such report had ever been heard about Susanna. They were therefore false witnesses, but known to God.

The household believed one thing; the Lord saw another. But what the Lord saw, human beings did not know, and it seemed right to believe the elders. Thus she had to die. Yet if the flesh died, chastity would be crowned.

The Lord was present to the woman praying; he heard the woman whom he knew. He did not abandon her so that she would die—the woman whom he assisted so that she would not commit adultery.

The Lord stirred up the [Col. 1506] Holy Spirit in Daniel, still young in age but mature in devotion. Since the prophetic Spirit was in him, he immediately saw the deceit of the wicked elders.

But what he saw had to be shown to the others. “These men,” he said, “are false witnesses; return to judgment.”

He knew that they were false because the prophetic Spirit had revealed it to him; those who did not know had to be instructed. Therefore, if the judges had to be instructed, the witnesses certainly had to be convicted.

In order to convict them, he examined the falsity of the testimony, which he already knew, and ordered them to be separated from one another. He questioned them individually. They could both have the same desire, but they could not have devised the same plan.

One was asked under what tree he had found the adulterers. He answered, “Under a mastic tree.” The other was questioned; he answered, “Under an oak.”

The disagreement between their testimonies revealed the truth and freed chastity (Daniel 13).

## 2. Susanna’s Deliverance Did Not Thereby Constitute Greater Happiness

Chastity, brothers, as I have already said, would have been freed and crowned even if the flesh had eventually died and had died under that judgment.

For we shall all die. No one who desires to escape death acts so as to remove death; he acts only to postpone what is owed.

This holds us all; this is what we shall all repay: what we drew from Adam. Since we do not wish to die, security is not granted to us by the collector of this debt; only postponement is requested.

Susanna, therefore, a religious woman and chaste wife, was certainly destined to die one day. And if that “one day” had been then, what would it have harmed her chastity, while her flesh was placed in the tomb and her chastity was returned to God and crowned by God?

Do you think, brothers, that it belongs to great merit if false witnesses do not prevail against an innocent person? It is not great merit if false testimony does not prevail against an innocent person. It would be great merit if it had not prevailed against the Lord.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself was crucified through the tongues of false witnesses. Yet although those false witnesses prevailed for a time, what harm did they do to the one who was going to rise again?

Thus, by his own example, our Lord God—in his flesh, in his weakness, and in the form of a servant, which he assumed in order to free a servant, seek a fugitive, redeem a captive, release one who was bound, and make a brother from a servant—coming in the form of a servant, he gave the servant an example, so that he would not dread false witnesses and would not fear when they were believed.

They can create a bad reputation, but they cannot kill a pure conscience.

Three men were delivered from a furnace of blazing fire. Their God was present; they walked unharmed among the flames, surrounded by burning fire but not consumed. As they walked, they praised God, and they escaped unharmed, just as they had been cast in. Their God was present (Daniel 3).

Was God absent from the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7)? The former escaped; the latter soon burned. Both were tested: these were consumed in the flesh, those were unharmed in the flesh; but both were crowned.

For the three men to escape the flames, it was granted to Nebuchadnezzar that he should believe in their God. For the one who could visibly free them could also crown them invisibly.

But [Col. 1507] if he had crowned them invisibly, he would not have freed the king who had raged against them. Their bodily salvation became his soul’s salvation.

They escaped by praising God, but from present fires. He escaped by believing in God, but from eternal hell. More, therefore, was granted to him than to them.

Antiochus, by whom the Maccabees were tortured, however, was not worthy that such things should be granted to him. Therefore, when they had been consumed by fire and tortures, he exulted. But “whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14).

## 3. Mary Freed from Joseph’s False Suspicion

The one who freed Susanna, a chaste woman and faithful wife, from the false testimony of the elders also freed the virgin Mary from the false suspicion of her husband.

That virgin was found to be pregnant, although no man had approached her. Her womb had indeed swollen with a fetus, but her virginal integrity remained.

She had conceived, through faith, the sower of faith; she had received God into her body, and he had not permitted her body to be violated. Nevertheless, she came under suspicion in the eyes of her husband, who was only a human being.

He believed that what he knew was not from himself came from elsewhere, and he suspected adultery from that other source.

He is corrected by an angel. Why was he worthy to be corrected by an angel? Because there was no malicious suspicion in him, such as the Apostle says arises among brothers (1 Timothy 6:4).

Malicious suspicions belong to slanderers; benevolent suspicions belong to those who govern. Anyone may suspect evil concerning his son, but he may not slander his son. You suspect evil, certainly, but you hope to find good.

The one who suspects benevolently wishes to be proved wrong. For he rejoices rightly when what he had wrongly suspected is found to be false.

Such was Joseph toward his wife. He had not been joined to her bodily, but he had already been united to her in faith.

The virgin, therefore, also came under false suspicion. But just as the Spirit was present in Daniel on Susanna’s behalf, so an angel was present on Mary’s behalf.

The angel said to Joseph: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what is born of her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:18–20).

The suspicion was removed because redemption was discovered.

## 4. The Chastity of Virgins and Married Women; Unequal but Eternal Reward for Both; Christ’s Yoke Is Easy and His Burden Light for Those Who Love

A little earlier the married women were rejoicing over Susanna; let the virgins rejoice over Mary. Let both preserve chastity: the former conjugal chastity, the latter virginal chastity.

Both kinds of chastity have merit before God. Although virginal chastity is greater and conjugal chastity lesser, both are pleasing to God, because both are gifts of God.

All reach eternal life, but in eternal life not all attain the same honor, the same dignity, or the same merit.

Eternal life and the kingdom of God will be like what we call the heavens, by way of comparison. All the stars are in the heavens; likewise, all the good faithful will be in the kingdom of God.

Eternal life will be equal for all. One will not live there longer and another less long, since we shall all live without end.

It is the denarius that the laborers will receive, whether those who worked in the vineyard from early morning or those who came at the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:9–10). That denarius is eternal life, which is equal for all.

But look at the heavens and remember the Apostle: “There are [Col. 1508] heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:40–42).

Therefore, each one of you, my brothers, should strive in this age according to the gift he has received, so that he may rejoice in the age to come.

Are you married? Your life is lower; hope for a lower reward, but do not despair of the eternal kingdom. The commandments of marriage must be retained by you.

For because you have a wife, should you not recognize that you are a pilgrim in this world? Should you not consider that you will die and leave the bed of pleasure? Consider where, however you proceed, you are going: toward the punishment of misery or toward the reward of eternity.

Think, therefore; preserve what you have received; carry your burden, because it is light if you love it, heavy if you hate it.

For the Lord did not say without reason—or was he truly speaking only to the continent?—“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls”—not for your bodies, but for your souls. “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30): light for one who loves, heavy for one who refuses.

Have you taken the Lord’s yoke upon your neck? It is easy if you strive well; harsh if you resist.

Temptations surround married life. Was this Susanna not tempted in her very chastity because she was joined to a husband? Are only those who are joined to men not tempted in this respect?

Behold, Susanna was another man’s wife; she had a husband. Yet she was tempted and tossed about in the storm. “I am distressed on every side,” she said.

She feared death from false witnesses, but she feared complete death from God, the true judge. From false witnesses she would die for a time; from God the judge she would be punished eternally.

She weighed the alternatives and chose. First she feared and weighed; she weighed and chose; she chose and conquered.

She taught religious married women to resist the tempter; she taught them to fight, to labor, and to implore assistance.

## 5. Susanna as an Example for Women; One Must Act Not Only So That Life Is Good but Also So That Reputation Remains Unharmed

If Scripture offers such testimony concerning a woman, did it abandon men? Did it permit them to lack an example for imitation?

We were watching Susanna, tempted by men who desired to violate her; we were watching her struggle. That reading was a theater for our hearts. We awaited the chaste spirit, God’s athlete; we saw the adversary fighting; together with the victorious woman, we triumphed over the defeated one.

Religious wives have their example; they have something to imitate. They should owe what they preserve to God, not to a human being. They preserve it when they owe it to God; they preserve it when they owe it to the one who sees what they preserve, which even a husband does not see.

For a husband is often absent, while God is always present. And sometimes, because a husband is human, he suspects falsely. Then let the woman pray for her husband who suspects falsely; let her pray that he may be saved, not that he may be condemned.

The man’s false suspicion does not close God’s eyes. Her conscience is naked before the one who created her. He himself frees her, though oppressed for a time, forever.

But let her pray for [Col. 1509] her husband and take care not only to have a good life but also an unharmed reputation.

Chastity itself frees a good life, so that it is not condemned. A good reputation, however, frees others, so that they do not slip by falsely suspecting and perhaps fall into sin while judging what they do not see.

Thus these judges fell, and holy Daniel—or rather, through Daniel, the Lord—freed those judges from inner death more than he freed Susanna.

He freed her so that she would not be condemned for a time; but he freed them so that, by judging wrongly and condemning an innocent woman, they would not fall into eternal punishment at the hands of the judge whom no one can corrupt and from whom no one can hide.

## 6. Joseph as an Example of Chastity for Men

I was speaking, then, about men, because they too have not been left without an example.

Chaste men, God-fearing men, men for whom their own wives are sufficient; men who do not violate what you do not wish violated in yourselves; men who have returned the fidelity you demanded—listen as I recall for you what your wives heard recited by the reader.

Nor has divine Scripture left you without an example. They heard about Susanna and rejoiced in her victory; you, pay attention to Joseph.

Not that Joseph to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed, she who bore Christ—for he was tested by suspicion and immediately healed by an angel.

Holy Scripture bears witness to another Joseph, whom an immoral woman tempted. She loved a handsome man, not with a chaste but with a perverse mind; she had no eyes for the spiritual and invisible beauty. She loved him as handsome but did not want him to be chaste.

She loved a man who belonged to another; she loved her own husband’s servant. But she did not love one who kept faith with his master.

Do you think she loved him, or rather herself? I think she loved neither him nor herself. If she loved him, why did she wish to destroy him? If she loved herself, why did she wish to perish?

Behold, I have proved that she did not love. She burned with the poison of lust; the flame of charity did not shine.

But he knew how to see what she did not know how to see. He was more beautiful within than without, more beautiful in the light of his heart than in the skin of his flesh. Where that woman’s eyes could not penetrate, there he enjoyed his own beauty.

Therefore, as he contemplated the inner beauty of chastity, how could he permit it to be stained or violated by that woman’s temptation?

She loved him, but he loved too. Yet what he loved was greater than what she loved, because he saw what she did not see.

## 7. Even the Immoral Love Chastity in Others

If you wish, in whatever way, to see the spiritual beauty of chastity, if you have eyes of any sort for it, I will propose something to you as an example: you love it in your own wife.

Therefore do not hate in another woman what you love in your own. What do you love in your wife? Surely chastity.

You hate this in another woman, although you love it in your wife. You hate it in another woman when, by sleeping with her, you wish to destroy her chastity.

What you love in your wife, do you wish to kill in another? What you love in your wife, do you wish to destroy in another?

How will you have a pious prayer, as a murderer of chastity?

Therefore preserve in another woman what you wish preserved in your own; love chastity itself more than the flesh.

Perhaps you think you are a lover of your wife’s [Col. 1510] flesh, not of her chastity. That is a filthy thought, but I will not leave you without an example.

For I think that you love chastity in your wife more than her flesh. But to show you most clearly that you love chastity more than flesh, you love it in your daughter.

What man is there who does not want his daughters to be chaste? What man does not rejoice together with his daughters in their chastity?

Do you love flesh there as well? Do you desire a beautiful body where you shudder at incest?

Behold, I have proved that you are a lover of chastity. If I have shown you to be a lover of chastity, why have you offended yourself so that you do not love it in yourself?

Here is a short rule for you: love in yourself what you love in your daughter; love it in another man’s wife, because your daughter too will be another man’s wife. Therefore love chastity in yourself as well.

If you love another man’s wife, you will not possess her immediately. If you love chastity, you will possess it at once.

Therefore love chastity, so that you may possess eternal happiness.

## 8. Chastity Must Be Loved and Defended in Temptation, Following the Example of Susanna and Joseph

Perhaps you will be tempted. An immoral woman will love you, find you in solitude, and try to force an embrace from you. If you refuse, she will threaten to accuse you and bring punishment upon you.

This is what the false elders did to Susanna; this is what her master’s wife did to holy Joseph.

But pay attention to the one to whom both Susanna and Joseph paid attention. Is God not present simply because there is no human witness?

Joseph did not wish to offend his master’s eyes—the eyes of his present Lord. He did not wish to consent to illicit intercourse with the immoral woman. He rejected another’s desire and embraced his own chastity.

Yet she did what she had threatened. She lied to her husband, and her husband believed her.

God was still patient. Joseph was handed over to prison and guarded as a guilty man, though he was one by whom God had not been offended. Yet God was not absent there either, because Joseph was not guilty.

The Lord was present with Joseph in his suffering. Because he did not help him immediately, he postponed his aid for greater rewards (Genesis 39; 41).

He made the one whom he had tested through punishment rejoice in his merit. For holy Joseph had to endure something harsh, that is, something bitter, for the sake of chastity itself.

If he perhaps loved that immoral woman, he would have been prepared to endure hardship for her. And she would not have proved his love for her unless he endured such troublesome or harsh things on her account; she would have returned affection—or rather, not affection but evil desire—with affection.

She would have burned for him in return, seeing him inflamed by such love for her that he did not refuse to endure any punishment for her sake.

If this is done for an immoral woman, how much more should it be done for chastity itself?

God therefore rightly sometimes postpones his help: to test a person, to exercise a person, and to make the person himself known to himself. For nothing is hidden from God.

## 9. Pleasures and Troubles Must Be Rejected for the Sake of Chastity

This, then, is what I would urge upon Your Charity, brothers: above all, place before carnal desires, worldly pleasures, empty display, and the fleeting vapor of this present life the dignity and beauty of wisdom; place before them the sweetness and pleasantness of wisdom; place before them the dignity of chastity and the [Col. 1511] beauty of purity.

All these things are hidden in the heavenly treasure. These precious gems lie naked before the eyes of God; they shine brightly. If you have eyes, you see them.

Therefore place these things before diverse and illicit pleasures. And if temptation goes so far that you must even suffer hardship, my brothers, who would not suffer for his purse? Who would not suffer for his field, or for a single boundary stone of his field?

If you suffer for these things, which you do not have the power to retain as long as you wish or to leave to whomever you wish—and which are often lost while we live, and often possessed after our death by those whom we hate—if for these goods, if they are even to be called goods, which do not make people good, human beings patiently endure such great evils, why are they sluggish for the sake of faith?

Why are they timid for the sake of those riches [Note: [Col. 1511] Earlier, the reading is “pro illis divitus”; perhaps one should read, “why are they not concerned?” or something similar.] which even shipwrecks cannot take away from us?

For the righteous person escapes shipwreck both rich and naked.

## 10. How Rich Job Was in the Dung

The holy Job was full of these riches. Everything perished in a single blow; nothing remained in his house. The man who had seemed wealthy shortly before suddenly became a beggar, covered from head to foot with swarming worms as he sat in dung.

What misery is more miserable than this? What is more blessed than his inner happiness?

He had lost all those things that God had given him, but he possessed God himself, who had given all things.

“Naked,” he said, “I came from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Surely he is poor? Surely he has nothing? If nothing remains, from what treasure were these gems of praise for God brought forth?

Afterward the tempter went so far as the flesh. When everything had been taken away, he left behind a temptress. He left Eve there; but that man was not Adam.

And how was he found there? How did he answer his wife, who was suggesting blasphemy?

“You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job 1–2).

O man rotten and whole! O vile and beautiful! O wounded and healthy! O sitting in dung and reigning in heaven!

If we love him, let us imitate him. To imitate him, let us labor. And if we begin to fail in our labor, let us implore assistance.

The one who established the contest helps the contestant. God does not await you in your struggle like a crowd awaiting a charioteer: it knows how to shout but does not know how to help.

Nor does God await you like a combat-trainer awaiting an athlete: he prepares a crown of hay but does not know how to supply strength to the laborer. For he is a human being, not God.

And perhaps, while waiting, he labors more by sitting than the other does by wrestling.

For when God awaits his contestants, he helps them when called upon. His athletes’ voice is heard in the Psalm: “When I said, ‘My foot is slipping,’ your mercy, O Lord, was helping me” (Psalm 93:18).

Let us not, therefore, be sluggish, my brothers. Let us ask, seek, and knock. “For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks will find; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8).

# SERMON CCCXLIV

[Note: [Col. 1512] Found only in v. and in Sirm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1512] Otherwise, no. 31 among the Sirmondian sermons.]  
On the love of God and the love of the world. [Note: [Col. 1512] Florus cites it on 2 Corinthians 5.]

[Col. 1512]

## 1. The Struggle Between the Love of God and the Love of the World

Two loves struggle with one another in every temptation of this life: the love of the world and the love of God. Whichever of the two conquers draws the lover thither, as though by its weight. For we come to God not by wings or feet, but by affections. Conversely, we cling to the earth not by bodily knots and bonds, but by contrary affections.

Christ came to change love and to make a lover of heavenly life out of one who was earthly: he was made man for us, he who made us human beings; and, God assuming humanity, in order to make human beings gods.

This is the contest set before us: this struggle with the flesh, this struggle with the devil, this struggle with the world. But let us trust, since he who has appointed this contest does not watch without giving his help, nor does he exhort us to presume upon our own strength. For whoever presumes upon his own strength, since he is a human being, presumes upon human strength; and “cursed is everyone who puts his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5).

The martyrs, burning with the flame of this pious and holy love, burned indeed the hay of the flesh by the strength of their minds; but they themselves, whole in spirit, came to him by whom they had been kindled. Yet in the resurrection of the dead the honor due will be granted even to that flesh which is now despised. For it was sown in dishonor in order that it might rise in glory.

## 2. God Is to Be Loved Above Parents

He says this to those inflamed with this love—or rather, so that they may be inflamed by it:

> “Whoever loves father or mother above me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37–38).

He did not abolish love for parents, wife, and children, but ordered it properly. He did not say, “Whoever loves,” but “whoever loves above me.” This is what the Church says in the Song of Songs: “He ordered charity in me” (Song 2:4).

Love your father, but do not love him above the Lord; love your parent, but do not love him above the Creator. A father begot you, but he did not himself form you—for when he sowed, who knew what sort of person or what kind of person he would be who was to be born? A father nourished you, but the father did not, from his own resources, provide bread for the hungry. Finally, whatever your father reserves for you on earth, he dies so that you may succeed him; by his death he will make room for your life.

But God the Father keeps what he stores up for you with himself, so that you may possess the inheritance together with your Father himself. You do not await him as a predecessor whom you will succeed; rather, cling to him who will always remain, and you will always remain in him.

Love your father, then, but do not love him above your God. Love your mother, but do not love her above the Church, which gave birth to you for eternal life. Finally, judge from your love for your own parents how greatly you ought to love God and the Church. If those who begot one destined to die are to be loved so greatly, with what charity must those be loved who begot one destined to come to eternity and remain in eternity?

Love your wife and love your children according to God, so that you may counsel them to worship God together with you. When you have been joined to him, you will fear no separation. Therefore you must not love those more than God whom you love wrongly if you neglect to lead them with you to God.

Perhaps the hour of martyrdom will come. You want to confess Christ. After confessing him, you will perhaps receive a punishment for a time; you will receive temporal death. Your father, or wife, or child will flatter you so that you may not die, and by flattering you will bring it about that you die. If they do not bring this about, then the saying will come to your mind: “Whoever loves father, or mother, or wife, or children above me is not worthy of me.”

## 3. Human Affection Must Be Overcome by Christ’s Example

Human willing in Christ recoiling from death.

But the carnal affection is swayed by the blandishments of one’s own people, and human softness slips, in a certain way. Gather up the folds of your flowing garment; gird yourself with strength. Does love of the flesh torment you? Take up your cross and follow the Lord.

Your Savior himself, although God in the flesh, although God together with the flesh, nevertheless displayed human affection when he said:

> “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

He knew that this cup could not pass; he had come to drink it. That cup had to be drunk by will, not by necessity. He was almighty: if he wished, it would certainly pass, because he and the Father are God together, and he and God the Father are one God.

But from the form of a servant, from what he assumed from you and for you, he uttered the voice of a human being, the voice of the flesh. He deigned to transform you into himself, so that you might speak of weakness from him and grasp strength in him. He displayed the will by which you could be tempted, and immediately taught which will you ought to prefer to that will.

“Father,” he said, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” This is the human will; I bear the human being, I speak from the form of a servant. “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass.” It is the voice of the flesh, not of the spirit; the voice of weakness, not of divinity. “If it is possible, let this cup pass.”

This is the will of which it is also said to Peter:

> “When you grow old, another will gird you and take you and carry you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18).

How, then, did the martyrs conquer? Because they placed the will of the spirit above the will of the flesh. They loved this life, and they weighed it carefully. From this they considered how greatly eternal life ought to be loved, if this perishing life is loved in such a way.

One who is going to die does not want to die; nevertheless, he will necessarily die, even though he continually does not want to die. You accomplish nothing by not wanting to die; you achieve nothing, extort nothing. You have no power to remove the necessity of death. What you fear will come, though you do not want it; what you delay will be present, though you resist it.

You strive, of course, to delay death; but surely not to remove it? If, then, lovers of this life strive so greatly to delay death, how much ought they to labor to remove it? Certainly you do not want to die. Change your love, and a death will be shown to you that will not come while you do not want it, but that, if you wish, will not exist.

## 4. Twofold Death: The First and the Second

The first death must necessarily be undergone by all; the other is prepared only for the wicked. From temporal death a person redeems himself with money; from eternal death, with righteousness. Christ’s blood was poured out for our redemption.

See, then, whether love has awakened somewhat in your heart; whether a spark has flashed from the ashes of the flesh; whether your heart has grasped some strength that the wind of temptation not only does not extinguish but makes burn more fiercely. See whether you do not burn like tinder, which is extinguished by a single light breath, but burn like solid wood, burn like a coal, so that you are rather stirred up by a breath.

Consider two deaths: one temporal, and also the first; the other everlasting, and also the second. The first death is prepared for everyone; the second only for the wicked, the impious, the unbelieving, the blasphemous, and whatever else opposes sound doctrine.

Keep these two deaths before you. If possible, you do not want to suffer either. I know that you love living and do not want to die; and you would wish to pass from this life into another in such a way that you would not rise again as one dead, but would be changed for the better while still alive. This is what you would wish; this is what human affection has, and what the soul itself possesses somehow in its will and desire. For by loving life it hates death; and because it does not hate its own flesh, it does not want what it hates to happen to it. “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29).

The Apostle displayed this affection when he said:

> “We have a dwelling from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed with our dwelling that is from heaven. In this,” he says, “we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

You do not want to be stripped; but you must be stripped. Nevertheless, you ought to act so that, stripped by death of the tunic of flesh, you may be found clothed with the breastplate of faith. For he adds, following this:

> “Provided that, when clothed, we are not found naked” (2 Cor. 5:1–4).

The first death strips you of the flesh, which is to be laid aside for a time and received again at its proper time. You will undergo this whether you wish it or not. You will not rise because you wish to; nor, if you do not wish to, will you fail to rise; nor, if you do not believe in the resurrection, will you therefore not rise. Rather, you must act so that, since you will rise whether you wish to or not, you may rise in such a way that you have what you wish to have.

For the Lord Jesus himself said:

> “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth,”

whether they are good or evil. All who are in the tombs will hear his voice, come forth, and be released from their hidden places. No creature will hold the dead beneath the voice of the living Creator.

When he said “all,” he seemed to make a confusion and mingling. But hear the distinction; hear also the separation:

> “Those who have done good,” he says, “will come forth to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

This judgment, for which the impious will rise to undergo it, is called the second death.

Why, then, Christian, do you fear this first death? It will come against your will; it will be present though you resist it. Perhaps you redeem yourself from barbarians so that you will not be killed. You redeem yourself at great cost; you spare none of your possessions and strip your children of theirs; and, once redeemed, you will die the next day.

You must be redeemed from the devil, who drags you with him to the second death, where the wicked, placed on the left, will hear:

> “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

You must be redeemed from this second death. You will ask, “From where?” Do not seek goats and bulls; finally, do not examine your strongbox and say in your heart, “To redeem myself from the barbarians I had money.” To redeem yourself from the second death, have righteousness.
