The barbarian could first take your money from you and afterward lead you away captive, so that you would have nothing with which to redeem yourself, since the one who possessed you would possess all your goods as well. You do not lose righteousness against your will; it remains in the innermost treasury of your heart. Hold it, possess it; from there you will be redeemed from the second death.

If you do not wish it, it will for that reason not exist, because that by which you redeem yourself from this death will exist if you wish it to. The will obtains righteousness from the Lord and drinks it as from its own fountain. No one is forbidden to approach that fountain if he approaches worthily.

Finally, consider your helper. Your silver redeemed you from the barbarians; your money redeemed you from the first death; the blood of your Lord redeemed you from the second death. He had blood with which to redeem us, and for this purpose he received blood, so that he would have blood to pour out for our redemption.

The blood of your Lord was given for you, if you wish it; if you do not wish to be his, it was not given for you. Perhaps you say: “My God had blood with which to redeem me; but when he suffered, he gave it all. What remains for him to give for me?”

This is the great thing: he gave it once, and gave it for all. Christ’s blood is salvation for the willing and punishment for the unwilling.

Why, then, do you hesitate—though you do not want to die—to be freed instead from the second death? You are freed from it if you wish to take up your cross and follow the Lord, because he took up his and sought a servant.

## 5. How Greatly Eternal Life Must Be Loved, Since Temporal Life Is Loved So Greatly

Against those who lose eternal life through love of temporal life.

Surely, my brothers, those who love temporal life so greatly do not most strongly urge you to love eternal life? How much people do in order to live a few days! Who could enumerate the efforts and contrivances of all those who want to live but will soon die? How much do they do for those very few days?

What so much do we do for eternal life? What shall I say about redeeming a few days—and those on earth? I call them only a few days if the man who has been freed grows old; I call them only a few days if the child who has been freed becomes decrepit. I am not speaking of someone who, redeemed today, may perhaps die tomorrow.

Look: for the sake of those few uncertain days, how much do people do? What do they devise? If through bodily illness they fall into the hands of physicians, and every hope of recovery is declared hopeless by those who pronounce judgment and examine them; if some physician is promised who is even capable of saving one given up for lost, what promises are made? What is given, despite the uncertainty?

In order to live a little longer, people surrender the means by which they live. But if someone falls into the hands of an enemy or brigand, and must be redeemed so that he will not be killed, even if a father has been detained, his children run and spend what he would have left to them, in order to redeem him whom they may be able to carry away.

What ambitions, what prayers, what efforts! Who could explain it all?

Yet I want to say something more serious, and, unless it happened, more incredible. What do I mean? People give money so that they may live; they leave themselves nothing. To live a few days—those same uncertain days—just a little longer, with fear and toil, how much do they spend? How much do they give?

Woe to the human race! I have said that, in order to live, people spend what they live on. Hear what is worse, more serious, more wicked, and, as I said, incredible unless it happens. In order that they may be permitted to live a little longer, they even give away what could enable them to live forever.

Hear what I have said and understand. It is still hidden, and yet it moves many to whom the Lord has already opened it while it was hidden.

Set aside those who give away and lose what they could live on, so that they may be allowed to live a little longer. Consider those who lose what could enable them to live forever, so that they may be allowed to live a little longer.

What is this? It is called faith; it is called piety. All this is like money by which eternal life is acquired. An enemy will suddenly come from the side, terrifying you, and will not say, “Give me your money so that you may live,” but will say, “Deny Christ so that you may live.”

If you do this so that you may be permitted to live a little longer, you will lose what could enable you to live forever. Is this loving life, when you were afraid of death?

Good man, why were you afraid of death, unless because you loved life? Christ is life. Why do you desire the lesser life, so as to lose the secure one? Or perhaps you did not lose faith, but did not possess what you would lose?

Hold fast, then, to what will enable you to live forever. Consider your neighbor and how much he does in order to live a little longer. Consider also the one who denied Christ and how great an evil he committed for the sake of a few days of life.

And you do not want to despise those same few days of life so that you may never die, live in an everlasting day, be protected by your Redeemer, and be made equal to the angels in the eternal kingdom?

What did you love? What did you lose? To follow the Lord, you did not take up your cross.

## 6. Losing the Soul So That the Soul May Be Found

See how prudent he wants you to be—the one who said to you, “Take up your cross and follow me.”

> “Whoever finds his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it for my sake will find it” (Matt. 10:38–39).

Whoever finds it will lose it; whoever loses it will find it. In order to lose it, you must first find it; and when you have lost it, finally you will find it again.

There are two findings, with one loss passing through the middle. No one can lose his soul for Christ unless he has first found it; and no one can find his soul in Christ unless he has first lost it.

Find it in order to lose it; lose it in order to find it.

How will you first find it, so that you may have something to lose? When you consider that you are mortal in part; when you consider the one who made you, who created a soul for you by breathing into you; and when you see that you owe it to the one who gave it, that it must be returned to the one who lent it, and that it must be guarded by the one who established it—you have found your soul by finding it in faith.

For you believed this, and you found your soul. You were lost before you believed. You found your soul: you had been dead in unbelief, and you came to life again in faith. You are one of whom it can be said, “He was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found” (Luke 15:32).

Therefore you found your soul in the faith of truth, if you came to life again from the death of unbelief. This is finding your soul.

Lose it, and let your soul be seed for you. For a farmer also finds wheat by threshing and winnowing it, and then loses the wheat again by sowing it. What had been lost in the seed is found on the threshing floor; what is found in the harvest is lost in the sowing.

Therefore, “whoever finds his soul will lose it.” If someone works to gather, why is he too lazy to sow?

## 7. For Whose Sake We Are Commanded to Lose the Soul

Consider, nevertheless, where you find it and why you lose it. For where would you find it unless he kindled a light for you to whom it is said, “You will light my lamp, Lord”? (Ps. 17:29.)

You have therefore found it, since he has kindled a lamp for you. Consider why you should lose it. What was found with such care must not be lost indiscriminately.

He did not say, “Whoever loses it will find it,” but, “Whoever loses it for my sake.”

If, after seeing on the shore the body of a shipwrecked merchant, you shed tears out of pity and say, “Woe to this man! He lost his soul for gold,” you grieve well and pity well. Give your tears to one to whom you cannot also give help. He was able to lose his soul for gold, but he will not be able to find it for gold. He was capable of bringing about the loss of his soul, but proved less capable of gaining it.

You must not consider what he lost, but why he lost it. If it was through greed, behold where the flesh lies; where is what was precious? Yet greed commanded it, and the soul was lost for gold; but the soul does not perish for Christ—indeed, let it not perish.

Fool, do not hesitate; hear the Creator’s counsel. He made you so that you might be wise—the one who made you before you existed as one who could be wise. Hear him; do not hesitate to lose your soul for Christ.

You entrust to the faithful Creator what you are said to lose. You will indeed lose it, but he receives it, for whom nothing is lost.

If you love life, lose it in order to find it. For when you have found it, there will no longer be anything for you to lose, nor any reason for you to lose it. The life that is found is found so that it cannot perish at all.

For Christ too, who gave you an example by being born, dying, and rising again, having risen from the dead no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9).

# SERMON 345

[Note: [Col. 1517] Found only in the Cluniac manuscript and in Sirmond.]

[Note: [Col. 1517] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons, no. 32.]

## On Contempt for the World

### 1. The Present Life Must Be Despised in Hope of the Future Life

#### This Life Is Sleep for the Rich

I shall speak to your Charity, brothers, about contempt for the present age and hope for the future age. If you ask what you should despise, every martyr despised the present life. If you ask what you should hope for, I speak of the resurrection, because today the Lord rose again.

O man, if you waver in the matter itself, be firm in hope; but if the task troubles you, let the reward itself lift you up.

The Apostle also admonishes us when he commands Timothy, saying:

> “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things richly. Let them be rich in good works, readily giving and sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may grasp the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

The rich especially ought to hear this. Hear, rich people, who possess gold and silver and yet burn with desire—those whom the poor look upon and murmur, groan, praise, and envy; they wish to be your equals and grieve that they are unequal. In the midst of their praise of the rich they commonly say, “These alone exist; they alone live.”

Because of these words with which poor people flatter the rich, saying, “These alone live,” do not be lifted up into pride, you rich people. Rather, hear the Apostle, the physician of disease, not a flatterer of words.

This life is your sleep; these riches flow like things seen in dreams. Paul says that they should grasp the true life. Hear Paul, and do not be proud.

Hear the Psalm also, O you very poor rich man: what do you have if you do not have God? Or what do you lack if you have God?

The Psalm says of the rich:

> “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

Sometimes even a beggar lying on the ground and trembling with cold, overcome by sleep, dreams of treasures. He rejoices, exults, grows proud, and is indignant at seeing his ragged father. What you see is in a dream, O beggar who sleeps and rejoices.

Nevertheless, until he wakes, he is rich; when he wakes, he finds what he can certainly lament. The rich man who is dying, therefore, is like that poor man who sleeps and dreams of treasures.

For that rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen—unnamed and not to be named—who despised the poor man lying before his gate and feasted splendidly every day, afterward died and was buried. He awoke and found himself in the flames (Luke 16:19–24). He slept his sleep, and after sleep found nothing, because he had done nothing with his hands—that is, with his riches.

### 2. Perishing Life Is Redeemed with All One’s Goods; At What Price Eternal Life Must Be Purchased

Riches are sought for the sake of life, not life for the sake of riches. How many have made agreements with their enemies so that they might redeem life alone? Whatever they had, they gave it all, only so as not to lose their life.

“You gave the barbarians everything you had, brother?”

“I gave everything,” he says. “I was left naked; but naked, I shall live.”

“And why?”

“I was going to be killed entirely; therefore I gave everything.”

“And why did this happen to you? Shall I tell you? Because before the barbarian arrived, you did not help the poor, so that through the poor your alms might reach Christ. You gave nothing small to Christ, and you gave the barbarians everything you had—and you gave it with an oath. Christ asks, and does not receive; the barbarian tortures, and takes everything.”

If you redeemed perishing life at such a price, at what price must eternal life be purchased? You who give to the enemy so that you may live as a beggar, give something to Christ so that you may live blessed.

To live a few days, you do what the enemy demands, and you despise what Christ demands? All the days of a person, from infancy to old age, are few. Even if Adam himself were to die today, he would have lived only a few days, because he had completed them all. He had certainly lived six thousand years, and yet they were few, because he had brought them all to an end.

You redeem a few laborious days, full of temptations, so that you may have a small piece of land—that is, an estate. Behold, the enemy who had captured you says, “Give me whatever you have.” To live, you gave everything: redeemed today, you will die tomorrow; redeemed from this man, you will be slaughtered by another.

See how much people suffer from barbarians for the sake of temporal life, and how they are reluctant to suffer anything for eternal life! Let these dangers instruct us, brothers.

You gave everything and cast it away, and you rejoice because you live. You say, “Even though I am poor, naked, needy, and a beggar, I rejoice because I live and have not lost this sweet light.”

Let Christ appear; let him also make a bargain with you—not the barbarian who captured you, but the one who was captured for you, who deigned to be killed for you. The one who gave himself for you says to you:

> “Make a bargain with me. Do you want to possess yourself? Possess me also. You must hate yourself and love me. By losing your life, you will find it, lest by keeping it you lose it.”

### 3. Riches Must Be Sent Ahead to Heaven So That They Do Not Perish Here

Concerning the riches you love to possess, which you are ready to give for the sake of the present life, I shall advise you what to do. If you love them too, do not lose them. But if you love them here, they will perish with you.

If you love them, send them ahead to where you will follow, so that, by loving them on earth, you may not lose them either while alive or when dead. I have already given my advice: I did not say, “Lose them,” but “Preserve them.”

Do you want to store up treasure? Good. I do not say, “Do not”; I say, “Where?” Accept me as an adviser, not as a destroyer.

It is written:

> “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither thief approaches, nor moth, nor rust destroys” (Matt. 6:20).

But perhaps you say: “I do not see a place in heaven where I can put them. What ladder, what machine shall I seek that reaches heaven, so that I may see where to put my money?”

What do you say? Do you see a place on earth where you bury it?

“I do,” he says.

That is good enough. If you are secure in burying it in the earth, why are you anxious about God, who made heaven and earth? Give securely to God. Entrust yourself to him who preserves your money for you in heaven, because he also governs you on earth as long as you live.

Do you want to preserve your money? Preserve it as you wish. If you find a better guardian than Christ, entrust your money to him.

“I entrust it,” he says, “to my servant.”

Good. How much better to your Lord? Do you place your servant before your Lord?

O Christian man! Your servant may perhaps take it away and flee. Surely Christ will not do this? Many servants suddenly became enemies of their masters and handed them over to their enemies together with their gold.

“To whom, then, do you entrust it?”

“To my servant,” he says.

“I know my servant’s fidelity, and therefore I entrust my gold to my servant.”

Very well: you prefer your servant; you entrust your gold to your servant. To whom do you entrust your soul?

“I entrust my soul to my God.”

How much better, O man, to entrust your gold also to the one to whom you entrust your soul! Or is he perhaps faithful in guarding your soul but unfaithful in guarding your money? He guards for you who also guards you.

“You praise your servant’s fidelity?”

“Yes, I know my servant’s fidelity.”

His entire fidelity consists in not defrauding and not taking it away. Surely he does anything to prevent its being lost? Behold, he put it down and it was not concealed; someone else found it and took it. Will anyone do this to Christ?

Shake off your laziness; accept the counsel. Give to Christ who is hungry; store up treasure in heaven.

Is it hard to store up treasure in heaven? Even if it were hard, it ought to be done in order to place your money in a secure location from which no one could take it. Yet when Christ says, “Store up treasure in heaven,” he does not tell you, “Seek ladders, fasten machines, fit wings.” He says this:

> “Give to me on earth, and I will preserve it for you in heaven.”

For this reason I came needy on earth, so that you might be rich in heaven. Make the transfer. Perhaps you fear a defrauder, lest you lose it, and you seek someone who will carry it and make the journey.

Christ is present to you in both respects. He will not commit fraud; he will also make the transfer.

### 4. Christ Receives What Is Distributed to the Poor

#### The Human Heart with Its Treasure

“But where do I find Christ,” he says, “on earth? Where do I find him so that I may give to him?”

My faith possesses what I hear in the Church. I learned this; I believed it; I was instructed in this creed: he suffered, died, and was buried; he rose on the third day; after forty days he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of the Father; at the end he will come. When do I find him here? To whom shall I give, so that he may carry it to him?

Do not be anxious; hear the whole matter. Or, if you heard or read the whole matter, did you never hear this—that when Saul was persecuting the Church, proud, cruel, thirsting for Christian blood, you heard what the one whom you confess to be seated in heaven cried out to him?

Recall it. What, then, did he say?

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4.)

The one whom Paul neither saw nor touched, who was in heaven, cried out, “Why are you persecuting me?” He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my family, my servants, my saints, or my brothers?” He said none of these things.

What did he say?

> “Why are you persecuting me?”

He meant, “My members.” For when these were trampled on earth, the head cried out from heaven. If someone tramples your foot on earth, your tongue cries out from your head—not, “You are trampling my foot,” but, “You are trampling me.”

Why, then, do you hesitate? What do you say? The one who said to Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” says to you, “Feed me.”

Saul was raging on earth and touching Christ in heaven. In the same way, you distribute on earth and feed Christ in heaven.

The Lord himself foretold this question that troubles you. Those who will be placed on the right will also be moved, and when he says, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” they will answer, “Lord, when did we see you hungry?” Immediately they will hear:

> “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:35–40).

If you had heard this, say openly, “I do not want to give,” and you have no means of excusing yourself; by your own voice you condemn yourself.

Your Lord, then, says this to you concerning your riches:

> “I gave you advice about what to do.”

“You love riches?”

“I do,” you say.

“Then transfer them, and once you have transferred them, follow them meanwhile in your heart while you live, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21).

But if you bury your heart on earth, be ashamed because you lie when you answer upon hearing, “Lift up your hearts.” For it is said, “Lift up your hearts,” and immediately you answer, “We have them with the Lord.”

You lie to God. For one hour in church you do not speak the truth; you lie to God, which you always do to human beings. You say, “We have them with the Lord,” while you have your heart buried on earth, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

### 5. The True Riches of the Kingdom of Heaven

#### Earthly Riches Bring Nothing but Anxiety

It is not enough to distribute your possessions unless you also follow Christ.

If you do with your riches what you have heard; if you are the kind of rich person whom the Apostle describes—not thinking proudly, nor hoping in the uncertainty of riches—so that you store up for yourself a good foundation for the future and grasp the true life, then ask your God and Lord and say to him:

“Behold, Lord, I have now transferred to heaven what I possessed; or, what I possess, I possess as though I did not possess it. Is the kingdom of heaven worth as much as my patrimony?”

“It is worth more.”

For it is not truly such that it could be valued at only that price. Your Lord, whom you asked about your patrimony, says this:

“You will live for a time, and afterward die; in my kingdom you will never die, but will live forever. There you will be truly rich, where you will never be in need.”

For that reason you seek many animals for transport, so that you may not fail; abundant banquets for food; costly clothing for dress. In truth, by possessing much you are rich, and is my angel poor? He owns nothing; he does not use a horse; he is not carried in a carriage; he does not fill a table with elegant furnishings; no garment is woven for him, because he is clothed with eternal light.

Learn, O rich man, to desire true riches. You want to have these riches so that you may have enough to eat much, because you are failing. But the one who gives you not to hunger forever makes you truly rich.

However much you possess, when the fifth hour comes, before you approach the table you are hungry and failing, because you are wretched.

Does an angel endure this? Far from it. An angel has neither hunger nor exhaustion.

Finally, you pant proudly after these banquets. This is not the satisfaction of needs, but the smoke of anxieties. When you think about increasing your riches, see whether you sleep easily. If I am not mistaken, when you found riches, you lost rest. When you are awake, you think about increasing your riches; when you sleep, you dream of thieves. Anxious by day and fearful at night, you are always a beggar.

The one who promises you the kingdom of heaven wants to make you truly rich. Do you think you will purchase those true riches, that true and blessed life, at the price you are prepared to pay to redeem these miserable and laborious days? Something that is much greater must be worth much more, because it is the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1521] This hour, namely, corresponds to our eleventh hour; in the ancient reckoning it precedes the sixth hour—that is, noon—and is the customary hour for the midday meal. Hence Martial, book 8, epigram 67:

> “The servant has not yet announced five hours to you,  
> and already, Caecilianus, you come to me as my guest.”]

### 6. The Same Argument Is Treated

“And what shall I do?” you say. “Behold, holy bishop, I have heard your admonitions, obeyed your counsel, and have not despised the Lord’s command. I gave what I possessed to the poor, and what I have I share with those in need. What more can I do?”

You still have something; you have yourself. You yourself are worth more; you are lacking from your possessions; you must be added.

“Did you carry out the counsel of your Lord?”

“I did,” he says.

“Why do you lie? You did not do everything. You did it on one side, but on the other you touched nothing. Hear what he commands:

> ‘Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor.’”

“Did he stop there?” And lest the man think that he had lost what he distributed to the poor, he made him secure by saying:

> “And you will have treasure in heaven.”

Is that enough?

No.

“What more?”

> “‘Come, follow me,’ he says” (Matt. 19:21).

Do you love him, and do you want to follow the one whom you love? He ran; he flew. Ask where.

“I do not know where.”

O Christian! You do not know where your Lord went? Shall I tell you where to follow him? Through hardships, reproaches, false accusations, spitting in the face, blows and scourging, a crown of thorns, the cross, and death.

Why are you lazy? Behold, the way has been shown to you.

“But the way is hard,” you say. “Who could follow him by this way?”

Be ashamed, barbarian, be ashamed! You are called a man because of your strength. Women followed him, whose feast we celebrate today.

[Note: [Col. 1521] Thus reads Colbertine manuscript 1785, which Sirmond elsewhere used under the name of the Pithoean manuscript to correct the text to “Tuburbitanarum.” By this expression he understands Perpetua and Felicity, whose bodies were buried in the Major Basilica at Carthage and whose anniversary is celebrated on March 7. Henry Valesius, however, contends in the preface to the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity that the women praised here are Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda, who are also said to have suffered at Thuburbo on July 30. See above, on Sermon 280.]

We are celebrating the solemnity of the Suburban women martyrs.

[Col. 1522]

Your Lord, our Lord, their Lord, the Redeemer of our life, went before you along the narrow and rough way and made it level for you—a safe and fortified road: Christ our Lord, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 346

[Note: [Col. 1522] This now comes forth for the first time from the old Michaeline manuscript, in which it is placed immediately with the two sermons that follow, under the same title, “On the Fear of the Lord.” Nevertheless, it seems to us to belong rather to the treatise listed in Possidius’s Index, chapter 8, “On the Pilgrimage of Christians, Which Is in This Life.”]

## On Our Pilgrimage in This Life, Through Faith
# Sermon 346

## On Our Pilgrimage in This Life, Through Faith

### Chapter VII

#### 1. This life is more truly death than life. True life is eternal alone

Recall with us, beloved brothers, that the Apostle said: “As long as we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). Our Lord Jesus Christ, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), wished us to walk both through him and toward him. For along what do we walk, unless along a way? And toward what do we walk, unless toward truth and life—that is, eternal life, which alone should be called life?

For this mortal life in which we now are is shown, by comparison with that life, to be death: it is altered by such great mutability, established by no stability, and brought to an end by an exceedingly brief course. Therefore the Lord replied to that rich man who had said to him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:16–17).

He was certainly in some kind of life; for he was not speaking to a corpse, but to a living man. Yet because that man had asked about attaining eternal life, the Lord did not say, “If you wish to enter into eternal life,” but, “If you wish,” he said, “to enter into life, keep the commandments”—clearly wishing this to be understood: that what is not eternal life ought not even to be called life, because true life is eternal alone. [Note: [Col. 1522] See Sermon 306, §§6–7.]

Hence, when the Apostle urged that the rich should be given the counsel of almsgiving, he said: “Let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (1 Tim. 6:18–19). What did he call true life except eternal life, which alone should be called life, because it alone is blessed?

Those rich people whom he said should be instructed to take hold of true life certainly possessed this present life amid an abundance of wealth. Yet if the Apostle judged this to be true life, he would not have said, “Let them store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life.” He was advising nothing other than that the life of the rich is not true—the life which fools call not only true but also blessed.

How, however, is that blessed which is not true? Therefore blessed life is not found except in true life; nor is true life found except in eternal life. The rich are understood not yet to possess it through whatever pleasures [Col. 1523] they may enjoy, and therefore they are urged to take hold of it through almsgiving, so that at the end they may hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food.” Since that kingdom itself is eternal life, the same Lord shortly afterward makes this clear, saying: “They will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:34–35, 46).

#### 2. Pilgrimage through faith in this life

Until we take hold of that life, we are pilgrims away from the Lord, because we walk by faith, not by sight. For he said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” In faith he is our way; in sight, our truth and life.

“Now we see through a mirror in an enigma”—and this is faith; “but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12)—and that will be sight. Again he says: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith in the inner person” (Eph. 3:16–17). This is the way, where “we know in part.” But shortly afterward he says: “To know also the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:19). That will be sight, when, in this fullness, “what is perfect has come” and “what is in part will be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10).

Again he says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” This is faith. Then he adds: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4). That will be sight.

John also says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” This is faith. Then he adds: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). That will be sight.

Accordingly, the Lord himself, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” was speaking to Jews, among whom there were some who had already believed in him. Directing his words to these people, he said: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” They had already believed; for the Evangelist says: “Jesus was saying to those Jews who had believed in him: ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free’” (John 8:31–32).

They had therefore already believed and had already begun to walk in Christ, as on the way. He therefore exhorts them to reach their destination by persevering. Where should they arrive except at what he says: “The truth will set you free”? What is that freedom except freedom from every mutability of vanity and from every corruption of mortality?

Therefore that is true life, eternal life, which we have not yet grasped so long as we are pilgrims away from the Lord. Yet we shall grasp it, because we walk through faith in the Lord himself, if we remain most steadfastly in his word.

For corresponding to what he said, “I am the way,” he said, “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” And corresponding to what he said, “and the truth and the life,” he said, “and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

In this pilgrimage, then, and on this way—that is, in faith—what do I exhort you to do, brothers, except what the Apostle says: “Therefore, since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord” (2 Cor. 7:1)?

[Col. 1524] Those who, before they believe, demand that the light of that utterly pure and unchangeable truth be supplied to them, although they cannot behold it except through faith with a cleansed heart—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8)—are like blind people who first desire to see the bodily light of this sun so that they may be healed of blindness, although they cannot see it unless they are healed beforehand.

# Sermon 347

[Note: Corrected likewise according to the manuscripts designated above and according to the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: Also elsewhere titled *On the Saints* 17.]

## On the Fear of God I

[Note: The Paris and Louvain theologians point out that Bede cites this sermon in his commonly circulated text; but this is mistaken. The error was occasioned by a fragment from Sermon 191, *On the Nativity of the Lord* 8, which had been attached to this sermon in the printed editions of Amerbach and the Paris editors.]

### Chapter I

#### 1. How frequently the fear of God is commended in Scripture

Many commands concerning the fear of God have been given to us, brothers, and the divine utterances have proclaimed countless times how useful it is to fear God. From this most abundant supply, listen attentively while I recall a few passages and discuss them as far as I can in the brevity of the time.

Who would not rejoice to be wise—or, if he is not yet wise, desire to become so? But what does Scripture say? “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

Who would not delight in reigning? But let us hear what the Spirit admonishes in the Psalm: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:10–11). Hence the Apostle also says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12).

We also read that it is written: “You desired wisdom; keep justice, and the Lord will provide it for you.” For we find many people extremely negligent of justice and extremely eager for wisdom. Through this the divine Scripture teaches them that they cannot attain what they desire unless they preserve what they neglect. “Keep justice,” it says, “and the Lord will provide for you the wisdom you desired.”

But who can preserve justice unless he fears God? For it says elsewhere: “The one who is without fear cannot be justified” (Sirach 1:16, 33; 1:28). Moreover, if the Lord provides wisdom only to one who preserves justice, while the person without fear cannot be justified, we are brought back to that saying: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

### Chapter II

#### 2. The stages from fear to wisdom

The prophet Isaiah also, when commending those seven well-known spiritual gifts, began with wisdom and arrived at the fear of God, as though descending from the heights to us in order to teach us to ascend. He therefore began from the point where we wish to arrive and arrived at the point from which we ought to begin.

“The Spirit of God,” he says, “will rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, the Spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:2–3).

Therefore, just as Isaiah descended from wisdom to fear—not by failing, but by teaching—so we ought to ascend from fear to wisdom, not by becoming proud, but by making progress. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

This is the valley of weeping of which the Psalm says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping.” For by the valley [Col. 1525] humility is signified. Who is humble except the person who fears God and, through that fear, crushes his heart in tears of confession and repentance? “For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19).

But let him not fear remaining in the valley. In that very contrite and humbled heart—which God does not despise—he himself has arranged the ascents by which we rise toward him. For the Psalm says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, to the place which he has appointed” (Ps. 83:6–7).

Where are the ascents made? “In the heart,” he says. But from where must one ascend? Certainly from the valley of weeping. And to where must one ascend? “To the place,” he says, “which he has appointed.” What is this place except a place of rest and peace? For there is that clear wisdom which never withers.

Therefore Isaiah descended to exercise us through certain stages of instruction—from wisdom to fear, that is, from the place of everlasting peace to the valley of temporal weeping—so that, grieving, groaning, and weeping in the confession of repentance, we might not remain in grief, groaning, and tears; but, ascending from this valley to the spiritual mountain where the holy city Jerusalem, our eternal mother, has been founded, we might enjoy undisturbed joy.

Thus, after placing wisdom first—that is, the unfailing light of the mind—he added understanding, as though replying to those asking how one reaches wisdom: “Through understanding”; how one reaches understanding: “Through counsel”; how one reaches counsel: “Through fortitude”; how one reaches fortitude: “Through knowledge”; how one reaches knowledge: “Through piety”; how one reaches piety: “Through fear.”

Therefore wisdom is reached from fear, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” From the valley of weeping to the mountain of peace.

# Chapter III

#### 3. The seven stages from Isaiah are compared with the eight beatitudes of the Gospel

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). They are the humble in the valley; they are in trembling; they offer to God a contrite and humbled heart. From there they ascend to piety, so that they do not resist his will—whether in his words, when they do not grasp his meaning, or in the very order and governance of creation, when many things happen otherwise than a person’s private will desires. There one must say: “Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance” (Matt. 5:4)—not the earth of those who die, but the earth of which it is said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6).

From this piety they will merit the stage of knowledge, so that they may know not only the evils of their past sins, which they lamented with sorrow in the first stage of repentance, but also the evil in which they exist amid this mortality and pilgrimage away from the Lord, even when worldly prosperity smiles upon them. For this reason it is written: “The one who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccles. 1:18).

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” From there they rise to fortitude, so that the world may be crucified to them and they to the world; so that amid the perversity of this life and the abundance of iniquity, love may not grow cold, but the hunger and thirst for righteousness may be endured until we arrive at its satisfaction [Col. 1526] in that immortality of the saints and fellowship of the angels.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:5–6).

Nevertheless, because of the restlessness of temptations and because of what was said, “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7), if certain sins should perhaps creep in little by little and stealthily, by which human weakness is overtaken, counsel must not be lacking.

For that stage of fortitude in this mortal life is not so powerful that a person who struggles continually with an exceedingly crafty adversary is never at times struck down—especially through temptations of the tongue, where, if someone says to his brother, “You fool,” he will be liable to the fire of Gehenna (Matt. 5:22).

What counsel is there, then, except what the Lord says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37)? Therefore, just as in the stages we learn through Isaiah the fifth is counsel, so in the Gospel, among the praises of the beatitudes, the fifth place is given to this: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

The sixth stage in Isaiah is understanding. At this stage hearts are cleansed of every falsehood of carnal vanity, so that pure intention may be directed toward the end. Therefore, in the sixth place, the Lord also said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:7–8).

When the end has been reached, one now stands, now rests, now triumphs in secure peace. And what is the end except God Christ? “For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). And who is the Wisdom of God except Christ? And who is the Son of God except Christ?

In him, therefore, all who become wise become wise, and in him all who become children of God become children of God; and this is complete and everlasting peace.

Therefore, since in Isaiah wisdom is the seventh stage for those ascending upward—the point from which Isaiah himself began to descend to us by teaching—the Lord, who raises us up, also placed this in the seventh place: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

Since, then, we possess these promises and are striving toward the Lord by these stages, let us endure all the rough and harsh things of this world. Let its savagery not break us; once it has been conquered, we shall rejoice in eternal peace.

To this the eighth saying exhorts us, having already shown the end: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:9–10).

# Sermon 348

[Note: [Col. 1526] Corrected according to the same manuscripts and editions designated in the preceding sermon.]

[Note: [Col. 1526] Also elsewhere titled *On Time* 214.]

## On the Fear of God II

[Note: [Col. 1526] Florus cites this sermon on Romans 11. But we do not know whether you have the sermon here in complete form, although Augustine says at the end that it is longer. Certainly it was much shorter in the earlier printed editions, in which everything contained here before Chapter III, beginning with the words “Therefore they must be mocked,” etc., §3, is entirely absent. We are now restoring this material from the old Michaeline manuscript.]

### Chapter I

#### 1. True strength is acquired through the fear of God. Fear must be expelled by love, not by vanity

I do not doubt, beloved brothers, that the fear of God has been implanted in your hearts, so that you may be led to true and solid strength. For although the person who fears no one is called strong, one is perversely strong who first refuses to fear God, so that by fearing he may listen, by listening love, and by loving cease to fear.

[Col. 1527] Then he will be truly strongest—not through proud hardness, but through secure righteousness. Thus it is also written: “The fear of the Lord is the hope of strength” (Prov. 14:26).

When the punishment that he threatens is feared, one learns to love the reward that he promises. Thus through fear of punishment a good life is preserved; through a good life a good conscience is acquired, so that through a good conscience no punishment is feared.

Therefore let the one who does not wish to fear learn to fear. Let the one who wishes always to be secure learn to be anxious for a time. For, as John says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

He certainly spoke correctly and truthfully. If you do not wish to have fear, then first see whether you already possess perfect love, which casts out fear. But if fear is excluded before that perfection has arrived, pride inflates rather than love builds up.

For just as hunger in good health is driven away not by disgust but by food, so in a sound mind fear must be driven away not by vanity but by love.

### Chapter II

#### 2. It must be examined by what kind of love one comes to be without fear

Examine your conscience, then, whoever you are who no longer wish to fear. Do not stroke its surface; descend into yourself and penetrate the inner recesses of your heart.

Investigate carefully whether some poisonous vein is sucking and swallowing a deadly love of the world; whether you are moved and captured by some enticement of carnal pleasure; whether you are puffed up and exalted by empty boasting; whether you are boiling over with some concern for vanity.

Would you dare to declare yourself pure and clear, however deeply you search out the hiding places of your conscience for evil deeds, words, and thoughts—if diligence in iniquity no longer exhausts you, and if no negligence in righteousness is creeping in?

If these things are so, you rightly rejoice; rejoice that you are without fear. The love of God has expelled it—of the God whom you love with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.

The love of your neighbor has also expelled it—the neighbor whom you love as yourself. Therefore you are concerned for him, so that he too may love God with you, with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind. For you do not rightly love even yourself except because you love God in such a way that you do not love him less on account of turning toward yourself.

But if, although no desire within you stirs you—something no one would dare boast about concerning himself—nevertheless you love yourself in yourself and take pleasure in yourself, you ought to fear this all the more, because you fear nothing. [Note: [Col. 1527] The Michaeline manuscript reads: “although no desire outside you ensnares you.”]

For fear must not be cast out by just any kind of love, but by the right love with which we love God with our whole mind and, for that reason, our neighbor, so that he too may love God. To love oneself in oneself and to please oneself is not the love of righteousness but the vanity of pride.

Accordingly, the Apostle struck with justified condemnation those who love themselves and please themselves (2 Tim. 3:1–5). Perfect love therefore casts out fear. But only that should be called love which is not baseness.

For what is baser than a human being without God? See what the person who loves himself not in God but in himself loves. To such a person it is rightly said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

Because he is high-minded and therefore does not fear, he certainly does not fear in a ruinous way: he is not placed on a solid foundation but is scattered by the wind of pride. [Col. 1528]

Nor is the person who loves and praises himself in himself gentle and devout; rather, he is puffed up and fierce. He does not know how to say: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33:3).

For what good does the person love who perhaps loves this very thing because of this very thing—that he fears nothing? He may persuade himself of this not through soundness but through savagery.

For example, there may be some exceedingly bold bandit who is perversely stronger in proportion as he is more dangerously cruel. Because of the very love by which he loves fearing nothing, he may devise enormous crimes so that he may practice what he loves and strengthen it by practicing it. The greater his offenses become, the greater will be the boldness of one who does not fear.

Therefore what can also be found in a very wicked person must not be loved as a great good.

#### 3. Epicureans and Stoics perversely love to be without fear

Therefore the philosophers of this world must be mocked—not only the Epicureans, who even hold justice itself for sale at the price of carnal pleasure. For they say that a wise person ought to be just for this reason: either to acquire bodily pleasure or to retain it.

These people also proclaim themselves exceedingly strong and say that they fear absolutely nothing. They believe that God does not care for human affairs, and that after this life has been consumed there will be nothing afterward. If some adversity befalls them in this very life, they consider themselves fortified because, when they cannot retain bodily pleasure in the body itself, they can nevertheless contemplate it in the mind and, delighting themselves through that contemplation, preserve the blessedness of bodily pleasure even against the assault of bodily pain.

Does love not also cast out fear among these people? Yes—but it is love of the filthiest pleasure, or rather love of the most disgraceful vanity. When pain, rushing upon the body’s limbs, has expelled pleasure itself, its false image will remain in the mind through vanity. That vanity is loved so greatly that when the vain person embraces it with all the strength of his heart, even the savagery of pain is softened.

Therefore not only must these people be mocked, but the Stoics themselves as well. For these two sects, the Epicureans and the Stoics, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, dared to vaunt their smoke against the light of our Paul (Acts 17:18).

The Stoics also present themselves as exceedingly strong. They preserve the same refusal to fear—not for the sake of bodily pleasure, but for the sake of virtue of mind—simply for the sake of not fearing. They are swollen with conceit, not healed by wisdom, but hardened by error.

They are all the less and less sound because they have believed that a sick mind can be healed by themselves. They think the mind’s health consists in saying that the wise person ought not even to pity. For if he pities, they say, he suffers; and what suffers is not sound.

O foolish blindness! What if he suffers less precisely because he is not sound? For it matters whether he does not suffer through perfect health. Such will be the body and mind of the saints in the resurrection of the dead, which these people do not believe, because they have ignorant teachers when they have themselves as their teachers.

It matters, therefore, whether something does not suffer through health or through numbness. According to the health of this mortal life, healthy flesh feels pain when it is pricked. Such also is the mind that is well disposed according to this life: when touched by the misery of one who is suffering, it suffers with him in compassion.

But flesh made numb by a more serious disease—or dead because it has even lost its spirit—does not feel pain when it is pricked. Such is the mind of those who philosophize without God, or rather, who are suffocated without God.

For just as a body lives when inspired by the mind, so the mind itself lives when inspired by God. Let these people, then, who neither suffer nor fear, see to it that they are perhaps not sound but dead.

### Chapter III

#### 4. In the Christian, one kind of fear must gradually be expelled, while another remains

Let the Christian fear before perfect love casts out fear. Let him believe and understand that he is a pilgrim away from the Lord so long as he lives in a body that is corrupted and weighs down the soul.

His fear should be less in proportion as the homeland toward which we travel is nearer. For the fear of those who are traveling should be greater; that of those who are drawing near, less; and that of those who have arrived, none.

Thus fear also leads to love, and perfect love casts out fear.

Let the Christian fear not those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more they can do, but the one who has power to kill both body and soul in the fire of Gehenna (Luke 12:4–5).

There is, however, another fear of the Lord, chaste and enduring forever and ever (Ps. 18:10). Perfect love does not cast this fear out; otherwise it would not endure forever and ever. Nor was it without reason that, when “the fear of the Lord” had been said, “chaste” was added, and the phrase was joined to “enduring forever and ever.”

Why is this so, except because the fear which love casts out pricks the soul lest it lose something loved in creation—whether bodily health and rest, or some such thing after death? For this is why the punishments, pains, and torments of Gehenna are feared even in the underworld.

But when the soul takes care lest God abandon it after it has abandoned him, that is the chaste fear which endures forever and ever.

I would speak about this at greater length, but the sermon has already grown long, and I am compelled to spare both my elderly strength and, perhaps, your weariness.

# Sermon 349

[Note: [Col. 1529] Corrected according to the designated manuscripts and according to the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1529] Also elsewhere titled *On Time* 52.]

## On Charity and on the Blind Man Who Was Illuminated I

[Note: [Col. 1529] Possidius notes in the Index, chapter 9: “Two treatises on Charity.”]

### Chapter I

#### 1. Some charity is divine, some human. Human charity is lawful or unlawful

The Apostle was speaking to us shortly ago about charity, when his Letter was being read. He commended it to us in such a way that we understood that all other things, however great the gifts of God, are of no benefit without it.

But wherever charity itself is present, it cannot be alone. Let us, then, in turn deliver a discourse on charity to your Charity.

There is one kind of charity that is divine and another that is human. Human charity is itself of two kinds: lawful and unlawful.

I shall speak, as the Lord grants, about these three kinds of charity or love—for Latin has two words for what in Greek is called ἀγάπη (*agapē*). This, then, is my first division: I said that one charity is human [Col. 1530] and another divine; and I divided human charity into two, since one is lawful and the other unlawful.

First I shall speak of lawful human charity, which is not condemned; then of unlawful human charity, which is condemned; and third, of divine charity, which leads us to the kingdom.

### Chapter II

#### 2. On lawful human charity

To indicate the matter briefly, human charity is lawful when a wife is loved; it is unlawful when a prostitute or another man’s wife is loved. In the marketplace and streets, lawful love is more readily tolerated than the love of a prostitute. [Note: Perhaps: “by which a prostitute is loved.”]

But in the house of God, in the temple of God, in the city of Christ, in the body of Christ, even love of a prostitute leads the lover to Gehenna.

Therefore possess lawful charity. It is human; but, as I said, it is lawful. It is not merely lawful in the sense that it is permitted; it is lawful in such a way that, if it is absent, one is condemned.

You may lawfully love your wives with human charity, love your children, love your friends, and love your fellow citizens. All these names contain the bond of relationship and, in a certain way, the glue of charity.

But you see that this charity can also belong to the impious—that is, to pagans, Jews, and heretics. Who among them does not love his wife, children, brothers, neighbors, relatives, friends, and so forth?

This is therefore human. If someone is carried away by such cruelty that he even loses the human affection of love, does not love his children, and does not love his wife, he should not even be counted among human beings.

The one who loves his children is not to be praised; but the one who does not love his children is to be condemned. Let him still see with whom this love ought to be shared.

Wild animals also love their young. Serpents love their young; tigers love their young; lions love their young. For there is no beast that does not murmur tenderly to its offspring. Though it terrifies human beings, it cherishes its little ones.

The lion roars in the forests so that no one may pass; it enters the cave where its young are, and lays aside all the rage of its wildness. It leaves that rage outside when it enters.

Therefore the person who does not love his children is worse even than a lion. These things are human, and they are lawful.

### Chapter III

#### 3. On unlawful love. The members of Christ. Beware unlawful love

You are members of Christ, and you are the body of Christ. Hear the Apostle and tremble. He could not have spoken more gravely, more forcefully, or more sharply have frightened Christians away from the love of fornication than when he said: “Therefore, taking the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute?”

To say this, he first said: “Do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her?” And he supplied a testimony from Scripture, where it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6:15–16; Gen. 2:24).

This was spoken by divine authority, but concerning a man and his wife—where it is permitted, allowed, and honorable—not where it is disgraceful, unlawful, and condemned in every respect.

Just as one flesh is made through the lawful union of husband and wife, so one flesh is made through the unlawful union of a prostitute and her lover.

When, therefore, one flesh is made, let what he added terrify you; let it horrify you: “Therefore, taking the members of Christ…”

Consider the members of Christ, Christian. [Col. 1531] Do not look for the members of Christ in someone else; look within yourself at the members of Christ—you who were purchased by the blood of Christ.

“Therefore, taking the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute?” Whoever does not shudder at this abhors God.

### Chapter IV

#### 4. Divine charity cannot coexist with unlawful love of a prostitute

By all means, by all means, I beg you, my brothers: let us suppose something that is not so—that God had promised such people immunity and had said, “Whoever does such things, I will have mercy on them; I will not condemn them.” Let us suppose that God had said this.

Even with immunity promised, does someone take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? He does not, if the third kind of love, divine love, is present.

For I have mentioned three kinds of love, and I promised that, as the Lord granted, I would speak about three: lawful human love, unlawful human love, and that excellent and divine love.

Let us question divine charity. Let us place the two human loves before it and say: “Here is lawful human love, by which a wife is loved, along with daughters and other worldly relationships. Here is another, unlawful love, by which a prostitute is loved, by which another man’s servant-girl is loved, by which another man’s daughter is loved without being sought or promised, by which another man’s wife is loved.

“Two kinds of love stand before you. With which of these do you wish to remain?”

The person who chooses to remain with lawful human love does not remain with unlawful human love. Let no one say to himself, “I have both.”

If you have both, admitting the love of a prostitute into yourself, you wrong the divine charity that dwells there, as though she were a married woman.

For I suppose that if you are a married man and love a prostitute, you do not bring the prostitute into your house to live with your wife. You do not go so far. You seek darkness; you seek hiding places; you do not openly profess your disgrace.

And those who do not have wives, and who are almost more freely lovers of prostitutes—I say “almost” because, if they are already believers, they too are condemned—I suppose that even a young man who does not yet have a wife, if he loves a prostitute, does not make her live with his sister, nor does he make her live with his mother, lest he wrong human modesty and offend the honor of his own blood.

If, then, you do not make the prostitute whom you love live with your mother or your sister, lest, as I said, you offend the honor of your blood, do you make the love of a prostitute live in your heart together with the love of God, and offend the honor of Christ’s blood?

### Chapter V

#### 5. Through love of the inner light, one must cry out by living well, following the example of the blind man. The world’s opposition. Love God; you will find nothing better

Love God. You will find nothing better. You love silver because it is better than iron and bronze; you love gold more because it is better than silver; you love precious stones more because they surpass even the value of gold.

Finally, you love this light, which everyone who fears death is afraid to leave. You love, I say, this light—just as the blind man who cried out after Jesus desired it with immense love: “Have mercy on me, Son of David!”

The blind man cried out to Christ as he passed by. For he feared that Christ might pass by and not heal him. And how loudly did he cry? So loudly that, although the crowd was forbidding him, he did not keep silent.

He overcame the one who opposed him; he held fast to the Savior. While the crowds made a din and forbade him to cry out, Jesus stood still, called him, and said to him: “What do you want [Col. 1532] me to do for you?”

“Lord,” he said, “that I may see.” “Receive your sight; your faith has saved you” (Luke 18:38–42).

Love Christ; desire the light that is Christ. If that man desired the light of the body, how much more ought you to desire the light of the heart?

Let us cry out to him not with voices but with our conduct. Let us live well; let us despise the world. Let everything that passes be nothing to us.

When we live in this way, those who love us as worldly people—who love the earth, who think in terms of dust, who draw nothing from heaven, who snatch the free air with their hearts and nostrils—will certainly criticize us and say, if they see us despising these human and earthly things: “What are you suffering? Why are you acting madly?”

That is the crowd opposing the blind man, so that the blind man would not cry out. There are also Christians who prevent people from living as Christians should. For that crowd too was walking with Christ, and yet it was preventing the man who was crying out to Christ and desiring the light from receiving Christ’s benefit.

There are Christians of this kind. But let us conquer them; let us live well. Let life itself be our voice to Christ. He will stand still, because he stands.

### Chapter VI
### 6. Christ’s Passing-By

For there too there is a great mystery. He was passing by when the man cried out; when he healed him, he stood still. Christ’s passing-by should make us intent on crying out. What is Christ’s passing-by? Whatever he endured for us temporally—that is his passing-by.

He was born: he passed by. Is he still being born? He grew: he passed by. Is he still growing? He nursed: is he still nursing? Weary, he slept: is he still sleeping? He ate and drank: is he still doing so? Finally, he was seized, bound, scourged, crowned with thorns, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, suspended on the wood, killed, pierced with a lance, buried, and rose again: he is still passing by. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father: he stood still.

Cry out as loudly as you can: now he gives you light. For even in the very fact that he was the Word who was with God, he was certainly standing still, because he was not changed. And the Word was God; and the Word became flesh. The flesh did many things and suffered many things in its passing-by; the Word stood still. By that very Word the heart is illuminated, because by that very Word the flesh which he assumed is honored. Take away the Word: what is flesh? It is what yours is. But in order that Christ’s flesh might be honored, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14). Let us therefore cry out and live well.

## CHAPTER VII

### 7. Parents Are to Be Loved, but Christ More

Love your children; love your wives—even in a worldly way. For you ought to love them according to Christ, so that according to God you may provide for them, loving nothing in them except Christ, and hating them among your own if they refuse to have Christ. For this is that divine love. What benefit will your transitory and mortal love bring them?

Nevertheless, when you love them as human beings, love Christ more. I do not say that you should not love your wife, but love Christ more. I do not say that you should not love your father; I do not say that you should not love your children; but love Christ more. Hear him saying this, so that you do not think these are my words: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

When you hear, “He is not worthy of me,” are you not afraid? Of the one whom Christ says is “not worthy of me,” he says that he is not with him. And he who will not be with him—where will he be? If you do not love being with him, fear being without him. Why fear being without him? Because you will be with the devil if you are not with Christ. And where will the devil be? Hear Christ himself: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

If you are not kindled by the fire of heaven, fear the fire of Gehenna. If you do not love being among God’s angels, fear being among the devil’s angels. If you do not love being in the kingdom, fear being in the furnace of burning, unquenchable, everlasting fire. Let fear first prevail in you [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions: “Let pious fear prevail in you.”], and love will follow. Let fear be a pedagogue; let it not remain in you itself, but let it lead you to love, as to a teacher.

# SERMON CCCL [Note: Corrected according to two manuscripts designated e., two designated t., the codex designated cb., and the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]  
[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 39 and in volume nine.]  
## On Charity, II

[Note: It appears at the end of Eugippius’s *Excerpta* under the title “On the Praise of Charity.” Bede and Florus likewise call it this in their treatments of 1 Corinthians 13 and 14, and of 1 Timothy 1. It was formerly read in volume nine as well, but there it is interpolated and was rejected by Erasmus’s judgment.]

### 1. The Praise of Charity

Through charity divine teaching is grasped without error and kept without labor. The new commandment makes a new human being.

My brothers, whoever’s heart is full of charity grasps, without any error, the whole rich abundance and the very broad teaching of the divine Scriptures, and keeps it without any labor. The Apostle says: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13:10); and elsewhere: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

What is the end of the commandment, then, except the fulfillment of the commandment? And what is the fulfillment of the commandment except the fullness of the law? Therefore, what he said there—“The fullness of the law is charity”—he also said here: “The end of the commandment is charity.”

There can be no doubt that a human being is the temple of God, in whom charity dwells. John also says: “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). When the Apostles said these things and commended the excellence of charity to us, they could only have belched forth what they had eaten. For the Lord himself, feeding them with the word of truth, the word of charity—which is himself, the living bread that came down from heaven—said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:34–35).

He came to destroy the corruption of the flesh through the mockery of the cross and to dissolve, by the newness of his death, the antiquity of the bond of our death. Through the new commandment he made a new human being. It was an old thing that a human being should die. But so that this might not always prevail in humanity, a new thing occurred: God died.

But because he died in the flesh, not in divinity, through the everlasting life of his divinity he did not permit the everlasting destruction of the flesh. Thus, as the Apostle says: “He died for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

Therefore, the one who brought the newness of life against the oldness of death sets the new commandment against the old sin. Consequently, if you wish to extinguish the old sin, extinguish desire through the new commandment and embrace charity. For just as desire is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all good things.

### 2. Through Charity the Whole Teaching of the Scriptures Is Possessed

Charity, by which we love God and our neighbor, securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances. For the one heavenly Teacher teaches us and says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37–40).

Therefore, if you do not have time to examine all the sacred pages, to unfold all the complexities of speech, and to penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, hold fast to charity, on which everything depends. In this way you will hold what you have learned there; you will also hold what you have not yet learned.

For if you know charity, you know something from which even that which you perhaps do not know depends. In what you understand in the Scriptures, charity is evident; in what you do not understand, charity is hidden. Therefore, the person who holds charity in conduct holds both what is evident and what is hidden in the divine utterances.

### 3. He Continues His Praise of Charity

Therefore, brothers, pursue charity, the sweet and health-giving bond of minds, without which the rich person is poor, and with which the poor person is rich.

It endures in adversity and exercises restraint in prosperity; it is strong amid harsh sufferings and joyful in good works; most secure in temptation and most generous in hospitality; most joyful among true brothers and most patient among false ones.

In Abel it was pleasing through sacrifice; in Noah secure through the Flood; in Abraham’s wanderings most faithful; among Moses’ injuries most gentle; in David’s tribulations most meek. Among the three young men it innocently awaits the soothing fires; among the Maccabees it bravely endures savage fires.

Chaste in Susanna toward her husband, in Anna after her husband, in Mary apart from a husband. Free in Paul for rebuking, humble in Peter for obeying; human in Christians for confessing, divine in Christ for forgiving.

But what greater or richer thing can I say about charity than the Lord proclaims its praises through the mouth of the Apostle, demonstrating “a still more excellent way” and saying:

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels but do not have charity, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so that I remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.

“Charity is magnanimous; charity is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not dishonored, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never falls” (1 Corinthians 13:1–8).

How great is this! The soul of the letters, the power of prophecy, the salvation of the mysteries, the solidity of knowledge [Note: The printed editions read: “How great is this salvation of souls, the solidity of knowledge.” Here we follow the manuscript codices.], the fruit of faith, the wealth of the poor, the life of the dying.

What is as magnanimous as dying for the ungodly? What is as kind as loving enemies? Charity alone is not oppressed by another’s happiness, because it does not envy. Charity alone is not exalted by its own happiness, because it is not puffed up. Charity alone is not pricked by a bad conscience, because it does not act wrongly.

Amid insults it is secure; amid hatred it is beneficent; amid anger it is calm; amid plots it is innocent; amid iniquities it groans, while in truth it breathes freely.

What is stronger than it—not for repaying injuries, but for disregarding them? What is more faithful than it—not to vanity, but to eternity [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “What is easier than it—not for vanity, but for truth”?]?

For this reason it bears everything in the present life, because it believes everything concerning the future life; and it endures everything imposed here, because it hopes for everything promised there. Rightly, therefore, it never falls.

Pursue charity, then, and, thinking of it in holiness, bring forth fruits of righteousness. Whatever richer things you discover in its praises than I have been able to say, let them appear in your conduct. For an old man’s speech ought to be not only weighty but also brief.

# SERMON CCCLI [Note: Corrected according to two manuscripts designated cl., and those designated f., gr., ph., r., rm., and s., as well as the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]  
[Note: Elsewhere, 50 among the fifty Homilies, and in volume nine.]  
## On the Benefit of Doing Penance, I

[Note: It existed in volume 9, mutilated in many places, in Erasmus’s copy. He judged this treatise and the one that follows to differ greatly from Augustine. Yet, in our judgment, each has Augustine’s doctrine and style. Possidius separately records both in the same chapter 8 of the *Index*. Florus frequently cites this first one, calling it the book *On Penance*, in his treatment of 1 Corinthians 5 and 6, and elsewhere. Some turns of phrase nevertheless have the flavor of a sermon, such as this one in chapter 2: “which your erudition recognizes with me.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Necessity of Humility in Penance

The high God is approached through humility. For what purpose the Law was given.

How useful and necessary the medicine of penance is is easily understood by those who remember that they are human beings. For it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The Publican, anxious in the confession of his sins, descended from the temple more justified than the Pharisee, secure in the enumeration of his merits.

For although the Pharisee also gave thanks to God, saying: “I give you thanks, God, that I am not like the other people: unjust, adulterers, robbers; or even like this Publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess”—nevertheless the one who stood at a distance was preferred to him. He did not dare raise his eyes toward heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:10–14).

For that Pharisee was rejoicing not so much in his own health as in comparison with the illnesses of others. Since he had come to the physician, it was more beneficial for him to show by confession the things from which he was suffering than to conceal his wounds and dare to glory in the scars of others.

It is therefore no wonder that the Publican departed more thoroughly healed, since he was not ashamed to display what caused him pain.

In visible matters, when a person wishes to reach high places, he is lifted upward. But since God is highest of all, he is reached not by exaltation but by humility. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord is near to those who have crushed their heart” (Psalm 33:19). And again: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, but the exalted he knows from afar” (Psalm 137:6).

By “the exalted” he means the proud. He regards the lowly in order to raise them up; he knows the exalted in order to cast them down. When he says that he knows the exalted from afar, he clearly shows that he attends to the lowly from nearby; yet he has declared that the Lord himself is exalted.

God alone is not arrogant, however much he may praise himself in proclamation. Let pride not suppose, therefore, that it is hidden from God’s eyes: God knows the exalted. Nor should it think itself joined to God: for he knows the exalted from afar.

Whoever therefore refuses the humility of penance has no thought of approaching God. For it is one thing to lift oneself up to God, another to lift oneself up against God. Whoever throws himself down before him is raised up by him; whoever raises himself up against him is cast down by him.

One kind of solidity belongs to greatness, another kind of emptiness to inflation. Whoever swells outwardly wastes away inwardly.

Whoever chooses to be cast down in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners—God chooses him to dwell in his courts; and he who claims nothing for himself, God takes up into the seat of blessedness.

Hence the Psalm sings most sweetly and truthfully: “Blessed is the person whose help is from you, O Lord.” Do not think that the person who humbles himself always lies prostrate, since it is said: “He will be exalted.” Nor should you suppose that his exaltation takes place in the eyes of human beings through bodily elevation. For after saying, “Blessed is the person whose help is from you, O Lord,” the Psalm immediately adds and reveals the spiritual height of that help: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, to the place which he established.”

Where, then, has he arranged the ascents? In the heart—in the valley, that is, of weeping. This is what it means: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” For just as ascent indicates exaltation, so a valley indicates humility, and a valley of weeping indicates tears.

For just as sorrow is the companion of penance, so tears are witnesses of sorrow. Very appropriately the Psalm continues and says: “For the one who gave the law will give blessing” (Psalm 83:6–8).

The Law was given for this purpose: to show the wounds of sins, which the blessing of grace would heal. The Law was given for this purpose: to make the proud person aware of his weakness and to urge the weak person to penance.

The Law was given for this purpose: so that in the valley of weeping we might say, “I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members.” And while we wept we might cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” And there might come to our aid, when he who raises the fallen, releases the bound, and gives light to the blind hears us (Psalm 145:7–8), “the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:23, 25).

## CHAPTER II
