### 2. Three Kinds of Penance

#### The First Penance, before Baptism

There are three acts of penance which your learning recognizes with me. They are customary in the Church of God and known to those who pay careful attention.

One is that which brings forth the new human being, until, through saving Baptism, the washing away of all former sins takes place. Then, as with a child who has been born, the pains by which the womb was pressed toward birth pass away, and joy follows sorrow.

Everyone who has already been established as the arbiter of his own will, when he approaches the sacraments of the faithful, cannot begin a new life unless he repents of the old one. Only little children are exempt from this penance when they are baptized, for they cannot yet use free choice.

Nevertheless, for the consecration and remission of original sin, the faith of those by whom they are brought forward benefits them, so that whatever stains of sin they contracted through others, from whom they were born, may also be cleansed through the questioning and response of others.

For it is most truly lamented in the Psalms: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquity, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7). Likewise, it is written that no one is clean in God’s sight, not even an infant whose life is a single day upon the earth (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

Apart from such children—it exceeds the measure of human beings to wish to inquire further concerning their order and merit in that future allotment of the saints which is promised—it is nevertheless devoutly believed that, for their spiritual salvation, they benefit from what the authority of the Church preserves throughout the whole world with such firm strength.

No other human being passes over to Christ, so as to begin to be what he was not, unless he repents of having been what he was.

This first penance is commanded to the Jews, when the Apostle Peter says: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38). The Lord himself commanded such penance when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4:17).

John the Baptist, also, full of the Holy Spirit, the forerunner and preparer of the Lord’s way, says concerning it: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:7–8).

## CHAPTER III

### 3. The Second Penance, Common and Perpetual in This Life

We ought to repent of this life because it is subject to corruption and temptations.

The second penance is that whose practice must be undertaken throughout this entire life, during which we dwell in mortal flesh, with perpetual supplicatory humility.

First, because no one desires eternal, incorruptible, immortal life unless he is dissatisfied with this temporal, corruptible, mortal life. For no one is born into a new life through the sanctification of Baptism in such a way that, just as he lays aside all former sins there, he immediately also lays aside mortality and corruption of the flesh.

If this were not so, then what is written—and what each person still feels in himself while he is in this life—would remain: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

Since this will not exist in that blessed state, when “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), who could doubt that, whatever temporal happiness we may experience [Note: The manuscripts lack the word “happiness”; perhaps “life” should be supplied instead.], we ought nevertheless to repent of this life, so that we may run with complete eagerness toward that incorruption?

Hence the Apostle also says: “As long as we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:6–7). Who, then, hastens and longs to return to his homeland and contemplate that vision which is face to face, unless he has become dissatisfied with his exile?

From this sorrow of the penitent there also bursts forth and resounds that mournful voice: “Alas for me, because my exile has been prolonged.” And lest you think that an unbeliever is speaking, see what follows: “I have dwelt in the tents of Kedar; with those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me fiercely” (Psalm 119:5–7).

These are the words not only of a faithful human being but also of a most steadfast evangelist and a most courageous martyr.

Hence also comes the Apostle’s statement: “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, longing to be clothed with our dwelling which is from heaven—if indeed, when clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we who are in this dwelling groan under our burden, not wishing to be stripped but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:1–4).

What, then, do we long for except not to be as we now are? And what do we groan over except that, in repenting, we are as we are? But when will we no longer be so, unless our earthly house has been dissolved, so that through the transformation of the whole human being, in soul and body, we may receive a heavenly dwelling?

Therefore holy Job did not say that there is temptation in this life; he said that this very life is temptation, speaking as follows: “Is not human life upon the earth a temptation?” At that point he also touched remarkably upon the mystery of fallen humanity, saying: “Like a servant fleeing from his master and finding a shadow” (Job 7:1–2, according to the Septuagint).

For this life ought rather to be called a shadow of life. And it was not without reason that the fugitive Adam, after the offense of sin, hid himself from the face of the Lord, covered by the leaves of trees which cast shade—as one fleeing from his master and finding a shadow, as it has been said.

### 4. The Humility of Penance Is Necessary Even for the Just

There is always reason for the just to repent, not to boast. The reason for penance among dispensers of God’s word and sacraments.

All these things have been said so that no one, though justified from former sins through Baptism, would dare to become proud if he commits nothing for which he should be separated from communion at the altar, as though already boasting of complete security. Rather, he should preserve humility, which is almost the one discipline of Christianity.

Let not earth and ashes become proud (Ecclesiasticus 10:9), until this entire night passes, in which all the beasts of the forest pass through, and the young lions roar, seeking their food from God (Psalm 103:21).

Job himself was sought out for this food, when he said: “Human life upon the earth is temptation.” The Lord also said: “In this night Satan asked to sift you as wheat” (Luke 22:31).

Who, then, in his right mind would not groan? Who would not be displeased, through penance, that this is his condition? Who would not, supplicating with complete humility, make himself heard by divine assistance, until all this material and earthly shadow of temptations passes away; until he who never fails shines upon us as everlasting day, illuminates the hidden things of darkness, reveals the thoughts of the heart, and then each person receives praise from God (1 Corinthians 4:5)?

Moreover, even if a person boasts that he has so subdued his body that, crucified to the world and freed from every evil work, he chastises his members by bringing them into servitude, so that sin no longer reigns in his mortal body by making it obey its desires; even if he worships the one true God alone, devoted to no rite of idols and entangled in no sacred rites of demons; does not take the name of the Lord his God in vain; confidently awaits eternal rest; renders due honor to his parents; is neither bloodstained by murder, defiled by fornication, fraudulent through theft, double-tongued through lying, nor polluted by desire for another’s property or wife; does not in his own affairs either dissolve into luxury or dry up through greed; is not quarrelsome, insulting, or abusive; finally, sells all that he possesses, gives it to the poor, follows Christ, and plants the root of his heart in the heavenly treasure—what could seem capable of being added to such complete righteousness?

Nevertheless, I do not want him to boast. Let him understand that all these things have been granted to him, not that they originate from him. “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Let him certainly distribute the Lord’s money; let him provide for his neighbor, just as he realizes that provision has been made for him [Note: The printed editions add, “or ought to be made,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]. Nor should he think it sufficient merely to preserve intact what he received, lest it be said to him: “Wicked and lazy servant, you ought to have given my money, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest.” Otherwise what he received will be taken away from him, and he will be cast into the outer darkness (Matthew 25:26–30).

If those who can preserve intact what they have received ought to fear so severe a punishment, what hope is there for those who wickedly and criminally squander it?

This person, then, will be occupied in human affairs, bound by the duty of spiritual rather than bodily acquisition—not indeed tied down by worldly businesses, but, because he serves as a soldier for God, not sluggish and cast down in the idleness of indolence.

Let him therefore give all his alms, if he can, with cheerfulness—whether he distributes something to the bodily needs of the poor, or whether, as a dispenser of heavenly bread [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “in the dispensation of heavenly bread.”], he builds an unconquerable camp against the devil in the hearts of believers. For “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Let him not therefore be broken by weariness amid the difficulties of affairs, which necessarily arise so that it may be shown to a person that he is human. Let anger not creep into him against someone who rushes in offensively, or who, compelled by need, asks at an inconvenient time; or who, while you are occupied with a greater matter, carelessly demands assistance in his own business; or who, through blind desire or pitiable sluggishness, resists an obvious word of justice.

Let him give neither more nor less than is appropriate. Let him not speak more than is necessary, or speak when there is no need. For “beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Romans 10:15).

Nevertheless, those feet draw dust from the dry earth; and this dust is rightly shaken off in judgment against those who, by perverse will, disdain this service offered to them.

Therefore, not only because of the mortality and ignorance of this life, and because of the evil of the day—which, if only it were enough, is described by the saying, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matthew 6:34), which we are commanded to bear and carry until it passes, and to endure by acting courageously so that we may bear fruit with perseverance—but also because of the very dust of this world, which clings to the feet of those who give counsel in the course of their journeys of counsel, and because of the losses that occur in the very busy work of administration—may the Lord grant that they be compensated with greater gains—we ought to practice daily penance.

### 5. The Daily Sins of the Laity

When Is the Use of Marriage Blameless?

If this is true of the dispensers of God’s word and ministers of his sacraments, the soldiers of Christ, how much more must it be true of the rest of the enlisted multitude, a kind of province of the great king?

Lest that most faithful and courageous soldier, the Apostle Paul, should offend anyone even through a false suspicion of greed, he served as a soldier at his own expense. And when necessary support happened to be lacking, he said: “I robbed other churches, receiving pay from them for your service” (2 Corinthians 11:8).

How much more, then, must the provincial churches [Note: Those whom we more commonly call laypeople, he calls “provincial” and “enlisted” members of the Church, beautifully alluding—as often elsewhere—to popular usage, according to which provinces that were responsible for paying soldiers’ wages were called *stipendiariae*, “enlisted” or “tribute-paying.” See above, Sermon 302, no. 15, and the passages from certain sermons on the Psalms cited there, as well as *Tractate 122 on John*, no. 3.]—those bound to worldly affairs—practice daily penance?

Although they ought to be free and pure from thefts, robberies, frauds, adulteries and fornications and every form of luxury, from the cruelty of hatred and the persistence of enmities, and finally from every foulness of idolatry, the frivolity of spectacles, the impious vanity of heresies and schisms, and all such disgraces and crimes, nevertheless, because of the management of household affairs and the very close bonds of marriage, they commit so many sins that they seem not merely to be sprinkled with the dust of this world [Note: The manuscripts read, “to be sprinkled with the dust of this world.”], but to be smeared with mud.

This is what the Apostle says to them: “There is already altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded?” For that execrable conduct he adds and says: “But you do injustice and defraud, and this to your brothers” (1 Corinthians 6:7–8).

Apart from acts of injustice and fraud, he says that the very fact of having lawsuits and disputes among themselves over worldly matters is a fault. Nevertheless, he advises that this should be tolerated if such disputes are brought to an end by ecclesiastical judgment.

Hence also comes the statement: “The unmarried person thinks about the things of God, how he may please God; but the married person thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.” He notes the same thing concerning a woman.

Or consider this [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read, “or that,” with one manuscript.], when he says: “And again, come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.” To show that this was a sin, but one conceded because of weakness, he immediately added: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (1 Corinthians 7:32–33, 5–6).

The sexual union of the two sexes is blameless only for the purpose of procreation.

How many other sins there are—whether in speaking about the affairs and business of others, which do not concern you; or in empty laughter, since it is written, “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise person will scarcely laugh quietly” (Ecclesiasticus 21:23); or even in food, when a greedier and more immoderate appetite for what is prepared to sustain this life often reveals an excess through the indigestion of the following day [Note: The manuscripts read *post triduana*, “after three days”; Louvain reads *postriduana*, “of the day after tomorrow.” The Parisian Nivellian edition is better with *postridiana*, “of the following day.”]; or in selling and buying, through perverse desires concerning high prices and low prices [Note: Louvain reads *nota perversa*, “perverse mark,” while other printed editions and the manuscripts differ.].

It is tedious to gather together all the things that each person more certainly understands and reproves in himself if he does not carelessly attend to the mirror of the divine Scriptures.

Although each of these may not seem to strike with a fatal wound, as murder and adultery or other things of this kind do, nevertheless, when all are gathered together, they are like scabies. The more numerous they are, the more they kill; or they so destroy our beauty that they separate us from the most chaste embraces of that bridegroom who is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44:3), unless they are dried up by the medicine of daily penance [Note: Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Louvain reads *desecentur*, “are cut away.”].

### 6. We All Contract Daily Sins through the Weakness of the Flesh

The Struggle of the Christian Soul

If this is false, why do we beat our breasts every day? We bishops do this as well, standing at the altar with everyone else. Why else, when we pray, do we say what we ought to say throughout this entire life: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12)?

We are not asking that sins be forgiven which we believe were already forgiven in Baptism—for if we did, we would doubt that very faith. Rather, we are speaking of daily sins, for which each person also never ceases to offer, according to his strength, the sacrifices of almsgiving, fasting, prayers, and supplications.

Therefore, whoever carefully examines himself and does not deceive himself through flattery understands well with what danger of eternal death and with what poverty of perfect righteousness he is an exile from the Lord, although he has already been placed in Christ—that is, on the way—and is trying to return.

For if we have no sins, yet beat our breasts and say, “Forgive us our debts,” then by this very act we certainly sin gravely, with no one doubting it, since we lie amid the very sacraments.

Therefore, insofar as we are joined to our God by faith, hope, and charity, and imitate him as far as we can, we do not sin but are children of God. But insofar as, through the occasion of bodily weakness—for it has not yet been dissolved by death or transformed by resurrection—blameworthy and wicked impulses creep in, we sin.

We ought certainly to confess this, lest, with hard necks, we merit not the healing of our sickness but the condemnation of pride.

Hence both statements have been written with complete truth: “Whoever has been born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9); and what we read in the same Epistle of John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

The first statement was made from the first fruits of the new human being; the second, from the remnants of the old. We enact both in this life. Gradually the newness advances, and as the oldness gradually yields, the new takes its place.

While both are being enacted, we are in the arena. We not only strike the adversary through good works; by avoiding sins less cautiously, we are also struck by them. At present it is not considered which of us has conquered, but who strikes more frequently and who fights more strongly—until he who, having fallen, begrudged the human being who stood upright drags others with him into eternal death, and the triumphant finally say to him:

“Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

Nor are we more easily thrown down by the enemy than when we imitate him through pride; nor do we overthrow him more forcefully than when we follow the Lord in humility; nor do we inflict sharper pains upon him than when, by confessing and repenting, we heal the wounds of our sins.

## CHAPTER IV
### 7. A third, stricter penance for deadly sins. The penitent’s tears are blood.

The third practice is penance, which must be undertaken for those sins contained in the Decalogue of the Law, and concerning which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21). In this penance, therefore, each person ought to exercise greater severity toward himself, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by the Lord, as the same Apostle says: “For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:31).

Let a man therefore set up the tribunal of his mind against himself, if he fears [Note: [Col. 1542] Lov., “suppose.” The other books more aptly read, “if he fears.”] that we must appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each person may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). Let him place himself before his own face, lest this later be done to him. For God threatens the sinner with this, saying: “I will reprove you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:21).

And when judgment has thus been established in the heart, let accusatory thought be present, conscience as witness, and fear as executioner. From this let a kind of blood of the confessing soul flow forth in tears. Finally, let the mind itself pronounce such a sentence that the man judges himself unworthy of participation in the body and blood of the Lord: so that the one who fears being separated from the kingdom of heaven by the final sentence of the supreme Judge may meanwhile, through ecclesiastical discipline, be separated from the sacrament of the heavenly bread. [Col. 1543]

Let the image of the future judgment be placed before his eyes, so that, when others approach the altar of God while he does not approach it, he may consider how greatly to be trembled at is that punishment by which, while others receive eternal life, others are plunged into eternal death.

To this altar, which is now set upon the earth in the Church and exposed to earthly eyes for the celebration of the signs of the divine mysteries, even many wicked people can approach, because in this present time God displays his patience, in order to exercise his severity in the future. For they approach without knowing that God’s patience is leading them to repentance. But “according to the hardness of their heart and their unrepentant heart, they are storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:4–6).

But to that altar into which Jesus, the Forerunner, entered on our behalf, where the Head of the Church went before, with the other members to follow, none of those whom—as I have already mentioned—the Apostle said “will not possess the kingdom of God” will be able to approach. For only the priest—but plainly the whole priest—will stand there, joined, that is, to the body whose Head has already ascended into heaven. He is the one to whom the Apostle Peter said: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9).

How, then, will one dare or be able to enter within the veil, into that invisible Holy of Holies, who, scorning the medicine of heavenly discipline, was unwilling for a little while to be separated from visible things? For whoever was unwilling to be humbled in order to be exalted, when he wishes to be exalted will be cast down; and whoever in this present time has not secured for himself a place in the body of the priest through the merits of obedience and the satisfaction of penance will be separated forever from the eternal saints.

For with what face of shamelessness will he then wish God to turn his face away from his sins, who now does not say with all his heart: “For I acknowledge my transgression, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5)? How, I ask, can God deign to forgive what a man himself disdains to acknowledge in himself?

### 8. Against those who promise themselves salvation apart from the kingdom of heaven. The final sentence sends one either into the kingdom or into the fire.

Or what is that supposed confidence in which those deceive themselves who flatter themselves through their own vanity? For while they persist in their wickedness and debauchery, when they hear the Apostle saying, “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God,” they dare to promise themselves, apart from God’s kingdom, the salvation they desire. And so they say among themselves, while they refuse to do penance for their sins and at some point to change their depraved conduct for the better: “I do not want to reign; it is enough for me to be saved.”

They are first deceived in this: that there is no salvation at all for those whose iniquity persists. For when the Lord says, “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13), he plainly promised salvation to those who persevere in love, not in iniquity. Where love exists, those evil works that separate a person from the kingdom of God cannot exist. For “the whole law is fulfilled in one saying,” namely, in what is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14).

Further, if there is some distinction between those who reign and those who do not reign, nevertheless all must be in one kingdom, lest they be counted among enemies or outsiders. All Romans possess the Roman kingdom, although not all reign in it; rather, the others obey those who reign. The Apostle does not say, “Those who do such things will not reign with God,” but, “will not possess the kingdom of God.”

The same was also said concerning flesh and blood: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” because “this corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:50, 53), so that it will no longer deserve the condition and nature of flesh and blood, but of a spiritual body derived from an animal body.

Or let them be terrified by that final sentence of our Judge, which for this reason he wished to be disclosed now, so that his faithful might guard against it, giving those who fear him a sign “that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. 59:6). For those who will judge together with him are excepted—those to whom he also promised, saying: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). In this number of judges all are understood who for the sake of the Gospel left everything they had and followed the Lord. For the number twelve refers to a kind of totality. The Apostle Paul will not be there merely because he was not among those twelve.

Excepting, then, those whom he also signified by the name “angels” when he said, “When the Son of Man comes to judge with his angels”—for angels are messengers, and we rightly understand as messengers all who announce heavenly salvation to human beings. Hence the Evangelists too may be interpreted as good messengers, and it was said of John the Baptist: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3:1).

Excepting these, then, as I had begun to say, the remaining multitude of all human beings will be divided into two parts, as is clear in the Lord’s own words. For he will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left, and it will be said to the sheep, that is, to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” This is certainly the kingdom of which the Apostle spoke when he enumerated evil works: “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Hear what those who will be on the left will hear: “Go,” he says, “into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:31–41).

Therefore, would anyone dare to presume upon the Christian name [Note: [Col. 1544] Manuscripts: “Who would rejoice,” with the verb “presume” omitted.] and not listen with complete obedience and fear to the Apostle saying: “For this you must know, understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not become partners with them” (Eph. 5:5–7)?

To the Corinthians he states this at greater length: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who have intercourse with males, [Col. 1545] nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. But see how he removed fear and despair of salvation from those who committed these things in their former life. ‘And such were some of you,’ he says, ‘but you were washed, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God’” (1 Cor. 6:9–11).

### 9. Penance must be embraced by those who have relapsed after Baptism.

Whoever, therefore, remains bound after Baptism by the practice of some former evils—is he so much his own enemy that he still hesitates to change his life, when there is time, while he sins and lives in this way? For by persisting in sin he is certainly storing up wrath for himself “on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.” But by continuing to live, God’s patience is leading him to repentance.

Thus entangled in the bonds of such deadly sins, he refuses, or postpones, or hesitates to flee to the very keys of the Church, by which he may be loosed on earth so as to be loosed in heaven; and he dares to promise himself some salvation after this life merely because he is called a Christian. Nor does he tremble at that truthful thunder of the Lord’s voice: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

What of the same Apostle’s words to the Galatians? Does he not conclude an enumeration of such things with the same ending? “The works of the flesh are manifest,” he says, “which are fornication, uncleanness, debauchery, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

Let a man therefore judge himself concerning these things by his own will, while he can, and change his conduct for the better, lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged by the Lord even against his will. And when he himself has pronounced upon himself the sentence of the severest medicine, yet still medicine, let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys are administered to him in the Church. Like a good son who is already beginning to be such, while preserving the order of his mother’s members, let him receive from the ministers of the sacraments the measure of his satisfaction, so that, in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart with devotion and supplication, he may do what benefits not only himself in receiving salvation but also others as an example.

If his sin consists not only in his own grave harm but also in so great a scandal to others, and if the bishop sees that it serves the Church’s welfare, let him not refuse or resist doing penance in the knowledge of many, or even of the whole congregation. Let him not add, through shame, swelling to a wound that is deadly and fatal. Let him always remember that “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

For what is more wretched, what more perverse, than not to be ashamed of the wound itself, which cannot be hidden, but to be ashamed of its bandage?

### 10. Against those who take from others an example for neglecting penance. They are not barred from communion unless they have confessed voluntarily or have been lawfully convicted.

Let no one, brothers, suppose that he ought to despise the counsel of this saving penance [Col. 1546] because he perhaps notices and knows that many approach the sacraments of the altar whose crimes of this kind he is not unaware of.

Many are corrected, as Peter was; many are tolerated, as Judas was; many remain unknown until the Lord comes, who will “bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of the heart” (1 Cor. 4:5). For many do not wish to accuse others because they desire to excuse themselves through them. Many good Christians, however, remain silent and endure the sins of others that they know because they are often deprived of evidence and cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know.

Although certain things may be true, they are not easily to be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by sure indications. We, however, cannot bar anyone from communion—although this prohibition is not yet fatal but medicinal—unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical court.

For who would dare to assume both roles for himself, so as to be at once another’s accuser and judge? The Apostle Paul is understood to have briefly indicated a rule of this kind in the same Epistle to the Corinthians, when, after mentioning certain such crimes, he gave from them a model of ecclesiastical judgment applicable to all similar cases.

He says: “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or robbers, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. For people living in this world cannot avoid living with such persons; nor can they win them for Christ if they avoid their conversation and company.”

Hence, when the Lord ate with tax collectors and sinners, he said: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:12–13).

And therefore the Apostle continues and adds: “But now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is a fornicator, or one who serves idols, or covetous, or slanderous, or drunkard, or robber; with such a person not even to eat. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside [Note: [Col. 1546] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Lovanii: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside?” M.]? Do you not judge those who are inside? But those who are outside God will judge. Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:9–13).

By these words he sufficiently shows that the wicked are not to be removed from communion with the Church rashly or in just any manner, but through judgment. If they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest, by perversely avoiding the wicked, someone himself depart from the Church and bind to Gehenna those whom he seems to flee [Note: [Col. 1546] The manuscripts read “conquers” (vincat).].

For this too the examples are set before us in the Holy Scriptures: as in a harvest, where the chaff is tolerated until the final winnowing fan (Matt. 3:12); or within those nets where good fish are tolerated together with bad until the separation that will occur on the shore, that is, at the end of the age (Matt. 13:47–50).

Nor is this passage contradicted by what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master” (Rom. 14:4). For he did not wish a man to be judged by another according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion, or even by an extraordinary judgment usurped without authority, but according to God’s law and the order of the Church—whether voluntarily confessed or accused and convicted.

Otherwise, why did he say, “If anyone is called a brother, whether a fornicator or one who serves idols,” and so forth, unless he wished that calling to be understood as one made against someone when a sentence is pronounced in due judicial order and with integrity? For if mere naming is sufficient, many innocent people must be condemned, since someone is often falsely named in connection with a crime [Note: [Col. 1547] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “crimes.”]

### 11. Against those who, acquiescing in wicked examples, despise penance. Bad superiors must not be imitated. An elegant comparison.

Therefore, those whom we urge to do penance should not seek companions for punishment, nor rejoice because they find more such people [Note: [Col. 1547] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “because they will have found.” Lovanii: “because they may find.”]. For they will not burn any less because they burn together with many. This is not a sound remedy, but a vain consolation of malice.

Or perhaps they observe that many, even among those appointed as ecclesiastical superiors and ministers, do not live in a manner consistent with the words and sacraments that they administer to the people. O wretched people, who, by looking at such men, forget Christ! Christ both foretold long beforehand that God’s law should be obeyed rather than those men imitated who say things they do not do (Matt. 23:3), and, while tolerating his betrayer to the end, sent him even to preach the Gospel together with the others.

Those people are just as absurd, misguided, and wretched when they choose to imitate the evil conduct of their superiors rather than keep the Lord’s commandments preached through them as someone would be if, while seeing milestones filled with letters teaching the way, he thought he ought to remain on the road and not walk.

Why, if he desires to arrive, does he not rather look to and follow such companions as both point out the way correctly and walk along it perseveringly and cheerfully?

But if such people are absent, or rather appear less often—for they cannot be absent—for people do not seek persons with zealous charity, so as to commend them for imitation, in the way that they seek with malicious suspicion what they may grumble about for deception. Some fail to find good people because they themselves are evil; others fear finding them because they always wish to remain evil.

Nevertheless, let us grant that people worthy of imitation do not now appear. Whoever you are who think this, look with your mind upon the Lord, who became human in order to teach human beings how to live. If Christ dwells in your inner person through faith in your heart, and you remember what John says—“Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6)—then you will not lack someone to follow, and when another sees you, he will cease complaining about the scarcity of good people.

For if you do not know what it means to live rightly, learn the divine commandments. Perhaps many live rightly, but no one seems to you to live rightly because you do not know what it means to live rightly. If you do know, then do what you know, so that you may both possess what you seek and show others what they may imitate.

Keep Christ before your mind; keep the Apostles before it, among whom the latest is the one who says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16). Keep in mind the thousands of martyrs. Why does it please you to celebrate their feast days with shameful banquets, while it does not please you to follow their lives in honorable conduct? There you will see not only men but also women, and finally boys and girls, neither deceived by ignorance, nor perverted by wickedness, nor broken by fear of danger, nor corrupted by love of the world.

Thus, when you find nothing with which to excuse yourself, you will be surrounded not only by the unavoidable uprightness of the commandments but also by the countless multitude of examples.

## CHAPTER V

### 12. Let no sinner despair, but flee to repentance. Change of life and satisfaction for sins committed.

But, to bring at last to completion what we undertook concerning the usefulness and healing power of repentance: if, already despairing of recovery, you add sins to sins, as it is written, “When a sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3), do not despise; do not despair. Cry even from the deep to the Lord, and say to him: “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication. If you mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure? For with you is propitiation” (Ps. 129:1–4).

The Ninevites cried from such a depth and found this propitiation; and the Prophet’s threat was more readily annulled than the humility of repentance (Jonah 3). Perhaps here you say: “But I have already been baptized in Christ, by whom all my former sins were forgiven me; I have become utterly vile by repeating my former ways, and, a dog horrible in God’s eyes, have returned to my vomit. Where shall I go from his Spirit? And where shall I flee from his face?”

Where, brother, except to his mercy through repentance—to him whose power you had despised by sinning? For no one rightly flees from him except to him: from his severity to his goodness. For what place will receive you as you flee where his presence will not find you? “If you ascend into heaven, he is there; if you descend into hell, he is present.” Therefore take up your wings straight, and dwell in hope at the ends [Note: [Col. 1548] The printed editions read “at the end”; the manuscripts, “at the ends.” Augustine, expounding the same Psalm 138, read “in the last things.”] of this age: for there his hand will lead you and his right hand will bring you through (Ps. 138:7–10).

Whatever you have done, whatever sins you have committed, you are still in this life, from which God would wholly remove you if he did not wish to heal you [Note: [Col. 1548] The manuscripts read, “if he did not wish you to be healed.”]. Why, then, do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance (Rom. 2:4)? He who, by crying out, did not persuade you not to depart, cries out by sparing you that you may return.

Look upon King David. He too had already received the sacraments of that time; he had already been circumcised, which our fathers had in place of Baptism. For this purpose the Apostle says that holy Abraham received the sign of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11). He had also already been anointed with the venerable anointing by which the royal priesthood of the Church was prefigured. Yet, suddenly made guilty of both adultery and homicide, he nevertheless cried out in repentance to the Lord from so monstrous and sheer a depth of crime, not in vain, saying: “Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” By what merit at last, except because he also says: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me”?

What, moreover, did he offer the Lord to make him gracious to himself? “For if you had wished,” he says, “I would surely have given sacrifice; you will not delight in burnt offerings. A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:11, 5, 18, 19). Therefore he not only offered devoutly, but also showed by saying these things what ought to be offered. For it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless satisfaction is also made to God for what has been done through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving assisting. For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

For it was not said that we should merely abstain from sins: “But also,” it says, “plead with the Lord concerning past sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclus. 21:1). Peter was already a believer, and had already baptized others in Christ. Look, then, at Peter: self-confident, accused; afraid, wounded; weeping, healed. Even after the Holy Spirit had come from heaven, a certain Simon, already baptized in Christ, wished to buy that same Holy Spirit with money, contemplating a most criminal and impious transaction; yet, rebuked by Peter himself, he received counsel to repent (Acts 8:13–22).

The Apostle Paul also, who was certainly sending epistles to believers, says: “Lest, when I come again to you, God humble me and I mourn many of those who previously sinned and did not repent of the uncleanness and debauchery and fornication which they committed” (2 Cor. 12:21). Thus both commands for right conduct and examples—not only of those acting rightly, but also of those repenting in order to recover the salvation lost by sinning—surround us.

But suppose it were uncertain whether God forgives. What does one lose by pleading with God, when he did not doubt that he would lose salvation by offending God? For who is certain that even an emperor will forgive? Yet money is spent, seas are crossed, the uncertainties of storms are undergone, and almost in order that death may be avoided, death itself is incurred. Then intercession is made through men to a man: these things are done without hesitation, though it is uncertain with what outcome they will succeed. Yet the keys of the Church are more certain than the hearts of kings: by these keys whatever is loosed on earth is also promised to be loosed in heaven (Matt. 16:19). And the humility by which each person humbles himself before the Church of God is much more honorable; a lesser labor is imposed, and eternal death is avoided with no danger of temporal death.

## SERMON 352

[Note: [Col. 1549] Corrected according to the editions of Erasmus, Paris, and Lovanii.]

[Note: [Col. 1549] Elsewhere numbered 27 among the 50 Homilies.]

### On the Benefit of Doing Penance, II

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. The occasion for the sermon provided by the reading.

The voice of a penitent is recognized in the words to which we responded while the psalm was being sung: “Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 50:11). Therefore, although we had not prepared a sermon for Your Charity, we learned that this was what we were to treat because the Lord commanded it.

We wished today to leave you to meditation, knowing how abundant a feast you have received. But because you receive what is set before you for your health, you are hungry every day. May the Lord our God himself therefore grant both us sufficient strength and you a profitable hearing. For we do not fail to recognize that we must serve your good and useful desire.

Let us therefore be helped by you both in prayer and in attention: in prayer directed to God, and in attention directed to the word. Then we may say what he himself judges to be useful for you, he who feeds you through us.

The voice of a penitent, then, is recognized in these words: “Turn your face from my sins, and blot out all my crimes.” We are therefore divinely commanded to say something about penance. For it was not we who ordered the reader to sing this psalm; rather, what he judged useful for you to hear, the Lord commanded even a child’s heart to receive.

Let us say something about the benefit of penance, especially since the holy anniversary day is now approaching, as it is fitting, when it draws near, to humble souls and discipline bodies with greater earnestness.

### 2. Three kinds of penance. The first belongs to those who are to be baptized. Penance commanded to the Jews before Baptism.

Sacred Scripture presents three considerations concerning the practice of penance. No one approaches the Baptism of Christ rightly—for in it all sins are blotted out—unless he does penance for his former life. For no one chooses a new life unless he is sorry for the old.

We must also prove this from the authority of the divine Books: whether those who were to be baptized did penance.

When the Holy Spirit, who had previously been promised, was sent, and the Lord fulfilled the pledge of his promise, the disciples, having received the Holy Spirit, as you know, began to speak in all languages, so that each of those who were present recognized his own language in what they heard.

Terrified by this miracle, they asked the Apostles for guidance concerning their life. Then Peter announced to them that they must worship the one whom they had crucified, so that, believing, they might now drink his blood, which they had shed in their violence.

When our Lord Jesus Christ had been proclaimed to them and they recognized their guilt, what the prophet had earlier foretold was fulfilled in them: “I turned my distress upon myself, while the thorn was being fixed.” They were pierced with remorse. For they were turned toward the distress of sorrow when the thorn of recollection of sin was fixed.

They had not thought that they had done anything evil; the thorn had not yet been driven in. But when Peter spoke, so that you may recognize that the thorn had been fixed, Scripture says: “When Peter was speaking, they were pierced in heart.”

Accordingly, in the same psalm, after it has been said, “I turned my distress upon myself, while the thorn was being fixed,” it follows: “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not hide my crime. I said, ‘I will confess my offense against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Ps. 32:4–5).

When, therefore, pierced by that thorn of recollection, they said to the Apostles, “What then shall we do?”, Peter said to them: “Do penance, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven” (Acts 2:37).

Therefore, for the moment, if any of those who are preparing to be baptized happen to be present—we believe they are present with all the greater devotion to the word because they are nearer to forgiveness—we address a few words to them first, so that they may lift their minds in hope.

Let them love becoming what they are not, and hate what they were. Let them already conceive by their desire the new person who is to be born. Whatever in their former life gnawed at them, whatever troubled their conscience, whatever in any way—great or small, speakable or unspeakable—let them not doubt can be forgiven, lest human hesitation hold against itself what God’s mercy wishes to forgive.

### 3. Our Figures in the Events that Happened to the Israelites

The rock was a figure of Christ. The crossing of the Red Sea was Baptism. The manna was a figure of Christ, the heavenly bread. How the Israelites received the same spiritual food and drink as we do. The rock struck with a rod.

Let each person faithfully remember also the example displayed in that first people. For the Apostle says—speaking of such matters—“All these things happened as figures for us.” What had he said? “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1–4).

He said that these things were our figures—he whom no faithful person has ever contradicted. And while he enumerated many things, he explained only one, because he said, “But the rock was Christ.” By explaining one thing, he left the others to be investigated. Yet, so that the investigator might not go astray by departing from Christ, but might seek firmly, founded upon the rock, he said, “The rock was Christ.”

He said that those things were our figures, and everything was obscure. Who could unroll these wrappings of figures? Who could open them? Who would dare to examine them? Amid certain extremely dense thickets and heavy shade, he kindled a light: “The rock,” he said, “was Christ.”

Now, therefore, with the light brought in, let us ask what the remaining things signify, what the sea, the cloud, and the manna mean. For he did not explain these, but showed what the rock was. The crossing through the sea is Baptism. But because Baptism—that is, the water of salvation—is not saving unless consecrated in the name of Christ, who shed his blood for us, the water is marked by his cross. To signify this, that Baptism was the Red Sea.

The manna is plainly explained by the Lord himself. “Your fathers,” he says, “ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.” For when would they have lived, if the figure could announce life but could not itself be life? “They ate manna,” he says, “and they died”—that is, the manna they ate could not free them from death; not because the manna itself was death to them, but because it did not free them from death. The one who was to free them from death was the one signified by the manna.

Certainly the manna came from heaven. Consider whom it signified: “I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:49, 51).

As attentive and watchful people, attend carefully to the Lord’s words, so that you may advance and learn how to read and hear. “They ate,” he says, “the same spiritual food.” What does “the same” mean, unless it means the food that we also eat?

[Col. 1552]

“But then,” someone says, “was that manna the thing I now receive? If so, nothing comes now, since it already existed before. Then the offense of the cross has been emptied.” How, then, does he say “the same,” unless he added “spiritual”? Those who received that manna in such a way that they thought only their bodily need was being satisfied and their belly fed, not their mind, ate nothing great; their need was adequately met. God fed some people; to others he announced something. These ate bodily food, not spiritual food.

Whom, then, does he say ate the same spiritual food as our fathers? Whom do we suppose, brothers, unless those who truly were our fathers? Indeed, they were not merely our fathers; they are. For all those people are alive.

Thus the Lord says to certain unbelievers, “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.” What does “your fathers” mean except “those whom you imitate in unbelief, whose ways you follow by refusing to believe and resisting God”? In accordance with this meaning he says to certain others, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). For the devil did not create or beget any human being either by power or by generation; nevertheless, he is called the father of the wicked, not because of generation but because of imitation.

Conversely, it is said of the good, “Then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. 3:29), although he is speaking to Gentiles who did not derive their bodily lineage from Abraham. They were his children, not by being born but by imitating him.

Abraham is abolished and disowned as father by the faithless when the Lord says to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). And so that evil trees boasting of Abraham’s fatherhood might be uprooted, children of Abraham are promised from stones (Matt. 3:9).

Therefore, when he says here, “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died,” they did not understand what they ate; and so, because they did not understand, they received nothing but bodily food. Likewise, the Apostle speaks of “our fathers”—not the fathers of unbelievers, not the fathers of the ungodly—eating and dying, but of our fathers, the fathers of believers, eating spiritual food, and therefore the same food.

“Our fathers,” he says, “ate the same spiritual food, and drank the same spiritual drink.” For there were people there who understood what they were eating; there were people for whom Christ tasted more deeply in the heart than manna in the mouth.

Why should we speak of others? Moses himself was there from the beginning, the servant of God, “faithful in all his house” (Heb. 3:2), knowing what he was administering, and knowing that at that time present realities ought to be administered as closed things and future realities as open ones.

Let me say it briefly: all who understood Christ in the manna ate the same spiritual food as we do; but all who sought only satiety from the manna—[Col. 1553] “the fathers of unbelievers”—ate and died.

The same is true of the drink: for the rock was Christ. Therefore they drank the same drink as we do, but spiritually—that is, it was received by faith, not swallowed by the body. You heard, “They drank the same drink: the rock was Christ.” For there was not one Christ then and another now.

There was one rock then (Exod. 17:6), another stone which Jacob placed beneath his head (Gen. 28:11); one lamb slaughtered to be eaten at Passover (Exod. 12), another ram caught in the thickets to be sacrificed when Abraham spared his son, whom he had been commanded to offer (Gen. 22:13); one sheep and another sheep, one stone and another stone—yet the same Christ. Therefore the same food, therefore the same drink.

Finally, the rock itself was struck with wood so that water might flow; for it was struck with a rod (Exod. 17:5–6). Why with wood, and not with iron, unless because the cross approached Christ so that he might offer us grace?

The same food, then, and the same drink—but for those who understood and believed. For those who did not understand, there was only that manna and only that water: that food was for the hungry, that drink for the thirsty; neither was for the believer. But for the believer it was the same as what exists now.

Then Christ was to come; now Christ has come. “To come” and “has come” are different words, but the Christ is the same.

### 4. Moses’ Doubt as a Figure

Since the matter has come before us, I also want to say something about the doubt of God’s servant Moses. This too was a figure of the saints of old.

Moses doubted at the water. When he struck the rock with the rod so that water might flow, he doubted. Someone reading about his doubt might perhaps pass over it without understanding, because he would not dare to investigate it.

But the Lord God was displeased with that doubt, and marked it—not only by rebuking it, but also by punishing it. For because of this doubt Moses is told, “You shall not bring this people into the land of promise” (Num. 20:12); and, “Go up into the mountain and die” (Deut. 32:49).

Here God clearly appears angry. What, then, shall we say about Moses, my brothers? Was all his labor, all his anguish for the people, and all that love of his—when he said, “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from your book” (Exod. 32:31–32)—condemned because of this sudden and unexpected doubt?

And what shall we make of what the reader concluded when he read the Apostle, “Love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8)?

While I was proposing certain things for solution, your eagerness led me to propose something else that perhaps you would not have sought. Let us see, then, and let us continue to attempt, as far as we can, to penetrate the mystery.

God is angry; he says that Moses will not bring the people into the land of promise; he orders him to ascend the mountain and die. And yet he gives that same Moses many things to do: he orders him how to act, how to organize the people, and how not to abandon them indiscriminately and carelessly. He would never deign to impose such duties upon a condemned man.

Receive something still more marvelous. Since it had been said to Moses—for this pleased God for the sake of a certain mystery and dispensation—that he himself would not bring the people into the land of promise, another Jesus, the son of Nave, was chosen. This man was not originally called by that name; he was called Auses (Num. 13:17). When Moses entrusted the task of bringing in [Col. 1554] the people to him, he summoned him, changed his name, and called him Jesus, so that the people of God might enter the land of promise not through Moses but through Jesus—that is, not through the law but through grace.

But just as that Jesus was not the true Jesus but a figurative one, so that land of promise was not the true land but a figurative one. It was temporal for the first people; the land promised to us will be eternal. Yet eternal realities were promised and foretold through temporal figures.

Therefore, just as that Jesus was not the true Jesus, and that land of promise was not the true land but a figure, so the manna was not truly heavenly food but a figure; so that rock was not truly Christ but a figure; and so with everything else.

What consideration, then, does Moses’ doubt demand? Perhaps a figure was also expressed there, giving a hint to the person who understood and stirring and urging the mind to investigate.

For I see that, even after that doubt, after God’s anger, after threats of death, and after Moses was removed from bringing the people into the land of promise, God continued to speak to Moses about many matters as to a friend, just as he had spoken before. Indeed, God sets Moses before Jesus the son of Nave as an example of obedience, admonishing him to serve God as Moses had served him, and promising that he would be with him as he had been with Moses.

Clearly, beloved, God himself compels us not to condemn Moses’ doubt indiscriminately, but to understand it.

The rock lying there was a figure; the rod striking was a figure; the water flowing was a figure; and Moses doubting was also a figure. And he doubted there, where he struck. Moses’ doubt arose when the wood came near the rock.

The swift may hurry ahead; or rather, let them patiently wait for the slow. Moses doubted when the wood came near the rock; the disciples doubted when they saw the Lord crucified. Moses bore the figure of them. He was a figure of that Peter who denied the Lord three times.

Why did Peter doubt? Because the wood had drawn near the rock. When the Lord foretold the manner of his death—that is, the cross itself—Peter was terrified: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen” (Matt. 16:22). You doubt because you see the rod hanging over the rock.

For this reason the disciples then lost the hope they had in the Lord. In a certain sense it was intercepted when they saw him crucified, when they mourned him as slain.

After the resurrection he found them speaking together about this matter in a sorrowful conversation. While holding their eyes so that he would not be recognized by them—not withdrawing himself from believers, but delaying himself for those who doubted—he joined their conversation as though he were a third speaker and asked them what they were discussing.

They were amazed that he alone was ignorant of what had happened in the very matter about which he was asking. “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?” they said. And they recounted what had happened concerning Jesus. At once they opened the innermost core of their despair and, although unknowingly, showed their wound to the physician: “But we were hoping,” they said, “that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:13–21).

Behold, the doubt arose because the wood had drawn near the rock; the figure of Moses had been fulfilled.

### 5. What Moses’ Death on the Mountain Foreshadowed

Let us also examine this: “Go up into the mountain and die.”

Through [Col. 1555] Moses’ bodily death, the death of his doubt was figured—but on the mountain. O marvelous mysteries! Once this has been explained and understood, how much sweeter it is than manna!

Doubt arose at the rock; on the mountain it died. When Christ was humble in his passion, like a rock lying before their eyes, it was fitting that people should doubt concerning him; that humility displayed nothing great. It was fitting that by this very humility he became a stone of stumbling. But once glorified by the resurrection, he appeared great; he is now a mountain.

Therefore, let that doubt which arose at the rock die on the mountain. Let the disciples recognize their salvation and recover their hope. Observe how that doubt dies; observe how Moses dies on the mountain.

He must not enter the land of promise: we do not want doubt there; let it die. Let Christ show us its death.

Peter was terrified and denied him three times. For the rock was Christ. He rose again and became a mountain; he strengthened Peter as well. But doubt dies.

How does it die? “Peter, do you love me?” The examiner and knower of the heart asks; he wishes to hear that he is loved, and once is not enough. He asks this and is heard almost to Peter’s annoyance. Peter is astonished that he is questioned by one who already knows, and also questioned so many times when it would have been enough to answer once even to one who did not know.

But it was as though the Lord were saying to him, “I am waiting; let the appointed number be completed: let him confess his love three times” (John 21:15–17), because he had denied him three times through fear (Matt. 26:69–74). Thus, by asking so many times, the Lord was killing that doubt on the mountain.

### 6. An Invitation to Baptism

Moses’ hands are now extended against Amalek, now lowered.

What, then, beloved, if these things are evident? They had been closed, not for deception but for delight. They would not be grasped so sweetly if, being readily available, they became commonplace.

Let the person preparing to receive Baptism, whom I began to address, therefore attend to his own affair. The Red Sea was Baptism; the people crossing through it were being baptized. The crossing itself was Baptism, but in the cloud. For what was being foretold was still clouded; what was being promised was still concealed.

Now the cloud has withdrawn, and the serenity of manifest truth has appeared, because the veil through which Moses spoke has also been removed. This veil hung in the temple as well, so that the temple’s secrets might not be seen; but on the Lord’s cross the veil was torn apart so that they might be revealed.

Come, then, to Baptism. Enter the road fearlessly through the Red Sea. Do not be anxious about your past sin as about an Egyptian pursuing you. Your sins pressed upon you with the heavy burden of slavery, but in Egypt—in the love of this world, in a distant exile. They compelled you to pursue earthly works; like people making bricks, you worked at things of clay.

Your sins press upon you; come [Note: [Col. 1555] Codex v. reads: “you worked while sin pressed upon you. Come.”] confidently to Baptism. The enemy will be able to follow you as far as the water; there he will die.

Have some fear concerning your former life. Believe that some of your sins may remain if any of the Egyptians remain. I hear the voice of the sluggish: “I am not afraid of my past sins. I do not doubt that everything is forgiven for me in the holy water, through the Church’s love as well; [Col. 1556] but I am afraid of future sins.”

So you prefer to remain in Egypt? For the present, escape the enemy who has already pressed upon you and already subdued you. Why do you imagine future enemies for yourself? What you have already done will exist even if you do not wish it; what you think you will do will not exist if you do wish it.

“But the road is dangerous. For even after I cross the Red Sea, I shall not yet be in the land of promise. That people was led through long deserts.”

For the present, let yourself be freed from Egypt. Do you suppose, then, that the one who rescued you from your ancient captivity will fail to assist you on the road? Will the one who freed you from your old enemies not restrain your new ones?

Only cross fearlessly, walk fearlessly, and be obedient. Do not embitter that Moses whose type he bore in this obedience.

I admit that enemies are not lacking. For just as there were people who followed those fleeing, so there were people who obstructed those walking. Indeed, beloved, these things were our figures.

For the present, let there be nothing in you that grieves Moses. Do not become the bitter water which that people could not drink after the Red Sea. For there too there was a temptation.

Yet when these things happen, when the people become bitter, we show them Christ—what he endured for them, how he shed his blood for them—and they become mild, as though we were casting wood into the water.

Certainly you will have Amalek as an enemy opposing your journey. Then Moses prayed; then he extended his hands. When he lowered his hands, Amalek grew strong; when he extended his hands, Amalek weakened.

Let your hands also be extended. Let Amalek, the tempter and obstructer of this journey, grow weak. Be watchful and sober in prayers and in good works, but not apart from Christ, because that extension of the hands was the cross of Christ.

The Apostle is extended upon it when he says, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Therefore let Amalek grow weak, let him be conquered, and let him not obstruct the passage of God’s people. If you lower your hands from good works, from the cross of Christ, Amalek will prevail.

Nevertheless, do not think that you will always and continually be strong, nor collapse entirely through despair. For that alternation of weakness and strength in the hands of God’s servant Moses was perhaps your own alternation.

Sometimes you fail in temptations, but you do not succumb. He lowered his hands for a little while; he did not fall completely. “I said, ‘My foot is slipping’; but your mercy, Lord, was assisting me” (Ps. 93:18).

Do not be afraid, then. The helper is present on the journey, the one who did not fail to be your liberator in Egypt. Do not be afraid; undertake the road and proceed confidently.

Sometimes Moses lowered his hands, sometimes he raised them; nevertheless, Amalek was defeated (Exod. 17:11–13). He could rebel; he could not conquer.

## CHAPTER II

### 7. The Second Repentance, Which Is Universal and Daily. The Remedy and Covenant in the Lord’s Prayer Concerning the Forgiveness of Debts. Forgiveness of a Brother

We are now reminded to speak about the second repentance. For I proposed that Scripture presents a threefold consideration of it.

The first belongs to those preparing themselves and thirsting to come to Baptism. I have shown this from the holy Scriptures.

There is also a daily repentance. And where have we shown this daily repentance? I have no better place to show it than in the daily prayer, where the Lord taught us how to pray and showed us what to say to the Father. Among these words he placed the following: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

What debts, brothers? Since “debts” here can mean nothing other than sins—sins whose debts were forgiven in Baptism—are we praying that they may again be forgiven? Certainly every Egyptian who was following us died. If nothing remains of the pursuing enemies, what are we asking to be forgiven except the lowering of our hands against Amalek?

“Forgive us, as we also forgive.” He established a remedy; he confirmed a covenant. Here he dictates the prayers; there he answers the one praying. He knows by what law the matter is conducted in heaven, and how the things desired may be obtained.

Do you wish to be forgiven? “Forgive,” he says. For what do you have to offer God that you wish to be offered to you by him?

Is Christ the Savior now walking on earth? Is Zacchaeus now joyfully receiving him into his house (Luke 19:6)? Is Martha now preparing him lodging and a meal (Luke 10:40)? He needs none of these things; he sits at the right hand of the Father. But, “When you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:40).

This is the extension of the hands under which Amalek was defeated.

You do indeed give to the poor when you give something to the hungry. Perhaps you will have less of what you give—but less in your house, not in heaven. Yet here too, on earth, the one at whose command you gave supplies what you gave.

Speaking of this, the Apostle says, “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply” (2 Cor. 9:10). You are God’s laborer when you give to the needy. You sow in winter what you will reap in summer.

Why, then, do you fear, unbeliever, that in this great household so great a master will not feed his laborer? It will also be there, but only what is sufficient for you. God will provide everything necessary, not everything desired.

Work, then, without fear. Extend your hands; let Amalek grow weak.

But here, as I said, when you give something from your household, you either see less of what you used to see there, or you do not see it there once you have given it, until God gives again.

Tell me: when you forgive from the heart, what do you lose? When you forgive someone who sins against you, what will you have less of in your heart? You forgive from it, but you lose nothing.

Indeed, a certain wave of love was flowing into your heart, issuing as if from an inner spring. You hold hatred against your brother and have blocked the fountain. Therefore, when you forgive, you not only lose nothing; you are watered more abundantly.

Love is not constricted. You place a stone of stumbling there and create difficulties for yourself.

“I shall avenge myself; I shall take revenge; I shall show him; I shall do this.” You rage and toil, though you could be secure by forgiving, live securely, pray securely.

For see what you are about to do. You are about to pray. What do I mean by “when”? You are going to pray today. Or are you not going to pray? Filled with anger and hatred, you threaten revenge; you do not forgive from the heart.

Look: the hour of prayer has come. You begin either to hear or to say those words. After the preceding words have been said and heard, you are going to come to this verse. Or if you are not going to come to it, where are you going?

Will you not forgive your enemy? Will you turn aside from Christ? Certainly, if you turn aside in prayer because you do not wish to say, “Forgive us our debts,” since you cannot say, “As we also forgive our debtors”—lest the answer quickly be given you, “So I forgive as you forgive”—then, because you cannot say this and do not wish to forgive, you will turn aside from this verse, pass it over, and say what follows: “Do not let us be led into temptation.”

There your creditor will seize you—the creditor whose face you were avoiding.

When someone is walking through a street and encounters a person to whom he owes something, if there is a side street at hand, he abandons the direction in which he was going and takes another route so as not to see the creditor’s face. You thought that you had done this in this verse. You avoided saying, “Forgive as I forgive,” lest he forgive in the same way—that is, not forgive, because you do not forgive—and you did not want to say it, avoiding the creditor’s face.

Whom are you avoiding? Whom are you going to avoid? Where will you go where you can be present and he absent? You are going to say, “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:7–9).

How far can a debtor flee from Christ, except by going to hell? This creditor is present there too.

What will you do except what follows? “If I take my wings in a straight direction and fly to the farthest parts of the sea”—that is, if I contemplate the end of the world in hope and live according to your commandments, I shall be lifted up on the two wings of love.

Complete, then, the two wings of love: love your neighbor as yourself, and do not hold hatred, from which you would flee your creditor.

## CHAPTER III

### 8. The Third Kind of Repentance, Mourning Repentance, for Mortal Sins. The Soul Is Suffocated by Despair of Forgiveness

There remains the third kind of repentance, about which I shall say something briefly, so that, with the Lord’s help, I may fulfill what I proposed and promised.

This repentance is more serious and more sorrowful. In the Church, those who undertake it are properly called penitents; they are also removed from participation in the sacrament of the altar, lest by receiving it unworthily they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

That repentance, then, is sorrowful. The wound is grave: perhaps adultery has been committed, perhaps murder, perhaps some sacrilege. It is a grave matter, a grave wound, deadly and fatal—but the physician is almighty.

After the suggestion of the deed, the pleasure, the consent, and the perpetration, let the sinner be thought of as a four-day-old corpse. Yet the Lord did not abandon even him; he cried, “Lazarus, come out!” At the voice of mercy, the mass of the tomb gave way; death yielded to life, hell yielded to what is above.

Lazarus was raised and came forth from the tomb, and he was bound, as are those who confess their sin and perform penance. They have already come forth from death, for they would not confess unless they were coming forth. To confess itself is to come forth from what is hidden and dark.

But what does the Lord say to his Church? “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18).

Therefore, when Lazarus comes forth, since the Lord has completed the good work of his mercy by bringing the hidden and putrefying dead man to confession, he now completes the rest through the ministry of the Church: “Loose him, and let him go” (John 11:39–44).

But, beloved, let no one choose this kind of repentance for himself; let no one prepare himself for it. Nevertheless, if it should happen, let no one despair.

Judas the betrayer was destroyed completely not so much by the crime he committed as by his despair of forgiveness. He was not worthy of mercy; therefore the light did not shine in his heart, so that he might run to the forgiveness of the one he had betrayed, as did those who had crucified him. Instead, he killed himself in despair; he hanged himself with a noose and suffocated himself.

What happened in his body happened in his soul. For this air, too, is called “spirit”—the wind of this atmosphere. Just as those who bind their own necks kill themselves because the air of this atmosphere cannot enter them, so those who despair of God’s forgiveness suffocate themselves inwardly through that very despair, so that the Holy Spirit cannot visit them.

### 9. Against Pagans Who Taunt Christians, Claiming That Permission to Repent Gives Permission to Sin

Pagans often taunt Christians about the repentance established in the Church. And against certain heresies the Catholic Church has maintained this truth concerning the practice of repentance. For there were people who said that repentance should not be granted for certain sins; they were excluded from the Church and became heretics.

Whatever the sins may be, the devout mother Church does not lose her compassion. Therefore Pagans also commonly taunt us on this account, not knowing what they are saying, because they have not yet reached the word of God, which makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

“You make people sin,” they say, “when you promise them forgiveness if they repent.” This is dissolution, not admonition. They enlarge upon this argument with as many words as each can muster; whether their tongue is eloquent or faltering, they do not remain silent. Yet even when we speak to them, although they are defeated, they do not agree.

Let your Charity understand briefly how they are defeated, because the Lord’s mercy has ordered everything most wisely in his Church.

They say that we give permission to sin because we promise the harbor of repentance. If the entrance to repentance were closed, would not that sinner add sin to sin all the more because he would despair of being forgiven? He would say to himself:

“Look, I have sinned; look, I have committed a crime; now there is no place for forgiveness for me. Repentance is fruitless; I shall be condemned. Why should I not live as I wish? Since I find no love there, here at least I shall feed my desire. Why should I restrain myself? There every place is closed to me; here I lose whatever I do not do, because the life that will follow this one will not be given to me. Why, then, should I not serve my lusts, fulfill and satisfy them, and do whatever is forbidden but desired?”
