Perhaps he would be told, “But, wretched man, you will be seized, accused, tortured, and punished.” Evil people know that these things are said by human beings and observed among human beings. They notice many people living wickedly and criminally while their sins remain unpunished. They can conceal what they have done; they can buy off what they cannot conceal; they can buy off, even into old age, a dissolute, blasphemous, sacrilegious, depraved life.

[Note: [Col. 1559] Thus the Victorinus manuscript. But the Amsterdam and Erasmus editions read: “they can conceal; what they have concealed, they cannot buy off. They enumerate to themselves, even into old age, a depraved life—its dissipations, blasphemies, and sacrileges: ‘Why did that man, who committed so many deeds, die old?’ Nor is the Louvain text much better.]

They list such examples to themselves: “What? Did that man, who committed so many deeds, not die an old man?”

Do you not consider that God allowed that sinful and criminal man to die old in order to demonstrate his patience, as he waited for repentance? Hence the Apostle says, “Do you not know that God’s patience [Col. 1560] is leading you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Rom. 2:4–6).

It is therefore necessary that this fear possess people’s minds. It is necessary that the person who does not wish to sin should think of God as present with him—not only in public, but also at home; not only at home, but also in his bedroom, at night, in his bed, in his heart.

Therefore, if you remove the harbor of repentance, they will increase their sins through despair.

“Look,” say those who think that sins increase because the harbor of repentance is offered in the Christian faith, “they say nothing.”

[Note: [Col. 1560] Perhaps: “to me.”]

What, then? Should God, lest sins increase again through that hope of forgiveness, not have provided against this as well? Just as he provided that sins should not increase through despair, so he ought to have provided that they should not increase through hope.

For just as the person who despairs can truly increase his sins, so can the person who hopes for forgiveness, saying to himself, “I shall do what I want; God is good; when I turn back, he will forgive me.”

Yes, say to yourself, “When I turn back, he will forgive me”—if tomorrow is certain for you. Does Scripture not admonish you with these words? “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for suddenly his wrath will come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Sir. 5:8–9).

Behold, God’s providence has watched over both dangers for us. So that we might not increase our sins through despair, the harbor of repentance has been provided; and again, so that we might not increase them through presumption, the day of death has been made uncertain.

## SERMON 353

[Note: Revised according to two “cl.” manuscripts and two “r.” manuscripts, with reference to the “gr. rm.”, Ambrose, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain editions.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 20 among the 50 Homilies.]

On the Octave of the Infants: in which he exhorts them with the words of the Apostle Peter, “Therefore, having laid aside all malice,” etc.

[Note: In Possidius’ Index, chapter 8, two sermons “on the day of the octave of the Infants” are noted; likewise, in chapter 10, “two treatises on the octave of the Infants.” All the manuscripts assign this sermon to this day. Its style shows that it belongs to Augustine’s earlier years and is plainly the same as that of Sermon 216, delivered shortly after he had become a presbyter. Verlinus and Vindingus wished to reject it, alleging a difference of style, but without justification.]

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1. He Exhorts the Baptized. The Innocence of Conduct Must Be Preserved. Humility Must Be Pursued

The sermon of an attentive shepherd should address the ears and minds of all whom our care embraces. Nevertheless, it is directed especially to you now, whose recent spiritual infancy has been marked by the cradles of the sacraments of regeneration.

For through the Apostle Peter the divine word thus speaks tenderly to you: “Therefore,” he says, “having laid aside all malice and all deceit and flattery and envy and slander, like newborn infants long for rational and innocent milk, so that by it you may grow into salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2:1–3).

Since you have tasted it, we are witnesses; we supplied this sweetness to you in the service of a nurse.

Therefore, instructed by the likeness of holy infancy, lay aside malice, deceit, flattery, envy, and slander. You must preserve this innocence in such a way that you do not lose it as you grow.

What is malice, [Col. 1561] except the love of doing harm? What is deceit except doing one thing while pretending another? What is flattery except seduction through deceptive praise? What is envy except hatred of another’s happiness? What is slander except criticism that is more biting than truthful?

Malice delights in another’s misfortune; envy is tormented by another’s good fortune; deceit gives the heart a double form; flattery gives the tongue a double form; slander wounds reputation.

But since this innocence of your holiness is the daughter of love, it “does not rejoice over wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. 13:6). It is simple as a dove and shrewd as a serpent (Matt. 10:16)—not intent on doing harm, but on avoiding the harmful person.

### CHAPTER TWO

I exhort you to this. “The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 19:14)—that is, to the humble, the spiritually little ones.

Do not despise this; do not shrink from it. This littleness belongs to the great. Pride, however, is the deceptive greatness of the weak. Once it possesses the mind, it casts down by raising it up, empties it by inflating it, and scatters it by distending it.

A harmful person cannot be humble; an innocent person cannot be proud.

I am speaking of the humility that does not wish to excel in things destined to perish, but truly contemplates something eternal, to which it may attain not by its own strength but with assistance.

[Note: The printed editions read, “but may attain to life through the strength of others.” The reading has been corrected in accordance with the manuscripts.]

Such humility cannot desire anyone’s harm, since another’s harm in no way increases its own good.

Pride, moreover, immediately gives birth to envy. And who is envious without wishing harm upon the person whose good fortune causes him pain? Therefore envy consequently gives birth to malice; from malice proceed deceit, hypocrisy, slander, and every evil deed which you would not wish to suffer from another.

If, then, you preserve devout humility—which in the holy Scriptures is commended as holy infancy—you will be secure concerning the immortality of the blessed.

[Note: The manuscripts read, “of the good.”]

“For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.”

2. Innocence must be preserved above all toward God. In the Israelites, a figure of Christian life was given to the baptized. Moreover, whoever is not proud toward human beings must certainly not be defiant toward God; for if one ought not to do to anyone what one does not wish another to do to oneself, and no human being wishes to suffer disobedience from someone subject to his authority, how much more must one beware that no one should be toward God the sort of person whom he does not wish a human being to be toward himself?

## CHAPTER III

They therefore deceive their own souls who think it sufficient if they do to no human being what they do not wish done to themselves, while corrupting themselves through a luxurious life in such a way that they attempt to do to God what they do not wish done to themselves by another person. For they do not wish anyone to corrupt their house, yet in their own selves, with pitiable blindness, they corrupt the house of God. Deaf to the Apostle crying out, they say: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone corrupts God’s temple, God will destroy that person. For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:16–17).

Let no one deceive himself. Why, then, do they think they are preserving their innocence toward other people when they harm themselves so greatly that they are deprived of God as an inhabitant and punished by him as avenger? Hence it also happens that, fallen and dissipated through harmful pleasures, they not only cease to be temples of God but even become ruins in which evil demons dwell; they begin to supplicate and worship those demons. Thus what was said comes to pass: “The final condition of that person is worse than the first” (Luke 11:26).

Therefore, you who have been regenerated by immortal seed, just as earlier the Apostle addressed you on account of the malicious desires to harm by which people do to others what they hate, so afterward he addresses you on account of the shameful and unlawful pleasures of the flesh and the wicked sacrileges by which human beings do not appear to harm other human beings—by refraining from doing to them what they do not wish done to themselves—but, through disobeying God, to whom all things are subject, do to the Lord of lords himself what they do not wish done to themselves by their own servants. The same Apostle Peter says: “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same disposition”—

## CHAPTER IV

“For whoever has died to the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live the remaining time in the flesh no longer for human desires but for the will of God.” For the past time is sufficient for having fulfilled the will of the Gentiles, living in debauchery, pleasures, drinking parties, drunkenness, and wicked service of idols” (1 Pet. 4:1–3).

The past time is sufficient for having served the muddy works of sins, as though under the domination of the Egyptians. The Red Sea—that is, baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ—has now cast down the true Pharaoh and destroyed the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 1562] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “consecrated, it led you across; the Egyptians,” and so forth.]. Fear nothing from past sins, as though they were enemies pursuing you from behind.

From now on, consider that you must pass through the wilderness of this life and reach the promised land, the Jerusalem above, the land of the living. Do not let your hearts become dull through contempt for the word of God, as though disgusted with manna; do not murmur, craving Egyptian foods, about the heavenly nourishment; do not commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication; and do not put Christ to the test, as some of them tested him.

If, while you thirst for the faith of the Gentiles, some bitterness from those who resist should confront you, like those waters which Israel could not drink, let it become sweet through imitating the Lord’s patience, as though the wood of the cross had been cast into it. If a serpent-like temptation bites you, let it be healed by the same medicine of the cross, when you behold the exaltation of that serpent as a sign of death conquered and triumphed over in the Lord’s flesh. If an Amalekite adversary attempts to block and obstruct your journey, let him be overcome by the most persevering extension of the arms, through the sign of that same cross.

Be true and genuine Christians. Do not imitate Christians in name who are empty in works [Note: [Col. 1562] The printed editions read “vain.” The manuscripts, however, read “empty.”]. I say again—and it must often be said: “The past time is sufficient for having fulfilled the will of the Gentiles.”

Detest and shun dogs returning to their vomit. Detest and shun the house that has been cleansed and left empty, into which seven other spirits, more wicked than the first, are brought, so that “the final condition of the person is worse than the first.” Keep your cleanser as your inhabitant. For, while giving commands, we beg you “not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6:1). The past time is sufficient for having fulfilled the will of the Gentiles [Col. 1563].

Hear also the Apostle Paul: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

# SERMON 354

[Note: [Col. 1563] Revised against three manuscripts: bn.; four copies: cl.; and a., cb., f., fs., g., Ir., m., pr., rm., vd.; and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1563] Otherwise, “On the Words of the Lord,” 53.]

Addressed to those practicing continence: first, he strengthens them against detractors and the envious; then he commands them to beware of pride [Note: [Col. 1563] Florus calls it “a sermon on the Words of the Lord,” referring to 1 Cor. 8 and 13.].

## CHAPTER I

1. Christ’s members must necessarily incur the world’s hatred, as he himself foretold. The Lord made this clear when the Gospel was read, because “whoever believes in him believes in the one who sent him” (John 12:44). Faith holds with complete certainty that the Savior of the world was sent to us, because Christ himself proclaims Christ—that is, Christ’s body spread throughout the whole world.

For he was in heaven, and he said to the persecutor raging on earth: “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Here the Lord likewise showed that he is in us. Thus the whole grows: for just as he is here in us, so we are there in him. The bond of love accomplishes this. He himself, who is our head, is the Savior of his body.

Christ therefore proclaims Christ; the body proclaims its head and protects its head. And therefore the world hates us, as we have heard from the Lord himself (John 15:18–21). He was not saying to only a few Apostles that the world would hate them, nor was it only to them that he said they ought to rejoice when people slandered them and spoke every evil against them, because for this reason their reward would be greater in heaven (Matt. 5:11–12). When the Lord said these things, he was not speaking only to them; he was speaking to his entire body, to all his members. Whoever wishes to be in his body and to be his member should not be surprised that the world hates him.

2. Christ’s members suffer not only enemies who are outside but also some enemies within. Many receive the sacrament of his body, but not all who receive the sacrament will have with him the place promised to his members. Almost everyone indeed calls the sacrament his body [Note: [Col. 1563] An old Fossatensis codex reads: “Almost all nations call the sacrament his body.” The Floriacensis likewise has this reading, omitting only the word “nations.” Nearly all the other manuscripts differ from the printed editions only in transposing the particle, reading: “Almost everyone indeed calls the sacrament his body.”], because all feed together in his pastures. But the one who will divide them is coming, and he will place some at his right hand and others at his left.

Both groups will say: “Lord, Lord, when did we see you and minister to you?”—or: “Lord, when did we see you and not minister to you?” Both groups will say this. Yet to one he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom”; to the other: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:31–41).

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, beloved, all of us who are Christ’s members with a good conscience must not count only our enemies as enemies; we must not think that only those who are openly outside are our enemies. Those who appear to be within but are outside are far worse. For they love the world, and therefore they are evil.

Indeed, they judge us according to what they themselves love, and they envy us in what seem to be the prosperity of this world—prosperities over which we groan. They think us happy where we are in danger. They do not know our inward happiness, because they have not tasted it. They do not understand that whatever in temporal matters pleases us in the world is more our danger than our adornment, because they do not know how to distinguish these joys.

3. The place of those practicing continence is more excellent in Christ’s body. Their continence is attacked by the envious so that it may be tested. The wicked are necessary to the good. Therefore we exhort Your Charity, especially because we see that you have gathered in greater numbers—those of you who have a higher calling: that is, by his gift, not through your merits, you hold a more excellent place in Christ’s body, possessing a conscience [Note: [Col. 1564] Perhaps “continence.”—In the Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice editions: “knowledge.” M.] that has been given by God.

For this very thing also becomes an object of suspicion to the wicked and to our envious opponents. Yet it is attacked for the purpose of being tested. If in professing continence we seek human praise, we fail under human criticisms. Suppose you are a chaste servant of God: behold, the world perhaps suspects you of impurity, attacks and reproves you, and willingly lingers over your slanders. For what a malevolent soul suspects most wickedly tastes, as it were, sweetly to that soul.

But if you wished to embrace continence for the sake of human praise, you have been defeated by human criticism and have lost everything you had purposed for yourself.

## CHAPTER III

But if you know how to say with the Apostle, “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12), criticism not only does not lessen your reward; it makes it greater. Nevertheless, pray for that person, lest he perish at the cost of your reward.

For by this also, beloved, we are tested: if we had no enemies, there would be no one for whom we could pray in obedience to the command of our Lord, who says: “Love your enemies, and pray for those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). How, then, do we test ourselves? How do we question our heart as to whether we are able to do this, if we encounter no enemy, no critic, no slanderer, no reviler?

You see, therefore, that the wicked are also necessary to the good. We are, in a certain sense, in the goldsmith’s furnace—that is, in this world. If you are not gold, you burn together with the rest. If you are gold, your straw is the wicked person. If you too are straw, you will both become smoke.

## CHAPTER IV

4. In Christ’s body, not only those practicing continence but also married people have a place. Humble married people are better than proud practitioners of continence.

Nevertheless, first know this, beloved: in Christ’s body the more excellent members are not the only ones. Married life is praiseworthy and has its place in Christ’s body. In our own body, too, only those parts that are placed more excellently do not have a place—for example, the senses occupy the higher part of the body, in the face—but unless the feet carried them, everything sublime would lie on the ground.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Those parts of our body that are dishonorable are more necessary. God has tempered the body so that there might be no divisions in the body” (1 Cor. 12:23–25).

We know that the members of Christ who live a married life—if they are members of Christ, that is, if they are faithful, if they either hope for or await the age to come, if they know why they bear the sign of Christ—we know that they show you honor. We know that they judge you better than they are themselves.

But in proportion to the honor they show you, you must also show them mutual honor. For if there is holiness in you, beware lest you lose it. How? Through pride. The holiness of a chaste person is lost in one way if he becomes an adulterer and in another if he becomes proud.

And I dare to say that those living a married life, if they preserve humility, are better than proud chaste persons. Consider carefully what I am saying. Look at the devil: must adultery or fornication be brought against him in God’s judgment? He does none of these things, because he has no flesh. Pride and envy alone send him into the eternal fire.

## CHAPTER V

5. Pride is the mother of envy. The virgin Agnes and the married woman Crispina, both martyrs. The person practicing continence should consider what is lacking, not what is present.

Therefore, in a servant of God whom pride has secretly entered, envy is immediately present as well. A proud person cannot fail to be envious. Envy is the daughter of pride; but this mother does not know how to be barren. Wherever she is, she immediately gives birth.

To ensure that envy may not be in you, consider this: during the time of persecution, not only was Agnes, a virgin, crowned, but also Crispina, a married woman. And perhaps—as cannot be doubted—some among those practicing continence then fell away, while many among the married fought and conquered.

Therefore the Apostle does not say without reason to all Christ’s members: “Considering one another superior to yourselves, and anticipating one another in honor” (Phil. 2:3; Rom. 12:10).

If you reflect on these things, you will not be great in your own eyes. You should consider more what is lacking in you than what is present in you. Take care not to lose what you have; beg to receive what you do not yet have. You should think about how much less you are, not how much greater. If you think about how far you have surpassed another, beware of swelling with pride. But if you think about how much is still lacking in you, you groan; and when you groan, you are healed. You will be humble, walk more safely, not fall headlong, and not be inflated.

## CHAPTER VI

6. Charity must be pursued in order to avoid being inflated. What pride is, and why it gives birth to envy. Should knowledge be avoided lest it inflate?

Would that everyone could think about the one thing, charity. For it alone conquers everything, and without it everything is worthless; wherever it is, it draws everything to itself. It is the one that does not envy. Do you ask why? Attend to what follows: “It is not inflated” (1 Cor. 13:4).

As I had begun to say, pride comes first among the vices, and envy follows. Envy did not give birth to pride; pride gave birth to envy. For no one envies except through a love of superiority. The love of superiority is called pride.

Since pride therefore comes first in order and envy follows, the Apostle, in praising charity, did not wish to say first, “It is not inflated,” and afterward, “It does not envy.” Rather, he said first, “It does not envy,” and afterward, “It is not inflated.”

Why is this? Because when he had said, “It does not envy,” you might seem about to ask the reason why it does not envy; he added, “It is not inflated.” Therefore, if it does not envy because it is not inflated, then if it were inflated, it would envy.

Let this grow in you, and the soul is strengthened, because it is not inflated. “Knowledge,” the Apostle says, “inflates” (1 Cor. 8:1). What then? Should you flee knowledge and choose to know nothing rather than become inflated? Why do we speak to you, then, if ignorance is better than knowledge? Why do we debate with you? Why do we make these distinctions? Why do we remind you of what you know and bring forward what you do not know, if knowledge must be avoided lest it inflate?

Therefore love knowledge, but place charity before it. If knowledge is alone, it inflates. But because “charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1), it does not allow knowledge to become inflated. Knowledge therefore inflates where charity does not build up; but where charity builds up, knowledge has been made firm. There is no inflation where the foundation is rock.

## CHAPTER VII

7. The thorn in the flesh given to the Apostle so that he would not become proud. We should desire to be heard, not according to our will but for our healing. How eternal things and temporal things should be requested.

Consider how greatly inflation—that is, elation—tempts us: on account of this vice, even that great Apostle said that a thorn in the flesh had been given to him, an angel of Satan, to buffet him [Note: [Col. 1566] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. Louvain reads: “But when inflation, that is, elation, tempts us, what then? Certainly wherever and whenever charity is lacking. For on account of this vice…” The other printed editions agree with our manuscripts, except that they read “When” instead of “How greatly.”].

When someone is buffeted, his head is struck so that it may not be raised. There too, therefore, there was fear of knowledge’s inflation—that is, elation. For he says: “To keep me from being exalted by the abundance of revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it might depart from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

A sick person asks that what the physician applies for his health be removed whenever the patient wishes. The physician says: “No; it bites, but it heals.” You say: “Take away what bites.” The physician says: “I will not take it away, because it heals.”

Why did you come to the physician? To be healed, or not to suffer discomfort? The Lord therefore did not hear Paul according to his will, because he heard him for his healing.

For it is not a great thing to be heard by God according to one’s will; it is not great. Do not think it a great thing when someone prays for something as though it were great and is heard. Ask what he is praying for; ask in what matter he is heard. Do not count it a great thing to be heard according to one’s will; count it a great thing to be heard for one’s benefit.

Even the demons were heard according to their will and were allowed to go into the pigs they had requested (Matt. 8:31–32). Their prince, the devil, too, was heard according to his will: Job, whom he requested to be tested, was not denied to him, so that Job might be proved and the devil confounded (Job 1–2).

The Israelites also were heard according to their will; and while the food was still in their mouths, you know what they received (Num. 11). Therefore do not count it a great thing to be heard according to one’s will.

Sometimes God, in anger, gives what you ask, and God, in mercy, refuses what you ask. But when you ask him for what God praises, what God commands, and what God promises in the age to come, ask confidently and devote yourselves to prayer as much as you can, so that you may receive it. Those things are granted by a merciful God; they are bestowed by his mercy, not by his anger.

But when you ask for temporal things, ask with restraint, ask with fear, and entrust the matter to him: if they are beneficial, let him give them; if he knows they will harm you, let him not give them. The physician knows what harms and what benefits, not the sick person.

## CHAPTER VIII

8. Against proud practitioners of continence.

There are humble practitioners of continence, and there are proud ones. Let the proud not promise themselves the kingdom of God. Continence leads to a more excellent place, but “whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

Why do you seek a higher place through a desire for exaltation, when you can attain it by holding fast to humility? If you exalt yourself, God casts you down; if you cast yourself down, God raises you up. This is the Lord’s judgment; nothing can be added to it or taken away from it.

Yet people practicing continence are so often proud that they are ungrateful not only toward any other people but even toward their parents, and exalt themselves against their parents. Why? Their parents gave birth to them, while they themselves rejected marriage. But how could those who rejected marriage be ungrateful if their parents had not given birth to them?

Still, a son is better than his married father because he himself did not take a wife; and a daughter is better than her married mother because she herself did not seek a husband. If she is prouder, she is in no way better; if she is better, she is unquestionably more humble.

If you wish to discover that you are better, ask your soul whether you see inflation there. Where there is inflation, there is emptiness. Wherever the devil finds emptiness, he tries to build a nest.

## CHAPTER IX

9. Pride must be avoided above all by those practicing continence. How much better a humble married person is than a proud practitioner of continence. A proud practitioner of continence has no place in the kingdom of God.

Finally, my brothers, I dare to say that it is beneficial for proud practitioners of continence to fall, so that in the very thing in which they exalt themselves they may be humbled. For what benefit is continence to a person in whom pride rules? He has despised that from which a human being is born, and desires that through which the devil fell.

You have despised marriage; you have done well and chosen something better. But do not become proud. Human beings are born from marriage; angels fell through pride.

If I consider your individual virtues, you are better than your father because you rejected marriage, and you are better than your mother because you rejected marriage. Indeed, virginal holiness is better than married chastity. If these two are compared together, one is better than the other—who doubts it?

But when I add two further things, pride and humility, I ask you about these two and ask you to answer me: What is better, pride or humility? You answer: humility. Join humility to virginal holiness. Let pride not only be absent from your virginity; let it not remain even in your mother.

For if you retain pride while your mother retains humility, the mother will be better than the daughter.

I shall compare you again. A little earlier, when I considered your virtues individually, I found you better. Now, when I consider them in pairs, I do not hesitate to prefer the humble married woman to the proud virgin.

And how do I prefer her? See how I prefer the woman whom I was comparing a moment ago. Married chastity is good; virginal integrity is better. I was comparing two good things, not evil and good; I was distinguishing good and better.

But when I place the other two together—pride and humility—can we say, “Pride is good, but humility is better”? What do we say? Pride is evil; humility is good. Pride is a great evil; humility is a great good.

If, then, one of these two is evil and the other good, evil is joined to your greater good, and the whole becomes evil. Good is joined to your mother’s lesser good, and the whole becomes a great good.

The mother will have a lesser place in the kingdom of heaven because she is married, and the daughter a greater place because she is a virgin. The virgin daughter will have the greater place, the married mother the lesser; yet both will be there—like a bright star and a dim star, yet both in heaven.

But if your mother is humble and you are proud, she will have whatever place she may have, while you will have no place. And who finds another place for one who will not have a place there, except with the one who fell from there and cast down the one who was standing?

The devil fell from the place from which he cast down the human being who was standing. He cast down the one who was standing, but Christ, descending, raised up the one who was lying prostrate.

Consider, nevertheless, how your Lord raised you. He raised you through humility, “becoming obedient unto death; he humbled himself” (Phil. 2:8). Your prince is humble, and you are proud? The head is humble, and the member proud? God forbid.

The one who loves pride does not wish to belong to the body of the humble head. If he does not belong to it, let him see where he will be. I do not wish to say it, lest I seem to have frightened you still more. Indeed, would that I had frightened you, and accomplished something! Would that whoever was such, whether man or woman, should no longer be so. Would that I had poured these words into you, and not poured them out.

Everything must be hoped for from the mercy of God: the one who frightens causes sorrow, and the one who causes sorrow consoles—but only if the one who has been saddened is corrected.

# SERMON 355

[Note: [Col. 1568] Corrected against the manuscripts cl., gr., and m., and against the editions of Ulm, Paris, and Louvain; against the old codex of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; and against the editions of the Council of Aachen.]

[Note: [Col. 1568] Otherwise, “On Various Matters,” 49.]

On the life and conduct of his clergy, I [Note: [Col. 1568] Possidius recalls in Augustine’s Life, chapter 23, the following sermons of Augustine, which he delivered before the people “when perhaps envy concerning possessions was directed against the clergy themselves.” They were formerly cited in councils and ecclesiastical documents. The second was cited more than eleven hundred years ago by Peter the abbot at the Council of Carthage in 525, volume 4 of the new edition of the Councils, p. 1647. Later, together with the authority of that same council, it was cited in the privilege of Landeric, bishop of Paris, granted to the monks of Saint-Denis, and in another granted by Bertefrid, bishop of Amiens, to the monks of Corbie, around the middle of the seventh century, volume 6 of the Councils, pp. 487 and 527. Finally, both the first and the second were presented at the Council of Aachen in 816. Florus cites the first on 2 Cor. 8.]

## CHAPTER I

1. Care must be taken that one’s reputation, as well as one’s conscience, be good.

For this reason I wished and asked yesterday that you gather today in greater numbers: namely, to hear what I am about to say. We live here with you, and for your sake we live; our purpose and desire is that we may live with you without end in Christ [Col. 1569].

I believe that our way of life is before your eyes, so that we too might perhaps dare to say—although we are far from deserving it—what the Apostle said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16).

Therefore I do not want anyone to find in us an occasion for living badly. “We take care to do what is good,” as the same Apostle says, “not only before God but also before human beings” (2 Cor. 8:21).

For our own sake, our conscience is sufficient for us; for your sake, our reputation must not be stained but must shine among you. Hold firmly to what I have said and distinguish it carefully. There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience belongs to you; reputation belongs to your neighbor.

Whoever, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel—especially when placed in this position, of which the Apostle says in writing to his disciple: “In all things present yourself as an example of good works” (Titus 2:7).

2. The common life, whose example was found among the first Christians. Augustine established a monastery, first in a garden and afterward in the episcopal residence. Salvation is found in a humble position; danger in a high one. The common life in the monastery. By the law of that life, no one is permitted to possess anything privately.

So that I do not detain you for long—especially since I am speaking while seated and you are weary from standing—you all know, or nearly all of you know, that we live in the house called the episcopal residence [Note: [Col. 1569] The printed editions read “the bishop’s house.” But the Colbertinus book, copied eight hundred years ago, reads “the episcopal residence.”] in such a way that, as far as we can, we imitate those holy people of whom the Acts of the Apostles speaks: “No one said that anything was his own, but everything was held in common among them” (Acts 4:32).

Perhaps some of you are not such diligent observers of our life as to know this in the way I want you to know it. Therefore I shall explain briefly what I have just said.

I, whom by God’s mercy you see as your bishop, came to this city as a young man, as many of you know. I was looking for a place where I could establish a monastery and live with my brothers. I had abandoned every hope of this world, and I did not wish to be what I could have been; yet I did not seek to become what I am.

I chose “to be despised in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). I separated myself from those who love the world, but I did not place myself on the same level as those who rule peoples. I did not choose the higher place at my Lord’s banquet, but the lower and despised one; and it pleased him to say to me, “Come up higher.”

I feared the episcopate so greatly that, because my reputation had already begun to carry some weight among God’s servants, I would not go to a place where I knew there was no bishop. I avoided this and did everything I could to be saved in a humble position, lest I be endangered in a high one.

But, as I said, a servant must not contradict his master. I came to this city to visit a friend whom I thought I could win for God, so that he might be with us in the monastery—almost without concern, because the place already had a bishop.

I was taken, made a presbyter, and through this step reached the episcopate. I brought nothing with me; I came to this Church with no clothing except what I was wearing at that time.

Because I was planning this—to live in the monastery with the brothers [Note: [Col. 1570] Thus the manuscripts and the Council of Aachen. The printed editions read: “And because I was planning to be in the monastery with the brothers.”]—the old man Valerius, of blessed memory, having learned of my institution and intention, gave me the garden in which the monastery now stands.

I began to gather brothers of good purpose, companions of mine, possessing nothing as I possessed nothing, and imitating me. Just as I had sold my small and meager property and distributed it to the poor, so those who wished to be with me would do likewise, so that we might live from a common fund. Our great and most abundant common possession would be God himself.

I reached the episcopate and saw that a bishop necessarily had to show constant kindness to all who came or passed through; if a bishop did not do this, he would be called inhuman. But if this custom were permitted in the monastery [Note: [Col. 1570] The manuscripts read: “if it had been sent into the monastery.” The same reading occurs in the Council of Aachen in the Binian edition. Is *missa* perhaps used there in place of *omissa*? Or perhaps one should read, “if it had been sent into the monastery,” so that the sense would be that, if this were done, it would be improper not for the monastery but for the bishop. He is speaking of the custom of receiving guests, which at that time especially flourished everywhere in monasteries. See Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*, book 3, chapter 4.], it would be improper.

And for this reason I wished to have a monastery of clergy with me in this episcopal residence.

## CHAPTER II

This is how we live. No one is permitted in our community to possess anything privately. But perhaps some do possess something. No one is permitted; if some do possess something, they are doing what is not permitted.

Yet I have a good opinion of my brothers, and because I have always believed the best, I avoided investigating this matter. For even asking such questions seemed to me almost equivalent to thinking badly of them. I knew—and I know—that all who lived with me knew our purpose and knew the rule of our life.

3. The presbyter Januarius retained private property contrary to the monastery’s rule. He made a will. Augustine does not wish to accept his inheritance for the Church. A dispute arose among Januarius’s children concerning his inheritance.

The presbyter Januarius also came to us. He seemed to have almost exhausted his property by distributing it honorably, but he had not exhausted it [Note: [Col. 1570] The manuscripts read: “What he seemed to have, he nearly exhausted by distributing it honorably, but he did not exhaust it.”].

Some money remained to him—namely, silver—which he said belonged to his daughter. By God’s mercy, his daughter is in the monastery of women and gives good hope. May the Lord govern her so that she may fulfill what we hope for concerning her, relying on his mercy, not on her merits.

Because she was underage and could do nothing with her own money—for although we saw the brilliance of her profession, we still feared the instability of her age—it was arranged that the silver itself should be preserved as belonging, so to speak, to the girl, so that when she reached the legal age she could do with it what was fitting for a virgin of Christ, when she would be fully able to do so.

While this was being awaited, he began to approach death. For a long time, treating it as his own, he had sworn that it was his, not his daughter’s, and he made a will [Note: [Col. 1570] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “living as though from his own.”]. The presbyter and our associate, I say, made a will: he who remained with us, lived from the Church, and professed the common life made a will and appointed heirs.

What sorrow for that community! What a fruit born not from the tree planted by the Lord! [Col. 1571]

But did he name the Church as heir? I do not want such gifts; I do not love the fruit of bitterness. I was seeking him for God. He had professed our community; he should have kept it and embodied it. He should have possessed nothing and should not have made a will.

Did he possess something? Then he should not have pretended to be our associate, as one poor before God. This causes me great sorrow, brothers. I tell Your Charity that, because of this sorrow, I have decided not to accept the inheritance itself on behalf of the Church. What he left should belong to his children; let them do with it whatever they wish.

For it seems to me that if I accept it, I shall become a participant in the very action that displeases and grieves me. I wanted Your Charity to know this.

His daughter is in the monastery of women; his son is in the monastery of men. He disinherited both: her with praise, him with an *elogium*—that is, with censure. I commended [Note: [Col. 1571] The manuscripts read “He commended.” This may be better, referring to Januarius.] to the Church that they should not receive those small portions belonging to the disinherited children until they had reached the legal age. The Church is reserving this for them.

Moreover, he left a dispute between his children, in which I am laboring. The girl says: “It is mine; you know that my father always said this.” The boy says: “My father should be believed, because in dying he could not have lied.”

And what sort of evil is this contention? But if these children are servants of God, we shall quickly end this dispute between them. I hear them as a father, and perhaps better than their father. I shall see what the law is, as God wills, with a few faithful and honored brothers—by God’s mercy, from among your number, that is, from this congregation.

I shall hear their case, and, as the Lord grants, I shall bring it to an end.

4. Augustine does not accept anyone’s inheritance when his children have been disinherited.

Nevertheless, I ask you: let no one criticize me because I do not want the Church to accept his inheritance. First, because I detest his action; second, because this is my established policy. Many praise what I am about to say, but some also criticize it. It is very difficult to satisfy both groups.

## CHAPTER III
You heard just now, when the Gospel was being read: “We sang to you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament. John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton, a drinker of wine, and a friend of tax collectors’” (Matt. 11:17–19). What am I to do among those who are preparing to criticize me and sink their teeth into me if I accept the inheritances of those who, in anger, disinherit their children? Again, what am I to do for those to whom I sing and who do not want to dance? They say, “See why no one gives anything to the Church of Hippo; see why those who die do not make it their heir: because Bishop Augustine, out of his goodness”—for while praising me they bite, they caress with their lips and fix their teeth—“gives everything away and accepts nothing.”

I certainly do accept; I openly acknowledge that I accept good offerings, holy offerings. But if someone becomes angry with his son and, at his death, disinherits him, would I not reconcile him to his son if he were alive? Should I not restore his son to him? How, then, can I want him to be at peace with his son when I am seeking his inheritance?

But certainly, if he does what I have often urged him to do: if he has one son, let him count Christ as another; if he has two, let him count Christ as a third; if he has ten, let him make Christ the eleventh—and I will accept it. Because, therefore, I have done this in certain cases, they now want to turn my goodness—or my reputation for goodness—into something else, so that they may criticize me in another way, because I do not want to accept the offerings of devout people.

Let them consider how many I have accepted. Why should I count them? Here is one example: I accepted the inheritance of Julian’s sons [Note: [Col. 1572] Some editions read “of Junianus.”]. Why? Because he died without children.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. Why he did not accept Boniface’s inheritance

I did not want to accept Boniface’s inheritance—not out of compassion, but out of fear. I did not want the Church of Christ to become a shipping company. There are indeed many who make acquisitions even from ships. Yet this would have been one temptation: the ship might have sailed and suffered shipwreck. Would we have handed men over to torture so that, according to the customary procedure, the shipwreck might be investigated and those who had been rescued from the waves tortured by the judge? But we would not hand them over. For the Church could not possibly do such a thing.

Would the fiscal burden, then, have been paid? But from what would it have been paid? We are not permitted to maintain a treasury [*entheca*] [Note: [Col. 1572] *Entheca* means a repository for treasure.]. For it is not the bishop’s role to store gold and to turn away the hand of a beggar. Every day so many ask, so many groan, so many appeal to us in our poverty, that we leave even more people sorrowful because we do not have what we could give to everyone. We therefore do not have a treasury.

I did this, then, to avoid shipwreck, not by giving anything away. Let no one praise me for it, but let no one criticize me either. Certainly, when I gave to the son what an angry father had taken away at his death, I acted well. Let those who wish praise me; let those who do not wish to praise me spare me.

What more, my brothers? Whoever wants to make the Church heir in place of a disinherited son should seek someone else to accept it, not Augustine; indeed, by God’s mercy, may he find no one.

How praiseworthy was the action of the holy and venerable bishop Aurelius of Carthage! How did it fill the mouths of all who know of it with praise of God! A certain man, having no children and no hope of children, gave all his property to the Church while retaining the usufruct for himself. Children were born to him, and the bishop returned to the man, who had not expected it, what he had given. The bishop had the power not to return it—but according to the law of the forum, not according to the law of heaven [Note: [Col. 1572] The manuscripts read “not according to the law of heaven.”].

### 6. He instructs his clergy that those who possess property should relinquish it promptly

He offers clerical office without taking it away from anyone who wishes to leave his fellowship. To pretend to a profession of holiness is worse than falling away from one’s profession. Clerical office is more a burden than an honor.

Your Charity should also know that I have told my brothers who remain with me that whoever possesses anything should either sell it and distribute the proceeds, or give it away and make it common property. He has a Church through which God feeds us.

I granted a delay until Epiphany on account of those who had either not divided their property with their brothers and had left what they possessed with them, or had not yet done anything with their property because the attainment of the legal age was being awaited. Let them do with it what they wish—provided that they are poor with me, together awaiting the mercy of God.

But if they do not wish this—and perhaps some do not—certainly I am the one who had decided, as you know, to ordain no one as a cleric except one who wished to remain with me. Thus, if he wished to withdraw from his profession, I could rightly remove his clerical office from him, because he would have abandoned the promise of the holy fellowship and the partnership he had begun.

Behold, in the sight of God and of you, I change my decision: those who wish to possess something of their own, for whom God and his Church are not sufficient, may remain where they wish and where they can; I do not take their clerical office away from them. I do not want hypocrites. For falling away from one’s profession is evil—who does not know this?—but pretending to the profession is worse.

Behold, I say it; listen: whoever abandons the fellowship of the common life already undertaken, which is praised in the Acts of the Apostles, falls from his vow and falls from his holy profession. Let him watch the Judge—but God, not me. I do not take his clerical office away. I have placed the danger before his eyes; let him do what he wishes.

For I know that if I should wish to degrade someone who did this, he would not lack patrons or supporters, here and among the bishops, who would say: “What evil has he done? He cannot endure this life with you; he wants to live outside the bishop’s residence and from his own resources. Must he therefore lose his clerical office?”

I know how great an evil it is to profess something holy and not fulfill it. “Vow and pay to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12); and, “It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay” (Eccl. 5:4).

Even if a virgin has never been in a monastery and is a consecrated virgin, she may not marry, although she is not compelled to live in a monastery [Note: [Col. 1573] The manuscripts read: “A virgin, if she has never been in a monastery, is not compelled. But if she has begun to be [in one], etc.”]. But if she has begun to live in a monastery, then abandoned it, and yet remains a virgin, she has fallen halfway.

So too a cleric has professed two things: holiness and clerical office. Holiness is the inward reality; for God has imposed clerical office upon his shoulders for the sake of his people, and it is more a burden than an honor. But “who is wise and will understand these things?” (Ps. 106:43).

He has therefore professed holiness; he has professed the fellowship of living together; he has professed “how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1). If he falls from this profession and remains a cleric outside, he too has fallen halfway.

What is that to me? I do not judge him. If he preserves holiness outside, he has fallen halfway; but if he has hypocrisy within, he has fallen completely. I do not want him to have the necessity of pretending.

I know how much people love clerical office. I take it from no one who is unwilling to live in common with me. Whoever wishes to remain with me has God. If he is ready to be fed by God through his Church, not to possess anything of his own, but either to distribute it to the poor or to place it in common, let him remain with me. Whoever does not want this has his freedom—but let him see whether he can possess eternal happiness.

### 7. He promises a subsequent sermon

Let these things suffice for the present, Your Charity. What I do with my brothers I shall announce to you. For I hope for good results. They all obey me willingly, and I shall not find any of them possessing anything except perhaps because of some necessity of religion, not through an opportunity for greed.

What I do after Epiphany I shall report to Your Charity according to the Lord’s will. I shall also not conceal from you how I settled the dispute between the two brothers, the sons of the presbyter Januarius.

I have said much. Forgive a talkative old age—and a timid weakness. As you see, I have become old only recently through age, but through bodily weakness I have been old for a long time. Yet, if it pleases God, may he himself give me strength for what I have just said; I shall not abandon you.

Pray for me, that as long as life remains in this body, and whatever strength is available, I may serve you in the word of God.

# SERMON 356

[Note: [Col. 1574] Corrected against all the manuscripts and editions identified in the preceding sermon.]

[Note: [Col. 1574] Elsewhere, *On Various Matters* 50.]

## On the life and conduct of his clergy, II

[Note: [Col. 1574] At the Council of Carthage in 525 it is called “the second book on the conduct of clergy.” In the privilege of Landeric and Bertefrid, these same sermons are called “books on the ecclesiastical degrees,” evidently because Augustine here proceeds through the individual grades of the clergy and says in §9, “For I wished to ascend to them in this way, step by step.”]

### 1. The form of life of the coenobites described in the Acts of the Apostles

Today a sermon must be given to Your Charity about ourselves. For the Apostle says, “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9). Those who love us seek something in us to praise; those who hate us disparage us.

We, however, standing between both groups, must, with the help of the Lord our God, guard both our life and our reputation in such a way that those who praise us do not blush because of our detractors.

But how we wish to live, and how, by God’s mercy, we already live—although many of you know it from Holy Scripture—the reading itself will now be recited to you from the Book of Acts of the Apostles, to show you where the form of life we desire to fulfill is described.

While it is being recited, I want you to listen with the greatest attention, so that after its recitation I may say what I have undertaken to say, with God granting it, in keeping with your attentiveness.

*(And the deacon Lazarus read:)*

> “When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence to everyone who was willing [Note: [Col. 1574] The printed editions read, “to everyone willing to believe.” “To believe” is absent from the manuscripts.]. The multitude of believers was of one soul and one heart; and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. For as many as were owners of estates or houses, selling them, brought the prices of what they had sold and placed them at the apostles’ feet. And distribution was made to each according to each one’s need” (Acts 4:31–35).

*(When the deacon Lazarus had recited this and handed the book to the bishop, Bishop Augustine said:)*

I too want to read. For I take greater pleasure in being a reader of this word than a disputant concerning my own word.

> “When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence to everyone who was willing. The multitude of believers was of one soul and one heart; and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. For as many as were owners of estates or houses, selling them, brought the prices of what they had sold and placed them at the apostles’ feet. And distribution was made to each according to each one’s need.”

*(When the bishop had read this, he said:)*

### 2. Why Augustine decided to discuss the life of his clergy before the congregation

You have heard what we desire; pray that we may be able to accomplish it.

A certain necessity arose which required me to deal with these matters more carefully. As you already know, a presbyter established in our fellowship—a fellowship to which the reading you have just heard bears witness—made a will at his death, because he had something from which to make one.

He had something that he could call his own, although he lived in a fellowship in which no one was permitted to call anything his own, but everything was held in common among them.

Suppose one of our admirers and praisers were to commend this fellowship to one of our detractors and say, “All those who live with Bishop Augustine live in this way, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles.” Immediately that detractor would shake his head, thrust out his tooth, and say:

“Is that really how people live there, as you claim? Why are you lying? Why do you honor the unworthy with false praise? Did not a presbyter who was recently part of their fellowship make a will, dispose of what he possessed as he wished, and leave it behind? Surely everything there is held in common? Surely no one calls anything his own?”

What could my praiser do under such words? Would not that detractor seal his mouth, as it were, with lead? Would he not regret having praised him? Would he not, overcome by shame and confounded by the detractor’s speech, curse either us or that testator?

This was the necessity that brought us to this careful examination.

### 3. All Augustine’s clergy are found steadfast in their profession of poverty: the deacon Valens and the subdeacon Patricius

I therefore announce to you something about which you may rejoice. I found all my brothers and clergy who live with me—presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and my nephew Patricius—to be as I desired.

But those who have not yet done what they had decided concerning whatever poverty they possess are two: the deacon Valens and my nephew, the subdeacon mentioned shortly before. His mother’s life was an impediment, because he lived from her resources. The attainment of the legal age was also awaited in his case, so that whatever he did he might do with the greatest firmness.

He has not yet acted, however, because he and his brother possess certain small fields in common, undivided. Once they have been divided, he wants to give them to the Church, so that those who live in the profession of holiness may be supported from them for as long as they remain in this life [Note: [Col. 1575] The manuscripts read: “Thus he wants them,” omitting “once they have been divided.” A little farther below, where the editions read “There are also slaves,” the manuscripts have “These are also slaves.”].

For it is written—and the Apostle says this—“If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for the members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

He also still has slaves in common with his brother, not yet divided. He plans to free them, but he cannot do so before they are divided. For he does not yet know which ones belong to whom. Since he is the elder, the division belongs to him; the choice belongs to his brother.

His brother too serves God: he is a subdeacon with my holy brother and fellow bishop Severus in the Church of Milevis. This must be done, and must be done without delay: those little slaves must be divided and freed, and then he must give them to the Church so that it may receive their maintenance from them.

My nephew too, from the time he was converted and began to be with me, was prevented from doing anything with his small fields because his mother, who held the usufruct, was unwilling [Note: [Col. 1576] The manuscripts read “with the usufructuary of his mother,” omitting “unwilling.”]. She died this year. Between him and his sisters there are certain matters that must soon be settled with Christ’s help [Note: [Col. 1576] The manuscripts and the Council of Aachen read “between him and his sisters.” The printed editions read “between him and his sister.”], so that he too may do what is fitting for a servant of God, what both his profession and this reading demand.

### 4. The deacon Faustinus

The deacon Faustinus, as nearly all of you know, was converted here from military service in the world to the monastery; he was baptized here and then ordained deacon.

But because what he appeared to possess was small, as the jurists say, he had left it by right, though not in actual possession [Note: [Col. 1576] Perhaps the reading should be “in actual possession, not by right.”], and it was held by his brothers.

From the time he was converted he never thought about it. He neither asked anything from his brothers nor was anything sought from him. Now, since the matter has reached this stage, he divided the property with my advice: half he gave to his brothers, half to the poor Church established in that same place.

### 5. The blind deacon Severus

You know under what discipline and scourging of God the deacon Severus lives; yet he has not lost the light of his mind.

He had bought one house here for his mother and sister, whom he wished to bring here from their homeland. He had bought it not with his own money, which he did not have, but from contributions made by religious men, whom he identified for me by name when I asked him.

Concerning the house itself [Note: [Col. 1576] The manuscripts read “concerning him himself.”], I cannot say what he has done or what he plans to do, except that he too placed the whole matter in my will, so that whatever I wished would be done with it.

He also has certain disputes with his mother and appointed me judge of those disputes. When those matters have been settled, the house is to be dealt with as I wish. And what could I wish, with God directing me, except what justice commands and piety requires?

He also has some small fields in his homeland. He plans to distribute them in such a way that there too, in that place, he may give to the poor Church.

### 6. The deacon of Hippo

The deacon of Hippo is a poor man; he has nothing to contribute to anyone. Nevertheless, from the proceeds of his labor before he became a cleric, he had bought some little slaves. Today, in your presence, he will free them by episcopal records.

[Col. 1577]

### 7. The deacon Heraclius

The deacon Heraclius is before your eyes; his works shine before your eyes. From his work and the money he spent, we have a memorial of the holy Martyr [Note: [Col. 1577] Perhaps it was built to house the relics of Stephen, which had been brought to Africa not long before the year 425. Thus, since this sermon was delivered shortly after Epiphany, it belongs to the beginning of the year 425. Augustine later designated Heraclius, of whom he speaks here and whom he subsequently made presbyter, as his successor in the episcopate in 426, on September 26, according to Letter 213.].

From his own money he also bought a property on my advice, for he wanted the money itself to be distributed through my hands as I saw fit.

If I were greedy for money, or if I were more concerned in this matter with the very needs that I have for the poor, I would accept the money. Why, someone asks? Because the property that he bought and gave to the Church still produces nothing for the Church. He had less than the purchase price, and because he had borrowed the remainder, it is still being repaid from the property’s produce.

I am an old man: how much produce can come to me from that property? Surely I do not promise myself that I shall live so many years that it will repay its own price? What it repays only slowly and over a long period, I could have had all at once immediately if I had wished to accept it.

I did not do so; I considered something else. I confess to you that I was still suspicious of his age, and I feared that, as happens with human beings, his mother might be displeased by it and say that I had induced the young man to consume his paternal property and leave him needy.

Therefore I wanted his money to be preserved in that property, so that if something happened otherwise than we wish—which God forbid—the estate might be returned [Note: [Col. 1577] The manuscripts and the Council of Aachen read “the estate might be returned.” The printed editions read “that it might be returned.”], lest the bishop’s reputation be blamed. For I know how necessary my reputation is to you; my conscience is sufficient for me.

He also bought a tract from the church behind this one [Note: [Col. 1577] The manuscripts read “from the church behind this one.”]—you know it—and built a house with his own money. You know this as well. A few days before I preached to you about this matter, he gave it to the Church. He had been waiting to complete it and then give it when finished.

He had no need to build the house except that he had considered that his mother would come here. If she had come, she would have lived in her son’s property; now, if she comes, she will live in her son’s work.

I bear witness for him: he remained poor, but he remained steadfast in the possession of charity [Note: [Col. 1577] The manuscripts and the Council of Aachen read “in the possession of charity.” Ulm reads “in the profession”; Lovaniensis reads “in the promise.”].

Some little slaves had been left to him. They are already living in the monastery, but today he will free them by the Church’s official records.

Let no one say, “He is rich”; let no one think it; let no one speak wickedly; let no one tear himself or his own soul to pieces with his teeth. He has no money kept in reserve. Would that he repay what he owes!

### 8. The subdeacons

The others—that is, the subdeacons—are poor, by God’s mercy, and await God’s mercy. They have nothing from which they can support themselves; possessing no resources, they have ended their worldly desires.

They live with us in a common fellowship. No one distinguishes them from those who brought something with them. The unity of charity must be preferred to the earthly advantage of inheritance.

[Col. 1578]

### 9. The presbyters

The presbyters remain. For I wished to ascend to them step by step. Let me say briefly: they are God’s poor. They brought nothing to the household of our fellowship except charity itself, than which nothing is more precious.

Nevertheless, because I know that rumors have arisen about their wealth, they must not be compelled by me to anything; rather, by my speech they must be cleared before you.

### 10. The presbyter Leporius

I speak to those of you who perhaps do not know—for many of you do know this—that although the presbyter Leporius was distinguished by worldly birth and born among his people in a position of the highest honor, I received him, already serving God, as a poor man, after he had abandoned everything he possessed—not because he had possessed nothing, but because he had already done what this reading urges.

He did not do it here, but we know where he did it. The unity of Christ and the unity of the Church are one [Note: [Col. 1578] The manuscripts read, “The unity of Christ exists; the Church is one.”]. Wherever he has done a good work, it belongs to us too, if we rejoice with him [Note: [Col. 1578] So in the manuscripts and in the Council of Carthage. The printed editions and the Council of Aachen read, “so that we may rejoice with him.”].

There is one garden, as you know; there he established a monastery for his own people, because they too serve God. That garden does not belong to the Church, nor does it belong to him. “To whom, then?” someone may ask. To the monastery that is there.

But the truth is that until now he managed their affairs in such a way that he kept with himself the expenses by which they are supported and, as it appeared, supplied them himself. But lest this provide an opportunity for people to gnaw at their suspicions without filling their stomachs, it seemed good both to me and to him that they should arrange matters as though he had already departed from this world.

For when he dies, will he be the one to administer anything to them? It is better that he see them living well there and, with God directing them, living according to the discipline of Christ, so that he may rejoice solely in them and not be burdened by their needs.

He has no money that he can call his own. He had a hospice to build, which you now see completed. I assigned it to him; I ordered him to do it. He obeyed me most willingly and worked, as you see.

At my command he also built a basilica for the Eight Martyrs, from what God gave through you. He began with money that had been given to the Church for the hospice; and once he had begun to build, religious people, desiring their works to be written in heaven, helped as each one wished, and he completed the building.

We have the work before our eyes; everyone sees what has been done. As for the money, since he has none, let them believe me; let them restrain their teeth, not break them.

From the money intended for the hospice he had bought a certain house in Carraria, which he thought would be useful to him because of its stones. But the stones from that house were not needed for the construction, since they were supplied from elsewhere. The house therefore remained as it was and produces rent—but for the Church, not for the presbyter.

Let no one say any longer: “Into the presbyter’s house,” “before the presbyter’s house,” “to the presbyter’s house.” Behold where the presbyter’s house is: where my house is, there is the presbyter’s house. He has no house elsewhere, but wherever he has God [Note: [Col. 1578] The printed editions read “unless wherever.” The manuscripts, “but wherever,” are far more correct.].

### 11. The dispute between Januarius’s children ended voluntarily

What more do you seek? Except that I remember having also promised to report to you what I had done between the two—the brother and sister, the children of the presbyter Januarius—because a financial dispute had arisen between them, though, by God’s mercy, their brotherly affection remained intact.

I had promised to hear the matter and settle whatever there was between them by judgment. I had prepared myself as judge. But before I judged, they themselves settled the matter on which I would have judged them.

I found nothing over which to judge, but something over which to rejoice. They entirely and harmoniously agreed with my wishes and advice that they should be equal in the money their father had left them, with the Church renouncing its claim.

### 12. The slanders of detractors are to be refuted without strife

After my sermon people will speak. Whatever people say, however, something will be carried to my ears on whatever breeze may be blowing. If it is such that it becomes necessary for us to clear ourselves again, I shall answer detractors, I shall answer slanderers, I shall answer unbelievers who do not believe us, their superiors [Note: [Col. 1579] So in the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “who do not believe you, their presbyters.”], as I am able; I shall answer what the Lord grants.

For now, however, it is not necessary, since perhaps they will say nothing. Those who love us will rejoice openly; those who hate us will grieve silently.

Nevertheless, if they exercise their tongues, they will hear, by God’s mercy, my answer in your presence—not my quarrel. For I shall not name people and say, “That man said this; this man slandered in such a way,” since perhaps what is brought to me may even be false—for that too can happen.

Whatever is brought to me, however, if it seems necessary, I shall speak about it to Your Charity. I want our life to be before your eyes.

I know that those who seek permission to do evil seek examples of people living badly for themselves, and defame many people so that they may appear to have found companions. Therefore we have done what belongs to us; we have no more that we can do. We are before your eyes. We desire nothing from anyone except your good works.

### 13. He wishes offerings made by the faithful to his clergy to be placed at the common disposal; Augustine’s modesty

And I exhort you too, my brothers: if you wish to give something to the clergy, know that you ought not, as though fostering their vices, to act against me. Offer whatever you wish to everyone; offer it from your own free will. Whatever is held in common will be distributed to each according to each one’s need.

Look to the treasury, and we shall all have enough. It greatly pleases me if it becomes our manger, so that we may be God’s beasts of burden and you God’s field.

Let no one give a *byrrhus*, or a linen tunic, or anything else, except into the common fund [Note: [Col. 1579] The manuscript codices read, “Let no one give a *byrrhus*, a linen tunic, except into the common fund,” omitting “or” and “or anything else.” Erasmus wanted *pyrrhus* read here, interpreting it in his note on the Augustinian Rule as a red cap ordinarily used by bishops. But the printed books and manuscripts are altogether more correct in reading *byrrhus*. To some this garment is clerical or episcopal; to others it is a more ordinary garment, also commonly used by laypeople. Augustine says above, in Sermon 161, ch. 10, §10, of a woman speaking to her lover: “She may say, ‘I do not want you to have such a *byrrhus*’; she does not have one. ‘Messianus,’ in the Life of Caesarius, §9, and Caesarius himself in his Testament, mention his little *byrrhus*. A white *byrrhus* was also called the garment worn by the newly baptized, according to Pope Gregory, book 7, indiction 2, letter 5.].

From the common fund I accept even for myself, since I want it understood that whatever I have is common.

I do not want Your Holiness to offer things of the sort that I alone might use more suitably. For example, offer me an expensive *byrrhus*. Perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit Augustine—that is, a poor man born of poor people.

People will now say that I have acquired expensive garments such as I could not have possessed either in my father’s house or in my former worldly profession. It is not fitting. I ought to have the kind of garment that I can give to my brother if he does not have one.

I wish to accept the sort of garment a presbyter can have, the sort that a deacon and subdeacon can decently have, because I accept it into the common fund. If someone gives something better, I sell it—which is what I usually do—so that when a garment cannot be common, its price can be common.

I sell it and distribute the proceeds to the poor. If it pleases him that I should have it, let him give me something for which I shall not be ashamed.

For I confess to you that I am ashamed of expensive clothing: it does not suit this profession, this admonition; it does not suit these limbs; it does not suit these gray hairs.

I say this also: if someone in our house or fellowship is sick, or recovering from illness, so that it is necessary for him to be refreshed before the hour of dinner, I do not forbid religious men or women to send them what they think appropriate to send. But no one else is to have lunch and dinner outside the common arrangement.

### 14. He decides that anyone who violates the profession of poverty is to be struck from the clergy

Behold, I say it; you have heard, and they hear it: whoever wishes to possess something of his own and live from his own resources, and to act against these instructions of ours—it is not enough for me to say that he will not remain with me; he will not be a cleric either.

I had said, and I know that I said, that if they were unwilling to accept our common life, I would not take their clerical office away from them: they could remain apart, live apart, and live for God as they knew how. Yet I also placed before their eyes how great an evil it is to fall away from one’s profession.

For I preferred to have even the lame [Note: [Col. 1580] The printed editions read, “the blind or the lame.” The word “blind” is absent from the manuscripts.] rather than mourn the dead. For whoever is a hypocrite is dead.

Thus, just as I would not have taken clerical office away from anyone who wished to remain outside and live from his own resources, so now—because, by God’s mercy, this common life has pleased them—whoever lives hypocritically, whoever is found possessing something of his own, I do not permit him to make a will concerning it; I shall erase him from the register of the clergy.

Let him appeal against me to a thousand councils, sail against me wherever he wishes, and be wherever he can be. God will help me so that, where I am bishop, he cannot be a cleric.

You have heard; they have heard. But I hope in our God and in his mercy that, just as they received this decision of mine cheerfully, so they will preserve it purely and faithfully.

### 15. The presbyter Barnabas

I said that my fellow-presbyters who live with me possess nothing of their own; among them is the presbyter Barnabas. But I have heard that certain things have been spread about him, above all that he bought a villa from my beloved and honored son Eleusinus.

This is false [Col. 1581]: he gave it to the monastery; he did not sell it. I am a witness. I do not know what more you could ask. I am a witness: he gave it; he did not sell it.

But because people did not believe that he could have given it, they believed that he had sold it. Blessed is the man who did so good a work that people did not believe it. Nevertheless, believe it now, and stop listening gladly to detractors. I have said it; I am a witness.

It was said of him [Note: [Col. 1581] Perhaps the reading is “It was also said of him,” namely of the presbyter Barnabas.] that during the year of his superintendence he incurred debts through his management, so that, when I wanted the debts repaid, I would give him permission [Note: [Col. 1581] The manuscripts lack the word “permission.” If it has been omitted, then instead of “to ask,” the text may originally have read “to the one asking,” or perhaps “for ten years.”] to request the Victorian estate—as though he had said to me: “To repay my debts, give me the Victorian estate for ten years.”

This too is false. But there was something from which the rumor arose: he incurred debts that had to be repaid. We repaid part of them from whatever resources were available. Something remained that was not owed [Note: [Col. 1581] In the Colbertine manuscript the first hand had written “was being given.”], even to that monastery which God established through him.

When something remained, we began to look for a way to repay the debt. No one came forward to lease the estate except one person offering a rent of forty solidi.
