But we saw that the estate could produce more, so that the debt could be repaid more quickly, and I entrusted it to his faithfulness, so that the brothers would not seek profits from the lease itself, but whatever the estate produced would be credited from its fruits toward the debt.

The matter is conducted in good faith. The presbyter is ready for me to appoint someone else who will repay the brothers from the produce [Note: [Col. 1581] The printed editions read, “who will repay the debt.” The manuscripts do not have “the debt.”].

Let someone from your number—someone among those who brought such matters to us—come to me, to whom I may entrust this. There are religious people among you who were distressed that the rumor had falsely criticized him, and yet believed that the deed had occurred.

Let one of them come to us, take possession of the property, faithfully sell all its produce at its proper prices, so that what is owed may be repaid more easily; and from that day the presbyter’s responsibility will cease.

The very place where the monastery was established by my aforementioned honored son Eleusinus was given to the presbyter Barnabas before he was ordained presbyter. He established the monastery in that place. But because the place had been given in his name, he changed the documents so that it would be held in the name of the monastery.

Concerning the Victorian estate, I ask, I urge, I beg: if there is any religious person, let him act in good faith and offer this service to the Church, so that I may repay the debt quickly. But if no layman is found, I shall appoint another [Note: [Col. 1581] The printed editions read “I propose.” The manuscripts’ “I appoint” is better]; this man will not approach it.

What more do you want? Let no one tear the servants of God to pieces, because it does not benefit those who do the tearing. The reward of God’s servants does indeed increase through false slanders, but the punishment of the slanderers increases as well.

It was not said without reason: “Rejoice and exult when they slander you, saying false things, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:11–12). We do not want to have a great reward there at your expense. Let ours there be smaller, provided that we reign there with you.

# SERMON 357

[Note: [Col. 1582] Corrected against the manuscripts and against Sirmond.]

[Note: [Col. 1582] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons 35.]

## On the Praise of Peace

Delivered at Carthage, when the conference with the Donatists was imminent, in the year 411, approximately on May 15.

[Col. 1582]

## 1. Praise of Peace

It is time to exhort Your Charity, according to the strength the Lord grants, to love peace and to beseech the Lord for peace. Let peace, then, be our beloved and friendly companion, with whom our heart may have a chaste bed; with whom there may be faithful rest and not bitter association; with whom there may be a sweet embrace and inseparable friendship.

To praise peace is more difficult than to possess it. For if we wish to praise it, we desire strength, seek ideas, and weigh our words; but if we wish to possess it, we have and hold it without any labor. Those who love peace deserve praise; but those who hate it should meanwhile be made peaceful more by teaching and silence than provoked by reproach.

The true lover of peace is a lover of its enemies. For example, if you loved this light, you would not be angry with the blind but would grieve for them. You would know what good you were receiving, and therefore, seeing how great a good they were deprived of, you would consider them worthy of mercy. If you had wealth, skill, or medicine, you would run to heal them rather than condemn them.

So, if you are a lover of peace, whoever you are, have mercy on the one who does not love what you love and does not possess what you possess. The thing you love is such that you do not begrudge your fellow possessor. He has peace with you, and he does not make your possession narrower. Whatever earthly thing you love, it is difficult not to envy someone who possesses it.

Suppose, moreover, that you conceived the idea of sharing the land you possess with a friend—perhaps an estate, a house, or something of that kind—in order that your benevolence might be praised and charity might also be celebrated in these temporal matters. You share it with one person, admit him to the partnership, and rejoice with him. You consider admitting a third person, perhaps even a fourth; then you begin to calculate how many the house can contain for living in it, or how many the field can support for grazing, and you say: “It cannot now contain a fifth; a sixth cannot live with us; when can such a small possession feed a seventh?”

Thus it is not you but narrowness that excludes the others. Love peace, have peace, possess peace; bring to yourself as many as you can to possess peace. It will be broader the more people possess it. An earthly house cannot contain many cohabitants; the possession of peace grows with many inhabitants.

## 2. To Have Peace Is to Love It

To have peace is to love it. How good it is to love! For this is to possess it. Who, however, would not want what he loves to grow? If you want only a few to be at peace with you, your peace will be small. If you want to enlarge this possession, add another possessor. For what I said, brothers—“It is good to love peace, and to love it is itself to possess it”—what does it cost? With what voice can it be praised, with what heart conceived: “To possess it is to love it”?

Consider the other things with which people burn in their desire. See one person loving estates, silver, gold, numerous children, costly and splendid houses, delightful and extremely valuable properties. Does he love these things? He does. Does the one who loves them already possess them? It may happen that a lover of all these things is empty-handed. When he does not possess them, he loves them and burns with desire to obtain them; but when he begins to possess them, he is tormented by fear of losing them.

He loves honor; he loves power. How many people deprived of positions of power sigh for them? Often the final day overtakes them before they reach what they love.

What, then, does it cost to have what you love once you have loved it? You do not seek what you love at a price; you do not go to a patron through whom you may attain it. Look: where you stand, love peace, and what you love is with you.

This is a matter of the heart. You do not share peace with friends in the same way as bread. If you wish to share bread, the more people among whom it is broken, the less there is to distribute. Peace, however, is like that bread which grew in the hands of the Lord’s disciples as it was broken and given.

## 3. Schismatics Are to Be Recalled Peacefully to Peace

### The Donatist Mind Is Estranged from Unity

Have peace, then, brothers. If you wish to draw others to it, possess it first; hold it first. Let what you possess burn within you, so that it may set others alight.

A heretic hates peace, as a person with inflamed eyes hates light. Is light therefore bad because one with diseased eyes cannot tolerate it? The person with inflamed eyes hates the light, yet the eye was created for the light.

Accordingly, those who love peace and wish what they love to be possessed with them work so that, when another possessor is added, the possession may grow. Let them therefore work to heal the eyes of those whose eyes are diseased, by whatever means and with whatever effort they can. The unwilling person is healed even though, while being healed, he does not want it; but when he sees the light, he will delight in it.

Suppose he is angry: do not grow weary through persistence. Lover of peace, pay attention and first delight in the beauty of your beloved; then burn with desire to draw the other to it. Let him see what you see, love what you love, and hold what you hold.

Your beloved, whom you love, addresses you. She says to you: “Love me, and you have me at once. Bring with you as many as you can to love me; I shall remain chaste and whole. Bring as many as you can; let them find me, hold me, and enjoy me. Many people seeing this light do not corrupt it; do many people loving me corrupt me?”

But they do not want to come because they lack the means by which they could see me. They do not want to come because the brightness of peace reflects the diseased eyes of dissension.

Listen to the pitiable voice of those with diseased eyes. They are told: “It has been decided that Christians should have peace.” When they receive such a message, they say among themselves: “Woe to us!” Why? “Unity has come.”

What is this? What kind of statement is “Woe to us, unity has come”? How much more rightly would you say, “Woe to us, dissension has come”! Far be it that dissension should come; these are darknesses belonging to those who see.

For unity has come, and we should rejoice, brothers. Why are you afraid? It has been said: “Unity has come.” Has it been said: “A wild beast has come,” or “Fire has come”? Unity has come; light has come.

If he wished to answer truthfully, he would say to you: “I was not afraid because a wild beast came—I am not timid—but I was afraid because light came, for my eyes are diseased.”

Work must therefore be done to heal them. What is not made narrower by being shared must be shared with them, according to our strength, as much as we are able and as much as God grants.

## 4. Gentleness Is to Be Shown to Heretics Who Quarrel and Revile

We must act against heretics not by quarrels but rather by prayers before God. Therefore, beloved, I exhort Your Charity to show them Christian and Catholic gentleness.

Now we are pressing on with their healing. The eyes of the wounded [Note: [Col. 1584] Perhaps, “of the wounded.”] are inflamed; they must be treated carefully and gently. Let no one enter into a dispute with anyone; let no one now wish even to defend his own faith by arguing, lest a spark arise from the quarrel and an opportunity be offered to those who seek an opportunity.

In short, when you hear an insult, endure it, disregard it, pass it by. Remember that the person needs healing. See how gentle physicians are with those whom they even treat by causing pain. They hear insults, provide medicine, and do not return insult for insult. Let there be word against word only in this sense: one is being healed, the other is healing; there are not two quarrelers.

Bear it, I beg you, my brothers.

“But I cannot bear it,” he says, “because he blasphemes the Church.”

This is what the Church asks of you: that you bear it because the Church is being blasphemed.

“He attacks my bishop; he makes an accusation against my bishop, and I remain silent?”

Let him make the accusation, and remain silent—not by acknowledging it, but by enduring it. You benefit your bishop if, for the time being, you do not involve yourself on his behalf. Understand the time; exercise prudence.

How many blaspheme your God? You hear, and He does not hear? You know, and He does not know? Yet He makes His sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). He displays patience and postpones the exercise of power.

So you too recognize the time. Do not provoke swollen eyes into disturbing themselves. Are you a lover of peace? Let your heart be well with your beloved.

“And what should I do?”

You have something to do. Remove quarrels and turn to prayers. Do not drive away the reviler by reviling him; pray for him. You want to speak against him concerning him: speak to God on his behalf.

I am not telling you to be silent; rather, choose where you will speak, before whom you will speak silently, with closed lips and your heart crying out. Where he does not see you, be good on his behalf.

To the one who does not love peace and wants to quarrel, answer peacefully: “Whatever you wish to say, however much you hate me, however strongly you detest me, you are my brother. What are you doing in order not to be my brother? Whether good or bad, willingly or unwillingly, you are my brother.”

And he replies: “How am I your brother, you enemy, you hostile man?” [Note: [Col. 1584] The Donatists evidently did not want to be called our brothers, although our people called them brothers. Optatus, Book 1 against Parmenianus, says: “They do not want to be called our brothers. Without doubt they are brothers, although not good ones”; and Book 4: “For you cannot fail to be brothers whom one mother, the Church, has brought forth from the same womb of the sacraments, whom God the Father has received as adopted sons in the same manner.” Augustine says much more of the same kind when he argues against the Donatists. SIRM.]

“Precisely because you say these things, you are my brother.”

It seems strange: he hates, he detests, and yet he is a brother? Do you want me to believe one who does not know what he is saying—one whose healing I desire, so that he may see the light and recognize his brother? Do you want me, then, to believe him when he says that I am not his brother because he detests and hates me, rather than the light itself?

Let us hear what that very light says. Read the prophet:

“Listen, you who fear, to the word of the Lord.”

The Holy Spirit speaks through the prophet Isaiah:

“Listen, you who fear, to the word of the Lord. Say, ‘You are our brothers,’ to those who hate you and who detest you.”

What does this mean? The light has shone forth and displayed brotherhood, yet the person with diseased eyes still says, “Close the window.”

Offer your eyes to the light. Recognize as your brother the one who is not in darkness, while you are in darkness, and say—say confidently: you are speaking God’s words, not mine.

“Say,” God says, “You are our brothers.”

To whom? To those who hate you. For what is remarkable if you say it to those who love you? Say it to those who hate you and detest you.

Why this? Listen, and consider the fruit of the matter.

Suppose you had questioned the Lord your God and said: “Lord, how can I say, ‘You are my brother,’ to one who hates and detests me? Tell me why.”

“So that the name of the Lord may be honored. Let him appear in joy, but let them be put to shame” (Isa. 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

See, I beg you, the fruit of patience and such great gentleness. “Say, ‘You are our brothers.’”

Why? “So that the name of the Lord may be honored.”

Why, then, does he not recognize you as his brother? Because the name of a human being has been honored by human beings.

Therefore say, “My brother.” Though you hate me, though you detest me, you are my brother. Recognize in yourself the sign of my Father. This is the word of our Father.

Bad brother, quarrelsome brother, you are my brother. For you say, as I do, “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). We say one thing; why are we not one?

I beg you, brother, recognize what you say with me, and condemn what you do against me. Pay attention to the words that come from your mouth. Listen—not to me, but to yourself. See to whom we say, “Our Father who art in heaven.” It is not a friend or a neighbor, but the very one to whom we say it commands us to be united.

Together we have one voice before the Father; why do we not together have one peace?

## 5. Pious Works for Obtaining Peace for the Church

### The Solemn Fast after Pentecost

### Hospitality toward Those Coming to Carthage for the Conference

Say such things fervently; say them gently. Speak with the fervor of charity, not the swelling pride of dissension, and beseech the Lord with us through solemn fasts.

We are already fasting solemnly after Pentecost; and certainly we would fast even if this cause did not exist. What, then, do we owe our brothers, whom we receive for healing and curing in the name of the Lord our God, our physician? We offer them to Him so that they may be healed, without presuming to place the physician’s hands upon ourselves.

What, then, are we to do? Let us beseech the physician himself, fasting with humble hearts, with pious confession, and with brotherly fear. Let us show devotion to the Lord and charity to our brothers.

For let our almsgiving increase, so that our prayers may be heard more readily [Note: [Col. 1585] In one manuscript: “Let your almsgiving also become more frequent, so that your prayers may be heard more readily.”].

Practice hospitality. The time has come: the servants of God are coming. The time has come; the opportunity is here. Why should it perish?

Consider what you have in the upper room of your house [Note: [Col. 1585] In the same manuscript: “Consider what you have in the purse of your house.”]. Consider also what you are storing above, what you are reserving for yourself, from what treasure alone you are secure.

Place it above; entrust it not to your servant but to your Lord. Do you fear there that a thief may creep in, a burglar break in, or a violent enemy seize it? Act so that you may have something returned to you.

Nor is only what you have deposited returned to you [Note: [Col. 1586] In one manuscript: “Nor is only what you have deposited returned to you.”]. The Lord wants you to be a lender—but His lender, not your neighbor’s.

# SERMON CCCLVIII

[Note: [Col. 1586] Corrected according to the manuscripts and editions designated above in the preceding sermon.]  
[Note: [Col. 1586] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons, 36.]

## On Peace and Charity

Delivered at Carthage, before the conference with the Donatists, II.

## 1. The Catholic Bishops’ Concern for Reconciling Peace

### Whoever Refuses to Be Defeated by Truth Is Defeated by Error

May your prayers, Your Holinesses, assist our concern for you, for our enemies and yours, and for the salvation of all, for quiet, for common peace, and for the unity which the Lord commanded and loves, so that we may speak about it to you repeatedly and rejoice with you.

For if we always love peace and charity, we must always speak about them. All the more, then, at this time, when peace is loved in such a way that those who do not return evil for evil, and with whom, as it is written, we are peaceful with those who hate peace, are placed in danger because of loving and preserving it; and because we speak peace to them, they want to wage war against us without cause (Ps. 119:7).

Those who are such are endangered between their love of peace and the confusion of shame. When they refuse to be defeated, they do not thereby become undefeated. For those who refuse to be defeated by truth are defeated by error.

If only charity rather than hostility overcame them! They would become victors precisely through what had defeated them.

As for us, we love, hold, and defend the Catholic Church, to whose peace, harmony, and reconciliation we invite its enemies—not by human opinions but by divine testimonies.

What am I to do with one who cries out for a part and quarrels against the whole? Is it not good for him to be defeated? If he is defeated, he will possess the whole; if he wins, he will remain in a part.

Indeed, that is so only if he seems to himself to win. For nothing wins except truth; and the victory of truth is charity.

## 2. Testimonies for the Unity of the Catholic Church

### The Catholic Argument Is a Matter of Love, Not Litigation

Why, then, brothers, should I commend to you in many words—and in my own words—the Catholic Church, which bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world? We have the Lord’s words on its behalf, and on ours.

“The Lord,” he says, “said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth’” (Ps. 2:7–8).

Why, then, brothers, do we quarrel over the possession instead of reciting the sacred documents? Let us suppose that we have come before a judge. The dispute concerns a possession, and this dispute is not litigation but love.

A litigant over an earthly possession quarrels in order to exclude his adversary; we quarrel in order to admit him. When the litigant over an earthly possession hears his adversary say, “I want to possess it,” he replies, “I will not permit it.”

But I say to my brother, “I want you to possess it with me.” He quarrels and says, “I do not want to.”

I therefore do not fear that the Lord will despise me and rebuke me as He rebuked those brothers—or that brother—who appealed to Him in the crowd and said: “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

Immediately the Lord pronounced a rebuke because He hated division: “Man,” He said, “who appointed me judge or divider of the inheritance between you?” But I say to you: “Beware of all greed” (Luke 12:13–15).

I do not fear this rebuke. I do appeal to my Lord, I confess that I do appeal to Him. But I do not say, “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Rather I say, “Lord, tell my brother to hold unity with me.”

Look: I am reciting the documents of this possession, not so that I alone may possess it, but so that I may convict my brother, who refuses to possess it with me.

Look at the documents, brother:

“Ask of me,” He says, “and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth.”

This was said to Christ. Therefore it was said to us, because we are members of Christ. Why do you run to a part? Why do you remain in a part? Hold the whole that appears in the documents.

You ask between whom and whom you are to possess it, as people customarily seek to identify the possessors in legal instruments by asking who their neighbors are. The one who gave you all the boundaries left no adjoining owners.

## 3. Testimony for the Catholic Church

Here is another testimony. Hear another testimony from the sacred documents. Of the Lord Christ, in the figure of Solomon, it is said:

“He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents. And all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 72:8–11).

When it was being said, it was believed; when it is being fulfilled, it is denied.

Hold the inheritance with me, then, from sea to sea, and from the river—namely, the Jordan, where Christ’s teaching began—to the ends of the earth.

Why do you refuse? Why are you hostile to this promise and inheritance, which are your riches? Why do you refuse? Because of Donatus? Because of Caecilianus?

Who was Donatus? Who was Caecilianus? Human beings, certainly. If they were good, that was to their credit, not mine; therefore, if they were bad, that was to their discredit, not mine.

Accept Christ, and consider the Apostle who was zealous for Christ:

“Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

And see what he recoiled from when he said this:

“Each one of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13).

If you were not baptized in the name of Paul, much less were you baptized in the name of Caecilianus, and still more—or much less—in the name of Donatus [Note: [Col. 1587] The words “in the name of Caecilianus, and still more, and much less” are absent from the Colbertine and Victorine manuscripts.].

Yet even after the apostolic words, after the Church’s declaration and its expansion throughout the whole world, I am still told: “I will not abandon Donatus; I will not abandon some Gaius, Lucius” [Note: [Col. 1587] Sirmond has “Carus, Lucius.” “Gaius, Lucius” seems preferable; these names are customarily used as substitutes for any person, as above in Sermon 42, chapter 3, section 3.], “Parmenianus”—a thousand names, a thousand divisions.

Will you deprive yourself, by following a human being, of so great an inheritance, of which you have just heard: “From sea to sea, from the river to the ends of the earth”?

Why do you not hold it? Because you love a human being.

What is a human being except a rational animal made from earth? Therefore you are hostile because you lick the earth. Rather despise this. Do not lick the earth, so that you may place your hope in the one who made heaven and earth.

This is our hope; these are the testimonies. “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Ps. 50:1).

Do not remain in the earth, but go where the earth has been summoned.

## 4. Charity Is the Broad Commandment by Which Peace Is Restored

Who could recite all the testimonies concerning this possession from the sacred documents? Why, then, do they not turn to the Church, unless it is because the Church’s own voice says:

“Let those who fear you turn to me and know your testimonies”?

The Church saw this when it said in the Psalm—you have just heard it; the words are still fresh in your ears and hearts:

“I have seen the end of every perfection.”

What does “I have seen the end of every perfection” mean? The end of perfection, not of destruction; I have seen the end of completion, not of abolition.

“I have seen the end of every perfection.”

What is this end?

“Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 119:96).

For the end of the commandment is—now you say it with me. [The people responded:] “Charity from a pure heart” (1 Tim. 1:5).

You have all said what you have always heard, not without fruit. The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart. The end by which we are perfected, not by which we are consumed.

This end is broad because it is God’s commandment, of which it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

“A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (John 13:34).

See the breadth of this commandment. Where is it broad? Is it in the flesh? Rather, it is in the heart. If it were broad in the flesh as well, attentive hearers, you would not suffer narrowness. It is broad in the heart.

See where it is broad, if you have something with which to see; and hear from the Apostle how broad the commandment of charity is:

“God’s charity has been poured out in your hearts” (Rom. 5:5).

He did not say “enclosed,” but “poured out.” The word “enclosed” suggests narrowness, while “poured out” indicates breadth.

“Your commandment, then, is exceedingly broad.”

Lord our God, show your approval, because it is on account of this very breadth that we invite our brothers to the possession of peace.

Do you wish to be bishops? Be with us. The people do not want two bishops. Be brothers with us in the inheritance. Let us not obstruct Christ’s peace because of our honors.

What honor will we receive in heavenly peace if we now defend our honor in an earthly quarrel? Let the wall of error be removed, and let us be together.

Recognize me as your brother; I recognize you as my brother—but with the schism excluded, error excluded, dissension excluded. Let these things be corrected, and you are mine.

Do you not want to be mine? If you correct yourself, I want to be yours.

Therefore, with error removed from our midst like a wall of rubble consisting of contradiction and division, be my brother, and let me be your brother, so that we may both belong to the one who is Lord both of me and of you.

## 5. With What Disposition Catholics Come to the Conference

We say this out of love for peace, not distrust of the truth. For this is what we wrote in reply, and this is what you read as our purpose (Letters 128 and 129): we do not avoid having the matter brought into conference; indeed, we insist that it be brought into conference, so that when I have demonstrated the possession, I may share the inheritance with him.

Let him come without fear; let him come confidently; let him come learned [Note: [Col. 1589] Manuscript v. reads: “Let him come unlearned.”]. I do not wish to prejudge the matter by authority. Let us open our eyes to the one who cannot err; let him teach us which is the Church.

You have heard his testimonies. Human offenses do not contaminate the one whom human justice did not redeem. Yet although the case of the Church is one thing and the case of human beings another, and although they are entirely distinct, we do not fear the case of the people whom they accused and could not convict.

We know that they were cleared; we read that they were cleared. If they had not been cleared, I would not establish the Church in their case, build upon sand, and cast it down from the rock.

“For upon this rock,” He says, “I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not overcome it” (Matt. 16:18).

The rock, however, was Christ.

“Was Paul crucified for you?”

Hold to this; love this; speak of this fraternally and peacefully.

## 6. He Asks That No One from the People Rush into the Place of the Conference

Let none of you rush into the place of the conference, my brothers. If possible, avoid even passing through that place, lest an opening for contention and litigation be found or some opportunity be provided, and those who seek an opportunity discover that very opportunity.

Especially since those who fear God little, or who regard our admonition lightly, or who love present things, should at least revere the severity of earthly authority [Note: [Col. 1589] Manuscript cl. reads: “They should at least fear the severity of earthly authority.”].

You have read the edict publicly posted by the illustrious man [Note: [Col. 1589] That is, Marcellinus, tribune and notary, who presided over the conference as judge in the name of the emperor Honorius. His edict, contained in the Acts of the first hearing, among other things required the people to be admonished by the bishops that “no layman or bishop should attempt to enter that most peaceful place of the council beyond the appointed number, contrary to the prohibition,” and so forth. SIRM.].

It was not posted on account of you, who fear God and do not despise the admonition of your bishops, but so that no one might fail to heed or despise these instructions.

Let them therefore consider what sort of people they are, lest what the Apostle says happen to them:

“For whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed. For rulers are not to be feared for good conduct but for evil” (Rom. 13:2–3).

Let us all avoid disturbances and every cause of disturbance.

Perhaps you say: “We are attentive; what are we to do?”

And what should we enjoin upon you? Perhaps abundant works of devotion.

Let us debate on your behalf; you pray on our behalf. As we have already warned you, support your prayers with fasting and almsgiving. Add wings to them, with which they may fly to God.

By conducting the affair in this way, you may perhaps be more useful to us than we are to you. For none of us presumes on himself in this debate [Note: [Col. 1589] Thus according to the same manuscript cl. [“presumes on his own behalf”].]; all hope is in God.

For we are not better than the Apostle who says, “Pray for us.”

“Pray,” he says, “for me, that speech may be given to me” (Eph. 6:19).

Pray, then, to the one in whom we have placed our hope, so that you may rejoice in our debate.

Hold fast to these things, brothers, we beg you. In the name of the Lord himself, the author of peace, the planter of peace, the lover of peace, we beg you [Note: [Col. 1590] This should be read according to one manuscript cl.: “Through the love of peace, through the planter of peace, we beg you.”] to pray to Him peacefully and beseech Him peacefully.

And remember that you are sons of the one who said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

# SERMON CCCLIX

[Note: [Col. 1590] Corrected according to manuscript cl. and Sirmond.]  
[Note: [Col. 1590] Elsewhere, On Various Matters 91, and among the Sirmondian sermons, 37.]

## On What Is Written in Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25:2: “The Concord of Brothers and the Love of Neighbors,” etc.

### On Quarrel and Concord with the Donatists

[Note: [Col. 1590] Florus cites this at 1 Thessalonians 3. Nicolaus Faber, in the preface to Hilary’s fragments, p. 49, thinks that it was delivered at Carthage for the dedication of the basilica of Florence, named after Aurelius the bishop, who was also called Florens. See note (b) below, p. 1597.]

Delivered after the conference.

## 1. Three Excellent Things

### Why Concord Is Rare

The first reading of the divine utterances, from the book called Ecclesiasticus, commended to us three things that are excellent and worthy of the greatest consideration: the concord of brothers, the love of neighbors, and a man and a woman agreeing with one another.

These are plainly good, pleasant, and praiseworthy things in human affairs; but in divine matters they are much more powerful.

Who is there who does not rejoice with brothers who are concordant? And, what is grievous, in human affairs so great a thing is rare: everyone praises it, but very few preserve it.

Blessed are those who embrace in themselves what they are compelled to praise in others. No brothers fail to praise brothers who are in agreement.

And why is it difficult for brothers to be in agreement? Because they quarrel over earth, because they want to be earth.

For from the beginning the sinful human being heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

Let us therefore examine and investigate the statement that the righteous person ought to hear in contrast. For if it was rightly said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” it is rightly said to the righteous person, “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go.”

Or are the righteous not heavens, since it is said most plainly of the evangelists: “The heavens declare the glory of God”?

And indeed, because this was said of them, what follows teaches it sufficiently:

“And the work of his hands the firmament announces.”

Those whom he called heavens, he also called the firmament.

“Day pours forth speech to day, and night announces knowledge to night. There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.”

You ask whose, and find no others except the heavens.

This, then, was said of the Apostles; it was said of those who announce the truth.

Thus it continues:

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (Ps. 19:2–5).

When the Holy Spirit came upon them and God began to dwell in the heaven He had made from earth, they spoke, as the Spirit filled them and granted them speech, in the languages of all nations.

Hence it was said: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.”

And because from there they were sent to preach the Gospel among all nations:

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Whose sound? That of the heavens, to whom it is rightly said: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go,” just as it is rightly said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

## 2. Love of an Earthly Possession Is the Cause of Discord

If brothers therefore wish to be in agreement, let them not love earth. But if they wish not to love earth, let them not be earth.

Let them seek a possession that cannot be divided, and they will always be in agreement.

Where does discord among brothers come from? Where does the disturbance of devotion come from? Where does one womb, but not one mind, come from? It comes from the moment their soul is bent downward, each looking to his own portion, laboring to enrich and enlarge his portion, and wishing to have unity in his possession while possessing division with his brother.

“This is a good possession. Whose is it?”

“It is ours.”

“A great possession!”

That is how people usually speak.

“Is it all yours, brother?”

“No; I have a partner here. But if God wills, he will sell me his share.”

The flatterer replies: “May God make it happen.”

What should God make happen? That the neighbor be crushed and sell his share to his neighbor.

“May God make it happen”—you are thinking well; may God fulfill it for you.

“For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts unjustly is blessed” (Ps. 10:3).

What is more unjust than wanting to grow rich through another’s poverty? Yet this is common: the one who acts unjustly is blessed.

Perhaps he prevailed; perhaps he pressured and crushed, twisted and extorted—not just any partner, but perhaps his own brother.

“It is better that I buy it than that a stranger do so.”

And the one easily oppressed, if he is righteous, has consolation. Let him hear the Scripture he has just heard.

He suffers from poverty; his brother is full of abundance. But the latter is full of earth and empty of righteousness.

Pay attention, earth, to what that poor man hears:

“Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, nor when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dies, he will not take these things with him” (Ps. 49:16–17).

Hold fast, poor man, to what you will not abandon when you die and what you will acquire while living eternally. Hold fast to righteousness; do not regret it.

Are you saddened because you are poor on earth? The one who created the earth was poor here. The Lord your God consoles you; your Creator consoles you; your Redeemer consoles you.

Your brother, who is not greedy, consoles you. For our Lord was willing to become our brother.

He is the one brother who is unquestionably most faithful, with whom concord must be possessed.

I called him not greedy, and perhaps I find that he is greedy. He is greedy—but he wants to have us; he wants to acquire us.

For our sake alone he paid the price of himself; nothing can be added to that price. He gave himself as the price and became our Redeemer.

For he did not give himself as the price in such a way that the enemy would release us and possess him. He gave himself to death, killing death.

By his death he killed death; he was not killed by death. Once death had been killed, he freed us from death.

For death lived while we were dying; it will die while we are living, when it is said to it:

“Where, O death, is your contention?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

[Col. 1592] **3. Why the Lord, when asked to order a brother to divide an inheritance, refused to do so. How the command that we give to everyone who asks is to be fulfilled.**

Thus the Lord was appealed to by one brother against another, between whom there was no harmony because of land. He said to him: “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. He has taken the whole of it; he does not wish to give me my share; he despises me. Let him at least listen to you.”

What concern was this of the Lord’s? If we think as humble people think—crawling on the earth, placed in this life, unwilling to distress anyone, and very often thereby distressing people more seriously—what would we say? “Come, brother, give your brother his share.” The Lord did not say this. And what was more just than he? Who would find such a judge to whom he might appeal against his brother’s greed? Was that man not rejoicing that he had at last found such a great consolation? Without doubt he hoped for great assistance when he said to so great a judge, “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

But what did he say? “Man, who appointed me a divider of the inheritance between you?” The Lord rejected him; he did not give what was requested; he did not grant a gratuitous favor. What great thing would it have been? What would he have lost by it? What effort, at least, would he have made in granting that favor? He did not give it.

Where, then, is “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30)? He who gave us an example of how to live did not do this. How are we to do it? Or how shall we give what costs us something, if we do not grant a favor where we expend nothing, where we disburse nothing, where we lose nothing?

The Lord did not give this, and yet he did not give nothing. He denied the lesser, but bestowed what was greater. He said plainly—he said, “Give to everyone who asks you.” What if someone asks you for something—not something useless to give, I say, but something shameful to give? What if some woman asks for what the woman asked of Joseph? What if some man asks for what the false elders asked of Susanna? Is that saying to be followed even here as though it were a universal rule: “Give to everyone who asks you”? Far be it from us. Shall we therefore act here against the Lord’s command? Rather, let us act according to the Lord’s command, and let us not give what is evil to those who ask for it; nor shall we act against this saying.

For it is said, “Give to everyone who asks you.” It was not said, “Give everything to everyone who asks you.” “Give to everyone who asks you”: give, certainly; and even if you do not give what he asks, still give him something. He asks for evil; you give good.

Joseph did this. He did not give what the shameless woman asked for, and yet he gave her what she ought to have heard, so that she would not be shameless by her example. He himself did not fall into the pit of lust, and he gave counsel concerning chastity. For this is what he replied: “Far be it from me to do this to my master, and to defile the bed of the one who has entrusted everything in his house to me” (Gen. 39).

If a slave bought with money preserved this fidelity toward his master, what fidelity ought a wife to preserve toward her husband? This was the admonition: “I am a slave; I will not do this to my master. You are a wife; ought you to do this to your husband?”

Susanna also gave, and did not send them away empty if they wished to be filled with the counsel of chastity. For she not only did not consent; she also did not remain silent about why she did not consent. “If I consent,” she said, “I perish before God; if I do not consent, I shall not escape your hands. But it is better to fall into your hands than to perish before God” (Dan. 13).

What, then, is “It is better to fall into your hands than to perish before God”? You have perished before God, you who seek such things.

Therefore hold fast to this rule. Give when you are asked, even if you do not give what you are asked for. The Lord did this. What was that man asking for? A division of the inheritance. What did the Lord give? The destruction of his greed.

What was he asking? What did he receive? “Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” “Man, who appointed me a divider of the inheritance between you?” But I say to you—what? “Beware of all greed.”

[Note: [Col. 1593] Here the Colbertine manuscript adds: “Did he send the petitioner away empty, and did he not rather fill him with the truth, if he wished to be filled by the one who says, ‘Beware of all greed’?”]

And I tell you why. Perhaps you are asking for half the inheritance in order to become rich. Listen: “The estate of a certain rich man produced a great harvest”—that is, it was made fertile by abundant crops.

[Note: [Col. 1593] The reading should be taken from the same Colbertine manuscript: “His estate produced a great harvest and was made fertile by abundant crops.”]

And he thought within himself, saying, “What shall I do? Where shall I gather my crops?” And, thinking carefully, he said, “I have found what I shall do. I shall destroy the old storehouses and make new ones; I shall fill them. For I shall make them larger than the old ones were. And I shall say to my soul: You have many good things; eat your fill, enjoy yourself.”

God said to him: “Fool, who seem to yourself to be very intelligent”—

[Note: [Col. 1593] The reading should be taken from the same Colbertine manuscript and from Lovaniensis, Sirmondus: “who seem to yourself to be very intelligent.”]

“for you know how to destroy old things and build new ones, yet you have remained amid the decay of old age, when you ought to have destroyed the old things in yourself, so that you would no longer savor earthly things. Fool, what did you say? To whom did you say it? You said to your soul, ‘Enjoy yourself; you have many good things.’ This night your soul will be demanded back from you, the soul to which you made such promises. The things you prepared—whose will they be?” (Luke 12:13–20).

Therefore, do not be afraid when a man has become rich, because when he dies he will not take these things with him.

**4. The harmony of brothers in the heavenly inheritance. Who should be considered to be quarreling.**

See what sort of counsel the Lord gave to the brothers who were at odds, so that they might be in harmony: they were to be free from greed and immediately filled with truth.

Let us therefore find such an inheritance. How long shall we speak about the harmony of earthly brothers—a harmony that is rare, suspect, and difficult? Let us speak of that harmony of brothers which ought to be real and can be real.

Let all Christians be brothers; let all the faithful be brothers; let those born of God and from the womb of Mother Church through the Holy Spirit be brothers. Let them be brothers, and let them also have an inheritance to be given—

[Note: [Col. 1593] Several books read: “to be held.”]

—and not to be divided.

[Note: [Col. 1593] Here the sermon formerly ended, *On Various Matters* 91.]

Their inheritance is God himself. He whose inheritance they themselves are is, in turn, their inheritance. How are they his inheritance? “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). How is he their inheritance? “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:5).

In this inheritance harmony is preserved; for this inheritance no quarrel is waged. Another inheritance is acquired by quarreling; this one is lost by quarreling. Those who do not wish to lose this inheritance avoid quarreling. And whenever they seem perhaps to be quarreling, they are not quarreling. They may seem to be quarreling, or may be thought to be quarreling, when they wish to care for their brothers.

See how united their dispute is, how peaceful, how kind, how just, how faithful.

For we seem to be quarreling with the Donatists, but we are not quarreling. The person who wishes his adversary evil is the one who quarrels; the person who wants his adversary to suffer loss while he himself gains, for something to be taken from the other and added to himself—that person quarrels. We are not like that.

You know, and so do you who quarrel outside the unity; you also know, you who have been acquired through division: you know that this dispute is not such a dispute, because it is not malicious and does not aim at the adversary’s loss, but rather at his gain.

For we wished those with whom we seemed, or still seem, to be quarreling to be acquired together with us—not to be lost, so that we might be acquired.

Finally, our voice is different from that of the brother who appealed to Christ while he was walking on earth. We also appeal to him in this matter while he sits in heaven, but we do not say, “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Rather: “Tell my brother to hold the inheritance with me.”

**5. The Catholics’ resolve and desire for the peace of the Church.**

For this is what we want, and the public Acts testify to it; and that we have wanted this is shown not only by our sermons but also by our letters sent to them.

Do you love the episcopate? Hold it with us. We hate nothing in you, we detest nothing, we abhor nothing, we anathematize nothing except human error. We said that we detest human error, not divine truth. What belongs to God in you, we acknowledge; what you have that is wicked and your own, we correct.

I recognize my Lord’s sign, the sign of my Emperor, the mark of my King in a deserter. I seek it, find it, approach it, draw near, seize it, lead the deserter back, and correct the deserter; I do not violate the mark.

If anyone notices this, if anyone pays attention, this is not quarreling but love.

We said that, for the sake of peace, concordant brothers could exist in one Church; for the harmony of brothers is a beautiful thing.

[Note: [Col. 1594] See Letter 128 among the Augustinian letters, and *Collation* 3, chapter 230.]

For we said that there cannot be two bishops. We said that both should sit—

[Note: [Col. 1594] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “that they should sit alternately.”]

—in one undivided basilica: one in the chair, the other as a stranger; one in the Christian chair, the other seated nearby as a colleague in the heretical one; and again one should preside in his own congregation—

[Note: [Col. 1594] The same manuscript reads: “again, the other should preside in the fraternal congregation.”]

—and in turn the other in his.

We said that repentance for the remission of sins had been preached by the Apostles, beginning from Jerusalem, among all nations. What will you answer to this Church, which was built among all nations by the Apostles, beginning from Jerusalem?

We said: “Let us suppose that Caecilianus had an entirely bad case”—

[Note: [Col. 1594] The same Colbertine manuscript reads: “Let us suppose that Caecilianus had a completely bad case.”]

—would one man with a bad case, or two, five, or ten men, prejudice so many thousands of faithful spread throughout the whole world with manifold fruitfulness?

We said these things. Abraham believed, and all nations were promised to him. Caecilianus sinned, and all nations perished—is what iniquity committed to count for more than what truth promised?

These things were said; they are read. Entirely contrary to the divine examples and testimonies that affirm that the Church is spread throughout the whole world—and whose unity we hold in the name of the Lord—they were unable to answer anything.

**6. They wished Caecilianus’s case to be judged while the Church’s case remained secure. Caecilianus was found innocent.**

With the Church’s case therefore secure, confirmed, immovably fixed and established—as though upon the foundation of a rock that the gates of hell cannot overcome—we came also to Caecilianus’s case, now secure regardless of what he might be found to have done.

For perhaps, if he were found to have committed some fault as a man, we would have had to quarrel, so that because of one man’s fault we might be judged worthy of condemnation or rebaptism?

And we said: “The Church’s case is secure; Caecilianus’s sin does not prejudice it; nor does Caecilianus’s righteousness crown the Church; nor does Caecilianus’s fault condemn the Church. Let us also see what his own case is like.”

We undertook to examine it, but as the case of a brother, not of a father or mother. God is our Father; the Church is our mother. Caecilianus was, or is, a brother: if good, a good brother; if bad, a bad brother—nevertheless a brother.

If we find him innocent, where will you then be, you who have failed even in this human calumny? But if he is found guilty, if he is found culpable, even then we have not been defeated, because we possess the unity of the Church, which cannot be defeated.

Let him be found entirely guilty: I anathematize the man; I do not abandon Christ’s Church. This is what we did and said: from then on we would not recite his name at the altar among bishops whom we believe to be faithful and innocent.

This alone we did.

[Note: [Col. 1595] See *Collation* 3, chapters 230, 233, 235.]

Are you going to rebaptize the whole world because of Caecilianus?

With this security established and strengthened, Caecilianus’s case began to be examined. He was found innocent; he was found to have been attacked by his accusers. Once condemned in his absence, he was acquitted three times in his presence—

[Note: [Col. 1595] He had been condemned by the Donatists in a synod at Carthage in the year 311. He was first acquitted at Rome in the council under Miltiades in 313; again at Arles by a general council in 314; and finally at Milan by the emperor Constantine, to whom the opposing party had appealed, in 315. The entire accusation against him was that he had been ordained by Felix, bishop of Aptunga, who was said to have handed over the sacred books under Diocletian. Even if this had been true, it would not have been sufficient for the cause of the schism, because the cause of the Church is one thing and that of individuals another. In any case, the public Acts established that Felix the bishop had not been a *traditor*. —Sirmondus.]

—condemned by a faction, acquitted by ecclesiastical truth.

These matters were read; these matters were approved. They were asked whether they had anything to say in reply. When all the evasions of their accusations had been exhausted, and they could produce nothing against the most evident documents or against Caecilianus’s innocence, a sentence was pronounced against them.

And yet they themselves say, “We have won.”

Let them win—but let them win over themselves, so that Christ may possess them; let the one who redeemed them win them.

**7. Many converted from the Donatist schism to the Church.**

And yet we rejoice over many. Many of them were defeated fruitfully, because they were not defeated. Human error was defeated; the human being was saved.

For a physician does not quarrel with a sick person; and if the sick person struggles with the physician, the fever is defeated and the sick person is healed. The physician’s aim is to conquer; the fever’s aim is also to conquer. The sick person has been placed, as it were, between them. If the physician wins, the sick person is safe; if the fever wins, the sick person will die.

In our struggle, therefore, the physician was struggling for health, while the sick person was struggling on behalf of the fever. Those who recognized the physician’s counsel won; they overcame the fever. We have them healthy and rejoicing with us in the Church.

Previously they blasphemed us because they did not recognize us as brothers; for the fever had disturbed their minds. Yet we love them even while they hate us and rage against us, and we served them while they raged.

We resisted, we struggled, and seemed almost to be quarreling; yet we loved them. For all who serve such sick people are troublesome; but they are troublesome for the sake of health.

**8. The foolish excuse of certain stubborn people. The madness and fury of others.**

Sometimes, however, we find people who are lazy and say: “It is true, lord, it is true; there is nothing to say.”

“What, then?”

“Come, act. My father died there; my mother was buried there.”

“You have named one who died and one who was buried. You are alive; there is still someone with whom you can speak. Your parents were Christians in the party of Donatus; their parents, perhaps, were Christians too, but their grandparents or certainly their great-grandparents were pagans.

When those who first became Christians carried out their pagan parents, were they perhaps cold toward the truth? Did they follow the authority of their dead parents, rather than preferring the living Christ to their dead parents?

If, then, the true unity is here, outside of which you must necessarily die forever, why do you wish to follow your dead parents—dead to you and to God? What do you say? Answer.”

“You speak the truth; there is nothing to say.”

“What do you want me to do?”

“Some sort of custom holds such people in its grip.”

They are lethargic; they suffer from the opposite disease; they are going to die while sleeping. Others are frenzied; they are troublesome. For even if the lethargic person is going to die, he is not troublesome to the one serving him.

The frenzied are troublesome: they have lost their minds, and, insane and furious, they wander armed here and there, seeking whom they may kill and whom they may blind. For new reports have reached us: they cut out the tongue of one of our priests.

[Note: [Col. 1596] See Augustine, Letter 185, no. 30.]

These people are frenzied. Charity must be exercised; they too must be loved. Many who were corrected wept—many who were corrected. We know them; they came to us from the number of those frenzied people. Every day they weep over their former conduct and are not satisfied with their tears, when they consider the frenzy of those who, their intoxication with vanity not yet digested, still rage.

What, then, are we to do? Charity compels us to serve such people. And although we are troublesome to both kinds—to the lethargic by awakening him, and to the frenzied by binding him—we love both.

**9. The harmony of brothers in Christ.**

Harmony among brothers is a good thing—but see where: in Christ, among Christians.

And there is also love of neighbors. What if someone is not yet a brother in Christ? Because he is a human being, he is a neighbor. Love him too, so that you may win him too.

If, then, you are in harmony with a Christian brother, but love your neighbor also, even one with whom there is presently no harmony because he is not yet a brother in Christ, because he has not yet been reborn in Christ and does not yet know Christ’s sacraments—whether he is a pagan or a Jew—he is nevertheless your neighbor because he is a human being.

If you love him too, you have advanced to another love through another gift, and thus there are two things in you: harmony among brothers and love of neighbors.

From all those who preserve harmony with their brothers and love their neighbor, the Church devoted to Christ and subject to her husband is constituted, so that the third thing may come to be: “A man and a woman agreeing with each other” (Sir. 25:2).

Therefore we admonish Your Charity, and exhort you in the Lord: despise present things, my brothers, which you will not carry away with you when you die. Beware of sins; beware of iniquities; beware of worldly desires.

Then our fruit is whole within us, and our reward before the Lord is full of joys. For even if we say what must be said, even if we preach what must be preached, and acquit ourselves before the Lord in the Lord’s sight because we have not been silent about what we fear or what we love, so that, when the sword of the Lord’s vengeance comes upon someone, he may find nothing to charge the watchman with—nevertheless, we do not want our reward to be secure because you are lost, but because you are found.

The apostle Paul was also secure concerning his reward, and yet what does he say to the people? “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8).

I speak to you and to Your Charity, according to the command of the Lord, fathers and brothers. I also speak on behalf of my brother, your bishop—

[Note: [Col. 1597] We suspect that the reading should be: “according to the command of the lord, father and brother. For I speak on behalf of my brother, your bishop.” He uses this conclusion when speaking to another people, among whom he perhaps was not accustomed to preach.]

—whose joy you ought to be by obeying the Lord our God.

Certainly, in God’s name, this church was made for you through his work, by the generous, merciful, and devoted contributions of faithful brothers. This church was made for you; but you are more truly the Church.

It was made for you so that your bodies might enter it; but your minds ought to be the place into which God enters.

You honored your bishop so that you wished to call this basilica “Florentia”—

[Note: [Col. 1597] Just as the basilica of Faustus and the basilica of Leontius were named after Faustus and Leontius, their founders, so here “Florentia” is a basilica named after Florentius the bishop. Which see he was bishop of is uncertain, unless Florentius of the Hippo-Diarrhytan see in the province of Proconsular Africa is intended. He took part with the others in the Donatist conference that year, as the Acts of the first hearing show, and several years later he subscribed, together with Augustine and others, to the letter of the monk Leporius to the Gauls. If this is true, it would be more fitting to say that the sermon was delivered not at Carthage or Hippo Regius but at Hippo-Diarrhytus. —Sirmondus.]

—but you are its Florentia. For the Apostle says: “You are my joy and crown in the Lord” (Phil. 4:1).

Whatever exists in this world fades and passes away. What is this life except what the Psalm said? “In the morning it will pass away like grass; in the morning it will flourish and pass away; in the evening it will fall, grow hard, and wither” (Ps. 89:6).

This is all flesh. Therefore Christ, therefore new life, therefore eternal hope, therefore the promised consolation of immortality—already fulfilled in the Lord’s flesh.

For that flesh which is now immortal was taken from us, and it showed us what it fulfilled in itself. For our sake he had flesh. But as regards himself: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Seek flesh and blood: where are they in the Word? Because he truly wished to suffer with us and redeem us, he put on the form of a servant. He who was here descended so that he might appear who was not absent; and he who made the human being wished to become human, and to be created from a mother who had been created by him.

He ascended even to the cross, died, and showed us what we already knew: birth and death. In himself, the humble one fulfilled these old, familiar, and known things of ours. We knew how to be born and die; we did not know how to rise again and live forever.

The humble one therefore assumed two of our old things; the exalted one fulfilled two other great and new things. He raised up the flesh, lifted the flesh into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father.

He wished to be our head; the head cried out for its members. For while he was here he said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

Let us hope for this also concerning our flesh: resurrection, transformation, incorruption, immortality, eternal dwelling. And let us act so that we may attain it.

This will be Florentia, the true Florentia.

# SERMON 360

[Note: [Col. 1598] Corrected from the Colbertine, Vatican, and Sirmondian manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1598] Elsewhere numbered among the Sirmondian sermons as 38.]

**At the vigils of Maximianus**

[Note: [Col. 1598] Manuscript R. does not prefer “at the vigil of Maximianus,” but “at Maximianus’s vigil”; perhaps he was an African martyr.]

**Concerning a certain Donatist who returned to the Church**

[Note: [Col. 1598] Rather, spoken in the mouth or under the name of a certain Donatist, but evidently dictated by Augustine.]

Thanks be to God. Brothers, rejoice with your brother, who was dead and came to life again, who had been lost and was found.

Thanks be to the patience and mercy of the Lord our God: to his patience, because he endured the one who delayed; to his mercy, because he deigned to receive the one who was returning.

This is the vineyard in which I did not labor, and I had spent my strength on another’s behalf. O vineyard beloved by my Lord, not only did my labor bring you no benefit, but I was also serving your enemy against you. With great sweat I was scattering seed when I was not gathering for you.

Thanks to your planter, with whom the laborers’ reward does not remain unpaid even when they are called at the last hour. I arrive late, but I do not despair of receiving the denarius (Matt. 20:9).

I was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent toward you; but I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance (1 Tim. 1:13). I held fast to the words of my parents—not of the Patriarchs, Prophets, or Apostles, but of my fleshly parents.

I did not listen to flesh and blood; rather, overcome by the truth, I listened and found rest when I was restored to unity.

Was I not reading the same Scriptures that I read now? Yet that teacher of the Gentiles, the vessel of election, Paul from Saul, the least from the proud, a shepherd from a plunderer, a ram from a wolf, was “a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee” (Phil. 3:5–6), and had been instructed in the law at the feet of Gamaliel the teacher (Acts 22:3).

And yet he did not recognize Christ, whom he was reading in the Prophets, as seated in heaven, nor did he permit him to be worshiped on earth. Unaware of the faith in his passion and resurrection, he sang of it with his mouth, while in his error he ravaged it in fury.

According to the Prophets, among whom he had been born and grown up, Christ had already risen from the dead and was sitting in heaven; yet he was still being blinded by his parents’ falsehood, that Christ’s disciples had stolen him from the tomb.

So I too was surrounded by the voices of the divine Scriptures concerning the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world; yet the false accusations of *traditores*—fabricated by my parents—made me deaf.

I do not compare myself with Paul in merits, but in sins. Even if I did not deserve to be so good, nevertheless I was not so bad that I could be without the medicine of correction.

He did not recognize the Bridegroom in the books he was reading, nor did I recognize the Bride. The one who revealed to him, concerning Christ’s glorification, what is written, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God,” himself revealed to me, concerning the Church’s diffusion, what follows: “Your glory is over all the earth” (Ps. 107:6).

Both testimonies are open to those who see, but closed to the blind. The baptism of Christ opened his eyes; the peace of Christ opened mine. That washing of holy water made him new; charity covered the multitude of my sins.

# SERMON 361

[Note: [Col. 1599] Revised from the Dominican, Roman, and Vatican manuscripts and from Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 1599] Elsewhere, *On Various Matters* 120.]

**On the Resurrection of the Dead, I**

[Note: [Col. 1599] Possidius, in the *Index*, chapter 1, notes “two treatises on the Resurrection.” Florus cites the first on 1 Corinthians 15; the second is cited by Florus himself and by Bede on 1 Corinthians 15 and Colossians 3.]

## CHAPTER ONE

**1.** When the Apostle’s Epistle was being read, we noticed the commendable movement of your faith and love: how you recoiled from people who think that this is the only life, the life we share with animals, and that after death everything human comes to an end. Corrupting the itching ears of evil people, they say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. 15:32).

Let this therefore be the starting point of our discussion, and let it be, as it were, the hinge of our sermon, to which the other matters that the Lord may deign to suggest will be referred.

## CHAPTER TWO

**2. Our hope and faith: the resurrection of the dead. Our love. Two questions concerning the future resurrection.**

Our hope is the resurrection of the dead; our faith is the resurrection of the dead. Our love also is aroused and kindled by the preaching of things not yet seen, and by the desire whose greatness makes our hearts capable of the blessedness that is promised to come, so long as we believe what we do not yet see.

Our love, therefore, ought not to occupy itself with these temporal and visible things, so that in the resurrection we may hope to have something like what we now live better and become better by despising—namely, bodily pleasures and delights.

When faith in the resurrection of the dead is removed, the whole of Christian teaching collapses. But when faith in the resurrection of the dead has been founded, there is not immediately security concerning the Christian mind unless that future life is distinguished from this passing one.

The matter must therefore be set out as follows: If the dead do not rise, we have no hope of a future life; but if the dead do rise, there will indeed be a future life, yet the second question is what kind of life it will be.

The first discussion, then, is whether there will be a resurrection of the dead; the second discussion is what the life of the saints will be like in the resurrection.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 1600]

**3. In one matter the unbeliever errs; in the other, the carnal Christian. The Christian must be led by the weight of authority.**

Those who say that the dead do not rise are not Christians. But those who think that, when the dead have risen, they will live carnally are carnal Christians.

Whatever discussion is directed against the opinion of those who deny the resurrection of the dead is directed against those who are outside, and I do not think that anyone from their number is present here.

Our exposition may therefore seem unnecessary if it lingers in an attempt to teach that the dead rise. For the Christian, who has already believed in Christ and in no way thinks that the Apostle lies, must be led by the weight of authority.

It is enough for such a person to hear: “If the dead are not raised, our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty.” “If the dead,” he says, “are not raised, neither has Christ been raised” (ibid. 14, 13).

But if Christ has been raised—and in him is the salvation of Christians—it is certainly not impossible for the dead to rise. For the one who raised his Son, and the one who raised his own flesh, gave the rest of the body, which is the Church, an example in the Head.

The discussion of the resurrection of the dead could therefore be unnecessary, and we could now undertake the discussion that Christians commonly have among themselves: When we have risen, what shall we be like? How shall we live? What shall our occupations be? Will there be any, or none? If there are none, shall we live idly, doing nothing? Or if we do something, what shall we do?

Further: shall we eat and drink? Will there be unions of men and women? Or will there be some simple and incorruptible common life? And if so, what will that life itself be like? What will the movement be like? What will the form of their bodies be like?

These are the discussions of Christians, with faith in the resurrection preserved.

## CHAPTER FOUR

**4. He undertakes to prove that the resurrection will occur.**

I would already pass to this discussion—to the extent that such things can be undertaken or promised by human beings to human beings, such as we are and you are—if a certain concern about our excessively carnal and almost pagan brothers did not compel me to linger somewhat over the question of whether the dead will rise at all.

For I do not think that any pagan is present here now, but that all are Christians. Yet pagans and mockers of the resurrection do not cease to murmur every day in the ears of Christians: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

And when the Apostle, expressing his concern and adding to this saying, said, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals,” we, fearing these evils and concerned for the weak—not only with a fatherly but also with a certain motherly love—shall say something about this, as much as may perhaps be sufficient for Christians. For today greater devotion to the Scriptures has brought together all who have assembled here.

No solemnity of any festive day has summoned theatrical crowds to the Church of God. Some people are accustomed to gather not from piety but for the sake of a celebration.

This consideration has caused us first to speak about the resurrection of the dead and then, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, about what the future life of the righteous will be like.

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 1601]

**5. Against those who decide that we should live here as though nothing remains after death.**

“I fear,” says the Apostle, “lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3).

Those conversations corrupt their minds: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

Let those who love these things, who pursue these things, who think that this is the only life, who hope for nothing afterward, who either do not pray to God or pray for this reason—let those for whom the speech of devotion is burdensome hear us saying these things with great sadness.

They want to eat and drink, for tomorrow they die. Would that they truly considered that they would die tomorrow! For who is so insane and perverse, who is so hostile to his own soul, that, being destined to die the next day, he would not think that everything for which he labors has come to an end?

For it is written: “On that day all his thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145:4).

Even if people, because of those whom they leave behind here, take care of their wills as the day of their death approaches, how much more ought they to think about something concerning their soul?

A man thinks about whom he will leave behind, but does not think about himself, who is leaving all these things behind? Look: your children will have what you leave, but you will have nothing; and your whole thought is consumed with how those who come after you may pass through this world, not with where those who pass through it may arrive.

Would that there were thought of death. But when the dead are carried out, death is considered, and people say: “Woe to the wretched man! Such was he; yesterday he was walking.” Or: “I saw him seven days ago; he spoke with me about this and that.” “Humanity is nothing.”

They murmur such things. But perhaps while the dead person is mourned, while the funeral is arranged, while the rites are prepared, while he is carried out, while people go along, while he is buried, this speech is vigorous. Once the dead person has been buried, even such a thought is buried.

Those deadly concerns return. The person forgets whom he has escorted and, though destined to depart, thinks about succession. He returns to frauds, robberies, perjuries, drunkenness, and the body’s countless pleasures—not merely pleasures that will perish when they have been exhausted, but pleasures that perish while they are being consumed.

And what is more destructive, an argument for burying the heart is taken from the burial of the dead, and people say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

## CHAPTER SIX

**6. The faith in the resurrection is mocked by unbelievers. Memorial observances for parents. Against those who object that no one has returned from the dead.**

They also mock the faith of those who assert that the dead will rise, saying to themselves: “Look, this man has been placed in a tomb; let his voice be heard.”

But his voice cannot be heard. “I shall hear the voice of my father, of my grandfather, of my great-grandfather. Who has risen from there? Who has reported what is happening among the dead? Let us do good for ourselves while we live. But when we have died, even if our parents, or dear ones, or relatives bring something to our tombs, they will be bringing it for themselves, since they are alive, not for us who are dead.”

Scripture also mocked this practice, speaking of some who do not perceive present goods: “It is as though you were placing delicacies around a dead person” (Sir. 30:18).

It is evident that this does not pertain to the dead, and that this custom belongs to the pagans. It does not derive from that lineage and vein of the righteousness of our fathers, the Patriarchs, for whom we read that funeral rites were celebrated, but not that offerings were made for the dead.

This can also be observed in the customs of the Jews. They did not retain the fruit of virtue from this, but they did retain, in certain solemn observances, the antiquity of the custom.

And when some people object from the Scriptures, “Break your bread and pour out your wine over the tombs of the righteous, and do not give it to the wicked” (Tob. 4:18), it is not necessary to discuss this here. Nevertheless, I say that the faithful can understand what was said.

For how the faithful religiously perform these things at the memorials of their own people is known to the faithful. And because these things are not to be offered to the wicked—that is, to unbelievers—for “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), this too is known to the faithful.

Let no one therefore seek a wound from a remedy, or attempt to twist a cord from the Scriptures, from which he may cast a noose of death around his soul.

It is evident how that passage is to be understood, and this Christian observance is open and salutary.

## CHAPTER SEVEN
### 7. Our faith in the heart, like Christ sleeping in the boat, must be awakened so that the storm may be calmed

Let us therefore consider what I had begun to say, on account of those who murmur into the ears of the weak, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” They say, “No one has come back from there; I have not heard anyone’s voice from the time my grandfather was placed there, nor from the time of my great-grandfather, nor from the time of my father. I have heard no one’s voice.”

Answer them, Christians, if you are Christians—lest perhaps, when you wish to become drunk among the people, you be reluctant to answer those who corrupt you. You have what you should answer; but you are tossed about by desire for pleasures, and you wish to gorge yourselves and be buried alive. The desire for drunkenness rises up, and, like a certain wave, rushes upon the soul, drawn on by the breath of an evil counselor.

You are therefore suffering a great storm. You do not wish to answer the corrupter while you favor the one who pours the drink; but the wave of desire rises too high and wants to overwhelm your heart as though it were a boat. Christian, Christ is sleeping in your boat: awaken him; he will command the storms, and everything will become calm (Matt. VIII, 24–26).

At that time, when the disciples were tossed about in the boat while Christ was sleeping, they signified that Christians are tossed about when Christian faith is sleeping. For you see what the Apostle says: “That Christ,” he says, “may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. III, 17). According to the presence of his beauty and divinity, he is always with the Father; according to his bodily presence, he is now above the heavens at the right hand of the Father; but according to the presence of faith, he is in all Christians.

And so you are tossed about because Christ is sleeping: that is, you do not overcome those desires which are aroused by the breath of evil counselors because faith is sleeping. What does “faith is sleeping” mean? It has been lulled to sleep. What does “it has been lulled to sleep” mean? You have forgotten it. What, then, does it mean to awaken Christ? To awaken faith, to remember what you have believed.

Therefore remember your faith; awaken Christ. Your faith itself will command the waves by which you are disturbed, and the winds of those who give perverse advice. Immediately they will depart; immediately everything will become quiet. For even if the evil counselor does not cease speaking, he no longer shakes the boat, raises a wave, or sinks the vessel in which you are being carried.

[Col. 1603]

### 8. The faith in the future resurrection is sufficiently confirmed by Christ’s resurrection

The whole world bears witness to our faith. Everything offers testimony to the resurrection. What, then, are you doing by awakening Christ? What had that evil speaker said to you? What had that corrupter said, who corrupts good morals through evil conversations? What had he said? Certainly this: “No one has returned from there. I have not heard my father, nor my grandfather. Let someone return from there and tell us what is happening there.”

### CHAPTER VIII
