Now that you have awakened Christ in your boat, recalling your faith, answer him and say: “Fool, if your father were to rise again, you would believe; the Lord of all has risen, and you do not believe? Why did he wish to die and rise again, except so that we might all believe in one person and not be deceived by many? And what would your father accomplish if he rose and spoke, only to die again?”

Consider with what great power he rose, who now dies no more, and over whom death will no longer have dominion (Rom. VI, 9). He showed himself to his disciples and to his faithful. The solidity of his body was handled, since for some it was not enough to see what they remembered unless they also touched what they saw. Faith was confirmed not only in human hearts but also in human eyes.

He ascended into heaven—the one who demonstrated these things—and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples; the Gospel was preached. If we are lying about these things, ask the whole world. Many things that were promised have come to pass; many things that were hoped for have been fulfilled. The whole world flourishes in the Christian faith.

Even those who have not yet believed in Christ do not dare to detract from Christ’s resurrection. There is testimony in heaven and testimony on earth; testimony from the angels and testimony from the underworld. What remains that does not cry out? And you say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!”

### 9. An example of the resurrection in a seed

But you have become sad because your beloved has been buried, since you did not immediately hear his voice. He was alive; he died. He ate; he no longer eats. He felt; he no longer feels. He does not share in the joys and gladness of the living.

### CHAPTER IX

Would you weep over a seed when you were plowing? Suppose, then, that someone were so inexperienced in these matters that, when the seed is carried out into the field, cast into the earth, and buried beneath the broken clod, he were ignorant even of things soon to come. Suppose he wept over the wheat because he remembered summer and said to himself:

“This grain, which has now been buried, was harvested, brought in, threshed, cleaned, and stored in the granary with such labor. We saw its beauty and rejoiced. Now it has been taken away from our eyes. I see plowed earth, but I can discern the grain neither in the granary nor here. He would mourn the grain as though it were dead and buried; he would weep abundantly, looking at the clods and the earth but not seeing the harvest.”

How would he be mocked by any unlearned people—not unlearned in that matter, but inexperienced in other matters and skilled in the very matter over which he was absurdly ignorant? And what would those who knew what was going to happen to the grain say to him, if he was mourning because he knew none of these things?

“Do not be sad. What we buried is certainly no longer in the granary and no longer in our hands. We shall come to this field, and it will delight you to see the appearance of the standing crop where you now mourn the bareness of the plowed ground.”

The one who knew what would happen to the grain would rejoice even during the plowing. But the incredulous—or rather foolish, and, to speak more accurately, inexperienced—person might perhaps mourn at first; then, believing the experienced man, he would depart comforted and would hope for the coming harvest together with him.

### CHAPTER X

### 10. Our resurrection exemplified in Christ. All creation speaks of resurrection. The awakening of animals. The new moons. The leaves of trees

Harvests of the same kind are seen every year, but one final harvest of the human race will arise at the end of the age. It cannot now be shown to the eyes, but an example has been given from one principal grain.

The Lord himself says, “If the grain remains thus and does not die, it remains alone” (John XII, 24), speaking of his own death, since the resurrection of the many who believe in him was to follow. An example was given in one grain, but it was such an example that all who wished to be grains would believe it.

Indeed, all creation speaks of resurrection, if we are not deaf. From this we ought to infer what God will do once, at the end, with the human race, since we see so many similar things every day. The resurrection of Christians will occur once; the sleep and awakening of animals occur daily. To sleep is like death; to awaken is like resurrection. From what happens every day, believe what will happen once.

The moon is born, grows, becomes full, wanes, disappears, and is renewed every month. What happens to the moon over the months will happen in the resurrection once over the whole course of time. As what happens daily with those who sleep, so what happens monthly with the moon.

Where do the leaves of the trees go, and from what hidden places do they return? It is winter. Certainly, the trees, now resembling dry things, become green in spring [Note: [Col. 1604] Manuscripts: “become green” (*viridescunt*).]. Is this happening for the first time, or was it so in the previous year as well? Indeed, it was so in the previous year too. It is taken away from autumn into winter and returns through spring into summer.

Therefore the year returns in its season, while human beings, made in the image of God, will perish when they have died?

### CHAPTER XI

### 11. How certain things are renewed from the earth

But someone who observes the transformations and renewals of things less carefully may say to me: “Those leaves have rotted; new ones are being born.”

Yet anyone who considers the matter well sees that even what rots contributes to the strength of the earth. For from what does the earth become fertile if not from the decay of earthly things?

Those who cultivate fields pay attention to this. Those who do not cultivate them, because they always live in the city, should at least learn from the gardens near the city how the most contemptible refuse of the city is preserved with great care, by whom it is even purchased for a price, and to what place it is carried.

Certainly, after all its usefulness has been exhausted, it might be thought contemptible by the inexperienced. And who considers it worthy to look at dung? What a human being recoils from seeing, he takes care to preserve.

Thus what already seemed consumed and cast away returns to the richness of the earth; richness becomes sap, sap becomes root; and what passes from the earth into the root migrates by invisible stages into the strength of the tree, is distributed through the branches, passes from the branches into shoots, and from the shoot into fruits and leaves.

Behold: what you dreaded in the decay of dung, you marvel at in the fruitfulness and greenness of the tree.

### CHAPTER XII

### 12. The objection that the body turns to ashes. The custom of the Egyptians. *Gabbarae*

Do not now bring against me the objection you usually bring: “The body of the buried dead does not remain intact. If it remained intact, I would believe in the resurrection.”

Then only the Egyptians believe in the resurrection, because they carefully preserve the corpses of the dead. For they have the custom of drying bodies and making them, as it were, bronze. They call them *gabbarae* [Note: [Col. 1605] The words “They call them *gabbarae*” are absent from the manuscripts.].

According to these people, then, who do not know the secret recesses of nature, where everything remains safe for the Creator even when it is withdrawn from mortal senses, only the Egyptians rightly believe in the resurrection of their dead, while the hope of other Christians is confined within narrow limits?

Often, when tombs have been opened or exposed either through age or through some non-sacrilegious necessity, bodies have been found to have rotted. People who are accustomed to delight in bodily appearance have sighed and said in their hearts:

“Will this ash ever again possess that beautiful appearance? Will it be restored to life, restored to light? When will this happen? When could I hope for anything living from this ash?”

You who say this: you see in the tomb either ash. Recall your own age. If, for example, you are thirty, fifty, or more years old, there is either ash in the tomb of the dead person. What were you fifty years ago? Where were you?

The bodies of all of us who are now speaking or listening will be ashes after a few years; a few years ago they were not even ashes. Will the one who was able to prepare what did not exist fail to restore what did exist?

### CHAPTER XIII

### 13. Faith strengthened by Christ against evil conversations

Let the murmurs of those who speak wickedly, and who corrupt good morals through evil conversations, cease. Plant your feet firmly on the road—plant them firmly—so that you do not leave the road, not so that you remain on the road, but, as it is said, “Run so that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX, 24).

May Christ always be vigorous in your heart, the one who wished to show in the head what the rest of the members should hope for. On earth we labor, but our head is already in heaven; he neither dies nor fails nor suffers anything, although he suffered for us. “He was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Rom. IV, 25).

We know this through faith. Those to whom he showed himself learned it through their eyes. Yet we are not rejected because he rose and we were unable to see him with bodily eyes. We have the testimony of the Lord himself on our behalf, which he gave to the doubting disciple who sought through touch what he should believe.

For when that disciple, overcome by touching the scars, cried out and said, “My Lord and my God,” the Lord replied, “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who do not see and believe” (John XX, 24–29).

Awaken, then, to your blessedness. Let no evil counselor shake from your hearts what Christ has fixed there.

### 14. Against those who say that only Christ was permitted to rise. The union of the members with Christ the head. An apt comparison

Nor should anyone say this to me. For this is said by all who, even against their will, have now yielded to Christ’s authority. Nearly all pagans—even those who are unwilling or delay embracing Christ in devotion—do not dare to criticize him. Although they dare to criticize Christians, they do not dare to criticize Christ. They yield to the head but still insult the body.

But when the body hears the insults of those who already yield to the head, it should not think itself cut off from the head but supported by it. For if we had been cut off, we ought to fear the voices of those who insult us. But the one who himself testifies that we have not been cut off said to Paul, who was still Saul and was persecuting the Church, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

He had already passed through the hands of the impious Jews; he had already entered the underworld; he had already risen from the tomb; he had already ascended into heaven; he had already enriched and strengthened the hearts of believers by the gift of the Holy Spirit; he was sitting at the right hand of the Father and interceding for us. He was not going to hand himself over to death again, but was going to free us from death. What could he suffer from Saul in his fury?

How could that hand touch him, even though Saul was, as it is written, “breathing out slaughter” (Acts IX, 4, 1)? He could attack Christians laboring on earth; but when and how could he attack Christ?

Yet Christ cries out on behalf of the other members and does not say, “Why are you persecuting mine?” If he had said, “Why are you persecuting mine?” we would have believed that they were servants. But servants are not joined to their master as Christians are joined to Christ. This is another kind of bond, another order of members, another unity of love.

The head speaks for the members. He does not even say, “Why are you persecuting my members?” but says, “Why are you persecuting me?” Saul was not touching the head, but he was touching what was joined to the head.

### CHAPTER XIV

We have often said this, but because the comparison is apt and conveys the matter well, it must be repeated.

Someone who steps on you in a crowd presses your foot but does nothing to your tongue. What, then, does it mean when the tongue cries out, “You are stepping on me”? The pressure is on the foot; the tongue has suffered no injury, but there is one bodily bond.

“And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (I Cor. XII, 26). If, then, your tongue speaks on behalf of your foot, does Christ in heaven not speak on behalf of Christians?

Your tongue does not speak for your foot by saying, “You are stepping on my foot,” but by saying, “You are stepping on me,” although it itself has not been touched. Recognize him as your head when he speaks from heaven on your behalf and says, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

Why, then, brothers, have we said this? Lest those of whom the Apostle says, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals,” should creep upon you, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (I Cor. XV, 33, 32).

They may say this to you. They do not dare to criticize Christ; they tremble before the authority of his majesty, established throughout the world. But, as it is written, “The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. CXI, 10). He can gnash his teeth and waste away, but he does not dare to blaspheme Christ.

Therefore, lest they speak in this way and say, “Only Christ was permitted to rise.” Sometimes they say it sincerely, but sometimes they say it out of fear. You, however, should observe both what they dare to say and what they do not dare to say.

### CHAPTER XV

### 15. Christ is deceitfully praised by unbelievers so that we may not hope for a similar resurrection

They will say: “You tell me that Christ rose, and on that basis you hope for the resurrection of the dead. But Christ was permitted to rise from the dead.”

And he begins to praise Christ—not to honor him, but to make you despair. This is the crafty destruction of the serpent: by praising Christ, he turns you away from Christ. He deceitfully proclaims the one whom he does not dare to criticize.

He magnifies Christ’s majesty in order to make him unique, so that you will not hope for something like what was displayed when he rose. He appears almost more religious toward Christ when he says:

“Look at the one who dares to compare himself with Christ: because Christ rose, he thinks that he too will rise.”

Do not be disturbed by the perverse praise of your Emperor. Hostile snares disturb you, but Christ’s humility and humanity console you. That man proclaims how greatly Christ has been exalted above you; Christ, however, tells you how far he descended to you.

Answer him, then. Awaken that faith. There is a storm; there are waves; the boat is in distress; Christ is sleeping. Awaken that faith. Do not forget what you believed (Matt. VIII, 24–26).

You will answer immediately when evangelical faith begins to keep watch within you. You will not be without an answer, for it will not be you who speaks. Christ dwelling in you will seize his instrument—your tongue—as his sword. Using your heart and your voice as a possessor dwelling within you, he will resist the adversary and make you secure.

You need only awaken the sleeper—that is, remember the faith you have forgotten.

### CHAPTER XVI

### 16. That Christ’s resurrection rightly brought us the hope of resurrection. The origin of Christ’s mortality. How Christ became mediator. How sins were in Christ. Mortality as the punishment of sin

What am I now going to say, by which you may answer such people? I will not say something new, but what you have believed. Awaken your faith, then, and answer the one who says, “Christ alone could do it; we cannot.”

Answer and say: “Christ could do it because he is God.” He could, certainly, because he is God. If because he is God, then because he is omnipotent. If because he is omnipotent, why should I despair that he can do in me what he demonstrated in himself for my sake?

Next I ask: from what did Christ rise? He will answer, “From the dead.” I ask why he died. For can God die?

Could that divinity—the Word equal to the Father, the art of the omnipotent Craftsman through whom all things were made, the unchangeable Wisdom, remaining in itself and renewing all things (Wis. VII, 27), reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly (ibid. VIII, 1)—die?

“No,” he says.

And yet Christ died. From what did he die? Clearly, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” What does he say before this? “Although he was in the form of God” (Phil. II, 6–7).

Had he received the form of God, or was he naturally in it [Note: [Col. 1608] Manuscripts: “Had he received the form of a servant, or was he naturally in it?”]?

The Apostle makes a distinction. When he spoke of the form of God, he said “was”; when he named the form of a servant, he said “taking.” Christ, therefore, was something and took something, so that what he had taken might be one with him.

He was equal to God in the form of God, as that fisherman evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). That is, “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized.”

For what is not naturally present but is illicitly usurped is seizure. An angel usurped equality with God, fell, and became the devil. A human being usurped equality with God, fell, and became mortal.

But this one, who was born equal because he was not born in time but was the eternal Son of the eternal Father, eternally begotten, through whom all things were made, was in the form of God.

In order to be mediator between God and human beings, between the just and the unjust, between the immortal and mortals, he assumed something from the unjust and mortal while retaining something with the just and immortal.

Retaining justice with the just and immortal, and assuming mortality from the unjust and mortal, he became a reconciler in the middle, casting down the wall of our sins. Hence his people sing to him, “And in my God I shall leap over a wall” (Ps. XVII, 30).

Restoring to God what sins had alienated, and redeeming with his blood what the devil possessed, he died for us and rose for us. He bore our sins—not by having them cling to him, but by enduring them—just as Jacob bore the skins of goats so that he might appear hairy to his father who was blessing him (Gen. XXVII, 16).

The wicked Esau had his own hair, but the good Jacob bore what belonged to another. Sins cling to mortal human beings. They did not cling to the one who had said, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

### CHAPTER XVII

Death, therefore, in our Lord was a sign of sins belonging to others, not the punishment of sins belonging to himself. In all other human beings, mortality is the punishment of sin. It is drawn from the origin of sin, from which we all come—from the fall of that man, not from the descent of this one.

For falling is one thing, and descending another. One fell wickedly; the other descended mercifully. “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22).

Bearing, therefore, sins belonging to others, he says, “Then I paid what I had not stolen” (Ps. LXVIII, 5)—that is, I died without having sin. “Behold,” he says, “the prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me.” What does “he will find nothing in me” mean? He will not find in me the merit of death. The merit of death is sin.

Why, then, will you die? He continues and says: “But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise; let us go from here” (John XIV, 30–31). And he rises and goes to his passion. Why? Because he was doing the will of his Father, not because he owed anything to the prince of sins, in whom there was no sin.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ brought divinity with him, but assumed mortality from us. He received it in the womb of the virgin Mary, joining the Word of God to human nature, as a bridegroom joins himself to a bride in the bridal chamber of the virgin, so that he himself might proceed as a bridegroom from his bridal chamber (Ps. XVIII, 6).

### 17. Mortality in Christ was real, not merited but merciful. Christ’s resurrection according to the flesh that was previously mortal. If they admit that he was just, he did not deceive us when promising resurrection

Return, then, to what I was saying. Mortality came from sin to all human beings; but in the Lord it came from mercy, and yet it was real, because that flesh was real flesh and truly mortal, “having the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII, 3)—not the likeness of flesh, but the likeness of sinful flesh. It was real flesh, but not sinful flesh.

For, as I said, he had not received that mortality as a merit of sin—he who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death.” What, then, was he, and what did he have? He was divinity possessing mortality. From what he died, from that he rose again.

### CHAPTER XVIII

Look now at those who say, “Christ alone could rise, but you cannot.” Answer and say: “Christ rose in that which he had received from us. Take away the form of a servant, and there would be nothing in which he could rise, because there would be nothing in which he could die.”

Why, then, do you wish to destroy my faith by praising my Lord, when my Lord built that faith in me? He died because he took the form of a servant. He rose according to that in which he died. Therefore I could in no way despair of the resurrection of servants, since the Lord rose in the form of a servant.

Or, if they attribute Christ’s resurrection from the dead to human power—for they also commonly say this, that he was such a just human being that he could even rise from the dead—then, for the moment, let me speak according to their position and say nothing about the divinity of our Lord: he was so just that he deserved even to rise from the dead. He could in no way have deceived us, since he also promised us resurrection.

### CHAPTER XIX

### 18. The future resurrection proved above

Everything that has been said, brothers, serves the purpose of instructing you if some people say that the dead will not rise.

The necessary things were said, if you remember, insofar as God deigned to suggest them. Testimonies were drawn from the nature of things and from daily examples; from the very omnipotence of God, for whom nothing is difficult—if he could make what did not exist, much more can he restore what did exist; and from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, whom we know to have risen, and whose resurrection occurred only in the form of a servant, since death—which would have required resurrection—could not have occurred except through the form of a servant.

Therefore, since we are servants, we ought to hope in our own form for what he deigned to demonstrate beforehand in the form of a servant.

Let the tongues of those who say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,” fall silent. Answer them yourselves and say: “Let us fast and pray, for tomorrow we shall die.”

### CHAPTER XX

### 19. We are admonished by Noah’s example to await the last judgment

It remains for us to say what the life of the righteous will be in the resurrection. But since you see that a moderate amount of time has already been taken today, meditate on what we have delivered; and pray that we may at some time deliver what we still owe.

Above all, hold fast to why we have spoken, especially because of these festival days, my brothers, which the pagans celebrate. Pay attention to yourselves. This world is passing away.

Remember the Gospel, where the Lord foretells that the final day will be as it was in the days of Noah: “They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, marrying and giving in marriage, until Noah entered the ark. The flood came and destroyed them all” (Luke XVII, 27).

You have the Lord most clearly warning you beforehand and saying elsewhere, “Let not your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (ibid. XXI, 34). “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” [Note: [Col. 1610] The printed editions add, “in your hands,” which is absent from the manuscripts—not only here but almost everywhere in Augustine. The Greek manuscripts likewise lack these words, nor does our Vulgate contain them in the ancient Corbie Bibles.]; “and be like servants waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding” (ibid. XII, 35–36).

Let us await his coming; let him not find us sluggish. It is shameful for a married woman not to long for her husband. How much more shameful is it for the Church not to long for Christ?

A husband comes to bodily embraces, and his chaste wife receives him with great desire. The Bridegroom of the Church is going to come to give eternal embraces and to make us his everlasting co-heirs, and yet we live in such a way that we not only do not long for his coming but even fear it!

How true it is that that day will come as it did in the days of Noah! How many will it find in this condition, even among those who are called Christians?

For so many years the ark is being built so that those who do not believe may awaken (Gen. VI). It was built for a hundred years, and they did not awaken to say: “The man of God is not building the ark without cause; surely destruction threatens the human race.” They did not turn to ways pleasing to God and appease God’s anger, as the Ninevites did.

### CHAPTER XXI

For they produced the fruit of repentance and appeased God’s anger.

### 20. Nineveh was overthrown according to the prophecy, but through repentance

Jonah announced not mercy but future anger. He did not say, “In three days Nineveh will be overthrown; but if you repent during these three days, God will spare you.” He did not say this.

He threatened and foretold only destruction. Yet they, not despairing of God’s mercy, turned to repentance, and God spared them (Jonah III).

But what shall we say? That the Prophet lied? If you understand it carnally, he appears to have spoken falsely. If you understand it spiritually, what the Prophet said came to pass. Nineveh was indeed overthrown.

Consider what Nineveh was, and see that it was overthrown. What was Nineveh? They ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built; they occupied themselves with perjuries, lies, drunkenness, crimes, and corruptions. This was Nineveh.

Now consider Nineveh: they mourn, grieve, and are afflicted in sackcloth and ashes, in fasting and prayers. Where is that Nineveh? Surely it has been overthrown, because it no longer exists in those former practices.

### CHAPTER XXII

### 21. Those who do not convert now while Christ is building the Church deserve greater condemnation than those who did not convert when Noah was building the ark

Therefore, brothers, the ark is also now being built, and those hundred years signify the present times. This entire span of time is represented by that number of years.

If, then, those who disregarded Noah while he was building the ark deservedly perished, what do those deserve who disregard salvation while Christ is building the Church?

The difference between Noah and Christ is as great as that between a servant and a Lord—indeed, as great as that between God and a human being. For a servant and a lord can both be called human beings.

And yet, because people did not believe while a human being was building the ark, an example was given to posterity that they should beware of such people. Christ, God who became human for our sake, is building the Church. He made himself the foundation of that ark. Every day imperishable timbers—faithful people renouncing this age—enter into the structure of the ark.

And still it is said, “Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die”?

You, then, as I said, brothers, answer them: “Let us fast and pray; for tomorrow we shall die.”

They say, “Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die,” because they do not hope for resurrection. But we, who already believe and proclaim the resurrection—believing it through the Prophets who spoke, and through Christ and the Apostles who preached it—who hope to live after this death, must not fail or weigh down our hearts with gluttony and drunkenness.

Instead, let us anxiously await the coming of our Lord, with our loins girded and our lamps burning. Let us fast and pray—not because we shall die tomorrow, but so that we may die securely.

What remains, brothers, demand from us at another time in the name of the Lord.

Turning toward the Lord, etc.

---

# SERMON CCCLXII

[Note: [Col. 1611] Corrected according to d. r. t. v. and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1611] Elsewhere *On Various Matters* 121.]

## On the Resurrection of the Dead, II

### CHAPTER I

### 1. It must be said what the resurrection of the righteous will be

Keeping our promise in mind, we also had the appropriate readings from the Gospel and the Apostle recited. For all of you who attended the previous sermon remember with us that the question of the resurrection was divided by us into a twofold discussion.

First, we were to discuss, on account of those who doubt or even deny it, whether there will be a resurrection of the dead. Afterwards, insofar as we are able and according to the Scriptures, we were to inquire what the life of the righteous will be in the resurrection.

In the first part, therefore, when we discussed the resurrection of the dead, we lingered so long—as you may recall—that time failed for treating the second question, and so we were compelled to postpone it until today. Your expectation therefore demands from us what we owe, and we recognize that the time has come to repay it.

### CHAPTER II

Let us therefore entreat the Lord together with devout intention of heart, so that we may suitably discharge our debt and you may profitably receive it. For this is, as must be admitted, the greater question. But charity is stronger than all difficult questions, and we must all serve it, so that God, who commanded this, may turn all our difficulties into ease and joy.

### 2. The same subject is treated

You remember that on that day we answered certain people who were saying, as the Apostle rebukes them, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” He added, saying, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals,” and thus concluded: “Be sober, righteous, and do not sin; for some have ignorance of God. I speak this to your shame” (I Cor. XV, 32–34).

May we all hear these apostolic words and commit them to our hearts. And whoever hears them and commits them to the heart should let his works reveal it.

For the one who hears is like a field receiving the seed of the sower. The one who commits it to the heart is like someone breaking the clod and covering what has been sown. But the one who acts according to what he has heard and committed to his heart is the one who rises into the harvest and bears fruit with perseverance—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold (Matt. XIII, 23; Luke VIII, 15). For him, barns are prepared—not fire, as for straw, but barns as for grain.

### CHAPTER III

In those hidden barns, therefore, in the resurrection of the dead, lies that perpetual blessedness—the very hidden places of the righteous—to which Scripture commends that they are to be received.

### 3. The hidden dwelling places of the blessed signified by the name “vessels.” The hidden place of God’s face

The Lord Jesus Christ also mentioned this matter elsewhere under the name “vessels,” when he said that the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet—that is, nets; for certain nets are called dragnets:

> “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore, they chose the good into vessels, but threw the bad outside” (Matt. 13:47–48).

Our Lord wished to signify that the word of God is now cast over peoples and nations in the same way that a dragnet is cast into the sea. Through the Christian sacraments it now gathers both the good and the bad; but not all whom the dragnet draws up are also stored in vessels. For the vessels are the dwelling places of the saints and the profound secrets of the blessed life. Not all who are called Christians will be able to reach them, but only those who are called Christians in such a way that they truly are Christians.

The good and bad fish, certainly, swim within the dragnet, and the good endure the bad until they are separated at the end. It is also said in one place: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face” (Ps. 30:21); for he was speaking about the saints. “You will hide them,” he says, “in the hiding-place of your face”—that is, where the eyes of human beings and the thoughts of mortals cannot follow. Signifying certain secrets that are exceedingly hidden and exceedingly concealed, he said, “in the hiding-place of God’s face” [Col. 1613].

Must we think in a carnal way that God has some enormous face, and that in his face there is some bodily receptacle where the saints are to be hidden? You see, brothers, how carnal such ideas are and how they must be rejected by the heart of every believer.

What, then, should “the hiding-place of God’s face” be understood to mean except that which is known only to God’s face—that is, only to God himself? When “granaries” are mentioned to signify hidden places, and elsewhere “vessels” are mentioned, neither the granaries we know nor the vessels we know are intended. For if one of these meant one particular thing, the other would not be mentioned. But because things unknown are conveyed, as far as possible, through comparisons familiar to human beings, accept both terms—“granaries” and “vessels”—as signifying a secret place. But if you ask what sort of secret place it is, hear the Prophet saying: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face.”

### CHAPTER IV

#### 4. We long for our homeland through faith

Since these things are so, brothers, we are still wandering as strangers in this life; we still long through faith for that homeland—I scarcely know how to call it—from which we are citizens. And why do I say “I scarcely know how to call it,” unless it is because, wandering far away, we have forgotten it, so that we are able to call our homeland “that which I scarcely know”?

The Lord Christ, the king of that homeland, comes to those who are wandering as strangers and drives this forgetfulness from the heart. Through his assumption of flesh, his divinity becomes a way for us, so that through the man Christ we may proceed and abide in Christ as God.

What, then, brothers? How are we to explain to you in words that secret place “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2:9)? Or by what eye shall we see it? Sometimes we can know something that nevertheless we cannot express; but what we do not know, we are at times unable to express at all. Since it could happen that, if I knew those things, I still could not express them to you, how much more difficult will my speech be when I too, brothers, walk with you by faith, not yet by sight?

But is this merely my statement, or is it also that of the Apostle himself? For he consoles our ignorance and builds up our faith when he says: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:13–14). Thus he shows that he is still on the way.

And elsewhere he says: “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). Again he says: “For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

### CHAPTER V

#### 5. The Church teaches what it has believed, not what it has known

Therefore, brothers, hear from me a voice that is found in the Psalms: devout, humble, meek—not proud, not turbulent, not rash, not presumptuous. For the Psalm says in one place: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” The Apostle inserted this testimony and added: “And we also believe, and therefore we speak” (Ps. 115:10; 2 Cor. 4:13).

Do you therefore want me to tell you things that I know? I am not deceiving you: hear what I have believed. Do not think it worthless that you hear what I have believed; for you hear a truthful confession. But if I were to say, “Hear what I know,” you would hear a presumptuous claim.

Therefore, brothers, if all of us—and, as we believe according to the sacred writings, all who lived in the flesh before us, through whom the Spirit of God, speaking, distributed to human beings as much as was sufficient to be signified to those wandering as strangers—all of us speak what we believe, the Lord alone spoke what he knew.

What, then, if the Lord alone could know the future life everlasting about which he spoke, while the others followed the Lord because they believed? We find our Lord Jesus Christ himself knowing what he was speaking about, yet not saying everything. For in one place he said to his disciples: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). He deferred saying what he knew because of their weakness, not because of any difficulty on his own part.

But we, because of the common weakness of us all, do not attempt to express with sufficient dignity what we know; rather, we explain as best we can what we rightly believe. And you, for your part, receive it as you are able. If perhaps one of you is able to grasp more than I am able to say, let him not attend to the little stream, but run to the most abundant spring; for with him is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light (Ps. 35:10).

### CHAPTER VI

#### 6. A Christian may not doubt the resurrection

Since, then, we have discussed the fact that there is a resurrection, we believe it in this way, we must believe it in this way, and we speak in this way because we have believed in this way—if we are Christians. We look upon the power of the Lord’s arm, which lays low the pride of the nations everywhere and builds up this faith throughout the whole world, as was promised long before it came to pass. Looking upon these things, we are built up so as to believe what we do not yet see, so that we may receive the vision itself as the reward of faith.

Since it is therefore evident that our faith concerns the future resurrection of the dead—and so evident that anyone who has doubted this may most shamelessly call himself a Christian—the question arises what sort of bodies the saints will have and what their future life will be. For many have thought that there will indeed be a resurrection, but only of souls.

### CHAPTER VII

#### 7. The question: what sort of bodies will there be? The rule of faith: the creed. An apt comparison

Since bodies too will rise, there is no need to argue at length after the previous sermon. But a question of this sort is raised: If there will be bodies, what sort will they be? Will they be such as they are now, or of another kind? If of another kind, what kind will that be? If they are such as they are now, will they therefore be suited to the same activities?

For the Lord prescribes that they will not be for the same activities, because the Apostle teaches that they will not be for such things. They will not be for the same life, nor for the same mortal, corruptible, perishable, and passing deeds; not for carnal pleasures, nor for carnal consolations. If, then, they are not for the same things, they will not be such bodies. But if they will not be such, how will the flesh rise?

We have the resurrection of the flesh in the rule of faith, and confessing it, we are baptized. Whatever we confess there, we confess from the truth and in the truth, in which we live and move and have our being. Through temporal events and through certain deeds that pass away and disappear, we are instructed for eternal life.

Everything that happened so that we might hear something salutary, so that miracles might occur, so that our Lord might be born, hunger and thirst, be seized, be subjected to insults, be beaten, be crucified, die, be buried, rise again, and ascend into heaven—all these things have passed away. When they are preached, certain temporal and transitory actions of our faith are preached.

Does the fact that these things themselves pass away mean that what is built through them likewise passes away? Let your Holiness attend, so that you may see this by means of a comparison. An architect builds a lasting house through temporary scaffolding. In this great and spacious building that we see, when it was being constructed there was scaffolding that is no longer here, because what was being built through it is now complete and standing.

So, brothers, something was being built in the Christian faith, and certain temporary instruments have been completed. Our Lord Jesus Christ’s resurrection is an event that has passed; he is not still rising. His ascension into heaven is an event that has passed; he is not still ascending. But the fact that he is in that life where he no longer dies and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9)—the fact that even the human nature in him lives eternally, that nature which he deigned to assume, in which he deigned to be born, die, and be buried—that is what has been built; that remains forever.

The instruments through which it was built have passed away. Christ is not continually conceived in a virgin’s womb, nor continually born from the virgin Mary; he is not continually seized, judged, scourged, crucified, or buried. All these things are counted as instruments, so that through them that which remains forever might be built. This resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has been established in heaven.

### CHAPTER VIII

#### 8. The building of the heavenly Jerusalem has its foundation above. Christ is both our foundation and our head

Let Your Charity attend to this marvelous building. Earthly buildings press down upon the earth by their own weight; the whole thrust of their weight in this structure tends downward toward the earth, and unless it is held together, it strives toward the lower regions, where its weight draws it.

Because it is built on earth, a foundation is laid on earth, so that the builder may safely construct upon the foundation. He therefore places the strongest masses at the bottom, so that they may properly bear what is imposed upon them above; and the size of the foundation is prepared according to the size of the building. Nevertheless, as I have said, it is on earth, because what is built above is itself placed on earth.

That Jerusalem of ours, in which we are strangers, is being built in heaven. Therefore Christ, our foundation, went before us into heaven. For there he is our foundation and the head of the Church. He is called both foundation and head, and truly he is both. For the head of a building is its foundation; the head is not where it ends, but where it begins its upward course.

The summits of earthly buildings rise up, but they establish their head upon the solidity of the earth. So also the head of the Church went before us into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Just as human beings, when establishing a foundation, bring something to place and secure at the bottom, for the safety of the mass that will be added in the future construction, so through everything that happened in Christ—being born, growing, being seized, suffering insult, being scourged, crucified, killed, dying, and being buried—a mass was, as it were, drawn toward the heavenly foundation.

#### 9. We must act so as to be built in Christ. Christ is the foundation if he holds the first place in the heart. How greatly the fire of Gehenna is to be feared

Since our foundation has therefore been placed on high, let us be built upon it. Hear the Apostle: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

### CHAPTER IX

But what follows? “Let each one see what he builds upon the foundation: gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw.”

Christ is indeed in heaven, but also in the hearts of believers. If Christ holds the first place, the foundation has been rightly laid. Therefore, whoever builds should build securely if, in accordance with the dignity of the foundation, he builds with gold, silver, and precious stones. But if he does not build in accordance with the dignity of the foundation, but with wood, hay, and straw, let him at least hold on to the foundation; and because of what he has built—dry and fragile materials—let him prepare himself for the fire.

But if the foundation is present—that is, if Christ has obtained the first place in the heart—while worldly things are loved in such a way that they are not preferred to Christ, but the Lord Christ is preferred to them, so that in the building of the heart he holds the foundation, that is, the first place, “he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:10–15).

This is not now the time to urge you to build gold, silver, and precious stones rather than wood, hay, and straw upon so great and strong a foundation. Nevertheless, take this brief statement as though it had been spoken at length and with many words.

For we know, brothers, that if any one of you were sent to prison because of the things he now loves, through the threats of some judge, and were made to suffer only smoke, he would prefer to lose all those things rather than endure that place. Yet somehow, when the fire that is to come on the day of judgment is mentioned, everyone makes light of it. They fear the flames of a furnace but regard the flame of Gehenna as nothing.

What kind of hardness is this? What such perversity of heart? If people feared, even in this way, what the Apostle says—“through fire”—then just as everyone fears being burned alive, an event that happens to him in a single moment, until his senses leave his limbs and make all those flames ineffectual, so they would fear it and would not do anything that is rightly forbidden, lest they come to that torment even for a single moment.

### CHAPTER X

#### 10. We must hope for a resurrection like the one that preceded us in Christ. The angels truly ate with Abraham

But, as I said, brothers, there is no time now to discuss this matter at length. I say this: in the resurrection of the dead we ought to hope for what has been manifested in our head, what has been manifested in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Whoever hopes for something else is no longer building upon the foundation—not gold, silver, and precious stones, but not even straw [Col. 1617]. For he places everything outside, because he does not place it in Christ.

Our Lord therefore rose in the body in which he had been buried. Resurrection is promised to Christians. Let us hope for a resurrection like the one that preceded the faith of us all in our Lord. He went before us for this reason: so that our faith might be built upon him.

What, then? How will we not be such as we are now? For the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ rose, but he ascended into heaven. On earth he retained human functions, so as to persuade us that what had risen was what had been buried.

But is there also such food in heaven? We read that angels too carried out human functions on earth. They came to Abraham and ate; an angel was also with Tobiah and ate. What are we to say? Was that eating a phantom, and was it not real? Is it not clear that Abraham killed a calf, made loaves, and set them on the table; he served the angels, and they ate (Gen. 18:1–9)? All these things are most clearly recorded and most clearly expressed.

### CHAPTER XI

#### 11. A human being eats from necessity; an angel eats by power

What, then, does the angel say in the Book of Tobit? “You saw me eat, but you were seeing according to your own sight” (Tob. 12:19). Was this because he did not eat, but merely appeared to eat? No, he truly ate.

What, then, does “you were seeing according to your own sight” mean? Let Your Holiness attend to what I am saying—attend more to prayer than to me—so that you may understand what we are saying, and so that we may speak in the way you ought to hear and understand what you hear.

As long as our body is corruptible and destined to die, it suffers the need for nourishment; hence hunger arises. Therefore we hunger and thirst. If we delay our hunger and thirst longer than the body is able to endure, it is brought to wasting emaciation and to a certain diseased thinness, as its strength departs without being replenished. If this continues further, death also follows.

For something is always departing from our body, as though by a kind of river of departure; but we do not notice our strength departing, because through nourishment we take in what replaces it. What arrives abundantly departs little by little. Therefore we restore ourselves in a short time, but over a longer time the strength that we received when we were restored leaves us.

It is like oil in a lamp: it is poured in over a short time but is gradually consumed over a longer period. When it has nearly been consumed, the dimness of that little lamp, like the lamp’s hunger, warns us; and we immediately come to its aid so that its appearance may be restored and the light remain in the lamp, replenished with its food when we add oil.

So our strength, which we receive by eating, continually departs from us, but gradually. Indeed, this very process is now taking place in us, and in all our actions, even in all our rest, what has been received does not cease to depart. When it has been entirely consumed, a human being dies just as a lamp is extinguished.

To prevent him from dying—that is, to prevent him from being extinguished—not because the soul dies, but so that this bodily life of ours may not be extinguished and a kind of waking state may continue in this body, we hurry and replace what has departed, and we are said to be restored. If someone says “restored,” what is he restoring if nothing is lacking?

Through this need and this corruption, therefore, we shall all die, because this body is of such a nature that death is reserved for it as its due. This mortality is signified by the skins with which Adam and Eve were clothed and sent out of paradise (Gen. 3:21–24). For skins indicate death, since they are customarily stripped from dead animals.

Although we carry this failing weakness—and even if food never fails but continually repairs our strength—it nevertheless does not prevent death from coming. For the entire condition of the body, through succeeding ages, even if one lives here longer, will eventually come to the limit of old age and will find nothing beyond which it can extend except death.

The lamp itself, even if you continually add oil to it, cannot burn forever; for although it may not be extinguished for other reasons, the wick itself fails and is consumed by a kind of old age.

As long, then, as we carry such bodies, we need because of their deficiency; because of need, we hunger; because of hunger, we eat. But an angel does not eat from need. For it is one thing to do something by power and another to do it from necessity.

A human being eats so as not to die; an angel eats so as to conform to mortals. If an angel does not fear death, he is not restored because of deficiency; if he is not restored because of deficiency, he does not eat from need. Those who saw the angel eating thought that he was hungry. This is what he means by saying, “You were seeing according to your own sight.”

For he did not say, “You saw me eating, but I did not eat.” Rather, he says: “You saw me eating, but you were seeing according to your own sight.” That is: I ate in order to conform to you, not because I suffered any hunger or need, which compels you to eat. Thus, when you see someone eating, you suppose that it happens from need; you measure what you see by your own experience. This is what “you were seeing according to your own sight” means.

### CHAPTER XII

#### 12. After the resurrection there will be the power to eat, as in Christ, but not the necessity

What, then, my brothers? We know, as the Apostle says, that “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again, and death will no longer rule over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6:9–10).

If, then, he no longer dies and death will no longer rule over him, let us hope that we too shall rise in such a way that we shall always remain in the condition into which we shall be changed by rising.

There will be the power to eat and drink, but there will be no necessity. At that time the Lord had reason to do this, because there were still people in the flesh to whom he wished to conform, and to whom he also wished to show his scars.

For the one who made the eyes of a blind man—eyes he had not received in his mother’s womb—was not unable to rise without scars. If he had wished, before his death, to change the mortal neediness of his own flesh in such a way that it would have no need of anything, he certainly could have done so. It was in his power, because he was God in the flesh, the almighty Son just as the almighty Father.

Indeed, before his death he changed his own flesh into whatever he wished. When he was on the mountain with his disciples, “his face shone like the sun” (Matt. 17:2). He did this by his power, wishing to show that he could also change his own flesh so as to remove every need from it, and thus not die if he did not wish to.

“I have power,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me” (John 10:18). Great is this power, by which he could also not die; but greater is the mercy by which he wished to die.

In his mercy he did what he could have refrained from doing by his power, so that he might establish for us the foundation of the resurrection: that what he carried for our sake as mortal, and what would die because we are destined to die, might rise to immortality, so that we might hope for immortality.

Therefore, before his death it is written not only that he ate and drank, but also that he hungered and thirsted (Matt. 4:2; John 19:28). After the resurrection, however, it is written only that he ate and drank, not that he hungered and thirsted. For in a body that would no longer die there was no longer that need of corruption requiring nourishment; there was instead the power to eat.

This happened in order to conform to them, not to relieve the poverty of the flesh, but to persuade them of the reality of the body.

### CHAPTER XIII

#### 13. The question: how will flesh and blood not possess the kingdom of God?

In opposition to such overwhelming evidence, some raise a question against us from the Apostle. Against this teaching, consider what they object: “The flesh will not rise. For if it rises, it will possess the kingdom of God. But the Apostle plainly says, ‘Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.’”

You heard this when the Apostle was read. We say that the flesh will rise, and the Apostle cries out, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” Are we therefore preaching against the Apostle, or did he himself preach against the Gospel?

The Gospel testifies with a divine voice: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). If he became flesh, he became true flesh. For if it was not true flesh, it was not flesh. Just as Mary’s flesh was true flesh, so Christ’s flesh was true flesh, since it was taken from her.

This true flesh was seized, scourged, struck on the face, and hung up. This true flesh died; this true flesh was buried. This true flesh also rose from the dead. The scars bear witness. The eyes of the disciples see, and amazement still wavers; the hand touches, so that the mind may not doubt.

In opposition to such overwhelming evidence, which our Lord Jesus Christ was thus able to impress upon disciples who would preach it throughout the world, the Apostle appears to fight against this evidence when he says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”?

#### 14. The question is resolved. The Apostle’s first interpretation

We could resolve this question in this way and resist the empty slanders of our opponents. Nevertheless, it will also be resolved in the manner that can be answered quickly, and we shall consider more carefully from what source the Apostle’s statement was made.

I shall therefore explain how we can answer most easily. What does the Gospel say? That Christ rose in the body in which he had been buried: he was seen, he was touched, and he said to the disciples, who thought that he was a spirit: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

What does the Apostle say in opposition? “Flesh and blood,” he says, “will not possess the kingdom of God” [Col. 1620].

I embrace both statements, and I do not say that they conflict, lest I myself fight against the goad. How, then, do I embrace both? Quickly, as I said, I could answer in this way: The Apostle says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God as an inheritance.” He is right. It is not the function of flesh to possess, but to be possessed.

For your body does not possess anything; your soul possesses through the body, and it also possesses the body itself. If, then, the flesh rises in such a way that it is held rather than holding, is possessed rather than possessing, what wonder is it if flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, since they will certainly be possessed?

For the flesh possesses those who are not the kingdom of God but the kingdom of the devil, and therefore they are subject to the pleasures of the flesh. Hence that paralytic was carried on a pallet; but after healing him, the Lord said: “Take up your pallet and go to your house” (Mark 2:11).

Thus, once his paralysis was healed, he holds his flesh and leads it wherever he wishes. He is not himself dragged by his flesh wherever he does not wish to go; rather, he carries his body instead of being carried by his body.

It is clear that in that resurrection the flesh will not have the pull of enticements, so as to lead the soul through certain ticklings and blandishments where the soul does not wish to go, and where it is often overcome, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

The paralytic is still being carried on a pallet; he does not yet carry it. Therefore let him cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” Let the answer be given: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

When, therefore, we have risen, the flesh will not carry us; we shall carry it. If we carry it, we shall possess it. If we possess it, we shall not be possessed by it, because, having been freed from the devil, we are the kingdom of God. And so flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.

Therefore let those slanderers be silent—those who truly are flesh and blood and can think nothing except in a carnal way. Since they persist in the same carnal understanding, and are rightly called flesh and blood, it could rightly be said even of them: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.”

### CHAPTER XIV

This question can also be resolved in this way: people who are called flesh and blood—for the Apostle also speaks of such people when he says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph. 6:12)—will not be able to possess the kingdom of God if they do not turn toward the spiritual life and put to death by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh.

#### 15. The Apostle’s more accurate meaning

Nevertheless, someone may say: What does the Apostle mean? For the more accurate meaning is disclosed by the context of the reading. Let us therefore listen to him himself and see, from the entire surrounding sequence of Scripture, what he wished to be understood in that passage.

For he says:

> “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven. As was the earthly, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven. Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God as an inheritance, nor can corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:47–50).

Let us therefore examine each statement. “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven. As was the earthly, so are those who are earthly”—that is, all who will die. “And as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly”—that is, all who will rise.

The heavenly man has already risen and ascended into heaven. By faith we are now incorporated into him, so that he may be our head; and his members, each in their proper order, may follow their head. What was shown beforehand in the head will in its proper time be shown in the members. For now, let us carry this by faith, so that in its proper time we may come to the reality and the visible form itself.

For he says elsewhere: “If, then, you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth” (Col. 3:1–2).

Therefore, just as, although we have not yet risen in ourselves as Christ rose in the body, we are nevertheless said to have risen with Christ through faith, so he commands us for the present to carry by faith the image of the heavenly man—that is, of the one who is already in heaven.

#### 16. How Christ is the heavenly man from heaven

If someone asks why he did not say that the second man was in heaven, but rather “from heaven,” since the Lord himself received a body from the earth—because Mary certainly was descended from Adam and Eve—let him understand that the earthly man is called earthly according to earthly desire.

That desire is earthly through which human beings are born by the union of male and female, also drawing original sin from their parents. But the Lord’s body was created from a virgin’s womb without any such desire. Although Christ assumed flesh from the earth, which the Holy Spirit is understood to signify when he says, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84:12), Christ is nevertheless not called an earthly but a heavenly man, and is said to be from heaven.

For if by grace he granted this to his faithful, so that the Apostle could rightly say, “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), how much more must he himself be called the heavenly man and the man from heaven, in whom there was never any sin?

Because of sin it was said to the human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). That heavenly man, therefore, is most rightly called heavenly and from heaven, whose way of life never departed from heaven, although the Son of God, having also become the son of man, assumed a body from the earth—that is, the form of a servant.

For no one ascended except the one who descended. Even if the others whom he grants to ascend do ascend—or rather, are lifted up to heaven by his grace—he nevertheless ascended in them, because they become his body. In this respect, one person ascended, since the Apostle explains the great mystery in Christ and the Church, concerning which it is written: “And the two shall become one flesh” (Eph. 5:31).

Hence it is also said: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. 19:6). Consequently, no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3:13).

For this reason he added, “who is in heaven,” lest anyone suppose that his way of life had departed from heaven when he appeared to human beings on earth through an earthly body.

Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven—for now through faith, through which we have also risen with him—so that we may have our hearts above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God [Col. 1622]. For this reason let us seek and set our minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 17. In the resurrection we must receive what preceded us in Christ. “Flesh and blood” means corruption

But because he was speaking about the resurrection of the body—for he had posed the question in this way: “But someone will say, How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come?” (1 Cor. 15:35)—he had therefore said: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven. As was the earthly, so are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are those who are heavenly.”

He said this so that we might hope that what occurred beforehand in Christ’s body will take place in our body, and although we have not yet received it in reality, we might meanwhile hold it by faith.

For this reason he had added: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.” Lest we think that we would rise to conditions like those in which we acted corruptibly according to the first man, he immediately added:

> “Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God as an inheritance.”

And wishing to show what he meant by “flesh and blood”—that the term does not signify the form of the body itself, but corruption, which will not then exist—he continued:

> “Nor can corruption possess incorruption as an inheritance.”

A body without corruption is not properly called flesh and blood, but body. For if it is flesh, it is corruptible and mortal; but if it no longer dies, it is no longer corruptible. Therefore, while its form remains without corruption, it is no longer called flesh but body. And if it is called flesh, it is no longer called so properly, but because of a certain likeness of form.

Perhaps, because of that same likeness, we could even call the bodies of angels flesh, since they appeared to human beings like human beings, although they were bodies, not flesh, because they did not possess the need arising from corruption.

Since, then, by way of likeness we can call even a body that no longer undergoes corruption “flesh,” the attentive Apostle wished to explain what he meant by “flesh and blood”: he said this according to corruption, not according to form. He immediately added: “Nor can corruption possess incorruption as an inheritance”—as though he were saying: “What I said, ‘Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,’ I said because corruption will not possess incorruption.”

## 18. How our body will be in heaven if corruption will not be there. The works of the flesh will not be the same after the resurrection. The error of the Jews and Sadducees concerning the resurrection. Resurrection to the life of angels.

And lest anyone should say, “If incorruption cannot be possessed by corruption, how will our body be there?” listen to what follows. It is as though the Apostle were being asked: “What, then, do you mean? Did we believe in the resurrection of the flesh for nothing? If flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, did we believe in vain that our Lord rose from the dead in the body in which he was born and crucified, and in that same body ascended into heaven before the eyes of his disciples—the heaven from which he cried out to you, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’” (Acts 9:4).

This question occurred to the holy and blessed apostle Paul, who in loving concern was giving birth to his children in Christ, those begotten through the Gospel (1 Cor. 4:15), whom he was still bringing to birth until Christ was formed in them (Gal. 4:19)—that is, until through faith they bore the image of the one who is from heaven.

For he did not want them to remain in that ruin, imagining that in the kingdom of God, in that eternal life, they would perform the same things they performed in this life: indulging in the pleasures of eating and drinking, marrying, taking wives, and begetting children carnally [Note: [Col. 1623] It might more correctly be read: “taking wives, begetting offspring, or children, carnally”; or, with Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 190: “taking wives and begetting children from them carnally.” M.]. These works belong to the corruption of the flesh, not to the very form of the flesh.

Since, then, we will not rise for such things, the Lord prescribed this, as I said earlier, in the Gospel reading that has just been recited. The Jews did indeed believe in the resurrection of the flesh, but they thought that it would be such that life in the resurrection would be like the life they led in this world. Thinking carnally in this way, they could not answer the Sadducees when they raised the question concerning the resurrection: Whose wife will the woman be, since seven brothers, succeeding one another, had possessed her, each wishing to raise up offspring for his deceased brother from that brother’s wife?

The Sadducees were a sect of the Jews that did not believe in the resurrection. Thus, when the Sadducees posed this question, the Jews, wavering and uncertain, could not answer them, because they supposed that the kingdom of God could be possessed by flesh and blood—that is, that corruption could possess incorruption.

Truth came. The deceived Sadducees, who were themselves deceivers, questioned the Lord, and that question was put before him. The Lord, who knew what he was saying and wished us to believe what we did not know, answered with the authority of his majesty what we are to believe. The Apostle, however, explained as much as was granted to him, so that we might understand as much as we are able.

What, then, did the Lord say to the Sadducees? “You are mistaken,” he said, “because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they do not begin to die, but will be equal to the angels of God.”

Great is the power of God. Why do they not marry or take wives? Because they will not begin to die. There, the successor exists wherever the predecessor has died. Therefore there will be no such corruption there.

That Lord, moreover, passed through the stages of life from infancy to youth because he still bore the substance of mortal flesh. But after he rose again at the age at which he had been buried, do we suppose that he grows old in heaven? “They will be equal,” he says, “to the angels of God.”

He removed the suspicion of the Jews and refuted the slanders of the Sadducees. The Jews did believe that the dead would rise, but they thought carnally about the works for which they would rise. “They will be equal,” he says, “to the angels of God.”

You have heard about the power of God; hear also from the Scriptures. “Concerning the resurrection,” he says, “have you not read how the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:23–32; Luke 20:27–38).

## CHAPTER XVI

### 19. Resurrection to life without corruption. The transformation of the flesh for the better belongs to the good.

That we shall rise, then, has been stated; and that we shall rise to the life of angels, we have heard from the Lord. But in what form we shall rise, he himself showed in his resurrection.

Since that form will not possess corruption, the Apostle says: “Now this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; nor can corruption inherit incorruption.” By the terms “flesh and blood,” he wished it to be understood that he meant the corruption of a mortal and living body.

Then he himself resolves the question which anxious listeners might ask him, since he was more concerned about his children’s understanding than children are about their parents’ words. He adds and says:

“Behold, I tell you a mystery.” Let your thought be still, whoever you are, O human being. You had begun to think, when you heard “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” that human flesh would not rise. But lend your ear to the words that follow, and correct the presumption of your thought.

“Behold,” he says, “I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed.”

What does this mean? Change is either for the worse or for the better. If, then, change has been mentioned, but we do not yet see what kind it will be—whether into something better or into something worse—let him continue and explain it himself. Why should we speculate?

Perhaps apostolic authority prevents you from slipping into error through human conjecture, and clearly explains what kind of change he wishes to be understood. What, then? When he had said, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed,” I see that all will rise, both the good and the wicked. But let us see who will be changed, and from this understand whether the change will be for the better or for the worse. If it belongs to the wicked, it will be for the worse; but if it belongs to the good, it will be for the better.

“In an indivisible moment,” he says, “in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

The change will therefore be for the better, since he says, “And we shall be changed.” But it has not yet been expressed as fully as necessary—namely, to what extent our body will be changed for the better. What this “better” is has not yet been said. For even when someone is changed from infancy into adolescence, it can be said that he is changed for the better, although, while less weak, he is still weak and mortal.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 20. The speed of the resurrection. What an indivisible moment is. An indivisible moment in bodies. An indivisible moment in time. The twinkling of an eye.

Let us therefore reconsider each point more carefully.

“In an indivisible moment,” he says. It seems difficult to human beings for the dead to rise, but it is remarkable how the Apostle removed every two-sided difficulty from the hearts of believers.

You say, “The dead do not rise.” I say not merely that a dead person rises, but that he rises with such speed as is greater than the speed with which you were conceived and born. How much time is required for a human being to be formed in the womb, completed, born, and strengthened through the succession of the ages? Will he perhaps rise in this way? No, he says, but “in an indivisible moment.”

Many do not know what an *atomus* is. The word *atomus* is derived from τομή (*tomē*), meaning “division” or “cutting”; ἄτομος (*atomos*) in Greek means “that which cannot be cut.”

The term *atomus* is used of a body and of time. It is used of a body if something can be found that is said to be incapable of division: some little body so minute that there is no longer any place in it where it can be cut. An *atomus* in time, however, is a brief moment that no longer has any point at which it can be divided.

For example, so that even slower minds may grasp what I am saying: there is a stone. Divide it into parts, and divide those parts into little stones; divide the little stones into grains, such as grains of sand; then divide those grains of sand again into the tiniest dust, until, if possible, you reach some minute particle of such a kind that it cannot be divided any further. This is an *atomus* in bodies.

In time, the matter is understood as follows. A year, for example, is divided into months; months are divided into days; days can still be divided into hours; hours can still be divided into certain longer portions of hours that admit division, until you come to such a point of time, such a drop of a moment, that it cannot be extended by any little interval and therefore cannot be divided any further. This is an *atomus* of time.

You were saying, then, that the dead do not rise. Not only do they rise, but they rise with such speed that the resurrection of all the dead will take place in an indivisible moment of time.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Explaining to you the speed of the indivisible moment, after he had said “in an indivisible moment,” he immediately added how much action and movement can occur in an indivisible moment of time: “In the twinkling of an eye,” he says.

He knew that he had spoken obscurely in saying “in an indivisible moment,” and wished to say it more plainly, so that it might be understood more easily.

What is the twinkling of an eye? It is not the movement by which we close or open the eye with our eyelids. Rather, by “the twinkling of the eye” he means the eye’s emission of rays for seeing something [Note: [Col. 1625] See above, Sermon 277, chapter 10.].

For as soon as you direct your gaze, the emitted ray reaches the heavens, where we contemplate the sun, the moon, the stars, and the constellations, separated from the earth by an immense interval.

By “the last trumpet,” he means the final sign. “For the trumpet will sound,” he says, “and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

By “we” he certainly means the faithful, who rise first to eternal life. Therefore that change, since it belongs to the godly and holy, will be for the better, not for the worse.

### 21. What the transformation of the saints will be in the resurrection. “Flesh and blood” are properly names of corruption and mortality.

But what is this change? What is meant by “we shall be changed”? Is the form that exists now lost, or is only corruption lost, on account of what was said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God; nor can corruption possess incorruption”?

Lest this move the listener to despair of the resurrection of the flesh, he added: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.”

And lest we think that the change would be for the worse, he says, “We shall also be changed.” It remains, then, for him to say what kind of change it will be.

“For this corruptible,” he says, “must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.”

If this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality, the flesh will no longer be corruptible. If, then, the flesh will no longer be corruptible, the name of corruption will cease in flesh and blood; the proper name of flesh and blood will also cease, because these are names associated with mortality.

And if this is so, the flesh will rise; yet because it is changed and becomes incorruptible, flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.
