If someone wishes to understand that change as applying to those whom that day will still find alive—so that those who have already died rise, while those who are still alive are changed, and the Apostle is thought to have taken upon himself their person when he says, “We shall be changed”—the same reasoning nevertheless follows, because that incorruption will certainly pertain to all, when “this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality.”

Then will come to pass the saying that is written: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”

A body that is no longer mortal, however, is not properly called “flesh and blood,” which are earthly bodies; rather, it is called a body that can now be described as heavenly.

Thus the same Apostle, when speaking about the differences among flesh, says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh. There is one flesh of human beings, another of animals, another of fish, another of birds, and another of serpents. And there are,” he says, “heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Cor. 15:39, 55).

He would by no means have called heavenly bodies “flesh,” although flesh can be called bodies—earthly bodies, that is. For every flesh is a body, but not every body is flesh: not only because a heavenly body is not called flesh, but also because some earthly things, such as wood and stones and anything of that kind, are not called flesh.

Thus, too, flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, because the flesh, when it rises, will be changed into such a body that mortal corruption will no longer be in it—and therefore neither will the name “flesh and blood.”

## CHAPTER XIX

### 22. The error of certain people concerning the truth of the resurrection.

But pay attention, brothers—we beg you. This is not a matter to be treated lightly; our faith is at stake. We must be on guard not so much against pagans as against certain perverse people who wish to be called and regarded as Christians.

Even in the time of the Apostles there were people who said that the resurrection had already taken place and subverted the faith of some. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They have erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they have subverted the faith of some” (2 Tim. 2:18).

It is not without significance that he did not say, “They have strayed from the truth,” but “they have erred concerning the truth”; nevertheless, they did not hold to the truth.

Death, then, is removed and will in a certain sense no longer exist, just as the Apostle says: “What is mortal will be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4). The same is said concerning the Lord, that “he swallowed up death” (1 Pet. 3:22).

Death does not withdraw as though it possessed some substance of its own. Rather, in the very body where it existed, it will cease to exist, so that you may see the form and retain the form, search for corruption and mortality, and find them no longer.

Has corruption therefore departed somewhere? No. It has been destroyed there; it has been swallowed up there.

For this reason, after saying, “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” he says: “Then will come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’”

He did not say, “Death has departed in victory,” but “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

How, then, did those people err concerning the truth? Because they affirmed one true resurrection but denied another.

## CHAPTER XX

### 23. The twofold resurrection, in spirit and in body. What the bodies of the wicked will be like when they rise.

There is a resurrection according to faith, in which everyone who believes rises in spirit. Indeed, the person who will rise well in body is the one who first rose in spirit.

Those who have not previously risen in spirit through faith will not rise to that transformation of the body in which all corruption will be taken up and swallowed. They will rise instead to that condition of punishment.

The bodies of the wicked will also be whole; nothing in them will appear diminished. But the wholeness of the body will be for punishment, and there will be, so to speak, a certain firmness of body—a corruptible firmness. For where pain can exist, it cannot be said that corruption does not exist, although that weakness does not fail amid the pains, lest the pain itself should die.

The corruption itself is not inappropriately believed to be signified prophetically by the name “worm,” and the pain itself by the name “fire.” But because their firmness will be so great that it will neither yield to pain in death nor be changed into incorruption, where there is no pain, it is therefore written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24; Mark 9:43, 45).

The transformation that will not contain corruption will belong to the saints. It will belong, then, to those who now possess the resurrection of the spirit through faith. Concerning this resurrection the Apostle says: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Just as we die according to the spirit and rise according to the spirit, so afterward we die according to the flesh and rise according to the flesh.

According to the spirit, death consists in no longer believing the vain things one used to believe and no longer doing the evil things one used to do. According to the spirit, resurrection consists in believing the saving things one did not believe and doing the good things one did not do.

A person who regarded earthly idols and images as gods came to know the one God and believed in him: he died in idolatry and rose in Christian faith. He was a drunkard; now he is sober. He died to drunkenness and rose in sobriety.

Thus, whenever one withdraws from all evil works, a kind of death occurs in the soul, and it rises in its good works.

“Put to death,” the Apostle says, “your members that are upon the earth: impurity, disturbance, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry” (Col. 3:1–5).

When these members have been put to death, we rise in the good things opposed to them: in holiness, tranquility, love, and acts of almsgiving.

Just as death according to the spirit precedes the resurrection according to the spirit, so death according to the flesh will precede the resurrection that will take place according to the flesh.

## CHAPTER XXI

### 24. Testimonies from the Apostle concerning the twofold resurrection.

Let us therefore recognize both—the spiritual and the bodily resurrection.

The spiritual resurrection is indicated by the saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Eph. 5:14); and by this: “Those who sat in the shadow of death, light has arisen for them” (Isa. 9:2); and by the passage I mentioned shortly before: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.”

The bodily resurrection is indicated by what the Apostle now says, after proposing this question to himself: “But someone will say, ‘How do the dead rise? And with what kind of body will they come?’”

He was speaking, then, about the resurrection of the body, in which the Lord preceded his Church. Concerning this he says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” This is in relation to what he had said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Elsewhere we have the Apostle Paul’s clearest testimony concerning the resurrection according to the spirit and the resurrection according to the flesh.

A mortal body that is or has been animated is called flesh. Thus the Apostle speaks: “But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

Here the resurrection of the spirit through righteousness is understood to have already taken place. See whether the resurrection of the body is also to be hoped for.

He did not wish to call the mortal body “mortal,” but “dead”; nevertheless, he makes clear in what follows that he meant the mortal body. He continues and says:

“If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

Therefore those people erred concerning the truth: they denied one resurrection. If they had denied it in every respect, they would have strayed from the truth, not erred concerning the truth.

But because they erred concerning the truth, they confessed one resurrection—the one that occurs according to the spirit—and denied the other, which is hoped for through the resurrection of the flesh, saying that the resurrection had already taken place. If they had not said this in such a way as to prevent people from believing and hoping for the resurrection that will take place in the body, it would not have been said of them: “They subvert the faith of some.”

## CHAPTER XXII

### 25. Both resurrections in the Gospel. The resurrection according to the spirit, which now takes place through faith.

But now hear the Lord’s most unmistakable testimony in the Gospel according to John. In one passage he declares both resurrections—the one that now takes place according to the spirit and the one that will later take place according to the flesh—in such a way that no one who in any manner calls himself a Christian and submits to the authority of the Gospel can doubt.

Thus no opening remains for slanderers who wish to overthrow Christians by means of Christian faith, inserting their poisons in order to destroy the souls of the weak.

But hear it from the text itself. For this reason I perform not only the office of a disputant but also that of a reader, so that this sermon of ours may be supported by the authority of the holy Scriptures and not built upon sand by human conjectures, should something not immediately occur to memory.

Hear, then, the Gospel according to John. The Lord speaks:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

“For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:24–29).

I think that many understand the Lord in this passage to have clearly and distinctly declared both resurrections: the resurrection according to the spirit through faith and the resurrection according to the flesh through that well-known trumpet.

Nevertheless, let us carefully consider these same words, so that they may be clear to everyone who hears them.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.”

This is the resurrection according to the spirit, which now takes place through faith.

But lest it appear to have been presented as though it were still far in the future—although he did not say, “He will pass from death into life,” but “He has passed from death into life”—lest he seem to have used the past tense figuratively, as in “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21:17), where something still future was being foretold, he continues and explains the same point more plainly:

“Amen, amen, I say to you,” he says, “the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.”

What he earlier said—“He has passed from death into life”—he now says as “they will live.”

But lest the phrase “the hour is coming” be understood as referring to the end of the world, when the resurrection of bodies will also occur, he added, “and now is.” He did not merely say, “The hour is coming,” but “The hour is coming, and now is.”

Those who hear this voice will live—that is, with the life he signified above when he said, “He has passed from death into life.”

Here, then, he signified those who do not belong to the punishment of judgment, because through their faith they anticipate judgment and pass from death into life.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 26. The resurrection according to the flesh, which is still to come.

It remains, then, for him to show the judgment that will come between the good and the wicked, since here he mentioned only the good as belonging to the present resurrection, which is according to the spirit.

He continues and says: “And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

He indicated in what respect he received authority to judge: “Because,” he says, “he is the Son of Man.” For insofar as he is the Son of God, he possesses eternal authority with the Father.

He next explains how the future judgment will take place:

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”

Above, when he said, “The hour is coming,” he added, “and now is,” so that the hour foretold would not be thought to be the one that will come at the end of the world, when the resurrection of bodies will occur.

Here, because he wished that hour to be understood, after saying, “The hour is coming,” he did not add, “and now is.”

Likewise, above he spoke of the dead hearing the voice of the Son of God, but he made no mention of tombs. This allows us to distinguish the dead through error of mind, who now rise through faith, from those dead whose corpses lie in tombs and will rise at the end of the world.

Here, therefore, so that the resurrection of bodies might be hoped for at the end, he says: “All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth.”

Likewise, above he says, “They will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.”

Why was it necessary to add “those who hear,” when it could have been said simply, “They will hear the voice of the Son of God, and they will live”? It is because he was speaking of those who are dead through error of mind, many of whom hear but do not hear—that is, they do not obey and do not believe.

But those who hear in the way he wished them to hear, when he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8), will live.

Many will hear, then, but “those who hear will live”—that is, those who believe. For those who hear in such a way that they do not believe will not live.

Thus it is clear what death and what life he meant in that passage: death, namely, which belongs only to the wicked by the very fact that they are wicked; and life, which belongs only to the good by the very fact that they become good.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Here, however, where he declares that they will rise according to their bodies, he does not say, “They will hear his voice, and those who hear will come forth.” Everyone will hear the last trumpet, and all will come forth, because we shall all rise.

But because we shall not all be changed, he continues and says: “Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”

Above, where people are revived according to the spirit through faith, all are revived for the same destiny, so that their life is not divided into blessedness and misery, but all belong to the good portion.

Therefore, when he had said, “Those who hear will live,” he did not add, “Those who have done good will enter eternal life, but those who have done evil will enter eternal punishment.” By saying “they will live,” he wished the expression to be understood only in a good sense, just as above he says, “He has passed from death into life,” without specifying into what kind of life, because to revive from death through faith cannot be an evil life.

Here, however, he did not first say, “They will hear his voice and live”—for throughout this entire passage he wished “they will live” to be understood in a good sense—but he said, “They will hear and come forth.” By this word he signified the bodily movement of bodies from the places of their burial.

But because coming forth from the tombs will not be good for everyone, he says: “Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life.” Here too he wished “life” to be understood only in a good sense. But “those who have done evil,” he says, will come forth “to the resurrection of judgment,” using “judgment” to mean punishment.

## CHAPTER XXV

### 27. What the body and life of the saints will be like after the resurrection.

Now, then, brothers, let no one ask with perverse subtlety what kind of form the bodies of the dead will have in the resurrection, what their stature will be, or what kind of movement and gait they will possess.

It is enough for you that your flesh will rise in the form in which the Lord appeared—in the form, certainly, of a human being.

But do not fear corruption on account of the form. If you do not fear corruption, you will not fear the saying, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” Nor will you fall into the snare of the Sadducees, which you could not avoid precisely because you imagine that human beings rise for the purpose of taking wives, begetting children, and performing the works of mortal life.

If you ask what that life will be like, who among human beings can explain it? It will be the life of angels. Whoever can show you the life of angels will show you their life, because they will be equal to the angels.

But if the life of angels is hidden, let no one ask further, lest through error he fail to reach what he seeks and instead reach what he has fashioned for himself.

He asks too hastily and seeks too quickly. Walk on the way; you will come to your homeland if you do not abandon the way.

Hold fast, then, to Christ, brothers; hold fast to faith; hold fast to the way. It will itself lead you to what you cannot now see.

For in that Head there appeared what is to be hoped for in the members. In that foundation was demonstrated what is built in our faith, so that afterward it may be perfected in form.

Otherwise, when you think that you are seeing, something may appear to you through a false image to be what it is not; you may leave the way and turn aside into error, and you may fail to reach the homeland to which the way leads—that is, the form to which faith leads.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 28. Life will be like that of the angels, free from works of corruption and want. The perpetual Sabbath. Why works of mercy will not exist there.

You say, “How do the angels live?”

It is enough for you to know that they do not live corruptibly. For it is easier to tell you what will not be there than what will be there.

I too, my brothers, can briefly run through certain things that will not be there. I can do this because we have experienced these things and know what will not be there. But we have not yet experienced what will be there.

For we walk by faith, not yet by sight. As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6–7).

What, then, will not be there?

There will be no taking a wife so that children may be propagated, because there is no death there. There will be no growing, because there will also be no aging. There will be no refreshment, because there will be no exhaustion. There will be no business, because there will be no need; nor will there be those praiseworthy works of innocent human beings that poverty and the necessities of this life compel them to perform.

I do not mean merely that the works of thieves or moneylenders will not be there. The very works that innocent people perform because of need, in order to relieve human necessities, will not be there.

## CHAPTER XXVII

The Sabbath will be perpetual. The Jews celebrate it temporarily, but we understand it as eternal.

There will be ineffable rest, which cannot be explained. Yet, as I said, it can to some extent be explained when we say what will not be there.

We are moving toward that rest; spiritually we are reborn for it. For just as we are born carnally for labor, so we are reborn spiritually for rest, while he cries out:

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

Here he feeds; there he perfects. Here he promises; there he gives. Here he signifies; there he makes manifest.

When we have been made perfect and saved in both spirit and body in that blessedness, these activities will not exist. Nor will those things exist there that are praised here among the good works of Christians.

Who is not praised as a Christian for offering bread to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, reconciling those who quarrel, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and consoling the grieving?

These are great works, full of mercy, praise, and grace. But even these will not exist there, because works of mercy have been created by the necessity of misery.

Whom will you feed where no one is hungry? To whom will you give drink where no one is thirsty? Will you clothe the naked where all are clothed with immortality itself?

You heard earlier about the garments of the saints, when the Apostle said: “This corruptible must put on incorruption.” Where “put on” is spoken, clothing is indicated. Adam lost this clothing and received skins instead.

Will you receive a stranger where all live in their own homeland? Will you visit the sick where all will flourish with the same incorruptible strength? Will you bury the dead where all live forever? Will you reconcile those who quarrel where everything is at peace? Will you console the sorrowful where all will rejoice forever?

Since misery will cease altogether, therefore these works of mercy will also cease.

## CHAPTER XXVIII
29. What the blessed will do after the resurrection. Amen and Alleluia will be our entire activity, without weariness. What, then, will be done there? Have I not already said that it is easier for me to say what will not be there than what will be there? This I know, brothers: we shall not be sleeping away our time in idleness, because sleep itself was given to the soul as a relief from exhaustion. For a fragile body could not endure the perpetual concentration that agitates mortal senses, unless, when the senses were lulled to sleep, that very fragility were restored so that it could endure the same agitation; and just as renewal will come from death, so now wakefulness comes from sleep. Therefore, sleep will not be there. For where there is no death, there will be no image of death either.

Yet let no one be seized by fear of boredom when told that he will always be awake and will do nothing. I can say—and I cannot say exactly how it will come to pass, since I cannot yet see it—but I can nevertheless say something without presumption, because I speak from the Scriptures, about what our activity there will be. Our entire activity will be Amen and Alleluia. What do you say, brothers? I see that you are listening and rejoicing. But do not again become distressed by carnal thought: for if one of you were to stand and say “Amen and Alleluia” every day, he would wither from boredom, fall asleep amid those very words, and eventually wish to be silent; and therefore he might think that such a life was to be despised rather than desired, saying to yourselves: “We shall always be saying Amen and Alleluia—who could endure it?”

I shall therefore say, if I can, as much as I can. We shall not say Amen and Alleluia with passing sounds, but with the affection of the soul. For what is “Amen”? What is “Alleluia”? “Amen” means “it is true”; “Alleluia” means “praise God.” Since God is unchangeable truth—without failure, without advancement, without loss, without increase, without any inclination toward falsehood [Note: [Col. 1632] Morel, *El. Crit.*, p. 316, reads *inquinatio* (“defilement”), a word that corresponds particularly well to the third part of the enumeration immediately following, namely, “incorruptible.” M.]—perpetual, steadfast, and always remaining incorruptible; and since the things we do in creation and in this life are like figures of realities, through bodily signs, and are things in which we walk by faith: when we see face to face what we now see through a mirror in an enigma (I Cor. XIII, 12), then with an entirely different and ineffably different affection we shall say, “It is true.” And when we say this, we shall certainly say “Amen,” but with an insatiable fullness.

For there will be no lack of anything, and therefore there will be fullness; but because what is not lacking will always delight us, there will be, if one may so speak, an insatiable fullness. Thus, as insatiably as you are filled with truth, so insatiably will you say, “Amen.” What will it be like? Who can say what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart (I Cor. II, 9)? Since, therefore, we shall behold the truth without any weariness and with perpetual delight, and shall contemplate it with the most certain clarity, inflamed by love of the truth itself and clinging to it in a sweet and chaste embrace, likewise incorporeal, we shall praise him with such a voice and say, “Alleluia.” For all the citizens of that city, rejoicing [Note: [Col. 1633] Perhaps, “exhorting.”] and impelling one another toward equal praise through the most ardent love, both for one another and for God, will say, “Alleluia,” because they will say, “Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

30. The rest and reclining of the blessed in contemplation and praise of the truth. This life of the saints will so fill their bodies also, transformed into a heavenly and angelic condition, and will so invigorate them immortally, that no corruption arising from necessity will turn or call them away from that most blessed contemplation and praise of the truth. Thus the truth itself will be their food, and their rest will be like reclining at table.

For when it is said that they will recline and feast, as the Lord says, “Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. VIII, 11), this signifies that they will be nourished in great rest by the food of truth. Such food restores and does not fail; it fills and remains whole: you are brought to completion, but it is not consumed. That food is not like this food, which is depleted in restoring, and which itself comes to an end lest the life of the one who receives it should end. That reclining, therefore, will be everlasting rest; that feast will be unchangeable truth; that feasting will be eternal life, that is, knowledge itself. “This is eternal life,” he says, “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

## CHAPTER XXX

31. The life of those who devote themselves with delight and supreme freedom to the vision of God. Prayer after the sermon. For this life will remain in the contemplation of truth not only ineffably but also delightfully, as Scripture testifies in many places, though we cannot recall them all. Hence there is the saying: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and I will love him, and will show myself to him” (John XIV, 21). For it is as though a fruit and reward were sought from him because his commandments are kept: “I will show myself to him,” he says, establishing perfect blessedness in being known as he is.

Hence also there is the saying: “Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). Therefore the Apostle Paul also says, “Then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12), because he likewise says elsewhere, “We are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18). And in the Psalms he says, “Be still, and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV, 11).

Then, therefore, he will be seen most perfectly when we are most perfectly free for contemplation. And when shall we be most free, unless when the difficult times have passed—the times of necessity by which we are now bound, as long as the earth produces thorns and thistles for sinful humanity, so that it must eat its bread in the sweat of its face? When the times of the earthly human being have entirely passed, and the day of the heavenly human being has been entirely perfected, we shall see most perfectly because we shall be most perfectly free.

For when corruption and want have ended in the resurrection of the faithful, there will be no reason to labor. Just as one might be told, “Recline and eat,” so one is told, “Be free and see.” We shall therefore be free and shall see God as he is; and seeing him, we shall praise God. This will be the life of the saints, this the activity of those at rest, because we shall praise without failure. We shall not praise for a single day; but just as that day has no limit of time, so our praise will have no limit of cessation. Therefore we shall praise throughout the ages of ages.

Hear Scripture also saying to God what we desire: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

Turning toward the Lord, let us pray to him for ourselves and for all his people standing with us in the courts of his house, which may he deign to guard and protect; through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with him throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCCLXIII

[Note: [Col. 1634] Corrected according to r. v. and Sirmond.]  
[Note: [Col. 1634] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons, no. 2.]

## On the Song of Exodus

[Note: [Col. 1634] The same title appears in Possidius, *Index*, chapter 8. John, deacon of the Roman Church, gives a more extensive excerpt from this sermon in his *Collections* on the first seven books of the Old Testament, not yet published. We possess a very ancient copy of these works from the library of Corbie, written perhaps in the author’s lifetime, or certainly not many years after the ninth century. The concise and somewhat obscure manner of exposition once caused us to doubt whether this sermon was genuine; but since it otherwise bears the strongest marks of Augustine, it is reasonable to believe that in certain places its obscurity was caused by scribal error, as may be seen in one or two passages that we have restored from John’s *Collections*. We further suspect that the sermon has been shortened to a considerable extent.]

*Chapter XV, verses 1–21.*

### 1. In considering the Holy Scriptures, we must be guided by the authority of those same Scriptures

In considering and expounding the Holy Scriptures, brothers most dear, our understanding must be guided by the clearest authority of those same Scriptures, so that from what is openly said for our nourishment, those things that are said more obscurely for our exercise may be faithfully explained. For who would dare to interpret the divine mysteries otherwise than they have been proclaimed and prescribed by the apostolic heart and mouth?

The Apostle Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ. But with most of them God was not well pleased. For they were struck down in the wilderness. These things happened as figures for us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them.” And shortly afterward: “All these things,” he says, “were happening to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (I Cor. X, 1–11).

### 2. The crossing of the Red Sea as a figure of Baptism

From this, therefore, beloved, let no faithful person doubt that the crossing of that people through the Red Sea was a figure of our Baptism. Through Baptism we were to be freed, under the leadership of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom Moses then represented, from the devil and his angels, who, like Pharaoh and the Egyptians, were wearing us down—enslaved to the mud of the flesh, as though to the work of making bricks. Thus we sing: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.”

Those who could no longer rule over us have died for us, because our very sins, which had made us subject to them, were washed away and destroyed as though submerged in the sea when we were freed by the bath of holy grace. Let us therefore sing to the Lord: “For he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea”—he destroyed pride and the proud person in Baptism. For now the humble person, subject to God, sings this song. The Lord was not gloriously exalted for the proud person who seeks his own glory and magnifies himself.

But the ungodly person justified by believing in him who justifies the ungodly, so that his faith is counted as righteousness (Rom. IV, 5), so that the righteous person may live by faith (ibid. I, 17), and so that, not knowing God’s righteousness and wishing to establish his own, he may not be subject to the righteousness of God (ibid. X, 3)—such a person most truly sings of the Lord as his helper and protector for salvation, his God whom he honors. For he is not one of those who are puffed up, who, although they knew God, did not honor him as God (ibid. I, 21).

He therefore says, “The God of my father.” For he is the God of my father Abraham, who believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (ibid. IV, 3).

[Note: [Col. 1635] Sirmond: “But he says to him, ‘God.’ For he is the God of Abraham’s father.” The passage is similarly corrupt in the manuscripts and is restored here from the unpublished *Collections* of the deacon John.]

Therefore, as little ones who presume not on our own righteousness but on his grace, we magnify the Lord, because he himself shatters battles—he who is our peace. Therefore “Lord” is his name, to whom we say through Isaiah, “Possess us” (Isa. XXVI, 13).

“Lord” is his name. We did not exist, and he made us; we had perished, and he found us; we had sold ourselves, and he bought us. “Lord” is his name. He threw Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea. He destroyed in Baptism worldly exaltations and the countless throngs of sins that had served the devil in us.

He had placed three charioteers upon the chariots [Note: [Col. 1635] In the Septuagint, “those who strike down.”], who pursued and terrified us with fear of pain, fear of humiliation, and fear of death. All these were submerged in the Red Sea, because we were buried with him through Baptism into death (Rom. VI, 4)—with him who was scourged, dishonored, and killed for us. Thus he covered all our enemies in the Red Sea, having consecrated Baptism by the bloody death through which our sins were to be consumed.

But if our enemies have descended into the depths like a stone, the hardness of the devil belongs only to those who are with them, of whom it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). For they do not believe that what they have done can be forgiven them, and in that despair they sink more heavily and more deeply.

“But your right hand, Lord, has been glorified in power; your right hand, Lord, has shattered the enemies; and in the abundance of your majesty, Lord, you have crushed your adversaries. You sent your anger, and it devoured them like straw.”

For we feared you when you were born [Note: [Col. 1636] Perhaps “when you were angry.” This reading fits the entire subject under discussion especially well. M.], and we believed in you, and all our sins were consumed.

For why was the water divided by the spirit of the Lord’s anger, and did the waves freeze like a wall of water? The waves froze in the middle of the sea, and through that division of the water, with the waves frozen, a way was opened for the people who had been delivered. Why, then, was the water not rather divided by the spirit of the Lord’s mercy, unless because the terror of God’s anger—which the sinner who descends into the depths of evils despises—drives him to Baptism, so that through water that does not suffocate us, but through which we pass by a road, we may be delivered?

The enemy said: “I will pursue; I will overtake; I will divide the spoils; I will fill my soul; I will kill with my sword; my hand shall rule.” The enemy does not understand the power of the Lord’s sacrament that is present in saving Baptism for those who believe and hope in him. He still thinks that sins can rule over the baptized, because they are tempted by the weakness of the flesh. He does not know where, when, or how the complete renewal of the whole human being is accomplished—a renewal begun and prefigured in Baptism and already held by the most certain hope.

For then “this mortal will put on immortality,” and when every principality and power has been completely abolished, “God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 53–54, 24, 28). But now, as long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. IX, 15), the enemy says, “I will pursue; I will overtake.”

“But you sent your spirit, and the sea covered them.” Here the spirit of God’s anger is not mentioned, whereas shortly before it was said, “By the spirit of your anger the water was divided,” although it was rather through this division that God’s passing people were delivered. But surely God seems not to be angry with the person whose sins go unpunished, and who thereby becomes more deeply burdened. Compared with lead, he descends into the depths all the more heavily as he sees those who have been justified by faith enduring present evils for the hope of future life and living amid hardships in which the Spirit of God strengthens them to persevere.

God therefore sent his Spirit to console and exercise the righteous in their labors, and the sea covered the ungodly—not merely because they thought there was no difference between themselves and the righteous, but rather because they judged that God was angry with those who were afflicted by such great tribulations and favorable toward themselves, who rejoiced in such great prosperity. Thus they descended like lead into the exceedingly mighty water.

“Who is like you among the gods, Lord? Who is like you? Glorious among the holy, who do not glory in themselves; wonderful in majesty, who perform miracles.”

For those things that happened then announced something that was to come, since they were figures for us.

“You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.” Certainly, at that time no chasm in the earth swallowed the Egyptians; they were covered by water and perished in the sea. What, then, does “You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them” mean?

Do we rightly understand God’s right hand to be the one of whom Isaiah says, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). He is the only Son, “whom the Father did not spare, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32). Thus on the cross he stretched out his right hand, and the earth swallowed the ungodly when they thought themselves victorious and considered him contemptible.

“For the earth was delivered into the hands of the ungodly, and he covered the face of its judge” (Job IX, 24)—that is, his divinity. Thus the Lord guided his people as though carried upon that wood, where the earth—that is, the Lord’s flesh—stretched out, swallowed the ungodly. The people did not cross the sea by ship, so that one could properly say that he guided them in that sense.

“But you guided your people in your righteousness”—a people not presuming on its own righteousness, but living by faith under your grace—“this people of yours whom you delivered.” “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19).

### 3. The passage through the wilderness as a figure of our pilgrimage in this life, in which we overcome our adversaries with Christ’s help

“You have strengthened them by your power,” that is, in your Christ. For “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I, 25). And “although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4).

“You have strengthened them by your power, and by your holy refreshment.” Since the mortality of the flesh was refreshed in him through the resurrection, and in him this corruptible nature has already put on incorruption, we have been strengthened by hoping for the future and enduring the present on account of all these things.

After Baptism, there remains the passage through the wilderness: the life lived in hope, until we come to the promised land, the land of the living, where the Lord is our portion, in the eternal Jerusalem. Until we come there, this entire life is a wilderness and an entire time of testing for us.

But in him who conquered the world, the people of God conquer all things. For just as in Baptism past sins are blotted out, like enemies pursuing us from behind, so after Baptism, on the journey of this life, when we eat spiritual food and drink spiritual drink, we overcome everything that opposes us.

The name of our Emperor terrified the enemies of our way. First the anger of the nations arose to destroy the Christian name; but when anger could accomplish nothing, it was changed into grief. As faith grew and increasingly took possession of everything, grief was changed into fear, so that even the proud people of this age, like the birds of heaven, might seek refuge and protection under the shade of that plant which grew enormously from the tiniest mustard seed (Matt. XIII, 31–32).

Thus in this song also, where the things that then happened to them in figure are recalled, the order of the nations’ anger, grief, and fear has been preserved. “The nations heard,” it says, “and were angry; anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the leaders of Edom hastened”—that is, they were thrown into confusion—“and trembling seized the princes of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.”

“Let trembling and fear fall upon them at the greatness of your arm. Let them become like stones, until your people pass over, Lord—until this people of yours whom you acquired passes over.”

So it happened; so it happens. Struck dumb with astonishment, the enemies of the Church become like stones until we pass into our homeland. And those who attempt to resist are overcome now by the sign of the Lord’s cross, just as Amalek was overcome then when Moses stretched out his hands (Exod. XVII).

Thus we are brought into and planted upon the mountain of the Lord’s inheritance, which grew from the small stone seen by Daniel and filled the whole earth (Dan. II, 34–35). This is the dwelling prepared for the Lord. “The temple of God is holy, and the sanctification of his house comes from him.” “The temple of God is holy,” says the Apostle, “which you are” (I Cor. III, 17).

And lest anyone should look toward the earthly Jerusalem, where that temple temporarily represented a figure, he appropriately indicated that he was speaking of the eternal kingdom, which is God’s eternal inheritance, the eternal Jerusalem. For he continues: “Which your hands have prepared, Lord, who reign forever, and throughout eternity, and beyond.”

Is there anything beyond eternity? Who could say so? Why, then, did he add, “and beyond”? Perhaps because “eternal” is sometimes understood also of an exceedingly long period, “and beyond” was added so that the true eternity, which has no end, might be understood.

Or is it because God reigns forever in the heavenly realms, which he established for the age of the age, and “he gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. CXLVIII, 6); and reigns throughout eternity over those to whom, after transgressing the commandment and later turning back, he forgave their sins, acquired them in time, and granted them endless blessedness; and still reigns over those whom he has ordered beneath the feet of his people in most just punishments?

For no one is removed from his kingdom, since by his eternal law all creatures are restrained through the distribution of giving and repaying, through the merits of rewards and punishments, and through the most just ordering of creation. “For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

“For Pharaoh’s cavalry entered the sea, with his chariots and riders, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea over them. But the children of Israel walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea.”

### 4. What Mary’s singing with a tambourine signifies

Moses and the children of Israel sang this song; Mary the prophetess and the daughters of Israel with her sang this song; and so do we now, whether men and women, or our spirit and flesh. For “those who belong to Jesus Christ,” says the Apostle, “have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. V, 24).

The tambourine that Mary took up is appropriately understood to signify this. For on wood the flesh is stretched out so that it becomes a tambourine, and from the cross they learn to confess the sweet sound of grace.

Having therefore been made humble through Baptism by the kindness of grace, and our pride—the pride by which the proud enemy ruled over us—having been extinguished there, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31), let us sing to the Lord: “For he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.”

[Col. 1639]

# CLASS V. DOUBTFUL SERMONS

Among these, those that seem less likely to belong to Augustine are printed in smaller type. (C, G, S)*

# SERMON CCCLXIV

[Note: [Col. 1639] Corrected according to b., cl., ful., r., and Am., Er., Par., Lov.]  
[Note: [Col. 1639] Elsewhere, *On Time* 107.]

## On Samson

[Note: [Col. 1639] Possidius, in his *Index*, chapter 10, lists a work “on Samson and on the verse of Psalm 57,” part of which we believe is represented in this sermon. It was formerly considered doubtful by the Louvain editors, but spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. Now, certainly, after correction according to various manuscript codices, it emerges much better than before, or at least less unworthy of Augustine; on the authority of these manuscripts we have restored some things and removed others. In earlier printed editions the beginning was as follows: “In the reading that has been recited to us, brothers most dear, many and exceedingly obscure divine mysteries are contained. Since these cannot be explained briefly, for this reason alone we wished to finish the morning Psalms earlier, lest a longer sermon weary you. And since you are about to leave the church at the customary hour, listen attentively, according to your custom, to what must be said, in silence and quiet. Samson, dearly beloved brothers,” and so forth. All of this is absent from the manuscripts.]  

*Judges, chapters XIII–XVI.*

### 1. Samson’s strength came from the Spirit of God

Samson had strength from grace, not from nature. For if he had been strong by nature, when his hair was cut away his strength would not have been taken from him. And where was that exceedingly powerful strength, unless in what Scripture says: “The Spirit of the Lord was walking with him”? That strength belonged to the Spirit of the Lord.

In Samson there was a vessel; in the Spirit there was fullness. A vessel can be filled and emptied. Every vessel, however, receives its fullness from elsewhere. Therefore grace itself was commended in Paul when he was called “a vessel of election” (Acts IX, 15).

Let us therefore see what sort of parable Samson proposed to the Philistines. “From the eater,” he said, “came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.” This parable was disclosed, reported to his companions, and solved; Samson was defeated.

If he is righteous here, his righteousness lies hidden; it is very deep indeed in this man. For to those who understand the secrets of truth less fully, both the fact that he is said to have been defeated by feminine blandishments and the fact that he entered a prostitute seem to make his merit falter.

A prophet, after all, is commanded by the Lord to take a prostitute as his wife (Hos. I, 2). Perhaps we may say that in the Old Testament these things were not criminal or condemnable, since what he said or did was prophecy.

Let us therefore inquire what was signified by his being defeated; what was signified by his being victorious; what was signified by his yielding to feminine blandishments; what was signified by his disclosing the secret of the parable; what was signified by his entering a prostitute; what was signified by his catching the foxes and, through the tails of the foxes to which he had attached fire, burning the enemies’ crops.

He could have burned those crops more conveniently if he had not intended a mystery in the foxes. For could dry straw not burn unless the foxes carried fire through it? Let us therefore understand that great mysteries lie hidden here.

[Col. 1640]

### 2. Christ figured in Samson. Samson’s wife. His riddle

What was Samson? If I say that he signified Christ, I seem to be speaking the truth; but at once this objection occurs to those who are thinking: “And was Christ defeated by feminine blandishments? And how can Christ be understood to have entered a prostitute’s house? Further, when was Christ stripped bare on the head, shaved of his hair, deprived of his strength, bound, blinded, and mocked?”

Awaken, faith; attend to what Christ is—not only to what Christ did, but also to what Christ suffered.

What did he do? He acted as the strong one. What did he suffer? He suffered as the weak one. In one person I understand both. I see the strength of the Son of God; I see the weakness of the Son of Man.

There is also another point: Christ in his entirety, as Scripture presents him, is both head and body. As Christ is the head of the Church, so the Church is the body of Christ (Eph. IV, 15; Col. I, 18). And lest it be alone, together with its head it is the whole Christ.

The Church therefore contains the strong and the weak; it contains those who feed on solid food and those who still must be nourished with milk. I add another point, which must be acknowledged: within the very fellowship of the sacraments, in sharing Baptism and participating in the altar, it contains the righteous and the unrighteous.

For now the body of Christ, which you know, is on the threshing floor; afterward it will be in the granary. Yet while it is on the threshing floor, it does not refuse to endure the chaff; when the time for storing it arrives, it will separate the wheat from the chaff (Matt. III, 12).

Thus Samson did certain things in the person of the head, certain things in the person of the body, yet everything in the person of Christ. In the fact that Samson performed mighty deeds and miracles, he signified Christ, the head of the Church; in the things he did wisely, he bore the image of those who live justly in the Church; where perhaps he was caught off guard and acted incautiously, he represented those who are sinners in the Church [Note: [Col. 1640] The manuscripts read, “who are weak.” Shortly afterward, in place of “prostitute,” it is more correctly read, “a woman from a foreign people,” as elsewhere in Augustine.].

The prostitute whom Samson takes as his wife is the Church, which before acknowledging the one God had committed fornication with idols, and which Christ afterward joined to himself. Once illuminated by him and having received faith, she also merited through him to learn the sacraments of salvation, and from him the mysteries of heavenly secrets were revealed to her.

For what else does the riddle itself mean—“From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness”—than Christ rising from the dead? From the eater, certainly—that is, from death, which devours and consumes everything—came forth that food which said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 41).

Human wickedness embittered him and gave him the bitterness of vinegar and gall to drink; from him the people of the Gentiles, converted, received the sweetness of life. And thus from the mouth of the dead lion—that is, from the death of Christ, who lay sleeping like a lion—there came forth a swarm of bees, that is, of Christians.

But when he says, “You would not have found my riddle unless you had plowed with my heifer,” this heifer is the Church, which has proclaimed throughout the ends of the earth, through the teaching and preaching of the Apostles and saints, the mysteries of faith, of the Trinity, of the resurrection, of judgment, and of the kingdom alike, and has promised the rewards of eternal life to those who understand and acknowledge them.

### 3. The companion taking Samson’s wife as a figure of heretics. Foxes dragging fire by their tails

It follows: “Samson was angry because his companion took his wife.” This companion bore the figure of all heretics.

A great mystery, my brothers. For the heretics who divided the Church wanted to take and carry away the wife of their Lord. Those who went out from the Church and from the Gospels attempt, through the adultery of impiety, to invade the Church—that is, Christ’s body—and make it their own.

Hence that faithful servant and friend of the Lord’s bride says: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.” And concerning the corrupted companion he touches upon the matter with faithful zeal and rebuke: “I fear,” he says, “that as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the truth that is in Christ Jesus” (II Cor. XI, 2–3).

Who are the companions—that is, the heretical deserters—who wanted to invade the Lord’s bride, except Donatus, Arius, Manichaeus, and the other vessels of error and destruction? The Apostle says of such people: “I hear that there are divisions among you. For one says, ‘I belong to Paul’; another, ‘I to Apollos’; and another, ‘I to Cephas’” (I Cor. I, 11–12).

Let us therefore see what this mystical Samson did when offended because another had taken his wife. He caught foxes—that is, adulterous companions—of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II, 15).

What does “Catch” mean? That is, seize them, convict them, refute them, lest they destroy the ecclesiastical vineyards. What else is catching foxes than overcoming heretics by the authority of divine law, and binding and constraining them as though with certain bonds through the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures?

He catches the foxes and attaches fire to their tied tails. What do the tied tails of the foxes signify? What are the tails of foxes except the latter parts of heretics, who have pleasant and deceptive beginnings? Their tails are tied—that is, condemned—and drag fire at the end, so that they consume the fruits and works of those who yield to their seductions.

He says to a person today, “Do not listen to heretics; do not yield to heretics.” The person replies, “Why? Did this or that person not listen to heretics? And did some other Christian not commit such great evils, commit such adulteries, and practice such robberies? And what evil happened to him?”

Those are the beginnings of the foxes, to which the deceived pay attention; the fire is behind them. “Nothing,” he says, “happened to him.” But because the fire comes behind, does it drag nothing after it? He is coming toward the fire that follows.

Do you suppose that because heretics drag fire in order to burn the enemies’ crops, they themselves will not burn? Certainly, when the foxes have set the crops on fire, they themselves also burn.

See, therefore, the judgment awaiting heretics behind them, and how they do not see what is behind them. They possess blandishments with which to soothe people; they display their first parts as free. But in God’s judgment they drag fire by their tied tails—that is, by what comes afterward—because their wickedness precedes its punishments.

[Col. 1642]

### 4. Samson’s approach to the prostitute. The city gates carried to the mountain after he arose from sleep

As for the fact that he entered the prostitute’s house: if he did so without cause, whoever did it is unclean; but if a prophet did it, it is a sacrament. If he did not enter in order to have intercourse with her, perhaps he entered for the sake of a mystery. But we do not read that he had intercourse with her.

It follows: “His enemies were waiting at the gates of the city to seize him when he came out from the prostitute to whom he had entered.” But he was sleeping. See how it is not written that he joined himself to the prostitute; rather, it is written that he was sleeping.

“When he arose,” it says, “at midnight, he went out and carried away the gates of the city with their bars, and lifted those same gates to the top of the mountain; and the Philistines could not hold him.”

He carried away the city gates through which he had entered the prostitute and lifted them to the mountain. What does this mean? Scripture joins together the underworld and the love of a woman. The prostitute’s house represented the image of hell. It is rightly used as an image of hell, because it repels no one and draws every person who enters toward itself (Prov. XXX, 16).

Here we recognize the work of our Redeemer. After the Synagogue, to which he had come, had been separated from him through the devil, and after it had trampled him—that is, crucified him at the place of the Skull—he descended to the regions below. His enemies guarded the place where he slept—that is, the tomb—and wanted to seize the one whom they could not see.

But he was sleeping there. I say this because it was a real death. When it is said, “He arose at midnight,” this signifies that he arose in secret. For he suffered openly, but after he rose he was revealed only to the disciples and to certain others. Therefore everyone saw that he entered; but few knew, held, and touched him after he had risen.

Nevertheless he takes away the city gates—that is, he removes the gates of hell. What is it to remove the gates of hell except to abolish the dominion of death? Death received and did not release. But what did our Lord Jesus Christ do? Having removed the gates of death, he ascended to the top of the mountain. For we know that he both rose again and ascended into heaven.

## 5. Strength in the Hair. Samson’s Blindness and Death

But what does it mean that he had his strength in his hair? Pay close attention to this also, brothers. He did not have his strength in his hand, nor in his foot, nor in his breast, nor in his very head, but in his hair, in his locks. What is hair? What are locks? We see this ourselves, and when questioned the Apostle answers us: “The long hair is a covering” (1 Cor. 11:15). And Christ had his strength in the covering, when the shadows of the old Law concealed him.

Samson’s hair, therefore, was a covering, because in Christ one thing was seen and another was understood. But what does it mean that the secret was betrayed and Samson was shorn? The Law was despised, and Christ suffered. For they would not have killed Christ if they had not despised the Law. They themselves knew that they were not permitted to kill Christ. They said to the judge, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (John 18:31).

Samson was shorn: the dense thickets were exposed, the covering was removed, and Christ, who had been hidden, appeared. But the hair that grew again covered his head, because the Jews did not wish to believe in Christ even when he had risen.

He was indeed blinded in the mill; he was in the prison-house. The prison-house or the mill is the labor of this present age. Samson’s blinding signifies those who, blinded by unbelief, recognized neither Christ working miracles nor ascending to the heavenly places. The blindness, therefore, which they inflicted signified the blindness of the Jews.

Christ was both seized and killed by the Jews; but he killed those who killed him all the more. His enemies brought him out in order to mock him. Here, then, observe the image of the cross. For he stretched out his hands to the two pillars, as though toward the two beams of the cross; but, once killed, he crushed and overwhelmed his adversaries, and his suffering became the destruction of his persecutors. Therefore Scripture concluded in these words: “The dead killed more than he had killed while alive.”

This mystery was clearly fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ. Our redemption, which while living he had in no way accomplished, he accomplished by dying—he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCCLXV

[Note: [Col. 1643] It does not exist in our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1643] Elsewhere, among the Vigneran editions, 28.]

Concerning verse 7 of Psalm 15: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1643] An excellent sermon against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, but its style does not appear to be Augustinian.]

## 1. God Must Be Praised with the Heart and with Love. Praise without Love Is Neither True nor Acceptable to God

We have sung and said, “I will bless the Lord”—if only with the heart, and not merely with the mouth! For if it is with the mouth and not with the heart, “the praise of the Lord is foul in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15:9); nor does confession of the mouth benefit a person if there is not within a profession of charity.

Consider, brothers: charity is not a virtue of the mouth. It fixes its seat where the bridegroom’s beloved is beautiful. But where is this beauty? “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). That glory is nothing other than beauty; that beauty is nothing other than charity; and charity is nothing other than life. Therefore, in order to live, love.

If you love, you are beautiful: love is good, love is beautiful. If that beauty is absent, you do not live; you have an outward appearance, but not life within. Let that tomb, supported by so many columns, be opened; let the marble be broken. What else will appear but a dreadful corpse, stinking bones, ashes, and worms? There is indeed an appearance, but it conceals a dead man, at the sight of whom you shudder and recoil.

Do you think that the dead man says, “I will bless the Lord”? No. Scripture testifies: “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, nor all those who go down into the underworld” (Ps. 113:17). Open the Gospel: you will hear the Lord rebuking and saying to the devil, “Be silent” (Mark 1:25). Why? Because “the dead shall not praise you, nor all those who go down into the underworld.”

No one praises someone whom he does not love; or, if an enemy praises him, he loves the virtue that he praises in his enemy. Whoever sins practices hostility against God. Therefore he does not praise God, nor does he praise God’s virtue, because praise is a good thing that does not fall into sin. Whoever praises someone while lying either slanders or mocks rather than praises him.

Take charity away from the heart, and only falsehood remains. Do you want falsehood to praise the truth, and God to receive a commendation from the source from which blasphemy proceeds? Wise people do not think highly of those who are praised by madmen and wicked people. Will God be praised by an impure and most shameless heart, by a blasphemous and utterly insane mind?

Say, then, “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” You are not insane; you have been healed; you possess understanding. Praise your God, who has given you understanding, who provides an eye: understanding, so that you may grasp; an eye, so that you may see. Grasp how great is the breadth and length of God’s love; look upon the author and perfecter of faith. Grasp charity; look upon Christ. Charity, so that you may love; Christ, so that you may bless. By loving and blessing, know the Lord who has given you understanding; and by knowing, live, because “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

## 2. Against Heretics Who Boast That They Possess Good Understanding from Nature, by Which God Is Blessed

But from where, I ask, do you have this understanding? Someone will come along from the side and say: “The one who gave nature gave understanding; good nature, good understanding. Let me draw this good nature as my lot, and that is enough. For understanding will not be degenerate; and from the source that gave me understanding—that is, from nature—I will bless the Lord.”

O heretic, then you have received a good nature as your lot? Let the Apostle be silent and be confounded: “The good that I will, I do not do” (Rom. 7:19). Yet he had received a good nature, and in that good nature he could not do the good that he wished to do. He wishes, desires, and strives: he wishes feebly, desires in vain, and strives fruitlessly; and contrary to what he wishes, desires, and strives for, he does not accomplish this good.

O good nature, whose will is weak, whose desire is fruitless, whose efforts are useless! Let the philosophers play their part, and they will owe you the greatest thanks, since you so freely bestow upon them a good nature. What follows from this? They have known the heavens; they have known the earth; they have known the sea; they investigate the abysses; they examine nature’s hidden things; they know the distinctions, differences, and essences of things; they give an account of all these things. What follows from this? Continue; say more.

After all this and so much more, they fail: “they did not glorify him as God, became futile in their thoughts, became foolish while judging themselves wise, and changed the likeness of God into the likeness of a calf that eats hay”; they poured themselves out into the error of Baalim; “the god of this age blinded them,” and they were handed over to dishonorable passions and became like those things which they worshiped (Rom. 1:21–28).

And yet they rejoiced in their good nature and in understanding through nature. Madman, do you see whether this nature gives understanding by which they may bless God? Rather, does it not give understanding by which they may curse God and rise up against the Creator?

Say instead, brothers: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” If he had not given it, I would not have understood; if I had not understood, I would never have blessed him. He gave understanding; he gave an eye.

Blind nature cannot provide what it itself lacks. Make understanding for yourself, and you will make yourself blind. “The light that is in you is darkness.” Say, then, “Enlighten my darknesses, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4).

What does it mean to sleep in death? To hope for something from nature; to make one’s own arm flesh; to fashion understanding for oneself. Whoever does this is not merely in death, but sleeps in death. He is more than four days dead; he already stinks (John 11:39).

If he were merely in death, he could be raised. But in death itself he sleeps a sleep harder than iron and rests in it. It is all over with him.

## 3. They Are Again Refuted by the Words of Solomon

But do you want to know what the man who had received a good nature did? Did he say, as you do: “In a good nature I have good understanding, and the one who gave me the one did not deny me the other”? Let us dash the scorpion to the ground; let us crush it; let its mouth be stopped against iniquity.

Read: “I received a good soul.” Continue; let us hear what sort of treasure you obtained—one that may perhaps be turned into coals; and would that it were into coals which, heaped upon your head, might consume what is superfluous.

“And when I was more good, I came into a body undefiled; and when I knew that I could not otherwise exercise self-control unless God gave it, and that this very knowledge was wisdom—to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wis. 8:19–21).

You truly received a good nature—who can deny it? For even the nature of the devil is good, and everything that God made is good. But in this nature, although it is good, will you have wise understanding by which you can abstain from desires and cravings that wage war against the soul, unless God gives it?

Learn, heretic; learn at last: “I knew that I could not otherwise exercise self-control unless God gave it.” The chief element of wisdom—which is entirely understanding—is to know from whom self-control comes, and that one cannot exercise it except through God alone.

O excellent nature, which can abstain from nothing and cannot do otherwise than fall unless God gives understanding by which it does not fall!

Let us therefore sing, brothers; let us sing: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” He gave nature; he gave understanding. He healed nature; he healed understanding. In both respects the merciful Samaritan showed compassion: he descended, bound up the wounds, cleansed them with wine—which we understand symbolically—treated them, carried the wounded man to the inn, that is, to the Church, and entrusted him to the innkeeper (Luke 10:33–35).

To what innkeeper? To the Holy Spirit, the inhabitant of the holy Church. After receiving the coin—but it was a coin poured out from a torn purse, since he paid for the wretched—he healed with his oil, his ointment, the wounds of fallen and expiring nature. With that same oil, which he kindled, he illuminated my darkness and made my understanding bright.

If you do not believe this, he will not be a Samaritan to you, and you will perish in your wound because you refuse to admit the hand of the physician.

## 4. Good Understanding Comes from the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit Is a Gift Purchased for Us by Christ’s Passion

Let the Apostles be questioned and say who gave them understanding on that fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection. Had they perhaps produced the terrible sound by which the place where they awaited the Father’s promise was shaken? Had they perhaps kindled that heavenly fire by which they were all burning? Had they perhaps themselves created those fiery tongues? Had they perhaps themselves procured for themselves those divine gifts, among which is understanding, and poured them out upon themselves according to the desires of their hearts?

Whoever says this has no share in this sacred fiftieth day; nor does he receive understanding who thinks that understanding is given according to nature.

When, then, was understanding given, if not when the Spirit was also given? Let us proceed together. Now you are confounded; now you blush. Would that you were so confounded that you might be built up, and so blush that you might be glorified.

What is the Holy Spirit except the promised gift of the Father, except the gift of the Son? If he is promised, you have one by whom he is promised, for what is promised is outside us. It would be promised in vain if, when it is promised, it were already in our power, or if, when it pleased us, it could already be possessed. I promise you what you do not have, and when I promise it, it is in me that what I promise may descend into you.

The Holy Spirit is also a gift—more than every gift, a gift owed to no one, a gift freely bestowed.

Christ was born and laid in a manger, so that he might become the food of devout beasts of burden. Yet he suffered thirst and weariness; he was sold by his own people, handed over and accused by the Jews, scourged by the Gentiles, crowned with thorns, crucified, and finally enclosed in a stone. Why all these things? So that he might purchase this gift for you and afterward distribute it to you when you believed—or rather, distribute it so that you might believe. For unless he had first given it, you would not have believed either before or afterward.

Therefore, if you possess this gift from nature, you make Christ’s death, passion, and cross empty. For he dies in vain to acquire for you what is already in you, and gives what you already possess. Give back to the Lord the humility of the manger; give back the curse of the cross; give back the abundance of the poured-out blood. All these things are in vain; they are empty for you. You are rich, and you count understanding among the goods of your rich nature: understanding given by nature, not by grace, and for which you are not indebted to the Creator except insofar as he gave you nature, which made understanding for you.

## 5. Finally, They Are Convicted by the Experience of Their Own Weakness and Desire

You recognize the error, I think. Would that “your kidneys corrected you” (Ps. 15:7), so that you might recognize it more fully, and, recognizing it, ask, and, asking, obtain the spirit of understanding, counsel, and fear—so that you might become wiser, more cautious, and more subject to the Lord.

These matters, brothers, even if I did not discuss them, would nevertheless have someone else to teach you; you yourselves would be their interpreters. For if—God forbid—you had fallen into so gross and stupid an error as to think that understanding was given to you by nature, although you possess it solely through the grace and mercy of God, your own kidneys would correct you and cry out, “Why do such thoughts rise in your hearts?” (Luke 24:38).

Let each person consult himself, touch himself, search himself, and not seek outside himself. Let him question his kidneys, and they will tell him that “there is another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23): “I am inclined toward every crime. The waves of desire overwhelm me so that every day I am submerged and fall into the depths of sins.

“Envy rises; pride rises; lust rises. They attack the wretched man in formation. If I avoid Charybdis, I run into Scylla. If I drive away lust, I succumb to anger. If greed does not subdue me, drunkenness strikes me. If I abstain from theft, I close my hand and my innards to the poor. If I stop my ears against slanders, death enters through the windows—that is, through my eyes I draw in the stimuli of lusts and pleasures. Finally, if I close one opening, a hundred remain open through which I may receive the enemy’s rain, until at last I collapse.”

These are the things that your kidneys discuss with you. Conscious of your weakness, they teach you, rebuke you, correct you, and do so “until night.”

What kind of night? The darkness of your conscience, whose shadows envelop you. If you could, you would wish to hold these shadows before the light of truth as a shield and place good hope in your own strength. But your kidneys correct you.

There is strength in the kidneys and loins, as Scripture says somewhere (Job 40:11). But since your loins are so lacking in strength and your kidneys so flaccid, they teach you and say: “If in the kidneys, from which strength comes, there is such weakness and infirmity, what will happen to the rest?”

When our loins have taught us and shown us how vain is the salvation of human beings, what remains except that we gird our loins so that they do not become slack?

When the wooden panels of our buildings gape open, whether through excessive age, excessive heat, the force of storms, or any other cause, we immediately fasten them together with nails and cords. Let this be done with your loins—that is, with your strength. They become loose, fall, and break apart; the whole structure is dissolved.

You have nails in the crucified one: drive them in firmly, and the deeper, the better. Do not place one against what is tottering merely to prop it up; thus the loosened structure will be strengthened. The nails of the cross have the power to raise those who lie fallen, restore the weak, and hold back those who are slipping.

Drive them in; strike them in, even to the marrow, even to the very soul. From this correction you will be healed, and once healed you will say to the Lord, “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. 58:10): “From you comes my strength; toward you is my strength.”

Turned toward the Lord, etc.

# SERMON CCCLXVI

[Note: [Col. 1646] Compared with two manuscripts, with the edition designated gr. rm., and with Sirmondus.]

[Note: [Col. 1646] Elsewhere, among the Sirmondian sermons, 9.]

Concerning Psalm 22: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.”

[Note: [Col. 1646] Sirmondus found it attributed to Augustine in three manuscripts, one from Germain-des-Prés and two Victorine manuscripts; in addition, we found it in the Remigian manuscript, nearly eight hundred years old. In all these books it is inserted as though belonging to the same collection, among various works of Augustine against the Pelagians. Its very style of expression, however, has almost persuaded us that the title of the sermon is false in the manuscripts, and we scarcely doubt that it is not Augustine’s.]

## 1. The Psalm Contains the Mystery of the Restoration of the Human Being

Beloved, to you who are hastening toward Christ’s Baptism, we entrust this psalm in the name of the Lord, so that you may commit it to memory. We must explain its mystery, with divine grace giving light.

For this psalm specially contains the restoration of the fallen human race, the discipline of the holy Church, and the sacraments together. Therefore let the ears of your hearts be opened in silence to hear, and let the furrows of your whole attention be ready to receive the seed of the word, so that what the thirsty earth has now received may, when the appointed time comes, be watered with Christ’s blood and, growing upon a tall stalk [Note: [Col. 1646] Sirmondus reads “fruitful.” But the manuscripts read “tall.”], bring forth abundant fruit.

## 2. The Figure of Fallen Humanity in the Man Who Descended from Jerusalem to Jericho

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.” A great beginning, beloved, for one who confesses. For “the Lord shepherds me” establishes confidence in defense; and “I shall lack nothing” strengthens the inexhaustible substance of riches.

But let us ask whose confession this is, how great it is, and what sort of confession it is. It belongs to him—yes, to him, beloved—who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers; who, stripped of the dignity of his first origin and struck down by the weapon of death, lay on the ground without strength and naked; who, while the trumpet of the Law and the Prophets sounded and he tried to rise by his own strength, was pulled back by the pain of his wound and fell more heavily into the fall in which he lay. For, as the Apostle says, “the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19).

Our Samaritan—that is, Christ, who was called a Samaritan by the Jews, a name interpreted as “Guardian”—passed along the same road and, taking pity on him, came in the flesh to die for us sinners.
