He lifted him from the ground, placed him upon his own beast, and, carrying him on his own shoulders like a wandering sheep, restored him to paradise, from which he had fallen, to the hundredfold—that is, to the perfect number (Luke 10:30–35).

For, as the prophet says, “he bore our sins and suffered for us” (Isa. 53:4). Speak now, human being; speak while upon the beast of mercy and seated on the shoulders of the Lord’s love. You recognize your Creator and Lord, who has recognized you: “The Lord shepherds me.”

You could not say this while lying there unless the Lord had raised you up. He therefore shepherds you who carries you. For when you say, “The Lord shepherds me,” there is nothing of your own in which you may trust. Therefore take care that you do not exalt yourself on account of your merits. You had none when the Lord came to raise you up.

In the end, he found you naked, not clothed; wounded, not healthy; lying down, not standing; wandering, not returning. Beware of boasting, beware! For he who in mercy lifted you, half-dead, from the ground carries the humble but casts down the one who exalts himself.

When you say with fear and by walking in innocence, “The Lord shepherds me,” you will confidently add, “and I shall lack nothing.” For “nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Ps. 83:13), and “the Lord will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things” (Ps. 33:10).

## 3. The Security of the Sheep Led Back by Christ to the Fold. The Pastures of the Christian Soul

To know that you will lack nothing, add what follows: “He has settled me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside the water of refreshment.”

Recognize, human being, what you were, where you were, and under whom you were. You were a wandering sheep, in a trackless and waterless place; you fed among thorns and thistles. Placed under a hired servant, you were not secure when the wolf came.

But now you have been sought out by the true shepherd, carried upon his shoulders in his mercy, and led back to the fold—that is, to the house of God, namely the Church—where your shepherd Christ and the gathered sheep dwell together.

This shepherd is not like the hired servant under whom you suffered miserably and under whom you feared the wolf. Do you want to know how much care this good shepherd has for you? He laid down his life for you. For he himself says in the Gospel: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.” This he did. When the wolf was lying in wait for you, he offered himself to be killed for you.

Now, therefore, you remain secure in the fold. Nor do you need anyone else to close and open the door of your fold [Note: [Col. 1647] Sirmondus reads “of your heart.” The manuscript reading, “of your fold,” is more correct.], because Christ is both your shepherd and your door; he is both pasture and provider.

“I am,” he says, “the door of the sheep. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will go in and go out, and will find pasture” (John 10:11, 9).

The pastures, therefore, which this good shepherd has prepared for you, in which he has settled you to be satisfied, are not a variety of green herbs, some possessing a sweet juice and others an exceedingly bitter one, and which, as time passes, are sometimes present and sometimes absent.

Your pastures are the words and commandments of God, sown for sweetness. He had tasted these pastures who said to God: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

From these pastures the same man cries out to the Lord’s sheep and says: “Taste and see how gracious the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

Read, therefore, the Decalogue of the Old Testament: “You shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20:13–16), and so forth. Read the praise of the commandments of the New Testament: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:3–4), and the other things that follow, or similar teachings, sown abundantly through the Prophets and Apostles.

From these pastures the shepherd cries to the sheep: “Work for the food that does not perish” (John 6:27). It does not perish because “the word of the Lord remains forever.” The word of the Lord is your food, and not only food but also drink.

Hear him speaking through the Prophet to the ancient people: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst” (Sirach 14:29). Likewise, he says through himself: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56).

These pastures, however, are not far from the water of refreshment. They have one place: the Catholic Church of God. There the commandments of life are your pastures, and there is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life. You will be refreshed by its streams when, being renewed in Christ, you are baptized.

Unless your pastures are watered by this water, you cannot be led out to pasture, because the commandments of God cannot sprout without Christ’s Baptism, nor can they be eaten to the soul’s satisfaction.

## 4. Conversion Comes from God’s Grace, Not from Merits. What Are the Paths of Righteousness?

When, therefore, through the water of Christ’s refreshment you have become fit to be satisfied with the flavor of sweet pastures, then you will recognize and cry out with joy, saying: “He has converted my soul; he has led me along paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.”

The devil overturned your soul through sin and turned it away from God. God the Father, through Christ, converted it—not on account of your merits, but for his name’s sake.

Now enlightened, converted, believing, and satisfied by the divine pastures through the water of refreshment, you will say: “He has converted my soul.” Your confession of glory is good if your conscience has not changed. You will say this with a true and unchanging conscience when you say it not on account of your merit, but for his name’s sake.

What are the paths of righteousness along which he has led you? Hear your guide. “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction; but narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:13–14).

Every path is short and direct. God has not appointed you to go to the kingdom of heaven through the pleasures of the world; through an abundance of gold and silver; through distinction in precious stones and clothing, furnished with every honor and nobility; or swollen with all the wisdom of philosophers. For all these things, and things like them—things which some use badly and which others are granted to use well [Note: [Col. 1648] Perhaps, “are not granted to use.”]—become for them a broad and spacious way, that is, only in a hope that is seen. When they have been deprived of the present life, this way leads them not to the hope in which they had no hope, but to destruction.

“For they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

He has appointed you to walk along the paths of righteousness—that is, through mercy and truth. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

He wishes you to reject the broad and spacious way and walk along narrow and direct paths—that is, through hunger and thirst, nakedness, fasting, obscurity, poverty, patience, and contempt for all present things, while truly possessing the promised hope [Note: [Col. 1648] Perhaps, “the hope of the promises.”].

Do you want to recognize clearly the shortness of the paths along which you have been commanded to walk? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.” For “on these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

Therefore, if you are hurrying toward the kingdom of heaven and wish to arrive quickly, walk along these two paths, which are the head of all paths and make one way. Then, when you arrive, you will rejoice that you have traveled all the others vigorously and without weariness.

## 5. The Shadow of Death Is the Way of Sin

Hold fast, therefore, to these paths. Let your steps remain in them amid the snares of the raging devil, so that you may safely sing to God and say: “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”

The shadow of death is the way of sin, in which the devil, that scoundrel and pirate, spreads nets of deception before those who walk aright. It is a shadow because light has nothing in common with darkness.

The Apostle teaches that the works of this shadow must be rejected, saying: “Let us cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the weapons of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and impurity, not in contention and jealousy” (Rom. 13:12–13).

Therefore, as long as you remain in this present life, you walk in the midst of vices [Note: [Col. 1649] Perhaps, “and”], amid worldly pressures, which are the shadow of death.

Let Christ shine in your heart. Through love of God and neighbor he illuminates the lamp of our mind, and you will fear no evil, because he himself is with you. “I will not abandon you,” he says through the Prophet, “nor forsake you” (Josh. 1:5). Likewise in the Gospel: “Behold, I will be with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Your guardian is capable. The Lord your God is with you. Take care that through boasting you do not abandon your companion and remain deserted in the shadow of death.

## 6. The Rod Signifies Discipline; the Staff, Assistance. The Table Prepared through Christ

When, therefore, you recognize that you are attacked by the enemy’s snares in the shadow and frightened by them, seize the rod of discipline and confidently lean upon the staff of mercy. Then, when Christ, the sun of righteousness, shines upon you with help, you may truly say: “Your rod and your staff have themselves comforted me.”

The rod governs the proud, according to what is said in the second Psalm concerning Christ: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them” (Ps. 2:9). The staff, however, supports the weak and the weary.

Remember, therefore, the correction and discipline of the rod, so that when you have been filled with the good gifts of God you may not be lifted up by pride and murmur against him, because, like a potter’s vessel, in his anger he will shatter you.

Remember also the help of the staff. Do not trust in your own strength, and do not say, “I am holy; I cannot stumble.” Our weakness has many falls, and, while still placed upon the earth that produces thorns and thistles, it is neither governed by the holiness of its works nor possesses the glory of purity. Until it returns to the earth from which it was taken, it cannot stand unless it is governed by the staff of divine grace.

Whether, therefore, you prosper in God or are troubled by the storm of temptations, throw your whole self upon the staff of God’s mercy. Then, when you recline upon it to be nourished by spiritual gifts and are delighted by the taste of its sweetness, you will fittingly say: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me. You have anointed my head with oil, and how glorious is your cup, which intoxicates!”

The whole Church, supported throughout the world by the staff of grace, sings this. Against the heretics, Jews, and Gentiles who trouble her by mocking her, she proclaims it, glorying not in herself but in the Lord.

The table of joy is Christ’s passion. On the table of the cross he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father, giving his Catholic Church a life-giving banquet: satisfying us with his body, that is, and intoxicating us with his blood.

Fed and given life by this table, the Church rejoices against those who trouble her, having the hope of eternal life through her life, the Lord Christ, who abundantly anointed her with the oil of gladness through the Holy Spirit.

On account of this table the Apostle rebuked the Corinthians who reclined at an idol’s feast, saying: “You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons; you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20–21).

## 7. Preceding and Following Grace

When divine grace, toward which you are hastening, has brought you in, you will recognize the table of the spiritual banquet. Having recognized the truth, each of you will rejoice, give thanks to God, and now fittingly and confidently say: “And your mercy will follow me all the days of my life.”

A great consolation of glory accompanies you. Because of the misery of your weakness, God’s mercy follows you. But first, in order to show you the way of eternal life, it goes before you—that is, it precedes you—according to what he says in another psalm: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11).

His mercy therefore goes before you: it leads you, ignorant of the way, onto the road; it calls you to God, though you have gone far from God; it draws the slave of sin so as to make him free, so that, by walking along the way all the days of your life, you may not go astray.

It also follows you, guarding your rear, lest the serpent-devil, lying in wait at your heel and with whom you are at enmity, trip you up. A robber kills either by encountering someone face-to-face or by rising up behind him. For this reason God’s mercy goes before you and follows you, so that you may walk safely and securely in the midst of it all the days of your life.

Therefore place your hope and glory not in yourself but in God’s mercy, which goes before you and follows you. Through it you were anticipated as a sinner, so that you might be saved; you were not found righteous so that you might glory in having pleased God.

## 8. The End of Grace and of the Christian Profession

Consider where he leads you, if you do not abandon the one who leads you. He does not lead you into the field of worldly misery, so that amid thorns and thistles you may seek bread through labor and sweat. He does not lead you into the dangers of the sea, so that for the sake of commerce you may pursue uncertain profits on a fragile piece of wood, where many have sunk while intent on gain.

He leads you to the house of God, not as a temporary guest, so that you may leave it, but as an inhabitant, so that you may remain in it. For what follows is: “And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.”

This house of the Lord is paradise. Length of days is eternal life. There you will neither hunger nor thirst, nor labor beneath the heat of sun and moon; you will not feel cold or the storms of winter. Sadness and sorrow are not there. You will be blessed forever in the fellowship of the saints. You will rejoice and exult with them, living and praising God for ages of ages.

For in another psalm he says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ages of ages they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

This is the hope of your faith, beloved. You have approached the Lord in order to believe. Hurry and strive to grasp, through a good manner of life, what you have believed. For you are not made Christians on account of the present life, but on account of the future life, which the Lord Christ himself grants to you who believe and persevere in him—he who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCCLXVII

[Note: [Col. 1650] Compared with two manuscripts designated bn. and four designated cl., and with cb., f., fs., g., lr., m., pr., rm., vd., and with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1650] Elsewhere, 25 among the sermons On the Words of the Lord.]

Concerning the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 16:19–31, where it speaks of the rich man and Lazarus.

[Note: [Col. 1650] All the manuscripts, in considerable number, attribute this sermon to Augustine. But the character of its diction—improper, inelegant, and ending rhythmically, with sentences often deliberately concluded by a similar sound of words—does not allow unquestioning confidence to be attached to them. The Louvain editors had doubts; Verlinus judged it spurious; Vindingus, moreover, held that it should rightly and deservedly be inscribed under Augustine’s name, if the style did not forbid it.]

# CHAPTER ONE
## 1. Comparison of the Rich Man with the Poor Lazarus. Insatiable Avarice

Your Holiness, dearest brothers, has observed and, as I think, perceived with the full attention of your mind the rich man’s abundance and the beggar’s poverty: one burning with food, the other wasting away from hunger. Both were human beings, both fleshly, both mortal—but they were not both equal. Their nature was one, but their lives were not one. Neither was exempt from the condition of death; yet one feasted splendidly, while the other lay filthy in rags and misery. The former rejoiced in delicate foods prepared by the ingenuity of cooks; the latter waited for crumbs to fall from his table.

Let the rich now hear, those who refuse to be merciful; let them hear that we are all born under one law, live beneath one light, breathe one air, and are likewise extinguished in one death. If death did not intervene, not even the poor man himself would endure. This Lazarus, lying ulcerous and naked, is carried by angels’ hands to Abraham’s bosom. Behold, the rich man, well fed and splendid, is shut up in a Tartarean prison. Where is that garment of fine linen? Where is that life abundant and overflowing with many possessions? Do not all things pass away in death like a shadow? “We brought nothing into this world,” says the Apostle, “and neither can we take anything away” (1 Tim. 6:7). We take or snatch nothing with us. If we were to take anything, would we not devour living human beings? What is this greed of desire, when even the beasts themselves have a limit? For they seize only when hungry, but spare their prey when they feel satiated. The avarice of the rich alone is insatiable. It always seizes and is never satisfied; it neither fears God nor respects man; it spares neither father nor acknowledges mother; it neither obeys brother nor keeps faith with friend; it oppresses the widow and invades the property of the orphan; it recalls freedmen into slavery and produces a false will. The possessions of the dead are occupied, as though those who do this did not themselves also die. What, then, is this madness of souls: to lose life and seek death, to acquire gold and lose heaven? But because no one thinks of God, judgment remains in death.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Why the Rich Man Was Condemned

It was rightly said to the rich man: “Because you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented.” Let the rich now hear who refuse to be merciful. Let them hear that punishments are imposed on those who refuse to distribute assistance. Let them hear of the poor man refreshed and of the rich man burning in heavier torments. “Father Abraham,” he says, “send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame.” But he replied: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

Punishment is weighed out in proportion to riches, refreshment in proportion to poverty, flame in proportion to purple, and nourishment in proportion to nakedness, so that the balance of equity may remain sound and the measure of that reckoning may not lie: “With the measure,” he says, “with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2). Therefore mercy is denied the rich man in his punishments because, while he lived, he refused to show mercy. Therefore the rich man, begging, is not heard in his torments, because on earth he did not hear the poor man who begged.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. An Exhortation to Almsgiving

The rich man and the poor man are two things opposed to each other, but again they are two things necessary to each other. No one would be in need if they supported one another, and no one would labor if the two helped each other. The rich man was made for the poor man, and the poor man was made for the rich man. It is the poor man’s part to pray, and the rich man’s to distribute; it is God’s part to weigh great things in return for small ones.

From His mercy, great abundance is born from a small gift. The field of the poor is fertile: it quickly returns fruit to those who rule it. The poor man is the road to heaven, by which one comes to the Father. Begin, therefore, to distribute, if you do not wish to go astray. In this life, loosen the fetter of your patrimony, by which you are bound, so that you may be able to approach heaven freely. Cast away from yourself the burdens of riches; cast away voluntary chains; cast away the anxieties and wearinesses that disturb you for many years.

Give to the one who asks, so that you yourself may be able to receive. Give to the poor, if you do not wish to be burned by flames. Give to Christ on earth what He may return to you in heaven. Forget what you are, and attend to what you will be. The present life is fragile and inclined toward death. No one can remain standing; all are compelled to pass on. We go unwillingly; we depart against our will, because we are evil. But if we were to send something ahead of us, we would not come to an empty lodging. What we give to the poor, we send ahead of ourselves; but whatever we seize, we leave here entirely.

## SERMON CCCLXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1652] Collated with two manuscripts, with gr. rm. v., and with Am. Er. Par. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1652] Elsewhere, 37 among the Fifty Homilies.]

On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter 12:25, “Whoever loves his life will lose it,” and on the words of the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter 5:29, “No one has ever hated his own flesh.”

[Note: [Col. 1652] The Louvain editors published it without Augustine’s name, as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus, however, rejected it as spurious. What both of them criticize in the words before the third chapter—“You certainly see now, if someone’s life …,” etc.—where they complain that a passage of Augustine from Sermon 161, chapter 4, has been reproduced or imitated unsuccessfully, may here have been inserted by the hand of some interpolator. In our opinion, the sermon is worthy of Augustine, and the title noted by Possidius in the Index, chapter 8, easily suits it: “On the Apostle, ‘No one has ever hated his own flesh,’ and from the Gospel, ‘Whoever loves his life,’” etc. In ancient lectionaries it is assigned to “the feast of Saints Fabian and Sebastian, martyrs.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. How Can Someone Love His Life and Yet Lose It?

Just now, brothers, when the divine reading was being read, we heard the Lord saying, “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” This statement seems almost contrary to what the Apostle says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” If, then, there is no one who hates his flesh, how much more is there no one who hates his life? For the soul is valued far above the flesh: the soul is the inhabitant, while the flesh is the dwelling; the soul rules, while the flesh serves; the soul is superior, while the flesh is subject.

If, then, no one has ever hated his own flesh, who is there who hates his life? For this reason the present Gospel reading has brought us no small question, since we heard: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” It is dangerous to love one’s life, lest it perish. But if it is dangerous for you to love your life lest your life perish, then you ought not to love it because you do not want it to perish. Yet if you do not want it to perish, you love it. What is this? If I love it, I lose it. Therefore, let me not love it, lest I lose it. But because I fear losing it, I therefore do not love it; and certainly I love what I fear losing.

The Lord also says elsewhere: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). Behold, the soul must be loved in such a way that it is preferred to the gain of the whole world; and yet the one who loves his soul must take heed, because if he loves it, he will lose it. You do not want to lose it? Do not love it. But if you do not want to lose it, you cannot fail to love it.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. A Certain Perverse Love and a Certain Proper Hatred of the Soul

There are, then, people who perversely love their souls. God’s word wishes to correct this—not so that they may hate their souls, but so that they may love them rightly. By loving it wrongly, they lose it, and something great takes place as though backward and contrary: nevertheless, it happens in such a way that if you love it perversely, you lose it; if you hate it rightly, you preserve it.

There is, therefore, a certain perverse love of the soul and a certain proper hatred of it. But perverse love comes from hatred, and proper hatred comes from love of it. What is the soul’s perverse love? It is when you love your soul in iniquities. Hear that this perverse love comes from hatred: “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

Now observe that proper hatred comes from love. The Lord continues in the same passage: “But whoever hates his soul in this world will find it for eternal life.” Certainly, whatever you wish to find in eternal life, you love greatly. For what benefit is it to love something temporarily? Either you will be taken away from it, or it will be taken away from you. When you have been taken away, the lover himself perishes; when it has been taken away, what you loved perishes. Therefore, where either the lover perishes or what is loved perishes, one must not love.

But what should be loved? What can remain with us forever. If you wish, then, to possess your soul eternally safe, hate it for a time. Proper hatred, therefore, comes from love; perverse love comes from hatred.

### 3. The Proper Way to Love the Soul. Two Kinds of Love

What, then, is the proper way to love the soul? Do you suppose that the martyrs did not love their souls? You certainly see now, if someone’s life in this present age is endangered, how his friends run on his behalf: how they hurry to the church and ask the bishop to interrupt whatever proceedings he may have, and to run and hasten. Why? For the sake of the soul. Everyone trembles, and, setting all other matters aside, decides that one must hurry. Every haste is praised; every delay is blamed. Why? For the sake of the soul.

What does “for the sake of the soul” mean? That the man should not die. The martyrs did not know how to love their souls—and yet this is “for the sake of the soul”: that a man should not die.

## CHAPTER III

### The Death of an Unrighteous Man

If you run a hundred thousand paces for this life, how many thousands ought you to run for eternal life? If you hasten to gain a few days, and even those uncertain—for today a man may have been freed from death, yet he does not know whether he will die tomorrow—nevertheless, if people run in this way for the sake of gaining a few days, since even the years leading to old age are few, how ought one to run for eternal life? And yet people are sluggish regarding this.

You scarcely find anyone who even moves slowly a single step for eternal life. Perverse love of the soul, therefore, is abundant; proper love is found among very few. For just as there is no one who does not love his soul, so there is no one who does not love his flesh. How, then, can what the Apostle says also be true—“No one has ever hated his own flesh”—while the soul is not loved?

Let us learn, therefore, brothers, to love our souls. Every pleasure of this world is passing. There is beneficial love, and there is harmful love. Love is obstructed by love: let harmful love withdraw, and let beneficial love take its place. But because people do not wish to withdraw from that harmful love, nothing else can enter them. So that they may not receive, they are full; let them pour out, and they will receive.

They are full of love for bodily pleasures, full of love for the present life, full of love for gold and silver and the possessions of this world. Those who are full are like vessels. Do you want honey to enter where you have not yet poured out vinegar? Pour out what you have, so that you may receive what you do not have.

Therefore the first renunciation is of this world, and afterward comes conversion to God. Whoever renounces pours out; whoever converts is filled—but only if this is done not with the body alone, but also with the heart.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. The Beginnings of Love

But, brothers, the question arises how this love grows. It has its beginnings, its increases, and its perfection. We ought to know who has begun, so that we may encourage him toward growth; who has not begun, so that we may admonish him to begin; and who has both begun and grown, so that we may urge him toward perfection.

First let Your Charity attend to this: all loves and affections in human beings are first directed toward themselves, and then toward the other thing they love. If you love gold, you first love yourself and then gold, because if you were dead, there would be no one to possess the gold. Therefore affection begins for each person with himself, and it cannot begin anywhere else. No one needs to be urged to love himself. This is present not only in human beings, but also in animals.

You see, brothers, how not only huge beasts and large animals, such as oxen, camels, or elephants, but also flies and the smallest worms do not wish to die and love themselves. All animals flee death. Therefore they love themselves and wish to preserve themselves: some by speed, others by hiding places, others by resisting and fighting back. Nevertheless, all animals fight for their lives; they do not wish to die; they wish to preserve themselves. They love themselves.

Begin to love something else as well. But what is this “something else”? Whatever you love is either equal to you, inferior to you, or superior to you. If what you love is inferior to you, love it for consolation, love it for handling, love it for use—not for enslavement.

For example, you love gold. Do not bind yourself to gold. How much better are you than gold? Gold is shining earth; you, however, were made in the image of God so that you might be illumined by the Lord. Although gold is God’s creature, God did not make gold in His image, but you. Therefore He placed gold beneath you.

This love, then, must be despised. These things are to be taken up for use; one must not cling to them as though attached by the glue of love. Do not make them your limbs, so that when they begin to be cut off you suffer and are tormented. What, then? Rise up from this love by which you love things inferior to yourself; begin to love equals—that is, what you are.

But why say more? If you wish, you can do this briefly.

## CHAPTER V

### 5. How True and Good Love Is Acquired in Its Proper Order

The Lord Himself told us in the Gospel, and clearly showed us, in what order we can possess true love and true charity. For He says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37, 39).

First, therefore, love God; then yourself; after this, love your neighbor as yourself. First, however, learn to love yourself; thus love your neighbor as yourself. For if you do not know how to love yourself, how will you be able to love your neighbor in truth?

Some people think that they love themselves in the proper order when they seize what belongs to others, when they get drunk, when they serve lust, and when they seek unjust profits through various slanders. Let such people hear Scripture saying: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

If, then, by loving iniquity you not only fail to love yourself but even hate yourself, how will you be able to love either God or your neighbor? If, therefore, you wish to preserve the order of true charity, practice justice, love mercy, flee lust; begin, according to the Lord’s commandment, to love not only friends but also enemies.

When you have faithfully striven with your whole heart to keep these things, you will be able, as though by certain steps, to ascend through these virtues, so that you may deserve to love God with your whole mind and all your strength. And when you have reached this blessed perfection, you will count all the desires of this world as dung; and with the prophet you will be able to say: “But for me, to cling to God is good” (Ps. 72:28).

## SERMON CCCLXIX

[Note: [Col. 1655] Collated with three manuscripts, with cb. and two n., with f. gr. r. t., and with Am. Er. Par. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1655] Elsewhere, On Time 5.]

On the Nativity of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 1655] The Louvain editors doubt whether it is Augustine’s. Vindingus, on the contrary, says that it contains nothing on account of which it should be denied to him; indeed, he asserts that it is Augustine’s on the authority of an ancient writer, in the *Conflict of Arnobius and Serapion*, at the end of which work this entire sermon is recited. But the author of this fictitious *Conflict*—the bishop Vigilius, who, according to Vindingus’s own conjecture in the *Augustinian Criticism*, volume 6—does not thereafter deserve any credibility in this matter, since he was convicted of publishing his own writings against the Arians under the falsely claimed names of earlier Fathers. He strives to imitate Augustine’s style, in order to prove that in this sermon Augustine preached Christ’s two births. Compare Sermon 117 of the Appendix.]

### 1. Christ’s Two Births: One Before Every Day, the Other on a Day. Christ’s Birth Illuminated by Divine Testimonies

Our Savior, born from the Father without a day, through whom every day was made, wished to have on earth this birthday—the day we celebrate today. Whoever marvels at this day—

[Note: [Col. 1655] The manuscripts read, “marvels in the day.”]

—should rather marvel at the One who remains before every day, creates every day, is born on this present day, and frees us from the evil of the day.

Marvel still further. She who gave birth is both mother and virgin; the one she gave birth to is both infant and Word. Rightly, the heavens spoke, the angels rejoiced, the shepherds were glad. The Magi were changed—

[Note: [Col. 1655] So the better manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read, “The Magi were invited.”]

—kings were troubled, and little children were crowned.

Nurse, mother, our food; nurse the bread coming from heaven and placed in a manger like food for pious animals. For there the ox recognized its owner and the donkey its master’s manger (Isa. 1:3)—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision, joined to the cornerstone, whose first representatives were the shepherds and the Magi.

Nurse Him who made you such that He Himself might become in you; who in His conception brought you the gift of fertility, and in His birth did not take away the honor of virginity; who chose for Himself, before He was born, both the womb from which He would be born and the day on which He would be born. He Himself also created what He chose, so that from there He might come forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, where He could be seen by mortal eyes, and by the yearly increase of light testify that He had come as the light of minds.

The prophets sang that the Creator of heaven and earth would be on earth with human beings. The angel announced that the Creator of flesh and spirit would come in the flesh. John greeted the Savior from womb to womb; the aged Simeon recognized God as an infant; the widow Anna recognized the virgin mother.

These are the testimonies to Your birth, Lord Jesus, before the waves were subjected beneath Your feet as You trod upon them, and before they yielded to You as You commanded; before the wind grew still at Your order, the dead lived when You called, the sun grew dark at Your death, the earth trembled at Your resurrection, and heaven opened at Your ascension; before You had performed these and other wonders in the age of Your now youthful body.

You were still being carried in Your mother’s hands, and already You were recognized as Lord of the world. The very child, a little one from the seed of Israel, was Himself God with us, Emmanuel.

### 2. Christ’s Eternal Birth

What is that generation of our Savior by which He is coeternal with the Father who begets Him, when the world shuddered at this generation from a virgin, which devout faith recognized and held, but unbelief mocked and pride feared after being overcome?

What is that generation in which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)? Or what is this Word, which did not remain silent before it was spoken, and which, once spoken, did not silence the One who spoke? What is the Word without time, through which times were made? The Word which no one’s lips opened by beginning, nor closed by ending; the Word which does not have its beginning from the mouth of speakers, and opens the mouths of the mute; the Word which is not made eloquent by the articulate tongues of nations, and makes the tongues of infants articulate.

What, I ask, is that generation in which the Father does not yield by dying, because He does not precede it by living? Let us raise our soul away from all intervals of places and times [Note: [Col. 1656] Here the printed editions and some manuscripts add “separated,” or “alien.”], from every extension of spaces that we are accustomed to perceive either in days or in bodies, as far as we can with His help, so that we may somehow comprehend both the One who begets without preceding the One born and the One born without following the One who begets—the Father and the Son—not equally fathers and not equally sons, but equally eternal; neither both begetting nor both being born, but neither living without the other.

Let us think, if we are able, that the Father eternally begot and the Son was eternally born; if we are not able, let us believe. There is nothing here that we can adequately say, and yet He is not far from each one of us: “For in Him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

Let us transcend our flesh, in which parents live before their children: they grew so that they could beget children, and when their children grow, they already grow old. Before their children were born, the parents lived; for after their parents have died, their children will also live.

Let us transcend our souls as well. They too give birth to something by thinking, something they possess with themselves through knowing; but they can lose it through forgetting, because they did not possess it beforehand by being born.

Let us transcend all bodily, temporal, and mutable things, so that we may see the One above all things through whom all things were made. Our ascent is in the heart, because the One to whom we ascend is also near. We are far from Him insofar as we are unlike Him. His likeness, therefore, which He made and remade in us, ascends to Him; but since it is not yet perfect, our weakened sight gropes and cannot behold the ineffable brightness of eternal light.

Whose radiance the mind’s vision does not yet grasp—who will recount His generation? (Isa. 53:8). But “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

### 3. Christ’s Temporal Birth

Let us therefore praise, love, and adore this generation whose day we celebrate today: the generation in which He deigned to come through Israel and become Emmanuel, God with us in the weakness of the flesh, though not with us in the iniquity of the heart; approaching us through what He assumed from us and freeing us through what remained His own.

For the Lord visited His servants through mortal weakness, so that He might make them free through unchangeable truth. Let us praise, love, and adore this generation, of which human frailty is in some measure capable—not that generation which remains without time and, without a mother, is above all things, but this one which took place in time and, without a father, is among all things: this son of a virgin and bridegroom of virgins, born from an incorrupt mother and bearing incorruptible truth.

Thus, through His mercy, let us triumph over the devil’s defeated cunning. The devil crept toward us to deceive us through a corrupted female mind; Christ came forth to free us through incorruptible female flesh also. He is blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCCLXX

[Note: [Col. 1657] Corrected against three manuscripts, against f. n. r. t. v., and against Am. Er. Par. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1657] Elsewhere, On Time 20.]

On the Nativity of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 1657] This sermon is doubtful to us because of its uncultivated and less careful style. For example, after the four modes of humanity’s creation have been listed, what follows—“But this fourth condition freed the three. For the first and second fell, they produced the third from their fall,” etc.—is expressed obscurely and improperly. Here and there one finds several things resembling genuine sermons of Augustine on the Nativity of the Lord.]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Four Kinds of Humanity’s Birth or Creation

The present day has brought great joy to the human race, so that it may possess hope of eternal life. For the first man, at whose fall we all fell, whose ruin is our mortality, was not born but made, with no father and no mother, but with God at work. This is the first condition of humanity: Adam from the earth.

The second condition of humanity is that by which woman was created from the man’s side. The third condition of humanity is that by which a human being was born from man and woman. The fourth condition is that of God and humanity, by which Christ was born without a man from a woman.

Of these four conditions, only one is familiar to us; the other three are not before the eyes of the flesh, but in the faith of the heart. We do not know from experience of a man made from earth without father or mother; we have believed what we read and heard about woman made from man’s side. The third is familiar to us: human beings are born every day from the union of man and woman.

There was already one birth without man and woman; there was already another from man without woman; there was already a third from man and woman; the fourth remained—without man, from woman. But this fourth freed the three. The first and second fell; they produced the third from their fall; in the fourth they found salvation.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Every Rank of the Faithful Bears Witness to the Savior Born for All

Let virgins rejoice: a virgin gave birth to Christ. Let them not think that anything they vowed was destroyed in her: she remained a virgin after childbirth.

[Note: [Col. 1657] Louvain reads “what she had vowed,” against the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

Let widows rejoice: the widow Anna recognized the infant Christ. Let married women rejoice: Elizabeth, herself married, prophesied the Lord Jesus Christ who was to be born. No rank has been omitted that does not possess testimony to the salvation of all.

For do only virgins reach the kingdom of heaven? Widows reach it too.

[Note: [Col. 1657] See Sermon 184, chapter 2, and Sermon 192, chapter 2.]

That holy widow Anna was of great merit. She had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; after his death she reached old age, and in holy old age awaited the Savior’s infancy, so that, being aged, she might see the little one; being an old woman, recognize the little one; and, about to depart from the world, see the Savior entering it (Luke 2:36–38).

The same three kinds are also commended in the male sex. Christ Himself was born a child; let boys rejoice, those who vow chastity to the Child. He truly consecrated the integrity of chastity: He brought fertility to His mother but did not take away her virginity.

That old man Simeon had lived for a long time, and his age is compared with Anna’s. He had received the revelation that he would not see death before he had first seen the Christ of the Lord.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. How Great Was the Desire of the Ancient Saints to See the Christ Who Was to Be Born?

Understand, brothers, how great was the desire of the ancient saints to see Christ. They knew that He would come, and all who lived piously said: “If only that birth should find me alive! If only I might see with my own eyes what I believe in the Scriptures of God!”

And so that you may know how great was the desire of the saints who knew from the holy Scriptures that a virgin would give birth, as you heard when Isaiah was read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). The Gospel explained to us what Emmanuel means, saying that it is interpreted, “God with us” (Matt. 1:23).

Therefore, let no unbelieving soul be astonished; let it not seem impossible to you that a virgin should give birth and remain a virgin while giving birth. Understand that God was born, and you will not marvel at a virgin’s childbirth.

And so that you may know that the ancient saints and righteous longed to see what was granted to this old man Simeon, our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking to His disciples, said: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17).

This old man was very late in hearing, but mature for seeing. He did not wait to hear Christ speaking, because he recognized Him as an infant. This too had been granted to him when he was already decrepit, as though he were longing, sighing, and saying daily in his prayers: “When will He come? When will He be born? When will I see Him? Do you suppose I will last? Do you suppose He will find me alive? Do you suppose these eyes of mine will see the One through whom the eyes of the heart will be opened?”

He said these things in his prayers, and because of his longing he received the response that he would not taste death before he had first seen the Christ of the Lord. Mary, His mother, carried Him as an infant. Simeon saw Him and recognized Him. Where had he known the One he recognized? Was He revealed within, the One who was born outside? He saw Him and recognized Him.

Simeon recognized the infant who was silent; the Jews killed the young man who performed wonders. When he had recognized Him, he took Him in his arms—that is, in his embrace—and embraced Him. He carried the One by whom he was carried.

For He is Christ, the Wisdom of God, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). How great was He there, and how great was He made here? He was made little and sought the little. What does “He sought the little” mean? Not the proud or the haughty, but He gathered the humble and gentle.

He deigned to be placed in a manger, so that He might be the food of pious animals. Simeon therefore took Him in his arms and said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.” You dismiss me in peace because I see peace. Why, then, do You dismiss me in peace? “Because my eyes have seen Your salvation” (Luke 2:25–30).

The salvation of God is the Lord Jesus Christ. “Announce His salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2).

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Children, Old Men, and Married People Bear Witness to Christ

You have, then, children, the child Jesus; holy old men, the old man Simeon. But if you seek a married man also to bear witness to the Lord, consider Zechariah.

Let no one, therefore, my brothers, faithful Christians, seek anything else—whether virgin, widow, married woman, child, celibate, or married man. Whatever further state anyone might wish to be, he finds no way in which he may belong to Christ.

We do not find adulterers, fornicators, or the impure bearing witness to Christ. Yet if testimony were to be borne to Him by such people, He Himself provided it; He Himself granted it. For no holy man possesses holiness by his own strength.

[Note: [Col. 1659] Similar material occurs in Sermon 196, chapter 2.]

Let us therefore rejoice, dearest ones. From this day onward the days grow longer. Believe in Christ, and the day grows in you. Have you believed? The day has begun. Have you been baptized? Christ has been born in your heart.

But did Christ remain as He was born? He grew and reached youth, but He did not decline into old age. Let your faith therefore also grow; let it find strength and know no old age. In this way you will belong to Christ, the Son of God, the Word in the beginning with God, the Word who was God—but the Word made flesh so that He might dwell among us.

Majesty lay hidden where weakness appeared. Simeon took weakness into his hands, but inwardly recognized majesty. Let no one despise the One who was born, if he wishes to be reborn. It belonged to Him to be born for our sake; let it belong to us to be reborn in Him. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCCLXXI

[Note: [Col. 1659] Missing from our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1659] Elsewhere, On Various Matters 52.]

On the Nativity of the Lord, III

[Note: [Col. 1659] It is read under Augustine’s name in the Paris Breviary. Certainly it contains many of Augustine’s opinions, especially in the first and second chapters, but these have been excerpted from the sermon on the Nativity of John the Baptist below, number 380, where everything is more genuine and more suitably connected. It also contains much that is manifestly foreign to Augustine’s spirit or style, such as the following: chapter 1, “And so that the servant might be changed into the lord”; and in the same place, “So that the day might rightly lengthen the sun’s course,” etc.; chapter 2, “And might establish for His future worshipers the mysteries of a repeated birth.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Christ’s Two Births

A Savior has been born for us today; and therefore today the true sun has risen upon the whole world. God became human so that the human might become God; and so that the servant might be changed into the lord, the Lord took the form of a servant.

The inhabitant of heaven dwelt on earth, so that the human inhabitant of earth might dwell in heaven. A Savior, therefore, has been born for us; He submitted to the day of birth, the conception of the rejected Law: born from the Father always, from His mother once.

For we have received two births of our Lord Jesus Christ: first the divine, then the human—but plainly both are wondrous. In the one, the functions of a mother ceased; in the other, those of a father ceased: one was eternal, so that He might create temporal beings; the other was temporal, so that He might grant eternal things.

He, therefore, in the form of God, was equal to the Father; He, in the form of a servant, was subject to the Father. He, the Creator of times, was born in time; and He was made so small that a woman could give birth to Him, yet He remained so great that He was not separated from the Father.

The beginnings of the two Gospels also bear witness to these births of the Lord. One evangelist speaks in this way of the divine birth: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

Of the human birth, another evangelist reports as follows: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matt. 1:1).

This, then, is the Lord’s birthday; this is the day of His second birth. Let us rejoice and be glad in it. Not without reason, since from this point onward the day has already begun to grow, today light receives increase, since on this day the true light came to the human race: so that the day might rightly lengthen the sun’s course, through which He brought us the One who would free us from the darkness of death.

The prophets, announcing Him as future like lamps, went before the day of His birth and proclaimed in the clearest testimonies the miracles He would perform in the flesh. For it was right that it should be preached that He would come, so that when He came there would be no doubt.

Thus our God lived as a human being among human beings. He appeared as human to those who saw, God to those who understood; offering humanity to those who looked upon Him, preserving God for those who believed. He therefore saved the weak by the appearance of His weakness; He seeks the strong for contemplation of His divinity.

## CHAPTER II
## 2. In the Incarnation God is made visible, so that man may follow him

I beseech you, dearly beloved, contemplate how great is this mystery of truth. For the salvation of human beings he had given the Law and sent the Prophets; and because these remedies had preceded for the healing of our sicknesses, God willed to offer himself to human beings for their salvation. Yet human beings could not see God himself in his substance, while they ought not to place their hope in a mere human being. What, then, was to happen? They ought not to follow a human being, but the one who could be seen was not to be followed; God, who could not be seen, was to be followed. Therefore, so that there might be presented to humanity one who could both be seen by humanity and followed by humanity, God became man.

Finally, when he was already moving among human beings and stood in their midst after taking the three apostles aside privately, he suddenly shone before them in that splendor of divine worship. The apostles who were present could scarcely gaze upon it because of the weakness of human feeling (ibid. XVII, 1–6). He willed to be born as a human being, so that we might be born in him, and so that he might establish for his future worshipers the mysteries of a repeated birth. Thus we, who were held captive and subject to that first birth, might, following the footsteps of our Savior, securely obtain the protection of a second birth; and, born in God and from God, might break the bonds of the ancient death when we received the pledge of salvation, the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when God wished to appear to human beings and also, while present, desired to teach them the things he had previously commanded, he moderated the divine power by assuming humanity, and “he made darkness his hiding place round about him” (Psalm XVII, 12), when he covered himself with the tabernacle of the flesh. Thus, through such a great and ineffable mystery, Christ our God is both held to be man and God: man through his mother, God through his Father. And so both of these statements are true which he made: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28), and, “I and the Father are one” (ibid. X, 30). For in divinity he is equal to the Father; in the Incarnation he is subject to the Father.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. How God and man could be mingled. The mingling of soul and body is more difficult

Yet some people customarily ask how man and God could be mingled. They seek an explanation of this mystery, which happened once, although they themselves can in no way explain what happens continually: namely, how the soul is mingled with the body so that a human being comes into existence. Therefore, just as a corporeal and an incorporeal thing are joined together so that a human being may be formed, so man was joined to God, and Christ came into being.

And yet, for Christ to come into being, those two incorporeal realities—that is, the soul and God—could more readily be joined and mingled than one incorporeal and another corporeal reality, namely soul and body, are mingled so that the person of a human being may exist.

[Note: [Col. 1660] See the letter to Volusianus, 137, no. 11.]

But if God, the creator of heaven and earth, although he was God, became man and “humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross” (Philippians II, 6–8), how much ought earth and ashes not to be proud? See, brothers, how greatly God humbled himself for human beings. How greatly ought a servant to humble himself, when the Lord descended to such profound humility?

This humility, dearly beloved, if it is possessed by human beings in its fullness, will also advance as far as love. For while each person considers the other superior, love creates equality. Therefore let a human being not despise himself, for whose sake God was willing to undergo these things.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Human dignity arising from God’s condescension toward humanity

And indeed, brothers, although I have always regarded you as great in my conscience—you for whom I desire to spend myself and be spent beyond measure—this very matter makes you greater in a certain way, when I consider how great was the condescension of my Lord toward humanity.

You are the price of the Lord’s Incarnation; you are the price of the Lord’s blood; you are members of Christ, and Christ is your head. For your sake he did not hesitate to be born; for your sake he did not hesitate to suffer all things. He even endured the cross for this purpose: to join you to himself as members of his household. You are called Christ’s brothers; you are called Christ’s heirs.

Therefore, dearly beloved, let each person regard himself as worthy of respect before one whom he ought not to sin; let him consider himself worthy of respect before one in whose presence he would blush if he conceived a sinful act. For you were bought at a great price: “glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians VI, 20).

He was born for your sake; he was offered for your sake; he also dwells in you, if you act worthily. Let us therefore act, meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, so that we may deserve to grasp him and see him. Let us act so that, since God deigned to descend for the sake of human beings, a human being may be able to ascend to God.

# SERMON 372

[Note: [Col. 1661] This sermon too is missing from our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1661] Elsewhere, *On Various Matters* 54.]

## On the Nativity of the Lord, IV

[Note: [Col. 1661] Not everything here has the character of Augustine. The opening, “Born from the Father without sexuality, from the mother without intercourse,” appears to have been expressed with insufficient accuracy. The first part of the same sentence, “He was born from the Father always,” etc., is also found in the preceding sermon. Before the end, Ambrose’s hymn on the Nativity of Christ is quoted; it had been sung shortly before. Perhaps the custom of singing Ambrosian hymns in church had been introduced into Africa by Augustine? He himself says in Letter 55, written around the year 400, that Catholics were reproached by the Donatists “because they sing soberly in the divine church the sacred songs of the Prophets, whereas they,” he says, “inflame their drunkenness with songs composed by human ingenuity to the accompaniment of psalms.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Christ’s two births

Your faith, dearly beloved, which has gathered this entire multitude together, knows that a Savior has been born for us today. He was born from the Father eternally, from his mother once; from the Father without sexual generation, from his mother without intercourse.

With the Father there was no womb of one conceiving; with his mother there was no embrace of one sowing. The first birth from the Father preserved nature; the second birth from his mother sowed grace. The former retained the majesty of divine substance; the latter accepted association with human mortality.

In this latter birth he deigned to come for the purpose of becoming “obedient even to death” (Philippians II, 6–8), and by dying to conquer death. Both births are ineffable; both are wondrous. What human heart could comprehend, or what tongue explain, how Christ was eternally born from God, or how recently from a womb? Who can understand the Father coeternal with the Son? Who can express the virgin mother? The one begetting without beginning and without end; the other conceiving without lust and giving birth without corruption?

[Col. 1662] Both births are marvelous because they are divine. Whether, then, the human mind considers the one or the other, it most rightly says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8).

And what shall we do, brothers? Since we cannot speak of it worthily, ought we to remain silent? Far be it from us—far be it that the tongue of a servant should be silent when it is the Lord’s birthday. Let us therefore say what we can, what we have read.

### 2. Jews and Gentiles invited to Christ’s wedding. We are nourished by Christ’s flesh and blood. Christ the bridegroom and giant, beautiful and strong

Blessed David, speaking of Christ, says in the Psalms: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant” (Psalm XVIII, 6).

For today he came forth from the sacred bridal chamber—that is, from the hidden and incorrupt secret place of blessed virgin limbs. From there came forth the son of a virgin, the bridegroom of a virgin: the son, clearly, of Mary; the bridegroom of the Church. For the Apostle was speaking to the whole Church when he said: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians XI, 2).

## CHAPTER II

To this kind of wedding of Christ, the Father of the bridegroom first invited the Jewish people. But what does the Gospel say? “Those who had been invited were not worthy” (Matthew XXII, 8).

Afterward the multitude of all the Gentiles was invited. It filled the Church; it received from the Lord’s table not cheap foods or lowly drinks, but tasted beforehand the flesh and blood of Christ himself, the shepherd himself, the one who was slain.

The innocent lamb himself was slain for his wedding; he was slain for the wedding, and he nourished all whom he invited with his flesh. Slain, he prepared the banquet; rising again, he celebrated the wedding. Slain, he endured a voluntary passion; rising again, he took the appointed bride as his wife.

In the virgin’s womb he accepted human flesh as a pledge; on the cross he poured out his blood as his most precious dowry; in his resurrection and ascension he strengthened the covenant of the eternal marriage. For “he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm LXVII, 19).

What gifts? The Holy Spirit, through whom love was poured into human minds, and the Church clung inseparably to Christ as to her husband.

Therefore today he came forth like a bridegroom from his sacred bridal chamber; and, as the Psalm continues, “he rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” He came forth as a bridegroom; he rejoiced as a giant. Beautiful and strong: beautiful as a bridegroom, strong as a giant. Beautiful so that he might be loved; strong so that he might be feared. Beautiful so that he might please; strong so that he might conquer.

Where is the beauty of this bridegroom found in the sacred Scriptures? “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Psalm XLIV, 3). Where is the strength of the giant found? “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm XXIII, 8).

Isaiah had seen and understood both in him—that is, beauty and strength—when he said: “Who is this who comes from Edom? The redness of his garments is from Bosor, so beautiful in his robe, with strength” (Isaiah LXIII, 1). This prophet, then, who called him both beautiful and strong, knew him as bridegroom and giant.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. How Christ ran the course

[Col. 1663] Ambrose’s hymn.

Therefore, dearly beloved, “he rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” What course, if not the mortal course which he deigned to share with us? This is the course through which the human race passes. For people pass through it, being born as they come and dying as they depart. And this stream of the human race flows continuously from the hidden veins of nature, from the beginning to the end.

Christ deigned to drink from this swift and turbulent stream. You have just heard in the Psalm: “He drank from the torrent on the way” (Psalm CIX, 7). This torrent brought us to birth and led us to death. As though from a hidden spring, Christ received the abyss of the sea. He was born and died for us both.

And because human beings, placed in the midst of this stream, are often delighted by the flatteries and enticements of the world—which are wrapped in the mud of this torrent and plunge into the depths of hell those who, while passing through its waves, draw from it in a foolish manner and are thus drowned, wishing to stand in the rushing torrent and seeking firm footing in the unstable commonwealth [Note: [Col. 1663] Perhaps one should read, “and seeking firm footing in an unstable reality.”]—therefore the Lord “drank from the torrent on the way.”

What does “he drank on the way” mean? He drank while passing through. For he drank and passed on; he did not remain, nor did he stand in the way of sinners.

Furthermore, human beings fear death, because all must necessarily be carried away by the force of this torrent. But Christ could not fear the death which he had willingly accepted. Therefore it was said: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course.”

He descended and ran; he ascended and sat down. You know that this is how you customarily profess your faith [Note: [Col. 1663] In the Creed]: after he rose again, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Blessed Ambrose sang of this course of our giant briefly and most beautifully in the hymn which you sang shortly before. Speaking of the Lord Christ, he says:

> “His going forth was from the Father, his return was to the Father;  
> his course extended to the underworld, his return to the seat of God.”

All these things, dearly beloved, if we ask why they happened, we shall find that they happened for us. He descended so that we might ascend; he died so that we might live; he rose so that we might rise; he ascended into heaven so that we might learn to despise earthly things and lift our hearts upward.

Finally, in order to lift our hope after him, he first lifted up his flesh; and so that we might hope that this would follow in us, that which he had received from us went before.

# SERMON 373

[Note: [Col. 1663] Revised against r, rm, v, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1663] Elsewhere, *On Various Matters* 66.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 1663] Some passages are ambiguous; after examining the ancient Floriacensis book, we readily believe that someone’s rashness has introduced a blemish into them, since that book generally omits whatever is objectionable in this sermon, as you will understand from the brackets placed around passages that the codex does not contain.]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Christ manifested to the Magi

The solemnity which we celebrate today received the Greek name *Epiphany* because of the manifestation of the Lord. For today, when the Magi worshiped him as the firstfruits of the Gentiles, the one who had been manifested was commended—the one who, only a few days before, is also said to have been born.

That cornerstone which, like two walls—the wall of circumcision and that of uncircumcision, that is, of Jews and Gentiles—coming from different directions, joined them in his unity, and “became our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians II, 11–22): in order that he might be announced to the Jewish shepherds, angels came from heaven; and in order that he might be worshiped by the Gentile Magi, a star shone from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1664] The oldest Floriacensis book reads: “and so that the Magi, as the first offering of the Gentiles, might be saved, they were warned by a new starlight.”]

Whether, then, through angels or through the star, “the heavens declared the glory of God,” so that, in the grace of the one who was born, the Apostles too might declare it, carrying the Lord like the heavens, and so that “their sound might go forth through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII, 2, 5). Since these words have also reached us, “we believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians IV, 13).

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The same subject continued

Many things, brothers, must therefore be considered in the Gospel reading we have heard. The Magi come from the East; they seek the king of the Jews—a king whom so many Jewish kings had never previously sought.

They seek not someone of mature or advanced age, visible to human eyes, conspicuous on a lofty throne, powerful with armies, terrifying with weapons, shining in purple, glittering with a diadem [or exulting from the cross, on which he would redeem all the confessing martyrs, or rising from the underworld, or ascending into heaven]; but one recently born, lying in a cradle, longing for the breast, distinguished by no bodily adornment, no bodily strength, no parental wealth, neither by his own age nor by the power of his relatives.

And they seek the king of the Jews from the king of the Jews: from Herod [a human being], Christ [God and man; from an earthly human king, the king of heaven who had created humanity]; from an old man, a little child; from one renowned, one hidden; from one exalted, one humble; from one speaking, an infant; from one wealthy, one poor; from one strong, one weak.

And yet [although Herod persecuted Christ, who was Lord over himself and others], they sought one to be worshiped by the very one who despised him: clearly, one in whom no royal pomp was visible, but true majesty was worshiped.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. Herod’s fear and his savagery in the slaughter of the infants. The Innocents endowed with the crown of martyrdom

Finally, Herod is afraid; the Magi desire. They wish to find the king; he fears that he will end the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1664] This is how the Floriacensis manuscript reads. The printed editions have: “He fears a successor; the Magi desire a redeemer. They wish to find the kingdom; he fears that the kingdom will end.”]

At last both seek: the Magi seek one through whom they may live; Herod seeks one whom he wishes to kill. Herod seeks one against whom he may commit a great sin; the Magi seek one who may forgive all their sins.

For Herod kills many little children while wishing to reach the death of one. And when he had carried out a most savage [Note: [Col. 1664] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “most celebrated.”] and bloody slaughter of so many innocent children, he first killed himself through such great wickedness.

Meanwhile our king [Christ], the infant Word [of God], the infant God, while the Magi worshiped him and the little children died for him, was either lying or nursing; and although he had not yet spoken [Note: [Col. 1664] So also that manuscript. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read: “whether he was rising and growing, and had not yet…”], he was finding believers; and although he had not yet suffered, he was already making martyrs.

O blessed little children, newly born, never tempted, not yet having struggled, already crowned! Let the one doubt your crown in suffering for Christ who does not believe that Christ’s baptism benefits little children.

You did not indeed have the age at which you could believe in Christ who was to suffer; but you had the flesh in which you could endure suffering for Christ who was to suffer.

In no way would the grace of the infant Savior abandon these infants. He had come to seek what had perished—not only by being born in the flesh, but also by hanging on the cross [descending to the underworld, ascending into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father].

For he who, at his birth, could have angels as proclaimers, the heavens as narrators, and Magi as worshipers, could also have ensured that these children would not die here for him, if he had known that they would perish through that death rather than live with greater blessedness.

Far be it, far be it that Christ, coming to free human beings, should have done nothing concerning the reward of those who were killed for him—he who, hanging on the tree, prayed for those by whom he was being killed.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. The wretched Jews resemble Noah’s ark-builders and milestone stones

What shall I say about the wretchedness of the Jews, who, when the Magi were seeking Christ, even produced a prophetic indication and designated the city of Bethlehem [which they themselves did not find]?

They resemble the builders of Noah’s ark: they provided others with a means of escape, while they themselves perished in the flood. They resemble milestones: they showed the way, but could not walk [because, foolishly, they remained on the road].

They were asked where Christ would be born. They answered, “In Bethlehem of Judea.” For it is written through the prophet [Note: [Col. 1665] In the Floriacensis manuscript: “They recited from memory what had also been written about this matter: ‘And you, Bethlehem,’ etc.]: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you will come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Matthew II, 1–6).

The seekers heard and departed; the teachers spoke and remained. Separated by contrary dispositions, the former became worshipers, the latter persecutors.

Even now the Jews do not cease to show us something similar. For some pagans, in order to learn that Christ was foretold beforehand, when we offer them clear testimonies from the Scriptures, suspecting that perhaps these things have been fabricated by Christians, prefer to believe the books of the Jews. And, just as the Magi then did, they leave the Jews to read vainly while they themselves go on faithfully to worship.

## CHAPTER V

### 5. A spiritual spectacle in this feast

Let us therefore celebrate, rejoicing in the Lord, the Lord’s feast—not only the day on which he was born from the Jews, but also the day on which he was manifested to the Gentiles.

It is pleasing to contemplate everything and, bringing it together into a single view, to behold it in the mind as a spiritual spectacle.

[Note: [Col. 1665] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “spiritual spectacles.”]

Christ is born: a virgin conceives, a virgin gives birth, a virgin nurses; fertility is present, yet virginity is not absent. Angels announce, shepherds glorify, the heavens declare, the Magi desire, kings fear, Jews point him out, Gentiles worship. The raging are frustrated, infants are crowned, believers marvel.

What is this humble loftiness, this weakness that is strength, this greatness that is small? Surely that Word has done all these things, the Word through whom all things were made.

[Col. 1666] The Word who was far from us became flesh so that he might dwell among us (John I, 3, 14). Let us therefore recognize in time the one through whom times were made; and as we celebrate his temporal feasts, let us desire eternal rewards.

# SERMON 374

[Note: [Col. 1666] Revised against r, rm, v, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1666] Elsewhere, among the Vignerian sermons 9.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 1666] He asserts without hesitation that the Magi, after seeing the star, were taught by angels that it was a sign of Christ: “And surely,” he says, “they heard it from angels, from some prompting of revelation.” Moreover, the preacher says that the Magi offered the objects as gifts according to their own custom, because they were accustomed to offer such things to their gods. But Augustine recognizes something of a mystery in their gifts in Sermon 202, no. 2.]

### 1. The Magi led to Christ by the star and by the revelation of angels

The anniversary celebration of this day requires from us an anniversary sermon, owed to your ears and hearts. Today our Savior brought the Magi to himself from so distant a people. They came to worship the infant, the Word of God.

Why did they come? Because they saw an unusual star. And how did they know that it belonged to Christ? They were able to see a star; could it speak to them and say, “I am Christ’s star”? Clearly, they were informed in another way, through some revelation.

Nevertheless, an unusual king had been born, one who was also to be worshiped by foreigners. Were not kings born previously in Judea, or throughout the earth among different peoples? Why was this one to be worshiped, and to be worshiped by foreigners—not terrifying with an army, but in the poverty of flesh, with the majesty of power concealed?

When he was born, he was worshiped by Israelite shepherds, to whom the angels announced him; but the Magi were not from the people of Israel. They worshiped the gods of the nations—that is, demons—and were deceived by their deceptive power.

They therefore saw an unusual star and marveled. Without doubt they asked whose sign it was that they had seen, so new and extraordinary. And surely they heard—certainly from angels, from some prompting of revelation.

Perhaps you ask: from good angels or from evil ones? Even evil angels—that is, demons—confessed that Christ was the Son of God. But why should they not also have heard from good angels, when their salvation was already being sought in worshiping Christ, and not wickedness ruling them?

The angels could therefore have said to them: “The star that you saw belongs to Christ. Go and worship him where he has been born, and at the same time make known what kind and how great a person has been born.”

Having heard this, they came and worshiped. They offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh according to their custom. For they were accustomed to offer such things to their gods.

### 2. Christ pointed out to the Gentiles by the Jews themselves

But before they did this, before they found him in the city where he had been born, they came asking, “Where has the king of the Jews been born?”

Could they not have learned this also through revelation, just as they had learned that the star belonged to the king of the Jews? Could not the same star have led them to that city, just as afterward it led them to the place where Christ was with his mother?

Certainly it could have, but it did not happen that way, so that they might inquire of the Jews. Why did God wish this to be sought from the Jews? So that, while they pointed out the one in whom they did not believe, they might be condemned by their own testimony.

Observe that even now the Magi become the firstfruits of the Gentiles—freed from so much greater impiety and therefore giving so much greater glory to the one who freed them.

They ask, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” Herod, hearing the name of a king, trembles like a rival. He summons the experts in the Law and asks them, according to the Scriptures, to indicate where Christ would be born. They answer, “In Bethlehem of Judea.”

The Magi went on and worshiped (Matthew II, 1–11); the Jews remained, though they had pointed the way.

O great mystery! Today we persuade people through the books of the Jews; people become believers through their books. We show pagans what they do not wish to believe.

For sometimes pagans raise this kind of question with us when they see the things that are written being fulfilled in such a way that they cannot altogether deny that, through the name of Christ, there are present among all nations the things foretold in the sacred books: in the faith of kings, in the overthrow of idols, in the transformation of human affairs.
