Sometimes they even dare to say: “You saw all these things happen, and you wrote them down as though they had been foretold.” One of their poets did this; those who have read him recognize it. He told how someone descended among the dead and came to the region of the blessed, and how the Roman leaders who were to be born were shown to him—leaders whom the writer himself already knew to have been born (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 752–887). He narrated past events but wrote them down as though they had been foretold as future.

“So too,” the pagans say to us, “you saw all these things happen and wrote books for yourselves in which they are read as though they had been foretold.”

O glory of our king! Rightly were the Jews conquered by the Romans but not destroyed. All the nations were subdued by the Romans and passed under Roman law. This people was both conquered and preserved in its Law; as far as the worship of God is concerned, it kept its ancestral customs and ritual.

Even after its temple was overthrown and its former priesthood extinguished, as the Prophets had said, they nevertheless preserve circumcision and a certain custom by which they are distinguished from the other peoples. Why, except for the sake of bearing witness to the truth?

The Jews are scattered everywhere, carrying the books in which Christ is proclaimed and presented as he was foretold, so that he can now be shown to the pagans.

I produce the book; I read the prophet; I show that the prophecy has been fulfilled. The pagan doubts, fearing that perhaps I myself have fabricated it. My enemy possesses this book, entrusted to him from ancient times by his ancestors. From it I convict both: the Jew, because I know that this was foretold and fulfilled; the pagan, because I did not fabricate it.

### 3. Sacrifice is owed to the one God

Therefore, let demons not mislead the unwary and those improperly curious about temporal matters under the appearance of divination; nor, deceiving the ungodly through proud arrogance, demand for themselves the honor of sacrifices.

Truly divine men, disciples of the one God, foretold divine things.

[Note: [Col. 1667] A perplexing passage, which stands in the Pithoean book as follows: “The true divine things were foretold; the divine men belong to the one God.”]

True sacrifice is owed to the one true God.

[Col. 1668] Before grace, figures of this were foreshadowed by sacrifices. What was going to happen in one way, divine providence announced beforehand in many ways, so that it might show how great it was.

He himself is the physician; he himself is the medicine: the physician because he is the Word, the medicine because the Word became flesh. He himself is the priest; he himself is the sacrifice.

He is the one who changed the way of the Magi; he is also the one who now changes the life of the wicked.

The nations justified in spirit celebrate together today the manifestation of him in the flesh, which in Greek is called *Epiphany*, so that the solemnity may renew memory, devotion may grow strong, love may burn through assembly, and truth may shine upon the envious.

# SERMON 375

[Note: [Col. 1668] Corrected against r, rm, v, and Vign.]

[Note: [Col. 1668] Elsewhere among the Vignerian sermons 9.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, III

[Note: [Col. 1668] We are uncertain about the author, because he speaks of Herod in such a way that he seems to have wished to confuse two different men: namely, the murderer of the infants and the other Herod mentioned in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 13. Augustine himself clearly distinguishes them in Book II of *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, chapter 7, and in Book XXII of *Against Faustus*, chapter 84.]

### Christ manifested first to the Jews and afterward to the Gentiles. The infants made martyrs. The two walls meeting at the corner. Epiphany means manifestation in Latin

The Lord Christ was manifested to the Jews through his birth a few days ago; today he was declared to the Gentiles through the star.

“The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isaiah I, 3). The ox is from the Jews, the ass from the Gentiles; both came to one manger and found the food of the Word.

The Magi who came to worship Christ, signifying the firstfruits of the Gentiles, did not receive the Law and did not hear the Prophets. The language of heaven was a star. It was as though it said to them, “What profit have I sought from you?”—“The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm XVIII, 2).

And yet Herod was troubled and asked the Jews where Christ would be born. They answered, “In Bethlehem of Judea,” and supplied prophetic testimony; while the Magi went on to worship, they themselves remained motionless.

They are stones piled beside the road: they point out the way, but they themselves do not walk.

Nevertheless the Magi went on to Bethlehem. But once they had found the city, how could they find the house? Behold, that star which had shone from heaven led them down to earth and stood over the place where the child was.

How great was the service of the elements—and the wickedness of the Jews! Herod was troubled, as though Christ had come to seek and find an earthly kingdom. The lion of heaven was born, and the earthly fox was troubled.

The Lord said of Herod, “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII, 32). What did he do when troubled? He killed the infants. What did he do? He killed infants for the infant Word (Matthew II).

Before they could confess the Lord with their mouths, they became martyrs through their blood. And Christ sent these firstfruits to the Father.

The infant came, and the infants departed: the infant to us, the infants to God. “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm VIII, 3).

Let us rejoice: the day has dawned upon us. The Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, signified us.

[Col. 1669] The Jews recognized him when he was born; the Gentiles recognized him yesterday [Note: [Col. 1669] Perhaps one should read “today.”]

Different walls came to the cornerstone: Jews from one direction, Gentiles from the other—not from different directions toward different destinations. You have seen and know that walls are as far from one another as they are distant from the corner. The closer they come to the corner, the closer they come to each other; when they reach the corner, they cling to each other.

Christ accomplished this. Jews and Gentiles had been far from each other: circumcision and uncircumcision, those under the Law and those without the Law [Note: [Col. 1669] Perhaps one should read, “hearers of the Law and those without the Law”], worshipers of the one true God and of many false gods. How far apart they were!

But “he is our peace, who made both one.” Those who came from the Jews are counted in the good wall, for those who came did not remain in the ruin.

We and they have become one—but in the One, not in ourselves (Ephesians II, 11–22).

From where was Christ born? From the Jews. Thus it is written: “Salvation is from the Jews” (John IV, 22)—but not for the Jews alone. For he did not say, “Salvation is for the Jews,” but, “Salvation is from the Jews.”

They grasped him, and they themselves lost him; they bound him, and he escaped from them; they saw him, and they killed him. We neither grasped him, and yet we hold him; neither saw him, and yet we believe. We are later, and we go before.

Those who preceded us lost the way; but we both found the way and, walking in it, shall come to our homeland.

# SERMON 376

[Note: [Col. 1669] Found only in the printed editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1669] Elsewhere, *On Time* 160.]

## Sunday within the Octave of Easter

[Note: [Col. 1669] We have found no handwritten copy of this sermon. The first part, to which what follows does not properly adhere, appears to have been taken from elsewhere. Compare Sermon 247, no. 2.]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The great miracle of entering through closed doors

Your Charity heard, when the holy Gospel was being read, that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, after his resurrection, entered to his disciples through closed doors.

A great miracle—but you cease to wonder if you consider that he is God. It would indeed be astonishing if a mere human being had done this. Refer it to omnipotence, not to an illusion.

He entered through closed doors. I answer you, so that you may know that it was true flesh: he showed scars to be touched (John XX, 19–27).

“But,” you say, “just as it is not the nature of a bodily thing to enter through a closed door, so it is not the nature of a bodily thing to walk upon the waves of the sea.”

He entered through closed doors. Answer me: give me the solidity of flesh. He walked upon the waters of the sea; you too give me the weight of flesh. Do you wish to know that this was an act of omnipotence? He also gave this power to Peter (Matthew XIV, 25–29).

He gave what he willed; what belonged properly to himself he kept. For the one who, while living, entered through closed doors is the one who, by being born, did not violate his mother’s virginity.

Therefore, brothers, let us marvel and believe; believing, let us obey; obeying, let us hope for the promises, if we do what has been commanded. For in order that we may do what has been commanded, he himself helps us—the one from whom we hope for the promises.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The octave of the infants. The old and the new human being

Today is called the octave of the infants; their heads are to be uncovered, which is a sign of freedom.

[Col. 1670] This spiritual birth possesses freedom; the birth of the flesh, properly speaking, possesses servitude.

There are, of course, two births of a human being: being born and being born again. We are born for toil; we are born again for rest. We are born for miseries; we are born again for eternal happiness.

For those boys, infants, little ones, nursing at their mothers’ breasts and unaware of how much grace is being bestowed upon them—as you yourselves see, since they are called infants—also have their octave today. And these old men, young men, adolescents: all are infants.

One infancy belongs to oldness; the other to newness. For those whom you see newly born from the womb are born old. Our old man is called Adam, from whom we are born; the new man is Christ, through whom we are born again.

These, therefore, are both new and born again to another life; and in them there is, if one may say so, a new oldness when they are born.

### 3. He exhorts the baptized not to imitate wicked Christians. The wicked mingled with the good in the Church

Behold, our infants are mingled today with the faithful, and they fly out as though from a nest. It is therefore necessary that we address them as they are being brought forth.

For, as you remember, my brothers, when the young of swallows or domestic sparrows begin to fly from the nest, their mothers fly around them with a great commotion, and with devoted cries bear witness to the dangers facing their offspring.

## CHAPTER III
We know, then, that many who are called faithful live wickedly and do not conform in their conduct to the grace they have received: they praise God with their tongue but blaspheme him by their life. Yet we know that others are found among these many, like grains groaning beneath the threshing, amid a great and abundant mass of chaff, but consoling themselves with the hope of the granary. We know that these two kinds of people exist in the Church. We recognize the Church as the Lord’s threshing floor; we hope for the winnowing on the day of judgment; we desire the mass of grain at the resurrection; we long to enter the granary in eternal life. There will be no chaff there, just as there will be no grain in Gehenna.

Now, therefore, my brothers, since we know that these two kinds of people exist in the Church—the godly and the ungodly, the good and the evil, those who fear and those who despise—we do not know with which of them these persons will be joined. What we desire, however, they themselves know. Whether our hopes concerning them will be fulfilled, human ignorance is wearied by anxious concern and is sometimes disturbed even by false suspicions. From these things one learns on this earth, where no one lives without temptation.

Therefore I admonish you, holy shoots; I admonish you, young plants in the Lord’s field, lest what was said of the vineyard of the house of Israel be said of you: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:2). May he find a cluster in you who was crushed for us as a cluster. Bear grapes; live well. For the fruit of the Spirit is, as the Apostle says, “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, faith, self-control, chastity” (Galatians 5:22).

When our farmer comes to us—the one whose laborers we are, the one who gives growth inwardly—for we know how to plant and water outwardly, but the Apostle says, “Neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7)—the one who now sees how you listen, who now observes how you [Column 1671] fear, or are already beginning to fear: when that farmer comes to you, may he find in you what the Apostle said: “My joy and my crown, all of you who stand firm in the Lord” (Philippians 4:1).

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Evil people who lead others into sin must be avoided. Illicit remedies of incantations. Almsgiving.

Brothers, dearest sons, most beloved sons, imitate the good and beware of the wicked. For I know that wicked men will come to you and persuade you to drunkenness, saying to you, “Why not? Are we not also thoroughly faithful?” I know it; that is why I grieve, that is why I fear.

If you say firmly, “Brother, I would not want you to do what you are doing; but if I cannot lead you to my good, at least do not drag me into your evil,” such men, as usually happens, will have a headache.

Your male or female neighbor will say to you, “There is an enchanter here; there is a healer here; and somewhere there is an astrologer.” You say, “I am a Christian; it is not permitted to me.” And if he says to you, “Why? Am I not also a Christian?” you will say, “But I am faithful.” And he will say to you, “I too have been baptized.”

They become angels of the devil, members of Christ. Because the enemy possesses that person, he seeks to drag another along as well. May he find you prepared—the one who has prepared these things for you.

That is why I speak; that is why I testify; that is why I do not remain silent; that is why I shake out my garments; that is why I consider myself acquitted before the tribunal of my God. I shall say to my God, “Lord, I did not remain silent; Lord, I did not hide the talent you gave me, but distributed it.” He will be able to say to me, “Wicked servant, you should have given it, and I would have demanded it” (Matthew 25:26–27). Behold, Lord, I have given it; you demand it.

And if perhaps an old habit should entice you, you have someone to whom you may appeal. The helper is greater than the attacker. That is why you groan; that is why you pray; that is why you say, “Do not lead us into temptation.”

Observe also, my brothers, what you say above, “Forgive us our debts,” so that you may do what follows: “as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. 6:13, 12). You give alms; you receive alms. You forgive; you will be forgiven. You distribute; it will be distributed to you. Hear God saying, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

Keep the poor in mind. I say to everyone: give alms, my brothers; give, and you will not lose. Believe God. I do not merely say to you that you will not lose what you do for the poor; I say plainly that this alone you will not lose, while you lose everything else.

Come, let us see whether you gladden the poor today. You are their granaries, so that God may give you something with which to give, and may forgive whatever sins you perhaps commit. “Store almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead with the Lord for you” (Sirach 29:15). To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 377

[Note: [Column 1671] Corrected against the readings of the manuscripts designated *f*, *gr.*, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Column 1671] Elsewhere numbered *On Various Matters* 57.]

## On the Ascension of the Lord

[Note: [Column 1671] The title prefixed in the printed editions was “On the Nativity of the Lord.” [Column 1672] It has been changed here according to the older copies, that is, the lectionaries, in the sole manuscript class in which we found this sermon, beginning with the words “On the eternal Word,” etc. It has something of Augustine’s style.]

### 1. The Word of God cannot be adequately praised by us. How he exulted to run his course. Why [Column 1672] “Lift up the gates” is said twice in the Psalm, etc.

Dearest brothers, who can worthily utter a temporal word about the eternal Word? How can what is lowly be sufficient for what is sublime? The heavens praise him, the virtues praise him, the heavenly powers praise him, the lights of heaven praise him, the stars praise him; and earth also praises him as it can—not so that it may praise him worthily, but so that it may not condemn itself for ingratitude.

Who can explain him, who can speak of him, who can even comprehend him who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1)? How did he exult to run his course, so that “his going forth was from the summit of heaven, and his return was to the summit of heaven” (Psalm 18:6–7)?

If he reaches everywhere, from where does he go out? If he reaches everywhere, where does he go? He is not extended through places, nor changed by times; he has neither arrivals nor departures. Remaining in himself, he moves everywhere in his entirety. What spaces do not have the Almighty, what spaces do not contain the Infinite, what spaces do not receive him when he comes?

[Note: [Column 1672] At this point the negative particle is absent from the manuscripts.]

If you are thinking of the Word, we have said nothing. But to teach the humble to say something about him, “he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:8). In this form he descended; in this form, according to the Gospel, he advanced in the pursuit of wisdom (Luke 2:52); in this form he suffered; in this form he fought valiantly; in this form he died; in this form he conquered death and rose again; in this form he returned to heaven, although he never departed from heaven.

Blessed, therefore, is he in the firmament of heaven who was made a curse for us, according to the Apostle, “so that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:13–14). “He exulted like a giant” (Psalm 18:6). What kind of giant? By dying, he conquered death. What kind of giant? He shattered the gates of hell; he went out and ascended.

Who is this King of glory, on whose account it was said to certain princes, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates”? Be lifted up—he is great. You are narrow; you cannot contain him. Be lifted up. Why this? So that the King of glory may enter.

They are terrified: “Who is this King of glory?” He is not recognized. He is not only God but also man; he is not only man but also God. He suffers—is he certainly God? He rises—is he certainly man? Or is he both God and man? For he truly suffers, and he truly rises.

Now, in one and the same Psalm, this is said twice: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” The same thing is then repeated after the same words, as though it might be considered superfluous and unnecessary.

But in the repetition of the same words, observe the endings, and notice why it was said twice. It is as though the gates of hell and of heaven were opened twice: once for him rising and once for him ascending. A new thing: God present among the dead. A new thing: man taken up into heaven. At both times and in both places the princes are terrified.

“Who is this King of glory?” How do we distinguish this? Hear what answer is given to both groups. To those who ask, it is said, “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” What kind of battle? To undergo death for mortals, to suffer alone for all, not to resist as the Almighty, [Column 1673] and yet to conquer while dying. Great, therefore, is this King of glory, even among the dead.

This is also repeated to the heavenly powers: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates.” Are they not eternal gates whose keys Peter received? But because he is raising a man with him, he is said there, as though unrecognized, to be, “Who is this King of glory?”

But there, because he is no longer a combatant but a victor, because he does not fight but triumphs, the answer is not, “The Lord mighty in battle,” but, “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Psalm 24:7–10).

# SERMON 378

[Note: [Column 1673] Corrected against the readings designated *cl.*, *r.*, *t.*, *vat.*, *v.*, and Vignerius.]

[Note: [Column 1673] Elsewhere numbered among the Vignerian sermons 24.]

## On the Day of Pentecost

[Note: [Column 1673] This sermon is either Augustine’s or that of someone deeply familiar with his teaching. Compare Sermon 23, chapter 8, and Sermon 156, chapter 15.]

### Love as the effect of the presence of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit as the pledge of eternal life. The distinction between a pledge and a security. The pledge of eternal life is given so that we may desire it.

A solemnity is pleasing to God when devotion is vigorous and love burns. For this is the effect of the presence of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle teaches when he says, “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

The coming of the Holy Spirit, therefore, filled the one hundred and twenty people gathered in one place. When the Acts of the Apostles were being read, we heard, “They were gathered together in one hundred and twenty, holding to Christ’s promise” (Acts 1–2). For he had told them to remain in the city until they were clothed with power from on high. “For I,” he says, “will send my promise upon you” (Luke 24:49).

He is a faithful promiser and a gracious giver. What he promised while he was on earth, he sent after he ascended into heaven. We possess the pledge of the future life and of the kingdom of heaven. Did he not defraud us by a recent promise, only to defraud us in the future by our expectation?

Whenever people enter into some transaction with one another and settle a financial matter by a promise, they generally either receive or give a pledge. A pledge that has been given establishes confidence that the matter for which the pledge preceded will indeed follow.

Christ gave us the Holy Spirit as a pledge. Although he could not deceive us, he nevertheless made us secure when he gave the pledge; and even if he had not given it, he would undoubtedly have fulfilled what he promised.

What did he promise? Eternal life, whose pledge he gave in the Holy Spirit. Eternal life is the possession of those who dwell there; the pledge is the consolation of those traveling as strangers.

For “pledge” is a better term than “security.” These two things seem similar to one another, but they nevertheless have a difference that must not be overlooked. Both when a security is given and when a pledge is given, it is done so that what is promised may be fulfilled. But when a security is given, a person returns what he received after the matter for which he received the security has been completed. A pledge, however, when it is given, is not taken back; rather, it is added to so that the promise may be fulfilled.

We have the pledge; let us thirst for the very fountain from which the pledge comes. We have the pledge—[Column 1674] the Holy Spirit, a kind of sprinkling in our hearts. If someone feels this dew, let him desire the fountain. For why do we have the pledge, unless it is so that we may not fail from hunger and thirst during this pilgrimage?

For we hunger and thirst, provided that we recognize ourselves as pilgrims. Whoever is a pilgrim and knows that he is a pilgrim desires his homeland; and while he desires it, the pilgrimage is burdensome. If he loves the pilgrimage, he forgets his homeland and does not wish to return.

Our homeland is not such that we should prefer anything to it. Sometimes, however, people become rich while they are traveling abroad. Those who were needy in their own country grow wealthy in their travels and do not wish to return.

We were all born as pilgrims, away from our Lord, from the time when he first breathed the breath of life into the first man. Our homeland is in heaven; its citizens are angels.

Letters have been sent to us from our homeland to encourage us to return; they are read daily before the gathered peoples. Let the world become worthless; let him be loved by whom the world was made.

[Note: [Column 1674] See Sermon 23, chapter 8, and Sermon 156, chapter 15.]

# SERMON 379

[Note: [Column 1674] Corrected against the readings designated *r.*, *t.*, *v.*, and Vignerius.]

[Note: [Column 1674] Elsewhere numbered among the Vignerian sermons 5.]

## On the Nativity of John the Baptist, I

[Note: [Column 1674] The style of this sermon does not differ greatly from Augustine’s.]

John was so great a man that he proclaimed Christ as God. Why so many prophets were sent beforehand before Christ.

Blessed John, dearest brothers, whose nativity we celebrate today, was so great among human beings that our Lord Jesus Christ bore him this testimony, saying, “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

We heard, when the Gospel was read, how wonderfully he was conceived from a state of hopelessness and with what great testimony of the Holy Spirit he was brought forth. His father became mute because he did not believe. Thus, announced by an angel and not believed, he took away his father’s voice; born, he loosened his tongue (Luke 1).

Receive, then, in the mystery of this event a great sacrament. Before the Lord Jesus Christ, John was sent ahead. Prophets were sent through the earlier ages, and there was no lack of those who proclaimed Christ. For so great a judge was to come that many heralds ought to precede him.

From the very beginning of the human race, Christ never ceased to proclaim himself and announce that he would come. Finally John was sent—a man, but no man greater than he had arisen. The Lord Jesus was to come, not merely man but also God: certainly both God and man; God always, man for a time; God before the ages, man at the end of the ages; God before the centuries, man at the end of the world.

God, who made man, deigned, for man’s sake, to become man—the man whom he had made. Since the Lord Jesus Christ was to come, being more than man, lest he be thought to be merely man, a great man ought to bear witness to him.

Christ, I say, the Lord, not merely God but God and man: God who made us, man who remade us. John, however, was merely man—but what a man! Hear God and man speaking about him.

“O Lord Jesus Christ, who [Column 1675] is John?” And God says, “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.”

“O great man John, than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women, tell me yourself, O great man: who is this one who is thought to be merely man?” Hear who he is: “Whose sandals,” he says, “I am not worthy to carry.”

[Note: [Column 1675] Perhaps one should read: “merely” (*solum*).]

Behold, through John we have learned both that Christ must be believed in as a man and that hope must not be placed in man but in Christ. Behold the great man, greater than whom no one has arisen—and he is John.

But observe that this John is the friend of the bridegroom; he is zealous for the bridegroom, not for himself. For he says to those coming to him, “I baptize you with water; but the one who comes after me is greater than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to untie; he, however, will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 3:11).

Come after me, but do not remain in me. Pass over to the one who created both you and me, because he will give life to both you and me.

# SERMON 380

[Note: [Column 1675] Corrected against the readings designated *cl.*, *d.*, *r.*, *t.*, *v.*, and Vignerius.]

[Note: [Column 1675] Elsewhere numbered among the Vignerian sermons 6.]

## On the Nativity of John the Baptist, II

[Note: [Column 1675] Sermon 371 contains an inserted notable passage from this sermon on Christ’s two births, as does Sermon 127 of the Appendix. We ourselves have no doubt that it is genuinely Augustine’s; nevertheless, we decided to place it among the doubtful works because it has been interpolated and corrupted from approximately the middle in all books, including the manuscripts. Here, contrary to our usual practice, we necessarily make two changes without manuscript authority. First, we move approximately one hundred lines, which belonged to Sermon 126, from their place. Second, we restore approximately forty more lines, found outside their proper position, to the very place occupied by that portion of Sermon 126. We have not been able either to remove or to expose the remaining defects, if any, because we lack the assistance of more reliable copies.]

### 1. John preceded Christ’s temporal birth. Christ’s two births. Pride and swelling. The reason for the Incarnation, so that God might provide man with an example. For quiet, even a small voice suffices.

If you wish, brothers, to listen quietly, do not have your heart in your ears, but your ears in your heart.

The Church both reports and believes that this day has dawned for the solemnity of blessed John the Baptist. It is proper to believe this about the day itself, which the whole world recognizes without variation. Since no one doubts that it is John’s day—not John the Evangelist who wrote the Gospel, but John the Baptist, the Lord’s precursor, who appeared so great because he presented himself as so humble, saying, when he himself was thought to be Christ, that he was not worthy to untie the strap of the sandals of the one whom he acknowledged as Lord (Matthew 3:11), so that he might deserve to be his friend—some people nevertheless think that his passion is celebrated today.

Let your Holiness know first that this is the day of his nativity, not of his passion. For from the Gospel reading it is found that his nativity precedes the Lord’s nativity by six months. And since the Church’s consensus hands down the day of the Lord’s nativity as the eighth day before the Kalends of January, it remains that today must be understood as the day of John’s nativity.

### 2. The same subject continued.

John therefore preceded the Lord, not as a teacher precedes a disciple, but as a precursor precedes a judge; not in order to impose authority, but in order to perform a duty.

[Column 1676] John’s testimony concerning him is as follows: “The one who comes after me was made before me, because he was before me.”

The Lord came after John by being born from the Virgin Mary, not from the substance of the Father. For we have received two births of the Lord, one divine and the other human, yet both marvelous: the first without a mother, the second without a father; the first eternal, so that it might create the temporal; the second temporal, so that it might bestow the eternal.

[Note: [Column 1676] The manuscripts read: “so that he might create temporal things; this temporal one, so that he might bestow eternal things.”]

The one of whom John speaks—not John the Baptist, but the Evangelist—because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1, 3): he, so great in the form of God and equal to the Father, he who fashioned times without time, he who was before all ages and before every age as the judge of the world, was made so small that he was born of a woman; yet he remained so great that he was not separated from the Father.

Serving him and bearing witness to him like lamps before the coming day, all the prophets came before him by being born and adhered to him afterward by believing. For it was necessary that the one who was to come and perform miracles be foretold. Through those miracles, he would be shown to the perceptive to be God; to those who saw him with human eyes, he would appear to be man—small among the small, but humble before the proud. By his smallness he taught man to recognize himself as small, lest, not growing great but swelling up, he should think himself great.

For pride is not greatness but swelling. Therefore, in order that this swelling of the human race might be healed, the physician himself, himself the medicine—not merely applying medicine but making himself the medicine—appeared among men as man. He offered man to those who saw, while preserving God for those who believed.

The sight of his humanity healed the weak; contemplation of his divinity requires the strong. At that time there were not yet people who could see God in man; they could see only man. Yet they ought not to place their hope in man.

What, then, was to happen? Man can see man, but man must not follow man. God had to be followed, though he could not be seen; man was not to be followed, though he could be seen. Therefore, so that man might be given one whom man could both see and follow, God became man.

O man, for whose sake God became man, you ought to believe yourself something great. But descend in order to ascend, because God too became man by descending.

Cling to your medicine, imitate your teacher, acknowledge your Lord, embrace your brother, understand your God. This is the one who is so great and yet so little, a worm and not a man—yet through him man was made.

This, then, is what he is. What is John except what the Lord says about him, what the truthful one says about him, what truth says about him? If we ought to believe John concerning the truth, should we not believe the truth concerning John?

### 3. From John’s words, the Arians’ slanders. The Word existed in the beginning; it was not made.

Let the one who shares in the truth first bear witness to the truth itself; and let the Creator of man bear witness to the man.

First [Column 1677] let us hear what John says about Christ, and then what Christ says about John. Let us hear the former first, but understand the latter afterward. Let the one who was born first speak first, but let his testimony be confirmed by the one by whom he was made.

“He came after me,” he says, “and was made before me.”

Now those who believe that the one through whom all things were made was himself made before all other things slander us with these words or through these words, saying, “Behold, he was made. John says, ‘He came after me and was made before me.’”

Explain to me what “he was made before me” means. I am stating their words and presenting them for examination.

“You customarily say,” they reply, “whenever something such as this is said about Christ as to show him lesser than the Father, that the statement must be referred to his humanity, so that what exists in the form of God is equal to the Father, while the Father is greater than the one who ‘emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man.’ What, then, will you say about John’s statement, ‘He was made before me’?”

Hear what we say. But first observe that the Apostle, distinguishing the two while commending one and the same person in both, did not say, “Taking the form of God.” What did he say about the form of God? “Being in the form of God”—looking back to the one who was called before him, in whose Gospel it is written, “In the beginning was the Word”; indeed, looking back to that light from which he too spoke this.

For John did not say, “In the beginning God made the Word,” although he could have said this just as Moses said it because he was speaking about creation made by the Lord God: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

Since John, if he held the belief that the Arians hold, could have said, “In the beginning God made the Word,” he did not say this. Rather, he said, “In the beginning was the Word.”

What was in the beginning had not been made. For nothing made preceded the Word. Everything that God made, he made through the Word: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5).

There is an immense difference between the one who says “Let it be made” and the thing made by the one who says it. But if he is one who speaks, he has the Word; if he has the Word, he made through the Word; if he made through the Word, he did not make the Word.

### 4. The Arians’ quibble: the same wording is used in Genesis, “The earth was.”

“Why?” they say. “Have you not also heard concerning the earth, ‘The earth was invisible and unformed’?” (Genesis 1:1–2). “If you say that the Word was not made because it is said, ‘The Word was,’ then the earth was not made either, because it is said, ‘The earth was.’”

O blind and heretical insanity! Pay attention, if you have the means to pay attention; listen, if you have the means to listen. Let not a sound strike the ear in vain while truth does not enlighten the heart.

I shall quote the words of that same Scripture which you found there when you were reading, but passed over when you were arguing. You think that something of this kind was said about the Word of God when it was said, “In the beginning was the Word,” as was said about the earth because it was said, “The earth was invisible and unformed.”

In this book of Genesis I shall recite to you the preceding words, so that it may be clear that before the divine writer and servant said, “The earth was,” he first said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

Behold, I first showed you the earth as made—and certainly made [Column 1678] by God—the Scripture resounding and bursting into the ears of one who resists it: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

These things had been made, but they had not yet been adorned or brought into visible form; the earth had not yet been distinguished, but it had already been made. And lest you think that the earth had immediately been made in such a way that there was nothing in it to be adorned, he continued: It had indeed been made, because “in the beginning God made heaven and earth”; but the earth that God made was still invisible and unformed.

He showed you what the earth that had been made was like, not that it existed though it had not been made.

John could therefore have said, “In the beginning God made the Word, but the Word was,” just as he said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth, but the earth was.” The order of the words would then have been: “In the beginning God made the Word, and the Word was with God,” so that we might understand that this Word was with God which God had made.

But now you hear, “In the beginning was the Word.” Why do you, having become more remote, seek what is prior? For you have become more remote in your error; you speak from below and look toward what is below.

I would wish, if you spoke from below, that you would direct your heart upward and cry from the depths to the Lord. He would break through the cloud of the darkness of your flesh; the light that came in humility would open your eyes to humility. You would see: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.”

Let Paul also speak: “Who, being in the form of God.”

What does John say about the human birth? “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:1–3, 14). Let Paul also speak: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7).

What, then, were you saying about the words of John the Baptist? Repeat those same words to me now; speak them now. What does John the Baptist say? “He came after me.”

I recognize the birth. One came from a barren woman; the other from a virgin. Barrenness was changed into fruitfulness; virginity remained after fruitfulness.

### 5. Objection: Christ is said to have been made insofar as he is the Word. Christ was made before John, that is, placed before him and preferred to him.

“But John,” he says, “if he had said ‘was made’ with reference to the fact that he was born from a virgin, would not have said, ‘He was made before me,’ because he was made from a virgin after John. Therefore, what does ‘he was made before me’ mean except that the Word was made in the beginning? For he existed before John in this way, since he was born from the virgin after John.”

Receive this, and, if you are not quarrelsome, pay attention. What you wish to understand may perhaps be somewhat obscure, so that by quarreling you increase the smoke that prevents you from understanding.

First look to that Scripture which teaches you to become teachable: “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand” (Sirach 5:13). Be patient, therefore, for a little while. Perhaps we shall discover how “he was made before me” was said, provided that we do not understand the Word through which all things were made to have been made.

“How?” he asks. If I can, I shall say. If I cannot say it, nevertheless there is still something for one who can say it to say. I believe and hope that the majesty of the Only-Begotten—who, although he was the Word, became an infant—will open the infancy of my tongue and bring about a birth in my mouth, just as he brought conception in my heart.

Behold, I shall speak as I can; understand as you can. And what you cannot understand, do not criticize as though you were already [Column 1679] great; rather, wait, so that you may deserve to grow.

Certainly what moves you is how it was said, “The one who comes after me was made before me.” Let it move you as one who is seeking, not as one who is quarrelsome.

Certainly I too seek with you. We shall find together if we seek together; we shall both receive if we both ask; it will be opened to both of us if we both knock.

“He came after me,” he says. Recognize the birth from the Virgin Mary. “He was made before me”—what does “he was made before me” mean? Understand: he was placed before me.

The one who came after me was made before me. It is as when two people are walking on a road, one slower and the other faster. The slower one goes ahead for a little while, and afterward the faster one follows. The slower one, who is ahead, looks back at the faster one following and says, “He came after me.”

And behold, when the faster one hastens, draws near, catches up, and passes him, the slower one sees ahead of him the one whom he had been regarding as behind. If he is in some way astonished and amazed at the other’s speed, could he not say these words: “Behold, the man was behind me, and he was made before me”?

What does this mean: “The one who was behind me was made before me”? The one who was walking behind me was made to be before me by his speed.

For wherever you read “was made,” you understand nothing except that one who did not exist was formed; and you will say that the Lord God was made, of whom it is said, “The Lord was made for me a refuge” (Psalm 94:22); “The Lord was made a helper” (Psalm 30:11); and “He was made my salvation” (Psalm 118:14).

How many times was he made? Yet he himself made all things.

Understand the words with me. For that same John did not remain silent about the fact that he was the Word, lest you think that he signified the Word there when he said, “He was made before me.” Thus you may know that “he was made before me” refers to this: he went before me; he was glorified more greatly than I; although people regarded me as the precursor, they recognized him as the Lord whom I preceded by birth and announced by serving him.

Their hope and their gathering became directed toward the Lord. He was glorified as the Son of God, “made before me,” according to what the Apostle says: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:9–10).

His glory, therefore, did not begin to exist; it became known. He was made before John because he preceded John in honor.

### 6. The Subsequent Words of John Accord with the Interpretation Given. But See Whether They Do So Justly.

Ask John himself: He who came after you, why was he made before you? He who followed you, why was he preferred to you? The text continues: “Because he was before me.” This means: “In the beginning was the Word.” Therefore he was rightly made before me, because he was before me.

He was before John, before Abraham, before Adam, before heaven and earth, before the Angels, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers. Why was he before them? Because all things were made through him.

Let the servant acknowledge his humility; let the Lord display his majesty. Let that same John say: “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.” He would have humbled himself greatly if he had said, “I am worthy.” For what if he had said that he was worthy? Would that mean he was worthy to sit in judgment at the right hand of the Father? Worthy to come to judge the living and the dead? What if he had said that he was worthy to untie the strap of his sandal? Great humility indeed, if he were worthy to be the bridegroom’s friend.

For he was going to say that he was the bridegroom’s friend; and lest someone imprudent should perhaps understand equality in that friendship, he calls himself a friend because of love, but casts himself down at his feet because of fear. And it is not enough that he lowers himself to the feet; he does not even call himself worthy to untie the strap of his sandal. He would certainly be humble if he were worthy to untie it; but because he does not even call himself worthy to untie it, he is worthy to be exalted from his humility.

Let him say it still more openly, let him say it more distinctly: what does “He came after me, he was made before me” mean? For he also gave the reason: “Because he was before me.” Since “in the beginning was the Word”; and “though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped.” “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

It was necessary that the one who came later should increase, and that the one who came earlier should decrease. If the one who came later increased, he was made before him by increasing. “He must,” he says, “increase, but I must decrease.” This is what “he was made before me” means.

And how did Christ increase while John decreased? John preceded the Lord in age, in his human birth; both grew as the years advanced in the stature of the flesh, and reached the measure fixed for human beings. But John was a human being, whereas Christ was God and man.

> **Note:** [Col. 1680] The sequence of the sermon had been interrupted because approximately forty lines had been transferred to this place. They are to be found below, no. 7, immediately at the words, “We too were once,” etc.

If we understand that Christ increased in divinity, we are absurd and greatly mistaken. Something grows in order to make progress. God has no room to grow; for if there were something by which he could grow, he was lesser before he grew.

Let us return to the form of the flesh. That form grew together with John; it did not grow by John’s decreasing. Let us therefore perhaps refer the matter to glory, and understand “He must increase, but I must decrease” according to the saying, “He came after me, and he was made before me.”

John was assuming the person of humanity and was speaking in the figure of the human race, for whose salvation Christ had come. We had said, brothers, that the humble God came to proud humanity. Let humanity acknowledge that it is human; let God appear to humanity.

For if Christ came for this reason—that humanity might be humbled and, through humility, might increase—it was necessary that human glory should now cease and that God’s glory should be commended, so that humanity’s hope might be in God’s glory, not in its own, as the Apostle says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Thus it is rightly said to humanity: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (ibid. 4:7).

By displaying this pattern of human humility, John showed that as Christ’s reputation and fame advanced—not Christ’s stature, Christ’s majesty, Christ’s wisdom, or the Word of God, but that fame which began from a very small beginning and now holds the whole world—Christ’s glory, not human glory, was to increase, so that humanity might acknowledge its humility and God might impart his divinity.

For God’s glory, brothers, is our glory. The more sweetly God is glorified, the more it benefits us. God will not be higher because we honor him; let us humble ourselves, and we exalt him.

For it is written: “I will exalt you, Lord” (Psalm 29:2). What does “I will exalt you” mean? Was he on earth, and did you place him in heaven? Does a human being exalt God? What does “I will exalt you” mean? “I will acknowledge you as exalted.” Let humanity therefore acknowledge itself as human; let it first decrease, so that it may increase.

Let John, by decreasing into humility, say that he is not worthy to untie the strap of the sandal, and let him understand that by sharing in the light he is made enlightened.

### 7. John the Baptist Was Not the Light, in Comparison with Christ, the True Light. Yet John Was a Light through Participation in Wisdom.

For the Evangelist John said this about him: “He was not the light.” Did he perhaps insult John by saying, “He was not the light,” when the Lord said to the Apostles, “You are the light of the world”? Did the Apostles place themselves above John? They do not, lest they judge the Lord himself a liar, since he said: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

Certainly this does not refer to bodily stature, but to the grace of shared wisdom and the grace of shared salvation. What, then, does “He was not the light, but to bear witness to the light” mean? Why did he say this?

“I know,” he says, “what I am saying: to bear witness to the light.” For there was a true light, distinct from John—not so that John was altogether no light, but so that the statement “He was not the light” might be understood in comparison with this light, according to the words: “There was the true light.”

How do you discern this true light? “It is the one,” he says, “that enlightens every human being coming into this world.” If every human being, then John also. But so that we may not appear to infer from the words something that was not said, although it must be understood consequentially, let John himself say: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:8, 9, 16).

There was therefore a true light. John was a light that had been enlightened; Christ was the light that enlightens. For so that you may know that John was a light, let the Lord now also bear witness to him.

John himself bore witness to his Lord—a testimony of truth concerning his Lord, which he possessed from his Lord. For he had received from his Lord the ability to speak about his Lord; but for the Lord to speak about his servant, he had not received it from his servant. Christ testified concerning John, and through John Christ testified concerning himself.

Let the Truth itself therefore bear witness. Let us hear that John is a light. The Jews are told concerning John: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (ibid. 5:35). A lamp is certainly a light—not like the light of day, but nevertheless a light.

A lamp is therefore kindled in order to shine, and John was enlightened in order to speak. If John was enlightened in order to speak, let him acknowledge that he is a lamp, lest he be extinguished by the wind of pride.

But perhaps the disciples are the light, and John is the lamp? For the Lord says concerning John, “He was the burning and shining lamp”; but concerning the disciples, “You are the light of the world.” Did the Lord place his disciples above John? And are those believers whom Paul addresses to be placed above John, when he says to them: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8)?

The Apostles are therefore light, and believers are light—those who were justified from sinners and made believers from unbelievers. Yet the disciples are not called lamps.

Pay attention: perhaps they were called lamps, but not in another place—in that very passage—in order to show how he called them light; for they are not the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.

Follow the words of the Gospel: “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” But did he speak about a city, not about light? Follow further: “Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel.”

You are such a light as John was: an enlightened lamp. It is as though the voice of one person, or of several, had gone before: “You will illumine my lamp, Lord; my God, illumine my darkness” (Psalm 17:29).

What darkness was there in the Apostles? “We too were once,” etc.

> **Note:** [Col. 1682] Something is missing by which the preceding words were connected with the subsequent ones. The latter had formerly occupied the place indicated above; instead of them, in other printed and manuscript books, the first part of Sermon 126 had been inserted here.

Such were the darknesses of that reprobate and blasphemer: “I, who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man.” Behold the darkness: let the lamp be kindled. “But I received mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13).

And so that you may know that the words refer to these very people—“Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house”—the text immediately continues: “Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works”; but this must be in humility, because humanity must decrease.

How, then, does God increase? “And let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:14–16).

The Father is glorified, and the Son is glorified, because the Father glorifies the Son and the Son glorifies the Father. Let humanity therefore acknowledge its humility; let it acknowledge the exalted God humbled for its sake, so that humanity, humbled in the confession of sin, may be exalted in the attainment of righteousness.

These two—Lord and John, humility and glory: God humble in glory, humanity humble in weakness; God humble for humanity’s sake, humanity humble for humanity’s sake. For God was humble in order to benefit humanity; humanity is humble so as not to harm itself.

### 8. The Difference between the Passion and the Birth. Christ Increases; John Decreases.

Let us therefore acknowledge these two things also in the very difference between their passions. We read that John suffered martyrdom for the truth. Was it for Christ? It was not for Christ if Christ is not the truth. It was not altogether for his name, but nevertheless for the truth itself.

For John was not beheaded because he confessed Christ. Rather, he urged self-restraint; he urged justice. He said: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18).

The law that had commanded this had commanded it concerning those who died without children, so that their brothers were to take their brothers’ wives and raise up offspring for their brothers. Where that circumstance did not exist, it was nothing but lust.

John condemned this lust; the chaste man condemned incest. For even what that law prefigured is of this character: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

It had already been commanded that if someone died without offspring, the one who was his closest relative should take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Why had God commanded this, unless it was to signify that the brother’s offspring was to be raised up in the brother’s name? For the command was that the one born from that union should bear the name of the deceased.

Christ died, and his Apostles received his spouse, the Church. Those whom they begot from her they named not Paulines or Petrines, but Christians.

Let these two passions therefore speak: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” He increased upon the wood; John was diminished by the sword. The passions have spoken this mystery; let the days speak it also.

Christ is born, and the days increase; John is born, and the days decrease. Let human honor therefore decrease, and God’s honor increase, so that human honor may be found in God’s honor.

---

# SERMON 381

> **Note:** [Col. 1683] Corrected from two manuscripts designated *cl. d. r. rm. t. vat.* and from Vignier.

> **Note:** [Col. 1683] In other copies, among the Vignier sermons, no. 6.

## On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul

> **Note:** [Col. 1683] Augustine’s name appears in the ancient lectionaries, and the style does not seem wholly foreign to him.

Today is the day of the Apostles Peter and Paul, on which, having conquered the devil, they deserved the triumphant crown, as the Roman faith bears witness. Since a solemn festival is being offered to them, let a solemn sermon also be delivered. Let them hear praises from us; let them pour out prayers for us.

As the memory handed down by the fathers preserves the tradition, they did not suffer on one single day as the course of heaven passed by. At Peter’s natal feast, therefore, Paul suffered—not on the day when he was poured forth from his mother’s womb into the number of human beings, but on the day when he was born from the bond of the flesh into the light of the angels. Consequently, the individual days were assigned to the two in such a way that one day is now celebrated for both.

This appears to me a great sign of concord: the one called last came to his fellow Apostle, the first, summoned to the same day and meeting him crowned on the same day. Peter was chosen before the Lord’s passion; Paul after the ascension. Unequal in temporal order, equal in the blessedness of eternity: one from a fisherman, the other from a persecutor.

In the one, “the weak things of the world were chosen, so that the strong might be confounded” (1 Corinthians 1:27); in the other, “sin abounded, so that grace might abound still more” (Romans 5:20).

In both, God’s great grace and his glory shone forth: he made their merits; he did not find them already present. For what else did he deign to demonstrate when he first wished to call fishermen to the kingdom and afterward to call emperors, except that “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31)?

Certainly he did not despise the salvation of the noble, learned, and powerful, to whom he preferred the ignoble, uneducated, and weak. But unless the lowliness of the weak were chosen first, the swelling pride of the haughty would not be healed.

If the rich had first been called by Christ, they would have thought and said that nothing had been chosen in them except wealth, eloquence, learning in rhetoric, the brilliance of knowledge, nobility, high birth, tranquility, and royal power. Thus swollen with temporal and worldly advantages, they would have imagined that they themselves had first contributed to Christ what they were, so that he seemed to restore to them, rather than give them, what they would become by God’s grace; and they would neither have understood nor retained this truth.

How much better, then, how much more orderly, that he first raised the needy from the earth and lifted the poor from the dungheap, “to set him with the princes of his people” (Psalm 112:7–8), so that the gift of understanding and teaching would not only come from God, but would also plainly be seen to come from God?

With what joy, therefore, and with what glory of God do we behold the wealth of an emperor despised by the heart of a fisherman? The prayers of an emperor poured out at the memorial of a fisherman? Thus neither does the one lie prostrate because of what he did not possess, nor does the other grow proud because of what he possessed.

Moreover, what Christ accomplished when he made Paul, his former persecutor, his preacher—what this contributes to the salvation of human beings, so that no one conscious of great iniquities should despair of God’s mercy—the Apostle himself should declare:

“Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, the first, Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:15–16).

Who would despair of salvation under the hand of the omnipotent physician, instructed by so great an example, when he considers that the one who once ravaged the faith later preached it—not merely escaping the punishment of a persecutor, but even earning the crown of a teacher—and that the blood he had desired to pour out in fury upon Christ’s members he afterward poured out in faith for Christ’s name?

Rome therefore possesses the head of the nations, the two lights of the nations kindled by him who enlightens every human being coming into this world: one in whom God exalted rejected humility; the other in whom he healed iniquity deserving condemnation.

From the one let us learn not to be proud; from the other, not to despair. How briefly, yet how greatly and beneficially, these examples have been set before us! Let us always remember them, and in praising them magnify the true light.

Let no one therefore exalt himself because of this world’s eminence: Peter was a fisherman. Let no one flee from God’s mercy by contemplating his own iniquity: Paul was a persecutor.

The one says: “The Lord has become a refuge for the poor” (Psalm 9:10); the other says: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will be converted to you” (Psalm 50:15).

---

# SERMON 382

> **Note:** [Col. 1684] Corrected from two manuscripts designated *c. b.* and two *n.*, from three copies designated *cl. gr. r. v.*, and from Am., Er., Par., and Lov.

> **Note:** [Col. 1684] In other copies, *On the Saints* 4.

## On Saint Stephen

> **Note:** [Col. 1684] This sermon appears to bear the form of a cento. The opening, “In speaking, my heart will no longer fear,” etc., is connected neither with what precedes nor with what follows. A little later, from “Let Your Holiness take notice” through “they received their reward,” Vindingus says that the whole passage is an addition by an unlearned hand. Besides several other passages, we have also come to suspect the words in section 3, “He was a deacon; he read the Gospels,” etc. For written Gospels did not yet exist before Stephen’s passion. Something similar was said above in Sermon 319, section 3, but there it is more easily excused and is not sufficient reason to reject a sermon that is otherwise sound.

## Chapter One

### 1. The Commandment to Love Enemies

Joshua the son of Nun was fighting in the wilderness, and Moses was praying. Not, indeed, were both fighting and both praying; rather, one was fighting and the other praying. The one who fought rightly did not fail, because the other conquered by praying.

So too I seem to be speaking, but I speak while others are praying, so that through their prayers what the Lord says may happen to me: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11).

If he was helped by one person praying, and was not overcome, how much more am I helped by the many who pray to God with me?

“In speaking, my heart will no longer fear, because my mouth will speak the praise of the Lord” (Psalm 144:21).

Our Lord Jesus Christ, brothers, commands something of us and promises something to us. What he commands is here; what he promises is elsewhere. What he commands comes to an end, because it is temporal; what he promises does not end, because it is eternal. What he commands is the work; what he promises is the reward.

Let Your Holiness take notice of how great his mercy toward us is: he has placed the labor here, where it has an end, and the reward in heaven, where it has no end.

Therefore we ought first to labor here and afterward receive the reward in heaven, rather than receive the reward here and labor afterward. For concerning certain people he says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2).

But perhaps you are eager for the reward and lazy about the labor. With what face do you ask for what God promised, if you do not do what God commanded? First listen to the warnings, and then demand the promises. First, I say, listen to the one who commands, and then demand from the one who makes the promise.

For he commands us and says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.” You have heard the work; await the reward: “So that you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (ibid. 5:44–45).

## Chapter Two

### 2. Christ’s Example of Praying for Those Who Killed Him

Christ prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us. Consider what the Lord himself, who gave this command, did.

After the impious Jews had committed so many things against him, repaying evil for good, did he not hang upon the cross and say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

He prayed in the human being, and the one who prayed was heard together with the Father. Even now he prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us.

> **Note:** [Col. 1685] See *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 85, section 1.

As our priest, he prays for us; as our head, he prays in us; as our God, he is prayed to by us.

When, therefore, hanging on the cross, he prayed, he saw and foresaw all his enemies. But he foresaw that many of them would become friends, and therefore he asked forgiveness for all.

They raged, and he prayed. They said to Pilate, “Crucify him” (Luke 23:21); he cried out, “Father, forgive them.” He hung upon harsh nails, but he did not lose his gentleness. He was already asking forgiveness for those from whom he was receiving such great injury.

They raged, they barked all around him, they shook their heads in mockery—heads that they did not possess in soundness, because they did not possess Christ, the head. Like madmen raging all around a single chief physician placed in their midst, they raged on every side. He was hanging, and he was healing.

“Father,” he says, “forgive them.” Take notice, brothers: great is his mercy. He was hanging, and yet he was asking.

> **Note:** [Col. 1685] Some manuscripts read: “and yet he was offering himself.”

He did not descend, because from his blood he was making medicine for the mad. Finally, after the resurrection, he healed those whom, while hanging, he had endured as utterly insane. They drank, in faith, the blood they had shed in their fury; and those who had been persecutors became followers.

Behold why Christ came: not to destroy what he had found, but to seek and save what had perished (ibid. 19:10)—so that by loving raging enemies he might make them believing friends.

## Chapter Three

### 3. Stephen’s Example of Praying for Those Who Stoned Him

But lest you say that you are far from imitating your Lord, who suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps (1 Peter 2:21), consider your fellow servant Stephen.

He was a human being, as you are; he was created from the mass of sin, as you are; he was redeemed at the same price as you.

He was a deacon; he read the Gospels that you too read or hear. There he found written: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44). He learned by reading and perfected the command by fulfilling it.

When the Jews were striking him with a hailstorm of stones, he not only did not threaten them but even prayed for forgiveness for those who were stoning him. Kneeling, he prayed, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

They were stoning him, and he was praying. They pursued him in fury; he followed Christ in peace. They were blinded by malice; he was enlightened by wisdom when he saw the Son of God in the opened heaven.

They were throwing stones; he was sending prayers ahead—as though he were saying: “Lord, if you kill these enemies now, whom will you later make friends?”

## Chapter Four

### 4. Grace and Salvation Obtained for Saul through Stephen’s Prayer

Finally, brothers, so that you may know how powerful the prayer of the holy martyr Stephen was, return with us to that young man named Saul.

When Saint Stephen was being stoned, Saul guarded everyone’s garments and, as it were, stoned Stephen with the hands of them all (Acts 7). Later, as you know, he received letters from the chief priests so that he might bring bound to Jerusalem whatever Christian men and women he found, to be tortured and punished.

As he was traveling along the road, suddenly a light from heaven shone around him, and he fell to the ground. He heard a voice from heaven saying to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” And he said: “Who are you, Lord?” And the Lord said to him: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad; for you will wound not the goad but the feet with which you kick.”

“What have I to do with you? Why are you persecuting me? Why do you rise up against me to your own harm, instead of humbling yourself to your own good? Against all the great evils you are committing against me, I ought long ago to have destroyed you; but my servant Stephen prayed for you.”

The raging man was struck down; the believer rose. The wolf was struck down; the lamb rose. The persecutor was struck down; the preacher rose.

Let me say it more plainly, more openly: the son of destruction was struck down; the vessel of election rose. Saul was struck down; Paul rose (ibid. 9).

For if the martyr Stephen had not prayed in this way, the Church would not have Paul today. But Paul was raised from the earth because Stephen, bowed down upon the earth, was heard.

## Chapter Five

### 5. How Wicked It Is to Pray for Evil against One’s Enemies

Behold why the Lord says: “Love your enemies.” By loving an enemy, you make him a friend.

But in the face of such and so great commands, who are you not to love? You kneel, strike your forehead against the ground, and say: “If only my enemy would die! God, if I have deserved anything from you, kill my enemy.”

And certainly you who pray that a human being may die are praying evilly against evil, and you have become two evil people: the other by doing evil, you by praying evilly.

You begin to be evil in your prayer when you say, “God, kill the evil person.” He himself answers you: “Which one of you? The evil person, or your enemy?”

Let Your Holiness take notice. A human judge does not kill the accused by his own hand; he gives the order, and the executioner kills. The judge says, “Kill,” and the torturer kills.

And when you say, “Kill my enemy,” you make yourself the judge and seek to make God the executioner.

> **Note:** [Col. 1686] See *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 33, section 9.

God answers you: “I will certainly not be that; I will not be the executioner of a sinner, but his liberator, because I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

For if I had your will, I would have killed you first, before you came when invited. Did you not blaspheme me? Did you not provoke me by your evil deeds? Did you not wish to erase my name from the earth? Did you not despise me in my commandments or in my servants?

If I had then killed you as an enemy, whom would I now make a friend? Why, then, by praying evilly do you teach me what I did not do to you?

Rather, God says to you, “I will teach you so that you may imitate me.” Hanging upon the cross, I said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

I taught this to my soldiers; I taught this to my martyrs. First become my martyr, my recruit, against the devil. Otherwise you will in no way fight unconquerably unless you pray for your enemies.

May he deign to grant this to us, and so forth.

---

# SERMON 383

> **Note:** [Col. 1687] Corrected from two copies designated *cl.*, from *gr. m. r. rm. t.*, and from Am., Er., Par., and Lov.

> **Note:** [Col. 1687] In other copies, no. 24 among the *Fifty Homilies*.

## On the Anniversary of His Episcopal Ordination

> **Note:** [Col. 1687] The style does not seem to be Augustine’s: it is carefully worked out, indeed, but ineptly, without art or talent. As a result, the sermon is somewhat obscure and, in the very matter that was especially suited by its nature to move the emotions of the hearers, extremely cold. Bossuet judged otherwise, believing that it should be listed among Augustine’s genuine sermons. —M.

[Col. 1687]

## Chapter One

### 1. He Leads Them to Consider with Him How He Bears the Episcopal Burden

Every day and every hour, and with wholly unceasing concern, beloved, a bishop ought to consider how great a burden of stewardship he carries and what account of it he will render to his Lord.

Nevertheless, when the anniversary of our ordination dawns, the burden of this office is considered especially—as though it were being imposed for the first time. There is, however, a difference: on the day when we first undertook it, we thought only about how it ought to be carried; but on the days that followed, and especially on the day when its solemnity is celebrated, we not only prudently consider how it must henceforth be carried in the future, but also recall with anxious remembrance how it has been carried in the past.

We do this so that we may imitate ourselves in good works; if anything blameworthy has passed, we may take care that it not be repeated; we may pray that it be forgiven; and we may flee the devil’s accusation, wherever we can, by diligently doing what is right, and wherever we cannot, overcome it by the piety of confession.

For just as future sins are committed by neglecting righteousness, so past sins are confirmed by defending injustice. Therefore, just as love takes care that sins not be committed, humility wipes away those already committed, so that what can no longer be avoided by right action may at least be forgiven through the absence of pride.

For we have learned to say to our Father, who is in heaven: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

To say this truthfully, we must certainly also love our enemies—though we ought not to have enemies unless justice compels it. For if people are our enemies because of our own evil merits, we should not be concerned to forgive debts owed to them; rather, we should fear that we may have to repay them. Since they hate us deservedly because of our iniquity, we—not they—are their debtors.

## Chapter Two

### 2. He Forgives His Debtors

On this solemn day of my episcopate, therefore, I shall first address briefly those who are my debtors—people who unknowingly support me before God while incurring debts that I may forgive, so that I may deserve to have my own debts forgiven.

To you, therefore, whether present or absent, who become my enemies when I preach the truth, to whom I seem burdensome when I give counsel, whose interests I am compelled to offend when I seek their benefit, I say:

“Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9). These beasts especially attack with hoof and bite those who care for them, when their wounds are being handled so that they may be healed.

You do not spare; I do not spare. You oppose; I oppose. You resist; I resist. The struggle brings us together, but the cause separates us.

You are the enemy of the physician; I am the enemy of your disease. You are the enemy of my diligence; I am the enemy of your pestilence.

“They repaid me evil for good; but I prayed” (Psalm 35:12). What did he pray except: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

“When they revile you,” he says, “and say every evil thing against you because of righteousness, rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5:11–12).

Nevertheless, correct your perversity; acknowledge our love; return love for love. We do not want a greater reward at the cost of your destruction.

Let these few words to my debtors, whom I forgive so that I may be forgiven, suffice for now.

## Chapter Three

### 3. He Wishes to Be Reconciled with Those Whom He May Have Offended

Next, I must address briefly those to whom I am a debtor. For as the Apostle says: “I am a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish” (Romans 1:14).

In this way I too, to the limited extent of my strength and my small share in the stewardship, am a debtor not to some but to all. But now I am speaking of debts that I wish to have forgiven, not collected from me.

I am not so lifted up by the swelling of an empty mind as to dare say that, from the time I began to carry the burden of this office, I have wronged no human being. For anyone occupied and burdened by so many and such troublesome activities, this is—not to say impossible—certainly difficult. How much more difficult for me, who know my weakness and offer it day and night to our Lord God for healing, together with your prayers for me and my own prayers with you.

Therefore, disturbed by the heat and difficulties of various concerns, if I have perhaps failed to listen to someone as he requested; if I have looked at someone more sternly than was necessary; if I have spoken a harsher word to someone than was proper; if I have troubled someone whose heart was broken and who needed help by giving an unsuitable response; if I have perhaps overlooked or delayed a poor person who was importunately pressing me while my attention was fixed on something else, or even saddened him by a harsh gesture; if I have become more bitterly indignant toward someone who, as a human being suspecting something about another human being, imagined something false about me, when that person did not recognize in his conscience what I had humanly suspected of him—you to whom I confess myself a debtor for these and similar offenses, believe me also to be your lover.

> **Note:** [Col. 1688] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “believe me to be your debtor.”

A mother often steps on the chicks she is warming when they are crowded together, but she does not put the full weight of her foot upon them; nor does she thereby cease to be their mother.

Forgive, so that you may be forgiven. Forgive the debts of difficulty owed by one who loves you; for you ought not to retain even against your enemies the debts of cruelty.

In short, I beseech you all: entrust to the Lord the care I have for you, for from this I justly seek your care for me, so that he may mercifully forgive whatever offenses of mine belong to the past and may not examine them with severity.
