As for what remains of my time under this burden, may he guide me as I travel, and make me pleasing in his eyes and useful to you, so that when his presence finds you, it may find not my horror and punishment but my joy and crown.

---

# SERMON 384

> **Note:** [Col. 1689] Corrected from two manuscripts designated *bn.* and three *cl.*, and from *cb. f. fs. g. lr. m. pr. rm. vd.*, as well as from Am., Er., Par., and Lov.

> **Note:** [Col. 1689] In other copies, *On the Words of the Apostle* 1.

## On the Trinity, or on the Old and New Scriptures against the Arians

> **Note:** [Col. 1689] With this title it occupies the final place in ancient books of the *Sermons on the Words of the Gospel*, all of which assign it to Augustine. Nevertheless, the Louvain editors reasonably doubted this attribution; indeed, Verlinus and Vindingus declared it spurious, saying that it has neither his style nor his talent.

[Col. 1689]

## Chapter One

### 1. What God Is

The holy and divine utterances, brothers, are continually—indeed, daily—recited to us for our salvation, so that our souls may be nourished and, in the future age, filled with eternal banquets, as the prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15).

What this future glory will be like, what riches adorn it, and with what splendor it shines forth, we can praise, but we cannot explain. Why? Because we read: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

If, then, such and so great are the eternal heavenly goods that the omnipotent Lord has prepared for his holy Catholic and faithful peoples, what is God himself, who has prepared such and so great things?

What, I ask, is God omnipotent? What is he except immeasurable, ineffable, incomprehensible, beyond all things, outside all things, surpassing all things?

For he exceeds all his creation, surpasses every created work, and excels the universe. If you seek greatness, he is greater; if beauty, more beautiful; if sweetness, sweeter; if splendor, brighter; if justice, more just; if strength, stronger; if mercy, more merciful.

For reason permits neither a created work to equal its maker nor a work to be compared with its craftsman, as we read in the prophet: “He who made mighty things is mightier than they, and he who made beautiful things is more beautiful than they” (Wisdom 13:3).

## Chapter Two
## 2. The Trinity Is One God. The Error of the Arians. Three Inseparable Things in the Sun. Three Likewise Inseparable Things in Fire

Thus we proclaim the exalted distinctions of this one divinity, while nevertheless confessing, not as the Jews do but as Christians do, the mysteries of the divine Trinity as well. For just as the Father is omnipotent and ineffable, so also is the Son omnipotent and incomprehensible; and likewise the Holy Spirit, inseparably joined with the Father and the Son, is ineffable and immeasurable. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one omnipotent God: one in the Trinity, one in power; unity, Trinity, eternal majesty. One who is powerful over all things, and a Trinity in unity, and a unity in Trinity, subsists; yet the Trinity is not divided, nor is the unity separated.

Armed and instructed, therefore, with this Catholic faith, dearest brethren, let us briefly ask the impious Arian heretics—who at this time boast impiously of themselves and, by seducing many of our Christians, corrupt and deceive them—how they pray to the Lord, since they think contrary to the Lord. They answer us, saying: “We certainly pray to the Lord in the Trinity; but, as we read, the Father is greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit lower, because Christ himself says, ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John 14:28).

## CHAPTER III

We answer them: “So, then, you pray and worship God in this manner?” “Yes, certainly; so we read, so we worship, so we pray.” To them we say: “If, then, you worship and pray to God in this way, this is not to worship and entreat one great God, but to make three gods. And where is what is read in the divine Law: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’? And again elsewhere it says, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve’” (Deut. 6:4, 5, 13).

For if the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, then it is no longer one Trinity but a divided power. How, moreover, can a discordant power stand, when, according to what we read in the Gospel, “A house divided against itself, or a kingdom, cannot stand” (Matt. 12:25)? How, then, can divinity be distinguished from itself, [Col. 1690] when the radiance of light or the heat of the sun cannot in any way be separated?

For behold, as we see, there are three things in the sun, and they absolutely cannot be separated. Let us see what these three are: movement, radiance, and heat. We see the sun moving, shining, and burning in the sky. Divide the sun, then, if you can, O Arian; and only then divide the Trinity.

But perhaps the matter of distinguishing the sun is difficult, because it is in the sky and far removed from us. Behold, we propose another element, one that is smaller and is with us on earth: I mean fire, which is held in our hands and yet is not divided. Fire, too, has three things and cannot be divided: movement, light, and heat. If, then, impious heretic, you cannot divide the created sun and fire, how can you divide God, the creator of all things?

## CHAPTER IV

### 3. Testimonies of Scripture Concerning the Divine Trinity. Praise of the Catholic Faith

Listen also and learn that this great and unique Trinity was shown from the beginning of the human race. Hear it declared in the Law and the Prophets, in the Psalms and in the Gospel; hear it plainly proclaimed in the Apostle.

Hear, I say, in Genesis: “God made man in the image of God.” In order at the same time to show the inseparable Trinity, that book says, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:27, 2).

Hear the prophet speaking in the person of Christ: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor” (Isa. 61:1).

Hear in the Psalms: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. 32:6); and again, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. 50:14).

Hear this same truth confirmed in the Gospel: The Lord Christ says to the Apostles, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:18–19).

Hear the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory for ever and ever” (Rom. 11:33–36).

Since, then, it has been sufficiently and plainly proved by both the ancient and the new Scriptures that the divine unity is an inseparable Trinity, let us utterly reject the heretics, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Avoid a heretic after one admonition” (Titus 3:10), and now strengthen our faithful peoples in this very Catholic faith.

For there are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no greater substance in this world than the Catholic faith. It saves sinful human beings, gives sight to the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the righteousness of the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins, widows, and married women in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, prepares people for the heavenly kingdoms, and grants them fellowship with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance.

As the Lord himself confirms by his promise: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be equal to the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30), through Christ our Lord.

# SERMON 385

[Note: [Col. 1690] Corrected against two codices, against the Greek, the Roman manuscript, the Vulgate, and the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1690] Elsewhere numbered 38 among the 50 Homilies.]

## On the Love of One Human Being for Another

[Note: [Col. 1690] Except for the opening, which seems ill-fitted here, and also the conclusion, which has the character of Caesarius of Arles, the whole body of the sermon presents Augustine’s teaching and ideas, though here and there perhaps collected and arranged from his writings by someone else. The style is certainly unpleasant, and the parts are joined together with less than elegance.]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Human Love Is Sometimes Right and Sometimes Perverse

We are admonished, dearest brethren, not only in the New but also in the Old Testament, concerning how we ought to maintain perfect charity. [Col. 1691] For the Lord himself said in the Gospel, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39).

Let us therefore discuss for a while the love of one human being for another, because there are perverse forms of human love. A person loves another perversely if he also loves himself perversely; but whoever loves himself rightly also loves another rightly.

For example, there are shameful and detestable loves: the loves of adulterers, the loves of those who corrupt others, unclean loves. All human laws and divine laws detest evil loves. Remove, then, these illicit loves, and let us seek those that are lawful.

### 2. Stages of Lawful Love

Lawful love begins with marriage, but it is still carnal. You see that it is shared with animals: those sparrows that fill the air with their cries have marriages, make nests, brood their eggs together, and nourish their young together. This love is indeed lawful among human beings, but you see that it is carnal.

The second love is that of children, but this too is still carnal. For one who loves children is not to be praised, but one who does not love them is to be detested. Am I going to praise in a human being as something great what I see in a tigress? Serpents love their offspring; lions and wolves love their offspring. Do not, then, consider it a great thing that you love your children. Even in this love you are comparable to serpents. If you do not love them, you are surpassed by serpents.

I am now speaking of honorable loves; I have excluded the shameful ones. Another love is that of relatives. This already appears proper to human beings, if it is not merely a matter of habit. For the love that extends beyond relatives is greater than that which is confined among relatives. Whoever loves his relatives still loves his own blood. Let him love those who are not relatives; let him receive a stranger. This love has already expanded greatly.

Yet it grows so far that it proceeds from a spouse to children, from children to relatives, from relatives to outsiders, and from outsiders to enemies. But in order to reach that point, it has many stages.

## CHAPTER II

### 3. One Friendship Arises from Habit, Another from Reason

Concerning friendship, then, see what I am saying. There are friendships—apart from that friendship which cannot even be called friendship, the kind produced by a bad conscience. For there are people who commit evil deeds together, and therefore seem joined to one another because they are bound by an evil conscience.

Apart from this wicked friendship, there is still a certain carnal friendship arising from the habit of living together, speaking together, and spending time together; so that a person is saddened when he is abandoned by the friend with whom he is accustomed to speak and to share companionship.

Two people meet, walk together for three days, and already do not want to part from each other. This too is a certain sweetness of friendship—honorable, certainly; but let us examine it, since we are seeking the stages of this love, and let us see how far we have advanced, up to the kind of friendship I have described.

This, then, is a friendship of habit, not of reason. Animals have it too. Let two horses eat together: they long for each other. If one goes ahead on another day, the other hastens after it, longing for it as for a friend. It can scarcely be restrained by its rider, and with its own impetus it presses onward until it arrives. When it reaches the one that went ahead, it is calmed. The weight was carrying it, and the weight of love was driving it; it arrived as though at its own place and came to rest.

This friendship of habit is still found among animals. [Col. 1692] Let us rise higher still and move beyond it.

There is another friendship superior to this—not a friendship of habit but of reason—by which we love a person because of faith and mutual goodwill in this mortal life. Whatever we discover above this is divine. Let a person begin to love God, and he will love nothing in another human being except God.

## CHAPTER III

### 4. The Love of Friendship Is Gratuitous

Let your Charity first consider how the love of friendship ought to be gratuitous. You ought not to have or love a friend so that he may provide something for you. If you love him so that he may provide you with money or some temporal advantage, you do not love him, but what he provides.

A friend is to be loved gratuitously, for his own sake, not for something else. If the rule of friendship urges you, a human being, to love gratuitously, how gratuitously must God be loved, who commands you to love a human being?

Nothing is more delightful than God. For in a human being there are things that cause offense; nevertheless, through friendship you compel yourself to tolerate even those things in another that offend you, for the sake of friendship. If, then, you ought not to dissolve friendship with a human being because of certain things that must be tolerated, by what things should God’s friendship be compelled to be dissolved from you? You find nothing more delightful than God. God gives you no cause for offense if you do not offend him: nothing is more beautiful than he, nothing sweeter than he [Note: [Col. 1692] Several manuscripts read “more luminous.”]

But you will say to me: “I do not see him. How am I to love one whom I do not see?” See how you may learn to love one whom you do not see. I shall now show you where you should try to see what you cannot see with these eyes.

Behold, you love a friend. What do you love in him? You love him gratuitously. But perhaps this friend of yours, to pass over other possibilities, is an old man; for it may happen that you have an elderly friend. What do you love in an old man? His bent body, his white head, the wrinkles on his forehead, his contracted cheek? If you love the body you see, nothing is more deformed because of old age; and yet you love something, and you do not love the body you see, because it is deformed.

Where, then, do you see what you love? For if I ask you, “Why do you love him?” you will answer me, “He is a faithful man.” Therefore you love faith. If you love faith, with the same eyes by which faith is seen, God is seen [Note: [Col. 1692] See *Expositions on the Psalms* 32, exposition 2, sermon 1, no. 6, and Psalm 64, no. 8.]

Begin, then, to love God, and you will love a human being for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. God Is to Be Loved Gratuitously

Hear a great testimony. The devil is certainly the accuser of the saints; and because he is not dealing with a judge whom he can deceive, he cannot bring false charges against us. He knows before whom he speaks. Since, therefore, he cannot speak falsely against us, he seeks true charges to bring. For this reason he tempts us, so that he may have something to say.

This adversary of ours, who envies us the kingdom of heaven and does not want us to be there, from which he himself was cast down, said: “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

Even now we are challenged by the adversary to worship God gratuitously, since when he was seeking something to accuse, he thought he had found something great when he said, “Does Job worship God for nothing?” He did not say this because he had seen Job’s heart, but because he saw his riches.

We must beware lest we love [Col. 1693] God for the sake of a reward. What then? Are you going to love God for a reward? What reward is it that God will give you? Whatever else he gives you is less than he himself. You worship him not gratuitously, so that you may receive something from him. Worship him gratuitously, and you will receive him himself. God keeps himself for you, that you may enjoy him.

And if you love what he has made, what must he be who made it? If the world is beautiful, what must the world’s craftsman be? Tear your heart away from love of the creature, so that you may cling to the Creator, and say what is written in the Psalm: “But for me, it is good to cling to God.”

## CHAPTER V

### 6. To Love the Creature After Abandoning the Creator Is Adultery

If you abandon the one who made you and love the things he made, then, having abandoned the one who made you, you are an adulterer. Thus the Epistle of James cries out, calling such people adulterers: “Adulterers!” And why adulterers? Do you ask why? “Do you not know,” he says, “that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4–5).

He made explicit what he said: “Adulterers.” The soul that abandons the Creator and loves the creature is an adulteress. For nothing is chaster, nothing more delightful, than love of him. When you abandon him and embrace this other thing, you become unclean.

O soul, if you wish to be worthy of his embraces, abandon these things and cling to him gratuitously. For this reason the Psalm said: “But for me, it is good to cling to God.” In the preceding verse it said: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:28, 27). And as though it were showing what fornication is, it added: “But for me, it is good to cling to God.”

I want nothing else, but him himself. To cling to him—this is my good; this is my gratuitous good. For this reason it is also called grace, because it exists gratuitously.

When, therefore, you begin to love God gratuitously, you are secure, because you also love a friend gratuitously, and you love him for this purpose: that he may love God with you.

Consider the ordinary friendship with which we began and through which we proceeded by stages; consider it. A husband loves his wife, and a wife her husband. Certainly he wants her safe, and she wants him safe. He wants him to be unharmed; he wants him to be happy. He loves her because he himself wishes to be safe and happy: what he wishes for himself, he wishes for her.

He loves his children. Who does not wish to have his children safe? He loves a friend. Who does not wish to have his friend unharmed? Indeed, if something should happen to him, he trembles, is saddened, is disturbed, runs to him, approaches him, and when he has approached, he mourns.

What, then, does he wish? To have him safe. If, then, everyone who loves wishes to keep safe what he loves; if he understands what true safety is, he begins to love it in himself, and is compelled to love that same true safety in his friend.

## CHAPTER VI

### 7. How Vain Is the Safety of This Life?

If you seek God with fleshly eyes, see the three boys delivered from the fire (Dan. 3). If you seek God through faith, see the Maccabees crowned in the fire (2 Macc. 7).

That salvation, then, is to be loved; this one is to be used. For this present salvation is necessary for use, since it will pass away.

The salvation that physicians speak of is not true salvation, brothers. In a certain way we are sick, for sickness is perpetual in this frailty of the flesh. Do you think that a person is sick when he has a fever and healthy when he is hungry? “He is healthy,” it is said. Do you want to see how great an evil hunger is? Leave him without medicine for seven days, and he dies. [Col. 1694] But because you apply medicine every day, he lives.

The medicine for hunger is food; the medicine for thirst is drink; the medicine for weariness is sleep; the medicine for sitting is walking; the medicine for walking is sitting; the medicine for fatigue is sleeping; the medicine for sleeping is wakefulness.

And see how weak the human body is: whoever takes the very remedy I have mentioned, if he persists in it, grows weak. You were seeking help against hunger through food: behold, the help of food is present; you eat and are restored. If you do more, you grow weaker.

You were seeking drink as help against thirst: by drinking too much you are choked, though you had been tormented by thirst. You became tired by walking and want to sit; sit continually and see whether you will not become tired.

Whatever it takes up in order to drive something else away, if it persists in that very thing, grows weak [Note: [Col. 1694] See *Expositions on the Psalms* 122, nos. 11 and 12.]

## CHAPTER VII

### 8. True Salvation Is Eternal Life. One’s Friend Must Be Loved for Eternal Salvation. Perfect Charity

What, then, is this salvation, brothers—passing, fragile, perishing, vain? Truly, how rightly it has been said: “For what is your life? It is vapor, appearing for a little while” (James 4:15).

Whoever, therefore, loves his life in this life will lose it. But whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life (John 12:25).

What is eternal life? True salvation. And if you see your friend, whom you loved in this world so that he might be safe, because you now desire the kind of salvation that is eternal, you love your friend for that salvation itself. Everything you wish to provide for your friend, you wish to provide for this purpose: that he may possess that salvation with you.

You love justice and want him to be just. You love being under God and want him also to be under God. You love eternal life and want him to reign there with you forever.

You see your enemy pursuing you [Note: [Col. 1694] In Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain, “him” is absent, and this seems better. M.]. It is wickedness that is pursuing you. You ought to be angry with him out of mercy; he is feverish in soul.

As, then, a worldly friend who loves his life according to the world wishes to drive a fever from his friend, whom he loves as himself, for the sake of present health, so love anyone you love for the sake of eternal life. When you find anger, indignation, hatred, and wickedness, try to drive away the sickness of the soul as a worldly friend drives away bodily sickness.

For this purpose you love: that you may make the other what you yourself are. And perfect charity will be in you.

If you discover this, love your spouse, your child, your relative, your neighbor, the unknown person, and your enemy for this purpose, and perfect charity will be in you.

If it is in you, you conquer the world, and the ruler of the world is cast out. For you have heard what the Lord said: “The ruler of this world has been cast out” (John 12:31), because he himself was going to suffer, and through his suffering was going to produce love in human beings.

“Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). In order that he might be loved, he first loved; so that no one would fear dying in his name, he first [Col. 1695] died for all.

For this purpose, then—to build charity in human hearts—he cast the devil out. Out where? From human hearts. Desire brings him in; charity sends him out.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9. Conclusion

We, brothers, carefully considering the stages of charity written above, must not repay the Lord evil for good.

And because, when he came, he bound the strong man, that is, the devil, and took all of us who had been his vessels away from his power, let us, emptied by his grace of every evil, strive to be filled with abundant good, fearing what the Lord himself said [Note: [Col. 1695] See Appendix, sermon 16, no. 4]:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. After this, returning and finding empty the house from which it went out, it brought with it seven spirits more evil than itself; and the later condition of that person became worse than the first” (Luke 11:21–26).

Therefore, lest we too suffer something of this kind, let us exert ourselves as much as we can to introduce virtues into the places formerly occupied by vices, so that we may reach God’s mercy.

# SERMON 386

[Note: [Col. 1695] Corrected against a codex and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1695] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 170.]

## On the Love of Enemies

[Note: [Col. 1695] The scholars of Louvain doubted the authenticity of this sermon. Verlinus declared that it contained nothing of Augustine. Vindingus, by contrast, wished only the opening and conclusion to be excepted, affirming that the rest was Augustine’s.]

### 1. Charity Must Extend Even to Enemies. Prayers Handed Down by Christ the Judge Himself. We Must Forgive in Order to Be Forgiven. Secure Before God Is One Whose Brother Denies Him Forgiveness When He Asks. We Must Pray for One Who Does Not Ask for Forgiveness

Pay attention, my brothers, to charity, which divine Scripture praises in such a way that it sets nothing equal to it.

When God warns us to love one another, does he merely warn us to love someone who loves us? This is mutual love, but it is not enough for God. For he wished us to go as far as loving our enemies, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:44–45).

What do you say? Do you love your enemy? You may answer: “Because of weakness, I cannot.” But make progress, and act so that you can—especially since you are going to pray to a judge whom no one can deceive, who is going to plead [Col. 1696] your case.

Appeal, then, to this judge, where no court clerk causes disturbance, no official removes anyone, and no advocate is purchased who might pour out prayers or speak words you have not learned. The only-begotten Son of God himself, equal to the Father, seated at the Father’s right hand, his assessor and your judge, taught you a few words that any uneducated person can retain and say. In them he established your case and taught you the heavenly law [Note: [Col. 1695] Perhaps, “the heavenly jurist taught you.”]—how you should pray.

But perhaps you will answer: “Through whom do I ask—through myself or through another?” The one who taught you to pray himself presents the prayer on your behalf, because you were the defendant. Rejoice, because the one who will then be your judge is now your advocate.

Therefore, because you are going to pray and conduct your case in a few words, you will come to these words: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

For God says to you: “What do you give me so that I may forgive you your debts? What gift do you offer? What sacrifice of your conscience do you place upon my altars?” Immediately he taught you what to ask and what to offer.

You ask, “Forgive us our debts.” And what do you offer? “As we also forgive our debtors.” You are a debtor to one who cannot be deceived; you too have a debtor.

God says to you: “You are my debtor, and he is your debtor. What I do to you, my debtor, I will do according to what you do to your debtor. You offer me a gift from that by which you spare your debtor. You ask me for mercy; do not be slow to show mercy yourself.”

Consider what Scripture says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). Do not offer a sacrifice without mercy, because your sins are not forgiven unless you offer it with mercy.

But perhaps you say: “I have no sins.” However cautious you may be, brother, while living in the flesh in this world, you act amid pressures and difficulties and move among innumerable temptations; you cannot be without sin.

Certainly God says to you: “Be secure concerning sin. Do not forgive if you have nothing that I should forgive you; rather, demand repayment if you owe nothing. But if you are a debtor, rejoice all the more that you have a debtor in whom you may do what is to be done to you.”

Listen to me and examine yourself, for perhaps you are among the few good people who can truly pray the Lord’s Prayer and truthfully say, “Lord, forgive me, as I also forgive.” Do not do this deceitfully or falsely; do it from a true heart, so that it may be true in you as well.

If the person who injured you, who sinned against you, asks your forgiveness and you forgive him, then you can say securely, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

But if you resist one who asks, you too will be rejected when you ask. You have closed the door against one who knocks; you will find it closed when you knock.

If you open the entrails of mercy to one who asks you, God will also open them to you when you ask him.

I am now addressing those who ask forgiveness from their Christian brothers and do not receive it. Behold, if you grant it, you will pray securely. But if he asks you and you do not grant it, how will you be secure [Note: [Col. 1696] Perhaps, “how will he be secure”?]

Whoever you are who have sinned and have not deserved forgiveness, do not fear. Appeal to his God and yours. These are debts. Can a servant demand debts that the master has forgiven [Note: [Col. 1696] See Sermon 211, nos. 3 and 4.]?

But if the person who sinned against you does not ask you—if he does not seek forgiveness, if he has sinned and, moreover, is still angry—what will you do? Will you forgive or not forgive?

Behold, you have not forgiven. Why? Because he did not ask.

If you did not forgive for this reason, do not hesitate in the Lord’s Prayer; say it securely and do not beat your breast, because you did not forgive one who did not ask.

Therefore, the one who did not ask remains; the debt is indeed demanded from him. Nevertheless, [Col. 1697] let perfect charity be in you: pray for the one who does not ask, because you are praying for one who is in great danger.

### 2. Christ’s Example of Praying for Those Who Insulted and Killed Him. The Example of Stephen

Now pay attention to your Teacher and Lord—not sitting on a chair, but hanging on a cross, surrounded on every side by crowds of enemies and saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Look at the teacher; listen to the imitator. Did the Lord Christ pray for those who were asking, and not rather for those who were insulting and killing him? Did the physician abandon his profession because a madman was raging?

Say, then, “Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” They are killing the Savior because they do not seek salvation.

Perhaps you, in turn, will say: “When will I be able to do what the Lord was able to do?” Why do you say this? Consider where he does this. Consider that he did it on the cross, not in heaven.

God is always in heaven with the Father; but on the cross he was a human being for you, where he offered himself to all as an example to imitate. For your sake he sent forth that voice, so that it might be heard by everyone. He could have prayed for them in silence, but you would not have had an example.

But if the Lord seems too great for you, let the servant not be too great for you. Can you not imitate your Lord while he hung on the cross? Consider Stephen, his servant, while he was being stoned.

First, as a servant addressing his Lord, he said, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” After this, kneeling, he said, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:58–59). And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the rest of love.

He found the richest peace, because he wished peace for his enemies. Did he then pray for those who were asking, and not for those who were raging, stoning, and killing him?

You have an example. Learn; see how he prayed standing for himself and knelt for them. Do we suppose, brothers, that he loved them more than himself?

When he stood for himself as a righteous man, he was easily heard. But for the unrighteous, he had to bend the knee.

Thus he displayed love extending even to enemies who were asking forgiveness [Note: [Col. 1697] Perhaps, “who were not asking forgiveness.”]

Therefore, brothers, for the sake of security in the Lord’s Prayer, forgive from your heart those who ask, so that the Lord may forgive you your sins in this mortal body and in the future, for ever and ever, etc.

# SERMON 387

[Note: [Col. 1697] Corrected against two codices, against the Greek, the Roman manuscript, the Vulgate, and the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1697] Elsewhere, 5 among the 50 Homilies.]

## On the Correction of One’s Neighbor

[Note: [Col. 1697] Neither the opening nor the conclusion suits Augustine. The parts are inelegantly connected with one another, and clarity and refinement in the sayings have been excessively neglected. We think that Augustine’s words or ideas have been gathered here.]

### 1. The Duty of Correction Is Imposed on Priests. The Word of God Is Our Adversary

Your Charity has often heard in the Holy Scriptures, dearest brothers, what danger priests are placed in if they do not fulfill what the Apostle charges: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2).

And because such a grave burden hangs over our necks—we are told, “If you do not announce his [Col. 1698] wickedness to the wicked person, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:18)—it is necessary for us to chastise all who are negligent, whether privately or publicly.

But when we correct someone, if the person we correct is evil, he considers who is correcting him; and more readily and willingly recognizes in his corrector than in himself something to correct. And if he finds true faults that he too can bring against the one correcting him, he rejoices.

How much better would a corrected person rejoice in his own health than, when rebuked, in another’s sickness? Suppose what you say is true. You have found something in the person by whom you were reproved. Yet through that person truth was speaking to you; through an evil and unrighteous person truth was speaking to you.

You seek something to criticize in a human being; instead, find something to criticize in the truth. Whether you wish it or not, the truth is your adversary, and in it you find nothing to accuse. Make it your friend, if you can.

Your adversary is the word of God. Let a sinner utter it, let a righteous person utter it: it is the word of God, and it is blameless. It is your adversary. Be reconciled with it while you are with it on the road.

This road is the present life. The word of God is the adversary of all unrighteous people.

Is it little that, while remaining in its most blessed and most secret dwelling, it came to you so that it might be with you on the road, and wished to accompany you? It did this so that, while you are walking and have the power, you might settle your case and say, “When will you finish the road?” Once you have finished the road, there will be no one with whom you can settle your case. Then the adversary will hand you over to the judge, the judge to the officer, and the officer to the prison. “You will never get out until you have paid the last penny” (Matt. 5:25–26).

The word of God is with you on the road, like an adversary. You have the power; settle the matter. What does this adversary ask of you, that you should be reconciled with him? What but your salvation?

He walks with his adversaries and tells them to be reconciled with him. Let it be done; the road is not yet finished. What was not done yesterday, let it be done today. The road is not yet finished. What are you waiting for, until it is finished? When it has been finished, there will be no other place where you can be reconciled with your adversary. The judge, the officer, and the prison remain.

For many people this road has ended suddenly, when they were promising themselves many more years on it.

But suppose your road will be long, and your adversary will always walk with you. Are you not ashamed to remain at odds for so long with such an adversary?

The word of God, insofar as it is concerned, is your friend; you make it your adversary. For it wishes you well, while you, on the contrary, wish yourself ill. It commands, “Do not steal”; you steal. It commands, “Do not commit adultery”; you commit adultery. It commands, “Do not commit fraud”; you do so. It forbids you to swear; you swear falsely. You act contrary to everything it says; you make the word of God your enemy. Nor is this surprising, when you yourself are your own enemy.

“Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). If, then, by loving iniquity you have hated your own soul, are you surprised that you have hated the word of God, which wishes your soul well?

## 2. Correction of One’s Neighbor Must Not Be Administered Out of Hatred

So shall we remain silent, then, and correct absolutely no one? By all means let us correct—but first ourselves. You wish to correct your neighbor: nothing is nearer to you than you yourself. Why go farther away? [Note: [Col. 1700] Corrected according to two codices, the Greek recension, the Roman, Venetian, and other editions, and according to Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Col. 1699] You have yourself before you. For what does the Lord say through Scripture? “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39). If, then, you do not love yourself, how do you love your neighbor? You have received the rule of love for your neighbor from yourself. “I do love him,” you will say. That is why I say: first love yourself, and speak to yourself. But if you truly say this out of love, it is clear that the word proceeding outward has accomplished something within. Yet we must fear that you do not love yourself and wish to correct someone else, and that you do this out of hatred.

But if you hate your brother, you accuse him of lesser faults than those you commit. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). You heard this; the Epistle of John was read today. Scripture says this so that people would not disregard what they have within their hearts and accuse only what is done through the body: now, whoever hates his brother, it says, is a murderer. His hand has not yet been armed; he has not yet occupied a narrow pass suitable for ambush [Note: [Col. 1699] That is, a place suitable for lying in wait.]; he has not yet prepared an ambush; he has not yet sought poison—and yet, in God’s eyes, he is already held guilty because of the hatred conceived within him. The one whom he seeks to kill still lives, yet he is already judged to have killed him.

If, therefore, you correct someone out of hatred, do you dare correct anyone as a murderer? Or because people do not seize you and lead you before a judge, do you therefore fail to recognize your crime in the eyes of the supreme God and Judge? If you do not wish to acknowledge your crime, you will acknowledge your punishment. For he does not spare murderers.

“But I correct myself,” you say, “while I am on the way.” Correct yourself, then, and afterward you will be able to correct your brother. You accuse him of lesser faults while committing greater ones. “You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam in your own eye” (Matt. 7:3). The Lord said this concerning people who correct others out of hatred.

You correct someone who is angry, while you yourself are wasting away with hatred? Weigh anger and hatred on the scales of reflection. What is anger? A kind of fervor of the spirit. At present, something displeases you. But that anger has now grown old within you, and for that reason it has become hatred. Anger is a speck; as it grows, it will become a beam. For just as a speck grows into a beam, so anger, when it grows old, becomes hatred.

You already hate, and you correct the angry person: in him you are displeased by the speck, while in yourself you are still pleased with the beam. Do you wish to know how great the difference is? We often find fathers angry with their sons; you will rarely find a father hating his son. A father can be angry with a son whom he loves: one may say, “He is angry and loves”; one cannot say, “He hates and loves.” I have said this concerning people who punish lesser faults in others but do not punish greater ones in themselves.

## 3. Conclusion

Therefore, dearest brothers, thinking rightly about these matters, let us “make friends with our adversary” while we are on the way with him; that is, let us agree with the word of God while we are still in this life, because afterward, when we have passed from this world, no settlement or any satisfaction will remain. The judge remains, and the officer, and the prison.

Therefore, so that with the Lord’s help we may be able to fulfill all these things, let us love with our whole heart not only our friends but also our enemies, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying in you: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14); and also: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

May he who is true love himself deign to grant this to us—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever, etc.

# SERMON CCCLXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1700] Elsewhere, 19 among the Fifty Homilies.]

## On Giving Alms, I

[Note: [Col. 1700] The Louvain editors were uncertain about this sermon; Verlin regarded it as spurious, while Vinding considered it interpolated and corrupted. Certain expressions are used improperly—for example, in section 2, “I extinguish all sins,” instead of “I redeem and abolish,” and shortly afterward, “yet you extinguish,” instead of “you finish with sins,” or “you cease to sin.” In general, the style indicates that the sermon is not wholly Augustinian. It is, however, very similar to the preceding three.]

### 1. At the Last Judgment Only Almsgiving Is Mentioned

This reading, brothers, which we have just heard from the holy Gospel, urges us to give alms; and it urges us in such a way that at his judgment the Lord counts only almsgiving that has been performed on the right, and only almsgiving that has not been performed on the left (Matt. 25:31, 46). [Note: [Col. 1700] See Sermon 60, section 9.]

This does not mean that other human deeds, whether good or evil, do not come under judgment; for it is written that “everything will come to judgment” (Eccles. 12:14). Yet our Lord Jesus Christ, announcing to us the judgment that was to come, chose nothing by which to admonish us except almsgiving.

Will nothing be said to those on the right: “Because you lived chastely, because you did not seize what belonged to others, because you confessed my faith even unto bloodshed”? All these good deeds must certainly be honored at the judgment of Jesus Christ.

Again, do you think nothing will be said to those on the left: “Because you were unchaste, because you committed fornication, because you seized what belonged to others, because through your pride and evil behavior you caused my name to be blasphemed,” along with all the other things that he enumerates?

Yet our Lord, announcing his judgment to us, was silent about all the other righteous deeds and deigned to mention almsgiving alone. He was silent about all the evil deeds of the wicked and judged that only the barrenness of almsgiving should be rebuked—not for any other reason than to admonish us.

Why is this? Because all crimes are redeemed by almsgiving. Therefore he praised the one’s fruitfulness and blamed and condemned the other’s barrenness.

### 2. Almsgiving Does Not Benefit Those Guilty of Graver Sins Unless Their Conduct Is Changed

No one here is without sin. But what you heard—that all evil deeds are redeemed by almsgiving—do not understand it in the way certain perverse people do. Almsgiving can benefit you in the erasing of past sins if you change your conduct. But if you persist in the same evils, your almsgiving does not corrupt the judge.

I am speaking about those wicked deeds and crimes that everyone who receives the body and blood of Christ ought now to avoid. As for the rest, I am not unaware that this mortal life, lived in corruptible flesh, cannot be without sins. But those daily and lesser sins also have their daily cleansings. This is why we beat our breasts and say in prayer to the Lord our God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). We do not say this without reason; nor would the heavenly Teacher himself have taught us this prayer unless he had foreseen that we would be sinners.

He saw what we ought to avoid, and he saw what is difficult to avoid. Yet he judged it impossible to avoid everything [Note: [Col. 1701] Perhaps, “he indicated.”]—he who taught this daily prayer not to ordinary Christians but to the very apostles, the leaders of the flock.

When the apostles beat their breasts and say, “Forgive us our debts”—that is, our sins—does any little sheep dare to boast of his righteousness? See what sort of man the apostle John was. He reclined upon the Lord’s breast and drank hidden things from that lofty fountain of wisdom. From there he drank what he poured forth in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Gospel also repeatedly testifies that the Lord loved him especially (ibid. 13:23 and 21:20).

And yet he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). But no one should become complacent because these words are spoken—no murderer should come and say, on account of his daily fornications and robberies, “Forgive us our debts.”

What God appointed to be said daily on account of lesser sins, that person thinks can help him with those grave sins from which he does not wish to depart but in which he desires to remain forever. Let him beat his breast over those sins also; let him give alms for them also—but with his life changed. Let him depart from there and come here.

But if he says in his heart: “If I commit robberies every day, if I defile myself with daily adulterous corruptions, if I seek out sorcerers, sacrifice to idols, consult astrologers, and do not withdraw from such a life at all, yet by giving alms daily I extinguish all my sins”—you do indeed extinguish them, but only when you have been extinguished. For this exchange of yours will be so evil that someone will say of you: “And yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more; you will seek his place, and you will not find it. I saw the wicked exalted like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought his place, and it was not found” (Ps. 36:10, 35, 36).

Your sins therefore perish—but with you. For you will not be permitted to sin in Gehenna, nor, when the eternal fire begins to torment you, will you think about satisfying your lusts. Your sins perish, therefore, but with you.

But if you change your life, they perish while you are found, and it will be said of you: “He was dead and came to life again; he was lost and was found” (Luke 15:24).

# SERMON CCCLXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1701] Corrected according to the Roman recension and according to Sirmond.]

[Note: [Col. 1701] Elsewhere, 40 among the Sirmondian sermons.]

## On Giving Alms, III

[Note: [Col. 1701] A sermon of sound character and worthy of Augustine; but its latter part is identical with the latter part of Sermon 60, except that there the entire account of the man who distributed the price of a solidus among the poor is omitted.]

### 1. The Heavenly Bread and the Earthly Bread. The Recommendation to Give Earthly Bread in Order to Obtain the Heavenly

The Lord’s Gospel reading admonishes us to speak to you about obtaining heavenly bread. This earthly bread is necessary for the earth, because our flesh is earth. But it cannot be that our flesh should have its bread and our soul should not have its bread.

Indeed, our soul too, in a certain poverty in this world, needs its own bread just as the flesh needs its own. For whoever does not need bread is God. God alone, therefore, does not need bread. He himself is the bread of our soul; he does not need another bread, but, sufficient in himself, nourishes us also.

The heavenly bread by which our soul is nourished is therefore evident. But how do we reach it, so that we may be filled with it, when for the moment we scarcely gather crumbs from it lest we perish in this famished wilderness? How, then, do we reach the fullness of this bread of which the Lord says, “Whoever eats this bread will not hunger, and whoever drinks the drink that I shall give will never thirst” (John 6:51)—promising a kind of fullness and satisfaction without disgust?

How, then, do we reach this satisfaction of bread, placed as we are in this hunger far from that fullness? We need advice. If we neglect this advice, we knock at that bread without reason. Rather, the advice I am about to give—or, better, to recall, for I shall not speak it as something learned from myself but as something I learned with you—this advice, I say, is not merely something that whoever despises it knocks at without reason; whoever despises it does not knock at all. To follow and practice this advice is to knock.

What do you think, my brothers? Does God truly have, as it were, a bodily hard door that he closes against human beings, and therefore tell us, “Knock,” so that we may come and beat upon the door until our knocking reaches the ears of the master of the house, seated in some hidden place, and he orders that we be admitted, saying: “Who is knocking? Who is troubling my ears? Give him what he asks and let him go away”? It is not so.

Nevertheless, there is something similar. Certainly, when you knock at someone’s door, you act with your hands. There is something for you to do with your hands when you knock at the Lord’s door. Act with your hands—knock with your hands. If you do not do this, I do not say that you knock in vain; I say that you do not knock. For this reason you will not deserve to receive, and for this reason you will not receive: because you do not knock.

“How,” he says, “do you want me to knock? Look, I ask every day.”

You do well. For this too has been said: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). Everything has been said: ask, seek, knock. You ask by praying, you seek by disputing, you knock by distributing alms. Let your hand therefore not rest.

When the Apostle was admonishing the people concerning almsgiving, he said: “I give advice in this matter: this is beneficial for you, who began a year ago not only to understand but also to will” (2 Cor. 8:10).

And Daniel said this to King Nebuchadnezzar: “Accept my counsel, O king, and redeem your sins with almsgiving” (Dan. 4:24).

### 2. Let the One Who Gives to the Poor Not Exalt Himself. By Receiving, the Poor Benefit the Rich More Than the Rich Benefit the Poor by Giving

If, then, the counsel we receive commands or admonishes us to provide something from what we possess to those in need, let us not become proud when we give. For if it is counsel, it benefits you more than the person to whom you give.

Let us not, therefore, exalt ourselves over our works, as though we should take pleasure in ourselves because we bestow benefits upon those to whom we give. Whoever wishes to receive counsel wishes to receive what benefits him; and whoever gives counsel gives advice. If he gives advice, it benefits the one to whom he gives it.

A poor person, as a suppliant, receives something from you. For if it is not fitting for you to give proudly, how much less is it fitting for him to receive proudly! He receives humbly; he receives with thanks. You, however, should know and remember not only what you give but also what you receive.

If this poor man were permitted to answer you—if he happened to perceive that you were becoming proud over him—and said to you: “Why are you proud? Why do you exalt yourself because you gave me something? What did you give me? Bread.

“If you had placed this bread in your house and neglected it, it would have gone into rust; from rust into decay; from decay into earth; and the earth would have returned to earth. You extended your hand to my outstretched hand so that it might receive. Remember from what your hand was made, and where you placed it upon mine: earth, from earth, into earth.

“Besides, what do I do with your bread? I eat it and restrain the distress of hunger; I receive a benefit; I am not ungrateful. Nevertheless, consider what the Lord himself, your Savior, admonished you: ‘Everything that enters the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled into the sewer’ (Matt. 15:17).

“And again, consider what the apostle Paul said to you: ‘Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, but God will destroy both it and them’ (1 Cor. 6:13).

“Bread, then, as I said, is earth: from earth, into earth; so that earth may be supported and earth restored. You consider what you have given, but you do not consider what you are going to receive. See, then, whether I benefit you more by receiving than you benefit me by giving.

“For if there were no one to receive from you, you would not distribute earth, and you would not receive heaven. I knock at your door, and you hear me; you order that something be brought to me by which my hunger may be sustained and restrained from the distress it inflicts upon me. You have done well.

“Do not listen to me knocking, if you dare. If you are not going to ask, despise the one who asks. Despise me if you ask nothing of the one who made both me and you.

“But if you are going to ask for what you give me, because you have heard me, you benefit yourself so that you may be heard. Give thanks to him who makes you purchase so precious a thing at so cheap a price.

“You give what perishes in time; you receive what remains forever. You give what, if you did not give it, you would shortly throw away; you receive what you may enjoy forever.

“You give what sustains human hunger; you receive what makes you a companion of the angels. You give what prevents a person from being hungry for a little while, only to suffer hunger again; you receive what prevents you from ever suffering hunger or thirst.”

When, therefore, you see what you give and what you receive, do not give—if you dare. Let us see who suffers the greater loss: I, to whom you do not give earth, or you, who will not reach the one who made heaven and earth.

### 3. Christ’s Counsel to Distribute Riches, So That They Do Not Perish Here

If, then, we receive counsel, let us act for our own sake; and let no one say that he benefits the poor. He benefits himself more than the poor.

If we think truthfully, my brothers, and understand according to the words of our Lord—for if we understand otherwise, we perish—if we live not according to our own counsel but according to his, then we truly live.

If we have something to give to the poor and do not give it, we leave it here; or perhaps, while we are alive, we lose it here. For how many people have suddenly lost all the possessions they had carefully stored away? In a single hostile assault, the entire treasures of the rich perished.

No one said to the enemy, “I am keeping this for my children.” You certainly see that [Note: [Col. 1704] In Sirmond, *quia* is lacking; moreover, the sense rejects the word. M.]—if they have any faith at all. For we must speak about those who, being Christians, suffered this. There is no mention here of those who did not know God. They lost in this life what they regarded as of greatest value, and they did not hope for another life. Darkness outside, darkness within: poverty in the chest, greater poverty in the conscience.

Of such people, then, as I said, we are not to speak at all; rather, we should speak about those in whom there is some Christian faith. I said “some,” not strong or complete faith, because if it had been strong and complete, they would not have despised the Lord’s counsel.

Yet certainly, dearest brothers, when they saw their houses empty—or perhaps were not even allowed to see the emptiness of their houses, having been led away captive, with flames following after their departure—when, therefore, they saw themselves stripped bare, how they regretted not having listened to the Lord’s counsel!

What did our Lord Jesus Christ say to that rich man who asked for counsel about attaining eternal life? What did he say to him? Did he say, “Lose what you have”? Certainly, even if he had said this—“Lose temporal things”—he would have said it so that you might acquire eternal things. [Note: [Col. 1704] Sirmond has this passage as follows: “What, then, did he say? Did he say to him, ‘Lose what you have’? It would be pleasing if he had said this: ‘Lose temporal things, so that you may acquire eternal things.’” M.]

Yet he did not say to him, “Lose what you have.” For he saw that the man loved his possessions. He did not say, “Lose”; he said, “Move to a place where you will not lose.”

“Do you love your treasures? Do you love your money? Do you love your riches? Do you love your estates? Whatever you love, you have on earth. There you have what you love—where you may lose it and perish.

“I give you counsel: move to heaven. If you have it here, you will lose what you have and perish with what you lose. But if you have it there, you have not lost it; rather, you follow it to the place where you sent it” (Matt. 19:16–21).

I give counsel, etc. [Note: [Col. 1704] Omitted material should be supplied from Sermon 60, section 7.]

[. . .]

Why did we despise the father who warned us and experience the enemy invading us?

Many, therefore, are regretful. For a certain man—poor, indeed, but nevertheless rich in the fatness of charity even from his slender resources, as is truly said to have happened—having sold a solidus, as people customarily do, ordered one hundred *folles* to be distributed to the poor from the price of the solidus [Note: [Col. 1704] He does not state for how much he sold the solidus; it may, however, be understood from Valentinian’s Novel 25 among the Theodosian Novels, where it is decreed: “A solidus may never be sold for less than seven thousand coins.” Cassiodorus says that it was formerly sold for six thousand, in Book 1 of the *Variae*, Letter 10: “They wanted a solidus to be six thousand denarii.” SIRM.].

[Note: [Col. 1704] He calls them bronze *folles*, not silver ones. One hundred silver *folles* would not have been a small fraction of a solidus. Just as they called both silver and bronze coins denarii, so some *folles* were silver and others bronze. The value of the bronze *folles* was either the same as that of the coins, or denarii, six or seven thousand of which were reckoned as one solidus, or there was little difference between the two kinds. What silver *folles* were worth in Augustine’s time may be estimated from Book 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On Swineherds*, which fixes the price of pork at six *folles* per pound, and from what is related in Book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8, concerning Florentius, a tailor from Hippo, who is said to have sold a large fish for three hundred *folles*. In both cases everything can fit if *folles* are taken as asses or solidi of our Gallic currency. Six solidi per pound of pork would indeed have been a fair price, and selling a large fish for three hundred of our asses is not at all absurd. It is therefore possible to conjecture that the value of *folles* and our solidi was the same or similar. These remarks, however, concern the *follis* insofar as it signifies a definite kind of coin. In monetary matters *follis* has other meanings that are irrelevant here. Sirm.]

It was done. There the ancient enemy—that is, the devil—brought it about that the man should regret his good deed [Note: [Col. 1705] Sirmond, from codex r.: “brought it about that he should regret.” *Egit* (“brought it about”) is absent from Michael’s manuscript.] and erase by murmuring what he had rightly done through obedience; he sent in a thief and took away everything from which the small amount had been given to the poor.

The devil expected the voice of one blaspheming, but found one praising; he expected hesitation, but found steadfastness. The enemy certainly wanted the man to regret it, and he did regret it. But see what he said:

“Wretched me, for I did not give everything! What I did not give is what I have lost. For I did not place it there, where the thief cannot approach.”

Therefore, if this is counsel, etc. [Note: [Col. 1705] The remainder is found in Sermon 60, sections 8 and following, through the end.]

# SERMON CCCXC

[Note: [Col. 1705] Corrected according to the Roman recension and according to Vignier.]

[Note: [Col. 1705] Elsewhere, 15 among the Vignerian sermons.]

## On Giving Alms, III

[Note: [Col. 1705] In the manuscripts it is assigned to the Saturday after the Fifth Sunday of Lent. The sermon is corrupt and mutilated, but otherwise contains almost nothing inconsistent with Augustine.]

### 1. Almsgiving as the Companion of Fasting among Holy Men. The Counsel to Send Riches Ahead to Heaven

We wish to exhort Your Charity to give alms, insofar as the Lord grants us the ability—almsgiving, which is accustomed to accompany fasting among holy and faithful men—so that what is taken away from the one who has may be added to the one who does not have; so that, when you deprive your soul of gain, you may withdraw from the flesh what you place in heaven.

You have your storehouse there; you have your guardian there. For wherever people wish to preserve safely on earth what they love, they obtain the most secure places for themselves and take the greatest care they can to keep it somewhere thieves cannot approach.

And when people desire and attempt this, how can it happen on earth? Perhaps the very guardian will be a thief.

The Lord Jesus Christ, observing what people want and strive for when they preserve their possessions on earth, gave this counsel: “Keep them in heaven; entrust them to me.” Therefore, he who commanded you to give did not wish you to be lost; he wished you to move elsewhere.

Let your possession go ahead of you, since you will follow it. What you do not send ahead to the place where you will not remain long [Note: [Col. 1705] Perhaps something is missing: “Here you leave it, where you will not remain long.”], you do not know who will possess after you what you have preserved.

Therefore, lift from here what you love, lest by loving it here you cling to it, and by clinging to it lose both it and yourself. Your Lord himself is the guardian of you and your possessions.

If an intimate friend should perhaps give advice to someone ignorant about preserving grain—telling him to move it from lower to higher places, where he could preserve it better—would you not accept his advice? [Note: [Col. 1705] See Sermon 60, section 7.]

Your Lord gives you that very advice: he does not want either you or your possessions to be corrupted. “Place it here, if you do not want to lose it.”

Do you wish to know what is happening? I know that no one can give better advice about this structure than the one who made it. You say, “Where shall I store it?” He replies, “In heaven.” For he says: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where the thief does not break in and the moth does not corrupt; for where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:20–21).

Accept the counsel, since you have been offered so great a storehouse, for which no notice has been posted assuring you that you will possess it forever.

### 2. Riches Are Lifted to Heaven by Being Distributed. Almsgiving as a Loan to God

Perhaps you will ask how you can lift your possession there. Do not become agitated and seek, by imagining ladders or some kind of machinery, how to do it. But, as is usually done by citizens living abroad, make a transfer [Note: [Col. 1706] See Sermon 42, section 2.].

Many certainly do this: when they find trustworthy agents, they give readily. Your Lord Christ did this—rich above, poor here. He hungers here; he asks you for a transfer. He will repay what is due.

Why, then, do you hesitate? Why do you delay giving? Is he not able to repay?

Give to the poor; you will not lose, do not fear. You give to him when you give to one of his least. Hear the Gospel. When those placed on the right were astonished, and after certain needs had been enumerated said, “When did we see you in these conditions?” the Lord replied: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:37–40).

“I,” he says, “received it when the poor person received it. In him I was hungry; in him I was satisfied.”

Give confidently: the Lord receives; the Lord asks. You would have nothing to give him unless you had first received it from him.

If you lent money to human beings, you would burden them with interest; but here there is no such borrower who is burdened by interest. If you wish to be a lender, be one with me, God says to you; give to me, and I repay with interest.

Now lift yourself up; extend your greed. For one solidus perhaps you will receive not ten, not a hundred, not a thousand, not earth, but heaven.

If you gave a pound of bronze and received silver, or a pound of silver and received gold, you would rejoice and count yourself fortunate. What you give will truly be exchanged—not for gold or silver, but for eternal life. It will be exchanged because you will be changed. The one who gave will become an angel; what he gave will become an angelic throne.

There is no remedy that frees anyone from death except almsgiving. It is difficult for any human being to pass through this life without sins. Therefore, my brothers, distribute your possessions; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, a treasure that remains in heaven.

Hear the Psalm: “Although a man walks in an image, he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasures and does not know for whom he gathers” (Ps. 38:7). “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38).

# SERMON CCCXCI

[Note: [Col. 1706] Corrected according to the Venetian recension and according to Amerbach, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1706] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 246.]

## To Young Men

[Note: [Col. 1706] The Louvain editors regard this sermon as doubtful; Verlin considers it spurious, as does Vinding. The latter says that it does not differ from the Ambrosian style; but certainly it does not differ any more from the Augustinian style of the earlier years.]

### 1. No Age Is Free from Temptation. Not Childhood

My address is to you, young men—the flower of life, the danger of the mind. No time and no age, so long as this corruptible flesh is carried about, can be free from temptations.

And a good person wrestles in the contest for as long as he struggles not to be overcome by the adversary and lives amid dangers, as long as he contends with him in this mortality as in a certain sandy arena.

As soon as a human being is born into the world and enters upon a life full of misery, announcing the labor that lies ahead as though he were a prophet of it through the proclamation of a tearful voice, he may already be tempted—not yet in his own mind, perhaps, but in the minds of his parents or of any people in whose hands his weakness lies to be nourished—and may be seized by the devil’s deceptions, whether through the bindings of accursed remedies, through the sacrilegious rites of the nations, or, if death should threaten, through neglect of renunciation in saving Baptism.

In short, that age is tempted when it is loved by its own people in the world but neglected in Christ.

For it carries with it the offspring of death and is rooted in that wound of sin which was inflicted upon the first man, from whom we derive the origin of corruption, by the serpent’s poisonous tooth.

Therefore holy Job says that no one is clean of the filth of sin—not even an infant whose life upon earth is only one day old (Job 4:14, according to the Septuagint).

But why should I speak of one already born, when David cries out in a voice of grief and says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:7)?

For the Baptisms of newborn infants might seem superfluous unless all died in Adam and original sin passed through the parents’ bodies along the path of mortality even to the offspring, since almighty God forms mortal creatures according to the law of his ordering, while the excellent Father supplies immortality through the grace of renewal.

### 2. Nor Old Age

If, then, even the infancy of mortal human beings is not free from temptations because of the bond of corruption, what shall I say about the other ages? Or is old age perhaps exempt, so that in flesh already near to becoming a corpse, the blood and limbs of unlawful desire have grown cold, and the material of temptation has withered away from a body already weary and almost dead?

By no means. In wicked old men there is often such a whirlpool of greed and such an insatiable gullet and appetite that, just as good old men are made serene by wisdom, so these are buried in drunkenness—as though their dry entrails, exhausted of moisture, were bent for this purpose: that they might be watered by a flood of drunkenness to restore their former vigor.

What of avarice, which is the root of all evils? Does it not burn more fervently in cold old men to acquire, the sooner they will have to leave behind what they acquire? A truly astonishing madness. They hasten to burden themselves with greater expenses when they have already reached the goal toward which they were advancing.

### 3. Youth Is Attacked More Forcefully

If neither childhood nor old age is free from temptations—one of them scarcely yet entering this life, the other already leaving it; one having been absent shortly before, the other soon to be absent—what should we think and say about the ardor of youth, which stands between the two, has already withdrawn from the weakness of childhood, and has not yet reached the sluggishness of old age?

This age is shaken by more numerous and greater storms of temptation; it is covered by the more frequent assault of the waves of the overflowing world. It presumes upon its strength, boasts of the dignity of its appearance, and either desires or rejoices in shining forth through the pomp of temporal things.

Thus, for youth, whatever truth commands is poison, while whatever the devil suggests is food. But the bitterness of justice is medicine for the wound of this age; the sweetness of injustice is a snare for its recklessness.

To this belongs what is written: “The wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6); and what David says: “Let the righteous strike me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5).

Let truth burn and nevertheless heal. For the sinner’s oil—the flattery of the flatterer—soothes but deceives. There pride is eased, but life slips away.

The Prophet speaks in the person of one who is already seeking a physician, who endures the hand of the healer even with the sharpness of pain, who desires his illness to be cured rather than praised.

The wound of youth is dangerous: it burns with desires, swells with hope, and wastes away in pleasures. But this is the hope of the hopeless—the hope of perishable things—which does not release the affection of the miserable soul but inflates it, making it unable to endure the touch of truth. Thus, even despairing of its own immortality, it loves to say—and loves those who say these things to it [Note: [Col. 1708] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, Venice, and Louvain have: “and loves even to have these things said to it.” M.]—“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die”; but it hates to say and to hear: “Be sober, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:32, 34).

It loves the destructive gentleness of the enemy and hates the wholesome harshness of the physician. This perversity, this madness, is especially to be feared in youth.

### 4. The Words of the Luxurious

Softness is followed by cruelty. From this arises the speech of men who dissolve into debauchery and then harden into crimes:

“For they said, reasoning unsoundly among themselves, ‘Short and sorrowful is our life, and there is no relief at the end of a man’s life, and no one has been known to return from the underworld.’” And a little later:

“Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as quickly as we can, as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes,”

and the other words of luxuriant desire that are appended in the same passage: the words of men who despair of eternal life and place their hope, as though on the sand of a torrent, in the temporal corruption of the flesh. But from this immoderation of lusts and the worms of rotting sins, see into what crimes and what monstrous wickedness they rush. For exhausted and overturned by the corruptions of immoderate and shameful offenses, while they hate the severity of truth that contradicts them, they say:

“Let us oppress the poor righteous man, and let us not spare the widow, nor respect the gray hairs of the aged. Let our strength be the law of justice; for what is weak is found to be useless. Let us therefore lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is of no use to us and is opposed to our actions.”

Such things the impiety of the Jews devised against our Lord Jesus Christ. This is found more plainly in the words that follow. For a little later they say:

“He professes to have knowledge of God, and calls himself a son of God.”

Then again, a little later, they say:

“Let us question him with insult and torture, so that we may know his reverence. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death; for there will be regard for him because of his words.”

But observe what judgment the Holy Spirit pronounces upon them when it immediately adds:

“These things they thought, and they went astray; for their wickedness blinded them” (Wis. 2).

See, then, from what defilement all the dreadful crimes feared in wicked men arise. For what is softer than that debauchery? What is harder than this cruelty? A little earlier they were saying, “Let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as quickly as we can, as in youth; and let us not miss the flower of the season, and everywhere let us leave signs of joy.” Now they say, “Let us oppress the poor; let us not spare the widow, nor respect the old man. Let us lie in wait for the righteous man; let us question him with insult and torture; let us condemn him to a most shameful death.”

Wine is followed by frenzy, perfumes by tortures, roses by blood, joy by anger. Bound, beaten, and killed by such men was the Lord. Who would have feared bloody chains from flowering crowns? Who would have foreseen the most savage pains from sweet cups? Who would have recognized so dreadful a wood of the cross in soft meadows? And yet, in that debauchery, no age but youth was compared with the flower of the season. For thus they said: “Let us use creation as quickly as we can, as in youth.”

### 5. Young Men Must Not Be Captivated by Sensible Things, but Turn to the Love of Wisdom

Youths, therefore, we especially admonish and exhort you to be captivated by the beauty of true virtue. Let no earthly appearance, no brilliance of metals, no loveliness of woods, no purple of flowers, no natural or artificially applied adornment of the flesh, no sound of any strings or flutes, no pleasantness of odors, no sweetness of flavors, no embraces, be compared with the beauty, inspiration, sweetness, and consolations of wisdom.

For we do not forbid you to love; we forbid you to love shameful things. Do you wish to love? Love wisdom; strive to reach her. So that her appearance may not horrify you, make yourselves ready in your inner person. Just as wanton eyes seek the adornments of the body, so she seeks the adornments of the heart. [Col. 1709] Do not bring these adornments out of your own riches, because she hates the proud and those who desire to boast as though what they possess were their own. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). She herself therefore gives you the means by which you may please her.

Only love her, and she will preserve you; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honor her, and she will embrace you, “so that she may place a crown of graces upon your head” (Prov. 4:9). “Bright is wisdom, and she will never wither, and she is easily found by those who love her” (Wis. 6:13). Resolve to attach her to yourselves; sigh for her, burn for her, perish with longing for her. Deny yourself to yourself, lest, while you please yourself, you deny yourself to her. “Her companionship has no bitterness” (Wis. 8:16).

If you are lovers, love her; if you are handsome, please God; if you are young, conquer the devil. Daniel was called by the angel “a man of desires” (Dan. 10:11). What were his desires except those by which he ardently yearned for the beauty of wisdom? For in his youth he trampled wantonness, though captive he subdued the pride of kings, and while confined he closed the mouths of lions.

### 6. These Words Also Apply to Young Women; They Must Not Display Themselves in Churches

Nor should you, young women, think that this sermon does not concern you. I say these things to you—not, however, to shame you, but to admonish you as my dearest daughters: flee youthful desires. Married women, think of Susanna; widows, of Anna; virgins, of Mary.

Do not therefore go out in public because you wish to display the flower of your hay before the eyes of men, and thus seek death in the house of life. “All flesh is grass, and the glory of man is as the flower of grass.” What will you do when the grass has dried and the flower has fallen? Do you think that the word of the Lord, which remains forever (Isa. 40:6–8), will easily find your ashes, when now you despise it in the proud greenness of youth?

Behold, I say again and solemnly declare: flee youthful desires. If you hear this, if you obey, if you receive it with honor and fear as the word of God, you will be not only beautiful in the sight of God but also healthy. But if you turn even this admonition of ours into amorous jokes, you will inflict deadly wounds upon yourselves with the very instruments of the physician.

Certainly the Jews who crucified the Lord—when we hear of it, we shudder and pursue them with immense condemnation—yet, when they were devising their own pleasures, they were imagining the solitude of luxurious fields, saying: “Let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through” (Wis. 2:8). How, then, would he spare Christ if he had found him on earth—he who chose not lonely meadows for the provocation of his lusts, but the most crowded churches of the One reigning in heaven?
