Behold, for the third time I solemnly declare and say: flee youthful desires. Burn with the desires of Daniel. “Children, choose instruction from your youth, and until your gray hairs you will find wisdom” (Sir. 6:18).

## SERMON CCCXCII

[Note: [Col. 1709] Corrected against two manuscripts of the first class, against the Greek, against the editions of the Fathers, against the Roman manuscript, and against the editions of Ambrose, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1709] Elsewhere numbered 49 among the 50 Homilies.]

### To Married People

[Note: [Col. 1709] In the manuscript books of the Homilies of Fifty it is entitled “On the Bent Woman.” In the Florus Collection, at 1 Cor. 7, it is called “A Sermon to Married People”; so also in the very old Phimarcon manuscript and several others. In these codices it begins with the words in chapter 2, “Hear, dearly beloved,” and does not contain what precedes concerning the healing of the bent woman. This sermon was composed from at least two sermons; it can scarcely be doubted that all its parts belong to Augustine.]

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1. The Bent Woman as a Symbol of the Human Race

We have heard the Apostle saying to us, “We are ambassadors for Christ, exhorting you to be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5:20). He would not exhort us to be reconciled unless we had been enemies. Therefore the whole world was an enemy of the Savior and a friend of its captor—that is, an enemy of God and a friend of the devil. And the whole human race, like this woman, was bent down toward the earth. Someone who understood these enemies cries out against them and says to God: “They have bent down my soul” (Ps. 56:7).

The devil and his angels bent the souls of human beings toward earthly things—that is, so that, bowed down toward temporal and earthly matters, they would not seek what is above. For this is certainly what the Lord says about this woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years: she ought already to have been released from her bond, and released on the sabbath day. But those who were themselves bent down—what else were they?—brought accusations against the One who raised her. For, not understanding what God had commanded, they looked with earthly hearts. They celebrated the sacrament of Baptism [Note: [Col. 1710] It seems that “sabbati” should be read.] carnally; they did not see it spiritually.

### CHAPTER TWO

#### 2. It Is Not Permitted to Keep Concubines, Nor to Marry Married Women or Women Repudiated by Their Husbands

Hear me, dearly beloved, members of Christ and children of the Catholic mother. What I say to those preparing for Baptism, let the faithful hear; what I say to the faithful, let those preparing for Baptism hear; what I say to those preparing for Baptism and to the faithful, let the penitents hear; what I say to the faithful, to those preparing for Baptism, and to the penitents, let the catechumens hear—let everyone hear: let everyone fear; let no one despise it.

May your hearing be a consolation to me, not a testimony against you in my sorrow. I say to those preparing for Baptism: you are not permitted to fornicate. Let either wives or no wives be enough for you: you are not permitted to keep concubines. Let God hear, if you are deaf; let his angels hear, if you despise it. You are not permitted to keep concubines.

Even if you do not have wives, you are not permitted to keep concubines whom you may later dismiss in order to marry wives [Note: [Col. 1710] Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “whom you may later marry as wives,” omitting “dismiss in order to.”]; how much greater will your condemnation be if you wish to have both concubines and wives [Note: [Col. 1710] The printed editions read, “and dismiss wives.” “Dismiss” is absent from the manuscripts.]?

You are not permitted to have wives whose former husbands are alive; nor are you women permitted to have husbands whose former wives are alive. Such unions are adulterous—not according to the law of the forum, but according to the law of heaven [Note: [Col. 1710] Sermon 355, no. 5.]. Nor is it permitted for you to marry a woman who has left her husband by divorce while her husband is alive. It is permitted to dismiss an adulterous wife for the sole reason of fornication; but while she is alive, it is not permitted to marry another.

And you women are not permitted to take as husbands those men from whom their wives have departed by divorce. They are adulteries, not marriages. Augustine is despised; let Christ at least be feared. Do not imitate the crowd of evil and unbelieving people, my children; do not follow the broad ways whose end leads to destruction. Whoever has been baptized must either vow continence to God, remain with his wife, or, if he has no wife, marry one.

### CHAPTER THREE

#### 3. Those Who Have Fallen from a Resolution of Chastity Must Embrace Penance. Public Penance. The Penance of Theodosius

Hear me, faithful—that is, baptized people. Why do you die, now that you have been reborn? When you who have been baptized walk along crooked, slippery, and unclean paths, do you not know that you are perishing? You are perishing, my children; believe me. You do not wish to believe? What can I do for you?

You who are faithful and hear me, if perhaps you have committed such acts, do not add to them; and pray that God may forgive you. If you could not have, or did not wish to have, conjugal chastity or continence, and you have strayed from your resolution either of the marriage bond or of vowed continence [Note: [Col. 1711] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “either from the marriage bond or from the vow of continence.”], let there be in you the sorrow and humility of penance.

I speak more plainly: let no one say, “I did not understand.” Those of you who have defiled yourselves by unlawful intercourse after your wives—if you have had intercourse with someone besides your wives—do penance, the kind of penance practiced in the Church, so that the Church may pray for you.

Let no one say to himself, “I am doing it secretly; I am doing it before God. God knows, who forgives me, because I am doing it in my heart.” Was it therefore said without reason, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18)? Were the keys given to the Church of God without reason? Are we frustrating the Gospel, frustrating the words of Christ? Are we promising you what he denies? Are we not deceiving you?

Job says, “If I have been ashamed to confess my sins in the sight of the people” (Job 31:33). Such a righteous man, refined gold of the divine treasury, tested in such a furnace, says this; and does the son of pestilence resist me? Does a proud neck, a twisted mind, blush to bend the knee beneath the blessing of God?

Perhaps—indeed, there can be no doubt that this was the reason—God willed that the emperor Theodosius should do public penance before the people, especially because his sin could not be concealed. Does a senator blush at what the emperor did not blush to do? Does not a senator, but merely a municipal councillor, blush at what the emperor did not blush to do? Does a commoner or a merchant blush at what the emperor did not blush to do? What kind of pride is this? Would it not alone suffice for Gehenna, even if there were no adultery?

### CHAPTER FOUR

#### 4. How Christian Women Ought to Be Jealous for Their Husbands

Finally, my brothers, let the men hear me, let the women hear me. Why are you angry with me? Would that you did what is written: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). I must fear that what happened to the Apostle Paul may happen to me—what you heard just now, if you were attentive, when it was read: “So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Gal. 4:16). And if that is so, let it be so. If it is necessary that I be your enemy, I prefer to be your enemy rather than an enemy of justice.

I commend you also to the care of your wives. They are my daughters, just as you are my sons. Let them hear me: let them be jealous for their husbands; let them not preserve for themselves that empty reputation by which matrons are accustomed to be praised by immoral husbands, because they patiently tolerate the immorality of their husbands.

I do not want Christian women to have such patience. Let them be thoroughly jealous for their husbands—not on account of their own flesh, but on account of their husbands’ souls. I admonish, I command, I order: the bishop commands; Christ commands through me. He knows before whom my heart burns. I say it again: I command it.

Do not permit your husbands to fornicate. Bring a case against them before the Church. I do not mean before public judges, not before the proconsul, the vicar, the count, or the emperor, but before Christ.

In all other matters be your husbands’ servants, submissive in obedience. Let there be no insolence in you, no pride, no insulting neck, no disobedience of any kind; serve entirely as servants. But when that matter is reached in which the blessed Apostle made you equal, saying, “The husband should render the wife her due, and likewise the wife to the husband,” he added: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.” Why do you exalt yourself? Hear what follows: “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7:3–4).

When this matter is reached, cry out in defense of your own concern. Your husband sells your gold because of his need: bear it, woman; bear it, servant; do not quarrel, do not object. Disregard for your gold is love for your husband. If he sells your estate because of his need—an estate that is also yours—for it cannot be his if it is not yours, if you possess the love that ought to be in a wife—bear it patiently; and if he hesitates, offer it yourself. Despise everything for the love of your husband.

But desire him to be chaste; contend for his chastity. Let your estate perish patiently, but do not, by your patience, let his soul perish.

### CHAPTER FIVE

#### 5. The Husband Is the Head of the Woman

Let him lead toward what is good; let her follow. I am not telling the men to be jealous of their wives in this matter. I know that they do so; I know it well. Who could tolerate an adulterous wife? And a woman is commanded to tolerate an adulterous husband! O justice! Why, I ask you—why? “Because I am a man.”

Are you a man? Let us prove that you are a man by your strength. Are you a man? Conquer lust. How are you a man when your wife is stronger than you?

You are the head of the woman, man; that is true. If you are the head, lead, and let the wife follow. But when the household is rightly ordered, the man is the head of the woman. If you are the head, lead; let her follow her head. But see where you are going. Do not go where you do not want her to follow; do not go where you fear that she may follow you, lest you both fall together into the pit of adultery, lest, while you do it, you teach her what you do [Note: [Col. 1712] Sermon 132, chapter 2, no. 2.].

Your soul grieves if you both fall together into the pit of adultery; let it grieve you if you alone fall. You are jealous and do not want her to fall: take care that you do not fall.

But do not imitate your immoral husbands, most chaste women. Far be it from you. Let them live with you, or let them perish alone. A woman does not owe chastity to an immoral husband; she owes it to God, she owes it to Christ. Let her do it not for the sake of the man who does not deserve it, but for the sake of Christ.

Let her consider her price; let her read her own title-deeds. Finally, let whoever is perhaps angry because I discuss such matters think as he pleases. For I know that those who are wise love me for this, because it is not without reason that it is written: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you; reprove a foolish man, and he will add to his hatred of you” (Prov. 9:8). It did not say, “He will begin,” but “he will add,” because he already hated you. Therefore I know that the wise love me in this matter.

Let those refrain from communion who know that I am aware of their sins, lest they be thrown out from the chancel rails. But those whose sins I do not know, I charge before God. Let them also do penance themselves and thereafter abstain from the uncleanness of their fornications.

### CHAPTER SIX

#### 6. Penitents Must Change; Catechumens Must Imitate the Good in the Church

I say to the penitents: what are you doing? Know that you are doing nothing. What good does it do that you humble yourselves if you do not change?

I say to the catechumens: burn with the desire to receive grace. But choose for yourselves in the Church of God those whom you may imitate. If you do not find them—alas for me, my God!—what am I saying, “If you do not find them”? Is there no one among the faithful people whom you can find?

For so many years, have we baptized so many people in vain, if there are not among them those who preserve what they received, who guard what they heard? Far be it from me to believe this. I would be better off not being your bishop if this were so. But I hope that such people exist; I believe that they exist.

My condition is miserable for this reason: I am often compelled to know adulterers, but I cannot know the chaste. In secret there is something from which I may rejoice; in public there is something from which I am tortured.

Therefore desire the grace of God; choose those whom you may imitate, with whom you may live, and with whom you may have the sweet conversations of charity. Do not admit evil whisperings. “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). Live like ears of grain among weeds; bear the tribulations of this age like grains on the threshing floor. The winnower will come. Let no one at this time be separated indiscriminately.

## SERMON CCCXCIII

[Note: [Col. 1713] Collated against three manuscripts of the first class, against the Corbie, Clermont, Florentine, Greek, Roman, and other manuscripts, and against the editions of Ambrose, Erasmus, Paris, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1713] Elsewhere numbered 41 among the 50 Homilies.]

### On Penitents

[Note: [Col. 1713] The Louvain scholars considered it doubtful; Verlinde and Vinding thought it spurious or composed, like a cento, from various fragments. It also exists among the minor works of Ambrose and Caesarius, but with substantial variation. In Ambrose and Caesarius, after the first twenty-five verses have been omitted, it begins with these words: “I admonish you, brothers, in the sight of God, to add my fear to your fear, etc. Hear, therefore, what I am about to say. I am certain,” etc. The same is true in an old book of the Church of Chartres, although it bears Augustine’s name.]

### Penance Is Not Genuine If Life Is Not Changed. How Uncertain Penance at the End of Life Is

Penitents, penitents, penitents—if indeed you are penitents and not mockers—change your life; be reconciled to God. For you also feed while wearing a chain.

“What chain?” you ask. The one concerning which it is said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). You hear of binding, and you think you can deceive God? You do penance, you bend the knee, and you laugh and mock the patience of God?

If you are penitent, let your sin cause you remorse; if it does not cause you remorse, you are not penitent. If you are sorry, then why do you do what you did wrongly? If you are sorry that you did it, do not do it. If you still do it, certainly you are not penitent.

Indeed, dearly beloved, people become ill, send for the Church, or are carried to the Church, and are baptized and renewed, and will depart from here blessed. But that is not itself the reason for penance. Whoever has not yet received Baptism has not yet violated the sacrament. But whoever has violated the sacrament by living wickedly and ruinously, and has therefore been removed from the altar lest he eat and drink judgment upon himself, must change his life, correct himself, and be reconciled while he is alive and healthy. Does he himself also expect to be reconciled only when he begins to die? We have known many to breathe their last while waiting to be reconciled.

And I say this also in the sight of God: I add my fear to your fear. Whoever does not fear despises one who fears—but to his own disadvantage.

Hear, then. I am certain that a baptized person who has led a life—not, I dare not say, without sin, for who is without sin?—but a life without serious offense, and has had only such sins as are forgiven daily in the prayer of the one who says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), when he has completed his day does not end his life but passes from life into life, from toil into rest, from misery into blessedness.

Whether he runs of his own will to Baptism, or is baptized when placed in danger and departs from this life, he goes to the Lord; he goes to rest.

But a baptized deserter and violator of so great a sacrament, if he does penance with his whole heart, if he does penance where God sees—the God who saw David’s heart when, rebuked by the prophet and severely rebuked, after the terrifying threats of God he cried out, saying, “I have sinned,” and immediately heard, “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Sam. 12:13)—how much three syllables accomplish!

There are three syllables: “I have sinned.” But in these three syllables the flame of the heart’s sacrifice rises to heaven.

Therefore, whoever has truly done penance, and has been released from the bond by which he was bound and separated from the body of Christ, and has lived well after penance, as he ought to have lived before penance, will go to God whenever he dies; he will go to rest; he will not be deprived of the kingdom of God; he will be separated from the people of the devil.

But if someone, placed in the final danger of his illness, wishes to receive penance, receives it, is immediately reconciled, and departs from here, I confess to you: we do not deny him what he asks, but we do not presume that he departs well. I do not presume this. I do not deceive you; I do not presume it.

The faithful person who lives well departs secure. The person baptized at the last moment departs secure. One who is doing penance and is reconciled [Note: [Col. 1714] The words that appear shortly afterward within parentheses are inserted here in the printed editions of Ambrose and Caesarius and in the Chartres manuscript, and are joined to what precedes as follows: “and is reconciled, if afterward he lives well, is secure. But you say: What does it mean, ‘if he lives well’? Or teach us this, good priest: you say that you do not know,” etc. After the words in the parenthesis, ending with “and better after penance,” there follows, “But one doing penance at the end and reconciled,” etc. Everything contained in the parenthesis is entirely absent from the manuscript books of the 50 Homilies.] while healthy, and afterward living well, departs secure.

One who does penance at the end and is reconciled—if he departs secure, I am not secure. From what I am secure, I am secure, and I give security; from what I am not secure, I can give penance, but I cannot give security.

[But someone may say: “Good priest, you say that you do not know and cannot give us any security if the person is saved and deserves to approach Christ—one to whom penance is given at the moment of death, who while he lived and was healthy was impenitent. Teach us, then, I ask, how we ought to live well after penance.”

I say: keep yourselves from drunkenness, from lust, from theft and abusive speech, from immoderate laughter, and from idle words, for which people will have to give an account on the day of judgment. See how slight the things I have mentioned are. Yet they are all serious [Note: [Col. 1714] In Ambrose: “See how slight the things I have mentioned, so that I may remain silent about serious things.” In the Corbie manuscript, “and I omitted those serious things.” In the other manuscript, this agrees almost entirely with the printed editions of Ambrose.], and deadly.

And I say something else: not only after penance must a person guard himself from these vices, but also before penance, while he is healthy; for if he remains until the end of life, he does not know whether he will be able to receive penance itself and confess his sins to God and the priest.

See why I said that one must live well both before penance and better after penance.”]

Pay attention to what I say. I must explain it more clearly, lest someone misunderstand me. Do I say, “He will be condemned”? I do not say that. But I do not say either, “He will be delivered.”

“What, then, do you say to me?”

“I do not know. I do not presume; I do not promise. I do not know.”

Do you wish to free yourself from uncertainty? Do you wish to escape what is uncertain? Do penance while you are healthy. For if you do true penance while you are healthy, and the final day finds you, run to be reconciled; if you act in this way, you are secure.

Why are you secure? Because you did penance at a time when you were still able to sin. But if you wish to do penance only then, when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.

“But how do you know,” you say, “whether God may perhaps forgive me?”

“You speak truly. I do not know. I know this; I do not know that. For that reason I give you penance, because I do not know. If I knew that it would benefit you not at all, I would not give it to you. Likewise, if I knew that it would benefit you, I would not admonish you or terrify you.”

There are two possibilities: either you will be forgiven or you will not be forgiven. Which of these will happen to you, I do not know. Therefore abandon the uncertain; hold fast to the certain.

## SERMON CCCXCIV

[Note: [Col. 1715] Brought to light by Holstenius from the Vatican Library.]

### On the Feast of Saints Perpetua and Felicity

Today two gems have shone in the Church, and one radiance, because Perpetua and Felicity are one solemnity; nor can there be doubt about the happiness of one who possesses perpetual dignity.

The custody of the prison joined them, and grace also joined them, because there was no discord between them. Together they sang in prison; together they went to meet Christ in the air; together they fought against the cow; together they would enter the everlasting homeland. Together they endured martyrdom: one was nursing, the other giving birth.

When she handed over the child and removed the nursing infant, Perpetua said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35).

Felicity groaned in childbirth and hurried fearlessly after her companions. Freed by her groaning, what did she say to Christ? “You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to you” (Ps. 115:17).

And blessed David, to console her in her groaning, said: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart and fulfill all your plans” (Ps. 19:5).

O frailty! The darkness was fleeing, but the human condition did not pass away. Yet the One who conquered death freed her from the danger of childbirth and lifted Perpetua from the burden of nursing.

When they climbed the steps of that ladder and trod upon the treacherous necks of the dragon, they came to the garden of the heavenly meadows. There they found the good shepherd laying down his life for his sheep and seeking milk from his flocks.

For, she says, a youthful and aged shepherd was sitting there, green in age and gray-haired, who knows no old age. His youthful face shone because he is the same One, and his years will not fail (Ps. 101:28). His head was becoming gray because the Lord is righteous, loves righteousness, and recognized equity in the martyrs.

Around him sheep lay, reclining. He milked them with his pastoral finger, and in them he found an abundance of milk and a fruitful consciousness of devotion. He milked with his fingers and addressed them with paternal consolations, prepared with heavenly promises, saying: “Come, blessed ones of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

And he showed them troughs of milk foaming with pure hearts through shining almsgiving, and said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:35).

Perpetua received new milk from the gentle shepherd before she poured out her precious blood. They answered, “Amen,” and began to seek mercy. They prayed in prison, already secure concerning the shepherd.

“Lord,” they said, “may our confession not be barren, so that we may also deserve to be joined to your precious flocks and not be separated from your martyrs.”

In a vision, an arena is set before them, a splendid arena in the amphitheater. The Egyptian appears—the one who had been the beautiful Lucifer in heaven. He himself rolls in the dust, ready to fight. Perpetua, destined to triumph in the Lord the Savior, stretched out her hands in the form of a cross, with a divine young man standing before her as her defender.

She receives the triumph of victory and obtains a branch from the crown. Let us also offer our gifts to her. Others offered them visits to the prison at the proper time; let us offer them the vow of the solemnity, so that we may deserve the kingdom with all the saints.

## SERMON CCCXCV

[Note: [Col. 1716] Now published for the first time, brought to light from the very ancient Remigius manuscript.]

### On the Ascension of the Lord, VI

#### 1.

Today we celebrate the Ascension of the Lord into heaven. Let us not hear “Lift up your hearts” in vain, and let us ascend with him with an undivided heart, as the Apostle teaches and says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1–2).

Let the necessity of action be on earth; let the will to ascend be in heaven. Hope is here; the reality is there. For the time will come when the reality will be there. When the reality is there, hope will be neither here nor there—not because hope is empty, but because it comes to an end when the reality arrives.

Finally, hear what the Apostle said about hope: “In hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

Consider this even in human affairs. If someone hopes to marry a wife, then he does not yet have one. For if he has her, what does he hope for? He marries the wife whom he hoped for, and he will no longer hope. Hope therefore comes to a blessed end when reality arrives.

A traveler hopes that he will reach his homeland. As long as he is not there, he hopes; when he arrives, he no longer hopes. Reality has succeeded hope. Hope comes to a blessed end when what was hoped for is possessed.

Therefore now, dearly beloved, when you have heard that we should have our hearts above, let us use that very heart to think of the future life. Let us live well here so that we may live there.

#### 2.

For behold the great condescension of our Lord: the One who made us descended to us, because we had fallen away from him. And in order to come to us, he did not fall himself but descended to us. If, then, he descended to us, he lifted us up. Already in his body he has lifted up our head; where he is, the members will follow. For where the head has gone before, the members will follow.

He is the head; we are the members. He is in heaven; we are on earth. Is he therefore far from us? Far be it from us. If you ask about distances, he is far away; ask love, and he is with us.

For if he were not with us, he would not say in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). If he is not with us, we lie when we say to you, “The Lord be with you.”

He would not have cried out from heaven to Saul, who was persecuting not him personally but his saints, his servants—or, to speak more familiarly, his members: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

“Behold, I am here in heaven, you on earth, and among the persecutors” [perhaps, as the note proposes: “you are on earth, and you persecute me”]. “Why me? Because they are my members; through those members I am there.” For if the sole of the foot is trampled, does not the tongue cry out?

Therefore the One through whom heaven and earth were made descended to earth for the sake of the one whom he made from earth, and from here lifted earth into heaven.

What has therefore gone before in him, let us hope will be completed. He will give us what he promised. We are secure; he has made a pledge; he has written the Gospel. He will give it to us.

What he has expended on us is greater. Do we suppose that he will not give us his life, when he has already spent his death for us? He accepted for us on earth the humility of passion, injuries, insults, and every indignity; will he not give us the kingdom, happiness, immortality, and eternity? He endured our evils; will he not give us his good things?

With this hope, because he is a truthful promiser, let us walk securely; but let us live in such a way that we may say to him with an open face: “We have done what you commanded; give back what you promised.”

## SERMON CCCXCVI

[Note: [Col. 1717] Possidius, in his Catalogue of Augustine’s works, lists sermons delivered by him on the deposition of certain bishops that have not survived to the present day. This sermon, moreover, is of that consolatory character. It had previously been counted among the spurious works of Fulgentius, but in the judgment of learned scholars it should perhaps be placed among Augustine’s genuine sermons.]

### On the Installation of a Bishop
1. You indeed seek a comforter, brothers; but we too need consolation. Yet our consolation is no human being, but he who makes human beings, because he who made us restores us, and he who created us renews us. Through weakness we cannot help grieving; but through hope we ought to be consoled. We all wish good people to live with us longer, and in this most harsh life we do not want to be abandoned by our companions. But those who have lived well and gone before us exhort us by their example: whether we live here for a long time or depart from here soon, let us live in such a way that we may come to them. For living here a long time is nothing other than enduring troubles for as long as [Col. 1718] one lives. But to live with God and in God is to live without any trouble and without any fear that the happiness which has no end might perish. Nor ought we think that your bishop, our brother, departed from here too soon or lived too little. For one does not live too little there where, however much is said, life does not end. Here, moreover, even what is long will be counted as nothing once it has ended. Yet he did not live too little here either, if we consider his works rather than count his years. How much that others perhaps did not accomplish over many years did he fulfill in a few? Therefore, to wish to keep him here was nothing other than to begrudge his happiness.

2. In this matter we grieve over a human being as human beings. What, then, shall we do so as not to be human? As human beings, therefore, we grieve humanly over the departure of a human being; but, as we heard in the divine reading, “being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long years” (Wis. 4:13). Let us therefore reckon time there as a day is reckoned. Whatever he did among you by exhorting, speaking, offering himself for imitation, and praising and worshiping God, hold fast to it; and you will be his most splendid memorial. For it is not a great thing for him to be enclosed in marble tombs, but to be preserved in your hearts. Let him live buried in living tombs. For your remembrance is his burial. He lives with God, so that he may be blessed; let him live among you, so that you may be blessed. We might exhort you to faithful prudence in many words, were we not also scarcely permitted by human grief to speak. Therefore, since God granted us to be present for a time at his death—and since he granted us to accompany his funeral, an escort owed to charity but adding nothing to his happiness—and since he also granted us to see your holiness and to address you, so that according to our limited ability we might console you by consoling you: whatever grief does not permit us to say, supply by reflection. Our spirit, in remembering so great a man, has human sorrow, but it does not have the despair of unbelief.

[Col. 1717]

## SERMON OF THE HOLY PRESBYTER HERACLIUS, DISCIPLE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, DELIVERED IN THE PRESENCE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Note: [Col. 1717] Extracted from a manuscript codex of the Church of Beauvais by the distinguished Godefridus Hermant, canon of that same church.] (C, S)

[Col. 1717]

1. I think, brothers, that you perceive the burden I bear; and I ask you to lift me up, as though with your fraternal prayers placed beneath my shoulders, while I labor under so great a weight. For I know that the most blessed Father, who placed this burden upon me, does not cease praying for me. For he would not burden me merely by command and deny me his pious prayers. Without doubt, he who commanded me to bear this prays that I may carry it through. What, then, is the meaning of his command, except that I must dare to display ignorance in the presence of wisdom, and speak of inexperience while instruction remains silent? And although Scripture says, “Speak, elder; for it is fitting for you” (Ecclus. 32:5), the Father says, “Speak, younger man; for it delights me.”

You know, brothers, that I had already begun to speak the word of God for you. Recently, compelled by the necessity of my office, I undertook this task, because I had no way to escape it. But it is easy for any disciple to fill the place of an absent teacher; it is arduous and difficult to teach one’s fellow disciples in the presence of the teacher—especially such a teacher, whose [Col. 1718] words possess greater authority because life accompanies the tongue that teaches. For every good thing commended to us by the word of instruction is preceded by the example of conduct. He goes before us—would that we might at least follow! Whatever we admire, venerate, and embrace in this man is then truly believed to be loved by us if we are not reluctant to imitate it.

Therefore, according to our limited ability, let each of us strive toward him, and let each of us pluck, as we are able, various branches of virtue from the root of his heart, which exists [Note: [Col. 1718] Perhaps: “which exist,” *existentes*.]. Whoever can, let him attain his eloquence; whoever cannot, let him hold fast to his self-restraint. Whoever can, let him fulfill his authority; whoever cannot, let him follow his humility. Whoever can, let him grasp his knowledge; whoever cannot, let him imitate his patience. And in all the ways of the Lord, let whoever can walk with him; and whoever cannot, learn from him.

Let us rejoice, brothers, that according to the distribution of divine gifts [Col. 1718] we possess in him what we do not possess in ourselves. For whatever we see in him is ours, if we love it.

2. While he is silent, therefore, we speak. While he is silent, I say, we speak. The cicada cries out [Note: [Col. 1719] Read *cicada*.], and the swan is silent; yet he is not silent while we speak, because he himself speaks in us. For if we tell you what we have learned from him, he himself teaches you, whether through himself or through me.

Nevertheless, brothers, what he has imposed upon us while we are still little is scarcely fulfilled even by the great. But we must not therefore despair, because we are small. For the Lord has blessed the little ones together with the great (Ps. 113:13). The things demanded of us are exceedingly difficult, and we are weak. We are weak, fragile, made of clay; but what of that? Will it not please the Lord to place his treasure in a clay vessel, so that we too may say with the apostle Paul, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7)?

For we and our words are in his hand (Wis. 7:16), and he gives speech to those who proclaim the gospel with great power (Ps. 67:12). What do you think, brothers? Would this steward, so wise, command you to distribute something unless he knew that he had placed the Lord’s money in us? He is conscious of his own works; he is conscious of his pious labors. He knows how much he has seasoned me with the salt of the word. For he himself is the living salt of the earth, conveying the flavor of apostolic teaching. But I fear that I have not brought his seasoning into an uncultivated heart.

He did well, therefore, to wish to taste our discourse. He did well to examine how much of his own flavor he might recognize in us. For what else are we to think was the reason that, among the other fathers and my fellow presbyters, he commanded me above all to speak in his presence—something he had previously been unwilling to do—except that, confident of their maturity and learning, he wished in this way to test our beginnings?

I obey, brothers, the commands that are more beneficial; and I do not withdraw myself from the one to whom I entrusted myself long ago in the Lord, to be nourished and instructed. Look upon me, pious Father and good Teacher. Question my tongue, and let it reveal to you the feeling of my heart [Note: [Col. 1719] Perhaps, “the feeling,” *affectus*.]. Whatever pleases you in our speech, recognize as yours; but whatever displeases you, forgive, because it is mine [Col. 1720]. Yet forgive in such a way as to correct; forgive in such a way as to punish. Forgive me because I have erred; punish me for having erred. Thus spare the human being, but not the error, until little by little everything that was not planted by you is abandoned.

3. But so that I may speak with you, beloved, rather than with him, lest I exceed in any respect the limits of my father’s command—for he commanded me to speak to you—let us think here of the apostle Paul, whose Letter we have just heard read. When he was preparing the young Timothy for the divine mysteries and filling the young man’s mind with heavenly teachings, he said, “Preach the word”; and shortly afterward, “Do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry” (2 Tim. 4:2, 5).

If Timothy had then said, “I cannot,” Paul would have replied, “Why can you not, my son? Have you not learned the sacred Scriptures from childhood?” (ibid. 3:15). This cannot be said to me, brothers. As many of you know, I came here already hardened. Throughout the period of childhood—for the rule of instruction more easily bends and directs that age—I was occupied with other matters. But, plainly, as must be admitted, after I came here the holy farmer worked in me as far as he could, and made great efforts to conquer my hardness. I have never lacked either rains or seeds; and therefore the one who sowed the seed now seeks fruit.

Let him pray that his grains have not degenerated in us; and whatever has emerged, whether in our words or in our conduct, while he cultivated us and the Lord gave the increase, let it be not a thorn but an ear of grain. Therefore, beloved, let us together entreat him for what remains: just as I have obeyed his commands beyond my strength, so may he not withdraw himself from the desire of us all, but, after this discourse of ours, deign to speak even a few words to you—words which you may delight to remember when you depart and may not be reluctant to ruminate upon profitably in recollection.

Nevertheless, lest I seem to have spent the entire sermon in making excuses and to have offered no admonition to your holiness, hear me, brothers. Whatever you have always heard, received, and learned from our Father, think upon these things and do them; “and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. 4:8–9). Amen.

[Col. 1719]

## FRAGMENTS OF CERTAIN SERMONS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, STILL OTHERWISE LOST, FOUND IN THE COLLECTIONS OF EUGIPPIUS, BEDE, FLORUS, AND JOHN, DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

(C, S)

### From a Sermon against the Pelagians, in Eugippius, volume 2, chapter 287 or 288

[Note: [Col. 1719] Florus cites this at 2 Cor. 13 and 1 Tim. 5.]

[Col. 1719]

1. **Bishop Urbanus.** The Pelagian error: that temptations can be overcome by the powers of free choice, and that the Lord’s Prayer does not concern temptations to sin.

When those two petitions—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matt. 6:12–13)—are brought against the Pelagians, what do you think they reply? I shuddered, my brothers, when I heard it. I did not hear it with my own ears; rather, our holy brother and fellow bishop Urbanus, who was once a presbyter here and is now bishop of Sicca, reported it after returning from the city of Rome. There, when he had disputed with someone who held such views—or reported that he had disputed with him—he pressed him with the weight of the Lord’s Prayer.

He pressed him, saying: “If it is in our power not to sin, and if it is in our power, by the strength of our will alone, to overcome all temptations to sin, why do we say to God, ‘Do not bring us into temptation’?” What do you think he replied? “We ask God,” he said, “not to bring us into temptation so that we do not suffer something that is not in our power: that I may not fall from a horse, break my foot, be killed by a robber,” and things of that sort. “For,” he said, “I do not have these things in my power. But to overcome the temptations of my sins, if I wish, I can; and I can do so without God’s help.”

2. **The malicious heresy refuted from the prayer commended by Christ and used for Peter.** You see, brothers, how malicious this heresy is; you see how all of you shudder at it. Take care that you are not captured by it. For I know the cunning and evasions of impious people who have turned away from the truth and, having fallen into their own opinions, refuse to be conquered. Look, I beg you.

He found something to say: that we therefore say, “Do not bring us into temptation,” so that nothing may happen to us which, according to bodily temptation, we do not have in our power. Was this then why the Lord said, “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41)? Did he mean, “Watch and pray, so that you do not break your foot, suffer a headache, or incur some loss”? He did not mean this. What, then, did he mean? What he said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

“I have prayed for you,” God says to a human being, the Lord to a servant, the teacher to a disciple, the physician to a sick person. “I have prayed for you”—for what? “That it may not fail.” What may not fail? Your hand? Your foot? Your eye? Your tongue, through some paralysis—that is, some dissolution of the limbs? No; “that your faith may not fail.” According to these people, we have it in our power to ensure that our faith does not fail.

3. **The Church’s prayers prove that the help of grace is necessary if we are not to sin.** Why is God entreated for us to grant us what these people say we ought not to ask from eternal majesty, but ought to possess in our own power? My brothers, our blessings—the blessings we pronounce over you—are emptied, nullified, and overthrown by their view.

You hear me, I believe, my brothers, when I say, “Turned toward the Lord, let us bless his name: may he grant us perseverance in his commandments, that we may walk in the right way of his instruction, that we may please him in every good work,” and other things of this kind. “Certainly,” they say, “all of this has been placed in our power.” Then we wish these things for you in vain. Let us defend both ourselves and you, lest we bless without cause and you say “Amen” without cause.

My brothers, your “Amen” is your subscription; it is your agreement; it is your affirmation. Lest some of them perhaps condemn both us and you, let us defend ourselves by the apostle Paul. Let us see whether he wished for his people things such as those for which we pray over you.

Hear what he said in one place. I will make the matter brief. What do you say, O new heretic—whoever you are who hears me, if you are present—what do you say? Do we have such power not to sin that we can fulfill this without the help of divine grace? Is this what you say? “It is,” he replies. “Then we have the power not to sin without God’s help?” “Certainly,” he replies. “Our free choice is sufficient for this.”

What, then, is the meaning of what the Apostle says when writing to the Corinthians: “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Cor. 13:7)? You have paid attention, heard, and received this; and because it is perfectly clear, you have undoubtedly understood what the Apostle prayed for. “We pray,” he says, “to God that you do no evil.”

He could have said, “We warn you not to do evil”; “We teach you not to do evil”; “We command and instruct you not to do evil.” If he had said this, he would certainly have spoken correctly, because our will does accomplish something. For our will accomplishes something; it is simply not sufficient by itself. Yet he preferred to say, “We pray,” in order to commend grace itself, so that they might understand that when they do no evil, they avoid evil not by their own will alone, but fulfill what has been commanded with God’s help.

4. **Free choice is shown by the command; the necessity of the help of grace by prayer.** Therefore, brothers, when a command is given, recognize the freedom of the will; when what is commanded is requested in prayer, recognize the benefit of grace. You have both in Scripture: a command is given, and prayer is offered; what is commanded is what is prayed for.

Observe what I am saying. A command is given so that we may understand. How is a command given so that we may understand? “Do not be like a horse or a mule, without understanding” (Ps. 31:9). You have heard that it is commanded; ask to be able to fulfill what is commanded.

“How,” you ask, “do I ask?” Hear Scripture. What has been commanded to you? “Do not be like a horse or a mule, without understanding.” Because it has been commanded, you have recognized the will; hear that it is prayed for, so that you may recognize grace: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:73).

We are commanded to have wisdom. I read that it is commanded, because it is commanded. “Where do you read this?” he asks. Listen: “You who are foolish among the people and senseless, gain wisdom at last” (Ps. 93:8). What does he say? You see how God has commanded us to be wise. Therefore, is wisdom in our power? I have already said: I heard the command and recognized the will. Hear the prayer, so that you may recognize grace.

Concerning the wisdom commanded to us, let us hear what the apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all” (James 1:5).

We are commanded to practice self-restraint. Where is it commanded? The Apostle says to Timothy, “Keep yourself pure” (1 Tim. 5:22). It is an order; it is a command. It must be heard and carried out. But unless God helps, we remain helpless. We try to act by our will, and the will exerts some effort; let power not presume unless weakness is helped.

Certainly it is commanded: “Keep yourself pure.” Hear another passage of Scripture: “And since I knew that no one can be continent unless God grants it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was—what did I do? I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wis. 8:21).

Why should I run through many examples, my brothers? Whatever is commanded to us must be prayed for, so that it may be fulfilled. But not in such a way that we abandon ourselves, lie helpless on our backs like the sick, and say, “Let God rain food down upon our faces,” so that we positively refuse to do anything; and when the food has rained down upon our mouths, say also, “Let God swallow us up.”

We too must do something; we must apply ourselves; we must strive. And for what we have been able to do, we must give thanks; for what we have not been able to do, we must pray. When you give thanks, you take care not to be condemned as ungrateful; but when you ask for what you do not yet have, you take care not to remain empty, because you are hindered.

5. **The Pelagian objection. How Pelagius was acquitted.** Consider these things, therefore, my brothers, whenever someone approaches you and says: “What, then, are we doing, if we have nothing in our power unless God grants everything? Then God will not crown us, but will crown himself.”

You see already that this comes from that vein. It is a vein, but it contains poison; it has been struck by a serpent and is not sound. For this is what Satan is doing today: through the poisons of heretics he seeks to drive people out of the Church, just as he once drove them from paradise through the serpent’s poison.

Let no one say that he was acquitted by the bishops. He was acquitted, but the confession was acquitted—the correction itself, as it were. For what he said before the bishops appeared Catholic; but what he wrote in his books was unknown to the bishops who acquitted him, and perhaps he was corrected. We ought not to despair of a human being who perhaps preferred to join himself to the Catholic faith and fled to its grace and help. Perhaps this is what happened. Nevertheless, it was not the heresy that was acquitted, but the man who denied the heresy, and so forth.

### From a Sermon on the Passion of the Lord, in the collection of Bede and Florus, on Romans 5

“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Rom. 5:10). Therefore Christ died for the ungodly. And Christ is God. How will he not reign, having been found righteous in the life of God, when the ungodly was sought, lest he perish, by the death of God?

For we shall be saved in the life of God, because we had perished in our own life. But when we hear both of the life of God and of the death of God, let us distinguish what comes from where. He brought us life, but he received death from us—not, however, on account of his own merit, but on our account.

### Also from a Sermon on the Passion of the Lord, Bede and Florus, on Romans 12

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). Therefore, when the Apostle admonishes us not to be wise in lofty matters but to associate with the humble (Rom. 12:16), let a person consider, if he can, into what precipice of pride he is driven if he does not consent to the humble God, and how pernicious it is for a human being impatiently to endure what the just Lord has willed, when God patiently endured what the unjust enemy willed.

### Also from a Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus, on Romans 15

Christ, therefore, is the King of the Jews, under whose gentle yoke the Gentiles too have been sent into salvation, because greater mercy has been granted to them. The Apostle himself shows this more clearly when he says: “For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers; but that the Gentiles might glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9).

For it was not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs, unless the dogs, humbled so as to gather the crumbs which they saw falling from their masters’ table, were exalted through that very humility, became human beings, and were deemed worthy to approach that table itself.

### Also from a Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus, on Galatians 6

[Col. 1724]

“Let us therefore also glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to us and we to the world” (Gal. 6:14). So that we might not be ashamed of that cross, we have placed it upon our very forehead—that is, in the dwelling place of shame.

### Also from a Sermon on the Passion, Bede and Florus, on Ephesians 4

For, contrary to what some think, the old human being is not the body and the new human being the soul. Rather, the body is the outer human being, and the soul the inner. This oldness and newness take place in the inner person.

When the Apostle said, “Put off the old human being and put on the new,” he was not commanding that the body be laid aside, but that one’s life be changed for the better. Finally, he taught this consecutively; for, wishing to explain what he had said, he continued: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Eph. 4:22–25).

### From a Sermon on the Resurrection of the Lord, Bede and Florus, on Romans 6

“For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 6:10–11). This is the sacrament in which those who are baptized experience the passing away of their former life and begin the entry into a new one. Hence he also says: “Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4).

Through this sacrament let us recognize that we have died to sin with Christ and live to righteousness in Christ. On the cross there is the pain of those who confess; in burial, the rest of those who have been absolved; in resurrection, the life of the righteous.

### From a Sermon for the Octave of Easter, among the unpublished collections of John the deacon, on Genesis

[Note: [Col. 1724] It is also cited by Bede, in his as-yet unpublished work on 2 Timothy 3.]

## GENESIS, CHAPTER 1, VERSE 3: “LIGHT WAS MADE”

1. “And God said, ‘Let there be light’; and light was made,” and so forth. By the name “light,” allegorically, we understand all the righteous and faithful to be designated, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

But this light was made: “There was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). That light was not made, but was born from God. That light was not made, and through the unmade light this made light came to be.

So also with the firmament: just as light was made by the God who gives light, so the firmament was made by the firm God. And we find that the firmament ought to be understood in the Church as the authority of the divine Scriptures. Therefore there is light first and afterward the firmament, because Scripture was produced through righteous human beings; and unless they were first justified, so that they might be light, Scripture could not be propagated so as to become the firmament between the waters and the waters—the intermediary between the lower peoples of human beings and the higher peoples of angels.

Why? Because angels do not desire to advance through the Scriptures; therefore they are not beneath the firmament, beneath the authority of the Scriptures, because they contemplate the form of divinity and wisdom. We, however, are rightly beneath the firmament, since God’s will is disclosed to us through the authority of the Scriptures, and so forth.

## THE SEA AND THE DRY LAND. GRASS FOR FOOD

2. We see the earth; we see the sea. They are works of God. The former lies beneath our eyes; the latter lies beneath our understanding. The former is known to our flesh; the latter is known to our mind.

What is the dry land in the Church? Every soul thirsting for God is called dry land. For the waters were separated, and the dry land appeared. This sea is the world, and the wicked are bitter waters. They were separated and gathered into a single gathering—that is, predestined to one end, toward which God directs all those whom he separates from the saints.

God separates them, for a human being cannot make these separations; and the dry land appears through separation. Place two people together: one desires a spectacle, the other the church. Joined in body, they are separated by their desires. The former belongs to the bitter water; the latter appears as dry land.

How do we prove that this earth, signifying people who desire good things, is dry land? The Psalm said to God: “My soul is like a land without water to you” (Ps. 142:6): my soul thirsts for you. It thirsts; it is dry; it has been separated from the waters of the sea.

Let it not matter that it has not yet been separated bodily. Desire has already effected the separation. Some desire God; others desire the world. What, then, does the dry land thirst for? Rain from heaven, rain from the clouds, rain from the Scriptures, rain from the firmament. When it desires rain, it desires sweet water, separated from bitter water.

But God knows that the dry land desires it, for the desire is hidden and lies concealed. The desires of the sea—that is, worldly desires—are visible. If someone desires money, he is moved toward that money and wants to acquire it; since money is a visible thing, its desire is apparent.

But the one who desires God has a hidden desire, because God, whom he desires, is hidden. It is inward; it is a hidden thing. He thirsts and is dry, but he appears to the eyes of God.

And God did not overlook the fruit. Immediately he said, “Let the earth bring forth grass for food.” Let the earth bring forth grass on the very day on which the dry land was made. That dry land could not remain without fruit for long.

Let us too hear the word of God: “Let the earth bring forth grass for food,” that is, good works of mercy, concerning which Isaiah says, “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house,” and so forth (Isa. 58:7).

The firmament, therefore, is the Scripture of God; the luminaries in the firmament are understanding of the Scriptures; and the lights in heaven are understanding within the Scriptures. Do you wish to reach the heavenly light? First become earth that bears fruit—that is, let works of mercy come first. For after works of mercy comes the illumination of that light which you desire, and so forth.

## THE GREATER LUMINARY AND THE LESSER LUMINARY

3. “And God said, ‘Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day and the night.’” The evangelists are luminaries; the Scripture of God is the firmament. The Gospel, which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets, consists of luminaries in the firmament of heaven.

The little one in the Church is not yet able to take solid food, but is content with milk; this signifies the lesser luminary and the stars. Therefore, the greater luminary is for ruling the day, and the lesser luminary for ruling the night.

As long as people are carnal and cannot contemplate that wisdom through which all things were made, they are in the night. But God did not abandon the night; he provided it with its luminaries. The day seeks the sun, and the sun is sufficient for it; the moon and the stars were given to the night and illuminate it. When the moon does not shine over the earth, the light in the air comes from the stars.

Thus it happens that at night we go outside and see the trees; and although we do not distinguish them clearly, we nevertheless see, in some fashion, the light of the stars. Therefore, when the clouds are thick, the light of the stars is also taken away, and the person is then beneath the open sky [Note: [Col. 1726] For *sub aere*, “under the air,” as in Horace, book 2 of the *Odes*, ode 3, and Pliny, book 14, chapter 21.] just as inside a room. Thus the night too has a certain light of its own.

Let us see what the Apostle says concerning those gifts and spiritual endowments: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. How is it given? To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12:7–8).

Whoever understands the difference between the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge has understood the difference between the greater luminary and the lesser luminary.

Let us hear the word of wisdom: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning,” and so forth. For those who comprehend this, it is day; the sun shines for them. But unless they first came from the night, they did not arrive at the light. For “darkness was over the abyss,” and God said, “Let there be light.”

Let no one say that he began from the light. For we are all justified from sinners. Let those who can grasp it understand what I have said about the Gospel. But they say to me, “We have not understood what ‘In the beginning was the Word’ means.”

If it is still night, observe that the Word assumed flesh and made himself for you like a nocturnal light: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–3, 14).

And in the thornbush God speaks through an angel to Moses. Hear where the word of wisdom is. “What are you called?” Moses said. “How shall I announce you to the people? If it is said, ‘Who sent you?’ what shall I say?”

Hear the word of wisdom: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” Who can grasp “He who is”? The other things are not. Who truly is? The one who does not pass away, who always remains immutable.

But this is food for the great; this is the sun of the day. It is as though Moses were saying to him, “I am still night; illuminate the night.” I shall say something that night can grasp, something that little ones can retain: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

Therefore, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14–15) belongs to the rule of the day; “I am the God of Abraham” belongs to the rule of the night. Faith dispensed in time shines for the night; wisdom, which always remains, shines for the day. It nourishes us in the night so that we may proceed into the day.

The stars, then, are the other gifts. For when he had said, “To one is given a word of wisdom,” as the sun for ruling the day, and “to another a word of knowledge,” as the moon for ruling the night, he also gives the stars: to one the gift of healings, to another prophecy, and so forth.

## LIVING SOULS. THE POWER OF THE SACRAMENT IS CHARITY

4. “God said, ‘Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls [Col. 1727] and birds.’ And the waters brought forth fish, and great sea creatures, and the birds of heaven. And God saw that it was good,” and so forth.

Let us therefore see what the Scriptures say. Light through light: the righteous through the Word. The firmament of heaven: the solidity of the Scriptures. The waters beneath the firmament: the earthly people. The waters above the firmament: the heavenly people. The dry land separated from the waters of the sea: souls thirsting for God, separated from the multitude of the world’s sins.

The earth brings forth grass for food and fruit-bearing trees: works of mercy. The luminaries in the firmament of heaven: preachers of the word, evangelists and apostles, spiritual gifts.

Let us therefore attend to the luminaries that travel throughout the whole world, and see how the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls. The evangelists travel about; human beings are evangelized. Therefore the reptiles with living souls are understood as the sacraments.

Why? Because the sacraments are necessary for this purpose: that the Gentiles may be evangelized and people may be separated from the Gentiles. That is, the bitter waters may bring forth these things and become sweet fish. For it is a remarkable thing: no one can taste seawater [Note: [Col. 1727] Perhaps *potest* is missing. This is the opinion of Morel, *Elementa Critica*, no. 211. M.], yet people can eat the fish. They are born from bitterness and nourished by it.

These are the sweet sacraments that have been sent throughout the whole world. But they are called reptiles with living souls—not yet a living soul. Why? This is somewhat dense and difficult to understand.

You heard just now, when the reading was read, that Simon Magus was baptized and did not put away his evil mind (Acts 8:13–23). He possessed the form of the sacrament, but he did not possess the power of the sacrament. Hear what the Apostle says about the impious: “They have the form of godliness, but deny its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

What is the form of godliness? The visible sacrament. What is the power of godliness? Invisible charity. Hear of the power of godliness: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze,” and so forth. “And if I have this and that, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

For the holy sacraments are great and holy; but a human being is nothing if he does not have charity. Therefore the power of the sacrament is charity. The heretic does not have this charity, although I find in him the form of the sacrament.

Thus, when a heretic comes to me, I respect the form of the sacrament, so that I do not rebaptize him; but I restore the power of the sacrament, so that I may implant the root of charity.

That, then, will be the living soul which the earth brings forth, so that it may be a living soul, already possessing the power of the sacrament. This, therefore, is what was said: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls,” and so forth.

## THE CREATION OF LIVING SOULS. THE LIVING SOUL. PIETY AS POWER. CHARITY. THE HUMAN BEING IN THE IMAGE OF GOD
5. God also said, “Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to its kind,” etc. On the sixth day God said, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul”: not creeping things of living souls, but a living soul. And the earth brought forth all cattle, beasts, serpents, and everything that creeps upon the earth. And God saw that it was good. And on that same sixth day, when the earth had brought forth a living soul, God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” etc.

We said that God made the light—that is, [Col. 1728] all the faithful. He made the firmament in the world, the heaven between the waters and the waters; he made the firmament in the Church, the authority of the Scriptures between the peoples of the angels, for whom this is not necessary, and the peoples of human beings, who would seek God there. God made in the world the separation of the sea from the land; God made in the Church the separation of the nations from his servants. The dry land thirsts for rain; human beings in the Church thirst for heavenly rain. The earth brought forth grass for pasture and fruit-bearing trees; human beings in the Church likewise bring forth works of mercy. Lights are made in heaven: the greater light, the word of wisdom; the lesser light, the word of knowledge; the stars, gifts of healings, faith, prophecies, etc.—all these in the firmament of heaven.

When, therefore, they had begun to walk and traverse the whole world, the waters brought forth—that is, from the Gentiles there arose—creeping things of living souls: the holy Sacraments, and consecrated people possessing the form. For the form of the Sacrament is present in a human being, and at times the power of the Sacrament immediately follows it; but this is already on the earth that has been separated. Therefore the earth brings forth a living soul.

And truly, brothers, it is necessary that there be a living soul. The brothers have received Baptism [Note: [Col. 1728] He indicates the newly baptized.]; let the power follow the form. Let Baptism not be for judgment, but for salvation. It was for judgment in the case of Simon Magus, for salvation in the case of Peter.

Let us therefore see what the living soul is that the earth brought forth. Consider the human being: he has a body, and he has a soul. In the soul itself he has many movements resembling those of beasts; and he has something else which beasts do not have.

What movements does he have that resemble those of beasts? Eating and drinking, sleeping and waking, and begetting. Are these not common to us and to beasts? Whoever casts these movements into lust has a dead soul, not a living soul.

How do we prove this? Hear the Apostle: “But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 6). What is “living in pleasure” except to release into pleasures and immoderate desires those movements of the soul that we share with cattle—to gluttony, drunkenness, fornication, and excessive sleep? Those who live in this way live in pleasure; yet while alive they are dead.

But if all these affections are restrained, and these movements are held to chastity and continence, the earth brings forth a soul. Since it was dead in pleasures, it remains that, once restrained from pleasures, it should begin to live and possess the power of piety.

What is the power of piety? Love of God and neighbor. Whoever possesses love restrains by faith all his lusts, all his desires, and all the movements of his soul that he shares with cattle; he will be a living soul. And it follows that the human being is now formed in the image and likeness of God.

He is formed when all these things that have been mentioned are brought together in that human being [Note: [Col. 1728] Perhaps, “are joined to the understanding of the human being.”]. For God made the light, and this was said of the human being in the Church; he made the firmament, on account of the authority of the Scriptures; he separated the waters from the earth, the Gentiles from believers; the earth brought forth grass for pasture, works of mercy; the lights in heaven, the holy Evangelists in the human being; and the earth brought forth [Col. 1729] creeping things of living souls, the Sacraments—and this too in human beings. Afterwards it brought forth a living soul, the restraint of all lusts—and this too in the human being.

Join all these things together in the understanding, and the human being has been made in the image and likeness of God.

Consider how we prove this. For that reason he said of each individual thing, “God saw that it was good.” But when he made the better thing, he did not say that it had become better. Rather, in the human being himself he gathered together all the things that had been made, and it was said, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” Earlier he had said of each individual thing that it was good; once the human being had been made, he named them all together. This is understood to mean that all those individual things are found together in the human being.

Do you seek light in the human being? You find faith. Do you seek the firmament? You find the authority of the Scriptures. Do you seek the separation of the waters? You find the faithful person separated from the Gentiles. Do you seek the earth’s putting forth grass and fruit-bearing trees? You find good works, works of mercy. Do you seek the lights of heaven? You find the Evangelists. Do you seek creeping things of living souls? You find the Sacraments. Do you seek a living soul? You find continence. Do you seek the human being in the human being? You find the image and likeness of God.

## From the Sermon on the Fiftieth Day of the Resurrection, Florus on I Corinthians I

The Lord Christ humbled himself so that we might learn to be humble. He was conceived while containing all things; he was born while bringing forth all things; he died while giving life to all things. But after three days he rose again and ascended into heaven, and he placed at the right hand of the Father the human flesh that he had assumed.

It is marvelous, brothers, and this is what the impious refuse to believe: it is marvelous that a human being rose again in the flesh and ascended into heaven with the flesh. But it is much more marvelous that the whole world believed something so incredible.

What is more incredible: that God did such things, or that the world was able to believe? Indeed, if we also consider the manner in which the world believed, that manner too is truly perceived as divine and is found to be exceedingly marvelous.

Christ sent to the sea of the world, with the nets of faith, a very few men untrained in the liberal disciplines and entirely unpolished in whatever concerns the learning of the world—unskilled in grammar and unarmed with dialectic—fishermen.

Why do I say “a very few”? He sent twelve; and yet through them he so filled the Churches with every kind of fish that many even of the wise men of the world themselves, to whom the cross of Christ seemed disgraceful, now sign themselves with it upon their foreheads; and the very thing of which they thought one ought to be ashamed, and for which they mocked us, they set up in the citadel of modesty.

## From the Sermon on the Apostle Paul, at the Conversion of a Certain Pagan, Faustus, Florus on Romans XIV

We can neither see nor display the human heart. God says, “The things that are manifest belong to you; the hidden things belong to me.” The Apostle Paul says, “Brothers, do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will manifest the counsels of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God” (I Cor. IV, 5).

You cannot inspect the heart of a new Christian. Can you inspect the heart of an old Christian? [Col. 1730] You will say, “He believed out of necessity.” The same might be said of the man of whom we were speaking shortly before: “Who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (I Tim. I, 13).

A certain necessity was also imposed upon him: he was struck down by a heavenly voice; so that he might have light, he lost the light. Threaten whatever you wish, and give whatever you wish to any human being: what is sweeter than this light? Yet Paul would not have received eternal light unless he had first lost this one.

“He believed out of necessity.” What did he fear? Let it be told me: what did he fear? Sheep crying out? Sheep can cry out; they cannot bite. Perhaps even in the very cry of God’s sheep he was able to perceive the glory of God and to fear the judgment of God. He was roused, as it were, from sleep, so that he might consider that the things foretold concerning Christ were being fulfilled: how powerful the name of Christ was, how greatly the glory of God prevailed.

Therefore I say briefly to your Charity—I address the Church of God, I address the people of God: if he believed, you found him; if he feared, you conquered.

Meanwhile, brothers, let us not claim for ourselves beyond what human beings are capable of, nor usurp what has not been granted to us. The Apostle says, “Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over thoughts” (Rom. XIV, 1). Let us not usurp the right to judge the thoughts of others; rather, let us entrust our thoughts to God, even on behalf of those concerning whom we perhaps have some doubt.

Perhaps his very newness causes him to doubt something. Love the one who doubts all the more abundantly; by your love heal the doubt in the weak heart. Look upon the inner face, over which you may rejoice; entrust the heart to God, for whom you pray.

Know that he is abandoned by the wicked; let him be received by you. Love the person more than you formerly hated the error. Thus Christ came to heal the sick, concerning whom we heard in the Gospel: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX, 12).

“And what person is there who, when he has lost one sheep, does not leave the ninety-nine in the mountains and go to seek the one that was lost; and when he has found it, does not rejoice over it? Thus my Father rejoices over one repentant person more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Matt. XVIII, 12–14, and Luke XV, 4–7).

Thus, indeed, Christ came to heal the sick; thus he knows how to avenge himself mercifully upon his enemies. Those whose companions have perhaps gone astray are grieved in spirit; for a time they are angry, but later perhaps they will imitate him.

Therefore, brothers, we commend him both to your prayers, to your love, to your most faithful friendship, and to your acceptance of his weakness. As you go before him, so he follows: teach him the good way, and let him find it exemplified in you.

Now that he has become a Christian, let him discern the difference between what he abandoned and what he found. His life and devotion concerning the faith of Christ will be confirmed by the times to come. But now, my brothers, it was neither necessary nor the counsel of shepherds to repel one who was knocking, or to delay one who was seeking. To wish to judge the hidden things of the heart and not to accept an open voice was neither our counsel nor our purpose.

For we know how that merciful avarice of God threatens—an avarice that seeks profits everywhere from its money—and how he speaks to the lazy servant who wished to judge what he did not see and who was sluggish in gathering the Lord’s profits:

“Wicked servant, I condemn you from your own mouth. You said that I was a demanding man, harvesting where I had not sown and gathering where I had not scattered” [Col. 1731] “You knew, then, that I was demanding. You ought therefore to have put my money with the money-changers, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest” (Luke XIX, 22–23).

We, therefore, could do nothing except distribute the Lord’s money. That exactor will be the exactor not only of him, but also of all of us. Let us fulfill the office of a distributor; let us not usurp the place of the exactor.

Therefore, my brothers, keep the work of God in mind. You were seeking one thing, planning another, and found something else. We commend the Lord’s work—servants to fellow servants. Let us love more in him what our Lord has done than what we wished to do. For his works are better.

We also heard his great and devoted declaration: “I do not want primacy; I want to be a Christian.” Rejoice; exult; love him more than you hated him. Commend his work to Christ in your prayers. Show a faithful, devout, and friendly spirit toward the first beginnings of an old man. For what does it matter that you see an already advanced age? He came to the vineyard at the ninth hour, intending to receive an equal wage, etc.

## From the Sermon on the Feast of Saint Quadratus [Note: [Col. 1731] Quadratus is celebrated in the Carthaginian Calendar in the month of August, and is called a martyr by Possidius in the *Indiculus*, chapter 9.], Bede, not yet published, on II Corinthians IV

The blessed Apostle Paul brought forward a testimony from the Scriptures in which he commended to us the glory of the martyrs. Therefore, he says, it is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” “And we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

For if they had believed only and had not spoken, they would not have suffered. By believing they seized life, and by speaking they found death—but death in which the corruptible body would be sown and incorruption reaped.

The same Apostle explained this meaning—that we believe and therefore speak—in another place as follows: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

## From the Sermon on the Three Rods, Bede and Florus on I Corinthians I
