Why, then, did the Lord first choose the lowly, the few, the unlearned, and the unpolished, although he had before his eyes a great multitude—indeed, fewer in comparison with those poorer people, but many within their own class—of rich, noble, learned, and wise people, whom he later also gathered? The Apostle explains the mystery:

“God chose the weak things of this world to confound the strong; and God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise; and God chose the lowly things of this world, and the things that are not—that is, that are not counted—in order to bring to nothing the things that are” (I Cor. I, 27–28).

For he had come to teach humility and to conquer pride. The humble God had come; in no way would he first seek the exalted, since he had come so humbly.

First, he chose to be born of that woman who was betrothed to a carpenter. He therefore did not choose illustrious ancestry, lest nobility on this earth should grow proud. He did not even choose to be born in the greatest city; rather, he was born in Bethlehem of Judah, which is not even called a city. Even today the inhabitants of that place call it a village. It is so small, so insignificant, almost nothing, except insofar as it was ennobled by the Lord Christ’s former birth.

Therefore he chose [Col. 1732] the weak, the poor, and the unlearned: not because he abandoned the strong, the rich, the wise, and the noble, but because if he had chosen such people first, they would have seemed to themselves to have been chosen on account of their riches, their possessions, and their ancestry. Inflated by these things, they would not have received the salvation of humility, without which no one can return to that life from which we would not have fallen except through pride.

## Also from the Sermon on the Three Rods, Bede, not yet published, on I Thessalonians II

“I became a little one in the midst of you, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (I Thess. II, 7).

For this reason he did not say “mother,” because mothers are sometimes either more tender or less loving toward their children, and after giving birth they hand them over to others to be nursed. Again, if he had said only, “Like a nurse cherishing,” and had not added, “her own children,” he might have seemed to have received children to nurse who had been born by another.

He called himself a nurse because he nourished them; and he called them his own children, whom he himself had begotten, saying, “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). He gives birth, however, just as the Church gives birth in her womb, not through her own seed.

## From the Sermon on the Good of Marriage, Bede and Florus on I Corinthians VII

“Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12).

“But I cannot,” he says.

“You cannot?”

“I cannot.”

Let a certain nourishing [Note: [Col. 1732] Bede’s manuscripts read *nutricatoria*.] authority of the Apostle support you: “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry.” Let there be something by which one may arrive at pardon. Let it contribute to pardon, lest one rush into eternal punishment. Let what is permitted be done, so that what is not permitted may be forgiven.

This is indicated by what follows: “I would rather that they marry than burn” (I Cor. VII, 9). I say that he conceded something to incontinence because he feared something greater: he feared eternal punishments; he feared what awaits and remains for adulterers.

I would also place among those things for which it is said daily, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12), the fact that married people, overcome by desire, use one another beyond the necessity of producing children.

## From the Sermon on What Is Written in Matthew XVI, 24, “If Anyone Wishes to Come After Me, Let Him Deny Himself”: Bede, Not Yet Published, on I Thessalonians V

“Correct the disorderly, console the fainthearted,” etc.

When a person sees someone living badly and perhaps contributing something to the Church, and does not correct him, he flees in his heart.

What does it mean to flee in one’s heart? To be afraid. Fear is an inward flight.

Why is he afraid? Because he is a hireling. He is afraid that the other person may take the correction badly and no longer give what he usually gives [Note: [Col. 1732] See Sermon 137, no. 12.].

He sees the wolf coming—that is, the devil breaking the neck of the person who lives badly—and he flees in his heart, refraining from useful correction, full of fear.

But whoever is a shepherd, and cares for the sheep, should not abandon him. He does what the Apostle says: “Correct the disorderly, console the fainthearted,” etc.

Therefore, let no one consider a pious shepherd—or one who calls himself a shepherd—to be someone who does not return evil for evil, when in fact he returns evil for good. For although that person is a sinful and wicked man, he gives some of his goods to the Church; but the other returns evil for good to him from whom [Col. 1733] he withholds correction.

But since all this must be done out of love, sometimes people think that those who correct them are their enemies. Therefore, after saying, “Correct the disorderly,” he added, “Console the fainthearted.” For perhaps the person begins to weaken because of the correction and is disturbed; then you ought to console him.

“Support the weak,” lest they fall because of their weakness. If weakness has made him stumble, let love receive him into its bosom.

And after saying these things, he added at the end, “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil” (I Thess. I, 14–15).

Correction, then, is not evil if it is given properly. But what does a good sheep say when he is corrected by his superior? “Let the righteous strike me in mercy” (Ps. CXL, 5).

## From the Sermon on What the Lord Says in Luke XI, 10–11, “Ask and You Will Receive”: Bede, Not Yet Published, on II Corinthians XII

We find that wicked people have asked and received, and good people have asked and not received. For who is worse than demons? Yet they asked for the swine and received them (Matt. VIII, 31–32). And we find that God did not fulfill the Apostles’ desire, while he fulfilled the demons’ desire.

What, then, are we to say, except that “the Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19), and that everyone of his who asks receives?

But a difficulty still remains concerning the Apostle. For he himself was surely among those who are his, since he said this sentence, “The Lord knows those who are his.” Therefore all who are his ask and receive.

But what do they ask for? Those things that are requested for this temporal life sometimes help and sometimes harm. And when God knows that they harm, he does not give them to his own who desire and ask for them—just as a physician does not give a sick person everything he requests; and out of love he refuses what, if he did not love him, he would grant.

He therefore hears all his own for eternal salvation; he does not hear all of them according to temporal desire. For this reason he does not hear them for one purpose, so that he may hear them for another.

Finally, consider the very words. When he did not receive what he had asked the Lord three times to remove, the Lord said to him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

What do you desire from me—that the thorn of the flesh be taken away from you, which you received so that you would not be exalted by your revelations? Certainly you ask this because you do not know that it benefits you.

Trust the physician. What he has applied is sharp, but useful; it causes pain, but brings forth health. “Power is made perfect in weakness.”

Therefore endure weakness if you desire health; endure weakness if you desire perfection, because power is made perfect in weakness.

## From the Sermon on the Apostle’s Words, “Our Struggle Is Not,” etc., Bede and Florus on Ephesians VI

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”

For it is not merely a human being who persecutes you; the devil does so through that person. And before he wounds you in the body, he kills himself in the heart.

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings, who are flesh and blood—“but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI, 12). For just as Christ governs and rules those who are light, so the devil drives and incites those who are darkness toward every evil.

The Apostle therefore exhorts us [Col. 1734] not to pray against the evil person, but against the devil who acts through him; and to do everything we can so that the devil may be driven out and the human being set free.

For just as, if an armed man mounted on a horse came against someone positioned for battle from the opposing side, that person would not be angry with the horse but with the rider, and would strive with all his might to strike the rider and take possession of the horse, so we must act toward evil people. We must labor with all our strength not against them, but against the one who incites them, so that when the devil is conquered, the wretched person whom he had begun to possess may be set free.

## From the Same Sermon, Bede and Florus on I Corinthians XII

“Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked” (I John II, 6).

What is this way on which Christ walked? What other way is there except love, concerning which the Apostle says, “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII, 31)?

If, then, we wish to imitate Christ, we must run along that very way on which Christ deigned to walk even while hanging on the cross. For he was fixed upon the cross, and while running the way of love he prayed for his persecutors. Finally, he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

Therefore let us also continually pray for all our enemies, so that the Lord may grant them amendment of conduct and forgiveness of sins.

## From the Sermon on What a Bishop Should Be, and Where Paul Rebuked Peter: Bede, Not Yet Published, on I Timothy III

“Therefore a bishop must be blameless” (I Tim. III, 2).

Who denies this? But since a bishop must be blameless, is it fitting for a Christian to be blameworthy?

“Bishop” is a Greek term; in Latin it can be called a superintendent or visitor. We are bishops, but with you we are Christians. We are properly called from visitation; all of us are commonly named from anointing. If the anointing is common, the struggle is common as well.

But why do we visit you, if there is nothing good that we see in you?

## From the Sermon on the Sabbath, Florus on II Corinthians III

“But when he turns to God, the veil will be taken away.”

The veil—not Moses—is removed; the veil—not the law—is removed. Consider how the Lord came, and the veil is removed. When he hung upon the cross, the veil was torn.

O great mystery! O ineffable sacrament! The transgressors of the law crucified him, and the secrets of the law were revealed.

Was that cross not the Lord’s key? It held him fast, and by closing it opened what had been closed.

But even though the veil has been torn, the Jews still have their face covered [Note: [Col. 1734] See Sermon 300, no. 3.].

“But we,” says the Apostle, “with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 16, 18).

## From the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon, on Leviticus

The Apostle Peter says to the Church, which is the body of Christ, “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II, 9).

At that time one priest was anointed; now all Christians are anointed. A king was anointed, and a priest was anointed; the others were not anointed. The Lord bore both persons—not in figure, but already in reality—both that of king and that of priest.

For this reason the Apostle says of the Lord himself, “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3).

Behold, then, the royal lineage. Christ is said to be from the seed of David on account of Mary, because she was from the seed of David.

But how is priestly lineage present in Mary [Note: [Col. 1735] Perhaps: “But how could priestly lineage be present in Mary?”]? It is written in the Gospel that the priest Zechariah had a wife, Elizabeth, from the daughters of Aaron. She was therefore of priestly lineage, since the whole tribe was that of Levi.

In the Gospel the angel says to the Virgin Mary, “Your kinswoman Elizabeth” (Luke I, 36). If, then, Elizabeth, one of the daughters of Aaron the priest, was Mary’s kinswoman, there is no doubt that the Virgin Mary belonged not only to royal blood but also to priestly blood.

Therefore, in the Lord according to the human being whom he assumed, there is both a royal and a priestly person. For this reason, then, two people were formerly anointed in figure—the king and the priest—which has been fulfilled in that head of ours, whose whole body, the Church, it is clear that we are.

Hence we are rightly called a royal and priestly race.

## Also from the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon, in the Same Place

In those ancient sacraments our one Lord Jesus Christ was prefigured. One priest entered the Holy of Holies; but all the people stood outside.

Are you now outside, when bishops are assisting at the altar, and not inside?

At that time one priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year. The year signifies the whole of time. Therefore, once in the whole of time, one priest entered the Holy of Holies—not a figurative one, but the true one—beyond the heavenly veils: our one priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead and offering himself for us.

He entered, and he is there. But the people still stand outside with us. We have not yet risen to go out to meet Christ and remain forever with him within, when he will say to the good servant, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21).

This, then, was formerly prefigured by the one priest entering alone into the Holy of Holies while the people stood outside. It has now been fulfilled by our Lord Jesus Christ alone entering above the heavenly mysteries, while the people still groan outside, saved in hope and awaiting the redemption of their body, which will take place in the resurrection of the dead.

## Also from the Sermon on the Kalends of January against the Pagans, John the Deacon, in the Same Place

For he himself is the high priest who offers our prayers, having offered himself as a burnt offering for us. He is the one who leads us forward, placing himself between us—not in order to block, but in order to direct; not in order to separate, but in order to reconcile; not in order to hinder, but in order to break apart hindrances.

He is the one pontiff and the one priest who was prefigured in the ancient priests of God. For this reason a priest without bodily blemish was sought, because he alone lived without the blemish of sin even in mortal flesh. For what was prefigured in their bodies signified what was to come in his life.

# Appendix to Volume Five of the Works of Saint Augustine, Containing Spurious Sermons, Now Arranged for the First Time in Four Classes

The first class contains sermons on the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. The second contains sermons on the seasons. The third contains sermons on the saints. The fourth contains sermons on various subjects.

Inserted among these classes are the sermons of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, except those entitled *To the Monks*.

[Note: [Col. 1735] We compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

[Col. 1735]

[Col. 1735]

## First Class: On the Old and New Testament (C, G)*

## Sermon One [Note: [Col. 1735] Elsewhere, in volume nine.] On the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Genesis II, 16–17 [Note: [Col. 1735] Attributed to Augustine in certain ancient books. In Bellarmine’s judgment it is doubtful; Erasmus, Verlinus, and Vindingus hold it to be spurious, and the Louvain scholars rejected it into the Appendix of volume 9. It was also wrongly ascribed to Ambrose [Col. 1736] and printed in volume 1 of his works with significant variation. It exists without an author’s name in an old Corbie manuscript apparently copied a thousand years ago.]

### 1. False Questions About the Tree of Paradise Are Resolved

We read in Genesis that the Lord said to Adam: “You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is in the midst of paradise, you shall not eat; for on the day on which you eat from it, you shall die.”

We know, dearest brothers, that many have raised false questions about this tree. They say that Adam did not sin willingly, because the knowledge of good and evil was in that tree. While trying to excuse the human being’s fault, they thus do injury to God the Creator.

An answer must be given to them, so that they may no longer raise false questions or continue to lie hidden in error by thinking in this way. But if they wish to know, let them be silent and listen, lest by speaking foolishly they insult God.

There was one tree in the midst of paradise, testing the human being’s will. Upon it life hung, and in it death lay hidden through transgression. In it the transgression appeared, in which the commandment of the law had been established.

God said, “You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from that tree which is in the midst of paradise you shall not eat, lest you die.”

In these words the law was established by God for the human being. In it a reward [Note: [Col. 1737] Two manuscripts read, “the reward of life.”] was appointed when, at the conclusion of the sentence, God said, “If you taste it, you shall die.”

But the devil said, “You shall not die,” and the human being stood between God the Maker and the devil the deceiver.

God threatened death if the fruit of the tree were touched; the devil promised that they would become gods if that tree were violated. Thus the poisonous sweetness was desired [Note: [Col. 1737] Several manuscripts read, “the sweetness of death.”], and the healthfulness of perpetual life was despised.

### 2. Death Was Not Made in the Tree

But some slanderer says, “You see that death was made in that tree?”

Let us answer this false question. It was certainly not made in that tree; rather, it was discovered through the human being. This was a test of the human being, not a deception by the Savior [Note: [Col. 1737] In a Roman manuscript, *salutis*; but in a Greek manuscript and in Erasmus, *salutaris*.].

For if God had not loved the human being, he would not have made him; nor would he have warned him beforehand if he had wished to destroy him. If he had not warned him beforehand, that would not have been mercy but impiety, nor justice but injustice: he would have made the human being mercifully, yet caused him to fall unjustly.

This impiety ought not to exist even in a human being; how much less should it be believed to have existed in God, who is the fountain of piety and goodness?

Who among human beings, my brothers, would allow his own work to perish, or hand over his own construction to ruin, or thrust a son whom he had begotten into a pit of death?

If such cruelty is not found in a human being, do not believe that it existed in God, who well ordered his own construction—that is, the human being—and supported the ruin threatening him with a prop of the commandment [Note: [Col. 1737] The printed editions read, “appointed for him by the commandment.” The manuscripts’ reading, “appointed as a support of the commandment,” is better. For *destina* is used of a support for a structure. Thus Bede, in *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book 3, chapter 17: “It happened that, leaning against the support which had been placed outside the church as a protection,” etc. In the title of that chapter, a new edition substitutes “placed against the church,” whereas the older edition has “the support of the church.” Augustine uses the same word at the end of Sermon 12; Saint Braulio uses it in the *Life of Saint Isidore of Seville*, April 4, in Surius.]

—but he could not stand. Why? Because he refused to obey God.

What, then, do we charge to God if Adam fell, when Adam despised God’s commandment in order to fall?

### 3. The Tree Was Not Evil: Evil Things Become So by Wrong Use

Tell me: was the tree itself good or evil? You will say, “Evil”—certainly evil, since by plucking its fruit the human being was punished with death [Note: [Col. 1737] Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read *mutatus est in mortem* (“was changed into death”).]. Therefore, was it the tree that was evil, or the transgression of the commandment? Clearly, the tree: for if it had not been evil, Adam would not have fallen [Note: [Col. 1737] The corrected manuscript reads: “if it had not been evil, it would not have brought death upon the human being.”].

You say this without paying attention to the force of Scripture. For just as it is written that the knowledge of good and evil was in that tree, so it is written: “And God saw the things that he had made, and behold, they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). Do you believe the one statement that leads you into error, and not the one that leads you to salvation?

Would you like to know, you slanderer, that the tree was not evil but good, and that death was not made by God in it, but that the human being created death for himself? Tell me, slanderer: is iron good or evil? Without doubt you will say, “Evil.” And why is it evil and not good, when everything that God made is very good? What sort of good do you say iron is, when people are killed by it?

Listen, then: iron is not evil; rather, the person who uses iron for a crime is himself evil. For would you like to know that iron is good? One person uses it for pruning a vineyard, another for committing murder; one sustains himself by means of iron, another kills an innocent person with a sword; one cultivates a field with iron, another sheds blood in a narrow passage by means of iron [Note: [Col. 1738] Ambrose has *in acie ferri* (“in the edge of the iron”). Our manuscripts read *in fauce*, which is better; that is, “in the narrowness of roads,” a place suitable for ambushes and robberies. Augustine uses the word in the same sense, *Exposition on Psalm 86*: “That robber did this, stronger on the cross than in the narrow passage”; also *Exposition on Psalm 55*, and *Tractate 7 on the Gospel of John*, no. 12.]. One works with iron to support his life, another takes another person’s life with iron. A judge, too, carries a sword so that he may punish the guilty and acquit the innocent.

Listen further, if you have the time, slanderer. Do you say that wine is good or evil? I think you will say that it is good, not evil—and this by a judgment of fairness, not by the benefit of drunkenness. Therefore wine is good—very good. Good: in the case of wine you have confessed that God’s creature is good, and I too confess that it is good.

Why, then, does one person take it with sobriety, while another takes it to drunkenness? Is God’s creature to be called evil merely because one person becomes drunk from it and appears disgraceful? Another drinks soberly and blesses God in that very sobriety; but the one who becomes drunk falls into a pit and sometimes incurs death.

The foods that the Lord has graciously granted us for our use are not evil but good; nevertheless, if they are consumed excessively, they are harmful and injurious. Is God’s creature therefore to be called evil because it causes harm or is destructive to some people? No; rather, because they consume more than is beneficial to the destruction of their own health, what God granted to the human race becomes harmful to them.

What I am about to say is well known to everyone. We know that some people have been suffocated by excessive wine and food. Was death in the wine or in the food? Far from it: it was the intemperance of their eating that caused them to fall into death.

So too, iron is not for that reason to be called evil because a robber commits murder with it; rather, the robber himself is evil, since he uses it to kill a human being. In the same way, that tree was not evil but good; what was plainly evil was that the human being transgressed God’s commandment. For whatever God has graciously granted the human being for use is good.

Behold, I produce testimony from the New Testament that everything God made is good. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that Peter fell asleep and saw a vision: a certain white vessel, like linen, was being lowered from heaven, in which were quadrupeds, birds, and reptiles of the earth. And a voice said to him, “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” Peter said, “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” The voice said to him, “What God has sanctified, you must not call common” (Acts 10:11–15).

What do you say, slanderer? Behold, we have proved by the divine mouth that all things are not only good but also sanctified.

### 4. Sin Is to Be Imputed to Adam Alone, Not to the Tree or to God

This tree was not evil but good, and nothing evil could be found in it. Rather, the human being was evil of his own accord, since he made wrongful use of the good that God had made.

Here the evil will of the human being is revealed: although the whole paradise lay subject to him, he extended his hand toward the forbidden tree and incurred death. If the divinity had granted him one tree and the whole of paradise had been forbidden, what God had granted him ought to have been sufficient. But because he wanted more than the will of the giver had allowed him, he lost even what he possessed and nevertheless incurred death.

To whom is Adam’s sin to be imputed—to God, who warned him, or to the one who refused to listen? To the physician who gave the wounded man instructions to observe, or to the wounded man who, contrary to the physician’s command, tasted harmful fruits and brought the cause of transgression upon himself?

It is the practice of physicians that, when they see people suffering from a serious illness, they prohibit those things that are harmful to health or that bring danger. If a sick person, contrary to the physician’s command, takes unsuitable things through intemperance and suffers death, what does this have to do with the physician, who foresaw the danger and imposed the requirement of observance?

In the same way, neither is it to be imputed to God, the physician of souls, that Adam fell, since God warned him beforehand and wished him to live forever.

### [5. A Request for Delay]

Much remains to be said about these questions, but the hour has passed for discussing each point, lest the length of the sermon weary the hearers. I declare myself a debtor and ask for a delay; but I fear that the debtor may appear and the creditor arrange to be absent.

I am concerned to pay the debt of the sermon, but I do not find my former creditors: I see some, and I look for others. O sluggish creditor, when you come [Note: [Col. 1739] Erasmus and several manuscripts read *conveneris* (“when you meet”), instead of *veneris* (“when you come”).] to demand the debt, why do you arrange for your absence? The debtor wishes to satisfy the creditor, and the lazy creditor makes himself absent. I see something new: the debtor presses the creditor to receive the debt, and he makes excuses.

But what does it matter if the creditor refuses to come? Let the debtor return what he promised [Note: [Col. 1739] The words enclosed in brackets, although found in all the manuscripts, appear to have been added so that two sermons might be made from one treatise. In several manuscripts the second begins with the words, “I am concerned to pay the debt of the sermon.” The interpolator imitates Ambrose, who begins his book *On the Incarnation* as follows: “Brothers, I am concerned to pay a debt; but I do not find my yesterday’s creditors.”].

### 6. Why, Knowing That Adam Would Sin, Did God Not Turn Him Back from Sin?

Even now that former slanderer, convicted by so many proofs, is not satisfied, but says: “Did God know that the human being could sin, or not?” Let us answer him, so that he may not think he has said something significant: certainly he knew.

“If, then, he knew that the human being could sin, why did he not turn him back from sin?”

Why? Because it was not fitting to crown someone against his will. Who ever gives a prize to one who does not fight, my brothers? Or what crown is given to one who does not contend? Or what victory is there without conflict?

Listen to the Apostle speaking with a divine voice: “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Adam neither fought nor undertook combat with the devil; at a single suggestion he lost the reward of immortality. He was defeated because he did not fight; he yielded to the will, not to necessity.

O slanderer, who do not know how to make your position clear, and who wish to slander God because Adam did not sin willingly! Surely Job was a human being like him. How much did he suffer and endure? He fought bravely and conquered. He was handed over by God into the power of the devil, and he endured it.

Certainly, if God knew that he could not be overcome at all, he ought not to have handed him over to the devil’s power. But God wished to test him in this way so that he might cut off from us every occasion for excuse and slander.

Stripped of his wealth and possessions, he could not be conquered, because he did not wish to be. He lost his children and blessed the Lord. That is little: afterward, covered with sores, he lay in dung; and although pain pressed him to speak, he could not utter anything evil against the Lord. His words contained no reproach.

His wife was now not a help but a deception: a help to the devil, but a deception to her husband. Suborned by the devil [Note: [Col. 1739] The corrected manuscript reads *subrogata* (“appointed in place”), rather than *subornata* (“suborned”).], she urged him with such words: “How long will you endure these things? Say something against the Lord, so that he may be angry with you and you may die” (Job 2:9).

O the affection of a wife! O the medicine of marriage [Note: [Col. 1739] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “O the malignity of marriage!” They also read shortly afterward, “For she could have said, ‘Confess to God,’” whereas the manuscripts read, “As if she said, ‘Confess,’” that is, she urged blasphemy against God and the provoking of his anger with the confidence with which she might have urged his confession and propitiation.]!

As if she had said, “Confess to God, so that he may be reconciled to you and you may live,” she instead said, “Blaspheme God, so that he may be angry with you and you may die.”

O the stratagems of the ancient serpent! Through his wife he thought to deceive Job, whose soul was full of wounds [Note: [Col. 1739] The word *plenum* (“full”) is missing in the corrected manuscript.], yet even so he could not incite him to blasphemy.

What had Adam suffered like this? What combat had he had with the devil? He had suffered nothing of the kind. Why, then, did he obey the devil rather than God?

### 7. Death Comes from Contempt of the Divine Command; Scripture Must Be Received with Reverence

But still, slanderer, you say: “Why did God say, ‘You shall surely die,’ unless it was because God himself made death, since he did not avert it?”

This too is answered for you, most foolish slanderer. Suppose that, as a human being with children, you warn all of them and give them all a command to follow and imitate you in everything; and suppose that one of them becomes contemptuous and incurs death through evil conduct. Is his death to be imputed to you, or rather to the one who, by despising your warning, incurred death?

In the same way, Adam’s death is not to be attributed to God, who warned him beforehand not to fall into death through transgression. For it is clear that the Lord warned him, did not wish the human being to die, and did not himself make death.

The most wise Solomon testifies to this statement, saying: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:13). Adam neglected God’s command and fell into death.

Truly, brothers, no one despises an imperial letter without endangering his own blood; rather, everyone receives it with trembling and reverence, and they adore a most worthless sheet of paper written in ink, treating its written characters as divine.

The divine Scriptures are read, the words of God thunder, and the Lord himself, in a certain way, speaks as present to those who are present. Yet he is not heard; people listen with distaste, or—what is worse—while sitting, occupy themselves with conversations.

An emperor far away speaks through a sheet of paper; people tremble, and, as if present, adore him in that sheet of paper. Yet when the Lord’s Testament is read, some people despise it.

The Prophets themselves cry out, the Apostles preach, the Gospels speak, and he himself converses with human beings—and he is not heard.

Hear the Lord present and speaking: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

### 8. Whether God Ought to Have Permitted Sin

“But surely,” slanderous people say, “God ought not to have permitted the human being to sin.”

O fools! Those who say this do not consider that God did not make a statue of stone or wood, but created a perfect human being and gave him the power of free choice, so that he might consider what good he should desire and what evil he should reject.

He ought to have feared what God threatened and rejected what the devil persuaded him to accept. With the reward of immortality set before him, he ought to have kept his heart prepared for it and preserved the command of his Creator, rather than listen to the counsel of the destroyer.

Do I not blame the human being rather than God? Would he who made the human being commit an injustice [Note: [Col. 1740] The corrected manuscripts read: “I do injustice.”]?

O foolish and empty question! People say, “God ought not to have permitted the human being to sin,” but they do not say that the human being did wrong by transgressing God’s command and thereby sinning. Surely the human being ought to have feared death and not approached the forbidden tree.

If any human being—I do not wish to say an emperor of this world—despised a judge’s herald, would he not be dragged away to punishment? Adam despised God’s command, and yet some people defend him!

Why do you blame God at your own peril [Note: [Col. 1740] The corrected manuscript reads, “at your own danger.” Shortly afterward it reads, “and not the human being without your own prejudice.”], and not the human being without endangering yourself? Why do you accuse the craftsman who built well, while defending the human being who refused to remain in his own building, who forgot the divine command, and fell into the wound of transgression?

### 9. Adam Was Not Evil Because He Was the Father of a Murderer

O you who defend Adam and do injustice to God, answer me this question. Was Adam good or evil?

You will say, “Good,” so that your defense may be complete. If he was good, why did he beget one good son and another robber? He ought to have created both good; or, if, as you say, Adam sinned because God caused it, he ought to have begotten both evil.

Why did he beget one innocent son and another who shed innocent blood? One dedicated martyrdom, and the other inaugurated parricide.

Therefore Cain is not guilty because he killed his brother, since his father, who created the son, assumed the guilt [Note: [Col. 1740] The corrected manuscript adds, “the robber. If Adam sinned unwillingly, then…”]. Therefore Cain drove the sword into his brother’s throat unwillingly.

Such is the justice maintained by those who strive to slander the law: that the offspring should not be guilty, while their parents are held bound by guilt.

Behold Adam, who begot a robber; behold Cain, who killed his brother. Which of these two is guilty: the father who begot him, or the son who destroyed his brother by a cruel death?

The slanderer yielded; the slanderer fell silent. Although the one who slanders the truth never says anything truer, where are you, slanderer? Answer me on behalf of your client [Note: [Col. 1741] Ambrose adds *munere* (“office”), but incorrectly; *susceptus* is an old term meaning “client.”], who was confident in you. Defend the one whom you have defended until now.

Why have you yielded? Why have you fallen silent? Behold, Adam is held guilty for the guilt of his son because he begot a parricide. Why do you not say, “He is not guilty”?

The one who was silent rose up: “I am not silent,” he says. “I answer plainly, and I defend him: neither is the son guilty on account of the father, nor the father on account of the son, because it is written: ‘The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it alone shall be punished’” (Ezek. 18:4).

That slanderer who was sleeping seems to have awakened. He opened his mouth and began to speak; but now he will be silent. Say, then, that neither the father is guilty on account of the son, nor the son on account of the father.

Answer on behalf of your client, and I will answer on behalf of my God. Defend Adam’s case, and I will defend my God’s honor.

You say that it is not just for Adam to be guilty on account of his son, and I agree. If the son’s guilt does not involve the father in sin, and if Adam is not to be judged on account of Cain, then neither should we impute to God the fact that Adam sinned. Let us act instead in such a way that we may come to God’s pardon.

## SERMON II

[Note: [Col. 1741] Formerly *On the Season* 51; later in Appendix 34.]

### On the Calling of Abraham: “Go Out from Your Land,” etc. (Gen. 12:1)

[Note: [Col. 1741] The Amerbach and Erasmus editions present this sermon among Augustine’s genuine sermons. The judgment of Louvain, followed by Verlin and Winding, places it among the spurious works. In the manuscripts it bears Augustine’s name, but falsely. It is one of those that we consider to belong to Caesarius, bishop of Arles.]

### 1. What It Means to Go Out from One’s Land

When the divine reading was being read just now, we heard the Lord say to blessed Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house.”

Everything, dearest brothers, that was written in the Old Testament bore the type and image of the New Testament. Thus Paul said: “All these things happened to them figuratively; but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

If, then, they were written for us, what we read as having happened bodily in Abraham we see fulfilled spiritually in ourselves.

“Go out,” the Lord says to him, “from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house.”

All these things, brothers, we both believe and perceive to be fulfilled in us through the sacrament of Baptism.

Our land is our flesh. We go out well from our land when, abandoning carnal habits, we cling to the footsteps of Christ.

Does it not seem to you that the person who changes from proud to humble, from angry to patient, from lustful to chaste, from greedy to generous, from envious to kind, and from bloodthirsty to peaceful has happily gone out from his land—that is, from himself [Note: [Col. 1741] Caesarius, Homily 10; also among those edited by Baluzius, no. 3.]?

Truly, brothers, the person who is changed in this way for the love of God happily goes out from his land. Indeed, even in private conversation we are accustomed to speak in such a way that, if some wicked person suddenly begins to perform good works, we say of him, “This man has gone out from himself.” And rightly is he said to have gone out from himself who, having rejected vices, takes delight in virtues.

“Go out,” the Lord says, “from your land.” Our land—that is, our flesh—before the grace of Baptism was the land of the dying; through Baptism it has become the land of the living.

This is the land of which the Psalmist speaks: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

Through Baptism we have become, as I said, the land of the living rather than of the dying—that is, the land of virtues rather than of vices—provided that after receiving Baptism we do not return to the mire of vices, and that, after becoming the land of the living [Col. 1742], we do not perform works subject to death and lust.

“And come,” the Lord says, “into the land that I will show you.” We come joyfully to the land that the Lord shows us only if, with his help, we first drive away vices and sins from our land—that is, from our flesh.

### 2. Going Out from Our Kindred

“Go out,” he says, “also from your kindred.”

By this kindred are understood the vices and sins that in a certain way are born with us in part [Note: [Col. 1742] Morel, *Éléments critiques*, p. 291, thinks that the reading should be *ex patre nascuntur* (“are born from a father”), which agrees very well with the context, where kindred is being discussed. M.], and from infancy are added to us and nourished through evil acts [Note: [Col. 1742] Thus one manuscript. Two others read, “are brought in by evil practices.” The printed editions read, “are added through evil habits.”].

We therefore go out from our kindred when, through the grace of Baptism, we are emptied of all sins and vices—but in such a way that afterward, with God’s help, we work as much as we can so that, once vices have been expelled, we may be filled with virtues.

For if, having been emptied of all evils through Baptism, we wish to be idle and sluggish [Note: [Col. 1742] The manuscripts read: “For if we refuse to be emptied of evil habits through Baptism and remain idle, I fear…”] [Note: [Col. 1742] Caesarius, among the homilies edited by Baluzius, no. 4.], I fear that what is written in the Gospel may be fulfilled in us:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places seeking rest and does not find it. Afterward, if on returning it finds the house empty, it brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself; and entering, they dwell there. And that person’s last state is worse than the first” (Matt. 12:43–45).

Let us therefore go out from our kindred—that is, from sins and vices—so that we may never afterward wish to return to these evils, like a dog to its vomit.

### 3. Going Out from One’s Father’s House

“Go out,” he says, “also from your father’s house.”

This too, dearest brothers, we must understand spiritually. Before the grace of Christ, our father was the devil.

The Lord rebukes the Jews concerning him in the Gospel, saying: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to carry out your father’s desires” (John 8:44).

He therefore called the devil the father of human beings, not because they were born from him, but because they imitated his wickedness—not because they could have been born from him, but because they wished to imitate him.

That the devil was formerly our father, the Psalmist recalls from the person of God speaking to the Church: “Listen, daughter, and see, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11).

Consider, brothers, what he said: “Listen, daughter.” The one who said, “Listen, daughter,” is certainly a father. And when he says, “Forget your people and your father’s house,” he is certainly urging her to abandon her father.

We are therefore invited by God the Father to leave the devil as father in a blessed and happy exchange. We leave the devil our father rightly if, with God’s help, we always strive to avoid or flee his cunning and wickedness.

### 4. Recapitulation of the Foregoing

All these things, brothers—that is, that, following Abraham’s example, we may go out from our land, namely, our carnal manner of life; leave our kindred, namely, vices and sins; and flee from the house of the devil, our father—we have merited not through our own strength but through the gift of Christ’s grace.

Therefore, as much as we can, let us labor with his help, lest we return to the companionship or friendship of the devil, or to vices or carnal desires, because of what is written: “You have become well; do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

Rather, by imitating Abraham’s faith and continually performing good works, may we reach not only pardon but also the companionship and friendship of God.

But also, dearest brothers, we must consider with great fear and trembling what the Lord spoke to Moses about this same matter. For he said:

“When the Lord delivers the land of the Canaanites to you, beware lest you ever make friendships with the inhabitants of that land, which would immediately become a ruin for you” (Deut. 7:1–4).

For even if we believe that through the grace of Baptism all crimes and sins have been expelled from us, if afterward we make friendships with those very vices and sins [Col. 1743], consenting to them in greed or lust, without doubt that friendship becomes a ruin for us.

Therefore, as much as we can, let us labor with God’s help for the salvation of our soul. Let us take care to bring virtues into the field of our heart, which sins and crimes had possessed, so that what blessed Isaac said when blessing his son in the type of Christ may be fulfilled in us:

“Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

May he deign to grant this, to whom honor and dominion belong with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen [Note: [Col. 1743] The manuscripts read: “May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father,” etc.].

## SERMON III

[Note: [Col. 1743] Formerly *On the Season* 68, and later in Appendix 37.]

### On Blessed Abraham

[Note: [Col. 1743] It is not found in our manuscripts. It was published by Amerbach and Erasmus among Augustine’s sermons, and later by the Louvain editors in the Appendix among the spurious works, with no one objecting. Compare Sermon 7 of the Appendix.]

### 1. Abraham Justified by Faith

“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6).

Behold: he is justified by faith without works, and whatever might have been conferred upon him through observance of the law, faith alone granted in its entirety. He was himself a law to himself, although he had not received the law; nevertheless, by nature he observed whatever belonged to the law (Rom. 2:14).

Our father Abraham possessed the root of faith and of the Christian name. When he was commanded to leave his own country for uncertain and foreign lands, he fulfilled the command with complete devotion. In so difficult a matter he had no doubt, but accepted God’s decision as though it were something he had desired.

“Go out,” the Lord says, “from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you” (Gen. 12:1).

What a new kind of test: to impose foreign exile upon one who possessed his own property; to impose the labor of a journey upon one at rest; to command poverty upon one who possessed abundance; and to impose the necessity of traveling upon the master of such great resources.

Yet faith readily accepted whatever seemed difficult to unbelievers. To whom is his own hut not sweeter than foreign palaces, or a voluntary cottage than ordered halls? It is not easy for anyone to leave his own things and pursue the uncertain belongings of others; to leave what one knows and seek what one does not know.

For who has ever abandoned his own possessions without pain, or left them without tears? To whom is it not hard to leave those walls that witnessed his birth, those sweet thresholds and beloved household shrine commended by the memory of his parents and by the beginnings of his own infancy—where the cradle served the newly born and soon-to-emerge human being; where carefree infancy played amid the first beginnings of light; or where the years of childhood, happy in their simplicity amid the playful pursuits and games of that age, found the necessities of life supplied by his native, ancestral soil?

Amid all these things, so gentle and so sweet, which had to be abandoned with every difficulty, the command was given: “Go out from your land.”

Who would willingly hear this without the strength of faith? It would have seemed easier if he had at least heard the name of the place to which he was to go.

He set out and proceeded, accompanied by faith, with his wife as his companion. He went secure and confident, intending to fulfill through the labors of faith what had been promised him, hoping more from uncertainty than he had been secure in what was his own.

He went through deserted solitudes, through pathless places, through the hidden regions of nature, where the still-untamed earth had not yet recognized a human footprint. Amid all those things that he had abandoned at God’s command, he found no hut, no cottage; amid the very fearful solitudes of silent fields, he found no shelter where he might turn aside, but was merely a guest of heaven and earth.

### 2. Abraham Receives Three Angels as Guests

Yet Abraham was received by a tree, a human-like oak, which refreshed him as he came, exhausted by the summer sun, beneath the shelter of its pleasant shade. The luxuriant foliage of the woodland suspended among its branches, during the summer season, the day and the burning, heat-bearing rays of the scorching sun, so that the density of its branches and leaves removed everything that the harshness of the weather inflicted.

Abraham therefore entered the grove of the tree, beneath which some kind of shelter was constructed: narrow indeed for a human being, but sufficient for majesty. Devoted faith nevertheless painted it as a palace worthy of God, in which heavenly majesty would dine.

While he was sitting there and gazing attentively at the sky with curious eyes, behold, suddenly incorporeal majesty descended in the form of three men. He runs up, hastens, stretches out his supplicating hands, and kisses the knees of those passing by.

“Lord,” he says, “if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant” (Gen. 18:3).

You see: Abraham meets three, and worships one. A threefold unity, and one Trinity.

“Let water be brought; wash your feet, and refresh yourselves beneath this tree. I will bring bread, and you shall eat; afterward you shall continue on your way.”

And they said to him, “Do as you have said” (Gen. 18:5).

Perfect justice always preserves its character in good works. He who had no roof offered hospitality to strangers; although deprived of every dwelling, he provided passing travelers with a dwelling of the kind that necessity made possible.

And although the things offered were small, faith had given greatness to the narrowness of the place, and this faith did not deserve to be despised by God.

They turned aside to the hospitality of the tree, which Abraham had already made worthy of God. Meanwhile, fine flour was kneaded, *encryphiae* were made [Note: [Col. 1744] Amerbach reads *engr usia*; Erasmus and Louvain read *encryphiae*, which is better.] [Note: [Col. 1744] These were ashes-baked breads, so called from the Greek verb *enkryptō*, “I conceal,” because while they are being baked they are hidden beneath the ashes.], and a calf was slaughtered.

Although the divinity had no need of these things, Abraham nevertheless offered what justice desired. Behold, heavenly majesty reclined at a human table; food was taken, the meal was eaten, and in the familiar conversation of companionship intimate words were exchanged between the human being and God.

### 3. Hospitality Is Not Without Reward

Because hospitality could not be fruitless before God, he immediately received the price of his reward: a son was given to an old man; offspring was given to one who had despaired; old age received what youth had been utterly unable to have.

“To this time,” he said, “I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. 18:10).

Although Sarah’s advanced years and lifeless womb denied that this could happen, faith nevertheless gave credence to the divine promise.

“I have made you the father of many nations,” he said (Gen. 17:5). He was filled with good things, because God fulfilled what he had promised him.

Behold, at the very edge of old age, before the laws had been delivered and recited, we affirm that Abraham was religious, and that the one who had been more righteous in worship was more approved in faith.

For behold, that aged husband, who as yet had no son, nevertheless received from God a promise of countless descendants through one child.

Behold, when his bodily powers were exhausted, God said to Abraham: “Look up at the sky and count the stars; so shall your offspring be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:5–6).

Sarah’s womanly functions had ceased, because her limbs had already grown weary and failed. Her whole body was furrowed with wrinkles; her forehead became plowed and exhausted by old age. With the blood failing in her veins, weary old age languished in sorrow; but by divine judgment the vigor of age was rekindled.

The divine promise made her a better mother than age had allowed her to become. The mother received a name that the barrenness of time had taken away from her.

Although her bodily powers were far gone, Isaac was conceived. Suddenly her empty and withering veins boiled with renewed blood, and the old woman’s lifeless womb, warmed and steaming with blood, was animated by inward heat until the birth.

Youthful age grew warm, and the warmed blood gave off heat. An old woman became fruitful; an old woman became pregnant. Her belly grew day by day, and as the pregnancy strengthened, the womb’s expanding cavity stretched to contain the swelling child.

She became a burden-bearer, and the longed-for affection became, from her weary womb, a burden—the greatly desired offspring. Such a mother carried a heavy womb, although in her emptiness she could scarcely walk.

But because what she had received was the result of faith, faith, stronger than weakness, enlivened her exhausted womb.

Her withered breasts, which the loss of withdrawn moisture had slackened into empty bags, were stretched by the abundance of a fountain of milk. She became a mother in her breast; she became a mother in childbirth. She became, I say, a mother who by age had been a grandmother.

Faith gave new fires to aged organs. Thus Isaac was born through faith, so that their faith might be proclaimed in their offspring throughout the ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV

[Note: [Col. 1745] Elsewhere *On the Season* 54.]

### On the Three-Year-Old Cow, Ram, or Goat, and Also the Turtledove and Pigeon (Gen. 15:9–17)

[Note: [Col. 1745] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. To the Louvain editors it seemed doubtful; Verlin and Winding considered it spurious. We think it belongs to Caesarius. Compare Augustine’s published allegorical exposition of Abraham’s same sacrifice, *Exposition on Psalm 103*, Sermon 3, no. 5, and *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 24.]

### 1. Carnal and Spiritual People Signified in Abraham’s Sacrifice

We heard, dearest brothers, the Scripture saying:

“The Lord spoke to Abram, saying: ‘Take for me a three-year-old cow, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram; also a turtledove and a pigeon.’ He took all these, divided them through the middle, and placed the two parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds. Birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

“When the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark terror seized him. When the sun had set, a dark gloom came to be, and behold, a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire passed between those divided pieces.”

What these things signify, brothers, we desire briefly to make known to the ears of Your Charity, insofar as the Lord grants it.

Blessed Abraham was called by the Lord the father of many nations. For all the nations that believe, and that will believe, in Christ are children of Abraham—not by being born according to the flesh, but by imitating his faith.

For just as the Jews, having become degenerate through unbelief, were called in the Gospel children of the devil and a brood of vipers instead of children of Abraham, so, conversely, all the nations that faithfully believe in Christ have merited becoming children of Abraham.

The three-year-old cow, the three-year-old ram, the three-year-old goat, and the turtledove or pigeon prefigured all the nations. They are said to be three years old because all the nations were going to believe in the mystery of the Trinity.

And because the whole Catholic Church has not only spiritual people but also carnal people—although some say that they believe in the Trinity, they are nevertheless carnal because they pretend not to avoid crimes and sins—because spiritual people exist together with carnal people, therefore the turtledove and the pigeon were added.

The spiritual may be signified by the turtledove and pigeon, just as carnal people may be understood in those three animals.

## 2. In the Catholic Church the carnal are set against one another, not the spiritual

Therefore attend carefully: Abraham is said to have divided those three animals into two parts and placed them opposite one another. “But the birds,” Scripture says, “he did not divide.” Why is this, brothers? Because in the Catholic Church the carnal are divided; the spiritual are not divided at all and, as Scripture says, are prepared against one another.

Why are the carnal divided and set against one another? Because all the lustful and lovers of the world never cease to have divisions and scandals among themselves. These, then, are divided because they oppose one another; but the birds—that is, the spiritual—are not divided.

Why are the spiritual not divided? Because they have one heart and one soul directed toward God; in them there is one will and one refusal. For those birds mentioned above—namely, the turtledove and the dove—are their likenesses. In the turtledove chastity is signified; in the dove, simplicity. All in the Catholic Church who fear God and are marked as chaste and simple can say with the Psalmist: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?” (Psalm 54:7). And again: “The turtledove has found a nest for itself, where it may place its young” (Psalm 83:4).

When the carnal, who can be divided, are weighed down in this world by the heavy fetters of vices, the spiritual are lifted high on the wings of various virtues; and, as though by two wings—namely, the two commandments, loving God and one’s neighbor—they are raised to heaven. With the Apostle they can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). And whenever the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” they confidently and faithfully say that they have them directed toward God. Yet very few and rare are those in the Church who can say this confidently and truthfully.

Abraham therefore did not divide the birds, because the spiritual, who—as I have said—have one heart and one soul, cannot be divided or separated from the love of God or of their neighbor. Rather, with the Apostle they cry out: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?”—and the other things that follow, up to the statement: “Neither any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35–39).

The spiritual, then, are not separated from Christ even by tortures; the carnal, however, are sometimes separated even by idle tales. The cruel sword does not separate the spiritual; carnal affection separates the carnal. Hard things do not break the spiritual; pleasant things corrupt the carnal. Abraham therefore divided those animals into two parts, but he did not divide the birds.

## 3. A figure of the final judgment

“When the sun had set,” he says, “a deep sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great and very dark terror; and there appeared a burning and smoking furnace, and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions.”

Observe, brothers, that this fire is said to pass between those divisions; yet it is not recorded as having touched the turtledove or the dove. That evening signified the end of the world. Those animals, as we have already said, represented all the nations believing in Christ. Since these nations, as has already been stated, contain within themselves not only the carnal but also the spiritual—that is, not only the wicked but also the good—those animals were therefore divided, and the fire passed through them, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “The Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire” (1 Corinthians 3:13).

That burning and smoking furnace and lamp of fire represented the day of judgment. For this reason a dark fear and terror fell upon blessed Abraham. From this we understand that if “the righteous man will scarcely be saved,” where will the sinner and the ungodly appear? (1 Peter 4:18).

The burning and smoking furnace therefore signified the day of judgment—the day, I say, of judgment in which there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, in which there will be wailing, lamentation, and belated repentance; when the foundations of the mountains will be shaken, and the earth will burn down to the depths of hell; when, as blessed Peter says, “the heavens, being on fire, will be dissolved, and the elements will melt with the heat of fire” (2 Peter 3:12); when, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “the powers of heaven will also be shaken”; when the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven (Matthew 24:29).

Where will the ungodly then see themselves? Where will adulterers, drunkards, and slanderers recognize themselves? Where will lovers of sensuality, robbers, the proud, and the envious appear? What will those wretched people say in their defense, whom that day will find so often warned, yet unprepared?

When the whole world begins to roar together at the trumpet of the Archangel, clearer than every trumpet; when, as the prophet says, the Lord comes “to make the world desolate” and destroy sinners from it (Isaiah 14:17); when, as Scripture says, sinners and the ungodly are cast into the lake of fire, and “the smoke of their torments will rise for ages of ages” (Revelation 14:19, 11)—what trembling, what darkness, what gloom will then seize all criminals, the negligent, and the lukewarm?

Therefore, lest we too come into this punishment, let us awaken while there is time for correction, and let us seek the will of our Lord as good and useful servants. Then, when that day of judgment arrives—the day signified by the burning and smoking furnace, a day terrifying and exceedingly dreadful even to the good—may we not be tormented in hell by avenging flames together with the carnal [Note: [Col. 1746] Perhaps, “the worldly” (carnalibus).], whom those animals represented and who can be divided through their various struggles for pleasure. Rather, bearing the simplicity of the dove and the chastity of the turtledove, may we be lifted to heaven on the spiritual wings of virtues, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Then we shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON V

[Note: [Col. 1747] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 70.]

## On the three men who appeared to blessed Abraham

[Note: [Col. 1747] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. You will understand the author’s method and skill by comparing it with Origen’s fourth Homily on Genesis, which he altered here and there by adding and removing certain words after prefixing a preface. We seem to discern Caesarius’s style especially in the beginning and conclusion of the sermon.]

### 1. In reading Scripture, one must attend not only to the letter

I have frequently admonished your Charity, dearly beloved brothers, that in these readings recited in the Church on these days we must not attend only to what we recognize as sounding from the letter; rather, once the veil of the letter has been removed, we must faithfully seek the life-giving Spirit. For the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

In the end, the unhappy Jews—and the heretics, who are more unhappy still—because they look only at the sound of the letter, like a body without a soul, have remained dead without the life-giving Spirit. Let us hear the Apostle saying that “all these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Let us therefore see what it is that we have just heard when the divine reading was read.

### 2. Lot far inferior to Abraham

“God appeared,” he says, “to Abraham as he sat at the door of his tent, by the oak of Mamre. And behold,” he says, “three men stood over him, and he went out to meet them.”

Attend, brothers, and observe how God appeared to Abraham and how he appeared to Lot. Three came to Abraham and stood over him; two came to Lot and sat in the street (Genesis 19:1–2). See, brothers, whether events are not ordered according to the merits of each by the dispensation of the Holy Spirit.

For Lot was far inferior to Abraham. If he had not been inferior, he would not have deserved to be separated from blessed Abraham, nor would he have been pleased to dwell among the Sodomites. Three men therefore came to Abraham at midday; two came to Lot, and they came in the evening. Lot could not endure the greatness of the midday light, whereas Abraham was able to receive the full brilliance of the light.

### 3. Praise of hospitality

Now let us see how Abraham and how Lot received those who came. Abraham took the initiative and went out to meet them. When he had met them, he hurried to the tent and said to his wife: “Hurry,” he said, “knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes,” which in Greek is called ἐγκρυφίας (*enkryphias*), indicating cakes that are hidden and concealed.

Abraham himself ran to the herd and took a calf. What sort of calf? Perhaps one that happened to come out first? It was not so; rather, he took a good and tender calf. He took the calf and gave it to the servant. “Servant,” he said, “hurry to prepare it.”

Observe, brothers, and consider with what fervent spirit you ought to receive guests. Behold, Abraham himself runs, his wife hastens, and the servant hurries. No one is sluggish in the house of a wise man.

Behold, Abraham and Sarah have equal duties of hospitality. Lot did receive them, but only two, not the whole Trinity, and not at midday, but in the evening. And what did he set before them? “He cooked unleavened bread,” it says, “and they ate.”

And because he was far inferior to Abraham in merit, he had neither a fattened calf nor any recognition of the mystery of the Trinity in the three measures of fine flour. Nevertheless, because he offered even what he could with a kindly spirit, he deserved to be saved from the destruction of Sodom. Attend, brothers: Lot too, because he did not reject guests, deserved to receive angels. Behold: angels enter a hospitable house, while houses closed to guests are consumed by sulphurous flames.

[Col. 1748]

### 4. Abraham recognized the mystery of the Trinity. The washing of the feet

Three men therefore came to Abraham and stood over him. Observe how significant it is that they came over him, not against him. He had subjected himself to God’s will, and therefore God is said to stand over him. “They stood,” he says, “over him”—not against him to repel him, but over him to protect him.

He received three men and set before them bread made from three measures. Why this, brothers, unless because he understands the mystery of the Trinity? He also sets before them a calf—a calf that is not hard, but good and tender. And what is as tender, what is as good, as the one who humbled himself for us even unto death? He is the fattened calf whom the father slaughters for the son who has returned in repentance.

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16). Abraham therefore goes out to meet three and worships one. In seeing three, as has already been said, he understood the mystery of the Trinity; in worshiping as though one, he recognized that there is one God in three persons.

He speaks to one, saying: “Turn aside to your servant.” He also adds, as though speaking to human beings: “I will bring water, and let your feet be washed.”

Learn, brothers, from blessed Abraham to receive guests gladly and to wash their feet with humility and devotion. Wash, I say, the feet of holy travelers, lest some dust remain on them which they might shake from their feet as a testimony against you.

For he said in the Gospel: “Whoever does not receive you, as you leave, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10:14–15).

Abraham foresaw this in the spirit, and therefore wished to anticipate it and wash their feet, lest some dust should remain which, once shaken off, could be preserved as testimony to unbelief on the day of judgment. Therefore wise Abraham says: “I will bring water, and let your feet be washed.”

Hear these things carefully, brothers, you who do not wish to practice hospitality, who receive a guest as though he were an enemy. Behold, blessed Abraham, by fervently receiving human beings, deserved through the practice of hospitality to receive God himself. Christ also confirmed this in the Gospel, saying: “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matthew 25:35).

Do not therefore neglect strangers, lest the one whom you did not receive should himself be Christ.

### 5. The same subject continued

Where, however, did this take place? At the oak of Mamre, which in Latin is interpreted as “vision” or “clear sight.” Do you see what sort of place it is in which the Lord can hold a banquet? Abraham’s vision and clear sight delighted him. For Abraham was pure in heart, so that he could see God.

In such a place and in such a heart the Lord can hold a banquet. Concerning this vision the Lord spoke in the Gospel to the Jews, saying: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

“He saw my day,” he says, because he recognized the mystery of the Trinity. He saw the Father as day, the Son as day, and the Holy Spirit as day, and in these three one day—just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and these three are one God. For each person individually is fully God, and all three together are one God.

Likewise, on account of the unity of substance, the three measures of fine flour can fittingly be understood as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This may also be understood in another way: Sarah may signify the Church, and the three measures of fine flour may signify faith, hope, and charity. For in these three virtues the fruitfulness of the whole Church is contained. Whoever deserves to possess these three within himself can confidently receive the whole Trinity at the banquet of his heart.

### 6. How God’s descent is to be understood

After this the Lord said to Abraham: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come up to me. Therefore I will go down and see whether the cry that has come to me is fulfilled in deed, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

These are the words of Scripture. Let us see what in them is worthy of understanding. “I will go down,” he says, “to see.” When responses are given to Abraham, God is not said to descend, but to stand above him; now, however, because the matter concerns sinners, God is said to descend.

Take care not to understand ascent and descent as movements through space. It is unworthy to think this of a substance that is incorporeal and wholly present everywhere. Rather, God is said to descend when he deigns to take care of human weakness. We ought to understand this especially of our Lord and Savior, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

### 7. How God does not know sinners

But let us see what he means when he says: “I will go down to see whether the cry that has come to me is fulfilled in deed, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

The pagans—and especially the most impure Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1749] Origen’s homily contains nothing about the Manichaeans, nor does it contain the word “Law,” which occurs shortly afterward.]—customarily attack us on this point, saying: “Behold, the God of the Law did not know what was happening in Sodom.”

We respond with sound understanding and say that God is said to know the righteous in one way and sinners in another. What is said about the righteous? “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). What is said about sinners? “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, because I do not know you” (Matthew 7:23).

And again the Apostle Paul says: “If anyone is the Lord’s, let him understand what I say; but whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:37–38).

What, then, does “I do not know” mean? “I do not know you”: I do not recognize you according to my rule; I do not recognize my image in you. My justice has recognized in you what it should punish, but mercy does not recognize in you what it should crown. Thus those whose deeds are unworthy of God are also said to be unworthy of God’s knowledge.

“I will go down, then, to see”—not so that I may know what they are doing, but so that I may make them worthy of my knowledge, if I should find any of them righteous, if I should find any repentant, if I should find any of the sort whom I ought to know.

Finally, because no one who would repent and no one who would turn back was found except Lot, he alone is recognized and he alone is rescued from the conflagration.

Let us, brothers, make every effort and labor with God’s help to become such people that we may be considered worthy of God’s knowledge, so that he may deign both to recognize us and to know us; through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

# SERMON VI

[Note: [Col. 1749] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 71.]

## On the Sacrifice of Isaac, I

[Note: [Col. 1749] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It was compiled by an uncertain author and interpolated. It contains some material from Origen’s eighth Homily on Genesis and some material gathered from elsewhere. In our manuscripts the beginning is somewhat more concise than in the printed editions, as follows: “The reading, dearly beloved brothers, in which blessed Abraham is read to have offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering, we shall now, if you wish, briefly expound to your Charity’s ears, insofar as we can, according to the way our fathers treated it under the inspiration of the Lord. ‘Take your son’ …” This little exordium appears to have been expressed from Caesarius’s words.]

### 1. Introduction

That reading, dearly beloved brothers, in which blessed Abraham is read to have offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering is not recited in its proper order during the days of Lent because, as you yourselves know, it is reserved for the vigils of Easter on account of the sacrament of the Lord’s passion. Since at that time there is no opportunity to say anything about it, let us now, if you agree, briefly present to the ears of your Charity an exposition of it according to the way our fathers treated it under the inspiration of the Lord.

### 2. The mystery of the Trinity

The Lord therefore said to Abraham: “Take your son, whom you love, Isaac, and offer him to me as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will show you.” He rose, saddled his donkey, took with him two servants and his son Isaac, and reached on the third day the place that the Lord had shown him (Genesis 22:2 and following).

When Abraham offered his son Isaac, he represented God the Father; Isaac, however, represented the Lord Savior. The fact that they reached the place of sacrifice on the third day reveals the mystery of the Trinity.

For the fact that the third day is understood in the sacrament or mystery of the Trinity is frequently found in the sacred books, as in Exodus: “We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness” (Exodus 5:3). Again, when they came to Mount Sinai, the people were told: “Sanctify yourselves and be ready for the third day” (Exodus 19:15). And Joshua, when he was about to cross the Jordan, warned the people to be ready on the third day (Joshua 1:11). Our Lord also rose on the third day (Matthew 28).

We have said this because blessed Abraham came on the third day to the place that the Lord had shown him.

### 3. The ram and Isaac as figures of Christ

The two servants whom he ordered to remain with the donkey represented the Jewish people, who, because they were not going to believe in Christ, could not ascend or reach the place where he was to be sacrificed. The donkey signified the synagogue.

The ram that was caught by its horns among the thorns also appears to have represented the Lord. Christ too was caught, as it were, by his horns among thorns when he hung upon the horns of the cross, fastened there by nails.

The fact that Isaac himself carried the wood for his sacrifice also represented Christ, who himself carried his cross to the place of his passion. Concerning this mystery it had been said long beforehand through the prophet: “The principality shall be upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6). Christ had principality upon his shoulders when he carried his cross with marvelous humility.

The cross of Christ fittingly signifies principality. For through it the devil is conquered and the whole world is recalled to the knowledge or grace of Christ [Note: [Col. 1750] Manuscripts: “renewed.”]. Finally, the Apostle said the same when speaking of the Lord’s passion: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9).

We say this, brothers, so that your Charity may recognize that the principality of Christ of which it is written, “The principality shall be upon his shoulder,” is none other than his cross. For this reason the reading itself is read at Easter, when the true Isaac—whose figure Abraham’s son carried—is fastened to the cross for the human race.

### 4. The Jews represented in Abraham’s servants

The reading itself says that blessed Abraham came with his son, saw the place from afar, and said to his servants: “Sit here with the donkey; I and the boy will go forward, and when we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

Why is it said to the servants, who represented the Jews, “Sit here with the donkey”? Could that donkey sit, dearly beloved? It is said, “Sit with the donkey,” because the Jewish people, who were not going to believe in Christ, could not stand.
