Rather, like a weak and languishing sinner, it was about to fall to the ground because it had despised the staff of the cross.

Blessed Abraham therefore said: “Sit here with the donkey; I and the boy will go forward, and when we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

What do you mean, blessed Abraham? You are going to sacrifice your son, and you say that you will return with your son? If you offer him as a burnt offering, surely he will not be able to return with you.

Blessed Abraham could reply: “I speak the truth. I am offering my son, and I shall return to you with my son. For my faith is so great that I believe that the one who deigned to give him to me from the womb of a barren mother can also raise him from the dead. Therefore I speak the truth when I say, ‘When we have worshiped, we shall return to you.’”

### 5. Adam buried at the place of Calvary

The ram was killed and Isaac was not killed because Isaac was a figure, not the reality. In him was signified what was later fulfilled in Christ.

See God contending with human beings in great compassion: Abraham offered his mortal son to God without allowing him to die, whereas God handed over his immortal Son to death for human beings.

The blessed Isaac and that ram may nevertheless also be understood in this way: in blessed Isaac the divinity of Christ was signified, and in the ram his humanity. Since in the passion it is believed that not the divinity but the humanity was crucified, it is not Isaac but the ram that is sacrificed.

The Son of God, the only-begotten, is offered, and the firstborn of the Virgin is sacrificed.

Hear another mystery. The presbyter blessed Jerome wrote that he had learned with complete certainty from the ancient and elder Jews that Isaac was offered in the very place where the Lord Christ was later crucified [Note: [Col. 1751] So in the manuscripts. In the printed editions, “sacrificed.”] [Note: [Col. 1751] This is found in the *Commentaries on Mark*, chapter 15, but they are incorrectly attributed to Jerome.].

Indeed, from the place from which blessed Abraham was ordered to depart, one reaches on the third day the place where Christ was crucified.

[This too is reported on the testimony of the ancients: Adam, the first man, was at some time buried in the very place where the cross was fixed. For this reason it is said to have been called the place of Calvary, because the head of the human race is said to have been buried there. And truly, brothers, it is not incongruous to believe that the physician was raised up where the sick man lay. It was fitting that where human pride had fallen, divine mercy should bow down; and that the precious blood, even in bodily form, should be believed to have redeemed the dust of the ancient sinner when it deigned to touch it by dripping upon it.]

[Note: [Col. 1751] The manuscripts do not contain the words enclosed in brackets.]

[Note: [Col. 1751] What is said about Adam’s burial at the place of Calvary is transmitted by Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 2; Origen, *On Matthew*, tractate 35; Basil, *On Leviticus*, chapter 5; Ambrose, *On Luke*, chapter 23; Chrysostom, *On John*, homily 84, and others. Jerome, however, rejects it in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 27.]

These things, dearly beloved brothers, we have gathered, insofar as we have been able, from various books of Scripture for the progress of our soul, and have offered them for the consideration of charity. You, for your part, with the Lord’s help, as you reread the divine Scriptures more frequently, may, if you attend carefully, be able to discover an even better exposition [Note: [Col. 1751] This sermon ends here in the manuscripts.]

### 6. The sacrament of baptism must not be sought negligently or too late

I ask you, brothers, that whoever wishes to have either his son or his servant baptized should not delay offering him to the Church now. It is not right that something believed to be so great and so splendid should be sought negligently or later than is appropriate.

For I fear that some women offer their infants later because they are reluctant to come with them to the Vigils. We firmly believe that those who, as soon as Lent begins, wish to offer those who are to be baptized and happily come with them to the Vigils will both have their children receive the sacrament of Baptism in due order and themselves obtain the forgiveness of sins, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

# SERMON VII

[Note: [Col. 1751] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 73.]

## On the Sacrifice of Isaac, II

[Note: [Col. 1751] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It is clearly not Augustine’s, but belongs to precisely the same author as the third sermon of the Appendix, which the Louvain scholars rejected long ago. In that sermon, shortly after the beginning, the divine command “Go out from your land” was explained as “A new kind of trial: to impose exile abroad upon one who possesses property.” Likewise, at the beginning of this sermon it says, “A new kind of command is to give a man a law of crime,” in order to interpret the divine command that should have preceded here, as it appears below: “Take your son and offer him to me.”]

### 1.

It is a new kind of command to give a man a law of crime and to regard him as religious if he wishes to perpetrate an impious deed. If Abraham commits parricide, he is righteous; if he does not, he is undevout.

What, then, does it mean that we never please God except through piety? He desires vows to be offered to him, not that he be worshiped cruelly. Behold: between the piety of the father and devotion to God, it is indeed a crime to kill one’s son, but it is more criminal still not to obey God.

Perfect righteousness has been placed in a narrow pass. You are commanded to commit parricide, to deprive yourself by your own hands. What is this? The one who forbids homicide commands parricide?

“You are commanded,” he says, “to sacrifice your son”—the comfort of your old age and the sole pledge of your posterity: the later-born, and therefore the sweeter; the solitary or only child, and therefore the dearer and more beloved.

In both parents, despair of producing offspring held sway: nature had deprived them of the proper time, age in the elderly father and barrenness in the aged mother. Sarah had already lost the function of her womb, and the power of begetting had exhausted the aged father, because the barren woman had no fruit.

Behold, suddenly the mother’s frozen womb grew warm—not through the impulse of lust, but through the fuel of virtue; the flower of youth returned. The limbs that had already mourned flourished; the withered members, pale with the decay of old age, blossomed with the blush of childhood; and the body already growing old in depleted warmth was invigorated, not as by intercourse, but by a promise.

His toga-covered head was already growing white with gray hairs, and the womb stretched its wrinkles within its belly. The pregnant uterus swelled; her steps trembled at the knee. She whose bent body could no longer support itself carried a burdened womb.

In her final years, a pregnant and weary woman who had not known how to conceive in youth learned how to nurse in old age. Married people, learn that the effect of seed is absent where the Creator’s gift is lacking, since he himself says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

### 2.

“Take,” he says, “your son and offer him to me upon one of the mountains that I shall show you” (Genesis 22:2).

The aged father and the mother of an only child, new parents and old progenitors, are not moved by so bitter a command. He who was neither afraid of the dreadfulness of the deed nor held back by a degenerate spirit from fulfilling what he had been ordered to do was girt with joy.

That future hope of so many nations is commanded to be killed by his father’s hand. The devout father undertook parricide with the same purpose with which he had accepted his son: it makes no difference whether he gives him up or loses him, so long as, by whatever means, he returns what he had received.

O most merciful Lord, you know that he is dear to his father—why do you command that he be sacrificed? Only recently you made an old barren man fruitful; so quickly have you demanded back what you gave? Where is what you granted to the aged?

Can you, when angry, harm him, just as in your favor you command bereavement? Far be such unbelief from us. God commanded that his own Son be killed for us, not that our sons be slaughtered.

He therefore commands the son to be killed so that what was already known to God might be made manifest to the world. For how can he desire the blood of the innocent who condemns the guilty on account of blood? He wished to demonstrate that devotion to all human beings by commanding that parricide be carried out.

He obeys the commands immediately; he submits to the orders; the executioner proceeds prepared. Indeed, the son departs with his father, destined to die—and would that he were only destined to die, and not also to perish by his father’s sword.

### 3.

They came to the place that God had named. Both together, as priests, build the altar; he places the wood upon the altar, binds his son, and, with sword extended, the angel cries out: “Do not strike the boy!” He looks with his eyes and sees the ram in the thicket.

See, brothers, Abraham strong in endurance and steadfast in devotion—not wrestling with some wild beast, but fighting against nature. Devotion said, “Strike”; piety cried, “Spare.” The one recalled him; the other urged him on.

The son lay there, about to die. Abraham raises his right hand to strike and searches out the place where he may willingly strike.

“Spare,” he says, “Abraham. The one who commanded you to strike now cries out that you should spare him. He knew that the father, proved and fervent in devotion, would restrain his sword and neither kill nor burn his son.

“Spare, devout father; parricide without guilt, spare him. Your sacrifice, which you had prepared, [the transmitted reading is obscure]; I have received what I commanded you to offer. I approved what you vowed, though I rejected it in deed; I accepted the vow and did not reject the sacrifice. I praise your faith, I do not condemn your piety, and I do not permit bereavement to be inflicted upon you.

“Everything is perfected, and everything remains unharmed. The innocent victim is overcome, lest the devotion of the one offering it think that he had presented something less if the victim, impatient under pain, had resisted.

“Behold, by spiritual foresight you have anticipated my purpose. For what I prepared for the whole world, you have already determined in your son. What I ordained in my only-begotten Son, you have accomplished in your only son. Therefore all nations shall be blessed in you.”

Amen.

# SERMON VIII

[Note: [Col. 1753] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 75.]

## On Abraham’s servant who was sent to Rebecca

[Note: [Col. 1753] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. The Louvain scholars, Verlinus, and Windingus considered it doubtful and spurious. We, however, think it belongs to Caesarius of Arles. It could not be found in our manuscripts.]

### 1. The oath by Abraham’s thigh

A little earlier, when the divine reading was being read, we heard that blessed Abraham called his servant and said to him: “Place your hand under my thigh, that I may adjure you by the God of heaven and earth not to take a wife for my son from the daughters of this region” (Genesis 24:2 and following). The servant obeyed, placed his hand under his thigh, and swore to him.

All these things, brothers, that are recited in the Old Testament, if we wish to receive them only according to the letter, will bring our souls little or no profit. For what benefit is it to us, who faithfully gather in church to hear the word of God, if we are told that Abraham sent his servant to bring a wife for his son from a distant region, when we frequently see such things happening in these regions as well?

But we, brothers, following the blessed Apostle Paul, should believe that all the things written happened to the Jews in figure, but were fulfilled for us in reality (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Abraham therefore said to his servant: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven and earth.” What does this mean, brothers?

Blessed Abraham said, “Put your hand under my thigh,” as though he were saying: “Put your hand upon the altar”; or: “Put your hand upon the Ark of the Testament”; or: “Extend your hand toward the temple of God, and swear to me.”

He touched the thigh and swore by the God of heaven and earth. Blessed Abraham was not mistaken when he ordered this to be done. Rather, because he was filled with the spirit of prophecy, he knew that Christ, the Lord of heaven and earth, would be born from his offspring.

Therefore, when his servant touched his thigh, he did not swear by a bodily member, but by the living and true God. For Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot Judah, from whose offspring Christ the Lord was born (Matthew 1:2–16).

## 2. Rebecca Meets Abraham’s Servant; with the Consent of Her Parents, Her Brother, and Herself, He Takes Her as a Wife for His Master Isaac

“And he stood beside the well and said in his heart: ‘Lord God of my master, if you have shown mercy to my master, behold, I am standing by the well, and let the girl who comes to draw water—if I say to her, “Give me a drink,” and she answers me, “You drink too, and I will draw water for your camels”—let her be the one whom you have prepared for my master Isaac.’”

The servant had not yet finished speaking these words in his heart when Rebecca appeared, with a jar on her shoulder. The servant said to her, “Give me a drink.” But she quickly lowered her jar and said, “You drink too, sir, and I will draw water for your camels.” When he asked whose daughter she was, she replied that she was the daughter of Bethuel and the sister of Laban. The man bowed and worshiped God, because he had recognized that they were the relatives of his master Abraham. He brought out earrings to adorn her face and placed bracelets on her hands.

Then she went and reported this to her parents. They came out, blessed God, and received Abraham’s servant with joy and honor. He spoke to them about Rebecca, asking that they give her to his master Isaac. But they said, “Let us call the girl and ask her wishes.” When she had been summoned, they said to her, “Do you want to go with this man?” She replied, “I will go.”

## 3. Abraham and His Servant as Figures; Rebecca Betrothed to Isaac as a Figure of the Church

Now, dearest brothers, let us see briefly, as far as we can, what these things signify. Blessed Abraham, when he sent his servant to take a wife for his son, represented God the Father; [Col. 1754] and when he offered him in the burnt offering, he likewise prefigured the image of God the Father. His servant, however, signified the prophetic word.

Abraham therefore sent his servant into a distant region to take a wife from there for his son, because God the Father had sent the prophetic word throughout the whole earth to seek the catholic Church as a bride for his Only-Begotten Son. And just as the bride is brought to blessed Isaac through Abraham’s servant, so through the prophetic word the Church of the Gentiles is invited from distant regions to Christ, the true Bridegroom.

But where is that bride, who was to be joined to Christ, found? Where else but at the water? It is true, dearest ones: unless the Church had come to the water of Baptism, she would not have been joined to Christ. Rebecca therefore found Abraham’s servant at the well, and the Church finds Christ at the sacrament of Baptism.

What happened after this? The servant brought out golden earrings and golden bracelets and gave them to Rebecca. The golden earrings signified the words of God; the golden bracelets signified holy works, since works are represented by the hands.

Let us see how Christ gave these things to the Church. The servant offered golden earrings to adorn Rebecca’s face, and Christ gave the Church divine words more precious than all pearls. He placed bracelets on Rebecca’s hands, and Christ placed holy works in the hands of the Church.

Consider this, dearest brothers, and rejoice and give thanks to God, because what was represented in those figures has been fulfilled in us through Christ’s gift. Just as Rebecca could have neither earrings nor bracelets on her hands unless Isaac had sent them through his servant, so the Church could have had neither divine words in her ears nor holy works in her hands unless Christ had bestowed these things upon her through his grace and through his Apostles.

When the girl was asked by her parents whether she wished to go with the servant and replied, “I will go,” we plainly see this fulfilled in the Church. There Rebecca’s will is asked; here the Church’s will is required. Rebecca is asked, “Do you want to go with this man?” and she answers, “I will go.” The Church is asked, “Do you believe in Christ?” and she answers, “I believe.” Rebecca would not have been led to Isaac unless she had said, “I will”; nor would the Church be joined to Christ unless she had said, “I believe.”

## 4. Isaac Coming into the Field as a Figure of Christ Who Was to Come into the World

The servant therefore took Rebecca and presented her to Isaac. Let us see, however, where he found him. He found him at the Well of the Oath. Observe, brothers: the servant found Rebecca at the well, and Rebecca in turn found Isaac at the well. It is true: neither Christ finds the Church nor the Church Christ except at the sacrament of Baptism.

As Scripture says, blessed Isaac had gone out toward evening into the field to meditate. That field represented the world. Isaac went out into the field because Christ was to come into the world: Isaac went out toward evening, while Christ came at the end of the world.

Isaac therefore went out into the field to meditate because Christ came into the world to fight against the devil and conquer him justly, while being unjustly killed by him; so that by dying he might destroy death and, by rising again, grant life to believers.

And just as Rebecca was joined to Isaac bodily, so the Church would be joined to Christ spiritually, receiving in the present the precious pledge—the blood of her Bridegroom—and later receiving the dowry of his kingdom. The blessed Apostle Peter clearly declares this, saying: “For,” he says, “you were not redeemed with gold or silver, but with precious blood, as of an unblemished lamb” (I Peter 1:18–19).

## 5. The Synagogue Prefigured by Sarah, the Church by Rebecca

Isaac therefore took Rebecca and brought her into the tent of his mother; Christ took the Church and established her in the place of the Synagogue. For the Synagogue, separated from God and dead through unbelief, was replaced by the Church, joined to Christ and given life through faith.

Isaac took Rebecca and loved her so greatly that he lessened the grief caused by his mother’s death. The death of Sarah signifies the unbelief of the Synagogue. Sarah dies, therefore, and Rebecca is brought in her [Col. 1755] place: the Synagogue is rejected so that the Church may be introduced.

Isaac took Rebecca and loved her so greatly that he lessened the sorrow caused by his mother’s death. Christ took the Church and loved her so greatly that he mitigated, through his love for the Church, the grief caused by the destruction of the mother, the Synagogue.

For just as the unbelief of the Synagogue brought sorrow to Christ, so the faith of the Church produced joy for him. And just as through the wickedness of the Synagogue he lost one nation of the Jews, though not even all of it, so through the faith of the Church Christ the Lord acquired the whole world.

And because Christ the Lord prepared for himself from among us, dearest brothers, a spiritual bride whom, as I have said, he also redeemed with precious blood, so, with his help, let each of us not only guard the benefits bestowed upon him by the divine gift but strive to increase them, so that nothing in him may appear defiled by lust, swollen with pride, consumed by anger, darkened by greed, or struck by the viperous poison of envy.

For it is just that the Bridegroom who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” should find nothing in us of the sins mentioned above that might offend the eyes of his majesty. To him belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON IX [Col. 1755]

*[Note: In other copies, among the Vignerian sermons, 12.]*

## On Holy Rebecca

*[Note: The epithet “holy” is always added to Rebecca’s name here and below in Augustinian manuscripts, but never in the books of Origen’s works.]*

*[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is attributed to Augustine in several manuscripts and had been published from them by Vigner, who found the same sermon cited under Augustine’s name by Bartholomew of Urbino in the* Milleloquium*. In Origen it is the tenth Homily on Genesis, though truncated in its latter part. The published and manuscript books of Origen’s works contain it in full; we have used them here to correct the more serious errors.]*

### 1. Those Who Rarely Attend Church or Neglect to Hear the Word of God Are Rebuked

“Isaac,” Scripture says, “was growing and becoming strong” (Genesis 21:8)—that is, Abraham’s joy was growing, because he looked not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen. Abraham was not rejoicing in present things, nor in the riches of the world and the activities of this age.

But do you wish to hear what made Abraham rejoice? Hear the Lord saying to the Jews: “Abraham your father,” he says, “desired to see my day; and he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56). Isaac was therefore growing through that by which Abraham’s vision—when he saw Christ’s day—and the hope that was in him multiplied his joys.

Would that you too might become Isaacs and be the joy of your mother, the Church. But I fear that the Church is still giving birth to children in sorrow and groaning. Is it not sorrow and groaning for her when you do not gather to hear the word of God, and scarcely come to church except on feast days—and even then not so much from a desire for the word of God as from a love of the celebration and, so to speak, under the pretext of a public relaxation?

What, then, shall I do, to whom the stewardship of the word has been entrusted? Although I am an unworthy servant, I have nevertheless received from God the task of distributing to his household its measure of wheat. But see what he adds: “Distributing,” he says, “the measure of wheat at the proper time.” What, then, shall I do? Where, or when, shall I find your proper time?

You spend most of it—or rather, almost all of it—in worldly occupations. One of you wastes it in the marketplace, another in business; one is occupied with fields, another with lawsuits. No one, or scarcely anyone, is free to hear the word of God.

But why do I blame you for your occupations? Why do I complain about those who are absent? Even those who are present and standing in the church are not attentive. Instead, you spend your time in ordinary and familiar chatter and turn your backs on the word of God and the divine readings.

I fear that what was spoken through the prophet may also be said to you by the Lord: “They turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jeremiah 32:33).

What, then, shall I do, to whom the ministry [Col. 1756] of the word has been entrusted? The things that are read are mystical and must be expounded through allegorical sacraments. Can I force the pearls of God’s word upon deaf and turned-away ears?

The Apostle did not act in this way. *[Note: In the Origenian books: “The Apostle does not speak thus.”]* See what he says: “You who read the Law,” he says, “have you not heard the Law? For Abraham had two sons,” and so forth; and he adds, “These things are allegorical” (Galatians 4:21–24).

Did he disclose the mysteries of the Law to those who neither read nor understand? Rather, he said to those who read the Law, “Have you not heard the Law?” How, then, can I open and reveal the mysteries and allegories of the Law, which I have learned from the Apostle, to those for whom both hearing and reading the Law are unknown?

### 2. Exhortation to Pray

Perhaps I seem too harsh to you; but I cannot plaster a wall that is collapsing. For I fear what is written: “My people, those who call you blessed, deceive you and confuse the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12).

I admonish you as my dearest children. I wonder whether the way of Christ is not yet known to you, whether you have not even heard that it is not a broad and spacious way but a narrow and constricted way that leads to life (Matthew 7:14).

You, therefore, enter through the narrow gate; leave breadth to those who are perishing. “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near,” says the Apostle. “Walk as children of light” (Romans 13:12; Ephesians 5:8). “The time is short. It remains that those who have should be as though they had not, and those who use the world as though they did not use it” (I Corinthians 7:29, 31).

The Apostle commands that we pray without interruption (I Thessalonians 5:17). You who do not gather for prayers—how do you fulfill without interruption what you always omit?

Christ also commanded: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). If those who watched and prayed, and always clung to the word of God, nevertheless did not escape temptation, what will happen to those who come to church only on feast days? “If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (I Peter 4:18).

### 3. Spiritual Betrothal

I am reluctant to say anything about the matters that have been read. For the Apostle says of such discourses that they are difficult to explain, “because,” he says, “you have become dull of hearing” (Hebrews 5:11).

Let us nevertheless examine what has been read to us. “Rebecca,” Scripture says, “was coming with the daughters of the city to draw water from the well” (Genesis 24:15–16).

Rebecca came to the wells every day and drew water every day. And because she attended the wells every day, she was able to be found by Abraham’s servant and joined in marriage to Isaac.

Do you think that these are mere stories, and that the Holy Spirit is narrating histories in Scripture? This is instruction for souls and spiritual teaching. It teaches you to come daily to the wells of Scripture, to the waters of the Holy Spirit, always to draw water, and to carry home a full vessel—just as holy Rebecca did.

She could not otherwise have been joined to the great patriarch Isaac, who was born according to the promise, except by drawing water—and drawing so much that she could not only give drink to those in the house but also to Abraham’s servant; and not only to the servant, but could draw such an abundance of water from the wells that she was able to water the camels as well, “until,” it says, “they ceased drinking” (ibid., 19).

Everything that has been written contains mysteries. Christ also wishes to betroth you to himself. He speaks to you through the prophet, saying: “I will betroth you to myself forever; I will betroth you to myself in faith and mercy, so that you may know the Lord” (Hosea 2:19–20).

Because he wishes to betroth you to himself, he first sends you this servant. This servant is the prophetic word. Unless you first receive him, you cannot marry Christ.

Know, however, that no untrained or inexperienced person receives the prophetic word, but only one who knows how to draw water from the depth of the well—and knows how to draw so much that it is sufficient even for those who appear irrational and perverse, represented by the camels—[Col. 1757] so that he too may say, “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14).

Finally, this servant had said in his heart: “Whichever of these virgins,” he said, “who have come to the water says to me, ‘Drink yourself, and I will water your camels,’ she shall be the bride of my master” (Genesis 24:14).

Thus Rebecca—whose name is interpreted as “Patience”—when she saw the servant and looked upon the prophetic word, lowered the jar from her shoulder. For she put down the arrogance of lofty Greek eloquence; bending toward the humble and simple prophetic word, she said, “Drink yourself, and I will water the camels.”

### 4. The Word of God Both Nourishes and Is Nourished

But perhaps you say: If the servant represents the prophetic word, how can he be given drink by Rebecca, when he himself ought rather to give her drink?

Consider, then, whether it may be that just as the Lord Jesus himself is the bread of life (John 6:35) and feeds hungry souls, yet again confesses that he is hungry when he says, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:35); and just as he himself is living water and gives drink to all who thirst, yet again says to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink” (John 4:7)—so the prophetic word, although it gives drink to those who thirst, is nevertheless said to receive drink from them when it accepts the diligence and vigilance of earnest students.

Such, then, is the soul that does everything patiently, that is ready and supported by such great learning, that is accustomed to draw streams of knowledge from the depths. It is this soul that can be joined in marriage to Christ.

Unless you come daily to the wells, unless you draw water daily, you will not only be unable to give drink to others; you yourself will suffer thirst for the word of God.

Hear also the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 7:37). But you, as I see, neither hunger nor thirst for righteousness. How, then, will you be able to say: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before his presence?” (Psalm 41:2–3).

### 5. Every Day Is the Lord’s Day for Christians

I beseech you who are always present in the audience for the word: listen patiently while we admonish those who are somewhat negligent and sluggish. Have patience, because our sermon concerns Rebecca—that is, patience. It is necessary for us to correct for a little while, with patience, those who neglect the assembly and avoid hearing the word of God: those who do not desire the bread of life or the living water; who do not leave the camp or go out from their clay houses to gather manna for themselves; who do not come to the rock to drink from the spiritual rock. “The rock was Christ,” as the Apostle says (I Corinthians 10:4).

Have, I say, a little patience. Our discourse is addressed to the negligent and the sick, for “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”

Tell me, you who gather for church only on feast days: Are the remaining days not feast days, or are they not the Lord’s days?

It belongs to the Jews to observe certain rare and appointed days as solemn. Therefore the Lord says to them: “I cannot endure your new moons and Sabbaths and great day; your fasting, holidays, and feast days my soul hates” (Isaiah 1:13–14).

God therefore hates those who think that only one day is the Lord’s feast day.

Christians eat the flesh of the Lamb every day; that is, every day they receive the flesh of the Word of God. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Corinthians 5:7).

And because the law of Passover is such that it is eaten in the evening, the Lord suffered in the evening of the world so that you might always eat of the flesh of the Word of God *[Note: At this point, the word “God” is absent from the books of Origen’s works.]* while you remain in the evening, until morning comes.

And if in this evening you are watchful and lead your life in weeping and fasting, or in every labor of righteousness, you too will be able to say: “In the evening weeping will lodge, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:6).

For you will rejoice in the morning—that is, in the age to come—if in this age you have gathered the fruit of righteousness through weeping and labor.

Come, therefore, while there is time. Let us drink from the well of vision, where Isaac walks about and where he goes forth for exercise.

# SERMON X [Col. 1758]

*[Note: In other copies, “On Time,” 78.]*

## On Rebecca’s Conception, Genesis 25

*[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars, Verlinus, and Vindingus considered it doubtful or spurious. Although it is attributed to Augustine in manuscripts, we place it as the fourth sermon of Caesarius. It was delivered during Lent. On section 5, see Caesarius, Homily 2.]*

[Col. 1758]

### 1. The Learned Should Adapt Themselves to the Ignorance of the Simple

If we wish to communicate the exposition of the holy Scriptures to the ears of your Charity in the order and style in which the holy Fathers expounded them, the food of doctrine will reach only a few learned people, while the rest of the multitude will remain hungry.

Therefore I humbly ask that learned ears be willing to bear rustic words calmly, provided that the whole flock of the Lord may receive spiritual nourishment in simple and, so to speak, pedestrian language.

And because the unlearned and simple cannot ascend to the heights of the learned, let the learned deign to bend down to their ignorance. What is said to the simple can be understood by the learned; but what is preached to the learned will not be grasped by the simple.

### 2. Isaac as a Figure of Christ, Rebecca as a Figure of the Church; Jacob and Esau in Rebecca’s Womb as the Good and Wicked in the Womb of the Church

A reading was recited to us concerning blessed Isaac, holy Rebecca, and the little ones who struggled in her womb.

*[Note: Manuscript reading: “On the third day, a reading was recited to us …”]*

That blessed Isaac was a type of the Lord and Savior is known to nearly everyone. Isaac therefore represented Christ the Lord, while blessed Rebecca represented the Church.

Although she remained barren for a long time, as an example of the Church herself, she conceived when blessed Isaac prayed and the Lord granted it. But the children struggled in her womb, and unable to bear their distress, she said: “If this was going to happen to me, why was it necessary to conceive?” And the Lord said to her: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be divided from your belly; one people will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger.”

All these things, dearest brothers, as the Apostle says, happened to them in figure; but they were written for our sake (I Corinthians 10:11).

Rebecca therefore conceived bodily from blessed Isaac because the Church was to conceive spiritually from Christ. But just as the two children struggled in Rebecca’s womb, so in the womb of the Church two peoples continually oppose one another.

For if there were only wicked people or only good people, there would be one people. But because both good and wicked are found in the Church, two peoples struggle as in the womb of spiritual Rebecca: the humble and the proud, the chaste and the adulterous, the gentle and the angry, the kind and the envious, the merciful and the greedy.

The good wish to win the wicked; the wicked seek to extinguish the good. The desire of the good is that those who are wicked be corrected; the aim of the wicked is that those who are good be destroyed.

There is one class of the godly and another of the ungodly. The class of the godly is raised to heaven through humility; the class of the ungodly is plunged into hell through arrogance.

All who in the catholic Church think in earthly terms, love the earth, desire the earth, and place all their hope in the earth belong to Esau. Whoever wishes to serve God in order to increase in honors and receive earthly profits is likewise recognized as belonging to Esau—that is, to earthly happiness.

In Esau the carnal are understood; in Jacob, the spiritual. These are the two peoples, as the blessed Apostle clearly distinguishes when he points out the carnal and indicates the spiritual.

For he says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, debauchery, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, angers, disputes, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and the like.” These are works belonging to Esau.

But what are the fruits belonging to Jacob? The same [Col. 1759] Apostle adds below, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” *[Note: A later manuscript adds three virtues: patience, gentleness, and chastity.]* “long-suffering, faith, goodness, kindness, modesty, self-control” (Galatians 5:19–21).

These are spiritual works belonging to blessed Jacob, that is, to the people of the godly.

### 3. The Greater People Are the Jews; the Lesser, the Gentiles

The statement, “One people will overcome another, and the elder will serve the younger,” is not seen to have been fulfilled literally in Esau or Jacob. Scripture does not report that Esau served blessed Jacob bodily.

How, then, should this be understood, or in what way does the greater people serve the lesser? We must understand it spiritually. Unless this had happened, holy Scripture would not have recorded it.

Whoever carefully observes how the greater people serve the lesser recognizes it among Christians and Jews. The greater and older people, the Jews, are shown to serve the younger—that is, the Christian people—by carrying throughout the world the books of the divine Law for the instruction of all nations.

The Jews were scattered throughout the whole earth for this reason: when we wish to invite a pagan to faith in Christ and testify from all the Prophets that Christ was the one announced, he may resist and say that the books of the divine Law were written by us rather than by the Holy Spirit.

Then we have a sound basis on which to refute him, saying: “If you have doubts about my books, here are the books of the Jews, who are certainly our enemies—books which, as is certain, I could neither write nor alter. Read them again. When you find in them what you find in mine, do not be unbelieving, but faithful.”

In this way the greater people are recognized as serving the lesser, since through their books the people of the Gentiles are invited to believe in Christ.

### 4. The Greater People Are the Wicked; the Lesser, the Good

The greater people also serve the lesser in another way. “In what way?” you ask. In the way the wicked serve the good—not by obeying them, but by persecuting them.

How do the wicked serve the good? As persecutors serve martyrs; as files or hammers serve gold; as millstones serve wheat; as ovens serve bread that is to be baked, so that the bread is cooked and the ovens are consumed.

How, I ask, do the wicked serve the good? As straw in a goldsmith’s furnace serves the gold, where unquestionably the straw is consumed and the gold is tested.

Therefore let the wicked not boast or exalt themselves when they inflict tribulations upon the good. For when they persecute them in body, they are shown to be killing themselves in heart. Before the adversity of the wicked reaches the good man, wickedness has already corrupted the soul of the wicked person.

Thus the person who, inflamed with the fury of anger and an evil disposition, tries to set a good man on fire: whether that good man can be burned is still uncertain; but that the wicked person is already burning is beyond doubt.

For perhaps the good man, filled with spiritual sap and the refreshment of the Holy Spirit, does not burn when the fire of persecution is applied. But the one who tries to burn him unquestionably cannot help burning himself.

*[Note: So the printed editions. But the manuscripts read: “can undoubtedly burn.”]*

From the one seed of Isaac, Esau and Jacob are born, just as from the one Baptism of the Lord and Savior and from the one womb of the Church the Christian people are brought forth. Yet, according to the diversity of their conduct, they are divided into two parts, as Esau and Jacob were: one part is recognized as carnal from the fruits of its works, the other as spiritual.

He said, “The elder will serve the younger,” because the number of the wicked is always greater than that of the good.

And just as those two children struggled in Rebecca’s womb, so these two peoples struggle in the womb of the Church until the day of judgment: as we have already said, the proud oppose the humble; adulterers persecute the chaste; drunkards, whose number is limitless, harass the sober; the envious rival the kind; robbers seek to destroy those who give alms; the angry seek to extinguish the peaceful; and the lustful try to drag back [Col. 1760] to earth those who think on heavenly things.

### 5. Virtues to Be Cultivated During Lent

Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, that whoever recognizes himself as entangled in these evils should, while there is time, strive with God’s help to be transferred to the right hand. Let them abandon the filth of vices and hasten to return to the adornment of virtues, so that on the day of judgment, freed from the hearing of evil, they may deserve to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

I ask and admonish you most earnestly, brothers, to strive to rise earlier for the Vigils and to come faithfully to Terce, Sext, and None.

*[Note: Concerning Caesarius, his* Life, *book 1, section 10, says: “He established that every day the clergy should sing the office of Terce, Sext, and None with hymns in the basilica of Saint Stephen, so that if any secular person or penitent wished to perform the holy work, he could attend the daily service without any excuse.” The office of Prime is omitted; Caesarius ordered it to be celebrated only on Sunday, Saturday, and solemn feast days, as is clear from the Appendix that he added to the first rule for nuns.]*

Above all, preserve chastity throughout Lent and until the end of Easter, even with your own wives. Give to the poor what you would have spent on your meal. Keep peace yourselves, and bring those whom you know to be in conflict back to harmony.

Receive strangers, and do not be ashamed to wash their feet. Let a Christian not be ashamed to do what Christ deigned to fulfill.

Give alms to the poor willingly and according to your means, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Corinthians 9:7).

If you cannot completely cut away the distractions of the world, at least moderate them in some measure, so that you may devote yourselves to reading or prayer.

*[Note: Manuscripts do not have “or prayer.”]*

Then, storing more abundantly in the holy receptacle of your breast the spiritual wine—that is, the word of God—and rejecting every crime and sin, you may serve God with a free and sincere conscience.

And when the holy solemnity of Easter arrives, may you preserve charity faithfully not only toward the good but also toward the wicked; and with the joy of exultation, pure in heart and chaste in body, may you approach the altar of the Lord, so that each of you may be worthy to receive his body and blood, not to the judgment of his soul.

Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

*[Note: In the manuscripts, the conclusion of the sermon reads: “Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with the Father,” and so forth.]*

# SERMON XI [Col. 1760]

*[Note: In other copies, “On Time,” 79.]*

## On Blessed Jacob I

*[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was considered doubtful by the Louvain scholars and spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. We count it among those that we consider the fifth sermon of Caesarius. It was delivered during Lent. On section 3, see the exposition of Psalm 30, section 3, and section 4 of Sermon 8 in this Appendix; on section 5, see the exposition of Psalm 44, section 20, and of Psalm 119, section 2.]*

### 1. The Mysteries of Christ Are Prefigured in Jacob

When the divine reading was being read, dearest brothers, we heard that, at the entreaty of holy Rebecca, Isaac called his son Jacob and told him to go to Mesopotamia of Syria and take a wife for himself there.

We heard that Jacob, humbly obeying his father, departed; that on the journey he came to a certain place, placed a stone under his head, and fell asleep; that in a dream he saw a ladder reaching to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it; and that the Lord was leaning upon the ladder and said to him: “Jacob, Jacob, do not be afraid. I am with you, and I will be your companion on your journey” (Genesis 28:1–5, 10–15).

Blessed [Col. 1761] Isaac, dearest brothers, when he sent his son to Mesopotamia, prefigured the type of God the Father; Jacob, however, designated Christ the Lord.

Blessed Isaac therefore, disregarding the women of the region in which he lived, sent his son to take a wife for himself in a distant region, because God the Father was to send his Only-Begotten Son, who, rejecting the Synagogue, would join to himself a Church from the Gentiles.

This was fulfilled in truth when the Apostles said to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

### 2. Jacob Carries a Staff; Christ the Wood of the Cross

We do not read that blessed Jacob went with horses, asses, or camels. We read only that he carried a staff in his hand. For when he entreated the Lord, he said: “Lord,” he said, “I am less than all your mercies. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Genesis 32:10).

Jacob therefore presented a staff when he went to take a wife; Christ carried the wood of the cross when he came to redeem the Church.

Jacob, while sleeping, placed a stone under his head and saw a ladder reaching to heaven, with the Lord leaning upon the ladder.

Observe, brothers, how many mysteries there are in this passage. Jacob bore the type of the Lord and Savior, and the stone that he placed under his head likewise represented Christ the Lord.

Why does the stone signify Christ as the head? Hear the Apostle: “The head of the man is Christ” (I Corinthians 11:3).

Finally, blessed Jacob anointed that very stone. Observe the anointed one, and you will understand Christ. “Christ” is interpreted from anointing—that is, from chrism.

### 3. What the Ladder Seen by Jacob Signifies

But if Jacob, sleeping on earth, represented the Lord, what does it mean that the Lord was leaning upon the ladder in heaven? How could Christ the Lord be seen both at the top of the ladder in heaven and in blessed Jacob on earth?

That Christ is both in heaven and on earth, hear Christ himself saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

Understand that the Lord himself said that he is both in heaven and on earth.

Dearest brothers, we confess Christ the Lord to be the head of the Church. If he is the head of the Church, then as head he is in heaven, and as body he is on earth.

Finally, when blessed Paul the Apostle was persecuting the Church, Christ cried out from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my servants?” Nor did he say, “Why are you persecuting my members?” Rather, he said, “Why are you persecuting me?”

It is as though a foot had been trampled and the tongue cried out, “You have trampled me,” although the tongue itself could not be trampled. Through the harmony of charity, the head cries out on behalf of all the members.

Jacob was therefore sleeping and saw the Lord leaning at the top of the ladder. What does it mean to lean upon the ladder except to hang upon the wood?

Consider, brothers, who prayed for the Jews while hanging upon the wood of the cross, and you will recognize who, leaning upon the ladder, cried out from heaven to Jacob.

But why did this happen on the journey, before Jacob took a wife? Because the true Jacob, our Lord, first suffered death upon the ladder—that is, upon the cross—and afterward joined the Church to himself, giving her in the present the pledge of his blood and later giving her the dowry of his kingdom.

### 4. The Lord Leaning upon the Ladder Prefigured Christ

But that both Jacob while sleeping and the Lord leaning upon the ladder prefigured Christ—pay attention and behold the greatness of this matter. For when our Savior, speaking about Nathanael, had called blessed Jacob, saying, “Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit,” he went on to say: “Hereafter you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man” (John 1:47, 51). What Jacob had seen figuratively in a dream, the Lord was proclaiming about himself in the Gospels. “You shall see,” he says, “heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man.” If the angels descended to the Son because he was on earth, how did these same angels ascend to the Son of Man, unless he was also in heaven? Thus, in Jacob, he himself was sleeping, and from heaven he himself was calling out to Jacob.

### 5. Preachers as Angels Ascending and Descending

All these [Col. 1762] things, brothers, as the Apostle cries out, were happening to them in figure; but they were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come (1 Corinthians 10:11). Yet how, brothers, do the angels of God ascend into heaven to the Son of Man and descend to that same Son on earth? Pay close attention.

When the preachers of God announce from the holy Scriptures lofty and profound matters that can be understood only by the perfect, they ascend to the Son of Man. But when they preach what concerns the correction of conduct, and what the whole people can understand, they descend to the Son of Man.

Thus the Apostle also says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this age, but a hidden and secret wisdom, which God predestined before the ages for our glory” (1 Corinthians 2:6–7). When the Apostle said these things, without doubt he was ascending to the Son of Man.

But when he said, “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18); when he said, “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18); when he declared, “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Timothy 6:10)—in these words, like an angel of God, he was descending to the Son of Man.

When he said, “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth” (Colossians 3:2), he was ascending. But when he said, “Be sober, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34), and preached the other things pertaining to the correction of conduct, supplying the milk of instruction like a nurse to little children, he was descending, because he was speaking of matters that even the uneducated could grasp.

In this order one both ascends and descends to the Son of Man: solid food is given to the mature (Hebrews 5:14), and the milk of instruction is not denied even to the inexperienced.

Blessed John also ascended when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He ascended very high when he said these things. But because the angels of God not only ascend but also descend, bending down to little ones, he said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

### 6. Recapitulation of the Foregoing

So that these matters which we have set before you above may cling more firmly to your holy hearts, we shall briefly repeat what has been said.

Blessed Isaac, as we have said, when he sent away his son, bore the figure of God the Father. Jacob, who was sent away, signified Christ the Lord. The stone which he had beneath his head and anointed with oil also signified the Lord Savior. The ladder reaching up to heaven bore the figure of the cross. The Lord leaning upon the ladder reveals Christ crucified.

The angels ascending and descending upon it are understood as the Apostles, apostolic men, and all the teachers of the churches: ascending when they preach perfect things to the perfect; descending when they convey to little ones and the inexperienced simple matters that they can understand.

But we, brothers, who see that all the things prefigured in the Old Testament have been completed in the New Testament—let us give God as much thanks as we can, for he has deigned to bestow such great gifts upon us without any preceding merits of ours. Let us labor with all our strength, with his help, so that these great and such remarkable benefits may bring us not judgment but progress.

Indeed, let us strive to live spiritually and to devote ourselves always to good works, so that when the day of judgment finds us chaste, sober, merciful, and devout, we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may deserve, with the just and those who fear God, to attain eternal blessedness; through the favor of our Lord, and so forth.

## SERMON XII

[Note: [Col. 1762] Elsewhere, On Time 80.]

### On Blessed Jacob, II

[Note: [Col. 1762] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful; Verlin and Winding regarded it as spurious. We, however, count it as the sixth sermon of Caesarius.]

### 1. Jacob as a Figure of the Savior. The Patriarchs’ Marriages at Wells

Very often, dearly beloved brothers, we have suggested to Your Charity that blessed Jacob bore the type and figure of the Lord Savior. Indeed, just as Christ was to come into the world to be joined to the Church, so this was prefigured in blessed Jacob [Col. 1763] when he journeyed into a distant region to obtain a marriage.

Thus, as you have heard, blessed Jacob went to Mesopotamia to take a wife. When he had arrived at a certain well, he saw Rachel coming with her father’s sheep; and when he recognized that she was his cousin, he watered the flock and kissed her (Genesis 28:6; 29:2–11).

If you listened carefully, brothers, you can recognize that it was not without reason that the holy Patriarchs found their marriages at wells or springs. If this had happened only once, someone might say that it had not occurred for any symbolic reason but rather by chance. But when both blessed Rebecca, who was to be joined to Isaac, is found at a well (Genesis 24:45), and Rachel, whom Jacob was to take, is recognized at a well (Genesis 29:9), and likewise Sephora, who was joined to Moses, is found at a well (Exodus 2:16), without doubt we ought to recognize certain mysteries in these events.

Because all three of these Patriarchs bore beforehand the type of the Lord Savior, they therefore find their marriages at springs or wells: Christ was to find the Church at the water of Baptism.

Indeed, when Jacob came to the well, he first watered Rachel’s flock and afterward kissed her. It is true, dearly beloved brothers: unless the Christian people are first cleansed from every evil through the water of Baptism, they do not deserve to possess the peace of Christ.

Could blessed Jacob, when he saw his cousin, not have kissed her before giving water to the flocks? Certainly he could have, but a mystery was being enacted. For it was necessary that through the grace of Baptism the Church be freed from every iniquity and discord, and thus deserve to have peace with God.

### 2. Leah and Rachel as Synagogue and Church

That Jacob received two wives during that journey signified the two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles. For at the coming of Christ, a considerable number even from the Jewish people is read to have believed in him. Thus it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles that three thousand believed on one day, another five thousand on another day, and afterward many thousands (Acts 2:41, 44).

That two peoples would believe in Christ the Lord himself also confirms in the Gospel, where he says: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; these also I must bring, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:11).

Those two women, therefore—Leah and Rachel, who had been joined to blessed Jacob—prefigured these two peoples: Leah the Jews, and Rachel the Gentiles.

To these two peoples, like two walls, Christ was joined as the cornerstone. In him they kissed one another, and in him they deserved to find eternal peace, as the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

How did he make both one? Certainly by joining the two flocks and binding the two walls together with one another.

### 3. Jacob Returning Rich as a Figure of Christ

Finally, observe what he obtained afterward. Scripture says that after these events blessed Jacob became rich (Genesis 30:43).

For just as holy Jacob grew, became wealthy, and returned to his homeland with an immeasurable substance, so also the true Jacob, our Lord Jesus Christ, came into this world, joined these two peoples to himself—the Gentiles and the Jews—and spiritually begot and created innumerable children from them, and became exceedingly rich.

Indeed, hear him himself saying: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). For after stripping the devil, he returned to the Father carrying great riches with him, in accordance with what the Psalmist had foretold about him long before: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Psalm 67:19).

### 4. Laban as a Figure of the Devil

When Jacob was returning to his homeland, Laban pursued him with his companions and searched all his property, but found nothing belonging to himself among his possessions. Since he found nothing of his own, he could not hold him at all (Genesis 31:23–35).

It is not unfitting to say that Laban here bore the figure of the devil. He served idols and was an adversary of blessed Jacob, who bore beforehand the type of the Lord. [Col. 1764]

Laban therefore pursued Jacob but found nothing belonging to himself with him. Hear the true Jacob also saying this in the Gospel: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John 14:30).

May divine mercy grant that our adversary also recognize nothing of his works in us. For if he finds nothing of his own, he will not be able to hold us or turn us back from eternal life.

And therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us carefully inspect the little chests of our conscience and search the hiding places of our heart. If we find nothing there that belongs to the devil, let us rejoice and give thanks to God. As far as we can, with his help, let us strive always to open the doors of our hearts to Christ and keep them closed to the devil until the end.

But if we recognize that something of the devil’s works or cunning is lurking in our souls, let us hasten to vomit or spit it out like deadly poison. Then, when he wishes to lie in wait for us and can find nothing belonging to him, he will depart in confusion, and we, giving thanks with the Prophet, shall cry out to the Lord: “You have delivered us from those who afflict us, and you have put to shame those who hate us” (Psalm 43:8).

Thus Leah, as we said above, signifies that people from among the Jews who was joined to Christ; Rachel, however, bore the type of the Church, that is, of all the nations.

Therefore Leah did not steal her father’s idols, but Rachel did (Genesis 31:19). For after the coming of Christ, the Synagogue is not known to have served idols everywhere, whereas this is most clearly established concerning the Church of the Gentiles. Consequently, we read that Laban’s idols lay hidden not with Leah, that is, the Synagogue, but with Rachel, who bore the type of the Gentiles.

### 5. Jacob’s Wrestling Signifies the Jews’ Persecution of Christ

When Jacob came to the Jordan, and after sending all his possessions across remained alone, and wrestled with a man until dawn, Jacob in that struggle prefigured the Jewish people; the angel who wrestled with him bore the type of the Lord Savior.

Jacob wrestled with the angel because the Jewish people would wrestle with Christ. Jacob overcame the angel because the Jewish people would persecute Christ even to death.

And because not the whole Jewish people was unbelieving toward Christ, as we have already said above, but a considerable multitude is recorded to have believed in his name, the angel touched Jacob’s thigh, and he began to limp.

That foot with which he limped represented the Jews who did not believe in Christ; the one that remained sound bore the type of those who received the Lord Christ.

Pay close attention, finally, because in that struggle Jacob both prevailed and asked for a blessing. When the angel had said, “Release me,” Jacob replied, “I will not release you unless you bless me.”

In the fact that Jacob prevailed, he signified the Jews who would persecute Christ; in the fact that he asked for a blessing, he prefigured that people which would believe in Christ the Lord.

What did the angel say to him? “If you were strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?” (Genesis 32:23–28). This was fulfilled when the Jewish people crucified Christ the Lord.

“Release me,” says the angel; “dawn has already risen.” This already prefigured the Lord’s resurrection, because, as you know very well, the Lord is read to have risen from the dead before daylight.

### 6. Jacob Carrying a Staff as an Image of Christ Bearing the Cross

We also recognize that Jacob prefigured the Lord from this: when he prayed to God to rescue him from the hand of his brother Esau, he said, “Lord, I am less than all your mercies; with my staff I crossed the Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Genesis 32:10).

It is true, dearly beloved brothers: by the staff of the cross Christ seized the world, and with two companies—that is, with two peoples—he returned to the Father in triumph.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, think on these things more frequently. Like clean animals spiritually chewing the cud, set before your souls the useful and necessary food—the food of which [Col. 1765] the Lord says: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life” (John 6:27).

May the Lord, in his mercy, lead you to that life; to him belong honor and dominion with the Father, and so forth.

## SERMON XIII

[Note: [Col. 1765] Elsewhere, On Time 81.]

### On Blessed Joseph, I

[Note: [Col. 1765] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors left it among the sermons of Augustine, but without Augustine’s name, as doubtful; Verlin and Winding counted it among the spurious works. It seems to us, however, that it should be numbered among the sermons of Caesarius, who here reproduced from Ambrose’s book On Joseph, chapters 2 and 3, generally the very same ideas and sometimes the very same words.]

### 1. Jacob Bore the Figure of God the Father, Joseph the Figure of Christ. Joseph’s Brothers Signify the Jews and Sinners

Whenever readings from the Old Testament are recited to you, dearly beloved brothers, as I have often admonished you, you ought not to attend only to what sounds in the words, but also to what is understood and perceived in the spirit.

Thus the Apostle also admonishes us, saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). For all these things that are read in the Old Testament, as the Apostle says, “were happening to them in figure, but were written for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

When the Christian people faithfully come to church, what benefit is it to hear how the holy Patriarchs took wives or begot children, unless they perceive with spiritual understanding why these things happened, or what the events themselves prefigured?

Behold, we have heard that blessed Jacob begot a son and called his name Joseph, and loved him more than all his other sons (Genesis 30:24; 37:3). In this passage blessed Jacob bore the figure of God the Father, and holy Joseph bore the type of the Lord Savior.

Jacob loved his son because God the Father also loves his Only-Begotten, as he himself said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

Jacob sent his son to inquire after his brothers; and God the Father sent his Only-Begotten to visit the human race, sick with sins.

While Joseph was seeking his brothers, he wandered in the wilderness; and Christ was seeking the human race, which was wandering in the world—and in that world he too seemed to wander, because he was seeking those who had gone astray.

Joseph was seeking his brothers at Shechem. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder.” Sinners always turn their back rather than their face toward the face of the righteous. For numbers are counted backward.

Just as Joseph’s brothers, struck by envy, offered their back rather than their face to brotherly love, so also the wretched Jews, when the author of salvation came to them, preferred to envy rather than to love him.

Of such people it is said in the Psalm: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and always bow down their back” (Psalm 68:24).

### 2. The Translations Do Not Agree about the Price for Which Joseph Was Sold

Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothaim. Dothaim is interpreted as “Defection.” Truly they were in a great defection, since they were contemplating fratricide.

When Joseph’s brothers saw him, they plotted his death, just as, when the Jews saw the true Joseph, the Lord Christ, they all decided with one accord to crucify him.

Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his multicolored and long robe; and the Jews, through the death of the cross, stripped Christ of his bodily garment.

Joseph, stripped of his robe, was thrown into a cistern, that is, into a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell.

After Joseph was lifted from the cistern, he was sold to the Ishmaelites, that is, to the Gentiles; and after Christ returned from hell, he was purchased by all the nations in the commerce of faith.

Joseph was sold through the counsel of Judah for thirty pieces of silver; and Christ was sold through the counsel of Judas Iscariot for the same number.

The fact that Joseph is reported in different translations to have been sold for unequal prices—some saying twenty pieces of silver, others thirty—signified spiritually that Christ would not be [Col. 1766] believed in or loved equally by all. Indeed, even now in the Church some love him more and others less. Christ is worth more to the one who loves him with greater charity.

Joseph descended into Egypt; Christ into the world. Joseph saved Egypt from a shortage of grain; Christ frees the world from hunger for the word of God.

For unless Joseph’s brothers had sold him, Egypt would have perished. Brothers, it is true: unless the Jews had crucified Christ, the world would have perished.

### 3. Through the Poison of Envy, Death Entered the World

Yet let us see, dearly beloved brothers, why Joseph’s brothers raged against him so cruelly. Why, unless because of the poison of envy, through which death entered the world?

Hear Scripture saying: “His brothers envied him, and they could not speak anything peaceful to him.”

Blessed Joseph had a dream: he seemed to be standing in a field with his brothers, binding sheaves, and his brothers’ sheaves were worshiping his sheaf (Genesis 37:4, 7).

This was fulfilled in that Joseph when his brothers worshiped him in Egypt. Nor is it unfitting that barren sheaves were compelled to worship the fruitful sheaf through which they were to be delivered from the danger of famine.

### 4. Joseph’s Dream Was Fulfilled Only in Christ

He also saw another dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were worshiping him. His father answered him: “Shall I and your mother and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” (Genesis 37:9–10).

This could not be fulfilled in that Joseph; but in our Joseph, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, the mysteries of that dream were completed.

The sun, moon, and eleven stars worshiped him when, after the resurrection, holy Mary, like the moon, and blessed Joseph, like the sun, together with the eleven stars—that is, the blessed Apostles—bowed and prostrated themselves before him. And the prophecy was fulfilled that had said: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light” (Psalm 148:3).

For the interpretation of this dream was so far from being fulfilled in that Joseph that his mother is read to have died many years before he saw those dreams.

And indeed, how could it apply to his brothers that they might worship him like stars, when the darkness of envy had made them obscure and gloomy? They had already lost the brightness of the stars, since they had extinguished the light of charity within themselves.

Therefore we rightly believe that this was fulfilled more truly in the Lord our Savior. As I have already said, we frequently read that blessed Joseph and blessed Mary, together with the eleven Apostles, worshiped him (Matthew 28:17).

And that the Apostles possessed the light of stars, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). And again concerning them and those like them: “Then,” he says, “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

[Note: [Col. 1766] “Like the sun,” that is, “like one of the parents,” represented by the sun in Joseph’s dream. Ambrose explained this in his book On Joseph, chapter 2, in these words: “Who is he whom his parents and brothers worshiped upon the earth, except Jesus Christ, when Mary and Joseph worshiped him with the disciples, confessing that he was the true God in that body? Concerning him it was said of the sun, ‘Praise him, sun and moon,’ and so forth.” Baronius, in the year of Christ 12, relying improperly on the authority of this sermon, makes Augustine a follower of the opinion held by Abbot Arnold of Bonneval in his book On the Cardinal Works of Christ, in the treatise On the Passion—namely, that Joseph was still alive after the Lord’s passion or resurrection.]

### 5. In Joseph Egypt Alone Increased; in Christ the Whole World Increased

“Who is it that repays evils for good?”

Joseph is interpreted as “Increase” or “Expansion.” But in that Joseph only Egypt experienced expansion; in our Joseph, the whole world deserved to experience increase.

That Joseph distributed grain; our Joseph deigned to distribute the word. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

We, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, who through the mercy of the true Joseph, our [Col. 1767] Lord Jesus Christ, have obtained such great blessings without any preceding merits of our own, and to whom not the shadow of the Old Testament but the truth itself has come—let us labor as much as we can, with the grace of God, so that what he bestowed upon us when he was judged may be found whole by him who will judge.

He who bestowed such great things upon you knows what he demands in return. He himself, when he comes, will give back what he promised; but he will require what he redeemed. What he gave at his first coming, he will exact at his second.

Let no one, therefore, repay our Lord Christ evil for good.

Who is it that acts so impiously? The one who receives sweetness and returns bitterness; who receives life and gives back death. For he gives back death who kills himself by living badly.

Who is it that repays evil for good? The one who, when he ought to give what belongs to him, seizes what belongs to another; who returns hatred for charity, envy for kindness, pride for humility, lust for chastity.

Who is it that repays Christ evil for good? The one who, when he ought to devote himself to reading and run to church, chooses instead to play at dice, to attend frenzied, bloody, or disgraceful spectacles; and who, when he ought to expend his sins through prayer, reading, and almsgiving, strives instead to increase and heap them up still further.

Who is it that repays evil for good? The one who returns darkness for light, wickedness for kindness, drunkenness for sobriety, rapacity for almsgiving, and iniquity for justice.

Therefore, whoever, with the Lord’s help, has not committed these evils should guard the divine gifts within himself as much as he can. But whoever feels himself subject to and enveloped by these evils should quickly have recourse to the remedies of repentance and, before his darkened soul departs from the body of its death, acquire a remedy for himself on the day of necessity through almsgiving, fasting, and prayers.

Let us act, then, brothers, so that before Christ’s tribunal both the good may obtain a crown and the negligent may obtain pardon; so that an upright life may adorn the former and a corrected life may avail to excuse the latter.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV

[Note: [Col. 1767] Elsewhere, On Time 83.]

### On Blessed Joseph, II

[Note: [Col. 1767] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The whole sermon has been compacted like a cento from the sayings of various authors—namely Pelagius, Ambrose, and Cyprian—and from a fragment of Sermon 343, On Susanna and Joseph. In other respects, a somewhat fuller and more authentic text is now published according to the Theoderician manuscript, copied seven hundred years ago. For section 1, see Pelagius’s Letter to Demetrias, chapter 5; for section 2, Ambrose’s book On Joseph, chapter 5; for sections 3 and 4, Augustine’s Sermon 343, sections 6–8; for section 5, Pelagius’s letter, chapter 5; for section 6 up to the middle, the same author’s letter, section 18.]

### 1. Envy Spares Not Even Brothers

It is written about blessed Joseph, dearly beloved brothers, that his brothers envied him, and therefore could not speak peacefully to him (Genesis 37:4).

It is true, beloved: the disease of envy is so destructive that it cannot spare even blood relatives, much less strangers.

Indeed, at the very beginning of the world, the unjust brother Cain killed righteous Abel (Genesis 4:8).

Thus holy and faithful Joseph, the Lord’s servant, is shown to be all the more righteous through his tribulations. First, because of envy, he was handed over by his brothers to the Ishmaelites as a slave and sold by those who had seen him worshiped; then, after being handed over to an Egyptian master, he nevertheless always retained the dignity of a free spirit.

By his example he taught both slaves and free people not to sin, and that it is not one’s condition but one’s mind that matters.

### 2. The Fault Lies in the One Who Sees Wrongly, Not in the One Who Does Not Wish to Be Seen Wrongly

Although he was handsome and beautiful in appearance, he did not turn the beauty of his face toward another’s injury but preserved it for his own honor. He judged himself more beautiful if he proved himself more beautiful not through the loss of chastity but through the cultivation of modesty.

That is the true beauty which does not seize the eyes of others or wound fragile minds.

The crime belonged to his mistress, who looked wrongly, not to blessed Joseph, who did not wish to be looked upon wrongly.

Nor is there guilt in the one who was seen, because it was not in a slave’s power not to be seen by his mistress. The husband ought to have guarded his wife’s eyes.

Let men, then, [Col. 1768] learn to guard against the eyes of women when they are loved, even though they do not wish to be loved.

Indeed, Joseph was loved by the woman whom he had rejected. Scripture rightly excuses him, saying: “His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph.” That is, he did not display himself, nor did he ensnare the unwary woman; rather, she cast out her nets and was caught in her own snare. She spread her chains and was bound in her own fetters.

Then she said to him: “Sleep with me” (Genesis 39:7).

The first arrows of adultery are the eyes; the second are words. But whoever is not captured by the eyes can resist words.

He is excused for entering; he is praised for escaping. He valued the clothing of his body no more highly than the chastity of his soul. He left behind as though it were not his own what the adulterous woman held in her hands, and judged as alien what could be seized by the touch of an immodest woman.

Truly he was a great man: though sold, he did not learn a slave’s mentality; though loved, he did not return the love; though asked, he did not consent; though seized, he fled.

### 3. Immodest Love Is Not Love

The mistress desired the young man, but he did not provoke her desire. She entreated him, and he refused. In this one matter she flattered and begged, though in all others she commanded.

Did she love him, or rather herself? I think she loved neither him nor herself. If she loved him, why did she wish to destroy him? If she loved herself, why did she wish to perish?

Behold, I have proved that she did not love: she burned with the poison of lust; the flame of charity did not shine.

But he knew how to see what she did not know how to see. Joseph was more beautiful within than without, more beautiful in the light of his heart than in the appearance of his body. Where that woman’s eye could not penetrate, there he enjoyed his own beauty.

Therefore, when he contemplated the inner beauty of chastity in the mirror of his conscience, when would he permit it to be stained or violated by that woman’s temptation?

What he saw, you too can see, if you wish: the inner and spiritual beauty of purity, if you have any kind of eyes with which to see it.

I offer you an example. Do you love chastity in your own wife? Then do not hate in another’s wife what you love in your own.

What do you love in your wife? Chastity, surely. You hate this in another woman when, by sleeping with her, you wish to destroy her chastity.

What you love in your own wife—do you wish to kill in another? How will you have a prayer of purity when you are the murderer of chastity?

Therefore preserve in another man’s wife what you wish to preserve in your own, because in your wife also you love chastity more than the flesh.

### 4. Chastity, Not the Flesh, Is to Be Loved

Perhaps, however, you think that you are a lover of your wife’s flesh rather than of her chastity. It is a filthy thought, a wretched and sensual lust—but I will not leave you without an example.

You think that you love the beautiful flesh of your wife. I say, rather, that you love chastity more in your wife.

To show you most decisively that you are a lover of chastity more than of flesh, you love it even more in your daughter.

For what man is there who does not wish his daughters to be chaste? What man does not rejoice with his daughters in their chastity?

Do you love the flesh even there? Do you desire a beautiful body where you shudder at incest?

Behold, I have convicted you of being a lover of chastity more than of flesh.

Finally, if you have a beautiful wife who perhaps is neither chaste nor sober, do you love the beautiful flesh, or do you rather detest it?

The beauty of the body is indeed considered outwardly, but inwardly the beauty of chastity is sought. If this is absent, all love of the body immediately grows cold. For although beauty is considered, a reciprocal love is required even more within.
