If, then, I have convicted you of being a lover of chastity, why are you offended, so that you do not love it in yourself?

Love in another man’s wife what you love in your daughter, because your daughter too will become another man’s wife.

Therefore love chastity also in yourself. For if you love another man’s wife, you will not necessarily possess her; but if you love chastity, you will immediately possess it, with the Lord’s help.

You ought to love a beautiful maidservant or another man’s elegant wife in such a way that you seek her as something outside yourself and external. If you love chastity, what you love is with you.

Holy chastity flatters you within, in the chamber of your heart. Her embrace is sweet; her companionship has no bitterness.

[Col. 1769] Chastity does not quarrel with you, does not overthrow you, and in no respect contradicts you in the house of your conscience.

Therefore love chastity both in yourself and in others, so that you may possess eternal blessedness.

If, then, you love in yourself this exceedingly beautiful thing called chastity, you will imitate blessed Joseph, who refused to consent to an immodest woman for unlawful intercourse. He rejected another’s lust and embraced his own purity.

Yet she did what she had threatened. She lied to her husband, and she was believed—God was still patient.

Holy Joseph was handed over to prison and guarded as though he were guilty, although God had not been offended by him.

But even there God did not abandon him, because Joseph was not guilty. The Lord was with holy Joseph.

Because God loved the holy man, his chaste spirit was not conquered by a woman’s love. The age of youth did not sway him, nor did the authority of the woman who loved him move him to frequent the mistress he had despised.

With her own mouth the young woman set a trap for him; secretly and without witnesses her shameless hand seized him; with bold words she urged him toward crime. Yet even there he was not overcome.

As he returned words for words, so he returned actions for actions: the man who had repeatedly refused when asked then fled when seized.

### 5. Joseph’s Kindness

You have admired Joseph’s chastity; now look upon his kindness.

He returned charity for hatred. When he saw his brothers—indeed, enemies descended from brothers—and wished to be recognized by them, he testified to his affection with devout sorrow.

He kissed each one and, bathing the necks of those who trembled with abundant tears, washed away their hatred with tears of charity. He had always loved them with brotherly affection, both while their father was alive and after his death.

He did not remember the pit into which they had thrown him to kill him; he did not consider the brotherhood that had been sold for a price. Returning good for evil, he then already fulfilled the apostolic commandments, although they had not yet been given.

Therefore blessed Joseph, reflecting upon the sweetness of true charity and recognizing the poison of envy with which his brothers had been struck, strove, with God’s help, to drive it from his heart.

### 6. Envy Compared with Rust and Vipers

And truly, brothers, what does envy provide for the unhappy envious person, whom resentment itself tears apart with certain hidden claws of conscience, and for whom another’s happiness becomes a torment? What reward, I ask, will he receive from his hatred except the horrible darkness of the soul and the terror of a confused mind? With a face and spirit always grieving, he torments himself with the desire by which he wishes to harm another; driven by the fiercest goads, he is cast down from every sound judgment and sober-mindedness.

Therefore, brothers, let us guard against the onset of this vice, lest perhaps we be found partners in the devil’s work and condemned with him by the same sentence. For it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his faction imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25). This evil injures somewhat even those against whom it is directed; yet it afflicts more gravely and destructively those from whom it first proceeds. For just as rust consumes iron, so envy destroys and consumes the very soul in which it dwells. And just as vipers are said to be born by tearing apart and rupturing the very maternal womb in which they were conceived, so envy consumes and destroys the very soul from which it was conceived [Note: [Col. 1769] From this point onward, much is taken from Cyprian, in the sermon *On Jealousy and Envy*.].

What a moth of the soul this is; what a wasting of the thoughts; what a rust of the heart: to envy in another the gift of God, to turn another’s good into one’s own evil, to make another’s glory one’s punishment, and, as though bringing executioners against one’s own breast, to apply torturers to one’s thoughts and feelings who tear one apart with inward torments! For such a person no food can be joyful, no drink pleasant. He is always sighing, groaning, and grieving; day and night his besieged breast is relentlessly mangled, because envy has no limit—it is an evil that continually remains, a sin without end.

And to the degree that the person whom he envies advances with greater success, to that same degree the envious person blazes into a greater fire, burning with the flames of resentment. Hence come pallor in the face, trembling on the lips, gnashing [Col. 1770] of the teeth, and rabid, unrestrained abuse. Whoever he is whom the envious person pursues with his jealousy may be able to evade and avoid him; but the envious person cannot flee from himself. Wherever he is, his adversary is with him; his enemy is always enclosed within his breast.

Finally, when the disciples asked the Lord in the Gospel which of them was the greatest, he replied: “Whoever is the least among all of you, he will be great” (Matthew 18:4). By this saying he removed and cut off every cause and source of biting envy.

### 7. Let Whoever Is Envious Vomit Out the Poisons of His Gall

Therefore, it is not permitted for the Christian people to be jealous; it is not permitted to envy. From humility one rises to the heights. Hear the blessed apostle John saying in his Epistle: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; and again: “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going” (1 John 3:15; 2:10).

For, ignorant and blind, he descends into Gehenna and is hurled into punishment, withdrawing from the light of Christ, who warns and says: “I am the light of the world”; and, “Whoever believes in me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

How, then, does a person who, through the vice of jealousy, can be neither peaceful nor secure, retain either the Lord’s peace or charity? But we, brothers, with God’s help, fleeing the poisons of jealousy and envy, must preserve the sweetness of charity not only toward the good but also toward the wicked, so that Christ may not reject us because of the evil of envy, but rather praise us and invite us to the reward, saying: “Come, blessed ones; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34).

Let divine reading be in our hands; let the Lord’s thought be in our understanding; let continual prayer never cease; let saving action persevere, so that whenever the enemy approaches to test us, he may always find us occupied with good works.

Therefore, let each person examine his conscience; and if he sees himself struck by the poison of envy because of his neighbor’s prosperity, let him pull thorns and thistles from his breast, so that the Lord’s seed may multiply in him like a rich harvest in fertile soil, and so that the divine and spiritual crop may swell into the abundance of a fruitful harvest.

Therefore, let whoever is envious vomit out the poisons of his gall; let him expel the venom of discord; with God’s help, let him cleanse the mind that serpentine resentment had infected. Let every bitterness of envy be soothed by Christ’s sweetness. Let him love those whom he previously hated; let him cherish those whom he envied with unjust slanders. Let him imitate the good and always rejoice in the progress of those who are better.

Let him not disparage priests, nor tear his superiors apart with poisonous teeth; let him make himself a participant with them through united love. He will be forgiven when he himself has forgiven; his sacrifices will be accepted when he too approaches God as a peacemaker.

Let each person think of the delights of paradise and desire the heavenly kingdom, to which Christ admits the merciful and those of one mind. Let us consider, brothers, that only those who are peacemakers can be called sons of God, according to what is written: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another”; and again: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:35, 34).

May the merciful Lord lead you to this love through good works and by his protection—he whose honor and glory are with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV

[Note: [Col. 1770] Elsewhere, *On the Seasons* 82.]

**On the Blessed Joseph, III**

[Note: [Col. 1770] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The judgment of the Louvain scholars remained doubtful; later Verlinus and Vindingus declared it spurious. We judge that it should be attributed to Caesarius, although at the end of section 6 it contains a small excerpt from Pelagius’ *Letter to Demetrias*, which was once believed to be by Augustine or Jerome. For section 3, see Caesarius’ Homily 14 in the editions published by Baluze; for section 6, see Pelagius’ *Letter to Demetrias*, chapter 5.]

### 1. Why Joseph Did Not Immediately Make His Circumstances Known to His Father

In blessed Jacob, dearest brothers, and in his holy son Joseph, anyone who pays careful attention recognizes that God did something exceedingly marvelous. First, I do not believe it was without cause that the Lord, who had so often deigned to reveal himself to blessed Jacob, did not wish to tell him for so many years that his son Joseph was alive, but allowed him to be consumed by prolonged affliction.

If anyone believes that this happened without a definite and evident reason, let him consider at least this: even Joseph, although he was so near, was not permitted to send word to his father to announce that he was not only alive but also established in great honor. For from the place where blessed Jacob was to Egypt there were scarcely three hundred miles. From Egypt, therefore, very many people were constantly hurrying to the place where Jacob was, and from that place innumerable crowds were continually traveling to Egypt.

But perhaps someone says that blessed Joseph left his father while still a little boy, and therefore could not have remembered him. It was not so, dearest brothers. A boy of sixteen could in no way have forgotten his parents. Indeed, he had not forgotten them so completely that, when he first saw his brothers, he recognized them.

### 2. By God’s Hidden Judgment He Did Not Send for His Father

But someone may say that, because he was serving an Egyptian master, he did not have the permission or power to send word to his father. Even if this may seem plausible, after he had been brought out of prison and had become ruler over the whole land of Egypt, during those seven years of plenty and the two years of famine that had passed before his brothers came down to him—during those nine years, could he not send to his father across three hundred miles? Without any doubt he could. But by his hidden judgment the Lord did not permit this to happen. So far did this extend that Joseph did not even reveal himself to his brothers when they had come to buy grain. On the contrary, speaking to them with the greatest severity, he kept their brother in confinement and ordered them to return to their father in great sorrow.

### 3. Why, by Retaining Simeon and Benjamin, He Increased His Father’s Grief

Pay attention further to another, greater marvel, and see how blessed Joseph, who knew that his father was enduring unbearable bitterness on his account—as though what he had previously suffered were little—also caused Benjamin to be taken from him. By doing this he certainly knew that he would suffer multiplied grief.

I believe that all these things were done through the providence of the Holy Spirit. God, whose judgments are often hidden but never unjust, did not wish to inform blessed Jacob that his son was alive. He likewise did not allow holy Joseph to announce his glory to his father. On the contrary, by keeping Simeon in confinement and taking Benjamin away, he increased the distress of that same father.

But if we attend to these things faithfully and carefully, dearest brothers, we recognize that the Lord did them with great mercy. From the beginning of the world God exercised this pattern in his saints, and with great compassion completed it in blessed Jacob. But pay careful attention to why this was done.

### 4. God’s Friends Are Not Without Minor Sins, Which Are Consumed by the Fire of Tribulation

Although servants and friends of God avoided grave crimes and performed many good works, we do not believe that they were without minor sins, because the one who said this does not lie: “No one is free from sin, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 15:15, according to the Septuagint).

And blessed John the evangelist, who certainly was not inferior in merit to holy Jacob, cries out and says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). And elsewhere it is written: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16).

Therefore, since, as has already been said, Jacob could not have been without these minor sins, God wished to consume those small sins in this world by the fire of tribulation. He fulfilled in him what he himself said through the Holy Spirit: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27:6); and: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6); and: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

Thus, in order that our God might present holy Jacob in the future judgment like gold purified, he first wiped away all the stains of sin from him, so that in that judging fire there would be nothing left for it to burn.

### 5. From Joseph’s Example We Learn That One Who Seeks Help from a Human Being Rather Than from God Is Disciplined

We recognize that this also happened in blessed Joseph himself. For when, as Scripture says, “the Lord was with him” and had given him favor with his master and with the prison governor (Genesis 39:2, 4, 21), he was nevertheless led to seek help from a human being, saying to the chief cupbearer: “Remember me when it goes well with you, and plead with Pharaoh to get me out of this prison” (Genesis 40:14).

And because it had not yet been written, “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in a human being” (Psalm 117:8), although he had merited God’s grace in all things, he was led astray into asking a human being for help. For this reason two years were added, during which he was still kept in prison, as though God were saying to him: “I am showing you that you ought to seek help from me rather than from a human being.”

Without any doubt we must believe that, as a discipline for holy Joseph, God did not permit the chief cupbearer to retain in his mind what holy Joseph had asked of him when he was released from prison. And because Joseph himself, although holy, could not at that time have been without sin, he was therefore kept shut up in prison for so long, so that what is written might be fulfilled in him: “Those whom I love, I reprove; and those whom I love, I discipline” [Note: [Col. 1772] The whole of section 5 is absent from the manuscripts.] (Revelation 3:19).

### 6. Why Joseph Dealt So Harshly with His Brothers

If we pay careful attention, dearest brothers, we recognize that what we believe God did with regard to blessed Jacob, Joseph also enacted with regard to his brothers. He was certainly so holy that he could not have hated them. We must therefore believe that he wearied them with such great tribulations in order to provoke them to confess their crime and seek the remedy of repentance.

Finally, they said with great sorrow that they deserved to suffer those things because they had sinned against their brother, when they saw his distress (Genesis 42:21). And because blessed Joseph knew that the crime of fratricide could not be forgiven his brothers without great repentance, once, twice, and a third time he boiled them in curative tribulation, as in a spiritual fire—not to avenge himself, but to correct them and free them from so grave a crime.

Accordingly, before they confessed their sin and consumed the crime they had committed through mutual chastisement, he neither revealed himself to them nor granted them the kiss of peace. But when he saw them humbly afflicted for the sin they had committed against him, he kissed each one, wept over each one, and, wetting the necks of those who trembled with the loving dew of his eyes, washed away the hatred of the brothers with tears of charity.

### 7. Fraternal Correction: We Must Forgive Others as We Wish God to Forgive Us

What God did in blessed Jacob, and what Joseph exercised toward his brothers, we too must fulfill toward those who have sinned against us: we must strive to hate not the persons themselves but their sins; and we must wish to correct them according to the gravity of their fault with the utmost severity, while always striving to love them in truth.

If we do this, dearest brothers, what is written will be fulfilled in us: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

To conclude everything I have said in a brief statement: let us forgive those who have sinned against us in the way we wish God to forgive us whenever we sin against him. If we do this, we can confidently say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” [Note: [Col. 1772] Here in the manuscripts the sermon concludes with the formula, “which may he himself deign to grant, who lives …”] (Matthew 6:12).

### 8. Because of the Poor Who Are Hurrying to Their Work, He Reserves Further Discussion of Joseph for the Following Day

We were still taking pleasure in speaking with Your Charity about blessed Joseph, but because of the poor who are hurrying to their work, it is better that we reserve this for tomorrow. Therefore, turning to the Lord, let us implore his mercy, that he may deign both to increase and always preserve the desire to hear the word of God which, in his graciousness toward us, he has bestowed upon us—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVI

[Note: [Col. 1773] Elsewhere, *On the Seasons* 84.]

**On the Statement: “Joseph Died, and the Children of Israel Increased,” etc. Exodus 1:6**

[Note: [Col. 1773] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars were doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus affirm that it is spurious. It contains certain excerpts from Origen, but it reflects the style and customary exhortations of Caesarius. For sections 1 and 3, see Origen’s *Homilies on Exodus*, homily 1.]

### 1. When Joseph Died, the Israelites Multiplied; When Christ Died, Christians Multiplied

We heard in the reading that was read, dearest brothers, how, when Joseph died, the children of Israel increased and multiplied greatly, and sprouted like grass. What does this mean, dearest brothers? As long as Joseph lived, the children of Israel are not said to have increased, nor to have multiplied greatly. But after he died, they are said to have sprouted like grass, although under Joseph’s protection or defense they ought rather to have grown and multiplied.

But these things, dearest brothers, were prefigured in that Joseph and fulfilled in truth in our Joseph, that is, the Lord Christ. Before our Joseph died—that is, before he was crucified—few believed in him. But after he died and rose again, the Israelites, that is, the Christian peoples, multiplied and grew throughout the whole world.

Thus the Lord himself also said in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24–25). After the precious grain of wheat had died and been buried through his Passion, the harvest of the Church sprang up from that single grain throughout the whole world.

For God is no longer known, as before, only in Judea, nor is his great name honored only in Israel; rather, from the rising of the sun to its setting, his name is praised.

### 2. The People of Israel in Egypt and the Soul in the Flesh, under Two Kings

Meanwhile, after Joseph died, a new king arose in Egypt who did not know Joseph, and he addressed his people so that they would persecute the children of Israel. While the king who knew Joseph was alive, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor to have been wearied with mud and brick, nor to have had their males killed and their females preserved [Note: [Col. 1773] Manuscripts *r. ful.*, “reserved.”—And not without reason, if one considers what is read a little later: “Let them kill the males and preserve the females”; and again: “To kill the men and preserve the females.” M.]. But after the king arose who did not know Joseph, all these things are reported to have happened.

For these things, brothers, according to what the Apostle says, happened to the Jewish people as a figure; “they were written for our sake” (1 Corinthians 10:11). What was figured carnally in them is fulfilled spiritually in us.

Therefore, if we pay careful attention, we too frequently recognize these things taking place inwardly within us, in the inner person. For our soul is either ruled by a lawful king or ravaged by a tyrant.

If, with God’s help, we live justly and holily; if we think about chastity, mercy, repentance, and other things of this kind; although we are still in Egypt—that is, in the flesh—we are nevertheless governed by Christ the King. He rules us and does not consume us in mud and brick; he does not wear us down and afflict us with earthly cares or excessive anxieties.

But if our soul begins to turn away from God and pursue things that are disgraceful and dishonorable, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, rejects Christ the King and submits its unhappy neck to the tyrant.

When this has happened, the tyrant addresses his people—that is, bodily pleasures—and, summoning the leaders of the vices to a council, deliberation begins against the children of Israel, that is, against thoughts that are holy and acceptable to God: how they may be surrounded and oppressed, how they may be afflicted with mud and bricks, how the males may be killed and the females preserved.

By the males is understood the rational faculty; by the females, the desire of the flesh. The devil therefore wishes to kill the men within us and preserve the women: that is, to extinguish within us the rational faculty that sees God, while preserving what belongs to the desire of the flesh.

### 3. The Things That Were Written Were Written for Our Instruction

These things were not written for us merely as history, nor should it be thought that the divine Books simply narrate the deeds of the Egyptians. Rather, as the Apostle says, “the things that were written were written for our instruction and admonition” (Romans 15:4).

Thus you who hear these things, who have already received the grace of Baptism, who have been numbered among the children of Israel, and who have received Christ the King within yourself—if after this you wish to turn aside and, out of desire, perform the works of the world, carry out the labors of the earth and the muddy—that is, luxurious—tasks, recognize and understand that another king has arisen within you, one who does not know Joseph.

It is certainly the king of Egypt who compels you to serve not justice but iniquity. He makes you work brick and mud for him. By placing taskmasters and overseers over you, he drives you with whips and blows toward earthly and luxurious works. He is the one who makes you run throughout the world and, out of desire, throw the elements of sea and land into turmoil [Note: [Col. 1774] Origen has, “to disturb the elements.”].

He is the king of Egypt who makes you bring lawsuits into the marketplace and, for a small patch of earth, wear out your relatives with quarrels. He is the one who persuades you, through luxury, to lay snares for chastity, deceive innocence, commit disgraceful things in your house [Note: [Col. 1774] Origen has: “to weary them with quarrels”; omitting, “not to mention laying snares for chastity, deceiving innocence, disgraceful things at home,” etc.], cruel things outside, and shameful things within your conscience.

If, therefore, you see that your actions are of this kind, know that you serve the king of Egypt—that is, that you are driven not by the spirit of Christ but by the spirit of the devil.]

### 4. It Is Not Enough for the Heart to Be Emptied of Evil Unless It Is Also Filled with Good

We, therefore, dearest brothers, who before the coming of the Lord and Savior were vessels and houses of the devil, and who through Christ’s grace have deserved to be freed from his power, must labor as much as we can, with his help, lest Christ, offended by our evil deeds, withdraw from us and the devil enter when he has departed.

Let us beware lest, after the true light has been driven away, dark night seize our heart, lest what is written in the Gospel be fulfilled in us:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept clean, and it brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Luke 11:24–26).

This, brothers, must also be understood of a Christian who has been baptized. Through the grace of Baptism everyone is emptied of all evils; afterward, however, he must labor with God’s help to be filled with every good.

For if the enemy finds someone freed from evils but empty of good, he brings with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and the person’s final state is worse than the first.

Therefore, where luxury has been expelled, let chastity be introduced; where greed has been uprooted, let almsgiving be planted; where malice or envy is driven out, let charity rule.

And because, when our Lord came, he bound the strong man—that is, the devil—and seized his vessels—that is, rescued us from his power (Matthew 12:29), let us strive as much as we can, with his help, to serve with all our heart and all our soul, until the end of our life, the one by whom we have been saved.

And because, after expelling the devil, Christ deigned to make of us a house for himself in which he might rest, and vessels in which he might dwell, let him not suffer insult in his own house. Let him find nothing dishonorable there, nothing filthy, nothing dark. Rather, let him always find the dwelling of our heart full of faith and empty of every evil, so that he may deign not only to visit us more frequently but also to dwell continually within us—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVII

[Note: [Col. 1775] Elsewhere, *On the Seasons* 85.]

**On the Struggle between the Egyptians and the Israelites**

[Note: [Col. 1775] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars left it among the Augustinian works, but without Augustine’s name. Verlinus and Vindingus asserted that it was falsely attributed to Augustine. We have no doubt at all that this sermon belongs to Caesarius.]

### 1. Temptations Grow More Severe as Easter Approaches

Although, dearest brothers, at every time we ought faithfully to hear the word of God with great desire, during these days we must devote ourselves especially to divine reading and think more attentively about the salvation of our soul. For although throughout the whole year the Christian people are harassed by many waves of vice through the devil’s cunning, when the solemnity of Easter approaches he customarily prepares himself with greater force against all the faithful and strives to pierce or disturb our hearts with more grievous goads of sin.

For just as during these days King Pharaoh and the Egyptian people, in the likeness of the devil and his angels, persecuted the children of Israel and afflicted them with mud and bricks, bringing them to bitterness, so at this time, as the solemnity of Easter approaches, because the devil grieves that the true Israelites who are to be baptized are departing from his army or possession, he customarily sends greater tribulations and stirs up greater scandals.

But if we follow Moses—that is, if we willingly hear the Law and do not wish to look back or long for Egypt—then, once Pharaoh has been drowned through the sacrament of Baptism, we are freed from his power and service as though by crossing the Red Sea.

### 2. The Devil Persecutes Only the Good; God and the Devil Have Their Own Ministers

It is absolutely certain, dearest brothers, that just as the Egyptians then brought the children of Israel to bitterness through many tribulations, so, as we have already said, even now the devil and his angels do not cease to attack or disturb faithful Christians devoted to good works.

But know this, brothers: the devil persecutes only the good. He is not accustomed to persecute the wicked, the luxurious, the greedy, and the proud. They are his friends and always do his will. Indeed, he does not persecute them to such an extent that he also uses them to persecute others.

The devil is accustomed to have wicked people as his hammers or whips. Finally, he does not persecute the good except through the wicked.

God therefore has his ministers, and the devil also has his helpers. God acts through good people, as through his ministers, in everything that is good; but the devil exercises everything evil through wicked people, as through his henchmen.

God clothes the naked through the mercy of good people; the devil strips the clothed through the greed of the wicked. God recalls those who are at odds to harmony through good people; the devil, through the impious and proud, provokes even those who seem to possess peace into scandals and quarrels.

Since it would take too long to go through each example, let Your Charity recognize and understand with certainty that just as God does everything good through good people, so the devil customarily carries out everything cruel and impious through wicked people.

Finally, consider, brothers, and you will see even with bodily eyes how the devil’s people persecute Christ’s people: adulterers persecute the chaste; drunkards harass the sober; the proud lay snares for the humble; the envious for the kind; the greedy for the generous; and the angry never cease afflicting those who maintain gentleness or patience.

Therefore, let each person examine his conscience. If he sees himself always loving what is good in thought, speech, and deed, and continually practicing what is honorable, let him recognize and rejoice that he is God’s minister.

But if, questioning himself inwardly, he sees that he not only thinks about what is evil but also speaks or practices it, let him understand and grieve that he is the devil’s helper. While his sinful and dark soul is still enclosed in his body, let him strive, with God’s help, to tear himself from the devil’s power, lest, if sudden death snatches him away while he persists in evil works, he deserve to hear, together with the devil whose will he has carried out: “Depart from me, you accursed ones, into the eternal fire.”

### 3. Let Us Heal Opposites with Opposites and, Having Destroyed Vices, Strive to Build Virtues

Let no one deceive himself, dearest brothers. Each person whose works or desires he exercises in this world will be with the same one afterward in the future. Thus every person will either reign with Christ or be tormented with the devil in the punishment of hell.

Therefore, while there is time and while, with God’s help, the matter remains in our power, let everyone who recognizes that he is on the left through evil works strive to cross to the right before he departs from this light. Then he will not hear with those on the left, “Depart from me, you accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” but will deserve to hear with the sheep on the right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:41, 34).

And so that with God’s help we may fulfill all these things, let us think more attentively about giving alms. How one passes from the left to the right is shown by a clear and evident rule.

Let the one who was drunk become sober; let the one who was angry become patient; let the one who used to steal other people’s property begin also to distribute his own to the poor; let the one who used to curse bless; let the one who used to swear falsely abstain even from taking oaths; let the one who was accustomed to slander always strive to speak what is good; let the envious strive to become compassionate; let the proud become humble.

In this way, let us always strive to heal opposites with opposites, and, once vices have been destroyed, hasten to build virtues. In this way, those who are on the left should attempt to cross to the right, so that whoever chooses to be such may deserve to hear before the tribunal of the eternal Judge: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21).

May the Lord lead you to that joy, to whom belongs honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1776] In the manuscripts the sermon’s conclusion is: “But to our God be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”]

## SERMON XVIII

[Note: [Col. 1776] Elsewhere, *On the Seasons* 86.]

**On Moses, I**

[Note: [Col. 1776] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It had already been considered doubtful by the Louvain scholars and was judged spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. Its author adopted certain interpretations and several expressions from Origen; we think the author was no one other than Caesarius. For section 1, see Origen’s *Homilies on Exodus*, homily 2; for section 8, homily 4.]

### 1. Christ Prefigured in Moses; the Church in Pharaoh’s Daughter

In the divine reading that was recited to us, dearest brothers, we heard that after holy Moses was born, he was placed in a basket of reeds and cast into the reeds of the river because of fear of Pharaoh.

If we pay careful attention, dearest brothers, we recognize that just as Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph prefigured Christ, so Moses also bore the type of Christ. Consider the matter more closely, and you will see how many mysteries were prefigured in him.

Moses was born of a Jewish woman and adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. Pharaoh’s daughter prefigured the Church, which had gone out from her father’s house and was coming to the water to be washed.

Pharaoh is understood as a type of the devil; his daughter, as I have said, signifies the Church. That her father had previously been the devil, the Lord says in the Gospel when rebuking the Jews: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

Therefore, we had the devil as our father—not by being born from him, but by imitating his wickedness. Pharaoh’s daughter had therefore gone out from her father’s house. Although she had an impious father, the prophet nevertheless says to her: “Hear, daughter, and see; forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

The one who says, “Hear, daughter,” is a father. And the one whom she is instructed to forget is nevertheless called a father—as though God the Father were warning her that she must abandon the devil as her father.

This, then, is the Church, which went out from the house of her father, the devil, and hastened to the water—that is, to the water of Baptism—to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house.

Finally, she immediately deserved to receive the compassion of her heart, and she gathered up Moses, who had been cast into the river by his parents. Moses, therefore, was cast away by his mother and found and gathered up by Pharaoh’s daughter; and the Lord Christ is rejected by the Synagogue from which he was born, and is found and received by the Church.

### 2. The Church Again Represented by Moses’ Ethiopian Wife

After Moses had grown up, he went away to a distant region and took an Ethiopian woman as his wife. Recognize, brothers, that this is no small mystery. That Ethiopian woman was from the Gentiles, whom blessed Moses took as his wife, because Christ too was to join the Church to himself from the Gentiles.

Moses left his own people in distant regions and was united to the Ethiopian woman; Christ, after abandoning the Jewish people, is joined from the farthest regions to the Church—to her, certainly, who says in the Psalms: “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you” (Psalm 60:3).

Hear the Church speaking in her own person in the Song of Songs: “I am black and beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:4). What does “I am black and beautiful” mean except black by nature, beautiful by grace; black through original sin, beautiful through the sacrament of Baptism?

### 3. The Synagogue in the Burning Bush

While Moses was tending the sheep of his father-in-law in the desert, the Lord appeared to him in a bush, and Moses said: “I will go and see why the bush is burning and is not consumed.” As he approached, the Lord said: “Do not come nearer; but remove the strap of your sandal, because the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:3, 5).

That bush is a kind of thornbush. It was burning but was not consumed. The Synagogue of the Jews was signified in the bush. For a long time there was fervor and the flame of the Holy Spirit among them. Yet they always resisted the Holy Spirit so rebelliously against God’s grace that their sins and sacrileges could not be consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

### 4. Good Words Are from God, Evil Ones from the Devil

The Lord said to Moses: “Come, and I will send you into Egypt.” And Moses answered, “Lord, I am not learned, and I am slow of speech.” And the Lord said to him: “I will open your mouth and teach you what you ought to say” (ibid., 10, and 4:10). Blessed are those whose mouth the Lord opens, so that they may speak. For all who speak for truth, justice, chastity, humility, and mercy—without any doubt, it is the Lord who opens their mouth.

But conversely, those who continually speak of lust, greed, pride, robberies, vulgarity, or wickedness: it is unnecessary to say who opens their mouth; anyone can recognize this without difficulty. Therefore, dearest brothers, with the Lord’s help let us think continually of good things, so that our mouth may be opened not by the cruel adversary but by the merciful God. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). Each of us habitually brings forth from his mouth the words of the one whose presence he has received in his heart.

Let our heart, then, be opened to Christ and closed to the devil, so that what is written concerning the Lord and the holy people may be fulfilled in us: “And I will dwell among them, and I will walk among them” (Leviticus 26:12); and again: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Whoever always speaks what is just—God dwells in him, and he himself dwells in God.

### 5. Moses’ Rod, the Mystery of the Cross

Then the Lord said to Moses: “What is that which you are carrying in your hand?” And he said: “A rod.” He said: “Throw it on the ground.” When he had thrown it down, it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it (Exodus 4:2–3).

That rod, dearest brothers, prefigured the mystery of the cross. For just as Egypt is struck by ten plagues through the rod, so also the whole world is humbled and conquered through the cross. And just as Pharaoh and his people are afflicted through the mystery of the rod, so that they may release the Jewish people to serve God, [Column 1778] so also the devil and his angels are wearied and oppressed through the mystery of the cross, so that they cannot call the Christian people back from God’s service.

### 6. Moses’ Hand

When Moses put his hand into his bosom and brought it out leprous, and then put it in again and brought it out healthy and like the rest of his flesh (Exodus 4:6–7), we must not understand this casually. That hand bore the type of the Synagogue or the Church.

Just as the Jewish people came first and the Gentiles afterward, so the Synagogue existed before the Church. But because the Church is chosen and the Synagogue rejected, Moses’ hand first becomes leprous and afterward is restored to resemble the rest of his flesh. Thus the Synagogue is left leprous on account of its unbelief, while the Church, like a healthy hand suited to every work, is preferred.

### 7. Moses Is Forbidden to Take His Wife with Him into Egypt

Moses therefore took Zipporah his wife and was coming into Egypt; and the Lord confronted him and wanted to kill him (Exodus 4:20, 24). Perhaps in this passage we can understand that God was displeased because Moses, who was about to perform such great wonders, wished to take with him into Egypt the hindrance of his wife.

Hence it may be understood that from that place he sent his wife back to his father-in-law. For he descended into Egypt without her, to such an extent that afterward, when Moses was already established in the wilderness, his kinsman Jethro brought his wife to him, as we read (ibid. 18:5–8).

### 8. The Serpent from the Rod

Let us see what it signifies that the rod thrown upon the ground was changed into a serpent. The serpent is regarded as a symbol of wisdom, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16).

We have said that the rod signified the cross. Therefore the cross, which is believed to be foolishness by unbelievers—as the Apostle says, “foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23)—after it was cast upon the ground, that is, prepared for the Lord’s passion, was changed into a serpent, that is, into wisdom; and into such wisdom as would devour all the wisdom of this world. Indeed, it swallowed all the serpents which the magicians had made by their incantations.

Thus Egypt is scourged by the rod; through the cross the world is conquered and the devil overcome. Let us therefore pray, dearest brothers, that Christ the Lord, in his mercy, may grant us to conquer the desire for this world and to carry away a happy victory over the devil and his angels before his tribunal—to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XIX

[Note: [Column 1778] Now published for the first time from an old Theoderician book, in which it appears without the author’s name together with the Homilies of Caesarius of Arles, whose style it also seems to reproduce. It is worth comparing with the sermon which, among the Augustinian sermons, we placed as the seventh, though not without some hesitation.]

## On Moses, II

### 1. The Flame Designates the Holy Spirit, the Thornbush the Jews

Great indeed are these things, dearest brothers, and like certain veiled mysteries of God’s sacraments. Although we cannot unfold them all, we nevertheless briefly offer to your Charity what we can.

It was not without cause, dearest brothers, nor without some hidden signification, that there was a flame in the thornbush and the thornbush was not consumed (Exodus 3:2). The thornbush is a kind of thorny growth, and it cannot be counted as anything praiseworthy that the earth produced for sinful humanity. For at the beginning, when the human being sinned, it was said: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3:18).

Nor is the fact that the thornbush was not consumed—that is, that the flame did not take hold of it—understood to signify anything good. In the flame the Holy Spirit is understood; in the thornbush and thorn the Jewish people are signified, hard and proud.

For that flame undoubtedly signified something good, in which either an angel or the Lord appeared. Finally, when the Holy Spirit came upon the Apostles, “there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire” (Acts [Column 1779] 2:3). Would that this fire might also take hold of us, lest it find us hard and be unable to consume us. Rather, let us pray that this fire may burn in us and destroy and consume the thorns of our sins.

### 2. Two Fires: of Charity and of Desire

There are two fires: there is the fire of charity from the Holy Spirit, and there is also the fire of desire. The former burns up everything evil; the latter consumes everything good. In the soul where the fire of charity has burned, it consumes every evil; conversely, in the one in whom the fire of desire has been kindled, nothing good will remain.

Therefore let each person hasten to his conscience. If he feels within himself any spark of compunction kindled by good works, let him preserve within himself the grace of divine mercy and kindle the fire of compunction—the fire of which the Lord said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

But whoever recognizes that the flame of desire is burning within him should, with God’s help, strive with all his strength to extinguish desire and kindle charity. Whatever good a person does while desire is burning in him will quickly perish. Conversely, if one in whom the fire of charity is present commits some negligence, it will consume it without delay and will not permit it to dominate at all.

The Jewish people were being burned by the fire of zeal or desire; therefore that thornbush signified the people who resisted God—the thorny people of the Jews, concerning whom it is written: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:2). Moses was being sent to that very people. Therefore the thornbush burned and was not consumed, because, as I said, the hardness of the Jews resisted the Law. For if that people had not been joined to thorns—

[Note: [Column 1779] Augustine, Sermon 7, section 2: “it would have been signified.”]

—it would not have been from them that Christ was crowned with thorns.

### 3. Moses and Joshua Are Commanded to Remove the Strap of Their Sandal

Then the Lord cried out to Moses: “Remove the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). We read that this same command was given not only to blessed Moses but also to his successor Joshua, when the Lord appeared to him.

When Joshua saw a man standing opposite him with a drawn sword and asked who he was, the man answered him: “I am the commander of the army of the Lord, and now I have come.” And he added: “Remove the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Joshua 5:13–16).

I ask you, dearest brothers, according to your holy custom, to listen more attentively to what we have learned concerning this matter through the revelation of the ancient Fathers. Since the matter is difficult and obscure to understand, receive it patiently, because we must often repeat certain things so that we may more easily bring them to your understanding.

### 4. Why the Command Was Given to Both; What Is Signified by Holy Ground

The Jews had been commanded by the Law that, if anyone died without children, his brother should take his wife, and whatever children were born from her should be reckoned in the name of the deceased brother. They were not to be registered as the children of the man who begot them, but of the man whose widow he had taken.

For this reason many among the people, unwilling that their children should be called by another man’s name, refused to take the widows of their brothers. Whoever wished to excuse himself was brought to the gate; the widow of his brother would remove his sandal and spit in his face, and his house was called “the House of the Barefoot Man.” Thus the straps of the sandal were removed from the one who was not to become the bridegroom; but for the one who consented, they were not removed at all (Deuteronomy 25:5–10).

I have said this, dearest brothers, so that, even if we cannot understand everything, we may try to understand why the Lord said to Moses and Joshua: “Remove the strap of your sandal; for the place on which you stand is holy ground.” Why was this said to them except because they were not the legitimate bridegroom?

For there could be no other legitimate bridegroom of the Catholic Church than Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Of him the Psalmist [Column 1780] had long before foretold: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm 18:6).

Blessed John the Baptist also spoke of him most clearly, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” He said this of Christ. But what did he say about himself? “But the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

And to show still more clearly that the Lord Christ is the legitimate bridegroom, he said: “This is the one whose sandal strap I am not worthy to remove” (ibid. 1:27). Why did he not presume to remove his sandal strap? Because he knew that Christ was the legitimate bridegroom of the Church.

Moses and Joshua are commanded to remove their sandals because they prefigured the bridegroom, but were not themselves the bridegroom. Finally, observe what the Lord said to Moses or Joshua: “Remove the strap of your sandal; for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

Can this be understood, dearest brothers, according to the literal sense? How could that ground which they trod be holy, when it was undoubtedly like the rest of the ground? But pay close attention to what was said: “For the place on which you stand is holy ground.” This means: Christ, whose figure you bear and whose type you appear to possess, is holy ground.

Truly, the holy ground is the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things heavenly and earthly have been sanctified, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Making peace through his blood, with the things in heaven and on earth” (Colossians 1:20).

### 5. The Apostles, the Brothers of Christ, Took the Deceased Man’s Wife

Therefore, dearest brothers, as I said above, the man who refused to take the wife of his deceased brother had his sandal removed and was spat upon. But the one who consented to take the widow of his deceased brother had children born to him who were called not by the name of the one who begot them, but by the name of the one who had died.

We see this fulfilled in the Apostles. For when the brother had died—that is, when Christ had died, he who had said, “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew 28:10)—the Apostles took his wife, that is, the Church.

For the Apostle Paul says: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). Yet all who were born into the Church through the teaching of the Apostles were called neither Petrans nor Paulans, but Christians, so that the figure previously set forth in the Law concerning the wife of a deceased brother might be fulfilled.

But the wretched heretics did not act in this way. Rather, like utterly cruel usurpers, seizing the wife of their deceased brother and tearing and dividing the Church into factions, they wished all who are born through the sacrament of Baptism to be called, with the most shameless boldness, not by Christ’s name but by their own.

Thus, in the Catholic Church, all who are born are called Christians by the name of the deceased one, that is, Christ. Among the heretics, however, some are called Donatists, others Manichaeans, others Arians, and others Fortians.

[Note: [Column 1780] Probably Photinians, that is, followers of Photinus.]

But because the leaders of the heretics were not legitimate bridegrooms, they imposed upon the peoples not Christ’s name but their own.

### 6. Hearers Should Examine More Carefully Whatever the Preacher Sets Before Them

Therefore I ask, brothers, that your holy Charity forgive me, because, while I have tried to suggest to you some understanding of what was said to Moses—“Remove the strap of your sandal”—I seem perhaps to have wearied you with a longer discourse than I ought.

And although there may be nothing in this sermon capable of pleasing you, I believe that our intention and desire ought not to displease your Charity, since I have attempted to explain so great a matter, even though I could not unfold it as adequately as it deserves. Nevertheless, I have tried to bring before your holy understanding certain outlines and whatever small indications I could, so that, examining them more attentively, you may, with Christ inspiring you, meditate on them even better than we have suggested.

# SERMON XX

[Note: [Column 1781] Also known as Sermon on Time 87.]

## On the Ten Plagues of the Egyptians

Exodus, chapters 7–12.

[Note: [Column 1781] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The whole sermon, except for the recapitulation, has been transcribed from Origen’s fourth homily on Exodus, with very few changes. Some material from the same source also appears in Jerome, Commentary on Psalms 77 and 104.]

[Column 1781]

### 1. Moses Is Understood as the Law; the Rod as Christ’s Cross

When Moses comes to Egypt, dearest brothers, he brings a rod with which he chastises and scourges Egypt with ten plagues. Moses is understood as the Law, which was given to this world to rebuke and correct it with ten plagues—that is, with the ten commandments contained in the Decalogue.

That Moses can be understood as the Law, the Lord said in the Gospel: “They have Moses and the Prophets” (Luke 16:29), that is, the Law and the Prophets.

The rod by which Egypt is subjected and Pharaoh overcome bore the image of Christ’s cross. Through the cross this world is conquered, and the ruler of this world is led in triumph together with the principalities and powers.

That the rod, once thrown down, becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptians signifies that the serpent is understood as wisdom, as it is written: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16). Therefore Moses’ rod, that is, Christ’s cross, after it descended to the earth—that is, after it came to human belief and faith—was changed into wisdom, and into such wisdom as would devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world.

### 2. The Plagues of the Egyptians

Blood. Frogs. Gnats. Dog-fly. Death of the Animals. Boils and Blisters. Thunder. Locusts. Darkness. Death of the Firstborn.

That the waters of the river are changed into blood is fittingly understood as meaning that the river to which they had handed over the Hebrew infants for a cruel death should return to the perpetrators of the crime a drink of blood, and that by drinking they should experience the gore of the polluted stream which they had stained with parricidal slaughter.

The second plague, in which frogs are brought forth, seems to me to signify figuratively the songs of the poets. Through a vain and inflated musical style, like the sounds and croakings of frogs, they introduced tales of deception into this world. For that animal is useful for nothing except that it produces the sound of its voice in disgraceful and importunate cries.

After this gnats are produced. This creature is suspended on wings as it flies through the air, but it is so subtle and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eyes unless the observer sees sharply. Yet it pierces the body on which it settles with a most painful sting, so that one who cannot see it flying nevertheless feels it stinging.

I therefore think that this kind of creature most aptly corresponds to the art of philosophy or to the cunning of heretics, which pierces souls with the minute and subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such cleverness that the deceived person neither sees nor understands the source of his deception.

In the fourth place the dog-fly, that is, the canine fly, is introduced. It is rightly compared with the sect of the Cynics, who, in addition to the other wickednesses of their deception, also proclaim pleasure and lust to be the highest good.

Since the world was first deceived through these several things, the word and Law of God come and rebuke it with such corrections that, from the nature of the punishments, it may recognize the nature of its own error.

In the fifth place Egypt is scourged by the death of animals or cattle. Here the senselessness and folly of mortals are rebuked—those who, like irrational cattle, gave the worship and name of God to images not only of human beings but also of animals. Hence by a just judgment it came about that in those things in which they believed divine worship to reside, they saw pitiable punishments.

After this, in the sixth plague, boils and blisters with burning heat are brought forth. It seems to me that deceitful and irritating malice is rebuked in the boils, swelling and inflated pride in the blisters, and the madness of anger and fury in the burning heat.

[Note: [Column 1781] Thus in the edition of Amerbach. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “purulent.” In Origen, “fraudulent.”]

Up to this point punishments are proportioned to the world through figures of its errors. Afterward, however, scourges come from above: voices and thunder, hail, and fire running [Column 1782] through the hail.

Observe the moderation of divine correction. He does not scourge in silence, but gives forth voices and sends teaching from heaven, through which the chastised world may recognize its guilt. He also gives hail, by which the tender beginnings of vices are still destroyed; and he gives fire, knowing that there are thorns and thistles of sins which that fire must consume—the fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). Through it the incentives to pleasure and lust are consumed.

That locusts are mentioned in the eighth place, I think signifies through this kind of plague the fickleness of the human race, which is either slanderous or always at variance with itself.

Although the locust has no king, as Scripture says, it leads forth an army arranged in one battle line (Proverbs 30:27). Human beings, however, although they were made rational by God, were unable to govern themselves in an orderly fashion, nor did they patiently endure the guidance of God their king.

The ninth plague is darkness: either so that the blindness of their minds may be rebuked, or so that they may understand that the reasons of divine dispensation and providence are exceedingly obscure.

For, as the Psalmist says, God “made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12). The proud, desiring to investigate these things boldly and rashly, and asserting one claim after another, have fallen into the dense and palpable darkness of errors.

Finally, the destruction of the firstborn is inflicted. The firstborn of the Egyptians may appropriately be understood as the principalities and powers of this world, that is, the devil and his angels, whom Christ is said to have destroyed at his coming—that is, to have led captive and triumphed over on the wood of his cross.

We may also understand the firstborn of the Egyptians as all the authors and inventors of the false religions that exist in this world, whom the truth of Christ destroys together with their authors.

### 3. Recapitulation of the Matters Stated Above

So that what has been said may cling more firmly to your memory, and so that you may turn it over in the mouth of your heart like clean animals and ruminate on it spiritually, we shall give a brief recapitulation.

When in the first plague the waters are changed into blood, the teachings of the philosophers are signified, teachings that deceive those who are little in understanding.

In the second plague, the multitude of frogs signifies the songs of the poets, which have never been able to benefit anyone.

In the third plague, gnats—that is, exceedingly small flies—are produced, piercing bodies with a very painful sting. In them are signified the cunning of the philosophical art and the poisons or exceedingly subtle arguments of unhappy heretics.

In the fourth plague the dog-fly is introduced, and it is rightly compared with the teaching of the Cynics, who, among their other evils, proclaim lust to be the highest good.

In the fifth place the animals are killed, signifying the senselessness or folly of human beings.

In the sixth place boils, pustules, and blisters with burning heat are sent forth. Deceitful and irritating malice is rebuked in the boils; swelling and inflated pride in the blisters; and the madness of anger and fury in the burning heat.

Afterward, in the seventh place, thunder and voices are sent from heaven, together with hail and fire. In the voices and thunder heavenly teaching is recognized; in the hail, the discipline received by sinners; and in the fire, the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the pleasures of lust and the thorns of sins are consumed.

In the eighth plague locusts are introduced, a creature harmful through its teeth. In them is signified the pride of wicked people who persecute one another with false testimonies and betrayals. Concerning them the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

In the ninth plague darkness is introduced, through which the blindness of the mind or heart is rebuked.

In the tenth plague the firstborn are struck. In them either spiritual wickednesses or original sins may be understood; these, when Christ came, are clearly shown to be erased or extinguished through the mystery of the cross and the grace of Baptism.

Therefore, dearest brothers, [Column 1783] let us rejoice and give thanks to God that what we read was done at that time through figures and images, we both feel and see completed in us through his mercy—our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXI

[Note: [Column 1783] Also known as Sermon on Time 95.]

## On the Ten Plagues and the Ten Commandments

Exodus, chapters 7–12; and chapter 20, verses 3–17.

[Note: [Column 1783] It is now placed in the Appendix of this volume for the first time. Formerly it appeared in two places in the Amerbach and Erasmus editions: namely, among the Sermons on Time and also among certain popular treatises which Erasmus arranged at the end of volume nine. There it was entitled “On the Correspondence of the Ten Commandments and the Ten Plagues.” In the manuscripts, however, it bears the title “On the Adaptation of the Ten Commandments,” and so forth. For the most part it contains a fragment of the eighth sermon among the Augustinian sermons, on the ten plagues, under a different preface. In the Royal and Sorbonne manuscripts this preface begins somewhat more fully with these words: “Since the sermon which has been read to us (perhaps, which is to be read) seems somewhat longer than necessary for the exposition, we shall bring the Psalms to an end more quickly, so that your Charity may not be wearied by standing longer and the poor may return to their customary work. It is not without cause, beloved brothers,” and so forth.]

### 1. In the Plagues Are Wounds; in the Commandments, Medicines

It is not without cause, beloved brothers, that the number of the commandments of God’s Law appears to correspond to the number of the plagues by which Egypt was struck. For just as there are ten commandments of the Law, by which the people are admonished to worship God, so ten plagues are recorded, by which the pride of the Egyptians is afflicted.

Let us therefore consider why ten commandments are mentioned there and ten plagues here. It is undoubtedly because in the former there were wounds and in the latter medicines; and because it was necessary that the medicines of the ten commandments should come to the aid of the dangerously severe wounds of the ten plagues.

Therefore I ask you, brothers, not to receive this carelessly. For if, with God’s help, you attend carefully, you will be able to recognize that those ten commandments are, in order, opposed to those ten plagues. The first plague corresponds to the first commandment, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so on until the tenth.

### 2. The Water Is Changed into Blood Because the Understanding of the Wicked Is Darkened

The first commandment in the Law concerns the one God: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” The first plague of the Egyptians is the water changed into blood.

Compare the first commandment with the first plague. Take the one God, from whom all things exist, as corresponding to water, from which all things are generated. To what does blood belong except mortal flesh?

What, then, is the changing of water into blood except that, concerning those who refused to believe in God, as the Apostle Paul says: “Their foolish heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:21–22)?

Thus water is changed into blood because the understanding of the Egyptians becomes obscure and dark. And by God’s just judgment it happened that they drank blood from that river in which they had been accustomed to kill the infants of the Hebrews.

[Note: [Column 1783] In most manuscripts: “except those who refused to believe God.”]

### 3. Frogs: Philosophers or Heretics

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” Whoever takes the name of his God in vain will not be cleansed.

The name of the Lord Jesus Christ is truth. For he himself says: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). And because truth cleanses while vanity defiles, let us see the plague opposed to this second commandment.

What is this second plague? An abundance of frogs. In the frogs heretics and philosophers are understood. The vanity of philosophers or heretics is fittingly signified if you consider the loquacity of frogs.

Philosophers or heretics, because they say that everything concerning Christ is false, [Column 1784] are frogs croaking in muddy marshes. They may have pride, empty disputes, and the noise of their voices, but they cannot convey the teaching of wisdom.

Those who contradict Christian truth and, deceived in their own vanity, deceive others are frogs bringing weariness to the ears, not nourishment to the minds.

### 4. The Spiritual Sabbath; Gnats, the Restless and Turbulent

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” In this third commandment a certain summons to rest is suggested—namely, rest of heart and tranquillity of mind, which a good conscience produces.

For sanctification is there because the Spirit of God is there. Finally, observe what rest means, namely quiet. “Upon whom,” says the Lord, “shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

The restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit: lovers of quarrels and sowers of slander. Through their restlessness they do not admit to themselves the quiet ones; they are lovers of contention rather than of charity, enemies of the spiritual Sabbath.

For they do not observe the spiritual Sabbath except those who so regulate their earthly activities that they nevertheless devote themselves, if not always, at least frequently, to reading and prayer, according to the Apostle’s words: “Attend to reading and teaching” (1 Timothy 4:13); and again: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Those who are such keep the Sabbath spiritually every day.

But those who are restless and continually entangled in earthly activities—and concerning whom it is written, “The distractions of the world have made them wretched”—cannot have a Sabbath, that is, rest.

Against this restlessness it is said that they should have, as it were, a Sabbath in their heart and the sanctification of God’s Spirit. “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand” (Ecclesiasticus 5:13). Cease from your restlessness. Let there be no tumult in your heart through the corruption of a fleeting fantasy, like flies that disturb or sting you.

You are going to understand God saying to you: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). Because of your restlessness you do not wish to be still, and, blinded by the corruption of your contentions, you demand to see what you cannot see.

Observe the third plague, which is opposed to the third commandment. Gnats are born in the land of Egypt from the mud: exceedingly small and restless flies, flying about without order, rushing into the eyes, and not allowing people to rest. When they are driven away, they return again and attack.

Such as these flies are, so are restless people who do not wish to observe the Sabbath spiritually—that is, to devote themselves to good works and attend to reading or prayer.

Such, undoubtedly, are the fantasies of contentious hearts. And just as the human body is afflicted by these flies, so the heart of such people is disturbed and stung by various thoughts.

Hold fast to the commandment; beware of the plague.

### 5. The Dog-Fly: Contempt for Parents

The fourth commandment follows: “Honor your father and your mother.” Opposed to it is the fourth plague of the Egyptians, the κυνομυῖα—that is, the dog-fly, for the word is Greek.

Whoever neglects to honor his parents is spiritually afflicted and tormented by the dog-fly, that is, by the devil’s wickedness. For it is canine not to acknowledge one’s parents; nothing is more canine than failing to recognize those who gave one birth.

### 6. The Adulterer Becomes a Beast

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery.” The fifth plague is death among the cattle.

Anyone who either uses his own wife immoderately, apart from the desire for children, or—what is a most serious crime—lies in wait for another man’s wife or daughter, or for his own or another’s maidservant, overcome by bestial desire, becomes a beast, as though he had lost his humanity.

He is not changed into the nature of cattle, but, while retaining the outward form of a human being, he possesses the likeness of cattle, because he refuses to hear God saying: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9); and again: “Though a man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13). [Column 1785]

But if you do not fear being a beast, at least fear dying like a beast.

### 7. Good Heat and Evil Heat

The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill.” The sixth plague is pustules on the body and boiling, bubbling blisters, with the burning of ulcers from the ashes of the furnace.

Such are murderous souls: they burn with anger, because through anger brotherhood perishes. People burn with rage, and they also burn with grace. For the one who wishes to help is fervent, and the one who wishes to kill is fervent: the one through obedience to the commandment, the other through disease; the one through good works, the other through festering ulcers.

If only we could see the souls of murderers! Without a doubt, we would grieve more over them than over the decaying bodies of those covered with ulcers.

### 8. Unjust Profit; Hunger of Soul and Body

The seventh commandment follows: “You shall not steal.” The seventh plague is hail upon the crops.

What you take away by theft against God’s commandment, you lose from heaven. For no one possesses unjust profit without just loss. For example, the one who steals acquires a garment but loses faith according to heavenly judgment. Where there is profit, there is loss: visible profit, invisible loss; profit through his own blindness, loss from the cloud of the Lord.

[Note: [Column 1785] Thus most manuscripts, together with Augustine. But manuscript s. reads, “loss from the Lord’s vision”; manuscript c. reads, “loss from the Lord’s equity.” The printed editions read, “because he now lives without equity.”]

Therefore those who steal outwardly through their evil desire are, by God’s just judgment, pelted inwardly with hail.

If only thieves or robbers could look upon the field of their heart! Surely they would mourn and grieve when they found nothing there to put into the mouth of the soul, even though in their theft they found something to swallow with the appetite of the throat.

The hunger of the soul is greater than that of the body; it is a greater hunger, a more dangerous plague, and a heavier death. What is worse, many walk about dead from this hunger of the soul and carry their own funerals while alive.

They seem to live in the body, but by their evil deeds they are proved dead in the soul. And many who are hungry in soul boast of empty pleasures.

Finally, Scripture says that a good Christian is rich within: “The hidden person of your heart,” it says, “is rich before God” (1 Peter 3:4)—not before human beings, but before God, where God sees.

What benefit is it to you, then, if you steal where a human being does not see, but where God sees, you are pelted with hail by just judgment?

### 9. The Locust: The Slanderer

The eighth commandment is: “You shall not give false testimony.” The eighth plague is the locust, a creature harmful through its teeth.

What does a false witness seek except to cause harm by biting and to consume by lying? Therefore the Apostle warns us not to attack one another with false accusations: “If you bite and devour one another,” he says, “see that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

### 10. When the Marriage Act Is Not Without Sin; Adulterers Are Blinded by Fury

The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” The ninth plague is dense darkness.

If it is a sin to have relations with one’s own wife except for the purpose of children, what sort of sin do you think it is not only to sin with one’s own wife but also to desire another’s?

Truly, the darkness is dense. Nothing causes such pain in the heart of the sufferer as the desire for his wife by another; and the one who does this to someone else has nothing he would be so unwilling to suffer himself.

People usually endure other evils patiently; but I do not know whether anyone has ever been found who could bear this tolerably. Oh, how dense a darkness is suffered by those who do such things and desire such things!

Truly, they are blinded by dreadful fury. For it is an untamed rage to wish to defile and pollute another man’s wife.

11. Desiring the Inheritance of Others. Faith, the Firstborn of the Heart

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.” The plague corresponding to this commandment is the tenth: the death of the firstborn. All the possessions people have they preserve for their heirs, and among heirs nothing is dearer than the firstborn. Those who want to possess another’s property as though by right seek to become heirs of the dying—for what seems more just than to possess something left to one? Someone says: “It was left to me; I am reading the will.” Nothing seems more just than this statement. You praise him as though he were possessing it lawfully; [Col. 1786] God condemns him for coveting it unlawfully.

Consider what sort of person you are when you wish to become someone’s heir. Do you therefore not want him to have his own heirs, among whom nothing is dearer than the firstborn? Accordingly, you will be punished in your own firstborn, because by coveting what belongs to another—that is, what is not legally owed to you—you seek it out as though under the shadow of law. Thus you destroy your own firstborn.

But it is easy enough, brothers, to lose one’s firstborn bodily. Human beings are mortal, whether they die before their parents or after their parents. What is grievous is that through this hidden and unjust covetousness you should lose the firstborn of your heart. The firstborn of our heart is faith, for no one does good works unless faith has gone before. All your good works are your spiritual children, but among them faith is your firstborn. Whoever secretly covets another’s property loses inward faith. For he will first, without doubt, become a hypocritical flatterer, serving not out of love but through deceit, as though loving the person from whom he desires to become heir. He says that he loves the one whose death he desires, and, in order to see himself in possession of that person’s goods, wishes that he leave no heir of his own.

12. Exhortation

This comparison, brothers, and, in a certain sense, this contrast between the ten commandments and the ten plagues, should make us watchful, so that we may keep our possessions secure in God’s commandments—our possessions, I mean, those within us and stored in the ark of our conscience. These are our treasures, which neither thief, robber, nor wicked neighbor will ever be able to take from us; there we need fear neither moth nor rust. These are the true riches: a good conscience, justice, mercy, chastity, and sobriety. Whoever is full of such things will be rich, even if he comes out of a shipwreck naked.

But if you attend carefully to these matters, and, with God’s help, wish both to flee what is evil and to practice what is good, you will be the Lord’s people. Freed from the wicked fellowship of the Egyptians—that is, from the persecution of spiritual powers of wickedness—you will be able happily to reach the promised land, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON XXII  
[Note: [Col. 1786] Also known as On Time 88.]  
On the passage that is written: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart.” Exodus, chapter IX, verse 12  
[Note: [Col. 1786] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It was doubtful to the Louvain scholars and was considered spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. It is among those sermons that we accept as Caesarius’s; see his Homily 14 among those edited by Baluze. In the criticism of this sermon, it was also thought to be the treatise On the Hardening of Pharaoh, concerning whose author the dispute against Hincmar was conducted in the work On Predestination, chapter 1, with some asserting that it was by Pardulus and Jerome. See the book of the Church of Lyons, On the Three Epistles, chapter 39.]

1. On the Hardening of Pharaoh

Whenever that reading is recited, dearest brothers, in which we frequently hear that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, it commonly causes scandal not only among laypeople but also among some clerics. For some say among themselves: “Why is that wickedness attributed to Pharaoh, when it is reported that the Lord hardened his heart?” And because the most unclean Manichaeans, in their sacrilegious madness, commonly attack the Scripture of the Old Testament on this matter, I ask you, brothers, to attend carefully. Although not as fully as we ought, at least as much as we can, we wish briefly to explain to your Charity how you should understand that hardening.
