2. Hardening of the Heart Arises from Despair. God Hardens through Patience, Not through Power

First, let your Charity believe faithfully and firmly that God never abandons a person unless the person has first abandoned God. For when someone has committed grave sins once, twice, and three times, God nevertheless waits for that person, as he says through the prophet: “That he may turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). But when a person begins to persist in sins, despair arises from the multitude of sins, and hardening is generated from despair.

When negligent people at first disregard their sins because they are small, their minor sins increase, they bring forth even crimes, heap them up, and sink beneath them. When this has happened, what is written is fulfilled: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Of such people the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II, 4–5).

And elsewhere we read of such hardening: “The untamed horse becomes hard to control, and the neglected son becomes headstrong.” Again, Scripture says concerning the correction of a son: “Strike the sides of your son while he is an infant, lest he become hardened and disobey you” (Eccli. XXX, 8, 12).

We wish to bring these testimonies of Scripture to your attention so that you may understand that hardening does not occur because God’s power compels it, but is generated through God’s release or indulgence. Thus we must believe that Pharaoh was hardened not by divine power but by divine patience. Indeed, whenever God’s plague struck him, he repented under affliction. But whenever divine indulgence granted him relief, he again rose up, lifted by pride.

Believe this most firmly, brothers, and understand it: whenever the Lord says, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” he intended nothing else to be understood than: “I will suspend my plagues and scourges”—

[Note: [Col. 1787] Manuscript C reads: “and by removing the scourges, him, etc.” Manuscript R, and S and F, read: “lest I scourge him, through which I will permit him, etc.”]

—“so that through my indulgence I may permit him to be hardened against me.”

3. A Second Objection Concerning the Same Subject

But perhaps someone will say: Why did God, by sparing him, allow him to be hardened, and why did he remove the scourges? Here I answer confidently: God removed the scourges so often because, on account of the immense accumulation of his sins, Pharaoh did not deserve to be corrected as a son for his amendment, but was permitted to be hardened as an enemy.

For such great iniquities had preceded, and so often had he contemptuously defied God with sacrilegious boldness, that in him was fulfilled what the Holy Spirit said of such people: “They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men; therefore pride held them fast; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity came forth as from fatness” (Ps. LXXII, 5–7). See how one is hardened who does not deserve to be chastised by the Lord for correction.

But what is written concerning those whom God’s mercy does not permit to be hardened? “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebr. XII, 6); and again, “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Apoc. III, 19); and again, “The Lord chastises the one he loves” (Prov. III, 12).

Concerning this hardening the prophet also cries out to the Lord in the person of the people: “You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you” (Isa. LXIII, 17). This means nothing other than: “You abandoned our heart, so that we would not turn to you.” We know that this was fulfilled among the Jewish people through many preceding sacrileges.

4. Hardening Follows from the Absence of Grace

Let no one, therefore, presume to criticize or blame God’s justice along with the pagans or Manichaeans. Let him believe most certainly that Pharaoh was hardened against God’s commands not by divine violence but by his own iniquity and untamable pride.

What else is meant by God’s saying, “I will harden his heart,” than: “When my grace has been removed from him, his wickedness will harden him”? To make this clearer, we offer your Charity a comparison drawn from visible things.

Whenever water is frozen by excessive cold, it is melted when the warmth of the sun comes upon it; when that same sun departs, it is hardened again. In the same way, through the coldness of sins the charity of many grows cold, and they are hardened like ice. When the warmth of divine mercy again comes upon them, they are melted—that warmth of which it is written: “There is no one who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. XVIII, 7).

We recognize that this also happened in Pharaoh’s case. Whenever the scourges were removed from him, he rose up in hardness against God; whenever he was afflicted, he humbly pleaded.

[Col. 1788] 5. Why God Does Not Mercifully Scourge Everyone. In What Sense He Is Said to Harden

Why, then, does our Lord not scourge everyone so mercifully that he permits no one to be hardened against him? This must either be attributed to the iniquity of those who deserve to be hardened, or referred to the inscrutable judgments of God, which are often hidden but never unjust.

Let it be enough for us, therefore, to believe piously and humbly what the Apostle said: “Is there injustice with God? By no means” (Rom. IX, 14); and what we are accustomed to sing in the psalm: “God is faithful, and there is no iniquity in him” (Deut. XXXII, 4).

Accordingly, as I have already suggested above concerning Pharaoh, let us believe without any hesitation that it was not so much God’s power as God’s patience that caused him to be hardened. We recognize this clearly from Pharaoh himself, who confessed it. For when he was being chastised, compelled by justice he declared: “The Lord is just, but I and my people are wicked” (Exod. IX, 27).

With what conscience, then, does a Christian complain that God is unjust, when even an impious king confesses him to be just? For God did not harden him irrevocably, since after the ten plagues he not only released God’s people but even compelled them to depart. What he is read to have done after being struck by ten plagues, we recognize that he could have accomplished after the first chastisement.

We customarily do something similar with our household servants whom we raise either too indulgently or too leniently, or whom we frequently forgive when they sin. When they become worse through that very leniency, we commonly reproach them, saying: “I made you such as this. By sparing you, I nurtured your insolence and negligence.”

[Note: [Col. 1788] In the manuscripts: “my negligence.”]

We do not say this because they have fallen into such great pride through our will, but because they have been hardened more through our goodness or indulgence. In the same way, God is understood to have acted toward Pharaoh: while in ineffable kindness he suspended the plagues from him, Pharaoh, with his heart hardened, rose up proudly against God.

6. Whenever We Sin, Let Us Hasten to Apply the Medicine of Almsgiving or Repentance to the Wounds of the Soul

Dearest brothers, in offering you these suggestions I have taken care to set before you, as it were, certain brief indications of obscure matters. But if with pious and faithful hearts, as you are accustomed to do, you consider the mysteries of divine Scripture, then, with the Lord’s gift, you will understand more fully what the truth of the matter is.

We, dearest brothers, recognize in truth that despair arises from the multitude of sins and that hardening is generated from despair, according to what was said above: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Therefore, whenever some sins have crept upon us, let us hasten without delay to provide the wounds of our souls with the medicine of almsgiving or repentance.

A soothing poultice is usefully applied while wounds are still hot, and a wound is quickly restored to health when it is not allowed to putrefy through prolonged abuse. Therefore, whenever we sin, let our sins recognize us as judges, not advocates; let them know that we are their accusers, not their defenders, according to what is written: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L, 5).

Acknowledge it, and God forgives. For how would God deign to forgive what a person disdains to acknowledge in himself? Just as, when some wound or injury appears on our body, we immediately seek a physician and hasten to apply medicines, so we ought to act with the wounds of the soul. Otherwise, if we are more concerned for the health of the body than for that of the soul, preferring the servant to the mistress by an unjust judgment, we may deserve to receive the prophet’s rebuke: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 13).

It is beneficial for us to care more for the soul’s well-being than for the body’s, and to strive to cultivate the image of God within us so that [Col. 1789] we may come without shame before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON XXIII  
[Note: [Col. 1789] Also known as On Time 89.]  
On Pharaoh’s Cruelty and Drowning. Exodus, chapters I, verse XIV  
[Note: [Col. 1789] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It appears to be by the same author as the third and seventh sermons.]

1. Pharaoh’s Cruelty toward the Hebrews

The Egyptian troops, entering upon a foreign path amid the waves of the sea, are punished by the avenging waters because they sought to bring back under their power those who had God as their special defender. Desperate boldness drew them into the middle of the sea’s channel; empty fury provoked their madness still further. As the waves confused them and returned to their proper nature, the shore soon received them harshly in different places, and the sand preserved them unburied as food for beasts.

God had chosen Moses to invite Pharaoh through mighty deeds, admonish him by signs and wonders, terrify him by vengeance, and restrain him, once terrified, through severity. But you say: How could the one who was already being dragged along by God’s sentence be set free by admonition? “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” he says (Exod. VII, 3). He uttered a sentence that he promised he would carry out, not one that he showed he had already carried out. “I will harden,” he says—not “I harden.” One thing is to do something; another is to promise that it will be done, though it is not yet fulfilled, so that those terrified by fear may be corrected.

He ordered the Hebrews to be worn down with clay, bricks, and a denial of straw, so that, once afflicted, they would eventually be unable to resist the Egyptians if war should arise. Thus the machines of war are raised up to heaven, towers rise high, and they construct the building with great skill—not because the city lacked buildings, but because he sought to destroy the people who enjoyed divine favor.

The people increase while being oppressed; while he thinks they are being diminished, they grow daily. He pursues them all the more, as though he could conquer those whom divine majesty had foretold would be victorious.

2. The Same Argument Continued

In the midst of these events he ordered midwives to be summoned. He commanded that if male children were born to Hebrew women, they should be killed, while the female sex should be preserved. O extravagant boldness of madness! Punishment is commanded against those not yet born, and danger is stirred up before life has begun.

Restrain your madness, wicked man. You pursue those whom you do not yet see—what could be more criminal? You kill those not yet born. Let your savagery keep the proper order: let those whom you will punish be born first.

Yet the midwives brought about the delivery. They refused to carry out for destruction what they had learned to do for salvation, saying that Hebrew women gave birth more easily than Egyptian women. Nor are the services of midwives necessary for those to whom God comes to free souls. O great ingenuity of humanity, and pious falsehood for the sake of salvation! The midwives feared God so greatly that they disregarded the king’s commands and preserved the women’s wombs.

But unbelieving Pharaoh turned to another means of inflicting harm, so that what he had previously attempted in secret he might make public among the people. He ordered every male Hebrew child to be killed. When rumor carried this to the ears of the mothers, the sky was struck with their lamentations. As the children were torn from the very breasts and carried off to death, a grief surpassing the pain of childbirth followed.

Yet no mother was more unfortunate than the one who was more fertile. All wished rather to be barren than to bear children. Why do you rage in impious madness? Why do you savagely rage? Although you inflict bitter deaths upon countless innocents and cruelly consume the souls of the wretched, your guilt for slaughter is increased, and the desert of punishment is not diminished.

3. The Mystical Meaning of Moses’ Name

As the little bodies of infants were being cast everywhere into the river, a human hand received Moses, whom they were seeking as the cause of vengeance upon the whole people. When Pharaoh’s daughter sought bathing in the flowing water on the verdant, trembling bank, she found him in a little chest—a child whom his father could not destroy by execution.

His mother was brought to nurse him (Exod. II, 5). Opportunity for feeding joined affection, which the king’s fear had separated. A new kind of miracle occurred: the daughter of a parricide performed an act of mercy. While unknowingly preserving the infant, she unwittingly deceived her father.

It was fitting that he who had forbidden mothers to give birth should perish through the provision made by his daughter. Divine vengeance proceeded fittingly, so that he might be punished through his own affections, and Moses might be drawn out in order to draw others out.

Finally, Moses received his name from the waves in mystical language, and in the river of the sea he found Pharaoh’s death, which Pharaoh had prepared in his name. Here, through the working of the staff, he displays steps through the middle of the waves as though across dust; by command he raises the suspended water high like mountains, so that he might bring God’s people safely through.

4. He Orders the Hebrew Male Children to Be Cast into the River

You have heard the impious and most cruel command of hard-hearted Pharaoh: “Cast the males into the river; keep the females alive.” The enemy orders the little ones to be cast into the river; he orders the innocent to be killed by a cruel death. He does not forbid birth, while decreeing that those born should be killed.

Nature had not yet granted those whom the sentence already holds for punishment the ability to live. O new and unheard-of cruelty! Judgment is carried out before the accused himself is condemned; sentence is pronounced before the one liable to sentence has been shown guilty. It is customary, of course, for the accused to await the sentence for his guilt. No accused person can be condemned before his fault has begun to be revealed.

But these children were neither born guilty nor handed over to the sentence for any deserved crime. They were born not to receive the fruit of life and salvation, but so that there would be those whose murder by cruelty would make the world mourn.

Now you command what you ought to have punished. Neither the tenderness toward the newborn nor the parents’ grief moves you, as you rejoice to fulfill your savage decree amid the death of infants and the sorrow of their parents.

O cruel wishes of parents, whose joy has been changed into mourning! Whatever proceeded from their happiness served the crime. The most joyful enemy rejoiced amid the tears of all.

How many prayers of the grieving perished? How many tears were poured out in vain? How many sighs and wailings of the multitude arose when parents saw their children exposed by their own hands, although they would shortly have done something similar anyway? Some saw their own fate in the fate of others. Some, holding their children when they could no longer hide them, exposed them; others exposed them immediately after birth, lest the longer they held them, the more cruelly they should release them.

How many wished to die for their children? How many wished to disregard the tyrant’s sentence? “Let us satisfy him,” they said, “and fill his savagery with our grief.”

5. The Just Striking of the Egyptian Firstborn

Egypt is struck through affection for its firstborn, so that the Egyptians might learn from their own experience how great is the grief of children, since they had killed the children of the Hebrews. Egypt, I say, is struck through affection for its firstborn, and a funereal cry arises.

No dignity excused anyone, nor did anyone’s condition escape the oppression. Neither the slave was spared for service nor the master for command. The king was not excused by honor, nor was the poor man exempted by necessity.

The Hebrews stood unharmed while vengeance prevailed. They were made joyful not only by their own salvation but even more by the plague upon their enemies. They departed joyfully; they departed safely, invincible under the Lord’s protection.

Then Pharaoh repented that he lived, and his great crimes would not allow him to remain escaped. Since he had amended none of his guilt through such great plagues, he sought the punishment that was fitting.

He yoked his chariots, prepared his army, and drew up his battle line. No one was left who deserved to be saved. The Hebrews were enclosed by the pursuing Egyptians between the sea and their enemies, between waves and swords. On one side the sea foamed; on the other weapons flashed. Here there was the roar of waters; there, the clamor of arms.

Thus God is accustomed to act for his own: when human counsel fails, divine assistance intervenes.

6. God Provides Wonderfully for His Own

When the people saw these things, they were terrified and afraid. When they saw the swift currents of the sea flowing toward the shores, and the waters, driven by the wind and colliding with one another, opening out, they all soon cried out to the Hebrew leader:

“While we wish to be free from Pharaoh’s rule, we have encountered danger; and when we refuse to serve willingly, we have reached peril. You present the evils that you have until now promised us, and you do not understand yourself to be the author of our destruction, while you fail to recognize that you have exposed us to such great evils.”

The most holy Moses said to them: “Do not be afraid, men. Be armed with faith. Believe the word that you will experience fulfilled; believe that your victory is already hastening, and that the raging nation is approaching destruction.

“Because the winds do not agree, the masses of water are held back in unfinished currents, so that they may not punish your enemies before they are commanded to do so.”

Immediately, at the divine command and by a blow of the staff, the sea was split, and, with its waters divided, it displayed fields unknown to nature. With the waters gaping open, the waves revealed the sea’s hidden depths and secrets. The sea was raised into a heap, and the suspended waves appeared like walls.

A shore came into being where the sea had been, and a road stretched in a straight line where the Lord’s people were to walk in wonder. When the Lord’s people saw these things, they understood that everything had been done for their sake, and they entered fearlessly at the divine command.

“He walked safely,” Scripture says, “invincible because the Lord was fighting.” Pharaoh’s army followed, destined to perish through the punishment of the waters. He thought he could fight there, though there he alone with his men was destined to perish.

Thus the Lord spoke to Moses: “Now the destruction of Egypt has arrived. Those whom I wished to destroy I have determined to remove through this punishment. Let the sea return to its former state, so that it may bring salvation to the just and destruction to the unjust.”

Immediately, at the divine command, the Egyptians were swept away in a violent rush; crushed by the collapse of the waters, they were cast upon the shore as the waves rolled over them. The Egyptians were dead before the Hebrews reached safety. Such vengeance was due, so that he who refused to pursue salvation might perish the sooner.

SERMON XXIV  
[Note: [Col. 1791] Also known as On Time 90.]  
On the Journey of Three Days. Exodus VIII  
[Note: [Col. 1791] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. Most of it is drawn from Origen, extracted from his Homilies on Exodus. For section 1 see his Homilies 5 and 3; for sections 2 and 3, Homily 3; for sections 4 and 5, Homilies 3 and 6.]

1. The Crossing of the Red Sea, a Figure of Baptism. Triple Immersion

In the divine readings recited to us on the preceding days, we heard Moses say to Pharaoh: “We shall go a journey of three days into the wilderness with all the people, to sacrifice to the Lord.” Let us see, dearest brothers, what Moses meant when he said: “We shall go a journey of three days into the wilderness, and we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God.” Moses indeed wished this, but Pharaoh opposed him and did not wish the children of Israel to depart far from him.

The ruler of this world did not wish the Lord’s host to know the sacraments of the three days—those sacraments of which the prophet said: “After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. VI, 3). The first day is the passion of the Lord and Savior; the second, that on which he descended into hell; the third is the day of the resurrection. Therefore God went before them on the third day, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire; and the people are led through the Red Sea.

We may also fittingly call the three days the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because the Father is day, the Son is day, and the Holy Spirit is day; and these three are one day. The journey of three days by which one departs from Egypt is rightly understood to be he who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6), because no one comes to the Father except through him. He is the way by which the people joined to God are led out of Egypt—that is, out of the observance of idols—and are rescued through the Red Sea, made red by Christ’s blood and already, as it were, consecrated at that time in mystery, as through the sacrament of Baptism, Pharaoh having been submerged.

And this is truly so, brothers. When Christians are immersed three times in the saving font, then the Egyptians—that is, original sins or actual crimes—are buried as it were in the Red Sea; and, while the children of Israel pass over into God’s service, sins alone suffer shipwreck. If anyone doubts and thinks that not all sins are wiped away by Baptism, let him know and understand that, just as not one of the Egyptians remained, so absolutely nothing of sins remains.

2. The Voiceless Cry of the Saints

But before the Red Sea was crossed, Moses cried out to the Lord. How does he cry out? No voice of his crying is heard, and yet God says to him: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15). I should like to know how the saints cry to God without a voice. The Apostle teaches: “God gave the Spirit of his Son in our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6). And elsewhere: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings”; and again: “He who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God” (Rom. VIII, 26–27). Thus, with the Holy Spirit inspiring, the cry of the saints is heard by God in silence.

[Note: [Col. 1792] In Origen: “Thus, with the Holy Spirit interceding with God.”]

3. The Mystery of the Cross in the Rod. Who Destroys the Spiritual Egyptian

After this Moses is commanded to strike the sea with the rod (Exod. XIV, 16). Recognize in the rod the mystery of the holy cross. It is true, brothers: observe and see that unless the rod is raised over the sea, God’s people are not delivered from Pharaoh’s power. So it is, dearest brothers. Unless the holy cross had been raised, the Christian people would have perished forever. But when the rod is raised—that is, when the cross is erected—the sea gives way, and its waves give way also: that is, the world and the powers of this world are conquered.

The wave is compelled into a heap, and the water, held back within itself, is bent. The liquid receives solidity, and the sea-bed dries into dust. Understand the goodness of the Creator. If you obey his will and follow his law, he compels even the elements themselves to serve you against their own nature. Let us therefore pray, dearest brothers, that what our Lord did to the Egyptians in the Red Sea, he may do in our heart and body: that he may grant us the power and help of the Holy Spirit, so that we may be able to destroy the spiritual Egyptians within ourselves.

For he destroys the spiritual Egyptian who does not perform works of darkness. He destroys the Egyptian who lives not carnally but spiritually. He destroys the Egyptian who either drives filthy and impure thoughts from his heart or does not receive them at all, as the Apostle also says: “Taking up the shield of faith, by which we may extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one” (Eph. VI, 16). In this way we too may today see the Egyptians dead and lying on the shore, their chariots and horses submerged. We may also see Pharaoh submerged if we live with such faith that the God of peace may quickly crush Satan under our feet.

4. What Is Meant by the Journey of Three Days

The journey of three days may also be understood as thinking well, speaking well, and doing well. Indeed, one who does this and guards it with all the strength of the mind walks not in night but in day, and becomes not a child of darkness but a child of light. In him is fulfilled what the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Eph. V, 8).

When were we darkness, brothers? Certainly when we walked the ways of night: when we thought evil, spoke evil, and also did evil. But after coming to Christ, let us through his grace leave behind the works of darkness, and, by thinking well, speaking well, and doing well, hasten to run the way of light. These, then, are the three ways by which one reaches heaven; just as there are three other ways by which lovers of the world reach hell: namely, thinking evil, speaking evil, and doing evil. This is the broad and spacious way that leads to destruction. By these ways the rich man clothed in purple descended into hell; by those other ways Lazarus deserved to reach Abraham’s bosom.

The enemy besieges these three ways, as we read concerning Pharaoh’s army: “He submerged in the Red Sea three chosen charioteers standing [there]” (Exod. XV, 4, according to the LXX).

5. The Same Argument Continued

Who are these chosen charioteers? Those chosen by the devil for lust, malice, and pride, the head of all evils. These, then, standing three by three, besiege these three ways, so that one may overthrow a person into evil works, another may draw forth an evil word, and another may force out a wicked thought.

But blessed is the one who, with God’s help, avoids all these three ways and throughout the whole three days departs from Pharaoh’s company, so that the prince of darkness may take no day from him or turn the brightness of his faith into night. Therefore, brothers, let us do what is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV, 23). With God’s help let us consider and guard both our heart and our consciences. If there is anyone among us into whom one of the princes of darkness has injected an evil thought, let him labor as much as he can not to sin even in speech. That is, if the devil has taken one day from him and turned it into night, let him at least be unable to gain possession of the second day.

But if by his most subtle cunning he has obtained even this, so that we think evil in our heart and speak it with our mouth—if we have already lost two days—let us, with God’s help, preserve at least one day, lest the enemy’s wickedness overthrow us as far as evil deeds also. And if this too has happened, nevertheless let us not despair of mercy; but let us hasten quickly through repentance to shake from the feet of our soul the mud of the dregs. For the Lord does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Yet let us turn in such a way that we do not look back again or repeat the evil deeds that we have done; nor let us return like a dog to its vomit. Rather, striving toward our precious and desired homeland, let us arrive at the kingdom by the way of good works, through the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON XXV  
[Note: [Col. 1793] Also known as On Time 91.]  
On Bitter Water and Manna. Exodus, chapters XV and XVI  
[Note: [Col. 1793] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It was transcribed from Origen’s Homilies on Exodus, except for very few words, together with the conclusion and preface. In the manuscripts the preface begins thus: “Yesterday, dearest brothers, when the divine reading was read, we heard that the children of Israel after the crossing,” etc.]

1. Bitter Water, the Letter of the Law

In the reading to be read to us at Mass, dearest brothers, we shall hear that after crossing the Red Sea the children of Israel came to Marah, that is, to bitter water; and the people could not drink the water because it was bitter. For this reason the Lord showed the blessed Moses a piece of wood, and he cast it into the water, and it became sweet.

[Note: [Col. 1793] From this point, Origen.]

It is very remarkable that God showed Moses the wood that he was to cast into the water and make it sweet—as though God could not have made the water sweet without wood, or Moses did not know wood, so that God had to show it to him. But we must see what inner beauty the meaning contains in these things. The Red Sea signified the sacrament of Baptism; the bitter water signified the letter of the Law. For if the Law is received according to the letter, it is quite bitter. How could that which kills not be bitter, as the Apostle says: “The letter kills” (II Cor. III, 6)? What could be so bitter as for a child to receive the wound of circumcision on the eighth day and for tender infancy to endure the hardness of iron? Such a draught of the Law is bitter, indeed exceedingly bitter, so much so that God’s people—not that people baptized into Moses in the sea and in the cloud, but the people baptized in spirit and water—cannot drink from this water. They cannot even taste the bitterness of circumcision, cannot endure the bitterness of sacrifices, nor the observance of the Sabbath. But if God shows the wood to be cast into this bitterness, so that the water of the Law becomes sweet, the Christian people can drink from it.

## [Col. 1794] 2. The wood by which the bitter Law is sweetened is wisdom

What is this wood that the Lord showed? Solomon demonstrates it when he speaks of wisdom, saying that it is “a tree of life to all who embrace her” (Prov. III, 18). If, then, the wood of Christ’s wisdom is introduced into the Law, and shows us how circumcision is to be understood spiritually, how the Sabbaths are to be understood, and how the Law is to be observed, then the bitter water becomes sweet, and the bitterness of the Law is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding; and then the people of God can drink from it.

Therefore, so that bitter water may be drunk, God shows the wood that is to be cast into it, so that whoever drinks from it may not die and may not feel its bitterness. Hence it is clear that if anyone wishes to drink from the letter of the Law without the tree of life—that is, without the mystery of the cross, without faith in Christ, and without spiritual understanding—he will die from its excessive bitterness. Knowing this, the Apostle Paul said that “the letter kills”: that is, he plainly said that bitter water kills if it is not changed into sweetness through the Spirit. The wood, therefore, is cast into the water so that it may be changed into sweetness.

This is true, brothers. The bitterness is removed from the water when the wood of the cross is joined to the sacrament of Baptism.

## 3. Manna began to be given on the Lord’s Day. Manna is the word of God. How it is to be eaten

And observe this also, brothers: on the Jews’ Sabbath God never caused manna to rain at all, nor did the Jews deserve that grace should descend to them from heaven on their Sabbath. But on our Lord’s Day manna not only always comes; its coming also began on that very day. Therefore the Lord always rains manna upon us from heaven.

For these words that have been spoken to us are heavenly utterances, and the words recited to us descend from God. Therefore, since we receive such manna, manna is always given to us from heaven. Hence the wretched Jews are to be mourned and lamented, because they do not deserve to receive manna as their fathers received it: they never eat manna. For they cannot eat that which is small like coriander seed and white like frost.

The wretched Jews perceive nothing small, nothing subtle, nothing spiritual in the word of God; rather, everything is fat, everything coarse. “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Matt. XIII, 15). The question contained in the name itself also signifies the same thing. For *manna* is interpreted, “What is this?” See whether the very force of the name does not summon you to learn, so that when you hear the Law of God being read in church, you always ask and say to the teachers, “What is this?” For this is what manna indicates.

Therefore, if you wish to eat manna—that is, if you desire to receive the word of God—know that it is small and exceedingly subtle, like coriander seed. For it contains something of a vegetable, by which it can nourish and refresh the weak, because “let the weak person eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV, 2). It possesses something of rigor, and therefore is like frost. But it possesses an abundance of whiteness and sweetness. For what is whiter, what more radiant than divine instruction? What is sweeter or more pleasant than the Lord’s utterances, which are “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. CXVIII, 103)?

## 4. What it means to gather twice as much on the sixth day. Worms from the manna

But what does it mean when he says that on the sixth day twice as much is to be gathered and stored, enough even for the Sabbath? According to our understanding, we must not pass over this idly or carelessly; rather, through almsgiving we must store up enough to suffice also for the coming day.

For if you acquire any good work here, if you store up any justice, mercy, or piety, this will be food for you in the age to come. The Apostle also admonishes us concerning this, saying: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. VI, 8).

What, then, are we doing, when we love to store up what will decay, rather than what will remain and endure until tomorrow—that is, in the age to come? The avaricious and greedy rich [Note: [Col. 1794] In Origen: “the rich of this age”; he does not have “avaricious and greedy.”] store up those things that will decay in this age—or rather, together with this age. But those who store up good works preserve them until tomorrow. Accordingly, it is written that those who were faithless “kept” some of the manna, and worms boiled out of it, and it became rotten. But what was stored up for the Sabbath did not decay, nor did worms boil out of it; rather, it remained whole.

You, too, therefore, if you hoard only for the sake of the present life and out of love for this age, worms immediately boil out. Hear, then, what the prophet says concerning sinners and those who love the present age: “Their worm,” he says, “will not die” (Isa. LXVI, 24). These are the worms generated by avarice. These are the worms generated by the blind greed for riches in those who possess money and, while seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts to them.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Command those who are rich in this present age not to be proud, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but to be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing, and storing up for themselves the true life” (I Tim. VI, 17–19).

## 5. For the sinner the word of God becomes a worm

But someone may say: If you say that manna is the word of God, how does it produce worms?

It is true, brothers: worms arise in us from nothing other than the word of God. For he says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV, 22). But after receiving the word of God, whoever sins finds that very word becoming a worm for him, continually gnawing at his conscience and eating away at the secrets of his heart.

## 6. The word of God tastes to each person as he wishes

Let us therefore now hasten to receive the heavenly manna. For this manna gives each person whatever taste he wishes in his mouth. Hear the Lord also saying to those who approach him: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. VIII, 13).

Therefore, if you receive the word of God preached in the church with complete faith and complete devotion, that very word will become for you whatever you desire. For example, if you are troubled, it consoles you, saying: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L, 19). If you are rejoicing in prosperity, it increases your future joys for you, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Ps. XXXI, 11). If you are angry, it calms you, saying: “Cease from anger and abandon indignation” (Ps. XXXVI, 8). If you are in pain, it heals you, saying: “The Lord heals all your diseases” (Ps. CII, 3). If poverty is consuming you, it consoles you, saying: “The Lord raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap” (Ps. CXII, 7).

Thus the manna of the word of God gives your mouth whatever taste you wish. Yet if anyone receives it faithlessly, and does not eat it but hides it, worms boil out of it.

Do you think the word of God should be brought to such a point that it is even thought to become a worm? Do not be troubled by hearing this. Hear the prophet speaking in the person of the Lord: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 7). For just as he himself becomes for some a ruin and for others a resurrection, so he himself now becomes in the manna sweetness of honey for the faithful, but a worm for the faithless.

## 7. Let us devote ourselves persistently to divine reading

And therefore, dearest brothers, let us, as far as we can with God’s help, devote ourselves persistently to divine reading, so that we may deserve to recognize the Law of God spiritually; so that the word of God may not become for us a worm that continually accuses and afflicts our consciences; but so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103)!

This is the grace that we pray God, in his goodness, may deem worthy to grant us—to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXVI

[Note: [Col. 1795] Elsewhere, *On Time* 93.]

## On Raphidim, the struck rock, and Amalek

Exod. XVII

[Note: [Col. 1795] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It contains almost nothing apart from allegories and words that are for the most part Origen’s own, from the eleventh homily on Exodus. In what the author says after Origen in no. 5—namely, that when the Israelites were fighting the Amalekites Moses did not extend his hands but merely raised them—Augustine dissents, *Sermon* 352, no. 6, and *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 30.]

## 1. What it means to come from the desert of Sin into Raphidim

“Everyone,” says the Apostle, “who wishes to live devoutly in Christ suffers persecution” (II Tim. III, 12), and is attacked by enemies. Therefore, as each person travels the road of this life, with Christ’s help he must be constantly armed and must always stand in the camp.

If, then, you also always wish to keep watch, so that you may know yourself to be serving as a soldier in the Lord’s camp, observe what the same Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (ibid. II, 4).

If you serve in such a way that you are free from worldly affairs and always keep watch in God’s camp, then what we heard a little earlier is said of you: that through the word of the Lord you should go out from the desert of Sin and come into Raphidim.

For *Sin* is interpreted as “Temptation,” while *Raphidim* means “health of judgment.” The person who comes out of temptation well, and whom temptation renders approved, is the one who comes to the health of judgment. On the day of judgment he will be saved, and health will be with the one who, in the temptation of the present life, never murmuring against God, has not been wounded at all.

As we read in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise” (Apoc. II, 7). Therefore the person comes to the health of judgment who, hearing another’s case well, orders his words in judgment and does not accept gifts against the innocent [Note: [Col. 1796] Origen has: “who orders his words well in judgment. What, then, ...”].

## 2. The many kinds of thirst

What, then, does Scripture recall in what follows? “The people thirsted there for water,” it says, “and murmured against Moses” (Exod. XVII, 3).

It may perhaps seem superfluous that it says the people thirsted for water. For when it had said, “The people thirsted,” why was it necessary to add “for water”? Thus the ancient translation has it. Why did it add this, unless because the person who ought to thirst for righteousness thirsted for water? “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V, 6). And again: “My soul thirsted for the living God” (Ps. XLI, 3).

For there are many kinds of thirst. The righteous thirst, and sinners also thirst: the former for righteousness, the latter for luxury; the righteous thirst for God, sinners thirst for gold. Therefore the people thirsted for water, though they ought to have thirsted for righteousness.

## 3. Christ is the rock struck, which brought forth springs. Whoever declares war on the devil

The Lord therefore said to Moses: “Take the rod and strike the rock, so that it may bring forth water for the people.”

Behold, there is a rock, and it has water. But unless this rock is struck, it has no water at all; once struck, however, it produces springs and rivers, as we read in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

For Christ, when he was struck and fastened to the cross, brought forth the springs of the New Testament. It was therefore necessary for him to be struck. For unless he had been struck, and blood and water had flowed from his sacred side, the whole world, suffering thirst for the word of God, would have perished [Note: [Col. 1796] In Origen: “we would all have suffered thirst for the word of God.”].

Moses therefore struck the rock with the rod twice. What does this mean, brothers? I do not think this is without a mystery. What does it mean that the rock was struck by the rod not once but twice? The rock is struck a second time because two pieces of wood are erected on the cross: on one piece of wood he spread out his sacred hands, while on the other he extended his immaculate body from head to feet.

The people therefore drank from the rock, and immediately entered into battle against Amalek. See, brothers, that after anyone has drunk water from the rock—that is, after he has received Christ’s sacraments—he must proceed to battle. No one will feel the devil fighting against him so long as he wishes to practice the devil’s works. But whoever abandons him and chooses to follow Christ, drinking from the rock, must necessarily endure the hostility of the one to whom he has chosen, by a just judgment, to prefer Christ.

Therefore whoever is joined to Christ must prepare himself not for delights or pleasures but for battle, because “everyone who wishes to live devoutly in Christ suffers persecution” (II Tim. III, 12); and again, “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21).

## 4. The first mention of the sacred name Jesus in Scripture

As battle was therefore approaching for the children of Israel, Moses called Jesus and said to him: “Choose men for yourself and fight against Amalek.”

Up to this point no mention had anywhere been made of this blessed name, Jesus. Here for the first time the splendor of this name shone forth. Moses calls Jesus; the Law invokes Christ.

“Choose,” he says, “powerful men.” Moses could not choose powerful men. Jesus alone can choose powerful men—he, certainly, who said to his Apostles: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). He is the one who entered the house of the strong man and plundered his goods (Matt. XII, 29).

## 5. Moses raised his hands; he did not extend them. What it means to raise the hands. Victory is won through prayer

Moses climbed to the top of the hill. “And it happened that whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed.”

Observe, brothers: Moses does indeed raise his hands, but he does not extend them. For whom, then, was it reserved to extend his hands, if not for our Lord Jesus Christ, who, extended upon the cross in order to embrace the whole world, spread wide the arms of his mercy? Moses therefore raised his hands; and although he did not spread them out, by that very raising he displayed the mystery of the cross.

See, brothers, that even then, through the sacrament of the cross, hostile nations were overcome. And we, dearest brothers, if, with the Lord’s help, we raise our hands, overcome the devil.

By “hands” we must understand works. If, then, your works are such that you can raise them on high in the Lord’s presence, you too can destroy your adversaries within yourself. Who raises his hands well except the one who continually stores up treasure in heaven through almsgiving? Who raises his hands well except the one who constantly supplies the poor with food and clothing?

Who raises his hands well? Certainly the one who fulfills the Apostle’s command: “Raising holy hands without anger or disputation” (I Tim. II, 8).

Since battle against hostile powers confronts us and you every day, if we wish to conquer, our hands—that is, our actions and our manner of life—must not be on earth; rather, as the Apostle says, “while walking upon the earth, let us have our manner of life in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

It is nevertheless written: “As a calf licks up green grass in the fields, so Israel’s people will lick up Amalek on the earth” (Num. XXII, 4). This seems to indicate that the people of God [Note: [Col. 1797] Here Origen adds: “as we have received from our elders.”] fought not so much with hand and weapons as with voice and tongue—that is, they poured out prayer to God—and therefore overcame their adversaries.

Therefore, if you also wish to conquer, hear the Apostle saying: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Col. IV, 2). This is the Christian’s most glorious battle: not to presume upon his own strength, but always to implore God’s help—to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXVII

[Note: [Col. 1797] Formerly, *On Time* 97; later, in the Appendix 39.]

## On the children of Israel

[Note: [Col. 1797] It is found among Augustine’s sermons in Amerbach and Erasmus, but among the spurious works at Louvain. In wording and style it differs little or not at all from the third, seventh, and twenty-third sermon of this Appendix.]

## 1.

“The Lord says this to Moses: ‘Leave me, so that I may make you into a great nation’” (Exod. XXXII, 10).

It is a grave matter to examine the person who falls into unbelief while losing the greater thing he had received. Which Jew does not know the insoluble knots [or: “inextricable difficulties”]? Who does not lay aside treachery and presumption? They read their own eulogies, that vengeance had not been absent in the transgression of their ancestors. Angry severity is brought forth, yet obstinacy is not corrected; mercy is less harsh in anger, because it pities more quickly.

The judgment belongs to him, both to prove what is worthy and to pardon sin in those who offend. What am I saying? Did God abhor them, or did he love them? Far from it. If he abhorred sinners, he despised them; but he loved them, and therefore frequently forgave them. “Return to me,” he says, “and I will return to you” (Mal. III, 7).

Their crimes are indeed present—either in a guilty tongue or in a criminal conscience. “You are from your father the devil,” he says (John VIII, 44). Vengeance cannot be deferred; punishment will not be postponed. For the crimes conceived through usurpation are so great that they do not spare the race, since they seem guilty along with their author.

“They cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted” (Ps. CVI, 6); a leader is sent who would restore the Israelite people to freedom. Plagues worthy of the Egyptians and beyond number are prepared as a disgrace: gnats advance for vengeance, the caterpillar takes possession of the vineyards, the locust devastates the fruit-bearing trees; terror and hail, ulcers, tumults, cries, flames, cattle struck down, herds prostrated, waters changed into blood, frogs laid low, fish killed.

The elements are hardened by no severity; streams are dried up, bent into this miraculous event, and the water is suspended like a wall. The waves marvel at the unfamiliar path, and the people also marvel.

## 2.

Why do you despair at night, unbelieving people? The pillar that Christ illumines will be a sign for you. Go confidently along the road you have undertaken; Christ will go before you. And because Christ accompanies you, there ought to be confidence, not terror. You will reach the promises securely—if only you do not rebel.

The Egyptians enter the sea openly, but the waves surrounding them rush upon them and destroy them. The sand of the sea’s midst felt the hoof; the sea halted the course of the horsemen. But this vengeance was deserved, so that the one who had refused to pursue salvation might perish all the sooner.

Why do you doubt concerning the enemy? Go forward yourself now; you will see him dead and prove him to be finished, the one whose slave you had previously been.

## 3.

They go out into the wilderness, and the insult is not delayed. They murmur; they ask for onions and melons, rightly tasteless people whom no seasoning of grace makes agreeable; they seek cheap food.

He says “onions,” so that tears might be wrung from them—tears gathered from their offense. The nature of the waters in the rivers did not degenerate; bitterness had darkened the common liquid. The wood is cast in, and sweetness is restored.

The struck rock supplied drink to the thirsty through the rod; nor were their age-worn garments torn apart; manna was not lacking in the sterile field. They ask for a savoury dish, and everything is supplied to their desires. Each person tasted whatever he wished in his mouth while he ate.

## 4.

They ask for something to worship—and would that they had asked simply. But the people who had received the marriage documents under the law of the husband make arrangements for corruption and think about adultery.

Why, unbelieving one, do you wish to join yourself to an unsuitable partner? Your mother displeased you; she was dismissed by a bill of divorce, as Isaiah declares (Isa. L, 1). Nor are you worthy of the highest grace, since by your detestable deeds you appear ungrateful.

“You shall not serve,” he says, “a foreign god” (Deut. VII, 16). Gold is placed in the fire, and the ungrateful seek an ill-fated crime: they worship the image that the blazing fire had cast out.

Where is what was commanded: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (ibid. VI, 4)? Where was your calf when Christ was preparing roads for you in the sea, opening the sea, supplying drink to the thirsty, and restoring those exhausted by fasting?

The licentious Gentile world seeks play after satiation. “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6). Would that these things had been spoken in words and not committed in deeds!

Behold, now father Abraham is transferred into a great nation. Behold what crime the firstborn commits, and what grace the second deserves. You sold me your birthright; through your sin you became a little servant to your brother. An alien root indeed carries me, but new grace makes my head flourish.

The Lord therefore presented himself as leader to an ungrateful people; the army of Christ was not disturbed by an unfamiliar journey through inaccessible places and the trackless wilderness of the earth. Thus, while the devil attacked, profane temptation arose; suddenly the people became ungrateful for divine benefits. Their mind turned away from the truth; they abandoned the giver of life and followed the author of death.

Whence comes the blind folly—or rather, the intolerable madness—of those who worship images: to think that a calf fashioned by mortal hands is divine? The indignity of the matter is all the more bitter because the form of an animal is made an object of terror, and although God subjected all animals to humanity, humanity itself voluntarily cast itself into the service of beasts.

Thus the calf is fashioned, gilded by the contributions of fools. No natural movement bent it in any direction, yet the madness of the faithless, with necks bowed beneath it, carried it. No hearing penetrated its ears, nor did any perceptible motion stir them; nevertheless the foolish prayer of the senseless people struck them in vain. It had no eyes with which the artisan’s fantasy, through moving eyelids, could give it the vital motion of sight, nor had mother nature bestowed such sight upon it; yet the ungrateful, seeing it, worshiped it as suppliants before God.

A calf without spirit went before the people in the wilderness, so that a mad people might use such a leader as it had itself become through its sins.

## 5.

And so that the example of so great an evil might not spread to posterity without vengeance, the guilty are immediately punished. For when a limit is imposed on evils, the license of sinners is broken. Discipline is frequently corrected through punishments when the exhortations of the righteous accomplish nothing; vengeance restrains people from damnable deeds when God’s benefits cannot keep them in good works.

For if divine judgment did not intervene at the first falls of sinners, but postponed the arrival of punishment for the future, then without doubt the boldness of all wicked people would have spread more widely.

Therefore, if you wish the discipline of your own people to prosper, exercise judgment. Where concern for God’s future vengeance is present, either sin does not occur or it occurs more slowly. For sometimes people accept punishment under judgment, so that many may be corrected through the few, lest afterward, angered, he begin to rage against many.

Frequent laughter corrupts morals and also relaxes the sinews held tight by strictness; but a severe countenance is the guardian of discipline. For if you frequently indulge those who offend, the sinner does not advance toward salvation.

# SERMON XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1799] Elsewhere, *On Time* 100.]

## On the spies and the cluster of grapes

[Note: [Col. 1799] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors left the matter doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious; we judge it to be Caesarius’s.]

## 1. Two men carrying the grape cluster: the two Testaments and the two commandments. Christ in the midst of the two Testaments

When the divine reading was being read just now, we heard that at the time when the twelve spies were sent to inspect the promised land, two of them carried a grape cluster of extraordinary size on a pole to the children of Israel (Num. XIII, 24).

These two, dearest brothers, can be understood in many ways. For they are not inappropriately believed to have signified the two Testaments, and also the two commandments by which God and one’s neighbor are loved. They can also be understood historically and allegorically [Note: [Col. 1799] Perhaps *enim*, “for.”].

That they bore the type of the two Testaments we recognize clearly from this: just as the grape is said to have been presented in the midst of those two, so the Lord Christ is clearly recognized in the midst of the two Testaments, according to what is written: “In the midst of two living creatures you will be known” (Hab. III, 2, according to the Septuagint), that is, in the midst of the New or Old Testament.

But when it says “in the midst,” it must not be understood as though Christ were in the middle between the New and Old Testaments in such a way that he was contained in neither the New nor the Old. It is not so, dearest brothers. Rather, when it says, “In the midst of two living creatures you will be known,” this must be understood to mean that he is in the midst of the Old Testament and in the midst of the New—that is, within, in the inner and spiritual understanding; not in the letter, which is accustomed to kill not only Jews but also all heretics, but in the Spirit, who gives life to all Christians who understand spiritually.

This, then, is “In the midst of two living creatures you will be known”: in the inner sense of either the New or the Old Testament.

## 2. Mary is the promised land

The grape cluster was therefore presented by two men. These two who deserved to bring the grape cluster from the promised land, as we have already said, can also be understood as the two commandments of love: “You shall love God” and “You shall love your neighbor.”

Finally, consider, brothers, that just as those two men brought the hanging grape cluster, so of these two—that is, of love of God and love of neighbor—it is said: “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. XXII, 37–40).

For just as that grape cluster represented Christ God, so the promised land in which he was born appears to have prefigured the image of holy Mary. In her was fulfilled what is written: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12).

How, moreover, was blessed Mary not the promised land, since she had been promised long beforehand through the prophet? For through blessed Isaiah the Lord promised her many years in advance, saying: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14).

The grape cluster was brought from the promised land. For this is the one of whom we read: “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the solid rock” (Deut. XXXII, 13). And of this same one it is written: “The rock, however, was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4); and also: “With the fat of kidneys and the blood of the grape”; and again: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX, 11).

This grape cluster, I say, hanging on the wood, is carried by the service of two men. It is represented for us, as has already been said, by the oracles of the two Testaments. It hung upon the wood of the cross, and its wine flowed forth as the price of our redemption through the outpouring of the Passion.

[Note: [Col. 1800] The grape cluster itself, namely Christ. The same is intended by the statement below, “And of this same one it is written.” Vindingus thought this referred to Mary, but he was not a fair critic of this passage.]

## 3. The two carrying the grape cluster are the Jewish and Christian peoples. Christ is salvation to the believer and a burden to the unbeliever

It is worthwhile, however, that the hidden mysteries should be opened through the effects of events. Two men carry this grape cluster, hanging from an inserted pole. These two can also represent the Christian or Jewish people.

These, then, are the two peoples of the Synagogue and the Church. Since the Jewish people came first, the Jew goes before and the Christian follows. One carries his salvation before his eyes; the other behind his back. One displays service; the other contempt.

Therefore the Prophet also testifies concerning the Jews: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bow down their back” (Ps. LXVIII, 24). The two proceed beneath the sacred burden in their proper order: one always sees, the other always leaves it behind.

The Jew considers himself to be near, but he remains absent. The Christian, therefore, enjoys the present gift; the Jew is weighed down by the burden alone, because Christ is salvation to the believer but a burden to the unbeliever.

For he was especially announced to the Jews, concerning whom it was said: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I, 11). He became for them “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Rom. IX, 32–33); and the one whom Israel did not recognize, the faith of the Gentiles received.

Therefore this one follows afterward; but, having his hope before his eyes, he goes ahead and makes progress. The other walks first, but abandons and withdraws. The Jew indeed carries Christ in the Law, but has turned away from the grace that he carries in its mysteries. For the chosen one received him through preaching, while the unbeliever loses him in his heart; and what one person scorns in the Law, another marvels at in the body.

Thus our Lord and Redeemer is carried by one who worships him and is suspended by the other who turns away from him. And so the following was fulfilled among the Jews: “They turned their backs to me and not their faces” (Jer. XVIII, 17).

## 4. Christ’s burden lifts; it does not weigh down. Everyone is under either Christ’s yoke or the world’s

Since we, who came later, deserved to worship and carry Christ the Lord—whom the earlier Jewish people both left behind them and crucified—according to what the Apostle says, “Glorify and carry God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20), let us labor as much as we can with his help, lest by evil works we lay down from our necks so holy a burden.

For Christ’s burden is accustomed to lift, not to press down. Thus he himself also said in the Gospel: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 30). If we receive Christ’s yoke with a submissive and humble neck, it carries us more than it is carried by us.

For just as the yoke of the world always presses down, so the yoke of Christ is accustomed to lift. Since every person is either raised up by carrying Christ or pressed downward by bearing the world’s yoke, let each person examine his conscience.

If he recognizes that he is carrying Christ’s yoke through holy thoughts and good works, let him rejoice, give thanks to God, and strive to persevere with great care and fear. But whoever recognizes that he is excessively burdened by the harshest yoke of this world through licentious thoughts and evil works should cast off the devil’s yoke through prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, so that he may deserve to receive Christ’s yoke.

Let him faithfully say with the prophet concerning all his evil deeds: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us” (Ps. II, 3).

Then we shall be able to drink with a secure conscience from that spiritual grape cluster, from which the press of the cross expressed the wine of joy, if neither luxury has defiled us, nor anger burned us, nor pride inflated us, nor avarice darkened us, nor envy struck us with its viper’s poison.

For whoever desires or hopes to approach the altar must drive all these things from his heart. Since the spiritual vintage—that is, the Paschal solemnity—is approaching, on which feast that grape cluster of which we spoke above was pressed through the violence and weight of the cross, we are about to receive the cup of salvation from so great and such a grape cluster and drink the wine of joy.

Let us therefore cleanse the receptacles of our hearts and breasts with great purity and diligence through fasts, vigils, prayers, almsgiving, and especially the radiance of chastity. Let us harbor hatred toward no one in our hearts, but love not only our friends but also our enemies and adversaries. With a secure conscience let us say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXIX

[Note: [Col. 1801] Elsewhere, *On Time* 102.]

## On the fact that the older people died in the wilderness and the younger entered the promised land

[Note: [Col. 1801] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, and Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. We have no doubt at all that it is Caesarius’s. On no. 2, toward the end, see Caesarius’s Homily 11 among those edited by Baluzius; on no. 4, Homilies 23 and 4.]

### 1. The Older People of Israel Symbolize the Jews, the Younger the Gentiles. God’s Justice and Mercy toward the Israelites

We must know and understand, beloved brothers, that the older people of the Jews, who died in the wilderness because of their unbelief [Note: [Col. 1801] This sermon has the following exordium in an old manuscript: “Those forty years, dearly beloved brothers, which we have just heard about when the divine reading was being read—years during which the children of Israel dwelt in the wilderness through the long circuits of their journey—expressed the difficult and harsh labors of the human miseries of the present life. Therefore, because of the excessive sins that abound in this life, out of six hundred thousand, no more than two men entered the Promised Land, just as the Lord himself says to the unbelieving: ‘Because,’ he says, ‘you murmured against me, you shall not enter the land concerning which I swore to your fathers; but I will bring in your little ones into the land that displeased you.’ That older people, dearly beloved brothers, who died in the wilderness because of their unbelief, etc.”], signified the former people of the Jews; but their little ones—that is, the younger people—symbolized the people of the Gentiles. For just as, when the older people had died, the younger received the Promised Land, so, when the people of the Jews had been rejected, the younger people of Christians obtained the grace of divine blessing.

Nevertheless, dearly beloved brothers, we must consider with great fear and trembling that of six hundred thousand, only two entered the Promised Land. Let those, therefore, hear this who want the Lord to be merciful in such a way that they do not believe him to be [Col. 1802] just. For if we pay careful attention, brothers, our merciful God was merciful toward those six hundred thousand who had died in the wilderness, and he appeared just toward those two who entered the Promised Land.

How was he not merciful when he preserved and awaited them for forty years, giving them opportunity for repentance? They not only refused to be converted, but, frequently rebelling and murmuring against the Lord, continually added a heavier burden to the accumulation of their sins. How is he not merciful when he waits for us so long, that we may be corrected? Can such prolonged mercy take justice away from God? For the longer he waits, the more severely he punishes. When we sin for prolonged periods and suffer no evil from the Lord, this is patience, not negligence: he has not lost his power, but has reserved us for repentance. Thus he was merciful even toward those who died in the wilderness, whom he endured with such great patience; and toward those two he fulfilled his promises, bringing them into the Promised Land because of the merit of their faith.

### 2. God’s Sentence against Sinners Is Not Unchangeable. Conversion Must Not Be Postponed

Someone may say that even if they had done penance, they could not have entered the Promised Land, because God had pronounced a fixed sentence upon them, saying: “You shall not enter the land concerning which I swore to your fathers, but your corpses shall lie in the wilderness” (Numbers 14:23, 29).

It is not so, dearly beloved brothers. Would that sinful man might rise to repentance as quickly as God is willing even to change a fixed sentence! Hear the Lord himself, promising the human race the greatest hope through the prophet: “Suddenly,” he says, “I will speak against a nation, to bring evil upon them for their sins; and if it repents of its iniquities, I too will repent of the evil that I had thought to do to them, and I will not do it” (Jeremiah 26:3).

See, brothers, how great is the compassion of our God toward us; and recognize whether he wishes to deny mercy, when he had said that he would change his sentence in response to our conversion [Note: The manuscript reads: “who desires to change his sentence in response to our return.”]. Let us therefore be converted, dearly beloved brothers, and let us not wish to defer our amendment until the final moment of our life. Rather, let us hear the prophet saying: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, nor postpone it from day to day” (Sirach 5:8) [Note: Thus according to manuscript t: “Do not delay in turning to the Lord, nor postpone it from day to day.”], because “you do not know what a day may bring forth” (Proverbs 27:1).

O man, why do you postpone it from day to day, when perhaps today you will have your last day? Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us always recall with great fear and trembling that our Lord’s justice is so great that, as has already been said above, of six hundred thousand, only two entered the Promised Land.

If we wish to think constantly about these things with a humble and contrite heart, by instilling a salutary fear in ourselves we make medicines for ourselves from the wounds of others, and the death of others contributes to our salvation [Note: After the words “contributes to our salvation,” manuscript t adds: “But pay careful attention to who these two are who invite the people of the Jews to the Promised Land, or what they signify spiritually. These two signify the Old and New Testaments. For by these two guides—that is, by the New and Old Testaments—one reaches the land of the true promise, namely, eternal blessedness. Of these two Testaments we read: ‘In the midst of two living creatures you will be known.’ For although the Old and New Testaments differ in the wording in certain places, they agree in truth; and, in different modes, the two speak as one. But these two may also be understood in another way. For one ascends to the Promised Land by two guides: one reaches Christ through history and allegory, through faith and works, through love of God and love of neighbor.” And immediately it continues: “Again and again I beg you, etc.”].

### 3. The Example of God’s Severity in Punishing the Israelites Should Move Us to Repentance. Proof of Eternal [Col. 1803] Punishments

Again and again I beg and admonish you, brothers, always to consider with great fear and concern that severity and just judgment of God by which that older people was consumed in the wilderness because of the sin of its murmuring; and so to love God’s mercy that we nevertheless fear his justice.

For now he spares and remains silent, but he will not always remain silent. At present, in his ineffable compassion, he not only admonishes us but even begs us to turn ourselves away from deadly sins. Let us listen to him while he begs, lest afterward he fail to listen to us when he judges.

Let us hear him saying through the prophet: “My son, have pity on your soul by pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24). What will human frailty answer to this? God begs you to have pity on yourself, and you are unwilling. He pleads your cause before you, and he cannot obtain anything from you. How, then, will he hear you supplicating on the day of judgment, when you refused to hear him begging you on your own behalf?

Who, dearly beloved brothers, would not be terrified and afraid that, for a period of forty days, the people of the Jews deserved to receive punishment in the wilderness for forty years? If punishment must compensate for a period of one year for the guilt of a single day, then we who commit so many sins every day—unless the remedies of almsgiving or repentance come to our aid—should fear that we may receive not temporal but eternal punishments.

### 4. The Wounds of Sins Are More Easily Healed While They Are Fresh

And because medicines usually help warm wounds more quickly, whenever we sin, let us not wait with deadly complacency for the wounds themselves to putrefy, nor add wound to wound. Instead, let us immediately return to the spiritual physician and hasten to receive salvation.

Thus, just as when we receive a wound in the body, if we seek medicines at once, we can quickly recover our health, so, if you delay, the wound itself must necessarily return to health more slowly, or some disfiguring scar will remain on our body.

If we do this for the body, how much more ought we to do so for the wounds of the soul, in which we have been made according to the image and likeness of God? If we devote such care to the body, which, whether we wish it or not, must be reduced to dust, how much concern and care ought we to devote to the salvation of the soul? We should do so in order that, as the Apostle says, we may deserve to appear before the tribunal of the eternal Judge “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

Otherwise, if we come to that wedding feast torn by many wounds of sin and wrapped in the filthy rags of vices, perhaps what the heavenly Bridegroom said in the Gospel will be said to us: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” May God turn away from us what follows. When that sinner heard this and fell silent, the master of the house said: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:12–13).

Behold the sentence those will receive who are more concerned about the body than about the soul, and who think more about how their flesh may live for a very brief time in the eyes of human beings than about how their soul, adorned with good works, may attain blessedness and the likeness of the angels.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we wish to think about these matters more attentively, as I begged above, we acquire remedies for ourselves on the day of necessity. Thus, when the day of judgment comes, we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may happily come with the righteous and those who fear God to eternal rewards, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX

[Note: Otherwise, *On Time* 98.]

### On the Censers

[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was copied from Origen’s Ninth Homily on Numbers. In an old Fuliensian manuscript it is attributed to Jerome.]

### 1. The Censers Represent the Scriptures. The Bronze Censers Signify Heretics [Col. 1804]. The Usefulness of Heresies. The Ambition of Clerics Is Cut Away

Just now, brothers beloved, when the divine reading was being read, we heard that the Lord told Moses to melt down the censers in which those proud and rebellious men had offered incense, and to make them into sheets and fasten them to the altar, so that they might serve as a testimony against the rebellious and proud.

“The censers,” says the Lord, “which have been sanctified in the deaths of sinners, make into beaten sheets and surround the altar with them, because they were offered before the Lord and have been sanctified” (Numbers 16:37–38). [Note: From this point onward, the text is Origen’s.]

By this figure, then, the following seems to be indicated: these censers, which Scripture calls bronze, represent an image of divine Scripture. Heretics place a foreign fire upon this Scripture [Note: The foreign fire had been placed not in the censers discussed in Numbers 16, which were ordered to be made into sheets and fastened to the altar, but in other censers, through the error of Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10. The confusion occurs here and in Origen.], that is, by introducing a perverse meaning and an interpretation foreign to God and contrary to the truth; and thus they offer the Lord incense that is not sweet but accursed.

If, therefore, we apply these bronze censers—that is, the voices of heretics—to God’s altar, where the divine fire and the true preaching of the faith are found, the truth itself will shine more brightly through comparison with falsehood. For if, for example, I set forth the statements of the Arians or Manichaeans [Note: Origen has “of Marcion or Basilides” instead of “of the Arians or Manichaeans.”], or of any other heretics, and refute them with the words of truth and the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, as with the fire of the divine altar, will not their impiety become more evident precisely through the comparison?

For if ecclesiastical doctrine were simple and were not surrounded externally by assertions of heretical dogmas, our faith could not appear so clear and so thoroughly tested. For this reason the Catholic doctrine is besieged by the assault of its opponents, so that our faith may not grow sluggish through idleness but may be refined through many exercises.

For this reason, finally, the Apostle also said: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19). This is to say: the altar must be surrounded by the censers of heretics, so that the difference between the faithful and the unfaithful may become certain and evident to everyone.

When the ecclesiastical faith has begun to shine like gold, and its preaching has gleamed before those who behold it like silver tested by fire, then, with greater shame and disgrace, the voices of heretics will be sullied by the cheapness of dark bronze.

We have said these things about the censers of those who were condemned, which are ordered to be fastened to the altar, so that through comparison with the impious the righteous may appear more brilliant. At the same time, an example was given to posterity, so that no one, through the presumption of a proud spirit, might seize for himself the priestly office that God had not given him; rather, it should belong to one whom neither human ambition nor corrupt favor has invited, nor profane offering of gifts installed, but whom awareness of his merits and God’s will have chosen.
