[What, therefore, those proud Levites endured, who, without the Lord’s command, claimed the priesthood for themselves, is suffered by all who shamelessly attempt to thrust themselves into the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, whether through gifts or through flattery. Just as those men were burned in the body, so these are burned in the heart.] [Note: Origen does not have this passage but has several other matters in its place.]

### 2. Aaron as a Type of Christ the Mediator. What the Destroying Angel Feared

Moses therefore urges the great high priest to offer incense in the camp and to intercede for the people. “The people,” he says, “has already begun to be destroyed.” Moses saw in the Spirit what was taking place.

“Then Aaron went, to offer incense for the people, and stood between the living and the dead; and the fury of God was appeased” (Numbers 16:46–48). [Note: In Origen, this is replaced by a more extensive description of the narrative.]

If you have understood the sequence of the narrative and, so to speak, have been able to see with your eyes the high priest standing in the midst between the living and the dead, now ascend [Col. 1805] to the loftier heights of this word and see how the true high priest, Jesus Christ, taking up the censer of human flesh and placing upon it the fire of the altar—the magnificent soul, undoubtedly, with which he was born in the flesh, together with the incense that is his undefiled spirit—stood in the midst between the living and the dead and did not permit death to rage any farther.

Rather, as the Apostle says, he destroyed “the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14), so that whoever believes in Christ the high priest may no longer die but live forever.

This, then, was the mystery that the angel who was destroying the people feared, though it was to occur later and was already present in figure. He recognized the figure of the censer, the fire, and the incense, and foresaw what kind of offering was to be presented to God by him who was to be established in the midst of the dead and the living. The prefigured image saved those people at that time; but for us the very truth of salvation has come.

For that destroying angel would not have been deterred by the high priest’s garments woven of purple, linen, and fine linen. Rather, he understood that these were the garments of our singular and great high priest, the Lord and Savior, which were to come; and he yielded to those before whom the whole creation was inferior.

### 3. Who Are the Living and Who Are the Dead on the Day of Judgment?

I think that this form was fulfilled not only at the first coming of our Lord and Savior, but perhaps will also be preserved at the second. For the Son of Man will come again; and when he comes, he will undoubtedly find some dead and others alive.

Here the dead may appropriately be understood as those who are proved to be dead in their sins through the enormity of their crimes, while the living are those who have persevered in works of life [Note: Origen prefers two other interpretations of this passage.].

Nevertheless, in either interpretation this great High Priest and our Savior will stand in the future also between the living and the dead.

He may perhaps also then be said to stand between the living and the dead when he sets the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left, and says to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” But to those at his left he will say: “Go into the eternal fire, workers of iniquity, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41), because “I never knew you.”

Those who are sent into the eternal fire are certainly dead; those who are sent into the kingdom are alive. May the merciful Lord deem you worthy to lead you to that kingdom, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI

[Note: Formerly *On Time* 99; later Appendix 40.]

### On Aaron’s Rod

[Note: This is the second part of Origen’s ninth homily on Numbers.]

### 1. The Rod Belongs to Rulers

Every ruler of a tribe of the people has a rod. For no one can govern a people unless he has a rod. Hence the Apostle Paul, because he was a ruler of the people, said: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4:21).

All rulers of the tribes must therefore have their rods. But there is one alone, as Scripture says—the true high priest, whom the priest Aaron prefigured—whose rod blossomed. For just as Aaron’s rod blossomed among the people of the Jews, so Christ’s cross flourished among the people of the Gentiles [Note: In place of this, Origen has: “The high priest Aaron, whose rod blossomed. But the true …”].

Since, as we have often shown, Christ is the true high priest, he alone is the one whose rod, the cross, not only germinated but also blossomed and produced the fruits of all believing peoples.

### 2. An Allegorical Comparison of the Nut with the Law

What, then, is the fruit that it produced? “Almonds,” he says. Almonds, brothers, are nuts [Note: Origen has: “A nut, he says. What fruit …”]. The fruit is bitter in its first covering, protected and enclosed by the second, and, in the third, nourishes and feeds the one who takes it.

Such, then, [Col. 1806] is the doctrine of the Law and the Prophets in the Church of Christ. The first appearance of the letter is sufficiently bitter: it commands circumcision of the flesh, gives instructions concerning sacrifices, and includes the other matters represented by the letter that kills. Cast all these away like the bitter shell of a nut.

In the second place you will come to the protective covering [Note: Origen has “shells”], in which either moral teaching or the discipline of self-restraint is represented. These things are indeed necessary for guarding what is kept within, but at some point they must undoubtedly be broken and dissolved.

For example, abstinence from food and discipline of the body are undoubtedly necessary as long as we are in this corruptible and suffering body. But when, at death, it has been broken and dissolved, and at the resurrection the incorruptible has been restored from the corruptible and the spiritual from the animate, then no corruption will dominate the body—not through the labor of affliction or the discipline of abstinence, but by the very nature of the body itself.

Thus even now [the stricter shell of the nut, as it were, [Note: The words enclosed in brackets here and shortly below were added to Origen.]] the discipline of abstinence seems necessary, but afterward it is not to be sought.

In the third place, you will find, hidden [as it were in the nut], the secret meaning of the mysteries of God’s wisdom and knowledge, by which holy souls are nourished and fed, not only in the present life but also in the future.

This is the priestly fruit promised to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because “they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

In this way, then, the principle of this threefold sacrament runs through all the Scriptures. Thus Wisdom also urges us to write it for ourselves three times in our hearts: “To answer,” it says, “with words of truth those who put questions to us” (Proverbs 22:20–21).

Since the priestly sacrament is the rod of a nut, I therefore think that Jeremiah too, who was one of the priests from Anathoth, saw a rod of almond wood and prophesied about it the things that are written—whether concerning the almond rod or concerning the boiling cauldron or pot (Jeremiah 1:1, 11–13)—as though he were showing by these things that there is life in the almond rod and death in the boiling cauldron.

Life and death are set before our face: Christ is life in the sacrament of the nut, while the devil is death in the figure of the boiling cauldron. If you sin, you will place your portion with the boiling cauldron; but if you act righteously, your portion will be made to lie with the almond rod, together with the great high priest.

In the Song of Songs also, the bride is said to descend into a garden of nuts (Song of Songs 6:10), where she is likewise described as finding, together with the nuts, an abundance of priestly fruits, so to speak.

### 3. God’s Generosity

Pay careful attention, brothers, because God promised that one thing would occur in the rod, yet he gave many things. It is true, brothers: our Lord made this an instance of his customary practice. He always gives greater things than he promises.

“And it shall be,” he says, “that the man whom I choose, his rod shall germinate.” This alone is what God promised: that the rod of the one he chose would germinate.

But when the matter is brought to completion, so that what was promised may be shown as fulfilled, it is not said that only the one promised thing was accomplished. See how many things are brought forth. Scripture says: “Behold, Aaron’s rod germinated in the house of Levi.” This is undoubtedly the one thing that had been promised. But other things are added, and it says: “It produced leaves, brought forth flowers, and germinated almonds” (Numbers 17:5, 8).

Thus, although only germination had been promised, see how generously God gives: it produced not only a shoot but also leaves; not only leaves but also flowers; and not only flowers but also fruit.

### 4. A Figure of the Resurrection and Its Four Privileges

Let us see, then, what we can gather and contemplate from these things.

First of all, we clearly recognize in them the mystery of resurrection from the dead. For a dry rod germinates when a lifeless body begins to live again.

What, then, are the four things that will be granted to the body when it rises? “What is sown [Col. 1807] in corruption shall rise in incorruption; what is sown in weakness shall rise in power; what is sown in dishonor shall rise in glory; and what is sown an animate body shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

These are the four things that the dry rod of our body will germinate in the resurrection. But let us return to what we began to say about the rod.

### 5. Four Stages of Spiritual Life Are Outlined

We can still understand in this way the differences among the things that had germinated on the rod.

Everyone who believes in Christ first dies, and after this is reborn. Here too there is a figure: the dry rod later germinates.

The first shoot, therefore, is a person’s first confession in Christ. Secondly, it puts forth leaves when, having been reborn, he receives the gift of grace through the sanctification of God’s Spirit.

Then it produces flowers when he begins to advance, to be adorned with the sweetness of his conduct, and to pour forth the fragrance of mercy and kindness.

Finally, it also produces the fruits of righteousness, by which he not only lives himself but also gives life to others. When he has reached perfection and has brought forth from himself the word of faith and the word of the knowledge of God, and has won others [through his teaching [Note: These words, “through his teaching,” were added to Origen.]], this is to have produced fruits by which others are nourished.

Thus each individual believer germinates from Aaron’s rod, which is Christ.

These four differences are designated in other passages of Scripture as four ages, which the Apostle John comprehended in a mystical distinction in his Epistle. For he says: “I write to you, little children”; “I write to you, adolescents”; “I write to you, young men”; and “I write to you, fathers” (1 John 2:12–14).

In these he establishes not bodily ages [Note: Origen has “of bodily age”], but differences in spiritual progress, just as we have observed them represented in the germination of the priestly rod.

### 6. Christ Is One Flower and One Rod, but Becomes Different for Different People

All these things are found not so much in Aaron’s rod as in that rod which came forth from the root of Jesse, and in the flower that rose from its root, upon which the Spirit of God rested (Isaiah 11:1–2).

Nor does it seem insignificant that the rod is said to come forth and the flower to rise. Although Christ is one in substance, he becomes different for each person according to the needs of the one who is at work.

For someone who is sluggish and negligent, Christ becomes a rod for discipline; and in the rod he is said not to rise but to come forth. The useless and idle person must come forth from the state in which he does not stand rightly and pass into another state, as though compelled by a rod—that is, by severity and the admonition of stricter teaching.

But the righteous person—because “the righteous flourishes like a palm tree” (Psalm 92:12)—has Christ said to rise in him.

Thus, the one who needs blows has the rod come forth toward him; but the one who advances toward righteousness has Christ rise for him into a flower.

He rises until he produces the fruits of the Spirit, which are love, joy, peace, patience, and the remaining virtues (Galatians 5:22–23), in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII

[Note: Otherwise, *On Time* 101.]

### On the Bronze Serpent and Moses’ Rod

[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Lovanienses had left it among the Augustinian sermons without Augustine’s name; Verlino and Vindingo counted it among the spurious works. We doubt whether it should be numbered among the Caesarian sermons.]

### 1. The Bronze Serpent as a Figure of the Incarnation. Death from a Bite. The Devil Acted Justly against Adam but Unjustly against Christ. Christ Paid Adam’s Debt

In the reading that was recited to us, dearly beloved brothers, we heard that at the time when, because of the Jews’ pride and their murmuring against the Lord, the people were being destroyed in the wilderness by royal serpents—that is, basilisks—the Lord commanded Moses to make a [Col. 1808] bronze serpent and hang it on a piece of wood, so that those who had been bitten might look at it and be healed from destruction (Numbers 21:4–9).

This serpent, dearly beloved brothers, although its meaning may seem very strange, nevertheless prefigured the Lord’s incarnation. This significance might seem difficult to someone unless the Lord himself had stated it in his Gospel. For he says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14).

The bronze serpent was therefore then suspended on a pole, because Christ was to be suspended on wood. At that time, whoever had been bitten by a serpent looked at the bronze serpent and was healed. Now, however, the human race, which had been bitten by the spiritual serpent, the devil, looks at Christ by believing and is healed.

Whoever had been bitten and did not look at that bronze serpent died. So it is now, brothers: unless someone believes in Christ crucified, he is destroyed by the devil’s poison.

Then each person looked at a dead serpent in order to escape alive; now whoever wishes to avoid the devil’s poison should look upon Christ crucified.

And because death takes its name from a bite, and death came upon the human race through the bite of the ancient serpent, and death could not be overcome except by death, Christ therefore endured death, so that an unjust death might conquer a just death, and might justly free the guilty while he was unjustly killed for them.

Whatever the devil had done against Adam seemed to have been done justly against a man who had sold himself for the delight of a single tree. In Adam, therefore, as in his own servant, he claimed dominion over him as his lawful master. But in Christ’s passion, in whom he found no stain of sin, he perpetrated every evil unjustly.

Thus the Lord himself also said in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30). What does “he found nothing” mean? No sin at all.

And in the Psalms: “What I did not steal,” he says, “then I paid back” (Psalm 69:4). Thus what Adam justly owed, Christ paid by unjustly receiving death.

The one stretched out his hand toward the sweetness of the fruit; the other toward the bitterness of the cross. The one displayed the tree of death; the other, the tree of salvation. The one raised himself against God and fell; Christ humbled himself in order to raise everyone up. Adam brought death upon all, and Christ restored life to all.

Each person, therefore, looked upon the bronze serpent and was healed from the poisonous serpents. The bronze serpent placed upon the wood overcame the poisons of the living serpents; and Christ, suspended and dead upon the cross, restrained the ancient poisons of the devil [Note: Perhaps “extinguished.”] and freed all who had been bitten by him.

### 2. Why the Bronze Serpent Was Not Made of Gold or Silver

Let us consider, however, why that serpent was made not of gold or silver but of bronze.

It seems to me that this can have two meanings: one because of durability, since bronze vessels usually last longer; the other because of clarity of sound, since among all metals bronze vessels generally produce a louder ringing and carry their sound farther.

The teaching was destined not to become known only among the one nation of the Jews but to reach throughout the whole world with the clear sound of saving proclamation. Therefore that serpent was made of bronze, so that Christ’s teaching might be preached more clearly throughout the entire world, according to what is written concerning the Apostles: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4).

### 3. Those Struck by the Devil’s Poisons Should Look Faithfully toward Christ

And yet, brothers, even according to the discipline of physicians of the flesh, who prepare healing antidotes from the death of a serpent against the poisons of living serpents, it is not inappropriate that the one who desires to be freed from the poisons of living serpents should look upon a dead serpent.

We have said all these things so that all whom the poisons of the serpent—that is, of the devil and his angels—have struck may faithfully look toward Christ, who was suspended upon wood in the likeness of that bronze serpent, so that they may be able [Col. 1809] to say with the blessed Apostle Paul: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

### 4. The Mysteries of the Cross in Moses’ Rod

And because it is both sweet and beneficial to speak at greater length about the mystery of the blessed cross, if you command it, we will briefly make known to the ears of Your Charity its remaining meanings.

For what can be thought or said that is sweeter or more pleasing than the mystery of the holy cross, through which we have deserved not only to be recalled from the underworld but also to be raised into the heavens? For without any doubt, where we believe that our head, Christ, has ascended, we trust that his members will follow.

The shadow or figures of the wood of the cross were also highly effective in the Old Testament. Moses performed no sign without the sacrament of wood.

Thus, in order to perform signs and wonders in Egypt, he received a rod from the Lord, and whenever he heard divine instructions concerning the signs, he was told: “Lift up your rod” (Exodus 7:9). God certainly did not need the aid of a rod; rather, it was raised so that we might know how great was the mystery of that future wood, whose shadow had been represented by the sacrament of that rod.

When the Red Sea was to be divided, Moses was commanded to lift up the rod; and the sea, recognizing the figure of the future wood, immediately opened an unusual path for the people (Exodus 14:16–22).

When they came to the bitter water of Marah, it did not become sweet unless it received wood into itself (Exodus 15:25). This indicated that the bitterness of the Gentiles would one day be transformed by the wood of the cross into a source of sweetness.

When the people had no water to drink, the rock was struck with wood; and by grace it gave what it had not possessed by nature.

When the fierce enemy Amalek appeared, Jesus the son of Nun was ordered to hold the rod in his hand, and Moses to extend his arms in the form of a cross. Thus, through the figure of the cross, the unconquerable enemy was defeated (Exodus 17).

Elisha too was not entirely ignorant of the power of this mystical wood. When an ax-head had fallen from its handle into a pool, he brought it up from the depths by throwing wood into the river (2 Kings 6:5–7). This signified that hard hearts and iron necks of human beings, raised from the depths of error, would henceforth be subdued by the wood of the cross.

O cross, from which such a great and such a kind of fruit is plucked! The fruit of the cross is a resurrection of glory.

This fruit of the wood was truly planted beside streams of water, for Baptism is always joined to the cross. This wood gave fruit in its time: it gave fruit meanwhile in the Lord’s resurrection; and it will give fruit when he appears from heaven, the one who was seen upon earth, when he comes from above with the already-glittering sign of the cross preceding him.

Then the bodies of the buried will rise; then the saints will exult in glory; then those who now are not ashamed of the cross of their King and Lord, but rather glory in it, will rejoice in their chambers.

## SERMON XXXIII

[Note: Otherwise, *On Time* 103.]

### On Balaam and Balak

[Note: This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It presents certain fragments from Origen’s Homilies on Numbers 13 and 14, which here do not form a connected sequence; but in the Fuliensian manuscript they are sometimes gathered together more suitably, and that manuscript is fuller with many sayings drawn from the same source.]

### 1. Introduction

The reading that has been recited to us today, dearly beloved brothers, says that, when the sons of Israel had set out, they pitched their camp west of Moab, beside the Jordan opposite Jericho; and Balak son of Sephor saw this, along with all the other matters that the narrative, full of events, records about Balaam and the ass (Num. 22). The inner meaning, however, is much more demanding; and I do not know whether it is easy even to explain merely the historical statements themselves. Nevertheless, with God’s help, we shall briefly touch upon what we can.

### 2. Balaam a magician rather than a prophet

This Balaam was exceedingly famous in the practice of magic and very powerful in harmful incantations. For he had neither the power nor the art of words for blessing, but he had them for cursing. Demons are summoned for cursing, not for blessing. And so, as one experienced in such matters, he was held in high regard by everyone in the East [Col. 1810]. For unless his many experiments had gone before—unless he had often turned an armed enemy back by curses—the king would certainly not have presumed that something could be accomplished by words which could scarcely be achieved by sword and battle line.

Balak, therefore, certain of this and frequently having tested him, sent messengers to him, setting aside all military equipment and assistance, and said: “Come now, curse this people for me, because it is stronger than we are; perhaps we may be able to strike some of them and drive them from the land.” And he added: “I know,” he said, “that those whom you bless will be blessed, and those whom you curse will be cursed.”

I do not believe that the king knew that those whom Balaam blessed would indeed be blessed. Rather, it seems to me that he said this in order to flatter him: by praising and exalting his art, he would make him more ready to commit the crime.

At length the messengers came to Balaam. “The elders of Moab and the elders of Midian came,” it says, “with divining instruments in their hands.” Balaam, therefore, having taken the divining instruments—for demons were accustomed to come to him—saw the Lord present, the demons having been driven away. He came to Balaam, not because Balaam was worthy that God should come to him, but so that those who were accustomed to assist him in cursing and doing harm might be driven away.

And God said to Balaam: “Do not go with them, nor curse the people, for it is blessed.” God forbids Balaam to go and summon demons for cursing—provided, that is, that he desist from his greed. But because he persists in his desire for money, God, indulging the freedom of his will, again permits him to go.

Balaam therefore mounted the ass. An angel who was keeping watch on behalf of Israel met him—the angel of whom the Lord says to Moses: “My angel shall go before you” (Exod. 32:34). Although he was permitted to continue on his way, the ass crushed him against the road. The magician sees demons but does not see the angel; the ass, however, sees him—not because it was worthy to see an angel, any more than it was worthy to speak, but so that Balaam might be confuted and, as Scripture says in one place, “a dumb animal, speaking with a human voice, rebuked the prophet’s madness” (II Pet. 2:16).

This ass—that is, the Church—formerly carried Balaam, but now carries Christ, since she has been released by the disciples from the bonds with which she was bound, so that the Son of God might sit upon her and enter with her the holy city of Jerusalem. Thus the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, gentle, seated upon a beast of burden” (Matt. 21:5), that is, upon an ass. By the ass, he undoubtedly means believers from the Jews; and by the young colt, those from the Gentiles who believe in Christ. [Note: [Col. 1810] Up to this point from Origen’s Homily 13 on Numbers; from here, from near the end of Homily 14.]

### 3. The figures represented by Balaam and Balak

This Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “Vain People,” seems to me to represent the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people. Balak, however, whose name is interpreted as “Exclusion” or “Devouring,” is likewise to be understood as representing some hostile power of this world, which desires to exclude and devour Israel.

Let us therefore first inquire concerning Balaam himself, why in Scripture he is now presented as blameworthy and now as praiseworthy. He is blameworthy when he builds altars, places victims upon them for demons, and seeks divine responses by magical apparatus. He is culpable when he gives the wicked counsel that the people should be deceived through the women of Midian and led into the worship of idols.

Yet again he is shown to be praiseworthy when the word of the Lord is placed in his mouth, when the Spirit of God comes upon him, when he prophesies about Christ, when he announces to Jews and Gentiles the mysteries that are to come concerning Christ’s advent, when he bestows blessings upon the people instead of curses, and when he adorns the name of Israel above its visible glory with mystical expressions.

### 4. Conclusion

These few remarks, dearly beloved brothers, drawn from many possible things, may suffice for you for the present. But retain everything most carefully in your hearts, and always turn your hearts toward recognizing spiritual realities, so that, since the Lord has now revealed every prophecy to us through the Gospel, we may deserve to attain that joy which the Lord has promised to those who live piously and justly. May he grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIV

*Formerly, On Time 105.* [Note: [Col. 1811] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time.]

## How, by the Just Judgment of God, the Sons of Israel Received the Promised Land after the Canaanites Were Expelled

[Note: [Col. 1811] It was left by the Louvain editors among the Augustinian works, without Augustine’s name, as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingius rejected it as spurious. It reflects Caesarius’s style and doctrine. At its end, however, it has an addition from Sermon 343, §§9–10, on Susanna and Joseph, above, col. 1497. For §1 see Caesarius’s Homily 14 among those edited by Baluze; for §3, Homilies 10 and 23.]

### 1. The Canaanites justly expelled from their lands

In the readings that have been recited to us, dearly beloved brothers, we heard that, after Moses had died, Joshua assumed the leadership, and that, having crossed the Jordan and expelled or killed the Canaanites, he handed over their lands to the sons of Israel for possession (Josh. 1 ff.).

Whenever these readings from the Old Testament are recited, the pagans—and especially the utterly impious Manichaeans—customarily blaspheme with sacrilegious speech and say: “What justice of God was it that he violently brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt and afterward, expelling the nations of the Canaanites, handed over their lands to them for possession?”

Therefore, lest this profane complaint perhaps deceive the simple or uneducated, I wish, insofar as I can, briefly and with God’s help to demonstrate to Your Holiness the true account handed down by the ancient Fathers, and to show that our God is not only merciful but also just, and that his judgments are for the most part hidden, but never unjust.

### 2. First reason: unlawful possession. Another reason: grave offenses

Our predecessors relate that, when the sons of Noah divided the whole earth among themselves, this land called the land of the Canaanites fell by the division of the world to Noah’s elder son, namely Shem, as his possession, and that he possessed it for a considerable time. But afterward, when the Canaanite peoples increased—those descended, of course, from Noah’s son Ham, who had been cursed by his father—they came to those regions and, violently expelling their brothers, that is, the sons of Shem, possessed their land in barbarous fashion.

And because blessed Abraham is read to have been descended from Shem, his sons—that is, the Israelite people—did not seize another’s land when the Lord gave it to them; rather, they recovered their own land, which their ancestors had lost through violence.

Moreover, apart from the sin by which they had invaded another’s possession, the Canaanites were committing many abominable and unheard-of crimes, to such an extent that, when the Lord was about to overthrow Sodom and Gomorrah, he is said to have declared: “For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. 15:16). The Lord was waiting either for them to turn and do penance, or, if they refused to convert, for them, by heaping crimes upon crimes and filling up the measure of their sin, to undergo the most just sentence of God.

Since, therefore, divine judgment found them guilty in two ways—both because they had invaded another’s lands and because afterward they had committed unheard-of wickedness and crimes—they are punished by a just judgment, and the possession of their ancient fathers is restored to the Israelite people.

This, then, according to the literal sense, as we have found it in the books of the saints, we have thought should be explained to Your Charity in a rustic and simple manner that everyone might understand, so that you may have something to answer the utterly impious and sacrilegious Manichaeans. Since, as has already been said, the sons of Israel receive the land of their ancient parents, they do not take away another’s land as though by injustice.

### 3. The promised land as humanity before sin; the heart’s natural possession restored to the virtues

These events are reported according to the literal sense as having been accomplished by the just judgment of God. But since, as the Apostle says, “all these things happened to them in figure, and they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. 10:11), if you carefully attend—as you are accustomed to do under God’s inspiration—you will recognize with the clearest reasoning what these things also signify spiritually.

The promised land, which God so often says flows with milk and honey, was ourselves before Adam sinned [Note: [Col. 1812] Manuscripts: “God praises, we were.”], when there was nothing else in us except what the mercy of the Creator had bestowed. But after we all sinned in Adam, of whom the Apostle says, “All die in Adam” (I Cor. 15:22), and again, “From one came condemnation for all” (Rom. 5:16, 18), through the transgression of the first man the Canaanites had begun to possess the promised land.

For the Lord’s will had naturally assigned possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. But after Adam’s transgression, when vices grew insolent like Canaanite peoples, the holy virtues were driven from their own region—that is, from the rational understanding or mind—and the vices remained.

When, however, through God’s grace, possession of our soul is restored once more to the virtues, we shall appear not so much to have occupied another’s lands as to have recovered our own. When, with the Lord’s help, vices have been overcome by the people of the virtues fighting against them, then chastity will occupy the place in our heart that the spirit of lust or fornication had held; wisdom will possess the place seized by rage; saving and joy-filled gladness will take over the place invaded by grief that works death; humility will ennoble the place devastated by sluggish apathy or negligence; mercy will restore to its former brightness the place darkened by greed; and kindly simplicity will adorn the place struck by envy’s poison.

Thus, when each vice has been expelled, the virtues will possess their places—that is, the affections—in their opposite form. The virtues themselves are not unjustly called the sons of Israel, that is, the souls of those who see God. And when, with God’s help, they have expelled all the passions from their heart, they should be believed not so much to have seized another’s possessions as to have recovered their own lands.

### 4. Recovery occurs only through Joshua, and after crossing the Jordan, that is, Baptism

Observe also, brothers, that this is understood especially to belong to the gift of grace. It is not achieved by the good of nature, nor by the letter of the Law; for the promised land is restored to the Israelite people not through Moses—that is, through the Law of the Old Testament—but through Joshua, Moses’ successor.

For the Apostle says: “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). It was not through the letter of the Law but through evangelical grace that cruel and exceedingly wicked nations—that is, original sins or actual crimes—could be driven out from the promised land, namely, from the hearts of Christians, under the leadership of Jesus. As he himself says in the Gospel: “No one can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12:29); and again: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Just as the old Adam, by consenting to the devil, expelled us from the promised land, so, conversely, the new Adam, Christ, by resisting the devil, recalled us to our ancient homeland.

### 5. The same argument continued

Pay attention also to this, brothers: the promised land is not received unless the Jordan River is first crossed while Joshua reigns. So it is, brothers, because one reaches the spiritual promised land—that is, a pure conscience—only through the sacrament of Baptism.

Through that river Joshua caused the Israelite people to pass; afterward the true Joshua consecrated it by his Baptism. [Note: [Col. 1812] These words, “afterward the true Joshua consecrated it by his Baptism,” are absent from the editions; that they are not alien to Caesarius is clear from Sermon 44, shortly to be presented, §4. In the manuscripts they conclude the sermon with the words “who lives,” etc.]

### 6. Adversity must be endured with equanimity

These matters that we have suggested to you, dearly beloved brothers, should be spiritually ruminated upon like clean animals. It is written: “Those whom God loves, he reproves and chastises” (Rev. 3:19); and, “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests just men” (Ecclus. 27:6).

Whenever, by the Lord’s dispensation, we are permitted to suffer tribulation, or endure any adversities contrary to justice, let us bear them patiently and calmly, with the Lord’s help, because of what the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

When we are afflicted, we are chastised by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world (I Cor. 11:32). We ought to fear more if we suffer either no tribulations or only small ones in this world; for if God scourges every son whom he receives, then undoubtedly the one whom he does not scourge he does not receive.

If people endure so many labors and such grave dangers with equanimity for earthly goods, why are we sluggish for the sake of faith, the eternal treasure? Why are we timid for the sake of those riches that even shipwrecks cannot take from us? For the just man escapes shipwreck both rich and naked.

The holy Job was full of these riches. Nothing remained in his house; everything by a single blow had perished, though shortly before he had seemed wealthy. Suddenly a beggar, he sat upon a dungheap, covered with worms from head to foot. What is more miserable than this misery? What is happier than this inward happiness?

He had lost all those things that God had given; but he possessed God himself, who had given everything. “Naked,” he says, “I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord forever.”

Certainly he is poor; certainly he has nothing. If nothing remained, from what treasury are these gems of praise of God brought forth?

Afterward the tempter approached his flesh. Once everything had been taken away, he left him a tempting wife. He dismissed Eve, but that man was not Adam. And how was he found there? How did he answer his wife, who was suggesting blasphemy?

“You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job 1–2).

O man corrupt and whole! O foul and beautiful! O wounded and healthy! O sitting upon dung yet reigning in heaven!

If we love him, let us imitate him; and to imitate him, let us labor. He who has called us to the contest helps the one who struggles.

God does not watch you struggling in the arena as the crowd watches a charioteer. The crowd knows how to shout, but does not know how to help; it can prepare a crown of hay, but cannot supply strength. It is human, not God. And perhaps, while watching, it labors more by sitting than the other does by wrestling.

When God watches his contestants, he helps those who call upon him. For his athlete’s voice is heard in the Psalm: “When I said, ‘My foot is slipping,’ your mercy, O Lord, was helping me” (Ps. 93:18).

Let us not be sluggish, then, my brothers. Let us seek, ask, and knock. “The one who seeks finds; the one who asks receives, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened” (Luke 11:10). This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXV

*Formerly, On Time 106.* [Note: [Col. 1813] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In the opinion of the Louvain editors it is doubtful; in the judgment of Verlinus and Vindingius it is spurious. Our judgment, however, is that it should be ascribed to Caesarius.]

## Concerning Jesus’ Command to the People to Prepare to Cross the Jordan, and Concerning the Overthrow of the Walls of Jericho

### 1. Moses as a figure of the Law; Joshua as a figure of the true Joshua; faith in the Trinity leading to Baptism

As we have often suggested to Your Charity, dearly beloved brothers, Moses is understood to have borne not only a type of Christ but also a figure of the Law. Accordingly, on the mountain where the Lord was transfigured, Moses and Elijah spoke with him (Matt. 17:3); and in those two figures the Law and the Prophets were signified.

When Moses had died, Joshua assumed authority; and, when the Law had ceased, our true Joshua, the Lord, obtained dominion over the whole world.

That Joshua, therefore, who prefigured the Lord, came to the Jordan and said to the people: “Prepare food for yourselves for the third day” (Josh. 1:11). The third day, dearly beloved brothers, we recognize as a mystery of the Trinity.

What food, then, ought we to prepare in order to come to the third day? It seems to me that this food should be understood as faith. For faith is what Christians possess, through which one believes in the Trinity and reaches the sacrament of Baptism.

What that Joshua then said to his people, the true Joshua now says through his ministers to the Christian people. For what else does it mean to say, “Prepare food for yourselves for the third day,” than, “Receive the sacrament of the Trinity”?

After this, when the Jordan had been crossed, as though the mystery of Baptism had been completed, the people of Israel entered the promised land. It is true, dearly beloved brothers: unless someone has passed through the sacrament of Baptism, he will not see the land of the true promise, that is, eternal blessedness.

### 2. The two spies as the two commandments

Joshua nevertheless sends two spies to the city of Jericho, and they are received by a prostitute (Josh. 2). In these two men who were sent, the two commandments of the twin love are understood. For what else do those whom the true Joshua sends announce to us than that we should love God and love our neighbor?

Joshua therefore said: “Prepare food for yourselves, and be ready for the third day.” Just as then, after the food had been prepared, they came to the Jordan River on the third day, so now in the Catholic Church, after spiritual food—faith, hope, and charity—has been received, one reaches the mystery of the Trinity and the sacrament of Baptism.

### 3. The stones in the Jordan as the patriarchs; those placed in the camp as the apostles

Joshua took twelve stones and placed them in the Jordan; from the Jordan itself he took another twelve and set them in the place of the camp (Josh. 4–5). The twelve who were sent into the Jordan seem to me to have represented the patriarchs; those who were lifted out of the Jordan, however, seem to have represented the apostles.

For after Moses’ death, when the patriarchs had been buried, the apostles rose up. Thus we read in the Psalm: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17).

Thus, when the patriarchs had been buried, the apostles rose up. Joshua sends two spies because the true Joshua was going to teach how, once the older people had been buried in the desert, the younger people, under Joshua’s leadership, would be brought into the promised land.

### 4. A figure of the Jews and the Gentiles

That older people represented the Jews; the younger people represented the Gentiles. The older people, after crossing the Red Sea, are buried in the wilderness; the younger people cross the Jordan River for this purpose, that they may receive the kingdom.

It is true, brothers: no one receives the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom unless he has first crossed through the sacraments of Baptism.

Of that older people, no more than two deserved to enter the promised land; and we recognize that something was figured in those two. For, as was said above, there are two commandments of love, which invite the Christian people to receive eternal life. In the same way, those two were the ones who gave counsel to the Jewish people that, if they believed in God, they would enter the promised land successfully.

### 5. Jericho as a type of the world; the priestly trumpet

After this they came to the city of Jericho, and its walls were thrown down to their foundations by the shouting of the people and the sound of trumpets (Josh. 6).

Jericho, brothers, represented this world. For just as then the walls of that city fell when the trumpets sounded, so now the city of the world—that is, pride—with its towers, namely greed, envy, and lust, together with its peoples, that is, all evil desires, ought to be destroyed and brought to ruin by the continual preaching of priests.

Priests ought not, then, to remain silent in the church; rather, they should hear the Lord saying: “Cry aloud; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes” (Isa. 58:1).

We are commanded to cry aloud, to cry out forcefully and spare our voice, so that we may spare their salvation. “Do not spare,” he says—that is, do not spare the sinner’s iniquity, lest by keeping silent you perish [Note: [Col. 1814] Manuscripts: “Do not pass over the sinner’s iniquity in silence.” The sense is incomplete unless one adds, “lest you perish.”], and, while attending to his shame, fail to attend to his health, so that the wounds which you could have cut away by crying out may instead be nourished for the worse by your silence.

We are commanded to cry aloud; and, lest anyone say that he did not hear, or lest the priest’s voice escape anyone, we are commanded to cry out forcefully.

And, as though this itself were not enough, he added, saying: “Raise your voice like a trumpet.” You know that the sound of a trumpet is accustomed to be not so much a source of pleasure as of terror, and not so much to offer delight as to instill fear.

A trumpet is therefore necessary for sinners, one that not only penetrates their ears but also shakes their hearts; one that does not delight them by its music but chastises them by what they hear, so that it encourages the vigorous toward good deeds and terrifies the negligent because of their offenses.

For just as in battle the trumpet casts down the spirit of a fearful soldier and inflames the courage of a brave man, so the priestly trumpet humbles the mind of a sinner and strengthens the mind of the just. With one and the same sound, this exhortation, insofar as it is stronger, instills in him fear that prompts him to conquer; but insofar as it is weaker, leaves him lax toward sinning.

Such is the function of the trumpet: to scatter the deeds of those who sin and to confirm the deeds of the saints.

### 6. The walls of Jericho fall through trumpets; iniquity through preaching

Accordingly, through the priestly trumpets the walls of Jericho, which enclosed within them a sinful people, fell. No battering ram struck them; no siege engine stormed them. Rather—and this is astonishing—the priestly sound and the terror of the trumpets overthrew them.

Walls that had proved impregnable against iron were shattered by the sacred voice of the trumpets. Who would not be astonished that, at that sound, stones were split, foundations were shaken by the clangor of irrational instruments, and everything collapsed so completely that, although the victors harmed nothing with their hands, nothing stable remained among the adversaries?

Although no one touched those walls, they were nevertheless attacked from outside by the sound of the righteous and from within by the sinners. Thus, by God’s equitable judgment, they opened a way for the just and denied defense to the faithless.

There is no doubt that all these things were done in figure. For what else do we believe that the trumpets of the priests of that time prefigured than the preaching of the priests of this time, who do not cease to announce a severe judgment to sinners in a terrifying sound, to preach the mournful destruction of Gehenna, and to strike the ears of wrongdoers with a certain threatening din?

Just as then the blast of the trumpets, after the walls of masonry had been destroyed, reached the people within, so now the preaching of priests, after wicked thoughts have been destroyed, passes through to the bare soul.

And just as the sound of the sacred voice destroyed and enslaved the rebellious people, so now the priestly preaching subdues and captivates the sinful people. As blessed Paul the Apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive into obedience to Christ” (II Cor. 10:4–5).

See, then, whether the tongues of priests, according to the Apostle’s statement, are not a kind of weapon of words, by which vain thought is destroyed and swollen pride is taken captive.

Thus, as Scripture says, for seven days the walls of Jericho were surrounded by the priestly trumpets and fell. Therefore, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things (I Cor. 2:13), we say that through this number seven the priests of God now destroy not so much one city as disperse the iniquity of the whole world.

For just as, under the name of a single city, the form of the whole world is represented, so the spaces of the whole world are divided by the cycle of seven days. Through these days the trumpets of priestly preaching announce destruction to the age itself and threaten judgment, as it is written: “The world shall pass away, and all that is in the world. But whoever does the will of God remains forever” (I John 2:16–17). This is granted by him who lives and reigns forever.

# SERMON XXXVI

*Formerly, On Time 108.* [Note: [Col. 1816] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. Apart from the recapitulation with which the sermon ends, it contains nothing other than the account of Gideon prefixed as a prologue to Book 1 of Ambrose’s *On the Holy Spirit*, though not in its entirety.]

## Concerning Gideon

### 1. An outline of predestination

Today we heard, brothers, that when Gideon son of Joash was cutting a harvest of wheat with a staff beneath an oak tree [Note: [Col. 1816] The Fulda manuscript has “yesterday,” etc. Ambrose, however, begins: “Jerubbaal, as we read, when beneath an oak tree…”], he was deemed worthy to hear the angel promise that he would rescue God’s people from the power of their enemies into freedom.

Nor is it surprising that he was chosen for grace, since even then he was established beneath the shadow of the holy cross and venerable Wisdom, within the predestined mystery of the future Incarnation. He was bringing forth the tangible grains of a fertile crop from hiding places and separating the election of the saints from the refuse of empty chaff.

Those who, as though exercised by the staff of truth, lay aside the superfluities of the old man together with his deeds are gathered, as in a winepress, into the Church. For the Church is the winepress of the eternal fountain, in which the fruit of the heavenly vine flows abundantly.

### 2. A figure of our redemption; Christ as the rock in relation to the flesh

When Gideon heard that through him the Lord would free his people from the multitude of their enemies [Note: [Col. 1816] Ambrose: “Moved by the oracle, Gideon, when he heard that, although thousands of peoples were failing, the Lord would free his people from their enemies through one man, offered…”], he offered a kid of the goats as a sacrifice. According to the angel’s command, he placed its flesh and unleavened bread upon a rock and poured broth over them.

As soon as the angel of God touched them with the tip of the staff that he carried, fire burst forth from the rock; and thus the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed. [Note: [Col. 1816] The Fulda manuscript, with Ambrose, reads *assumptum est* (“was taken up”) rather than *absumptum est* (“was consumed”).]

By this sign it appears to have been declared that that rock represented the body of Christ, because it is written: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. 10:4).

This was referred not to his divinity but to his flesh, which flooded the thirsty hearts of the peoples with the perpetual stream of its blood.

Thus it was already declared in the mystery that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would abolish the sins of the whole world—not only the offenses committed in deeds but also the desires of souls.

The flesh of the kid refers to guilt in action; the broth, to the allurements of desire, as it is written: “The people desired an evil desire, and they said, ‘Who will give us flesh?’” (Num. 11:4).

Therefore, when the angel extended the staff and touched the rock from which fire came forth, he showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human condition. Hence the Lord also says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

### 3. The abolition of the ancient sacrifices revealed; Christ as kid, sheep, and calf; the mystery of the cross

The learned man, foreseeing future events, perceived the heavenly mysteries. Therefore, in accordance with the oracles, he killed the calf dedicated by his father to the idols, and sacrificed another seven-year-old calf to God.

By this action he most clearly revealed that, after the Lord’s coming, all the sacrifices of paganism were to be abolished, and that the one sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion was to be offered to God for the religious worship of the people. [Note: [Col. 1816] Ambrose reads “for redemption.”]

That calf, indeed, bore a type of Christ. It was seven years old because, as Isaiah said, the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues dwelt in Christ (Isa. 11:2).

Abraham also offered this calf when he saw the Lord’s day and rejoiced (John 8:56). This is the one who was offered now in the figure of a kid, now of a sheep, now of a calf: a kid because it is a sacrifice for sins; a sheep because it is a voluntary victim; a calf because it is an unblemished victim.

Holy Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery. Accordingly, he chose three hundred men for battle, to show that the world was to be freed from the attack of powerful enemies not by the number of the multitude but through the sacrament of the cross (Judg. 7:7).

For three hundred, according to the Greek reckoning, display the likeness of the cross in the letter T, tau.

### 4. The dew on the fleece and then on the threshing floor; faith first in Judea, afterward among the Gentiles

Although he was strong and confident, Gideon nevertheless sought fuller assurances from the Lord concerning the future victory, saying: “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, Lord, behold, I shall place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor; and if there is dew upon the fleece while the whole earth is dry, I shall know that by my hand you will deliver the people according to your promises.”

And so it happened. But afterward he added that dew should once again flow over the whole earth, while there was dryness in the fleece [Note: [Col. 1817] At this point Ambrose briefly resolves this question: “Does he not seem almost unbelieving, asking for still more signs after having been instructed by repeated indications?”] (Judg. 6–7).

The dew upon the fleece was faith in Judea, because the words of God descend like dew. Hence Moses also says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and my words like dew” (Deut. 32:2).

Thus, when the whole world was parched by the fruitless heat of Gentile superstition, that heavenly dew of visitation was upon the fleece, that is, in Judea.

But after the sheep that had perished—the sheep of the house of Israel, from which I think the figure of the Jewish fleece was sketched out—had denied the fountain of living water, the dew of faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine fountain diverted its channels into the hearts of the Gentiles.

Hence the whole world is now moistened with the dew of faith. The Jews, however, lost their prophets and counselors.

Nor is it surprising that those who have been deprived by the Lord God of the abundance of prophetic rain should fall into the dryness of faithlessness, since he says: “I shall command the clouds not to rain upon this vineyard” (Isa. 5:6).

There is a salutary rain of the prophetic cloud, as David also said: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth” (Ps. 71:6).

The divine Scriptures promised us this rain upon the whole world, which would water the world with the dew of the Spirit under the advent of the Lord and Savior.

The dew has now come, and the rain has come; the Lord has come, bringing heavenly drops with him. Therefore we now drink, though formerly we thirsted, and we drink that divine Spirit with inward draughts.

This, then, holy Gideon foresaw: that the Gentiles and nations also would drink the true and spiritual dew by receiving faith.

### 5. Why the fleece was placed on the threshing floor

Gideon did not place the fleece carelessly, neither in a field nor in a meadow, but on the threshing floor, where there is a harvest of wheat—for “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37)—because through faith in the Lord there was to be a fruitful harvest of virtues in the Church.

Nor is it without significance that he dried out the Jewish fleece and poured its dew into a basin, so that it was filled with water, yet did not himself wash his feet with that dew. The privilege of so great a mystery was owed to another.

Christ was awaited, the one who alone could wash away the filth of all. Gideon was not great enough to claim this mystery for himself. For it was not Gideon but the Son of Man who came “not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28). [Note: [Col. 1817] Up to this point, Ambrose.]

## 6. Recapitulation

I ask you, dearly beloved brothers, not to take it amiss that, for the sake of those who are slower and more simple, we sometimes briefly repeat what has been said. For those who are educated and learned, by God’s favor, understand what is said without difficulty; but for the rest—that is, for the uneducated and simple—I fear that, unless a brief recapitulation is given, they may grasp little of what is said.

Gideon, dearly beloved brothers, bore the type of the Lord and Savior. And because, according to the Greek reckoning, three hundred makes the sign of the cross, so at that time Gideon, with three hundred men, rescued the people of the Jews from the most savage nations; just as afterward Christ, through the mystery of the cross, liberated the whole human race from the power of the devil.

The winepress where he threshed the harvest bore the type of the Church because of its continual tribulations. The harvest that was cut down signified the Christian people, whom Christ, at his coming, separated from the chaff—that is, from all sins—by the rod of discipline or by the staff of his cross.

[Col. 1818] For that angel also who came to him is himself understood as a type of the Lord and Savior. It is evident that the tree under which he stood and the staff which he held signified the cross. That rock upon which Gideon offered the burnt offering was Christ; for the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ.” That kid which was offered designated the human race subject to sins. When the angel touched the rock with his staff, fire went out and consumed that kid: the cross touched Christ, and from the rock—which was Christ—there went out the fire of love, which consumed the sins of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 1818] In the Fulda manuscript: “The cross touched the rock which was Christ, and fire,” etc.]

For the true Gideon, Christ, says of himself in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” But the bull which he killed also represented the Lord, who was offered for the redemption of the human race. And because it was seven years old, it seems to have signified the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit that came upon Christ.

The fleece which he placed on the threshing floor and asked the Lord to have dew on the fleece alone, while there was dryness over all the earth—and it happened so—and then again asked that the fleece remain dry while there was dew over the entire threshing floor: the fleece signified the people of the Jews, while the threshing floor signified the people of all the nations throughout the whole world.

And because, in the first age, the dew of God’s word was found in Judaea alone, while the whole world remained in dryness, the dew first came upon the fleece and the threshing floor was dry. But afterward, when the Jews killed Christ the Lord, the fleece was wrung out through the outrage of his Passion, and the Jewish people remained arid and dry; while over the entire threshing floor—that is, throughout the whole world—to all the nations, there reached not only the dew but also the rain of God’s word and the streams of the Apostles.

Finally, throughout the whole earth, like a threshing floor, the Church is watered with the dew of spiritual grace; while the unhappy Synagogue remained dry and arid, deprived of all moisture and of the rain of the divine word.

Therefore, so that this spiritual rain and the dew of divine grace may persevere in us, let us profitably ponder everything that is preached, and let us ruminate upon it with one another in conversation like clean animals, so that we may possess a wholesome sap by which our soul can live forever, and, filled with such delights, may deserve to say with the prophet: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, O Lord!” (Ps. 118:103).

But then the sweetness of God’s word will be able to remain in us if we also wish, with full and perfect love, to communicate it frequently and impress it upon others, so that we may be able to gain spiritual profit not only from our own salvation but also from that of others; with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1818] Elsewhere, *On Time* 197.]

## On David and Jesse his father, and on Goliath

[Note: [Col. 1818] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. Having been left by the Louvain editors among the Augustinian works as doubtful, it lacked Augustine’s name. Later, Verlin and Vinding proved with certainty that it was not his. It more readily recalls Caesarius of Arles than Augustine, although in many Breviaries it is read under the latter’s name on the fourth Sunday after Pentecost. Not long ago it was removed by the Parisian editor.]

### 1. One person can be a figure of different things. Jesse a type of God the Father

In the divine Scriptures, dearly beloved brothers, one and the same person can have a different significance according to the time and place. For blessed Isaac—as Your Holiness knows very well—when he was offered by his father, represented Christ the Lord; but when he blessed his son Jacob and sent him to Mesopotamia to take a wife, Jacob bore the type of Christ, while Isaac bore the image of God the Father.

Again, blessed Jacob bore the type of Christ when he took a wife; but he bore the figure of God the Father when he loved blessed Joseph more than all his sons and made him a many-colored tunic, which signified the incarnation of the Lord and Savior.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, just as this happened then among the blessed Patriarchs, Isaac and Jacob, so we recognize that it was also prefigured in Jesse, the father of David. For when David was sending his son to seek his brothers, he seems to have borne the type of God the Father. Jesse sent David to seek his brothers; and God the Father sent his Only-begotten, concerning whom it is written: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23).

[Col. 1819] Christ had come to seek his brothers when he said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

### 2. David a figure of Christ

Jesse therefore said to his son David: “Take an ephah of meal and ten cheeses, and go; seek your brothers.”

An ephah, my brothers, is a measure of three modii; and in the three measures the mystery of the Trinity is understood. Blessed Abraham also knew this mystery well. For when, beneath the oak of Mamre, he was granted to see the sacrament of the Trinity in three persons, he ordered three measures of fine flour to be mixed. Three measures are three quantities. Jesse therefore also gave this measure to his son.

In the ten cheeses the Decalogue of the Old Testament is understood. David therefore came with three measures and ten cheeses to visit his brothers who were stationed in battle, because Christ was to come with the Decalogue of the Law and the mystery of the Trinity in order to free the human race from the power of the devil.

### 3. The brother rebuking David signifies the Jews or the devil, envious of Christ’s coming

When David came, one of his brothers rebuked him, saying: “Why have you left those few sheep and come to the battle?” (1 Sam. 17).

This older brother, who maliciously rebuked David as he bore the type of the Lord, signified the Jewish people, who, out of envy of Christ the Lord, who had come for the salvation of the human race, slandered him and frequently inflicted many injuries upon him.

“Why,” he said, “have you left those sheep and come to the battle?”

It is as though the devil, envying the salvation of humanity, were speaking through his mouth—as if he were saying to Christ: “Why have you left the ninety-nine sheep that did not go astray and come to seek the one that had perished” (Matt. 18:12), so that, having rescued it from the hand of the spiritual Goliath—that is, from the power of the devil—by the staff of the cross, you might bring it back to its own sheepfold?

“Why,” he says, “have you left those few sheep?”

Although he spoke with an evil and proud intention, he was nevertheless speaking the truth: for Jesus, as has already been said, was going to leave the ninety-nine sheep in order to seek the one and bring it back to its own sheepfold—that is, to the fellowship of the angels.

### 4. David killed the lion and the bear; Christ stripped the devil

Before David came, after he had already been anointed by blessed Samuel—as he himself had told King Saul—he killed both the lion and the bear without weapons. But both the lion and the bear prefigure the devil: because they dared to seize something from David’s sheep, they were strangled by David’s own strength.

All this, dearly beloved brothers, which we read as having been prefigured in David, we recognize as fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ. For he strangled the lion and the bear when, descending to the realm of the dead, he freed everyone from their jaws.

Finally, hear the prophet supplicating in the person of the Lord: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog; save me from the mouth of the lion” (Ps. 21:21–22).

And because the bear has strength in its paw while the lion has it in its mouth, the same devil is represented in these two beasts. This was therefore said in the person of Christ, so that his one Church might be taken from the hand—that is, from the power—of the devil.

### 5. Before Christ there is neither courage nor strength for battle. After Christ’s coming the devil is bound

David came, then, and found the Jewish people stationed in the Valley of the Terebinth, preparing to fight against the Philistines, because the true David, Christ, was to come in order to raise the human race from the valley of sins or of tears.

They were standing in the valley against the Philistines. They were in the valley because the weight of their sins had oppressed them. They were standing, but they did not dare to fight against their adversaries.

Why did they not dare? Because David, [Col. 1820] who bore the type of Christ, had not yet come.

It is true, dearly beloved brothers. For who could fight against the devil before Christ the Lord freed the human race from the power of the devil? David is interpreted as “strong of hand.” What is stronger than he, brothers, who conquered the whole world armed not with iron but with wood?

The sons of Israel therefore stood against their adversaries for forty days. The forty days, because of the four seasons and the four regions of the earth, signify the present life, in which the Christian people do not cease to fight against Goliath and his army—that is, against the devil and his angels. Yet they could not conquer unless the true David, Christ, had descended with the staff—that is, with the mystery of the cross.

Before the coming of Christ, the devil was unbound. Christ came and fulfilled in him what was said in the Gospel: “No one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12:29). Christ therefore came and bound the devil.

### 6. He can bite no one except one who is willing

But someone may say: “If he has been bound, why does he still prevail so greatly?”

It is true, brothers, that he prevails greatly—but over the lukewarm and negligent, and over those who do not fear God in truth. For he is bound like a dog fastened with chains, and he can bite no one except one who voluntarily joins himself to him with a deadly security.

Now see, brothers, how foolish is the man whom a dog held on a chain bites. Do not join yourself to him through the desires and passions of this world, and he will not dare approach you. He can bark; he can trouble you; he cannot bite unless you are willing.

For he harms not by compulsion but by persuasion; he does not extort consent from us but asks for it.

[Note: [Col. 1820] These words are taken verbatim from Pelagius’ letter to Demetrias, chapter 25, whose words Caesarius also imitates elsewhere.]

### 7. David with a staff against Goliath. Christ with the cross against the devil. Goliath struck with his own sword, the devil struck by his own iniquity. Our members are the devil’s weapons or God’s temples

David came, then, and found the Jewish people fighting against the devil. Since no one dared to go forth to single combat, he who bore the figure of Christ advanced to battle, took a staff in his hand, and went out against Goliath.

What was then prefigured in him was fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ. For the true David, Christ, came to fight against the spiritual Goliath—that is, against the devil—and himself carried his cross.

See, brothers, where blessed David struck Goliath: on the forehead, certainly, where he did not bear the sign of the cross. For just as the staff represented the cross, so also that stone with which he was struck represented Christ the Lord. He is the living stone, concerning whom it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22).

But the fact that David, having no sword, mounted upon Goliath and killed him with his own sword signified that, at Christ’s coming, the devil was conquered by his own sword. Through his own wickedness and the unjust persecution which he exercised against Christ, he lost his dominion over all who believe in him.

The fact that David placed Goliath’s weapons in his own tabernacle signified that we were the devil’s weapons. Thus the Apostle says: “Just as you presented your members as weapons of unrighteousness for sin, so now present your members as weapons of righteousness to God”; and again: “Do not present your members as weapons of unrighteousness for sin” (Rom. 6:19, 13).

Christ placed the weapons of our enemy in his tabernacle when we, who had been the house of the devil, through his grace were deemed worthy to be the temple of God. For it is also recognized that Christ dwells in us and we in Christ.

The Apostle proves that Christ dwells in us when he says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts, in the inner person (Eph. 3:17). And the same Apostle indicated that we dwell in Christ when he said: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). [Col. 1821]

And the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you” (John 14:11).

### 8. The spiritual Goliath struck on the forehead

But the fact that he was struck not in another bodily member but in the forehead signifies what is now enacted in our Candidates: when a catechumen is signed on the forehead, the spiritual Goliath is struck and the devil is put to flight.

And because we recognize and likewise perceive that the devil has been driven from our hearts through the grace of Christ, let us labor as much as we can with his help, lest by our evil deeds and by impious or lustful thoughts we again wish to invite him into us.

[Note: [Col. 1821] The remainder is from the manuscripts. In the printed editions, the following few words occur in its place: “that, inspired by him, we may deserve happily to attain eternal rewards. May he himself deign to grant this,” etc.]

Lest perhaps—which God forbid—there be fulfilled in us what is written:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept clean; then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matt. 12:43–45).

Therefore, since we have been emptied of all evils through the grace of Baptism, without any preceding merits, let us strive, with God’s help, to be filled with spiritual goods, so that whenever the devil wishes to tempt us, he may always find us full of God’s Spirit and occupied with good works; so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

May he himself grant this, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1821] Elsewhere, *On Time* 198.]

## On the plague among the people on account of David, and on the building of an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite

[Note: [Col. 1821] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. To the Louvain editors it seemed doubtful; Verlin and Vinding consider it spurious. It is not unworthy of Caesarius.]

### 1. A figure of the rejection of the Jews and the election of the nations

When the reading from the Books of Kings was being read a short while ago, we heard that, while God’s plague was raging among the Jewish people, the angel of the Lord who was striking them stood beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. And the Lord said to the angel who was striking the people: “Enough; now hold back your hand.” And the plague ceased among the people.

Araunah, dearly beloved brothers, was king of the Jebusites, and he seems to have possessed some portion of Jerusalem. For although all the surrounding nations had been subjected to King David, God nevertheless did not permit the Jebusites to be completely destroyed, just as he says elsewhere: “I will not destroy all the nations, so that through them I may test whether they fear me” (Judg. 2:21–22).

The prophet therefore says to David: “Go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”

That pagan king represented the people of the nations. Pay attention, brothers: in the land of the Jews no worthy place was found where the Lord’s altar could be set up; rather, a place is chosen in the land of the nations, where the angel is seen, where the Lord’s altar is built, and where the wrath of the almighty Lord is thus appeased.

Even then it was being prefigured that no worthy place could be found in Jewish hearts for offering spiritual sacrifices; rather, the land of the nations—that is, the conscience of Christians—is chosen as the place where the temple of the Lord should be established.

The Apostle clearly shows this when he rebukes the Jews, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13:46).

This is to say: “Because you rejected Christ and did not prepare a worthy place where the Lord’s altar could be set up, we establish the Lord’s altar in the land of the nations—that is, in the hearts of all peoples.”

Hence the same Apostle cries out to us: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17).

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, pay attention: the land of a gentile king is chosen precisely when the Jewish people are struck by God’s plague. We see this fulfilled in the Passion of the Lord. [Col. 1822] For when the Jewish people are rejected for crucifying the Lord, then in the threshing floor of the nations—that is, throughout the whole earth—the altar is consecrated to the Lord.

The angel of the Lord therefore stood on the threshing floor of the gentile king; and the true angel, that is, Christ, visited the people of the nations.

### 2. The same subject continued

That king therefore offered blessed David the threshing floor and the oxen for a burnt offering; but King David refused to accept them unless he first paid the price. This was fulfilled in the coming of the Lord and Savior.

For because grace is given freely, without preceding merits, he did not wish to take the hearts of the nations for himself unless he first paid the price of blood for them.

What did he give? “Fifty shekels of silver,” it says (2 Sam. 24).

In the number fifty, the grace of the Holy Spirit is understood, and the remission of sins is signified. For on the fiftieth day the Holy Spirit was sent to the Apostles; and in the Old Testament the fiftieth year was consecrated to remission and pardon.

David gave that king silver; but our David, of whom the former was a type, poured out precious blood. Thus, in order to purchase the threshing floor of the pagan king, David offered fifty shekels; and the true David, Christ, in order to establish an altar for himself on the threshing floor of the nations, gave the grace of the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of sins on the fiftieth day.

And therefore, brothers, since he has deigned to make a temple for himself in us and from us, let us not permit injury in his house. For if he suffers injury from our sins, he quickly departs; and woe to the miserable soul from which he departs! Without doubt, the one abandoned by the light is seized by darkness.

Let us therefore strive, with his help, to act in such a way that we may deserve not only to receive so loving a Lord as a guest but also to have him as a permanent inhabitant; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1822] Elsewhere, *On Time* 200.]

## On Solomon’s judgment between two prostitutes: against the Arian heresy

[Note: [Col. 1822] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was copied from the sermon *Against Five Heresies*, chapter 6.]

### 1. The Catholic Church and the Arian heresy in the two prostitutes. The Son’s equality demonstrated from the Father’s omnipotence and goodness
