Concerning the two prostitutes, dearly beloved brothers, who came to Solomon’s judgment and about whom the reading is to be recited for us at Vespers—one of whom was not only lustful but also cruel and impious and was crying out to the king that the infant should be divided—if you willingly receive it, we desire to make known to the ears of Your Charity what our holy Fathers have expounded concerning them.

The woman who cried out that the child should be kept whole bore the type of the Catholic Church. The other, cruel and impious, who cried out that the child should be divided, represented the Arian heresy.

For the Catholic Church, like a most devoted mother, cried out to all heretics: “Do not make Christ lesser than the Father; do not divide unity; do not, by dividing the one God into different degrees, fashion in your hearts something like the idols of the nations. Possess the whole with us. If you wish to have peace, do not tear unity apart.

“For if you possess the whole, nothing remains for us.” His omnipotence is so great that everyone may possess him whole, and each one may possess him whole.

But the impious and cruel heresy cries out: “No, let him be divided.”

What is “Let him be divided” except “The Son is not equal to the Father”? For by taking equality away from the Son, it has denied a good and omnipotent Father.

For if God the Father was able to beget a son like himself and did not wish to do so, he is not good; if he wished to do so but was unable, he is not omnipotent.

Be certain, my brothers, that no Arian will ever be able to answer this argument. Whenever they are constrained by the most truthful reasoning, they flee like a slippery snake to any other crafty and tortuous questions.

[Col. 1823]

### 2. The inheritance left in Christ’s testament

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, I bring forth a testament and repeat the words of the testator. If it contains something that can be divided, I find it there; if it contains nothing that can be divided, I resist them from the testament itself.

O unhappy heretic, what does the testament contain? Hear: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

This is the inheritance of Christians. And who is the testator himself? Read the testament and you will find him. When the prophet was speaking of the Lord, he said: “He will be magnified to the ends of the earth, and he will be peace” (Mic. 5:4–5).

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14)—not to those who divide holy unity, but to people of good will.

He himself is the inheritance; he himself is the testator. Are you seeking to divide him? Why do you divide the one? If you divide the one, you have nothing whole.

### 3. The division of God

O cruel and impious Arian heresy, be ashamed! When Solomon was judging, the prostitute, lest she betray the one living child, the one conceived and born from anywhere at all, did not permit her son to be divided. And you divide your God?

Although she was a prostitute, she was nevertheless devout, because she was a mother. You, heresy, are impious, because you are not a mother. What you give birth to, you strangle; what you do not give birth to, you gather together. Your wombs have grown hard; hers trembled.

What does the woman who bore the type of the Catholic mother say? “Give the child to her, and do not divide him” (1 Kings 3).

“He is my son; but let him better go alive, let him go whole, with her; nevertheless, let the mother’s affection remain with me. Give the child to her; let the vows not be taken away; let the integrity of his limbs not be divided, lest my devotion be taken from me.”

What she says—“Give the child to her, and do not divide him”—I too say: “Possess the whole, and do not divide God.”

“No,” he says, “but if you wish to have peace, divide the inheritance.”

I speak without prejudice. How am I to divide it? Hear: “The Father is greater than I; the Son is lesser; the Spirit is a creature.”

What portions! What justice! What fairness! I make a portion because I divide peace. For if peace is broken, it is no longer peace.

But how is peace undefiled with you, when faith is not whole? Since you wish to possess with me and wish to divide peace, do you not wish to divide the inheritance?

### 4. Unity must be preserved in the Lord

Finally, if, as is your custom, you pursue not peace but faithlessness, go and appeal to Christ the Judge; let us see what he will say to you.

Tell him what was said in the Gospel: “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

Without doubt he answers you: “Friend, who appointed me judge or divider?” (Luke 12:13–14).

You wish to divide peace and seek to have peace as judge; I do not wish to be your judge. I am peace: I sit beside those who agree, and I flee from those who quarrel.

For if I grant all my Christians to have one heart through one will, how can I divide the unity between myself and the Father, when I grant all my faithful one heart and one love?

What does the Lord say to Philip? “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known me? Philip, I came to join you to my Father; do not separate me. Why do you seek someone else besides me? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

Such is the likeness among us, such the unity, such the love, that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.

By this unity may the Lord deign to join you to himself and preserve you; through that same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XL

[Note: [Col. 1823] Elsewhere, *On Time* 201.]

## On Elijah

[Note: [Col. 1823] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors left it doubtful; Verlin and Vinding prove it spurious. We judge that it should be attributed to Caesarius. It is read in the Roman Breviary on the ninth Sunday after Pentecost, but it has been excluded from the new Parisian edition.]

### 1. Elijah a type of the Savior. The nations represented by the ravens. The Church black and beautiful

In the readings that are being recited for us these days, dearly beloved brothers, I have frequently admonished you not to follow the letter that kills and [Col. 1824] abandon the Spirit that gives life. Thus the Apostle says: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

If we wish to understand only what sounds in the letter, we will derive little or almost no edification from the divine readings. For all those things that are recited were types and images of future events. What was prefigured among the Jews has been completed in us by the gift of God’s grace.

Blessed Elijah bore the type of the Lord and Savior. Just as Elijah suffered persecution from the Jews, so the true Elijah, our Lord, was rejected and despised by those same Jews.

Elijah left his own people, and Christ abandoned the Synagogue. Elijah went into the desert, and Christ came into the world. Elijah was fed in the desert by ravens ministering to him, and Christ in the desert of this world is refreshed by the faith of the nations.

For those ravens that, at the Lord’s command, ministered to blessed Elijah represented the people of the nations. Therefore it is also said concerning the Church of the nations: “I am black but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem” (Song 1:4).

From where is the Church black and beautiful? Black by nature, beautiful by grace.

From where is she black? “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

From where is she beautiful? “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:7, 9).

From where is she black? The Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin.”

From where is she beautiful? “Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23–25).

Truly, the Church of the nations was like ravens when it despised the living Lord and, before receiving grace, ministered to idols as though to rotting corpses.

### 2. God speaks inwardly to everyone who does a good work. The widow who received Elijah as a figure of the Church

After this Elijah is commanded to go to Zarephath of Sidon, so that he might be fed there by a widow. For the Lord said to him: “Go to Zarephath of Sidon; I have commanded a widow there to feed you.”

How, and through whom, did God command the widow, when at that time there was scarcely any other prophet with whom God spoke more openly than with blessed Elijah? For although there were at that time some of the sons of the prophets, they feared Jezebel’s persecution so greatly that they could scarcely escape even by remaining hidden.

“I,” says the Lord, “have commanded the widow.”

How does the Lord command, except by inspiring inwardly in the soul what is good through his grace? Thus every person who does something good has God speaking inwardly to him. Therefore let no one glory in himself, but in the Lord.

Were there not then many widows in Judaea? Why was it that no Jewish widow was found worthy to minister food to blessed Elijah, but he was sent to a gentile widow to be fed by her?

The widow to whom the Prophet was sent bore the type of the Church, just as those ravens that had ministered to Elijah represented the nations. Elijah therefore came to the widow because Christ was to come to the Church.

### 3. Spiritual death necessary for the believer

But let us see, dearly beloved brothers, where blessed Elijah found that widow. She had gone out to draw water and gather wood.

Let us see what the water and the wood signify. We recognize that these two things are sufficiently both friendly and necessary to the Church: wood and water.

Thus it is written: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. 1:3). For in the wood the mystery of the cross is shown, and in the water the sacrament of Baptism.

She had gone out to gather two pieces of wood. For she answered blessed Elijah in this way when he asked her for food. She said: “As the Lord lives, I have nothing except a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a vessel. And behold, I am going out to gather two pieces of wood, and I will make food for myself and my son; and we shall eat and die” (1 Kings 17).

As I said above, that widow bore the type of the Church, while the widow’s son represented the Christian people. When Elijah came, the widow went out to gather two pieces of wood.

See, brothers, that she did not say three, or four, or only one piece of wood; she wished to gather two pieces of wood. She gathered two pieces because, in the type of Elijah, she was receiving Christ. She wished to gather two pieces [Col. 1825] because she desired to recognize the mystery of the cross.

For the cross of the Lord and Savior was fashioned from two pieces of wood. That widow therefore gathered two pieces because the Church was going to believe in him who hung upon two pieces of wood.

The widow said: “I am gathering two pieces of wood, so that I may make food for myself and my son; and we shall eat and die.”

It is true, dearly beloved brothers: no one will be deemed worthy to believe in Christ crucified unless he dies to this age. For whoever wishes to eat the body of Christ worthily must die to the things that have passed and live for those that are to come.

### 4. A figure of the resurrection of the nations. This is accomplished by the whole Trinity

That widow, as we have said, represented the Church; the widow’s son bore the type of the gentile people.

The widow’s son lay dead, because the son of the Church—that is, the people of the nations—was dead through many sins and crimes. When Elijah prayed, the widow’s son was raised; when Christ came, the son of the Church—that is, the Christian people—was brought back from the prison of death.

Elijah bent down in prayer, and the widow’s son was brought to life; Christ fell down in his Passion, and the Christian people were raised.

The fact that blessed Elijah bent down three times to raise the boy also shows the mystery of the Trinity. Before I say this, I believe that the understanding of Your Charity has anticipated it.

For the fact that he bent down three times reveals the mystery of the Trinity. The widow’s son—that is, the people of the nations—was raised not by the Father alone without the Son, nor by the Father and the Son without the Holy Spirit, but by the whole Trinity.

Finally, this is also demonstrated in the sacrament of Baptism, when the old person is immersed a third time, so that the new person may deserve to rise.

### 5. A figure of the grace to be bestowed through Christ’s coming. Christ preached for three years and six months

After this blessed Elijah showed himself to the king, went up Mount Carmel, placed his head between his knees, and prayed that the Lord would give rain upon the earth.

And he said to his servant: “Look toward the sea.”

The servant reported that he had seen absolutely nothing. And he said to him: “Go and look seven times.”

The seventh time he reported and said: “I see a little cloud, like a man’s footprint, rising from the sea” (1 Kings 18).

And suddenly the heavens grew dark, and there was heavy rain.

Elijah, as we have said, bore the figure of the Lord and Savior. Elijah prayed and offered sacrifice; Christ offered himself as an immaculate sacrifice for the whole world.

Elijah prayed on Mount Carmel; Christ on the Mount of Olives. Elijah prayed that rain would come upon the earth; Christ that divine grace would descend into human hearts.

The fact that Elijah said to his servant, “Go and look seven times,” designated the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit that was to be given to the Church.

And because he said that he had seen a little cloud rising from the sea, it represented the flesh of Christ, which was to be born in the sea of this world.

Therefore, lest anyone perhaps doubt that the cloud had the form of a man’s footprint, he said so: that is, the footprint of the man who said, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13).

Just as, when Elijah prayed, rain descended from heaven after three years and six months, so, at the Savior’s coming, during the three years and six months in which he deigned to preach, the rain of God’s word happily watered the whole world.

And just as at Elijah’s coming all the priests of the idols were killed and destroyed, so at the coming of the true Elijah—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—the sacrilegious observance of the pagans was destroyed.

### 6. Recapitulation

By briefly bringing these matters to the attention of Your Charity, as though they were a few chapters or certain little indications, we display them before the eyes of your faith, so that your holy desires may thereby be salutarily stimulated to examine the divine mysteries; and so that, by sound counsel, we may continually provide spiritual nourishment for your holy souls to ruminate, lest it perhaps slip from memory. If you wish, then, let us make a recapitulation from what has been said.

As we said above, understand that the holy Elijah bore a type of the Lord and Savior. Thus, just as the Lord, after He had performed many miracles, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, so Elijah, after the wonders God performed through him, was lifted up to heaven in a chariot of fire [Col. 1826]. Elijah’s abandonment of Judea signified that Christ left the Synagogue. The ravens who ministered to Elijah, as has already been said, displayed a figure of the Gentile people. That widow who received him at Zarephath bore the type of the Church. The two pieces of wood that she gathered signified the mystery of the cross.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if you receive these things with sincere goodwill, as we believe, and, like clean animals, ruminate upon them continually in your hearts, what is written will be fulfilled in you: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI, 20). He is our God Jesus Christ, who reigns, and to whom belong honor and dominion, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLI

[Note: [Col. 1826] Formerly, *On Time* 204.]

### On Elisha I

[Note: [Col. 1826] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors regarded it as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. It seems to us to belong to Caesarius. See his Homily 14 among those edited by the distinguished V. C. Baluzius.]

### 1. Why the Manichaeans blaspheme the Old Testament. The prophets were despised in Elisha’s age. The striking of the children was an act of mercy more than cruelty. An example of this severity from the New Testament.

When the divine reading was being read, we heard that, as blessed Elisha was passing by, some boys cried out mockingly, “Go up, baldhead!” For this reason, when Elisha prayed, two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two boys to pieces (IV Kings II, 23).

The utterly filthy Manichaeans, enemies of God and of their own souls, who not only refuse to accept the Scripture of the Old Testament but also presume to blaspheme it with savage mouths, commonly say: “What great cruelty was there in Elisha, that because of the playful words of children he caused forty-two boys to be torn to pieces?” Therefore we shall briefly suggest to Your Charity how their madness should be answered.

At the time when blessed Elisha lived in Judea, he and the other prophets were not only not honored by the greater part of the people, but were also held up to ridicule and reproach, and were believed to be mad and possessed. So great was this contempt that, when blessed Elisha sent one of the sons of the prophets to anoint Jehu as king, the leaders sitting with Jehu said: “Why has this madman come to you?” (ibid. IX, 11).

They saw the Lord’s prophet and blasphemously called him possessed. For at that time the holy prophets were held in such great contempt and reproach that even the undisciplined boys cried out to blessed Elisha, who performed so many miracles, as we said above: “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” We should believe that they did this at the prompting of their parents also. Clearly, the boys would not have shouted this if it had displeased their parents.

Thus blessed Elisha, grieving over the destruction of the people—or rather, the Holy Spirit through blessed Elisha, wishing to restrain the pride of the Jews—caused two bears to come, and they tore the forty-two boys to pieces. By striking the children, He intended the elders to receive discipline, so that the death of the sons might become the discipline of their parents, and so that they might learn at least to fear the prophet whom they were unwilling to love while he performed miracles.

But the Jews persisted so greatly in their evils that they turned medicines into wounds for themselves, and acquired death from the very source through which they could have obtained salvation. They turned light into darkness for themselves and changed sweetness into bitterness. Thus what is written was fulfilled in them: “I struck your children, and you did not accept discipline” (Jer. II, 30).

Therefore let no one presume, with a viperous tongue, to disparage blessed Elisha, since what happened to those boys should be believed to have been done not so much by his own power as by the Holy Spirit through him. But this, as I said, was done out of great piety and ineffable mercy: because the Jews were unwilling to believe the prophets who preached humbly in God’s name [Col. 1827], they might at least fear Him when He inflicted punishment with severity, and, fearing the death of their bodies, might in some way seek the salvation of their souls.

We read that this was fulfilled not only in the Old Testament but also in the New, through the blessed Apostle Peter, in the case of Ananias and Sapphira. Peter’s sentence condemned them so that no one might presume to lie to the Holy Spirit in his offerings or gifts.

### 2. The madness of the Jews in the Lord’s Passion. Their punishment is prefigured by Titus and Vespasian. How many Jews were then killed and how many taken captive.

Indeed, dearest brothers, we should believe literally, as we suggested above, that blessed Elisha, moved not by the disease of anger but inflamed with zeal for God, permitted those children to be torn apart in order to correct the Jewish people—not to exact vengeance, but rather to reform them. Nevertheless, it is also clearly shown that the Passion of the Lord and Savior was prefigured in this event.

For just as those undisciplined boys cried out to blessed Elisha, “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!”, so at the time of the Passion the senseless Jewish people sacrilegiously cried out to the true Elisha, Christ: “Crucify him! Crucify him!” (Luke XXIII, 21). What is “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” except “Go up onto the cross at the place of Calvary”?

And observe this, brothers: just as forty-two boys were torn apart under Elisha, so, forty-two years after the Lord’s Passion, two bears came—Vespasian and Titus. Consider this also, brothers: the siege of the Jews began at the solemnity of Passover, so that, by the just judgment of God, the Jews gathered from all the provinces might suffer the punishment they deserved on the very days on which they had suspended the true Elisha, our Lord and Savior, on the cross.

In that year—that is, the forty-second year from the day of the Passion of our Lord—the Jews, as though driven by the hand of God, had gathered at Jerusalem, as they customarily did, to celebrate Passover. We read in the histories that at that time three million Jews gathered at Jerusalem. Of these, eleven hundred thousand are said to have been destroyed by the sword and famine, while one hundred thousand young men were led to Rome in triumph. For that city was besieged for two years, and so great was the multitude of the dead thrown out of the city that the corpses themselves reached the height of the walls.

That devastation, therefore, was prefigured by the two bears who are said to have torn apart forty-two boys because they mocked blessed Elisha. What the Psalm said was fulfilled: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Ps. LXXIX, 14). For, as has been said, after forty-two years that sacrilegious people received what it deserved from the two bears, Vespasian and Titus.

### 3. Warned by the misfortune of the Jews, let us hold the true faith, preserve complete charity, and strive to serve the Lord.

Since the unhappy Jews deserved, because of their pride, to be rejected and despised and scattered throughout the whole world, let us, to whom divine mercy has granted such great benefits, hold the true faith with all humility. So that pride may find no place in us, let us preserve complete charity toward all people and strive to serve the Lord with a pure heart and chaste body until the end of our life.

Then, after the labor of good works, may we deserve to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21): “Because you have administered temporal life well, receive eternal life; because you have guarded the price of my blood, share in my kingdom.”

May divine mercy deign to lead you to that kingdom, which lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLII

[Note: [Col. 1827] Formerly, *On Time* 206.]

### On Elisha II

[Note: [Col. 1827] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It belongs to the number of those which remain doubtful according to the Louvain editors and are asserted to be spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus [Col. 1828]. It will be restored to Caesarius by us, with no one, as we hope, resisting.]

### 1. Christ is represented in Elisha. The Church in the poor widow. The former released from debts by oil, the latter from sins by charity.

As we said concerning blessed Elijah, dearest brothers, that he bore a type of the Lord and Savior, so we confidently and securely assert that holy Elisha also displayed the image of our Savior.

For, as you heard in the divine reading, a certain widow cried out to blessed Elisha and pleaded in a tearful voice, saying: “My husband is dead, and behold, the creditors are coming and want to take my sons from me.” He then asked her what she had in her house. The woman answered: “As the Lord lives, I have nothing except a little oil with which I may anoint myself.” And Elisha said: “Ask vessels from your neighbors and, having shut the door, pour from that oil into all the vessels; and when they are full, sell it and pay your creditors.”

This widow, dearest brothers, bore the type of the Church, just as did the woman who was worthy to receive blessed Elijah. This widow, therefore—that is, the Church—had contracted a heavy debt, not of coins but of sins. She had a debt and endured a most cruel creditor, because she had made herself liable to the devil through many sins. Thus the prophet foretold: “You were sold because of your sins, and in your crimes I dismissed your mother” (Isa. L, 1).

That widow, therefore, was held captive, so to speak, because of so great a debt. She was captive because the Redeemer had not yet come. But after Christ the Lord, the true Redeemer, visited this widow, He set her free from all her debts.

Let us see from what this widow was freed. From what, except the increase of oil? Oil signifies mercy. Therefore the widow’s debt had increased because, by sinning, she had lost the oil of mercy.

Consider, brothers: the oil failed, and the debt increased; the oil increased, and the debt disappeared. Greed had increased, and charity disappeared; charity returns, and iniquity perishes. When Elisha, Christ the Lord, came, the widow—that is, the Church—was freed from the debt of sins through the increase of oil, that is, through the gift of grace and mercy, or through the richness of charity.

### 2. The empty vessels are the Gentiles.

Let us see, nevertheless, what blessed Elisha said to her: “Ask many vessels from your neighbors and close relatives, and, having shut the door, pour into the little vessels of your neighbors.”

Who were these neighbors except the peoples of the Gentiles? Although that widow bore the type of the Church, she was nevertheless a widow; and therefore the neighbors from whom vessels were requested represented the people of the Gentiles.

These vessels were presented empty so that they might deserve to receive the oil of mercy, because all the Gentiles, before they obtain the gift of grace, are shown to be empty of faith, charity, and good works. Thus all who are brought to the Church to receive saving Baptism receive chrism and the oil of blessing, so that they may deserve to be no longer empty vessels but full of God, and to be the temple of God.

### 3. Self-love is poor and needy. Charity is rich and abundant. It grows by being distributed.

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers: as long as that widow kept the oil in her own vessel, it was sufficient neither for herself nor for paying her debt. It is true, dearest ones, that whoever loves only himself is sufficient neither for himself nor for paying the debt of his sins.

But when he begins to pour the oil of charity into the vessels of others—that is, into all neighbors and relatives and absolutely all people—then he will be able both to suffice for himself and to free himself from all debts.

Indeed, brothers, such is the nature of holy love and true charity: it grows by being distributed, and the more it is spent on others, the more abundantly it is accumulated within oneself.

If you wish to give bodily food to someone in need, you cannot retain for yourself what you have given him at that moment. But if you give the bread of charity to a hundred people, it remains whole; if you wish to distribute it to the whole world, you lack nothing. Indeed, it not only does not diminish, but the profit of all those to whom you have given it increases for you many times over.

For example, you had one loaf of charity. If you had given it to no one, you would have only that one. You gave it to a thousand people, and you acquired a thousand loaves, because such is the possession of charity that it can be wholly possessed by each individual and remain whole for everyone.

Therefore you gave to others and lost absolutely nothing yourself. Indeed, you not only did not lose anything, but, as I have already said, whatever you bestowed upon others, you acquired a hundredfold.

Therefore, dearest brothers, recognize that the widow was released from her creditors by nothing other than oil; and understand that the Catholic Church was freed from her crimes by no other means than the oil of God’s mercy.

### 4. The vessels of charity are human beings; they are filled when they are loved.

But observe this, brothers: as long as that woman had vessels into which she could pour the oil, the oil continued to increase. For she said to her son, “Bring me a vessel.” He answered, “I have none.” And Scripture says that the oil stopped after she found no place in which to put it.

Thus, beloved brothers, charity increases as long as it is given. Therefore we ought deliberately to seek vessels into which we may pour the oil, because we have proven that, while we pour it into others, we possess more.

The vessels of charity are human beings. If we wish to abound in the oil of charity, we must love not only the good but also the wicked: the good because they are good; the wicked so that they may become good. For the oil of charity has this power: it makes the good better and brings the wicked back from the darkness of sins to the light of truth.

### 5. Who acts with the door closed or open.

When Scripture says that the widow poured the oil into the little vessels with the door closed, it signified that each person should give alms with the door closed—that is, for the love of God alone—not in order to be praised by human beings, but in order to deserve to find grace with God.

Whoever gives alms for human praise gives with the door open, because what is open is visible to everyone. But whoever performs good works for the sake of eternal life alone and the remission of sins gives with the door closed, even if he does so publicly, because in that almsgiving he seeks not what is seen but what is unseen.

Human praise is visible; eternal reward is not visible. But hear what the Apostle says: “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV, 18). Let each person therefore give alms confidently, provided that he does not seek human glory for it.

### 6. The woman of Shunem, passing from barrenness to fruitfulness, is a type of the Church.

After this we heard that, as blessed Elisha was passing through Shunem, a certain prominent woman received him and said to her husband: “I perceive that this man is a holy man of God. Let us make a small upper room for him and place there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that whenever he comes, he may stay there.”

That woman was barren, but, when Elisha prayed, she bore a son. So also the Church was barren before Christ came. And just as that woman bore a son when Elisha prayed, so the Church, when Christ came to her, bore the Christian people.

But the woman’s son died while Elisha was absent. So also the son of the Church—that is, the people of the Gentiles—was dead in sins before Christ came. When Elisha descended from the mountain, the widow’s son was restored to life; when Christ descended from heaven, the son of the Church—that is, the people of the Gentiles—was raised up. But let us see how this happened.

### 7. What the command in Scripture not to return a greeting forbids. Like Elisha’s servant, Moses could not restore life.

After her son died, the woman went and prostrated herself at the feet of holy Elisha. Blessed Elisha gave his staff to his servant and said to him: “Go and place my staff upon the boy’s face. If anyone greets you, do not return the greeting” (IV Kings IV).

Here, brothers, take care lest an impious thought enter anyone’s mind and he say that blessed Elisha wished to observe an omen, and therefore ordered his servant not to return the greeting of anyone who greeted him on the road.

We frequently read this in Scripture. It was said for the sake of speed, not as a command involving some superfluous and sacrilegious observance—as if he had said: “Walk so quickly that you do not presume to become occupied with or delayed by any conversations on the road.”

The servant went, therefore, and placed the staff upon the boy’s face, but he did not rise at all. This servant bore the type of blessed Moses. God sent him into Egypt with a staff, but the staff without Christ could strike Egypt; it could not free anyone from original or actual sin, nor could it raise anyone from death. For, as the Apostle says, “the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebr. VII, 19).

It was necessary that the one who had sent the staff should himself descend. The staff was powerless without Elisha, because the cross could do nothing without Christ.

### 8. Elisha, bending over the boy, and Christ, humbling Himself, raised up the world.

Blessed Elisha came, therefore, and went up into the upper room, because Christ was to come and ascend the gibbet of the cross. Elisha bent over in order to raise the boy; Christ humbled Himself in order to lift up the world lying in sins.

Elisha placed his eyes upon the boy’s eyes and his hands upon the boy’s hands. See, brothers, how greatly that man of mature age contracted himself in order to correspond to the dead and prostrate child. What Elisha prefigured in the boy, Christ fulfilled in the whole human race.

Hear the Apostle saying: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 8). Because we were little, He made Himself little; because we lay dead, the merciful physician bent down. For indeed, brothers, no one can raise up someone lying down if he is unwilling to bend down himself.

The fact that the boy yawned seven times displays the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which is granted to the human race at Christ’s coming so that it may be raised from death. Concerning that Spirit the Apostle says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 9).

The Lord also gave that same Spirit to the disciples when He breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22). He placed mouth, so to speak, upon mouth when He gave the Spirit by breathing upon him.

Let us therefore give thanks to our most merciful Redeemer, who raised us up without any preceding merits of ours, and who not only rescued us from perpetual death but also, with His grace assisting us, promised eternal rewards if we should act well.

May He Himself deign to grant this—He who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII

[Note: [Col. 1830] Formerly, *On Time* 207; later, Appendix 62.]

### On Naaman the Syrian

[Note: [Col. 1830] Of uncertain authorship, and unworthy of John Chrysostom, to whom it is attributed in two manuscripts.]

### 1.

When Naaman, the commander of the king of Syria, had been covered with leprosy, and, afflicted with the spotted contagion of a dreadful disease, had become abhorrent both to himself and to everyone else, the king of Syria grieved that he had been deprived of such a man’s assistance. Through Naaman he had waged many wars, subdued nations, won victories, and liberated the Syrian people from the hand of their enemies.

Then Naaman heard that among the people of Israel there was a most holy prophet, Elisha, renowned for wondrous powers and famous for extraordinary deeds, through whom he might be freed from the danger of his condition and cleansed of his destructive discoloration.

He immediately went to his own king and asked that he be commended by a letter to the king of Israel. At once the king sent a letter to the other king in these terms: “I have sent my servant Naaman to you, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.”

### 2.

When the king received and read this letter sent by the other king, he tore his garments, saying: “See, see! This man is looking for an occasion of hostility. He has sent a man to me so that I may cure him of his leprosy. Am I God, that I can kill or give life?”

O the faith of the Syrian commander Naaman! O the faithlessness of this king! Naaman the Syrian hastens faithfully to God, while the faithless king tears his garment. Those who knew did not believe; those who did not know believed. Those of the household resist; outsiders hasten. The king of Syria believes that what he has heard can happen, while the king of Israel does not believe that what he knows can happen.

Strangers run to obtain help; those who belong deny the heavenly gift. The one who ought to have preached destroys; the one who could have destroyed hastened, so that glory might be all the greater among outsiders, in proportion as the king’s faithlessness had become known.

### 3.

When the king’s agitation reached Elisha, he said: “Send Naaman the Syrian to me, send him, so that he may know that there is a God in Israel.”

Naaman the Syrian was therefore brought to the door of the man of God with chariots and horsemen and magnificent power. The man of God came out to him and said: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and you will be cleansed.”

When he heard this, Naaman was troubled and rushed away, saying: “I thought he would come out to me, place his hand upon me, invoke the Lord his God, and cure me of my leprosy. If I must be cleansed in water, are not the waters we have better?”

Then one of his men said to him: “Is the word that the prophet has spoken to you difficult? Why do you not do what he said?”

Naaman then returned and went down into the Jordan. After he had been baptized seven times, he came up cleansed, and his flesh became like the flesh of a little child.

Then Naaman marvels, then he is astonished; then he looks upon the prophet, then he turns his attention to heaven. He marvels that power was present at a single command; he marvels that God has acted; he marvels that a disease of such long duration has been wiped away; he marvels that he has been changed in body and in mind.

The destructive contagion is driven from him, and the desired health is restored. The whole man is returned to his natural state, because perfect power operates through the most holy prophet. Naaman rejoices; the prophet rejoices; the Lord is praised by both.

Naaman rejoices that he has received what he desired and found what he had lost [Note: [Col. 1831] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “believed.”]. The prophet rejoices in the deed, and the people rejoice in the power. Judea rejoices that she provides assistance to those coming to her; the Gentiles say that Israel possesses what they cannot find among themselves.

The glory of God is sown among the Gentiles. The one who has been cured proclaims; the one who has experienced it announces it. What is said is no longer doubtful, since Syria bears witness to what it sees in Naaman.

### 4.

Then joyful Naaman offers gifts to Elisha; then, in his desire for health, he begs him to accept presents. “Accept,” he says, “accept the gifts I offer you. What I give, I freely bestow; take it. This is not the price of the cure that I give, nor do I purchase the health I have received with this gift. Indeed, the health I have obtained could neither be bought with a price nor found through any gift.”

Elisha replied: “I do not accept what you offer; I reject as belonging to another what you press upon me. For I did not give you the health in which you rejoice; I myself did not correct the destructive disease in you, nor did I restore you to nature, as you suppose. Rather, there is a powerful God in the heavens, whose command I serve, whose office I obey, whose service I pursue, and to whom alone your mind must be dedicated, your understanding prepared, and your service offered.

“For if you serve Him alone, or bind yourself to the obedience due to Him, consider how great a reward you will deserve, since before you served Him you had already deserved such great health.”

### 5.

At once Naaman renounced the worship of false gods and cut off his superstitions. At once he professed that he revered God and detested idols. At once he declared that he worshiped the Lord whom he had recognized and abhorred the images he had worshiped.

“Now,” he said, “I know that the Lord alone is to be worshiped. Now for the first time I have learned that there is one God who must be revered. For the other gods of the Gentiles can neither save nor harm, since, being themselves dependent upon human assistance, they cannot provide assistance.

“Those who are saved cannot save; those who do not live cannot give life; and those who cannot defend themselves against those who do not worship them cannot make any of their worshipers healthy.”

Then Naaman set out for Syria rejoicing; then he hurried back to his people in good health. All who had come with him in sorrow rejoiced; all who had dreaded his condition were glad; all spoke among themselves of God’s mighty works, and together they recounted His powers.

### 6.

Immediately Gehazi, the prophet’s servant, said to himself: “Since my master did not wish to accept anything from Naaman the Syrian, I will go and take what he refused.”

He went quickly and hastened after him. When the Syrian servants saw him hurrying behind them and reported it to their master, Naaman immediately stopped his chariots, drew back his vehicles, turned his animals around, and, hurrying and hastening, returned to meet him. He asked the reason and demanded an explanation for his coming so quickly.

That deceitful and fraudulent man prepared a lie and fabricated a false story. He said that the prophet had sent him a message, as though Naaman should send some silver which the prophet would distribute to the sons of the prophets who had come to him.

Naaman promptly gave the servant twice as much as he had asked for—more than he himself, as a suppliant and petitioner, had been able to give the prophet. After receiving it and placing it in safekeeping, he appeared before Elisha and took his usual position in his presence.

“Where have you been,” the prophet asked, “or what business have you conducted?”

“Nowhere,” he replied. “I did not leave that place; I was nowhere absent from your sight.”

Then the most holy prophet exclaimed: “Was not my heart with you? I know how Naaman hurried to meet you and from whom you received the silver. You shall possess from it fields, vineyards, olive groves, male servants, and female servants; and the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian shall cling to you and to your offspring forever.”

Immediately he departed from him, leprous like snow (IV Kings V).

O wondrous power of God! O sublime merit of Elisha! At one and the same time a double power is displayed and a twofold authority is shown in the most holy prophet. Naaman the Syrian is cured, and the servant Gehazi is covered with leprosy.

Faith brought glory to the Syrian; faithlessness brought punishment to the servant. The one came from Syria and received what he desired; the other left the prophet’s house and acquired a wound through his faithlessness.

Naaman is cured and rejoices; Gehazi is wounded and mourns. One is restored healthy to his own people; the other is displayed to all as blemished. One is shown as an example of virtue; the other demonstrates the consequence of deceit.

The one who had been blemished is cured by faith; the one who had been healthy is blemished by faithlessness. Naaman invites people to God; Gehazi is displayed to each person as an example. Through Naaman the Lord is praised; through Gehazi heavenly judgment is feared.

From the one comes salvation; from the other fear. From the one glory is sought; from the other the trouble of fraud is dreaded, so that through these examples the value of faith and the punishment of faithlessness might be shown to all nations.

## SERMON XLIV

[Note: [Col. 1832] Formerly, *On Time* 208.]

### On Elisha and His Servant Gehazi

[Note: [Col. 1832] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It seemed doubtful to the Louvain editors and spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. The latter observes that the allegory presented here in section 2—namely, “The people of the Gentiles heard the prophecy and came to Christ”—corresponds to what is found above in section 3 of Appendix Sermon 8, in these words: “Thus through the prophetic word the Church of the Gentiles is invited from distant regions to the true bridegroom Christ.” We regard Caesarius as the author of both sermons. Moreover, the third part of the Sermon, which was absent from the printed editions, has here been restored from manuscripts.]

### 1. Elisha represented the Lord; Gehazi Judas or the Jews. The greedy are lepers.

We have frequently suggested to Your Charity, dearest brothers, that blessed Elisha bore a type of the Lord and Savior; while his disciple Gehazi, not unfittingly, is understood to have represented Judas the traitor or the Jewish people.

For just as Gehazi served blessed Elisha in order to acquire money, so Judas had attached himself to the Lord and Savior in order to commit fraud and gather earthly riches. Thus it is written about him in the Gospel: “Because he was a thief, and had the money box, and carried what was put into it” (John XII, 6).

Gehazi, who could have earned the grace of his master, just as his master had obtained that of blessed Elijah, overcome by greed deserved to be covered forever with a cruel leprosy. Judas, however, for the love of money lost the grace of the apostleship and ended his life by a noose.

Thus we understand that all greedy and covetous people are inwardly covered in their souls with the leprosy of sin.

### 2. Naaman, obeying the girl’s prophecy, represented the people of the Gentiles.

Naaman, the commander who was a leper and who came to blessed Elisha to be healed at the suggestion of a servant girl, represented the people of the Gentiles [Col. 1833].

That girl had been taken captive from Judea and had told her mistress that, if her master went to blessed Elisha, he would recover his health. That girl, I say, bore the image of prophecy. For although at that time the grace of prophecy flourished in Judea alone, it could not happen that this blessed knowledge did not also reach the neighboring nations.

Naaman therefore heard the girl and came to Elisha; the people of the Gentiles heard the prophecy and came to Christ. Naaman came to Elisha and was healed of leprosy; the people of the Gentiles came to Christ and were cleansed from every leprosy of sins.

### 3. The Jews were struck with leprosy when the Gentiles were freed from it.

Nevertheless, as I have already said, Gehazi can also represent the Jewish people, who were struck by the leprosy of sin at the very time when the people of the Gentiles were freed from it.

Thus the unhappy Jews cried out during the Lord’s Passion: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). They deserved then to be covered with the leprosy of sin, when with sacrilegious mouths they cried out against the heavenly physician: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him!” (John XIX, 15).

Therefore the leprosy remained in them at the time when grace passed over to us. Thus the Apostle Paul also spoke to them, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46).

When the apostles’ teaching passed to the Gentiles, the leprosy of sin remained in the wretched Jews.

### 4. The calling of the Gentiles to faith is figured through Baptism.

Let us see, nevertheless, what blessed Elisha commanded Naaman the Syrian. “Go,” he said, “and wash seven times in the Jordan.”

When Naaman heard that he was to wash seven times in the Jordan, he became indignant and was unwilling to agree. But after receiving counsel from his friends, he consented to wash and was cleansed.

This signifies that the people of the Gentiles, before Christ was crucified, did not by themselves believe Christ when He spoke; but afterward, when the apostles preached, they came faithfully to the sacrament of Baptism.

Elisha told Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan. Observe, brothers: Elisha sends Naaman to the river Jordan because Christ was going to send the people of the Gentiles to Baptism.

The fact that Elisha did not himself touch or baptize Naaman signifies that Christ did not come personally to the people of the Gentiles, but through His apostles, to whom He said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Observe this also: Naaman, who represented the people of the Gentiles, received health in that river which Christ later consecrated by His Baptism.

But when Naaman heard that he should wash seven times in the Jordan, he became indignant and said: “Are not the rivers of my country, the rivers of Damascus, the Abana and the Pharpar, better, so that I may wash and be cleansed in them?”

When he said this, his servants advised him to submit to the prophet’s counsel. But consider carefully, brothers, what this signifies.

Holy Elisha, as we have said, bore a type of the Lord and Savior; Naaman represented the people of the Gentiles. What did it signify that he believed he would receive health from his own rivers? It indicated that the human race presumed upon free will and its own merits.

But personal merits can possess leprosy without the grace of Christ; they cannot possess health. Therefore, unless the human race, following Naaman’s example, had listened to Elisha’s counsel and humbly received the gift of Baptism through Christ’s grace, it could not have been freed from original and actual leprosy.

“Wash seven times,” he said, referring to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which rested in Christ the Lord. Thus, when the Lord was baptized in that river, the Holy Spirit came upon Him in the form of a dove (John I, 32).

### 5. Those who are baptized begin to be born

When, therefore, Naaman had descended into the river as a figure of Baptism, “his flesh,” it says, “became like that of a little child” [Col. 1834] (2 Kings 5). See, dearest brothers, how this likeness is fulfilled in the Christian people. For you know that all who are baptized—whether they are old or young—all are nevertheless born as infants. The first generation brings forth for death; the second generation brings forth for life. The first generates children of wrath; the second generates vessels of mercy. As the Apostle says: “In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22).

Just as Naaman, though he was an old man, was cleansed by washing seven times as though he were a little child, so the person who has become old through former sins and is covered, like a leper, with the many stains of iniquities is so renewed by the grace of Baptism that in him neither the original nor the actual leprosy of sin remains. And he who had always been bent beneath the weight of crimes is renewed by the saving bath, after the example of Naaman, as a little child, so that in him is fulfilled what the Apostle says of Christ concerning the Church: “That he might present the Church to himself without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27).

### 6. The great gifts of the Lord should bring us not judgment but progress

The fact that, after Naaman had been cleansed, he offered gifts to blessed Elisha, while Elisha refused to accept them, signified the grace of Christ. It is called grace because it is given freely. Thus the Lord said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cast out demons; you have received freely, give freely” (Matt. 10:8).

And because we see that all the sacraments and mysteries of our Lord, which had been prefigured among the Jews, have been fulfilled in us, even if we cannot give God as much thanks as we ought, let us give him as much as we can; for he has deigned to bestow such great blessings upon us without any preceding merits of good works. For our salvation he sent not only his disciples, but he himself descended; and for us he patiently received scourges, insults, and the other injuries that we read of. He was wounded to heal our wounds; he died to free us from everlasting death; he descended to the underworld to snatch us from the jaws of the most savage dragon; he rose again to give us the hope of resurrection; he ascended into heaven to show us where we ought to follow him.

What, then, shall we render to the Lord for these gifts, which we are unable even to contemplate, much less explain to you, except that—as I have already said—we should continually offer as much thanks as we can and, with his help, strive that his gifts and benefits may bring us not judgment but progress? Let us also labor to fulfill his commandments, so that when the day of judgment comes, and we have been delivered from the sound of evil, that desirable voice may be directed to us: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 25:34). May the Lord bring us to it under his protection. Amen.

## SERMON XLV

[Note: [Col. 1834] Elsewhere, *On the Season* 210.]

### On Elisha and the axe-head that fell into the pool

[Note: [Col. 1834] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors have the same doubts about this sermon as about the preceding one; Verlini and Vinding likewise condemn it. You will readily judge that it should be attributed to the same author, Caesarius. For no. 3, see his Homily 16; for no. 4, Homilies 12 and 37.]

### 1. The figure of the fall of the human race

When the divine reading was just being read, dearest brothers, we heard that blessed Elisha was going with the sons of the prophets to the Jordan River. While they were cutting wood for themselves, an axe fell into the water. The man from whose hand it had fallen cried out to blessed Elisha, “Alas, my lord! And I had borrowed it!” After this, in the place where the axe had fallen, blessed Elisha threw in a piece of wood, and the iron floated (2 Kings 6:4–7).

We have often suggested to Your Charity, beloved brothers, that Elisha bore the figure of the Lord and Savior. But in the young man who was one of the sons of the prophets, from whose hand the axe fell, the Lord Christ may also appropriately be understood. That axe which fell is said to have signified Adam, or the entire human race.

The son of the prophets, therefore, held the axe in his hand; and our Lord and Savior held in the hand of his power the human race that he had created. But just as that axe fell from the prophet’s hand into the depths, so the human race shook itself loose from the hand of almighty God through pride, fell, and submerged itself in the river of lust, in the pool of all sins. That axe therefore lay in the depths because the human race had fallen through an unhappy ruin into the abyss of every crime. As it is written: “I am fixed in the mire of the deep”; and again: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68:3), and so forth.

For that river in which the axe fell signifies pleasure—or the lust—of this world, which flows past, flees, and descends into the abyss. The river receives its name from flowing. And because all sinners are said to flow away, clinging to or longing for passing pleasures, that axe therefore lay submerged in the river and in the mire.

### 2. The figure of its restoration; the need to beware of falling again

Elisha came, therefore, threw in a piece of wood, and the iron floated. What does it mean to throw in wood and bring the iron into the light, except to ascend the gallows of the cross, raise the human race from the depths of hell, and free it from the mire of all sins through the mystery of the cross?

After the iron had floated, the prophet stretched out his hand, took it, and restored it to the useful purposes of its master. So it has happened to us, beloved brothers. We had fallen through pride from the hand of the Lord, but through the wood of the cross we deserved to be brought back again to the Lord’s hand, or to his power. Therefore, as far as we can, let us strive with his help not to fall again through pride from the hand of the Lord.

And because without any preceding merits we have been brought from darkness into light, recalled from death to life, and led back from many errors onto the way, let us run while we have the light, lest we neglect the passing opportunities for salvation. Let us not delight in the badly sweet and exceedingly dangerous joy of this world, lest we fall again from holy works and from the way of righteousness, as though from the hand of the Lord, and return to the lustful river of this world, where we may once more be submerged in the mire of all sins through an unhappy fall.

But let us hear the Apostle saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above” (Col. 3:1–2). Why does he say, “If you have risen,” unless it is because we had fallen? And elsewhere the same Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Does this not seem like a cry to the axe lying in the mire? “Rise,” he says, “you who sleep in the deep pool; and through the mystery of the cross Christ will enlighten you.”

### 3. Whoever sins destroys the temple of God

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, with God’s help strive to carry all these things out through the sacrament of Baptism, so that the benefits of our Lord may bring us not judgment but progress. Let us preserve the sweetness of charity, purity of heart, and chastity of body, lest the sacraments of God suffer injury in us.

For if it is true—indeed, because it is true—that the Apostle says, “We are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in us” (1 Cor. 3:16), whenever we complete some sin by thinking, speaking, or acting, we destroy the temple of God and inflict injuries upon the one who dwells in us.

Therefore, if anyone has defiled within himself the temple of God with shameful thoughts, polluted it with lustful speech, or perhaps destroyed it down to its foundations through whatever crimes, while there is still time let him strive, with God’s help, to restore what has been lost, raise up what has fallen, and rebuild what has been destroyed. Thus, when the day of judgment comes, even if he does not deserve to receive a crown, he may at least deserve to attain forgiveness for his sins.

When I said “or at least to attain forgiveness for his sins,” I seem to have spoken out of the humility that is very necessary for us. For that heavenly physician is accustomed to repay repentant penitents who give alms generously not only with forgiveness but also with a crown.

[Col. 1836]

### 4. Conclusion

Therefore, dearest brothers, although negligent, nevertheless appointed by the Lord as a herald of truth, I say, proclaim, and admonish what it is useful for you to hear and necessary for me to say. If I do not suggest as much as I ought or as much as I can, still I do proclaim and admonish.

Whoever despises the herald should fear the judge. None of you will be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of Christ by saying that he was not admonished to resist every vice and devote himself to the virtues. And because you have often been shown what you ought to avoid or flee, and by constant preaching have been taught what you ought to do or seek, act, with God’s help, so that our admonition may serve you more for reward than for judgment before the tribunal of the eternal Judge.

May he himself deign to grant this to you, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI

[Note: [Col. 1836] Formerly, *On the Season* 211; later, in Appendix 63.]

### On the famine of Samaria

[Note: [Col. 1836] By an uncertain and unlearned author.]

### 1. When an ungodly people depart from the worship of God, they are crushed by dreadful famine and troubled by just necessity

“The son of Adadezer, king of Syria, came,” it says, “against Samaria and besieged it. And there was a great famine, so that the head of a donkey was sold for fifty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a cab of dove’s dung for five shekels of silver.”

Why do you suffer famine, most miserable man? Why do you feel such appalling want? Why are you torn apart by such poverty? The punishment of famine increases daily because guilt also increases daily. The scourges continue because sins also continue among the people. For on your account the enemy has rushed in, the foe has besieged you, and the adversary has devoured your provisions. You hunger, while he grows fat. You suffer horrible famine, while he feasts on your provisions.

You purchase the carcasses of donkeys and the dung of pigeons with silver. Henceforth, live wisely: condemn sins, restrain offenses, turn back to God, leave the idol, abhor the image. Then, with divine help, you will be able to conquer your enemies and overcome them in heavenly battle. No one will be able to harm you any longer if, once wickedness has been condemned, divine worship takes root in you.

Shame upon this outrage! A sinful people eats dreadful carcasses and pigeon dung and does not seek the worship of God. Famine and necessity demand polluted flesh and horrible food, yet the stubbornness of human beings still worships an image. Provisions are denied, while unlawful things are offered by sinners. God is not sought by the sinful people, and the idol is worshiped.

The worship of God is changed into an image; religion is changed, and food is changed as well. The holy worship of God is changed, and human provisions are changed too: forbidden things are eaten. For just as what is worshiped is alien, so what is unlawfully hungered for is alien. It is not difficult for a people to experience physical famine when it is clear that, by living wickedly, it has hungered spiritually.

### 2. As vices increase, famine also increases; sins lead mothers to desire the corpses of their children

Meanwhile, as vices increase, famine also grows, and sins lead mothers to desire the corpses of their children. Two women, in turn, plan to devour their own children. Alas for the sorrow! Piety is turned into food; the child received into the womb is changed into nourishment. Parricide is committed before the women come to the fatal meal. The soul is torn from the limbs, and the mothers’ wombs are polluted. Innocent blood is poured out so that the parents’ raging hunger may be fed.

For among them everything is cruel and, I say, unspeakable: to pour out innocent blood, digest innocent flesh, and swallow cooked limbs with greedy mouths, so that she may turn into food the child whom God created for consolation.

But after they had come to the fatal meal, one woman exhorted the other: “Take him,” she said, “take him, wretched mother, into your womb—the son recently begotten from your own womb. Be the tomb of your child; be the lodging place of his body; be, so to speak, his monument. Let the infant who, from hunger, could scarcely continue living return within you after being eaten. Let the maternal bosoms that had nourished him within and brought him forth alive into the light recognize him, piece by piece, as he is returned to them. Let the womb now receive the child it had given birth to alive. Let the dead return to the dwelling from which he had recently emerged alive, since hunger presses and necessity compels. Why should I die while my child survives, and why should I not rather, as his mother, consume my child?”

### 3. One woman rescues her son from the calamity

When this woman was already looking upon the child who had been eaten, she withdrew her own son from this calamity. She refused to do to her own child what she had done with the other woman’s child.

“It is enough,” she said; “it is enough for me, woman, that I consented to your crime. It is enough that I tasted the fatal meal and polluted my entrails with the flesh of an innocent. I shared with you the cruel plan of committing unspeakable parricide against my son. What I committed with you I cannot atone for; I cannot reject the unspeakable crime. At least, let your burden be lightened through my child, since you are so heavily burdened through yours. Stop with my crime; stop with the graver crime that you have committed.

Would that you had not done what you did, and that I had not committed the crime into which I fell: that I should commit homicide and perpetrate parricide. Learn from me what you have done, since through you I have suffered the loss of what I had. Therefore I will not do what you compel me to do; I flee what you urge; I shudder at what you thrust upon me.”

### 4. The matter is brought before the king

Then one woman dragged the other before the king and brought her to judgment. She made public the cause of such a great crime, for the enormity of the deed compelled her to disclose it. Then, I say, grief exposed the wicked deed; then treacherous piety laid bare the monstrous crime.

The mad woman burns because she committed parricide; she burns because she devoured her son. But she burns even more because, in that calamity, the other woman did not sacrifice her own son.

“Either I will die with her,” she said, “or certainly, just as she attacked my child, so I will attack hers. O just king, confirm our unjust agreement: for I would never have killed my child unless she had placed her own child, to be killed, in the bargain by her hateful decision. Therefore, lord king, let her either return my child who was eaten, or reveal her own child who has been hidden. Certainly, as is fitting, strike us both with the same sentence, lest I live after so great a crime, or she rejoice that she was not a parricide toward her own son.”

### 5. The prophet announces abundance, but unbelief is punished

When the king heard this, he tore his garments and changed his expression. Immediately the prophet sent word to the king: “Thus says the Lord: At this hour tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley will be sold for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.”

The most holy prophet announces from heaven the abundance that faith alone could believe and unbelief deny could happen. He announces that an abundance of fine flour will replace the famine; he announces that famine will cease and plenty will follow. He announces that the great works of God will suddenly follow through the power of the Most High—and human unbelief is added to its own crime.

Then the man who had been sent by the king said: “Even if the cataracts of heaven were opened, could what is being announced happen?”

O human unbelief! He does not believe that the promised abundance can come about, though he had experienced dreadful want. He does not consider that God promised abundance, though he had inflicted scarcity upon the people.

Most wicked man, why do you not believe in miracles? Why do you not accept the grain? Why do you shudder at the Lord who promises? Believe what is given to those who believe. Believe that it will happen to the people whose fellowship you have already denied yourself. And because you are unworthy of such great blessings, you are permitted to see them, but denied the ability to enjoy them.

### 6. God drives away the Syrians by a sound of armies

While these things were taking place, the Lord caused a sound to be heard in the camp of the Syrians in order to grant the people the abundance that had been promised. He chose to make the clatter of chariots, the noise of wagons, and the tumult of armed enemies resound in their ears, so that he might now set his people free.

Struck by this sound, the enemies fled; without a battle they turned their backs and abandoned their equipment. The Israelites went out from the city, entered the enemy camp, and plundered it. As the people returned laden with goods, the man who had not believed fell down; and when he saw the abundance among the people, he fell and was crushed (2 Kings 6–7).

## SERMON XLVII

[Note: [Col. 1838] Formerly, *On the Season* 226; later, in Appendix 65.]

### On blessed Tobit

[Note: [Col. 1838] By an uncertain and unlearned author.]

[Col. 1838]

### 1. Blessed Tobit, who knew how to break his bread for the hungry, prepares swift payment for the laboring hireling

After receiving the reading that was recently recited with patience, we marveled at the conduct of father and son: how the angel counsels them, whom they thought to be an earthly hireling beneath heavenly glory. For this reason he fell into the calamity of blindness, so that he might receive an angel as physician, who, kindled by divine torches, breathed forth these words:

“Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is honorable. The prayer of the righteous is the key of heaven. Prayer ascends, and God’s mercy descends. Though earth is high and heaven higher, God nevertheless hears the human tongue if the conscience is clean. He speaks with the senses if our only speech is a groan. A rain of tears is enough for his ears; weeping is heard more quickly than voices. The prayer of the envious is usually driven away from his ears.”

The father and son had one soul, though their limbs were distinct; they possessed a singular kinship of spirit.

“Son,” he said, “let us dismiss this man, adding to the agreed payment, because through his work he has brought us many good things.”

And the son, recounting what had happened, addressed his father:

“Father, should this blessed worker really be paid only the agreed wage, whose excellent guidance cannot be valued? We shall give him too little honor if we set a limit to his merits. Did he provide only what had been agreed? It had been agreed that he should show me the region and the man to whom you entrusted the money. First, setting out on what was almost a heavenly journey, he prepared for both you and me the necessary eye-salve from the fish; he led me there, recovered the money, and betrothed Sarah to me as my wife.

“He is worthy of more than the agreed payment, he who proved to me like a heavenly matchmaker. And what is more, good father, he cured the spots from your eyes by removing the whiteness and illuminated our entire house by lighting the lamps of your eyes. Now I see more clearly because I look upon you seeing. Is this man not worthy, excellent father, of half our property? Let such a guide and provider, physician and guardian, as I have said, receive half the property which he himself carried with me, since by his guidance he showed me such great kindness.”

The good father was pleased by his wise son’s answer. He began to ask the hireling to take the substance of his payment.

“Brother,” he said, “take what is yours, and then go in peace. Receive your payment, because you have shown mercy to me and to my son. Take, as I have said, half the property that you brought back with my son; for the gratitude we owe you cannot be weighed.”

### 2. The angel refuses human payment

Immediately the angel rejoiced at the payment they had conceived, though he had been sent freely to perform an act of kindness.

“Tobit—or Tobias,” he said, “why are you thinking so excessively about my payment? Keep what that heavenly Father has given you. I am the minister of healing; he is the author of health. You do not know through whose hireling service you have deserved to benefit.

“You did not fear to bury the dead of the captivity, Tobit; your works ascended to the Lord, because, leaving your meal, you gave a dead man burial. I offered to the Lord rich sacrifices for the venerable burial; I was sent as a worker of the heavenly marketplace. You buried the dead and did not fear the sting of death. The one who was buried proclaimed for you with a silent voice.

“The blindness of your eyes was a test, through which your patience might deserve more splendid heavenly adornment. I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before the glory of God. I do not need the fruit of human payment; communion with majesty makes me rich. Rich is the one who sent me, who commanded that I be expended freely, who himself freely granted what you received.

“Do not even count the honor of thanksgiving as owed to me, because you received nothing through my powers. Bless God, confess to him, and glorify him, because he has done good things with you” (Tob. 12).

### 3. The identity of the angel is revealed

Suddenly, when the heavenly mystery had been revealed, Tobit and Tobias, struck with astonishment at the voice of the angel Raphael, fell prostrate upon the earth and concealed their trembling voices completely, because they had heard an unfamiliar voice.

What had you deserved, father Tobit and son Tobias? To have a heavenly hireling and to hire as a worker one who was earthly? The angel concealed his name:

“I am Azariah,” he said, “the son of the great Ananias” (Tob. 5:18),

and he did not say, “I am the angel Raphael.” He concealed his dignity under the first name so that he would not terrify those who were hiring him. For if he had said, “I am an angel,” he would not have been Tobias’s hireling. The dignity of the name was withheld so that at the end the greatness of his dignity might become clear.

See, beloved, how great is the merit of almsgiving: it deserved to have an angel as its worker. You see how much good comes from burying the dead, so that his offering might ascend through the angel Raphael to the heavenly majesty. You see that almsgiving delivers from death and itself cleanses sins. It purifies the eyes and frees them from the darkness of sins. Tobit is led along his way; Sarah, saddened by so many husbands, is joined in marriage through the angel.

## SERMON XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 1839] Formerly, *On the Season* 228; later, in Appendix 66.]

### On Judith I

[Note: [Col. 1839] By an uncertain and unlearned author.]

### 1. Judith conquers Holofernes

Mortal eloquence is not sufficient to recount all the outstanding prayers of the righteous, their triumphs, and the weighty virtues that almighty God gave to those to whom he is accustomed to grant victory. He allowed men and women to be strong; he scattered the flame of the furnace with cooling relief and exposed treacherous armies by striking off their leader’s head.

For when that Holofernes, the enemy of the sons of Israel—or rather of his own head—claimed authority over foreign nations and fought by siege, arms, and fire, even turning the fields of many peoples, heavy with harvests of flesh, into ashes as the flame fed upon them, the most holy Judith, for whose prayers heaven was opened, fashioned victorious weapons by the art of prayer. With them she could engage her adversaries and, as a woman, avenge men who were trembling.

The city was squalid under the siege of barbarous savagery. Everything was languishing so greatly that its inhabitants were already judging it more tolerable to be handed over to the enemy than to be tormented by the ravages of destructive famine.

Behold Judith: after prayer and sackcloth, after ashes, she returns to the adornments of a young woman. The hope of all the peoples goes forth. About to make anxious peoples secure, she consoles them by her wisdom. Promising a victory that every nation would marvel at, she asks that the gate be opened for her a little after the barriers have been moved aside.

She went forth secure, content with the company of one young woman, and hastened with confident steps into the camp of the enemy. Within the walls she had been anxious; she became secure when she reached what was to be feared. At the sight of this woman’s novel and deceitful beauty, the hostile army was so greatly terrified that they lost their strength in her service, threw down their arms, and bowed their necks.

### 2. Judith deceives Holofernes

The deception of Holofernes and the victory of the mourning city were brought in due order to the praetorium. When Holofernes saw her, his senses deserted him, and he was about to lose his soul together with his head. The disgrace of young men lay captive before a woman’s face. A woman was permitted to disarm young men, defeat conquerors, defend an anxious city, and overthrow a barbarian warrior.

She deceived the corrupted man by her sincerity; she outwitted the polluted man by her chastity; the modest woman defeated the adulterer; the sober woman struck down the drunkard. For by the deceit of her treacherous appearance she had so confounded those barbarous minds that she bound him by a web of many speeches, making him defeated amid his armies and captive amid his weapons.

A feast was prepared for the king, and Judith was ordered to attend. She consented in order to conquer. She approached the feast, intending to taste none of the food or drink of the enemy, for she wished to be content with her own provisions. Although that warrior, unsound in mind, gazed upon the face of the most chaste woman, she nevertheless kept in mind why she had come: she was thinking about his head, which, once removed, would aid the exhausted citizens and protect, defend, and avenge many heads.

[Col. 1840]

### 3. Judith kills Holofernes

But when the fullness of the feast had passed its limits and heavy sleep followed the cups, Judith saw the necks of the enemy’s body bowed by drunkenness. She rose, seized his bloody neck, and also grasped the hair of the barbarian’s head in her hand.

“Lord,” she said, “strengthen my arm.”

She struck his neck three times and cut off his head. She went outside, handed Holofernes’ head to the young woman, and put it into the bag. A little later she went outside as though to pray, according to her custom.

Behold chastity. Through the favor of prayer, chastity preserved her own modesty intact and undisturbed, while deceiving another’s. The corpse lay enclosed, while the head was already outside.

With the palm-bearing victory of chastity, Judith hastened anxiously to the citizens. She was not prevented from returning, since she had been permitted to go forth as though to prayer. Now the astonished city received the triumphal return of so great a victor; mourning was changed into joy; the gates were opened in complete security; the victorious head hung upon the walls.

There was victory throughout the city, while terror and flight prevailed in the enemy camp (Judith 10–15). Judith was secure in the city among those made secure. For wherever heaven is struck by persistent prayers, the power of arms is always trampled underfoot.

Behold, prayer preserved the chastity of the glorious woman, while the multitude could not preserve the enemy. One woman was able to avenge the mourning city, while such a great army could not protect its king.

## SERMON XLIX

[Note: [Col. 1840] Formerly, *On the Season* 229; later, in Appendix 67.]

### On Judith II

[Note: [Col. 1840] By an uncertain and unlearned author.]

### 1. Judith prepares for battle

Whenever a warlike rumor grows through a terrifying report, or a deadly murmur resounds with the terrifying blare of trumpets or the hoarse sound of bronze, the image of death appears frightening to women and the weak. But the fearless hearts of brave men are accustomed to burn with love of praise.
