In the fortunes of war, when the combatants, thickened by a deadly rain, have covered their joined ranks with a fatal shadow and the whistling course of weapons, they draw near to triumphal palms with headlong ardor, though already wandering toward a deadly outcome.

Judith, a warrior in spirit, besieged the enemy’s breast. Casting away the fear proper to women, she sought victory amid dangers, neither fearing death in danger nor dreading uncertainty.

When Holofernes therefore trod upon the walls of Bethulia in a hostile siege and, diverting the watercourses, first proclaimed the battle of thirst, Judith preserved in mournful lament the covenant of her marriage, broken by bitter separation. When she discovered that a respite had been requested for the capture of the city, her private grief was immediately joined to the common grief of the city.

When she had been entreated, she rose, washed her body with water, put on adornments, hung down golden riches as earrings, and placed jeweled, shining bracelets upon her hands. She gathered the flowing folds of her purple garment across her gemmed breast. With a chaste expression she prepared to fight before taking up the sword.

The weapons of necklaces, always opposed to modesty, learned to strike the enemy. The avenger of her people took up the weapons of adornment. She was not going to a wedding after the war; rather, as a bride and warrior, she went forth from the city to war. Nor was the adornment frivolous, since it was being prepared for the murder of so great a leader.

Led by the divine Spirit, she went forth, content with the companionship of a single maidservant. She guarded her appearance, which was alluring; and lest the chastity she guarded be violated by force, she addressed Holofernes so that an empty desire might be conceived:

“I, your maidservant,” she said, “have been sent by the Lord God to do a deed at which everyone who hears of it will marvel, because your maidservant worships the God of heaven. Now I will go out by night and pray to the Lord of heaven; and he will announce to me when he will do these things. I will lead you through the middle of Judea, set your seat in the middle of the city, and no dog will bark its tongue against you, because these things have been shown to me by the Lord.”

It was not fitting for a chaste woman to lie. She did not say this to those who understood; she fulfilled by her actions what she promised.

### 2. Judith defeats the enemy

While she flattered the king with lofty speech and imaginary words, the warrior’s spirit was dissolved by lust. The countless strength of the soldiers grew sluggish in the love of arms. Amid royal luxury, the pomp of a wedding was constructed though no one was marrying, and all were undone by drunkenness.

It was not a delicate matron who fought; rather, sleep prepared you, Holofernes, for the blow. Once the bridal chamber had been arranged, she was stirred toward the commander, who was prone with love, overcome by sleep, and laid out upon his bed. She entangled the warrior’s hair with the beauty of her fingers; after the soft body had been stretched out, she sought the hilt of the ebony sword.

The sword did not terrify the matron; it armed her, and thus she fought. The flashing blade removed the enemy’s head; the victory was accomplished and hung upon the walls of her homeland (Judith 10–15).

The ranks gather in astonished columns and triumph in an inverted order. The army follows, poured out in wine and loosened by sleep; they rise to battle without a cry summoning them. Mountains are covered with flashing weapons.

“Why do you rage, foreigner? Why do you arrange battles? Why do you prepare your battle line when you have someone whom you must seek in the bedroom? Restrain every varied assault of fury. We have left you only your commander; we have his recognizable portion hanging at the gate.”

The spirit received from God as great a generosity as faith was able to claim for itself.

## SERMON L

[Note: [Col. 1841] Formerly, *On the Season* 224; later, in Appendix 64.]

### On blessed Job I

[Note: [Col. 1841] By an uncertain and unlearned author.]

### 1. Job’s faith withstands every trial

Your Holiness’ prompting warns me to be readier to speak. The confidence to speak, which has long been suggested by the Scriptures, is also granted with complete devotion, since God has shown that you gladly listen to me. Thus may Your Holiness receive me speaking about Job as though you were listening to a rustic.

Do not suppose that the man who professes to speak simply under Job’s instruction is uttering speeches tainted with artificial coloring. The devil obtained permission to fight against Job. When the ruin destroyed his children, he became poor after being rich; alone after having a household; after a numerous offspring, the father of no one; shipwrecked in his possessions. In his body he endured devouring torments with the single strength of faith.

His riches fell into poverty. Here a new awakening occurred through nakedness: no one was near, because friendship is rare for the miserable. The health of his body was changed into wounds; joy was turned into pain; there was no limb that was not agitated by the scourges of illness.

At last, illustrious righteousness lay beneath the dung heap. While wounded flesh was being tested in his limbs, his breast within remained unharmed. From head to foot there was nothing that pain did not afflict. Surrounded on every side by encircling torments, he stood firm. From the very point where the devil’s envy burned, victory was drawn forth in exhaustion.

He was tortured in body and tested in spirit. His body endured doubled punishments from restless worms, while a fruitful calamity hardened the putrefaction of his flowing flesh. There was no rest by night, no respite by day. He was tortured, and he prayed. The enemy sought one thing; the confession of the sufferer’s cry asked another.

His nerves loosened, the harsher potsherd scraped away the flow of pus, and the terrible torture changed. He did not recognize kings, and his pierced body reclined in the dung. In his shipwrecked body, uninjured righteousness was protected; amid limbs in peril, his breast was preserved for the author of his wounds. The enemy had occupied everything except his spirit.

### 2. The restoration of Job

There was no one to return an equivalent gift in payment. The delicate matron served in other people’s houses, she who had been accustomed to command. When, after sunset, she had endured the hardships of the day with difficulty, she awaited rest; and with her matronly fingers exhausted, she drew out the succeeding day with tearful eyes.

The woman bereft of her children and sunk in mourning was placed in service, with no time even for tears. Still a matron, now a widow, everywhere a hireling and nowhere a mistress, she wept over the destruction of her womb, neither childless nor a mother.

“Behold, husband,” she said, “what you are suffering. Say something against God, and die.”

She alone sinned, because she denied mercy to her husband. Job’s wife had learned to forget him in his children, while, though everything in his body was flowing away, his spirit alone faithfully resisted.

The warrior of the world was tortured in one man; while the punishment itself inflicted torment, it turned back upon its author.

“Behold,” says the Lord, “I hand him over to you; only preserve his life” (Job 1–2).

He fights securely who is preserved while the enemy fears. Thus the enemy raged that he might fear. Cruelty inflicts pain and then fails in its own strength. Once the punishment was driven away, health returned; and medicine, made more fortunate by its scars, was restored.

The Lord heals more swiftly than the enemy wounds. Groans migrated into joys, and in the pits of the wounds the monuments of victory were counted. Because of Job she became a queen, because of him she had been a hireling. She returned with double interest, so that what had been lost might be received back twofold.

## SERMON LI

[Note: [Col. 1842] Elsewhere, *On the Season* 225.]

### On blessed Job II

[Note: [Col. 1842] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, and Verlini and Vinding considered it spurious. It is by an erudite and pious author, but one unknown to us.]

# 1. Job victorious in prosperity and adversity. The faith of the righteous is a treasure

In the reading that has been read to us, dearest brothers, we heard that the most glorious athlete of God fought wondrously against a most cunning enemy; and, according to what the Apostle says, “a spectacle to God and to his angels and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9), we have been permitted to hear it with immense wonder and, in a certain way, to see it with the eyes of faith. We saw blessed Job fighting bravely and successfully not only against the prosperity of the world, but also against poverty, the harshest sufferings, and the bereavement of his children. When he was rich, he despised no one; when he suffered want, he blasphemed no one, nor dared to murmur against God’s dispensation. Rather, while wealthy, he said: “My house was open to all travelers, and the shoulders of the weak were warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (Job 31:19–20). Later, when he was oppressed by poverty, he said in his distress: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (ibid. 1–2).

The devil wrestled fiercely, but could not overcome God’s athlete. He raised monstrous waves, but could not move the firmest rock. He employed his schemes, but did not overthrow the strongest tower. He shook a tree, but could not knock down its fruit; he broke its branches, but harmed nothing at the root. He bored through a wall, but could not carry away the treasure. And by “treasure” I mean not gold and silver, but the faith of the righteous. For this was the treasure the devil hastened to plunder when, after stripping him of all his possessions, he tortured him with an intolerable affliction.

You saw the waves increase; you saw the firmest rock; you saw the impregnable tower; you saw God glorified and the devil shattered. By what name should I call this righteous man, I do not know. Shall I call him an athlete? Yet he surpasses it through the abundance of so many crowns. Shall I call him a rock? Yet I see one still firmer. Shall I call him a soldier? Yet I perceive one stronger in steadfastness. Shall I call him a tower? Yet wisdom rises above it. Shall I call him a tree? Yet he is found more beautiful. Shall I call him a fruit? Yet he is shown to be more precious. Shall I call him a treasure? Yet he is recognized as more abundant. By what word I should call that holy man, I cannot find.

# 2. A rich person too can be good, and a poor person blessed. The contempt of the poor must be avoided

Let the rich hear this, and let the poor hear this: how this blessed man, in his wealth and prosperity, proved a kindly steward of his riches, and in the trial of poverty endured patiently and bravely. You see, therefore, that it is not impossible for a rich person to abound in good works, nor impossible for a poor person, through patience in want, to be blessed.

Do not tell me, “I fear poverty.” You fear poverty, and do not fear sin? I do not want you to fear poverty; fear iniquity, which is the mother of torments. The Lord asks you for a payment, and you do not wish to give it. For when you hear him say, “As long as you did it to one of these least ones” (Matt. 25:40), surely, if you give to the poor, you lend to Christ. If you withdraw your hand from the poor, how and with what confidence will you then ask mercy from the Lord on that day? Will he not accuse you, saying: “You saw me naked, and did not clothe me; hungry, and did not feed me” (Matt. 25:43)? What will you answer to this, and what pardon will you beg? Will not your conscience make you guilty, and will you not fall silent?

You are sometimes filled to surfeit with many costly and choice delicacies, while you pretend not to have anything to give the poor with which to drive away his hunger or provide him a simple meal. You walk about dressed in excessively expensive clothing, yet give the naked poor person not even the cheapest garment. You strive to arrange and adorn your house with every display of magnificence; perhaps you do not receive a stranger or poor person even in one corner of it.

But such a person, when his irrevocable end arrives, if repentance has not come to his aid, will go naked of good works to hell, while his house remains with all its adornment as a testimony to his greed. Every passerby will say: “This was the house of that robber, plunderer, and miser. How many widows he afflicted, how many orphans he stripped, how many wretched people he made, in order to erect this house at such great expense from goods acquired through iniquity!”

# 3. It is not the dignity of the noble that is to be condemned, but arrogance. How dear human beings are to God

But someone says: “I am noble and hold an honored position.” No one condemns nobility; no one disputes those dignities that God graciously grants to human beings. Therefore, no one ought to condemn the rich who hold positions of honor, if they live justly, chastely, and mercifully.

But those deserve pity and lamentation who, puffed up by the pride of their dignities, think that they will be immortal together with those dignities; they do not consider their condition, that they are from the earth and will be reduced to dust, and that, for the sake of the brief pleasure of this life—if indeed it should be called either pleasure or life—they will endure everlasting torments.

You look upon a poor person and despise him, and do not reflect that he is a human being, just as you are: a human being, God’s dear and beloved possession; a human being for whose sake heaven was established, the sea stretched out, and the earth founded; for whose sake the sun rises and sets, the moon waxes and wanes, and the shining stars arise.

Do you then despise a poor human being, for whom God established such great and marvelous things—and, to say even more, for whom the Son of God assumed human flesh, endured insults and scourging, bore the cross, felt the bitterness of the scourging, tasted death, descended to the underworld, and freed, at the price of his blood, those who were held captive there by the devil?

Behold how many and what great gifts divine mercy has granted to the human race. See, therefore, whether it is just that any poor person should be despised by us, when divine mercy bestows so many benefits upon him.

# 4. God’s favor toward the poor

Let us therefore love, dearest brothers, and not despise the poor or strangers, lest he despise us who, though rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8:9).

Consider, brothers, and pay close attention: from the beginning God did not wish any poor person to be despised. For, as you have often and carefully heard in the divine Scriptures, in order to restrain the pride and vanity of the world, God did not choose rhetoricians, eloquent men, consuls, rich people, or powerful people to whom he would entrust the secrets of his word. Rather, he chose shepherds, such as the patriarchs and blessed David, or fishermen, such as blessed Peter and the other Apostles, so that through the weak he might destroy the strong, and through the humble cast down the exalted and proud.

Let us therefore love the poor, so that we may be able to share in the portion of him who said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Because the human race had received a mortal wound through pride, Christ offered the remedy of humility.

Do not despise the humble poor person: though he is poor in himself, he can make you rich. Let those who are rich imitate blessed Job, who humbly gave abundant alms. Let them not become elated in prosperity; and if, with the Lord permitting it, they suffer some misfortune, let them not be crushed by adversity. Let them murmur against God’s judgments in nothing, but with a humble and devout conscience say with blessed Job: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord,” to whom belong honor and sovereignty with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LII

[Note: Formerly, On Time 222.]

On blessed Job, III; and on the words of Psalm 97:5–6, “Sing praises to the Lord with the lyre,” etc.

[Note: Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the judgment of the Louvain editors it had remained doubtful among Augustine’s sermons. After Verlino, Vinding observed that most of what is found in it had been transferred here from Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 97.]

## 1. Who sings on the psaltery and lyre. Job as a beaten-out trumpet. Job afflicted for the purification of slight sins

Blessed Job, dearest brothers, about whom yesterday’s reading was recited to us, was so holy that in him was fulfilled what the Holy Spirit said in the Psalm: “Sing praises to the Lord with the lyre and with the voice of the psalm.” Take up not the voice alone, but works as well, so that we may not merely sing but also work with our hands.

Whoever sings and works sings on the psaltery and lyre. Whoever sings on the psaltery proclaims divine words from heaven; whoever works with his hands accomplishes human works. Stretch out your hands and give to the poor; clothe the naked; receive the stranger into hospitality. But when you do so, do it devoutly and cheerfully. Remember that you are doing it for him who will say: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35).

See what instruments are joined in the comparisons: “With beaten-out trumpets,” he says. Blessed Job, dearest brothers, was so full of God’s Spirit that, like a beaten-out trumpet, he sweetly sang the praises of the Lord. For this is the sound concerning such things: “With beaten-out trumpets and with the voice of the horn.”

Trumpets are of ductile bronze and are shaped by hammering. When are they stretched? When we suffer the persecution of wicked people, if we endure everything patiently and never murmur against the Lord’s dispensation. By being beaten, we become trumpets beaten out for the praise of the Lord, if we advance through tribulation. Tribulation is the hammering; progress is the stretching.

Blessed Job was a beaten-out trumpet when, struck by the devil and afflicted by such great losses, including the bereavement of his children, he murmured against the Lord in nothing. Through that hammering of such great tribulation he became a beaten-out trumpet.

Let us therefore hear whether that trumpet sounded well. Hear: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” See, brothers, how and how carefully it sounded, what a sweet sound it gave.

Nor is this alone sufficient, unless he is hammered further. He was handed over to Satan’s power, so that his flesh might be struck. He was struck and began to putrefy, so that swarms of worms furrowed him as they poured out.

Yet blessed Job, however righteous he was, was not without sins. For he was not better than the holy evangelist John, who says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). Through that most cruel punishment, his lesser sins were being purified. Understanding this himself, he also gave thanks to God; and, like a most truthful judge of his negligences, he scraped away the flowing corruption not with a soft linen cloth but with a potsherd.

## 2. Afflicted Job better than Adam in his integrity. Of all his goods, the devil leaves him only a woman

Eve, his wife, was left behind, as though for his seduction. It was necessary that his wife be left to him—not, to be sure, for the comfort of her husband, but for the devil’s service.

The woman suggested blasphemy; Job did not obey but refused. Adam did not repel Eve in paradise; Job repelled Eve on the dung heap. Job sat on the dung heap while he flowed with worms and putrefied; yet Job, full of wounds on the dung heap, was better than Adam whole in paradise. His wife was still indeed Eve, but that man was no longer Adam.

What, then, did the woman say? “Blaspheme God and die.”

## 3. The devil, the hammer of the whole earth

Behold, we have heard how this trumpet is hammered. The devil struck him with a grievous wound from head to foot, and, putrefying with worms, he sat on the dung heap.

We have heard how he was hammered; if it pleases you, let us hear the sweet voice of this beaten-out trumpet. For he answered his wife: “You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 1–2).

O strong sound! O sweet sound! Whom would this sound not awaken from sleep? Whom would confidence in the Lord not rouse to proceed fearlessly into battle against the devil—not seeking protection in his own strength, but in God’s help?

For he himself gave the assistance who permitted him to be tested. The devil could not hammer on his own initiative; he will be able to do nothing except what divine dispensation has permitted.

The prophet, speaking of the future punishment of that devil, says: “The hammer of the whole earth has been shattered” (Jer. 50:23). By “the hammer of the whole earth” he wished the devil to be understood. With this hammer, placed in the Lord’s hand—that is, in God’s power—the beaten-out trumpets, that is, holy souls, are hammered so that they may resound with God’s praises.

## 4. The righteous and the unrighteous are hammered by the devil

By this hammer the righteous person too is hammered, and the sinner: the one so that he may be tested, the other so that he may be punished—or rather, so that the righteous may increase in goodness and the sinner be corrected from his evils.

Under this hammer, established in the hand—that is, in the power—of the Lord, not only the humble but also the proud are hammered. The humble are stretched out; the proud are shattered like glass.

One and the same hammering advances the good toward glory and reduces the wicked to ashes, so that what is written may be fulfilled in them: “And he will be like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4).

Whenever holy souls are hammered by this hammer, through God’s dispensation or permission, they murmur in nothing and wholly contradict in nothing. Rather, humbly, like a beaten-out trumpet, they cry out: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are just” (Ps. 118:137); “we suffer less than we deserve.”

These are the words of holy souls. But proud souls, burdened by sins, whenever they are struck by some adversity, presume to murmur rebelliously against the Lord, saying: “God, what have I done to you? Why do I suffer such evils?”

Divine justice answers them in their conscience: “You say well, ‘O God, what have I done to you?’ It is true that you have done nothing to me, but everything to yourself. If you had done something good, you would have done it to me. But when you committed sins and crimes, you did everything to yourself, not to me.”

And because “whatever a person sows, that he will also reap,” it is not unjust that the sinner who sowed wickedness should gather thorns and thistles.

But let us, dearest brothers, hear the Apostle saying: “Let us sow what is good toward all, especially toward those who are of the household of faith.” Let us beware lest, if we sow in the flesh, according to the Apostle, we reap corruption from the flesh. Rather, with his testimony, let us sow in the Spirit, so that from the Spirit we may reap eternal life (Gal. 6:8–10). May the Lord lead us to it under his protection, to whom belong honor and sovereignty throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LIII

[Note: Formerly, 2 from the Fifty Homilies; later, Sermon 13 in the Appendix.]

On the words of Psalm 49:20–23, “Sitting, you spoke evil against your brother,” etc.

[Note: Taken from Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 49, with certain changes and additions. The additions are enclosed in brackets.]

## 1. Almsgiving without zeal for justice

Frequently, dearest brothers, we sing with the Psalmist that verse by which slanderers are struck with a spiritual sword. For he says: “Sitting, you spoke evil against your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.”

By saying “sitting,” he wished to show that the person did not slander in passing, nor was he carried away so as to speak evil of his neighbor. “Sitting,” that is, out of idleness—as though you were free for this purpose, to disparage your neighbor.

“You did these things, and I was silent.” Let no one, brothers, deceive himself with false security and think that he will not come before Christ’s tribunal or render an account of his own deeds. For the Lord our God will come, and he will not be silent.

He is said to be silent now because he appears still to defer vengeance. “You did these things, and I was silent.” What is “I was silent” except “I did not take vengeance; I postponed my severity; I prolonged my patience toward you; I waited a long time for your repentance”?

“You did these things, and I was silent.” While I was still waiting for you to repent, you both despised me and refused to listen to the Apostle [Note: Thus the printed editions. But Mss. gr. and rm. read: “You despised both me and the Apostle.” Manuscript gr., however, adds “to listen.” Immediately afterward both have “according to the hardness of your heart,” without the particle “but.” Augustine has it somewhat differently in his exposition of the same psalm.]; but “according to the hardness of your heart and your unrepentant heart you stored up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5).

## 2. The same subject continued

“You have wickedly supposed that I would be like you.” It is not enough that your evil deeds please you; you think that they please me as well. Because you do not immediately suffer God as your avenger, you want to make him your accomplice; and, as though you had corrupted the judge, you want to have him as a partner in your plunder.

[By making small almsgiving from the many things you have stolen, and still not abandoning your sins, you think that you can buy off the judge as though he were corrupt. Even if you gave everything and did not abandon those sins themselves, you would deceive yourself—losing your money without redeeming your sins.]

“You have wickedly supposed that I would be like you. I will accuse you.” For when the Lord our God comes, he will not be silent. “I will accuse you.” And what will I do by accusing you? What will I do to you? At present you do not see yourself; I will make you see yourself. For if you saw yourself and disliked yourself, you would please me. But because, not seeing yourself, you pleased yourself, you will displease both me and yourself: me when you are judged, yourself when you burn.

“For what will I do to you?” he says.

## 3. Good deeds are to be placed behind one’s back, evil deeds before one’s face

“I will set you before your own face.” Why do you want to hide from yourself? You are behind your own back; you do not see yourself. I will make you see yourself. What you placed behind your back, I will place before your face. You will see your foulness, not so that you may correct it, but so that you may be ashamed.

[Now, dearest brothers, all lovers of luxury, and those who commit iniquity with delight, throw their sins behind their backs. But if they happen to do something good by chance or on some occasion, they place it before themselves; they boast about it continually and say: “I freed him; I did him a favor; I gave him so much.” And while they attribute to themselves the good things God did through them, through vanity they lose what they seem to acquire through almsgiving.

Thus, before Christ’s tribunal, once the good things they had placed before themselves have been lost, the sins they had thrown behind their backs are recalled before their faces. Without end they will endure punishment because, while they lived, they refused to provide themselves a remedy. These are the deeds of those who love present things more than future ones.

But those who think more attentively about the salvation of their souls do the opposite. Whatever good they have done, they throw behind their backs; whatever evil has slipped into them, they place before their eyes. While they are ashamed of these things in the present age, they strive with complete devotion of faith to heal what is wounded, raise what is dead, and wash what is filthy.

Thus, when they come before Christ’s tribunal on the day of judgment, the evils they had placed before their faces—and which have been redeemed by good works—will be taken away; the good deeds they had cast behind their backs through vanity will be placed before their eyes; and they will deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34).

Yet, although these things are so, we must not despair of those who still refuse not only to correct their evils but are even unashamed to defend them. Nor was that city without hope of which it was said: “Three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). Within those three days, however, it was able to convert, pray, mourn, and merit mercy concerning the punishment that threatened it.]

Therefore, let those who are such people listen while it is possible to hear him who is silent [that is, who does not take vengeance in the present]. For he will come and will not be silent; then he will accuse, when there will be no opportunity for correction.

“I will set you,” he says, “before your own face.” Therefore, now, as has already been said above, whoever you are who are such a person, do what the Lord threatens to do to you: take yourself from behind your back, where you do not wish to see yourself, dissimulating your deeds; and set yourself before yourself.

Ascend the tribunal of your mind; be your own judge. Let fear torture you; let confession burst forth. Say to your God: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). What was behind you must become before you; and when it has become before you, let it be punished by you [Note: The words “and when it has become before you, let it be punished by you” are found neither in the manuscripts nor in Augustine.], lest afterward you yourself become before God the judge, and there be nowhere for you to flee from yourself.

## 4. The wicked do not praise God, nor do the proud righteous

Understand these things, you who forget the Lord.

You were not thinking about your evil life. Understand yourself, you who have forgotten the Lord, lest at some time he seize you like a lion and there be no one to rescue you. What does “like a lion” mean? Like one who is powerful, strong, one whom no one can resist.

[Those whom we mentioned above—that is, lovers of the world—appear to praise God with their mouths, but are proved to practice something entirely different in their deeds, according to what the prophet says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). But the Holy Spirit cries out to them:]

“But to the sinner God said: ‘Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth?’” As though he were saying to him: “It does you no good that you praise God.” For those who live well, their praise is beneficial; but if you praise while not abandoning your sins, it does you no good. “Why do you praise me?” [Hear Scripture saying:] “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

If you live badly and speak good words, you do not yet praise. But again, if you begin to live well and attribute it to your own merits, you still do not praise. I do not want you to be the thief insulting the Lord’s cross; but neither do I want you to be the man in the temple boasting of his merits and concealing his wounds.

If you are wicked and persist in that wickedness, I do not merely say to you, “Praise will not benefit you”; rather, “You do not praise me.” I do not count this as praise. Again, if you are supposedly righteous—that is, humble and devout—but walk about puffed up by your righteousness, despise others in comparison with yourself, or exalt yourself as though boasting of your merits, you do not praise me.

Neither does the person who lives badly praise me, nor does the person who lives well as though by his own power praise me. But was not that Pharisee such a person, as though righteous by his own power, when he said: “I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity”? He gave thanks to God for the good he possessed. Therefore, however much good there may be in you, confess that what is good is not from you, but that you received it from God.

Yet even in this matter, if you exalt yourself above another who does not possess it, you will be held guilty of pride; you will not yet be my praiser.

First, therefore, correct yourself from your most evil way. Begin to live well. Understand that you are not corrected except by God’s gift: “For the steps of a person are directed by the Lord” (Ps. 36:23).

When you have understood this, favor others also, so that they may become what you are, because you too were once what they are. Favor them as much as you can, and do not despair. God is not rich only as far as you are concerned. [Believe that what he has given you he both wishes and is able to give also to others.]

The person who, having begun to live well, thinks that his good life comes from himself and not from God does not praise him. Nor does the person who knows that he received his good life from God, yet [Note: Thus in the manuscripts; the printed editions have “only.”] wishes God to be rich only as far as he is concerned [and does not want God also to be merciful to others].

Thus the man who said, “I thank you, God, that I am not like the rest of humanity—unjust, robbers, adulterers, or like this tax collector”—could he not also have said there: “Lord, grant this tax collector what you granted me; supply me also with what you have not yet given me”? But he was already belching as though he were satiated.

What did that poor man, the tax collector, say? “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Therefore the tax collector went down justified more than that Pharisee (Luke 18:10–14).

Hear, then, you who live well; hear, you who live badly: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me.” No evil person offers me this sacrifice. I do not say, “An evil person does not offer me this” [Note: Augustine has “let an evil person offer this.”]; rather, “No evil person offers me this.” For whoever praises is good: if he praises, he also lives well. Whoever praises does not praise with the tongue alone; his life also agrees with his tongue.

## 5. Exhortation

[And therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, that as far as we can, with God’s help, we strive so that just as we praise God with our voices, so also we may praise him with good conduct. For it is better to be silent and do good than to praise God and commit sins.

Whoever praises God with both life and tongue, with voice as well as good works, calls God’s grace upon himself in two ways. But if he is not able to praise God with his voice, let him praise him through good works, constant prayers, and holy thoughts.

For if we attend carefully to these things, then in this age we can praise the Lord with a secure conscience, and in the future we shall happily come to eternal joy.]

[Note: The style of Caesarius seems to be present both here and in other passages where Augustine’s words are interpolated with additions.]

# SERMON LIV

[Note: Formerly, 33 from the Fifty Homilies.]

On what the Prophet says in Psalm 83:3–4: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.”

[Note: Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. Earlier, in the Louvain edition, it had been left without Augustine’s name as doubtful. Together with Verlino and Vinding, one can readily judge from its style and method of interpretation that it was falsely attributed to him.]

## 1. Perfect love of God excludes love of the world. How heart and flesh rejoice in God

According to the Apostle, dearest brothers, whoever loves the world too much does not possess the full affection of divine love. For you have heard it read: “Whoever loves the world, the perfect love of God is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

Therefore, a Christian begins perfectly to love the future and eternal life when he begins not to love the present life. For this reason the Psalm immediately continues: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” It confirms what he had said above: that he loves God, not the world.

He rejoiced in the living God; he did not rejoice in this world, nor in any pleasures that belong to the world—that is, not in riches, not in honor, not in luxury, not in drunkenness, not in dead vanities that soon die together with all their love—but in the living God.

Why did he not say merely “in God,” but added “in the living God”? Clearly, to show that everything that did not belong to the worship of God ought to be regarded by us as dead.

At the same time, consider the subtlety of sacred speech in this saying: “My heart,” he says, “and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” Would it not have been enough to say, “My heart has rejoiced in the living God,” unless he had added, “and my flesh”?

Let us see, then, how both the heart and the flesh of a human being rejoice in God. How, unless so that a person may serve God both with flesh and with heart?

The heart rejoices in God when it thinks honorable and holy thoughts, when it desires religious works that please God. The flesh rejoices when it is chaste, when it is sober, when it is polluted by no impurity, when it is defiled by no unclean acts.

Consider the opposite and recognize how true what I say is. If one of you sees a person speaking unjustly, can he say that this person’s heart rejoices in the living God? Or if someone sees another person drunk, immodest, or fornicating, can he say that this person’s flesh rejoices in the living God?

No flesh that lives in vice rejoices in God. Therefore the Prophet said: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God,” because in his heart he retained the fullness of religious faith, and in his flesh he preserved devoted bodily purity.

[Col. 1849]

## 2. Christ as the turtledove and sparrow. The turtledove’s voice as the teaching of chastity. Christ’s house, the Church. The young birds, Christians

Nor without cause did the Psalmist immediately add what follows, saying: “For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young.”

Our Savior is signified in the turtledove and the sparrow, dearest brothers. The sparrow, as you know, is a very small bird; the turtledove, as we read, is exceptionally chaste. Therefore our Savior was called a sparrow because he was the first to teach humility; he was called a turtledove because he was the first to teach chastity.

Hence the prophet also says in the Song of Songs: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2:12). The turtledove’s voice is understood as the Savior’s teaching. Whoever began to hear it loved the purity of chastity.

“For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young.” For what is Christ’s house except the Church of God? What is Christ’s house except the assembly of the Christian people?

The Savior sought and found this house with immense mercy; he loves it in a special way. He rightly loves in a special way what he specially purchased with his own blood.

In this house, therefore, the Savior gathers his young. Whom do we believe to be Christ’s young? Whom but the Christian peoples? Indeed, today your assembly itself shows who our Lord’s young are. For when I look upon your gathering, I see the Savior having gathered his young in the church.

Although in other books we read, as I said above, “And the turtledove a nest for itself, where it may place its young,” both expressions fit well when understood of the Church: namely, that the Savior both gathers us and provides us a place.

He gathers us so that we may hear his teaching; he shelters us so that we may be safe from the devil’s snares. Let us pray to God our Savior that he may do this and continue to do it each day. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LV

[Note: Formerly, 4 from the Fifty Homilies; later, Sermon 14 in the Appendix.]

On what is written in Psalm 118:66: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”

[Note: By an uncertain author, though not an unlearned one.]

## 1. What should be prayed for. Discipline is necessary for goodness, and knowledge for both

Among the many things by which blessed David heals the weaknesses of our souls, he taught us, like a most skilled master, to maintain a pattern of prayer according to a kind of trinity, saying: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, O Lord.”

Therefore, brothers, pay close attention to the virtues that the prophetic king especially asks to be granted him: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, O Lord.”

The person who knows how to pray rightly truly knows how to live rightly. For he did not ask for treasures of worldly riches, neighboring kingdoms, or a longer span of life; instead, he asked to be taught goodness together with discipline.

Goodness makes discipline lovable, and discipline makes goodness blameless. I think no one can fail to understand that goodness without discipline is the mother of offenses, while discipline without goodness is a certain sad bitterness of life.

He likewise begs that knowledge be granted him, so that he may distinguish knowingly and wisely what the boundaries of goodness are and what measure discipline should have. Otherwise, goodness might be disfigured by the fault of excessive leniency, or harsher discipline might become cruel through its own austerity.

Do you wish, brother, to be good to a sinner? You act kindly indeed; but, if you wish truly to be good, apply the strength of discipline to him, so that your goodness may advance his salvation. If you do not terrify him with any rebuke of corrective judgment, this goodness of yours will be harmful to him, because you permit the sinner to perish whom you could have saved through correction.

Again, if through excessive severity of discipline you offer no remedy informed by knowledge of goodness [Note: In Ms. f.: “of healing goodness.”], then, while the sinner flees your harshness, you will not cure the sickness of sin.

[Col. 1850]

And what, finally, will the rule of life be, or what justice, if relaxed leniency offers indulgence [Note: Or “connivance”; both words were used by the ancients in the sense of “connivance.” M.] to the sinner, or immoderate severity does not recall the offender from his fall?

To learn more fully and perfectly that the teaching of this goodness and discipline existed among our forefathers, let us review a few examples from the many venerable fathers.

## 2. Peter displayed these virtues in himself

Without doubt blessed Peter fulfilled the pattern of this goodness and discipline when, as one truly good, he is said to have healed the sick brought to him, and, as a lover of heavenly discipline, is reported to have punished liars with a just retribution.

The grace of his goodness is certainly attested by that disabled Aeneas who, lame from infancy, sat at the gate of the Lord’s temple begging, and in the name of Jesus Christ, at the Apostle’s command to heal, received his former health (Acts 9:34).

Ananias and Sapphira also demonstrated the severity of his discipline. They sold a field that no one had compelled them to sell, but, when they lied to the Apostle about the amount of the price, they purchased death for themselves through their falsehood (ibid. 5:1–11).

By this deed the most glorious Peter showed that goodness and discipline were present in him: he provided a remedy for the sick and exacted an appropriate punishment from liars. The agreement of heavenly judgment shows that he acted rightly and holily.

Who could doubt the perfection of his knowledge, since, with the Father revealing it to him from heaven, he recognized that Christ the Lord was the Son of the living God? And because goodness, discipline, and knowledge were not lacking in him, the Lord entrusted his little sheep to him to feed (Matt. 16:16–19).

### 3. Paul likewise

The most glorious Paul likewise possessed goodness and discipline. As his writings testify, he held before his disciples both the rod of correction and the spirit of gentleness; for this reason his goodness made him lovable to all, while his discipline made him formidable. Indeed, even at the very beginnings of the world, so that he might teach the churches the goodness and discipline of Christ, he both ordered the sinner to be removed from the communion of the saints (1 Cor. 5:5) and received him back once he had been corrected (2 Cor. 2:6–9). But what shall we say about his knowledge, when everyone knows that he learned in heaven the things he was to teach on earth? There, he recalled, he was taught such things as it is not permitted mortals to utter (ibid. 12:1–4).

### 4. John the Baptist likewise

John, the Lord’s witness and baptizer, likewise possessed goodness and discipline. By the utterance of prophetic compassion he washed away the sins of those who repented of their transgressions through the baptism of repentance. And, as a true and unwavering guardian of the legal commandments, he both accused King Herod concerning his unlawful wife and charged all who flocked to him with the precepts of a purer life. But who can acknowledge the fullness of his knowledge, since he was the first to reveal to everyone the one who came from heaven for the salvation of the world?

### 5. Conclusion

See, then, brothers, with what brevity of prayer and with how few words the venerable Prophet sought perfection of life. In the shortest possible utterance he summed up everything contained in the multitude of spiritual virtues. If, therefore, that foremost of the prophets prayed so earnestly that God would teach him this way of holier living, what ought we to do, who both grow sluggish through the weakness of our slow understanding and are corrupted by the harmful habit of a more careless life?

We, I say, ought to pray even more, saying: “Teach us goodness, discipline, and knowledge, O Lord,” so that in us goodness may overcome wickedness, discipline may restrain vices and pleasures, and knowledge of the truth may illumine the blindness of ignorance. For if you know that almighty God the Father and his only-begotten Son are of one substance, and if you likewise believe that the Holy Spirit reigns with equal eternity, no empty persuasion of the pagans or treacherous impiety of the Arians will ever disturb you. If knowledge of the future judgment fills your heart and mind, you will possess discipline in your conduct.

[Col. 1851] Again, if you observe the measure and rules of discipline itself, you will maintain appropriate goodness in all things, because goodness is the tempering of discipline, and discipline is the seasoning of goodness. Take care, therefore, brother, that you do not wish to appear so good that you cast discipline aside, or pursue discipline so harsh that you remove goodness. For this reason blessed David prays that knowledge be added, so that by the upright judgment of our mind we may know how both stricter goodness and gentler discipline can exist in us.

## SERMON LVI

[Note: Formerly 46 among the fifty Homilies; later Sermon 20 in the Appendix.]

On the words of Psalm 135:1, “Give thanks to the Lord,” etc., and also of Proverbs 3:11–12, “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God,” etc.

[Note: Of uncertain authorship, although in a certain manuscript of Victorinus this same sermon, abridged in its earlier part and beginning only with the words “For whom God loves, he corrects,” is assigned to Caesarius.]

### 1. The necessity of confession; God’s readiness to forgive

“Give thanks to the Lord, dearest brothers, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” We learn, with the Holy Spirit instructing us, the remedies for cleansing a crime; we cannot otherwise merit pardon unless, at God’s command, we confess our crimes to him. For what does the sinner conceal when he committed it in the presence of God as witness? Why is he ashamed to confess, when he was not ashamed to be defiled by sins?

Let him therefore wash away through confession what he had infected by sinning; let him cleanse through satisfaction what he had soiled with the stains of transgressions. After his offense, let him be more cautious who before the offense had been more negligent; let him follow Christ in good works who in evil works had followed the devil.

“Give thanks,” he says, “to the Lord, for he is good.” He who persuades us to confess our transgressions does not wish to avenge wickedness: he desires to release those who confess, lest he be compelled to punish the obstinate. Therefore let God’s admonition make you heedful, lest his severity make you punished.

For that we are often scourged on account of the merits of our sins—[Note: Thus Lov. and Er. At Am. and the manuscripts of the better class: “By the admonitions of sins.” Other manuscripts: “By the death of sins.” Immediately afterward, in the Greek, “no one who is imprudent.”]—no prudent person denies, and no fool fails to understand. God wishes those whom he considers corrected to be admonished frequently [Note: In one manuscript, “whom he considers in need of correction.” In Lov., “whom he considers reproved.”]; he wishes to correct by the severity of temptations those whom he sees to have been corrupted by his patience [Note: Manuscripts of better quality read “uncorrupted.”]. He wishes, I say, to reform sinners in this way, to correct those who offend, to call back those who wander, and to raise again to the hope of recovering salvation those who are already dead.

For God rejoices when he sees those whom he corrects brought to amendment; and he is glad when he sees those whom he scourges changed for the better and made righteous. Therefore, from that disposition, he desires the terror, threats, and blows sent against sinners to benefit the correction of the wicked rather than the punishment of the guilty. For God wishes to have mercy on all; he wishes to forgive; he wishes to show himself gracious if he sees someone corrected after changing his conduct.

“If your sons forsake my law,” he says, “and do not walk in my ordinances; if they profane my statutes, I will visit their crimes with the rod and their offenses with scourging; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:31–34).

### 2. God’s scourges are benefits and remedies; indifference is a cause for grief

These are the remedies by which God cares for us; this is the medicine by which the wounds of human beings are healed. Through these beneficial means vices are amended and human wickedness is restrained. These are divine benefits, not blows; those things are not inflicted by God in order to harm, but come so that paternal clemency may care for human beings.

“I reprove and chastise those whom I love,” he says (Rev. 3:19). And again: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him. For whom God loves, he corrects” [Note: In the manuscripts r., cl., and V., the sermon begins with these words, “For whom God loves, he corrects,” and is prefaced by the title *On the Scourges*.]; “moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives.”

Therefore, if he scourges everyone in order to correct them, and corrects them in order to make them worthy of the Father—that is, of God—let the one who is not scourged be afraid that he may be unable to be a son. Let the one whom God does not wish to correct in this world be afraid, because he has destined him for punishment after this world. Let the one who still rejoices and delights in this world be afraid that he may grieve and weep forever [Note: Here and below, some manuscripts r. and cl. read “so that” instead of “lest.”]. Let the one who does not grieve in this world with the righteous be afraid that he may tear himself apart with sinners in everlasting punishment.

### 3. Sinners are afflicted so that they may be corrected; the righteous so that they may be tested and advance

“But if sinners,” he says, “suffer these things in this world because of the deserts of their offenses, why are holy men sometimes afflicted equally and together with sinners?” [Note: Two manuscripts read “affected.” Others read “visited.”]—unless it is because these things benefit sinners for correction, but the righteous for testing? For just as sinners are corrected from evil by these remedies, so the righteous are thereby increased in goodness.

God corrects the former in order to reform them; he tests the latter in order to increase them. He recalls the former from guilt; he preserves the latter for himself as holier. In the one case sins are corrected; in the other the merits of virtue are increased—in the one, a remorseful remembrance; in the other, the joyful delight of a pure mind.

The one longs for divine indulgence; the other already considers the promised rewards. The one asks pardon from the merciful Judge; the other awaits the just Rewarder. The one is anxious, so that he may obtain what he asks; the other is confident, because he can receive what he deserves.

For God at least crushes those who sin through correction, lest, as wickedness grows, he find something for which to exact vengeance. He hates punishment, since he first takes precautions [Note: Thus the manuscripts, with the exception of one more recent manuscript, which, along with the printed editions, has “he has first taken precautions.”] so as not to condemn.

Let the Christian rejoice in adversity, because if he is righteous, he is being tested; or if he is a sinner, he is being corrected. Let the one whom divine scourges cannot correct truly grieve; let the one who in the present world has despised the remedy of the Judge fear the punishment of the future judgment.

Let the sinner rejoice if he grieves with the righteous in this world, so that after this world he may be rewarded with the same righteous person. “You,” says the Lord, “will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20).

Who would not desire to grieve for a short time, so that he might triumph with Christ in everlasting and perpetual joy? Who would not desire to balance the tears of the present time against future joy? Whatever good or evil exists in this world is small, momentary, and brief.

“Temptation,” he says, “has not overtaken you except such as is human. But God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tested beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13). Yet God also grants security and for a time shows indulgence toward our weakness [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Two others read: “Or even God will grant security for a time from our weakness.” A certain more recent manuscript, along with the printed editions, reads: “Yet God grants security, showing indulgence toward our weakness for a time.”].

### 4. Christ’s soldier must always be vigilant; he must be more vigilant in peace

Let Christ’s soldier be armed, concerned, cautious, and secure in God alone. Let him be more watchful in peace than he has been accustomed to be in war. Let him not become slack through security, lest the enemy creep in from some quarter.

“Be sober and watchful,” he says, “because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). The more diligently the enemy watches in order to harm, the more diligently the Christian must watch in order to conquer. The enemy never steals upon those who are vigilant; the adversary never deceives those who are watchful.

For he must not be guarded against only when he declares war on God’s servants. We must be more vigilant in peace: the mind must be exercised, virtue must be exercised, and the attention of the mind must be strengthened by the fear of God.

The enemy makes secure those whom he wants to make captive; he makes them secure, I say, so that he may subdue them when they are off guard [Note: Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions omit “subdue them.”], and overwhelm them when asleep and unarmed, wounding those whom he has seen to be least watchful.

If some soldier entered combat with the enemy in the presence of his commander, with what eagerness and with what courage would he fight so that he might please the one under whom he serves! Nor could he obtain pay or promotion unless he had bravely conquered the enemy by overcoming him [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “He will be unable to despise him if, after overcoming the enemy, he has conquered him bravely. Indeed, he is ashamed to be despised unless he overcomes the enemy by a courageous victory.”].

Watch, Christian, beneath the eyes of God, so that you may be crowned with perfect victory. Fight the devil, since you are already armed by Christ. God is with you, who desires you to conquer; Christ is with you, who desires to reward you.

Despise present things so that you may receive future things; spurn temporal things so that you may be able to receive eternal things. You will possess the heaven that the devil could not possess; you will have the paradise from which the enemy was excluded; you will receive the eternity that the transgressing enemy lost.

Perfidiousness cast him down to earth; faith raises you into heaven. By despising, he was deprived of heavenly virtue; by serving, you are supported by angelic majesty. Eternal punishments have been destined for him; divine rewards have been prepared for you. He, the faithless one, will perish with the faithless; you, sanctified, will reign with the saints, so that you who were temporal and needy may be adorned with eternal glory.

You will fear nothing in this world, because you have rejected, together with the world, the author of fear, the devil [Note: Three manuscripts read “you have overcome.”].

Amen.

## SERMON LVII

[Note: Also *On Time*, 218.]

On the strong woman and on the Church, from Proverbs, chapter 31:10–31.

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It has been copied from Augustine’s Sermon 37, with several changes and with an added introduction that closely approaches the style of Caesarius.]

### 1. The word of God must be cherished with fervor of heart

I ask you, dearest brothers, to receive in the customary manner of the faithful, with silence and quiet, the things preached to you. For when our mind, by God’s gift, has been able to conceive something from the reading of the holy Scriptures, it desires to find a spiritual nest in your hearts.

Therefore, like the most chaste turtledoves, strive to cherish the divine words in the nest of your heart with the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Do not allow the seed that is the word of God to freeze within you through the coldness of sins, in accordance with what is written: “Iniquity abounded; charity grows cold” (Matt. 24:12). Rather, as the Apostle says, “Be fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11).

For just as doves or turtledoves, after laying eggs, lose the fruit of those eggs if they allow them to grow cold, so you too cannot have the desired fruit if you allow the word of God, once conceived, to grow cold through forgetfulness.

Provide within yourselves a nest for holy sermons, as it is written: “The turtledove found for herself a nest in which to place her young” (Ps. 83:4). And because Solomon’s Scripture commends to us a great woman who has a great husband, saying, “Who will find a strong woman?” we wish to speak briefly to your ears about her, according to what God deigns to suggest.

### 2. The Catholic Church cannot remain hidden

“Who will find a strong woman?” It is difficult to find her, and difficult not to know her. Is she not the city on a mountain that cannot be hidden (Matt. 5:14)? Why, then, is it said, “Who will find her?” when it ought to have been said, “Who will not find her?”

But you see the city placed upon a mountain. Yet in order for it to be placed upon the mountain, it had to be found. For it is that sheep which had been lost. And truly, brothers, it is the Catholic Church, which has now been illumined; who, then, does not see her?

When she was hidden, who found her? For just as she has been called the city, so also she is the sheep whom the shepherd sought when she was lost. The shepherd himself is the mountain. The sheep, therefore, carried upon his shoulders, is the city on the mountain. It is easy to see her placed upon the mountain. But how could you have found her when she lay hidden among the brambles and thorns of her sins? It is a great thing that he sought her there; it is marvelous that he found her there.

Her difficult discovery is commended when it is said, “Who will find a strong woman?”—that is, the Church. Who does not see her now found by Christ, now exalted [Col. 1854], now conspicuous, now glorious, now adorned, now radiant, and, to put it briefly, spread throughout the whole world?

Christ is recognized as the one who sought and found this woman, the Church. And after he found her, he not only rescued her from the thorns of her sins but also adorned her with precious stones. Therefore it is said of her: “She is more precious than precious stones.”

I wish to commend something else to your Charity, as much as you understand, as much as I fear, and as much as you ought to fear concerning these precious stones. There are precious stones in the Church, and there always have been: namely, learned people, rich in knowledge and eloquence and in every kind of instruction in the Law. These stones are truly precious. Cyprian was among them; Ambrose was among them [Note: In Augustine, “Donatus.”], and others like them. Some among their number wandered away from the adornment of this woman.

## SERMON LVIII

[Note: Also *On Time*, 217.]

On the same passage of Proverbs, chapter 31, verses 10–31.

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It has been drawn from the same source as the preceding sermon. The conclusion seems to reflect the character of Caesarius. We have distinguished the other principal additions with small brackets.]

### 1. The Church prefigured in many ways

The Catholic Church, dearest brothers, was not preached only after the coming of our Lord and Savior; from the beginning of the world she was also represented by many figures and more hidden sacraments. For the Catholic Church was present in holy Abel, and in Noah, and in Abraham, and in the others down to the coming of the Lord and Savior.

For Solomon says of her: “Who will find a strong woman?” When he said “who will find,” we must understand difficulty of finding, not impossibility. This strong woman is the Church. How could she not be strong, since from the beginning of the world she has been wearied by such great tribulations and yet is not overcome?

“Who will find a strong woman?” Who else but Christ? He did not find her strong; rather, by finding her, he made her strong. For in order to find her, he left the ninety-nine in the mountains, sought the one that had gone astray, placed her upon his shoulders, and brought her back to his own fold (Luke 15:4–5).

### 2. What wool and linen signify

“She made wool and flax with her hands.” The sacred word describes this matron as one who works both wool and flax. Perhaps you ask us what wool and flax signify. Wool signifies something carnal, while flax signifies something spiritual, because in the arrangement of garments linen garments are inner garments, whereas woolen garments are outer garments.

[Wool also arises from the mingling of animals. Flax, however, is produced from the earth without the pleasure of the flesh; therefore it seems to bear the image of chastity, to such an extent that, by the command of the Law, the priests of the Old Testament wore linen undergarments as an indication of chastity. Thus wool signifies something carnal, while flax signifies something spiritual. They are also used as terms of praise.]

You find a person extending his hand in alms to a poor man, yet not thinking there of God, but desiring to please human beings. He has a woolen garment, which can be seen, but he does not have the inner linen garment.

You find another saying to you: “My conscience is enough for me. I worship God; I adore God. Why do I need to go to church or visibly associate with Christians?” He wants to have linen without a tunic. This woman neither knows nor commends such works.

This woman found wool and flax and made them useful. Many people find them, but do not make them useful with their hands. When you listen willingly, you find; when you live well, you make useful.

### 3. The distaff and the spindle

“She strengthened her arms with the spindle.” I shall speak about this spindle as the Lord grants me to do; for such wool-working is not alien to men. In the spindle, wool-working is signified; in wool-working, a good work, like that of a chaste woman and an industrious matron.

Pay careful attention, however, to the two instruments used in wool-working: the distaff and the spindle. On the distaff is wound the wool that is to pass by thread onto the spindle. What is wound on the distaff is still on the left hand [Col. 1855] and is not yet on the spindle [Note: Augustine: “It is still in the future; what is on the spindle.”]. What has been gathered onto the spindle is already past.

Let your work therefore be on the spindle, not on the distaff. On the distaff is what you are going to do; on the spindle is what you have done. See, then, whether you have anything on the spindle. For there your arms are strengthened; there your steadfastness will be strong; there you will confidently say to God: “Give, because I have given; forgive, because I have forgiven; do, because I have done.”

What hangs on the distaff must be transferred to the spindle; but what has been gathered onto the spindle must not be returned to the distaff. See, then, what you are doing, so that you may have something on the spindle, so that you may strengthen your arms on the spindle—something that may console you, strengthen you, and give you confidence to pray and hope.

### 4. Christ must be praised in two ways and simply

Next: “She opened her hands to the poor.” Come, brothers, practice the holy wool-working. If someone has a full storeroom, a full granary, all these things are on the distaff; let them pass onto the spindle.

[They are on the left as long as you have not distributed them to the poor; but once you begin to give alms, they are transferred to the right, and a work is produced from which a garment can be made.]

“All her household are clothed.” Surely her husband, having such a wife, will be concerned about the nakedness of his servants? [Who is this husband except Christ? And who is the wife except the Church [Note: This is now absent from Augustine; nevertheless, it is found in Bede’s authentic Collection on Galatians 1.]?]

All who have been baptized in Christ are clothed. The good servants and the evil servants are clothed. That woman does not cease to clothe everyone, so that no one may complain and say: “I have not done good works because I have not been well clothed.”

“She made double garments for her husband.” The garments are praises, faith, and confessions. You praise God; you praise the human being. You praise in two ways, and you praise simply: in two ways because he is human and God; simply, not so that you may be deceptive.

Photinus, from whom the heretics are called Photinians, made what was, as it were, a single garment for her husband. For he believed Christ to be merely human and refused to honor him as God.

Another appears, weaving for her husband a ragged garment. For he says: “Christ is God alone, having nothing whatever of a human being.” The Manichaeans say this. The Photinians say, “He is human alone”; the Manichaeans say, “He is God alone.”

[Behold from what kind of church such precious garments proceed. And therefore it is written of her that she] made double garments for her husband. Double garments: for we confess God in the human being and the human being in God.

“She prepared spiritual garments from fine linen and purple.” From fine linen, a white confession; from purple, a glorious passion. We recognize fine linen when we confess God; in the martyrs we praise purple with honor.

### 5. Let us hasten to draw alms from the distaff onto the spindle

[Let us hasten, in giving alms, to draw them from the distaff onto the spindle and transfer them from the left hand to the right. We, brothers, to whom God has deigned to grant so great a benefit that we were born neither from Jews nor from heretics, but were deemed worthy to be children of the Catholic Church, should give thanks to God as much as we can. He has deigned to inspire or instill in us a right faith that pleases him.

And with all our strength—for faith cannot save us without works—let us prepare our minds for that spiritual wool-working. Therefore, continually giving alms, let us hasten to draw them from the distaff onto the spindle and transfer them from the left hand to the right, so that through the alms given to the poor each one of us may prepare a robe for eternity. Thus, as the Apostle says, we may be found clothed and not naked at the heavenly banquet (2 Cor. 5:3), lest it be said to us: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22:12).

Rather, freed from the evil proclamation, may we be found worthy to hear that blessed and desirable voice: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 25:34), which may he himself deign to grant.]

## SERMON LIX

[Note: Also *On Time*, 240.]

On the three boys sent into the fiery furnace.

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The author is uncertain [Col. 1856], and he tests his own ability and eloquence in speaking. The same character is evident in certain other sermons printed above, namely 3, 7, 23, 27, 46, and others, as well as in the one that immediately follows, 60.]

### 1. The tyrant’s cruelty toward the three boys

The tyrant orders the furnace to be set alight, and to the degree that he himself was burning with the fire of fury, he consumed the holier boys. Now the sky is covered with the density of billowing smoke; now all the Chaldeans are terrified by the horrific roar, so that the greatness of divine severity might be displayed through punishments.

The violent enemy raged, seeking punishment for his servants. He raged, not in order to slaughter the righteous, but to bring destruction upon his own men. He raged, not so that the increase of punishments might grow, but so that divine power might be displayed to all: while the impious gloried in punishments, they would be devoured by the force of the flames.

The wicked Chaldeans raged, destined to perish in the punishments before them, and ignorant of those to come. The servants hasten to carry out the command; they prepare the conflagration and increase the flames. His cruelty possesses the mind; his savagery changes the will.

### 2. The three boys unharmed in the furnace

The holy men are thrown into the furnace. The flames flee; the fires yield; the conflagration is afraid. The fires fear injuring those whom they had been ordered to preserve unharmed.

They display the merit of the righteous while they disregard the tyrant’s command. The saints may play with fire, since they were not permitted to dwell among human beings. In the furnace they were permitted to worship God, whom among human beings they were not permitted to honor.

They may deserve the service of the flames, although they had not deserved the punishments of the Chaldeans. They may be preserved unharmed by the fires, although the tyrant had handed them over to be burned. They may be secure amid punishment, although outside punishment they had not been permitted to remain untouched—so that where there was destruction, there they might find salvation; where there were punishments, there they might find refreshment.

Receive an example from punishments, enemy, you who have lost the counsel of humanity. The fires flee the righteous whom you unjustly condemned. The flames recoil and proclaim innocent those whom you judge worthy of punishment; and those flames accustomed to rage saw holy men worthy of honor in the furnace.

The enemies condemn, and the fires absolve. The Chaldeans add to the punishment, and the punishments defend. Human beings rage, and punishments show reverence.

The tyrant thought that tortures could rage only as far as he, the sacrilegious one, believed himself to possess power. The fires yield to the righteous; the heat of the flames turns into refreshment; and the devouring forces established in nature forget their accustomed behavior, so that they fear while honoring the righteous and punish their persecuting enemies.

The fires receive the righteous as guests with every honor and willingly offer their service. The enemy rages by a changed method; he is moved by no compassion and softened by no humanity. He could conquer if he commanded the fires.

The righteous, therefore, are offered to the fires clothed and bound with chains. The righteous are defended by the heat, and those whom human power condemned are absolved by the fire.

He thinks of nothing and fears nothing. Thus tyrannical cruelty is overcome and cast down, while its own attendants are devoured. It sees the punishment and beholds the glory of God’s servants.

The fires offer service to the righteous and provide destruction to the unjust. While the flame avenges, the impious are killed and the righteous are saved.

### 3. The tyrant recognizes the miracle

When the tyrant hastened to the furnace, he was amazed at the praise-worthy spectacle, marveled at what had happened, and honored God with the three boys in the furnace. He saw those whom he had recently ordered to be violently destroyed protected by a just and divine surrounding.

In them, in the furnace, he sees the one whom he had previously thought was not among them. Terrified by this sight, he adds gentleness to his fury. He suddenly becomes a confessor who had recently been a persecutor. He proclaims the one whom shortly before he denied; he orders him to be honored, though he had condemned those who honored him.

He asks the righteous to come out of the furnace; he begs God’s servants to leap forth from the fire. “Come out,” he says, “servants of the Most High God. Now I proclaim myself the defender of the God whose enemy I plainly was, so that, as an advocate, I may punish his enemies, whose servants I persecuted in ignorance.”

Then the Hebrews emerge unharmed from the furnace; safe, they rejoice and triumph as victors, because they faithfully served God and despised the tyrant’s fury (Dan. 3).

## SERMON LX

[Note: Formerly *On Time*, 242, and later Sermon 69 in the Appendix.]

On Susanna.

[Note: Of uncertain and unlearned authorship. It is worth observing that it is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, volume 3 of the Cologne edition and volume 2 of the Paris edition, although somewhat shorter and varied in places, and that there, as also in the Remigian manuscript, it is attributed to Zeno of Verona.]

[Col. 1857]

### 1. The righteous are victorious amid the world’s snares because God delivers them

Whenever, in this perverse world, manifold snares are laid against praiseworthy men, or various causes of calumny arise, the righteous will not fear what the pestilential human being contrives or what the devil devises, because Christ is with him.

Let a person be chosen as a soldier stationed in battle, always exercising the duties of the virtues. He therefore embraces one of two outcomes: either, when the snares have been exposed, his innocence shines among the people; or, overtaken by pursuing enemies, once he has passed beyond the condition of death, freed from worldly troubles, he enters the harbor of security.

The prophet Daniel was not terrified or shaken by fear when he was thrown into the lions’ den. Rather, standing amid those beasts’ mouths, he pleased the Lord with his whole mind and escaped the tyrannical designs unharmed.

The high priest Zacharias, for the worship of God, for the sacred laws, and for discipline in the priestly temple, rebuked a rebellious people and steadfastly accepted death; the detestable host of the Jews stained the pavement with his blood.

Zacharias the martyr triumphs, and Daniel the confessor rejoices: the one dies and triumphs; the other escapes and reigns. Nor is the female sex deprived of its examples, since it has commendably preserved the adornment of chastity.

### 2. Susanna’s danger and deliverance

The noble Susanna, the glory of chastity, overcame the shamelessness of the judges and restrained the audacious insolence of the elders, so that chastity might suffer no injury in her.

Susanna stood in court, oppressed by the false testimonies of condemned liars. She stood not as a guilty woman, but as one firmly prepared to die for chastity. Thus the chaste woman went to punishment—not the body of adulterers, in which extreme lust had blazed and the devil had kindled it. What virtue had protected and modesty had adorned went unharmed toward the end of death.

She bore an excellent head, whose face an undefiled conscience raised toward heaven. Because of the threatened loss of modesty, she suppressed her desire for life; and for her, to whom the rewards of chastity were dear, the joy of life was not lost.

She despised one thing and gained the whole. She who wished to die escaped with the glory of chastity; and she whom an evil sentence had cast down was raised up by the integrity of her illustrious conscience, by the fear of God, and by her unshakable belief in the approaching sacred judgment.

O love of honor and of the Law! Susanna judged consciousness of adultery more grievous than punishment. When she was led away, she did not grieve over the punishment, because she rejoiced over the false testimony.

The innocent woman is accused by the sentence, but by God’s will the punishment is suspended, so that the falsehood of the judges might be exposed and the innocent woman cleared.

The weaker sex rises against men with greater strength. Chastity and honor conquer lust; the dreadful wickedness driven by wantonness is cast down.

Susanna preserved her own strength of spirit and steadfastly endured the judgment of the people. False charges are fabricated against an innocent woman. For the one who has God as his defender is protected.

Finally, the prophet Daniel, warned by divine inspiration, cried out: “Return to the judgment!” The people are amazed at the sudden judgment; the condemned woman is recalled; fear seizes the false witnesses.
