The devil groans because his schemes are exposed. The angels rejoice when the integrity of her modesty is recognized, because the truth, wearied on earth, is defended.

They were asked in what place Susanna had committed the crime of which she was accused. One says, “Under the mastic tree”; the other, “Under the holm oak.” When their answers therefore differ, the contradiction of their statements exposes the facts, so that, when the people had been rebuked and the witnesses confounded by force of mind, the truth might be shown.

The people rejoice at the integrity of her modesty. Her husband triumphs because he has found a faithful wife. Her household rejoices because it has found nothing in her deserving punishment, because it has found no act of adultery, and because the devil has not accomplished the murder he was plotting (Dan. 13).

## SERMON LXI

[Note: Formerly *On Time*, 169, and later Sermon 57 in the Appendix.]

On peace, concerning the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 5, verse 9, “Blessed are the peacemakers,” etc.

[Note: This is Sermon 53 of Peter Chrysologus, but here it has been interpolated in various places, or enlarged by many sentences, as the brackets indicate. Compare Alcuin’s book *On Virtues and Vices*, chapter 6.]

## 1. The fruit of peace. The harmony of the brethren

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” The merit of Christian virtue is diminished in everything if it does not possess the unity of peace; nor does one attain the title of son except through the name of peacemaker. Peace is what strips a person of servitude, gives him the name of a freeborn person, and changes the person along with his condition: from a servant it makes him free, from a slave it makes him a son; [it calls God “Father,” changes the servant into a son, makes a friend out of God, and makes the Lord a father. Thus, thus does the one who does not wish to perish act. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Behold, the one who has begun to be a peacemaker begins to be a son of God. The one who refuses to be found a peacemaker does not wish to be called a son; the one who could not become an heir of peace denies God as his Father [Note: [Col. 1858] Alcuin, in his book *On Virtues and Vices*, chapter 6: “who disdains to be a peacemaker.”]. He will find God severe, whom he disdained to have as a merciful and gracious father. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Let us rejoice in this name as sons and heirs of God, and indeed co-heirs of Christ. How great is the reward of this peace: to possess an inheritance with Christ, to have the Father’s substance with the Son, to share the heavenly kingdom with the Lord, and to be admitted with the Lord into fellowship with eternity! What perversity of character is this—to envy those who are better and cling to those who are more degraded; to lose the victory of adoption and refuse to possess the inheritance of the heavenly kingdoms? For he denies himself to be a son of God and a co-heir of Christ who refuses to be governed by the Father’s rule. Peace is the harmony of the brethren, as it is written: “There are three things that pleased my spirit, which are approved before God and human beings: harmony among brothers and sisters, love of one’s neighbors, and a man and a woman agreeing with one another” (Sirach 25:1–2).] Accordingly, the harmony of the brethren is the will of God, the joy of Christ, the perfection of holiness, the rule of justice, the substance of teaching, the safeguard of conduct, and, in all things, a discipline worthy of praise. Peace is the support of prayers, an easy and effective way of supplication, because it is the fitting fullness of all desires [as it is written in the Apostle (Philippians 4:7). Thus the peace of fellowship makes the brethren pleasing to God, for it shows the testimony of charity]. Peace is the mother of love, the bond of harmony, and the manifest sign of a pure mind, because it obtains from God whatever it wishes: whatever it wishes, let it ask, and whatever it wishes, let it receive.

## 2. Whoever does not preserve peace despises Christ

Peace must be preserved by royal commands, as the Lord Christ says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27). [Whoever is Christ’s disciple keeps Christ’s commands; to keep the commandment is to preserve peace in everything. For to divide unity is not to follow the teacher, but to trample upon his command. To follow Christ is to possess peace; and not to follow what belongs to peace is to accept from the teacher, on the one hand, what you love and, on the other, what you condemn. It is to love the teacher to keep the teacher’s commands in everything—he who says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.” It is pleasant, brothers, to linger over peace; it is delightful to have said this often and to proclaim it again and again: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.”]

“I leave you in peace; I left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.” As he departed, he wished to give what he desired to find in all things when he returned. [He wished the one to whom he had given it to be secure, since he commanded him to preserve what he had granted until his return. What, then, will a human being do when God comes and does not find what he gave, though he sought it? What excuse will the one who could not preserve peace use? “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.”] “I left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.” Preserve the royal command: it is the divine voice. I shall find what I left.

## 3. Peace is the work of God; discord, of the devil

To plant peace deeply is God’s work; to uproot it entirely is the work of the enemy. Love of a brother comes from God; hatred arises from the devil. Therefore hatreds must be condemned, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Let us restrain anger, because it is written: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22). Peace is to be loved, and harmony is to be cherished. These are the things that produce [Note: [Col. 1859] Chrysologus adds, “and nourish”] charity; and you know, according to the Apostle, that “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). Whoever does not have charity is without God. [A fatherly affection cannot fail to love what it teaches.]

The peace of the people is the glory of the priest; and the joy of parents is the perfected charity of their children [Note: [Col. 1859] In Alcuin: “The peace of the people is health, the glory of the priest, the joy of the homeland, and the terror of enemies, whether visible or invisible.”]. It is the priest’s task to admonish concerning what is fitting; it is the people’s task to hear what he commands. Whatever is not permitted, it is the shepherd’s task to forbid lest it be done; it is the flock’s task to listen, so that it may do what is commanded [Note: [Col. 1859] Chrysologus: “and to wish that it not be done.”]. Let both sides agree, and everything is saved: God finds nothing among the people to punish, nor can the priest have anything over which to grieve.

Let us keep the commandments, which lead to life. Let the brotherhood, bound together by the deep bonds of peace, hold fast, and let it bind itself together by the saving bond of charity in mutual love, because love makes one magnanimous. [Love is gracious; it does not envy, it is not jealous. Love does not speak falsely, it is not puffed up, it admits nothing shameful, it does not seek its own interests, it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth. It believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7).]

Therefore love is to be embraced with every vow and desire, since it can possess as many blessings as it has rewards. Peace must be guarded with every strength [Note: [Col. 1859] In Chrysologus: “Above all virtues, peace must be guarded”], because God is always in peace. Let there be no place for the enemy to creep in, lest he be able to sow weeds among the wheat, and lest, when the farmer is already secure and deceived in his hope of long labor, the expected fruit be taken away at the very ripening of the harvest; or lest wine, made sweeter by age, suddenly be changed into something harsher by treachery and join itself to the mixture of poured-out lees; or lest, amid sweet honey, he pour in poisons more bitter than gall [or, amid fields blooming with flowers and glittering with the varied beauty of meadows, kill souls of pleasant fragrance by inserting thorns].

Let quarrels be sent far away, lawsuits far away, hatreds far away, curses far away. And because the tongue of the whisperer and the double-tongued person is a snare of death, let each one spare his own soul, lest he bring upon himself the bonds of death for his punishment. Love peace, and all things are tranquil. Thus you may preserve rewards for yourselves and joys for us, so that, founded in the unity of peace, the Church of God may hold perfect discipline, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXII

[Note: [Col. 1859] Formerly *On Time* 59; later in *Appendix* 35.]

Concerning the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 5:43–48, and chapter 6:1–6: “But I say to you, Love your enemies,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1859] It consists of sentences and interpretations borrowed from Augustine, book 1 of *On the Sermon on the Mount*; Jerome, on Matthew, chapters 3 and 6; Caesarius, homily 7 among those edited by Baluze; and the sermon that follows here, along with others.]

## 1. How the enemy is to be loved. Who one’s neighbor is

That there is some degree in the righteousness of the Pharisees, which pertains to the Law, is understood from this: many people hate even those by whom they are loved, as dissolute children hate parents who restrain their dissipation. Therefore, someone ascends a certain degree when he loves his neighbor, although he still hates his enemy. But by the command of the one who came to fulfill the Law, not to abolish it, he will complete benevolence and kindness when he extends it even to love of the enemy. For although that degree is something, it is nevertheless so small that it can be shared with tax collectors.

Nor should what was said in the Law—“You shall hate your enemy”—be understood as the voice of one commanding the righteous, but of one permitting the weak. An enemy is to be loved, not insofar as he is an enemy, but insofar as he is a human being, so that you may wish for him what you wish for yourself—that is, that, corrected and recalled, he may reach the kingdom.

Every human being is one’s neighbor. We are all neighbors by the condition of earthly birth and mortality, and also by hope of the heavenly inheritance, because we do not know what anyone may become: whether a Jew, a heretic, or a pagan. For perhaps, through the mercy of God, he may be converted to God and deserve to hold the first place among the saints. In the Law the Lord commands that one’s enemies—not “enemy” in the plural, but “enemy” in the singular—be hated, so that those who were spiritual in the Law might hate only the devil, whose hatred Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill.

## 2. God’s commandments are not impossible. No one can excuse himself from love

“But I say to you, Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.”

[Many people, judging God’s commandments by their own weakness rather than by the strength of the saints, think that what is commanded is impossible. They say that it is enough, as a virtue, not to hate enemies, but that to love them is commanded beyond what human nature can endure. Therefore it must be understood that Christ does not command impossible things, but perfect things—things David did toward Saul and Absalom. The martyr Stephen also prayed for those who were stoning him, and Paul desired to be anathema for his persecutors. Jesus both taught and did these things, saying: “Father, forgive them”] (Luke 23:34).

[In other good works someone may sometimes put forward some sort of excuse; but in possessing love no one will be able to excuse himself. Someone may say to me, “I cannot fast.” Can he possibly say, “I cannot love”? He may say, “Because of the weakness of my body I cannot abstain from wine and meat.” Can he possibly say, “I cannot love”? Someone may say that he cannot preserve virginity; he may say that he cannot sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor. Can he possibly say, “I cannot love my enemies”? For in this matter neither do the feet grow tired from running, nor the ears from hearing, nor the hands from working, so that we might try to free ourselves by that excuse [Note: [Col. 1860] Caesarius: “so that we might excuse ourselves by that very fatigue.”]. We are not told, “Go east and seek charity; sail west and you will find love.” It is within our heart, where we are commanded to return, as the prophet says: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isaiah 46:8). For what is asked of us is not found in distant regions.]

“And pray for those who persecute and slander you.” What else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies except what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive” (2 Timothy 2:25–26)?

## 3. Nothing in Scripture is contrary to the commandment about loving enemies. For whom one should not pray. The sin unto death

Here a question rightly arises: how is this commandment of the Lord not contradicted by the many imprecations against enemies found in the Prophets, which are considered curses? For example: “Let their table before them become a snare” (Psalm 68:25), and the other things said there. The apostle John also says: “If anyone sees his brother committing a sin that is not unto death, he shall ask, and life will be given to the one who sins not unto death. There is sin unto death; I do not say that he should pray for that” (1 John 5:16).

First, it must be observed that the Prophets, through imprecation, foretold what was going to happen—not by the desire of one wishing it, but by the spirit of one foreseeing it. They especially tend to proclaim future things in the form of one who is uttering an imprecation, just as they often sang of things that were going to happen in the figure of past time. [Col. 1861]

Second, in the Apostle’s words it must be understood that there are certain brothers for whom we are commanded not to pray, although the Lord commands us to pray even for our persecutors. This question cannot be resolved unless we admit that among brothers there are certain sins more grievous than the persecution of enemies.

“Brothers” signifies Christians, as can be proved by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Therefore, I think that a brother’s sin unto death occurs when, after coming to know God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is driven by the torches of envy against that very grace by which he was reconciled to God [Note: [Col. 1861] *Retractations* I, chapter 19, no. 7].

But the sin that is not unto death occurs when someone has not alienated love from his brother, but through some weakness of spirit has failed to provide the duties owed to the brotherhood. For this reason the Lord also says on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” For they had not yet become participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit or entered into the fellowship of the holy brotherhood.

And blessed Stephen prays in the Acts of the Apostles for those by whom he is being stoned (Acts 7:59), because they had not yet believed in Christ and were not fighting against that common grace. But I think that the Apostle Paul does not pray for Alexander because he was a brother and had sinned unto death—that is, by attacking the brotherhood through envy. Yet he prays for those who had not broken off love but had succumbed through fear, asking that they be forgiven. For he says:

“Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also must avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words.” Then he adds for whom he prays, saying: “At my first defense no one came to my assistance, but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them” (2 Timothy 4:14–16).

And note that the Apostle does not say, “May he repay,” but “The Lord will repay him according to his works.” This is the word of one foretelling, not of one invoking a curse, just as it was said concerning the hypocrisy of the Jews, whose impending overthrow he saw: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23:3).

## 4. What the saints are praying for when they ask for vengeance. How the kingdom of sin is to be overthrown

It is asked how that commandment—by which we are ordered, “Pray for those who persecute and slander you”—is not contradicted by what is read in the Apocalypse: that the martyrs pray to God to be avenged (Revelation 6:10).

But this ought not to trouble anyone. For who would dare to assert that, when those holy ones in white robes asked to be avenged, they asked for vengeance against the people themselves or against the kingdom of sin? For this is the martyrs’ sincere and wholly just and merciful vengeance: that the kingdom of sin, under whose reign they suffered so much, be overthrown.

The Apostle strives for its overthrow when he says: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:12). The kingdom of sin is destroyed and overthrown partly by the correction of human beings, so that the flesh may be subjected to the spirit, and partly by the perversion of those who persevere in sin, so that they may be so ordered that they cannot trouble the righteous who reign with Christ.

Who, then, can prove that the saints did not ask the Lord for such vengeance on their behalf?

## 5. Who are the sons of God

What follows—“So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven”—must be understood according to the rule by which John says: “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

There is one Son by nature, who knows absolutely nothing of sin. We, however, become sons by the power we have received, insofar as we fulfill what he commands. Therefore apostolic teaching calls this adoption, by which we are called to an eternal inheritance, so that we may be co-heirs of Christ (Romans 8:17; Galatians 4:5).

We become sons through spiritual regeneration, so that we may be adopted into the kingdom of God—not as outsiders, but as those made and created by him. Thus he does not say, “Do these things, you who are sons,” but, “Do them so that you may be sons of your Father.” [Col. 1862]

When we suffer enemies, we ought to cry out: “Father, forgive them.” For they are deranged and possessed by an opposing spirit, so that they persecute us; and they suffer a greater persecution from the devil.

“He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.” It is written: “For those who fear you, the sun of justice will rise, so that you may also receive the rain, the watering of the teaching of truth” (Malachi 4:2), because Christ appeared to the good and the evil and was proclaimed in the Gospel to the good and the evil.

Or, if you prefer to understand this sun as the one brought forth not only for human beings but also for animals’ bodily eyes, and this rain as that by which fruits are produced, which have been given for the nourishment of the body—which I consider the more probable interpretation—then that spiritual sun rises only for the good and the holy. For this is what the wicked lament in the book entitled *The Wisdom of Solomon*: “The sun has not risen for us” (Wisdom 5:6). And that spiritual rain waters only the good, because the wicked were signified by the vineyard of which it was said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

## 6. Who are tax collectors and Gentiles. Enemies are to be loved more than friends

“For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have?”

A robber loves his children and parents; a lion loves them; a dragon loves them; bears love them, and wolves love them. If we do not love those who love us—children or parents—we are worse than lions or the beasts mentioned above. But if we return love to those who love us, we still appear to differ in nothing from these beasts.

“Do not even tax collectors do this?” Tax collectors are those who pursue profits and exact taxes through commerce, fraud, theft, crimes, and perjuries.

“And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this?” *Ethnici* is translated from Greek into Latin as *Gentiles*. For ἔθνος (*ethnos*) in Greek means “nation” or “people.”

Therefore, he says, if even sinners—tax collectors and Gentiles—know by nature’s guidance how to be kind toward those who love them, how much more ought you, for whom the dignity of your profession is greater, to have a more abundant concern for truth, to embrace those who do not love you with a wider breast of love? For God commands the love of enemies.

Thus, by the affection of public charity, you break the insolent movements of human minds, not only driving anger away from vengeance but also softening the wrongdoer into love. For it belongs to the Gentiles to love those who love them, and it is common to love those who love us.

Enemies are to be loved more than friends. For enemies oppose the body and prepare eternal rewards for the soul, since those who seize our carnal and earthly possessions gather heavenly and spiritual things for us. Is the one who gives us eternal riches not more to be loved than hated? Friends, however, strive to urge upon our flesh pleasant things that prepare eternal death for our soul.

## 7. The same subject is treated

“Therefore you shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” Who does these things except one who is fully and perfectly merciful? By this one policy misery is avoided, with the help of him who says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

For the perfection of mercy, by which the suffering soul is helped to the greatest extent, cannot extend beyond the love of enemies. Therefore it is concluded in this way: “You shall be perfect, as your Father is perfect.” Yet this must be understood so that God is perfect as God, while the soul is perfect as a soul.

## 8. The commandments are observed in two ways

“Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

“Take care,” he says, “to perform your righteousness before human beings”—that is, to live justly with this disposition of mind, and to establish your good in this, that people may see you.

“Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven”—not if you are seen by human beings, but if you live justly for the purpose of being seen by them. For the Apostle also says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” [Col. 1863] (Galatians 1:10), although elsewhere he says: “Just as I also please everyone in everything” (1 Corinthians 10:33).

He removes all concern for present things and commands us to be attentive only to the hope of the future. We must not pursue either human favor through a display of goodness or the boastfulness of religion through the abundance of public prayer; rather, the fruit of good works must be kept within the conscience of faith, because the pursuit of human praise will receive only the reward that it expects from human beings.

Righteousness is nothing other than not sinning; and not sinning is to keep the commandments of the Law. The observance of the commandments is contained in two forms: that you do none of the things that are forbidden and strive to fulfill all the things that are commanded. This is what the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:15).

If you turn away from evil and do not do good, you are a transgressor of the Law, which is fulfilled not only in the rejection of evil acts but also in the perfection of good ones. You are not commanded merely not to strip those who are clothed of their garments; you are also commanded to clothe those who have been stripped with your own.

## 9. The hypocrite. No one is without the stain of hypocrisy

“When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and streets, so that they may be honored by human beings.”

The Greek word *hypocrite* is interpreted as “pretender”: one who, although evil within, displays himself publicly as good. The term *hypocrite* was transferred from the appearance of those who walk about in spectacles with their faces covered, distinguishing their features with blue and snow-white colors and other pigments. They had face-masks, linen cloths coated with plaster and marked in various colors, and sometimes smeared their necks and hands with chalk, so that they might achieve the color of the character and deceive the people while acting in the games—now in the appearance of a man, now in the form of a woman, and through other deceptions.

This type of image was transferred to those who walk about with a false face and pretend to be what they are not. But to be without the stain of hypocrisy belongs either to very few or to no one. For whoever wishes to appear to be what he is not is a hypocrite.

[Whoever sounds a trumpet while giving alms is a hypocrite. Whoever prays in the synagogues and street corners so as to be seen by human beings is a hypocrite. Whoever fasts and disfigures his face to display the emptiness of his stomach in his appearance is also a hypocrite. From all these examples it is understood that hypocrites are those who do anything whatsoever in order to be glorified by human beings.

It seems to me that the person who says to his brother, “Let me remove the speck from your eye,” is also a hypocrite, for he appears to do this for the sake of glory, so that he himself may appear just. Therefore the Lord says to him: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye” (Luke 6:42).

It is not the virtue but the motive for the virtue that has a reward with God. And if you deviate even slightly from the straight path, it makes no difference whether you go to the right or to the left, once you have lost the true road. Significantly, he says: “They have received their reward”—that is, not God’s reward, but their own.]

For they were praised by human beings, whose approval was the reason they practiced their virtues.

## 10. What the left hand is; what the right hand is. Another explanation of the right and left

“But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.”

The love of God is understood by the right hand; vanity or desire for the world by the left. If you give alms for the sake of human praise, the whole act is performed by the left; but if you give for the remission of sins, the whole act is performed by the right.

What, then, is meant by “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” except that what the love of God does must not be corrupted by vanity or desire for the world?

If someone believes that this can be fulfilled literally, what will he do? If his right hand hurts, should he not give alms with his left? In the preceding passage he says: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings,” where he named righteousness generally; then he explains it in particular. For the work done through almsgiving is one part of righteousness, and therefore he connects the statements by saying: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you.”

This refers to what he said above: “Take care to perform your righteousness before human beings,” namely, so that you may be seen by them. What follows—“Truly I tell you, they have received their reward”—refers to what he previously stated: “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Then follows: “But when you give alms.” When he says “But you,” what else does he mean except “Not as they do”? What, then, does he command me? “When you give alms,” he says, “let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.”

Thus they act in such a way that their left hand knows what their right hand is doing. What is condemned in them is therefore forbidden to you. What is condemned in them is that they act in such a way as to seek human praise.

Accordingly, nothing seems more naturally signified by the left hand than the very delight in praise. The right hand signifies the intention of fulfilling the divine commandments. Therefore, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing—that is, let the desire for human praise not mingle with your conscience when you strive to fulfill the divine commandment in giving alms.

“So that your almsgiving may be in secret.” What is “in secret” except in the good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes or revealed in words? Many give alms outwardly but not inwardly, wishing to appear merciful either out of ambition or for the sake of some temporal thing.

“And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” Entirely right and entirely true. For if you expect a reward from the one who examines the conscience, let that very conscience be sufficient for you to win God’s favor.

## 11. The chamber. The door. What the wings of prayer are

“And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by human beings.”

Nor is it wrong here to be seen by human beings; rather, it is wrong to do these things in order to be seen, expecting from them the fruit of pleasing people.

The streets are the continuous and broader roads of cities; according to the character of the Greek language, they are named from breadth: for πλάτη (*platē*) means “broad.”

“Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.” Here also the Lord shows that he forbids the pursuit of the reward in which fools rejoice when they are praised by human beings.

“But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret.” The chamber he names does not indicate a hidden house, but the secret place of our heart. Hence the Psalmist says: “What you say in your hearts, be pierced with compunction upon your beds” (Psalm 4:5).

“And having shut the doors,” he says, “pray to your Father in secret.” It is not enough to enter the chambers if the door remains open to intruders, through which the things outside thrust themselves in improperly and lay open our inner selves.

By “outside” we mean all temporal and visible things, which enter our thoughts through the door—that is, through the bodily sense—and the crowd of empty imaginings makes noise around those who pray.

Therefore the door must be shut; that is, resistance must be offered to the bodily sense, so that spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father. This prayer takes place in the innermost heart, where the Father is prayed to in secret.

Whoever wishes his prayer to fly to God should give it two wings—that is, almsgiving and fasting. Then it will ascend swiftly and be heard.

“And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” This was rightly and fittingly brought to an end by such a conclusion. For he is not now urging us to pray, but teaching us how to pray; nor, as above, urging us to give alms, but teaching us with what disposition to give. For he commands the cleansing of the heart, and nothing cleanses it except a single-minded intention toward eternal life, through the sole and pure love of wisdom.

# SERMON LXIII

[Note: [Col. 1864] Elsewhere, *On Time* 60.]

Concerning the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 6:1–6: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1864] It is now placed in the *Appendix* for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain editors; Verlin and Vinding consider it spurious; to us it appears to be a genuine offspring of Caesarius.]

## 1. Almsgiving in public and yet in secret

The Gospel reading, dearest brothers, which has just been read to us, seems to me unable to be understood according to the literal sense. Therefore, with God’s help, let us inquire [Col. 1865] how we may reach its spiritual meaning.

For the Lord says: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them”; and again: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret.”

How can we understand this literally, since the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16)?

How does he say here, “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” when elsewhere he says, “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works”?

Pay close attention, brothers, and seek the meaning of divine Scripture humbly and wisely. For the Lord cannot contradict himself in the Gospel reading.

Since he himself has said that almsgiving is to be done both secretly and publicly, a sober understanding is needed so that his commandments may not appear contradictory.

Whoever gives alms for the purpose of desiring to be praised by human beings gives publicly, even if he does so secretly, because he seeks praise from human beings. But whoever gives alms solely out of love for God, so that others may imitate him in the good work and not he himself but the Lord may be praised, gives alms secretly even if he does so publicly. For in that almsgiving he desires not what is seen but what is unseen; he hopes to receive not praise from human beings but a reward from God.

## 2. Public fasting. What the right hand is, and what the left hand is

We must understand the same thing about fasting. Since the Lord himself says, “Anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting” (Matthew 6:17), are we therefore acting against Christ’s commands when we proclaim a public fast and fast together with the whole people watching?

Here too it must be understood that no one should fast for human praise, but for the forgiveness of sins or for divine mercy. Each person should question his own conscience. If he gives alms for God alone, let him do so confidently and publicly, so that whoever sees him may imitate him.

The Lord’s statement, “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” is also understood to belong to what we said above. The love of God is understood by the right hand; vanity or desire for the world by the left.

If you give alms for human praise, the whole act is performed by the left hand; the right hand does absolutely nothing. But if you give alms for the remission of sins and the love of eternal life, the whole act is performed by the right hand.

What, then, is meant by “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” except that what the love of God does must not be corrupted or destroyed by vanity or desire for the world?

For if someone believes that this can be fulfilled literally, what will he do if his right hand hurts? Can he not give alms with his left? Or if he wishes to redeem a captive, how could he loosen his purse or open his chest if he does not join his left hand to his right? Or if he wishes to welcome a stranger and, according to the Lord’s command, wash the feet of the saints, I do not see how this could be done with the left hand unaware.

### 3. Public Prayers: That They Are to Be Made with the Door Shut; Where Temporal Things Are to Be Asked

To this also belongs what he said: “When you pray, do not pray in the corners of the streets; but enter,” he says, “into your room, and with the door shut pray to your Father in secret.” You yourselves rightly recognize that this cannot always be fulfilled according to the letter. For we ourselves, and the whole people, pray not only in our rooms; we also assemble publicly in the church and kneel together with all the people. Are we therefore, in doing these things, contrary to Christ’s commands, since he said that we ought to pray in our rooms with the door shut? It is not so.

Therefore this meaning also agrees with the preceding statement. Pay attention, then, to how this should be understood. Whenever you pray to God and ask from him for something visible, you pray publicly and with the door open, because you wish to receive from God something visible. But if you wish to plead for the forgiveness of sins [Col. 1866] and for eternal life, even if you pray publicly, you pray with the door shut, because you are not asking for what is seen, but for what is unseen. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. 4:18).

If you seek temporal things, as I have already said, you pray publicly and with the door open. If you seek eternal things, your prayer is secret, because you desire to receive not the things that are seen, but those that are not seen. Whoever, therefore, seeks in truth the things that are not seen will also receive the things that are seen, when God rewards him; for he who says this does not lie: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33).

Nor do we say this in such a way that we should not pray to God for temporal matters—that is, for bodily health, peace in our times, or abundance of crops. We ought also to ask God for these things, but in the second and third place, so that in all the intention of our prayer the love of the soul and the desire for eternal life may hold first place. Let us pray for the body, then, but without comparison let us plead much more for the soul.

And therefore, beloved, whenever this Gospel reading is read to you, you ought to receive its meaning in the order we have indicated above: whether in almsgiving, fasting, or prayer, whether in the right hand or the left, let us strive to observe this—that whatever we do, we do not for the vanity or desire of this world, but for the love of eternal blessedness. May he himself deign to grant this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIV

[Note: [Col. 1866] Formerly, *On the Time*, 182.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 6: “When you fast,” etc., and on the Lord’s Prayer, chapter 6, verses 1–18.

[Note: [Col. 1866] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It contains certain excerpts from Book 2 of *The Sermon on the Mount*, but its preface and conclusion have been taken from elsewhere.]

### 1. Two Things Especially to Be Considered by Man; The Fall to Be Mourned

There are two things, dearest ones, to which human prudence ought principally to attend: the dignity of its condition and the excellence of its restoration. It should attend to the dignity of its condition, so that it may fear to sin; and to the excellence of its redemption, so that it may not prove ungrateful to redeeming grace.

By the sole will of the Redeemer, man was raised from the lowliness of the earth and exalted, through the privilege of reason, to the likeness of God. Wretched man lost this when, seduced by the devil’s persuasion, he withdrew in pride from the institution of his Creator. Considering this fall, the Psalmist said, as though in grief: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Falling by his own choice from the highest exaltation, he was rightly condemned to the lowest abasement: he was able to fall by himself, but by himself he was not able to rise again. Human frailty ought to mourn this fall with daily lamentation, so that through daily lamentation it may return to the place from which it fell through empty pleasures, and so that what fell by the foot of pride may strive to rise by the foot of obedience.

Attending to this, the Psalmist said: “Let not the foot of pride come to me”; and, “There they fell who work iniquity; they were cast out, and were unable to stand” (Ps. 35:12–13). “They were cast out” from intimate rest; “and were unable to stand,” that is, to persevere. As the same Psalmist says of them: “For they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:39).

### 2. The Redeemer’s Healing Grace Is Necessary; Christ Taught by Word and Example

For this return, or resurrection, the healing grace of the Redeemer was necessary, so that by humility it might heal what had been corrupted by the exaltation of pride. Therefore the Word of God assumed the form of a servant, in which he could instruct his fellow servants by word and shape them by the discipline of his life as an example.

He taught humility and obedience by word and example when he exhorted his disciples, saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29–30). His yoke is rightly easy because it is obedience, and to serve him is to reign; and the burden of his commandments is light, for it does not weigh us down by pressing upon us, but assists us by enabling us to fulfill them through grace.

By word he also taught sobriety, when he said: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with drunkenness and intoxication” (Luke 21:34). By example he taught it, for he did not feed the crowd that followed him with luxurious delicacies, but with barley loaves (John 6:5–13).

Directing our intention toward inward goods, he also taught how we should fast when he said: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, gloomy”—indicating those who simulate the severity of abstinence through mournful squalor, so that they may appear to people to be fasting.

He did not wish to pass over in silence how almsgiving should be performed, when he said: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” By this instruction he indicated that the almsgiving and every work of mercy that we perform should be done not in pursuit of human praise, but with the intention of eternal life, which is signified by the right hand.

He also taught how one should pray when he said: “But when you pray, enter into your room”—that is, keep your heart tranquil and free from all the disturbance of external things—“and with the door shut”—that is, with the crowd of phantasms excluded—“pray to your Father.”

### 3. A Summary of Whatever Is to Be Asked; Three Petitions for Eternal Life and Four for the Present Life

It has now been said how one should pray. He also adds what one should pray for, continuing as follows: “Thus you shall pray: Our Father, who are in heaven,” and so forth.

This prayer, in concise words—that is, in seven petitions—embraces all the forms of prayer by which we appeal to God, whether for desired goods, for the avoidance of evils, or for the blotting out of sins. Of these seven petitions, the first three concern eternity; the four that follow concern the necessities of the present life.

For the sanctification of God’s name, the coming of his kingdom, in which he will come in glory, and the fulfillment of his will “as in heaven, so on earth”—whether we understand heaven and earth as the righteous and sinners, soul and body, or Christ and the Church—although they take their beginning from Christ’s humble coming, will be completed only at the end of the age. All three will remain forever.

The remaining four, however, appear to pertain to this temporal life. For daily bread, both bodily and spiritual, although it is everlasting, pertains to this time only insofar as it is ministered to the soul through certain signs and words, whether spoken or written. It is therefore called bread because it is learned through labor and exposition, and thus is swallowed, as it were, by chewing.

Now also sins are forgiven us, and we forgive others; this is the second of the four petitions. Now temptations also trouble our life, and deliverance from evil itself pertains to this life, because through God’s justice we incur death, from which we are to be delivered by his mercy.

Since this is so, the words of the petitions must be treated more carefully, so that, once understood, they may produce a greater affection of the heart and bring what is requested to more rapid fulfillment.

### 4. In What Christians Are Distinguished from Jews, and in What They Are Indistinguishable from One Another; The Awakening of Charity; Confidence in Obtaining What Is Asked; Why We Turn toward the East When We Pray

Let us say, then, “Our Father,” whom we serve not through fear but through love.

This was not said to the former people, that they should pray to the Father. The Lord was indeed made known to them, but they did not obey him with filial love; rather, they were subjected to him through servile fear.

By this word, however, the rich and noble are admonished, once they have become Christians, not to exalt themselves against the poor and lowly, since together they say, “Our Father,” which they cannot say truly and devoutly unless they recognize that they are brothers.

By this name charity is also awakened, for nothing ought to be dearer to children than their father. A suppliant affection is also awakened when people say, “Our Father,” as well as a certain confidence of obtaining what is asked, since even before the petition we have received so great a gift that we are able to say, “Our Father.” For what will the Father not now give to his children when they ask, who has already given them this very thing—that they should be children?

Finally, how greatly does the thought of the one who says “Our Father” touch his mind, so that he may not prove unworthy of so great a Father?

Let the people of the New Testament, therefore—the new people called to eternity—use the words, “Our Father.” The prayer is fraternal: it does not say, “My Father,” as though one were praying only for oneself, but “Our Father,” embracing in one prayer all who recognize that they are brothers in Christ.

“Who are in heaven”—that is, in those whose manner of life is in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1868] Augustine: that is, in the saints and the righteous.]

This likeness is highly appropriate: spiritually, the distance between the righteous and the sinner is to be understood as great as the bodily distance between heaven and earth. For it was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

To signify this, when we stand for prayer we turn toward the east, from which heaven rises—not because God is there, as though he had abandoned the other parts of the world, but so that the mind may be admonished to rise toward a more excellent nature, that is, toward God.

### 5. The Beatitudes Enumerated; The Fear of God

Now let us consider what should be asked for: “Hallowed be your name.”

This is not asked as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be regarded as holy by human beings, and so that God may become known to them in such a way that they consider nothing to be holier. Thus they may fear to offend him, because it is right to sanctify the name of God and to fear God, of whom it is said: “The Lord is his name” (Amos 9:6).

This fear is the first degree among the beatitudes. Of it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16); and elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10).

### 6. Piety

It follows: “Your kingdom come,” that is, “Let it be manifested to the world.”

Just as present light is absent to the blind, so God’s kingdom, although it is everywhere, is absent to those who do not know it—or in this sense: that you reign in us and we in you, by your gift.

This petition pertains to piety, which is the second degree among the beatitudes. For if piety is that by which the meek are blessed, let us ask that God’s kingdom come into us—that is, that we may become meek and not resist.

### 7. Knowledge

It follows: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”—that is, as in the angels, so also in human beings; and as in the righteous, so also in sinners. Or: let the flesh consent to your will, as the spirit does.

This petition pertains to knowledge, which is the third degree among the beatitudes. For if knowledge is that by which those who mourn are blessed, let us pray that God’s will may be done on earth as in heaven—that is, that the flesh may consent to the spirit. Human misery ought to grieve for nothing so much as for this: that the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), so that with the Apostle we may be compelled to cry out: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

### 8. Fortitude

The fourth petition follows: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

This may be understood simply of bodily food, and spiritually of the bread of the divine word. If it concerns bodily food, this petitioner does not extend his request far into the future; he follows the Gospel command, where it is said: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow. Tomorrow will take care of itself” (Matt. 6:34).

Thus also the blessed Apostle admonishes us: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. 6:8).

But if you understand this bread spiritually, understand either Christ himself, who is the soul’s supersubstantial bread—for he surpasses every substance—and who said of himself, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41); or understand the very meaning of the divine word, which is necessary for us to restore the ruins of the soul, as long as it is called “today.”

This petition pertains to fortitude, which is placed fourth among those ascending toward supreme blessedness. For if fortitude is that by which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, we must pray that this daily bread be given to us, so that, strengthened by it, we may be able to arrive at that perfect fullness.

[Col. 1869]

### 9. Counsel

It follows: “And forgive us our debts.”

If someone has perhaps sinned against you, forgive him when he asks forgiveness from you, lest, while you deny mercy to your brother, you close to yourself the Father’s indulgence. As the Apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

This petition is related to counsel, which is placed fifth among the degrees of the beatitudes. For if counsel is that by which the merciful are blessed, let us therefore forgive our debtors their debts, and let us pray that our debts—that is, our sins—may be forgiven, on account of which we are kept from obtaining pardon unless the forgiveness of our brothers hastens it.

### 10. Understanding

It follows: “And do not lead us into temptation”—that is, “Do not allow us to be led into temptation.”

To be tempted is one thing, and no one has been approved as righteous without it; to be led into temptation, that is, to be led in by the tempter, is another.

This, then, is what we pray: that God may not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but may provide a way of escape along with the temptation, so that we may be able to endure it (I Cor. 10:13).

This petition pertains to understanding, which is placed sixth in the enumeration of the beatitudes. For if understanding is that by which the pure in heart are blessed—that is, those whose mind’s eye has been cleansed of earthly dust—let us pray not to be led into temptation: that is, not to have a divided heart, but to seek one simple good.

### 11. Wisdom

It follows: “But deliver us from evil”—not only from the evil into which we may be led, but also from that into which we have been led, after which nothing will remain to be mourned.

Wisdom corresponds to this petition, and it holds the seventh place among the beatitudes. For if wisdom is that by which the peacemakers are blessed—that is, those who, by ordering their conduct, compel all things to serve the spirit—we must therefore pray that we may be delivered from evil.

This deliverance itself makes us free, that is, children of God, so that by the Spirit of adoption we may cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15).

“Amen” in these petitions signifies that what is asked is certainly conferred by the Lord, provided the agreement of the final condition is firmly maintained.

### 12. Three Remedies for Sins; Three Kinds of Sinning

The heavenly Physician has commended to us these three kinds of remedies in a spiritual sense—almsgiving, fasting, and prayer—so that by these medicinal antidotes we might heal long-standing evils, drive away present ones, and avoid future ones by preserving our health.

There are appropriately three kinds of treatment, just as three kinds of corruption precede them. Every sin is either committed in the soul, through consenting to an evil suggestion in order to violate God’s temple; or it is committed through the wrongful use of the body to injure one’s neighbor, which is a crime; or it is committed through the wrongful use of the body to corrupt oneself, which is a disgraceful act.

Crimes, although they are committed through the body—such as murders, robberies, and thefts—do not thereby affect or corrupt the body of the one who commits them. Concerning these the Apostle said: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body.”

Disgraceful acts, however, are committed through the body and also affect and defile the body. Concerning these the Apostle says: “The one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (I Cor. 6:18).

Therefore crimes committed outside the body are rightly cleansed by almsgiving as by an external medicine, because just as the crime harmed one’s neighbor, so almsgiving, which is outside us and yet is given through the body, ought to benefit one’s neighbor.

Disgraceful acts, however, are appropriately cleansed by the medicinal discipline of abstinence, because just as a pampered flesh drew one toward guilt, so afflicted flesh ought to lead one back to pardon.

But if there are some for whom these remedies are unsuitable—whether because they cannot give alms on account of extreme poverty or cannot fast on account of weakness of the stomach—they possess a third kind of medicine, from which no one will be able to excuse himself except those who have refused to heal the diseases of their souls.

Let us therefore diligently and devoutly practice this medicine, which cannot be lacking to any sound mind, fulfilling the apostolic command: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. 5:17).

For this antidote confronts every illness in such a way that, when practiced continually, it drives away all diseases and restores everything corrupted to wholeness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXV

[Note: [Col. 1870] Formerly, *On the Time*, 126.]

Again on Matthew 6:9–13: On the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1870] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It appeared doubtful to the Louvain editors; Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious, observing that Augustine usually explains the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer differently. Whoever the author may ultimately be, he generally agrees with Cyprian.]

### 1. By the Words “Our Father” We Proclaim God’s Goodness and Grace

Since, with the Lord’s help and guidance, you have already been established in the royal palace, and the day is near when you will come, as it were, to the court of the heavenly King, I urge you, beloved, first to learn the proper prayer to be offered to the Father and God.

For since the human mind, disdainful and ignorant of heavenly things, could neither know nor discover how it ought worthily to pray to God, the true Lord and Teacher himself showed and taught—through the holy Apostles, and through them to us—how we ought to pray.

“Thus,” he says, “you shall pray: Our Father, who are in heaven; hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done,” and so forth.

O truly heavenly prayer, which is wholly prayer! For if we wished to treat each word more fully as it stands, the day would end before the sermon did. Nevertheless, let us run through it briefly.

We say: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” By beginning in this way, we proclaim God’s goodness and grace. For when would we, earthly and wretched, weak and useless servants, dare to raise our faces toward heaven and say, “Our Father,” unless he himself had granted us this confidence through his Only-Begotten?

As it is written: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

Having therefore received this power, we call God “Father,” because through faith we have received the Spirit of adoption, so that we may rejoice that we have been made children of God.

### 2. Those Who Have Received Grace Ought to Give Thanks; What the Words “Your Kingdom Come” Signify; We Must Always Regard God’s Will, Not Our Own

Next we say: “Hallowed be your name.” This is an act of thanksgiving, as though one were saying: “May your name be holy and blessed.” For those who have received grace ought to give thanks.

“Your kingdom come.” Certainly this does not mean that he should begin to reign whose kingdom is of all ages. Rather, we desire that he bring an end to our evils and, coming from heaven, take us up into his kingdom.

By saying this we are admonished where we ought to hope for life, substance, and kingship.

Similarly we say: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.” For who can hinder God, so that his will is not done everywhere?

[Note: [Col. 1870] Cyprian: “For who can resist God, so that he does not do what he wills?”]

But we pray that just as God’s will is done in heaven, where no one offends, so he may grant strength to our souls, so that we who are on earth may be able to do and fulfill his will.

Or certainly, when we say, “Your will be done,” we are taught always to regard God’s will, not our own, because in our will there are sometimes opposing desires, whereas in the Lord’s will there is always life and goodness.

### 3. The Eradication of Greed, and the Remembrance of Death in the Word “Today”

After heavenly matters, we consequently ask also for earthly things, but only what is necessary.

For we say: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

O true wisdom and divine providence, which taught us both to ask only for bread and to name “today”! By this saying both craving and avarice are removed, and the uncertainty of human life is impressed upon us, according to the word: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34).

Indeed, it would be unfitting for someone to ask for necessities for many years and times—or even for another day—when his life might perhaps be ended during the night.

Thus also that exceedingly greedy rich man, who, after rebuilding his barns and filling them, said to his soul, “You have many good things laid up for many years; feast,” heard from the Lord: “Fool, this night they demand your soul of you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:19–20).

[Col. 1871]

[Note: [Col. 1871] In manuscript R: “This night your soul will depart from you.” In Cyprian: “Your soul is being demanded.”]

We therefore appropriately pray that our daily bread be given to us today, because we do not know what tomorrow may bring.

### 4. One Must Forgive One’s Brother So That the Father May Forgive One

Next we say: “Forgive us our debts.”

“Debts,” brothers, means sins. A debt is contracted whenever one commits an offense, and that debt must eventually be paid in Gehenna.

And because human frailty is not without daily occasion for sinning, we ask that our debts be forgiven while we are in the body, lest we labor until the final farthing.

It is rightly added: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

You see, beloved, by how great a condition the divine word binds us.

[Note: [Col. 1871] Cyprian: “He gave a law, binding us by a definite condition and pledge.”]

Forgive, then, so that you may be forgiven. You have someone who owes you a debt, who has sinned against you, who perhaps has inflicted an injury: forgive him when he asks, show indulgence to him when he pleads, spare him when he repents, lest, while you deny mercy to your brother, you close to yourself the Father’s forgiveness.

### 5. Why God Tempts

The sacred prayer is completed with a most useful conclusion when it prays against temptation and evil. For we say: “And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

God leads a person into temptation when he permits him to be tempted, in order to test him, not to destroy him.

He does not tempt as though he were ignorant of human minds, but in order to make his faithful ones manifest in the world, as it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6).

Thus he tested Abraham through his son and honored him (Gen. 22); thus, by giving Job over to various temptations, he tested him (Job 1–2); thus he crowned the holy Apostles and the blessed martyrs even through fire and swords.

From this it is evident that temptations of this kind proceed from God, and that the devil can do nothing without God’s permission.

Therefore God alone is to be worshiped, for he can lead us out of temptation. He leads us out when he delivers us from evil; and he delivers us from evil when he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear.

### 6. Summary of the Lord’s Prayer

You have, brothers, been shown both whom you ought to pray to, to whom you ought to give thanks, whose kingdom you ought to desire, and whose will you ought to await. You have also heard from whom help is to be awaited against temptations and evil.

Behold, everything is contained in a few words and completed in brevity. Since it is not difficult to learn, indeed since it is easily retained, I urge all of you, men and women, to learn to keep it, so that when you have obtained the Lord’s grace which you desire, you may be able to utter this prayer with one voice among all the saints and love it with a pure heart.

Thus may Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father, see his words in your mouth and his commandments in your heart, guard you in this life, and make you worthy in the age to come.

[Note: [Col. 1871] Perhaps: “in the kingdom.”]

To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXVI

[Note: [Col. 1871] Formerly, *On the Time*, 202.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 7:1–5: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1871] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. The Louvain editors left it among the Augustinian works as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus judged that it should be removed along with the spurious works. It certainly reflects the style and thought of Caesarius. In the manuscripts it begins as follows: “Just now, when the Gospel was being read, we heard the Lord saying,” etc.]

### 1. Manifest Evils Are to Be Judged, but Not Things Unknown or Doubtful; It Is Better to Think Well of the Wicked Than Ill of the Good

Manifest evils may and ought to be judged, but with charity.

We heard the evangelist saying, dearest brothers: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

What does this mean, brothers, when the Lord himself said elsewhere in the Gospel: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (John 7:24), and elsewhere it is said: “Judge true judgment” (Zech. 7:9)?

The divine reading cannot contradict itself; rather, it seeks a sober understanding.

In human conduct, beloved, there are some things that are reasonably reproved, but there are others that cannot be judged without sin. Manifest evils ought both to be judged and reproved; but those things that we do not know, or whose performance with a good or evil intention we cannot determine, we ought not to judge at all.

For example, you see someone fasting frequently. Rejoice with him, but do not praise him excessively, because he may be doing this for human glory. But do not censure him either, because he may be fasting for God and for the healing of his soul.

You see another person wishing to eat during a publicly proclaimed fast. Admonish him with love. If he says that he is unable to fast because of weakness of the stomach, believe him and do not judge him. Both possibilities exist: he may wish to eat through gluttony or luxury, or he may be unable to fast because of illness.

You see another imposing discipline upon his subjects with severity and granting indulgence slowly. Do not judge him cruel, because perhaps he does this not from the disease of anger, but from zeal for discipline and love of justice, on account of what is written: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10).

Perhaps one of your neighbors or friends, while his mind is occupied with matters sufficiently necessary to him, greets you later than he should or comes to meet you later than he ought. Do not judge him proud; do not think him malicious. Rather, believe that this happened through forgetfulness or negligence rather than through contempt or pride.

For perhaps this also frequently happens to you, as human frailty dictates: being too intent upon other matters, you may appear to have done something less carefully or less attentively, although you did not wish to be judged with an evil intention on that account.

In these and similar matters, where we cannot know whether something is done with a good or evil intention, it is better that we incline our minds toward the right-hand side. It is more tolerable for us to anticipate this error by believing those who are evil to be good than, through the habit of judging, to suspect evil even of those who are good.

In such matters, which are known to God but unknown to us, we judge our neighbors dangerously. Concerning these the Lord said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

But concerning those evils that are manifest and public, we both can and ought to judge and reprove them—with charity and love, however—hating not the person but the sin, not the vicious person but the vice, detesting the disease rather than the sick person.

For if a public adulterer, robber, habitual drunkard, traitor, or proud person is neither judged nor disciplined, what the blessed martyr Cyprian said of such people will be fulfilled in them: “Whoever strokes the sinner with flattering words supplies fuel for sin.”

### 2. Sudden Anger Is a Speck; Anger That Has Grown Old Is a Beam; Anger Disturbs the Eye of the Heart, Hatred Blinds It

To this matter, dearest brothers, also belongs what we heard in this very Gospel reading: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not see the beam in your own eye?”

You have seen someone suddenly become angry. Do not judge him immediately, but wait a little. Perhaps just as quickly as he becomes angry, he is appeased.

Let us see, however, what the speck and the beam signify.

Sudden anger is a speck; but anger prolonged for a long time becomes a beam.

[Note: [Col. 1872] The printed editions add here: “while it is nourished by hatred through false suspicions.” These words are absent from the manuscripts.]

Thus, as becoming angry and quickly being reconciled is a speck, so anger long preserved in the heart is a beam. Old anger therefore is transformed into a beam.

With what face, then, does one who keeps hatred in his heart presume to judge someone in whose eye he recognizes not a beam but a speck?

For a speck disturbs the eye of the heart, while a beam blinds it.

What I have said, brothers, I ought to confirm by testimonies from Scripture. Hear how anger disturbs the eye of the heart, as the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8).

But how hatred blinds the eye of the heart is attested by the evangelist John: “The one who hates his brother,” he says, “is in darkness and walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John 2:9, 11).

Accordingly, through sudden anger the eye of the heart is disturbed; through hatred the light of charity is extinguished.

### 3. Recapitulation; Rash Judgment Is No Small Sin

Therefore, dearest brothers, I offer you certain headings and brief indications of how you ought to understand and receive these matters. By God’s favor you are able to grasp and observe them better.

So that what I have said may be more firmly implanted in your hearts, I briefly repeat what I have proposed.

In these matters, as I said above, we judge others dangerously when it is uncertain whether they are done with a good or evil intention: fasting, keeping vigils, giving alms, abstaining or not abstaining from wine and meat, and other similar practices, which may be undertaken either for God or for human glory.

Because we do not know with what intention they are done, we ought not to judge them at all.

For this reason the Lord said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

But concerning manifest iniquity it was said: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (II Tim. 4:2). And there is also what we mentioned above: “Judge a just judgment.”

If we wish carefully to consider these things, as we believe, and by God’s gift to observe them with great diligence, then with God’s help we are delivered from no small sin.

For the greater part of the human race is shown to be ready and eager to censure by indiscriminate judgment, although it does not wish to be judged by others in the way it wishes to judge others.

For this reason divine Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Before you ask questions, do not blame anyone; and when you have asked, reprove justly” (Ecclus. 11:7).

Every person wishes first to be questioned, and afterward, if guilty, patiently tolerates reproof. Since we all wish others to act in this way toward us, it is right that we should strive to fulfill this toward others.

Let us first question with patience and be attentive. When we have learned something more certainly, then let us wish either to reprove it, if it is evil, or to defend it, if it is good, in accordance with what is written: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them. For this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12).

And therefore, turning to the Lord, let us implore his help, so that in his mercy he may deign to grant us true discernment and perfect charity. To him belong glory and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.

[Note: [Col. 1873] In place of this conclusion, the manuscripts have the following: “And since, as you yourselves see, many of our people now appear to be absent from the church, let us reserve for them whatever admonition we may give in another basilica; and perhaps God will inspire them also, so that they may assemble there for the salvation of their souls. To him belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.” Perhaps on the same day he preached in two basilicas, using in the first sermon the conclusion preserved in the manuscripts and the other in the second.]

## SERMON LXVII

[Note: [Col. 1873] Now brought forth for the first time from the Theoderic manuscript, where it is attributed to Augustine, but falsely. It appears to exhibit the teaching and style of Caesarius, whose are nearly all the other sermons contained in the same old codex.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 7:13–14: “Enter through the narrow gate,” etc., and on the two ways, the narrow and the broad.

### 1. Free Will

You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, when the Gospel was read, that the Lord mentioned two ways: one fearful and terrible, the other to be sought and greatly desired; one by which, after a little labor, the righteous are raised to heaven, the other by which, after a brief sweetness, lovers of the world are dragged into hell. “Enter,” he says, “through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow,” he says, “is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it!” Behold, dearly beloved brothers: God has set before the whole human race what we ought to expiate, what to avoid, what to desire, what to flee, what to fear, and what to love with our whole heart. And as he himself had foretold through the prophet: “Before man are life and death; whichever he chooses will be given him” (Ecclus. 15:18); and again: “Behold, you have fire and water, death and life; choose life, that you may live” (Deut. 30:19). Everything we have said above—that is, good and evil—is contained in these two ways. For in them hell and the kingdom, Christ and the devil, height and depth are set before us. By God’s grace, each person has in his power what he will love and toward what he will stretch out his hand.

### 2. Christ presides over the narrow way, the devil over the wide way. Both ways must be judged not by the eyes of the flesh but by those of the heart.

Christ presides over the narrow and constricted way; the devil rules the broad and spacious way. Christ invites us to the kingdom; the other lures us to hell. The one raises us on high; the other thrusts us down into the depths. The devil displays false sweetness in order to draw us toward true bitterness; Christ invites us to brief hardship in order to lead us to lasting blessedness. If only the bodily eye is opened, the broad and spacious way deceives us; but if we attend with the eyes of the heart, what is hard and rough makes us secure.

### 3. Christ is both the way of pilgrims and the homeland of the angels.

Therefore, dearest ones, let us admonish one another and continually invite one another with true charity, so that we may choose rather the brief and narrow way by which we may deserve to reach the spaciousness of paradise. But that way which, after brief breadth, customarily plunges its lovers into the depths of hell, we must reject and despise as far as we can, with God’s help. Let us therefore leave the left-hand way, whose end leads into Gehenna, and follow the right-hand way, which leads to eternal life.

We must reach him who is the way, the life, and the truth (John 14:6). Nor is it surprising if we faithfully reach him through whom we faithfully walk. Since he himself is the way, we run through him; but since he himself is the homeland, when our course is completed we arrive at him. For although according to his divinity he is the rest and homeland of the angels, according to his humanity he became the way of pilgrims. Because he is the rest and homeland of the angels and of all the faithful: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; because he is the way of pilgrims: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

### 4. The benefit of redemption.

When, after the sin of the first man, we were cast from paradise into this world, as into a valley of tears, and lost both the way and the homeland, we traveled through difficult deserts; but “we did not know the way of the Lord” (Wis. 5:7). Yet the pious and merciful king of our homeland not only took care to send his servants to us frequently; he also deigned to descend himself and prepare the way by which we might return to our homeland.

O man, if you were too lazy to seek the way, the way itself deigned to seek you; if you were too lazy to come to the way, the way itself came to you. Rise and walk. Flee the broad and spacious way of the world, which delights you for a time and torments you forever. Run along the way of Christ, on which you will labor for the briefest time and afterward rejoice without end with the angels.

### 5. Two feet for running along Christ’s way: twofold charity.

Perhaps you say: “How ought I to run along Christ’s way?” If you have both feet sound, you will run happily. What are these two feet? If you love the Lord and love your neighbor. On these two commandments, as the Apostle says, the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40; Gal. 5:14).

If you love the Lord but do not love your neighbor, you have only one foot and cannot run. If you love your neighbor but do not love the Lord, you remain lame and useless.

Run, therefore, along Christ’s way, for it is itself the way. Along this way of love the Lord himself also ran while hanging on the cross, when he prayed for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Along this way blessed Stephen also strove to run manfully, so that he deserved to see heaven opened and Christ standing as if to meet him or to help him (Acts 7:55).

### 6. Let humility be the companion of charity.

But because you must run humbly if you wish to arrive quickly, observe that you are running toward him, through him, and to him who said: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Whatever good work you may wish to offer to God—whether almsgiving, fasting, or prayers—you lose it all if you are unwilling to be gentle and humble in heart with true charity.

Therefore, as I have already urged, strive to hold fast above all, among your other good works, to humility and charity, so that with these two holy and spiritual feet you may faithfully run and happily reach eternal blessedness; through him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXVIII

[Note: It was the thirteenth homily among those published among the sermons of Caesarius by V. C. Stephanus Baluzius from the royal manuscript.]

On the same words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 7:13–14: “Broad and spacious is the way,” etc.

*(This admonition explains how, through the sin of the first man, we were cast from paradise into the hell of this world, so that we might not deserve to come, under the weight of sins, to the lower hell, but might strive with all our strength to ascend, as though by certain steps of good works, to the higher and principal homeland.)*

### 1. Two hells. After the fall, Adam is between paradise and the lower hell.

I know, dearest brothers, that your holy Charity cannot be unaware that our father Adam had been placed amid the delights of paradise; but, persuaded by the devil, he despised God’s commandments and was cast into the miseries of this world, as from a higher place to a lower one.

[Note: Undoubtedly one should read *contemnentem* (“as he was despising”).]

Paradise, therefore, is above; this world is hell. There is another hell, into which sinners and the impious are plunged after death. That there are two hells the prophet clearly demonstrates when he says: “God, you have rescued my soul from the lower hell” (Ps. 85:13). He would not have said “the lower hell” unless he knew that there was also a higher one.

Now when our merciful and compassionate God, patient and greatly merciful, cast us in our father Adam from the height of paradise into the hell of this world by his just judgment, he did not, in his ineffable goodness, wish us to reach the lower hell by ruin.
