Rather, in a certain sense he placed us midway between paradise and the lower hell, so that, if we wished to do penance, we might deserve to ascend to the height of the principal homeland; but if we wished to remain continually in that tyranny of pride through which we fell at the devil’s persuasion, we might be pressed down by the weight of sin into the depths of the lower hell, from which return would no longer be possible.

### 2. The broad way leads to the lower hell; the narrow way leads to paradise.

Therefore, dearest brothers, considering these things not casually but with great fear and trembling, let us understand that by God’s mercy we have been placed in this higher hell, so that we may desire rather to return by steps of good works to him who created us than to descend with him who deceived us into the depths of the lower hell.

And because we have been placed as if between water and fire, between the highest good and the highest evil, between the ruin of the lower hell and the height of paradise, let us hear the Lord crying out in Scripture with admirable compassion: “I have set you,” he says, “between death and life; choose life, that you may live” (Deut. 30:19).

The Lord admonished us in the Gospel concerning these two ways when he said: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and there are many who enter through it; narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and there are few who find it.” And because through the narrow and constricted way one returns to paradise, while through the broad way one descends into that lower hell, let us, while we are still able with God’s help and the matter remains in our power, as I have already urged above, strive rather to climb to paradise through the narrow and constricted way than to reach the punishments of hell through the broad and spacious way.

### 3. Who walk by the broad way and who by the narrow way. The way of each is brief, whether in labor or joy.

But perhaps someone says: “I would like to know who those are who descend with perilous joy by the broad way, and who those are who climb with labor by the narrow and constricted way.”

All lovers of the world—proud people, the greedy, robbers, the envious, drunkards, those who commit adultery, those who use dishonest scales and double measures, those who harbor hatred in their hearts, repay evil for evil, and love spectacles that are bloody and frenzied or shameful—are shown to descend by the broad and spacious way.

But the chaste and sober, the merciful, those who uphold justice, those who give alms according to their means with a willing and cheerful spirit, and those who harbor hatred in their hearts against no one ascend by the narrow and constricted way to the heights. Although they still appear to dwell here on earth in the body, nevertheless, according to the Apostle, “their citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), so that when the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” they may confidently answer that they have them directed toward the Lord.

Consider, I beg you, brothers, and reproach those who are being hurled along the broad and spacious way, not only with sorrow but also with fear, saying and testifying to them that after brief joy they will have punishment without end. But rejoice with those who strive to ascend by the narrow and constricted way; faithfully join yourselves to them, and strive to reach with them the height and blessedness of eternal life.

Do not fear because you will have labor on the way; rejoice because you will find a great reward in the homeland. Therefore, again and again I beg you, dearest brothers, let us consider the eternal joy of the righteous after brief labor, and fear the endless punishment of sinners after transitory delight, recognizing that even those who appear to ascend with labor by the narrow and constricted way do not seem to labor for a long time.

For just as those who serve avarice or lust with unhappy joy will, when the journey along the broad way is completed, burn with the devil in hell, so, conversely, those who despise the false joys of the broad way and the luxurious life will, when they have completed the course of the narrow way, deserve to reach the fellowship of the angels in heaven.

### 4. Let the sick person join himself to the physician, not to the disease.

Since we have spoken of the higher paradise, the place where true blessedness is, and of the two hells, and have briefly shown, according to the ability God has given us, what we ought to flee and what we ought to desire, there are three further matters related to the same subject that we wish to make known to your Charity.

There are three things about which we both can and ought to think usefully and faithfully; and we frequently recognize these three as occurring in human life even with bodily eyes. There is a physician, a sick person, and a disease.

If the sick person joins himself to the physician, the two of them overcome the disease. If the sick person wishes to join himself more to the disease than to the physician, then, because there are two of them, the physician is overcome. For if he consented to the physician, the sick person would escape when the disease perished; but the disease could in no way defeat two opponents fighting against it.

Pay close attention to why I have offered this comparison. The physician is God; the sick person is man; sin is the disease. If the sinner joins himself to God, who is the true physician, the disease immediately perishes. But if the unhappy sinner loves his disease, wishing to join himself more to his sins, as to deadly illnesses, than to cling to the heavenly physician, he not only refuses to accuse his disease—that is, his sin—but strives to defend it with the most shameless face. By wishing to join himself to his sins, he seems, as it were, to overcome the heavenly physician; but through this unhappy victory, as through a broad and spacious way, he descends into Gehenna. For if he had wished to consent to the physician, when sin, like a most cruel disease, perished, he would have deserved to ascend into heaven by the narrow and constricted way.

### 5. Exhortation to almsgiving, prayers, and fasting.

Therefore, dearest brothers, thinking faithfully about these matters, while with God’s help the matter still remains in our power, let us shudder at the wounds of our sins as at deadly poisons. Let us devote ourselves to almsgiving, prayers, and fasting, and especially to charity, which loves not only friends but even enemies themselves. Like spiritual medicines, let us turn to the mercy of that heavenly physician for the healing of our souls.

For he said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live”; and again: “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved” (Ezek. 33:11). May he bring us, in his goodness, to this salvation—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIX

[Note: It now appears for the first time from two Corbie manuscripts that bear the name of Caesarius in their books, except that in one of them, the older, several sermons of Caesarius are attributed to Augustine by the first hand, but to Caesarius by the second. Compare Sermons 67 and 68 above. Moreover, concerning no. 7, see Caesarius, Homily 19, at the end; concerning no. 8, Homilies 21 and 10, and no. 4 of Sermon 29 of this Appendix.]

On the same passage of Matthew, chapter 7:13–14: concerning the pilgrimage of Christians and the two ways, one to heaven and the other to hell.

### 1. Those absent in body are together in love.

Our sermon to you, dearest brothers, concerns what you heard in the Gospel: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and spacious is the way that leads to death,” or, concerning the pilgrimage of Christians.

If the demands of time permitted, dearest brothers, we would wish to visit you not only once a year but also a second or third time, so that we might satisfy both our own longing and yours by seeing you. But desire wishes it, while the demands of time do not permit it. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us or you from being together, although we see one another bodily only after a delay, since in love and charity we are always together.

For in this pilgrimage of the present world, even if we could be in one city, we could not be together. There is another city where good Christians are never separated from one another.

### 2. There are two cities: the world and heaven. Let the one who wishes to be a citizen of heaven be a pilgrim in this age. The homeland, city, citizens, kindred, and king of Christians.

There are two cities, dearest brothers: one is the city of the world, the other the city of paradise. In the city of the world, the good Christian is always a pilgrim; in the city of paradise, he is known to be a citizen.

This city is laborious, that one peaceful; this one miserable, that one blessed. In this one there is labor; in that one there is joy and rest. Whoever lives badly in this one will not be able to reach the other.

We must be pilgrims in this age so that we may deserve to be citizens in heaven. Whoever loves the world and wishes to be a citizen in the world has no share in heaven. For we prove that we are pilgrims by desiring our heavenly homeland.

Let no one deceive himself, dearest brothers: the homeland or city of Christians is not here. The true blessedness and eternal happiness of Christians are not here. Whoever seeks happiness in the world will not have it in heaven.

Our homeland is paradise; our city is that heavenly Jerusalem. Our fellow citizens are the angels; our parents are the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs; our king is Christ. Let us therefore live in this pilgrimage in such a way that, while we are here, we may desire such a homeland. For whoever wishes to live badly cannot desire that homeland.

### 3. The joy of the saints over our good life and their sorrow over our evil life.

The glorious army of many patriarchs and prophets, as well as of apostles and martyrs, many thousands of confessors and virgins, and a considerable number of faithful peoples has already gone before us to that homeland. All of them, now established in blessed rest, daily await us with arms extended in charity, desiring and praying together that, from the arena of this world, where we must fight against the devil, they may receive us as victors, with triumph and exultation, into that homeland of paradise.

For if we act well, if in this world we despise demonic sins and deadly pleasures, we generate joy for all those in heaven. But if we despise God, love the world, and embrace crimes and sins, we grieve all those—angels, apostles, and martyrs, as we said above—in heaven, and prepare eternal fire for ourselves.

### 4. Christ watches over and helps those who fight for him. The different promises of Christ and the devil.

Behold, Christ awaits us in heaven with his angels, watching how we fight against the devil and his angels. Let us not fear, brothers, because Christ not only awaits us but also helps us. Do not fear; do not despair. The devil indeed rages, but Christ will extend consolation.

He awaits you while you fight, helps you while you labor, and crowns you when you conquer. Do not despair; do not yield. You have such a commander over you, and yet you fear?

Consider what the devil promises you and what Christ will give you. The devil promises false sweetness; Christ true blessedness. The devil thrusts upon you the empty joys of the world; Christ the true blessedness of paradise.

Through adultery the devil provides the pleasure of lust for a single hour, in order to destroy an immortal soul. Christ commends to you chastity for the few days during which you live in the world, so that he may make you like the angels in heaven. In exchange for the broad and spacious way of lust, the devil lures you into hell; in exchange for the narrow and constricted way of chastity and mercy, Christ invites you into heaven.

### 5. Freedom to choose the right-hand or left-hand way. The sweetness of the broad way is brief and false, but its punishment is long; the opposite is true of the narrow way.

Behold, man: you have water and fire, life and death; before you are good and evil, hell and the kingdom, the false sweetness of the world and the true blessedness of paradise. Through the grace of Christ, power has been given you: stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. “Choose life, that you may live” (Deut. 30:19). Leave the left-hand and spacious way, which drags you toward death, and hold to the right-hand and narrow way, which happily leads you to life.

Let the left-hand way neither hold nor delight you. Its breadth is indeed ample and level, and adorned with various flowers; but its flowers quickly wither, and poisonous serpents frequently hide among them, so that while you run toward false joys, you may be struck by deadly poison.

It is broad, but not long. You pay attention to the kind of way along which you are going, but not to the kind of homeland to which you arrive. If you do not believe me, you draw yourself toward death; rather, if you do not believe in Christ, you will perish in hell.

For the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and there are many who enter through it.” It delights, indeed, but it deceives.

Conversely, let the right-hand way neither sadden nor frighten you. It is narrow, indeed, but not long. There is no prolonged joy in the broad way, nor prolonged labor in the narrow one. The former, after brief breadth, drags one into eternal straits; the latter, after brief straits, leads one to eternal blessedness.

### 6. We must labor so that by good works we may obtain joy in heaven.

Therefore, brothers, let us strive to labor with God’s help and, rejecting sins, adorn ourselves with good works, so that our king Christ, our fellow citizens the angels, and our parents—the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—who have already gone before us happily into our city, the heavenly Jerusalem, may receive us with joy and exultation.

Let us act, brothers, so that through our good works there may be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, as the Lord himself previously deigned to proclaim (Luke 15:7). If, then, we cause joy in heaven when we do penance, surely we generate sorrow when we return to the pleasure of our sins.

### 7. Wholehearted charity.

Therefore, dearest brothers, so that with God’s help we may escape all sins, let us strive to preserve complete charity, loving not only friends but also enemies, and desiring to entreat for everyone and pray for all human beings.

For if you do for all people what you would wish done for yourself, you close the door of sins completely. There will be no opening by which sin can enter your soul if you are willing to love not only friends but also enemies with your whole heart.

### 8. Exhortation to almsgiving.

I beg you, brothers, let us live in this world as guests and pilgrims. Whatever we acquire through any labor, through any just business, or through any legitimate service, let us send ahead by almsgiving to our eternal homeland, except for daily food and simple clothing.

Let luxury not consume us in this pilgrimage; rather, let mercy send us onward to our homeland. We are traveling, brothers; we are making our way toward our homeland. Let us not indulge in luxury along the journey of this life, and let us never feel secure. Rather, always watching carefully and cautiously, let us not prepare delicacies for ourselves on the road.

If we spend here in luxury, gluttony, and drunkenness whatever we can labor to obtain, how will we come to that homeland? With what face could we enter among angels and archangels, naked of good works, wrapped in the filthy rags of sins, and wounded by evil deeds?

Whatever gluttony was going to squander, let almsgiving lay up. Whatever avarice has buried on earth, let mercy send to heaven. Thus, when the soul leaves this body, may it be adorned with splendid garments and with the pearls of chastity, mercy, patience, humility, and concord, so that we may deserve to hear from the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and what follows.

These are the things we ought to desire, and we ought to dread that other sentence which the soul, naked of good works and wrapped in the filth of vices, will hear. For concerning such a soul the Lord speaks in the Gospel, saying: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” And when he was silent, he said to the attendants: “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:12–13).

May God turn away from us this sentence, which all those will hear who now set aside nothing or little for heaven through almsgiving. Of such people the Apostle says: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

When such people leave their bodies, they are not lifted by angels with Lazarus into Abraham’s bosom; rather, with the rich man dressed in purple they are plunged into the depths of hell.

Considering these things, let us reduce our food and clothing as much as we can while we are in this world, so that after our death we may deserve to be clothed in heaven with the most precious and splendid garments of our almsgiving and hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

May the Lord bring us to that joy under his protection—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God in the Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXX

[Note: Formerly, On Time 48; later, in Appendix 33.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 11:25–30: “I confess to you, Father,” etc.

[Note: It is composed from two Augustinian sermons, 67 and 71, with some inserted fragments from Ambrose and others.]

### 1.

When the holy Gospel was read, brothers, we heard the Lord Jesus rejoice in the Spirit and say: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

For now, let these words of the Lord suffice. If we consider them worthily, diligently, and—what is most important—devoutly, we discover first of all, etc.

### 2.

Finally, he discloses the heavenly mystery: it pleased God to reveal his grace more to little ones than to the wise of this world. The Apostle Paul set this out more fully in writing, saying: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:20–21).

He therefore says: “Yes, Father, for thus it was pleasing before you.” The secrets and powers of heavenly words are hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones: little ones in wickedness, not in understanding; but to the wise they are hidden because of the presumption of folly, not for reasons of prudence.

The Lord confirms the justice of this act by the judgment of the Father’s will, so that those who disdain to become little ones before God may afterward become fools in their own wisdom. You see how terrible the Lord is in his counsels. Learn the examples of true humility, and do not rashly scrutinize the plans of the heavenly dispensation.

For when he had stated both things—namely, that he had revealed the mysteries of his coming to some and hidden them from others—he did not immediately give the reason, but said that this was pleasing to God, clearly showing that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust.

And lest he be regarded as in any respect less than what is in God, he immediately added: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” A most beautiful passage concerning faith is joined here, when he says that all things have been handed over to him by his Father.

When you read “all things,” you recognize the omnipotent one, not unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you read “handed over,” you confess the Son, to whom all things properly belong by right of his nature and unity of substance, not as gifts bestowed by grace.

He says that all things have been handed over to him—not only the heavens and the earth and the other elements that he himself created and made, but also those who through the Son have access to the Father, who were formerly rebellious against God and afterward began through faith to perceive him. Hence elsewhere he says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37).

“And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” When he said, “No one knows the Son except the Father,” he did not say, “and the one to whom the Father wishes to reveal him,” as, when he said, “No one knows the Father except the Son,” he added, “and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

This is not to be understood as though no one could know the Son except the Father alone, while the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son revealed him. Rather, it was said so that we might understand that both the Father and the Son himself are revealed through the Son, because he is the light of our mind. Thus, when he later added, “and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,” understand that this refers not only to the Father but also to the Son, for the addition applies to the whole statement.

For the Father declares himself by his Word. The Word declares not only what is declared through the Word but also himself.

To know that, just as the Son reveals the Father himself to those whom he wishes, the Father also reveals the Son, hear the Lord Jesus himself praising Peter because he had confessed him to be the Son of God: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

Let us therefore hear what follows, where he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened.”

### 3.

It seems strange to some, dearest brothers, when they hear the Lord saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. My yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

They consider those who bear that yoke itself, etc.

## SERMON LXXI

[Note: Elsewhere, On Time 233.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 13:24–30: “While people were sleeping, an enemy came and sowed weeds over the field,” etc., and on other passages, an exhortation to good works.

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors had doubts about it; after Verlinus, Vindingus declared it spurious. Here he censures, first, the confusion of dissimilar matters; second, expressions unfamiliar to Augustine; third, a doctrine contrary to sound theology in chapter 4, where the question “Why does the Lord call one person to himself and not another; why does he help one and not another?” is answered: “He considers this one worthy because of his good works, and that one unworthy because of his evil works.” A little later it concludes: “And when you have done these things, you will receive my grace.” These words appear to contain the Pelagian doctrine, “Grace is given according to our merits.”]

### 1. The enemy is symbolically called man.

Our Lord and Redeemer speaks in his Gospel, saying: “While people were sleeping, an enemy came and oversowed weeds.” Symbolically, the enemy is called man.

Hear the Apostle saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). Hear, man: the one who gave you light did not give you darkness.

Where are you going, man? Where are you being dragged? Why do you pursue carnal desires when you hear: “Walk by the Spirit, and do not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5:16)?

Listen instead to the Lord saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3). “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:6).

Hear, man: if you withdraw from God, you will not escape his hand; but if you approach him, you will immediately have him, because he withdraws nowhere.

Hear the prophet saying: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:8). Where, then, is there no God from whom you flee?

You are evil, because you flee the good; you are death, because you flee life. You wish to wrap yourself in darkness in which you may hide, but you cannot escape him whose eyes see everything.

The Apostle says: “What fruit did you have then from those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21). The voice of the judge follows, saying: “Go away, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

Therefore, whoever flees the Lord and withdraws from God is confounded and perishes in his ungodliness. So that he may not perish then, let him now return to the Lord; and he will be enlightened, and his face will not be ashamed.

### 2. Who the weeds in the Church are. Love of Christ above all.

Nevertheless, my brothers, I will say what I think; understand what I say. Among you, the grain of God is mixed with weeds—that is, lovers of the world, lovers of money, lovers of pleasures, devisers of trivialities, all seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

Those who enter Christ’s Church hypocritically, promising and not doing, making vows and not fulfilling them, renouncing evil and doing the same again—those who love such things are weeds.

They do not love Christ if they love anything more than Christ. Hear, man, the voice of the Lord your God: “Whoever loves father or mother or wife or sons or daughters or brothers or fields more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

If you wish to hold what you do not have, let go of what you have, so that the love of Christ may be in your heart.

### 3. Whoever desires what belongs to God must relinquish his own things.

Behold, you ask something from God and say: “Lord, give me.” What will he give you when he sees your hands occupied elsewhere? Behold, the Lord wishes to give what belongs to him, but he has nowhere to put it.

See, then: let go of what you are holding, and you will receive what you seek. Let go of temporal and perishable things, and you will receive eternal and everlasting life. Let go of earthly things, and you will receive heavenly things.

Now someone said to Jesus: “Good Teacher, what good must I do to have eternal life?” Surely the one who said, “What good must I do?” desired eternal life, but he loved more what he was holding.

The Lord saw that his hands were occupied. He wishes to give, but has nowhere to put what he would give: the hands of those who would receive are occupied.

For the Lord says to you: “Go, sell everything and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:16, 21), and place it in heaven, because on earth it is an impediment.

### 4. What Is Given to the Poor Is Not Lost

Why are you afraid, man, to give to the poor? You will not lose these things; rather, they are being kept for you in heaven. “I did not command you to give them in order to lose them,” says the Lord, “but I advised you where to put them.” After this, man, you will have a treasure not destined to perish on earth, but destined to remain in heaven.

At some point trouble comes upon a man, [Col. 1882] the fear of loss comes. You are afraid, man, lest you lose your money; you are afraid lest you lose your silver; you are afraid lest you lose your property—and are you not afraid lest you yourself perish altogether? For this you give false testimony; for this you lie and seize what belongs to another; for this you swear and perjure yourself, which the law entirely forbids. When you do all these things, are you not wholly hay, wholly stubble, wholly straw? And are you not afraid lest you burn altogether? Your soul is always disturbed by the loves of this world. Say: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. XLI, 6).

### 5. Gold Is in the Earth, from the Earth, and Is Earth

The miser suffers sadness on account of his gold, undergoes trouble, and faces dangers from servants and dangers from robbers. The miser loves gold more than his own soul; you, Christian, love Christ more than all that is yours. He burns with love of gold; you, Christian, burn with love of Christ, and you will be blessed in the kingdom of Christ.

Hear, man: gold is in the earth, it is from the earth, it is earth, and it is a portion of the earth. The ungodly person, while loving the creature, offends the Creator and loses Him who created all things from nothing. Hear, man: it is not you who lose God; rather, you perish away from God. He is the redeemer of your soul—the one you wish to lose. “For what will it profit you if you gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of your soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26).

### 6. Why God Calls One Person and Does Not Call Another

Awaken at last, man, and love Christ. For this is true wisdom: to love Christ. Many people say, and wish to know, why the Lord calls one person to Himself and does not call another; why He helps one and not another; why He considers this one worthy and that one unworthy; why He honors this person and torments and afflicts that one.

Hear, man. He considers this one worthy because of his good works; He considers that one unworthy because of his evil works—for the Lord is a debtor, and He will repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

Perhaps you will say, “Why is that person treated so?” Your Lord God answers you: “Because I did not withhold what is good. Rather, I said beforehand, ‘Wash yourselves; be clean’” (Isa. I, 16). What did you want? What did you seek? What did you desire? The grace of God. Therefore, if you seek the grace of God, first remove wickedness from your soul and from before my eyes; cease from evil now and do good; seek peace and pursue it with all your strength (Ps. XXXIII, 15). And when you have done these things, you will receive my grace; my eyes will be upon you and my ears attentive to your prayers; and before you seek me, I will say, “Here I am.”

### 7. Good Things Must Be Provided Here. Hope of Mercy Belongs Only to the Merciful. Whoever Does Not Forgive His Enemy Becomes His Own Enemy. One Should Pray for Him Before He Prays. What Praise of God Ought to Be Like

Let us do good, dearest brothers, so that in the age to come we may deserve to find the rest that our Lord promised us when He said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7). And, rejoicing with the prophet, let us say to the Lord: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

Those who are merciful find mercy. Let the despisers fear judgment—those who spare neither themselves nor show mercy to others, saying: “Let us sin, and God will spare us, because He is merciful and good.” God is altogether merciful and good; but because He spares now, He will not spare in the future. The ungodly have judgment prepared for them without mercy.

Let us understand, brothers, and see where we ought to place our hope. Mercy belongs to the one who has shown mercy. Blessed are the merciful, because God will have mercy on them. There is hope in mercy if we have not become barren in the work of mercy.

O man, why do you seek mercy from God if you yourself are not merciful? Why do you seek forgiveness for your sins from God when you yourself do not forgive someone like yourself? Hear, man; hear the voice of the Lord your God, where He Himself says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, 37, 38).

Hear again where you yourself say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” For if you do not forgive your adversary, you yourself are first your own adversary. He injured you by taking your money; you injure yourself by refusing to forgive your adversary.

Perhaps you will say: “I will not spare him, because he injured me greatly and sought my blood.” If you do not forgive him, you will possess the destruction of your soul. Moreover, you still say: “I will not spare him, because he was my adversary.” Believe me, man: you will be a worse adversary to yourself if you do not spare him.

You say, “He does not ask me.” If he does not ask you, pray for him, so that what he did against you may be forgiven him by the Lord. For if you say, “I will not spare him,” you wish to quarrel, not to forgive. And with what face or confidence will you say to your Lord, “Forgive, because I have forgiven”?

Consider, man, and see another law in your members fighting against the law of your mind and taking you captive in the law of sin (Rom. VII, 21). You yourself are already being dragged away captive, and you are angry with the one who stripped you?

Let no one charge us, my brothers, if through you we have not been able to double the Lord’s money. We shall be bad servants if we do not do what has been commanded us; but if we do it, we shall be good servants, and we shall rejoice with the Lord without end.

Let us all love Him through whom we were made; let us love Him through whom we were redeemed. For His sake, let us love one another in this age, so that we may deserve to rejoice together with Him in the age to come. For thus it has pleased our Lord God concerning us: that, established here, we should sing to Him with your Charity.

Let us praise the Lord, brothers, with tongue, heart, mouth, and voice. For He wishes praise to be given to Him in such a way that there is no discord among us; rather, He wishes harmony to exist in us, in our voices and our conduct.

O blessed praise in heaven, where the angels are the temple of God! There is the perfect harmony of those who praise, where no law in our members fights against another law; there is no strife and no desire. Here, then, let us sing praise to the Lord with anxious care, so that there we may be secure.

### 8. Here There Must Be Not Security but Concern. The Body Is a Prison

Why, then, should we be concerned here, my brothers? Hear why: because “human life is a trial” (Job VII, 1). For the Lord exhorts us in His own words, saying: “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41).

Do you not wish to be concerned when you hear yourself saying, “Forgive us our debts”? How are you secure when every day you hear yourself asking for the remission of sins? How are you secure when you still say, “Forgive me my sins,” and again say, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (ibid. VI, 12, 13)?

How, then, do you dare cry out, “Deliver us from evil,” if you are secure? Hear, man; hear. You are evil when God delivers you from yourself, who are evil. You see another law in your members fighting against the law of your mind and taking you captive in the law of sin.

Hear what we are and what we carry with us. As long as we are enclosed in this body of death, we carry vice with us. Hear the prophet saying again: “Lord, bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. CXLI, 8). My prison is this, as long as I am in the body of death. For when I have been freed from this body, earth is returned to earth and the spirit is received into heaven.

I go, then; I leave the earth, because as long as I am here, I serve the law of God with my mind, but with the flesh I serve the law of sin.

### 9. In the Resurrection the Whole Human Being Will Be Spiritual

One of the faithless may say: “Then, when you have been freed from this flesh, you will be nothing but spirit.” Hear, then, heretic. The flesh of which I speak I do not consign to eternity; I lay it down here.

The unbeliever answers: “Then will you return to this body of death?” And from where did you cry out with such a devout voice, “Bring my soul out of prison”?

Hear, ignorant man, and deaf against the daily readings. I shall return to a body that is not this body of death, because “this corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality.” Now it is animal; then it will be spiritual. No one can receive what is eternal unless he has first laid aside what is temporal. Therefore, lay aside this temporal evil, so that you may receive that eternal good.

### 10. The Land of the Living and the Land of the Dying

Hear, brothers, and beware. Here we are traveling, and we are placed on the journey; we have not yet reached our homeland. Let us beware of those who lie in ambush for us on the journey, because here they act against us so that we may not return to our homeland—that is, to paradise. This land is the land of the dying; but that land is the land of the living, of which the prophet said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

In that land one will live forever and never die. That land shines more brightly than the appearance of silver; there the angels are citizens among the righteous. They rejoice in that land; let us mourn in this land, so that we may deserve to reach their joys.

See, brothers: here we are placed on the journey; our ambusher, the devil, opposes us on the way and seeks to harm us, so that we may not return to the land of the living.

For there are two commandments, dearest ones, which we must observe in every respect: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind,” and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37–40).

Whoever walks in these two commandments should hasten along the road; and he will reach the homeland of paradise, where all the saints rejoice in the glory of their Redeemer and praise His holy name—those who have been rescued from the distress of this pilgrimage and live forever in everlasting joy.

## SERMON LXXII

[Note: [Col. 1884] Elsewhere, *On the Words of the Lord* 14; and later, in the Appendix 2.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XIV, 23–32, where the Lord walked upon the waters and Peter faltered

[Note: [Col. 1884] In the books printed earlier, as well as in the manuscripts of those who attribute this sermon to Augustine, it was mutilated by more than a third, beginning as follows: “When the holy Gospel was being read, we heard of a little boat in danger, and Christ coming to the aid of those in danger.” Here it is published restored from several manuscripts of excellent quality, in which it bears the name of the presbyter Heraclius—namely, the man whom Augustine designated as his successor in the episcopate.]

### 1. Explanation of the Text

We heard, and in a certain sense saw in the present reading, a little boat in danger, Christ coming to the aid of those in danger, and Peter going out to meet the Christ who was coming. In all these things we expected a miracle; let us seek the mystery.

For when, with the inspiration of Him who performs them, we are able to carve out some understanding of mystical significance from the divine works that are read, we are, as it were, bringing honey from the hidden cells of honeycombs. Or, imitating Christ’s disciples, we rub ears of grain in our hands (Luke VI, 1), so that we may reach the grains hidden within and find life in them.

Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore went up, as has been read, onto a mountain by Himself to pray. A mountain is a height; for what in this world is higher than heaven? And who ascended into heaven, your faith knows very well. Why, then, did He ascend alone? Because “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

Although, at the end, when He comes and gathers all of us, His members, and raises us into heaven, He will then also ascend alone, because the head together with its body is one Christ. But now only the head ascends: “the man Christ Jesus, mediator of God and human beings” (I Tim. II, 5). He ascended alone to pray because He ascended to intercede for us with the Father.

### 2. The Little Boat Is the Church; the Sea Is the World; the Mast Is the Cross. Persecution Enlarged the Church and Enriched the World

Nevertheless, dearest ones, while He is praying on high, the little boat is being tossed by waves in the depths. Since waves rise up, the little boat itself can be shaken; but because Christ is praying, it cannot sink.

Understand this little boat, brothers, as the Church, and the turbulent sea as this world. When someone of impious will and great power declares persecution against the Church and, so far as he can, tries to extinguish the Christian name, a great wave rises up against Christ’s little boat.

But in these temptations let the mast be raised, so that, suspended from the tree, it may represent the cross of Christ. Let the Christian look upon it and not lose heart, because, as the apostle Peter says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in His footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21).

Blessed John also says: “Just as Christ laid down His life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (I John III, 16). To this mast—that is, to the cross of Christ—let simple conduct and pure confession be fastened like shining sails. Let these sails of ours be washed by the waves, and let the garment be stretched out so that it may be found without stain or wrinkle.

However fiercely the sea may rage, however the wind may press upon it, however this ship may be tossed amid blasts and waves, let it only not sink, and let it continue on its course.

[Note: [Col. 1885] Lovaniensis has *and let it continue on its course* (*et currat*); these words are absent from some manuscripts.]

Finally, after this ship had been built in Jerusalem and from there sent out into the midst of this roaring sea, the rolling masses of the swelling waves and the blasts of the raging winds, as they carried it here and there, brought it to the shores of all nations. Wherever it came, it brought foreign merchandise.

For what is so foreign in our land as the remission of sins through repentance and the kingdom of heaven? And yet it was necessary for Christ to suffer, to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the remission of sins to be preached in His name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke XXIV, 46). For from that harbor this ship first raised its anchor.

[Note: [Col. 1885] The following material up to the beginning of section 4 is restored from books of sound quality. In their place, other manuscripts have: “Therefore the Lord came to visit His disciples, who were troubled on the sea during the fourth watch of the night. The fourth …,” as below, section 4.]

### 3. The Christian Should Be Secure and Concerned. Flatterers Are Hidden Rocks; Slanderers Are Sea Dogs. They Cannot Bite One Who Clings to the Cross

Let this ship of the Lord sail, then, dearest ones; let it sail safely through the storms of the world under Christ’s protection, and, by God’s gift, with concern. For because the helmsman is watchful in the ship, the sailor ought not therefore to sleep.

He is watchful of whom it is truly written: “He will neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Ps. CXX, 4). Yet He Himself also says: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41).

From what source, then, ought we to be concerned, and from what source secure? Concerned because He said, “In this world you will have distress”; but secure because He immediately added, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33). Concerned because He foretold to us the temptations that would come; secure because He does not cease to intercede for us.

Therefore, my brothers, being steered cautiously and attentively amid the waves of the world, embark upon the voyage in your good works. Let neither the tooth of the slanderer break you nor the tongue of the flatterer deceive you.

Watch your flatterers as hidden rocks beneath the waves. For when the sea is calm, the hidden rocks are not seen; but if a storm of tribulation rises, then they lift their peaks among the mountains of the waves, and the danger that was concealed appears in them. For it is not enough for such people to abandon the one suffering; they also try to attack and oppress him.

Let the Christian avoid this type of human being, like the roughest cliffs hidden by the winds beneath the calm surface of the sea. We have spoken briefly about flatterers.

Slanderers must be utterly despised, because they are sea dogs. They can bark from the depths of bitterness; they cannot bite. But how long can they not bite? As long as you remain seated in the ship.

What does “as long as you remain seated in the ship” mean? As long as you hold fast to the cross of Christ and do not depart from His little boat. Let us raise our minds to heaven and not concern ourselves with an envious mind.

[Note: [Col. 1885] Perhaps *an envious tooth*, as Morel conjectures, *Elem. Crit.*, pp. 254–255. The relevance of this correction is better understood by reading what precedes. M.]

In this stormy and turbulent sea, the devil too, breathing upon it, rages, terrible with an armed fleet, and, ranging everywhere, blockades the supplies of the innocent. He is the one of whom the apostle Peter says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour.” And because he added, “Resist him, firm in faith” (I Pet. V, 8–9), the daily battles of those who are making progress are waged against him.

That great teacher of the field described this warfare; he described it when he said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12).

Therefore, brothers, established in these things, in this labor and in this contest, let that apostolic saying console you: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Phil. IV, 5–6).

### 4. The Watch

Christ therefore came to His ship during the fourth watch of the night and visited it. The fourth watch of the night is the final part of the night. One watch has three hours, and therefore the night has four watches, distributed in three-hour periods for each watch. The fourth watch of the night thus means that the night was almost finished.

So He will come at the end of the world, when the night of iniquity has passed, to judge the living and the dead. For now He came, as you heard, walking in a most wondrous manner upon the waters. The waves rose up, but they were trodden down; the roaring sea murmured beneath the Lord’s footsteps, yet, willingly or unwillingly, it carried Him.

However greatly the swelling forces of the world may rise up, He presses down their head—our Head. When He drew near the little boat, the disciples were troubled with fear and cried out, thinking that He was a phantom. The Lord said to them: “Have confidence; it is I; do not be afraid.”

What does “It is I” mean? “I am not the phantom you suppose. Recognize the one you see.”

At this voice Peter leapt forth and said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” If it is you, I do not marvel that you suspend solid flesh upon the back of a flowing element. For what is astonishing if creation serves its Creator? I do not marvel at this; do what will astonish me: let Peter walk.

### 5. The Death and Resurrection of Faith

“Do what will astonish me: command me to come to you upon the waters.” For I know that the law of nature does not allow a human body to plant firm footsteps upon liquid waves. But let the gift of grace approach, and let this law of nature pause for a little: “If it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.”

You are God; I am a human being. You wished to possess from me the weakness of the flesh that you bear; let me also possess from you the power by which the wave may carry me. “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” For how will there not be a way for me in the sea if you command, you who for our sake became the way?

And the Lord said, “Come.” Peter did not hesitate; he heard the Lord’s word and immediately ran toward the Word. He believed quickly because he was a faithful man. But when a strong wind arose, he faltered because he was a human being.

This faltering, brothers, was like the death of faith; but when he cried out, faith rose again. He would not have faltered unless he believed; but neither would he have cried out unless he believed.

[Note: [Col. 1886] So the manuscripts that we have followed throughout. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read: “He would not have walked unless he believed; but neither would he have been submerged unless he had doubted.” The words that follow, up to “Why did you doubt?” in “In Peter, therefore …,” have been drawn from the same sources from which the preceding material was taken.]

“Lord,” he said, “save me!” And the Lord stretched out His hand, lifted him up, and said to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”

Could the wind have thrown you down, whom the wave could not swallow? Could the wind have overturned you, whom the wave could not cover? What you had done was greater: you had trodden upon the sea, pressed down the waves, and conquered the winds. Why did you doubt?

In Peter, therefore, the common condition of us all must be considered: if the wind of temptations tries to overturn us in some way, or the wave to submerge us, let us cry out to Christ.

What does “let us cry out” mean? Let us pray. He will extend His hand and rescue us from the depths. For His hand will lead us, and His right hand will hold us, until He brings us to His eternal promises.

## SERMON LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1886] Elsewhere, *On Time* 230.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XVII, 20: “This kind is driven out by nothing except prayer and fasting”

[Note: [Col. 1886] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Lovanienses allow doubt concerning this sermon; Verlinus and Vindingus, however, reasonably maintain that it is not Augustine’s.]

### 1. The Effect of Fasting

We ought certainly to retain the weapons that the Lord showed us against the wickedness of demons. “This kind,” He said, “is driven out by nothing except prayer and fasting.” When these are practiced with full faith, they constitute piety. And piety is useful for everything, possessing the promise of the present life and of the life to come (I Tim. IV, 8).

Let us therefore usefully examine the fruits of prayer and fasting, because these themselves are weapons against evil thoughts. Fasting purifies the mind, lifts the understanding, and subjects the flesh to the spirit. Fasting makes the heart contrite and humbled, which God does not despise. Fasting scatters the clouds of desire, extinguishes the fires of lust, and kindles the true light of chastity.

Fasting does not love excessive speech; it condemns the superfluity of riches; it despises pride; it commends humility. It enables a person to understand himself as weak and fragile. And while he understands himself to be so feeble, he more readily seeks and receives the help of God’s power. He seeks it through frequent prayers and supplications.

### 2. Prayer, the Refreshment of Fasting. What Prayer Is

Prayer is the refreshment of fasting and summons the grace of the Holy Spirit. Prayer softens the hardness of the heart, moderates austerity, and sweetens fasting. For just as refreshment is not complete without drink, so fasting without prayer cannot perfectly nourish the soul.

What, then, is prayer except an ascent of the soul from earthly things to heavenly things, an inquiry after what is above, a desire for invisible things? Let the discord of worldly conduct, by which the human mind is daily oppressed, depart.

Prayer is union with the Holy Spirit—provided that the mind is attentive in prayer—as the prophet cries: “My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh thirsted for you.” What must be thirsted for follows: “That it may see your power.”

Believe me: if the soul of human substance thirsts fully to see the full power of God, and does not pretend indifference after being overcome by distaste, it will be filled with spiritual richness and abundance. And, thirsting for that visitation of God, it will cry out with its own understanding and with faith: “My soul clung after you; your right hand received me” (Ps. LXII, 2, 3, 9).

Fasting removes sluggishness and takes bodily impediments away from the mind. Persevering prayer, however, joins one to God; and thus, rejoicing to stand before the Lord, the soul glories in Him.

When the soul clings to the Lord, it begins to possess security and freedom; it endures neither terrors nor fears. Once it has received so great a protection from God’s right hand, how could it be harmed by any power? As it is written, no one snatches it from the Father’s hand (John X, 29). This is what fasting accomplishes; this is what prayer accomplishes.

## SERMON LXXIV

[Note: [Col. 1887] Elsewhere, *On Time* 247.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapters XXII, 2–14: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son”; and concerning the adulterous dress of men and women

[Note: [Col. 1887] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In the Lovanienses edition it bears the mark of a doubtful sermon; according to Verlinus and Vindingus, it is plainly unlike Augustine in style and character. It was first published under the name of Ivo of Chartres by Juret from the Victorinus codex, and then revised by Gussanvilla according to the Regius and Petavian codices. From that edition it was possible to correct several things here.]

### 1. The Master of the Household Is God

We heard from the evangelical parable that a certain master of a household made a wedding feast for his son and invited very many people to it. Among them, when one person entered without a wedding garment, he was seen by the master of the household and ordered not only to be excluded from the wedding feast but also to be thrust into the outer darkness.

This parable clearly rebukes the senseless people of the present age, although something more hidden and sacred may be understood through a deeper investigation. Let us first ask, then, who this master of the household is, who this son is, and what this wedding feast is. Once these matters have been examined, we shall more easily understand why the person who approached this wedding feast in adulterous clothing was excluded from it.

We understand, therefore, that this master of the household is God the almighty Father, whom all the households of the nations serve, who begot for Himself in heaven a Son coeternal and coequal with Himself, without a mother, and on earth without a father. He made a wedding feast for Him when He joined the Church to Him from every kind of human being. To this union of Christ and the Church the noble and ignoble, the rich and the poor, every condition, every sex, and every age have been summoned.

### 2. Many Reprobates Are One

Among these there entered one person who alone deserved to be excluded, because he did not possess the garment appropriate to the sanctity of such a wedding feast.

Pay attention, brothers: this one person is many; and yet this entire multitude is comprehended under the name of unity. They are many with respect to the number of individual distinctions, but they are one through agreement in a single perversity. For just as the Church is one through faith under Christ the head, so the entire multitude of the reprobate, whether it is manifest or hidden, is one body under the devil as its ruler.

Therefore, whoever openly departs from God through unbelief does not approach this wedding feast. Whoever is faithful approaches bodily but departs in mind; he enters the church with us and shares Christ’s table with us. Good and bad fish still lie hidden within the nets until they are separated on the shore. The chaff is still tolerated until the threshing floor is winnowed. Then it will plainly appear that “many are called, but few are chosen.”

### 3. Immodest Dress of the Body in Men and in Women. Adulterous Dress Is an Insult to the Creator

Then this adulterer of the wedding garment will, at the command of the master of the household, both be openly excluded and thrust into prison. In the meantime, however, the friends of the bridegroom do not fail to recognize such an impostor, because immodest dress of the body is a messenger of an adulterous heart.

Among men, immodest dress of the body consists in excessive and disorderly hair, an affected imitation of women’s clothing, and a contrived length of footwear exceeding the limits of necessity. Among women, it consists in an artificially made-up face, imitation of men’s clothing, and alteration of the natural color of the hair.

This dress is adulterous in both sexes, unworthy of fellowship in the holy wedding feast, and entirely to be removed from the sight of so great a bridegroom and so great a bride. Nor should the friends of the bridegroom, who love the beauty of God’s house, pass over these matters in silence. They ought publicly to bark against adulterers of this kind, lest it be said of them: “They are mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. LVI, 10).

For whoever tries to transform into something else the size or form that the almighty and most wise creator fashioned—does he not plainly seem to say to the one who fashioned him, “Why did you make me like this”? It is wicked presumption to degrade the Creator’s handiwork in this way, so that, as far as lies within him, he transforms his own size and form into something else—something whose possession, had he received it from nature, he would grieve over incomparably more.

### 4. Condemned by the Fathers. The Work of the Devil Is the Alteration of Nature

Nor do we say these things as though they came from us. We have our fathers, outstanding teachers, who wrote against these practices before us and condemned them with irrefragable authority.

Let us hear Paul, the teacher of the nations, speaking to the Corinthians about excessive hair: “If a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him” (I Cor. XI, 14). Since, by God’s ordering, a man holds primacy over a woman, the man who, contrary to the honor of his sex, veils his head with an excess of hair deprives himself of his primacy. Thus it is rightly said of him: “When a man was in honor, he did not understand; he was made like”—to speak truthfully—not only to women but also to foolish animals (Ps. XLVIII, 21).

For by the judgment of the laws, a person is rightly cast down from the dignity he has obtained when he abuses the privilege granted to him.

Let us also hear blessed Cyprian, an outstanding martyr and most gracious teacher, discussing adulterous dress. For in the letter he wrote *On the Dress of Virgins* he says:

“The work of God, His creation, and His handiwork must in no way be adulterated in dress with yellow coloring or black, or with any cosmetic that corrupts the natural features. For God says, ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness’ (Gen. I, 26). And does anyone dare to change and transform what God has made? They offend God with their hands [Note: [Col. 1889] In Cyprian: “they bring [an offense] upon God.” And immediately afterward: “not knowing that it is the work of God,” etc.] when they try to remake and transform what He formed, knowing that everything that is born is the work of God, while whatever is altered is the devil’s.”

[Note: [Col. 1888] Cyprian has “when they apply.”]

“If a painter wished to mark the face, appearance, and bodily form of someone with a rival color, and, after the likeness had been marked, completed, and finished, another person brought his hands to it in order to remake what had already been formed and painted, as though he were more skilled, this would plainly seem a serious insult to the first artist and a just cause for indignation.”

And later:

“Do you not fear that, when the day of resurrection comes, your artist will not recognize you and will remove and exclude you, when you come to receive your rewards and promises? Will he not rebuke you with the authority of a censor and judge, saying: ‘This is not my work, nor is this image ours,’ because you polluted yourself with yellow cosmetic, because you disfigured by falsehood the form I gave you? Your face has been corrupted; your limbs are foreign. You will not be able to see God, because you do not have the eyes that God made, but eyes that the devil has stained?”

[Note: [Col. 1889] Cyprian has “with false cosmetic applied to the skin.”]

### 5. Who Should Bear God in the Body

Hear me, then, as a father. Hear me, I ask, as I teach and admonish you alike. Hear me as I faithfully counsel what is useful and advantageous for you.

Be such as God the artificer made you. Be such as the hands of the Father fashioned you. Let your face remain uncorrupted, your neck pure, your appearance genuine; let your feet be free from superfluous footwear, your hair uncolored by any dye, and your eyes worthy to behold God.

It is the voice of the apostle, whom the Lord called a chosen vessel. For he says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 47, 49).

Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; holiness bears it; truth also bears it. Those who remember God’s disciplines bear it, retaining justice with religion, steadfast in faith, humble in fear, strong in enduring everything, gentle in bearing injury, ready to show mercy, united and harmonious in fraternal peace.

[Note: [Col. 1889] From *On the Dress of Virgins*, chapters 2 and 4.]

We must observe, love, and fulfill all these things so that we may complete the apostle’s command: “You were bought with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20).

For we bear God in our body when we do not disfigure His image through filthy and profane inventions, when in every act of service we strive to obey the command of our Redeemer. Thus He will recognize His image in us and will not exclude us, adorned with the wedding garment, from the fellowship of Himself and the saints. May He mercifully grant this to us, the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXV

[Note: [Col. 1889] Elsewhere, *On the Words of the Lord* 20; and later, in the Appendix 4.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapters XXIV, 19: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1889] It contains excerpts from Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 39, section 28. In most other respects it seems to us to refer to Caesarius. Compare section 2 with Caesarius, Homily 24.]

### 1. What the Scriptures Promise Here

We must know and understand, dearest brothers, that while Christians live in this body, tribulation cannot be absent. For, as you heard, the apostle testifies to us, saying: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12); and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV, 21).

Days of tribulation and days of grievous tribulation are coming; they are coming, as Scripture says. And as the days approach, tribulations increase. Let no one promise himself what the Gospel does not promise. For as the end of the world approaches, as the Gospel says, “iniquity will abound and charity will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12); so, because of those very iniquities, adversity will never be absent.

We must prepare our minds not only for repentance but also for endurance. My brothers, I beg you, pay attention to the Holy Scriptures: have they deceived us in anything? Have they said anything whose outcome was different from what they said? It is necessary that everything happen to the end just as they have said.

Our Scriptures promise us nothing in this age except tribulations, pressures, difficulties, increasing sorrows, and an abundance of temptations. As the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “In the world you will have distress”; and again: “The world will rejoice, and you will be sorrowful; but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI, 33, 20).

Let us prepare ourselves especially for these things, so that we do not fail when unprepared.

## 2. Pregnant Women and Nursing Mothers. The Craftiness of the Avaricious

For when the Gospel was being read concerning those very tribulations, you heard: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing.” Pregnant are those who swell with hope; nursing—that is, suckling—are those who have already obtained what they desired. For a pregnant woman swells with the hope of a child, though she does not yet see the child; but she who is already nursing embraces what she hoped for. Pregnant is the person who covets another’s property; nursing is the person who has already seized what he coveted.

And so that even the simple may understand this more clearly, let us offer an illustration. Someone covets another man’s estate and says: “That estate of my neighbor is a good one. If only it were mine! If only I could join it to my own and make one property from this land and that!” Avarice too loves unity: what it loves is good, but it does not know where it ought to be loved.

Perhaps that neighbor who has the fine estate is rich, and the coveter suspects that he cannot take it away from him because the man is powerful and able to defend himself against him. Thus he neither covets nor becomes pregnant; hoping for nothing, he does not conceive, and in his mind he is not pregnant.

But if a poor neighbor lives nearby—someone who is either in such need that he might be able to sell, or who could be oppressed and forced to sell—the eye is cast upon him. The coveter hopes that he can take either the poor neighbor’s estate or his farm, and he brings various troubles upon him. For example, he acts secretly through those who have influence, so that tax collectors either oppress the man who is already afflicted or constrain him through some public office. As a result, burdened with many debts, the unfortunate man is forced to sell the little farm from which either he himself or his children had been supported.

Driven by necessity, therefore, he comes to the man whose wickedness is pressing and afflicting him. Unaware that he is suffering this because of the other’s instigation, he says to him: “Give me, sir, I beg you, a few solidi. I am in need and pressed by a creditor.” And the other replies: “I do not have any in my hands at present.” He says that he does not have it in hand so that the man, oppressed by the false accusation, will be forced to sell.

Finally, when the poor man tells him that, because of his excessive affliction, he is being compelled to dispose of his property, the other immediately replies: “Even if I do not have my own money, I will do my best to borrow it somewhere, so that I may assist you, my friend; and if necessary, I will even sell my own silver, so that you do not suffer injustice.” When he was asking for assistance, the man had declared that he had absolutely nothing; but when the poor man said that he would sell his property, he claimed that he would assist him as a friend. Yet after bringing him to this necessity, he tells him that he must make the sale; and for the little farm for which earlier—let us suppose—he had offered perhaps one hundred solidi, once he sees the man oppressed, he is unwilling even to give half the price.

It is against such people as these, as has already been said above, that the Evangelist cries: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing.” Woe will indeed be theirs on the day of judgment, and they will not be able to escape the evil proclamation; rather, they will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink” (Matthew 25:41–42).

Here let Your Charity pay close attention. If the person who did not give away his own property is sent into the fire, where do you think the one who seized another’s property will be sent? If the person who did not clothe the naked must burn with the devil, where do you think the one who stripped another will burn?

## 3. “Woe to Those Who Are Pregnant” Is Not to Be Understood Literally

Every human being conceives: one person conceives from Christ, another from the devil. Therefore, whenever the Gospel reading is recited to you in which it says, “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing,” do not believe that this concerns women who have legitimate husbands. What evil did the woman do who conceived by her own husband? Why should it go badly for her on the day of judgment when she did what God commanded?

It is not, then, to be believed that this concerns women who conceive and give birth lawfully; rather, it concerns those whom we mentioned above, who, by unjustly coveting another’s property, appear to have become pregnant. Of such people we read: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (Psalm 7:15).

Every human being conceives, and no one can exist without conception; but some conceive from Christ, while others conceive from the devil. For just as it is said of those who conceive from the devil, “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity,” so it is written of those who conceive from the Holy Spirit: “Because of your fear we conceived in the womb, and we gave birth to the spirit of your salvation” (Isaiah 26:18).

## 4. Lift Up Your Hearts

Those who pay careful attention to what we have said, dearest brothers, and recognize that the evils described above have either been in them or perhaps still are in them, should correct themselves quickly. Past evils do not harm us if we no longer approve of them; there is still an opportunity for repentance and correction.

The separation in which some are placed at the right and others at the left has not yet occurred (Matthew 25:33); we are not yet in the underworld, where that rich man is thirsty and longing for a drop of water (Luke 16:22). Let us listen while we are alive, and let us correct ourselves. Let us not covet what belongs to others and swell with pregnancy; nor let us strive to reach those things and, once we have obtained them, kiss them as though they were children.

For when someone covets another’s property, as has already been said, his soul appears to have conceived. But if, through some trickery or wickedness, he is able to obtain what he covets, he is understood to kiss and nourish a son who has been born.

Let us not, then, love these earthly things in such a way, brothers, that we lose the heavenly ones. The heart must be changed; the heart must be lifted up; let us no longer dwell here in heart. The love of the world is a wretched region; let it be enough that we still appear to be here in the flesh. Let us hear the Apostle saying: “If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on the things that are above; seek the things that are above, not those that are on earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

What has been promised to you is not visible; it is already prepared, but it is not seen. Do you wish to become pregnant through coveting? Become pregnant here instead: covet eternal life. God invites you to that life; let it be your hope. Your delivery will be certain; there will be no miscarriage. You will not embrace temporarily what you have brought forth; you will possess it forever.

## 5. The Certainty of the Promises in Scripture

What has been promised must undoubtedly be given, but it still lies ahead: it will not be given now, but it will be given later. Consider how many things have already been given, brothers. Who is able even to count them?

Of all the things promised to us in the divine Scriptures, only one remains. Will God, who spoke truthfully about so many things, deceive us concerning one? It was written concerning the Church that it would exist, and we see that it does. It was written concerning idols that they would not exist, and we see that they do not. It was written that the Jews would lose their kingdom, and we see that they have. It was written concerning heretics that they would arise, and we see that they have.

The day of judgment has been written about; the rewards of the good and the punishment of the wicked have also been written about. Let no one deceive himself, brothers: just as all the things that were promised have come, so the day of judgment, the punishment of the wicked, and the rewards of the righteous will undoubtedly come.

Therefore, while it is permitted and while, with God’s help, it remains within our power, let each one of us strive both to avoid sins and to practice what is good. Thus, when that terrible and fearful day arrives, he will not be burned in everlasting fire with the wicked and sinners, but may deserve, together with the righteous and those who fear God, to attain the eternal reward. May he himself deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and dominion forever, etc.

# SERMON LXXVI

[Note: It was added long ago to the Caesarian Homilies in the Cologne edition of the Library of the Fathers, 1618, volume 5, part 5, page 790, and exists under the name of Caesarius in one German manuscript and another of the Carthusian monastery of Portes. On section 2, see Caesarius, Homily 13; on section 5, Homilies 35 and 18; on section 6, Homily 32.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 25:1–13: “The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” etc.

## 1. The Sleep of the Virgins Is Death. Midnight Is the Day of Judgment

In the Gospel reading that was recited to us concerning the ten virgins, dearest brothers, it was said that all the virgins trimmed their lamps, but the foolish did not have oil prepared with their lamps [Note: [Col. 1892] Thus the Carthusian manuscript of Portes: “oil prepared for the lamps.”]; the wise, however, took oil in their vessels.

While the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep. But at midnight a cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. When the lamps of the foolish virgins began to go out, they asked the others, in whose vessels there was oil, to give them some of their oil. But those others said: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.”

While they were going to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him to the wedding, and the door was shut. Later the remaining virgins came, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” They were told: “I do not know where you are from.”

When it says, “While the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep,” that sleep signifies death. Thus the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, brothers” (1 Thessalonians 4:12). Midnight, when the great cry was made, signifies the day of judgment. It is called midnight because of our ignorance [Note: [Col. 1892] The same manuscript has: “it was said at midnight”]; for no one knows when or at what hour the day of judgment will come.

## 2. Oil Means Mercy or Charity. The Obligation to Give Abundant Alms

The fact that all the virgins trimmed their lamps shows that even the foolish had some oil, but it was too little to suffice for them at all; consequently, it immediately began to go out [Note: [Col. 1892] The same manuscript has: “they trimmed their lamps; and those foolish ones,” etc.].

Therefore, dearest brothers, with God’s help we must labor as much as we can to store in the vessels of our souls as much oil as will suffice for us eternally, since oil signifies mercy or charity. Little is sufficient for no one, brothers, except perhaps the person who, because of poverty, is unable to give more.

The lamp of the soul must be full, so that through the oil of charity our light may shine forever. The person to whom God has given greater possessions should open his hands as widely as he can for almsgiving, and should not believe that a little can suffice for him. Rather, each person should consider, from the time when he began to understand, how much he owes for the things he has thought, said, or done wrongly.

Let him attend to the multitude of his sins and carefully weigh the price of each one. Let him see how much he owes for lies, oaths, perjuries, curses and slanders, drunkenness, gluttony and lust, filthy thoughts, and idle words. Let each person consider all these things and others like them, which cannot even be counted. Then he will recognize how much almsgiving he ought to practice.

Even if we give everything, unless God’s mercy outweighs it, we cannot redeem all our sins. Let us therefore do what we can with humility [Note: [Col. 1892] The same manuscript has: “with humility, with a contrite,” etc.], with a contrite and remorseful heart; and let us do it not for human praise, but because of God’s commandment and in contemplation of eternal life.

## 3. Why the Wise Virgins Were Afraid. The Poor as Merchants. Oil in the Vessels Means Good Works in the Conscience. Flatterers as Sellers of Oil

When the foolish virgins said to the wise, “Give us some of your oil,” and the others replied, “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you” [Col. 1893], I think this was said humbly [Note: [Col. 1893] The Portes manuscript has: “This was said humbly out of fear.”], because such great terror and such a strict examination will occur on the day of judgment that even those who understand themselves to have prepared an abundance of the oil of mercy will fear that it may not suffice to redeem all their sins.

What was said—“Go instead to those who sell it, and buy some for yourselves”—can be understood as referring to the poor. They are the merchants who sell the oil necessary for the lamps of souls. Through them Christ is accustomed to conduct this business. In them he receives earthly things, intending to repay eternal things. Thus he himself said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40).

The lamps signify souls. The vessels in which the oil is stored signify good consciences. What does it mean to have oil in the vessels, except to store good works within the conscience?

And because some perform good works for the love of God, while others do so out of a desire for human praise, those virgins—although they were virgins in body and exercised themselves in vigils [Note: [Col. 1893] Thus from the same manuscript: “both those who were virgins in body and those who exercised themselves in vigils,”], psalms, readings, or prayers—did all this for human praise, not for God or eternal blessedness. Therefore, when death intervened and human praise ceased for them, their oil also failed at the same time.

What was said to them—“Go instead to those who sell it, and buy some for yourselves”—can also be understood in this way: the sellers are those who praise foolish virgins with flattering compliments.
