Hence it is understood that all who desire to receive human praises for what they appear to practice in God’s work sell it through human flattery, receiving empty praise and losing eternal rewards.

But those virgins who had oil in their vessels placed every good work within their consciences, because they did it not for praise but for divine mercy.

## 4. The Practices of Virgins, So That Virginity May Not Be Fruitless

Keeping these things faithfully in mind, dearest brothers, since this parable concerns the whole Church, those who cannot preserve bodily virginity should preserve purity of heart. Thus, if they cannot attain the crown of martyrs or virgins, they may at least deserve to receive forgiveness for all sins.

But virgins who, with God’s help, preserve bodily purity should strive with all their strength and with God’s assistance to avoid excessive talk; reject slander, complaining, and murmuring as the poisons of the devil; fear the disease of envy and pride as though it were an enemy’s sword [Note: [Col. 1893] The same manuscript has: “the disease of envy or pride.” Caesarius commonly joins these two together]; preserve obedience humbly; never despise the commands of an elder; persist in reading and prayer; and, if illness does not prevent it, rise to the vigils with complete eagerness, whether in the oratory or in any other place.

They should always strive to bring from their mouths whatever pertains to obedience or humility. If they see someone sad, let them console that person; if they recognize someone as disobedient, let them not cease to correct him.

## 5. Helpers of Christ and of the Devil Are Found Everywhere. Ministers of the Devil in Monasteries

Since both good and bad are found in every profession, and since in the Church of Christ there is not only wheat but also chaff, there are also—what is worse—clerics, monks, and nuns so negligent and lukewarm that they do not, like spiritual bees, produce the sweet honey of souls. Rather, like utterly savage wasps, they strike the hearts of their brothers with the poisonous stings of their tongues.

Such people prove to be not helpers of Christ but defenders of the devil. If they happen to see a brother or sister acting proudly against an elder [Note: [Col. 1893] Thus from the same manuscript: “acting proudly against an elder.”], they do not merely try to calm the person [Note: [Col. 1893] Perhaps: “they do not merely fail to try to calm the person.”]; rather, through malicious words they strive to inflame him to even greater fury [Col. 1894], saying that this cannot and ought not to be endured any longer. They even urge him to make the elders regret having wished to admonish or correct him with paternal kindness.

But since, as we have already said, in every way of life there are not only helpers or ministers of the devil who kindle disobedience and pride through crafty whispering, but also helpers of Christ who strive through gentle exhortation and holy, salutary counsel to recall people to humility and gentleness, those who are placed in the clergy or monastery and raise themselves and others up in pride are like quivers full of the devil’s arrows: they strive to pierce the hearts of the simple and extinguish charity, humility, and gentleness in them.

## 6. Those Who Belong to Christ

But since, by God’s favor, wheat is also found amid the chaff, there are holy souls who prove to be like storehouses of Christ filled with spiritual antidotes. Whatever the others have wounded, these do not cease to heal by applying heavenly remedies.

To any proud person they say: “Do not be proud, brother, for it is written, ‘God resists the proud’” (James 4:6). “Do not be angry, for it is written, ‘Anger rests in the bosom of a fool’” (Ecclesiastes 7:10); and again, “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

If they see someone disobedient, they say gently and humbly: “Do not be disobedient, brother, for it is written, ‘Obedience is better than sacrifice’” (1 Samuel 15:22). The Apostle also cries out: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account” (Hebrews 13:17).

If these souls, full of God, see someone lukewarm and negligent, they bring forth remedies from the spiritual storehouse—that is, from a good heart—and strive to kindle him toward remorse. If they see someone slandering or murmuring, they say to him the words of the blessed Apostle: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10:10). “Do not slander, for it is written, ‘The one who slanders his brother slanders the law’” (James 4:11); and elsewhere, “The one who slanders his brother will be uprooted.” Through this holy admonition they deter him from evil speech and begin to urge him to praise God.

If they recognize someone as talkative or quarrelsome, they apply the remedy of silence, saying to him what is written in the Old Testament: “Hear, Israel, and be silent”; and what was prophesied concerning the Lord Savior: “As a lamb before its shearer, so he will be silent; and as a mute who does not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7); and also: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

With such remedies and others like them, whatever the vessels of the devil have tried to wound, the vessels of Christ strive and labor to restore to health.

Whether he is a cleric, a monk, or a nun, let each examine his conscience. If he recognizes that, by speaking well, he is a helper of Christ and a defender of righteousness [Note: [Col. 1894] The text is restored in accordance with the Portes manuscript: “For it is written, ‘The one who slanders his brother will be uprooted.’ Whoever recognizes himself, by speaking in such a way, as a helper and defender of righteousness…”], let him rejoice and give thanks to God, and, with God’s help, persevere to the end. For it is not the one who has begun but the one who has persevered to the end who will be saved (Matthew 10:22).

But whoever feels that through pride, disobedience, or envy he is a helper or deputy of the devil should grieve over the past and beware of the future. Through humility he should rebuild what he destroyed through the tyranny of pride; let gentleness calm what anger inflamed [Note: [Col. 1894] Thus corrected according to the same manuscript: “what he destroyed through the tyranny of pride, let gentleness calm.”]; let the sweetness of charity set right what malice or disobedience had embittered.

And while that dark soul, which had been accustomed to serve the devil, is still held in this mortal body, let it acquire a remedy for itself on the day of need, so that, transferred from the left to the right with Christ’s sheep, it may deserve to hear: “Come, you blessed; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Col. 1895] (Matthew 25:34).

And although these things are so, dearest brothers, it is nevertheless necessary that the good not become exalted over their holy merits, nor those who have been bad be crushed by excessive despair [Note: [Col. 1895] Thus the Portes manuscript has: “those who have been bad.”]. Rather, let the former persevere humbly in good works, and let the latter quickly correct their evil, so that when the day of judgment comes, an upright life may enable the good to be crowned and corrected conduct may be able to excuse the bad, by the granting of the Lord, etc.

# SERMON LXXVII

[Note: Elsewhere, On the Saints 38.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 25:34–43: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1895] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is among those that the Louvain editors left doubtful, while Verlinus and Vindingus declared them spurious. Two Corbie manuscripts attribute it to Caesarius, although one of them, corrected by a second hand, had previously attributed it to Augustine. On section 5, see Caesarius, Homily 24 and Homily 4 among those edited by Baluzius; on section 6, Homily 12 among the same.]

## 1. Sacred Reading Should Be Used Frequently. God Punishes Unwillingly

Just now, while the Gospel was being read, dearest brothers, we heard the Lord saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Therefore, in order that you may hear this desirable voice and escape the evil proclamation, attend with all your strength, with God’s help, and gladly and obediently arrange for this divine reading to be read and heard frequently in your homes or in the church.

For just as that voice is desirable by which the merciful are told, “Come, you blessed; receive the kingdom,” so, by contrast, the voice that the wicked and unmerciful will hear is dreadful and greatly to be feared: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.”

May God turn this away from us, dearest brothers, and deign to free us from the evil proclamation, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “The righteous will be held in everlasting remembrance; he will not fear an evil report” (Psalm 111:7). For this will be the evil proclamation that the wicked will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.”

The sentence will be irrevocable. The most merciful God proclaims it long beforehand for this reason: so that we may guard ourselves from it with all our strength. If our God wished to punish us, he would not warn us beforehand through so many ages. In a certain sense he punishes unwillingly, since he shows long beforehand how we may escape. For he does not wish to strike you who cries out to you, “Take heed.”

## 2. Heaven Predestined for Us, Not Gehenna

Consider, nevertheless, what he will say to those placed at the right: “Come,” he says, “you blessed; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Pay attention, dearest brothers: the kingdom of heaven has been predestined for us, whereas Gehenna was prepared not for us but for the devil. Thus those placed at the left will hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared.” He did not say, “for you,” but “for the devil and his angels.”

## 3. The Necessity of Giving Alms

I ask you, brothers, to attend faithfully and carefully both to the sentence that the wicked will hear and to the one that the saints will hear.

“Come,” he says, “you blessed; receive the kingdom.” Why? “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth.

But to the sinners he says: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food.”

Therefore, those who will be at the right will not receive the kingdom because they never sinned, but because they strove to cleanse their sins through almsgiving. And those who will be at the left will not be sent into the eternal fire because they were sinners, but because they were unwilling to redeem their sins through almsgiving.

Thus generosity alone will glorify the former, and barrenness alone will condemn the latter. For just as it is impossible for any human being to exist without sin, so, through God’s mercy, it is possible for each person to redeem himself from sin through good works, especially almsgiving.

Thus what is written will not be fulfilled in him: “Judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13). Rather, the sentence will apply to him: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7); and: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Psalm 111:9).

## 4. Barrenness Alone Is Responsible for Condemnation. Who Do Not Come to Judgment

Consider this also, brothers: for what reason will they be sent into the eternal fire? They will not be told, “Because you committed murder, because you committed adultery, because you seized another’s property.” Rather, this alone will they hear: “Because I was hungry, and you did not give me food.”

I ask you, dearest brothers, do not think about these matters superficially [nor believe that this was said only concerning Jews, pagans, or heretics; but believe with complete certainty [Note: [Col. 1896] The manuscripts omit the words placed in brackets, which nevertheless are not at all unlike Caesarius’s style; the expression “believe with complete certainty” occurs frequently among his other expressions.], because Christians and Catholics who wish to persist in evil works will hear this].

Pagans, heretics, and Jews do not come to judgment, for it is written concerning them: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Therefore, among those who will be sent to the left there will be not only laypeople, but also many bishops—what is worse—bad clerics, greedy or proud monks, as well as angry, proud, or greedy nuns. Unless fruitful repentance comes to their aid, they will hear that fearful and irrevocable voice: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.”]

This sentence, if we are willing to hear it faithfully and with immense trembling, will be able to turn us back from every evil work.

## 5. The Torments of Robbers; Those of Evil Doers

Pay careful attention, therefore, to what the Truth said: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire; for I was hungry, and you did not give me food.”

If the person who did not give his bread to the hungry is sent into the fire, where do you think the one who took what belonged to another will be sent? If the person who did not clothe the naked is sent into the fire, where will the person who stripped the clothed be sent? If the person who did not offer his house to guests is condemned to burn with the devil, where do you think the person who took another’s house will be sent? If the person who did not visit someone in prison will perish [Note: [Col. 1896] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have: “If the person who did not visit the prison will perish.” M.], what will happen to the one who perhaps unjustly sent someone to prison?

I ask you, brothers, pay attention here. What hope can those who do evil have, when those who do not do good will perish?

Finally, in another place the Lord solemnly warns us, saying: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7:19). He did not say, “the tree that produces bad fruit,” but “the tree that does not produce good fruit.”

From this we can clearly recognize what punishments the thorny tree will suffer on the day of judgment, when the tree that has not produced fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

## 6. Faith Without Works Profits a Christian Nothing

Let no one deceive himself, dearest brothers; let no one mislead himself with a false hope. The dignity of bearing the Christian name alone does not make someone a Christian. It profits nothing that someone is called a Christian by name if he does not demonstrate this in his conduct.

For it is written: “Faith without works is dead.” To the one who believes but does not practice good works, the divine Scripture cries out: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and they tremble” (James 2:17, 19).

Thus those who believe but do not do good works appear to possess the faith of demons. Those who do not believe are proved to be worse than demons.

This too must be considered carefully: the Lord says, “The one who hears my words and does them is the one who loves me”; and again, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments” (John 14:21, 23). Without doubt, the one who does not keep them does not love him.

We must also greatly fear what the Lord says again: “What benefit is it that you say, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Matthew 7:21; Luke 6:46).

We must know, dearest brothers [Col. 1897], that it profits nothing to profess faith with words [Note: [Col. 1897] The word “faith” is absent from the manuscripts] and abandon the truth in deeds.

For just as we are not pleased when our servants profess in words that they belong to us, yet are unwilling to perform their duties, so God is not pleased when someone declares himself a Christian in words alone and neglects to fulfill the works that Christ commanded.

Finally, when the blessed Apostle was speaking about rendering an account on the day of judgment, he declared: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then he will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

He did not say, “according to his faith,” but “to each according to his works,” because, as I have already said above, the Apostle James cries out: “Faith without works is dead.”

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to escape punishment and attain eternal blessedness, let us not merely believe in God, but also love him with our whole heart. And, as far as we can, with his help, let us strive to do good works, so that, when with his assistance we have done what he commanded, by his rewarding we may deserve to receive what he promises.

This is through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one God in the Trinity, living and reigning forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1897] Manuscript cl. has: “may we deserve to receive what he promises, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”]

# SERMON LXXVIII

[Note: The Vatican and Remigius manuscripts give the name of Augustine in the title. But in the Library of the Fathers it is the thirty-ninth homily of Caesarius, and more probably so, in our judgment, although the sermon there was printed more corruptly in other respects and appears somewhat different from the manuscripts mentioned above, which we have followed. On section 1, see Caesarius, Homily 4; on section 3, Homily 24; on section 5, Homilies 2 and 22; on section 6, Homily 22.]

Again on Matthew 25:34–43, “Come, you blessed of my Father,” etc., an exhortation to give alms.

## 1. The Force of This Reading

When the Gospel was being read, we heard a terrible voice, the sentence of our Lord, at once fearful and desirable. It is terrible because of what he says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.” It is desirable because of what he says: “Come, you blessed; receive the kingdom.”

For who, on hearing this voice, would not tremble and rejoice at the same time? Let him rejoice because Christ has deigned to promise the kingdom to his Christian servants; let him tremble because he threatens sinners with eternal fire.

I ask you, brothers, always to hear this reading with attentive hearts and the most vigilant understanding. Since it is not burdensome to prepare for, keep it always in memory and continually reflect upon its power.

For the person who attends carefully to this reading—even if he has not been able to read the rest of the Scriptures—can find in this reading alone enough to lead him to perform every good work and flee every evil.

## 2. The Basis of Salvation or Condemnation

Pay attention, therefore, brothers, and see what Christ promises to say to those who will be at the right: “Come,” he says, “you blessed; receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink,” and the other things that follow.

But what will he say to those who will be at the left? “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” and the rest.

Pay attention, therefore, brothers, and see that he did not say, “Depart from me, you accursed, because you committed theft, because you gave false testimony, because you committed murder or adultery,” which are unquestionably more serious [Col. 1898]. He did not say this. Rather, he said: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink.”

He did not say, “Because you took what belonged to others,” which is more unjust; rather, he said: “You did not give the poor from your possessions.” He did not say, “Because you did evil works,” but “Because you were unwilling to do good.”

Thus mercy alone will free those who will be at the right, and avarice alone will condemn those who are at the left.

What was said to those at the right—“Come, you blessed; receive the kingdom”—will not be heard by them because they did not sin. Nor will he say to those at the left, “Depart from me, you accursed, because you sinned,” but because you were unwilling to redeem your sins through almsgiving.

No human being can exist without sin; nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, every human being can redeem his sins through almsgiving.

## 3. How Great Will Be the Punishment of Evil Doers

In this sentence of the Lord, in which he said that the one who does not feed the hungry and clothe the naked will be sent into the eternal fire, we can clearly recognize what sort of torment and punishment await those who do evil, since those who do not do good are sent into the fire.

If the one who did not give his bread to the poor is condemned with the devil, where will the one who took what belonged to another be condemned? If the one who did not clothe the naked is sent into the fire, where do you think the one who stripped the clothed will be sent? If the one who did not welcome a stranger into his house is condemned to hell, where do you think the one who took another’s house will be sent?

## 4. Exhortation to Good Works

Therefore, dearest brothers, thinking faithfully on these things, let us strive, as far as we can, to perform good works, and according to our means let us distribute from our little resources to strangers and the poor, so that we may both redeem the sins we have committed and prepare eternal rewards for ourselves through those very good works.

Let us hear the Lord saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). For you have heard the true sentence of our Lord, by which the kingdom of heaven is promised to us if we give alms, if we feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked according to our means, and welcome strangers. If we faithfully do all these things, we shall come confidently before the tribunal of the eternal Judge; and then we shall be among the righteous in everlasting remembrance, and we shall not fear the report of evil (Psalm 111:7). What is this “report of evil” except that which—may the Lord deign to avert it from us—the wicked placed on the left will hear: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire”?

## 5. Praise of Almsgiving

Therefore, brothers, hold fast to almsgiving or mercy, because almsgiving delivers from death and does not allow its worker to go into darkness. Let each person, according to his means and as much as he is able, extend his hand to the poor. Whoever has gold, let him give gold; whoever has silver, let him give silver. But whoever has no money should offer the stranger a morsel with a good disposition; and if he does not have a whole loaf, let him break off and give some of what he has.

For the Lord deigned, through the prophet, to offer the poor such consolation and assurance that he did not say, “Give all your bread to the hungry,” but rather, “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58:7); and if you do not have a whole loaf, at least share some small portion.

## 6. Giving with a Joyful Spirit. The Giver Gains

And so that you may know how acceptable to God is whatever you offer with a good disposition, hear the Lord in the Gospel speaking about that widow who offered two coins: “This widow has put in more than all the others, because the others who were rich gave something from what they had in abundance, but she offered all that she had” (Luke 21:3–4). Therefore she deserved that the Lord himself should praise her with his own mouth.

Let each person, then, do what he is able; and, except for reasonable food and simple clothing, let him joyfully and cheerfully give to the poor whatever remains for him. Why joyfully and cheerfully? Because he gives little and receives much; he offers a coin and acquires a kingdom; he gives a small sum of money and receives eternal life. He gives temporal things [Col. 1899] in order to merit eternal ones; he offers things that perish and receives what will endure without end.

See, then, why we ought to give with a joyful and good disposition. If a faithful human being were to say to you, “Give me one gold coin, and I will repay you one hundred solidi,” would you not gladly give one in order to receive a hundred? How much more, since the God of heaven and earth says to you, “Whoever gives to the poor lends to God” (Proverbs 19:17); and, “As long as you did it to one of these my least brothers, you did it to me”; and in the Psalm, “The good man is gracious and lends” (Psalm 111:5). You ought to lend to God on earth, so that you may receive many times over in eternal life.

Then, when you have deserved to come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge in the presence of the angels, you may say with a confident and free conscience: “Give, Lord, because I gave; have mercy, because I showed mercy. I fulfilled what you commanded; repay what you promised.”

Again and again I admonish you, brothers, always to keep this Gospel reading in your memory and to labor with all your strength, with God’s help, so that you may escape the eternal fire and happily reach the kingdom of heaven; through him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1899] Elsewhere, *On Time* 124.]

On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 26:31–35, 69–75: “You will all be scandalized,” etc.; concerning Peter’s fall.

[Note: [Col. 1899] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered its authenticity doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. Its style truly does not resemble Augustine.]

## 1. Man without God’s Grace. Why God Withdrew His Support from Peter

In the Gospel reading recited to us yesterday, dearest brothers, we heard the Lord say to his disciples: “You will all be scandalized because of me this night.” Blessed Peter said to him: “Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized.” But the Lord, who examines the heart, answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” He, however, said: “Even if I must die for you, I will not deny you.”

Observe, dearest brothers: the true and heavenly physician had examined the vein of the heart and had foretold at what moment the weight of temptation or the chill of unbelief would come. The physician foretold it, and the sick man denied it; but when the moment arrived, what the man had promised proved false, while what God had foretold appeared true.

For what man can do without God’s grace is clearly shown by the fear of blessed Peter the apostle. Relying on free will alone, without the addition of God’s help, he had promised that he would die for the Lord. But what is a human being without God’s grace except what Peter was when he denied Christ, and what the prophet said: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6)?

Therefore the Lord allowed blessed Peter to fall for a little while, so that in him the whole human race might recognize that it can accomplish nothing without God’s grace, and so that a certain rule might be established for the future ruler of the Church concerning forgiveness toward sinners.

## 2. Peter Naturally More Severe

The keys of the Church were to be entrusted to the apostle Peter—indeed, the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to him. An innumerable multitude of peoples was also to be entrusted to him, a multitude entangled, because of the defects of its nature, in passions, faults, and sins.

Thus the Savior says to him: “To you,” he says, “I have given the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Then he continues: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19), so that in the keys he might be a faithful doorkeeper, and in his judgments a most merciful steward.

For this Peter was in truth somewhat hard and severe, as is shown by the ear of the high priest’s servant, cut off because of the injury done to Christ, revealing his harshness. If, therefore, one so hard and severe had obtained from the Lord the gift of not sinning, what forgiveness would he grant to the peoples entrusted to him?

For this reason divine providence arranged and permitted the matter in this way: Peter himself should first slip and fall into sin, so that, by considering his own fall, he might temper a harsher judgment toward sinners. [Col. 1900] Consider, therefore, how much divine generosity, how much care and solicitude, are expended for the salvation of human beings. He cures the illness of the whole body in the very head of the Church and restores the health of all its members in the very summit—in that foundation of the confession of Christ, in that immovable foundation of faith, namely in that Peter who had said, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”

## 3. Peter’s Fall and Repentance

This is Peter, who by divine revelation was the first of all to deserve to confess the truth, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matthew 16:16). So great and such a man came to that night on which the Lord was being handed over. When he wished to warm himself by the coals, a girl approached him and said: “You too were with this man yesterday.”

He immediately replied: “I do not know the man.”

What are you doing, Peter, future ruler of the Church? What are you saying? Consider what you were asked, and what you answered the one who asked you. Your voice has suddenly changed. Is this the whole of what you had quickly, though not cautiously, promised? Is this all that you had sworn you would maintain even if everyone denied you, even unto death?

No one had yet tested or examined your faith; no adversary had yet dragged you before the public because of your denial of Christ; you had not yet been brought before kings and governors because of his name. No whips had been applied to you; no tortures.

Who, then, is questioning you, whom you denied so quickly? It is not a servant, not a free man, not a Pharisee, not a scribe, not a priest, not a soldier, not a centurion, not an executioner—in short, no one who by his authority could instill fear in someone making a confession. A woman questions you in a simple voice, and perhaps would not even have betrayed the person she had heard confessing. Indeed, she is not merely a woman but a girl; and not merely a girl but a doorkeeper, plainly a lowly and despised slave.

O astonishing event! A girl approached and shook Peter’s faith. And is it surprising that Peter’s solidity was pierced not by a whirlwind or a rainstorm but by the lightest drop of dew? Peter did not endure the girl’s words [Note: [Col. 1900] Perhaps, “endured.”]; but when she spoke, he was disturbed. The girl’s speech went forth, and the immovable pillar was shaken.

Nevertheless, she persisted in questioning him and said: “You too were with this man yesterday.” But Peter, overcome all the more by fear, denied that he knew the man. Christ looked at him and made him remember his words. Understanding what had happened, he turned to repentance and wept most bitterly. For he recognized that, as a human being, the destruction of sin had crept into him. Everything that followed was, as I recall, arranged by divine providence.

## 4. Peter’s Fall Permitted for Our Sake

Observe, therefore, dearest brothers, how so great an apostle is permitted to fall under a small fault, so that, corrected and cured of the vice of arrogance, he may be clothed in the complete garment of moderation and mercy.

You have now been instructed and taught in Peter how the Lord, for your sake, allowed him to be circumscribed by sin; how he permitted the standard-bearer of faith and devotion, the pillar of the human race, to be shaken by the domination of fear, so that he might be an example to teachers and instructors of peoples: God has not granted them the grace of not sinning, as the apostle Paul says, “Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

When someone in the Church has been overtaken by a fault, therefore, let no one immediately cast him away or condemn him; rather, let him sympathize and grieve, console and recall him, offer affection to the one lying fallen, extend a hand, raise up the one who has fallen, and promise him hope in divine mercy—under which even this service is shown to be sanctioned by the example of such great teachers.

We have said these things, as we mentioned above, not to blame the righteous but to raise sinners toward hope. First, indeed, we praised Peter’s virtues, so that we might show the righteous a model of caution and sinners an example of salvation.

# SERMON LXXX

[Note: [Col. 1901] Formerly *On Time* 128, and later Appendix 48.]

On Matthew, chapter 27:3–10: concerning Judas the betrayer and the field purchased for the burial of strangers from the price of Christ’s sale.

[Note: [Col. 1901] Long ago restored to its true author, Maximus, bishop of Turin, whose name it bears in manuscripts and printed books.]

[Col. 1901]

## 1. Judas, the Most Severe Judge of Himself

You remember, brothers, that we preached to you last Sunday [Note: [Col. 1901] The words “last Sunday” are absent from the manuscripts; the printed editions also omit the particle “now.”] that Judas Iscariot, condemned by his own judgment, brought to the Pharisees the price of the Lord’s blood and, moved to repentance, returned the price of the sale; but he did not undo the crime from his conscience.

Finally, after returning the money, he hanged himself, so that the man who had punished himself with money might also punish himself with his life. [Note: [Col. 1901] In manuscripts n. and cl.: “so that the man who had changed himself through money might also change his life.”]

For, understanding how great a crime he had committed, it was not enough for him to be without the profit of sacrilege unless he was also without salvation. He judged himself worthy of death because he had handed over Christ, the life of all.

Judas, therefore, the most severe judge of himself, confesses in avenging himself against the one whom he had denied in handing him over. He returned the money to the Pharisees, but the Pharisees did not willingly accept it either; for they said that it was unlawful for them to keep it in their treasuries.

See, then, how great is the power of the Lord’s money: Judas rejects it on one side, while the Pharisees on the other do not put it into their purses. Iniquity fears possessing the price of righteous blood.

## 2. God’s Providence in the Use of the Price of Christ. The Potter’s Field, the World

Nevertheless, the Pharisees reach the decision that a potter’s field should be purchased with it, in which the bodies of strangers might be placed.

I believe this happened by God’s providence, so that the Savior’s price might not provide resources for sinners but supply rest for strangers; might not serve sacrilegious people for luxury but serve the dead as a burial place; so that from then on Christ might redeem the living through the passion of his blood and receive the dead through a precious possession. [Note: [Col. 1901] In Saint Maximus: “receive the dead through a precious passion.” In one manuscript: “offer a precious passion to the dead,” and so forth.]

Thus the potter’s field is purchased with the price of the Lord’s blood. We read in Scripture that the salvation of the entire human race was redeemed by the Savior’s blood, as the apostle Peter says: “Knowing that you were not redeemed from your vain manner of life inherited from your fathers with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, as of an immaculate and undefiled lamb” (1 Peter 1:18–19). [Note: [Col. 1901] So the printed editions. In Maximus: “For you were not redeemed with perishable gold or silver, but with precious …” The manuscripts, however, read: “For you were not redeemed with gold or silver,” and the rest.]

Therefore, if the Lord’s blood is the price of our life, see that what was redeemed was not so much the earthly fragility of a field as the eternal safety of the whole world. For the evangelist says: “Christ did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17).

Consider, I say, whether not so much a small portion of a field was purchased with that money as the abundant possession of the whole world, as the prophet David says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

This field, therefore, is the whole world, in which we, scattered and sown, produce for the Lord the fruit of good works. [Note: [Col. 1901] Ambrose has similar material in chapter 22 of his exposition of Luke.]

## 3. The Potter, Lord of the World

But perhaps you will ask me: if the field is the world, who is the potter who can possess dominion over the world?

Unless I am mistaken, he is the potter who made the vessels of our bodies from clay, of whom Scripture says: “And God made the human being from the clay of the earth” (Genesis 2:7). He is the potter who animated the muddy clay of our flesh with the breath of his spirit and baked our fluid, earthly material with fiery heat.

He, I say, is the potter who formed us by his hands for life and reformed us through his Christ for glory, as the apostle says: “We are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). That is, although we fell from our first formation through our own faults, in a second birth we are restored by the mercy of this potter; that is, although we fell into death through Adam’s transgression, through the Savior’s grace we rise again.

He is plainly the potter of whom the apostle says: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” And again: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20–21).

For from the same clay of our bodies God nevertheless, according to the merits of each person, preserves some for the kingdom and reserves others for punishment.

## 4. Strangers, Devoted Christians. Christ Is Their Burial

The field of this potter, therefore, was purchased with Christ’s blood for strangers—strangers, I say, who were without a home, without a fatherland, and scattered as exiles throughout the whole world. Rest is provided for them through Christ’s blood, so that those who have no possession in the world may have burial in Christ.

But whom do we say these strangers are, except the most devoted Christians, who renounce the world, possess nothing in the world, and rest in Christ’s blood? For the Christian who does not possess the world possesses the Savior in his entirety.

Burial in Christ is promised to strangers for this reason: whoever guards himself from carnal vices as a stranger and outsider will merit Christ’s rest. For what else is Christ’s burial except the Christian’s rest?

We, therefore, are strangers in this world and live in this light as though we were guests, as the apostle says: “For while we are in the body, we are strangers from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

We are strangers, I say, and a burial place has been purchased for us at the price of the Savior’s blood. [Note: [Col. 1902] We have taken the words “at the price of the blood” from Maximus’s edition, since they are absent from the other printed editions and from our manuscripts.]

“For we were buried with him,” as the apostle says, “through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4). Baptism, therefore, is Christ’s burial for us. In it we die to sins, are buried with respect to crimes, and, with the conscience of the old person dissolved, are restored in a reborn infancy to another birth.

Baptism, I say, is the Savior’s burial for us, because there we lose what we previously lived, and there we receive anew the means of living. Great, therefore, is the grace of this burial, in which both a beneficial death is inflicted upon us and a more beneficial life is granted. [Note: [Col. 1902] So manuscript cb. Others read, “is bestowed.”] Great, I say, is the grace of this burial, which both purifies the sinner and gives life to the dying, with the help of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXXI

[Note: [Col. 1902] Elsewhere *On Time* 209.]

On the words of the Gospel of Mark, chapter 8:1–9: “When there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1902] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. Among works associated with Augustine it had been left as doubtful by the Louvain editors without Augustine’s name. It was later rightly rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus, who observed that the error of Eutyches condemned here began to arise somewhat after Augustine’s death. The author took the beginning of chapters 1 and 2 from Augustine’s Sermon 252, which begins: “In many and various ways, and the height of his divinity,” etc.]

## 1. Christ’s Divinity and Humanity Shine Forth in Many Ways. The Error of Eutyches Refuted

Our Lord Jesus Christ displayed the height of his divinity and the mercy of his humanity in many and various ways in the holy Scriptures, as he is accustomed to do in mysteries and sacraments, so that those who ask may receive, those who seek may find, and to those who knock it may be opened.

For all the miracles that he displayed in this world amid our frailty benefit us. The Lord did not perform them without reason, as though uselessly and in vain. Christ is the Word of God, who speaks to human beings not only through sounds but also through deeds. This too, then, which has been read today from the holy Gospel, seeks an interpreter; and when it has been understood, it produces spiritual joy.

In this reading, too, we must consider together, in our one and the same Redeemer, the distinct operation of divinity and humanity, as well as the utterly detestable error of Eutyches, who presumes to teach that there is only one operation in Christ.

For if someone asserts one side or the other—either that Christ was only human, or that he was only God—he will deny either the glory of the Creator or the mercy of the Redeemer. When the Lord takes pity on the crowd, lest it fail either from hunger or from the labor of a long journey, we recognize in this the feeling and compassion of human frailty. But when he fed four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish, we believe this to be the work of divine power.

## 2. The Crowds, the Nations. The Food of Which They Lacked: the Law of Moses

Let Your Holiness attend, therefore, because this is what has been set before us for discussion with your charity: what is the meaning of so great a mystery in this event, in which holy Scripture testifies that God showed himself to his disciples in the manner narrated by the Gospel?

For the evangelist says in today’s reading: “When there was a great crowd with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat, he summoned his disciples and said to them: ‘I have compassion on this crowd.’”

But let us examine what is said above: “In those days, when there was a great crowd.” Earlier, the Jews had approached the Savior, accusing his disciples because they ate without washing their hands. The Lord rebuked them, because the things that proceed from the heart are what defile a person.

After leaving them, he came into the territory of the Gentiles, where the Canaanite woman, who is the mother of the Gentiles, pleaded with the Lord for her daughter—that is, for the Church. She persisted in asking until she received what she sought. After this he again healed a man who was mute and deaf (Mark 7).

Therefore, in those days, when a multitude of people had gathered and they had nothing to eat—for here we understand the crowds to signify all the Gentile peoples, for whom the Lord himself is moved with compassion because they had nothing to eat—we must understand this spiritually. They had nothing to eat for this reason: the Gentiles did not possess the Law, that is, the five books of Moses; nor the Prophets; nor the preaching of Saint John. For the Gentiles came to the Redeemer not through the Law but through faith.

Therefore they persevere for three days—that is, in the Lord’s birth, passion, and resurrection; or in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. To persevere means to remain in confession, as the Lord himself says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

The Lord therefore says: “They have nothing to eat,” because they do not have the Law; and, “I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way,” so that those who have believed through the faith of Christ might be saved through the faith of Christ.

Some of them, however, came from far away. The Gentiles were far from God, wandering among idols. And now everyone who sins is far from God.

## 3. The Unbelieving Apostles, until the Mysteries Were Revealed

His disciples say: “Where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?” The Apostles were still held by unbelief until the mysteries were revealed; they did not remember what he had done with the five loaves and two fish.

And Jesus asked them how many loaves they had. They said: “Seven.” He commanded the crowd to sit down on the ground. Taking the loaves, he gave thanks and gave them to his disciples to distribute. He likewise blessed the fish and set them before the people.

They ate and were satisfied, and they collected seven baskets full. Those who ate numbered about four thousand, apart from women and children.

We most certainly believe that the Lord’s miracles were performed in the present event; but, with his grace granting it, let us seek what lies hidden in the mystery.

## 4. Comparison of the Two Multiplications of the Loaves. The First Represents the Jews, the Second the Gentiles

In the preceding reading, he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves and two fish; here he satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves. [Col. 1904]

There the disciples advise the Lord, saying: “The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed; dismiss the crowds, so that they may go to the villages and buy food for themselves” (Mark 6:31–44). Here the disciples are completely silent; the Lord himself is concerned for them.

Let us see why they are silent. Because they had not yet been sent to preach to the Gentiles, but rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

The first parable, therefore, pertains to the Jews; this one to the Gentiles. There were five loaves, that is, the five books of Moses; here there are seven loaves, which are the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, as the holy prophet Isaiah says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:2–3).

There, twelve baskets are filled with the Holy Spirit; here, seven churches, or seven golden lampstands.

There, there are two fish, which are the two Testaments, or the one book of all the Prophets, or [Note: [Col. 1904] Perhaps, “and.”] the preaching of Saint John; here, an indefinite number is given, signifying the gifts of graces, as the apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8–11).

There they recline upon grass; here, upon the earth. In both places there is one way of life, one grace, one power, one divinity.

There they recline upon grass, that is, upon the works of the flesh that have been put to death, because the prophet says, “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6). Here they recline upon the earth, that is, they trample upon earthly works.

There, five thousand are fed—a number that pertains to the Jews; for after the Lord’s ascension, when Saint Peter was speaking, five thousand were baptized (Acts 4:4). Here, however, there are four thousand, that is, all the Gentiles from the whole earth, from the four quarters of heaven, are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit for eternal life.

## 5. Exhortation

Therefore, beloved, we who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ not through the Law but through faith; who have been redeemed not from works but by grace itself; who have been filled not from five loaves—that is, from the five books of Moses—but from the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, as blessed Isaiah had prophesied, saying, “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him”—

Let us remain in this sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, in which we have been called and filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of that same Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXXII

[Note: [Col. 1904] Formerly *On the Words of the Lord* 19, and later Appendix 3.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 3:12–14: “Tax collectors also came to John,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1904] The Louvain editors rejected it long ago, observing that it belonged to Maximus the bishop and was found among the works of Ambrose. In many manuscripts it is consistently attributed to Augustine. Certainly it does not belong to Augustine, but perhaps it does not belong to Maximus either.]

## 1. No Condition Excuses the Sinner. Pay. The Christian’s First Service

Some brothers who are either bound by the soldier’s belt or employed in public office, when they commit serious sins, customarily excuse themselves at the outset by saying that they are soldiers; and, to prevent themselves from ever doing good, they complain that they are occupied with evil activities—as though it were military service rather than the will of human beings that was at fault. Thus they attribute to their offices what they themselves do.

For serving as a soldier is not a crime; but serving as a soldier for the sake of plunder is a sin. Nor is holding public office criminal; but acting in public office in order to increase one’s private wealth appears condemnable.

For this reason, pay was established for those serving in the army by a certain providence, lest, while expenses were being sought, the robber might run rampant.

But what of this? When they are reproved by their superiors for some error, and one of them is asked why he was drunk, why he seized another person’s property, or why, in his disorder, he committed murder, he immediately replies: “What was I supposed to do? I am a secular man and a soldier. Have I professed to be a monk or a cleric?”

As though everyone who is not a cleric or a monk might be permitted to do what is not permitted.

Therefore, sacred Scripture prescribes a norm of life for every office, and every sex, age, and rank is summoned to live well. Let no one, then, excuse himself on the basis of public duties; let no one complain about the occupation of military service. Among all Christians, the first service ought to be the service of uprightness.

## 2. Just Taxes. Public Robbers

To confirm what we are saying by evangelical authority, let us consider the reading that was just recited. The Gospel says: “Tax collectors also came to John to be baptized by him, and they said to him: ‘Teacher, what shall we do?’ He said to them: ‘Exact nothing beyond what has been appointed for you.’”

A thoroughly honorable question from the tax collectors, and a just response from the holy prophet. They ask carefully so that, either by exacting more through ignorance they may fall into sin, or by ceasing to perform their public function they may deceive the public. He commands moderately, so that injustice may have no place and the appointed tax may be collected.

For he did not say, “Exact nothing,” but “Exact nothing beyond what has been appointed.” From this we understand that before God it is not exacting itself but unjust exaction that is condemned. The Lord himself says: “Give to God what belongs to God, and to Caesar what belongs to Caesar” (Matthew 22:21).

Therefore what Caesar commands must be borne; what the emperor imposes must be tolerated. But it becomes intolerable when plunder is added to the exaction.

What of this, however: those very people who administer such necessities double their sins by their sins? They call their frauds and robberies “profit,” although the plunder itself produces loss. They add this to their crimes: they persecute precisely those whom they see to be defenseless. They think they have deceived public necessities unless they have deceived the homes of orphans.

Thus the children of one whose father perhaps only two days before had been their friend, colleague, or brother are, after death intervenes, treated as though they were unknown, worthless, and miserable.

If there is a widow, she is either harassed by such injuries that she remarries, or, if she wishes to persevere in her resolve of chastity, she can scarcely maintain herself by giving gifts.

After filling their purses with these frauds, you may see them hurrying happily and carefully to church and giving thanks to God, as though this money had been granted to them by him. They commit this further sin: they want God to share in their plunder.

## 3. The Name “Soldiers” Extends to More People

The holy Gospel says: “The soldiers also questioned him: ‘And what shall we do?’ John said to them: ‘Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages.’”

Here every person who serves should recognize himself. For Scripture is not speaking only about those soldiers who are engaged in armed service. Anyone who uses the belt of his office is reckoned a soldier of his rank. Therefore this sentence can be applied, for example, to soldiers, protectors, and all governors.

Whoever receives wages publicly assigned to him, if he seeks more, is condemned by John’s sentence as a slanderer and extortioner. This evil has become so deeply rooted that now, as though by custom, laws are sold, rights are corrupted, judgment itself is for sale, and no case can any longer exist without a case being manufactured.

## 4. Clerics as Soldiers. Their Belt. Their Pay. A Cleric Who Is No Cleric

This divine sentence, which addresses soldiers, can also be applied to clerics. For even if we do not appear to serve the world as soldiers, we nevertheless serve God and the Lord, as the apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2:4).

I say that we do not appear to serve as soldiers in loose and flowing tunics; but we have the belt of our service, by which we bind the inner parts of chastity. Concerning this belt the Lord says to his apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). [Col. 1906]

We are therefore soldiers of Christ, and we have received from him pay and a gift, [Note: [Col. 1906] So the printed editions. The manuscripts read: “and we receive a gift.”] as blessed Paul the apostle says: “He gave us the pledge of the Spirit”—that is, he enriched us with the reward of the Holy Spirit.

If, then, any Christian is not content with this gift and seeks more, he begins to lose the very thing he has earned. This applies especially to the Arian heretics: while they seek I know not what more, they found the spirit of error and lost the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The Catholic cleric, too, is held by this sentence. If he is not content with the wages that, at the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but conducts business, sells intercessions, and willingly accepts gifts from widows, he may be seen more as a merchant than as a cleric.

Nor can we say, “No one accuses us of seizing things; no one accuses us of violence,” as though at times flattering words did not extract a greater plunder from widows than tortures. Before God it makes no difference whether someone takes possession of another’s property by force or by deception, provided that he holds what belongs to another by some means or other.

# SERMON LXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1906] Elsewhere, 14 among the Vignerian sermons.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 7:36–50: “A woman who was a sinner in the city came.”

[Note: [Col. 1906] Found in four manuscripts: the Royal manuscript attributes it to Augustine; two Corbie manuscripts attribute it to Caesarius; the Navarre manuscript contains it without the name of an author.]

## 1. Everyone Must Do Penance; Who Especially Should Fast

The days of fasting, dearest brothers, the days of supplication—or, to put it more plainly, the season of penance—have now come upon us. We must all do penance, because we have all gone astray. For if, according to the testimony of Scripture, not even an infant of one day is clean (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint), who would dare claim to be free from guilt and reject the remedies of penance, when he understands that they have benefited even the saints?

The days of fasting are days of reconciliation. For through food we fell into Adam’s sin, and through fasting we were reconciled to God in Christ, as the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). God requires fasting from us so that the snare of the appetite [Note: [Col. 1906] In manuscript cb., “the place of the appetite,” erroneously. Better in n., “the knot of the appetite.”], by which Adam was strangled, may be undone; and he wishes us to abstain not only from foods, but also from vices and wickedness. Thus the Lord cries out through the prophet, saying: “Cease from your evils [Note: [Col. 1906] So the r. codex. But manuscripts cb. here and a little above have, “Cease from your evil deeds”; n. has, “Depart from your wickedness.” The Septuagint, “Rest from your wickedness.”]; learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16–17).

For what benefit is it to abstain from meat while refusing to lay aside carnal deeds, since the Lord Jesus says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matt. 15:11)? For this reason God rejected the fasts of the Jews, because they said that one should abstain from foods, not from sins. Hence he rebukes them, saying: “For on the days of your fasts your own desires are found, and you exact payment from all your debtors” (Isa. 58:3).

Let this be far from the Christian people, who during the time of fasting know nothing else but mercy, by which they themselves have been saved. And therefore, since the season of fasting is at hand, let us approach the Lord’s table and be refreshed by Christ’s banquet, so that, like Elijah, we may be able to endure prolonged fasts in the strength of that food.

## 2. The Sinful Woman Is the Church

You heard in the Gospel that, while the Lord was reclining in the house of the Pharisee, “a woman who was a sinner in the city came, bringing with her an alabaster jar of ointment; and standing behind him at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, and anointed them with ointment.”

This is no insignificant mystery. We see that in the house of the Pharisee—that is, in the Synagogue—the Lord was reclining [Col. 1907], not resting. But how could he rest in the Synagogue, where he could not find anyone humble and peaceful upon whom he might rest?

Behold the sinful woman. Who is this woman except the Church from the Gentiles, which was sinful as long as the forgiveness of sins had not yet come? But when the Lord came, she approached baptism and became without stain or wrinkle. For by following the immaculate Lamb, she laid aside all the stains of sins.

The sinful woman approached the feet of Christ. The sinner approaches the feet; the righteous approaches the head. The sinner washes the Lord’s feet with tears; the righteous pours precious ointment over his whole body.

But the Pharisee, ignorant of the mystery, said within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him.” This unbeliever wrongly supposed that the Lord ought to drive sinners away from himself. But since he had come not to call the righteous but sinners, how could he avoid the company of sinners? He is not defiled by sinners who cleanses sinners by the touch of his body. The eternal fountain cannot be polluted, but by its overflowing it washes everyone.

## 3. Christ’s Mouth, Hands, Shoulders, and Feet

Therefore, turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she has bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not give me a kiss, but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet. Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she has loved much.”

When the Lord entered the Pharisee’s house, he did not ask for water for his feet, because he was reserving them for sinners’ tears; he did not desire the Pharisee’s kiss, because he judged the kiss of sinners more worthy. Indeed, he did not wish even his head to be anointed with ointment, lest it be made fat with a sinner’s oil.

For we are all one body in Christ, but different members, some weaker and others stronger (Rom. 12:4–5). His mouth was the blessed apostle Paul, who said: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, namely Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3). His hands are the venerable Apostles, through whom he performed many healings and countless wonders. His shoulders are the holy martyrs, on whom he was scourged by various persecutors; hence through the prophet he says: “I gave my shoulders to the scourges” (Isa. 50:6, according to the Septuagint).

If his upper members are the saints, whom else can we understand the Lord’s feet to be except sinners, whom the holy Church soothes with her tears and cherishes with the precious ointment of mercy? Do not despise these sinners, because they are Christ’s feet. Rather, seek them diligently: seek them in prison, seek them in custody, seek the poor and needy. When you have found them, offer them the oil of mercy; pour ointment upon Christ’s feet, so that it may also be said of you: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she has loved much.” For the one to whom little is forgiven loves little.

Therefore, brothers, let us love more, because more has been forgiven us, and let us give more generously, hoping to receive mercy from the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 1907] Formerly, On the Words of the Lord 28; later, in the Appendix, 5.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 11:1–4, “Lord, teach us to pray,” etc., with an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1907] The whole sermon is copied from Ambrose’s *Book 5 on the Sacraments*, chapter 4.]

## 1. God Is Christ’s Special Father and Our Father in Common; Heaven, Where Sin Is Absent

The holy Apostles said to the Lord Jesus: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” Then the Lord gave this prayer:

“Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not allow us to be led into temptation, which we cannot bear [Col. 1908], but deliver us from evil.”

Do you see how brief this prayer is, yet how full of every virtue? What grace there is in its first utterance! O human being, you did not dare raise your face toward heaven; you directed your eyes toward the earth. Then suddenly you received Christ’s grace: all your sins were forgiven. From an evil servant you became a good son. Therefore, rely not on your own work but on Christ’s grace. “By grace you have been saved,” the Apostle says (Eph. 2:8). Here, then, there is no arrogance but faith; to proclaim what you have received is not pride but devotion.

Raise your eyes, therefore, to the Father who gave you birth through the washing of baptism, to the Father who redeemed you through the Son, and say: “Our Father.” It is a good presumption, but a restrained one. You call him Father because you are a son; but do not claim anything for yourself in particular. He alone is Christ’s special Father; for all of us together he is Father, because he begot Christ alone but created us.

Say, then, by grace, “Our Father,” so that you may be worthy to be a son; commend yourself by the Church’s regard [Note: [Col. 1908] Thus Lovaniensis together with manuscript cl. But these two words, “by the Church’s regard,” are divided by a point in other printed editions and manuscripts; several manuscripts have “look upon yourself” instead of “by regard.”] and consideration.

“Our Father, who are in heaven.” What does “in heaven” mean? Hear Scripture saying: “The Lord is exalted above all the heavens” (Ps. 112:4). Everywhere you find that the Lord is above the heavens of heavens—as though the Angels were not in heaven, as though the Dominions were not in heaven—but he is in those heavens of which it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2). Heaven is where guilt has ceased. Heaven is where there are no crimes. Heaven is where there is no wound of death.

## 2. The Kingdom of God Is Grace

“Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your holy name in us” [Note: [Col. 1908] Lovaniensis omitted the words “holy” and “in us” here and below.].

What does “hallowed be” mean? Is it as though we were asking that the one who said, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 19:2), should be made holy—as though something of sanctification were added to him through our prayer? No. Rather, may he be hallowed in us, so that his sanctification may be able to reach us.

“Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your holy name in us. Your kingdom come.” As though God’s kingdom were not eternal! The Lord himself says, “For this I was born” (John 18:37), and you say, “Father, let your kingdom come,” as though it had not come? But God’s kingdom comes when you have received his grace. For he himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21).

“Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us this day our daily bread.”

All things, whether in heaven or on earth, have been reconciled by Christ’s blood (Col. 1:20); heaven has been sanctified, and the devil has been cast down. He is in the place where the human being whom he deceived also is.

“Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—that is, let there be peace on earth as in heaven.

## 3. The Consecration of Christ’s Body; The Greeks Receive Communion Rarely; Daily Communion Is Recommended

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

I remember my sermon when I was treating the sacraments. I told you that before Christ’s words are spoken, what is offered is called bread; but when Christ’s words have been uttered, it is no longer called bread but is named the body.

Why, then, does he say in the Lord’s Prayer that follows, “Our bread”? He did say “bread,” but he said ἐπιούσιον—that is, “supersubstantial.” It is not this bread that passes into the body, but that bread of eternal life which sustains the substance of our soul.

That is why it is called ἐπιούσιον in Greek. The Latin speaker, however, called this bread “daily,” because the Greeks speak of the coming day [Note: [Col. 1908] Most manuscripts omit the word “day,” which nevertheless occurs in Ambrose.]. Therefore, what the Latin and the Greek have said both seem useful. The Greek expressed both meanings in one word; the Latin said “daily.”

If the bread is daily, why do you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily. Live so that you may deserve to receive it daily. One who does not deserve to receive it daily does not deserve to receive it after a year.

As holy Job offered sacrifice daily for his children, lest they had sinned in either heart or speech, so you hear that whenever the sacrifice is offered, the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, and the Lord’s ascension are signified, as well as the forgiveness of sins—and you do not receive this bread of our daily life [Note: [Col. 1909] In some manuscripts, “daily”]? One who has a wound seeks medicine. There is a wound because we are under sin; the heavenly and venerable sacrament is medicine.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” If you receive it daily, every day is for you “today.” For you Christ is today; for you he rises daily. How so? “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). It is “today” when Christ rises. “He is the same yesterday and today” (Heb. 13:8), the apostle Paul says. But elsewhere he also says: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12). Yesterday’s night has passed; today’s day has drawn near.

## 4. We Must Forgive Others So That God May Forgive Us; One Who Entrusts Himself to God in Temptations Does Not Fear the Devil

It follows: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

What is a debt except sin? Therefore, if you had not received another person’s money at interest, you would have no debt; and for this reason sin is charged against you. You had money with which you could have been rich from birth. You were rich, having been made in the image and likeness of God; you lost what you possessed—that is, humility. While you desired to claim arrogance for yourself, you lost the money. Like Adam, you were made naked; you accepted from the devil a debt that was unnecessary. Thus, although you had been free in Christ, you became a debtor to the devil.

The enemy held your bond, but the Lord nailed it to the cross and erased it with his own blood. He took away your debt and restored your freedom.

He therefore rightly says: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Consider what you are saying: “As I forgive, so forgive me.” If you forgive, it is right that you be forgiven; if you do not forgive, how can you make such a claim?

“And do not allow us to be led into temptation, which we cannot bear, but deliver us from evil.” Consider what he says: “which we cannot bear.” He does not say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” but, as an athlete, he desires such temptation as the human condition can bear, so that each person may be delivered from evil—that is, from the enemy and from sin.

The Lord is powerful: he has taken away your sin and forgiven your offenses. He can protect and guard you against the hostile snares of the devil, so that the enemy who habitually generates guilt may not creep upon you.

But one who entrusts himself to God does not fear the devil. For “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. 8:31). To him, therefore, be praise and glory from the ages, and now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON LXXXV

[Note: [Col. 1909] Formerly, *On Time* 171.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 11, “Which of you will have a friend,” etc., and also of John, chapter 16, “Until now you have asked nothing,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1909] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It remained doubtful in the Lovaniensis edition; Verlini and Vindingi later declared it spurious. We suppose that no one who has spent even a little time reading Augustine will now be found to defend it.]

## 1. Encouragements to Pray to God; God Is Merciful and Rich; Access Is Easy; Angels Are Ready to Announce to the Lord Who Has Knocked; Prayer Must Be Insistent and Persevering

The gracious and gentle Lord, dearest brothers, has a door of mercy. He does not drive away those who knock there; rather, he blames the negligent. For nothing is asked that he does not possess, so that, when he has not given it, he might be ashamed. He is rich and merciful, overflowing and kind; he gives and does not reproach. Indeed, the treasures of his house suffer sadness when the agreeable annoyances of petitions are absent.

The Lord himself says: “Until now you have asked nothing. Ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened to you. I am the door and the gate. Why does your hand grow fearful as it knocks, and why does your conscience grow drowsy in poverty? I am the door of life. I do not shrink from a filthy knocker; I do not reject a poor petitioner. Let no one neglect his own poverty.

“Knock, and it will be opened. The Angels stand at the door, to admit, not to repel; to suggest, not to terrify. There is no pomp at my door. I am the door, I who endured the disgrace of the cross. Why should those who ask fear want, when he has never denied mercy to anyone? Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?

“If those who desire chastity knock, he immediately gives them grace and holiness and says to them: ‘Do not walk polluted; do not proceed stained. Be holy, because I am holy’” (Lev. 19:2).

If an orphan approaches to knock at his father’s door with a small hand, the Angels announce him to the Lord: “The orphan is knocking; he awaits the mercy of protection. Answer him, Lord, for the poor man has been left to you; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 10:14, according to the Hebrew text).

The one who is rich and full of mercy, who is a father to the afflicted, answers him: “I am the judge of widows and the father of orphans. Let no one injure those whom I receive; let no one strip those whom I defend.”

Those who approach this very door, although they utter prayers of differing voices, all receive mercy from the house of one rich head of a household. The Savior’s door loves this: that it should always abound in suitable and importunate knockers.

Therefore, when the Lord sees his door silent from the voices of petitioners and the cries of those who knock, he invites everyone to prayer, ready to show mercy to all. “Ask; and if you do not receive, ask again, and persist in knocking. Do not give up, because God does not kill the soul of the righteous by hunger.”

Whoever wishes to be humbly and gently good stands secure, as though in the safest harbor.

## 2. The Mystery of the Trinity

He therefore sets forth the parable of a certain man whose unexpected guest arrived, and the host received his guest. Ashamed, he went immediately to the house of a rich man. It is not without sacramental meaning that he asks for three loaves, because the guest was one in the grace of mercy but three in the substance of the Trinity.

Was there not one guest in three persons who came to Father Abraham? Guest and friend, diner and resident—the services of human hospitality were all offered to him in a trinitarian form, because the glory of the Trinity shines forth. The father brought a three-year-old calf; the future mother, who was to bear the son for whom the father would slaughter the lamb, mixed three measures of fine flour; and she had already made the body of Christ a sacrament in the Trinity.

So this friend too, when a guest arrived, went to the house of the rich man and pleaded the necessity of three loaves. He knocked, but none of the doorkeepers answered, because sleep held them all: neither Angels, nor Archangels, nor Prophets, nor ministers. Yet he continued knocking, although no one answered.

## 3. Sometimes One Must Knock with Persistence So That the Head of the Household May Open

At times the head of the household answered the persistent knocker from the inner holy places, from the throne of rest:

“Why do you knock at an unsuitable time, you who were lazy when there was time? It was day, and you did not walk in the light; night came, and you began to knock. The time excuses the shameless desire that seeks what it wants. The children are already resting, and it is not right that they should suffer injury on your account. Before you came, they stayed awake longer; now they have rested at the proper time. There is no one who can give you an answer.”

And he replied: “Lord, I ask from you; I knock at you—or rather, I knock upon you. You are the door. Rise; give me mercy, you who did not disdain to form my limbs from clay and mud. You have no need of a servant, because you can do everything.

“But if your children are sleeping, you do not sleep, you who guard Israel. I ask freely; under grace I beg, not under the Law do I presume. The Law and the Prophets lasted until John, but your grace has no end.

“I know where your children, your Prophets, have gone. But you, Lord, who are the beginning and the end, the first and the last (Rev. 22:13), do not grow weary of me, who ask at the final [Col. 1911] hour of the night—you who at midnight led captivity captive.”

What will the head of the household do, constrained by the voice of such a persistent person? He does not awaken a prophet; he does not send an Angel or an Archangel. He himself rises and gives him as much as he desires.

That persistent petitioner and nocturnal beggar rightly returned to his own guest, became rich, and refreshed him; nor did the guest depart from his host unrefreshed.

## 4. The Guest at Night Is Grace in Ignorance; The Guest from Heaven Is a Good Thought—Christ

Who, I ask you, brothers, is this guest who comes at night and finds the host unprepared? Indeed, why does the guest come at night except because of perpetual and failing poverty?

The guest comes at night: grace comes amid profound ignorance and great want. He introduces sadness when the nocturnal petitioner says: “In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a spacious place” (Ps. 117:5); and again: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all” (Ps. 33:20), because he is near.

Therefore the guest suddenly arrives unexpectedly when someone is wearied by the burden of afflictions. The desire to pray comes upon him, seizing the resolve to weep. At that hour the guest comes as grace, to prick the conscience so that it may not die in its poverty; but may go and ask the rich man—not on the basis of its own merits, but on the merits of the arriving guest—and receive three loaves, so that in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit he too may feed other needy people.

Whatever good a person thinks when suddenly struck in the heart, let him know that this guest has come from heaven. And he comes rightly, because he comes at night: he helps in tribulation, not bringing weariness but affection.

Since the Lord Christ came to his disciples behind closed doors in their tribulation, unexpected but desired, greeted them with peace, and refreshed his guests in peace (John 20:19), is he not the guest who says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter and dine with him, I and my Father” (Rev. 3:20)?

What a good house, where the Father and the Son enter as a friendly guest—and the Holy Spirit as well! There he provides, in the house of the poor and the lodging-place of purity, various dishes for the Lord’s supper.

What are these dishes? Joy, patience, self-restraint, faith, and chastity.

Only let it not be burdensome to receive the Lord as guest. He himself carries with him the sweetness of delights, so that there he may feed the rejoicing hosts of Angels.
