With that guest there are peace and gladness. He comes to his host not to torment but to feed; not to strip but to clothe; not to strike but to heal.

Let us always receive him with the doors of our hearts open, and never let the tyrannical enemy rule over us. By Christ’s gift, let us keep his commandments in all things.

# SERMON LXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 1911] Formerly, 48 among the Fifty Homilies.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 12:16–21, “The possession of a certain rich man brought forth abundant crops,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1911] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Lovanienses; to Verlini and Vindingi it is spurious. The preacher’s warning here in section 3 concerning tithes is wholly incompatible with Augustine’s period.]

## 1. The Blindness of the Avaricious

“The possession of a certain rich man brought forth abundant crops, and he thought within himself, saying: ‘What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my crops?’ And he said: ‘I will do this: I will tear down my storehouses and barns and build larger ones, so that I may gather my crops there; and I will say to my soul, You have many good things stored up; rejoice and be glad.’ But God said to him: ‘Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; whose will those things be which you have gathered?’”

O the blindness of the avaricious, dearest brothers! One night remained to him, and he was concerned about a life of many years. He rejoiced because he saw that much was going to be born for him, and he did not know that he would take nothing away with him but would leave everything here. Night was driving life away from him [Note: [Col. 1911] In manuscript v., “For night was driving it away.” In others, “But night was driving it away.” No manuscript has the word “life.”], and he was thinking about tomorrow. What he expected in others, he did not expect for himself. Certainly he too had seen people dying; he had seen people possessing; he had seen that no one took the earth away with him.

How many even now speak in this way: “I have so much; I do so much; I am worth so much!” They must be answered: “Fool, this night your soul is taken from you. Whose will the things you have gathered be?”

The foolish rich man rejoices, though he is going to die at night. However widely greed spreads its roots everywhere, however much it snatches, it must leave everything behind in a single hour.

## 2. The Avaricious Man Does Not Love His Children; Care for Children Should Be Entrusted to God

But you will say: “I have children for whom I labor; I have children for whom I must provide; I have children for whom I must exercise the greatest care.”

What kind of care do you show your children, if you overwhelm them with the tears of the poor? This is not loving children, but rather strangling them.

Do you not know that a tree is recognized by its fruit? Do you not know that what is hidden in the root is revealed in the branches, and that what lies hidden among the leaves shines forth in the fruit [Note: [Col. 1912] All manuscripts have “in the fruits.”]?

I do not want your children to find such a father in you; I do not want you to provide for them in such a way that you seem rather to begrudge them. O how many poor people are born and later become rich! How many receive a great inheritance and are later reduced to poverty!

Therefore, if it belongs to God to make someone poor, it belongs to God to make him rich. Why, then, do you act as though you must provide for your children? Why do you seize what you do not know will perhaps remain after you, nourish eternal punishment for yourself, and leave grief to your children?

That wisest man Solomon says: “The one who gathers another’s possessions leaves grief to his children” (Ecclus. 14:15). And again it is said in the Psalms: “Nevertheless, a human being walks about in the image of God and is troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38:7).

What are you storing up, avaricious man, when you do not know for whom? Why do you delight in the weight of gold and silver and hide it away? Why do you preserve the image of the king engraved on coins, while you detest the image of the Creator in human beings?

## 3. Tithes and Almsgiving Must Be Given; Excusing Oneself from Almsgiving on Account of Children

It has been said: “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). Our ancestors therefore abounded in every resource, because they gave tithes to God and paid tribute to Caesar. But now, because devotion to God has departed, the fiscal imposition has come upon us. We were unwilling to give the Lord a share through tithes; now everything is taken away. The fiscal authority takes what Christ does not receive; what is not distributed to the poor is given all the more.

“Do not spare your treasures,” Solomon says (Ecclus. 29:13). Alms must be given according to one’s means and resources, as it is written: “As you have, my son, give alms; if you have little, share even that little with the hungry” (Tob. 4:8–9). “Hide your alms in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you before the Lord” (Ecclus. 29:15).

But you said: “I have children to whom I will leave them.” Suppose your children will have what you leave behind; you will have nothing, because you sent nothing ahead of you. You cared for your children, but you did not wish to benefit yourself.

Behold, after you, strangers pass on—and they too. You ran without purpose, though the Apostle says: “We brought nothing into this world, and certainly we can take nothing out of it” (1 Tim. 6:7), because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1).

You hear, “Lift up your hearts,” and you hurry to say [Note: [Col. 1912] In the manuscripts, “and you run to say”]: “We have them toward the Lord.” If you have sent something there, you have something to seek there. If you have sent nothing upward, you have nothing to seek there. Seek on earth where you have placed your treasure, because it is written: “Where your treasure is, there your heart is also” (Matt. 6:21).

## 4. Lawful Interest; Debtors Should Not Be Pressed Excessively

And hear what God says to you. What? Do you wish to lend at interest—to give less and receive more? “Give to me,” the Lord says; “I accept less, and I will give more.”

When you ask where money may increase, you seek a human being who rejoices when he receives but weeps when he repays; who begs in order to receive but raises objections so as not to repay. Give to a human being, then, and do not turn your face away from one who asks for a loan [Col. 1913]; but accept only as much as you gave. Otherwise you have lost your act of kindness, and even what you are going to give is being demanded.

Perhaps he does not have the means at hand to repay. You endured the petitioner; wait for the one who does not have the means.

Do not shout and say: “Am I asking for interest? I ask only as much as I gave; I will receive that back.” You have not lied; you speak the truth. You are not a moneylender, yet you want the person to whom you gave the money to find a moneylender in order to repay you.

But if for that reason you do not charge interest, so that God will not judge you a moneylender, yet you pressure, suffocate, and demand—if you demand only as much as you gave, nevertheless, by suffocating him and keeping him in distress, you have not done a kindness but inflicted greater distress.

Perhaps you say: “He has the means to repay. He has property; let him sell it. He has a house; let him sell it. He has a household; let him sell it.”

When your brother asked you, he asked you precisely so that he would not have to sell. Therefore, let him not sell because you helped him, so that he would not have to do so [Note: [Col. 1913] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “so that he did not do so.”] This is what God wishes; this is what God commands.

But if you are avaricious, now hear what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you. Whose will the things you have prepared be?” So is the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

# SERMON LXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1913] Formerly, *On the Saints* 31; later, in the Appendix, 81.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter 13:18–19, “To what is the kingdom of God like?” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1913] Formerly published among the Sermons of Ambrose and found under his name in the manuscripts; but there it is somewhat longer, beginning with this opening: “It is clear that we willingly preach and gladly do God’s work; but when we see many of the brethren coming to church rather sluggishly,” etc. It is also noted that it was delivered on the feast of Laurence the martyr.]

## 1. The Mustard Seed Is Great in Power; Christian Faith Is Small in Appearance but Great in Power

The Lord says in the Gospel: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a mustard seed, which a man took and cast into his garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air rested in its branches.”

Perhaps this troubles your understanding: why should the kingdom of God, so glorious and magnificent, be compared with a tiny mustard seed, and such great consolation for our hope in it be said to resemble something so insignificant—especially since elsewhere the same Lord says to his disciples: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matt. 17:19)?

Therefore, if faith is so great that it can move the foundations of mountains from their very bases, the mustard seed too must necessarily be great, since we are compelled to have faith resembling it. We shall call it great not in appearance but in power; it is not to be compared with faith according to the quality of a vegetable, but to be equated with it in the force of its pungency.

For if we pay close attention, we find that the Lord rightly made this comparison. A mustard seed, at first sight, is small, cheap, and despised according to its appearance; it offers no flavor, gives off no fragrance, and does not reveal any sweetness. But when it begins to be crushed, it immediately releases its fragrance, displays its pungency, exhales food of fiery flavor, and is kindled with such heat of fervor that it is astonishing that so great a fire was enclosed in something so insignificant.

People also take food made from this seed, especially in winter, because of its great pleasantness, so that it may drive away chills, expel fluids, and warm the inner parts of the body. Often it is also applied as a remedy to the head, so that if anything is weak or diseased, it may be cured by mustard’s fire.

So too Christian faith at first sight seems small, cheap, and thin. It does not display its power, does not present itself with pride, and does not supply grace. But when it begins to be crushed by various temptations, it immediately reveals its strength, displays its pungency, breathes forth the warmth of the Lord’s faith, and is tossed about with such ardor of divine fire that it both burns itself and compels the one who shares in it to burn.

Thus, as two of the disciples said in the holy Gospel [Note: [Col. 1913] The manuscripts omit the words “two of the disciples” and substitute: “Emmaus and Cleopas said.” Nor does this add the slightest authority to the manuscripts that attribute this sermon to Ambrose, for it is characteristic of him to have believed that Emmaus was the name of one of the two disciples to whom Christ showed himself visibly after the resurrection.], while the Lord was speaking with them after his passion [Col. 1914]: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, while the Lord Jesus opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

The mustard seed therefore warms the bodily organs, but the strength of faith burns away sins from the heart. The former removes the harsh chill of cold; the latter drives away the diabolical cold of sins. The mustard seed, I say, cooks away harmful fluids from the body, but faith consumes the streams of lust. Through the former, medicine is provided for the head; through faith, our spiritual head, which is the Lord Christ, is repeatedly refreshed.

Moreover, in accordance with the comparison with mustard, we enjoy the holy fragrance of faith, as the blessed Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

## 2. Lawrence, the Mustard Seed

Accordingly, we may compare the holy martyr Lawrence with a mustard seed. Worn down by various sufferings, he deserved, throughout the whole world, to diffuse the fragrance of his martyrdom. For while he had previously been established in the body, he was humble, unknown, and of little account; but after he had been tormented, torn, and burned, he poured the fragrance of his nobility into all the churches throughout the world.

Rightly, therefore, is this comparison applied to him: when the mustard seed is crushed, it becomes hot; when Lawrence suffers, he is set aflame. The former arouses heat through its crushing [Note: In the manuscripts: “he breathes forth the heat of his crushing.”]; the latter sighs out fire amid countless torments. The mustard seed, I say, is boiled in a heated vessel; Lawrence is roasted on a gridiron in the fire of the flames.

Thus blessed Lawrence the martyr was burning outwardly in the fires kindled by the raging tyrant; but inwardly he was being scorched by a greater flame, the love of Christ. And although the wicked ruler added wood and placed greater fires beneath him, holy Lawrence nevertheless did not feel those flames, because of the warmth of his faith. While he reflected on Christ’s commands, everything that he suffered was cold to him.

For one who possessed the refreshment of paradise in his inward senses could not feel the torments amid the flames. Let his burned flesh and lifeless body lie before the tyrant’s feet: he suffers no loss on earth whose soul dwells in heaven. He is stretched out, therefore, upon the unknown masses of flame and turned repeatedly from side to side; but the more punishment he suffers, the more deeply he fears the Lord Christ.

In a new kind of marvel, one man tortures him, while the torments inflicted by another advance his cause. More atrocious punishments made Lawrence more devoted to his Savior.

# SERMON LXXXVIII

[Note: Formerly, *On the Saints* 33; later, in the Appendix 82.]

Again, on the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XII, verses 18–19: “To what is the kingdom like?” and so forth.

[Note: We also find this sermon attributed to Ambrose both in the published editions of his works and in manuscript books, in which it begins with these words: “On the preceding Sunday, while discussing the Lord’s parable in which he says, ‘To what is the kingdom of heaven like?’” and so forth. Toward the end, that version is fuller by much material lacking here.]

## 1. The Christian faith is the kingdom of God; mustard is the symbol of its vigor

“To what is the kingdom of heaven like? And to what shall I compare it?” says the Lord. “It is like a mustard seed,” and so forth.

We have touched upon many points by which we could prove that the kingdom of God is not unfittingly compared with a mustard seed, and that the difference lies only in the wording of the comparison, not in the correspondence of their powers. For the Christian faith, which is the kingdom of God, possesses the same vigor that the nature of mustard displays.

When we take mustard juice, our face becomes sorrowful, our brow contracts, we are moved to tears, and we receive the very health of our body together with a certain austere weeping. Its bitterness irritates us, its sharpness penetrates us; then the heat of its fiery flavor kindles us. Thus, when our whole body has been disturbed, we become healthier precisely when we lament more deeply.

So also, when we receive the commandments of the Christian faith, we are saddened in spirit, afflicted in body, moved to tears, and attain our very salvation with a kind of weeping and grief. Fasting irritates us; the conscience of our sins torments us; the loss of our possessions disturbs us. And when our whole condition has been saddened, we attain salvation more fully if we weep more abundantly, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16:20).

Again, when the head must be treated with mustard, we are ordered to remove the shorn hair and lay aside every obstacle of the skin, so that the medicine may reach the uncovered body more effectively. Likewise, when the soul must be healed through faith, we are commanded to remove worldly possessions from ourselves and lay aside the impediments of gold and silver, so that spiritual medicine may more suitably reach the soul when it is naked and alone.

Whoever is wrapped up in the things of the world and in worldly riches will gain no benefit from the medicine of faith. Therefore, what mustard juice accomplishes in the body, Christian faith accomplishes in the soul.

## 2. Christ in humility is the mustard seed; he becomes a glorious tree, whose branches are the saints

But since the same Gospel saying also records: “A man took it and put it in his garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds rested in its branches,” let us inquire more carefully who this may be to whom all these details apply.

Earlier we said that the nature of mustard could appropriately signify the holy martyrs, who have been worn down by various sufferings. But since Scripture says, “It grew and became a tree, and the birds rested in its branches,” I think this is more properly compared with the Lord Christ himself, who, by being born as a human being, was humbled like a seed, and, by ascending into heaven, was exalted like a tree.

Christ is plainly a seed while he suffers; he is a tree when he rises again. He is a seed, I say, when he endures hunger; he is a tree when he satisfies five thousand men with five loaves. There he suffers the barrenness of human condition; here he bestows satiety from his own divinity.

I would call the Lord a seed when he is struck, despised, and rebuked; but a tree when he gives sight to the blind, raises the dead, and forgives sins. [Note: Much is omitted here.]

If you seek the branches of this tree, you will find that Peter is a branch, Paul is a branch, blessed Lawrence is a branch, whose festival we celebrate today; all the apostles and martyrs are branches. Whoever wishes to hold firmly to them will not be submerged by the waves of the world. Rather, sheltering beneath their shade, he will not suffer the heat of Gehenna, secure both from the storm of the devil’s tempest and from the fire of the consuming judgment—through the help of him who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

# SERMON LXXXIX

[Note: This was Caesarius’s homily 19 in the order of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.]

On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XVII, verse 21: “The kingdom of God is within you”; and on the words of the Apostle to the Romans, chapter XIV, verse 17: “The kingdom of God is not food,” and so forth.

## 1. Introduction

We heard, when the Gospel was read, that the Lord said: “The kingdom of God is within you.” And because he knew that not everyone could understand what he was saying, after he had said, “The kingdom of God is within you,” as though someone had asked him, he added: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, I ask you to examine our consciences and see whether we have the kingdom stored within the little chambers of our souls. If righteousness, peace, and joy are there, we are secure, because we know that the kingdom of God is within us. But what is this righteousness, what is this peace, and what is this joy? Attend carefully.

## 2. Perfect righteousness

True and perfect righteousness is that which does not do to others what one does not wish done to oneself. But someone may say: “Who can do good to all people?” Yet he can wish good to all people. When you have done this, the evangelist says to you: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Someone may say: “I do not have the means.” Can he possibly say: “I cannot have good will”? True righteousness, then, is that which wishes for all people what it wishes for itself, desiring that what it wishes for itself may happen to them. True righteousness is that which, for the love of God, loves not only friends but even enemies themselves.

But, brothers, we extend this true righteousness to others only if we also desire to possess it ourselves. For how can anyone give to others what he is not known to possess within himself? Perhaps, however, someone asks how we ought to preserve righteousness within ourselves.

## 3. Righteousness derives its name from judging between two opposing parties; the law of the soul and the law of the flesh. No one can be just toward others who is not just within himself

Attend, brothers. It seems to me that righteousness received its name from this: it is accustomed to judge justly between two opposing and mutually contrary parties. Come, brothers, let us recognize that there are also two things within us that are opposed to one another. “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17).

We therefore have both an inner person and an outer person; we have flesh and soul. That is, we have a mistress and a servant. If you want me to believe that you can judge another person’s case justly, I want first to recognize this in you yourself. Be a just judge within yourself [Note: Thus an old book of the College of Clermont. “Be the judge of this within yourself.”]: assign to the soul what is worthy; reserve for the flesh what it needs. Give the mistress what will suffice for her forever, and reserve for the servant only enough by which she can live in this world.

For if the mistress is humbled and the servant is raised up; if little or nothing is stored for the mistress in heaven, while everything is reserved for the servant in the world—behold, we are already recognized as unjust within ourselves. And how can another person’s case be heard by us in due order, when no justice is preserved within us and in our own case?

This alone I know, brothers: the person who has refused to maintain justice between his soul and his flesh will never be able to judge another person’s case justly. In soul and mind we were made in the image of God; according to the flesh, however, we were formed from the clay of the earth.

Therefore, whoever loves his flesh more than his soul wishes to set the image of God below and raise the earth above. And whoever is so unjust within himself will certainly not preserve justice if he hears another person’s case.

Thus whoever desires to maintain justice should begin with himself. Let him first maintain justice within himself, and become accustomed to being a just judge between his flesh and his soul. Let him reserve for the flesh simple and moderate food and clothing in this world, and let him place what is better—his soul—through almsgiving in heaven.

For if he acts otherwise and does not reform himself, if he wishes to persist in this, then just as he judges in this age, so he will be judged in the age to come. Let this, then, suffice as a brief statement concerning true righteousness [Note: Thus two manuscripts: “concerning your righteousness.”]

## 4. True peace. Many people displease God; perfect peace is peace with God

You ought to recognize what true peace is. It is not the supposed peace that robbers and drunkards, slanderers and the proud, appear to offer one another. That should not be called peace which does not arise from the root of charity.

Whoever, therefore, desires true peace should first strive to have peace with God. But someone says: “Who is there who does not wish to have peace with God?” The one, certainly, who does not live in the way God commanded people to live.

Who is this person who does not have peace with God? The person to whom God is displeasing. But someone says: “Who is so insane that God should be displeasing to him?” If I examine you, perhaps I will find that you are the one to whom God is displeasing.

Tell me, I ask you: have you never grumbled about excessive rain? Have you never complained about the dryness of drought? Have you never grumbled against the prosperity of wicked people? Have you never been angry at the violence of the winds? And, to say something more serious, have you never blasphemed when you gathered fewer fruits from your vineyards?

If, in all these matters, you recognize and understand that you have not grumbled against God, know that you have true peace with God in all that happens to you. Cry out what blessed Job cried out with a secure conscience: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

For if, when things go well for you, you praise the Lord, but when things go badly for you, you grumble against the Lord, you do not have peace with God, nor can you say with the Psalmist: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Psalm 33:2).

Who is the person who blesses the Lord at all times? The one whom prosperity does not corrupt and adversity does not terrify. The first and true peace, then, is that we be at peace with God. When this has been accomplished, we will also be able to have peace within ourselves. For whoever refuses to have peace with God cannot have peace within himself.

Let our soul, then, be at peace with God, so that our flesh may be subject to our soul. For if what is above you does not rule you, what is below you tortures and afflicts you. Let your soul incline its neck beneath the yoke of God, so that your flesh may also place its neck beneath the yoke of your soul.

Then there will be true and perfect peace, when we are at peace not only with others but also with ourselves. But because we are still in battle and fight against the devil, let us not despair of victory if we are at peace with God.

And if we are joined to God, how can it happen that we should fear the devil? You have such a commander with you, and do you fear the devil? You serve beneath such a king, and do you doubt victory?

The devil opposes us daily, but Christ is present. The one wishes to press us down; the other to raise us up. The one wishes to kill; the other to give life. But take courage, brothers: Christ is stronger for raising us up than the devil is for casting us down.

If, then, as we said above, we preserve righteousness and peace with all our heart, we will also be able to possess true joy.

## 5. True joy is the kingdom of heaven, and this is Christ; it is the fruit of righteousness and peace

What is true joy, brothers, except the kingdom of heaven? And what is the kingdom of heaven except Christ our Lord?

That true joy is Christ we read in the Gospel. Thus the angels said to the shepherds: “Behold, we announce to you great joy.” Attend, brothers, and see that there is no true joy except Christ our Lord [Note: Thus according to two manuscripts: “What is the kingdom of heaven except Christ our Lord? Thus the angels also …”].

The angels confirmed this by their testimony. For when they had said, “We announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people,” they immediately added: “For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:10–11).

I know, brothers, that all people wish to have true joy. But the person who does not wish to cultivate the field yet wishes to rejoice in its fruit deceives himself. The person who does not wish to plant a tree yet wishes to gather its apples deceives himself.

True joy is possessed only when peace and righteousness are maintained. Righteousness is first, as it were, the root; peace is second; joy is third. Peace is born from righteousness, and joy is generated from peace.

Righteousness and peace appear to be good works; joy, however, is understood to be the fruit of good works. Thus, by doing righteousness and maintaining peace, we labor for a short time, as it were, in a good work; but afterward we will rejoice without end in the fruit of good works.

Hear the Apostle speaking of Christ: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). We have already said that joy itself is Christ. And the Lord Jesus Christ, speaking with his disciples in the Gospel, encouraged them in this way: “Again,” he said, “I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

What does “No one will take your joy from you” mean [Note: Thus according to the same manuscripts: “What does ‘No one will take your joy from you’ mean? Attend, then …”] except “No one will take me, the Lord himself, from you”?

Examine your consciences, dearest brothers. If righteousness is in you—that is, if you wish, desire, and pray for all people to have what you wish for yourselves; if peace is in you, extending not only to friends but even to your enemies—know that the kingdom of heaven, that is, Christ the Lord, remains in you.

But whoever, returning to his conscience, finds there not righteousness but greed; not peace but discord; not joy founded on the hope of eternal life but carnal delight arising from love of lust—let him recognize and understand that it is not Christ, the king of the Law, who reigns in him, but a cruel tyrant.

Now, brothers, while we still live in this body, we can, with God’s help, amend and correct ourselves. But if the last day finds us entangled in many crimes, there will be no time for correction.

For then, just as there will be eternal joy for all the saints, so there will be punishment without end for sinners—but this will be for those who refused to amend themselves through repentance. Then Christ will say to those placed on the left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire”; but to those placed on the right: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:41, 34).

May the Lord bring us to that blessedness under his protection—he to whom belong honor, glory, and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XC

[Note: Formerly, among the Vignerian sermons, 10.]

On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter II, verses 1–10: “On the third day there was a wedding,” and so forth.

[Note: This is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is not Augustine’s, to whom it is assigned in some manuscripts, but belongs entirely to Caesarius. The sermon itself is found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* among those attributed to Eusebius Gallicanus, fifth in order, though with considerable variation and with the material contained here in section 6 omitted. The same sermon is truncated at this same point in a manuscript at Vendôme and is there attributed to Faustinus. On section 6, see Caesarius’s homilies 7, 9, and 11, from the editions published by Baluze.]

## 1. What this wedding signifies; what the six water jars signify; what the two or three measures signify

That the wedding took place on the third day and that water was changed into wine—you heard this when the Gospel was read. Let us now examine it. What is that wedding?

Here our acquisition and restoration are represented through the vows and celebrations of a wedding, just as elsewhere the return of the younger son is received with chorus and music.

The six water jars are the six ages of this world, through which the righteous prefigured and typified the Lord. Each holds two or three measures, because they contain within themselves faith in the Trinity.

But let us see what the divine discourse says; let us review the sacred declarations of the Gospel itself.

## 2. The mystery of the restoration of humanity. Christ gave the Church a pledge and a dowry

At Cana of Galilee he changed water into wine and revealed the divine power concealed beneath his human form.

“On the third day,” it says, “there was a wedding.” What is this wedding except the joys of human salvation? Why on the third day? Either because he showed us the mystery of the Trinity, or because he rose again on the third day.

Thus, as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, he descended to earth, having assumed incarnation, in order to be joined to the Church gathered from the Gentiles. To this Church—which, of course, is us—he gave both a pledge and a dowry.

He gave a pledge when he was promised to us through the Law; he gave a dowry when he was sacrificed for us. It may also be understood in another way: let us take the pledge as present grace, and the dowry as eternal life.

Let us see what he does at Cana of Galilee. Here let the Lord’s astonishing miracles now appear to us.

## 3. The symbol of regeneration

Water jars are set up, each holding two or three measures. A *metreta* derives its name from *metrum*, that is, “measure.” The jars are filled; suddenly the waters are changed [Col. 1919], and afterward human beings are changed.

As they are reformed for the better, they speak, as it were, of the power of baptism; in them, in a certain way, the likeness of regeneration is expressed. When one thing is made from another, when an inferior creature is transferred into a more gracious form, the mystery of a second birth is revealed.

Nothing of the quantity of the water itself is diminished. While it remains within itself, it is wholly transformed from what it was through a noble change. Its former substance perishes, and another is acquired. A stronger flavor is added to a thin substance; a hidden power is infused into the light streams; the nature of water is made intoxicating. Thus, in a new manner, they confess the power of their Creator.

Who can change these things except the one who was also able to create them?

## 4. Wine signifies Holy Scripture; water becomes wine, grace succeeding the Law

When the wine failed, his mother said to Jesus: “They have no wine.”

Let us first inquire what the wine is that is said to have failed, and what the other wine is that is wonderfully prepared, which the chief steward declares to be better, saying:

“Every man first sets out the good wine; and when they have become drunk, then the inferior wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”

In many passages we understand wine as the divine commandments and the holy Scriptures, which contain the purest vigor of heavenly wisdom. Through them the senses are inflamed with fear of God and the affections are made drunk, according to what is written about Wisdom: “She has prepared her table; she has mixed her wine in the bowl” (Proverbs 9:2).

When the power of the divine Scriptures has filled someone’s inner being, he will be able to say with the prophet: “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Psalm 59:5), and, “How excellent is your cup, which makes drunk” (Psalm 22:5)!

When Christ was at work at Cana of Galilee, the wine failed and wine was made—that is, the shadow is removed and the truth is presented. The Law withdraws; grace succeeds. Carnal things are exchanged for spiritual things. The old observance is transferred into the New Testament, as the blessed Apostle says: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Just as those jars, when filled with water, were diminished in nothing from what they had been, yet began to be what they had not been, so the Law does not perish when it is fulfilled through Christ’s coming; rather, it advances.

When the wine fails, therefore, another wine is supplied. The Old Testament is good, certainly, but without spiritual understanding it fades into the letter; the New Testament, however, gives forth the new fragrance of life in grace.

## 5. The greatest miracle: the conversion of the sinner

Since these things are so, let us consider the chief steward himself, the official placed over the bridegroom’s house, whom we may identify. And whom else should we understand him to be except blessed Paul?

After the letter of the Law, having received the exceedingly sweet mystery of the New Testament, filled and intoxicated by the fragrance of spiritual perceptions, he cries out and praises it: “You have kept the good wine until now.”

Let us nevertheless see how he praises the wine itself: “Eye has not seen,” he says, “nor ear heard what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Behold the true miracles; behold the miracles that ought to be proclaimed, which he works in us when he makes good people from the worst, humble people from the proud, chaste people from the dishonorable, and friends of God from followers of the world.

What greater miracles can he perform than when he deigns to raise a human being—who is a worm and corruption—to an angelic state; to place him among heavenly beings instead of earthly ones; and to receive him into the grace of his adoption?

## 6. Gifts pleasing to God

What, then, shall we render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to us? Or when will we be able to repay what we are not even sufficient to conceive?

Nevertheless, we must not despair because we can repay nothing. For so great is the compassion of our Lord that, in his sight, the perfect intention to do something is reckoned in place of the deed itself.

He has fulfilled everything who has done what he could. What, then, shall we render to the Lord except that, humbly bowing the body and with a contrite heart, we say: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13)?

For he loves holocausts who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. He does not demand from us what he knows we cannot fulfill.

Therefore, those who cannot distribute more generous alms should, according to their means, give something small with good will. Those who cannot attain the glory of virginity should strive, with God’s help, to preserve chastity with their own wives. Let them love justice, maintain charity, cultivate patience, flee drunkenness as though it were a pit of hell, and love all people with a perfect heart.

Let them pray for the good, that they may not withdraw from holy conduct; let them plead for the wicked, that they may quickly turn to better things.

These things and those like them, dearest brothers, are shown to be neither excessively difficult nor impossible to bear. Where good will alone is present, nothing will be impossible.

God does not send us to acquire eternal life through arduous journeys, either to the East or to the West. He directs us toward ourselves; he requires from us what he has bestowed within us by his grace. For he himself said in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21).

Therefore, let true charity and good will be in us, so that this Gospel may be fulfilled in us: “Peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

May he deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XCI

[Note: This now appears for the first time from four manuscripts, where it is appended without the author’s name to certain Augustinian sermons. It presents Augustine’s teaching, but its style is entirely Caesarius’s; here he imitates the ninth tractate on the Gospel of John.]

Again, on John, chapter II, verses 1–10: the six water jars changed into wine at the wedding of Cana of Galilee.

## 1. The six water jars signify the six ages of the world; the six ages of human life. These jars are filled with the mysteries of Christ

As we have already sometimes suggested to your Charity, dearest brothers, those six water jars mentioned in today’s Gospel reading, whose water was changed into wine, signified the six ages of this world.

As you commonly hear, the first age extended from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, as the evangelist also recalls, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to John the Baptist; and from John the Baptist and the coming of the Lord Savior the sixth age is now being conducted (Matthew 1).

This same pattern is also clearly recognized in the course of human life. The first stage, or first age, is infancy; the second, childhood; the third, adolescence; the fourth, youth; the fifth, old age; and the sixth is extreme old age, which is also called decrepitude.

Therefore, do not find it strange when you hear that this world is completed in six ages, since you see the same thing fulfilled in the ages of human beings.

In these six ages of the world, as in six water jars, prophecy was not absent. Those jars, therefore, were full of the mysteries of the Old Testament. But when Christ was not understood in them, it was not wine but water that was drunk from them.

## 2. Christ in Adam

The first jar was filled in the time of Adam, when the Lord cast a deep sleep upon him, took one of his ribs, and fashioned it into a woman (Genesis 2:21–22).

What else did this signify at that time except the passion of the Lord Savior? Adam sleeps, and Eve is fashioned from his side. Christ slept on the cross with his head bowed, and the Church was formed from his side.

When he was pierced in the side, blood and water came out (John 19:30, 34): the blood of redemption and the water of baptism.

As though, brothers, God really could not have made Eve from the same place from which he had made Adam! But already then, in that old Adam from whose rib Eve was fashioned, the new Adam was signified, from whose side the Church was to be formed.

But because the people of the Jews did not understand Christ in that prophecy, it tasted not of wine but of water.

## 3. In Noah

The second jar was filled in Noah’s time. In his days, through the mystery of the ark or the flood, the human race is saved (Genesis 6 and following), just as, through the sacrament of the cross and baptism, at the coming of the Lord Savior, the whole world is rescued from eternal death.

## 4. In Abraham

The third jar was filled in Abraham, whom the Lord commanded to offer his son as a holocaust, in a likeness of the Lord Savior (Genesis 22:1–19).

For just as blessed Isaac himself carried the wood to the place of the holocaust, so the true Isaac himself carried the wood of the cross to the place of his passion (John 19:17).

## 5. David prefigured Christ in many ways

The fourth jar was filled in David, who prefigured the Lord Christ in humility, gentleness, and many tribulations.

Among the other things through him that the Lord deigned to speak, he also cried out this: “Arise, O Lord, judge the earth.”

To whom is it said, “Arise,” except to the one who slept? “Arise,” he says, “O Lord, judge the earth.” You slept, judged by the earth; arise, so that you may judge the earth, in order that what Scripture foretold may be fulfilled in you: “For you will inherit among all the nations” (Psalm 81:8).

## 6. Prophecy concerning Christ in Daniel

The fifth jar was filled in Daniel’s time. He said that he had seen a stone cut from a mountain without hands, and that this stone had grown and filled the entire surface of the earth (Daniel 2:34–35).

See, brothers, that the mountain from which the stone was cut filled the whole earth. That mountain signifies the kingdom of the Jews; from that mountain the stone was cut—that is, Christ was born.

When he says “without hands,” this means without the work of marriage, for works are signified by the hands.

That mountain, therefore—that is, the kingdom of the Jews—did not fill the earth, because before Christ came, God was known only in Judea. But after Christ came, he so filled the whole world with his grace that the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world.

## 7. The calling of the Gentiles in John; stones signify the Gentiles. To those who do not understand Christ, the Law is water; otherwise, it is wine

The sixth jar was filled through blessed John the Baptist. When he saw Jews coming to his baptism, he said to them:

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce fruits worthy of repentance. For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:7–9).

Whom did he wish to be understood as the stones from which children of Abraham could be raised? Surely none but all the Gentiles.

And why were all the Gentiles stones? How were they not stones, when they worshiped stones?

But someone says: “Even if some worshiped stones, are they therefore stones?” Hear Scripture saying: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 113:8).

These six ages of the world, therefore, like six jars, were filled by servants—that is, by the patriarchs and prophets.

When Christ came, he did not throw away that water and provide another; he himself changed that water into wine. Why? Because he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

He did not reject the Old Testament and then establish the New; rather, what tasted like water in the letter of the Law he changed into wine by causing it to be understood spiritually.

## 8. The disciples were unbelieving after Christ’s death

Indeed, before Christ’s coming the Old Testament was so much water that those who read it without understanding Christ were called foolish by the Lord Christ himself.

After the passion of our Lord, two disciples were traveling and wished to go to a village named Emmaus. The Lord and Savior joined them and said to them:

“What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?”

Among other things they replied:

“Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet, powerful in deed and word.”

O blessed disciples! Your faith has become so weak that you call the Lord of the prophets a prophet?

Did you not hear blessed Peter the apostle confess in this way? Do you not remember what Peter answered when the Lord questioned him?

“You are,” he said, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16).

He confessed the Son of the living God, while you believe him to have been a prophet?

This name does indeed also suit the Lord Savior, according to what Moses said: “Your Lord will raise up for you a prophet; you will hear him as you hear me myself. Every soul that does not hear that prophet will be destroyed from among the people” (Deuteronomy 18:18–19).

Nevertheless, when those disciples said this, they certainly did not believe Christ to be the true God.

Finally, see what they said: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

O disciples, you were hoping—have you now despaired? The thief says on the cross: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom”; but you say, “We were hoping.”

Behold, you did not even believe that he would rise again, while the thief believed that he would also reign.

When faith had grown so cold in the disciples that they spoke in this way, the Lord answered: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe” (Luke 24:13–25).

Why were they foolish? Because they were still drinking water. Christ had not yet caused the water to be changed spiritually into wine.

## 9. The two or three measures signify the mystery of the Trinity and the commandments of charity

“Each holding two or three measures.”

He did not say, “Some held two, others three,” but said of all of them that each held two or three measures.

Since this cannot be understood according to the letter, let us see what we may perceive spiritually in them. We have already said that the water in the jars could signify prophecy or the Old Testament. Why, then, two or three measures?

Without doubt, because of the mystery of the Trinity. Why also two? Because of the two commandments of love.

For in the Law and the Prophets not only is the mystery of the Trinity acknowledged, but the two commandments of charity are also continually proclaimed.

Let us nevertheless see whether we can find two or three measures in the Gospel as well.

“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—there you have two.

“Go,” he says, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)—there you have three.

### 10. How the Soul’s Fervor Is to Be Fostered

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, since Christ has deigned to accomplish in us also what he did in the Apostles—so that we who were lukewarm and cold through unbelief might deserve to become fervent through faith in the work of God—let us labor, with his help, as much as we can, so that we may deserve to maintain perseverance in good works to the end. Let us continually strive to exercise ourselves in the readings of the holy Scriptures, so that with the Prophet we may say, “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction” (Psalm 59:5); and again, “How splendid is your cup, which makes drunk!” (Psalm 22:5).

For just as through the love of God our water has been changed into wine, so conversely we must fear lest, by loving the world and cherishing its desires, our wine be changed into water. And therefore, devoting ourselves as much as we can to good works, let us implore God’s mercy, so that he himself, in his goodness, may preserve in us his works and gifts; he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCII

[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 41.]

Also on John, chapter 2:1–10, concerning the wedding at Cana of Galilee. [Col. 1922]

[Note: [Col. 1922] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave its authenticity doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus assert that it is spurious. For here, in section 3, the author does not think that Mary is called “woman”; Augustine, on the contrary, does so in Sermon 52, section 10, and frequently elsewhere.]

### 1. Why Christ Came to the Wedding. Why He Said, “My Hour Has Not Yet Come”

The power of our Lord and Savior, dearest brothers, is clearly displayed in the present reading, since his miracles are narrated not with obscure language but with pure expression. Indeed, the Evangelist guards the inner meaning of the mystery in such a way that he sets forth the event itself in faithful speech. For he says: “The Lord Jesus was invited to the wedding, and his mother.” He did not disdain human society, since he had assumed the use of the flesh; nor did he despise secular institutions, since he had come to correct them. [Col. 1923]

He was present at the wedding in order to strengthen the laws of concord; he was present at the wedding and did not reject the wedding feast, so that he might stir up psalms and tambourines [Note: Perhaps, “compose them harmoniously” (*concinnaret*).] for the proclamation of the glory of God the Father, so that the Father might be honored in the Son and the Son might be known from the Father.

“He says, ‘His mother was there.’” How willingly Mary came to this wedding, at which the miracles of God are confirmed. The wine is suggested—by divine prompting—to have run out. Could God be unaware of what was happening in the house in which he was present? Yet God, who was not ignorant of events, replied: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

From this reply we should meanwhile observe that perhaps some of the wedding wine still remained. Therefore the Lord’s full hour of exercising his powers had not yet come, lest he appear to mix the elements rather than change them. But he said, “My hour has not yet come,” so that God’s miracles might be made manifest in such a way that the enemy could not prevail by argument [Note: [Col. 1923] Perhaps read *tegumento velet*, “veil [them] with a covering.”], nor the Jew accuse them through unbelief.

### 2. The Soul That Faithfully Confesses God Is Not Deceived

And Mary says to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do.” How well the Lord’s mother urges the servants to believe, so that the diners may not lack wine: “Whatever he tells you, do.” We understand that there is already a mystery here, since the attentive mother urges them to recognize the commands of God.

The Lord Jesus says to the servants: “Fill the jars with water.” And when they had filled them, he said: “Draw some out now and take it to the chief steward.” When the chief steward had received it, he immediately perceived that the wine brought later was superior. Since he did not know what the Lord had done, he said to the bridegroom: “Why do you bring out the better wine so late, when it ought to have been served first?”

We have therefore seen that the mystery agrees with what the Savior says, “My hour has not yet come.” And when the chief steward accuses the bridegroom of delay, let us examine more attentively the manifest mysteries of this order which the Evangelist sets forth. Let us see what the wedding is, who the servants are, who the chief steward is, who the bridegroom is, how God comes to the wedding, how Mary does so; whence the wine comes from water, why the better wine appears later, and why God wished to delay until the appointed hour.

Indeed, among the minds of believers no mysteries are hidden. The soul that faithfully confesses God is not deceived. For whoever knows that the Savior’s coming is the remedy of our life easily recognizes, in pure truth, the mercy of his power.

### 3. The Church Calls Christ to the Wedding and Desires Wine from Him. What Held Christ Back

The Savior is called to the wedding; that is, the Holy Spirit is invoked at the Church’s desire. He comes with his disciples, that is, in this setting, with a crowd of saints. What could be said more plainly?

Mary, the mother of God, was awaiting the divine miracles; that is, the Church awaits Christ’s power. She compels him to draw near, for Mary says: “Behold, the wine is running out”—that is, “Why does the people no longer find a remedy?” Mary hastens to test God; the Church desires to receive wine, so that a spiritual banquet may be made from the wedding feast.

For she says: “What is there between me and you, woman?” Does he call Mary “woman,” who was found to be a virgin even after giving birth? But [Note: Supplied editorially: “he says.”] he calls the Church “woman,” which is named not only woman but also prostitute; she received as a bride, like a prostitute, the wandering people—lascivious through all the ages and through the slippery season of life—and, like a learned mother, adorns it.

“My hour has not yet come,” he says; that is, the time of the Passion still remains. “My hour has not yet come”: the people have not yet believed; the Jew does not yet persecute; the devil still has something over which to rejoice; the palm of my triumph has not yet been revealed; he does not yet know the place where he will pursue the cross; and Judas has not yet played false.

“My hour has not yet come”: there are first things that must be cleansed in the world, and thus life advances among the people.

### 4. The Church Teaches Obedience to the Teacher. The Best Wine Comes Only after the Inferior Has Been Exhausted. The Best Wine Is Christ’s Blood

Mary says to the servants, “Do whatever he commands.” That is, the Church commands the servants to obey the teacher. [Col. 1924]

Who are the servants except the ministries of the Levites, which have been assigned to the mysteries of God? The jars are filled with water; that is, once emptied of wedding wine—that is, of a sordid drink—they are replenished with the purity of the spring and changed by the Lord’s blessing into the taste of wine, so that the drink of the Spirit, which had already failed the diners, might be restored.

He changes water into wine; power is increased for human weakness. The chief steward tastes the better wine; that is, human hearts have perceived the taste of the Lord’s vigor. For the one who first judged the wine to be better was also the first to believe.

What is the wine judged to be best, which the chief steward complains was brought out late, except the blood of the Lord’s Passion? This is what God delayed until the appointed hour; this is what the servants receive; this is what the bridegroom preserves; this is what the chief steward, who is first in faith, venerates.

Let us therefore attend with an attentive heart when we hear the holy Scriptures, so that we may recognize heavenly teaching with faithful belief and be freed from every impediment of this world; with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCIII

[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 92.]

On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter 4:5–13: “Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar,” and so forth; and on not delaying Baptism. [Col. 1924]

[Note: [Col. 1924] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was likewise considered doubtful by the Louvain editors, while Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. It contains the style and wording of Caesarius. For section 4, see Appendix Sermons 45, section 6, and 46, section 3.]

### 1. Christ Became the Legitimate Heir of Jacob

In the Gospel reading the holy Evangelist has shown us most fully that the Lord Jesus Christ assumed the weakness of the human race. For after saying that the Lord had come to the city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph—an estate in which Jacob’s well was located—he added: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus beside the well.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ came to the estate that the holy Jacob had left to his son Joseph. I think that this estate was left not so much to Joseph as to Christ, whose figure the holy patriarch Joseph bore—he whom truly the sun and moon worship, and whom all the stars bless.

The Lord came to this estate so that the Samaritans, who wished to claim for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch of Israel, might recognize their possessor and be converted to Christ, who became the patriarch’s legitimate heir.

### 2. Christ Is Weary Because of Our Weakness. He Rests in the Faithful

“Jesus,” he says, “wearied from the journey, was sitting thus beside the well.” Observe the difference in the mystery. Among the Apostles, when he was situated on the mountain, he rejoiced in spirit; he not only strengthened them but also showed them their own glory. But when he was situated in Samaria, he sat beside the well, wearied from the journey.

Could God’s power grow weary? Certainly not. Rather, he was weary because he could not find a faithful people. Christ is therefore weary whenever he recognizes no virtue in his people. Even today our disobedience makes him weary; our weakness makes him weary. For we are weak when we pursue not what is strong and lasting but what is temporal and perishable.

He rightly says, “He was sitting beside the well,” not “he was resting,” because he could not rest among the Samaritans. “And it was,” he says, “about the sixth hour.” On the sixth day God formed the human being from the clay of the earth; at the sixth hour he came to visit Samaria, so that, when the Samaritans believed in him, he might begin to rest in them and celebrate that true Sabbath of rest.

The Lord was therefore sitting beside the well.

### 3. Why Christ, the Fountain, Sat beside the Well

“And a Samaritan woman came to draw water.” A great mystery. The woman came to the well and found the fountain she had not expected.

The Lord says to her: “Give me a drink.” The good Lord freely offers himself to one who does not seek him, so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled: “I appeared openly to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not inquire after my name” (Isaiah 65:1, according to the Septuagint).

He asks for a drink in order to give one. He sat beside the well [Col. 1925] so that we might not seek water on high, but draw saving drinks from that fountain which is above all waters.

What is the fountain except our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is said: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10)? A good fountain, which has refreshed us from the burning heat of this life and, by its flood, has overcome the dryness of our hearts.

### 4. Those Who Delay Baptism Do Not Know God’s Gift. The Grace of Christ’s Coming

Hence it is also said to the woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

Not everyone knows God’s gift, because not everyone desires living water. For if they desired it, they would never put off the sacrament of Baptism. Thus they pronounce judgment on themselves and lose [Note: Perhaps, “expose” (*produnt*).] the testimony of their own lives—those who want to be baptized later for the purpose of committing many shameful acts and crimes.

Do not delay, O human being, the remedies of your salvation, because you do not know when your soul will be demanded back from you.

Finally, the Samaritan woman, unaware of the mystery, said: “Lord, you have neither a bucket, and the well is deep.” Before the Lord’s coming, the well was indeed deep, and without a bucket no one could draw water for himself.

The Lord, the living fountain, came to wash the hearts of the Pharisees, quench their thirst, and satisfy their breasts—not seeking a bucket, but freely pouring himself into the minds of individuals.

And he added: “Everyone who drinks from this water that I shall give him will never thirst forever; but it will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

He teaches one Baptism, which does not allow any one of us to thirst after entering into the mystery of the eternal fountain and heavenly drink.

And therefore, since divine mercy has bestowed such great gifts upon us without any preceding merits of ours, let us labor as much as we can, with his help, so that the grace of such great goodness may produce in us not judgment but progress. May he himself deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCIV

[Note: Formerly Sermon 22 among the Fifty Homilies; later Appendix 18.]

On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter 5:20–30: “As the Father raises the dead,” and also chapter 6:37–40: “Everything that the Father gives me.” [Col. 1925]

[Note: [Col. 1925] The second part of this sermon is excerpted from Augustine’s commentary on John.]

### 1. One Judgment Is of Discernment, Another of Condemnation

You heard, dearest brothers, in the Gospel reading the Lord saying: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. And he will show him works greater than these”—that is, not only healing the weak but also raising the dead.

When he says, “The Father judges no one,” this may refer to his divinity, because no one can behold or hear him, as in the saying, “No one has ever seen God.” But “he has given all judgment to the Son”—that is, the one who was judged according to the flesh will judge all people.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but passes from death into life.”

When he says, “He does not come into judgment,” referring to the one who hears his word and believes him who sent him, it is clear that the Lord has made a distinction between the righteous and sinners. It is as though he said: The one who does this will not come among the number of sinners, but will pass from death to life—that is, from pride to humility, from hatred to charity, from temporal things to eternal ones.

“Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear will live.”

The dead are understood as sinners, who heard Christ but did not believe. And when it is added, “Those who hear will live,” this is repeated because shortly before he had spoken of the resurrection of sinners, whereas here he speaks of the resurrection of the dead.

“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

The Father therefore gave the Son life by begetting him, just as he himself has life. When it says, “He has given him authority to execute judgment,” we understand that the Father is said to have given the Son judgment on account of the portion of flesh that he assumed. This signifies the future judgment, in which the Lord Jesus Christ will stand and repay each person according to his works. For here we understand judgment as the condemnation and punishment of sinners.

But where the Psalmist says, “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause” (Psalm 42:1), we recognize a judgment of discernment.

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth: those who have done good, into the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, into the resurrection of judgment.”

“I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own glory but the will of him who sent me.”

Here he most plainly announces the future resurrection. And when he says, “I can do nothing of myself,” it is as though he were saying: “For this reason I can do nothing of myself, because I did not come from myself but from the Father.” When he says, “As I hear, I judge,” and so forth, that hearing is signified to have taken place in eternity.

### 2. The Humble Person Given to Christ Cannot Perish. The Twofold Resurrection

“Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out.” [Note: Here are omitted words found in Augustine: “What sort of inner place is that from which one does not go outside?”] [Col. 1926]

A great inner chamber and a sweet secret place, without weariness, without the bitterness of evil thoughts, without the interruption of temptations and sorrows. Is it not that secret place into which the one will enter to whom the Lord will say: “Good servant, deservedly [Note: Augustine has, “Good and deserving servant.”] enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21)?

“And whoever comes to me,” he says, “I will not cast out.” Whoever comes to me becomes humble; whoever clings to me will be humble, because he will not do his own will but God’s. Therefore he will not be cast out.

“This is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that of everything he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day.”

He is given to the one who preserves humility, and Christ receives him. Whoever does not preserve humility is far from the teacher of humility.

“That of everything he has given me I should lose nothing.” “This is not the will before my Father that one of these little ones should perish.” The swollen may perish; none of the little ones will perish, because unless you are among these little ones [Note: Augustine has, “like this little one.”], you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3).

“Everything that the Father gives me I will not lose, but I will raise it up on the last day.” Observe how here also he defines that twofold resurrection. Whoever comes to me now rises, having been made humble in my members; but I will raise him up on the last day—that is, according to the flesh.

“For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”

Above he said, “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me”; but now, “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him.” He did not say, “He sees the Son and believes in the Father.” For to believe in the Son is the same as to believe in the Father, because just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself.

Thus everyone who sees and believes in him has eternal life: by believing and passing into life, as in that first resurrection. And because that resurrection is not the only one, he says, “I will raise him up on the last day.”

## SERMON XCV

[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 104.]

On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter 11:1–44: “Lazarus our friend is sleeping; but I am going to awaken him from sleep,” and so forth. [Col. 1927]

[Note: [Col. 1927] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful, but Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. Compare Treatise 49 on John. In any case, it bears the marks of a devout author practiced in the Holy Scriptures.]

### 1. Christ’s Divinity Is Demonstrated in the Raising of Lazarus. The Apostles Did Not Raise the Dead by Their Own Power

Our Lord and Savior Christ Jesus declared the power of his divinity through many signs and miracles, but especially in the death of Lazarus, as Your Charity heard in the present reading. He showed himself to be the one of whom it was written: “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector” (Psalm 45:8).

Our Lord and Savior worked these miracles in two ways: bodily and spiritually—that is, visibly and invisibly—so that through a visible work he might display invisible power.

Earlier, by a visible work, he gave sight to a man blind from birth (John 9:1–7), so that by that invisible power he might illuminate the blindness of the Jews with the light of his knowledge. In the present reading he gave life to the dead Lazarus, so that he might raise unbelieving Jewish hearts from the death of sin into life.

Indeed, many of the Jews believed in Christ the Lord because of Lazarus. For in the resurrection of Lazarus they recognized the manifest power of the Son of God, because to command death by one’s own power belongs not to human condition but to divine nature.

We read that the Apostles also raised the dead (Acts 9:40; 20:9, 12), but when they raised them, they prayed to the Lord. They raised them not by their own virtue or power but by invoking the name of Christ, who rules over death and life. The Son of God, however, raised Lazarus by his own power.

Therefore, as the Lord said, “Lazarus, come out,” he immediately came forth from the tomb. Death could not hold the one whom Life was calling. The moisture of burial was still in his nostrils; Lazarus stood alive.

Death did not wait to hear the Savior’s voice a second time, because it could not endure the power of life. At the Lord’s one command, death released both Lazarus’ body from the tomb and his soul from the underworld; and the whole Lazarus came forth alive from the tomb, although the whole of him had not been there.

Someone is awakened from sleep more slowly than Lazarus was raised from death. The body’s moisture was still in the nostrils of the Jews, and Lazarus stood alive. [Col. 1928]

But let us now examine the beginning of the reading itself.

### 2. Why Christ Rejoices and Weeps over Lazarus’s Death. The Power of Christ’s Tears

The Lord therefore said to his disciples, as Your Charity heard in the present reading: “Our friend Lazarus is sleeping, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.”

The Lord rightly said, “Our friend Lazarus is sleeping,” because he truly was going to rise from death as from sleep. But the disciples, not understanding why the Lord had said this, replied to him: “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will be well.”

Then he answered and told them plainly: “Lazarus has died; but I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.”

But if the Lord says here that he rejoices for the disciples’ sake over Lazarus’s death, what does it mean that he is later reported to have wept at Lazarus’s death?

Let us consider the reason for his rejoicing and his tears. The Lord rejoiced for the disciples; he wept for the Jews. He rejoiced for the disciples because their faith in Christ was to be strengthened by the resurrection of Lazarus. He wept over the Jews’ unbelief because they would not believe in Christ the Lord even when Lazarus had risen.

Or perhaps the Lord wept for this reason: that by his tears he might wipe away the sins of the world. If Peter was able to remove his own sins by the outpouring of his tears, why should we not believe that the sins of the world were wiped away by the Lord’s tears?

Indeed, after the Lord’s tears, many from the Jewish people believed. The feeling of the Lord’s compassion overcame, in part, the Jews’ unbelief, and the first outpouring of tears softened their divided minds.

And perhaps this is why both things are reported of the Lord in the present reading: that he rejoiced and that he wept. For, as it is written, “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm 125:5).

The Lord’s tears are therefore the joys of the world, because he shed tears for this reason: that we might deserve joys.

But let us return to the order of the passage.

### 3. Christ Both Absent and Present at Lazarus’s Death

He therefore said to his disciples: “Our friend Lazarus has died; but I rejoice for your sake, so that you may know that I was not there.”

Here also let us attend to the mystery: how does the Lord say that he was not there? For when he plainly says, “Lazarus has died,” he clearly shows that he was present there. The Lord could not have said this without someone informing him, unless he had been present.

How was the Lord not present in the place where Lazarus died, when by the divine power he encompasses every place throughout the whole world? But here too our Lord and Savior reveals in himself the sacrament of flesh and divinity.

He was not there according to the flesh; he was there according to divinity, because God is everywhere.

### 4. Why God Asks about Things He Does Not Ignore. Adam Is Saved by Confessing His Guilt; Cain Is Condemned for His Denial

When the Lord had therefore come to Mary and Martha, Lazarus’s sisters, and saw the crowd of Jews, he said: “Where have you laid him?”

Did the Lord not know where Lazarus had been laid—the Lord who, while absent, had declared that Lazarus was dead, and who by the majesty of his divinity was everywhere?

But the Lord did this according to an ancient custom. For he likewise said to Adam: “Where are you, Adam?” (Genesis 3:9). He did not ask because he did not know where Adam was, but so that Adam might confess his sin with his own mouth and thereby be able to obtain forgiveness for his sin.

He also asked Cain: “Where is your brother Abel?” And he replied: “I do not know” (Genesis 4:9). Cain was not questioned because God did not know where Abel was, but so that, when Cain denied it, God might expose the fratricide he had committed against his brother.

Thus Adam, because he confessed to the Lord who questioned him the sin he had committed, was restored to forgiveness; Cain, because he denied the fratricide he had committed, was condemned to eternal punishment.

So here too, when the Lord says, “Where have you laid him?” he does not ask because he did not know where Lazarus had been laid, but so that the Jewish crowd might follow him to Lazarus’s tomb. Then, seeing Christ’s divine power in the resurrection of Lazarus, they might themselves become witnesses against themselves if they did not believe in such great power.

For the Lord had said to them earlier: “If you do not believe me, believe the works at least, and know that the Father is in me and I am in him” (John 10:38).

### 5. God Leaves to Human Beings What Belongs to Human Power

Then, when he had come to the tomb, he said to the Jews standing around: “Take away the stone.”

What shall we say? Could the Lord not have commanded the stone to be removed from the tomb, when by his own power he had removed the gates of the underworld?

But what human beings could do, he commanded human beings to do. What belonged to divine power, he demonstrated by his own power.

To remove the stone from the tomb belongs to human power; to call the soul back from the underworld belongs to divine power alone.

Yet, if he had wished, he could easily have removed the stone from the tomb by the command of a single word, since by his word he created the world.

### 6. The Power of Christ’s Voice. Another Miracle: Lazarus Walks with His Feet Bound

When they had therefore removed the stone from the tomb, he cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!” He showed himself to be the one of whom it was written: “The voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in majesty” (Psalm 28:4); and again, “Behold, he will give his voice to his power” (Psalm 67:34).

This is plainly a voice of power and majesty, which immediately recalled Lazarus from death to life. His soul was restored to his body before the sound of the voice had gone forth. Although the body was in one place and the soul in another, the Lord’s voice immediately restored the soul to the body and presented the body to the soul.

Death was driven away when it heard a voice of such power. [Col. 1929]

Nor is it surprising that Lazarus could rise at the Lord’s one command, since in the Gospel he himself declared that all who are in the tombs will rise at one voice, saying: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will rise” (John 5:25).

Without doubt, then, death could have released all the dead from itself when it heard the Lord’s voice, unless it had recognized that Lazarus had been called by name.

As the Lord said, “Lazarus, come out,” he immediately came forth with his hands and feet bound, and his face covered with a cloth.

What shall we say here also? Could the Lord not have broken the bonds of burial in Lazarus, when he had broken the bonds of death?

But here our Lord and Savior displayed in Lazarus a twofold power of his work, so that he might in this way pour the faith of belief into the unbelief of the Jews. For it is no less astonishing that Lazarus could walk with his feet bound than that he rose from the dead.

## SERMON XCVI

[Note: Formerly *On the Words of the Lord* 52; later Appendix 6.]

Again, on John’s Gospel, chapter 11:1–44, concerning the raising of Lazarus.

[Note: [Col. 1929] The author is uncertain and plays the rhetorician ineptly.]

### 1.

Although human beings may admire all the miracles that the Son of God performed on earth in order to reveal his majesty, so greatly that they cannot define them in words, the miracle that Christ performed concerning Lazarus surpasses every other.

He did not restore health to a sick man, nor immediately restore strength by his word to one weakened by illness [Note: In most manuscripts: “nor did he banish the sickness of debility, nor [restore] strength, etc.”]; nor, finally, did he restore life to someone who still possessed the remnants of a soul. Rather, he commanded a man who had already been buried, already placed in a tomb, already assigned to the underworld according to the proper intervals of time—an inhabitant of the pale seat itself—to return to the upper world. He destroyed the law of Tartarus and made the captive of death return above.

After the assemblies of the shrieking shades, after the deep darknesses of eternal night, he made him live, recline at a banquet, enjoy conversation with those reclining, eat, and rejoice.
