And, to increase the miracle of divine power, while the guests asked about the sorrowful regions of punishment [Note: Many manuscripts read *tristega poenarum*; thus the old codex cited by the editor may perhaps be corrected, where it reads *tristitia capitenarum*.] and the dwellings forever darkened by deep night, Lazarus described them in careful narrative and in order. At last, the underworld’s betrayer, long sought and unknown for a long time, was found.

### 2.

Nor had various powers in many healings been insignificant beforehand. For, apart from Lazarus, the things Christ accomplished were neither slight nor trivial: the lame ran with restored steps and gave thanks to the Lord after receiving the benefit of health; the maimed raised both hands toward heaven with praises; the barriers of the tongues of the mute were loosened, and after the dreadful bellowing of inarticulate sound, once the knot binding the tongue had been broken, intelligible words emerged from the divided mouth.

The blind man received the light that violent pain had snatched away from the seat of his eyes by a cloud of thick fluid; and, shaking off the night that had buried his brow, he received full sight and, blind though he had been, deserved the resurrection of his eyes.

One man indeed recovered his eyes; another received them. What nature had not given, Christ’s hand fashioned. [Col. 1930] For he placed upon the man’s brow dust mixed with spittle, and, at the touch of the sacred hand, the skill of the work hastened to set shining jewels into prepared eye-sockets. What nature had not given, Christ the craftsman restored.

All these things were miraculous to everyone as they occurred. Who, however stony-hearted, would not immediately be compelled to marvel when he saw all injuries of the limbs restored not by medicinal compounds, nor by any craft, nor by remedies, but solely by the command of a word?

Yet these things appeared small in comparison with Christ’s power, unless Christ’s friend Lazarus had died. Christ restored him to the nature of life for this reason: to change nature and overturn the order of life; so that one human being might learn to be born once and die twice, and so that he might disturb the condition of death by a new law of resurrection.

### 3.

An enemy plague of illness therefore attacked Lazarus. Scorching his panting body with the furnace of fevers, an ever-devouring fire consumed the wretched man’s strength day by day.

He lay there, burning with heaving entrails, while his body, shaken by frequent sobs, announced that the soul was about to depart from its bodily dwelling.

Neither friends, nor counsel, nor soothing remedies, nor medicines supplied by the art of healing came to his aid. Everything that had been provided for his health was turned to the contrary.

For this illness could be ended not by any remedy but only by death—and death itself had to be conquered through Christ’s resurrection.

Two sisters were present with the sick man, and, grieving over the young man’s plight, they clung constantly to the bed of the sick man. They frequently encouraged the one lying there with such words:

“Endure patiently,” they said. “Bear it bravely; do not collapse in despair. While you tolerate this illness with courage, while you endure and cherish it, Christ will come amid these things, as we believe; perhaps you will even be healed.”

But why does such great grief burn you, O Mary and Martha, on behalf of your brother? Why do you desire with continual sighs to die with your brother? Rather, change the wishes of your hearts in the opposite direction. Pray for the illness to intensify; seek an increase of fevers; desire that the storm of raging disease strike more quickly against the farthest boundaries of life.

For your brother Lazarus, whose illness you lament with such deep affection, will not recover health unless he has died.

### 4.

The persistent fever therefore burned the sick man, and a devouring flame dried him with penetrating heat. Pain, like a torturer, pressed upon his body; the whole man was weighed down by the burdens of raging illnesses, so that the soul might be released from the bonds of the body.

At last the disease overcame the body’s vital fluid, and the furnace of fevers forced the soul to emigrate from the seat of the body in its final separation.

Mary and Martha, the sisters, tore their garments, lacerated their cheeks with angry fingernails, scattered their torn-out hair, and struck the stars with their wailing.

Yet, as they bent over the corpse and embraced the lifeless body, pressing empty kisses upon it, they repeatedly said:

“You could, poor man, have neither been sick nor died if no circumstance had caused Christ to be absent. For among all those to whom he granted what they desired by his healing word, if he had also encountered or seen you while you were sick, we would not see you overcome by the cold sleep of the body, nor deprived of light. Indeed, if he had been present, fever would not have approached you, pain would not have attacked you, and illness would not have devastated you.

“For his omnipotence is so great that even if you had already died, you would rise again if he came.”

Meanwhile the funeral procession advanced, and, adorned with mournful rites in a long procession, the body was carried to the tombs. It was hidden in a hollowed stone, and mournful voices cried out over it.

5. Christ therefore came to Bethany to destroy the bars of death by divine power. The weeping sisters came to meet him, bearing witness to the man’s death and seeking God’s help (for Lazarus was deeply loved by him, and there was a certain affection for his sisters in the Lord’s sight) [Note: [Col. 1930] Thus in several manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read: “for there was an affection for him,” etc., and shortly afterward, “a certain delight.”]. By inwardly laying down a pledge of their loving service, they seemed to hold the Lord in the depths of their hearts. Yet God asks about their tears; although he knew what had happened, he still desired to hear it from their own voices. “Lazarus,” they said, “the one you loved, has died.” O envy! O faithless circumstance! While you still remained in the world, Lazarus, your friend, dies. If a friend dies, what must an enemy suffer? It is not enough that the beings above do not serve you alone: behold, the beings below have snatched away your beloved. “Lazarus,” they said, “the one you loved, is dying.” That cry set aside the customary language of humanity and mortality: “God’s friend ought to have lived longer”; but he dies.

6. Our Lord Jesus Christ, gazing upon the tears of the women who, with continual sighs, desired to die with their brother, hastened with his disciples and the great crowds to Lazarus’s tomb. For he had already lain for four days inside the hollowed rock; the most dreadful stench of his disintegrating limbs already prevented approach; his eyes, decaying in their sunken sockets, had already settled into a putrid state; the softness of his nostrils was already failing; his mouth gaped horribly, its teeth exposed; and, with the skin stripped bare, the slackened temples revealed the seat of the brain, growing pale beneath its thinning covering, while the hair gradually became sparse. Mary and Martha, Lazarus’s sisters, who had often seen Christ raise the dead, no longer believed at all that their brother could be raised. There Christ was truly proved to be God, where he did as much as faith itself had not dared to hope. Moved in spirit, he said: “Where have you laid him?” Yet he should not be thought to have been ignorant of the place of burial; rather, he wished to approve the faith of the people. Christ therefore came to the tomb in which Lazarus slept and immediately summoned him from the grave, not as a dead man but as one who was healthy, alive, and ready to hear: “Lazarus,” he said, “come out.” He names him, so that all the dead would not be compelled to come out. Yet he cries out to the tomb: the beings below are thrown into turmoil; all the dead await the summons and seek to have their names called. “Will the Lord,” they ask, “raise us also?” Wherever Christ had stood, the realm below lay open. Suddenly one voice silenced the others: “Lazarus, come out.” No delay holds back the one rising; no slowness impedes the soul’s return; no bonds of burial hinder him. Wrapped in linen and entangled in linen knots, he comes forth more swiftly at Christ’s voice; he rises, walks, and runs. And lest anyone say that the one rising still lacked anything, he gives thanks to the Redeemer before them all.

## SERMON XCVII

[Note: [Col. 1931] Formerly, *On the Words of the Lord* 57; later, in the Appendix, 7.]

On the words of the Gospel according to John, chapter 14:27: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.”

[Note: [Col. 1931] Its style agrees with the sermon in Appendix 73, and also with 61, which is attributed to Chrysologus. In the royal manuscript marked 3793, it is attributed to Ambrose.]

What peace is; what it accomplishes; what kind it is; how great its loss; the crime of obstinacy; discord.

The Lord’s word, dearest brothers, is: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.” Since we are going to speak about peace, let us first consider peace’s benefits. Peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of spirit, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, and the fellowship of charity. It removes hostilities, restrains wars, suppresses anger, tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms the quarrelsome, reconciles enemies, and pleases everyone. It does not seek what belongs to another; it counts nothing as its own. It teaches love, since it does not know how to hate. It does not know how to be exalted or puffed up.

Therefore, let the one who has received peace hold fast to it; let the one who has lost it seek it again; let the one who has missed it search for it, because whoever is not found in it is rejected by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and likewise made a stranger to the Holy Spirit. For the one who despises the goodness of the law given has rejected the gift offered; nor can the one who refuses to observe the testament reach the Lord’s inheritance. One cannot have concord with Christ while choosing to be at odds with a Christian.

It is therefore the crime of obstinacy to despise what is commanded, refuse what is prescribed, and avoid what is ordered. What have you in common with discord, Christian? Why do you love hostilities, which could not please the author of peace? Why do you practice enmities, which even the one who first devised them could not escape? At the beginning, when the serpent displayed enmity against the first-created man, he was killed; when he envied the human being, he himself was overthrown; when he desired to deceive Adam, he himself was first slain. Therefore either embrace Christ’s charity, Christian, or recognize that, in the likeness of your deeds, you are equal to the author of discord.

[Note: [Col. 1931] All manuscripts add the word “his”: some place it after “deeds,” others after the particle “you.”]

### The same sermon in a fuller form

As it appears in the royal manuscript and also in the Colbertine manuscript, where it is prefaced by this title: “Sermon of Saint Augustine at the Lord’s Supper, on the peace commended to the disciples.”

This is the Lord’s word: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.” Since we are going to speak about peace, let us first hear what peace’s benefits are. For peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of spirit, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, and the fellowship of charity. It removes hostilities, restrains wars, suppresses anger; it tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms discord, reconciles enemies, and is pleasing to all. It does not seek what belongs to another; it counts nothing as its own. It teaches love, since it does not know how to hate. It does not know how to be exalted or puffed up: it is humble toward all and gentle toward all. In it there is rest; in it, tranquility.

The peace exercised among Christians is brought to perfection in Christ. Whoever loves it is God’s heir; whoever despises it is Christ’s rebel. For the Lord Christ, returning to the Father, left his worshipers an hereditary good—that is, his peace—saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.” Let the one who has received this peace hold fast to it; let the one who has lost it seek it again; let the one who has missed it search for it, because whoever is not found in that peace is rejected by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and, stripped and naked, will be found alienated from that same Lord. The one who despises the goodness of the law given will reject the gift offered; nor can the one who refuses to serve the testament reach the Lord’s inheritance.

Embrace the peace Christ left you, Christian; cling as a worshiper to God’s inheritance; show that the Lord’s will has been poured into you. “Blessed are the peacemakers,” he says, “for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). This has been written for the quarrelsome; this has been written for enemies: no one can be a son except one who is peaceful. He has rejected enemies and made peaceful people his sons. Either preserve the peace given to you, Christian, or recognize that the glory of salvation has been taken from you if you do not love peace.

The one who refuses to be reconciled with his brother cannot receive Christ’s promises; one cannot have concord with Christ while choosing to be at odds with a Christian. If Christ were to demand from us a vicarious suffering, and the blood of the Son of God, poured out for us, were sought to be repaid with our blood, with what urgency and devotion ought we to hasten, so that we might fulfill the commands of such great majesty, rejoice in paying through vicarious suffering, acquire life in exchange for death, and make compensation through reciprocal suffering? But now, how will you be able to lay down your life for Christ if you refuse to preserve the peace entrusted to you by that same Christ?

It is therefore the crime of obstinacy to despise what is commanded, refuse what is prescribed, and avoid what is ordered. Christ’s peace is good; discord is the devil’s evil. Whoever chooses one rather than the other answers to its author. What have you to do with discord, Christian, which killed its own prince, the devil? Why do you love hostility, which could not please its author? Why do you practice enmities, which even the one who first devised them could not escape? When the serpent practiced enmity against the first-created man, he was killed; when he envied the human being, he himself was overthrown; when he deceived Adam, he was slain.

Christ, by contrast, clung to humanity with such great charity and loved it with such singular kindness that, descending and assuming flesh for its sake, he commended it to the Father and joined it to himself. It is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world. But those who belong to him imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25). Let what falls upon the devil not fall upon a Christian, because it is fitting for a Christian to preserve what he has plainly learned from the Lord. For this reason we ought to embrace Christ’s charity, so that we may live with him in eternal blessedness. Amen.

## SERMON XCVIII

[Note: [Col. 1932] Formerly, *On Time* 166.]

On the same words of the Gospel according to John, chapter 14:27.

[Note: [Col. 1932] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It contains chapter six from Alcuin’s work *On Virtues and Vices*. The second part of the same sermon should be added: from the words in section 4, “This unanimity therefore existed under the Apostles,” etc., it is taken from Cyprian’s book *On the Unity of the Church*.]

### 1. Peace, Christ’s inheritance. The peacemaker, a son of God

We read in the Gospel, dearest brothers, that when our Savior and Lord was approaching his passion and announcing to his disciples his departure from this world to the Father, among the other words he gave his beloved companions for remembrance, he especially commended the good of peace and unity to them as a particular gift, saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace”—as though he were saying, “I left you in peace; in peace I shall find you.” As he departed, he wished to give what he desired to find in all of them when he returned. He gave this to his own as an inheritance, and promised all the gifts and rewards of his pledge in a life of peace [Note: [Col. 1933] Perhaps, “preservation.”].

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be Christ’s heirs, we must be and remain in his peace. As you have heard, Christ gave us peace, commanded us to be harmonious and united, and enjoined us to keep the covenants of love and charity uncorrupted and inviolate. Elsewhere he wonderfully displayed the adornments of this peace, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). If the one who has begun to be peaceful begins to be called a son of God, then the one who refuses to embrace peace does not wish to be called a son of God: the one who disdains to be peaceful denies that God is his Father. God’s sons, therefore, ought to be peaceful: gentle in heart, simple in speech, united in affection, and faithfully joined to one another by bonds of unanimity.

### 2. With whom peace must be preserved. The effects of peace

But this peace must be maintained with the good and with those who keep God’s commandments, not with the wicked and criminal, who have peace among themselves in their sins. Christ’s peace advances salvation to eternity; the peace that exists in the devil leads to everlasting destruction. We must always have peace with the good and war against vices; the evils of wicked people are indeed to be hated. The people themselves, however, although they are wicked, must be loved, because they are God’s creatures [Note: [Col. 1933] In Alcuin: “Not people,” with the following words omitted: “must be loved.”].

The peace that exists among the good joins together the concord of brothers and the charity of neighbors. Peace specially wins the favor of God’s Spirit; peace is the mother of love; peace is the sign of holiness. Concerning it the Lord says through the prophet: “Love peace and truth” (Zechariah 8:19). Peace is the health of the people, the glory of the priest, the joy of the homeland, and the terror of enemies, whether visible or invisible. Peace must be guarded with all our strength, brothers, because whoever remains in holy peace always remains in God and has fellowship with God’s saints.

### 3. The priest’s duty. Without peace, prayer and offering are not accepted

It is the priest’s duty to admonish the people in peace concerning what they ought to do; it is the people’s duty to hear humbly what the priest advises. Whatever is not permitted, the shepherd must prohibit from being done; the people must hear and refrain from doing it. All, leaders and subjects alike, must preserve in every respect the bond of unity in faith and love, because without peace the priest’s prayer is not received, nor the people’s offering.

If, then, we wish to be heard swiftly by God and to have our gifts gratefully accepted by him, we must certainly live in peace. The Truth itself deigned to instruct us about this: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” he says, “and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24).

### 4. Peace and unity often commended in Scripture

Since God desires our unity and concord, the Savior himself shows this in the Gospel, speaking thus to the Father: “Holy Father,” he says, “keep in your name those whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John 17:11). Hence the Apostle also exhorts the faithful, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, to think the same thing and all to say one thing” (1 Corinthians 1:10); and again: “Let there be no jealousy and strife among you” (Romans 13:13). “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice” (Ephesians 4:30). Elsewhere he says: “Bearing with one another in charity, eager to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (ibid. 4:2–4).

This unanimity, therefore, existed formerly under the Apostles. Thus the new people of believers, keeping the Lord’s commandments, maintained their charity. Scripture proves this when it says: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32); and again: “They all continued steadfastly with one accord in prayer, with the women and Mary, who was the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1:14). Therefore they prayed with effective prayers; therefore they could confidently obtain whatever they requested from God’s mercy.

### 5. The diminishing of charity, the failure of faith

Among us, however, unanimity has diminished to such an extent that the generosity of our deeds has also been weakened. At that time they sold their houses and, storing up treasures for themselves in heaven, offered the proceeds to the Apostles for distribution to the needs of the poor (Acts 2:45). But now we do not even give tithes from our property; and although the Lord commands us to sell, we instead buy and increase our possessions. Thus the vigor of faith has withered in us; thus the strength of believers has grown weak.

Therefore the Lord, looking upon our times, says in his Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). We see what he foretold taking place. Faith exists in the fear of God, in obedience to the law of justice, in love, and in works. No one considers the fear of future things. No one considers the Lord’s day and anger, the punishments destined for unbelievers, or the eternal torments appointed for the faithless—things our conscience would fear if it believed. Because it does not believe, it does not fear at all; but if it believed, it would beware, and if it were wary, it would escape.

### 6. Vigilance

Let us rouse ourselves as much as we can, most beloved brothers, and, breaking away from the sleep of our former sluggishness, let us keep watch over the Lord’s commandments, observing and carrying them out. Let us be such as he himself commanded us to be, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning; and be like men waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:35–37).

We ought to be girded, so that when the day of departure comes, it may not find us hindered and entangled. Let our light shine and gleam in good works, so that this very light may lead us from the night of this world to the light of eternal charity. There, with Christ, who is the author of true peace, and with his holy angels, may we enjoy eternal peace and everlasting happiness; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCIX

[Note: [Col. 1934] Formerly, *On the Words of the Apostle* 26; later, in the Appendix, 10.]

On the words of Acts, chapter 3:1–8: “Peter and John were going up into the temple,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1934] By an uncertain author, who appears to have transferred a fair amount here from Augustine; perhaps he is no different from the author who wrote Sermons 3, 7, and 23. Indeed, just as we read in Sermon 3, section 1, “A new kind of trial, to impose exile on one who possesses property”; in Sermon 7, section 1, “A new kind of commandment is to give a man a law of crime”; and in Sermon 23, section 3, “A new kind of miracle: the daughter of a parricide showed mercy”—so here too we have, in section 3, “Gold is then more beneficial in a new way, when it is despised.” The rest of the style is likewise not inconsistent. The same may be said of Sermon 135, in which we similarly find, in section 4, “By a new kind of sanctification, the water did not so much wash Christ as was itself washed.”]

### 1. Praise of evangelical poverty

After Christ’s resurrection, the reading you heard explained by whose works the Apostles’ preaching was fortified. “Peter and John,” it says, “went up into the temple”; through signs they prepared the material for their discourse—that is, for their preaching. Amazement ought to precede, so that an explanation of the wondrous event might follow. The brilliance [Note: [Col. 1934] In most manuscripts, “flash.”] of the signs therefore struck the hearts of the people.

For there was a certain man lame from birth, who was carried in people’s hands and, as it says, begged at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. When he saw the Apostles entering, he customarily asked them for alms. But when they turned their gaze toward him, the lame man, expecting nothing beyond the familiar consolation, believed that a paltry gift would flow from the Apostles’ hands. The Apostle Peter said to him: “Look at us.” When he had looked at them, he said: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk.”

We must carefully explain the order of these words. For once the riches of virtues were to follow, there would have been no point in mentioning poverty of means unless the Apostle wished to present the virtue together with his own testimony. So that you would not be amazed at the possessor of virtues, he first professed his renunciation of riches. It rightly followed that the one who had despised wealth should bestow signs. What is richer than this poverty? What is poorer than this virtue?

A profession of poverty therefore follows as testimony to virtue. Hence the Apostle also said: “As having nothing, and possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10). What, then, is richer than this poverty? “Silver and gold I do not have.” But what does the one who has no silver possess? A forceful utterance, an utterance purified by fire. The one who has no gold possesses faith.

### 2. The low value of gold. Why it is so deeply hidden

Let us see what more brightly glitters than gold, which is so hidden that nature seems deliberately to have condemned it for human beings and not exposed it to the eyes of the greedy, lest they should be inflamed. To assist poverty by making wealth difficult to obtain, nature made what it did not wish to be found difficult to seek. Let us therefore see: what does the one who has no gold possess? He possesses faith; he possesses virtue.

Let us weigh what we have said. What more brightly glitters than gold, which hardship seeks, greed desires, and anxiety guards? Gold is the material of labors, a dangerous thing for its possessors; gold is the weakening of virtues, a bad master, a treacherous servant. What, then, does the one who has no gold possess? He possesses faith.

Let us see, as we said, what more brightly glitters than gold, which no one safely possesses unless he always hides it; gold that shines to the ruin of its master; gold sought through darkness and guarded through darkness; gold whose pursuit condemns those who pursue it; gold whose love made Judas—and, so that no one may be unfamiliar with the name, an apostolic traitor; gold that is preferred to Christ in the avaricious heart. Against the desire for it the Teacher of the Gentiles thundered with fitting authority, saying: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5:5).

What, then, more brightly glitters than gold, which a sordid master possesses; gold that torments most severely the one who has the most of it; gold that permits the one who loves it nothing of his own possession, returning his guilt to him while the heavy acquisition, the burdensome possession, denies him its use [Note: [Col. 1935] Thus Lovaniensis and Erasmus. But Amerbach, with the manuscripts, reads “heavy accusation.”]?

### 3. The use of gold is condemned, not its nature. It is dangerously possessed and profitably renounced

Yet when we say these things, God’s creation is not condemned. Rather, because human judgment, blinded, has accepted gold as something of great value, whatever is acquired through evil desire now redounds to the object’s disgrace. Thus the thing is blamed so that avarice may be condemned.

In any case, the Lord says through the prophet: “The gold and silver are mine” (Haggai 2:9). But if the thing were evil in itself, it could not belong to God. Instead, it provides material for mercy in good hearts; and in a new way it is then more beneficial when it is despised, so that its very condition may testify that possession of the thing whose renunciation is fruitful is evil.

It therefore provides material for helping others: “He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Psalm 111:9). Do you wish to know how truly gold and silver are the possessions of a just judge? Through them the avaricious person is tormented; through them the merciful person is helped. Let the despising of the object therefore be practiced through a useful renunciation. Not everyone is suited to possess it; everyone is suited to despise it.

No one, therefore, can fail to be counted among those who scattered and gave to the poor, whose righteousness remains forever; no one who wishes to please God through contempt for fleeting things can fail to be counted among them.

### 4. The value of poverty

The condition of Christians is one of great happiness, since the splendor of the kingdom is placed in poverty [Col. 1936]. To possess what is sought with labor belongs to a few; to despise what may be despised with profit belongs to all. Great, then, is the happiness of Christians, to whom it has been granted to purchase the kingdom of heaven through poverty.

Do not be displeased with your poverty: nothing richer than it can be found. Do you wish to know how wealthy it is? It purchases heaven. With what treasures could what we see granted to poverty be compared? If a rich person wished to enter the kingdom of heaven, he could not obtain it through his possessions; now he obtains it by reaching it through contempt for them.

Faith therefore shines far more brightly than gold. Gold grows dark in its hiding places, a friend to darkness [Note: [Col. 1936] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “mind.”]; faith is conspicuous with its inborn splendor. Gold cannot safely be brought into the open; faith always shines for the public good, and faith’s own confidence testifies to its dignity. Gold is not safe even among those who agree with one another; faith is secure even among those who are fighting.

### 5. The poor man’s riches

What, then, the Apostle, poor in wealth but rich in faith, gave is proclaimed by the order of the reading: “Silver and gold I do not have.” But what does he have instead? “What I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.”

Let the value of things be assessed by their effects. Those who gave gold filled the poor man’s belly, which would become a greater burden for his weak feet; they relieved his distress but could not restore health. The one who possessed no gold, however, gave health. He is rich in God, poor in gold. “Silver and gold I do not have”; for this very reason he displayed such great riches of virtues.

“What I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” This was plainly held not in a purse but in the heart. What did he give him? “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” The infirmity feared the poor man, though by an equal law and equal power it binds kings and captives; it could not withstand the command of the poor man who ruled over kings. It is too little to call it infirmity: even nature could not endure the poor man’s command.

For the man had been lame from his mother’s womb. The weakness that birth had imposed upon him was driven out by the power of the poor man’s command. This certainly would not have happened unless the poor Apostle had been filled with that God who is the author of nature.

Nothing, therefore, is richer than this poverty. What does the one who has no bronze give? He bestows virtue; he confers it freely. For what can he not do? “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.”

What came by necessity is subjected to obedience. The man is told, “Rise,” which he had always desired; but because he was hindered by natural bonds, he could not do what he wished. Now, however, insensible things serve with such ease that at the command of the one ordering it, the infirmity flew away from his feet. “Rise and walk.” And, it says, “he immediately rose and stood.” The command is given to the mind, and the feet serve. “They shall leap,” says the prophet, “like calves released from their bonds” (Malachi 4:2).

### 6. The speed of the resurrection

And the bases of his feet were strengthened. Observe how swiftly the event took place. The words of the one commanding had scarcely entered the invalid’s ears when the power of health immediately rushed in, and, the infirmity expelled, his limbs were restored to use. The speed with which the one rising from weakness rose is testimony to the speed of resurrection.

“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). Measure future things by things already done. Believe the natural footsteps of the weak, and you will understand in what brief moment the dead will be raised.

“He rose; the bases of his feet,” it says, “were strengthened.” It was not enough to say that the lame man had returned to use: strength was restored to him along with health. For it did not say, “They were restored,” but “the bases were strengthened.” They receive such abundant health that they can endure exertion.

“He leaped,” it says, “and walked.” A leap is often burdensome even for the healthy. Those feet did not experience sluggish remedies, nor were their footsteps recalled as though merely smeared with ointment. The power of the medicine rushing in is revealed in an instant, and the flight of the expelled infirmity is marked. Thus does the one healed by the poor man leap.

### 7. Flesh is of good nature and from God. All vice lies in the will

The flesh, then, is healed by the Apostles, thereby indicating what it deserves from its God the Creator. Let the Manichaeans therefore be refuted by all these signs: every kind of salvation conferred upon the flesh is testimony to its good nature. What is shown worthy of divine work is proved worthy of benefits, since it is not believed unworthy of them.

The limbs recognize the name of their author when they are told: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” If the flesh were from the devil, it could have feared Christ’s name. The obedience of the healed is testimony to the Creator: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” Nature had imposed the weakness; the authority of the invoked name is directed toward that very weakness. The flesh recognizes the one who commanded, obeys its Lord, and resists the adversary.

If the flesh is from the devil, it must be conquered by Christ’s disciples, not healed. If you ask reason, whatever is hostile must be bound. I do not want you to trust only your own reflection on this; let divine authority support this understanding. The Lord says in the Gospel: “No one enters the house of the strong man to plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matthew 12:29).

The devil therefore had to be bound in his own works. But now the devil is not bound; rather, he is honored if his property is healed by signs. Christ would be greatly indebted to the flesh for a benefit if he demonstrated in its salvation what he is able to do. There would be no material for this discourse if healed flesh had not provided testimony to mercy. The flesh supports Christ’s preaching; in it the administration of signs takes place.

The lame man rises so that the Apostles may speak. We have said that if the flesh were not the work of this God, the lame man ought not to have been healed in his feet but bound in his arms. Now, however, the lame man rises so that the Apostles may speak, and becomes the forerunner of their preaching. The lame man leaps so that Christ’s Gospel may resound.

The Apostles acted shamelessly if the flesh were not the work of their God. But since saying that is sacrilege, the Apostles do not act shamelessly. The flesh, then, is God’s work: when it is formed, it is God’s work; when it is created, it is God’s work; when it is brought forth, it is God’s work; when it is regenerated, it is God’s work; when it is marked, it is God’s work; when it is healed, it is God’s work.

How often, then, does God’s possession owe anything to the devil? Let the Manichaeans therefore be mocked, and, for the honor of God, let the nature of the flesh be praised. Let every vice be placed in the will, and let hope of correction be suggested to human beings, so that they may understand that they sin not through the necessity of the flesh but solely through the perversity of the will.

We, however, attribute the flesh to God’s work. We see that in Christ’s resurrection it has attained the glory of divine fellowship, which it received from Christ its Creator, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON C

[Note: [Col. 1937] Formerly, *On the Words of the Apostle* 25; later, in the Appendix, 9.]

On the words of Acts, chapter 4:32–35: “No one said that anything of what he possessed was his own.”

[Note: [Col. 1937] It also appears among the sermons of Ambrose and Maximus. Vinding considers it to be Maximus’s after the Louvain editors.]

### 1. The fervent charity of the first believers. The brotherhood of charity is greater than that of blood

We read in the book attributed to the Acts of the Apostles that among the men just mentioned there was such devotion among the people, and that the beginnings of the Christian people flourished so greatly, that after receiving the faith no one claimed his own house for himself and no one asserted anything as his own. Rather, by the law of brotherhood, everything was held in common among them: namely, those who were held together by the same fellowship of religion should also enjoy the same fellowship of life. That is, those who had one faith should have one substance, and those who had Christ in common should also have their means in common.

For religious men considered it wrong not to admit as a sharer in their possessions one who was a sharer in grace. Therefore they all used their possessions together in the brotherhood of charity—except that Christ’s brotherhood is greater than brotherhood by blood. Brotherhood by blood reflects only a bodily likeness; Christ’s brotherhood demonstrates unanimity of heart and soul, as it is written: “The heart and soul of the believers were one.”

He, therefore, is truly a brother who is a brother both in body and in unanimity; truly, he is a brother whose spirit and will are the same in his brother. As I said, Christ’s brotherhood is better than brotherhood by blood, because the latter is sometimes hostile to itself, whereas Christ’s brotherhood is peaceful without interruption. The former divides what it holds in common with rivalry; the latter shares even with rejoicing. The former often despises its kinsman in fellowship; the latter frequently takes in a stranger.

As I said, the devotion of the Christian people at that time was so great that no one called his house his own, and no one claimed anything as his own, as Saint Luke says: “No one said that anything of what he possessed was his own.” For, I say, there was no needy person among them.

Blessed, then, is the people who, while having many rich in Christ, has no needy person in the world; who, while thinking upon eternal riches, drove temporal poverty away from the brothers. For, as Scripture says, they sold their estates and houses and placed the proceeds of what they had sold at the Apostles’ feet, so that it might be distributed according to each person’s need.

Observe the faith of these holy men: how, for Christ’s sake, they stripped themselves of their entire property and left nothing for themselves. They did not fear that they themselves would hunger while fearing that someone else might hunger.

### 2. Charity now growing cold. A truly rich person is scarcely found

This, then, was the devotion of the people under the Apostles. What similar thing do we find now? Certainly the same Christ is among us, but not the same spirit is among us. The same faith exists among the people, but the same generosity is not found among the people.

Thus one person gives no thought to another’s poverty, so that what the Apostle says is true: “One is hungry, while another is drunk” (1 Corinthians 11:21). For many Christians not only fail to distribute their own possessions; they also seize what belongs to others. They not only fail to gather their money and lay it at the Apostles’ feet; they even pull their brothers away when they flee to the priests’ feet.

Now is the time described by the blessed Apostle when he says: “In the last days the iniquity of many will abound, and charity will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). For now avarice and iniquity abound, though previously they were restrained by the goodness of generosity; and the charity of brotherhood grows cold, though formerly it burned with love of Christ.

The love of brotherhood under the Apostles was so great that at that time no need was found in their assembly. Now, however, there is such indifference among Christians that in our gathering you can scarcely find a wealthy person. By “wealthy” I do not mean one who is scarcely found in possessions, but one who is scarcely found in deeds. For the Apostle says: “Let them be rich in good works” (1 Timothy 6:18). He wished the wealthy person in the Church to be understood as one who is rich in Christ.

For when he says that under the Apostles no one was needy, he clearly shows that they were all endowed with such abundant grace through faith that they all overflowed with the generosity of heavenly riches. Rarely, then, do we find a wealthy person among the Christian people in this age. And even if many are rich in gold in their houses, in the Church they are beggars in righteousness.

### 3. Almsgiving Given Without Generosity. Ananias Guilty of Fraud and Sacrilege

For when people do not act toward the poor in proportion to their means, neither is what they offer pleasing, nor is what they retain sufficient. The Lord says to Cain, when he was offering gifts: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint). So too you, Christian, do not divide rightly, since from your great store of gold you keep for Mammon a larger portion than you give to the Lord.

Thus Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles, while thinking that he was making a proper offering but not dividing properly, lost the money he offered and forfeited what he had kept at home: he lost, I say, both his money and his salvation. For when he withdrew a portion from what he had promised, he was condemned at once for sacrilege and fraud: for sacrilege, because he had deceived God in his promise; for fraud, because he had thought that a certain portion could be withheld from a complete offering. For the apostle Peter says: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts 5:4).

If, then, brothers, Ananias is condemned because he did not give all that he himself had promised from his own possessions, what should we think of one who does not wish to fulfill what he has promised to others? Consider, therefore, brothers, what you promised God when you first received the grace of faith. Look: visitors abound in our city. Do what you promised, lest it also be said to you what was said to Ananias: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God.”

[Col. 1939]

## SERMON CI

[Note: Formerly numbered 45 among the Homilies 50, and later placed in Appendix 19.]

### On the words of Acts, chapter 10:1–28: “Peter went up to the upper room about the sixth hour, and when he was hungry, he wished to taste,” etc.

[Note: In the manuscripts this sermon bears the title: “Extracts from the work of Saint Augustine the bishop, on the vision of the blessed apostle Peter and on Cornelius the centurion”—that is, from Sermon 149 among Augustine’s sermons, which in earlier editions was Sermon 26 among the sermons On Various Subjects. A preface and a recapitulation were added to these extracts.]

### 1. What the Clean and Unclean Animals Signify. Who Belongs to the Church. Why the Church Reads the Jewish Precepts. Christian Food. The Vessel Shown to Peter as the Church

When the reading from the Acts of the Apostles was being read just now, we heard that the blessed Peter went up to the upper room about the sixth hour; and when he was hungry, he wished to taste some food. While the disciples were preparing it, he fell into an ecstasy of mind, and saw a large vessel, like a great linen cloth, being let down from heaven, suspended by its four corners, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth. And a voice sounded from heaven: “Peter, kill and eat.” But he said: “Lord, you know that I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” And the voice came again: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.” This happened three times, and the vessel was taken back into heaven.

What these things signify, then, we desire, if you command it, briefly to explain to the ears of Your Charity. All the animals that the Jews were forbidden to eat are signs of realities and, as it has been said, “shadows of things to come”: for example, the command given to them that they should eat those animals that chew the cud and have a divided hoof, but that they should not eat those in which one or both of these features were lacking (Deut. 14:6–7).

In these animals certain human beings are signified who do not belong to the fellowship of the saints: the divided hoof pertains to conduct, while chewing the cud pertains to wisdom. Why does the divided hoof pertain to conduct? Because it slips with difficulty; for a fall is a sign of sin. How does chewing the cud pertain to the wisdom of doctrine? Because Scripture says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it” (Prov. 21:20). Whoever hears and then, through negligence, becomes forgetful is like one who swallows what he has heard, so that it no longer has savor in his mouth, burying the hearing itself in forgetfulness. But whoever meditates on the law of the Lord day and night is like one who chews the cud, delighting in the flavor of the word upon a kind of palate of the heart.

What was therefore commanded to the Jews signifies that those who are either negligent hearers, or have evil conduct, or are reproved for both faults, do not belong to the Church—that is, to the body of Christ, to grace, and to the fellowship of the saints. Thus the other commands given to the Jews in this manner are symbolic representations of things to come.

After the Lord our Jesus Christ, the light of the world, came, these commands are read only so that they may be understood, not also so that they may be observed. Christians have therefore been granted permission not to act according to this empty custom, but to eat whatever they wish, with moderation, with blessing, and with thanksgiving.

Perhaps, then, Peter was also told, “Kill and eat,” so that he would no longer maintain the observance of the Jews; yet he was not commanded to become a glutton or to indulge in filthy voracity. Nevertheless, so that you may understand that this was shown to him in a symbolic figure, there were reptiles in that vessel. Could he possibly eat snakes? What, then, does this signification mean?

[Col. 1940]

### 2. The Animals as the Gentiles. Peter Represents the Figure of the Church

That vessel signifies the Church; the four corners by which it hung signify the four parts of the world through which the Catholic Church extends, since it has been spread everywhere. Whoever, therefore, wishes to go off into one part and, through some heresy, to be cut off from the whole does not belong to the sacrament of the four corners. But if he does not belong to Peter’s vision, neither will he belong to the keys that were given to Peter.

For that vessel was let down by four corners because God says that at the end his saints will be gathered from the four winds (Mark 13:27); for now the evangelical faith is spreading over all these four cardinal regions.

The animals, then, are the Gentiles. For all the Gentiles were unclean through errors, superstitions, and their own desires before Christ came; but when he came, their sins were forgiven and they were made clean. Why, then, should they no longer be received into the body of Christ, which is the Church of God, whose person Peter represented?

Peter is shown in many places to represent the person of the Church. If Peter represented the figure of the Church, and the Church is the body of Christ, let it receive into itself, as into its food, the Gentiles who have now been cleansed and whose sins have been forgiven.

### 3. The Killing and Eating of the Gentiles

For this reason Cornelius, a Gentile, sent to Peter; Cornelius’s almsgiving, having been accepted, had cleansed him in a certain manner, together with those who were with him; what remained was that, like clean food, they should be incorporated into the Church, that is, into the body of the Lord.

Peter, however, hesitated to deliver the Gospel to the Gentiles, because those who had believed from the circumcision were forbidding the apostles to give the Christian faith to the uncircumcised. They said that the latter ought not to approach participation in the Gospel unless they had received the circumcision that had been handed down to their fathers.

That vessel therefore removed Peter’s hesitation. After the vision, he was instructed by the Holy Spirit to descend and go with those who had come from Cornelius, and he went.

Cornelius and those who were with him were regarded as belonging to the animals displayed in the vessel; yet God had already cleansed them, since he had accepted their almsgiving. They were therefore to be killed and eaten—that is, the former life in them, in which they had not known Christ, was to be put to death, and they were to pass into his body as into a new life in the fellowship of the Church.

When Peter himself came to them, he briefly recalled what had been shown to him in that vision. For he said: “You know how unlawful it is for a Jewish man to join himself to or approach foreigners; but God has shown me that I should call no human being common or unclean.” God had surely shown this then, when that voice sounded: “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”

### 4. The Linen Cloth as a Symbol of Incorruption. Let Down Three Times from Heaven as a Mystery of the Trinity. The Four Corners as the Four Regions of the World

Perhaps the question may also be asked why the cloth in which those animals were contained was linen. This was certainly not without reason. For we know that the moth does not consume linen, although it corrupts other garments. Therefore whoever wishes to belong to the mystery of the Catholic Church must remove from his heart the corruption of evil desires, and must be established so incorruptibly in the faith that he is not penetrated by perverse thoughts as by moths, if he wishes to belong to the sacrament of that linen cloth by which the Church is signified.

But why was it let down from heaven three times, unless because all the Gentiles are baptized in the name of the Trinity? They belong to the four regions of the earth through which the Church is spread, signified by the four corners by which that vessel was fastened. Believers are renewed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that they may belong to the fellowship and communion of the saints.

Thus the four corners signify the four regions of the world, while the threefold descent displays the mystery of the Trinity. This event also indicates the number twelve of the apostles, as though they were assigned in groups of three to the four regions: for four times three makes twelve. And because the twelve apostles were to preach the mystery of the Trinity throughout the four regions of the earth, the four corners were let down from heaven a third time.

[Col. 1941]

### 5. Recapitulation

As was said above, the blessed Peter bore the type of the Catholic Church. That he went up to the rooftop signifies that the Church was to rise spiritually above earthly desires and have its heart above, according to what the Apostle said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

That Peter was hungry signified that the Church would hunger for the salvation of the Gentiles. That linen cloth let down from heaven signified the Church. The animals that were in the cloth bore the image of all the nations. The four corners by which the vessel hung seem to have signified the four regions of the world in which the Gospel of Christ is preached.

That the vessel was let down a third time signified the mystery of the Trinity and the sacrament of Baptism. What was said to Peter, “Kill and eat,” signified that the Catholic Church would first kill and afterward eat all who believe in Christ—that is, it would kill unbelief in them in order to implant faith.

No one can believe in Christ unless he first dies to what he was, according to what the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). Just as those who are ensnared by heretics are devoured alive by death, so those who come to Christ die to what is past so that they may live for what is to come; they perish to the devil and are acquired for Christ; they die to death and are happily grafted into life.

Let us beseech God in continual prayers that divine mercy may deign to fulfill and confirm this also in us, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CII

[Note: Formerly On Time 43, and later placed in Appendix 31.]

### On the words of the Apostle, Romans, chapter 7:15: “For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate”

[Note: The beginning is indeed Augustine’s, extracted from his Sermon 151; but what follows thereafter differs greatly from his manner of interpretation. Nevertheless, it is the work of a learned and devout author.]

### 1. Care Must Be Taken Lest the Apostle’s Passage Be Misunderstood

Whenever the divine reading from the Epistle of the apostle Paul is recited, we must fear that, if badly understood, it may give an opportunity to people who are looking for an opportunity. Human beings are inclined toward sin and scarcely restrain themselves. When, therefore, they hear the Apostle saying, “For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate,” they do evil and, as though displeased with themselves because they do evil, think that they are like the Apostle, who said, “For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will.”

This passage is read from time to time, and now it imposes upon us the necessity of discussing it, lest people who receive a salutary food wrongly turn it into poison. Let Your Charity therefore pay attention until I tell you what the Lord grants me, so that when you perhaps see me laboring amid the difficulty of some obscurity, you may assist me by the devotion of your affection.

[Note: Up to this point, Augustine.]

We must therefore measure the meaning of the virtues from the innermost disposition of the speaker. What the blessed Apostle called good, and what he pronounced evil in comparison with it, must be examined not by the bare meaning of the words, but with the same outlook with which he examined it. We must pronounce its meaning according to its dignity and search out its merit.

For we shall then be able to comprehend the statements spoken under God’s inspiration according to his purpose and will, when, weighing the condition and merit of those by whom they were proclaimed, we have adopted—not merely in words, but in experience—a corresponding disposition. According to the quality of that disposition, all meanings are undoubtedly either conceived or expressed.

### 2. What Is the Good That the Apostle Could Not Perfect? The Merit of Contemplation. Things Good in Themselves Cease to Appear Good When Compared with a Greater Good

[Col. 1942]

Let us therefore investigate more carefully what is principally the good that the Apostle could not perfect when he wished to do so. We know many good things that we cannot deny the blessed Apostle, and all men of his merit, both possessed by nature and acquired through grace.

Chastity is good, continence praiseworthy, prudence admirable, kindness generous, sobriety watchful, temperance modest, mercy devout, and justice holy. There is no doubt that all these qualities were so full and perfect in the apostle Paul and his companions that religion was taught by them more through the authority of their virtues than through their words.

What shall we say of the constant care of all the churches and the unceasing vigilance by which they were always consumed? How great a good of mercy, how great a perfection it is to burn for those who are scandalized and to become weak with those who are weak!

Since, then, the Apostle abounded in such great goods, what is that good whose perfection he lacked? We shall not be able to recognize it unless we advance into the disposition in which he himself spoke.

All the virtues we have mentioned, although they are like splendid and precious gems, nevertheless, if they are compared with that renowned and supreme pearl which the Gospel merchant sought and desired to purchase by selling all that he possessed, their worth becomes so diminished and despised that, once they have been sold without hesitation, possession of that one good enriches the seller of countless goods.

What, then, is that one thing which is set so incomparably above such great and innumerable goods that, when all the others have been despised and rejected, it alone ought to be possessed?

Surely it is that better portion whose magnificence and perpetuity Mary chose when she left aside the task of hospitality and service. It is praised by the Lord in these words: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but few things are necessary, or even one. Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

There is therefore one and only one contemplation of God, to which, rightly, all the merits of justification and every pursuit of virtue are subordinated.

All those things that we said shone in the apostle Paul are not only good and useful, but also great and illustrious. Yet, just as the metal tin, which was thought to possess some usefulness and value, becomes very cheap in comparison with silver, and silver in turn loses its worth in comparison with gold, and gold itself is despised when compared with gems, and the multitude of gems, however distinguished, is surpassed by the brightness of a single pearl—so all those merits of human capacity, although they are not only good and useful in the present but also acquire the gift of eternity, will nevertheless be judged cheap and, so to speak, saleable when compared with the merits of divine contemplation.

### 3. Why Created Things Are Very Good. Yet Why They Are Vanity

To confirm this same comparison by the authority of Scripture, does Scripture not say generally concerning all things created by God: “And behold, all the things that God made were very good” (Gen. 1:31); and again: “All the works of God are good in their season” (Ecclus. 3:11)?

These things, then, which in the present are pronounced not only simply good but, with an added qualification, very good—for they truly are useful to us who dwell in this world, whether for the necessities of life, the healing of the body, or some purpose of usefulness unknown to us; or, certainly, they are very good also because through them they cause us to perceive the invisible things of God, understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20), and to contemplate his eternal power and divinity from so great and well-ordered a structure of the world and of all that exists within it—nevertheless, none of these things will retain the name of good if they are compared with that future age in which there is no alteration of good things and no corruption of true blessedness to be feared.

The blessedness of that world is described thus: “The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26).

Great, therefore, illustrious, and wonderful as these things are when viewed and compared with the future promises made in faith [Col. 1943], they will immediately appear vanity, as David says: “They shall all grow old like a garment, and as a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:27–28).

Since, therefore, nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, and nothing good except the Godhead alone, while all creatures will obtain the blessedness of eternity or immutability not through their own nature but through participation in the grace of their Creator, they cannot retain the merit of goodness when compared with their Creator.

### 4. Human Goodness Is Evil in Comparison with Divine Goodness

If we wish to establish the reasoning of this statement with still clearer testimonies, do we not read in the Gospel that many things are called good, including a good tree and a good treasure? It speaks of a good person and a good servant: “A good tree,” it says, “cannot bear evil fruit” (Matt. 7:18); “A good person brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (ibid. 12:35); and, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (ibid. 25:21).

There is no doubt that all these are good according to their own nature. Yet if we look to the goodness of God, none of them is called good, since the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19).

In view of this goodness, even the apostles, who by the merit of their election had surpassed the goodness of the human race in many ways, are called evil by the Lord, who speaks to them as follows: “If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (ibid. 11:13).

Finally, just as our goodness is turned into evil when compared with heavenly goodness, so our justice, when compared with divine justice, is judged like a menstrual cloth; the prophet Isaiah says: “All our righteousness is like a menstrual cloth” (Isa. 64:6).

### 5. The Law Is Good in Itself, but Not Good in Comparison with the Gospel. Scripture Justifies Those Who Sin Less by Comparison with the Wicked

To add something still more evident, even the life-giving precepts of the Law itself—which are said to have been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator (Gal. 3:19), and concerning which the same Apostle says, “Thus the Law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. 7:12)—are declared not good by the divine oracle when compared with evangelical perfection.

For he says: “I gave them commands that were not good, and ordinances by which they would not live” (Ezek. 20:25).

The Apostle likewise asserts that the glory of the Law is so dimmed by the light of the New Testament that, in comparison with the splendor of the Gospel, he declares that it was not glorified, saying: “For even that which was glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Cor. 3:10).

Scripture preserves this comparison also in the opposite direction—that is, in the balancing of the merits of sins—so that it justifies those who have sinned much less by comparison with the wicked. It says: “Sodom was justified in comparison with you” (Ezek. 16:52); and again: “For what sin did your sister Sodom commit?” (ibid. 16:48); and: “Apostate Israel has justified herself in comparison with sinful Judah” (Jer. 3:11).

Thus also the merits of all the virtues that I described above, although they are good and precious in themselves, are darkened in comparison with the radiance of contemplation. For they greatly draw and hold back even holy people, occupied though they are with good works, from contemplation of that supreme good.

## SERMON CIII

[Note: Formerly On Time 47, and later placed in Appendix 32.]

### On the words of the Apostle, Romans, chapter 7:24–25: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person,” etc.

[Note: It presents exactly the same author as the preceding sermon, of which it seems to be a continuation.]

### 1. Even the Saints Have Constant Cause for Groaning. The Struggle of the Inner and Outer Person

Since the saints therefore feel themselves every day weighed down by the burden of earthly thought, falling from that elevation of mind [Col. 1944] and being carried, against their will—or rather, even without knowing it—into the law of sin and death, and since, to pass over everything else, they are drawn away from the presence of God by even those good and just things that I described above, though they are nevertheless earthly, they certainly have cause to groan continually to God.

They have cause to humble themselves and, truly contrite, to pronounce themselves sinners—not merely in words but in feeling—in order to ask continually for forgiveness from the Lord’s grace for all the things into which they fall daily, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, and to pour out unceasingly the true tears of repentance.

For they see that, entangled in those very things by which they are continually tormented with grief, they groan continually even to God, and that they cannot offer even their prayers without anxiety of thought.

Having therefore experienced that by human strength they cannot attain the faith they desire, because of the burden of the flesh, nor unite themselves to that chief and supreme good according to the desire of their heart, but are led captive from its contemplation to worldly things, they flee to the grace of God, who justifies the ungodly, and with the Apostle they proclaim: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

They feel that they cannot perfect the good they desire, but that what they do not desire and hate—the evil, that is, the movements of thought and concern for bodily matters—continually intrudes.

They delight, indeed, in the law of God according to the inner person, who, transcending all visible things, strives always to be united with God alone. But they see another law in their members—that is, implanted in the nature of the human condition—which fights against the law of their mind and drags their understanding by the violent law of sin, compelling them, having abandoned that principal good, to submit to earthly thought.

Although this may appear necessary and useful to the body when it is expended in the service of some religious necessity, nevertheless, in comparison with that good which delights the contemplation of all the saints, it is judged by them to be evil and something to be avoided, since through it they are in any way, even for a brief time, held back from the joy of that perfect blessedness.

### 2. The Law of Sin Is Universal

Truly it is the law of sin that the transgression of its author brought upon the human race, through the guilt of the one against whom the sentence of the most just judge was pronounced: “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat your bread in the sweat of your face” (Gen. 3:17–19).

This, I say, is the law implanted in the members of all mortals, which fights against the law of our mind and keeps it from the contemplation of God. After the knowledge of good and evil, this cursed earth began to bring forth thorns and thistles of thought in our works. Their spines choke the seeds by dulling the flesh, so that we cannot eat without the sweat of our face that bread of ours which came down from heaven and strengthens the human heart.

The whole human race is therefore subjected generally to this law without exception. No one, however holy, receives the bread mentioned above without the sweat of his face and the attentive concentration of his heart. Yet, as we see, many rich people eat this ordinary bread without any sweat of their face.

The blessed Apostle also declares this law to be spiritual, saying: “For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14).

The law is spiritual because it commands us to eat, in the sweat of our face, that true bread which came down from heaven; but that sale under sin made us carnal.

### 3. Adam Sold His Liberty. Hence His Descendants Are Born Slaves

What, I ask, is this, and whose sin is it? Without doubt, Adam’s. Through his transgression and, so to speak, his ruinous bargaining and fraudulent exchange, we were sold.

For, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion and by eating the forbidden food, he handed over all his offspring, alienated, to the yoke of perpetual slavery. It is customary, indeed, between seller and buyer that one who wishes to surrender himself to another’s dominion receives from his purchaser some payment as the price for the loss of his own liberty and the imposition of perpetual [Col. 1945] servitude.

We see this fulfilled most clearly between Adam and the serpent. Adam received from the serpent the price of his liberty by eating from the forbidden tree and departed from his natural freedom. He preferred to sell himself into perpetual servitude to the one from whom he had received the deadly price of the forbidden fruit. Bound thereafter by this condition, he not unjustly subjected all the offspring of his posterity to perpetual service to the one whose slave he had become.

For what else can a servile marriage produce except slaves?

### 4. Yet the Lord Did Not Lose His Right by This. To Free a Person Against His Will Would Be Both Unjust and Evil

What then? Did that clever and crafty purchaser deprive the true and rightful Lord of his right of dominion? It is not so. He did not so seize all God’s possession through the deceitfulness of a single fraud that the true ruler lost the power of his dominion; for he also restrains that purchaser himself, though a fugitive and rebel, beneath the yoke of servitude.

But because the Creator had granted freedom of choice to all rational creatures, he ought not to force back into their innate liberty those who had sold themselves against the law through the transgression of greedy desire.

Whatever is contrary to goodness and equity is abhorrent to that author of justice and mercy. It would have been evil if he had withdrawn the benefit of the liberty he had granted; unjust if, by his power, he had oppressed and taken captive a free human being and had not allowed him to exercise the privilege of the liberty he had received.

He reserved that person’s salvation for future ages, so that the fullness of the appointed time might be completed in due order. His offspring had to remain under the ancestral condition until, freed from their original bonds, they might be restored by the grace of their former Lord to their ancient state of liberty at the price of his blood.

He could have saved them even then through an impulse of mercy, but he did not wish to do so, because equity did not permit him to violate the sanction of his decree.

### 5. Our Iniquity Was the Cause of Our Sale and an Obstacle to Redemption

Do you wish to know the cause of your sale? Hear your Redeemer himself proclaiming it most clearly through the prophet Isaiah: “Where is this bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities, and because of your crimes I dismissed your mother.”

Do you also wish to understand clearly why he did not wish to redeem you, though you were bound to the yoke of slavery, by the power of his might? Hear what he added to the preceding words, in which he reproves those same servants for the cause of their voluntary sale: “Has my hand been shortened and made too small, so that I cannot redeem? Or is there no strength in me to deliver?” (Isa. 50:1–2).

But the same prophet shows what has always stood in the way of his most powerful mercy: “Behold,” he says, “the Lord’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; nor is his ear burdened, that it cannot hear. But your iniquities have separated you from your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear” (ibid. 59:1–2).

### 6. The Power of the Law of Sin

Since that first curse of God made us carnal and condemned us to thorns and thistles, and since our father sold us through such an unjust bargain, so that we cannot do the good we wish to do—being separated from the memory of the supreme God and compelled to think about the things of human weakness—and since, while we burn with love of purity, we are often pricked against our will by natural impulses that we would wish utterly to ignore, we know that “good does not dwell in our flesh” (Rom. 7:18): that is, the perpetual and unbroken tranquility of the contemplation and purity of which we have spoken.

A most grievous and lamentable divorce has taken place, so that although we wish to serve the law of God with our mind and never willingly to turn our gaze away from divine charity, nevertheless, surrounded by carnal darkness, we are compelled by a certain law of sin to be drawn away from what we know to be good: namely, toward earthly cares and thoughts, falling from that elevation of mind to which the law of sin [Col. 1946]—that is, that sentence of God—justly condemned us, the sentence that the first transgressor received.

Hence the blessed Apostle, while openly confessing that he and all the saints are constrained by the unavoidable necessity of this sin, nevertheless boldly declares that none of them is to be condemned because of it, saying: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:1–2).

That is, the daily grace of Christ absolves all his saints from this law of sin and death, into which they are continually compelled to fall, even against their will, when they ask the Lord for forgiveness of their debts.

## SERMON CIV

[Note: Elsewhere, On the Saints 41.]

### On the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians, chapter 3:11–15: “No one can lay any other foundation,” etc.

[Note: It was the eighth homily of Caesarius in the Library of the Fathers.]

### 1. Only Minor Sins Are Purified by Fire

In the apostolic reading, dearly beloved brothers, we heard the Apostle say: “No one can lay any other foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire.”

There are many who, misunderstanding this reading, are deceived by false security, believing that if they build capital crimes upon the foundation of Christ, the sins themselves can be purified by a temporary fire and that they can afterward attain eternal life.

This interpretation, dearly beloved brothers, must be corrected, because those who flatter themselves in this way are deceiving themselves. By that temporary fire of which the Apostle said, “He himself will be saved, yet as through fire,” not capital sins but minor sins are purified.

And although—and this is worse—not only greater sins but even minor ones, if they are too numerous [Note: Perhaps “certainly” (*nimirum*).], overwhelm a person, we must mention at least some of these greater or lesser sins, even if not all, lest anyone try to excuse himself vainly and say that he does not know which are minor sins or which are criminal and capital sins.

[Note: Caesarius, in the Library of the Fathers, has: “which are criminal and capital.”]

### 2. Capital Sins

Although the Apostle has mentioned several capital sins, nevertheless, so that we may not seem to cause despair, we shall briefly state what they are: sacrilege, homicide, adultery, false testimony, theft, robbery, pride, envy, avarice; and anger, if it is maintained for a long time. Drunkenness too is counted among them if it is habitual.

Whoever recognizes that any of these sins dominates in him will not be able to be purified by that temporary fire of which the Apostle speaks unless he has corrected himself worthily, and, if he has had the opportunity, has done penance for a long time, distributed abundant alms, and abstained from the sins themselves. Otherwise the eternal flame will torment him without any remedy.

### 3. Minor Sins. No One Is Free from Them. They Do Not Kill the Soul, but Defile It

Although everyone knows what minor sins are, nevertheless, because it would take too long to repeat them all, it is necessary to name at least some of them. Whenever anyone takes more food or drink than is necessary, let him know that this belongs among minor sins. Whenever he speaks more than is proper, or is silent more than is useful. Whenever he irritates a poor person who is persistently begging. Whenever, while physically healthy, he wishes to eat lunch while others are fasting; or, devoted to sleep, rises late for church. Whenever [Col. 1947] he has intercourse with his wife for any reason other than the desire for children. Whenever he visits those shut up in prison and placed in chains later than he should. Whenever he visits the sick later than he should. If he neglects to restore those who are at odds to harmony. If he irritates a neighbor, wife, child, or servant more than is proper; if he flatters more than is useful. If he wishes to flatter any person of higher rank, whether voluntarily or from necessity. If he does not give food to the poor who are hungry; or if he prepares for himself excessively luxurious or costly banquets. If he occupies himself in church or outside church with idle tales, for which an account must be rendered on the day of judgment. If, while swearing carelessly, we are unable to fulfill what we have sworn through some necessity, then certainly we commit perjury. And when we curse with complete ease or recklessness, although it is written, “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI, 10). And when we rashly suspect something which nevertheless is usually not proved to be as we believe, we sin without any doubt.
