For there is no doubt that these things, and things like them, belong among minor sins. As I have already said, they can scarcely be enumerated, and not only the Christian people, but no saint, has ever been or can be entirely free from them. Although we do not believe that the soul is killed by these sins, they nevertheless make it ugly, filling it as if with pustules and with a dreadful scab, so that they scarcely permit it—or permit it only with great shame—to come into the embrace of that heavenly Bridegroom, of whom it is written: “He prepared for himself a Church without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27).

### 4. They Are Cleansed Either by Good Works, by Fire, or by Punishments Inflicted Here by God. The Benefit of Punishments Inflicted by God

And therefore they must continually be redeemed by prayers without interruption, by frequent fasts, by more generous almsgiving, and especially [Note: [Col. 1947] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* the word *praecipue*, “especially,” is omitted. And below, after the word *demergant*, the word *animam*, “the soul,” is missing.] through forgiveness toward those who sin against us, lest perhaps, gathered together all at once, they form a heap and sink the soul.

Whatever of these sins has not been redeemed by us must be cleansed by that fire of which the Apostle said: “Because it will be revealed in fire; and if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” Either, while we live in this world, we wear ourselves out through penitence; or certainly, when God wills or permits it, we are afflicted with many tribulations on account of these sins; and if we give thanks to God, we are freed.

This happens, for example, whenever a husband, wife, or child dies; or when property that we love more than we ought is taken away from us. Although we love Christ more than that property, and, if necessity demanded it, would prefer to lose the property rather than deny Christ, nevertheless, since—as I have already said—if we love it more than we ought, we cannot lose it, whether during life or at death, without great sorrow. Yet if we give thanks like good children to God, who like a loving father permits it to be taken away from us, and if we declare with true humility that we suffer less than we deserve, then those sins themselves are cleansed in this world, so that in the future that purifying fire either finds nothing, or at least very little, to burn.

But if we neither give thanks to God in tribulation nor redeem our sins through good works, we shall remain in that purgatorial fire for as long as the minor sins mentioned above, like wood, hay, and straw, are consumed.

### 5. The Nature of the Punishment of Purgatorial Fire

But someone may say: “It does not matter to me how long I remain there, provided that I proceed to eternal life.” Let no one say this, dearest brothers, because that purgatorial fire will be harsher than anything that can be imagined, seen, or felt as punishment in this world.

And since it is written concerning the day of judgment that “one day will be like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day” (Ps. LXXXIX, 4), [Col. 1948] how does anyone know whether he will pass through that fire for days, months, or perhaps even years? And whoever now does not wish to put even one of his fingers into a fire must necessarily fear being tortured there, even for a short time, with soul and entire body.

Therefore let everyone labor with all his strength to escape capital crimes and to redeem minor sins through good works in such a way that nothing of them seems to remain for that fire to consume.

But those who commit capital crimes, if they do not wish, as long as they live, to redeem them through the remedies of penitence, will not be able to come to that fire of which the Apostle says, “He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire,” as has already been said; rather, they will hear that harsh and irreversible sentence: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41).

Therefore those who desire to be freed from that perpetual punishment and from that purgatorial fire must not commit capital crimes; or, if they have already committed them, they must perform fruitful penitence and must not cease redeeming those small, daily sins through good works.

### 6. By What Works Minor Sins Are Redeemed

I desire to explain to you more fully by what works minor sins are redeemed. Whenever we visit the sick; seek out those shut up in prison and placed in chains; restore those who are at odds to harmony; fast when a fast has been proclaimed in the Church; wash the feet of guests; frequently assemble for vigils; give alms at the door to poor people passing by; forgive our enemies whenever they ask—by these works and similar ones, minor sins are redeemed every day.

### 7. By What Means Capital Sins Are Blotted Out. Public Penitence

For capital crimes, however, this alone is not sufficient. Tears, weeping, and groaning must be added; fasts must be continued and prolonged for a long time; more generous alms must be distributed [Note: [Col. 1948] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* there is added here: “even more than we ourselves are able to afford.”]; we must voluntarily remove ourselves from communion with the Church; remain for a long time in mourning and sadness; and also perform penitence publicly. For it is just that he who has destroyed himself together with the destruction of many should redeem himself together with the edification of many.

Finally, what I suggest is neither impossible nor burdensome: let us mourn our extinguished soul as we mourn the dead flesh of another. If a wife, child, or husband has died, people throw themselves upon the ground, pulling their hair and beating their breasts, and continue for no little time in mourning, penitence, and tears.

I beg you, brothers, let us show our soul what they show to another’s flesh. And observe this, brothers: how evil it is that we seek what we cannot do and do not seek what we can [Note: [Col. 1948] Thus Caesarius in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. But Augustine has: “that we mourn what we cannot raise up”—the flesh, and so forth.].

We mourn flesh that we cannot raise up, but we do not mourn our dead soul, which through penitence we can restore to its former condition. Worse still for us, we mourn a dead body that we love; but we neither grieve nor mourn the dead soul that we do not love.

Therefore, reversing our priorities, let us begin to love the Lord more than the servant—that is, the Maker of the body more than the body; the mistress more than the maidservant—that is, the soul made in the image of God more than the flesh formed from the mud of the earth. Thus, when on the last day our flesh begins to decay and be devoured by worms in the grave, may the soul be lifted into Abraham’s bosom by the hands of angels; and, on the day of judgment, having received the body through the resurrection, may we deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21).

[Col. 1949] ### 8. Recapitulation. The Threefold Lot of Human Beings at the Judgment

And so that what we have said above may remain more firmly fixed in your hearts, and so that the apostolic reading itself may be understood more fully, I wish briefly to repeat it for your Charity.

All the saints who faithfully serve God strive to devote themselves to reading and prayer and to persevere in good works. They neither build capital crimes nor minor sins—that is, wood, hay, and straw—upon the foundation of Christ; instead, building good works—that is, gold, silver, and precious stones—upon it, they will pass through that fire of which the Apostle says, “Because it will be revealed in fire,” without any injury [Note: [Col. 1949] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: “without violence.” In the Sorbonne manuscript: “without delay.”].

Those, however, who do not commit capital crimes but are ready to perpetrate minor sins and negligent about redeeming them, will come to eternal life because they believed in Christ and did not commit capital sins. But first they must either be purified in this world through the justice or mercy of God by the most bitter tribulations, as has already been said; or, through many alms, and especially by mercifully forgiving their enemies, they must be freed by God’s mercy; or else they must be tortured for a long time by that fire of which the Apostle speaks, so that they may reach eternal life without spot or wrinkle.

But those who have committed homicide, sacrilege, adultery, or other similar crimes, if worthy penitence does not come to their aid, as has already been said, will not deserve to pass through purgatorial fire into life; rather, they will be plunged into death by eternal burning.

### 9. We Must Strive, with God’s Help, to Avoid Greater Sins and to Redeem Minor Ones through Love of Enemies and Generous Almsgiving

Therefore, whenever you hear in the apostolic reading, “If anyone builds upon the foundation of Christ gold, silver, precious stones,” understand this of holy and perfect Christians, who, like purified gold, will deserve to attain eternal rewards.

But those who build wood, hay, and straw are to be understood, as has often been said, as good but negligent Christians who fail to cleanse their minor sins. If divine justice does not cleanse these sins through many tribulations, and if each person does not redeem them through generous almsgiving, then, not without great sorrow, what the Apostle says will be fulfilled in them: “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.”

Nevertheless, as has already been said above, let no one deceive himself into believing that this can also happen with capital crimes if they remain unhealed. Therefore, as I have often said, let us labor as much as we can, with God’s help, so that we may escape greater sins and continually redeem those minor sins without which we cannot exist, through love of our enemies and generous almsgiving.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 105

[Note: [Col. 1949] Formerly numbered 15 among the *Fifty Homilies*, and later placed in the Appendix as 17.]

On the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. XII, 26: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1949] In the manuscripts it is entitled as follows: “Extracts from the books of Augustine: how true and perfect love is to be preserved; and concerning the love of the members, how all the members serve when a thorn is stepped on.” The passages are excerpts of ideas, not words, and perhaps are by Caesarius. For nos. 1 and 2, see Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 130*, no. 6; for no. 3, *Exposition on Psalm 86*, no. 5; for no. 4, *Second Exposition on Psalm 30*, no. 3.]

### 1. The Mutual Love of the Members Teaches Love of One’s Neighbors

How we ought to love one another, dearest brothers, we can clearly recognize from the health or sickness of the bodily members. For if we wish to love one another as [Col. 1950] the members of our body love one another, perfect charity can be preserved in us.

Consider and see what happens to us physically when the head is healthy: how all the members rejoice together, and how the remaining members are pleased with each one. But, on the other hand, when one member suffers some harm, all the members suffer with it.

Look: the foot [Note: [Col. 1950] Some manuscripts read *spinam habet*, “has a thorn”; perhaps two others, which read *cavet*, “avoids,” should be corrected accordingly.] steps on a thorn. What is farther from the eyes than the foot? It is far away in place, but near in loving affection. The thorn pricks slightly and occupies a very small place in the foot; see how all the members turn toward that spot.

First, the back itself bends, and all the members lower themselves toward it. Do the eyes cease seeking? Do the ears cease hearing? Perhaps those who see where it is say, “There it is.” At once the ears hear this and follow the instruction; there the eyes search, the hands work, and, as I have said, the whole body bends toward that place. Nothing in the person remains idle in coming to the aid of the injured part. The wound has been made only in the foot, yet everything that is in the person is at work.

Are all the members wounded? Pay attention. Do they all suffer pain? The hand is healthy, the eyes are healthy, the head is healthy, and the other members are healthy; the foot itself is healthy except for the place that was pricked. Therefore the calamity is not common to all; but through the compassion of charity all come to offer aid, and all wish to help. Thus what the Apostle said is fulfilled: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.”

### 2. The Envious Person Is a Rot That Must Be Cut Away. Through Charity, the Virtues of Others Become Our Own

What, then? Someone has a gift from God in the virtues; you do not have it. Do not be envious, lest you be cut off from the body.

See, brothers: the envious person is like rot, like a wound, like an abscess. You do not wish to rejoice with the one who has been glorified? That heavenly physician sees the disease of envy in you and will cut you off from the body. Therefore do not be envious.

But what do you do? Rejoice. Do not say in your heart, “If I were a Christian, and therefore belonged to God, I could do what another does.” It is as though [lacuna] the ear were to say, “If I belonged to the body, I could see the moon and the sun.” Yet neither the ear nor the hand possesses that ability. Each performs what it can, and all the members serve one another in harmony.

So you too should rejoice with the one to whom God has given some grace in a special way. In him you can possess what you cannot possess in yourself. Perhaps he has virginity: love him, and it is yours. Again, you may have greater patience: let him love you, and it is his. He may be able to keep vigil abundantly; if you are not envious, his devotion is yours. Perhaps you can fast more extensively; if he loves you, your fasting is his.

This is because you are in him: by individual possession you are not in him, but through charity you are.

### 3. The Example of Charity in Christ

Consider, brothers, and see the example of our Lord, who made us pilgrims and commanded us to hasten along the way of charity until we come to the heavenly city.

Can anyone say that the Lord became sick here? What, then, does he mean when he says, “I was sick, and you did not visit me”? What does this mean except what they themselves confess: “When did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?” And although he sits in heaven, nevertheless, because he suffers with his afflicted members, since he is the head of the members and of the whole body, he says: “When you did not do it for one of the least of mine, you did not do it for me” (Matt. XXV, 43–45).

Again, he was certainly already in heaven when he transformed Paul from a persecutor into a preacher. For, having shown him mercy and incorporated him into his whole body, he said from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4).

Was he persecuting Christ himself in heaven? What, then, is the meaning of “Why are you persecuting me”? Saul [Note: [Col. 1950] The manuscripts read: “Paul.”] was persecuting Christians—not Christ, who was seated in heaven. But because Christ himself [Col. 1951] was in the Christians, he suffered with all the members.

So that what he said might be true in him—“If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it”—what did he say? “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Certainly I am already in heaven; nevertheless, when you persecute my least ones, I myself still suffer persecution in my members.

### 4. Those Who Rejoice in the Tribulation of Others Are Dead Members

And consider this too, brothers, something we ourselves sometimes do. Pay attention. When people are standing in a crowd and there is some jostling, if one person steps on another, the tongue says, “You are stepping on me.” Has the tongue itself been stepped on? What, then, is the meaning of the sound, “You are stepping on me”? If the other person responds, “You are free, O tongue; you have a voice in your mouth. If I stepped on anything, I stepped on the foot,” charity says, “You are stepping on me.” It is the compassion of unity and the bond of fellowship speaking.

As I had begun to say, let all envious people recognize that those who rejoice in the tribulations of others, even when those others are their enemies, are rotten, severed, and dead members. Therefore they have no sensation; and when they separate from the other members, they do not feel it, because they were without sensation.

Our sensation, brothers, is one faith; charity is one health [Note: [Col. 1951] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “one faith, one charity, one health.”]. Let us hold faith as our sensation and charity as our health.

And although different members have different functions, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1951] In the manuscripts the word *tamen*, “nevertheless,” is absent. Shortly afterward they read *teneantur*, “may be held together,” for *tenentur*, “are held together,” and *ibit*, “will go,” for *ivit*, “has gone.”] they are held together by the unity of charity, and all deserve to follow the head. The head is in heaven; let us labor here and bear one another’s burdens. For where the head has gone, the other members will go.

Certainly you heard what was said a little earlier: the Lord cried out from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

### 5. Whoever Does Not Suffer with the Suffering Person Is Outside the Church

I ask you, brothers: if our Lord and Savior, who had no sin, deigns to love us sinners with such affection that he testifies that what we suffer, he himself suffers, why do we, who are not without sin and who can redeem our sins through charity, not love one another with such perfect love that, whatever evil another endures, we suffer with him through the affection of charity; and whatever good another receives, rejoice as though we ourselves had received it, giving thanks to God on behalf of the one who received it?

Look: as has been said, someone is suffering either tribulation or loss. If you grieve for him, you are established in the body of the Church; if you do not grieve, you have been severed.

For charity, which gathers and gives life to all the members of the Church, sees you rejoicing over another’s ruin and immediately cuts you off from the body. And perhaps you do not grieve for this reason: because you have been severed. For if you were still there, you would certainly grieve.

Consider, brothers, and pay close attention: a member suffers only as long as it remains in the body. But if it has been cut off, it can neither suffer nor feel. When the hand or another member has been severed from the body, even if the whole body is afterward divided into many parts, that hand does not feel, because it has already been separated and detached from the fellowship of the remaining members.

Such is the Christian who not only does not grieve another’s losses, afflictions, or even death, but—what is worse—perhaps even rejoices. Because he has become alien to the body, he does not retain the affection of charity in his heart.

But if we wish to preserve true and perfect charity, let us all strive to love one another as ourselves. Thus, because Christ is our head and we have deserved to be his members, when Christ, our glory, appears, may we also deserve to appear with him in glory through the harmony of charity, as his true and perfect members, loving all people as ourselves, without any deceit of malice or envy.

## SERMON 106

[Note: [Col. 1952] Elsewhere, *On the Liturgical Year* 46, and in volume 9.]

On the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. XIII, 4, 7, 8: “Charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”

[Note: [Col. 1952] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. Erasmus long ago rejected it from Augustine in volume nine; Verlinus, Vindingus, and others likewise observe that the method and manner of argument are not Augustine’s, and still less does it suit him that the preacher says at the beginning of the sermon that he learned the sacred Scriptures from childhood. It is nevertheless not unworthy of being assigned to one of Augustine’s pupils.]

[Col. 1952]

### 1. Introduction

The desire of your Charity demands from us the duty of delivering a sermon. But so many things frighten and restrain our mind that, if we wish to comply with your desire, it will not be without danger to us.

First, I am compelled, as a young man, to speak before elders. Moreover, I consider it rash for one who is inexperienced [Note: [Col. 1952] In an old Dijon manuscript: *in peritia*, “in expertise.” Perhaps one should read *in imperitia*, “in inexperience.”] to wish to speak among those whom ancient teaching has strengthened. I therefore wished to pass by in silence and choose that safest position: to listen rather than say anything.

But what am I to do? Your love presses me, our modesty calls me back, and the command of the holy fathers compels me. If I wished to beg pardon from them, saying, “Forgive me, holy fathers, forgive me; spare our modesty, spare our youth,” especially as I recall that it was commanded to you, “Speak, elders; for it is fitting for you” (Eccli. XXXII, 4), they themselves, through the holy charity in which they prevail, would answer me: “Speak, young man; for it delights us.”

If I then asked them again, “Holy fathers, what shall I speak about?” they would answer me once more: “Remember, son, what you have often heard from us: you learned the sacred Scriptures from childhood” (2 Tim. III, 15).

But even then I shall not be able to excuse myself to you, whose hearts will strike me with these words: “Why are you afraid to utter a word? If age holds you back, Paul commanded the young Timothy, saying: ‘Let no one despise your youth’ (1 Tim. IV, 12). ‘Preach the word’ (2 Tim. IV, 2). If speech is lacking, ask, and you will receive. For it is not you who speak; rather, you minister to us what has been given to you.”

Pressed by these difficulties, where shall I turn except to the holy footsteps of charity? I beseech it to grant me something worthy to say about itself, something that may both complete my ministry and satisfy your desire.

### 2. The Four Virtues of Charity. They Do Not Exist Apart from One Another. No Saint Is Without Them

Among the other virtues of that same charity which the Apostle Paul mentions—that charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not irritated, is not puffed up, does not think evil, and so forth—he briefly gathers four of its virtues at the end, saying: “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails.”

It is therefore fitting to speak to your Holiness about these four virtues of holy charity. It is pleasing first to contemplate how, like four hinges holding together the world, it has possessed the whole world.

Let us therefore, if it pleases you, seek examples among certain saints—namely, those who were possessed by these virtues of holy charity—and let us assign one virtue to each in such a way that we may recognize all of them in everyone. For everyone who patiently bears rightly believes; everyone who rightly believes hopes for something; and whoever hopes endures, lest he fall from hope.

But let us now see who these people are, whose faith we may attain insofar as we are helped from above. The virtue of charity that bears all things was prominent in holy Noah; that believes all things, in holy Abraham; that hopes all things, in our fathers—that is, in the people of Israel, from whom our Lord himself arose; and that endures all things, in our very head, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is true charity, which never falls.

Let your Charity not suppose that the other saints are alien to these virtues. Understand that they have been passed over in this brief treatment and because of the sermon undertaken, yet know with complete certainty that all are in Christ and Christ is in all.

[Col. 1953] ### 3. The First Virtue of Charity: To Bear All Things

Let us now see how holy Noah possessed, or was possessed by, the virtue of charity that bears all things.

God foretold to him that, as human wickedness increased, he would destroy the world by a flood. At once, warned by God, Noah took refuge in wood and, after the open beauty of the fields, shut himself within the confined space of the ark. He bears the roar of heaven, the sound of the waters, and the crash of the storms. After all this, he who was accustomed to rejoice in the company of human beings becomes, in a certain sense, the companion of serpents and wild beasts.

Yet this man is not terrified that wild beasts are with him in the ark. Rather, there the ferocity of the beasts recognizes its order, because humanity recognized its own; and they obey the man who commands them because they recognize that man has obeyed the higher Lord.

In Noah it was shown what Adam lost by despising the commandment; and it was demonstrated that human beings can even rule over beasts if they submit themselves in obedience to the Creator.

This holy man waits for and endures the end of the flood. The ark is not abandoned for the sake of the beasts before the flood has ended (Gen. VI–VIII). The good person endures evil people; and until, at the end, they are separated even in body, he remains within, separated in heart but not in body.

### 4. What Must Be Done by One Who Desires This Virtue

If you are a soul that desires to possess the virtue of charity that bears all things, leave the world, take refuge in the wood of the cross, and do not fear the storms and whirlwinds of this flood. You will not be drowned if you are carried by the wood. The one who deigned to create knows how to steer; let only the virtue of charity that bears all things be present.

Let nothing tear you away from the solidity of the ark. Remain good and endure the wicked. For it is better to remain inside and endure the wicked for the sake of the good than to go outside, perish, and abandon both the good and the wicked.

If, then, wild beasts are with you—that is, if within the Church there are people teaching perversely, thinking falsely, heretics or schismatics, or even wicked Catholics themselves, seeking to devour souls like wild beasts—let them be endured until the end of the world, as though until the end of the flood.

Even if they roar, gnash their teeth, and attempt to break the ark itself, do not be frightened. When the flood has ended, an empty and thorny forest will seize them, while a fertile land receives you. After the end of the world, the wicked will be carried away into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth; but the pious will be received into the land of the living (Matt. XXV, 30, 46).

For holy Noah himself also offered sacrifice to God after the end of the flood—but from clean animals, not unclean ones (Gen. VIII, 20). Clean and unclean animals could swim together in the ark, but the evil ones did not reach the sacrifice of God.

### 5. The Second Virtue of Charity: To Believe All Things. It Shines Forth in Abraham When He Leaves Everything. He Does Not Doubt Concerning His Son

But let us now move on, so that we may examine the remaining matters. Let holy Abraham come forward and teach us by his example to possess the virtue of charity that believes all things. At the first call he did not hesitate to leave his native land, home, and family.

Everything is abandoned so that he may obey the Lord who commands. God says to him: “Go out from your house and from your kindred, and come into whatever land I shall show you” (Gen. XII, 1). This holy man did not think or say to himself, “Where shall I go? To whom shall I entrust myself? To what land shall I go?” Rather, as soon as he hears, he rises, runs, hurries, and hastens.

He does not see the promised land, but by believing he holds it firmly. He walks on the straight path and does not turn aside with wandering steps elsewhere than he ought, because the one who sent him to an unknown land did not abandon him after sending him.

Nor did that one deceive him. The reward is given to the believer. He reaches the land, expands and multiplies; from poor he becomes rich, from obscure powerful, and he is enriched with every good. In him is fulfilled what the Lord promised his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone has left a house, or a field, or parents for the sake of my name, he will receive a hundredfold in this life and will obtain eternal life in the age to come” (Matt. XIX, 29).

The reward of this faith is increased further, and a son is promised to the old man. The virtue of charity that believes all things is present. He hears, rejoices, loves more deeply, receives a son from a barren wife, [Col. 1954] whom age and barrenness had already deprived of hope of bearing a child, and in him holds most firmly the blessing promised to all nations (Gen. XVIII, 10).

### 6. He Offers His Son. He Becomes God’s Friend. What Makes Friends

But charity still tests him, commends him once tested, and shows future generations how he preferred nothing to God.

The Lord calls him from heaven, saying, “Abraham! Abraham!” And he, like an obedient servant, says, “Here I am.” And the Lord says: “Take your son, that one whom you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I shall tell you.”

Even by this command the faithful servant is neither disturbed nor broken, for the virtue of charity that believes all things is present in him. He rises, goes home, saddles the donkey, cuts the wood, takes the sword and fire, brings the boy with him, and proceeds to the place.

Then Isaac, becoming attentive, asks his father: “Father.” And he replies, “What is it, son?” And the son says: “Behold, here are the fire and the wood; where is the sheep that you are going to sacrifice as a burnt offering?” And the father replies: “God will provide himself a sheep for the sacrifice, my son.”

Here I see a great and profound mystery. Abraham carried one thing in his heart and promised another to his son. Yet neither did what he promised deceive his son, nor did any weakness alter his heart from its purpose.

What more need be said? He proceeds along the road, sees the place from a distance, and, leaving his servants there, says these words to them: “Remain here with the donkey; I and the boy will go as far as that place, and when we have worshiped, we will return to you.”

O holy Abraham, what is this that you say, when you have to do something else with the boy? Are you deceiving either yourself or your servants? “No,” he says. “But the virtue of charity that believes all things, remaining in me, both does and says what I utter prophetically or enact.”

For I hear it speaking inwardly to my heart without any sound of voice and saying to me: “Although you believe that he will rise again and are leading your son to be sacrificed with a full and perfect resolve, the son is not burned in this sacrifice, because the resurrection is reserved for the Son of God.”

Rightly, when recalling the faith of this Abraham, the Apostle James says: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (James II, 23).

As we know, friendship is produced by the union of minds. Hence a certain wise man of this world said: “To wish and not wish the same things—this, finally, is firm friendship” (Sallust, *Catiline*, chap. 12).

Therefore, as we know, friendship is produced by the union of minds. Do you wish to know how this holy man united his mind to God so that he might be called God’s friend?

Just as God the Father did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all (Rom. VIII, 32), so this man also did not spare his only son. When commanded to sacrifice him, he offered him with devoted heart to the one who had given him.

### 7. Isaac as a Type of the Suffering Christ

But let us see what follows. With the help of our Lord God, it delights us to give you a full account of this story.

After leaving the servants behind, the father comes with his son to the place of sacrifice. He builds an altar, arranges the wood, binds the son’s hands, places him on the altar upon the wood, lays aside the signs of human paternal affection, assumes the dreadful steadfastness of a priest, and draws the sword to kill his son.

What do you see, brothers? We perceive nothing human here, because we recognize everything as divine.

But the son himself, who a little earlier was asking about the sheep, silently perceives that these things are being done to him. He is found to be so patient as though he were already the one who, like a sheep, was led to slaughter, and, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open its mouth (Isa. LIII, 7).

O holy Isaac, you too, tell us the great secret of this silence. A little earlier you felt nothing being done to you and were asking your father for the ram; but now your hands are bound, you are placed upon the altar, and in a certain sense suspended upon the wood. And now you are silent.

“I am silent,” he says.

“Tell us why, I beg you, so that we may know.”

“Do you wish to know why I am silent now?” he says. “Because I bear the figure of the one who lays down his life by his own will, not by necessity” (John X, 17–18).

In this great mystical sacrament of faith, holy Abraham was shown to have been tested, and the son was freed in the present, in whom Christ was foretold (Gen. XXII).

[Col. 1955] **8. What God expects from one who practices charity, which believes all things.** If you are a soul that desires to follow the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, go out from your land and from your kindred; leave your people and your father’s house: that is, faithfully renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels; and follow the straight path that will lead you to a land in which you may grow rich and become eminent, and become Abraham’s companion.

But when you have done all these things, if the virtue of charity, which believes all things, is in you, it will still test you; and, once you have been proved, it will crown you. It asks from you the sacrifice of your beloved. What does it ask from you? What was said to Abraham: “Give me your only beloved”; Wisdom says to you, “Give me your heart, my son” (Prov. 23:26). He is that only beloved. Why are you afraid to offer your heart? Offer the sacrifice of a contrite heart to the Lord your God, and say to him with the prophet: “You will not be pleased with burnt offerings. The sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:18–19). Fear nothing after offering such a sacrifice:

[Note: [Col. 1955] In manuscript ful., the word *Deo* is lacking, and *tibi* is substituted for it in the others. But above this word, in cl., *illi* is written by a second hand.]

it will be acceptable to God, and what you have offered will remain whole.

**9. The third virtue: to hope for all things.** Would you like us to examine another virtue of charity, which hopes for all things? We recognize that earlier we assigned this to the people of Israel and to our fathers. For its voice is heard in that prophetic verse: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them” (Ps. 21:5). They themselves were commanded to flee from Egypt, and a land flowing with milk and honey was promised to them (Exod. 3:8). They crossed the Red Sea and came to the wilderness: the hope of charity led them, so that they might first learn to love God freely. The reward of faith is also given to them; for he cannot fail to repay who deigns, by giving himself, to make himself a debtor. After the wilderness they sucked honey from the rock and ate the bread of heaven (ibid. 14–16); they were not deprived of what they desired and hoped for, and they also received the promised land.

**10. The exercises of this virtue.** Let the soul that has been seized by the virtue of this charity arise and flee from Egypt—that is, from the desire of this world—and proceed to the Red Sea, namely, the Baptism of Christ; it is called red because it has been dyed purple with Christ’s blood.

Let the enemies pursue: sins, together with their author the devil, like the Egyptians with their king Pharaoh, may rage and pursue the fugitives. Why are you afraid? They rage only as far as the water. You will enter, and they too will enter after you; but when the water is turned, it will be their destruction and your salvation. It will overwhelm them and wash you; it will condemn them and free you.

After this you will receive honey from the rock, with which you may satisfy your thirst. For “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), and from his precepts, as from springs of sweetness, you will be satisfied. You will also taste the bread—the one who said, “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). You will taste, “and you will see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

[Note: [Col. 1955] The printed editions read, “because the Lord is sweet”; the manuscripts, “how sweet the Lord is.” Augustine himself likewise regularly uses the latter when citing this verse.]

And if the virtue of charity, which hopes for all things, excels in you, you must pass through the wilderness; that is, use this world as though you did not use it (1 Cor. 7:31); and recognize that you are a pilgrim on this road, if you desire to enter the promised land. This is the land of which the prophet sings and says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

**11. The fourth: to endure all things. How much Christ endured.** The final virtue of charity remains: it endures all things and never fails. We know that this belongs to our head, the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore it is mentioned last, since “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4).

How much he himself endured for us, I think your Charity cannot fail to know. Yet I shall say something about it, if only I can worthily say something about so great a subject. First, consider this: God became man; the Word became flesh (John 1:14); he did many good things and suffered evils; he raised the dead and died himself; that singular patience endured the tempting devil and the betraying disciple. Before Judas revealed himself as a traitor, it endured him as a thief; and before experiencing bonds, the cross, and death, it did not deny him the kiss of peace on his deceitful lips.

But in death itself, how much did he endure? He endured the flames of hatred and the tongues that served an evil heart. The Jews cried out, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21). Thus, while the Jews remained guilty, the innocent Son of God was crucified by them. He is led to the cross and struck with open hands—he who is the true palm of victory. He is crowned with thorns—he who came to break the thorns of sins. He is bound—he who frees the fettered. He is hung upon wood—he who raises up the fallen (Ps. 145:7–8). The fountain of life is given vinegar to drink; discipline is beaten; salvation is wounded; life dies. For a time death killed life, so that death might be killed by life forever.

**12. The Jews defeated in Christ’s death. How they serve Christ.** What did the Jews gain by exulting in this death of Christ as though they were victors? While they feared losing an earthly and transitory kingdom, they did not hesitate to kill the King of heaven and earth. Yet they did not emerge victorious as they thought. If they conquered, how did they lose the kingdom? How have they remained servants to this day?

This is the reason: Christ was killed by them. The rulers of the Jews said among themselves, as the Evangelist relates: “You see,” they said, “that the whole world has gone after him? If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away our place and our kingdom” (John 11:47–48). They killed Christ, and lost both their place and their kingdom.

What did it profit you, insane Jews, that you committed so great a crime? Was it because you refused to serve Christ the Lord as you ought that you were deprived of his dominion? While kings serve him, to whom you yourselves are subject, you have become bad servants of Christ’s good servants. Through them he crushes your obstinacy, through them he scatters your plans, and through them he repays your crimes upon your own heads.

Yet the Lord whom you killed desired that you should be not slaves but free, when he said: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (ibid. 8:36). But you not only rejected the Lord God and King, and true freedom itself; desiring even to kill him, you cried out, “We have no king except Caesar” (ibid. 19:15).

Nor should you glory in having killed Christ; rather, it was done to you, and you did not know it. Hear the Lord himself saying through the prophet: “I slept and took my rest” (Ps. 3:6), calling the death inflicted by you sleep. But how could the death of one who says elsewhere through the same prophet, “Will not one who sleeps rise again?” (Ps. 40:9), last three days—especially his death? “I,” he says, “slept: I who have power to lay down my life. I slept—not because you raged, not because you went mad. I fulfilled what I willed; you remained in your crime.”

**13. The powers of charity.** What, brothers, demanded such great things from our God for our redemption and salvation, except charity, which never fails? O charity, how great are your powers, since you brought God down from heaven! O dear holiness, O holy and true charity, as great as you are on earth, how great will you be in heaven? What power you possess now, while still anxious in this struggle of mortality—how much greater will your power be in that perfect peace, secure and at rest?

**14. Imitation of Christ’s patience.** Wake up, therefore, every Christian soul. If the virtue of charity, which endures all things, excels in you, imitate the footsteps of your Lord. For “Christ,” the apostle Peter says, “suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

If he descended for your sake from his heavenly seat to earthly things, then for your own sake flee earthly things and seek heavenly ones. If the world is sweet, Christ is sweeter; if the world is bitter, Christ endured all things for you.

The Savior himself has become your way: rise and walk; you have somewhere to go—do not grow sluggish. Perhaps you ask, “Where?” You see the way and ask where this very way leads. It leads to the truth and to life. If you love the truth, if you love life, and desire to come to the truth and to life, do not stray from the way.

“I see the way,” you say, “and I desire to walk it; but it is bitter and rough, for the way that leads to life is narrow and confined” (Matt. 7:14). Christ passed along it, and is it still rough? The head has passed through, and the members hesitate? “But Christ,” you say, “was God and man, whereas I am only human.” Thousands upon thousands of martyrs have passed through it; and is it still rough for you? Old men have passed through, young men have passed through, boys have passed through, girls have passed through. They have made smooth for you the way you feared by treading it.

Walk, then, along the way; walk securely. What do you fear on this way? Death? Do you fear death when you are running toward life? If you are good, you are running well on this way. Death will be a door for you, presenting you to life, not taking life away.

Walk, then, along the way—or rather, may the one who became the way for you lead you through himself to himself. For he is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Say, then, to your God, O faithful and devout soul; say it, say it, say it confidently, and cry out truthfully with the prophet: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. 85:11). Then I shall reach you securely, if I am not abandoned by your grace until the end.

These things, dearest brothers, which have been spoken to your Holiness through the gift of that very charity, should cling to your hearts and minds, so that this same charity may find in you the fruit of works, not merely the leaves of praise.

# SERMON CVII

[Note: [Col. 1957] Formerly, *On the Season*, 42.]

Again on the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 13:1: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing,” etc. On love of God and neighbor, of friends and enemies.

[Note: [Col. 1957] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors wished it to remain among the Augustinian sermons, but without Augustine’s name, as a doubtful work. Verlinus and Vindingus judged that it should be removed. It contains a thought and certain words taken from Augustine’s Sermon 350. If you compare it with Caesarius’s other homilies, you will readily agree that it is a work of Caesarius. It falsely bears Augustine’s name in books copied more than seven hundred years ago, namely, the Colbertine and Theoderician manuscripts. See the note on Sermon 112 of this Appendix. On section 1, see Sermon 69 of the Appendix, section 1; also Caesarius, Homily 10, in the editions published by Baluzius, and Augustine, Sermon 350. On section 2, Caesarius at the end of Homily 36. On section 4, Sermon 69 of the Appendix, section 7.]

**1. Charity makes those bodily separated be together.** How greatly your Charity desires us, dearest brothers, I recognize from my own feelings. And although you continually wish to see my humility, yet, if it could be done, I would more frequently wish to satisfy both your desires and mine by being in your presence.

[Note: [Col. 1957] The printed editions read: “and I would wish to satisfy both your desire and mine.” In manuscript t.: “I desire, by our and your presence, to satisfy my and your soul.” Here we follow cl.]

But we must patiently bear what, because of the necessities of the times, we cannot fulfill. Although, because of many necessities, we cannot see one another bodily, nevertheless through charity and holy love we are always together.

[Note: [Col. 1957] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “and having used holy love, we are together.”]

Therefore bodily separation does no harm where there is a true and sincere union of souls. For charity itself is true charity, which habitually unites and joins together spiritually those separated bodily. Two people who love each other with holy love—even if one is in the East and the other in the West—are joined by charity’s bonding so closely that they are never separated from one another.

Hear the Apostle praising true and complete charity. For he says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing,” and so forth. A little later he adds: “Charity is patient, it is kind,” and the rest.

Although the Apostle Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, has sufficiently proclaimed its praises, nevertheless, because holy charity is a sweet and salutary bond of minds, let us, little ones also, according to our measure, seek to speak about it as much as we can.

**2. The good use of riches must be learned from charity. Charity is oil. Charity is a good steward.** Great are the riches of charity, dearest brothers, without which the rich person is poor, and with which the poor person is rich. For if the rich person does not have charity, what does he have? However great his wealth may be, without charity it is empty and void.

Even if charity possesses nothing of earthly resources, it is full. Therefore, however abundant someone’s riches may be, if charity is not in him, he will be able to do no good with them, because without the true mother and teacher of heavenly virtues he does not know at all what he ought to do, or when or how much he ought to give.

And so let each person strive as much as possible to have charity, to have light, to have oil. Charity is compared to oil. For just as oil is known to be above all liquids, so charity is proved to be higher than all virtues.

If someone possesses limitless riches but does not have charity, he is like someone who has many lamps and numerous lanterns without fuel. A lamp or lantern lit without oil can smoke and stink, but it cannot give light. So also the person who has riches without charity can burn with anger, smoke with pride, and stink with greed; but without charity he absolutely cannot have light.

If charity is in you, however great your wealth may be, it knows what should be done with it. It knows very well to whom and how much to extend, what to give, and what to reserve. It understands how much to store up for the soul in heaven and how much to reserve for the body in the world.

It is a sufficiently good steward, brothers, and knows well how to gather in summer what one may have in winter. That is, it knows through almsgiving how to provide in this world what one may find in the future.

[Note: [Col. 1958] The printed editions read, “A lamp or lantern lit can smoke from anger,” omitting the intervening words, “it can stink, it cannot have light,” and so forth. We have restored these words from the manuscripts.]

Have charity, brothers; because without it, whatever other good there may be in a person can amount to nothing.

**3. True charity embraces enemies. Charity is the root of good works.** But have true charity also, brothers. What is true charity? It is that which loves every person as itself. True charity does not extend only to friends, but reaches even to enemies themselves.

Let no one deceive himself, brothers. Whoever does not have this charity will not be able to see God, nor will he deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” Surely you see that in the Gospel reading the Lord named no other virtue among all virtues except almsgiving, which works together with charity.

He was silent about the branches and named only the root, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom; for I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:34–35). And again the Lord himself says: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Everyone who wishes to have charity in the world to come should make it his patron in this world, so that he may find it favorable to him forever. For just as a tree, however beautiful and fruitful it may be, cannot live without a root, so no good works can persevere without charity. For it is of charity that the Apostle says: “Rooted and grounded in charity” (Eph. 3:17).

**4. Charity is always sweet.** Let us therefore have such charity, brothers, that we may be able to love all people with our whole heart. If you love the whole human race as you love yourself, no door remains through which sin can enter you. You close every entrance by which the devil enters the soul, if you love all people as yourself.

Indeed, brothers, how can anyone do evil to another person if he loves him as himself? Love, then, and do whatever you wish. Love with all your heart, and practice toward your neighbor whatever you wish.

If you become angry, it is sweet, because it proceeds from charity; if you correct, it is pleasant; even if you chastise and scourge, it is acceptable. Why, brothers? Because it is true love when you correct and chastise.

When you even cast someone out of the Church, bitterness seems to rage in your mouth,

[Note: [Col. 1958] In the manuscript of the first class, “seems to sound.” And shortly afterward: “sweetness is preserved.”]

but sweetness is preserved in your heart [Col. 1959]. You do not hate your brother as an enemy; rather, you pursue sin as though it were a disease.

On the contrary, there are people who, under false flattery, customarily offer sweetness from their mouths while keeping deceit or bitterness in their hearts. But you, dearest brothers, holding true charity, flee what is false.

Hear the Apostle saying: “Charity is from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

Brothers, when I speak about charity, I cannot be silent. Why? Because charity is exceedingly sweet. Whoever has it understands what I am saying; whoever does not have it perhaps mocks and despises me. Why does he mock? Because he has not tasted how sweet charity is.

Let him taste, then, and see how sweet the Lord is. God is charity. What is sweeter than God, brothers? Whoever does not know should hear the prophet saying what I mentioned a little earlier: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9).

O how happy and blessed is the soul that deserves to have charity! Charity, brothers, is drink for the thirsty, food for the hungry, sweetness for those placed in bitterness, true and complete consolation for those in sorrow, a harbor for those tossed about, a way for those who wander, and a homeland for pilgrims.

Hold fast to it, then, brothers; love it with your whole eagerness. If you are lovers, love charity; if you are strong, conquer desire; if you are pilgrims, long for your homeland.

If you are willing to hold charity fast, charity itself both governs you in this world and leads you to the kingdom, through the favor of our Lord, who lives and reigns forever. Amen.

# SERMON CVIII

[Note: [Col. 1959] Formerly, *On the Season*, 53.]

On the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 13:13: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greater of these is charity.”

[Note: [Col. 1959] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was regarded as doubtful in the Louvain edition; Verlinus and Vindingus censured it as spurious. Among other points, they observe that in this sermon every Christian is called one’s neighbor, whereas Augustine, in his Exposition of Psalm 11, in Sermon 359, and likewise in Sermon 90, section 7, wishes every human being to be understood as one’s neighbor. It is compiled from Alcuin’s work *On Virtues and Vices*, chapters 2–4.]

**1. Faith is necessary for the Christian. Its effect. What it must be like.** Whoever bears the Christian name, and whoever has been imbued with the divine sacraments, dearest brothers, must know the meaning of the Christian religion and recognize the truth of the faith—that faith which, as the Apostle says, works through love (Gal. 5:6), which strengthens and confirms believers in the present and leads them in the future to the contemplation of God.

For the blessed and distinguished Teacher of the Gentiles set before our soul three things necessary to it, saying: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greater of these is charity.”

First, therefore, Catholic faith is necessary for the Christian, because by it the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil, and the children of light from the children of darkness. Through it we are reborn in Baptism and obtain eternal salvation, as it is written: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). This is the gate of life; this is the door of the kingdom.

Through it the knowledge of truth is learned and the understanding of divinity is received; through it we find the grace of God. We cannot please God in any other way, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

Truly blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, preserves right faith. Therefore, just as faith without good works is useless, so good works accomplish nothing without right faith.

Hence the blessed apostle James said: “What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him? Faith without works is useless. For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James 2:14, 17, 26).

Strive above all, my brothers, to have faith that is right and undefiled. According to the rule of apostolic teaching, hold by heart the Creed established by the holy Fathers, and, living religiously, take care to observe it.

Flee the poisonous doctrines of heretics; dread the deadly poisons of sorcerers and enchanters; utterly reject the wicked traditions of diviners and practitioners of magic, which have fellowship with demons. Thus may you hold in mind, profession, and conduct nothing other than what the Catholic faith praises, loves, and proclaims.

**2. Firm hope. Concerning forgiveness of any sins, provided one ceases from sinning; and concerning God’s consolation in afflictions.** After this faith, learn to have firm hope. It draws our spirit toward invisible things, implants our purpose in heavenly and eternal things, and binds it, as it were, with unbreakable bonds. It does not deceive, but faithfully leads those who obey it to eternal blessedness.

Therefore no one, however great the burden of sins pressing upon him, ought to despair of the goodness of divine mercy. Rather, in hope of certain mercy, he should daily ask for forgiveness with tears. He may rightly hope for it if he ceases from doing evil.

We must not persist in sinning because we hope for forgiveness; nor, because God justly punishes sins, must we despair of forgiveness. Thus we should neither sin presumptuously nor despair of our sins; but, avoiding both dangers, turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from the mercy of God.

Likewise, in the distress of every tribulation, we must run in hope to the consolation of heavenly mercy, because in God alone all hope and salvation unquestionably consist, as the prophet says: “In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God” (Ps. 61:8).

**3. Charity is greater than hope and faith. It is the reward of the saints.** When we commend right faith and firm hope to you, brothers, our chief exhortation is that you strive in every way to have charity in yourselves and to show it in your works.

Know that through charity and with charity you will have true blessedness, because without it no one will see God. The Apostle says that it is greater than faith and hope because, when the others depart, it alone will remain.

Hope succeeds faith, and blessedness succeeds hope; but charity has not transformation awaiting it—only perfection. It is the citadel of all virtues, the promise of the kingdom, and the highest reward of the saints in heaven, because in everlasting joy the saints have nothing more pleasing or sweeter than perfect love of God. Since they see him present, they love him more sweetly and enjoy that good more delightfully.

**4. It holds primacy among God’s commandments.** You ought to know, brothers, that in all God’s commandments charity holds first place. Without its perfection, nothing can please God, as the apostle Paul testifies (1 Cor. 13:1–3), for he shows that neither martyrdom, nor contempt of the world, nor generosity in almsgiving can profit anything without the service of charity.

Accordingly, when a certain scribe asked the Lord which commandment was greatest, he replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” He added: “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22:37, 39–40).

When he says, “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” this means that God is to be loved with the whole understanding, the whole will, and the whole memory.

The love of God consists entirely in observing his commandments, as he says elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words” (John 14:23). Hence Truth itself says elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid. 13:35).

The Apostle likewise says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10). The evangelist John likewise says: “We have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his neighbor” (1 John 4:21).

**5. Every Christian is one’s neighbor.** If someone should ask who one’s neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called one’s neighbor, because in Baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that spiritually we may be brothers in perfect charity.

Spiritual birth is nobler than bodily birth. Of it Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

Whoever, understanding this, loves his neighbor will undoubtedly possess true charity within himself.

Consider these things carefully, brothers, so that with faith and love you may always work out your salvation, holding firm hope that whatever good you do in the present will be repaid to you immeasurably in the future by him who is the author and protector of our salvation, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

# SERMON CIX

[Note: [Col. 1961] Formerly, *On the Words of the Apostle*, 34; and afterward in the Appendix, 11.]

On the words of the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 5:10: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.” On the certainty of the future resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1961] The author is uncertain.]

**1. Christians’ joy in hope. The chief distinction between Christians and pagans. In what state we shall rise.** The hope of all Christians, dearest brothers, extends into the future, so that we may rejoice elsewhere in having served God here. Here our struggles are placed; but in the future world the rewards of our struggles are reserved. For divine wisdom has justly and prudently separated the time of labor from the time of reward.

Here, therefore, we labor; here we serve God and keep his commandments, so that in the future world—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—we may receive eternal rewards.

We must know, dearest brothers, what divine Scripture commends to us: namely, that there will be a judgment of God, which will be completed after the resurrection of the dead.

This is what chiefly separates Christians from pagan error: they believe that this life alone exists, and therefore do not fear being without God or defiling themselves with various sins and crimes. We, however, conduct ourselves in this life in such a way as to prepare ourselves for another, in which good things will be repaid to the good and evil things to the evil, as the Apostle said: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

Just as we now stand in the church and look upon one another as present, so after the resurrection of the dead we shall stand before the tribunal of Christ.

For at that time we shall have the very soul that we now have, and in this very body with which we are now clothed we shall be raised. We were not made like dumb animals, nor like horses and oxen, to perish in eternal death. After we have lived here, we shall be judged elsewhere, so that we may receive either punishment for sins or eternal rewards for good works.

**2. The resurrection is demonstrated from God’s omnipotence and truth.** Therefore, dearest brothers, let no one despair of the resurrection, in which the whole hope of Christians consists.

Believe, brothers, the Apostle who preaches; and, doubting nothing about the resurrection, prepare yourselves for the day of judgment.

Or perhaps, like the impious and unbelieving, you do not think it possible for us to rise from the dead? Let the person who says this say it because he does not believe that God is omnipotent, although God promises that this will happen.

But we, who know that power belongs to the omnipotent God, because we read that he has promised to bring about the resurrection of the dead, cannot doubt the resurrection which he has promised to accomplish—he who is both omnipotent and unable to lie.

[Note: [Col. 1961] Thus Am. and Er., with certain manuscripts. But Lov. and manuscript fs. read, “by which he promised”; manuscripts cl. and rm., “who promised.” The Divionensis manuscript, however, reads, “whom he sent.”]

**3. Likewise from creation, and from the enlivening of seeds.** But I address you, whoever you are who doubt the resurrection with an unbelieving mind and think that the dead cannot be raised.

Which is greater: to make living human beings from nothing, or to restore after death those who were made and lived? Certainly it is greater to make what never existed than to restore what once existed.

How, then, can you say that God cannot restore the human being whom he formed from nothing? How can he not raise us when we have been turned to dust, if, even had we returned to nothing, he could make us exist—just as he did make us exist when previously we had never been?

For the blessed apostle Paul said: “But some will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?’ Foolish person, what you sow does not come to life unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of one of the others. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body” (1 Cor. 15:35–38).

Do not doubt the resurrection, unbelieving human being. He who gives life to the dead and rotting seeds, through which you live in this world, will much more raise you yourself so that you may live forever.

He restores the things necessary for you; how could he not restore you yourself, for whose sake he has also deigned to restore other things?

**4. Created things bear witness to the future resurrection.** If we wish to consider what we see in this world, the works of divine administration are signs of what is to come. The whole government of this world is therefore a testimony to the future resurrection.

Certainly we see that, when winter comes, trees are stripped of their fruit and left bare of leaves; but in spring they again express the form of resurrection. First they begin to swell with buds, then are adorned with flowers, clothed with leaves, and afterward weighed down with fruit.

I ask you, unbelieving human being who doubt the resurrection: Where are the things that are produced at the time God has appointed? Tell me, where do they lie hidden before they are produced? They are nowhere seen, yet God, who is omnipotent and created them from nothing, brings them forth by his hidden power.

Look now at the fields and meadows. When summer has passed, they are stripped of their grasses and flowers, and the expanses of earth remain bare. But again, in springtime, they are clothed anew, and the farmer rejoices everywhere as new growth begins.

Certainly the grass that previously lived and dies comes to life again from seed. So also our body comes to life again from dust.

**5. Christ’s resurrection, the pledge of ours.** But you say, unbelieving human being: “We believe that trees, grasses, and everything else will come to life again because we know that these things have already happened. But how can we know that the dead rise, since no one has yet risen from the dead?”

Whoever says or thinks this, listen patiently and understand wisely. Our Lord Jesus Christ wished to die and rise again precisely so that you would not doubt the resurrection.

How can you doubt that we shall rise from the dead when God promises it—God who cannot at any time lie, who can do whatever he wills because he is omnipotent, and who fulfills everything he promises because he is truthful and there is no falsehood in him?

The merciful and compassionate Lord gave us a pledge of his power and showed us the hope of the resurrection through great testimony, because he raised from the dead his only-begotten Son, who was made human for us and died.

For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born from a human being, that is, from the Virgin Mary; to be crucified by the Jews; and to rise on the third day: so that, encouraged by such an example, we might believe with complete certainty in the resurrection from the dead.

Whoever does not believe that it will happen does not even believe that Christ rose from the dead. Whoever confesses that the Lord Jesus rose from the dead will not be able to doubt his own resurrection.

Therefore abstain from every evil work: from enmities, drunkenness, fornication, theft, perjury, false testimony, and slander. God hates all these things and will punish those who do them in the future.

But be kind and merciful, honoring one another, and always practice the things that God loves in his saints, so that you may reach eternal and immortal glory with his saints, and live forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CX

[Note: [Col. 1963] Formerly, *On the Words of the Apostle* 35; and later, in Appendix 22.]

On the same words of the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 5:10.

[Note: [Col. 1963] Among Augustine’s sermons *On the Words of the Apostle*, in whose class it formerly stood in the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, it is not found in the manuscripts. This very treatise, under the name of Faustus, but somewhat longer and in the form in which it is presented here, was first published by Henricus Canisius, and then in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. But anyone who carefully considers the genuine and certain little works of Faustus and of Caesarius will unquestionably assign this one to Caesarius, not to Faustus. Indeed, the sermons of the writers of Lérins are so confused that works known to be Caesarius’s are seen attributed to Faustus, while those of Faustus are attributed to Caesarius; and we may even find some works of both, and perhaps of Hilary, Eucherius, and others, included in that collection to which the general name of Eusebius was given—as though it meant “a pious man,” which is how it sounds in Greek. The greater part of this sermon, namely everything from section 2 to the end, is presented in Homily 1 of Eusebius Gallicanus *On the Epiphany*. In addition, concerning section 1, see Sermon 29 of the Appendix, section 1; and concerning section 3, see Caesarius, at the beginning of Homily 13, and the same passage at the end of Homily 31.]

[Col. 1963]

## 1. God is merciful here, just in the future. Remembering the day of death

Just now, dearest brothers, when the divine reading was being read, we heard the blessed Apostle admonishing us both terribly and salutarily. For he says: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through his body, whether good or evil.” The Lord also announces this in the Gospel, saying: “The Son of Man will come in his glory with his angels; and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

Please attend carefully, dearest brothers, and tremble together with me, because he did not say that he will repay each according to his mercy, but according to his works. Here he is merciful; there he is just. For the fact that he does not immediately take vengeance on sinners is patience, not negligence: he has not lost his power, but has spared us for repentance. Hence we must fear greatly that, the longer he waits for us to be corrected, the more severely he may punish us if we refuse to amend.

Since this is so, dearest brothers, we must know and understand that nothing is more salutary for us than, having condemned the pleasures of all present things, to think instead about when we shall depart from this world, or when, on the final day, we shall lay down the tent of our body and receive it again at the time of the resurrection, so that with that same body we may receive according to what we have done, whether good or evil.

## 2. To present the final judgment to oneself

And therefore I ask you, brothers, to think every day what sort of people we shall be when we are presented before the purest sight of the angels on the day of judgment and render an account to the eternal Judge from the books of conscience. When all other proofs have been removed, it is certain that on that day the person himself will be set before himself, and his very life [Note: [Col. 1963] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: “his soul itself.”] will be displayed in the mirror of his heart, and witnesses against him will be brought forth not from elsewhere outside him, but from within, from the soul itself.

The testimonies to be added will not be foreign but exceedingly familiar ones—namely, one’s own works. His sins or crimes will be set in order before the unhappy soul, so that proof may convict it and recognition may shame it, according to what is written: “I will rebuke you, and set you before your own face” (Psalm 49:21).

Whoever now, while it is permitted, has neglected to amend himself will first have to receive the punishment of shame before that heavenly people. And the soul that now, through a brief repentance, pretends not to heal the rottenness of its completed sins will remain before that fearful tribunal, without any remedy, forever in Tartarus [Note: [Col. 1963] In the aforementioned book: “will remain perpetually wounded.”].

## 3. To forestall unfruitful repentance with fruitful repentance

Since this is so, we would be well served if even now we repented of our evils in the way that then, without any remedy, we shall repent—if we could now see and dread our foulness and shame as we shall then see them.

[Col. 1964]

Oh, if only we were now permitted to behold with the eyes of the body the face of the sinful soul, and were allowed to bring the countenance of our conscience into the presence of our eyes! If this were permitted, it cannot be said with what zeal and fear we would be driven to set right what had been defiled, wipe clean what had been stained, and heal what had been wounded.

Therefore, since we cannot inspect ourselves with the eyes of the body, let us look at ourselves, insofar as we can, with the eyes of the heart; and let each person place his conscience before the sight of the inner man. Let us punish ourselves; let us ourselves render an account to ourselves of our daily conduct. Let each soul speak to itself in secret and say:

“Let us see whether I have passed this day without sin, without envy, without detraction, without murmuring. Let us see whether today I have done what pertains to the progress of the soul. I think that today I have lied; I have been overcome by anger or desire; I have done good to no one, nor have I groaned out of fear of eternal death. Who will give me back this day, which I have squandered on empty things, which I have consumed in harmful and most wicked thoughts?”

And so, brothers, let us be pierced by sorrow over all our negligences; in our chambers—that is, in our hearts—let us ourselves condemn ourselves, let us ourselves accuse ourselves daily before our Judge. And while we are in this flesh, let us, with the Lord’s help, fight daily against the flesh itself; let us conquer our pleasures and delights, so that that most longed-for and most blessed time may follow for us in the happy transformation of eternal life, when what the Lord said will be fulfilled: “They will be like the angels” (Matthew 22:30); and again: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (ibid. 13:43).

## 4. The condition of the blessed

What, do you suppose, will then be the splendor of souls, when the bodies’ light possesses the brightness of the sun? For then, when we have come to this blessedness, there will be no sadness, no fear, no weakness, no death. Nothing will hinder us from serving our God; no weakness will hinder us any longer; no adversity of miserable flesh will resist us; no necessity of fighting will remain any further.

The time will come, I say, when no food or refreshment will be desired; no weariness of fasting will be felt; no anxiety will be feared, whether concerning the flesh or concerning temptation from the enemy. But after the adversary has been thrust into the depths of hell, we shall first enjoy this happiness: that we shall begin neither to wish to sin any longer nor to be able to do so.

When all iniquity, all misery, and all sorrow have ceased, innocence will possess everything, and happiness everything. No one who is lower will fear misery; no one who is happier will fear envy, because misery and envy, emptied out and utterly extinguished, will have passed away.

In the breasts of human beings there will be the love of angels; and human beings, now joined to them and clothed in heavenly flesh, will shine without the weakness of flesh. Therefore they will no longer suffer any weariness of their Lord’s everlasting power, nor any failure amid the perpetual exultation of their praises.

We shall possess complete blessedness, brothers, amid those immense benefits of our Lord, so that we may never cease to give him thanks for the blessedness in which we shall rejoice, having been made co-heirs of him who will say: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 25:34). This he grants, to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXI

[Note: [Col. 1964] Formerly, 10 among the 50 Homilies; and later, in Appendix 16.]

On the words of the Apostle, Ephesians 5:15–16: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

The manuscripts add: “And on the saying, ‘Give money so that you may buy bread for yourself; give something to the evil man so that you may buy rest for yourself.’”

[Note: [Col. 1964] This is an entire sermon, number 167; but many passages are interspersed throughout, and we have distinguished them with brackets.]

## 1. Evil and misery make the days evil

You heard the Apostle when he was read—indeed, we all heard him—saying to us: “See carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

Two things, brothers, make the days evil: wickedness and misery. The days are called evil because of the wickedness of human beings and the misery of human beings. Otherwise, insofar as the periods of the hours are concerned, these days are ordered, they follow their appointed turns, they carry out their seasons. The sun rises and sets; the sun rises again and sets; seasons come, seasons pass.

Who would find the seasons burdensome if human beings were not burdensome to themselves? Therefore, as I said, two things make the days evil: the misery of human beings and the wickedness of human beings. But the misery of human beings is common; wickedness ought not to be common.

## 2. Regeneration frees from misery—and by what means [uncertain fragment]. The reward of Christian service is not in this life. The Christian spirit concerning temporal and eternal goods

[From the time Adam sinned, we have all been born miserable; misery is therefore common. But against the generation that made us miserable, God provided regeneration, by which he would free us from misery. Generation sends us into misery; regeneration appoints us to blessedness.

For I did not mean, when I said that regeneration frees us from misery, that we are immediately blessed as soon as we have been regenerated. If we were blessed immediately upon regeneration and were living through good days, the Apostle would not say to us—he who speaks to those already regenerated and faithful—“Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
