Even after being regenerated, we live through evil days until the punishment of mortality comes to an end and the grace of supreme happiness follows.

If our worship of God benefits us nothing in the world to come, why do we worship him? So that we may have happiness here? How many possess it who do not worship God? So that we may grow old here and become decrepit? How many blasphemers of God grow old?

Is God therefore to be worshiped so that his worshipers may have children and not be barren? God gives children to lions, wild asses, and serpents as well. Therefore, what is also given to Jews, pagans, heretics, and even beasts should not be sought as a great and true good.

For even the wicked possess gold and silver, honors, children, and extensive estates. The person who is truly a Christian ought not to seek all these passing things; rather, he ought to expend the entire weight of his intention and prayer in seeking eternal blessedness.

For these temporal goods, both when God gives them and when he takes them away, let thanks be given equally. Let him grant them when he wishes and take them away when he wishes; only let him not take himself away from us.]

## 3. The present times are not more unhappy than earlier times

Therefore, brothers, when you hear this reading of the blessed Apostle—“Redeeming the time, because the days are evil”—let no one say in his heart: “Our parents had good days; we have evil days.”

Why our parents? Were they not Christians? Was this reading not recited in the very times of the Apostles? So many years ago, when it was recited, did people not groan under it and recognize the truth of what it said?

[Col. 1965]

Ever since Adam fell and was expelled from paradise, there have never been days except evil days.

Let us ask these children who are born why they begin with crying, though they are also able to laugh. A child is born and immediately cries; only after I do not know how many days does he laugh. When he cried at birth, he was a prophet of his own calamity, for tears are witnesses of misery.

He does not yet speak, and already he prophesies that he will live in labor and fear. And even if he lives well [Note: [Col. 1965] Thus Lov. The manuscripts have: “if he lives well, well, if he lives,” etc.; Amerbach and Erasmus repeat *bene*—“well”—a third time, evidently meaning: “if he lives well.”] and is righteous, certainly, placed amid temptations, he will always be afraid.

[What does it matter that he is righteous? Look, he is righteous.]

What does the Apostle say? “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12). Look: because the days are evil, the righteous cannot live here without persecution.

## 4. The persecution of the godly in a time of peace. Danger from false brothers

[But you say to me: “What do you mean? When there is peace, when the judges of the provinces honor the Church, when the Church suffers no hostile kings, [Col. 1966] when all the laws are on its side, how do those who live piously suffer persecution? Those who live among the wicked suffer persecution. Why?”]

Because all wicked people persecute the good—not with sword and stones, but by their life and conduct.

Was anyone persecuting the holy Lot in Sodom? No one was troubling him; and yet he lived among the ungodly, among the impure, unclean, proud, and blasphemous. He suffered persecution, not by being beaten, but by living among the wicked.

[For every person who is righteous and godly, when he sees some people living wickedly, serving luxury, failing to uphold justice, pursuing pride, and scorning love—when those who are good see such people, they grieve, are afflicted, and are saddened. For with the Apostle they mourn those who have sinned and have not repented (2 Corinthians 12:21).]

Whoever hears me and does not yet live piously in Christ, begin to live piously in Christ. And why do I say this?

[Did the Apostle Paul, who lived at a time when faith was still newly spreading throughout the world and therefore had to endure many adversaries—since this was said of Christ, “A sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34)—did he mention only those persecutions that he suffered from Jews or from Gentiles? Not only those, for he describes them as follows: “From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one; I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:24–25), and the other things we know when we read them.

But there were also persecutions without which no righteous person can live in this world: “Battles without, fears within” (ibid. 7:5).]

Finally, when he was recounting his dangers, he says: “In dangers at sea, in dangers in rivers, in dangers in the desert, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from false brothers” (ibid. 11:26). The other dangers can cease; dangers from false brothers do not know how to cease until the end of the world.

## 5. Redeeming the time

Let us therefore redeem the time, because the days are evil. Perhaps you expect me to explain what it means to redeem the time, how we are to redeem the time. I shall say something that few hear, few endure, few undertake, and few put into practice. Nevertheless, I shall say it, because the few who will listen to me live among the wicked, because the days are evil.

“Redeeming the time”: that is, when someone brings a lawsuit against you, give up something so that you may be free for God; do not lose yourself in lawsuits [Note: [Col. 1966] Thus Amerbach and Erasmus with the manuscripts. Lov. has, with Augustine’s *On the Words of the Apostle*: “so that you may be free for God, not for lawsuits. Therefore give up,” etc.]. From what you give up comes the price of time.

Certainly, when you go out into the marketplace for your needs, you give money and buy bread, or wine, or oil, or wood, or clothing, or some piece of household equipment, or whatever you need. You give and receive; you lose something and acquire something. This is buying.

For if you lose nothing and have what you did not have, either you found it, or you received it as a gift, or you acquired it by inheritance. But when you lose something in order to have something, then you buy: what you have is purchased; what you lose is the price.

Therefore, just as you spend money to buy bread for yourself, so spend money to buy rest for yourself. This is what it means to redeem the time.

[Note: [Col. 1966] The manuscripts add after the word “redeem”: “Hear an ancient proverb,” and omit what follows. In the printed and manuscript Augustinian texts, after the words “It is a Punic ancient proverb,” there follows: “Pestilence seeks a coin,” etc.]

## 6. A Punic proverb. Avoiding lawsuits

There is a well-known Punic proverb, which I shall tell you in Latin, because not all of you know Punic. It is an ancient Punic proverb: “To have rest, give up something.”

Hear an ancient proverb, useful and necessary: “Pestilence has come to the door and asks for a coin; give it two, and let it go on its way.”

[Pestilence is the wicked person who wants to strip you through false accusation. Pestilence is a wicked person, an accuser, a betrayer. Such a person is like a bad pustule on the body.

For when a person develops a pustule, he wants it to come quickly to a head and wishes that, without any delay, the evil pustule itself might take away some portion [Col. 1967] from the body and depart with it, lest its poison seize the whole body and attack the soul.

So also, when an unjust and wicked person, who wants to do nothing except occupy himself with lawsuits, brings some accusation against you, consider him a bad pustule and consent to lose whatever small portion of your property may be necessary. Otherwise, while you occupy yourself excessively with litigation, you will be unable to have a peaceful heart and devote yourself to God.]

Does not the proverb just mentioned seem to have arisen from the Gospel? Did the Lord say anything else than “Redeem the time” when he said: “If someone wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40)?

He wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic? He is going to draw you away from your God into lawsuits. You will not have a peaceful heart; you will not have a tranquil mind. Your thoughts will be overturned; you will be irritated against your adversary. Look: you have lost time. How much better it would have been to lose a coin and redeem the time!

Certainly, what has been said has pleased everyone.

[I come to your own affairs, and there I find you.]

## 7. What follows concerning lawsuits

And yet, my brothers, in your cases and your business affairs, when they come to us for judgment, if I say to a Christian that, in order to redeem time, he should give up some of what belongs to him, with how much greater concern and confidence must I tell him to return what belongs to another?

For I hear both of them as Christians. The accuser who wants to bring a case against another and take something from him, rejoices at these words as though they were spoken for his own advantage: “The Apostle said, ‘Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.’ I shall bring an accusation against a Christian; whether he wishes to or not, he will give me something in order to redeem his time, because he has heard the Apostle.”

[See to it that perhaps, while you think yourself clever, you may prove litigious, and that he may prefer to spend something in order to defeat you rather than lose something in order to be rid of you.]

Nevertheless, if I am going to say to that good and just person, “Give up something, [Note: [Col. 1967] Perhaps: “rather.”] redeem the time; you have heard the Apostle, because the days are evil; if I say to him, ‘Give up something so that you may be at peace,’” am I not going to say to you, accuser, spendthrift, son of the devil: “You have no case, and you are trying to take another’s property; you have no case, and you are full of accusation”?

You are a Christian. Surely I do not want him to gain and you to perish? If I say to him, “Give him something so that he may withdraw from his accusation,” where will you be—the one who will have money from the accusation?

He who redeemed time from you by paying to avoid accusation is enduring evil days here. You who feed on accusations also have evil days here, and after these days you will have worse ones on the day of judgment.

But perhaps you laugh because you are looking at the coin. Laugh, laugh, and despise it; I shall spend, and the one who will demand payment will come.

[But we trust in God’s mercy that the merciful Lord himself will deign to inspire not only all the holy and God-fearing Christians, but also those who disturb themselves and others with many lawsuits, so that, setting aside all contention and rivalry, they may devote themselves so fully to peace and love that they may not incur God’s anger on account of discord, but rather, through love and peace, may deserve to reach eternal rewards; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.]

# SERMON CXII

[Note: [Col. 1967] Formerly, *On Time* 44.]

On the words of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 1:5: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

[Note: [Col. 1967] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is among those that are doubtful to the Louvain editors but spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. In its entirety it represents the style and character of Caesarius together with Augustine’s teaching. For section 1, see Caesarius, Homily 20; for section 2, Homily 10 among those published by Baluzius; for section 5, Homily 32.]

## 1. Love is something brief and great. Love is sweet

If, with Christ’s help, dearest brothers, we could present ourselves to your love more frequently, from the abundant fountains of the holy Scriptures we might pour into your holy souls, if not overflowing streams, at least drops of some kind [Col. 1968], so that the most fertile and fruitful soil of your hearts, having received the rain of God’s word, might produce an abundant harvest of good works; so that, when the Lord comes, he may rejoice to find in the field of your hearts not only a thirtieth-fold fruit but also a sixtieth-fold and hundredfold fruit. By these fruits may he prepare a granary in heaven, not a fire in hell.

But because we are hindered by many occupations, if we can present our humility to you according to your desire [Note: [Col. 1968] Thus manuscript T. The printed editions have: “we cannot represent,” without the particle “if.”], we wish, with God’s gift, to suggest to you something brief in speech but very great for the salvation of souls. If you attend carefully to this brief teaching, you can discover what is fitting for your souls.

What, then, is this brief thing, and so great that it can suffice for the human race? The Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

Attend, brothers: what could be found briefer in words and more magnificent in reality than love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith? This brief teaching is pleasant to retain in memory and sweet to keep faithfully.

What is sweeter than love, dearest brothers? Whoever does not know should taste and see. What, then, must the person taste who wishes the sweetness of love to be pleasing to him? Hear the Apostle saying: “God is love” (1 John 4:16). What is sweeter, brothers? Whoever does not know should hear the Psalmist saying: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33:9).

God, then, is love. Whoever has love has God dwelling in him, and he himself dwells in God.

## 2. It makes rich

If you have love, you have God; and if you have God, what do you not have? If a rich person does not have love, what does he have? If a poor person has love, what does he not have?

Perhaps you think that the person is rich whose chest is full of gold, and that the person is not rich whose conscience is full of God? It is not so, brothers. The one in whom God deigns to dwell truly appears to be rich.

What could you fail to understand from the Scriptures if love—that is, God—has begun to possess you? What good works could you fail to accomplish if you have deserved to carry within your heart the fountain of good works? What adversary will you fear if you have deserved to have God the King within you?

Therefore, dearest brothers, hold and guard the sweet and salutary bond of love. But above all, hold true love—not the love that is merely promised with the mouth and is not kept in the heart, but the love that is uttered from the mouth in such a way that it is nevertheless held continually in the heart—so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in you: “Rooted and founded in love” (Ephesians 3:27).

For love is the root of all good things, just as greed is the root of all evils. Just as nothing evil can ever be found in love, so nothing good can ever be found in greed.

## 3. Two roots planted in human hearts: from one nothing evil, from the other nothing good proceeds

These two roots, dearest brothers, are planted in two fields by two farmers. Christ plants one in the hearts of the good; the devil plants the other in the hearts of the wicked.

Nothing evil is born from the root of love, nor anything good from the root of greed. For Truth does not lie. When speaking in the Gospel about these two roots, it defined them as follows: “A good tree produces good fruits”; and again: “A good tree cannot produce evil fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits.”

This saying is not mine, brothers, but the Lord’s.

Therefore, let there be in us such an abundance of love that it reaches not only to friends but even to enemies themselves. And because you have heard both praise of love and condemnation of greed, let each person attend and examine the field of his heart.

If someone sees love in himself, let him rejoice and, with all the vigilance of his heart, guard the holy shoots within him. But whoever notices in the field of his heart any growth of greed should, with Christ’s help, uproot [Col. 1969] greed and plant love. For as long as he refuses to do this, he will not be able to bear good fruits.

And when he has not borne good fruits, the Lord Christ, Lord of heaven and earth, says of him: “The tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7:17–19).

If you take no delight in bearing the sweet fruits of love, should you not at least fear the fire on account of the thorns of your sins? “Every tree,” he says, “that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

As long as you have not changed the root, you will not be able to bear proper fruits. And you promise in vain with your mouth what is good, because you cannot fulfill it as long as the root of goodness is not held in your heart.

Therefore, as I said above, two farmers customarily plant these two roots. Christ plants one in the hearts of the faithful; the devil plants the other in the hearts of the proud. Thus one is planted in heaven, the other in hell.

## 4. The hearts of the faithful are heaven; the hearts of the greedy are earth

But someone says: “If it is planted in the hearts of the faithful, the faithful evidently still appear to be in the world. How, then, is that root planted in heaven?”

Do you want to know how? Because the hearts of the faithful are heaven, since they are raised daily into the heavens. For when the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” they confidently respond, “We have them with the Lord,” because, as the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

If, then, the citizenship of the faithful is in heaven because true love is in them, the root of love has been planted in heaven.

Conversely, the root of greed, which is in the hearts of the proud, has been planted in hell, because they always desire earth, savor earth, love earth, and place all their hope in earth.

## 5. The wicked must avoid despair; the righteous must avoid presumption. Repentance must not be postponed

Although this is so, proud sinners ought not to despair, nor should humble righteous people grow proud in any way, as though relying on their own merits. For if the righteous presume upon themselves, they quickly lose the root of love; and if sinners turn to repentance, once greed has been uprooted, they quickly receive the plant of love.

Therefore, let those who are good guard what they have received by God’s gift; and let those who are evil strive to restore what they have unhappily lost.

Let no one reserve himself for that time when, at the point of departure from this life, he will repent or retain the sweetness of love. Let no one reserve himself for old age, intending then to flee to the remedies of repentance, because he does not know what the coming day may bring.

With what face does he postpone his salvation until old age, when he cannot be certain even of the span of a single day?

Therefore, if we do not wish to fear death, we must always be ready, so that when the Lord orders us to be called away from this world, we may come before the sight of the eternal Judge with a secure conscience—not in despair, but with joy—and may there happily hear:

“Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

May the Lord, in his mercy, lead us to that joy—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXIII

[Note: [Col. 1969] Formerly, *On Time* 190.]

On the words of the Apostle, Hebrews 1:3: “For he is the radiance of eternal light and the image of the invisible God.”

[Note: [Col. 1969] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was copied from Vigilius of Tapsus, *On the Faith against the Arian Palladius*, book 2, chapters 5–7, in the edition of Francis Chiffletius, page 516 and following. The first two verses were added in place of a preface.]

## 1. The nature and greatness of God are not to be judged. What God is

You heard the Apostle’s reading together with me, beloved. For he says of the Lord Jesus Christ: “For he is the radiance of eternal light and the image of the invisible God,” since the light of the sun is itself an image of the sun, proceeding from that same sun.

Since it is established that this light of divinity cannot be estimated, comprehended, or defined, I therefore first warn you to believe spiritually only in the unity of substance and to recognize the true Son from the true Father.

You ought not to inquire into the quality of the reality, because God wished to be believed, not judged or examined; for what he is or how great he is cannot be known. The Prophets and the Apostles proclaimed this.

Finally, according to our capacity, strength, and faith, let us contemplate what God is and see whether anything can be compared with him.

Certainly, God is this: when he is spoken of, he cannot be spoken; when he is estimated, he cannot be estimated; when he is compared, he cannot be compared; when he is defined, he grows through the very definition. He is the one who covers heaven with his hand and encloses the entire circuit of the world in his fist; whom all things do not know in his entirety, yet know in fear; whose name and power this world serves, and whose own momentary succession of the elements testifies that it must serve him [Note: [Col. 1970] The word “must serve” is found neither in Vigilius’s work nor in the Remigian manuscript.]

## 2. The Son’s various names and the reasons for each

See, then, whether anything can exist with which the Father and the Son may be compared, because the Son is such as the Father is. For he would not himself say that he is one with the Father unless he knew himself to be such from the Father as the Father is.

There is a certain Reason, called **λόγος** (*logos*) among the Greeks, which distinguishes the persons or names of the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1970] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov. read: “Indeed, the Reason which is called *Logos* among the Greeks, between the Father,” etc. M.], because the Son himself is also called Reason. Yet this Reason is called by many names: now Word, now Power, now Wisdom, now Right Hand, now Arm, now Pearl, now Treasure, now Nets, now Plow, now Fountain, now Rock, now Cornerstone, now Man, now Lamb, now Calf, now Eagle, now Lion, now Way, Truth, and Life—while he is God, all things in all things.

These names are given so that the mysteries of the divine dispositions may be understood, not so that the majesty of the Son of God itself may be properly defined or displayed.

For the Son of God is what the Father is, not another—namely, the one through whom all things were made [Note: [Col. 1970] Manuscript Remigianus has “the same.”].

He is also called the Word because he is always in the Father and from the Father, and the Father has commanded or done nothing without him.

He is called Power because he is properly from God and all power rests in him.

He is called Wisdom because, coming from nowhere other than the Father, he has opened the heavenly mysteries to believers.

He is called the Right Hand because through him all divine works have been perfected.

He is called the Arm because all things are held together by him.

He is called the Pearl so that nothing may be considered more precious than he.

He is called the Treasure because in him all the resources and riches of the heavenly kingdoms are known to be stored.

He is called Nets because through him and in him the multitude of the various nations is gathered from the sea of the world, like fish, into the Church through Baptism, where the distinction between the good and the wicked is recognized.

He is called the Plow because, by the sign of his cross, hardened hearts are subdued [Note: [Col. 1970] In the Remigian manuscript: “are broken up,” or “are tilled,” *subiguntur*.], so that they may be prepared for the necessary seed.

He is called the Fountain of living water because from him thirsty hearts are watered by the grace of heavenly water.

He is called the Rock because he grants strength to believers and hardness to unbelievers.

He is called the Cornerstone because, himself alone and the mediator, holding both walls—the New and the Old Testament—in himself, he joined them together.

He is called the Lamb so that the innocence and Passion of Christ may be shown.

He is called Man because, according to the flesh, he deigned to be born for us human beings.

He is called the Calf because he endured being sacrificed for our salvation.

He is called the Eagle because, after his venerable resurrection, he flew back to the seat of his Father.

He is called the Lion because he is the King of kings, because by the power of his strength he crushed death and the devil.

He is the Way because through him there is access to the Father.

He is the Truth because he knows no falsehood.

He is the Life because he gives life.

He signifies all things.

[Col. 1971]

## 3. The equality of the Son with the Father

The Father, therefore, is God, immeasurable, eternal, incomprehensible, beyond estimation. The Son also is God and our Lord, as great as the Father, but from no one other than the Father, because he says: “I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:27–28)—that is, light from light.

But lest a heretic take from this an opportunity, and, when I establish two names or two persons—that is, of the Father and the Son—imagine that I am fabricating two gods on account of their distinction, we name the Father and the Son in such a way that we assert one God in these persons and in all things.

Moreover, although the Father and the Son are believed to be two persons, they are one in reason and substance. For an association between unequal persons is an offense against the better, and it is an insult to him who is the true God if another who is not true is compared with him. For whoever unjustly compares God violates him.

When, therefore, I establish the Father and the Son, I affirm the unity of kind. And if I distinguish that unity among the persons, nevertheless the distinction of the persons again consigns those same names to their unity, according to the law of their natural covenant.

# SERMON 114

[Note: [Col. 1971] Also titled *On Various Matters* 97.]

On the words of the Apostle, Hebrews, chapter 12, verse 1: “Since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1971] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. Verlinus and Vindingus declare it spurious; the hardness of its style and its method of interpreting Scripture support their judgment.]

## 1. A great struggle in the contest

My brothers, the apostolic reading recently sounded in our ears; and how greatly it was desired that it be implanted in our hearts! For it exhorted us with patience toward the prize of the contest promised to us. In this respect, I confess, it greatly stirred the spirit of my weakness. For who can run with patience? There is usually a great struggle in a contest; each person strives not to be defeated by another. How, then, will the one who is striving to overcome be patient? If he is slow, he is defeated; if he runs, impiety contends, sweats, and fights. What patience does he preserve? Unless perhaps, brothers, this contest of ours is not of the body but of the soul; and our running is not a matter of place but of the mind.

## 2. The saints are a cloud

For the saints there is already rest and patience. Above, the blessed Apostle showed to what sort of contest he had summoned us. For he names, one by one, the contests of all the saints; and after enumerating the multitude of the saints, he says: “Since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses.”

If they are witnesses, they are not obscure. How, then, are they clouds? Not through obscurity, but through height. For he was speaking of those who were already resting with God and, from above, concealed us here on earth; and yet he says: “After they had contended, they await us, so that they may not be made perfect without us” (Hebr. 11:39–40). They ran and arrived; yet they have not received the prize, because they await us. There too, then, there is patience, until the Lord comes, “and brings to light the things hidden in darkness and reveals the counsels of the heart; and then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5). Then there will be praise. What is there now? Rest and patience.

Since, then, we have so great a cloud of witnesses—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Joseph, Elijah, Elisha, Paul, and James—and who could count so great a cloud of witnesses?

## 3. The patience of Stephen

Among this number of holy men was the most blessed Stephen, who was the first to run with patience in this stadium of the world. While the unbelievers repeatedly struck him with a stony rain, he did not lose patience from his holy heart.

Then an unhappy, countless multitude of Jews was stirred up against him; roaring, they hurled hard stones at his delicate limbs.

Why do you roar, mad Judea? Why do you fix your hard eyes upon the martyr? The one whom you think is dying from your stones has already begun to behold heaven’s secrets. He no longer fears your hands, raging to stone his body, because Christ has already opened heaven to him.

## 4. We must run, and therefore lay down the burden of sin

Sin is agile.

Let us too, brothers, run with patience toward the contest of faith set before us. How do we run when we are weighed down? Burdens oppress us. For no one runs while loaded down, when even a light person scarcely arrives with sweat.

We are called; let us come. And lest we fail to arrive, let us run. What counsel is there for those who are burdened? “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28).

“We wish to, Lord, we wish to—and we cannot; or perhaps we do not even wish to. We are burdened because the load has come upon us [Note: [Col. 1972] Perhaps, ‘because the load presses upon us.’], and we do not wish to. Help us and have mercy on us. You said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5).

Because of this burden, let us implore God’s help and hear Paul’s counsel. For see what he added next. When he had shown us so great a cloud of witnesses—as though we were thinking and saying, “Who can rise up there? Who can reach those people?”—he saw our burden and oppression. He gave counsel to the weak, infirm, and burdened, saying: “Laying aside every burden.” And to show what the burden is, he added: “And the agile sin.”

A slow burden—perhaps anyone might be able to avoid such a sin. What does it mean to avoid agile sin? It suddenly rises in the mind and produces pleasure; immediately it drags the mind along. O certain agility! Run against it, lest it overcome you. Anticipate it; watch for it; lay the sin aside; throw out iniquity, suggestion, and pleasure.

But so that you may be able to do this, implore him without whom you can do nothing. Frustrate the sin; offer the remedy.

## 5. Patience belongs to God

Let us run with patience. Let us not stand still, but neither let us be disturbed—rather, with patience.

What, then? Is patience yours? By no means. Hear the blessed martyr Cyprian: in one of his chapters he says, “Patience is God’s affair” (*Sermon on the Good of Patience*). Hence he himself also says by the Holy Spirit, through David: “You are my patience.” And to show by what means he would run and where he would arrive, he says: “Lord, you are my hope from my youth” (Ps. 70:5).

When Paul offered the many-clouded host of witnesses, he presented the sun by which we ought to see the light. For he says, as though to people established in darkness: “Looking to Jesus, the pioneer of faith and its perfecter.”

If he is himself the pioneer and himself the perfection, it is true that without him we can do nothing.

But what did he do that we ought to imitate? Was it that he is God? Was it that he is equal to the Father? Was it that he is the creator of heaven and earth? Who could imitate this? O human being, when will the creature be made equal to the Creator?

Do not think arrogantly; hear what you ought to imitate. “For the joy set before him, he endured the cross.” As an example of suffering, he offered the vine to its branches. Whatever is superfluous among the branches must be cut away, so that it may bear abundant fruit.

## 6. The praise of Stephen, the protomartyr

Most beloved, how did he endure suffering except through patience? The most blessed and first martyr Stephen was of such a branch; he was the first to follow, clinging to the vine.

When he saw, without fear, the blood of the vine, he shed his own blood. Stoned for Christ the Lord, the king of the ages, he was the first to merit receiving the unfading crown of his martyrdom.

---

# CLASS II OF THE APPENDIX

SERMONS FOR THE LITURGICAL YEAR. (C, G)*

# SERMON 115

[Note: [Col. 1973] Also titled *Sermon for the Liturgical Year* 1.]

On the Advent of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 1973] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition it had remained among the doubtful works; Verlinus and Vindingus later added the judgment that it was spurious, both on account of the simplicity of its style and because, among those men, the practice of daily Communion—which Augustine in his time attested to be customary in the Western Church, in *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book 2, section 26, and Letter 54, section 4—was not accepted. For here the hearers are invited to change their lives so that, on the Lord’s Nativity, “they may approach the altar with a pure heart and a chaste body.” Its style and method of argument compel us to restore it to Caesarius of Arles, although some manuscripts attribute it to Augustine. In those manuscripts the sermon begins with these words: “By the favor of God, most beloved brothers, the day has now arrived on which we desire to celebrate with joy the Nativity of the Lord our Savior. And therefore I ask and urge you, as much as we can, let us labor so that on that day, with a sincere and pure conscience,” etc. It is also found published among the Ambrosian sermons with this same beginning. For section 1, compare Caesarius, Homily 2 and Appendix Sermon 5, section 5; for section 3, Caesarius, Homily 3 from the editions published by Baluze, as well as Homily 32; for the end of section 4, Homily 21, where Caesarius imitates Augustine’s *Enchiridion*, chapter 74.]

## 1. What must be done before the celebration of the Lord’s Nativity

We must labor so that Christ’s body may be received worthily.

As the most sacred solemnity approaches, on which our Savior mercifully willed to be born among human beings, consider more attentively, most beloved brothers, how we ought to prepare ourselves for the coming of such great power, so that we may deserve to receive our King and Lord joyfully and gladly, with glory and praises, and may exult in his presence while rejoicing among the happy assemblies of the saints, rather than, rejected by him because of our foulness, deserve eternal shame among sinners.

And therefore I ask and urge you: as much as we can, let us labor with God’s help so that on that day, with a pure and sincere conscience, a clean heart, and a chaste body, we may approach the Lord’s altar and deserve to receive his body and blood, not for judgment but as a remedy for our soul.

For our life consists in Christ’s body, just as he himself said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Therefore, let the person who wishes to receive life change his life. For if he does not change his life, he will receive life for judgment; and he will be corrupted by it rather than healed, killed rather than given life.

For the Apostle said: “Whoever eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:27).

## 2. The conscience must be cleansed

Although it is fitting that we be adorned and radiant with good works at all times, nevertheless, especially on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, as he himself said in the Gospel, “your works must shine before people” (Matt. 5:16).

Consider, I ask you, brothers, when some powerful or noble person wishes to celebrate his own birthday or that of his son, with what care, many days beforehand, he orders everything dirty that he sees in his house to be cleaned, everything useless and unsuitable to be thrown out, and everything useful and necessary to be brought in. If the house is somewhat dark, it is whitewashed; the floors are cleaned with brooms and decorated by being sprinkled with various flowers. Everything that contributes to cheerfulness of mind and bodily pleasures is provided with the greatest care.

Why do people do all these things, most beloved brothers, except so that the birthday of a mortal person may be celebrated with joy?

If, then, you make so many preparations for your own birthday or your son’s, how many and what sort of preparations ought you to make when you are about to celebrate the Nativity of your Lord? If you make such preparations for one who will die, what preparations ought you to make for the Eternal One?

Therefore, whatever you do not wish to find in your house, labor as much as you can so that God may not find it in your soul.

## 3. The soul must be adorned with good works

Repentance must immediately follow fault.

Certainly, if an earthly king—or any head of a household—invited you to his birthday celebration, in what sort of garments would you strive to appear adorned? How new, clean, and splendid they would be, so that neither their age, nor their cheapness, nor any foulness would offend the eyes of the one giving the invitation?

With such zeal, then, as far as you are able, strive with Christ’s help so that your soul, arranged with various ornaments of virtue and adorned with the jewels of simplicity and the flowers of sobriety, may proceed to the solemnity of the eternal King—that is, to the Nativity of the Lord and Savior—with a secure conscience: shining with chastity, radiant with charity, and white with almsgiving.

For if Christ the Lord knows that you have arranged yourself in this way to celebrate his birthday, he himself will deign to come, to visit your soul, and not only to visit it but also to rest and dwell in it forever, as it is written: “I will dwell in them, and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). And again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone rises and opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3:20).

How happy is the soul that, with God’s help, has striven to govern its life in such a way that it may deserve to receive Christ as guest and inhabitant! Conversely, how unhappy is that conscience—one to be mourned with a whole fountain of tears—which has bloodied itself with evil works so that Christ cannot rest in it, but the devil begins to rule there!

For such a soul, unless the remedy of repentance quickly comes to its aid, is abandoned by the light and occupied by darkness; it is emptied of sweetness and filled with bitterness; death invades it, and life rejects it.

Yet the person in such a state should not despair of the Lord’s mercy or be broken by deadly despair. Rather, let him flee quickly to repentance. While the wounds of his sins are still fresh and hot, let him apply healing remedies to himself, because our physician is almighty God, and he is accustomed to heal our wounds in such a way that, after his medicines, not even traces of scars remain.

Therefore you too ought to abstain for many days before his Nativity from every impurity.

## 4. Vices to be avoided before solemnities

Hatred especially.

Whenever you plan to celebrate either the Lord’s Nativity or the remaining solemnities, flee drunkenness above all; resist anger as though it were a most savage beast; drive hatred, like deadly poison, from your hearts. Let such charity exist among you that it extends not only to friends but even to enemies themselves, so that you may confidently say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

For whoever knows that he hates even one person—I do not know how he can approach the Lord’s altar with confidence—especially since the blessed evangelist John cries out terrifyingly and says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

It is for you to judge whether a murderer ought, before doing penance, to presume to receive the Eucharist.

The holy John adds further and cries out, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes.” And again he says: “Everyone who does not love his brother remains in death.” And again: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 2:11; 3:14; 4:20).

Therefore, whoever keeps hatred or anger in his heart and is neither terrified nor awakened by such thunder should be considered not asleep but dead.

## 5. Exhortation

Thinking about these things daily, most beloved brothers, let those who are good, with God’s grace, strive to persevere in good works, because “it is not the one who begins but the one who perseveres to the end who will be saved.”

But those who recognize that they are slow to give alms, quick to anger, and headlong in practicing lust should hasten, with the Lord’s help, to rescue themselves from evil, so that they may deserve to accomplish what is good.

Thus, when the day of judgment comes, may they deserve to arrive not with the ungodly but with the just and merciful at eternal rewards; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 116

[Note: [Col. 1975] Also titled *Sermon for the Liturgical Year* 2.]

On the Advent of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 1975] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition it had remained among the doubtful works; it was rejected by the judgment of Verlinus and Vindingus. A comparison with his other sermons will establish that this too belongs to Caesarius, to whom it is attributed in the Corbie manuscript. For sections 1 and 2, see Appendix Sermon 29, section 4; for section 5, above, Sermon 104, section 3; for section 6, Appendix Sermon 10, section 5.]

## 1. Let the Lord’s Nativity not find us unprepared

As we are about to receive with the most faithful devotion this holy, desirable, glorious, and unique solemnity—that is, the birth of the Lord and Savior—most beloved brothers, we must prepare ourselves with all our strength and with his help. We must carefully examine every hiding place of our soul, lest there perhaps be some hidden sin within us that both confounds and gnaws at our conscience and offends the eyes of the divine majesty.

For although Christ our Lord rose after his passion and ascended into heaven, he nevertheless considers and carefully observes, as we believe, how each of his servants strives to prepare and arrange himself for celebrating his birth: without greed, anger, pride, or lust. And according to how he sees each person adorned with good works, so he will dispense to that person the grace of his mercy.

For if he sees someone clothed in the light of charity, adorned with the pearls of justice and mercy, chaste, humble, merciful, kind, and sober, then to such a person he will dispense his body and blood through the ministry of his priests, not for judgment but as a remedy.

But if he sees someone adulterous, drunk, greedy, and proud, I fear that what the Lord himself said in the Gospel may be said to him: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?” And, God forbid, may what follows come to pass: “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:12–13).

Behold what sentence will meet on the day of judgment the person who, without the remedy of repentance, approaches the Lord’s festival stained with the filth of vices.

## 2. The day is Christ’s wedding

At Christ’s wedding, who is the bride and what is the food?

On the Lord’s Nativity, most beloved brothers, as though at a spiritual wedding, Christ was joined to his bride, the Church. Then truth arose from the earth; then justice looked down from heaven (Ps. 84:12). Then the bridegroom came forth from his bridal chamber (Ps. 18:6)—that is, the Word of God from the Virgin’s womb.

For he came forth with his bride, the Church; that is, he assumed human flesh.

Invited, then, to this most holy wedding and about to enter the banquet of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, see with what sort of garments we ought to be adorned. Therefore, with God’s help, as far as we can, let us cleanse both our hearts and our bodies, so that the heavenly inviter may find nothing dirty, nothing foul, nothing obscure, and nothing unworthy of his eyes in us.

These things, then, most beloved brothers, we must attend to not superficially but with great trembling. For we have been invited to a wedding at which, if we act well, we ourselves will be the bride.

Let us consider what sort of wedding, what sort of bridegroom, and what sort of banquet we have been invited to. For we have been invited to a table where the food is not human food, but where the bread of angels is set forth.

Therefore let us take care lest, within our souls—where we ought to be adorned with the pearls of good works—we appear wrapped in the old rags of vices. And when chastity makes those who are good white in God’s eyes, lust will make those who are evil soiled.

## 3. What must be done before the solemnities

Therefore, whenever either the day of the Lord’s Nativity or the other festivals arrive, as I have often admonished you, abstain for many days beforehand not only from the wretched intercourse of concubines but also from your own wives. Keep yourselves free from every form of anger.

Let past sins be redeemed through almsgiving and repentance. Let no hatred be held in the heart against anyone. Let what vanity used to squander through gluttony begin to be distributed by justice through mercy to the poor. Let what lust or gluttony dissipated in the world be restored by piety in heaven.

## 4. The poor must be invited to the banquet

Although it is beneficial that we should always give alms, nevertheless, especially during the holy solemnities, let us give more generously according to our means. Above all, let us invite the poor to our banquets more frequently.

For it is not right that in a holy solemnity, among a Christian people belonging to one Lord, some should be made drunk while others are tortured by the danger of hunger.

Both we and the whole people are servants of one Lord. We were redeemed at the same price; we entered this world under the same condition, and we shall depart from it by a similar exit. And if we act well, we shall likewise arrive at one blessedness.

Why should the poor person not share food with you, when he will receive the kingdom with you? Why should the poor person not receive at least an old tunic, when he will receive with you the robe of immortality? Why should the poor person not deserve to receive your bread, when he deserved to receive with you the sacrament of Baptism? Why is he unworthy to receive the leftovers of your food, when he will come with you to the banquet of angels?

Listen, brothers; listen—not to my command, but to the Lord’s common command. For he says in the Gospel: “When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite the rich, who may invite you in return and so repayment be made to you. Instead, invite the poor and the lame; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the just” (Luke 14:12–14).

## 5. Friends may also be invited, but less often and to modest banquets

But someone says: “Then ought I not invite friends or relatives to a banquet?”

Parents and neighbors should be invited, but they should be invited less often. And banquets should be prepared for them not excessively costly or luxurious, but so modest, sober, and decent that something remains with which the poor can be refreshed and something can be distributed to those in need.

Then, when the day of judgment comes, may we not hear with the ungodly, who now despise the poor, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” but may we deserve to hear with the just and merciful: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:41, 34–35).

May that desirable word also be addressed to us: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid. 21).

## 6. Recapitulation

But so that these things which we have suggested may remain more firmly in your loving hearts, let us briefly repeat what has been said.

We have admonished you, brothers, that since the Lord’s Nativity is near, we should prepare ourselves through Christ’s help as though for a nuptial and heavenly banquet, cleansed from every lust and adorned with good works; that we should distribute alms to the poor; and that we should reject anger or hatred from our hearts as the devil’s poison.

Preserve chastity faithfully even with your own wives. Invite the poor to your banquets more frequently. Rise earlier for the vigils [Note: [Col. 1977] The manuscript vd. reads, “rise for the vigils of the martyrs.” The manuscript Cb. instead reads, “rise more frequently for the vigils.”].

Standing in church, either pray or sing psalms. Do not yourselves utter idle words [Note: [Col. 1977] In the Cb. manuscript: “lustful words.” A little later, where the text has “or worldly,” vd. reads “or jocular.”] or worldly words from your mouths, and correct those who wish to utter them.

Keep peace with everyone, and bring those whom you know to be in disagreement back to harmony.

If, with Christ’s help, you faithfully wish to fulfill these things, then in this world you will be able to approach the Lord’s altar with a secure conscience, and in the future you will happily arrive at eternal blessedness; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 117

[Note: [Col. 1977] Also titled *Sermon for the Liturgical Year* 7.]

On the Nativity of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 1977] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was regarded as doubtful by the Louvain editors, but Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. Its style is simple and more like Caesarius than Augustine. Nevertheless, as everyone will admit, it shows the character of a serious and devout author; nor is it unworthy of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in whose name a fragment was published in the fifth volume of the *Spicilegium* on the authority of a Vatican manuscript. That fragment contains the final part of this sermon, namely from section 7 to the end.” M.]

## 1. The grace of this day

I ask you, most beloved brothers, to receive with willing hearts the sermons which the Lord will grant on this sweetest day: the day on which even unbelievers are moved to compunction, the wicked are touched by mercy, the repentant hope for pardon, the captive does not despair of return, the wounded longs for a remedy, and the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world is born.

At his birth, the person who has a secure conscience rejoices more sweetly; the person who has a miserable conscience fears more attentively. The good person prays with affection; the sinner begs with the deepest devotion.

A sweet day, truly sweet, bringing pardon to all who repent.

I promise you, my little children, and I am certain: on this day, if anyone repents from the heart and does not return to the vomit of sin, whatever he asks will be given to him—provided only that he does not doubt in faith and does not seek his former pleasure again.

Today the sin of the whole world is taken away, and the sinner despairs?

## 2. What makes repentance genuine

True or freely offered repentance.

But consider what repentance ought to be. Many people constantly say that they are sinners, and yet they still take pleasure in sinning. It is a confession, not a correction; the soul is accused, not healed; the offense is pronounced, not removed.

Nothing makes repentance genuine except hatred of sin and love of God.

When you repent in such a way that what was previously sweet in life tastes bitter to you in your soul, and what formerly delighted you in the body now torments you in your heart, then you are truly groaning before God and saying: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6).

Well said: “Against you alone have I sinned,” because no human being is without sin; and therefore, “Against you alone have I sinned,” because you alone among human beings are without sin [Note: [Col. 1977] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain editions: “because no one is without sin.” M.].

Grant mercy, Lord, to the wretched person whom you have spared for so long in his crimes. Let the humility of the penitent incline you toward a remedy, since the long duration of his sin could not move you.

Say to him in the tears of your heart: “Look upon the unhappy person, boundless compassion; look upon the cruel person, universal mercy. I come to the Almighty in despair; wounded, I run to the physician. Preserve the compassion of your gentleness [Note: [Col. 1977] Some manuscripts: “preserve the habit of compassion”; others: “preserve the compassion of habit.”], you who have suspended the sword of vengeance for so long. Erase the multitude of my crimes through the multitude of your mercies.”

This, my little children, is true repentance [Note: [Col. 1977] Most manuscripts read “free repentance” instead of “true repentance.”], when someone is converted in such a way that he does not return to sin; when he repents in such a way that he does not repeat it.

## 3. The emptiness of passing pleasure

The true happiness of this life.

Let us see whether some of you are strong and exercising the virtue of your souls [Note: [Col. 1978] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice: “Indeed, we see some of you displaying strength and exercising the virtue of your spirits.” Louvain: “Indeed, let us see whether some of you are so strong and are exercising the virtue of your spirits.” The same books shortly afterward read “soft vices,” and three times “fights.” M.].

On this day, let them hear my words for their salvation in such a way that they manfully cast off the softness of vices, like those who are fighting. In truth, those fight more courageously who fight against themselves.

Let them open their ears to Christ’s commands—ears which perhaps until now were open to hear mockery. Let them open their eyes to radiance—eyes which until now were open to disgrace.

Let repentance for crimes pierce the one whom the pleasure of delights has pierced until now. Let the virtue that has been added raise up the one whom vices have cast down.

Let them open their nostrils to the remedy, since the habitual practice of sin stinks to them [Note: [Col. 1978] The printed editions add here the word “of repentance,” and shortly afterward, instead of “for whom that stinks,” they read “for whom those things stink.” We have followed the manuscripts.].

May he open the eyes of your hearts who today deigned to be born for us, so that we may see him.

What is thought to be sufficiently sweet now, within the brevity of time—how bitter will it be in the eternal fire! With how severe and perpetual a punishment will the brevity of pleasure have to be punished!

Pleasure kills, and then passes away; it wounds, and then departs; it makes a person wretched, and then leaves; it makes a person unhappy, and then abandons him.

How beautiful is the soul’s radiance! How happy is the conscience full of good works!

If the person who possesses what he will leave behind after death is considered blessed, how secure is the person who hopes for the reward he will never lose throughout eternity!

If the one who rules the world is called powerful, how blessed is the one who bears God in a pure conscience!

Therefore, sweetest children, desire purity of heart; possess love of God and neighbor.

Sinners, forgive, so that you may be forgiven. Just people, do not sin, so that Christ may remain in you [Note: [Col. 1978] Here the Remigianus manuscript concludes this sermon with the words, “through him who lives with the Father,” etc.].

## 4. Vows to be made to the newborn God

Different vows. The best vow.

Since these things are so, it seems to me, most beloved, that today we should promise vows to the Lord and Redeemer who is being born, and fulfill them, as it is written: “Vow, and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12).

Let us make our vows to him sweetly and confidently. He will grant the ability to fulfill them; we need only hope in him for whatever we promise him.

But perhaps you ask me what you ought to vow or fulfill today. Many people make vows: one, a cloak; another, oil or wax for the night lamps; another, not to drink wine for several years; another, to fast for a certain period; another, not to eat meat.

This is not the best or perfect vow. I want something better.

God has no need of your appearance, your oil, or your fasting. Today offer him the very thing that he redeemed in you—that is, your soul.

And if you ask me, “How shall I offer my soul, which he himself holds in his power?” I will answer you how: through holy conduct, chaste thoughts, and fruitful works; by turning away from evil and turning toward good; by condemning vice and loving God; by loving your neighbor and showing mercy to the miserable—for we too were miserable before we were redeemed; by forgiving those who sin against us—for we were all under sin; by trampling down pride—for through pride the first human being was deceived; by casting away envy—for through envy the devil deceived the human race.

## 5. How each person should vow from his own condition

The angry person. The unchaste person. The envious person. The murderer. The slanderer. The harsh person. The proud person. The drunkard.

Since these things are so, lift up all your spirits, and let no one—whether free, enslaved, or freeborn—fail to offer and fulfill a vow to God today.

For it is exceedingly wretched if we offer God nothing of our own, when he laid down his soul for us; and for our sake, although he was eternal, he assumed flesh.

Therefore, whoever now holds anger against another should forgive for the love of God—and he has offered a vow.

If someone has become accustomed, over a long period, to wallow in lust, let him come to his senses at last and shake off his filth through compunction. Let him cry out more secretly in his heart, in prayer, to the Lord:

“Most merciful Lord, most compassionate God, let it be enough for me that until now I have sinned, that I have despised you, that I have satisfied the foulness of my flesh. Now, with your inspiration, I vow that I will turn away from my wickedness.”

When he has done this, he too has offered a vow.

Again, if someone is held by envy of his brother and does not rejoice in that person’s happiness or prosperous action—which is a sin unto death—let him also promise in his heart that he will imitate good deeds rather than retain envy of that person [Note: [Col. 1979] So read the better manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read “will contemplate” instead of “will imitate.”]. When he has done this, he too has offered a vow.

But if someone is conscious of murder, let him himself declare repentance in his heart, punish his own evil deeds, and appoint for himself before God the suffering and duration of repentance. Let him torment through abstinence and humility the soul full of poison, which the shedding of his neighbor’s blood previously wounded.

And let him presume in no way to receive Communion, lest the unhappy man condemn himself doubly by dangerously presuming to receive the most sacred body of the Lord while his heart is full of the horrors of crimes.

If someone recognizes himself as such and does these things, he too offers a vow.

If someone, as often happens, has become accustomed always to slander and to criticize the actions of others without considering his own, let him vow to God today in his heart and say:

“Until now I have spoken about others and have not examined myself. I was more wretched, yet I considered others wretched. Therefore, now let it be enough that my tongue has sinned; from now on I resolve to correct myself.”

Behold: the person who does this offers a vow.

If someone feels himself to be cruel, let him vow mercy of spirit to God. If someone is proud, let him vow humility. If someone is excessively devoted to wine, let him vow sobriety to God.

If someone has sinned against his superior, let him ask forgiveness; and if that superior does not know how to ask for it, let the other nevertheless forgive him.

## 6. The fruit of such vows

The guardian angels offer our vows to God.

And when you have done all these things, most beloved, you offer God a vow pleasing to him and, as it were, repay Christ.

After this, blessing will come to you, and your vows will be offered before Christ’s tribunal. And, as Solomon said, “your memorial will not be forgotten” (Wis. 2:24).

It will be said of you: “Behold my people, whom I acquired with my blood. They have satisfied me with vows; they have filled me with fragrances. I will be to them as a Lord, and they will be my people; and captivity or desolation will no longer exist among them.”

Let us consider how sweet it will be when the angels who guard our lives have offered such vows as I have described before the presence of the divine majesty.

If we offer something of ours to an earthly and mortal human being, and nevertheless hope to receive much from him and to be helped by him, then if we offer God something from our conduct, how much shall we receive?

## 7. The fruit of remembering Christ’s incarnation

Therefore, let us now exult in the Lord; let us rejoice with tears; let us remember the divine condescension and our captivity.

Whenever power elevates anyone, let Christ’s humility come to mind, so that this sentence may not be directed at him: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9).

Whenever we see someone miserable or needy, let God’s mercy come to mind. Whenever we see a captive, let the redemption of our Lord come to mind.

Whenever any sin delights us or steals upon us, let it remain in our memory that our sins have already been erased.

Let us not squander the price of Christ’s blood, nor stain the robe of the soul through iniquity, robbery, or lust.

We had fallen; now we have been raised. We had been wounded; now we have been healed.

There will be no excuse of any kind. The devil can invite us to evil, but he cannot drag us into it; he brings pleasure, but not power; he introduces a proposal, but not compulsion.

[Col. 1980] **8. What virgins should pursue or avoid.** Now, therefore, on account of the birth of blessed Mary, let my speech be addressed to virgins—whether men or women, widows or penitents, poor or slaves. With God there is no distinction except that of merits. Hear me, then, all of you who by Christ’s gift are virgins in body. I speak generally to everyone: hear me. Whoever recognizes that he is what I describe should strive to be a virgin in body and heart. Let him rejoice in the gain of the body, provided he suffers no loss of soul. Yet let him rejoice in so precious a gift of Christ; let him rejoice with humility and weep with devotion. Let him give thanks because he bears such happiness in purity; let him rejoice because he will follow the Lamb wherever he goes—provided that, as we read in the Apocalypse, no lie is found in his mouth (Apoc. 14:4–5). Let him pray for perseverance, so that no worldly pleasure or diabolical envy may take away so great a gift, cloud so great a brightness, or darken so great a radiance. Let him hold fast firmly; let him not lose what cannot be restored; let him not forfeit the grace of bodily purity in a single moment of pleasure; let him not contract defilement of soul through the beauty of a corrupted form; let lust not conquer him. If he listens to me, he will remain steadfast; but if he does not listen, he will lose what he will never restore.

**9. What married people, widows, and women should do.** Once again my speech is addressed to you who have wives: I warn you to keep them chastely. For Elizabeth too, who had lived chastely with her husband for many years, and both of whom had been faithful before the Lord, deserved to have a son from seed already dead, one who would adorn his parents with holiness and convert many unbelievers by his preaching (Luke 1). Again I speak to you who are widows: guard your widowhood; do not be talkative, but await the Lord in silence—the Lord who receives the orphan and the widow; yet a good widow, one who is ready in prayer, humility, and almsgiving. If, certainly, she has no means by which to do this, let her have good will and sincere thought. Women, do not curse, do not swear, do not be quick to speak. Perhaps you say that what I am saying is intrusive. I may not keep silent: I fear the one who commands more than the one who slanders. I say: let whoever recognizes this amend it; whoever does not recognize it in himself should listen and retain it, so that he may be able to speak to others for their salvation.

**10. What penitents should do. To weep wisely.** Now I speak to you, penitents, who have received penance in the Church and are practicing it. Persevere in weeping; weep wisely in compunction. What does “weep wisely” mean? It means that in prayer you should not seek temporal things, but eternal blessedness and the forgiveness of sins. Whoever prays in this way weeps wisely. Your tears will not fall to the ground, because he is truthful to whom the prophet said: “You have placed my tears in your sight” (Ps. 56:8). You ought now to love God greatly, and already to pass from fear to love, because this is what we read in the Gospel concerning that sinful woman: “To whom much is forgiven, he loves much” (Luke 7:47). Therefore you ought to love God greatly, since by waiting for you and not punishing you, he has deigned to lead you to repentance.

**11. An address to the poor.** Now once again my speech is addressed to you, poor people. I mean you poor who beg, who live from the alms of Christians. “Be comforted, be comforted”: your tribulation will be turned into joy, and your sorrow into gladness. Do not regard it as a grievance that you beg, nor therefore say anything in your heart against God, because he is just and merciful in all his works. For this reason he made you poor: so that by enduring brief want you might acquire eternal life. And for this reason he made the other person rich: so that, while giving you what was surplus, he might acquire a remedy for his sins. Therefore be patient and await the Lord.

**12. To slaves.** My speech is also addressed to you, slaves, all of you who have earthly masters, to whom you owe the condition of servitude: obey your masters; love them from the heart, serving not merely for appearance, but performing your service [Col. 1981] out of love (Eph. 6:5–7). For God established them to rule over you, and you to serve. Serve well for God’s sake, because you will receive a reward for good service. If you are good, you will be better than bad masters, because before God the soul of each person is not distinguished by nobility but by conduct, nor by birth but by action. Therefore my speech has now been addressed to everyone, because Christ died for all (2 Cor. 5:15). Preserve, then, what I have said, so that I may obtain fruit from you, and so that the merciful Lord may admit you all into the heavenly storehouses where the grain is to be gathered—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1981] Formerly *On Time* 8.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, II**

[Note: [Col. 1981] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. Concerning this sermon, the Louvain scholars, Verlinus, and Vindingus reached the same judgment as concerning the preceding one. It seems to have been composed to assert the divinity of Christ, perhaps by Vigilius of Tapsus, who published several short works of this kind against the Arians under the names of ancient Fathers.]

**1. The Son of God is not changed when he becomes human.** Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the day of the Lord’s Nativity, that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ. Although he possesses with the Father an equal Trinity [Note: [Col. 1981] Perhaps “divinity.”], and although with the Father’s equal power he established heaven, earth, and the seas, and everything that is in them, in the last times the Son of God deigned to be born human from a human being. He assumed our nature in such a way that he did not alter his own. For, while the condition of his divinity remained wholly intact, the Son of God assumed humanity; he did not lose what he was, but joined to himself what previously had not been in him. Thus the Son of God, invisible according to his divinity, assumed visible humanity; the immortal assumed mortality, the impassible assumed passibility [*passibileni* in the source]; and, to encompass everything briefly, God assumed humanity. Whatever weakness we read of in Christ—that he was hungry, that he suffered grief, and that he even endured death for our sins—let us attribute to the humanity he assumed for our salvation, while preserving reverence for the one who assumed it, namely, the Word of God. He joined humanity to his divinity in such a way as to make it impassible after the Passion, not in such a way that—an impious thought—divinity itself should become passible.

**2. Christ’s birth was true, but not customary. Through it he did not condemn marriage.** Yet by this he did not condemn marriage. For although there is one person in the Son of God, from divinity and humanity, when you hear that the Son of God was born from a human being, do not suppose that the origin of this birth arose there from the common work of marriage, which indeed was established by God so that humanity might be propagated. I say that the origin of humanity there was different, wholly unlike our birth. For although Christ was born in the same true flesh in which we naturally exist, he was not conceived and born in the manner in which we are through marriage—that is, in the manner from which the rest of us have arisen—although all human beings are procreated.

For he was also procreated wondrously. That lawful union of man with woman, although, in accordance with divine authority, it is not free from fault [Note: [Col. 1981] Perhaps, “is free from fault.”], is nevertheless not glorious as well. In Christ’s birth, however, propagation without intercourse is endowed with every glory and honor. Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, except for the order of his birth, was truly begotten from a virgin, conceived and born by the same sign of omnipotence. He had a virgin as his mother both when he was carried in the virgin’s womb and when he was brought forth from the womb. Yet this birth did not condemn marriage; it honored the power of divinity.

**3. God with us.** Long ago the prophet Isaiah foretold the sign of this new fertility: “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). This was most clearly prophesied concerning Christ our Lord, for *Emmanuel* is interpreted as [Col. 1982] “God with us.” Thus our Savior also received this name from the effect of events, so that he might be called “God with us.” At that time he himself deigned to be God with all of us, when he assumed this flesh, so that through the human being who was visible he might be seen dwelling on earth.

For the prophet Jeremiah had promised this, saying: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. He discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38). Hence the Lord himself also says to his disciples in the Gospel: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Whoever sees me sees also my Father” (John 14:9), and the rest that follows. The Son of God performed such works through the human being he assumed that from the very splendor of the works the divinity both of the Father and of the Son might be recognized. If we carefully consider the reason for which the Lord deigned to fulfill this entire mystery of the humanity he assumed, then we shall truly understand that the prophetic word has been fulfilled for us.

**4. The twofold purpose of the Incarnation: our restoration and instruction.** There are principally two reasons why the Son of God became the son of man. One is that, suffering everything for us according to his humanity, he might free us from the bonds of sins. Thus the prophet Isaiah had foretold: “He himself bore our sins and grieves for us”; and again: “He was wounded because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:4–5).

The other reason for the Lord’s Passion was that he might kindle in us, whom he redeemed from faults and crimes by his blood, a zeal for holiness not only through the assistance of teaching and grace but also through his example. Thus we would follow with greater eagerness not only the Lord who commands us, but also the one who by his example calls us to the heights of virtue; and, according to the judgment of blessed Peter, we would honor the most just Lord and merciful Father by imitating the Son.

For Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was cursed, he did not curse; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness” (1 Pet. 2:21–24).

May our Lord Jesus Christ grant that, aided by his grace, you hasten to follow his footsteps; and that, having been put to death with respect to all sins and vices, you may live solely for the practice of works of righteousness, giving thanks to God the Father, to whom belong glory and dominion, and to our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CXIX

[Note: [Col. 1982] Formerly *On Time* 9; later Appendix 21.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, III**

[Note: [Col. 1982] It is by an unknown author and was not unjustly rejected by the Louvain scholars, although we have not found it well established that, as they claim, it contains most of the sentences from St. Bernard’s Homilies on the Gospel *Missus est*. For sections 1 and 2, see Eusebius, Homily 2.]

**1. The proud human being is restored by the humble God. The procreation of the first human being is renewed.** We read and hold faithfully that, at the very beginning of the world’s creation, God made us in the first human being according to his image and likeness. Behold, on this day the roles are reversed: God has been made according to our image and likeness. In the first case he bestowed what was better from his own; in the second he assumed what was lower from ours.

Through the taste of the forbidden tree, the unwary weakness of the first human being attempted, with damnable ambition, to desire the divinity of his Lord, persuaded by the devil, who said: “If you taste from this tree, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Therefore let us recognize the wondrous goodness of our merciful Father. Humanity, urged on by the enemy, wanted to be God through pride; and God became human through mercy.

In a certain way the appearance of that ancient and dawning age is renewed in us through Christ’s divinity, when the first Adam was fashioned from the material of clay. For behold, now the second Adam is formed, as it were from untouched and unworked earth, from the flesh of a virgin. Behold, I say, once again, with the laws of nature suspended, the new human being is brought to completion in a new life, with God alone at work.

**2. The operation of the Holy Spirit declares Christ’s holiness and divinity.** A son is therefore promised to the virgin through the visitation of the Holy Spirit. Is it surprising that he is born without corruption, who is conceived through sanctification? For it was not fitting that the one who brought salvation to us should deprive his mother alone of dignity. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you.” It was entirely fitting that she who was to be burdened with a royal birth should first be sanctified by the entrance of the heavenly King.

Therefore let us not believe that our Lord and Savior is merely human because we see him born from a human being. It is not permissible not to believe him God, for whom a dwelling place is prepared by God as he descends to earth. Thus, through divine power at work, the womb of the believer is made fertile; the tree of life is grafted onto mortal wood; the power that bears all things is borne by weakness; and he whom earth, sea, and heaven cannot contain is received within the limbs of a tiny body.

The Creator of all is procreated from his own creation; from his own stream the great spring arises. The root of all is born from its own shrub, and the true vine becomes the fruit of its own branch. Behold, the long-desired day is present, shining with doubled grace, illumined indeed by the brightness of its accustomed light, but especially flashing with the radiance of the resplendent womb.

O day, novelty of all days, gain of light and loss of blindness, on which the eternal Sun, descending from the highest height of the Father’s splendor, opened the entrance of the virgin womb and drove back the darkness of the whole world with a dazzling flash!

**3. Prophecy concerning the virgin birth.** Lead forth, faithful people of Christ, the most festive joys. Today a new event has been accomplished for us, one that was formerly promised: that the mother’s breasts might nurse a son without any loss to virginal modesty. This is the novelty announced in the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah: “The Lord,” he says, “will make something new upon the earth.” And as though lighting a lamp in this darkness, he immediately added: “A woman will encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). That is, he says, this is the new thing that I declare the Lord will do upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man.

Pay attention, brothers, and let your understanding anticipate me rather than the reverse: “A woman,” he says, “will encompass a man.” O woman blessed above women, who neither knew a man nor encompassed a man in her womb; who was not touched by carnal intercourse and yet rejoiced in fleshly offspring from spiritual seed! Mary encompasses the man by giving faith to the angel, because Eve lost the man by consenting to the serpent. “The Lord,” he says, “will make something new upon the earth.”
