**4. The angel’s address to Mary.** When the time for presenting this novelty arrived, a heavenly messenger was sent in advance to the Virgin. The angel greets the girl who was unfamiliar with a man’s greeting; the virgin is frightened by the novelty of the words. To her the angel says: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord. Do not,” he says, “be frightened at the sight of me, Mother of my Lord. I have come as the minister of your conception; he who is to be born from you sent me to you. Through me he announces to you the joy of one who has chosen to join a mystical marriage with human nature in your womb. You have found grace with the Lord. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son—not a human being of some ordinary merit, but the Savior of the whole world.”

“Do not,” he says, “be afraid. Cast away from you every fear of the world, you who are to conceive the joy of the world. Recall, Mary, the prophetic reading; for knowledge of the divine books cannot pass you by, since you are to give birth to the very fullness of the prophets. Recall the virgin whom you read of in the book of the prophet Isaiah, and rejoice because you have deserved to be she. You are the virgin prefigured there. Behold, you will conceive in your womb, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit; you will be pregnant and will remain incorrupt; you will bear a son and suffer no loss of virginity.”

But she said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

[Col. 1984] **5. The grace of the Word’s self-emptying.** Immediately, then, after receiving the Virgin’s consent, the angel returned to the inhabitants of the heavenly region; and suddenly ineffable power penetrated the Virgin’s secret. The Maker of the world enters the confines of a human womb; the untouched mother becomes pregnant. And behold, like a bridegroom from the bridal chamber, Christ proceeds from Mary’s womb.

The power of majesty is concealed in the limbs of an infant; God hangs at his mother’s breasts. He is covered by the squalor of cheap swaddling clothes; he endures the cramped confines of the hardest manger; and, in his mercy, he humbly suffers everything, provided that the world which had perished might be set free.

O blessed infancy, through which the life of our race has been restored! O most welcome and delightful cries, through which we have escaped the gnashing of teeth and eternal lamentation! O happy swaddling clothes, with which we have wiped away the filth of sins! O splendid manger, in which there lay not merely hay for animals, but food for angels was found!

Nurse your Creator, Mary; nurse the bread of heaven, the price of the world. Offer your breast to him who sucks, so that he may in turn offer his cheek to the one who strikes him for your sake. Let the infant be nourished by the milk of your breasts, so that for your sake he may also receive the drink of vinegar. Let your hands now carry him, so that later his hands may be fastened to the cross for you. Finally, as a mother, minister temporal substance to him, so that he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, may grant everlasting life to us and to you.

May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and is glorified as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

---

## SERMON CXX

[Note: [Col. 1984] Formerly *On Time* 21.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, IV**

[Note: [Col. 1984] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain scholars, and spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. Petavius found its style, in book 14 of *On the Incarnation*, excessively elevated. Compare Sermon 194, where not a few things are repeated in the very same words as here.]

**1. Through a woman sin arises; through a woman it is uprooted.** Today a child has been born to us; today a son has been given to us (Isa. 9:6). A child, I say, not weak through the tenderness of his limbs, but glorious through an untainted generation. For on this day the Holy Spirit is declared to be the author of the mother’s innocence and purity.

Today a son has been given to us. He is now given to us who was born before the ages: given in the Virgin’s childbirth, a son from the substance of the Begetter. When, therefore, the formerly rejected Ruler entered the slave’s cottage through the door of faith [Note: [Col. 1984] Thus the Greek manuscript. The printed editions have *speratus*, “awaited”], inviolate virginity blushed. He did not break the bolt of modesty, and a ray of eternal splendor shone forth in the sacred womb.

Let every exile of this world rejoice, let the age that had shortly before been captive exult. God sent his Son to be born and to terrify, to die and to conquer. For his birth terrified Herod; innocent, crucified, he conquered the devil.

Hide, Lord, beneath the skin of flesh the weapons of your power; conceal for a little while the appearance of majesty. Cover yourself in the Virgin’s womb; come forth and engage battle from the tent of the holy Virgin. Prepare a trap for me, where you may set the whole creation free. Let us therefore examine both the reason and the wonder of so great a conception and birth.

When the world, worn out and horribly fouled by the filth of vices, had been captive from its origin already in paradise, a woman was the cause. For it is written: “From a woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die” (Eccli. 25:33). And the apostle Paul says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was made a transgressor” (1 Tim. 2:14).

Through her, therefore, the world, weighed down by grievous servitude, had bent its anxious neck beneath the yoke of the devil; for each person is made a slave to the one by whom he has been conquered. When, therefore, the joined structure of the elements was dissolved, the Flood destroyed the human being but could not destroy the crime.

Isaac, the son not of a virgin but of a barren woman, deserved to bear the signs of the cross; he deserved to be seized and bound, but he did not deserve to be killed. Moses was exposed for the purification of the waters; by God’s sending he rescued the Jewish host, but did not free the whole world; he destroyed Egypt, but not sin; he killed King Pharaoh when the sea opened, but did not slay the devil with his legions.

David confesses that he was conceived in iniquities; therefore he too could not take away the sin of the world. As the course of the world rolled on through the turning cycles of the ages, and no one brought healing; as guilt grew heavier, and the members of the whole world were reduced to dust by the blow and crash of impending ruin, with no one coming to their aid: the cause returns to a woman, and the origin is cut off by an origin.

The origin of sin was extinguished through Christ’s Mother; the lineage of impiety was removed through the lineage of piety; the stock of death through the stock of life. Thus far we have addressed the reason; now let us also reveal to miracles eyes that have been veiled [Note: [Col. 1985] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions: “now let us reveal eyes fitted to miracles.” Manuscript.]

**2. The miracles of the virgin birth.** A virgin gives birth to Christ; nature is changed, and guilt is erased. That unhappy saying of Eve has been cut away: “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16), because this woman bore the Lord in joy. The one mourned; this one shone again. The one carried tears in her womb; this one carried joy, because the one brought forth a sinner, while this one brought forth the innocent one.

The Spirit sowed, not lust; God planted, not a husband. A virgin gave birth because a virgin conceived. She gave birth inviolate because there was no desire in the conception. There is a miracle in both respects: pregnant without corruption, and a virgin mother in childbirth; marriage in faith, childbirth in a virgin.

**3. Gabriel’s words are examined. The greatness of Mary’s faith.** That Gabriel was the intermediary of these betrothals. Let him report what he said and what he heard: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace; the Lord is with you.” He begins with a greeting, he who carried salvation on his tongue.

Let the evil-persuading hiss of the crooked serpent now fall silent among women. The angel spoke to the mother of our Lord: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace; the Lord is with you.” Grace is given in place of guilt; she is called full, not empty. Grace, therefore, has been filled, and guilt has been emptied.

In this way that venerable Virgin of ours also applauded in her Canticle: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.” “Hail,” he says, “full of grace; the Lord is with you”—with you in heart, with you in womb, with you in the belly, with you in aid.

Rejoice, Virgin: Christ the King has come from his heaven into your womb. From the Father’s bosom he deigned to descend into his Mother’s womb. Yet infinite majesty neither abandoned its own realm nor, once received, was confined by the Virgin’s palace. Faith was raised from earth to heaven; Christ mounted upon it, and through it entered the temple of modesty.

**4. Eve’s curse is erased through Mary. A woman who is also a virgin.** “Blessed,” he says, “are you among women,” you who have brought forth life both for men and for women. Give birth, blameless woman, to the inviolate man; and thus you will save both woman and man.

The mother of our race brought punishment upon the world; the Mother of our Lord carried salvation both to woman and to man. That author of sin was accursed; for the sentence of the original decree is directed against her: “Cursed are you among women.” This author of merit, therefore, is blessed; for the heavenly messenger says to her: “Blessed are you among women.”

By sexual kind all are commonly called women, although some differ through incorrupt virginity, the distinctive quality of modesty. The one did harm by killing; this one did good by giving life. The one struck; this one healed. For disobedience is exchanged for obedience, and faith makes compensation for faithlessness.

**5. Mary’s song of exultation.** Once again let Mary play her instruments, and let drums resound among her nimble fingers. Let songs echo from her fingers [Note: [Col. 1985] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions: “let songs be excluded by the fingers.” Manuscript.]; let her give birth to Christ amid playful psalms.

Let rejoicing choirs sing together, and let sweet melodies mingle in alternating modes. Let Mary perform a musical melody among the young women, because she brought forth on earth in Judaea the sweet word of the Holy Spirit through sounding plectra [Note: [Col. 1985] In the Greek manuscript, “she was present also in Judaea.”], while Judaea itself was preparing the drum of cruelty and stretching Christ upon the wood.

After the wandering hand of crime had faltered in disordered rhythms, that barbarous crash of savage shrieking immediately thundered: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21). When, therefore, the day was repeated on which criminal Egypt was swallowed up, the drum struck by our Mary produced the Word, and our mother, by the striking of her tongue, poured forth joyful songs from her mouth.

Let us hear, then, how our drummer has sung: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid. For behold, from this time forth all generations will call me blessed. For he who is mighty has done great things for me.”

Thus the miracle of the new birth overcame the cause of the strengthening error, and Mary’s song drove out Eve’s lamentation.

**6. God is the author of the offspring.** Finally, after the foretelling and triumph of that blessed salutation, the silent Virgin struggles inwardly with an argument in her mind, wondering what sort of greeting this might be. Meanwhile the heavenly messenger continues: “Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found grace with God. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.”

But while she asks about the manner, she hears that God is the author of the offspring. “How,” she says, “will this happen, since I do not know a man?” “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore what will be born from you will be holy; it will be called the Son of God.”

Now let faith spread out the beautiful tents of its radiant womb; let power overshadow it; let the Spirit whisper; with natural warmth driven away, let a gentle breeze refresh the virgin, and let the womb be fanned by heavenly breath through flowing coolness. Let the virgin womb be crowned with garlands of modesty. Let the fiery radiance of the rose breathe there; let the white lily gleam; let the tender violet glow red; let purple flowers be scattered; and let Christ’s bridal chamber, painted with varied brilliance, be adorned.

**7. The world’s salvation hung upon Mary’s consent. Mary’s faith opens heaven.** Answer now, sacred Virgin: why do you delay life for the world? The angel awaits your consent; that is why this messenger lingers. You have already heard how this will happen: the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you, so that you may bear offspring without losing your virginity.

The gate of heaven, once closed through Adam, has now sounded; through it this messenger has passed. God is at the gate; he awaits the angel whom you delay. O blessed Mary, the whole captive world begs your consent. The world has made you a pledge to the Lord of its faith; through you it begs that the injuries of its ancestors be wiped away [Note: [Col. 1986] Greek manuscript: “through you the parent begs concerning the injuries of his own.”].

The one who was offended first himself sent the messenger and unlocked the barrier that our iniquity had fastened upon heaven. We have an entrance, if your consent is granted. You come to our aid, and to your own, because punishment came upon both us and you. God has prepared a wedding for his Son in your bridal chamber; in that very joy of betrothal he has released whatever in the world had offended him.

O you also, angel, messenger of so great a King and herald of the divine secret, who have brought indulgence to the guilty from the palace of imperial majesty, life to the dead, and the mysteries of peace to captives: urge the virgin, who does not distrust God’s gift but considers the greatness of the gift. Favor the cause of the world, as one acquainted with heaven’s secrets.

Your companions will rejoice if you assist the world’s cause. The sword of our impiety divided us from your fellowship; through you our return is being arranged. Look upon the squalid misery of our prison and speak quickly to Mary: “How long will you delay, Virgin, the messenger who hastens? Behold God waiting for me in the vestibule of heaven. Speak your word and receive the Son; give faith and experience power. Open your rose-colored bosom, perpetual Virgin: your faith now either opens heaven or closes it.”

**8. Christ’s betrothal with humanity and with the Church.** “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:26–38, 46–52). Without delay the messenger returns, and Christ enters the bridal chamber. He receives the garment of flesh within the Virgin’s bridal chamber; within the treasure of majesty, the little purse of flesh. Humanity is betrothed to divinity; the flesh receives its reward.

Christ proceeds like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. As a foretelling of the wedding, he went out onto the field of the world; he ran like a giant rejoicing on his way. He reached the bridal bed of the cross and there, by ascending, established the marriage. When he felt creation panting in sighs [Note: [Col. 1987] Printed editions: “when he consented to creation alienated amid sufferings.”], in an exchange of mercy he gave himself for his bride to punishment.

He also gave her a carbuncle, as a jewel of his blood, and joined the matron to himself by perpetual right. “I betrothed you,” says the Apostle, “to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Behold, what had been foul has become beautiful; what had been captive has become free. But Judaea, which had been free, became a slave, because it saw its life hanging on the wood and did not believe in the one who set it free.

Let us therefore rejoice, brothers, in the exchange between God and humanity, bridegroom and bride, Christ and the Church, Savior and Virgin. Let us exult in faith and at the Virgin’s childbirth: while she was betrothed to a craftsman, she was married to the Architect of heaven.

Let us venerate Christ in the manger, who filled the fourfold world with faith. Let us adore the swaddling clothes of infancy, through which we have deserved the remedies of nature. Honor the shepherds, who first learned the mystery from the angels. Let us all applaud together with the heavenly angels and with the divine ministries, and let us announce peace from heaven and earth to people of good will.

“Give glory to God in the highest.” Redeemed people, believe that peace has been given to captives. Be people of good will, so that you may deserve the reward of freedom, through the gift of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CXXI

[Note: [Col. 1987] Formerly *On Time* 10; later Appendix 22.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, V**

[Note: [Col. 1987] It is found in various manuscripts with notable variation. Some omit everything enclosed in brackets, from the words “We preach today,” etc., through the end of section 3. Moreover, different beginnings occur in different codices, and in some the name of Peter of Ravenna is prefixed. In section 4, certain—not by any means all—words from the passage that Cassian cites in book 7 of *On the Incarnation* from a hitherto unknown sermon of Ambrose on Christ’s Nativity are read here, namely, “Behold the miracle,” etc. For section 4, see the same material in Sermon 194, chapter 1.]

**1. Bearing witness to the Savior.** Who could be so equipped with an abundance of subjects and words as to proclaim the grace of this day with worthy praises? Since no such person exists, we are not ashamed if we lack a more polished eloquence of speech. Nevertheless, by discussing in ordinary language the childbirth of the holy Virgin and the origin of the Lord’s body, we shall try to explain them.

Today, then, is the Savior’s Nativity, beloved ones, on which light has been added to the world, and immortality, which had perished through sin, has been restored to mortals. Today is the Savior’s Nativity, concerning which the angel says to the shepherds: “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2:11); concerning which the prophet also says: “A son has been given to us; a child has been born to us” (Isa. 9:6).

He is therefore born whom another prophet testifies to be the King of the nations; and he is born from a virgin, as it is written: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel” (ibid. 7:14). This, translated from the Hebrew language into Latin, is interpreted as “God with us.”

[We preach today the Savior born from a virgin, and, instructed by angels, we adore the infant placed in a manger together with the watchful shepherds. Let us offer faith to the miracles; let us show reverence to the holy witnesses: to Simeon, who recognized him; to Anna, who confessed the Lord; to John, who baptized; to the purification of the Jordan; to the Holy Spirit, who descended; to the opened heavens; to the Father, who bore witness; to the virgin, who remained a virgin; to the shining star; to the descending dove; and to the Lord himself, who overcame every temptation of the devil.]

[Col. 1988] **2. The excellence of virgin birth.** Virginity bears in the mind the one whom Mary bore in her womb. Today, therefore, the Virgin gave birth to him who would make human beings children of God, annul the sentence of transgression, rescue them from the penalty of death, and grant everlasting life to believers. As a mother she carried in her womb a son greater than all nourishment that had gone before; and she brought forth on earth, in the form of a servant, the one whom the angels have as their ruler in heaven. A mother gave birth to the son by whom she herself would rather be nourished than nourish him: a mortal womb received an immortal guest, and in an earthly dwelling the virgin received the heavenly ruler.

Blessed virginity has now ceased to be death’s servant, because she bears within herself in her mind the one whom Mary carried in her womb. Virginity submits to no slavery, because it loves him who brought freedom to the human race. A heavenly offspring was budding in the womb, and in this extraordinary birth the virgin limbs shone forth. A divine conveyance was carried on human feet, and in the narrow chamber of modesty the holy Virgin carried enclosed the one whom the heavens cannot contain; and she gave birth to him—not one who by being born would defile the woman giving birth, but one who would wash the world from defilement. The holy woman believed, the holy woman conceived, and after giving birth she became holier.

**3. A wondrous birth. The world becomes consolation.** The very son who was the bridegroom was present to the Virgin herself, and the very one begotten was the begetter. There, belief was the bridesmaid and the archangel the groomsman; the mother was the bride, and the one whom she bore, Christ the bridegroom, was joined to her by the Holy Spirit, announced by the angel Gabriel, celebrated by the host of angels, and displayed by the shining star.

He made the Virgin pregnant who himself was destined to be born from the Virgin. The mother was suddenly terrified at her own labor: God was speaking through an angel, and the Virgin was being made pregnant through her ears. Let every age hear what it has never heard. The Virgin married through her childbirth; while giving birth she doubled her virginity; and she adored the son whom she had borne.

Let every anxiety cease: Christ, our true security, has come. Let every weakness cease: today the Savior has appeared. Let wars cease and quarrels end: today true peace has descended from heaven. Let every bitterness cease: today the heavens have become honey-sweet throughout the whole world. Let death flee, because today life has been given to us from heaven.

Today on earth the angels sing, the archangels rejoice, the prophets glory, the saints are invited, the wicked are thrown into confusion, the good rejoice, the blind receive sight, the deaf hearing, the lame the use of their feet, lepers are cleansed, the sorrowful are gladdened, the sick are healed, and the dead are raised. Only the devil and all the demons with him tremble, because the human race is restored through the destruction of the devil. Today Christ has appeared to you as Redeemer.

**4. The power of the Lord shown in the order of his birth, and various testimonies concerning him.** The order of his birth proves the Lord’s power. A virgin, ignorant of the embrace of a man, conceives; the womb is filled without being defiled by any human embrace. Behold the miracle of the mother of the Lord’s body: a virgin conceives, a virgin is pregnant, a virgin gives birth, and a virgin remains after giving birth. Thus that virginity is glorious, and that fertility splendid.

The world’s power is born, and the woman giving birth feels no pain. The womb is emptied and the infant is received, yet virginity is not violated. For it was fitting that, when the Lord was born in the flesh from a virgin, the merit of chastity should increase, lest his coming violate what was intact, since he came to heal what was corrupt.

A child is therefore born and placed in a manger—for these are the Lord’s first cradle, and the ruler of heaven does not disdain this confinement. Mary stands there, joyfully marveling that she is a mother, and rejoicing that she has brought him forth from the Holy Spirit. She is not frightened because she has given birth unmarried; rather, she marvels with exultation that she has become a mother.

For when the Savior’s advent, owed to the world, was hastening, the Holy Spirit came to the virgin Mary, as had been foretold beforehand by the angel, who said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Rightly, therefore, we venerate heavenly realities at his coming, since we clearly know that he came from heaven, and we learn that he was born for our salvation through the power of God the Father and the Holy Spirit. For a new offspring destined to come from heaven had been announced beforehand by many signs.

You see, dearest one, that the Savior’s birth is the power of God, since the prophets do not remain silent about him and the Holy Spirit acknowledges him. What is more splendid than the star’s announcement? What than the Magi’s open confession? What than the prophets’ judgment, so harmonious and so continuous? Everywhere the Lord is known; everywhere he is announced as born from a virgin.

**5. The Blessed Virgin as a type of the Church.** Since we have said that he was born in the flesh from a virgin, let us now discuss what we can understand spiritually. Let us see, then, who that virgin is—so holy that the Holy Spirit deigned to come to her; so beautiful that God chose her as his bride; so abundant that the whole world might receive her offspring; so chaste that she could remain a virgin after giving birth.

Do we not see, in the figure of Mary, a type of the holy Church? To her, certainly, the Holy Spirit descended; over her the power of the Most High overshadowed; from her Christ, powerful in his strength, came forth. She is undefiled in intercourse, fertile in childbirth, a virgin in chastity. She conceives not from a man but from the Spirit; she gives birth not in sorrow but in joy; she nourishes not with bodily breast but with the milk of a teacher.

She is therefore Christ’s bride and the mother of the nations, who marvels that she is full and rejoices that she is fruitful. On this day, then, when the Savior is born, the splendor of light increases and the darkness of shadows diminishes. On this day heavenly light is restored to believers, and in the eternal night the devil’s fictions are condemned. On this day light grows from light, the power of virtues is raised up, the glory of eternity is lifted high, and the world embraces its restoration as the Lord is born in the flesh.

Let the celebration of this day therefore be complete, on which God, mindful of us, deigned to visit earthly things and restored to mortals the light they had lost through the radiance of his coming. For he is the splendor and eternal glory, our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

---

# SERMON CXXII

[Note: [Col. 1989] Formerly, *On the Season* 11; later, in Appendix 23.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, VI**

[Note: [Col. 1989] In manuscript and printed books it is attributed to Bishop Maximus.]

**1. The benefits of Christ’s birth.** At the Lord’s coming, dearest brothers, every fear of the ancestral transgression was dissolved—the fear into which mortal humanity had long ago fallen, deceived by the devil’s frauds. For the Judge of heaven and earth is present among us, and, having torn up the bond recording our sins, he has mercifully absolved us from our guilt.

That Lord is present who, releasing the yoke of ancient captivity from our necks, gladdens the world’s sorrow with eternal freedom. That gentle King is present who, walking throughout the expanses of the whole world with the steps of heavenly justice, crushes the tyranny of the raging enemy in his pride.

Today, while Mary gives birth, the Son of God has been born for us, so that, produced through the genuine conception of our flesh, he might extend both the Father’s tenderness and a brother’s affection to the human being created by him.

**2. The manner of birth proves him God and man.** He was indeed born from an untouched woman, so that human birth might testify that he was man, while enduring virginity proved that he was God. For just as flesh could be born only from flesh, so the flesh of God could not emerge from a woman’s womb except without a begetter.

Therefore the angel said to the blessed Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you.” For this reason, brother, the angelic speech sets before you the power of the Holy Spirit, lest, dulled by the suppositions of carnal argument, you confuse the heavenly mystery for yourself with earthly reasoning.

**3. The possibility of this manner of birth. Three wondrous kinds of birth.** Or do you think that he could not form a new child in the Virgin’s womb, who, when he first created man, sought neither a father’s seed nor a mother’s womb? Tell me, then, whoever you are, judge and examiner of the heavenly dispensation: which power seems greater to you—to give a virgin childbirth, or to create a complete human being from earth?

For, as the Apostle says, “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47). If you insist that it is contrary to nature for a girl to be said to have conceived without a man in the mystery of our redemption, then, I ask, what sort of nature is it that flesh was formed without flesh in the parent of our race?

What kind of reasoning—or rather, what blind contention—is it to refuse to believe that God can make a human being from a woman, when he is believed to have made one from dust? If, O man, you see the will of the Almighty in such a matter, why do you recoil from the work? For, as we read, “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6).

And if you investigate carefully, you will find that, beyond the ordinary human manner of conception, the Trinity brought about three highly wondrous kinds of birth. The first is that Adam was formed from clay; the second, that woman was formed from a male; the third—and this is heavenly—that Christ came forth from a virgin.

Which of these is not new? Which is not wondrous? Which of them could human inquiry comprehend, unless we follow faith? But the fact that the Son of God deigned to visit his world through this mystical conception was demanded by the necessity of our salvation—namely, that heavenly generation might at last restore what earthly birth had lost.

**4. Christ’s humility is revealed by signs of power. The virtues commended on this day.** Perhaps, however, you doubt that the one proclaimed as born from a woman is God while he is wrapped in cheap cloths, content to lie in a manger, crying out with tearful wails, and being nursed at his mother’s breasts.

Rather, brother, through these things recognize him: as man, he endured weakness for the weak; as God, he exercised heavenly power. He who is wrapped in soiled cloths is honored with royal gifts by the Chaldaeans. He who lies humbly in a manger shines from heaven with the light of a new star. He who utters the cries of infancy is praised by the voices of the angelic hosts. He who is nourished by a woman’s milk satisfied many thousands of people with a very small amount of bread.

Why should I add that Lazarus, rising from the dead, proves him to be God and truly the Son of God; that the blind man, restored to light, proclaims him; that the wave of the sea, trampled beneath his revered footsteps, bears witness; and—what surpasses all these—that the Father’s voice resounding from heaven confirms it?

Therefore, beloved, let us honor this great mystery of the Lord’s birth with worthy voices. Above all, let us love chastity, because, to show that Christ approved it, he chose the purity of a virgin womb. Let us pursue mercy, because it is through compassion that we are saved. Let us carefully hold fast to justice, because for this the Only-Begotten Son of God deigned to become human: so that, proclaiming the truth, he might cleanse the whole face of the world from condemned iniquity.

---

# SERMON CXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1990] Formerly, *On the Season* 15; later, in Appendix 24.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, VII**

[Note: [Col. 1990] It had previously circulated among the sermons of Fulgentius. The Louvain editors note that in manuscripts it is attributed either to Fulgentius or to Severianus. In our copies it bears no name other than Augustine’s, but falsely. Concerning section 1, see the words of Ivo of Chartres in his sermon on the Annunciation of Blessed Mary.]

**1. The wondrous birth of Christ. A virgin before and after childbirth.** Today the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ has flooded the entire world with the new light of his coming. Today God descended from heaven to humanity, in order to prepare humanity’s ascent into heaven. Today we have received the one born as God, the son of a virgin, the Savior of all believers: God from the Father, man from his mother; God hidden, man manifest.

And since the devil, speaking through the serpent to Eve, brought death into the world through Eve’s ears, God brought forth his word through an angel to Mary and poured life upon all ages. The angel uttered the message, and the Virgin conceived Christ.

O union accomplished without defilement, in which the husband is a word and the wife a little ear! In this splendor the Son of God is conceived; in this purity he is generated. No pregnancy could become burdensome to the woman conceiving, no sadness to the woman giving birth. For he who had come to gladden the sorrowful world did not make the dwelling of his womb sorrowful.

The physician from heaven passed through the Virgin and, after his passage, caused her to remain an unharmed virgin. For if, by touching them, he could restore in others limbs that had been torn apart, how much more could he, by being born, avoid violating what he found intact in his mother? At his birth, bodily integrity increased rather than diminished, and virginity was enlarged rather than driven away.

Within the narrow member of a body he sustained whatever the heavens sustain. Her womb was full, and the Virgin’s conscience knew no [lacuna or unspecified object; Note: [Col. 1991] Thus the manuscripts and printed editions. In the Louvain edition, however, *contagium* (“contagion”) is added; in one manuscript, by a recent hand, *virum* (“man”).]. While she was pregnant, she rejoiced with healthy lightness; for the light that she held within her could not have weight.

**2. Mary, window and ladder of heaven. Restorer of women. Mary’s blessings against Eve’s evils.** Mary became heaven’s window, because through her God poured true light upon the ages. Mary became the heavenly ladder, because through her God descended to earth, so that through her human beings might merit to ascend to heaven. Only those will be permitted to ascend there who believe that God descended to earth through the virgin Mary.

Mary became the restoration of women, because through her they are shown to have been rescued from the fall of the first curse. Finally, three evils of Eve are shown to have been excluded by three blessings of Mary.

For it was said to Eve: “In pains and sorrow you shall give birth; your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). Women who do not follow Mary are therefore subjected to these three evils: pain, sorrow, and servitude.

But hear with what splendid threefold blessings Mary, by contrast, is exalted: angelic greeting, divine blessing, and the fullness of grace. For we read that the angel greeted her thus: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28).

When he said “Hail,” he offered her a heavenly greeting. When he said “Full of grace,” he showed that the anger of the first sentence had been wholly excluded and that the full grace of blessing had been restored. When he said, “Blessed are you among women,” he expressed the blessed fruit of her virginity, so that every woman who perseveres as a virgin may be called blessed on account of it.

“Blessed are you among women”—for Eve had been accursed, and we now believe that through Mary she has returned to the glory of blessing.

**3. Mary assumed every condition of women.** Come, virgins, to the Virgin, and rejoice. Lay aside the curse of transgression and take up the blessing of restoration. Cast away the pains that Eve received through the serpent, and take up the honors that Mary received through the angel. Drive away the sorrow of conception [Note: [Col. 1991] Thus the Louvain edition and Erasmus, with manuscripts n and the second hand of the Greek manuscript. The first hand of the Greek manuscript, as well as manuscripts rm and cb, have *concupiscentis* (“of the desiring woman”). Another copy, together with vd, reads: “Drive away sorrow; cast away desire.”], cast away the groans of childbirth, so that this Son of the Virgin alone may rule over you.

Come, virgins, to the Virgin; come, women who conceive, to the one who conceived; come, women giving birth, to the one who gave birth; come, mothers, to the mother; come, nursing women, to the one who nursed; come, young women, to the young woman.

The virgin Mary assumed all these stages of nature in our Lord Jesus Christ in order to assist all women who flee to her. Thus she restored the whole race of women who come to her, preserving virginity as the new Eve, just as the Lord Jesus Christ, the new Adam, restores the whole race of men. He lives and reigns as one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever, and so forth.

---

# SERMON CXXIV

[Note: [Col. 1992] Formerly, *On the Season* 24; later, in Appendix 26.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, VIII**

[Note: [Col. 1992] Author uncertain.]

[Col. 1992]

**1. Christ is born for me, not for himself.** So that today, dearest brothers, the majesty of the Lord’s birth may be proclaimed by me, you must obtain for me from the Lord the ability to speak, so that he himself may place the word in the mouth of his priest and not disdain the service of our mouth—he who today deigned to enter into communion with our flesh.

For, brothers, we do not claim to disclose the ineffable mystery of the divine generation; rather, we undertake to announce the great and wondrous joy of our salvation, as the angel said: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10).

Let no conception, brothers, let no birth terrify anyone today. For where virginity conceives and integrity gives birth, God’s power is the witness, not desire. Hear the angel saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Today, brothers, deity does not begin, but humanity is renewed. Today Christ was born not for himself, but for me. “Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6), because today, as the prophet said, “he has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18:6).

**2. Virginity is never naked.** What is happening, dearest brothers, is divine, not human. Virginity is never naked when it has adorned itself with the covering of modesty [Note: [Col. 1992] Thus manuscript cb. Another cb manuscript reads, “she is adorned in her eternal modesty.” The printed editions, however, have, “she is adorned with the eternal honor of her modesty.”].

An angelic mediator came to the dwelling of chastity, in order to prepare a palace for the King, a temple for God, and a bridal chamber for the heavenly bridegroom. When the Lord was born, virginity was not taken away but consecrated. She herself gave birth to the bridegroom of her modesty; she herself offers faithful service to her guardian: fruitful, yet a virgin; a virgin, yet a mother. She lacked fruitlessness, not modesty.

Holiness, sincerity, purity, chastity, integrity, faith, and all the virtues were present together, so that the fearless servant might carry the author of her womb and, about to give birth to heavenly power, know neither the pain nor the groan of her sex. Blessed fertility, which both acquired the honor of motherhood and did not lose the reward of chastity.

**3. The mysteries of Christ’s birth in the flesh, his having no place in the inn, and his being wrapped in cloths.** He does not disdain to inhabit what he deigned to fashion, nor does he disdain to touch in himself the flesh that he had previously handled with a heavenly hand in the dust.

He came to your face, O man, because you could not reach his face; and he who was invisible became visible for your redemption. He came, summoned by your ancestors. Hear the voice of one crying: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 79:4).

There stands a witness to innocence and defender of modesty. He does not grieve at having lost his bride but rejoices that he has recognized God. He follows not as a husband but as a servant, and rejoices to offer service to the one whom he sees all the angels serving.

At his birth, therefore, Christ found no place in the inn, though through him every place was created. Like a stranger he was born, though he is Lord of the whole world, so that he might make us citizens of our heavenly homeland.

He is wrapped in cloths so that in his own body he might restore the unity of the human race, which had been torn apart, and carry into the heavenly kingdoms the entire garment of immortality, shining with the purple color of blood.

He is born, brothers, so that he might improve the very nature that the first man had corrupted. He lies in cloths, but reigns in heaven; he is humbled in a cradle, but thunders in the clouds. He is placed in a manger (Luke 2:7), because Isaiah’s statement shows that “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

O grass, brothers, whose flower is changed into heavenly bread, by eating which we reach eternal life!

[Note: [Col. 1992] Thus the manuscript. The printed editions have: “We are grass, brothers, and by its flower we are cleansed into heavenly …,” and so forth.]

---

# SERMON CXXV

[Note: [Col. 1993] Also known as *On the Season* 17.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, IX**

[Note: [Col. 1993] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful; Verlin and Winding considered it spurious. It does not sound like Augustine, though it contains something from Ambrose’s commentary on Luke.]

[Col. 1993]

**1. Why God assumed humanity from the Virgin.** The Evangelist demonstrated the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh so plainly that he showed him to have been born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, because of the cunning of the heretics who deny that God assumed humanity.

Our Lord therefore sought a virginal dwelling for himself so that he might show us that God ought to be carried in a chaste body. For this reason God assumed humanity into himself: so that we too might receive God into ourselves, as he himself says, “Remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

O sacred and heavenly mystery in the Lord’s birth! The Virgin conceived before she had a husband; she gave birth before she married; and—to the praise of the Lord’s name—after giving birth she began to be both mother and virgin. A virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, and after giving birth a virgin remained undefiled. When she carried him, she feared; when she gave birth, she adored; and after she had given birth to him, the mother was lesser than the son.

**2. Christ’s generation prefigured in Adam.** In the figure of Adam, the divine majesty sent us a great mystery beforehand. For when our God first wished to make Adam, he did not make a human being through the union of a man and woman. Rather, taking earth—the material from which he made man—he formed him by a certain divine art.

In the same way, without union with a man, he arranged for God to be embodied in a virgin’s womb. Therefore, if at that time it was permitted for a man to be born without a man, why was it not permitted for a man to be produced without a man through the virgin Mary?

For just as Adam was formed from virgin earth, so Christ is recognized as born from a virgin. There, then, God’s breath caused a living man to rise from earth into life; here, the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary formed Christ as a man for the world [Note: [Col. 1993] Thus manuscript cb. The printed editions have *mundum* (“the world”) rather than *mundo* (“for the world”). Manuscript n, however, reads: “Here, the Holy Spirit formed Christ as a man from the virgin Mary, so that God might dwell in him for the restoration of humanity.”], in whom God would dwell for humanity’s restoration.

Adam was then born; here he is renewed and raised again in Christ. The restoration was therefore similar, just as the creation of humanity had been. Finally, just as the Savior then fashioned Adam’s limbs in the womb of the earth, so now Christ fashioned his limbs in the Virgin’s womb.

O great patience of the Savior: he waits to be born as the limbs he himself made! But he wished to be born for this reason, so that we might live again.

God was hidden in a human being. Power was humbled so that compassion might increase; and, to the praise of his name, his power appeared to will less than it was able to do. He humbled himself as a man; nor did God shrink from putting on the human being whom he had formed in the image of himself and of the Father. Thus the Son of God willingly chose to be what he had made.

For this reason our God sent his Son to liberate humanity, so that he who had said, “Let us make man” (Genesis 1:26), might himself also be the liberator who had been the creator.

**3. Why Christ came from a woman. Why women are said to have announced the resurrection.** Why, then, did our God wish to restore us to life by being born through a Virgin? So that, since death entered this world through a woman, salvation might be restored through a Virgin.

Finally, when Christ rose from the dead on the third day, women were the first to encounter him, worshiping through an angel. They were therefore ordered to announce the resurrection to the apostles, so that it might be shown to men: “Behold, through the one by whom you fell into death, the resurrection of the dead is announced to you.”

Because the woman had tasted first, she is also shown to have seen the resurrection first, so that she would not bear among men the disgrace of perpetual guilt. She who had transmitted guilt to us also transmitted grace.

**4. The necessity of chastity for one who wishes to be a Christian.** Finally, our Lord came to earth through the limbs of a chaste virgin in order to show that God is the author of chastity.

Therefore, just as our God received us into himself, let us also receive God into ourselves. Let us carry God in a chaste body, whom the chaste limbs of the Virgin carried. For Christ is the teacher of chastity; and therefore one who does not possess chastity cannot carry Christ.

But we too, beloved, who believe in God, must show ourselves chaste and pure from every sin, so that we may always be able to carry Christ in our hearts and so that Christ may dwell in us. For one who does not have Christ within cannot be called a Christian.

Nor should anyone exalt himself so far as merely to call himself a Christian by name while showing himself by his actions to be Christ’s enemy. How is one a Christian who strives to live contrary to Christ’s commandments?

But you who serve God and keep his commandments—he is powerful enough to grant you eternal life, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

---

# SERMON CXXVI

[Note: [Col. 1994] Also known as *On the Season* 22.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, X**

[Note: [Col. 1994] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. According to the Louvain editors’ judgment it is doubtful; Verlin and Winding, however, regard it as spurious. The latter particularly observes that the opening of section 4 is alien to Augustine’s style: “The entire school of this birth, then, is a workshop of humility, a mass of patience, an agony of virtue.”]

**1. Christ’s two generations compared with one another. Christ’s mother always a virgin, who is always a bride. The two generations incomparable.** The venerable birth of the Savior, who was born in the flesh, is an instrument of humility, a mystery of compassion, and an evident remedy of eternal hope.

On this day he was born from a virgin mother, though before the ages he was eternally begotten from God the Father. In that birth he is born from an impassible Begetter; in this one he is born from an incorrupt virgin. Only the Father himself, who begot him, knew that birth; this one was known only by the Virgin and undefiled mother, who did not endure a man in conceiving.

In the Father there is impassibility; in the mother, incorruptibility. In the Father, perpetual divinity; in the mother, eternal virginity. Thus the Lord speaks to her through the prophet: “I will betroth you to myself forever” (Hosea 2:19).

She is therefore always a virgin who is always a bride; and she who did not lack the name of bride remained a virgin forever. “I will betroth you,” he says, “to myself forever,” because she who is called an eternal bride is proved to be an eternal virgin.

From the Father invisibly, from the mother visibly; but incomparably from the Father and incomparably from the mother. For in that birth he has God the Father without a human mother, incorruptibly; in this one he has a virgin mother but no human father.

In that birth he is coeternal with the Father and coeternal with his Author; in this one he is the Virgin’s son and the author of his mother. For he himself formed the womb who descended into the womb; he came forth from the womb and did not corrupt the womb, so that he who has God the Father in heaven might have a virgin mother on earth.

In the first he was begotten without time; in the second he was born at the end of time. In the first he is born without end; in the second he is conceived without seed. In the first, without a beginning of generation; in the second, under the condition of the Law and the flesh.

In the first, invisible God; in the second, visible man through the body, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In the first, impassible; in the second, mortal. In the first, most exalted; in the second, subject—subject, indeed, to the injuries of suffering and death, and death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

Yet through all these things he is glorious in heaven, since he is found victorious in all things on earth.

**2. The privilege of Christ’s birthday. The day of Christ’s resurrection is the same as that of his conception.** He chose for himself the day on which he was to be born—the one who made every day. This day must be regarded as surpassing the others, not without the grace of precedence, because on it God is taught to have been advanced into humanity.

Indeed, from today the day received increase, and the course of its progress takes on growth, since this day is known to have been chosen for the glory of God. He was conceived at the spring equinox and born at the winter solstice. And on the day on which he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, on that same day he rose from the underworld with the glory of his passion.

Both at his conception and at his birth, the day received increase; and as the true light was born, the function of light and day was enlarged.

Meanwhile, brothers, perceive—perceive the Lord’s mystery. At his birth the day advances; in his passion it declines, because “from the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour” (Matthew 27:45). What was diminished in the passion was enlarged in the resurrection.

Behold: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night reveals knowledge to night” (Psalm 18:3): the day of birth to the day of passion, and the day of passion to the day of resurrection; the night of birth announces the word to the night of passion, and the night of passion to the night of resurrection. There he was born; here he suffered. In the one there was the angels’ joy; in the other, the mourning of the whole world; yet in the resurrection there was the triumph of all.

“For weeping will remain for the evening, and joy for the morning” (Psalm 29:6): the evening of the passion, when a crowd of people followed him and the women lamented and wept; the morning of the resurrection, when the women ran joyfully from the tomb and the disciples hurried joyfully to the tomb.

**3. The mystery of the growing day at Christ’s Nativity.** He therefore chose this day for his birth, for our happiness; for his service, for our joy. Thus the angel proclaimed to the shepherds: “Behold,” he said, “I announce to you joy, which will be for the whole earth. Why? Because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:10–11).

Rightly, therefore, we ought to sing today: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24).

Behold, the day grows with the rising of the one being born, increasing through profitable progress and the advances of each moment; and as the course of night diminishes, the works of darkness feel their decline.

When the eternal Day was born, the temporal day ought to receive increase—not because the day contributed anything to the one being born, but so that from the one being born the day might acquire the privilege of increase and happiness, and become festive for the whole world, in which the true God was born perfect in the flesh as man.

**4. Christ’s power shines forth in his self-emptying.** The entire school of this birth, then, is a workshop of humility, a mass of patience, an agony of virtue.

First, because the immense and omnipotent Son of God, whose uncontainable power and incomprehensible greatness contains, surrounds, embraces, and surpasses heaven and the world at once, wished to contract himself with such confinement and subtlety that, shut within the Virgin’s womb, he both compressed what he possessed in majesty and concealed what he was in power.

He humbled himself so greatly that he wished to be the Son of Man, while never ceasing to be the Son of God. But only God could do this. To have hidden himself within his own greatness, when he possesses the power to do so, is not a work of human weakness but of divine power.

No human being can hide or conceal what is born, because although mortal nature exists in everyone, no one can deprive himself of the fact that he has been born. Our God, however, disclosed the power of his majesty when he hid himself within the limits of human weakness. In this mystery above all he showed himself omnipotent, subjecting to his power what, through the power of heavenly nature, remained free from every subjection.

God, born from God the Father, wished to be man; but he did not lose what he had previously been born as God. He wished to be man in such a way that what belonged to humanity did not remain in the condition in which he had been born.

For from the virgin Mary he assumed a true human being, whom through the glory of the resurrection he raised into heaven. Christ’s humility, therefore, is the exaltation of our body: when the Lord is humbled, humanity is exalted; and the servant is so exalted that in the Lord he himself also becomes what the Lord is.

The most blessed Paul proves this, saying: “He will transform the body of our humility to conform to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is able to subject all things to himself” (Philippians 3:21).

And again: “Although he was established in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself unto death, and death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:6 and following).

---

# SERMON CXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1996] Also known as *On the Season* 26.]

**On the Nativity of the Lord, XI**

[Note: [Col. 1996] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It contains several sentences from the other sermon cited above, namely Sermon 371, but they are neither similarly connected nor always preserved intact. We therefore judge that this sermon derives from that other one, rather than the reverse.]

# Two Nativities of the Lord. Pride is not greatness but swelling.

The necessity of humility. Christ the Only-Begotten and Firstborn.

The annual celebration of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the very frequent gathering of your Fraternity, requires from us the proper duty of preaching. Therefore, brothers, let us knock with pious affection and devoted heart at the Lord’s door, so that he may grant us confidence to say what is useful and to your Charity the fruit of hearing. May our Savior and teacher of humility, our Lord Jesus Christ, assist us, his most humble servants: the son of a virgin, the bridegroom of virgins, bodily born from a virginal womb and spiritually joined in a virginal marriage.

Today, therefore, he has deigned to be born through whom all things were made: remaining what he is, he displayed to you what you are; remaining with the Father in divinity, he assumed our weakness in humanity. For we acknowledge two nativities of the Lord, one divine and the other human, yet both wonderful: the former without a mother, the latter without a father; the former eternal, so that he might create temporal beings; the latter temporal, so that he might grant eternal life.

For he of whom the evangelist John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and that “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John 1:1–3)—he who was so great, who in the form of God was equal to the Father, who without time fashioned time, who belongs to no age, before all ages, the judge of the world—was made so small that he was born of a woman; yet he remained so great that he was not separated from the Father.

All the Prophets, offering him service and witness like lamps before the coming day, came before him by being born and adhered to him afterward by believing. For it was necessary that the one who was to come and perform miracles should be foretold; through those miracles it would become clear to those who understood rightly that he was a little man among little ones, but humble among the proud. By his smallness he taught the human being to recognize himself as small, lest, by growing larger in his own estimation, he should believe himself great.

For pride is not greatness but swelling. What is swollen appears large, but it is not healthy. Therefore, to heal this swelling of the human race, the Creator himself, both physician and medicine, appeared among human beings as a human being—not merely applying a remedy, but presenting a human being to those who saw him while preserving God for those who believed. The sight of his humility healed the sick; contemplation of his divinity seeks those who are strong.

And while there were human beings who would see God in a human being, yet would not place their hope in a human being whom one ought not to follow—for God, who could not be seen, was to be followed [Note: This entire passage is corrupt. It can be corrected better from section 2 of Sermon 371 above, p. 1660, note 2, than from the manuscripts. Some manuscripts here read, “And while he was among human beings”; shortly afterward others read, “nor yet ought they to place their hope in a human being.” Then one manuscript, omitting the word “who,” adds: “one ought not to follow God; he is to be followed,” and so forth. Three others omit the words “whom one ought not to follow, God.”]—in order that God might be presented to humanity, seen by humanity, and followed by humanity, God became human.

You ought to consider yourself something great. But when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–3, 14), that same Wisdom which was begotten of God deigned also to be created among human beings. To this belongs the statement, “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. 8:22), for its beginning is the head of the Church, which is Christ. He created a human being through whom an example of living might be given to us—that is, a sure way by which we might reach God.

For we could not return except through humility, although we fell through pride, just as it was said to our first-created ancestor, “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). An example of this humility, therefore—that is, of the way—had to be sought. Our Restorer himself deigned to demonstrate it in his own person. He “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7), so that a human being might be created at the beginning of his ways by the Word through whom all things were created.

For this reason our Lord is proclaimed by the authority of the divine Scriptures as both Only-Begotten and Firstborn: Only-Begotten from the Father, Firstborn from the dead. Accordingly, insofar as he is Only-Begotten, he has no brothers; insofar as he is Firstborn, he has deigned to call brothers all those who, after his primacy and through his primacy, are born in grace by adoption as sons, as apostolic teaching commends.

Therefore, according to what he is as Firstborn, the natural Son is our brother; born alone from the very substance of the Father, he exists as the Father is: God from God, light from light. We, however, are not naturally light; rather, we are illumined by that light, so that we may shine with wisdom through him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXVIII

[Note: Also known as *On Time* 13.]

## On the Nativity of the Lord, XII

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors and was judged spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus, who observe that it has been clumsily assembled from various passages of Augustine. They also note that it embraces almost the whole sermon which elsewhere stood as *On Time* 5 (now 369). They especially object to the statement in section 3 that Simeon was “renewed in age,” since Augustine’s wording has been corrupted: in his exposition of Psalm 39, section 18, he said, “Made a child in the Child, renewed in faith.” Moreover, in the manuscripts—apart from certain ones that have the sermon shortened by more than a third—the following introduction precedes it: “You have heard, brothers, how the blessed Evangelist today related the mystery of Christ’s generation. ‘The generation of Christ,’ he says, ‘was thus.’”]

## 1. The remedy of our restoration. Christ alone was born without sin

Our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, who is eternally the Creator of all things, today, by being born from a mother, has become our Savior. Today he was born for us in time by his will, so that he might lead us to the Father’s eternity. God became human so that the human being might become God. So that the human being might eat the bread of angels, the Lord of angels today became human.

Today that prophecy has been fulfilled which says, “Drip down, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). Therefore the one who had made all things was made, so that the one who had perished might be found.

Thus the human being confesses in the Psalms, “Before I was humbled, I sinned,” and again, “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost” (Ps. 118:67, 176). The human being sinned and became guilty; God was born as a human being so that the guilty one might be set free.

The human being fell, therefore, but God descended: the human being fell miserably, God descended mercifully; the human being fell through pride, God descended with grace. For thus the mother of the Lord heard from the angel: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28).

He who was first born without a mother in heaven was today born without a father on earth. O miracles! O wonders, dearest brothers! The laws of nature are changed in a human being: God is born, a virgin becomes pregnant without a man. Immediately the Word of God espouses one who had known no man; she became at once both mother and virgin—a mother, yet undefiled; a virgin with a son, knowing no man; always closed, yet not unfruitful.

For he alone was born without sin, whom, without the embrace of a man, not the desire of the flesh but the obedience of the mind brought forth. The virgin conceived; she alone could give birth to medicine for our wound, since she did not bring forth the offspring of holy love from the wound of sin.

## 2. Christ yesterday and today

O wondrous and carefully fashioned union! O new and unheard-of mingling! God, who is and who was, becomes; the Creator, a creature. He who is immeasurable is contained; he who makes others rich becomes poor. The incorporeal is clothed with flesh; the Word grows substantial; the invisible is seen; the intangible is handled; the incomprehensible is comprehended; the immortal is killed.

He whom heaven and earth bless is placed in a narrow manger. He who exists before the ages is numbered among the ages. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). “Yesterday” refers to mortality; “today,” to eternity.

Rightly today the heavens spoke, the angels rejoiced, the shepherds were glad, the Magi were invited [Note: The manuscripts read, “the Magi were changed.”], kings were troubled, martyrs were crowned, and demons were driven away.

Therefore, with joy, let us speak to the holy virgin Mary, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us speak and not be ashamed: “Nurse Christ, mother, and our Lord and food. Nurse the bread that comes from heaven and is placed in the manger like food for pious beasts.”

For there the ox recognized its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger (Isa. 1:3)—that is, circumcision and uncircumcision, joined to the cornerstone, whose first representatives were the shepherds and the Magi [Note: In a German manuscript, the words “and placed in the manger” through “Nurse him” are absent.].

Nurse him who made you such that he himself might also be made in you; he who, by being conceived, brought you the gift of fertility, and by being born did not take away the gift of virginity. Before he was born, he chose for himself the womb from which he would be born, the city in which he would be born, and the day on which he would be born; and he himself created what he chose.

For thus it was foretold long ago: “The mother Zion will say, ‘A man, and a man was born in her’; and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5).

## 3. Simeon’s desire

O omnipotence of the one being born! O majesty of the one descending from heaven to earth! He was still being carried in the womb, and from his mother’s womb he was greeted by John the Baptist. He was presented in the temple and recognized by the famous, aged, proven, crowned old man Simeon.

Then he recognized him, then he worshiped him, then he said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

He was delayed from departing this world so that he might see the one who was born through whom the world itself had been founded. The old man recognized the infant; he became a child in the Child. He was renewed in old age, though he was full of devotion.

The old man Simeon carried the infant Christ; Christ guided Simeon’s old age. The Lord had told him that he would not taste death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord born.

Christ was born, and the old man’s desire was fulfilled in the old age of the world itself. He came to an old human being who found the world grown old. Simeon did not wish to remain long in this world, yet he desired to see Christ in this world, singing with the prophet and saying: “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8).

Finally, so that you may know that his joy was indeed of this kind, he concluded by saying: “Now you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation.”

## 4. Testimonies to Christ’s birth

The Prophets sang that the Creator of heaven and earth would be on earth with human beings. The angel announced that the Creator of flesh and spirit would come in the flesh. John greeted the Savior from womb to womb. The old man Simeon recognized God as an infant; the widow Anna recognized the virgin mother.

These are the testimonies to your birth, Lord Jesus, before the waves of the sea would be subjected to you as you trod upon them and yield as you commanded; before the wind would fall silent at your order, the dead rise when you called, the sun grow pale at your death, the earth tremble at your resurrection, and heaven open at your ascension.

For you were still being carried in your mother’s hands, and already you were recognized as Lord of the world.

## 5. Christ beautiful everywhere

For everywhere Christ the Lord appeared beautiful: beautiful in heaven, beautiful on earth; beautiful as the Word in the Father, beautiful as flesh and Word in the mother; beautiful in the Virgin’s womb, where he did not lose his divinity when he assumed humanity.

For while he was here, while he was carried in hands, the heavens spoke, the angels rejoiced, and the star guided the Magi. He was worshiped in the manger as food for the gentle; the child Christ was worshiped in the temple by the old man Simeon and was carried in the arms of one whom he himself was guiding.

Christ was therefore beautiful in miracles; beautiful in scourging, in speeches, and in blows; unconcerned with death and raising the dead; beautiful on the wood, beautiful in heaven, beautiful also in the tomb.

Who, therefore, dearest brothers, would not worship the first and the last, the beginning and the end, “the Alpha and the Omega” (Rev. 22:13)? Who, I ask, would not worship him through whom day breathed forth and the shadows were driven away?

## 6. What Christ purchased from us and what he gave back

The emperor was born so that the sinner might be released. For it is written: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

The Lord Jesus Christ, through the flesh that he assumed, granted us great hope, great consolation, and great grace. He was born—something we did not know; he was nursed by his mother—he sucked what we knew. He purchased from us what is abundant here: to be born and to die. To rise again and live forever did not belong here.

He found here cheap earthly goods and brought to earthly beings foreign and heavenly ones. If you fear Christ’s death, whoever you are who hears me, love Christ’s resurrection.

Many despised Christ in his humility and did not reach the height of Christ. But those who worshiped him in his humility found him exalted.

## 7. The figure of the Law: Elisha’s staff. The foundation of Christian faith

The Jews hear this and say, “Christ is ours.” O blind Jews, if you recognized what was yours, why did you kill him?

The Lord indeed accepted circumcision in order to remove circumcision itself; he accepted the shadow in order to give the light; he accepted the figure in order to fulfill the truth. He himself gave you the Law. But the Law was given in the same figure in which Elisha acted when he raised the dead son of a devout woman.

This is what happened. The dead child was announced to Elisha. He gave his servant a staff and said to him: “Go,” he said, “and place the staff upon the boy, and he will revive” (2 Kings 4:29). The servant took the staff and placed it upon the boy, but he did not rise.

For this reason the Jews were able to receive the Law, but they were not able to live in it. O Jew, hear the Law changed, if you wish to be changed; if you do not wish to be changed, you are condemned in your old state. Do not love the old garment.

Your father crucified Christ; you hate him. He did it with his hand, you with your heart; both of you completed the crime. Let what your father did displease you. Hear what your Lord says: “The Father who remains in me himself gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak; and I know that his commandment is eternal life” (John 12:49–50).

If the Father’s commandment is eternal life, if the Father’s Word is eternal life, then the one who was speaking was eternal life. Therefore he did nothing from himself, because he is not from himself.

But from whom is he? From the Father. The Father is God, but not God from God; the Son is God, but God from God. Therefore he is Son, because he was begotten from God—always Son, begotten without beginning, and yet begotten.

And you are waiting to hear from me how this can be understood. Hear the prophet through me: “Who can recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). Yet we have said much about his generation—but about the generation that is from his mother.

But how he was born from the Father in heaven—who can explain it? Who can recount or investigate it? Let us hold fast to this human birth, through which God granted us grace.

Grace, I say, was granted, not paid as a reward, because the one who created also heals. Through it he raises the fallen, through it he cures the sick, through it he crowns the victor.

This is faith; this is truth; this is the foundation of Christian faith: one human being through whom came the fall, another human being, Christ, through whom comes the structure. The former fell because he did not remain; the one who did not fall raises him. The former fell because he abandoned the one who remains; Christ, remaining in the Father, descended to the one lying fallen.

## 8. Christ’s divine generation

He himself is the little child from the seed of Israel, and he himself is Emmanuel, God with us.

What is that generation of our Savior by which he is coeternal with the Father who begets him, when the world was astonished at this generation from a virgin, which devout faith recognized and held fast, while unbelief mocked it and pride feared it after being overcome?

What is that generation by which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)? Or what is this Word which, before it was spoken, did not remain silent, and when spoken did not silence the one who was speaking?

What is the timeless Word through which times were made; the Word whose beginning no lips opened and whose ending no lips closed; the Word that has no beginning from the mouth of speakers and opens the mouths of the mute; the Word that does not become eloquent through the articulate tongues of nations but makes the tongues of infants articulate?

What, I say, is that generation whose Father does not yield by dying, because he does not precede it by living; a generation foreign to every interval of place and time, to every extension of space that we are accustomed to perceive either in days or in bodies?

## 9. The mind contemplating this must be raised above all created things

A person is as far from God as he is unlike him.

Let us raise our souls toward him as far as, with his help, we can, if somehow we may be able to grasp both the one who begets, who does not precede the one born, and the one who is begotten, who does not follow the one who begets; the Father and the Son, neither both fathers nor both sons, yet both equally eternal; not both generating, nor both being born, but neither living without the other; the eternal Father having begotten, and the eternal Son having been born.

Let us think, if we can; if we cannot, let us believe. What we wish to say is not found here, yet it is not far from any one of us: “For in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

Let us transcend our flesh, in which parents live before their children. To be able to beget children, they grew; and when their children grow, they already grow old. Parents lived before their children were born, since after their parents die the children will also live.

Let us transcend our souls as well. They too give birth to something by thinking, something they possess with themselves by knowing; but they can lose it by forgetting, since they did not possess it before by being born.

Let us transcend all bodily, temporal, and changeable things, so that we may see above all things the one through whom all things were made. Our ascent is in the heart, because that toward which we ascend is also near; but we are far from him insofar as we are unlike him.

His likeness, therefore, ascends to him—the likeness that he both made and remade in us—because our weak sight does not yet beat perfectly and cannot gaze upon the ineffable brightness of eternal light. Since the mind’s vision does not yet grasp its radiance, who can recount his generation?

But “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Let us therefore praise, love, and worship this generation, whose day we celebrate today: the generation in which he deigned to come through Israel and to become Emmanuel, God with us in the weakness of flesh, but not with us in the iniquity of the heart; approaching us through what he assumed from us and freeing us through what remained his own.

For the Lord visited his servants through mortal weakness, so that he might make them free through unchangeable truth. Let us praise this generation, which human frailty is in some measure capable of grasping—not that generation which remains timeless and, without a mother, is above all things, but this one which occurred in time, without a father, among all things.

Let us praise, love, and worship this son of a virgin and bridegroom of virgins, born from an undefiled mother and bearing fruit in incorruptible truth, so that in his mercy we may triumph over the devil, whose cunning has been defeated.

Let us come to him by believing; let us advance by giving thanks; let us acknowledge him by persevering. Let us come to him and be reconciled among ourselves. Why do we quarrel over his birth? Is it so that we may not hear the physician calling us?

O unhappy sickness! The physician comes to the sick person, and the sick person occupies himself with disputes.

Let us therefore celebrate the Lord’s Nativity, dearest brothers; let us celebrate the advent of God and humanity, so that we may return to God. Let us therefore celebrate the feast—not of human devotion but of divine condescension; not of weakness but of eternity; not of formation but of the reformation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

# SERMON CXXIX

[Note: Also known among the Viguier sermons as 14, in the first part of the Supplement.]

## On the Kalends of January, I

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. An ancient manuscript, now in the Colbert Library, ascribes it to Augustine; Vignerius seems to have used it.
