But the belief that it is Augustine’s is opposed both by its manner of expression, which resembles Caesarius more closely, and by the fact that it belongs to a later period, since the observation made here in section 3 concerning a public fast throughout all the churches on the Kalends of January, ordered by the holy ancient Fathers, can scarcely be placed before Caesarius’ time.

Another manuscript from Navarre, after completing the sermon on the Circumcision to which this one is immediately appended, has the following: “Here ends the sermon on the Circumcision of the Lord. Here begins the sermon of Saint Maxentius on the Nativity of the Lord. On the Kalends of January.” Immediately afterward follows the sermon beginning, “The day of the Kalends,” and so forth. But in this sermon there is no mention of the Lord’s Nativity.

Under the name of Bishop Faustinus it was published by Bollandus in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume 1, from an old copy of Acy, or Acinctum, at the monastery among the Burgundians. Sermons 129 and 130 are found in the *Life of Caesarius*.]

## 1. Who Janus was. The origin of idolatry. Why Janus had two faces. The superstition of the Kalends of January

The day of these Kalends, dearest brothers, which they call the Kalends of January, received its name from a certain Janus, a lost and sacrilegious man.

This Janus was a certain leader and prince of the pagan people. When ignorant and rustic people feared him as though he were a king, they began to worship him as a god. They paid him unlawful honor, being terrified by the royal power they saw in him.

For foolish people who did not know God then considered those to be gods whom they saw to be more exalted among human beings. Thus it happened that the worship of the one true God was transferred to many names of gods—or rather of demons.

They therefore named the day of these present Kalends after Janus, as has already been said. Since they wished to confer divine honors upon that man, they designated it as the end of one year and the beginning of another.

Because among them the January Kalends were said to complete one year and begin another, they placed Janus, as it were, at the beginning and the end, so that he might be said both to complete one year and to begin another.

Hence the worshipers of idols fashioned two faces for Janus: one in front of him and the other behind him; one that seemed to look upon the past year and another upon the future. Thus, by assigning two faces to him, foolish people who wished to make him a god made him a monster.

The pagans wished their god to possess as something exceptional what is monstrous even among beasts. Therefore, in the clearest revelation and indication of their error, while they wished through religious vanity to make him appear a great god, they proclaimed him a demon.

## 2. Those who make themselves into a little deer. Men dressing as women

This is why on these days pagan people are covered with obscene distortions, with the order of all things perverted, so that those who worship this being may make themselves like the one who is worshiped.

On these days miserable people—and, what is worse, some who have been baptized—assume altered forms and monstrous appearances, among which are things that ought first to cause shame, or rather grief.

For what wise person could believe that some sane people are found who, making themselves into little deer, wish to change themselves into the appearance of wild beasts? Some clothe themselves in the skins of animals; others put on the heads of beasts, rejoicing and exulting if they have transformed themselves into animal shapes so completely that they do not appear to be human beings [Note: This explains canon 1 of the Council of Auxerre, held in 578, which says: “It is not permitted on the Kalends of January to make an old woman or a little deer, or to observe diabolical gifts.” One should read “to make an old woman or a little deer,” as in the *Life of Saint Eligius*, book 2, chapter 15, or in the treatise *On the Right Conduct of Catholic Life*; see also Halitgar, *Penitential*, chapter 6; Burchard, book 19, chapter 5; and the letter of Boniface, bishop of Mainz, to Pope Zacharias, chapter 6.].

By this they indicate and prove that they possess not so much a beast’s outward appearance as its mentality. For although they wish to express in themselves the likeness of various animals, it is nevertheless certain that in them the heart of beasts is more present than the form.

Now what is that practice, and how shameful, by which men who were born male put on women’s tunics and finally, through a most disgraceful transformation, weaken their masculine strength into feminine figures? They are not ashamed to insert military arms into women’s tunics; they display bearded faces and wish to appear as women.

And rightly they no longer possess masculine strength, since they have passed into the dress of women. For it must be believed that by God’s just judgment they lost military valor because they had disfigured themselves in the appearance of women.

## 3. Other superstitions. New Year’s gifts

Since God, being gracious to you, has deigned to inspire you so that, for love of the faith, this miserable custom might be completely removed from this city, I ask you, dearest brothers, not to be satisfied merely that you yourselves, by God’s gift, do not commit this evil.

Wherever else you see it being done, rebuke, discipline, and correct it; by your salutary counsel remove foolish people from this miserable sacrilege.

And so that you may dedicate yourselves wholly to divine mercy, reject also those other observances as poisons of the devil—observances which, what is worse, many people in the Christian community are not ashamed to practice.

There are some who observe omens on the Kalends of January, so that they will not give fire from their house, or any other benefit, to anyone who asks. They both receive diabolical New Year’s gifts from others and pass them on to others themselves.

Some rustics also set out small tables on the past night, laden with many things necessary for eating, and want them to remain arranged in this way throughout the night, believing that the January Kalends can grant them that their banquets will continue throughout the entire year in such abundance.

And since, as it is written, “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 5:9), remove from your well-ordered households these practices and others like them—which would take too long to mention and which the ignorant consider either small or no sins. Command this also: that they observe these Kalends in the same way they are accustomed to observe those of the other months.

For those who wish to observe anything from pagan custom on these days must fear that the name “Christian” may be of no benefit to them.

## 4. The fast formerly ordered on the Kalends of January. Masked people are not to be looked upon

Therefore, because our holy ancient fathers considered that most people on these days served gluttony or lust and raged in drunkenness and sacrilegious dances, they decreed throughout the whole world that a public fast should be proclaimed in all the churches [Note: The Council of Toledo IV, canon 11, and the Council of Tours II, canon 17, mention this solemn fast. Long ago Augustine likewise exhorted the people in Sermon 198, *On the Kalends of January*: “They become drunk; you fast.”].

Thus miserable people might recognize that they were doing so much evil that all the churches had to fast on account of their sins.

Let us therefore fast on these days, dearest brothers; and with true and perfect charity let us mourn the folly of miserable people, so that at least in this way they may understand their evil when they see a public fast being observed on their behalf.

For we must not despair that God may correct them through our prayer or discipline. Through his apostle, in ineffable goodness, he promised, saying: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20).

Whoever on these foolish Kalends offers any kindness to people playing luxuriously must not doubt that he makes himself a participant in their sin. For one who thinks wisely about the salvation of his soul ought to grieve or weep over them rather than relax his mind into unhappy laughter with them or about them.

But you, brothers, who by God’s favor are accustomed to cry out daily, “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15), and again, “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1), ought not to allow your eyes—which, by keeping constant watch in church, are sanctified toward God—to be polluted by looking upon the revelry of foolish people.

You ought rather to disdain and despise the works of the devil, so that the love of Christ may remain whole in you.

Cry out, therefore, with the prophet, saying, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118:37), fearing what the Apostle says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20–21).

But I trust in God’s mercy that through your correction their folly will be amended, so that the Lord may repay you with double rewards—not only for yourselves but also for the correction of those who will advance through your example—through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, to whom are glory and honor forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXX

[Note: Also known among the Viguier sermons as 15, in the first part of the Supplement.]

## On the Kalends of January, II

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It certainly has the same author as the preceding sermon. In a very ancient manuscript from Fleury it is entitled: “Here begins the sermon of Saint Sedatus, bishop, on the Kalends of January.” We scarcely doubt that “Saint Caesarius” should be read there instead of “Saint Sedatus.”

Although there was a certain bishop of Béziers named Sedatus, who subscribed to the Third Council of Toledo in 589, and although some consider him the author of the homily on the Epiphany entitled “of Saint Sedatus, bishop,” printed in volume 15 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, this work, as must now be observed, is nothing other than a cento consisting of many poorly joined fragments of other sermons.

For its first part, beginning “Recently, dearest brothers,” and so forth, is found in the sermon numbered below as 136. The middle section, beginning with the words “That matter, dearest brothers, which on the third day,” and so forth, is found in Caesarius’ sermon numbered above as 90. For the later part, see sermon 135 here, and so forth.]

## 1. Pride and error are the sources of all sins. Error. How it passes into pride. The madness of the masked. How the demon rules them

The devil introduces every sin, dearest brothers, either through pride or through error: error through ignorance, pride through contempt. These two things are the origins of all sins.

Error is, as it were, the lighter offense: the pursuit of pleasures, immoderate gluttony, the shameful delight of brazen joking, eagerness for spectacles, an unrestrained tongue, thoughtless and disordered presumption. Error also includes the useless observance of auguries, the worship of days belonging to ancient superstition, and inquiry into the future.

But these things pass into pride when, once recognized, they persist without amendment. Thus it happens that, for the sake of foolish pleasure, while the days of the Kalends or the vanity of other superstitions are observed, through the license of drunkenness and the shameful singing of games, demons are invited as though to their sacrifices.

For their sacrifice is sweet when something is either said or done by us through which moral decency, the friend of justice, departs after being violated by wicked acts.

What is more insane than to change the male sex into the form of a woman through shameful dress? What is more insane than to disfigure the face and put on expressions at which even the demons themselves shudder? What is more insane than to sing, with disordered movements and immodest songs, the praises of vices with shameless delight?

To put on the appearance of a beast and become like a doe or a stag, so that a human being made in the image and likeness of God becomes a sacrifice to demons—this is how that craftsman of evils insinuates himself, so that, gradually capturing minds through the likeness of games, he may rule them.

Therefore, when the things mentioned above have gained strength, pride, hostile to God, follows. Through neglect of religion and contempt for fear of God, it first introduces disputes even against the holy Scriptures. Then, raging with ambition, swelling with vanity, desiring dishonorable things and despising honorable ones, it advances with the spirit of arrogance into the shipwreck of morals, like an unrestrained storm of a whirlwind.

From this comes envy, the root of all evils. It burns at another’s advancement as though at its own misfortunes, and, like the future fire of Gehenna, already consumes the souls of the living with a hidden flame and torments them with biting anxieties.

For what can be more miserable than one whom another’s happiness makes unhappy? Or where can one find a remedy who is wretched not only through his own misfortune but also through another’s good?

From this comes anger, which is always hostile to counsel and lays down both a pit into which it may fall and snares by which it may itself be caught.

## 2. Such People Must Be Restrained

But you, dearest brothers, to whom God has graciously granted honorable and sober conduct, pass on to your neighbors or household members, through constant admonition, the holy way of life that you have received by divine gift, and do not allow them to utter shameful words or sing wanton songs. For every sin rebounds upon the one who does not wish to restrain sinners when he is able to do so.

Therefore, whoever on the Kalends of January gives any form of human kindness to wretched people who rage with sacrilegious ritual—rather than celebrating—should recognize that he has given it not to human beings but to demons. And so, if you do not wish to share in their sins, do not allow a little stag or heifer [Note: [Col. 2004] An old codex has *sive anulas*, “or little old women.” Of two manuscripts, one has *sive agniculam*, “or a little lamb”; the other, *sive anniculam*, “or a yearling.”], or any other such monstrosity, to come before your houses. Instead, rebuke and correct them; and, if you can, constrain them even with severity, so that, with God as your rewarder, you may receive a double recompense: for your own salvation and for the correction of others.

I ask you, beloved brothers, since by God’s favor we trust in the faith and uprightness of your conduct, not to be satisfied merely that you yourselves are good. Rather, as I have already urged above, strive through your admonition to correct the negligence of others as well, so that you may gain eternal rewards not only for your own holy way of life but also for the correction of others. Therefore admonish your households not to observe the sacrilegious customs of the wretched pagans.

## 3. New Year’s Gifts. Fasting on the Kalends of January

There are some, what is worse, whom hostile observance so overturns that, if on the day of the Kalends they happen to be needed by neighbors or travelers, they even pretend not to be able to provide a fire. Moreover, many are accustomed both to offer New Year’s gifts themselves and to receive them from others.

Above all, brothers, in order to confound the carnal and wanton joy of the pagans, let us all fast with God’s help, except those who cannot abstain because of illness; and let us pray to God as much as we can for those wretched people who, because of gluttony and drunkenness, honor these Kalends with sacrilegious custom. While we shudder at the things they do, let us also pray for them; and let us rejoice doubly—both in our own kindness and in their correction—if God grants it.

With God propitious, dearest brothers, you listen to us faithfully and willingly for the salvation of your souls, so that we may freely and with complete confidence lovingly suggest to you what we know to be necessary for your salvation, and show you what you ought to do and what you ought to avoid. Therefore I ask you, brothers, since, inspired by God, you yourselves despise the ancient pagan custom out of devotion to religion, that you correct with charity and gentleness any others whom you see observing it.

## 4. The Empty Honor Paid to the Planets. Why the Days Are Called by the Planets’ Names. Their First Naming. The Name Should Be Taken Up Again

For some fall into these evils, carefully observing on which day they should set out on a journey, paying honor either to the Sun, or to the Moon, or to Mars, or to Mercury, or to Jupiter, or to Venus, or to Saturn. In their misery they do not know that, unless they amend themselves through repentance, they will have a share in hell with those to whom they seem to pay empty honor in this world.

Above all, brothers, flee all these sacrileges and avoid them as the deadly poisons of the devil. God established both the sun and the moon for our sake and for our benefit, not so that we should worship these two lights as gods, but so that we should give as many thanks as we can to the One who gave them to us.

For Mercury was a wretched, greedy, cruel, impious, and proud human being. Venus, however, was an utterly shameless prostitute. These monstrous figures—that is, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn—are said to have been born at the time when the children of Israel were in Egypt. If they were born then, certainly the days that are called by their names already existed at that time. According to what God had instituted, they had names such as first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day [Note: [Col. 2005] The word *feria* (“day”) seems to have been added here, whereas the word perhaps to be understood in its place was *dies* (“day”). In an old codex it is omitted, and the text reads: “and the fifth and sixth.”].

But wretched and ignorant people, who—as we have said—worshiped these most filthy and impious men more through fear than love, consecrated the days of the whole week to them individually, assigning each day the name of one of them, as though, by venerating their sacrilegious rites in their hearts, they might seem to have their names more frequently on their lips.

But we, brothers, who are known to place our hope not in ruined and sacrilegious human beings but in the living and true God, should judge that no day is worthy of being called by the name of demons. Nor should we observe on which day we ought to set out on a journey. Rather, we should disdain even to utter those most filthy names, and should never say “the day of Mars,” “the day of Mercury,” or “the day of Jupiter” [Note: [Col. 2005] Augustine also disapproves this manner of speaking, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 93.3, and wishes Christians to correct it and speak according to ecclesiastical usage.]. Instead, let us call them the first, second, or third day, as it is written.

Also admonish your households about these names. The health of your soul will then remain perfect in you, if through your admonition spiritual medicine reaches those who have been wounded by many sins. Therefore correct not only your own people frequently and severely, but also admonish outsiders continually with charity, so that the gracious and merciful Lord may repay you with eternal rewards not only for your own salvation but also for the salvation of others. To him belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXXI

[Note: [Col. 2005] Formerly numbered 1 among those added by the Paris editors.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 2005] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Leuven editors regarded it as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. Its style is plainly very different from Augustine’s; moreover, the statement here that the star appeared two years before Christ was born is contrary to his teaching. Augustine assigns the appearance of the star to the day of Christ’s Nativity in his sermons on the Epiphany, 200, 201, 202, and so forth.]

### 1. The Unique Star. It Did Not Identify Christ but Stirred People to Seek Him

Just as this present day, returning each year, reminds us that the Magi worshiped our Lord Jesus as the firstfruits of the nations, so our sermon too is owed to this solemnity because of so great a mystery.

Therefore I remind Your Charity: recall the recent preceding day on which the Lord was born, and join to it this present day on which he was worshiped by the Magi. The star could not speak to them to say whose it was or whose greatness it foretold. Yet a new and unique star shone forth, and by a new miracle it terrified even those who are accustomed to observe the stars carefully. No one had ever been signified by such a star, because no one like this had ever been born.

Nevertheless, although the star remained silent, it shone forth to indicate who he was, where he was, and whose king he was. But God, who does not disappoint those who seek and knock with their hearts, undoubtedly revealed in another way to those who asked what the star could not indicate. Scripture does not say what that method was, but it left it to the prudent to understand; and in the narrative itself it shows where we may learn this.

### 2. Then Another Revelation Made It Clear

Since the city of Bethlehem had been identified by the Jews from the Scriptures as the place where Christ ought to be born, and since the house where the infant Word lay hidden, the same star led the Magi to the house beneath whose roof lay the one who had made the world and whom heaven had announced. Thus far the radiance of the star that went before them was evident.

But so that they would not return to Herod, king of the Jews, who had said that he wished to worship the one he wanted to kill, they are said to have been warned in a dream. Thus God showed by another revelation what the star could not express.

This must be understood as follows: it was not by the star alone—although it shone before their eyes with an unusual and unfamiliar light—that the Magi in the East could learn who was worthy of being signified by so great a star, whose radiance was its witness, whose great brightness announced him, or where they should seek him so that, once found, he might be worshiped. Rather, by another divine revelation it was certainly indicated what the light of the star silently signified.

As they sought with great wonder what the new appearance in the heavens meant and to whom it referred, it was communicated—not by the star itself speaking, but in another way—who had descended from heaven and, while presiding over heaven in his divinity, lay in the flesh beneath heaven. It was then understood whose star it was, the star that had already been visible for a long time, when the one signified through it was born.

### 3. The Star Appeared for Two Years

For nearly two years it was seen while people wondered what it was. But after Christ was born, it was revealed to the Magi that the star was no longer to be wondered at, but that the one foretold by the star was to be worshiped, and that he was king of the Jews.

They came from the East and worshiped today the one whom they had learned had been born a few days earlier, and whose was the star that had appeared to them for two years.

Someone may ask: Where is it shown that the star appeared for two years? Let us recall the words of the Gospel. Herod, king of the Jews, having been deceived by the Magi because they had been warned in a dream not to return to him and reveal where Christ had been found, killed all the children from two years old and under.

The Evangelist does not remain silent about why he did this—that is, why he ordered the little children from two years old and under to be killed. He says that it was according to the time which he had carefully learned from the Magi (Matt. 2:16). There we see the proof that the star did not first appear when Christ was born, that is, only a few days earlier, but had shone beforehand for a period of two years, and that its significance became known when the Magi were sent to worship on earth the one whom they had already seen marked out in heaven.

### 4. What Is Signified by the Two-Year Appearance. The Two Commandments of Love. The Two Testaments. The Two Advents of Christ. The Two Births of the Human Being

If anyone asks why the star shone for two years as a sign announcing Christ, the two years may be understood as signifying the two commandments: one, love of God; the other, love of neighbor. On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend (ibid. 22:40).

Thus what seemed to be spread out infinitely through many things has been brought together in this brevity. Here we may understand the prophet to have said: “For the Lord, completing and abbreviating, will make a brief word upon the earth” (Isa. 10:23). He therefore completed the word in the two commandments, and the star foretold his coming through two years.

These two years may also be understood as the two Testaments, the Old and the New. The author of the Law by which we are frightened is not one person, and the author of the grace by which we are helped another, since he himself said: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). He himself is the wisdom of God, of which it is said: “But he bears law and mercy upon his tongue” (Prov. 31:26).

But since the two years may more properly be taken as signifying two periods, we may also understand them as the two advents of Christ: one in humility, the other in glory. And we may understand them as our two births, since the one through whom all things were made is certainly the author of both: one birth by which we are born in the flesh, and another by which we are reborn in faith.

### 5. The Union of Jews and Gentiles

Let us therefore rejoice and exult in him whom swaddling clothes enclosed and angels proclaimed; who lay in a manger and shone among the stars; whom the star of heaven showed to be the eternal king to be worshiped by the nations—not a jewel in a diadem; who suckled at the breast and made martyrs of nursing infants.

Let us acknowledge the cornerstone in which two walls coming from different directions—one from the circumcision of the Jews, the other from the uncircumcision of the nations—are joined by a faithful kiss. “For he is our peace, who made both one.” Coming, as you have heard through the Apostle, he preached peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near (Eph. 2:14, 17).

The shepherds were near; the Magi were far away. Both recognized him; both came. And according to the prophet Isaiah, both found their food in the manger, like an ox and an ass (Isa. 1:3). Christ, glorified, took up these peoples from Jews and Gentiles and received them as his firstfruits when he was born.

The rejoicing of this day therefore pertains especially to us, who have come from the Gentiles.

### 6. The Mystical Gifts of the Magi

When the Magi worshiped Christ, they brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. 2:11): gold, because they saw a king; frankincense, because they understood him to be God. They also recognized that he would suffer in the flesh, for they brought myrrh for his burial.

That was according to their understanding. But from us he receives gold if we give alms; frankincense if we pour out prayers; myrrh if we die for him.

Therefore, since *Epiphany* indicates “manifestation” in the Greek word—for the infancy of the Lord, hidden from the Magi who desired to worship him, was manifested by the sign of the star—let us follow the way of the radiant Gospel and worship in holiness the one to whom we have been manifested. Thus, when God comes openly, and he will no longer be an infant, because he will not be silent (Ps. 49:3), may we deserve to appear at his right hand.

# SERMON CXXXII

[Note: [Col. 2007] Formerly *On Time* 35.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 2007] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It seemed doubtful to the Leuven editors, but Verlinus and Vindingus judged it false, on the same indications and arguments by which the preceding sermon was rejected.]

### 1. Today Jews Are Joined to the Gentiles

The coming in the flesh of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ began to be manifested to the Gentiles at his very first appearance, when he was born from the Virgin and the Magi came from the East to worship him.

This most solemn day has rightly been made a holy observance of the Church, especially of the Church that grew from the Gentiles and, by a more abundant structure, joined the second wall to the cornerstone, so that “he might make both one” (Eph. 2:14), forming the Church from circumcision and uncircumcision.

Hence he was also called the cornerstone, as one joining together those who came from different origins, so that he might transform both into one body for God, as prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teaching bears witness.

When the Lord was born from the Virgin—the day we celebrated most recently—the shepherds, warned by angels according to the evangelist Luke, came to the manger of the infant Word (Luke 2:9). Those shepherds were Israelites. Behold, one wall was marked out: it ran from the circumcision toward the cornerstone.

A few days later, the Magi are believed to have come today from the East and to have recognized the greatness of that little child, as the evangelist Matthew records (Matt. 2:1–12). Behold, the other wall, coming together from the despair of uncircumcision, represented us specifically and doubled this feast day for us in familiar joy.

### 2. The Star Appeared Two Years Earlier. What Led the Magi to Worship

For they saw in heaven a completely unfamiliar star—not a few days earlier but nearly two years earlier, as they disclosed to Herod when he inquired. Hence, according to the time he had learned from the Magi, he killed the infants from two years old and under, as it is written.

As they understood, they admired this star and, by a subsequent revelation, were granted knowledge of whose star it was: namely, that it belonged to the king of the Jews. When they also learned that he had been born for this purpose, they were able to come today to worship him.

They certainly did not suppose that such great honor was owed to this king of the Jews as other kings usually were, by distant foreigners entirely outside that kingdom. Rather, they had learned that one had been born in whom, by worshiping him, they would undoubtedly obtain the salvation that comes from God.

He was not even of an age to which human flattery might be offered. No royal seat lay beneath his knees; no purple hung from his limbs; no diadem shone upon his head. No procession of attendants, no terror of an army, no reputation for glorious battles had drawn these men from distant lands to him with so great a desire for supplication.

A newly born child lay in a manger, small in body and despised in poverty. But something great was hidden in the small one. These men, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, had learned it not from earth bearing witness but from heaven proclaiming it. From so far away and with such humility they came to him, seeing him but not perceiving what they saw, and desiring through worship to gain his favor.

The queen of the South had come from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; she too was moved not by the elevation of his kingdom but by the light of her mind (1 Kings 10:1; Matt. 12:42). Yet Solomon possessed teaching which, spread abroad through his words far and wide, could stir eager minds to learn. Therefore she had not come to worship a hidden God but to hear a speaking human being.

But here was the one who had given Solomon that wisdom and who was the power and wisdom of God. Clothed in the weakness of the flesh, he was still silent on earth because of his tender age, yet already shone in heaven through the greatness of his majesty [Note: [Col. 2008] Thus all the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *clamabat*, “he cried out,” instead.]

### 3. Herod’s Detestable Cruelty, but the Jews’ Still More Astonishing Folly

What are you afraid of, Herod? Why are you disturbed in your wicked mind? If you had wisdom for your own salvation, he has been born through whom you might see the kingdom of God, not one whose human kingdom you should envy.

Why do you rage? Why do you kill infants? Why, guilty yourself, do you pursue an innocent age with a guilty sword [Note: [Col. 2008] The words *noxio gladio*, “with a guilty sword,” are absent from the manuscripts.]?

No one will be secure from the sword of this king through cruelty, but through piety.

The madness of King Herod is therefore detestable, but the folly of the Jews is still more astonishing. It was on their account, by divine providence, that the star briefly withdrew from the sight of the Magi who were seeking Christ, in order that they might be judged. For the star had appeared in order to show the place where the child was.

It could certainly also have served as a guide to the city. But when questioned about where Christ would be born, the Jews ought to have brought forth from the holy books that he would be born in Bethlehem of Judea—ready to read, blind to understand, hard-hearted toward belief.

Let us therefore leave them in the antiquity of the letter and, aided by their books, recognize with these foreigners the Christ who is to be worshiped.

# SERMON CXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 2008] Formerly *On Time* 33; later Appendix 28.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, III

[Note: [Col. 2008] This is Pope Leo’s eighth sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord, and it is attributed to him in all the manuscripts.]

### 1. The Cause and Meaning of the Solemnity

Beloved, the cause and meaning of today’s solemnity have often been made clear to you both by the Gospel narrative and by the custom of observance. There is no need now to repeat in such a way the events of our Savior’s human beginnings that we discourse on the brilliance of the new star, the Magi and their gifts, Herod’s savagery, and the slaughter of the infants.

For, as you know, the radiance of the star prefigured the grace of God, the three men the calling of the Gentiles, the impious king the cruelty of the pagans, and the killing of the infants the pattern of all martyrs.

But since on this most sacred day the duty of priestly speech must answer your expectation, let us strive, with the help of God’s Spirit, to reach as far as we can by the paths of understanding, so that we may recognize that the mystery of this present feast pertains to the times of all the faithful. Let it in no way be considered strange that, within the order of God’s dispensations, what is ancient is worshiped.

### 2. The Necessity of the Incarnation

Although every Christian soul ought to think nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Son of God, and although, once the rudiments of beginning faith have been surpassed, each person ought to advance toward higher things, nevertheless the weakness of the human mind must tremble when it receives Christ as a true human being and must approach with difficulty, through the beginnings or growth of bodily existence, the recognition of the one divinity he shares with the Father.

But when a ray of heavenly light shines through thoughts obscured by darkness, let the splendor of truth break through the delays of hesitant faith. Let the heart, set free and released from visible things, follow the light of understanding as its guiding star. For, as the Apostle says, “The Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). Thus the one whom it reverently worshiped lying humbly in a cradle, let it worship without distinction reigning with the Father.

This manifestation, beloved, dissolves the clouds of hesitant souls and makes the Son of God known in such a way that the fact that he is also the Son of man causes no obstacle. It belongs to the dignity of the present feast. The Savior’s true infancy declares his divinity when the perception of the flesh is transferred from human things to divine things, so that the signs of power lift up those whom experiences of weakness cast down.

Our nature and our condition needed such assistance, so that the human race might be restored: humility could not do so without majesty, nor majesty without humility.

### 3. Here No One Should Feel Secure

When, together with the progress of individual believers, the guardianship of the divine commandments shines forth, and what was said is fulfilled—“Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16)—who would not understand that divinity is present where he sees true virtue appearing?

Such virtue certainly does not exist without God, nor does it possess the character of divinity unless it is enlivened by the Spirit of its author. Since the Lord says to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), there is no doubt that a human being who does good receives from God both the accomplishment of the deed and the beginning of the will.

Hence the Apostle, the most abundant encourager of the faithful, says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13).

This is also why the saints have cause to tremble and fear: lest, exalted by the very works of piety, they be abandoned by the help of grace and remain in the weakness of nature.

### 4. Signs of God’s Indwelling in Us. Love, the Mother of All Virtues

Whoever wishes to discover whether God dwells within him—of whom it is said, “God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. 67:36)—should examine the inner places of his heart by sincere scrutiny and carefully ask:

With what humility does he resist pride? With what goodwill does he struggle against envy? Is he not captured by flattering tongues? Does he rejoice in the good of others? Does he refuse to repay evil with evil? Does he prefer to forget injuries without taking revenge rather than lose the image and likeness of his Creator?

The Creator calls everyone to knowledge of himself through universal gifts; he makes his rain fall on the just and the unjust and makes his sun rise on the good and the wicked (Matt. 5:45).

And so that this examination of careful discernment may not labor over many things [Note: [Col. 2009] Manuscripts *cb* and *n* read: “And so that he may not labor in vain over many things, let him examine discernment carefully.”], let him seek in the secret places of his mind love itself, the mother of all virtues. If he finds that his whole heart is intent upon love of God and neighbor, so that he wishes his enemies also to receive the same kindness that he desires for himself, then anyone of this kind should have no doubt that God is both his ruler and his inhabitant.

He receives God more magnificently the more he glories not in himself but in the Lord, since those to whom it is said, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21), are governed only by the Spirit whose authority rules them.

Knowing, therefore, beloved, that love is God, who works all things in all, pursue love, so that the hearts of all the faithful may converge in one pure affection.

Let vain things pass away from us; and, so that they may not occupy us, let us direct our constant desire toward the things that will always remain.

The mystery of the present feast must therefore be perpetual within us. It will indeed be celebrated without end if the Lord Christ appears in all our deeds, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 2010] Formerly *On Time* 37; later Appendix 29.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, IV

[Note: [Col. 2010] In manuscripts and printed books it is attributed to Maximus.]

### 1. Different Traditions Concerning the Celebration of the Epiphany

Although, beloved brothers, the tradition of the ancients concerning this day’s solemnity is diverse, the faith of holy devotion is nevertheless one.

Some today believe that our Lord Jesus Christ was worshiped by the Magi who came from the East under the guidance of a star; others assert that he changed water into wine; and still others affirm that he was baptized by John. In all these accounts the Son of God is believed, and in all of them our feast is present [Note: [Col. 2010] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *vera*, “true,” instead.].

For the fact that the Magi—who were certainly Gentiles—were permitted both to worship the Lord and to offer gifts prefigures the calling of the Gentiles. The transformation of water into wine signifies the hidden mystery of our religion. The fact that Jesus was baptized in the waters of the Jordan consecrates water for our Baptism.

It is therefore fitting, dearest ones, that we now say something to Your Holiness about that very baptism, insofar as the Lord grants it, so that you may recognize both the humility of our Savior and the glory of the mysteries.

### 2. John’s Baptism Did Not Remove Sins. Christ’s Humility

John preached in the desert a baptism of repentance to a sinful people [Note: [Col. 2010] The printed editions read “to the people for the remission of sins.” We have followed the manuscripts.], not one that erased committed crimes, but one that corrected those who had gone astray; for the remission of sins was reserved for the grace of Christ.

A very great multitude of various kinds therefore streamed to the Jordan, desiring the washing. Their deeds were so wicked and their lives so depraved that the venerable Baptist compared them to a brood of vipers.

Among such people the Lord of heavenly virtues, the one who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps. 103:32), Christ Jesus, did not disdain, in humility and quietness, to hasten to the baptism of his servant.

But why should we marvel at the Savior’s gentleness, since he bowed before the hands of a prophet, when he allowed himself to be crucified by his enemies?

### 3. John’s Testimony Concerning Christ

As he hastened toward the river, John suddenly cried out to the crowds standing around him:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

This is as though he were saying:

“Cease now, cease from my baptism, by which repentance is received” [Note: [Col. 2010] The printed editions have “by which repentance began.”]. “Behold the Baptizer through whom crimes are forgiven. Do not wish to be baptized any longer by your fellow servant.

“The Lord of us all is present, the one who baptizes unto life. Follow him; believe in him; with your whole mind, humbly ask from him the washing of salvation. From him even I, your own baptizer, desire to be baptized.”

Jesus did not reject the testimony of this voice. But because he wished to fulfill everything in due order, he nevertheless sought to be baptized by John.

The devoted Baptist, shaken by the power involved in baptizing him, said:

“I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”

That is: “I am a creature, but you are the Creator; I am a servant, but you are the Lord; I am the figure, but you are the Truth.”

But Jesus said:

“Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

That is: “Why do you now bring these things forward? The purpose of the humility undertaken must be fulfilled” [Note: [Col. 2011] The printed editions have “I have undertaken the purpose.” A manuscript of the *rm* group has “the purpose of holy humility.”].

Then the one who had been afraid to presume quickly obeyed the command of the one giving orders.

### 4. The Manifestation of the Trinity and Christ’s Power

Jesus is therefore baptized not for himself but for us; he is baptized not to be purified by water but to sanctify the waters himself. The new human being is baptized in order to establish the sacrament of the new Baptism.

“The heavens were opened to him,” it says. I think this happened so that in the heavens there might be a miracle concerning the things being done on earth, as Scripture says: “Into which things the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12).

For how could the Powers and Dominions of heaven, the Cherubim and Seraphim, fail to marvel when they saw the Lord of hosts being baptized in the river by a human being?

And so that John’s testimony might also be confirmed by heavenly testimony, he sees the Holy Spirit in bodily form, descending like a dove and remaining over Jesus. He also hears the Father saying:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:14–17).

Notice, beloved brothers, how great a grace was revealed to us in the baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by what subtle mystery the Trinity revealed itself to humanity today. The Father is heard in the voice; the Son is manifested in the human being; the Holy Spirit is recognized in the dove.

By what wondrous mystery does our Lord Jesus Christ, through either the touch of his body or the passing of his glory, sanctify, give life to, and illumine every creature, at least for a moment?

He consecrates the waters when he is baptized; he sanctifies the earth when he is buried; he raises the dead when he rises again; he glorifies the heavenly things when he ascends into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

# SERMON CXXXV

[Note: [Col. 2011] Formerly *On Time* 36.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, V

[Note: [Col. 2011] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Leuven editors considered it doubtful, while Verlinus and Vindingus regard it as spurious. It contains not only words unusual for Augustine, such as “submerged in pure water,” “Mary’s purification,” “he bound the seas with pebbles,” and “the blessed embassy of the Magi,” but also statements contrary to his teaching and dangerous in their implications, such as the claims that Christ “is now reborn through the sacraments,” “was consecrated in the Jordan,” and “was begotten through the mystery.” These expressions favor the heresy of Felix of Urgel, against whom Alcuin argues in book 2: “In John’s baptism, in which Christ was baptized, there was no regeneration.” On this matter see Augustine’s notable statement in Letter 187.31: “Certainly he alone was born in such a way that he did not need to be reborn.” The Remigian manuscript attributes the sermon to Ambrose. This is certainly false, but the sermon may perhaps have been printed from sermons falsely attributed to Ambrose, or from the same author from whom the sermon printed among Ambrose’s works as sermon 17, *On the Baptism of Christ*, derives. There the Lord himself is likewise said to have been “consecrated, born, and generated through the mystery,” so that this very day is called his Nativity, just as in this sermon one reads: “Therefore today is, in a certain way, another Nativity of the Savior.” Moreover, the comparison made here between Joseph and God the Father is expressed in nearly the same words in sermon 10 among the works of Ambrose. There are also other points of agreement with certain other Ambrosian sermons.]

### 1. The Water Enriched More Than Mary

We can understand, dearest brothers, how great a grace we owe to Christ the Lord, who heaps vows upon vows and multiplies joys by joys.

Behold, we are still rejoicing that Christ the Lord was born, and already we are glad that he was baptized for the salvation of the human race. The celebration of his birth has not yet ended, and already the solemnity of his baptism must be celebrated. He has scarcely been born for human beings, and already he is reborn through the sacraments.

Today, although many years have passed, he was consecrated in the Jordan. Thus the Lord arranged matters so as to join vows to vows—that is, so that at one and the same time he would be brought forth through the Virgin and be begotten through the mystery—and so that the celebration of his birth in the flesh and of his baptism would be continuous.

Thus, just as we then marvel that he was born from an incorrupt mother, so now we receive him submerged in pure water; and we glory in both events, because a mother gave birth to a son and remained chaste, and because water washed Christ and became holy.

For just as Mary’s chastity was glorified after childbirth, so the purification of the water was confirmed after the baptism—except that the water was enriched with an almost greater gift than Mary. She earned chastity for herself alone; the water bestowed sanctification upon us. She earned that she should not sin; the water that sins should be cleansed. She rejects personal offenses from herself; the water, through God’s grace, forgives in itself offenses belonging to others. Virginity was bestowed upon her; fecundity was granted to the water. She bore one, and remained a virgin; the water gives birth to many, and remains pure. She knows no other son besides Christ; with Christ she is the mother of peoples.

## 2. Christ’s Second Nativity

Today, then, is in a certain sense another birthday of the Savior. For we recognize that he was born through the same signs and the same miracles, but now baptized with a greater mystery. Indeed, the Holy Spirit, who was present with him then in the womb (Luke 1:35), now surrounded him with radiance in the depths of the river; he who then kept Mary chaste now sanctifies the waters. The Father, who then overshadowed [Mary] with his power, now cries out with his voice; and, as though with a more mature purpose, he who then provided the shadow for his birth now bears witness to the truth.

For God says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). This is more illustrious than the first. The second nativity is plainly more glorious than the first. The first gave birth to Christ silently and without a witness; the second baptized the Lord with a profession of his divinity. In the first, Joseph, who was thought to be his father, excuses himself; in this one, the Father, who was not believed to be such, makes himself known. There the mother struggles beneath suspicion, because the father was absent from the declaration; here the mother is honored, because the divinity proclaims the Son. The second nativity, I say, is more honored than the first: for here God the Father is named as the Father of majesty, whereas there Joseph is regarded as a craftsman. And although in both cases the Lord was born and baptized through the Holy Spirit, nevertheless the one who cries out from heaven is more honored than the one who labors on earth.

## 3. God the Father, the Craftsman

Joseph, then, a craftsman on earth, was thought to be the father of the Lord and Savior (ibid. 13:55), nor is God, who truly is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, excluded from this work: for he too is a craftsman. He is the artisan who fashioned the structure of this world by power that is not only wondrous but also ineffable; like a wise architect, he suspended heaven with subtlety, founded the earth with its mass, and bound the seas with pebbles.

He is the artisan who lowers the heights of pride to a certain measure and exalts the lowest places of humility. He is the artisan who cuts away superfluous works from our conduct and preserves whatever is useful. He is the artisan whose axe John the Baptist threatens has been placed at our root, so that every tree that has exceeded the rule of just discernment may be cut down at the root and handed over to the fire (ibid. 3:10), while whatever has kept the measure of truth may be assigned to the heavenly structure.

## 4. When Christ Is Baptized, He Cleanses the Waters

Today, then, the Lord is baptized in the Jordan. What sort of baptism is this, in which the one who is immersed is purer than the spring; in which, while the water washes what it has received, he is not stained by defilements but honored by blessings? What sort, I say, is the Savior’s baptism, in which the waters are cleansed rather than cleansing?

For by a new kind of sanctification, the water did not so much wash Christ as become washed itself. From the moment the Savior immersed himself in the water, he consecrated by the mystery of baptism the courses of all rivers and the veins of every spring, so that wherever anyone should wish to be baptized in the Lord’s name, the water of the world might not so much wash that person as Christ’s water purify him.

The Savior therefore wished to be baptized, not in order to acquire purity for himself, but to cleanse the waters for us.

## 5. Mystical Gifts

Meanwhile the blessed embassy of the Magi, led to the sacred cradle, marvels at the ray proceeding from above. Ethiopia precedes Judea, destined to be stripped of the blackness of sin and clothed in the whiteness of faith.

What an astonishing condescension! He who embraces heaven and earth is enclosed in his mother’s arms; he who surpasses the Father’s kingdom lies hidden in his mother’s lap. Through a simple service, a spiritual secret is revealed: humanity is seen, and divinity is worshiped.

They present gold, frankincense, and myrrh, offering more in their mystical significance than in their own understanding. In the gift of gold, royal dignity is shown; in the vapor of frankincense, divine majesty; in the form of myrrh, humanity destined for burial. Thus the number of the offerings speaks of the Trinity, while one devotion bears witness to unity.

Therefore, if we desire to reach Christ, let us always strive to gaze upon heaven with vigilant attention of heart. Let the perfect star of righteousness guide our paths of life—the one who said, “You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Exodus 23:15). Let us offer him the gold of faith, the spices of devotion, and the holocausts of chastity. Let us also possess within us spiritual myrrh, which may so season our souls that it preserves them unharmed from the corruption of sin. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: The whole of this section 5 is absent from manuscripts r and rm. It is found, however, in the printed editions and in the sermon of Sedatus, mentioned above in connection with Sermon 130.]

# SERMON CXXXVI

[Note: Otherwise, On the Season 29.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, VI

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave the matter doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus assert that it is spurious. And rightly so, indeed: not to linger over the miracle of the five loaves, which is said here to have been celebrated on the feast of the Epiphany, just as in the preceding sermon, so in this one Christ’s baptism is called regeneration. In both sermons the same words are pronounced: “The water did not so much wash Christ the Lord as become washed itself.” Moreover, this subsequent treatise contains several passages both from the sermon on the Epiphany attributed to Sedatus and from another attributed to Eusebius in the Library of the Fathers. Furthermore, in the Navarre manuscript the sermon is not incongruously divided into two, the second of which begins with these words in section 5: “Recently, most beloved brothers, from this day,” and so forth.]

### 1. Christ’s Fourfold Manifestation on This Day; the Mysteries of Our Salvation Are Contained in Each

Recently, most beloved brothers, we celebrated the sacrament of our redemption by which God clothed himself with humanity together with its weaknesses. Today, however, we honor that by which God revealed himself in humanity through his powers, because on this day either the star gave notice of his rising in the heavens (Matthew 2), or he changed water into wine at the wedding feast in Cana of Galilee (John 2), or he consecrated the waters in the Jordan for the restoration of the human race through his baptism (Matthew 3:13), or he fed five thousand people from five loaves (ibid. 14:19). In each of these events the mysteries and joys of our salvation are contained.

For he was born for us from the Virgin, as the star showed; for us the washing of baptism was granted, which he consecrated in the channel of the Jordan; and he also showed beforehand, by the miracle of his deed, that we are to be changed for the better when he changed water into wine.

[Note: Up to this point, several matters agree with Eusebius.]

Therefore, most beloved brothers, let us prepare the star of faith in all our conduct, and let us celebrate Christ’s baptism by guarding purity, because this regeneration of Christ is the confirmation of our faith. He intimated to us the benefit of his gift through the example of his second birth, and what he wished to do, he himself first did.

We read that the Jews had various baptisms under the Law; but none of them could provide a general remedy against the evil of transgression. Therefore, for the absolution of the whole world, they needed the waters of regeneration to be sanctified from heaven.

[Note: Thus the old manuscript vd; the others, with the printed editions, have “water.”]

And because the sacrament of Baptism was necessary for the human race throughout the whole world, he gave a blessing to all waters when, with unique and singular mercy, he descended into the channel of the Jordan. Then the water did not so much wash Christ the Lord as become washed itself.

[Note: In the preceding sermon, section 4.]

Christ therefore came to you by being born; he served you by living; he contended with death for you by dying. When you see that he died for you, understand that he was baptized for you.

### 2. All Waters Blessed in Christ’s Baptism

He was altogether such even before his baptism; and therefore his precursor and baptizer addresses him in this way when he came to him to be baptized: “Lord, I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me!” What could be clearer concerning the purity of Christ before his baptism, or stronger?

“I ought to be baptized by you”—that is, by you who are the fountain of innocence and the fullness of righteousness, who, needing nothing, know how to give and do not know how to receive. “I,” he says, “ought to be baptized by you,” because with you and in you you possess the gifts of purity and the sacraments of baptism; and what I shall give, through your giving it by grace, you possess by nature (ibid. 14).

At his touch, limbs are bathed and the waters are enriched: life-giving grace is not borrowed by the body from the river, but by the river from the body. The blessed water marvels that its own source has descended into it, conceiving eternal remedies in a single moment and giving birth to God through the new fecundity of regeneration; returning what it had received and receiving what it did not have.

Amid all this, it would be astonishing that the Lord subjected himself to the blessing of a servant, if he had not also subjected himself to the cross and to death.

[Note: The contents of this section 2 are absent from the manuscripts.]

### 3. The Gravity of Sin Must Be Measured by Its Remedy; How Carefully Sin Must Be Avoided

He taught that humanity is precious to him by the dignity of its price, so that from this also we may understand how greatly our God esteems the causes of human crimes, on account of which he sent to earth not an angel, not an archangel, but God himself. How serious sin is, and how harsh its condition, the greatness of the remedy reveals.

What a reckoning of evils there will be when the wicked are condemned—the concern with which the righteous are redeemed indicates.

[Note: Here the word “wicked,” and below the word “righteous,” were absent from the printed editions. Both, however, are found in the manuscripts.]

Therefore, with every diligence and vigilance, let us beware lest the devil wound what God has healed; lest, through the consent of our heart or the disgrace of our body, we be found to offer the enemy more readily the servitude we owe the Lord.

Indeed, if some violent and powerful person had seized something from our means and property, would we not regard it as worthy of the greatest hatred? Would we not rightly detest him as an enemy? Why should we consent through sin to the devil, who wishes to take from us not our substance but our life; not to defraud us of earth but of heaven; not of the boundaries of a narrow possession but of the infinite expanses of eternity?

Amid all this, O human being, if you wish to assess the dignity of your creation and the mercy of your Lord toward you by the price paid for you, you cannot doubt the kingdom.

### 4. The Faith of the Trinity and the Incarnation in the Gifts of the Magi; How the Magi Are to Be Imitated

The Magi themselves, who came by the indication of the star to the venerable cradle of the heavenly child, what else did they express in those gifts except our faith? In the fact that three gifts are offered, the Trinity is understood; in the fact that there are three and each offers one gift, unity in the Trinity is declared.

By gold the king is shown; by frankincense, God is recognized; by myrrh, which is suitable for preserving bodies, the burial of the human being destined to be crucified is proclaimed.

Accordingly, beloved, let us also imitate the person of the Magi through spiritual acts of service. Above all, let us seek Christ until we deserve to find him. Let the light of faith provide us with guidance, like the star of heaven. Let it show him to us—not now wailing in a manger, but reigning in the highest citadel of heaven; not to be worshiped in his mother’s lap, but on the Father’s throne; not to be judged any longer in humility, but coming with majesty for judgment.

Let there be, as it were, an offering of three gifts, a perfect confession of the Trinity. Let us believe in unity joined without confusion and in Trinity distinguished without separation: let the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be believed to be one God—three persons, but not three substances.

[Note: These are the words of Eusebius.]

As far as concerns the order of the heavenly nature, one divinity must be confessed in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in such a way that neither a single person is thought to exist in the Trinity nor a threefold substance in the unity. Rather, plurality must be assigned to unity in such a way that equality is not taken away from the Trinity. Although a numerical plurality is introduced into one Godhead, difference must nevertheless not be admitted.

Thus the worship of God must be established in the hearts of the faithful so that neither separation is admitted in unity nor confusion in the Trinity.

### 5. In Christ’s Baptism We Are Baptized; the Waters Are Cleansed; the Effect of Baptism Is Explained

[Note: Here, with the particle *enim* removed, the second sermon begins in the Navarre manuscript.]

Recently, before this day, most beloved brothers, the Lord was born on the sacred day of his Nativity; now he has been baptized. Then he gave us birth for life; now he regenerated us for salvation. Then he received the lost Adam; now he washed the sinner.

He therefore came to baptism, as it is written. But what would one who was pure wash? Certainly, so that the pure one might wash the impure.

The flowing waters then poured themselves over him, but they carried our sins with them. Drops of baptism flowed from him, but our crimes flowed away in the drops.

O mercy and power of God together! We did not yet exist in the world, and already we were being washed in baptism; we were cleansed in him before we were born. For this was the very purpose of baptism: that the waters which were to cleanse us might first be cleansed by him.

“And when he had risen,” Scripture says, “from the water, he saw the heavens opened” (Matthew 3:16). Had heaven then been opened for him whose eyes saw the inner regions of the heavens? But heaven is opened for this reason: so that the mystery of Baptism might be declared in this event, because when a person emerges from Baptism, then the door of the heavenly kingdom is opened to that person.

### 6. The Source of the Magi’s Great Devotion; Their Mystical Gifts; Gifts Pleasing to God

What, indeed, is this: that the Magi come to the God who has been born—or rather, are led to him? They see him placed in a manger, and yet the lowliness of his birth does not diminish the reverence due to his divinity in their senses. They worship with their bodies, honor him with gifts, and venerate him through their services.

They see a human being with their eyes, but confess God through their acts of devotion. For they saw in the one who had been born that there was more than human minds could perceive, or than eyes could see.

The Lord who was then born bodily had brought all things into being through himself. He was seen in a manger, but ruled in heaven; he was within a little body, but contained all things within himself. He had indeed been born from his mother, but he himself had created his mother.

Therefore the Magi humbled themselves before him, because they saw the stars serving him. They recognized that he was God, since the heavenly powers served him.

For this reason their gifts themselves were also full of divine mystery. As you have heard, they offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh (ibid. 2:11). The number of the three gifts therefore contains a threefold meaning: in frankincense they signify the honor of God; in gold, royal dignity; in myrrh, the burial of the body.

Let us therefore also offer, most beloved brothers, sincere and holy gifts to our God: chastity, faith, patience, love, humble minds, upright conduct, and souls worthy of having God dwell within them.

These are the gifts pleasing to God, these are the acceptable offerings, which are indeed offered to him but benefit those who offer them. For he needs nothing, no thing and no gift; rather, this is the best gift to him: that he have reasons for giving gifts.

He demands nothing more from us and asks nothing more than our salvation. For he regards everything as being done for him by us if we act in such a way that all things may be done for us by him—with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXXVII

[Note: Otherwise, among the Vignerian sermons 3, in the first part of the Supplement.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, VII

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. Several manuscripts bear the name of Augustine. In the Corbie manuscript, written more than 800 years ago, it is found without a name after Jerome’s letter. The Remigian manuscript, however, attributes it to Ambrose, among whose sermons it was also published, with a few changes. In Ambrose it begins in this manner: “This baptism of Jesus Christ,” and so forth, and it is numbered 18.]

### 1. Christ First Became Known in His Baptism

The days of the Epiphany are so called by a Greek name. What we call an apparition or manifestation, the Greeks call *epiphaneia*—“epiphany.” We say this because today our Lord and Savior appeared on earth according to the flesh.

Although he had long ago been born from Mary and had already completed thirty years of age, he was nevertheless unknown to the world. He became known at the time when he came to John the Baptist to be baptized in the Jordan, and the voice of the Father, thundering from heaven, was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

The Holy Spirit wished to reveal by a tangible sign him whom the Father had pointed out from heaven by his voice, appearing as though in a dove and resting upon his head, lest anyone else from among the people should be thought to be the Son of God.

What is more sublime than this humility, or nobler than this lowliness? He is baptized by a servant and called the Son by God. He comes to the washing among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners, yet he is holier than his baptizer. He is baptized by John in the flesh, but he himself washes John in the Spirit.

The waters that had been accustomed to cleanse other things were cleansed when our Lord washed them. The river Jordan, which in the time when Joshua son of Nun led the people of Israel and brought them into the promised land had been dried up, now wished, if it could have done so, to gather all its waters into one place so that it might touch the Lord’s body. “The Jordan turned back” (Psalm 113:3).

### 2. A Brief Exposition of Psalm 28; the Fruitfulness of the Church, Formerly Desolate

See, brothers, how what was read in the Gospel had earlier been foretold in Psalm 28: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters.” For the Son of God said to John, “Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

It continues: “The Lord of majesty thundered,” when the Father bore witness to the Son, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:15, 17).

“The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars.” For Christ was baptized, and the demons, previously erect and exalted, fell. The Lord cut them down like the cedars of Lebanon and shattered them like calves, scattering the fragments of the trees and dispersing the stumps in every direction with his feet.

By contrast, what is said about the Savior? “And the beloved one like a son of unicorns.” The beloved Lord and Savior is the Son of God: the son of unicorns, the son of the cross, of whom it is said in the song of Habakkuk, “Horns are in his hands; there he hid his strength” (Habakkuk 3:4).

[Note: In Ambrose: “and is the son of unicorns.”]

After this beloved one was crucified, what follows in the Psalm was fulfilled: “The voice of the Lord dividing the flame of fire.” For when he had been baptized, and the whole world had been cleansed by Christ’s washing, the fire of Gehenna was extinguished.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness.” The Church was a wilderness, for previously she had no children. At Christ’s preaching this wilderness was shaken; she went into labor, gave birth, and an entire people was born in a single day.

At the same time, she who was formerly called the wilderness of Kadesh—that is, the wilderness of holiness, since she had not possessed holiness—began to give birth to stags and send forth the herds of her saints, who kill serpents and disdain poisons. As they run throughout the world and preach Christ’s Gospel, “in his temple all shall say glory to God.”

It continues: “The Lord makes the flood dwell.” Let us consider the whole world; let us look upon the barbarian nations; let us also survey in our minds the Roman Empire. Everywhere they believe in Christ; everywhere they are baptized into our Lord. Thus it comes about that there is not one water only, but, in a certain sense, a flood of baptisms.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, since the Tabernacle has been completed—for this is indicated beforehand in the title of this Psalm—and since the Church has been built with living stones, let us bring to the Lord the sons of God; let us bring him the sons of rams, the Apostles and the saints.

Let us imitate our Savior, who is himself called both shepherd and lamb; who is sacrificed for us in Egypt; who is held in place of Isaac among the thorns. And let us say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture he has settled me; beside the water of refreshment he has led me” (Psalm 22:1–2). To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXXXVIII

[Note: Otherwise, On Various Matters 65.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, VIII

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The opinion of Verlinus and Vindingus, by which it is withdrawn from Augustine, is one to which we willingly subscribe.]

### 1. Human Beings Made Like the Angels

Today, most beloved, let every mouth be opened, and let every word praise the Word of God who has shone forth from heaven. Let every soul rejoice, let every tongue sing together, and let the whole earth of the Lord sing psalms.

Today, on the day of light, the Son of light irradiates the grace of light. Let earthly things agree with heavenly things; let all that is seen in the world sing a hymn with the highest Powers.

Today the truth has shone forth together with the heavenly King. For Christ’s presence is the arrival of the true light and the complete freedom of the whole world.

Therefore observe, beloved, the Church’s discipline worthy of God; observe the unquenchable flame of heavenly desire; observe how this nature of the body is made equal to the ministries of the angels.

Human beings are from the earth and dwell on the earth, and the earth also nourishes them, yet they rival the heavenly Powers. For through the love of Christ they deny the claims of bodily nature and undertake the ministry of angels.

What else do the angels do in heaven except obey the divine commands? And what are the works of the saints on earth except to live an angelic life on earth and proclaim God with worthy praises? Since their office is the same, there is no doubt that their dignity too can be the same.

### 2. John, the Lamp

Today, therefore, most beloved, our Lord Jesus Christ descended into the waters of the Jordan—not to be sanctified himself, but himself to provide sanctification to the waters that would bring life.

John was therefore fulfilling the office of a priest. The Redeemer of the world came to him to be baptized in water, while he illuminated the baptizer in the Spirit. The King therefore came to his precursor, God to the prophet.

John, then, most beloved, was not ignorant of the mystery of the dispensation by which the Lord was preparing a remedy for the human race. Nor did the appearance of his body deceive him, nor did the flesh that was visible mislead him.

For this reason he was called by the prophet a lamp for my Christ, because he was the first to recognize by the light of his heart the Son of God, who lay hidden beneath the obscurity of the flesh, and he pointed him out with his finger to those who did not know him.

This, then, is that wondrous lamp of which it is said: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 131:17). The Father prepared him for the Son—not because the Word of God, who was the true light and the Sun of righteousness, needed the light of a lamp, but because, as we said above, he was the first to recognize the Redeemer of the human race.

### 3. When John Baptized the Lord, the Mystery of the Trinity Was Manifested

Observe, beloved, the miracle of the Lord’s majesty. When the Lord who came to us determined to come in the flesh, he deigned, out of love for humanity, to become human. And there was a new miracle: God among human beings, the Lord among servants, the Creator among creatures, the sanctifier among those being sanctified.

Then John baptized the Lord Jesus and Redeemer of all, a human being who had himself been redeemed—not moved by self-confidence, but subjected to the command.

Then twin prophetic voices resounded: “The voice of the Lord in the wilderness,” and “the voice of the Lord over the waters” (Psalm 28:3, 8). The herald of truth cried out, and the God of glory thundered. There was present, united in one, the whole glory of the Trinity to be worshiped.

The Father proclaimed the Son from above; the Son on earth fulfilled the order of the most sacred dispensation; and the Holy Spirit bound together the indissoluble mystery of the Trinity.

This, therefore, most beloved, is the Trinity of unity, which is the unity of the Trinity. May it protect us through countless solemnities and guard us here and forever, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

# SERMON CXXXIX

[Note: It exists among the Ambrosian sermons as number 12, but must altogether be counted among the Caesarian sermons. Caesarius, Homily 16, and number 9 among those published by Baluzius.]

## On the Epiphany of the Lord, IX

### 1. On the Word “Epiphany”

This day and feast which you celebrate today, brothers, is called Epiphany—that is, appearance or manifestation—because on it Christ was manifested to the Gentiles under the guidance of the star (Matthew 2), and today is said to have been baptized by John (ibid. 3:16), and is related to have changed water into wine by divine power (John 2).

Would that just as Christ our Redeemer was shown today to the Gentiles through a new star, so he might always make himself manifest to your hearts through heavenly desire; and that he who today wished to be baptized by his servant might grant you the ability, through the virtue of humility, to keep what you promised in Baptism; and that he who today changed water into wine might transform whatever is tasteless in you into spiritual understanding.

### 2. How We Should Imitate the Magi

Raise your souls to God, brothers, and examine your hearts and thoughts, so that you may give thanks to God for your good deeds and cast your evils far from you.

Imitate these Magi, so that you may always come to church with the same zeal and ardor with which they came from distant regions in their desire to worship Christ.

They offered precious gifts; you too should offer your souls to him, if you love faith, hope, charity, penitence, humility, and chastity. Offer him rational gifts—that is, yourselves—for God loves you yourselves more than your possessions.

There are many who give alms and nevertheless do not cease sinning. Such people offer what is theirs to God, as it were, but themselves to the devil. God has no share with the devil (2 Corinthians 6:15). Therefore, whether theft, lust, hatred, pride, or whatever evil there may be, drive it away from you with God’s help, so that your Creator may possess you wholly.

Observe that Herod sought Christ, but did not find him because he sought him wrongly. You too seek Christ wrongly if you perform good works for human praise. Beware lest by seeking him in this way you neither find him nor lose yourselves.

When the Magi entered Herod’s presence, they lost the star. And if you approach the devil by sinning, you will not have spiritual light, unless perhaps you withdraw from him again through confession and penitence.

I warn you not to enter Herod’s presence, because it is better to avoid sin than to correct it. For if, at the devil’s persuasion, you sin, but then, with God’s help, withdraw from him through penitence, you will recover the grace you lost. Thus, after the Magi had departed from Herod, they were worthy to see again the star they had lost.

### The Gifts of the Magi

The Magi are said to have been three kings, and they offered three gifts—that is, gold, frankincense, and myrrh—because they recognized that the true God, the King, and the true human being had appeared in mortal flesh.

And you, brothers, offer him the gold of heavenly wisdom, the frankincense of pure prayer, and the myrrh of perfect mortification.

And just as they returned to their own country by another road (Matthew 2:12), so you, who departed from paradise through pride, disobedience, and eating the forbidden food, should take care to return there through humility, obedience, and abstinence.

This present life is a pilgrimage; your homeland is paradise. And because those who love exile instead of their homeland are exceedingly foolish, despise this miserable and uncertain life so that you may be able to reach the most certain happiness of your heavenly homeland.
