For this purpose the Son of God came from heaven to earth: so that, by following his example, you might be able to ascend from earth to heaven. May he grant this to you, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end forever and ever.

# SERMON CXL

[Note: Otherwise, On the Season 55.]

## In Lent, I

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors and was declared false by Verlinus and Vindingus. It has the greatest similarity and kinship with the sermon immediately following and with other Caesarian sermons. For section 1, see Appendix Sermon 11, section 6, and also Caesarius, Homily 37 among those published by Baluzius; for section 2, Appendix Sermon 10, section 5, and Sermon 69, section 5; for section 4, Appendix Sermon 10, sections 5, and 28, section 4; for section 5, Caesarius, Homily 21, at the end.]

[Column 2019]

### 1. Lent Beneficial to Body and Soul; To Whom It Is Harmful

Behold, most beloved brothers, by God’s favor the season of Lent has arrived. Therefore I ask you, beloved, to celebrate these days with God’s help in a holy and spiritual manner, so that they may be healthful for our bodies and medicinal for our souls; so that the observance of holy Lent may produce not judgment for us but progress.

For if we act negligently, if we entangle ourselves in excessive occupations, if we do not wish to preserve chastity, if we do not devote ourselves to fasts, vigils, and prayers, if we either do not read the divine Scriptures ourselves or do not willingly listen to others reading them, the medicines themselves become wounds for us; and we shall have judgment from the very things by which we could have obtained a remedy.

### 2. Devout Exercises of Lent

Therefore I ask you, most beloved brothers: rise earlier for the Vigils; above all, gather for Terce, Sext, and None. Let no one withdraw from this holy work, except someone whom illness, public duty, or perhaps some definite and serious necessity has kept occupied.

Nor should it be enough for you that you hear the divine readings in church. In your homes also, either read them yourselves or seek out others who are reading and listen willingly.

Remember, brothers, the saying of our Lord, in which he says: “If a person gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul, what exchange will he give for his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). Above all, retain in memory and continually fear what is written: “The obstacles of the world have made them miserable.”

Therefore occupy yourself in your house in such a way that you do not neglect your soul. Finally, if you cannot do more, at least labor for your soul as much as you observe yourself laboring for your flesh.

### 3. Good Works Are Followed by Sweetness, Evil Works by Bitterness

Therefore, most beloved brothers, do not love the world or the things that are in it, because the world and its desire are passing away (1 John 2:15, 17).

What, indeed, remains in a person except what each one has stored in the treasury of conscience for the salvation of the soul, whether by reading, praying, or doing good works?

Unhappy pleasure, and still more unhappy greed and lust, prepare eternal bitterness through transitory sweetness. Abstinence, vigils, prayers, and fasting, however, through very brief hardships lead to the delights of paradise, because the Truth does not lie when it says in the Gospel: “The way that leads to life is narrow and constricted, and few are those who find it” (Matthew 7:13–14).

There is no long-lasting joy on the broad road, nor is there prolonged labor on the narrow and difficult one. For those on the narrow way receive eternal life after brief sadness, while those on the broad way suffer punishment without end after brief joy.

### 4. During Lent, Food for the Soul Must Be Provided for the Whole Year; Losses Must Be Repaired

Therefore, most beloved brothers, during these forty days we ought, as it were, by fasting, reading, and praying, to provide food for our souls for the whole year.

For although throughout the entire year, by God’s favor, you frequently and faithfully hear the divine readings, nevertheless during these days we must take refuge, as from the sea and waves of this world to the harbor of Lent, and rest there; we must receive the divine readings in the receptacle of our hearts with silence and peace.

Thus, by God’s favor, being free for the sake of the love of eternal life, we should strive during these days with every concern to repair and restore whatever in the little boat of our soul has been broken, loosened, corrupted, or lost throughout the year amid many storms—that is, amid the waves of sins.

And because, while we are still in this little body, we must endure the storms and whirlwinds of this age, whenever the enemy wishes either to turn us aside through the harshest storms or to deceive us through the softest pleasures, let him always find us prepared against him, with God’s help.

### 5. Worldly Occupations Must at Least Be Moderated; Either We Laugh at the World or It Laughs at Us

Therefore I ask again that during these days of holy Lent, if you cannot cut off the occupations of this world, you strive at least to moderate them to some extent, so that, cutting away the loss and pursuing the most glorious fruit, you may flee this age and withdraw some hours from earthly business in which you can devote yourselves to God.

For this world either laughs at us or is laughed at by us. Either we submit and are despised, or we despise it so that we may obtain eternal rewards. Thus you either despise and scorn the world, or you submit and are oppressed or trampled down by the world.

But it is better for you to trample upon the world and, once it has been trampled, make for yourself a step by which you may climb upward.

These things, most beloved brothers, which we suggest for the common salvation, presuming upon your obedience—if, according to your custom, you both listen willingly and strive faithfully to fulfill them—will enable you to celebrate Easter with joy and to come happily to eternal life.

May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CXLI

[Note: Otherwise, On the Season 56.]

## In Lent, II

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The judgment of the Louvain editors regarding it is the same as that concerning the preceding sermon, as is the judgment of Verlinus and Vindingus. It is found as number 25 among the Ambrosian sermons. Nevertheless, both the authority of the two Corbie manuscripts, which attribute it to Caesarius, and especially the agreement of its style recommend attributing it to Caesarius.]

## 1. The Days of Lent Signify the Present Life; the Days of Easter, the Life to Come

Our Lord and Savior, dearly beloved brothers, exhorts and admonishes us through the prophet concerning how we ought to come to him after many negligences, saying: “Come, let us adore and fall down before God, and let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94:6); and again: “Turn back to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2:12).

For the days of holy Lent, dearly beloved brothers, if we attend carefully, signify the life of the present age, just as the days of Easter prefigure eternal blessedness. And just as in Lent we experience something like sadness so that in Easter we may rejoice in due order, so also in this present age, for as long as we live, we ought to practice repentance, so that in the future we may receive forgiveness of sins and attain eternal joy.

But each person ought to sigh over his sins, shed tears, and give alms in such a way that, with God’s help, for as long as he lives he always strives to flee those very sins. For just as no one ever was or could be without minor sins, so, by God’s gift and help, we can—and ought to—be entirely without capital sins.

[Note: [Col. 2020] In the manuscripts and in Ambrose, *possumus* (“we can”) is absent.]

## 2. Lent: The Season of Spiritual Harvest and Vintage. What Food Is to the Body, the Word of God Is to the Soul. Canava

And so, if we wish to obtain this, let us meditate day and night on the law of the Lord during the days of holy Lent, if at another time the world’s distractions keep us bound and occupied, as it is written (Psalm 1:2). Let us so fill our hearts with the sweetness of the divine law that we leave within ourselves no vacant place for vices to seize, but fill every place with virtues.

For just as during the season of harvest or vintage produce is gathered by which our flesh may be sustained, so during the days of Lent, as though in a [Col. 2021] spiritual season of vintage or harvest, let us gather what may enable our soul to live eternally. For just as any negligent person who gathers nothing during the season of vintage or harvest will be tormented by hunger throughout the entire year, so whoever neglects to provide and gather spiritual wheat and heavenly new wine in the storehouses of his soul during this season—through fasting, reading, and prayer—will suffer everlasting thirst and cruel deprivation.

Know with complete certainty, dearly beloved brothers, that what the flesh is like when it receives food only after many days, such is the soul that is not continually nourished by the word of God. And just as through hunger and want the flesh becomes thin and dry, like some sort of image, so also the soul, if it is not nourished by the food of God’s word, is found to be arid, useless, and unfit for any good work.

Consider, brothers: if we fill our granary, *canava*, and storeroom every year, so that our flesh may have food for one year, how much ought we to store up so that our soul may be sustained forever?

[Note: [Col. 2021] Here we have restored from the manuscripts the word *canava*, that is, a provision-room or wine-cellar, in French *cave*. Caesarius himself uses the word in the sermon that was formerly numbered 61 among Augustine’s sermons on Time and is now Appendix 273; he also uses it in chapter 30 of his Rule for Virgins, where he says, “Those who are placed over the storeroom, whether the *canava* or the clothing,” and so forth. See Saint Aurelian’s Rule for Monks, chapter 21, and Isidore in the *Glossary*. Victor, in book 2 of *On the Vandal Persecution*, uses it for a workhouse or cage.]

## 3. Occupations Should Be Changed. Board Games

Therefore, brothers, at least during these few days let the world’s distractions withdraw—those distractions which, according to Scripture, make many negligent people wretched. Let carnal joy withdraw; let the world’s blandishments, full of poisons, withdraw. Let bodily pleasures be diminished so that spiritual gains may be prepared for the soul, because of what is written: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25); and again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

The time which the furious game of *tabula* used to take away from us should now be occupied by sacred reading.

[Note: [Col. 2021] Canon 79 of the Council of Elvira and canon 50 of the Sixth Council of Constantinople concern those who play at dice or *tabula*. At one time the game of *tabula* was also prohibited by civil laws; see Justinian’s *Novels* 123, Julian the Antecessor, *Constitutions* 115, chapters 4 and 9. Gregory of Tours nevertheless relates in his *History*, book 10, section 16, that an abbess who presided over the monastery of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, accused of having played at *tabula*, replied that it was prohibited neither in the Rule through Scripture nor in the canons. Those who play at *tabula* are reproved again below in sermon 146, section 4, and in Caesarius’s third homily published by Baluze; especially in the treatise circulated among Cyprian’s works, *On Gamblers*.]

Let conversations about the holy Scriptures replace idle stories, biting jokes, and poisonous slanders. Let the hours during which we used to remain detained to the detriment of our souls be devoted to visiting the sick, seeking out those confined in prison, receiving strangers, and restoring those who are at odds to peace. If we do this, brothers, we can prepare medicines for ourselves from the very place where we had inflicted wounds upon ourselves.

## 4. Lunches Should Be Given to the Poor. Supper Foods Should Be Neither Delicate nor Excessive. The Flesh Should Be Treated as a Servant, the Soul as Mistress

Above all, during the days of fasting let us give to the poor what we used to consume at lunch, lest someone strive to prepare for himself expensive suppers and meals with elaborate flavors, and seem to have exchanged the abundance of food rather than diminished it.

It does no good to have prolonged a fast throughout the entire day if afterward the soul is overwhelmed by the pleasantness or excess of food. At once the filled mind grows sluggish, and the soil of our body, watered in this way, will produce the thorns of lust.

Let food therefore be moderate, and let the stomach never be filled to excess. Let us always think more about food for the heart than food for the body, because inwardly, in the inner person, we have been made in the image of God, whereas in the flesh we were formed from the mud of the earth.

And consider, brothers, whether it is just that our flesh, made from the earth, should sometimes receive food twice a day, while the soul in which [Col. 2022] the image of God resides scarcely receives God’s word after many days, although it is more beneficial for us to honor God’s image within us than our own flesh.

Those who think only about the flesh are like beasts and cattle; and those who act in this way have already crushed the image of God within themselves. Let the flesh therefore be governed like a servant, and let the soul, as its lawful mistress, be refreshed.

For if it is done otherwise—if we do not recognize that we were made in the image of God, and think more about the flesh than about the soul—I fear that the Holy Spirit may rebuke us through the prophet, saying: “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13).

## 5. Sacred Readings in Church, at Home, and During Meals

Listen willingly to the sacred readings in church, as you are accustomed to do, and read them again in your homes. If someone is so occupied that he cannot devote himself to divine Scripture before eating, let him not hesitate to read something from the divine Scriptures during his small meal, so that, just as the flesh is nourished by food, the soul may be refreshed by God’s word, and the whole person—that is, both the outer and inner person—may rise satisfied from a holy and health-giving banquet.

For if only the flesh is refreshed and the soul is not nourished by God’s word, the servant is satisfied while the mistress is tormented by hunger; and Your Holiness cannot be unaware of how unjust this is.

Therefore, as I have already said, you ought both to read and to hear the sacred readings with such desire that you may also be able to speak about them in your homes and wherever you may be, and to teach others. Like clean animals, ruminating God’s word through constant reflection, you should be able, with God’s help, to take for yourselves and offer to others its useful nourishment—that is, its spiritual meaning—so that what is written may be fulfilled in you: “And your cup that makes drunk, how excellent it is!” (Psalm 22:5).

Thus you will fulfill what the blessed Apostle exhorts and admonishes, saying: “Whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do all things for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

If illness does not prevent you, fast daily. Rise for the Vigils with eager and fervent devotion, because it is written: “In the night my spirit keeps watch for you, O God” (Psalm 62:2); and again: “To you, Lord, I will pray in the morning, and you will hear my voice” (Psalm 5:4); and again: “At midnight I rose to confess your name, O Lord” (Psalm 118:62).

Our Lord and Savior also exhorts and admonishes us concerning this in the Gospel, saying: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). May he himself deign to grant this, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

# SERMON 142

[Note: [Col. 2022] Formerly *On Time* 62.]

## In Lent, III

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars counted it among the doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus among the spurious. It is also sermon 26 among Ambrose’s spurious sermons. But it is more truly represented among Caesarius’s sermons in the *Library of the Fathers* and in the Lérins Library; nearly every word unmistakably proclaims Caesarius, so that the more recent manuscripts that attribute it to Faustinus scarcely deserve credence. For section 3, see Caesarius, homily 22, and Appendix sermon 78, section 5; for section 5, Appendix sermon 142; for section 6, Caesarius, homily 24, and the preceding sermon, section 4; for section 7, Caesarius at the end of homily 35; for section 8, Caesarius, homily 1.]

## 1. Whoever Cannot Fast Should Give More Generous Alms

I ask and admonish you, dearly beloved brothers, that during this lawful and most sacred season of Lent, except on Sundays, no one presume to eat lunch, unless perhaps he is one whom illness does not permit to fast. For on other days fasting is either a remedy or a reward; in Lent, not fasting is a sin. At another time, whoever fasts will receive forgiveness; in Lent, whoever can fast but does not will experience punishment.

Even the person who cannot manage to fast should prepare privately for himself alone—or, if there is another sick person, together with that person in his own home—[Col. 2023] what he is to eat. He should not invite healthy people who are able to fast to lunch. For if he does this, not only God but also human beings may understand that he cannot fast not because of illness, but because he is unwilling to fast on account of gluttony.

Let it be enough for him that he cannot fast; and let him eat with groaning, sighing, and sorrow of heart because, while others are fasting, he cannot abstain. What need is there for a sick person to invite a healthy person to lunch and thereby increase the other’s sin through gluttony?

Instead, because he cannot fast, he ought to give more to the poor, so that the sins he cannot cure through fasting he may redeem by giving alms.

## 2. Almsgiving Is Better Than Fasting

It is good to fast, brothers, but it is better to give alms. If someone can do both, there are two good things; but if he cannot, it is better to give alms.

If the ability to fast is absent, almsgiving is sufficient by itself without fasting; fasting without almsgiving is entirely insufficient. Therefore, if someone cannot fast, almsgiving without fasting is good; but if he is able, fasting together with almsgiving is a double good.

Fasting without almsgiving, however, is no good—unless perhaps someone is so poor that he has absolutely nothing to give. For the person who has nothing from which to give, good will is sufficient, according to what is written: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

## 3. No One Is Easily Excused from Almsgiving

But who could excuse himself when the Lord has promised that he will repay even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42)? And why did he say “cold”? Perhaps so that some poor person might not excuse himself on account of a shortage of firewood, or say that he did not have a vessel in which to heat the water.

[Note: [Col. 2023] Here the manuscripts, omitting the intervening material, add: “For he has fulfilled everything who did what he could,” and so forth. These words occur near the end of the sermon.]

Finally, through the blessed prophet, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord so exhorts and admonishes us to give alms that scarcely any poor person can excuse himself. For he says: “This is the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord: Break your bread for the hungry.” He did not say that he should give the whole loaf, since perhaps the poor man had no other; rather, he says, “Break it”—that is: Even if you are so poor that you have only one loaf, break from that very loaf and give it to the poor.

“And bring,” he says, “the needy and homeless into your house” (Isaiah 58:6–7). If someone is so poor that he has nothing from which to give food to the poor, let him at least prepare a bed for a stranger in one corner of his house.

What will we say to this, brothers, or what excuse will we be able to offer, since we have broad and spacious houses and scarcely ever deign to receive a stranger? We do not know—or rather, we do not believe—that Christ is received in every stranger, as he himself says: “I was a guest, and you welcomed me”; and: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:35, 40).

## 4. Christ Must Be Received in the Poor, So That He May Himself Receive Us into Our Homeland

It is burdensome and unpleasant for us to receive Christ in the poor in our homeland. I fear that he may repay us in heaven by not receiving us into his blessedness. We despise him in this world; I fear that he may despise us again in heaven, according to what he himself said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food”; “I was a guest, and you did not welcome me”; and: “As long as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me.”

And what follows after this, brothers? May God avert it from us. For afterward he added: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:42–46).

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us not hear these things superficially or only with the ears of the body. Rather, having heard them faithfully, let us teach them by word and example, so that others too may retain and fulfill them.

[Note: [Col. 2023] In the printed editions this sermon ended with the clause, “our Lord [Col. 2024] granting it,” and so forth. The second part of the sermon, which is presented by several manuscripts, had already been published separately by Marus Vignerius in the *Supplement*.]

[Col. 2024] ## 5. Those Who Hoard Wealth Are Rebuked

What, then, did the Lord say afterward through the prophet? “If you see someone naked,” he says, “cover him.” I judge no one in this statement; let each person attend to his own conscience.

Yet I accuse and reproach myself, because it may perhaps have happened several times through negligence that my little garments, which ought to have gone to the poor, were devoured by moths. I fear that these very clothes may be brought forward as testimony against me on the day of judgment, in accordance with what the apostle James terrifyingly rebukes when he says: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will consume your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasures on earth, and you have nourished your hearts in luxury on the day of slaughter” (James 5:1–5).

Although all these things, as I have said, dearly beloved brothers, which Christ threatened through the Apostle terrify us greatly, we must not despair of God’s mercy. Still I and others like me, negligent people, can, with God’s help, amend ourselves if we wish—if we give more generously the alms that we have given too sparingly until now, and if, for our past sins, with sorrow and groaning and with hope of restoration, we beseech God’s mercy.

## 6. Fasting Must Not Be Without Almsgiving. Lunches Should Be Given to the Poor

Therefore, as I suggested above, dearly beloved brothers, let the richness of almsgiving commend our fasts. For fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil.

Just as a lamp lit without oil may produce smoke but cannot give light, so fasting without almsgiving does indeed afflict the flesh, but does not illuminate the soul with the light of charity.

[Note: [Col. 2024] This is how the manuscripts read. In Caesarius and Ambrose, however, the reading is *claritatis* (“of brightness” or “of light”).]

Meanwhile, brothers, in what is being done at present, let us fast in such a way that our lunches are given to the poor; let us place what we would have eaten not in our purses but in the bowels of the poor. For the hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury: what it receives, he stores in heaven so that it does not perish on earth. Although the food that the poor person receives is consumed, the reward of the good deed is stored up in heaven.

For if we take pains to spend our lunches at supper on elaborate flavors and multiplied courses, and if delicacies are not taken away from our bodies but even doubled, then just as nothing is diminished from the body, nothing is increased for the soul.

## 7. Chastity Must Be Maintained Throughout Lent

I admonish you concerning this, brothers, fearing it more than believing anything sinister about you. For I know that, by God’s favor, many of you continually receive strangers and frequently give alms to the poor.

Therefore, may what I suggest serve this purpose: let the person who was already doing these things do them more abundantly; and let the person who was not doing them—or perhaps was doing them too slowly—make such a holy and God-pleasing practice habitual.

Although I believe that, with God inspiring you, whenever the feasts approach Your Charity preserves chastity for many days beforehand, even with your own wives, nevertheless—even if this is superfluous—I remind you, out of charity, of what I believe you already do. With God’s help, preserve chastity throughout Lent and until the end of Easter, so that at that most holy Easter solemnity, clothed in the light of charity, radiant with almsgiving, and adorned with prayers, vigils, and fasts as with heavenly and spiritual pearls, you may approach the Lord’s altar in peace not only with friends but also with enemies, with a free and secure conscience, and receive his body and blood not for judgment but for healing.

[Col. 2025] ## 8. The Poor Fulfill the Commandment of Almsgiving Through Good Will

But when we speak about almsgiving, let narrow poverty not be disturbed. For the person who did what he could has fulfilled everything, because a perfect willingness to do the deed will be reckoned in place of the deed itself.

Yet the person who wishes to fulfill this must regard every poor person as though he were himself, so that he gives to the poor what he would wish to be done for himself if he were in such need.

Whoever does this will fulfill the commandments of both the New and the Old Testament, fulfilling the Gospel command: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 7:12).

May the merciful Lord lead you to this law of true and perfect charity under his protection—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 143

[Note: [Col. 2025] Formerly *On Time* 64.]

## In Lent, IV

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars allow that it may be doubtful, but Verlinus and Vindingus rightly wish it to be rejected.]

## 1. Lent Celebrated by the Examples of the Saints: Moses, Elijah, and Christ Himself

We ought to regard the whole period of our life as a kind of contest of virtues and strive with all our strength for the heavenly prize. But this must especially be fulfilled during the days of Lent. Dedicated to abstinence and fasting, these days contribute as much to the virtue of the spirit as they remove from bodily pleasure.

This number of fasting days is lawful, and it is celebrated by the examples of these saints. Moses, about to receive the Law from God, spent forty days and nights without food or drink, and prepared himself fasting to receive the Lord’s will (Exodus 34:28). After forty days of fasting, Elijah was transferred from this world to the heights of heaven in a fiery chariot (1 Kings 19:8). Our Lord and Savior himself, fasting for forty days, triumphed over the devil’s temptations so that he might approach the preaching of the Gospel already victorious (Matthew 4:2).

Therefore, we too ought rightly to observe this number of days in fasting, since we read that it was consecrated by such examples.

## 2. Virtue Is Easier Then

Let us therefore celebrate these days with complete eagerness of mind and joy, and prefer them to all banquets and all bodily delicacies. For during these days especially the spirit is inflamed to fulfill the Lord’s will, when the pleasure of the flesh is most extinguished through abstinence.

Then the whole mind, made purer, hastens toward the Lord and his future promises, when it is not made gross by any gluttony or satiety of food and drink. Hence the Savior said in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and worldly cares; and that day come upon you suddenly, for it will come like a snare upon the whole world, and no one will escape” (Luke 21:34–35).

There is also this great benefit during the days of Lent: while we abstain even from what is lawful, we are increasingly admonished to avoid what is unlawful. If we abstain from meats that are permitted to us on other days, then, since we avoid what is sometimes lawful, let us above all flee sins, which are never lawful at all.

## 3. The Principal Fast Is from Vices

Therefore, if we wish to fast properly from foods, let us first of all fast from vices as well. What good does it do to empty the body of food and fill the soul with sins? What good does it do to be pale from fasting if you are livid with hatred and envy? What good does it do not to drink wine while becoming drunk on the poison of anger? What good does it do to abstain from meats created for eating while tearing the members of your brothers apart with malicious slanders?

What good does it do if we abstain from what is sometimes lawful but do what is never lawful? For God honors and loves those who flee what is unlawful.

Thus, as I have said, let us fast from foods so that we may fast much more from vices, and be filled with the abundance of holy works, so that in the future we may deserve to be satisfied [Col. 2026] by the reward of those works, just as we read in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

## 4. Through Frugality, the Poor Should Be Refreshed

We ought rather to choose this exchange: let us give to the poor and weak the foods from which we abstain, according to what is written: “Blessed are those who are content to hunger so that others may be refreshed.”

A gift is very pleasing to God when the needy person is fed, when the naked person is clothed, when anger is not carried through to its conclusion and no opportunity for wrath is reserved, and when evil is not repaid with evil.

Our fasts are pleasing to God when those who fast out of necessity are refreshed by us. Then we shall deserve to hear the Lord’s declaration: “Amen, I say to you, as long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40).

O most merciful Lord, who, to tame human greed, says that what is given to the least poor person is given to him!

And for you, brothers, may the Lord’s mercy grant that you serve him through fasts and almsgiving in good works, so that he may lead you to eternal and true life—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 144

[Note: [Col. 2026] Formerly *On Time* 65.]

## In Lent, V

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars leave it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus assert that it is spurious. In the Remigian manuscript it is attributed to Jerome, and in nearly all the other manuscripts to Augustine, but the attribution is false, as the style demonstrates. Most manuscripts begin the sermon with the words, “Moses, for forty days and nights,” and so forth. Otherwise they vary somewhat in places, especially at the end, where they omit the words, “But in order that our fasts may be complete,” and so forth, and conclude the sermon as follows: “At least for a few days we ought to live for the Lord.” Moreover, what is read here in section 1 about Adam is said in nearly the same words below in sermon 147, section 2.]

## 1. The Benefit of Fasting Demonstrated by the Examples of Moses and Adam

The venerable and healing season of Lent is here for us, dearly beloved, during which we ought, by fasting, to heal the wounds of our sins. Let us therefore discuss briefly, adding examples, how great a good fasting is and how much grace it confers upon a human being.

Moses was the first: after fasting for forty days and nights, he deserved to receive the Law of the Lord, by which he would govern the peoples. The fasting of one man obtained what the satiety of an entire people had despaired of obtaining.

Let us observe, therefore, how great is the difference between fasting and satiety, between an empty stomach and lungs heated by banquets. Moses, because he fasted, saw the Lord (Exodus 24:18); the people, because they ate and drank, made idols.

But why should I speak of Moses and the Israelite multitude? Adam, that prince of the human race, remained in paradise for as long as he fasted while keeping the commandment; but when he ate, he was expelled from paradise (Genesis 3). And he who had been a virgin in God’s paradise, once expelled from paradise, came to know a wife.

For wantonness is always joined to satiety. The stomach and the genitals are close to one another, and the order of vices follows the order of the limbs. Food therefore expelled us from paradise; let hunger, let fasting, bring us back.

We have said what holy Moses deserved by fasting; next let us consider everyone else as well.

## 2. Likewise, Elijah

Even the elements served holy Elijah when he was fasting. In the end, he shut up heaven for three years and six months (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17); at his word fire also descended from above (2 Kings 1:10).

When Queen Jezebel wished to kill him, and he, exhausted, lay beneath a leafy tree in the wilderness, an angel was sent to him and said: “Take a little bread and water” (1 Kings 19:5).

See how great God’s clemency is toward those who fast, dearly beloved. It was not enough that the Lord had sent an angel to the fasting man to admonish him to take food; he also commanded him to flee farther from his pursuer.

He therefore said: “Take a little bread and water.” For he was going to continue through the desert for forty days until Mount Sinai.

Could the Lord, who had made heaven and earth and whose is every creature, [Col. 2027] not have sent him a meal in the wilderness through an angel, just as he sent one to Daniel in the lions’ den through Habakkuk (Daniel 14:33)?

But God knew that his prophet could not overcome the devil’s temptation in any other way than by being trained through fasts to repel the assaults of the enemy who lay in wait.

## 3. Likewise, Daniel, John the Baptist, and the Gospel Itself. The Difference Between Fasting and Satiety

Daniel, that knower of future things, conscious of the Lord’s coming, and most explicit preacher of Jerusalem’s overthrow, was therefore called “a man of desires,” because he did not eat the bread of desire or drink the drink of lust, since he desired Christ more than banquets.

John also, the Lord’s forerunner, was nourished in the wilderness by locusts and wild honey, not by the flesh of animals or the delicacies of birds. Certainly, stationed beside the Jordan, he could have provided himself with the pleasures of fish; but because he was going to preach repentance, he ought by his example to teach a doctrine of rigor and fasting more through his conduct than through his voice.

In the Gospel, too, when a man full of a demon was brought before the Lord, one whom the Apostles had been unable to cure, they asked and heard from the Lord that this kind of spirit could be expelled only through prayers and fasts (Matthew 17:20).

See, therefore, dearly beloved, how great is the power of fasts, since fasts can do what the Apostles could not.

I omit the rest; but let each person consider how great is the difference between fasting and satiety, between an empty stomach and one that is filled, between a flushed face and pale features, between a fasting mouth and lips loosened by gluttony, between a mind weighed down by banquets and one kept watchful by the thinness produced by hunger.

## 4. From What One Should Abstain and Why. Fasts Must Not Stand Alone

I do not speak of fasting for weeks, or doubled, or multiplied fasts; but let us at least pass individual days without the luxury of food. Let baths, wine, and meats cease—not because we judge God’s creation to be condemned, but because we have lived for ourselves throughout the whole year; let us at least live for the Lord for a few days.

But in order that our fasts may be complete and enduring, let them be nourished by the richness of mercy; let us give our lunch to the hungry. Do not suppose that fasting alone is sufficient to heal the wounds of sins unless it is restored by the medicine of almsgiving.

Let your fasting therefore chastise you but make another person joyful; and your hardships will be fruitful if they provide another person with relief. Fast in such a way that, when someone else is eating, you rejoice that you have eaten lunch through him.

For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). When the poor person eats from your goods, Christ is dining, for he testifies that he himself hungers in the poor person.

# SERMON 145

[Note: [Col. 2027] Formerly *On Time* 69.]

## In Lent, VI

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain scholars and judged false by Verlinus and Vindingus. In the Remigian manuscript it bears the name of Maximus. It contains several sentences from sermon 31 among Ambrose’s sermons; concerning that Ambrosian sermon, see again below under sermon 147.]

## 1. The Length of Lent Must Not Be Disliked

These days of holy Lent, dearly beloved brothers, ought to be received with every form of reverence, and we must not be annoyed by the greater length of this season. For the more numerous the days of fasting, the greater the cause of healing; the longer the course of abstinence, the more abundant the redemption of salvation; the more severe the treatment of wounds, the more health-giving the medicine of sins.

For God, who is the physician of our souls, established a suitable season—one sufficient for the righteous to pray and adequate for sinners to make petition: for the former to ask for rest, and for the latter to beg forgiveness.

Lent is a suitable season. It is neither too short for entreating nor too long for gaining favor. Through forty days of fasting, any sin of a sinner can be pardoned, and however great the severity of the judge can be appeased.

The season may seem long and wearisome to the person who neither prays over his guilt nor hopes for forgiveness. For despair knows neither how to confess a crime nor how to hope for pardon from the judge.

Holy, therefore, and salutary is the [Col. 2028] course of Lent, by which the judge is led to mercy, the sinner to repentance, and the righteous to rest. During these days, divinity shows mercy more than usual, guilt makes its plea, and righteousness wins favor.

[Note: [Col. 2028] Manuscript n. reads, “and diligence makes its plea.” Manuscript rm. reads, “and the righteous person’s supplication earns rest.”]

For everything lies open: heaven for granting forgiveness, the sinner for confessing, and the tongue for making petition.

## 2. The Mystical Significance of the Number Forty. The Flood as an Act of Mercy

The number forty, I say, is salutary and mystical. For at the beginning, when human iniquity possessed the face of the world, over the course of so many days God poured out rain from heaven and flooded the entire earth (Genesis 7:4).

You see, therefore, that already at that time the mystery was arranged in a figure. For just as then it rained for forty days to cleanse the world, so now he shows mercy for forty days in order to purify the human being.

Indeed, the flood of that time must also be called mercy, since iniquity was overwhelmed and righteousness preserved. It was done as an act of mercy so that the righteous might escape and the wicked might sin no more.

Clearly, we see that flood as an act of mercy, by which, as though through a kind of baptism, the face of the whole world was renewed: so that what had been defiled by the crime of ruined humanity might flourish in grace through the dwelling of blessed Noah; and what had then been a brothel of iniquity might now become a dwelling-place of holiness.

[Note: [Col. 2028] Thus read two manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read *purgatorium* (“place of purification”). Manuscript rm. reads *pyraterium* (“pirate-place” or “place of piracy”).]

### 3. The Flood as a likeness of our Baptism, and likewise of the Lenten fast

The Flood, I say, was a likeness of this Baptism of ours. For what was then accomplished is now being accomplished: namely, that as the springs of water overflow, vices should be endangered, righteousness alone should reign, sins should be submerged in the depths, and holiness, near to heaven, should be carried aloft. For then, as I said, what is now being accomplished in the Church of Christ was being accomplished. Just as Noah’s ark, when all the vices of sinners had been submerged, was carried aloft [Note: [Col. 2028] Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 82, considers that *ad alta ferebatur* should be read. This reading is all the more commendable because immediately afterward the Church is represented as near to heaven. M.]; so through the baptismal font the Church, near to heaven, is carried aloft; and when all the superstitions of idols have been destroyed, faith reigns on earth, proceeding from the ark of the Savior.

The season of Lent, therefore, is holy and consecrated. From its very beginning it began to distinguish between the just and the unjust, and by a kind of judgment to separate the good from the wicked. We plainly see the same thing taking place in our observance of Lent. For during these forty days the wicked are separated from the good: the lustful from the chaste, the intemperate from the fasting person [Note: [Col. 2028] In manuscript *rm.*, *prandens* (“one who lunches”).], the Gentile from the Christian. The wicked, I say, is separated from the good: that is, the sinner from the righteous, the devil from the holy person, the heretic from the faithful. For when all these have been left behind, as in a shipwreck amid the world, the Church alone, like that ark, is raised aloft with her virtues.

### 4. The Church, an ark with three chambers. The voice of Noah preaching the destruction of the world

For we too, although sinners, following the example of holy Noah, announce to you that the destruction of the world is to come; and we say that only those will escape the danger whom the threefold ark has enclosed within the bosom of religion. For the Church is a threefold ark, because it contains the mystery of the Trinity. When Scripture says that it was two-chambered and three-chambered, it surely shows that the ark was distinguished by the threefold grace of the Godhead (Gen. VI, 16, according to the Septuagint).

We therefore announce, like Noah, that the world’s shipwreck is to come, and we admonish all people to flee for refuge to this house. Just as Noah received his sons into the ark, so we too desire to receive our children into this ark. Whoever wishes to dwell with us in this house is our son.

But someone may say that the voice of holy Noah’s preaching is nowhere recorded in Scripture. Listen, then. Although Noah was silent in his voice, he spoke by his work; his tongue was silent, but his construction cried out. For when he was undertaking a new work, unknown to anyone before, he warned everyone that new shelters were being prepared against new dangers. He therefore spoke by his work and uttered that evangelical saying of the Lord: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John X, 38); and by believing, you will be able to escape the danger—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 146

[Note: [Col. 2029] Elsewhere, from the Vignerian collection, 13.]

### On Lent, VI

[Note: [Col. 2029] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In an old Remigian manuscript it is attributed to Ambrose, and among the Ambrosian sermons in later printed editions it is numbered 41, beginning, “We said on the preceding Sunday.” This opening perhaps identifies a sermon among Ambrose’s works, Sermon 29, which begins, “He bears witness.” For these words are read there: “This, however, is his first commandment: that during these forty days we devote ourselves to fasting, prayers, and vigils.” It seems to have the character of Caesarius, who, in the conclusion of the homily published by Baluze, extracted from the third sermon what is said here at greater length and with greater force about hunters. On section 4, see above, Sermon of the Appendix 141, no. 3, and Homily 3 from those published by Baluze; on section 5, see above, Sermon 141, no. 4, and 142, no. 5.]

### 1. Fasting is useless for those who do not turn away from wickedness

Last Sunday we said that the first work of our faith is this: that throughout these forty days we should fast with the utmost devotion, and that our salvation depends upon our devoting ourselves to abstinence during this season. Therefore, dearest brothers, we must examine the character of this fast, so that we may consider how great its usefulness is.

For sometimes fasting is useless and empty. Although it empties the stomach and all the organs of the nourishment of fullness, it is nevertheless not acceptable to God, because it does not empty the mind and innermost feelings of the bond of wickedness. What benefit is there in fasting with the organs while indulging in hunting; abstaining from food while wandering into sins; chastising the body with hunger while exercising the mind in wickedness; not drinking strong wine while proceeding drunk with thoughts of malice?

Except that the case of the full or drunken man is easier than that of one who is both wicked and fasting. The former sometimes ceases to sin because he sometimes falls asleep drunk; but the latter does not cease to go astray, since he is continually practiced in evil and constantly vigilant in fasting. Such fasting is useless and empty: it weakens the limbs through hunger but does not free the soul from destruction. Concerning this fasting the holy prophet speaks in the person of the Lord: “Why do you fast for me? I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord” (Isa. LVIII, 5).

### 2. Those who do not devote themselves to pious exercises but to hunting

Do you think, brothers, that the man fasts who at first light does not keep vigil at church and does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his servants, arranges his nets, brings out the dogs, and searches through thickets and forests? He drags his servants along with him—perhaps servants more eager to come to church—and piles up the sins of others upon his own pleasures, unaware that he will be held guilty both for his own offense and for the destruction of his servants.

Thus he spends the whole day hunting, now raising an immoderate shout, now secretly imposing silence; joyful if he finds something, angry if he loses what he did not have. He conducts himself with such zeal as though fasting had been prescribed for this very reason, so that he might hunt.

In these indulgences, brothers, tell me what worship of God there is, what devotion of mind can exist in the man who fasts for this reason—not to devote himself to God or to prayers, but so that, idle and free all day, he may pursue his own pleasures. Even if you, brother, return home in the evening and eat when the sun is already declining, you may appear to have taken your meal late, but you have not fasted for the Lord. Nor can you be seen to have done the will of the Lord merely by pursuing your own will.

For this is the will of the Lord: that we fast equally from foods and from sins. We prescribe abstinence for the body so that we may be more able to keep the soul from vices. An exhausted body is a kind of bridle for the soul that luxuriates. Whoever fasts and sins appears to have gained the profit of food, not of salvation; by sparing his provisions he has filled his storeroom, not fattened his mind with virtues.

### 3. The wickedness of masters toward their slaves. The slave is a brother, yet is treated as inferior to dogs

Some people, forgetful of the divine commandments, exercise their power of domination over their servants and subjects in such a way that during these days they do not hesitate to beat them with whips, afflict them with punishments, or fetter them with chains. If, when the time comes to eat, a servant happens to arrive late, they immediately tear him with blows and satisfy themselves first with the servant’s blood before enjoying the pleasure of the banquet.

Such is the fasting of these people—as though they fasted for this reason, not to call forth the mercy of the Godhead, but to produce the cries of a groaning household. Whoever wishes to merit God’s mercy must himself be merciful first. For it is written: “With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you” (Luke VI, 38).

And what is more grievous, a Christian master does not spare a Christian servant during these days, paying no attention to the fact that although he is a slave by condition, he is nevertheless a brother by grace. For he too has put on Christ, he too shares in the same sacraments, and he uses the same God as Father that you do. Why should he not use you as a brother?

There are many who, returning from the hunt, take more care of their dogs than of their servants. They arrange for the dogs to lie or sleep beside them, supplying them with their daily food by their own presence, while they do not know whether their servants are dying of hunger. And what is worse, if food has not been carefully prepared for them, the servant is punished on behalf of the dog.

You may even see sleek and fat dogs running about in some people’s houses, while human beings walk about tottering and pale. Will such people ever have pity on the poor, when they have no pity for their own servants?

### 4. Fasting acceptable to God

We must know, therefore, brothers, that fasting is acceptable to God not merely when we discipline our bodies through abstinence, but also when we clothe our souls with humility. Let us be gentle toward servants, gracious toward strangers, merciful toward the needy, and peaceful toward everyone.

At first light let us rise and hasten to church; let us give thanks to God and ask forgiveness for our sins, requesting pardon for past offenses and protection against future ones. Throughout the entire day, let prayer or reading be constant for us. Whoever does not know letters should seek out a holy teacher and feed upon his conversation.

Let no worldly activity hinder the activity of God. Let no game of dice distract the mind; let no pleasure in dogs lead the senses astray; let no profit from business pervert the soul through greed. Whatever else you do apart from God’s commandment, even if you abstain, you are not fasting.

For this is saving fasting: just as the body abstains from banquets, so the soul is restrained from vices.

### 5. Meals should be distributed to the poor. Fasting without almsgiving is a form of business

This too, brothers, must not be left unsaid for the perfection of fasting: those who abstain and do not eat lunch should distribute their meals to the poor during this season. For this is true righteousness: if, while you are hungry, another is filled from your food; if you ask the Lord on account of your sins, and the one who has been fed intercedes for you. Both your hunger and the beggars’ fullness will benefit you.

But whoever abstains in such a way that he gives nothing from his meals to the poor appears to have made his fasting a profit for himself and to have conducted a business by economizing. He abstained for this purpose—not to please God, but so that he would not have to give more away. Therefore almsgiving together with fasting is good.

It is, as it were, a kind of business to live so sparingly that one’s abstinence surpasses that of monks and clergy. The difference is that they do this for the sake of profit, whereas we do it for salvation: they mortify their souls for the sake of financial gain, while we chastise our bodies for the sake of gain for our souls.

## SERMON 147

[Note: [Col. 2031] Formerly, among the sermons *de Tempore*, 77; afterward, in the Appendix, 38.]

### On Lent, VIII

[Note: [Col. 2031] It appears among the Ambrosian sermons as number thirty-nine. It perhaps belongs to the same author as Sermon 145 of this Appendix. For the words in this sermon, “We preached this on the preceding Sunday,” and so forth, likewise seem to indicate Ambrose’s thirty-first sermon, in which one finds: “For the Lord consecrated this Lent for us by his fast. What I said, ‘by his fast’...” Just as here the fasting body is called “a desert,” there it is said: “Every fast is a desert.” On section 2, see above, Sermon 144, no. 1, and Sermon 125, no. 2; on section 4, see the sermon numbered 31 among the Ambrosian sermons.]

[Col. 2031]

### 1. Lent was consecrated by Christ and must necessarily be observed

If your Belovedness remembers correctly, brothers, last Sunday we preached that the Lord himself consecrated holy Lent through abstinence, and that by abstaining altogether from food throughout so many days and nights he made one complete and unified body of fasting [Note: [Col. 2031] In the earlier editions of the Augustinian Sermons, *tempus* (“period” or “time”).]. To fail to observe it entirely is sacrilege; to violate it in part is sin.

He did this for the sake of our salvation, so that he might not only teach a useful thing in words but also instruct us by example, so that we might advance toward abstinence by the same footsteps by which we run toward faith.

But let us see what reason there was for the Savior to prescribe fasts for himself, and why he himself, the first good physician of the human race, fasted. A good physician first tastes the potion he is going to give to a sick person, in order to demonstrate his medical skill in himself beforehand, so that the sick person, having received the test, may be secure about the potion and more secure about his health.

Next, let us consider in what setting he established this time of fasting. The evangelist says that the Lord abstained for forty days and nights in the desert (Matt. IV, 2).

### 2. The reason for that institution. Fullness that squanders chastity. Comparison of the first and second Adam

I therefore judge that the reason for this fast is the following: because the first Adam, placed in paradise, had lost the glory of immortality through intemperance of the appetite (Gen. III, 17), the second Adam, Christ, would restore that same immortality through abstinence.

And because, by tasting from the forbidden tree against the commandment of God, he had fallen into the sin of death, now, by fasting according to the Lord’s commandment, he would merit the righteousness of life.

This is what the Savior accomplishes: that the offenses may be cleansed by the same footsteps through which they were committed. That is, because man had sinned by eating, he should correct himself by abstaining; or because he had known the woman through feasting, he should now reject her through fasting.

For Adam knew Eve only when intemperance provoked him. As long as their untouched restraint remained, so long did unpolluted virginity remain; and as long as they fasted from forbidden banquets, so long also did they fast from shameful sins.

Hunger is the friend of virginity and the enemy of lust; fullness, however, squanders chastity and nourishes enticement. Thus, as I said, the Lord accomplishes this: that human beings may be freed from the very precedents by which they had become subject to sins.

For this reason he wished to be born in every respect in the likeness of Adam, so that in the likeness of Adam he might undo all human sins. Adam was born from virgin earth, and Christ was brought forth from the Virgin Mary. The maternal soil of the former had not yet been split by ploughshares; the maternal secrecy of the latter had never been violated by desire. Adam was fashioned by God’s hands from clay; Christ was formed in the womb by God’s Spirit.

Both, therefore, arise from God the Father; both have a virgin as mother; both, as the evangelist says, are sons of God. But Adam is God’s creature, whereas Christ is his substance (Luke III, 38, and I, 32).

### 3. Why Christ fasted in the desert. How dangerous the presence of a woman is

The Lord therefore acts as the second Adam: what the first man had lost by eating, the other recovers by fasting, and he observes in the desert the law of abstinence given in paradise.

For he knew that God’s commandment was not the law of one place but of the world. It makes no difference to the Godhead whether you keep the commandment at home or in the field, since the one who gave the commandment is everywhere.

Thus in the desert the Savior fulfills God’s commandment, so that he might save wandering Adam there, where Adam had been expelled from possession of paradise. For Adam, expelled from paradise, endured the uncultivated deserts of the world.

In the desert, therefore, salvation is first restored to humankind: where there are no banquets, no luxuries, and—what is the cause of all evils—no woman. Adam could have stood unshaken amid the delights of paradise if Eve had not been there with the devil’s snares [Note: [Col. 2032] In Ambrose, *illecebris* (“enticements”).].

The desert is therefore suited to salvation, where there is no Eve who persuades and no woman who flatters. Consider this remarkable thing: in paradise the devil contends with Adam; in the desert the devil fights with Christ. Everywhere he lies in wait for man; everywhere he engages him. But where he finds a woman, he conquers; where he does not find a woman, he departs defeated.

### 4. The fasting and chaste body as a kind of desert

God therefore gave us a pattern in this event: during the time of fasting, let us live as though in a desert, abstaining from banquets, pleasure, and women [Note: [Col. 2032] The manuscript of Lyon reads, “pleasure of women.”]; and let Eve not be joined to us, lest she overthrow us from our chaste observance through seductive persuasion.

For in a certain sense the person who is fasting and chaste during Lent seems to dwell in a desert. Indeed, the Christian’s body itself is a kind of desert when it is not filled with food or watered with drink, but is neglected in the parched squalor of hunger.

Our body, I say, is a desert when the flesh withers through abstinence, pallor is spread over it by thirst, and through contempt for worldly things the appearance of the whole person grows unkempt and filthy.

Then Christ the Lord dwells in the desert of our breast, when he finds our land made squalid by hunger and dry through thirst, according to what the prophet David says: “As in a desert and pathless and waterless land, so I appeared to you in the holy place” (Ps. LXII, 3).

For we cannot appear to him in the holy place in any other way unless the land of our body has become a desert from worldly pleasures, pathless to diabolical desires, and waterless with respect to lustful enticements.

Then, dwelling in this desert of our body, the Savior overcomes all the devil’s conspiracies there and makes it his secluded and secure dwelling, free from worldly thoughts. Thus, henceforth, established within ourselves as though in solitude, we may look only toward heaven and earth—that is, think of no one but the Lord of the heavenly kingdom and the author of the earthly resurrection.

## SERMON 148

[Note: [Col. 2032] Formerly, among the sermons *de Tempore*, 63; afterward, in the Appendix, 36.]

### On Lent, IX

[Note: [Col. 2032] This is the fifth of Pope Leo’s sermons on Lent, and it is attributed to him in the manuscripts.]

### 1. We must continually devote ourselves to renewal. The undivided cooperation of God and man. Why God gives commandments

The apostolic teaching, dearest brothers, admonishes us that, laying aside the old man with his deeds, we should be renewed day by day through holy conduct (Eph. IV, 22–23).

For if we are God’s temple and the Holy Spirit dwells in our minds, as the Apostle says, “For you are the temple of the living God” (I Cor. III, 16), we must labor with great vigilance so that the dwelling-place of our heart may not be unworthy of so great a guest.

And just as, in buildings made by human hands, one must provide with commendable diligence that if anything has been damaged either by the infiltration of rain, by the violence of storms, or by age itself, care may quickly restore it to wholeness, so we must constantly and anxiously take precautions lest anything disordered or anything unclean be found in our souls.

Although our building cannot stand without the help of its own craftsman, and our structure cannot remain unharmed unless the protection of its creator is present, nevertheless, because we are rational stones and living material, the hand of our maker builds us in such a way that the one being restored works together with his craftsman.

Therefore let human obedience not withdraw from God’s grace, nor fall away from that good without which it cannot itself be good. If it discovers that something in the fulfillment of the commandments is impossible or difficult, let it not remain within itself but turn to the one who helps—the one who gives the commandment for this reason: to arouse desire and provide assistance. As the prophet says: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV, 23).

Or does anyone perhaps presume with such insolent pride to be so unharmed and so spotless that he no longer needs any renewal? This conviction is entirely mistaken, and through excessive vanity grows old: whoever, amid the temptations of this life, believes himself immune from every wound.

### 2. This life is full of dangers. The dangers of the righteous: the tongues of slanderers and scandal arising from the prosperity of the wicked. The stars have no power

Everything is full of dangers; everything is full of snares. Desires incite; enticements lie in wait; profits flatter; losses terrify. The tongues of slanderers are bitter, and the mouths of those who praise are not always truthful.

From one side hatred rages; from the other deceptive courtesy misleads, so that it is easier to avoid a quarrelsome person than to evade a deceiver.

Even in acquiring virtues, the way is so uncertain and discrimination so precarious that, if anyone is able to preserve measures amid the boundaries between good and evil with the finest discernment, it is still difficult for the integrity of a good conscience not to be bitten by the tongue of slanderers, and for the person whose companion is righteousness to escape the reproaches of the wicked.

When human thought turns to the very changes of temporal affairs, what darkness confronts it, and what errors of perverse opinions arise, so that complaints find their material in the collision of opposites!

For although the hearts of all the faithful do not doubt that divine providence is absent from no part or period of this world, and that the outcomes of worldly affairs do not depend upon the power of the stars—which has no power—but that everything is arranged by the most just and merciful decision of the supreme King, since, as it is written, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10), nevertheless, when certain things do not proceed according to our desires, and under the mistaken judgment of human beings the cause of the wicked is often superior to that of the just, it is very easy—even for great spirits—to be shaken by such things and driven into some unlawful complaint.

Indeed, the most excellent prophet David confesses that he was so disturbed by these changes that he was almost in danger, saying: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 1–2).

Since only a few possess such solid strength that they are shaken by no disturbance caused by wickedness, and since many of the faithful are corrupted not only by adversity but also by prosperity, diligent treatment must be applied to heal the wounds by which human weakness is injured.

For this reason I have briefly reviewed some of the dangers with which the world is full, so that, as Scripture says, “Who will boast that he has a clean heart, or that he is pure from sin?” (Prov. XX, 9), everyone may understand that the forgiveness of sins and the medicine of restoration are necessary for him.

### 3. Penance is necessary for everyone. God knows all things

When, dearest brothers, do we turn more appropriately to divine remedies than when the very sacraments of our redemption are presented to us according to the order of the seasons?

To celebrate them more worthily, let us most beneficially prepare ourselves through forty days of fasting. Not only those who, through the mystery of Christ’s death and resurrection, are to be regenerated into new life by Baptism, but also all the people of the reborn should usefully and necessarily take up the protection of this sanctification: the former, so that they may receive what they do not yet possess; the latter, so that they may preserve what they have received. The Apostle says: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12).

No one is so supported by strength that he ought to feel secure about his own stability. Let us therefore, dearest brothers, use the venerable institutions of this most salutary season, and with more anxious care wipe clean the mirrors of our hearts.

However chastely and soberly this mortal life may be lived, it is nevertheless sprinkled with a certain dust from earthly conduct. The brightness of minds created in the image of God is not so removed from the smoke of all vanity that it cannot be darkened by any stain and does not always need polishing.

If this is necessary even for the most cautious souls, how much more should it be desired by those who have perhaps spent the whole year either too securely or too carelessly? We admonish them with the charity that is their due not to flatter themselves because the consciences of individuals cannot be open to us, since the eyes of God, who sees everything at once, are shut off neither by hidden places nor by walls. Not only what has been done and thought is known to him, but also what is to be done and thought.

This, then, is the knowledge of the supreme Judge; this is the fearful gaze for which every solid thing is passable and every secret is open; before which obscure things shine, the mute reply, silence confesses, and the mind speaks without a voice.

Let no one despise the patience of God’s goodness because of the apparent impunity of his sins, nor therefore judge that God is not offended because he has not yet experienced him as angry. The intervals of mortal life are not long, nor is the license of foolish pleasures lasting: it will pass into the pain of eternal punishments if, while the sentence of justice is suspended, the medicine of repentance is not sought.

### 4. How dangerously the person eager for vengeance prays. Mercy is present to the merciful

Let us therefore flee to the mercy of God, which is present everywhere, so that the holy Pasch of the Lord may be celebrated with worthy observance and the hearts of all the faithful may be sanctified.

Let cruelty grow mild and anger become gentle. Let everyone forgive one another’s offenses, and let the person who asks forgiveness not demand vengeance.

For when we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12), we bind ourselves with the hardest chains unless we fulfill what we profess. Therefore, if the most sacred covenant of this prayer has not been kept in all its terms, then at least now let each person examine his conscience and, by forgiving the offenses of others, obtain the abolition of his own sins.

For the Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matt. VI, 14; Luke VI, 37). What each person asks is not far from him, since the judgment of the one who judges depends upon the kindness of the one who pleads.

As the merciful and just hearer of human prayers, God prescribes this for his own equity: that he should not exercise the right of severity against those whom he does not find eager for vengeance.

A generous spirit also becomes those who are merciful and gentle. For nothing is more fitting than that a human being should imitate his creator and, according to the measure of his own ability, carry out a divine work.

When the hungry are fed, the naked clothed, and the sick cared for, does not the Lord’s aid complete the work through the minister’s hands, and is not the servant’s kindness the Lord’s gift? Although he needs no helper for the effects of his mercy, he has so tempered his omnipotence that he assists human beings through human labor; and gratitude is rightly returned to God for acts of devotion whose work is seen in his servants.

For this reason the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Let your light shine before people, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16), through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON 149

[Note: [Col. 2034] Formerly, among the sermons *de Tempore*, 127.]

### On the Lord’s Supper

On what is written in the Gospel of John, chapter XIII, 4–8: “He rises from supper and lays aside his garments,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 2034] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful, while Verlinus and Winding regarded it as spurious. Certainly the statement at the end of section 1—that the washing of the feet cleanses not only minor but also capital sins—does not have the character of Augustine. He is much more cautious in Sermon 9, *On the Ten Strings*, chapter 11, no. 17. Nevertheless, this sermon contains some Augustinian expressions and is composed like a patchwork from various fragments. On section 2, see the exposition of Psalm 33, Sermon 1, no. 6.]

### 1. The washing of guests’ feet should be offered following the Lord’s example

[Note: [Col. 2034] This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have, “we heard.”]

[Col. 2035]

Today, dearest brothers, we are going to hear the evangelist saying: “When the Lord had risen from supper, he laid aside his garments, girded himself with a towel, and began to wash the feet of his disciples.”

What shall we say here, beloved? What excuse can we offer, when we disdain to provide strangers with what he deigned to provide for his servants?

But perhaps there are certain powerful and noble men, and certain delicate matrons, who disdain to bend down to the feet of the holy people journeying as strangers in this world. They themselves do not deign to wash the feet of their guests, nor even to command any of their own people to do it in their place.

Perhaps noble men with delicate hands, or Christian women, are ashamed to touch the feet of the saints in this world because the privilege of their birth does not permit it. It is a bad nobility that makes a person ignoble before God through pride.

Noble and powerful people are therefore ashamed to wash the feet of the saints and strangers in this world. But if they do not correct themselves, they will have still more reason for shame and sorrow when they are separated from the company of those people in the future.

Then they will be afflicted without any remedy of repentance, when they see those whom they had despised receiving the kingdom because of their humility, while they themselves have deserved punishment because of their pride.

Let us therefore fear, brothers, what blessed Peter feared when he heard the Lord saying: “If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me” [Note: [Col. 2035] The printed editions add here: “And while Peter refuses, Christ denies him the kingdom unless he accepts the service.” This is absent from the manuscripts.], lest perhaps we too, if we disdain to wash the feet of the saints, fail to merit having a part with them.

Rather, let us bend ourselves down to the feet of the saints or of strangers. For when we accomplish this with holy humility, we touch their feet with our hands, but through faith and humility we wash away the filth and stains of our souls, and cleanse not only minor but also capital sins. [Note: [Col. 2035] What follows through the end of section 3 is absent from the manuscripts; and in them, after the words “cleanse sins,” there follows immediately: “Therefore, dearest brothers...”]

### 2. Mysteries instituted on the day of the Supper

Rejoice, therefore, beloved, and exult in the Lord, who on this day consecrated for us the mysteries of saving consolation.

But from what did the Lord commend his body and blood? From what, if not from his humility? For if he were not humble, he could neither be eaten nor drunk.

Consider his height: “In the beginning was the Word.” Behold what kind of food is eternal. Angels eat it; the powers above eat it; the heavenly spirits eat and are nourished by it; yet what satisfies and gladdens them remains whole.

But what human being could ascend to that food? Since man could not ascend to that bread, the bread itself deigned to descend to man. This was accomplished with ineffable goodness, because it was necessary that the table of the angels should become milk for little ones and reach them.

Thus the Wisdom of God acted; thus, by assuming flesh, he fed us with heavenly bread, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 1, 14).

Consider, then, the humility: man ate the bread of angels; that is, man ate the eternal Word by which angels are nourished, the Word that is equal to the Father.

### 3. Nothing should be presumed upon except with God’s help. Peter’s presumption

And therefore, dearest brothers, because our Lord taught us patience, freed us from punishment, and redeemed us by his death, let us always hope in the Lord and presume to do nothing without his will and help.

For you know what blessed Peter rashly promised Christ: “Even if all are scandalized because of you,” he said, “I will never be scandalized.” The Lord, who knew human frailty and knew that strength lies not in the promise but in its fulfillment, said: “Amen, I say to you, that this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

Blessed Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”

Observe, brothers, the disciple’s reply and understand that what he said arose from love. But because he wished his promise to rest upon the zeal of his own love alone, without the added help of the Lord, what depended upon divine power could not be sustained by a human being.

The will was present, but the strength was not, just as the Lord himself says: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 33–35, 41); and again: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

He promised to the point of death, and denied in fear. He would have had a remarkable confession if he had possessed strength in its fulfillment.

### 4. The conscience must be cleansed of sins

Therefore, dearest brothers, I beg and admonish you: let each person turn to a suitable witness, namely, his own conscience. If he finds there any wounds of sin, let him flee to the remedy of tears; let him repent of having done what he did; let him begin, with a most vigilant heart, to care for the past, avoid the present, foresee the future, and, with God’s help, drive it away.

For no one knows how long he may be able to live in this world, nor is escape possible unless repentance goes before him.

Above all, dearest brothers, think with devout faith and complete devotion of soul about this matter, which especially concerns the faithful: you are going to approach the altar of the Lord our God.

Examine every hiding place of your heart, lest there be there any sins not yet healed by almsgiving and fasting. Fear the Apostle’s warning: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and thus let him eat of that body and drink from the cup” (I Cor. XI, 27–28).

Let none of you retain hatred in his heart against anyone, so that you may be able confidently to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

Above all, guard chastity, restrain the appetite, flee drunkenness, and give alms to the poor according to the strength available to you.

### 5. Perseverance in Pious Works

And this above all I ask, dearest brothers: that the joy which you have given us up to now by your devotion you complete tomorrow, that is, on the Lord’s Passion. For it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved (ibid. 24:13). And therefore you ought to act in such a way that, through the negligence of a single day, you do not lose what you have acquired throughout the whole of Lent. For it is like abstaining, praying, or chanting psalms throughout the whole of Lent, and then withdrawing from the church on the Lord’s Passion—that is, on Parasceve [Good Friday]—as though someone labored greatly to cultivate the earth and did not deserve to receive the harvest. And therefore I ask you: let no one withdraw from the church, unless perhaps bodily illness or some great and public necessity has kept him occupied. For he will be able to celebrate legitimate joy at the Paschal solemnity if he does not wish to withdraw from the assembly of the church on the Lord’s Passion. Whoever willingly listens to me in this exhortation, I trust that God will repay him with glorious rewards both in this world and in the world to come. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CL

[Note: [Col. 2036] Formerly, *On the Seasons* 121; later, in Appendix 46.]

### On the Passion of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 2036] By an uncertain author.]

#### 1. Judas Did Not See Jesus, Although He Had Not Changed

“All of you,” says the Lord Jesus, “will suffer scandal on this night.” The disciples are terrified at such a saying, but Judas is not terrified by the thought of so great a crime. Apostles, consult the Lord; disciples, question the Master. “The one,” he says, “who dips his hand with me into the dish is the one who will betray me.” O hardened brow!
