He hears such things said about himself and still delights in reclining at table; he sees his conscience being made public and still extends his hand toward the morsel. “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” O Judas, to whom do you say, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” Say now, “It is I.” This is not the forgetfulness of one who does not know, but the mercy of one who pities. You, Judas, whom greed has possessed, the divinity knows everything about you; but woe to you, in whom humanity has once and for all perished.

“All of you,” he says, “will suffer scandal on this night.” And Peter: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I nevertheless will not be scandalized.” The physician and the sick man began to argue: one thought himself free of illness, while the other saw the coming attack. To him the Lord says: “Let us withdraw for a little while, until we confirm the outcome of the matter.” And Judas: “The one whom I kiss is he; seize him” (Matt. 26:31, 23, 25, 33, 48). O sacrilegious sign, O agreement to be shunned, where war begins with a kiss and the sacrament of peace is broken by the sign of peace!

They came into the garden, having already lost paradise, seeking the Lord Jesus Christ. Those who had come ahead previously now go out seeking him. Jesus stands, and they say, “We are looking for Jesus.” The Savior himself looks upon those whom the dark guide Judas was leading. He was providing guidance, yet he did not see the Master—not because Jesus was changeable; he was what he was. They were seeking light in darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend the light.

But let us hear the voice of the light, who says to those who came with lanterns into the darkness, “Whom are you seeking?” They said, “Jesus.” Jesus answered, “I am he”; and, having heard the voice, they went away, cast prostrate on their faces by blindness (John 18:4, 5, 7, 6). But because “the light shines in the darkness” (ibid. 1:5), he raises from death those who had been struck down. Again he says to them, “Whom are you seeking?” “Jesus,” they reply. And he says to them, “I am he.”

O senseless Jews! You asked, and you fell; you were raised up, and you are ungrateful. By what threat or terror will you be shaken, when you fell at a single, simple utterance? Say, Israel: “You have come to seize me, because I defended you from those who persecuted you”? Would that you had seized me and not destroyed yourself. In the waters I built up walls; I raised a torch upon a shining pillar; I struck the Egyptians with blindness; throughout the whole night I fought for you. Morning came, and you crossed the sea unharmed. You seek me wrongly; therefore you have fallen. Behold how those who seek the Lord wrongly fall.

#### 2. Peter’s Fall and His Weeping

Meanwhile the Lord is seized and is to be led before the chief priest. While the disciples were stumbling, Peter, that outstanding promiser, began to walk farther away and arrived at the chief priest’s house. Because the cold was pressing Peter, he stood there attentively, seeking warmth. Behold, the man who thought he had no weakness at all gradually began to encounter the physician’s words. Terrified, he denies Christ, although he had promised that he would lay down his life for him. A decrepit old woman overthrew him, as though with a slight fever. A lethargic sleep weighed him down, and an active herald of the morning seized him. He heard the cock crowing and saw that he, the disciple, had offended the Lord.

Under a maidservant he began to be bent down and submerged by the weight; no one could help him unless the Lord, from within the governor’s court, had looked upon Peter. When midnight suddenly held the onset of decline, the cock crowed, and the shipwrecked man breathed again in the night. He found the generous pole of faith, with which to propel the ship so that, amid the reefs, it might seek the harbor of tears. He saw the ship of his heart stripped bare, without cargo; he began to weep because he had begun to love—he had begun to love his Lord.

Jesus terrified the sailor upon the sea; Peter hoped for security from the helmsman. “Lord,” Peter says, “where have you left me? I see your light, but I do not yet see you. You washed my feet and wiped them with your towel; by your light open my eyes. When can I see you, unless you look upon me?” Thus he remained in the bitterness of tears until the Lord burst forth from the gates of hell. Peter poured out tears of confession, while Judas extends a kiss of falsehood.

#### 3. The Price of Christ’s Sale

“Pray,” he says to the disciples, “that you do not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). An agitated night drove the fishermen into flight. The shepherd is seized, and Peter is troubled. The shepherd himself was sorrowful, his soul was troubled, but his divinity rejoiced unshaken. He prays once, prays again, and prays a third time. Like an eagle, he covered his nest with the shelter of his wings; and, after praying anxiously, he returned to his young, for whom he was suffering sorrow. The Jews offered thirty pieces of silver. He must be purchased at such a price, for whom nothing can be valued.

Well, Synagogue, you weighed out thirty silver staters when you suspended the Son of God. Judas therefore went away and hanged himself with a noose. See, Judas, the sentence of divine majesty, which did not wish you to be punished by the hands of others. You hang from the noose, and the silver lies in the temple. No one rejoices in such a transaction, because he declares the price sacrilegious. It is not permissible to put it into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.

Behold, the wickedness of the Jews condemns the deed committed, but does not condemn the sacrilege. If it is not permissible to take up the price, why do you hasten to complete the murder? Or was it not permissible to put the price of innocent blood into the treasury, while it was permissible to kill the innocent man himself? “They bought,” he says, “the field for the burial of strangers.” At last the blind mind found a remedy. They assign the price to the burial-place of the Savior’s strangers. Although they do not recognize it, the sacramental mystery is nevertheless fulfilled.

#### 4. Signs Appear at Jesus’ Death

Pilate questioned Jesus: “Are you the king of the Jews?” And Jesus: “You have said so.” The one who says to the crowd, “Whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus?” The crowd cries out, “Let him be crucified!”

O disordered wickedness of the judge! He declares him innocent and grants the power of choosing. “For I have suffered many things this night because of that righteous man,” his wife sends word. At the world’s birth, a wife leads her husband to death; in Christ’s Passion, a wife urges her husband toward salvation. There the serpent’s cunning precipitates; here angelic terror recalls—so that forgiveness might begin from the place from which sins seem to have burst forth.

Water washes his hands, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27). Through the mystery of water the judge’s understanding is enlightened, and he declares Christ righteous in order to make the people guilty. You claim for yourself a great primacy in guilt. Behold, the judge excuses himself out of love for the Savior, while the betrayer condemns himself, together with the Jews, by his own voice.

All the elements are disturbed; heaven is not at rest when the Lord’s head is beaten with blows. The heavenly court did not remain content with heaven, because all were in commotion. The lights of heaven are troubled, and sulfurous stars fall from their stations into ruin. Golgotha is split by the point of the wood; hammers and axes resound as they strike; the rocks of the sacred mountain are torn apart. That Peter alone who had been upon the rock was being dissolved from the rock as though into soft and yielding sand.

The robber asked for forgiveness and received it through the generosity of the Godhead. He asked that the Savior remember him; the Savior promised that he would come with him into paradise.

## SERMON CLI

[Note: [Col. 2038] Formerly, *On the Seasons* 117; later, in Appendix 43.]

### On the Passion of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 2038] It consists of fragments excerpted from Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, chapters 22–24; passages not found in Ambrose are distinguished by brackets.]

#### 1. Why Christ Was Sorrowful

The Lord took upon himself our sorrow in order to bestow his joy upon us. He descended along the paths of our footsteps even to the anguish of death, so that by his own footsteps he might recall us to life. “I will strike the shepherd,” he says, “and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matt. 26:31). He was sorrowful because he was leaving us as little ones. His soul was sorrowful not on account of his own Passion, but on account of our dispersion.

He willingly received the betrayer with a kiss [Note: [Col. 2038] Ambrose: “in the service of charity”]; not because God the Son feared death, but because he did not wish even the wicked to perish on his account. “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). You had been practicing the discipline of virtue, and have become a disciple of a plan of wickedness? Do you shed blood in the performance of a duty? Do you inflict a wound in place of a pledge of love? Do you bring death by the sign of peace? Do you, a servant, betray the Lord; do you, a disciple, betray the teacher? [Note: [Col. 2038] In place of these words, “He willingly received the betrayer with a kiss,” etc., Ambrose’s *Commentaries* read: “Take this cup away from me, not because God, etc.”]

“The wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6). When the sign was given, he was detained by those who had come with clubs. The crowd lays hands upon him, bonds are tied, justice is mocked, and he is handed over by injustice.

#### 2. Why Peter Struck the Ear; Why He Was Cold; Whom He Denied

Peter therefore struck the ear of the chief priest’s servant. Why Peter? Because he himself received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and obtained the power of loosing and binding [Note: [Col. 2039] It does not seem beside the point to report here Ambrose’s omitted words: “He condemns who also absolves, since the same man has the power of binding, etc.”].

The servant’s ear was cut off because he heard badly; it was the inner ear of one who misunderstood Christ badly. He did not allow Christ to be regarded as a prophet, but taught, by a faithful confession, that he should be marked as the Son of God. Clay recognizes its own maker, and flesh follows its own female maker. He could have commanded; he preferred to work—the one who formed the members of the body from the clay of the earth, the one who did not permit his enemies to be wounded. They were inflicting death upon the righteous man; he was healing the wounds of his persecutors.

Peter followed from a distance; for he could not have denied him if he had clung to Christ the Lord. “Three times,” he says, “you will deny me.” In the house of the chief priest a fire was burning, where Peter sat concealed. There was cold where Christ was not.

Peter, exposed by a maidservant, denies him. I would rather Peter had denied the Lord than that Judas had sold the Lord [Note: [Col. 2039] Ambrose has it thus: “Let us suppose that Peter denied him, because the Lord said, ‘You will deny me three times’; I prefer that Peter denied him to the Lord’s being deceived.”].

Peter was questioned: “You too,” he says, “are one of those who were with the Galilean.” For he was not the one who was in the beginning [Note: [Col. 2039] Ambrose: “He avoided the Word of eternity . . . he alone was the one who was in the beginning.”]. He denied the man; he rejected the company of men. For he was not an apostle of a man, since he had been a disciple of Christ.

#### 3. Peter’s Weeping; The Potter’s Field

And so he wept bitterly (Luke 22:50, 54, 34, 56, 62). He preferred to accuse his own sin, so that he might be justified by confessing, rather than burdened by denying. I read of tears; I do not read of satisfaction. Peter denied at night, but confesses in the day.

Peter had tears, which he poured out with pious feeling. The betrayer did not have the tears by which he might wash away his guilt; so that, while the guilty man is condemned by his own judgment, the voluntary crime might be expiated [Note: [Col. 2039] In Ambrose: “and the crime is expiated by spontaneous punishment, the Lord’s mercy being shown because he himself did not wish to avenge it, and the divinity being demonstrated because he questioned the conscience of the mind by invisible power.”].

“I have sinned,” he says, “because I betrayed innocent blood.” And the Jews: “What is that to us? You see to it” (Matt. 27:4). With stubborn determination they claim for themselves the deadly auction of blood, even as the seller returned to so great a debtor the bond for an enormous debt.

While the price of blood is separated from the Jews’ treasury, and the potter’s field is bought with Christ’s money as a place for burying the remains of strangers, the testimony of prophecy is fulfilled and the mystery of the rising Church is revealed (Zech. 11:12). Therefore the world is bought with the price of blood: for he came so that the world might be saved. The world did not recognize him who had been pure while in the world.

#### 4. Christ on the Cross as Worm and Scarab

He is accused, and he is silent. He is right to be silent who has no need of defense; let those who fear defeat seek to be defended. He does not excuse himself by remaining silent as though guilty [Note: [Col. 2039] Perhaps, “he accuses.” See Ambrose’s words in the following sermon, no. 1], but despises the deceitful by not refuting them. Pilate indeed washed his hands, but he did not wash away his deeds. The wife is stricken during the night and warns her husband in the day. Truth is wearied, and the Lord is judged by a servant.

They crown his head by pressing upon it a crown fastened with thorns, and they worship him in mockery. He is greeted as king and crowned as victor; and he is worshiped as God and Lord. Beautifully he ascends the cross; he stands victorious in judgment. Such, then, is the one who ascended, preparing to conquer the world.

They placed a written title: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.” A worm on the cross, a scarab on the cross. A good worm, who clung to the wood; a good scarab, who cried out from the wood. What did he cry out? “Do not hold [Note: [Col. 2039] In Ambrose: “Father, forgive them; that is, do not hold, etc.”] this sin against them.” He was certainly asking forgiveness for those from whom he was receiving injury.

“Today,” he says [Note: [Col. 2040] Add: “to the robber.”], “you will be with me in paradise.” Nor is it surprising that he forgave the guilt of the converted man, since he released forgiveness to those who insulted him.

“They gave him vinegar to drink” (Matt. 27:48). It is fitting that, to bring all things to completion, corruption is drawn from sincerity. Thus vinegar is drunk, while wine mixed with gall is not drunk. Bitterness ought not to be mixed with sincerity, because he taught [Note: [Col. 2040] The copyist departs from Ambrose, who gives another account of the mystery: “so that,” he says, “the immortality of those who rise might be shown to be without bitterness.”] that the Lord was crucified for us without sin [Note: [Col. 2040] Morel, *Critical Elements*, p. 164, thinks *decuit* (“it was fitting”) should be read instead of *docuit* (“he taught”). The sense does not require this correction, although it is not to be dismissed. M.].

“Father,” he says, “into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:38, 34, 43, 46). He surrendered it well, since he did not lose it. The spirit is commended to the Father so that the bonds of sins may be loosed.

The sun sets for the sacrilegious, so that it may cast a shadow over the spectacle of the wicked. The rocks are split, while the hearts of the Jews are hardened. The elements flee, the earth is shaken; the judge reproves, the soldier guards, the tombs are opened, and the Jews’ faithlessness is exposed.

#### 5. Why Joseph Secretly Asked for Jesus’ Body

[The disciples keep watch, and envious sleep seizes their sorrowful eyes with tears. Jews, why are you curious about where the crucified flesh remained? He appeared in the flames with the three boys, he who afterward deigned to be born as a little child.]

Nevertheless the women stood watching these things (ibid. 23:49), and the mother of the Lord also stood, bearing witness to her son (John 19:25). Joseph and Nicodemus bury Christ (ibid. 19:39). One was righteous; the other was one in whom there was no deceit.

For if the Apostles had buried him, they would have said that the one whom the Jews reported to have been stolen had not been buried. Nicodemus came at night because of fear of the Jews. Simplicity is sought; ambition is not desired. How could a righteous man fear the hiding places of danger, when he did not fear burying the body? Therefore he asked secretly so that he might conceal the body [Note: [Col. 2040] Ambrose: “might obtain it”], not so that he might avert danger.

The women stood at a distance, carefully guarding the place. Their sex wavers; their devotion burns. And although the disciples were exhausted, they alone are warned by the angel not to be afraid.

“Do not touch me,” he says, “for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” I have not yet ascended to you, who seek the living among the dead. Why first to a woman? Through a woman death was formerly announced; through a woman life is restored to humanity.

“Woman, why are you weeping?” (ibid. 20:17, 15). The woman saw Christ, but thought he was the gardener. He who is worshiped is God; he who was being held was a human being. He does not [Note: [Col. 2040] Perhaps, “for.” M.] refuse to be touched by a woman, because not everyone can touch Christ risen who had touched him while he dwelt in the body.

## SERMON CLII

[Note: [Col. 2040] Formerly, *On the Seasons* 118; later, in Appendix 44.]

### On the Passion of the Lord, III; and on Susanna

[Note: [Col. 2040] The Louvain editors note that Maximus is credited with it in manuscripts and printed editions. It is the same sermon that appears in his books of Homilies after the first homily for Palm Sunday, and which is cited in the homily following it there. Nevertheless, some words from Ambrose’s *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 23, are interspersed here and there.]

#### 1. Why Christ Is Silent When Accused

Perhaps it seems strange to you, brothers, that the Lord is accused before the governor Pilate by the chief priests and does not now refute any of them with an answer, since an accusation that is not accepted is ordinarily repelled only by the defense that follows. It is strange, I say, brothers, that the Savior is accused and remains silent. For silence is regarded as consent: he seems to confirm what is alleged when he does not wish to answer what is asked.

The Lord therefore does not establish his accusation by remaining silent, but despises it by not refuting it. He is right to be silent who has no need of defense. Let those who fear defeat seek to be defended. Let those who fear being conquered hasten to speak.

But when Christ is condemned, he surpasses; when he is judged, he conquers, as the Prophet says: “So that you may be justified in your words and may prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6). What need, then, was there for him to speak before the judgment, when the judgment itself was his complete victory? Christ conquers, then, when he is judged, because in this way he is shown to be innocent. Hence Pilate says, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27:24).

Better, therefore, is the cause that is not defended and yet is proved; fuller is the justice that is not supported by words but upheld by truth. The tongue must be silent where truth itself is present. Let the tongue be silent in a good case, although it has been accustomed to prevail in bad [Note: [Col. 2041] Morel, *Critical Elements*, p. 255, thinks it would be better to read *in malo causas obtinere* (“to prevail in bad cases”). We disagree with that view; there is no reason to alter the text. In Latin, *in causas obtinere* can be said in the neuter sense, meaning “to be engaged in cases.”] cases.

I do not want justice defended in the way in which wickedness is ordinarily excused. Christ’s victory does not belong to eloquence but to virtue. The Savior, who is wisdom, knew how to conquer by remaining silent and how to overcome by not answering. Therefore he preferred to prove his case rather than state it. What could compel him to speak, when silence was sufficient for victory?

Perhaps fear would have forced him, lest he lose salvation—except that this itself was the whole cause of his victory. He lost his own life so that he might gain salvation for all. He preferred to be conquered in himself so that he might be victorious in everyone.

#### 2. Susanna Defended by Chastity; She Deserves a Virgin Judge

But why should I speak of God Christ? Susanna, a woman, was silent and conquered her enemies [Note: [Col. 2041] A manuscript, by a second hand, reads “conquered by remaining silent.” Ambrose, however, omits “her enemies.”]. For before Daniel the judge she did not defend herself by a rational speech, nor protect herself by a lawyer’s argument. Rather, while the holy woman’s tongue was silent, chastity spoke on her behalf.

Chastity was present with Susanna in judgment and defended her in paradise: there it safeguarded her honor, here her life; there, so that her purity would not be stained; here, so that her innocence would not be condemned.

For Susanna’s chastity both convicted the shameless elders in paradise and overcame false accusers in judgment. Twice victorious, it makes them guilty through their testimony, whom it had made guilty of adultery. At last chastity deserves Daniel as judge, a younger boy, not yet of mature age. Chastity therefore receives much from God, since it earns a virgin judge. Chastity is secure of victory when virginity is to judge. The causes of modesty ought not to be heard except by a modest man. Such an arbiter is deserved by chastity, before whom modesty will not be endangered.

#### 3. Daniel’s and Pilate’s Identical Judgment; Pilate’s Injustice

When Daniel therefore learned of Susanna’s case, while the ignorant crowd wished to condemn her by false accusations, he said the same thing: “I am innocent of the blood of this woman” (Dan. 13:46). By this utterance he recalled the sinful people from their error.

Thus Daniel uses concerning Susanna the same words that Pilate used concerning the Lord. Pilate says, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27:24). By the same sentence, therefore, chastity is acquitted by which justice also was acquitted.

But Daniel was better than Pilate. The former does not condemn chaste blood, but sets it free; the latter confesses the blood of the righteous and yet hands him over. What good did it do to testify to innocence and, as though he were guilty, condemn him—unless it is that it is a more serious sin both to declare the same man righteous and to hand him over to criminals?

He himself is the witness to his injustice: with his mouth he absolves, but in his heart he condemns. Though Pilate washed his hands, he did not cleanse his deeds. Although he thought that he had wiped the blood of the righteous man from his limbs, his mind nevertheless remained stained by that same blood. For the one who handed Christ over to be killed killed him himself.

A good and steadfast judge ought neither to condemn innocent blood nor yield to envy or fear. Daniel, then, was better than Pilate. He recalled the sinful people from their error; Pilate, however, confirmed the sacrilege of the raging Synagogue.

## SERMON CLIII

[Note: [Col. 2042] Formerly, *On the Seasons* 114; later, in Appendix 41.]

### On the Passion of the Lord, IV

[Note: [Col. 2042] It is perhaps by the same author as most of the Homilies circulated under the name of Eusebius. Indeed, nowhere there is a more solemn turning toward humanity than in that appeal, using the same words employed here, to consider how much one is worth by the Creator’s estimation and how much one owes him. Thus, in Homily 2 *On Easter*: “Consider, O man, how much you are worth, and weigh how much you owe. Consider how much you are worth, so that at last you may cease to be contemptible in your own eyes, and so that, blushing at this very fact, you may disdain to lie subject to vices.” Likewise in Homilies 1 and 2 *On the Creed*, in the exposition of the words “From there he will come to judge,” etc. Finally, in Homily 6 *On Easter*, he says: “Let us consider how greatly he could have loved his servant before the fault, whom he so glorifies after the fall.” These very words occur here in no. 2. See the following sermon, no. 8. For no. 1, see Eusebius at the end and around the middle of Homily 6 *On Easter*; for no. 2, see Eusebius, Homily 1 *On the Creed*.]

[Col. 2042]

#### 1. The Whole World Redeemed

The one whose Passion even the mute elements did not keep silent summons us, dearest brothers, to the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion. Let the light of faith celebrate it with human tongues, a Passion proclaimed even by the silences of darkness.

Today our Lord hung the price of our salvation upon the scales of the cross, and by one death, as the creator of all, he absolved the whole world as the restorer of all. Let us believe without hesitation that he redeemed the whole world, who gave more than the whole world was worth. The dignity of the redeemed reward surpassed the value of the great price. Between the redeemed and the redeemer there was a dispensation, not an equivalence.

Therefore he who had no sins of his own rightly erased the sins of others. He alone fell as a pious victim on behalf of all, so that he might raise all. And because he alone had no debt, he rightly paid out the interest of mercy on behalf of debtors.

Consider in this regard what sort of return he who gave such money for us will demand from us. On this day, therefore, the faith of prophetic proclamation was fulfilled, as it says: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn my face away from the disgrace of spitting” (Isa. 50:6). He took upon himself our evils so that he might bestow his goods.

#### 2. How Dear Man Is to God, How Much He Is Worth, and How Much He Owes; The Mysteries of the Scarlet Cloak, the Crown of Thorns, Thirst on the Cross, the Torn Veil, and the Opened Tombs

From this let us understand how greatly he deigned to love humanity before its guilt, since he loves it in this way after its fall. Recognize, O man, how much you are worth and how much you owe; and when you perceive the greatness of the dignity of your redemption, impose upon yourself the shame of sinning.

Behold: for the impious, piety is scourged; for the foolish, wisdom is mocked; for the liar, truth is killed; for the wicked, justice is condemned; for the cruel, mercy is afflicted; for the wretched, sincerity is filled with vinegar; sweetness is intoxicated with gall; for the guilty, innocence is condemned; for the dead, life dies.

The nature of things shuddered at the crime of humanity. The trembling earth testifies that the one whom the rebellious creation does not recognize is Lord of the world, and the fleeing sun confesses him king of heaven.

He is clothed in a scarlet cloak, because the body of the Church is adorned with the blood of its martyrs. A crown of thorns is placed upon his head, because the pricking of our sins—by whose remission the glory of the Redeemer is built—is compared to dry thistles. Let us now strive, in the opposite direction, that the life of the members may be the crown of the head.

When he says that he is thirsty while hanging on the cross, he desires the faith of the unbelieving nation. But in return they offer vinegar of wickedness, because by sinning they had corrupted the wine of wisdom that they had received from God.

The veil of the Temple is torn, because the Synagogue is stripped of its honor; the ancient observance is dissolved; the unity of the Church is foreshown. The tombs are opened because the rights of death are rightly overcome. When the seat of hell has been loosed by the Lord of all things, the prisons of deep night are opened, and the underworld recognizes that the one whom human beings do not receive is God.

#### 3. The Mystery of Judas’ Returning the Price of Christ’s Sale

But the fact that Judas, the profane seller, returned the thirty pieces of silver indicated that Christ’s price would profit him nothing, but that the benefit of salvation would be conferred upon others through his crime.

Let us see what the divine words testify was bought with this returned price. “They bought,” he says, “from it the potter’s field for the burial of strangers” (Matt. 27:7). Christ is the potter; the field is Christ’s Church; the acquisition of strangers is the people of the Gentiles.

It remains, dearest brothers, that we strive to be cultivators of this field, daily and perpetual. Let us sow in it the fruit of a good conscience, so that when the time of harvest—that is, of consummation—and the day of rendering an account arrive, we may bring back with confidence and exultation the sheaves of good works. After the affliction of the fasts of the present Lent, clothed in the brightness of praiseworthy deeds and adorned with the garment of chastity, let us proceed to the coming festivals and, incorporated into the assemblies of the devout, celebrate that eternal Passover; with our Lord Jesus Christ granting this, who with the Father, etc.

## SERMON CLIV

[Note: [Col. 2043] Formerly, *On the Seasons* 120; later, in Appendix 45.]

### On the Passion of the Lord, V; and on the Blessed Robber

[Note: [Col. 2043] It is published among the Homilies in the *Library of the Fathers* under the name of Eusebius; there, as in the manuscripts, it begins with these words: “God was in Christ,” etc. It is not unworthy of Faustus the semi-Pelagian. If you inspect his *On Free Choice*, book 1, chapter 7, and book 2, chapter 6, you will soon recognize as his own the turns of expression found here in no. 3, “newborn faith”; no. 7, “the disposition of belief”; and no. 9, “the happiness of belief, the devotion that belief makes concise.” For no. 4, see Eusebius, Homily 10 *On Easter*; for no. 8, compare Eusebius, Homily 2 *On Easter*, and above, Sermon 153, no. 2.]

#### 1. Christ’s Purpose in the Mysteries of the Flesh

We have often heard, dearest brothers, the blessed Apostle Paul saying, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19)—that is, the Godhead was at work in the body; humanity appeared in frailty, and majesty in power.

For this purpose he lived with us in the flesh: to set before us examples of righteousness. For this purpose he underwent death for us: to bestow the gifts of eternal salvation. For this purpose he put on humanity: to instruct; for this purpose he handed himself over: to redeem; for this purpose he took it up again: to take humanity into God.

For this purpose he laid down life: to give it; for this purpose he accepted death: to conquer it. Yet to the death that was about to return its presumed dominion, he submitted as a servant, but commanded as Lord. For neither could the gate of hell hold his soul, nor could the tomb hold his body. During those three days the tomb in no way violated the flesh with mortal corruption, because in hell, during the same interval, his soul was destroying the kingdom of death.

#### 2. God’s Immense Condescension toward Humanity; Christ’s Death Reveals the Human Being, His Resurrection Reveals God; The Robber’s Absolution Becomes the World’s Hope and Consolation; The Hope of Salvation from Two Things

What shall we repay the Lord for gifts of such condescension? From heavenly fullness the Maker emptied himself into his own work; the potter entered into his own vessel; and the King of heaven served as a soldier for humanity. I said, “served as a soldier,” for the cross indicates one who fights, while the resurrection indicates one who triumphs.

Who could relate such piety [Note: [Col. 2043] The words “Who could relate such piety?” are absent from the manuscripts and from Eusebius.]? “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18:7), and his descent reaches to the depths of hell. In one and the same person, how well are human and divine things equally manifested! For as he descended to penetrate the seat of Tartarus, he confessed himself human; as he returned, he revealed himself as God.

To redeem the impious, as the divine word says, “to redeem the wicked, he was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12), among the two whom we read hung on his right and left (Luke 23:33). He handed himself over to shame and the disgrace of the cross in order to glorify the robber.

But if we look carefully, we discover that this was not granted to him alone. For while he releases so notable a criminal, while he cancels so great a debtor’s enormous written obligation, he drafted a guarantee for the human race, so that the absolution of one desperate man might become the consolation and hope of the whole people, and a private gift might grow into [Col. 2044] a public benefit.

Therefore it must be believed without hesitation that, in commendation of his faith, that robber also received this for the sake of our hope and benefit. For the immense goodness of our God gladly grants what he foresees will also be beneficial in general.

And therefore, in keeping with our confidence in such great mercy, if any one of us condemns his sins by a worthy manner of life and believes in Christ with his whole heart, let him know that even now he has opened, in himself, the entrance to paradise for the robber [Note: [Col. 2044] Thus the manuscripts and Eusebius. The printed editions, however, read: “even with the robber.”].

How much the greatness of faith and the height of the riches of God’s mercy accomplish in the hope [Note: [Col. 2044] The Augustinian printed editions read: “How great is the matter in the hope,” etc.] of human salvation [Note: [Col. 2044] The printed editions added here: “and the greatness of patience is shown when he,” etc. We have followed Eusebius and the manuscripts.]! Behold, punishment sent a man wrapped in crimes toward innocence, and offense led him to glory [Note: [Col. 2044] Beware of the semi-Pelagian.]. The one whom guilt had destroyed for salvation was found by destruction; suffering absolved him; condemnation consecrated him.

#### 3. The Robber Deservedly Obtains Salvation by Believing in Christ When He Was Abandoned

But he did not deserve so much without cause. Let us see at what moment he appeared faithful. Behold: amid signs and virtues, with miracles bearing witness and acclaiming, the mind already strong sometimes faltered among the disciples; and now, when Christ’s sufferings in a certain way contradicted him, new faith grew strong in the robber.

At the very time of the Passion, when one of the disciples, blessed Peter, who was especially known to Christ, was questioned by a maidservant, he answered: “I do not know this man” (Matt. 26:72). But this man, who previously had not known him, cries out: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

How singular and how astonishing was his devotion! The guilty man believed at the very time when the chosen one denied. This was therefore more praiseworthy and more magnificent in the robber: that he believed the man condemned and failing amid the final torments to be God, rather than if he had believed amid the works of miracles. He did not, then, deserve so much without cause.

### 4. Confessing God while suffering

Let us consider more fully at what time he confesses the Lord. The wickedness of the persecutors was raging, the impiety of the blasphemers was exulting; crushing, bruises, and wounds showed Christ only as a human being. The stretching out of his sacred hands upon the wood of the cross, and the reverent nailing of them there—hands which condemned the hands of Adam and Eve, stretched out through the ages in lamentable transgression toward the forbidden food of the tree—this nailing, I say, asserted in every respect the weakness of a human being. The dreadful blow inflicted by the spear against his side showed him to be human to the extent that it concealed him as God. While the Apostles were despairing after the divine miracles, this man alone did not yield to the scandal of the cross and death; this man alone is a witness to his majesty, who is proved to be a companion in suffering, and therefore, although still engaged in brigandage, already sees the invisible God with angelic eyes. I believe that the divinity which had drawn nearer in bodily form to the side of one already believing in Christ had illumined the faith that was being born—a divinity which had poured itself forth more abundantly at that moment, when redemption was to be accomplished.

### 5. The faith of his prayer. The brigand a martyr

Let us consider, moreover, what sort of entreaty the confessing man himself made. “Remember me,” he says, “Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” He did not say, “If you are God, rescue me from my present punishment”; rather, “Because you are God, deliver me from the judgment to come.” How quickly the instruction of the Holy Spirit filled him—an instruction by which, while thinking of the day of the future examination, he recognizes that although what he is suffering is intolerable, what he fears is still more grievous.

He proclaims the Judge and King of the ages: not yet summoned, and already chosen; not yet a servant, and already a friend; not yet a disciple, and already a teacher—and, from a brigand, a confessor. “Remember me,” he says. With this glorious voice he moderates his present sufferings. I said “moderates,” because although punishment had begun for the brigand, it is brought to completion in a new manner in the martyr. From the wood of the cross he cries out, but he is already thinking of the times of recompense.

### 6. The reward promised to the brigand

Let us see what the rich and generous goodness of God replies amid these circumstances—a goodness which, just as it surpasses one’s prayers, so adds grace to merits.

“Today,” he says—as though he were saying: “What do you think, O most faithful companion and unique witness of so great a triumph? What do you think you must entreat me so earnestly for—that I should remember you on the day of my judgment? Why do you postpone me, who am ready for present recompense, to such distant times? Why do you weary your perfect faith in me by consigning it to future ages? Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Therefore, as though it were an hereditary and paternal dwelling—the dwelling which, after Adam was expelled, and after the expulsion of the two, was closed to countless peoples—it will be opened when you enter. Enter there first, but with a happier entrance than the first man. Enter paradise, no longer destined to see hell with Adam. Fear no deadly food there, no law now, no tree: I shall be your food and your life there. And lest you perhaps fear that some enemy may lie in wait for you in that blessed grove, lest that ancient brigand may ambush you, your possession there will be secured by my bringing you in.

Let unbelief, then, withdraw—the unbelief that recognizes neither God nor man. For just as it is the devil who expelled him from paradise, so it is God who brings him back.

### 7. Christ’s divinity attested on the cross by his judgment concerning the brigands, by his wondrous patience, and by the whole creation. The great hardness of the human being

In accordance with these things, dearest brothers and sisters, let us recognize throughout the whole order of events God working beneath the human appearance. Placed upon the gallows like a judge in the midst of the condemned, he drove away the one who denied him and received the one who confessed him; he assigns this man to the kingdom and leaves that one to hell.

Through these events, therefore, let us believe that the one whom we now see exercising both mercy [Note: [Col. 2045] In the manuscripts and in Eusebius, the words “and mercy” are lacking; they may have been added here, perhaps contrary to the author’s Pelagianist intention.] and judgment on the cross will judge in majesty. Let us believe, I say, that he is God, even from the sole virtue of his patience: while he is handed over by a human being to the cross and to death, he nevertheless promises glory to that human being; and he turns those very insults and blows heaped upon his body into the price of our redemption.

But the rational creation of the whole world itself also speaks of God through its movements. For in the midst of the Lord and Savior’s passion, heavenly and earthly things are disturbed; light is mingled with night, the elements are shaken, and they flee from their ancient services. Nature plainly appears to be thrown into commotion, as though it wished to arm itself in vengeance for its Creator.

The earth itself, shaken from its foundations, as though it could scarcely endure the Lord’s cross [Note: [Col. 2045] Eusebius reads: “as though it could scarcely endure God upon the cross.”], trembles as if over its own crime. The day, deprived of its returning light, takes up lamentation as best it can, and clothes itself in the dark and mournful garment of shadows, like one who is grieving. And just as the whole face of heaven bears witness to the glory of the Lord’s birth by a new light, so it denounces the outrage of the cross by new darkness.

And what hardness of the human heart! Woe to those who do not believe amid these events, since insensible creation, which cannot receive the feeling of faith, nevertheless gives God the obedience of confession. Although Christ died for the human being alone, even that part of the world to which the benefits of the passion did not reach nevertheless bears witness to his divinity.

### 8. How much the human being is worth and owes. How guilty one is when sinning. Forgetfulness of the future judgment, a great punishment for sin

Since these things are so, dearest brothers and sisters, let the human being recognize how great is his worth, and how greatly either nature or grace makes him indebted to God. Let the human being recognize how much God expects from him, and how precious in conduct God wishes the one whom he has held dear with such great condescension to be.

Let the human being recognize how much he is worth and how much he owes. While he considers his price, let him cease to be contemptible in his own eyes, and rather repay his Savior a fitting return for the gift from his very own good—that is, from the salvation that has been preserved.

Let us therefore carefully guard what Christ redeemed at the cost of such great suffering. The person who violates and stains a soul cleansed by the blood and passion of Christ will therefore be guilty of no small price, but of Christ’s blood: he will be a blasphemer, a murderer, a betrayer of chastity. These three sins bring death in the gravest sense.

We testify to your Charity concerning the causes of eternal evils. The blasphemer, the murderer, and the betrayer of his own chastity, the violator of another’s—that is, the person who transgresses the rights of the lawful marriage bed, who wanders outside his spouse in deadly embraces—will be guilty of eternal death, because he has regarded the blood of the Redeemer as worthless in himself.

And because the Apostle cries out, “Neither the greedy nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10), let us keep our hands from what belongs to others, and guard our eyes from another’s wife, lest we do injury in our own body to that body which Christ assumed from our body.

Let us beware of betraying our life through sins and crimes, lest that terrible prophecy apply to us: “There is no God before his eyes; his ways are polluted at all times; your judgments are removed from his sight” (Psalm 9:5).

It is an irremediable danger to loosen the reins to vices and desires so far that one no longer remembers having to give an account to God. For I think that the punishment of sin is already great when one has lost fear and remembrance of the future judgment.

Let the spoils of the poor not be so sweet to us, since afterward they will become exceedingly bitter. Likewise, as has been said, let us flee the abominable contagions of another’s flesh and avoid the obscene fires of hostile pleasure.

The person who does these things, dearest brothers and sisters, kindles for himself perpetual fires from the straw and wood of iniquities and prepares vapors that will never be extinguished. Life is not worth so much if a person lives in order to consume eternity during the few years of this life and, within a brief end, gather punishments that will remain without end.

### 9. The example of the brigand must not become an occasion for a more lax life, since few possess the brigand’s faith and many have been deceived by this empty hope

But lest, dearest brothers and sisters, such a new happiness of faith make anyone overly secure or lax, lest someone say in his heart: “Let not a guilty conscience trouble and torture me so greatly; let not a culpable life sadden me so greatly. I see that, in a moment, in a brief interval, the brigand’s crimes were forgiven, and for me they are conceived with an unburdened mind” [Note: [Col. 2046] Perhaps one should read, “are granted to me.” Or else the words “and for me they are conceived with an unburdened mind” are superfluous. Eusebius’s manuscripts themselves omit them.].

First, in that brigand we must consider not only the concise devotion of his faith, but also the circumstance of that time in which these things were happening—a time at which the perfection of the righteous is read to have faltered.

Then show me the brigand’s faith before you claim the brigand’s blessedness for yourself. The devil introduces security in order to bring destruction, and it is impossible to count how many this shadow of empty hope has deceived.

May countless peoples, stripped and empty of good things and full of evil under such security, snatched away from this light, deter us, I beg, from this persuasion.

### 10. To postpone the time of salvation is extremely dangerous, extremely foolish, and hateful to God. The brigand did not postpone the work of salvation

Every day we must fear the uncertain hour of our departure and migration—an hour which is sometimes unexpected or sudden even now, and which, if missed, will lack remedies forever. The day that is accustomed to overtake us must be anticipated.

A person deceives himself and toys with his own death when he thinks: “The indulgence of the final hour may come to my aid.” This is not so. First, because security promised for the last day is extremely dangerous; then, because it is extremely foolish to entrust a matter concerned with eternal necessities to the final moments of a failing life, when they are useless.

It is hateful to God when a person sins more freely in the confidence of repentance reserved for old age. Believe me, dearest brothers and sisters, it is difficult for a clever pretense concerning an ordered completion to be worthy of obtaining the opportunity: before him who interprets the heart, cleverness is not admitted to salvation.

But that blessed brigand of whom we have spoken—blessed, I say, not now lying in ambush beside the road, but holding the road itself in Christ and suddenly snatching the prize of life, carrying away new spoils from his own death after his condition had been transformed—he neither postponed the time of salvation because he did not know it, nor placed the remedies for his condition in the final moments through an unhappy deception, nor reserved the hope of his redemption for the last extremity of despair. He had previously known neither religion nor Christ. If he had known them, perhaps he would not have been last in number among the Apostles who became first in the kingdom.

Therefore, even in this respect he pleased God at the end, because that final hour was not his last hour for attaining faith but his first.

It is therefore necessary for a person to provide for himself through daily action and to secure a good completion. It is necessary that our whole life be such in conduct that we may deserve to be free at the end.

Thinking unceasingly of the day of our departure and the time of judgment, let us too continually proclaim with the brigand: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.”

## SERMON CLV [Note: [Col. 2047] Formerly, *On Time* 130; subsequently, Appendix 49.]

### On the Lord’s Passion, VI; or, On the Cross and the Brigand [Note: [Col. 2047] This is a homily of John Chrysostom, but here abridged and given in another old translation—the one found in manuscripts and in the older printed editions of Chrysostom—which is inferior and agrees less closely with the Greek wording.]

### 1. The cross now glorious, the cause of innumerable gifts

On this day our Lord hung upon the cross, and we feast [Note: [Col. 2047] Thus the printed editions, with two manuscripts. But the other translation in the manuscripts and older printed editions of Chrysostom has, “we celebrate the feast with excessive joy.” The Greek edition has *heortēn agomen*, “we celebrate a feast.” Gretser translates, “we keep a feast.”], so that we may learn that Christ’s cross is a festival and a spiritual fair. For formerly the cross was the name of condemnation, but now it has become a thing of honor; formerly it stood in the condemnation of the accursed, but now it has been raised as the occasion of salvation.

For this cross has proved the cause of innumerable good things for us: it freed us from error; it enlightened us while we sat in darkness; it reconciled us, conquered by the devil, to God; from aliens it restored us to members of the household; from those far off it made us near; from strangers it made us citizens. This is the destruction of enmities, the foundation of peace, and the treasury of all good things for us.

Because of it we no longer wander in deserts, for we have known the way of truth; nor are we any longer outside the kingdom, for we have entered the King’s gate. We no longer fear the devil’s fiery arrows, for we have found the fountain of life by which they are quenched. Because of it we are no longer in widowhood, for we have received the bridegroom; we do not dread the wolf, because we have found the good shepherd—for he says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:14). Because of it we do not fear the tyrant, for we cleave to the King. Because of it we keep a feast day, celebrating the memory of the cross.

### 2. The festival of the cross instituted by Paul. The cross an altar. Christ priest and victim

Thus also the Teacher of the Gentiles teaches that an annual festival is established because of the cross [Note: [Col. 2047] In Chrysostom, Paul urges us to celebrate the feast. Gretser: “Paul exhorts us to keep a feast.” Another ancient translation: “Paul commanded that the festival be celebrated because of the cross.” He immediately adds, “Therefore let us keep the feast day,” where the Greek has *heortazōmen*, and Gretser, “let us celebrate.” This is certainly better than “let us feast.”]. “Let us feast,” he says, “not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Then, adding the reason for observing the solemnity, he says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us” (1 Cor. 5:8, 7).

Where there is sacrifice, there is also the destruction of sins; where there is the destruction of sins, there is reconciliation with God; where there is reconciliation with God, there is “the voice of rejoicing and salvation in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. 117:15). Let all the earth also rejoice: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us. And where, tell me, was he sacrificed? Upon the height of the cross. The altar of this sacrifice is new, because the immolation also is new and wondrous. For he himself was both victim and priest: victim according to the flesh, but priest according to the Spirit. The same one both offered according to the Spirit and was offered according to the flesh.

Hear, then, how Paul made both of these things clear [Col. 2048]: “Every high priest,” he says, “who is taken from among human beings is appointed for human beings; therefore it is necessary that he also have something to offer” (Heb. 5:1). Behold, he offered himself. Elsewhere it is said: “Because the Lord was once offered for the offering of himself, henceforth to take away the sins of many [Note: [Col. 2048] The old translation has: “Christ, offered once, took away the sins of many.” Behold, here he is offered; there, etc. Chrysostom says nearly the same.] he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation” (Heb. 9:28). Behold, there he was offered; here he offered himself. Do you see how he became at once both victim and priest, and how the cross was the altar?

### 3. Why he was sacrificed under the open sky, not in the temple. The cross consecrated every place as a temple

Why was this victim offered not in the temple, but outside the city and beyond the walls? So that what is written might be fulfilled: “He was numbered among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12). Why, then, was he sacrificed upon the height of the cross rather than beneath a building’s roof? Clearly so that he might cleanse the nature of the air; for this reason he was not offered upon an altar or beneath an overhanging roof, but under heaven. For the air was purified when the Lamb was sacrificed on high; the earth also was purified, because the Lord’s blood dripped upon it.

Therefore he was not beneath a roof, nor in the temple of the Jews, so that the Jews might not remove the saving sacrifice [Note: [Col. 2048] The old translation just cited adds: “and claim it for themselves.”]. Nor should you suppose that this victim was offered for that nation alone: it was outside the city and beyond the walls so that you might understand that it is a common victim, offered for the human race; and consequently the purification is universal, not partial, as it had been among the Jews.

For God commanded the Jews to leave all the land and offer sacrifices and pay vows in one place, because at that time the whole earth was unclean with the smoke of altars, the odor of pyres, and the other defilements brought upon it from the profane sacrileges of the Gentiles. But now, since Christ by his coming has expiated the whole earth, every place has become a place of prayer. Therefore the blessed Paul exhorts and commands us to pray everywhere without ceasing: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands” (1 Tim. 2:8).

Do you see how the world has been cleansed? We can therefore lift holy hands everywhere, because the whole earth has been sanctified, so that it is holier than the Holy of Holies in the inner part of the old temple. For there an irrational animal, a sheep, was offered; here a spiritual sacrifice has been offered. And the greater the offering, the more exalted is the sanctification. Therefore Christ’s cross is a festival of feasting.

### 4. The cross opened paradise

Do you wish to learn another benefit of the cross? Paradise, closed to us about five thousand years or more ago, he opened today. For on this day and at this hour Christ, introducing the brigand, accomplished a double benefit: first, he opened paradise; second, he introduced the brigand. Today he restored to us our original homeland; today he led us back to our fatherland city and gave the eternal home back to the common nature of humanity. “Today,” he says, “you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

What are you saying? You are crucified and nailed fast, and yet you promise paradise? “Yes,” he says, “so that you may recognize my power upon the very cross.” Since this appeared to be a matter of sorrow, he acted thus so that you might not attend to the wood of the cross, but might learn the power of him who was crucified. In the cross he performed this miracle by which the Almighty especially reveals his power: not by raising the dead, commanding sea and winds, or casting out demons, but by being crucified, spat upon in the face, and nailed fast; when he endured injuries and curses, ridicule and contempt, he was able to change the brigand’s malicious mind, hardened by long practice in crimes. Thus you may behold his power in both respects [Col. 2049].

For at the same time during his passion, while crucified, he disturbed all creation and shattered the rocks; yet he drew to himself and honored a soul harder than stones, saying: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” Certainly a cherub guarded paradise, but he is also Lord of the cherubim. There the flaming sword turns; but he has authority over flame, Gehenna, life, and death.

### 5. The brigand’s entrance into heaven greatly commends the Lord

No king has ever allowed a brigand, or any other fellow servant of the same nature, to enter a city with himself in this way; but Christ did so. Victorious over death and the devil and entering the most holy homeland, he brings the brigand in with him. By this work of mercy he does not trample down paradise, but honors it; nor does the brigand’s entrance disgrace it, but illumine it.

For it is the honor of paradise to have such a Lord, who can make even a brigand worthy of the paradise of delights. Indeed, when he brings tax collectors and prostitutes into the kingdom of heaven, he does not disgrace but exalts the kingdom of heaven; he does not cast down but rather honors paradise. For, as we have said, it is paradise’s honor to have such a Lord, who can make even a brigand worthy of the delights and possession of paradise.

Such is the Lord’s kingdom of heaven that it renders even prostitutes and tax collectors so acceptable that they appear worthy of the grace and glory which are there. Just as we most admire a physician when we see him curing difficult human illnesses and overcoming the perils of death by the art of healing, so it is right to admire Christ when he heals incurable wounds in bodies and minds, when he brings a tax collector and a prostitute to such health that he shows them worthy even of heaven.

### 6. The brigand’s merit. The brigand a teacher

And what had the brigand done that was such that, after the cross which he had deserved, he should suddenly be judged worthy of paradise? Do you wish me briefly to state the power of his faith? When Peter denied below, that man confessed above. I have not said this to accuse the most blessed Peter—far be it—but wishing to show the brigand’s greatness of spirit. The disciple could not bear the threats of a lowly maidservant; but the brigand, seeing the crowd of the whole people standing around and shouting, hurling mad blasphemies, reproaches, and curses, paid them no attention. He did not consider the visible abasement of the one being crucified; but passing over all these things with the eyes of faith, and passing by and abandoning those abject and slight impediments to the truth, he recognized the Lord of heaven and said: “Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom.”

Let us not, then, dismiss this brigand with a brief mention, nor be ashamed to receive as a teacher one whom our Lord was not ashamed to introduce first into paradise. Let us not, I say, be ashamed to have as master a man who, before all human nature, deserved to be accounted worthy of the kingdom of heaven. Rather, let us investigate each point more intently, that we may recognize the power of the cross.

The Lord did not say to him as he said to Peter, “Come after me; I will make you a fisher of men” (Matt. 4:19). Nor did he say to him as to the twelve disciples, “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid. 19:28). He did not even deem him worthy of saying any word to him; he showed no miracle: no dead person raised, no demon cast out, no sea obeying. Finally, he spoke to him neither of the kingdom of heaven nor of the threat of Gehenna; yet the brigand, before them all, confessed him, and did so while the other brigand reproached him. For that other brigand was reproaching him.

### 7. Brigand and brigand. The brigand’s charity and preaching

You have seen brigand and brigand: both on crosses, both from a life of brigandage, both coming from the same wickedness; but no longer were both established in the same minds and merits. For one was attaining the kingdom, while the other was being sent to Gehenna. Thus on the preceding day there was a similar distinction among the disciples. Judas too was a disciple, as were the eleven; but they said to the Lord, “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” while he was preparing to betray the Lord and said, “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. 26:17, 15). They were preparing themselves for divine service, but he was hastening to betrayal.

Thus here also, brigand and brigand: one reproached, the other worshiped; one blasphemed, the other praised and rebuked the blasphemer, saying, “Do you not even fear your God?” You have seen the brigand’s confidence; you have seen free will upon the cross; you have seen philosophy in tribulation and reverence for divine fear in punishment [Note: [Col. 2050] The old translation has, “and prudence in punishment.” It then adds: “For that he was mindful of himself, that he kept watch with a sound mind while constrained by the fastening of the nails—who,” etc. But Chrysostom’s later translator has: “For that he was present to himself, that he was not cast down from his mental state, though fastened with nails,” etc. In both, however, the word “is pierced with compunction” is lacking.].

Who would not admire and be pierced with compunction that, so far as concerned himself, even though nailed fast, he did not have a wounded understanding or a pierced perception? Indeed, leaving not only what concerned himself but also what surrounded him, he cared for the other man on the cross, becoming a teacher, rebuking him and saying: “Do you not even fear your God?” “Do not,” he says, “attend to this judgment below; there is another, invisible judge. Therefore do not consider that he has been condemned below by a mortal judge: for the heavenly judgments are not like this.

“Here, in earthly judgment, both righteous persons are condemned and unjust persons escape; the guilty are acquitted and the innocent punished. For those who judge, whether willingly or unwillingly, are greatly mistaken: being ignorant of justice, they are led astray; or, though knowing it, they are corrupted by greed so as to sell innocent blood. But above there is nothing of the kind. For the judge is righteous, and his judgment has gone forth like light, having neither darkness nor ignorance.”

So that he might not say that, because he was condemned below on earth and sentenced to punishment, the Lord led him to the heavenly judgment and recalled that dreadful tribunal, as though saying to him: “Look, and you will not bear the sentence of eternal condemnation, nor stand in the lot of corrupt judges; look to the judgment above, which will be for salvation” [Note: [Col. 2050] The Corbie-manuscript translation has: “Nor will you stand below with corrupt judges; but you will receive the true judgment above”; Greek: “nor will you stand with the people below, but you will marvel at and accept the judgment from above.”].

You have seen the brigand’s philosophy; you have seen his understanding and teaching. In an instant, he leapt from the cross into heaven. So abundantly had he received righteousness that he rebuked that neighbor, once his companion, saying: “Do you not fear, since we are in the same judgment,” that is, in the same condemnation? “Are you not also on the same cross? Why then, in reproaching your companion in punishment, do you make yourself guilty in his place?” For just as one who is in sins, if he ventures to accuse others, accuses himself before them, so one placed in affliction, if, forgetful of himself, he reproaches others with it, first speaks reproach against himself: “For we are in the same judgment.”

### 8. The brigand’s confession and its fruit

What are you doing, O brigand? In beginning to make satisfaction, have you made the Lord your companion? “No,” he says; “I correct this opinion of me in what follows.” For lest you suppose that, because they shared a condemnation, he made the Lord also a partner in his crime, he supplied the correction, saying: “And we indeed justly, for we suffer things worthy of what we have committed.” You have seen a perfect confession; you have seen how upon the cross he stripped himself of sins. “State your iniquities first,” he says, “that you may be justified.” No one compelled him, no one forced him; but he himself disclosed himself, he himself condemned himself, saying: “And we indeed justly; we receive what is worthy of our deeds. But this man has done nothing evil. Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom” (Luke 23:40, 41, 42).

He did not dare first to say, “Remember me, God,” until, through confession of his former iniquity, he had laid down the burden of sins [Col. 2051]. Do you see what a great thing confession is? He confessed and opened paradise; he confessed and received such strength of confidence that, though a brigand, he asked for the kingdom, considering how great are the benefits which the cross brings us.

### 9. The cross, the emblem of the kingdom. Christ took it hence into heaven

Tell me, brigand: you ask for a kingdom; what do you see in him from whom you ask it that is such? [Note: [Col. 2051] The Erfurt, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions have: “Tell me, brigand, asking for a kingdom, what do you see in him from whom you ask it that is such?” M.] Tell me, for what is visible is nails and a cross. “But,” he says, “this cross itself is the emblem of the kingdom; and therefore I call Jesus king, because I see him crucified. For it is the work of a king to lay down his life for those over whom he rules; hence he says that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11, 27–29). “Therefore the good king too lays down his life for those of whom he is prince. Since, then, he has laid down his life, I recognize him as king and call him Lord: ‘Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom.’”

Have you considered how the cross is also the emblem of the kingdom? If you wish to learn this same thing from another source, he did not leave it on earth, but drew it into heaven. How can you know this? Because it will come with him at his second and glorious advent, so that you may learn how wondrous and magnificent the cross is. Hence he called it glorious, while the Apostle gloried in it.

### 10. He will bring it at the second advent. Christ’s second advent will not be hidden, and why. The sun, moon, and stars will be darkened by the cross’s splendor. The angels will tremble at the final judgment, and why

But let us see how he will come with the cross, for it is necessary to show this also. “If they say,” he says, “Behold, Christ is in the inner rooms; behold, he is in the wilderness, do not believe it,” speaking of the second coming of his glory because of false Christs, false prophets, and Antichrist, lest anyone, forestalled by error, fall among false christs.

Because Antichrist will precede the advent of Christ the Savior, one must carefully beware lest, seeking the shepherd, one find the wolf. For this reason I tell you how you may recognize the advent of the true shepherd. Since his first advent took place secretly, do not suppose that his second advent will be like it. He gave this sign: “As lightning coming forth from the east appears in the west, so will be the advent of the Son of Man.” He will suddenly appear to all, and no one will need to ask whether Christ is here or there. For just as, when lightning flashes, we have no need to inquire whether there has been a flash, so when the revelation of his presence shines forth, we shall not need to ask whether Christ has come.

But since the question is whether he will come with the cross, let us inquire into it; for I have not forgotten the promised explanation. Hear what follows: “Then,” he says, “when he is about to come, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light.” For the splendor in Christ will be so surpassing that even the brightest lights of heaven will be hidden before the radiance of the divine light. “Then the stars will fall, when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven.” Have you considered how great the power of the sign, that is, of the cross, is? The sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light, but the cross will shine; when heaven’s lights have been darkened and the stars have fallen, it alone will beam forth. Thus you may learn that the cross will be brighter than the moon and more splendid than the sun, surpassing their brightness when illumined by the radiance of the divine light.

Just as, when a king enters a city [Note: [Col. 2051] The Erfurt, Lyons, and Venice editions have: “Just as a king entering a city.” M.], an army goes before him, bearing royal signs and standards upon its shoulders and announcing the king’s entry with the circuit of its martial preparation, so, when the Lord descends from heaven, an army of angels will precede him. Bearing that sign, that is, the triumphal standard, upon their lofty shoulders, they will announce to the trembling earth the entrance of the divine heavenly king [Col. 2052].

“Then,” he says, “the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matt. 24:26): he speaks of the angels, for trembling and great fear will seize them. Why, then, tell me? Because that judgment will then be so terrible that even the angels will fear it. For all the nature of the human race will begin to be judged and stand before the terrible judge. [Note: [Col. 2052] In the manuscripts the word “judge” is lacking; Chrysostom has in its place *bēmati*, “tribunal.”] Why, then, will the angels tremble then, and whence will trembling seize them? They are not themselves to be judged. But just as when a prince judges, not only the accused but also the officials, who are conscious of nothing against themselves, are seized with fear and trembling because of the judge’s terror, so, when the human race is judged, the heavenly ministers too will be afraid; beholding the judge’s terrible array, they will tremble with dreadful fear.

### 11. Why the cross will appear at the judgment

But why will the cross then appear, and for what reason will the Lord come with it borne before him? The reason is clear: so that those who crucified the Lord of majesty may recognize the purpose of their iniquity; for by this sign the shameless impiety of the Jews is convicted. And how he will come bearing the cross for this very reason, hear him himself declare in the Gospel: “Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn,” seeing their accuser, that is, the cross itself. When it accuses them, they will recognize their sin too late and will vainly confess their impious blindness.

Why are you surprised [Note: [Col. 2052] The Corbie-manuscript translation, in accordance with the Greek, has: “Seeing the accuser and recognizing the sin; and why are you surprised if,” etc.] that he will come bringing the cross, when he will also display the wounds themselves? “Then,” he says, “they will see him whom they pierced” (John 19:37). Just as he did in Thomas—wishing, for the faith of many, to correct the disciple’s unbelief and error—he showed and presented to him the marks of the nails and the very wounds from the nails, saying: “Put your hand, and see; for a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have” (John 20:27; Luke 24:39). Then he will show the wounds and make the cross manifest, to show that he is the one who was crucified.

## 12. Christ’s Prayer on the Cross for His Enemies. The Effect of That Prayer

Not only from the cross, but also from the very words he spoke upon the cross, can we consider his immense mercy. For while he was still fastened to the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them their sin; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). And he prayed for those who had crucified him; while they, on the contrary, were saying, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” But he did not come down from the cross for this very reason: because he is the Son of God. For this is why he came, that he might be crucified for us. “Come down from the cross,” they said, “and we will believe in you” (Matthew 27:40, 42).

These words are occasions of unbelief. For he did more than he would have done had he come down from the cross. It was much greater to rise again after the stone had been placed at the tomb than to come down from the cross. It was also greater to raise Lazarus, already four days dead and stinking in the grave, than to come down from the cross.

They were saying, “If you are the Son of God, save yourself” (Mark 15:30); but he endured everything in order to free those who had crucified him. “Forgive them their sin,” he said. Certainly he forgave them, if they were willing to repent. For if he had not forgiven them their sin, Paul would not have become an apostle after persecuting the Church; if he had not forgiven them their sin, immediately after his assumption three thousand, five thousand, and many thousands would not have believed. For it says: “Many thousands of Jews believed” (Acts 2:41; 4:4). Hear what they say to the apostle Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed” (Acts 21:20).

## 13. The Imitation of Christ. It Is Not Impossible. Stephen, the Apostle

Therefore we must be imitators of the Lord and pray for our enemies, following the example of the one who, when he was crucified, asked the Father on behalf of those crucifying him to forgive them their sin. “And how,” you ask, “can I imitate the Lord?” If you wish, you can. For if it were impossible to imitate him, how could he say, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29)? If it were impossible to imitate him, Paul would never have said, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).

But if you do not wish to imitate the Lord, imitate his servant Stephen, whom I also call an apostle; for he too imitated the Lord. Just as Christ, among those crucifying him, leaving the cross and leaving behind his own persecution, prayed to the Father for those crucifying him, so also his servant, among those stoning him, receiving the stones hurled at him and the pains they caused, said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

You have heard how the servant spoke in accordance with the Lord. The Lord says, “Father, forgive them their sin; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). But Stephen says, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And so that you may learn that he prayed with all earnest concern, it says: “Having knelt down, he prayed, saying, Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59)—you who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CLVI

[Note: [Column 2053] Elsewhere, *On Time* 122.]

## On the Passion of the Lord, VII

[Note: [Column 2053] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars regard it as doubtful; Verlino and Vindingo consider it spurious. The manner of expression, manifestly differing from Augustine’s style, absolutely compels us to assign to this place a sermon which we searched for in vain among the manuscripts. For no. 1, see Sermon 160, no. 5, and Sermon 163, no. 1; for no. 3, compare Sermon 159, no. 3.]

### 1. The Benefit of Our Redemption. What God Requires in Return

Dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ has brought us salvation, while diminishing nothing of the divine nature. Let us therefore give thanks for his mercy, who composed for our weakness a life-giving medicine from his humanity. Let us magnify him, because, while coming to our aid, he caused no loss to divine power.

Truly merciful, truly the Savior, who loved his work so greatly, who valued his servant—namely, the entire human race—so highly that he expiated its guilt by his scourging and healed its wounds by his bruises. In the end, one sins and the other is beaten; one transgresses and the other is crucified. Who could believe this, and who could conceive it? Who could repay the Lord, who deigned to die for servants? And for whom did he do this? For criminals, for the ungodly.

What will your good work, O Lord, return to you—your work made by you, perverted by its own will, but restored by your mercy? What do you seek from it in return for such great benefits? Do you need anything from it, or will you demand from it something you did not give it? Or perhaps—indeed, this is what you seek—that you may make fit the one on whom you will have mercy; that you may establish as worthy the one whom you will make a participant in your immortality; that you may make good the one whom you will crown forever?

### 2. God’s Art by Which He Came to the Aid of Earth and Satisfied Justice

But what did you receive from us in return for granting this? Certainly nothing—or something? May the Lord pardon the wretched earth if earth and ashes have presumed to say anything. Let him not reject the foolish, but look upon the penitent.

Let earth speak to its Lord; let humanity speak to its Maker: Surely you received from me something that you did not possess in yourself. For, wishing to come to earth’s aid but unwilling to exceed the measure of justice, you planned to redeem a mortal by your death; yet you still had nothing in yourself by which you could die.

You are omnipotent; I am needy. You are immortal; I am mortal. You received from me the poverty of dust; you took from me the death of the flesh; you poured out for me the price of redemption. O precious price of the lost!

Let those whom the Lord has redeemed, whom he has delivered from the hand of the enemy, now say: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 106:2, 1). Let redeemed earth, watered earth, speak to him—redeemed by blood, watered by baptism: “Great is my iniquity, but greater is your redemption.”

### 3. From This the Devil Was Deceived and Overthrown

Let the adversary of the human race hear the voice of my Lord and no longer exalt himself with complacency, because our Lord Jesus Christ hung upon the cross for the crime of the whole world. “Now,” he says, “is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I have been lifted up from the earth, will draw everything to myself” (John 12:31–32).

O devil, how well you struck yourself by your own attack! Your credulity brought destruction upon you and benefit to us. While you spared no one, you finally destroyed yourself. Through the offense of one person you captured everyone; through the righteousness of one person you nevertheless lost everyone.

If you attacked the one who had consented to you, why did you unjustly kill this one in whom you had found nothing? You poured out innocent blood; give back the condemned race.
