Surely you are the one who, in your pride, claimed for yourself the likeness of divinity; now you are overthrown and defeated by the divine human being.

And what is astonishing if divine power had overcome you, its own creature? But this is great and marvelous: that from dust it should take what would overthrow and crush your wickedness, so that you, who had lifted yourself proudly above the stars, would now be defeated by flesh.

That blood which you poured out conquered you and redeemed me. In the end, I drink it; and, saved, I no longer fear the destruction caused by your poison. You prevailed in paradise, but you were defeated on the gallows.

Why do you set against me the flaming sword placed around paradise? Behold, the stream flowing from the lifted-up Crucified One has quenched the revolving flame. Paradise is now open to the human race, and the Lord Jesus Christ has led the confessing thief back into it.

### 4. From This Paradise Was Opened. Conversion Is Never Too Late. The Thief’s Faith. The Reason for This Change

O what a great mystery! Paradise, which had been closed to the transgressor, is now opened to the thief. Perhaps in this thief too it is appropriate to recognize the whole human race, or even that first parent of the human race. For if the one who inflicted death on others by killing them received the name “thief,” how much more did the one who, by sinning, discovered death itself—though it had not existed—rightly incur the crime of a thief?

Christ says to the thief: “Today,” he says, “you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). To whom, dearest ones, could conversion ever seem too late, when the confession of a thief already hanging and already dying was not rejected?

O the abundant mercy of the Lord, who forgets the crime of the unjust, receives the faith of the penitent, makes one condemned for wickedness chosen, and makes a debtor to death a participant in eternal life!

Yet certainly this thief’s faith was at the very end, but not the least: he was worthy to recognize and confess the Lord when he was not raising the dead but dying for sinners. Peter alone, terrified by fear of the Passion, denies him as though he were merely human; the thief worships him crucified. But the Lord corrected Peter by looking upon him, whereas he blessed the thief by taking him into glory.

O thief worthy of praise, marvelous, worthy of imitation—raging with the sword, violently seizing heaven, intent on theft, yet fervent in faith! But this change is “the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11), for Christ was returning the reverse of the devil’s deed: just as the devil, by corrupting the first human being, had taken him away from paradise, so Christ would snatch the confessing thief from hell.

The devil deceived the presumptuous one through the forbidden tree; Christ redeemed the one hanging upon the tree of punishment.

### 5. The Thief’s Words Must Be Taken Up by Us

Therefore, brothers, let us also take up the voice of this thief, if we do not wish to be thieves. Let us too say: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.”

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, utter with the firmest devotion the confession of that holy thief which we have expressed in song and made our own by answering with our voices. Let us speak in such a way that we may be heard; let us confess in such a way that we may be saved. Let us speak in faith, let us cry out with our hearts.

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself will certainly hear the voice of our cry if he approves the complete devotion of our mind. May he himself lead us to the tree of life, who delivered us from the pit of misery. May he himself open for us the gates of paradise, who broke the gates of hell. May he himself deliver his people from the scourge, who allowed himself to be held before the governor Pontius Pilate. May he himself lead those who confess him into his kingdom, who, innocent, deigned to suffer for the ungodly; so that the name of the Lord may be blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CLVII

[Note: [Column 2055] Elsewhere, *On Time* 134.]

## At the Vigil of Easter, I

### On the Words of Genesis, Chapter 1:1–61: “In the Beginning God Made Heaven and Earth,” etc.

[Note: [Column 2055] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain scholars, but Verlino and Vindingo consider it spurious. They observe that Augustine, in Book 13 of the *Confessions*, chapters 6–9, and elsewhere, emphatically asserts precisely what is denied here—namely, that the Spirit of God who was borne over the waters was God. They also observe that in Book 2 of *To Simplicianus*, Question 1, he expressly disapproved the opinion of those who understood that spirit to be “that by which,” he says, “the whole corporeal mass of the world is, as it were, animated for the service of all things that are generated and for the preservation of corporeal creatures in their proper form.”]

### 1. Opening of the Sermon

There are many great mysteries of venerable Easter, consecrated in the divine Books and preserved in the ancient archives of the Jews. Their admirable order and marvelous faith, their sincere religious devotion, concealed their holiness in hidden places as though under a kind of veil; the ancient priests saw them in shadowy outline and offered bloody sacrifices as gifts.

The Craftsman painted this holiness not with earthly colors but with heavenly virtues, with a shield gleaming with the gold of devotion. Loving the soul tenaciously, he dedicated it in the very temple of the human body, assigned functions to its complete and keen senses, and enclosed love within its heart.

And when that illustrious ruler of the stars, father of the heavens, leader of the day, emperor of light, interweaver of seed, and temperer of autumn had completed the course of the year and the fourfold periods of the seasons, he taught us to celebrate the solemnity of this day.

How many blessings the admirable triumphs of the Lord’s Passion have conferred upon us, I am unable either to proclaim in mortal human speech or to enumerate from memory. From that heap of benefits, therefore, which heavenly generosity has bestowed upon the human race, I shall place one grain of faith—containing within itself a manifold principle of life—in the lap of wisdom, so that, sown by the rain of the divine word, it may grow together in the furrow of prudence, produce great and marvelous things from a small shoot, and, under the shade of prayer, yield abundant growth.

### 2. Created Light, as Much as Mortal Eyes Could Receive. The Invisible Earth Becomes Visible

“In the beginning,” he says, “God made heaven and earth.” He excluded the errors of all the unhappy; he showed one God the Father as ruler and indicated one Son as creator of the universe.

“Let there be light,” and light came to be. “And God saw that the light was good”—not because God had previously been unaware of the light and praised it only after seeing it, since he himself alone is the light of all, as the Evangelist testifies: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12); and the Apostle: “He dwells in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:16).

He said that this light exists in the world because it is good according to humanity, not according to God. For God did not bestow as much of this light as he himself could give, but only as much as mortal eyes could receive. Nor would the one who illuminates the entire world have bestowed a brightness that mortal eyes could not receive or endure.

“The earth was invisible and unformed.” But the earth could not be invisible. To whom, then, was it invisible? To angels? Where could so great a mass be concealed? To human beings? Human beings did not yet exist.

For God founded the earth upon the waters, placed half the waters above the heavens, submerged half in the abysses, and gathered them into the seas; thus the earth appeared. And God said: “Let there be a firmament between water and water.” And God called the firmament “heaven.”

You see that he placed water above the firmament of heaven; and, through the separation of the waters, dry land appeared, and, as the waters withdrew, he made it visible. But it was called invisible and unformed because it had not yet been ordered and was not yet filled with different fruits.

### 3. The Spirit over the Waters Was Not God but a Thing of God. It Is the Seed-Bearer of Animated Creation. Two Spirits: God’s and the World’s

“Darkness,” he says, “was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” For if you bring a torch into darkness, everything is immediately illuminated. How much less could darkness exist where God was?

This spirit is indeed a thing of God; yet it is not to be understood as God himself. For although it is called spirit, not every spirit is God. It is called the Spirit of God in the same way as the angel of God—that is, a thing of God, but not God himself, who is the Spirit of God.

This spirit, therefore, which was borne over the waters, is the seed-bearer of animated creation. Hence, at God’s command, both the waters and the earth soon brought forth; for neither water nor earth could live or generate anything unless this Spirit of God animated them. Thus the earth produced crops and the water produced fish.

The Apostle says that there are two spirits, one of God and the other of this world: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). He thereby showed that there is one Spirit of God, who is God, and another spirit of this world, by which all things are animated.

The prophet Amos says: “He makes the thunder firm and created the spirit”—that is, the spirit which could not be called God, but which was generated.

### 4. Allegorical Interpretation of the Invisible Earth, the Division of the Waters, the Sprouting Earth, the Sun, Moon, Stars, and Fish

“In the beginning,” therefore, he made heaven and earth: heaven, the spirit; earth, the flesh—that is, the spiritual human being; “in the beginning,” that is, in Christ.

The Jews asked him, “Who do you claim to be?” He answered, “The Beginning, who am also speaking to you” (John 8:25).

“The earth,” he says, “was invisible and unformed.” Because Christ intended to assume human flesh, it was called unformed. It was not yet formed because it had not yet been formed by the annunciation of the angel Gabriel, had not yet been made visible by the Lord’s assumption of flesh, and was not yet full of the fruits of virtue.

The division of the waters signifies the peoples of the Jews and of the Christians, as in the Apocalypse: “The waters which you saw are peoples and nations” (Revelation 17:15). When he says that the waters were placed above the heavens, he announces the Christian people.

On the third day the earth sprouts the grass of pasture according to its kind and every tree producing fruit. When, therefore, he commands the earth to sprout, the catechumens in the Church are like grasses; when they believe, they rise up like stalks. The faithful also grow mature in the ear of grain; hence the grains of the saints are stored in the heavenly granaries.

The fruit-bearing tree signifies the various classes of saints. These trees can be overturned neither by the storms of desire nor consumed by the flames of burning lust.

“Let there be,” he says, “a greater light at the beginning of the day, and a lesser light at the beginning of the night.” The sun is Christ; the moon is the Church, complete throughout the world and daily illuminated by the sun’s brightness.

The shining stars are also the thousands of saints—that is, apostles, patriarchs, martyrs, virgins, priests, and all the righteous and faithful, radiating together with the flame of their virtues.

On the fifth day it came to pass that the waters produced their offspring, fish and birds. By the comparison with fish we designate the saints who live in the water of Baptism. Therefore the fish were worthy to receive the blessing first, because the faithful could be blessed in the sacrament of Baptism.

On the sixth day God made the human being in his own image and likeness.

# SERMON CLVIII

[Note: [Column 2056] Elsewhere, *On Time* 132; and later, Appendix 50.]

## At the Vigil of Easter, II

[Note: [Column 2056] Of an uncertain author. Vindingo, Verlino, and the Louvain scholars hold that the author appears to err against Luke, chapter 18, and John, chapter 20, because he says that Peter knew of the resurrection of the Son of God before the crucifixion, and that, when he saw the resurrection foretold by the Son of God fulfilled, Peter—who had come anxiously—departed secure. What it relates in no. 2 about Mary Magdalene being rebuked by the angel agrees almost entirely with the beginning of the sermon numbered 56 among the Ambrosian sermons, which is also the fourth among Maximus’s *Homilies on the Burial of the Lord*; a large part, however, has been excerpted from Ambrose’s commentary on Luke.]

### 1. Joseph Asks Pilate for Jesus’ Body

After the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ had been completed, and after the resurrection on which the whole substance of our faith rests, a certain Joseph appears—formerly a lover and disciple of the Lord, and one who, according to the circumstances of the time, was secretly providing funeral rites for the dead, since even the compassion of acquaintances was prevented by the fury of the persecutors.

The Evangelist John related the event as follows: “Joseph secretly asked Pilate, because of fear of the Jews; and he asked for the body of Jesus, and Pilate permitted it” (John 19:38).

While fear and devotion were struggling in his religious heart, he immediately devised a course that would satisfy both faith and fear: he asked secretly so that he might commit the slain man to the earth and avoid the Jews’ madness.

The judge preserves the same disposition toward the dead that he had shown when he heard the case: the one whom he had compelled to punishment, he willingly hands over to burial.

But after Jesus’ body had been buried, he immediately recovered the power with which the returning majesty had come. For the one whose birth had shown him to be human, death revealed to be God.

### 2. Peter Knew of Christ’s Resurrection before the Crucifixion

When Mary Magdalene came to the tomb, devotion, which remembered the Savior but had lost faith, compelled her to tears. Seeing that the stone had been rolled away from the entrance and not finding the Lord in the tomb, she began to grieve more bitterly because she had lost even the dead man.

At once she hurried to Peter, his disciple, whom, because of his merit and faith, greater concern over the Lord’s death affected. She announced that the tomb was empty; the stolen body was sought.

But Peter, who knew even before the crucifixion of the resurrection of the Son of God, which the Son of God himself had foretold that he would undergo, did not weep or grieve at such a report. Maintaining his customary confidence in divine acts, he hurried to test what he believed.

He therefore hastened at a swift pace to the Lord’s tomb, intending to return happier if he did not find the one he was seeking.

The blessed Evangelist also proves the power of the one who rose by what follows: “Simon Peter came and entered the tomb; and when he had not found the Lord, he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth which had been over his head” (John 20:6–7).

God was already manifest, about to carry into heaven the one whom he had made alive; he emptied both death and the tomb. For when the linen in which the body had been wrapped was exposed, majesty, already clothed with a living body, left the spoils of death to the earth.

Thus Peter, seeing that the resurrection foretold by the Son of God had been fulfilled, came anxiously but departed secure.

### 3. Mary Rebuked by the Angel

Mary, however, ignorant of the resurrection, did not cease shedding tears, not knowing that what she regarded as an injury was the glory of the Lord’s body.

The angel restrains her empty grief more than he consoles it, as the Evangelist also testifies: “Mary, why are you weeping?” If you understand the intention of the divine speech with spiritual discernment, he does not ask the cause of her tears as though unaware, but rebukes the mourner’s untimely weeping.

“Mary,” he says, “why are you weeping, when, because the tomb was empty, the power had claimed Jesus Christ’s body for itself—not as the result of funeral loss, but as the merit of the one rising again?” At the very time when she ought to have rejoiced, he reproves Mary for shedding tears.

“Why are you weeping, or whom are you seeking?” The angel instructs the ignorant woman with sound counsel, so that she would not seek the living among the dead.

Because this woman, even though rebuked, did not recognize that the one for whom she was mourning had come back to life, she was afterward recalled from her unnecessary tears by the voice of the risen one.

Jesus addresses Mary in similar words: “Woman,” he says, “why are you weeping, or whom are you seeking?” (John 20:13, 15). This is to say: “While I am already living, why do you shed tears for me as though I were dead? Or, while I am present, whom are you seeking?”

But when she recognized Jesus after being called by name a second time, through the operation of divine power she found alive the one she had been seeking as dead: Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father, be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CLIX

[Note: [Column 2058] Formerly, *On Time* 136; and later, Appendix 51.]

## On Easter, I

[Note: [Column 2058] The Louvain scholars say that it is found among the sermons attributed to Eusebius, although in those sermons only the content of the ideas is found. The entire text, in wording as well as content, is found in volume 9 of Jerome, among the spurious works.]

[Column 2058]

### 1. This Day Is Brighter Than the Others. The Mother of All Days

I cannot, dearest brothers, express with my mouth what I conceive in my mind; my tongue cannot unfold the joy of my heart. Yet this is not suffered by me alone, who desire to relate what I feel; you suffer it with me as well, rejoicing more in your awareness than expressing it in words.

It seems to me that this day has dawned brighter than the other days, that the sun has shone more brilliantly, and that the stars and all the elements are rejoicing. Those which, while the Lord was suffering, had withdrawn their own light and refused to look upon their crucified Creator—behold, now they follow him as victor and risen from the dead with a new service of their brightness.

[Note: [Column 2058] So the manuscripts read, with the exception of one, cb., which has “proclaim.” The printed editions, however, have “venerate.”]

Heaven believes, earth believes, and the net that fished the whole world could not hold the Jews.

“This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24).

Just as Mary, the virgin mother of the Lord, holds primacy among all women, so among the other days this is the mother of all days. I speak of something new, but something confirmed by the words of Scripture.

This day is both one of the seven and outside the seven. It is the day called the eighth; hence in certain Psalm titles it is superscribed, “For the eighth” (Psalm 6, etc.).

This is the day on which the synagogue comes to an end and the Church is born; the day in whose number eight souls were saved in Noah’s ark.

And why do I need to repeat endless things? The day would fail me if I wished to expound the entire mystery of this day.

### 2. All the Grace of the Sabbath Has Been Transferred to This Day. The Righteous Are Christ’s Crown, by Which He Is Also Adorned

I say only this: all the grace of the Sabbath and that ancient festival of the Jewish people have been transformed into the solemnity of this day.

On the Sabbath they did no servile work; we, on the Lord’s day—that is, on the day of the resurrection—do no servile work, because we do not serve sins and vices: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

They did not leave their houses; we too must not leave the house of Christ.

[Note: [Column 2058] Manuscript cb. adds, “that is, let us not depart from his commandments”; nor does it have “for we are in the Church.”]

For we are in the Church.

They did not kindle a fire on the Sabbath; we, on the contrary, should kindle in ourselves the fire of the Holy Spirit and melt away every vice of sins. Concerning this fire the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

The Lord desires this fire to burn in us, according to the Apostle—that is, he desires the Holy Spirit to boil fervently (Romans 12:11), so that the love of God may not grow cold.

They did not travel on the Sabbath day; for they had lost the one who said, “I am the way” (John 14:6). But we say: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord”; and again, “I have chosen the way of truth”; and, “Teach me the way of your statutes” (Psalm 118:1, 30, 26).

They crowned the Lord with thorns; but if we are precious stones, we crown our Lord.

Diadems adorn the heads of the rulers of this age; we are placed upon the head of our King for this reason: that we may be adorned by the Head.

[Note: [Column 2058] In manuscript cb.: “For this reason we place upon our heads the seal of our King, that we may be adorned by Christ.”]

They did not receive Christ, and they will receive the Antichrist; we have received the humble Son of God, so that afterward we may possess him in triumph.

Finally, our goat is sacrificed upon the altar before the Lord; their goat, the Antichrist, is spat upon and cursed and cast into the wilderness.

Our thief entered paradise with the Lord; their thief, a murderer and blasphemer, dies in his sin.

The thief Barabbas is released for them; Christ is killed for us.

[Column 2059]

### 3. Today the Gate of Heaven Is Opened. The Gate of the Church, the Gate of Paradise

For all these things, dearest brothers, let us sing with one united voice: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

Today Christ opened with the thief that flaming sword and gate of paradise which no one had been able to break through.

Today Christ said to the angels: “Open for me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and confess to the Lord.” Once opened, this gate is never closed to believers.

From the time when the Lord suffered until the present day, this gate has been both closed and opened: closed to sinners and unbelievers, opened to the righteous and believers.

Through it Peter entered; through it Paul entered; through it all the saints and martyrs entered; through it, every day, the souls of the righteous enter from the whole world.

For there are two gates: the gate of paradise and the gate of the Church. Through the gate of the Church we enter the gate of paradise.

Therefore we must live in such a way that we are not cast out of that house and, once cast outside, devoured by beasts. Fearing them in another place, the prophet mentions them and says: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul confessing you” (Psalm 73:19).

Behold, now the Lord, standing at the gate of paradise, speaks to us who have been gathered in his house and says: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117:19–20).

May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Column 2059] Thus most manuscripts. Manuscript cb., however, has: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. Let us hasten, therefore, my brothers, as the Apostle exhorts, to that rest, lest anyone, by wandering, fall into temptation and the snare of the devil; but let us hasten to the eternal rewards which he himself promised, who died and rose again for us; to whom be honor and power forever and ever. Amen.”]

# SERMON CLX

[Note: [Column 2059] Elsewhere, *On Time* 137; and later, Appendix 52.]

## On Easter, II

[Note: [Column 2059] Composed from the ideas of Gregory and Eusebius. Indeed, several passages enclosed in brackets here are not found at all in the manuscripts; once they are removed, the remainder would fit together more suitably. For no. 1, see Pope Gregory’s Homily 22 on the Gospel; for no. 2, see Eusebius’s Homily 1 on Easter; for no. 3, compare his Homily 1 on the Ascension of the Lord; for no. 5, see Appendix, Sermon 163, no. 1.]

### 1. How Christ Acted Freely. How He Became the Death of Death and the Bite of Hell

Although all the books of the Old Testament had foretold long beforehand the Passion or resurrection of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, the Holy Spirit also clearly revealed it through the mouth of the prophet David, saying: “God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance acted freely” (Psalm 93:1).

For he alone acted freely, who today showed us what he had done. He acted freely, of whom it had been prophesied long before: “He became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5–6).

Do you nevertheless wish to know what he did? Hear what he accomplished. Under no compulsion, but by his own will, he allowed himself to be hung upon the tree; he did not refuse to have his body pierced with nails; by laying down his soul, he endured death; he placed his flesh in the tomb; and, with his soul accompanying him, he descended to the regions below.

[Through him the elect, who, although held in the bosom of tranquility, were nevertheless confined within the prison of hell, were led back to the delights of paradise. What the Lord had said before his Passion, he fulfilled in his resurrection: “When I have been lifted up from the earth,” he says, “I will draw everything to myself” (John 12:32).

For he drew everything to himself, since he left none of his elect among the dead; he took away everything that was elect. For the Lord did not restore unbelievers, delivered over to eternal punishment for their crimes, to forgiveness by rising again; rather, he snatched from the prison of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds.

Therefore it is rightly also said through Hosea: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” (Hosea 13:14).

What we kill, we act so that it may no longer exist at all; but from what we bite, we remove one part and leave another. Therefore, because in his elect he utterly killed death, he became the death of death; but because from hell he removed one part and left another, he did not utterly kill hell but bit it.

He says, therefore, “I will be your death, O death,” as though he were saying openly: “Because I utterly destroy you in my elect, I will be your bite, O hell, because, after my own have been taken away, I pass through you only in part.”

Then our Lord Jesus Christ bound that prince of darkness and death and threw his legions into confusion; he broke the iron bars of the gates of hell; he released all the righteous who had been held bound by original sin; he restored the captives to their former freedom; and he flooded with splendid light those blinded by the darkness of sins.]

### 2. The Voices of Tartarus at Christ’s Coming

Behold, you have heard what our Defender, the Lord of vengeance, is described as having freely done.

After he had been lifted up—that is, suspended upon the cross by the Jews—to summarize all this briefly, as soon as he gave up his spirit, his soul, united to his divinity, descended into the depths of hell.

When, like a splendid and terrifying plunderer, he reached the boundary of darkness, the impious and infernal legions saw him and, terrified and trembling, began to inquire, saying:

“Who is this terrifying one, flashing with snowy brightness? Never has our Tartarus received such a one; never has the world vomited such a one into our cavern. This is an invader, not a debtor; an exactor, not a petitioner. We see a judge, not one pleading. He has come to command, not to submit; to snatch away, not to remain.

“Where were our gatekeepers sleeping when this warrior was shaking the prison? If he were guilty, he would not be so powerful. If any sins darkened him, he would never scatter our Tartarus with his radiance.

“If he is God, why has he come? If he is human, what has he presumed to do? If he is God, what is he doing in the tomb? If he is human, why is he releasing sinners? Has he perhaps made a pact with our ruler? Or has he perhaps confronted him, defeated him as well, and thus ascended to our kingdoms?

“Certainly he was dead; certainly he had been defeated. Our warrior has been deceived. He did not know what devastation that deceptive cross would bring upon hell—deceiving our joys and giving birth to our losses.

“Through the tree we were enriched; through the tree we are overthrown. That power always feared by the peoples is perishing. No living person ever entered here; no one ever terrified the executioners; never did a joyful light appear in this filthy place, always blinded by black darkness.

“Or perhaps the sun has departed from the world? Yet neither heaven nor the stars appear to us, and nevertheless hell shines. We cannot defend the guard of our prison against him.

“We entered badly.”

[Note: [Column 2060] In Eusebius: “We have been blackened”; this may perhaps be the reading that should correct the manuscripts, which have “we entered.”]

“We have been unable to darken so great a light; moreover, we fear for our own destruction.”

[Note: [Column 2060] In the printed editions Eusebius’s homily ends here. But in our manuscripts—one of which bears Eusebius’s name—it is much longer and contains most of the statements that are explained hereafter.]

### 3. The Denizens of Tartarus Address Their Prince

“Whence is this one so splendid, so strong, so glorious, and so terrifying? That world which was subject to us and always paid tribute to Death for our uses has never sent us such a one, never assigned such gifts to the underworld. Who, then, is this who enters our borders so fearlessly, and who not only does not dread our punishments but even releases others from our chains? Or is he perhaps the one of whom our prince said shortly before that, through his death, he would receive power over the whole world?

“But if this is he, our warrior’s judgment has been turned against him: while he seemed to himself to conquer, he himself has rather been conquered and struck down. O our prince, is this the one whose future death you were always celebrating to yourself? Is this the one on whose cross you believed the whole world would be subjected to you? Is this the one whose departure you promised would bring us such great spoils? What have you done? What did you intend to do?

“Behold, he has already driven away all your darkness by his splendor, broken all your prisons, [Col. 2061] cast out the captives, released those in chains, and changed their mourning into joy. Behold, those who once used to sigh beneath our torments now mock us because they have received salvation; and they not only fear nothing any longer, but even threaten us. Never had the dead here been so proud, nor had the captives ever been able to rejoice in this way. Why did you wish to bring this one here, at whose coming all those who had previously despaired have been restored to joy? None of their customary howling is heard here now; no groan resounds.”

[The captives’ ransom-exchange took place.]

“O our prince, those riches of yours that you first acquired through the loss of paradise you have now lost through the cross. All your joy is perishing; your pleasures have been turned into mourning. While you hang Christ upon the wood, you do not know what losses you are suffering in the underworld. Could you not foresee that you were bringing the overthrower of your kingdom to death, without any guilt? If you had examined the case, you would have sought the fault. In him whom you had recognized to possess nothing evil, why did you bring him to our realm? You brought this man, who was free, here—and you lost all those who were subject to you.”

### 4. The Just Address Christ with Entreaty

After these words of the cruel infernal ministers, and without any delay, all the iron bars were shattered at the command of our Lord and Savior. And behold, suddenly innumerable crowds of saints, who had been held captive in death, fell about the knees of their Savior and implored him with tearful entreaty, saying:

“You have come, Redeemer of the world; you have come, whom we desired and awaited daily; you have come, whom the Law and the Prophets announced as destined for us; you have come, granting in the flesh indulgence to the living sinners of the world. Release the dead and the captives of hell.

[You came after long tears; rescue us, you alone who suffered for us. Creator of heaven, you deigned to enter the underworld: our sighs were calling for you, our abundant lamentations were seeking you—hope for the despairing, consolation amid torments. At your coming our chain fell; night fled. When Life comes, death dies; neither torturer nor executioner remains. The condemned receive their desires; the Creator commands, not an invader. The chain is fastened upon the tyrant, and our torturer is tormented by punishment. Release, Redeemer of the world, the dead and the captives of hell.]

“You descended to the underworld for us; do not abandon us when you are about to return to the heights. You have set up a title of glory in the world [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read ‘in heaven.’]; set up the sign of victory in the underworld.”

### 5. They Turn Their Torments upon Their Torturers

Nor was there any delay. Once the petition and dispute of the innumerable captives had been heard, immediately, at the Lord’s command, all the ancient righteous received the rights of authority and at once turned the torments upon their own torturers. With humble supplication and ineffable joy they cried out to the Lord, saying:

“Ascend, Lord Jesus, with the underworld despoiled and the author of death entangled in chains; now restore joy to the world. Let your faithful rejoice at your ascension as they behold the scars of your body.”

Christ did this, as has already been said above. After plundering the underworld, he came forth alive from the tomb. By his own power he raised himself and clothed himself again in undefiled flesh. He appeared to his disciples in order to remove unbelieving doubt; he displayed the wounds of the nails so that he would leave no suspicion for the Manichaeans. He plainly ate and drank; afterward he appeared in the sight of many. Through a cloud he ascended into heaven and placed himself upon his throne at the right hand of the Father, from which the Word had never departed.

Let the Christian peoples therefore rejoice, for whom Christ’s blood was poured out. Let us all rejoice in the Lord, who solemnly celebrate the resurrection of the flesh in Christ. Let the Catholic Church throughout the whole world rejoice, because Christ the Lord neither diminished anything of his divinity nor failed to free the human being whom he had made.

Therefore, rejoicing, let us humbly entreat him with our voice that, for the sake of those for whom he endured these things when he came into the world, he may deign to raise us, once freed from the hand of the underworld, with himself into heaven. To him be honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CLXI

[Note: Formerly *On Time* 156, and later in Appendix 54.]

### On Easter, III

[Note: This homily is the ninth on Easter in the first Eusebian collection. It is plainly by the same author, as is evident from its style and subject matter, as the homilies there *On the Nativity of the Lord* 2, *On Easter* 2, 6, 7, 10, and 11, and the one that follows *On the Blessed Thief*, together with many others—namely, in our opinion, the offspring of the semi-Pelagian Faustus. It is clear that very many of his sermons were inserted into that collection of homilies under the name of Eusebius. This unfortunate teacher is especially represented by the statement in Homily 4 *On the Epiphany*: “Divine grace … wherever it finds the desire of our weakness, supplies assistance.” Likewise by this passage from Homily 11 *On Easter*: “Captivity was accepted through free choice; through free choice liberty was again to be restored. For the Lord, who opens the door, also awaits the concern of the one who knocks.” Nor may one pass over the words found immediately before that passage: “Therefore, if a human being had been seduced by the devil through a fall into disobedience and through the assent of a free mind, not under compulsion, he was to be invited by the author of all reason and justice, not dragged. For it seems utterly unjust that one who had fallen voluntarily should be raised against his will.” These same statements may be read in this Sermon 161, no. 2, without any variation in meaning. Finally, the semi-Pelagian heresy is suggested by the doctrine that Thomas did not deny the Lord’s resurrection but “wished it to be taught and desired it to be confirmed”; that Christ in him “formed not the vice of doubt but the disposition of concern”; and that, finally, “diligence in curious investigation was not excluded.” For no. 1, see Eusebius, Homily 7 *On Easter*; for no. 2, compare Sermon 103 of the Appendix, no. 4, and Eusebius, Homilies 6 and 11 *On Easter*; for no. 3, compare Eusebius, Homily 2 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, *On the Creed* 1, *On Easter* 10, and *On the Ascension* 1; for nos. 4 and 5, compare Eusebius, Homily 10 *On Easter*.]

[Col. 2062]

### 1. The Effects of Christ’s Descent into the Underworld

Rightly, dearest brothers, let us rejoice in Christ with devout zeal during this present solemnity, in which the third day has restored to us the one rich in the spoils of the underworld: exaltation from the depths, light from darkness, life from the dead.

Behold how widely the kindly concern of the merciful shepherd extends for the salvation of his lost sheep. At one and the same time he deigns both to restore the human being to paradise and to pursue death even into the underworld, there to be more gloriously captured in his kingdom and more magnificently triumphed over in its own dwelling.

At the descent of the heavenly Lord, therefore, the depth of the underworld is opened, and eternal night marvels at the light that is strange to it. The night was suddenly terrified—not by its own dead, but rather by its own death. For he was present who had said earlier through his prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O underworld” (Hos. 13:14).

And therefore death could not find in him anything that it might hold; indeed, it saw those whom it had previously retained being recalled to the heights against its will. It discovered that the one whom it had thought its debtor was instead its exactor; and the one whom it had believed must be bound as a captive by the chains of the underworld, it marvelled to see returning as a liberator, with his captivity recovered. Thus, the one whom by his descent it had judged to be human, by his return it recognized as God.

### 2. Humanity Could Have Been Freed without the Incarnation of the Word, but This Was Not Fitting

Our Lord, dearest brothers, could indeed have struck down the enemy of the human race by majesty alone, without the humility of incarnation and without the struggle of suffering. But the human being, who was held liable by the guilt of his own transgression and had fallen into slavery through his own fault, was not to be freed by violence but redeemed by mercy.

And because God is equity and justice, he is a law to himself. Since the human being possesses judgment, legal right, and the will of free choice, it would have been unjust for one who had fallen voluntarily to be raised unwillingly.

It was more equitable and more salutary that the one who, persuaded by the devil through pride, had been led to death should be summoned to life by God through humility [Note: So the better manuscripts read. Manuscript N has “raised up.” The printed editions read “strengthened,” and below, “strengthens and rescues to life.”].

Therefore, according to a just order, the one who through the cunning of the malevolent serpent had been led to destruction—not driven, but deceived—is again led to salvation through the wisdom of the benevolent Redeemer—not compelled, but guided. Thus the one who seemed to have fallen by his own will might be restored again by his own will [Col. 2063], so that there might be room for virtue and reward.

He does not therefore seize him by violence; rather, through just benevolence he summons and instructs him toward life, because the kindness of the one who invites also desires the merit of the one who consents, and the devotion of the most worthy physician requires the patient’s assent.

The present Gospel reading likewise declared his ineffable condescension in instructing us.

### 3. Christ, Born of a Virgin, Could Enter through Closed Doors

For he says, as you heard: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, Jesus came with the doors closed and stood in the midst of the disciples.”

What is surprising if the Lord introduced his glorified body through astonished barriers to his disciples, when he entered through the door of this world without violating the seal of his mother’s modesty—he whose birth nature did not know?

Do not doubt when you see the triumphant exercise of power in the one whom you perceive to have performed such wonders at his birth. What will the Jews say to this, when they left the Lord buried and sealed the stone with guards? Since these things are so, how could the obstacle of a barrier repel him whom the weight of the tomb had not restrained? Or how could a locked house exclude him whom the gate of death had not been able to contain?

What is surprising if he conveyed the substance of our body through closed doors, when even the innermost places of heaven, the secret familiar to the angels alone, are accustomed to lie open to him?

### 4. In Thomas, the Disposition Was Not One of Doubting but of Inquiry

His inquiry became instruction for the whole world. Why Christ Displayed His Scars.

When the other disciples had said, “We have seen the Lord,” Thomas answered and said to them: “Unless I see,” he said, “the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

What good ignorance, which instructed the ignorant and taught the unbelieving! What good unbelief, which served the faith of the ages!

“Unless I see,” he says, “the mark of the nails in his hands.” This is the voice of one inquiring, not denying. By saying this, he wished to be taught and desired to be confirmed; therefore the Lord said to him: “Put your finger here and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side.”

While Truth offers a gracious and measured answer, in his Apostle he formed not the vice of doubt but the disposition of concern. Since at that time the novelty of so great a mystery was at issue, diligence in curious investigation was rightly not excluded.

Moreover, these words of the Apostle concern the welfare of the world: the inquiry of one became the instruction of all. Therefore he showed his hands and his side. It was necessary that the visible presentation of the scars of the crucified body should establish faith, because the splendor of the new light had obscured the former reality, and brightness had in a certain way darkened recognition.

After seeing the scars, Thomas answered and said: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:19–28)! In a new manner, the traces of wounds bear witness to divinity, because the garment of the wounded body was the temple of God.

Here admire two substances in Christ. He sees the mark in the body and proclaims the God of majesty.

### 5. We Shall Rise with the Same Bodies

Why Death Is Compared to Sleep, and the Resurrection to a Grain of Wheat.

Where are those who say that souls are to be clothed with new bodies in which they had not previously lived? Behold, in the author of the resurrection I see that the very thing which fell has risen again. Therefore the dead are said to sleep, according to the prophet: “Will not one who sleeps rise again?” (Ps. 40:9).

Why did he compare death to sleep? Is there, in one and the same person, one who is dissolved in sleep and another who, in the stupor of that same sleep, is raised to the duties of waking? Certainly not. Rather, those very limbs which were relaxed by the stupor of sleep must plainly be believed to have awakened.

Thus, when the death of the body has taken it to be reduced to dust, it will restore that very body once its dissolution has been dispelled. The kindred spirit will recognize not an alien but a restored vessel.

For this reason, when explaining the mystery of the resurrection even from small things, the Apostle [Col. 2064] speaks in this way, comparing the resurrection to a grain of wheat: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.”

When, as is customary, the farmer entrusts crops to decaying furrows as though lending them out, is what is buried as seed one thing and what grows green in shoots another? No. Each body is produced not from nothing but from its own origin, and new things are renewed from old.

When the Apostle spoke of the resurrection, saying, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies,” you see that death returns what it has received. “To each of the seeds,” he says, “its own body” (1 Cor. 15:36, 38): not something alien to its kind, but what belongs to its nature and is restored from the quality of its own material.

The unity of soul and body will therefore be recalled into their former companionship, and their kinship will never again be separated throughout any ages.

It is for us to rely upon the grace of the Author and Redeemer, so that we may seem to belong to those of whom the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up together to meet Christ in the air and in the clouds, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16).

For he judged it fitting that the kindred substance of body and soul should reign together with Christ in heaven, since it served Christ on earth.

## SERMON CLXII

[Note: Formerly *On Time* 161, and later in Appendix 56.]

### On Easter, IV

[Note: Perhaps by the same author as the preceding sermon, which seems to be designated at the beginning of this sermon and which immediately precedes it in the Corbie manuscript. For no. 1, compare the preceding sermon, no. 4.]

### 1. Thomas’s Concern Strengthened Everyone’s Faith

Thomas the faithful did not doubt.

You remember, brothers, the preceding treatment, in which we wrote that the holy apostle Thomas, in order to confirm everyone’s faith, touched the members of the Lord’s body after the resurrection, and, to dispel everyone’s uncertainty, wished to examine the scars of his wounds.

For the blessed Apostle did not do this only for himself: what he did for himself benefited everyone. By exercising his own concern, he confirmed everyone’s faith.

Who, after this, could doubt that the Savior returned from the dead, when the eye recognizes his presence after the underworld, the hand touches him, and the finger examines him?

Although a Christian might be a man of modest faith or weak understanding, he could never have equated his own concern with Thomas’s inquiry. After recognition, association, and conversation, he would never have dared to ask to examine Christ also by touch: in Christ, to investigate a human body; and to believe his resurrection not so much through the glory of miracles as through the evidence of the injury of his passion.

Thomas, then, being holy, faithful, and just, diligently sought all these things—not because he himself doubted anything, but so that he might exclude every suspicion of unbelief.

For it was enough for his own faith that he had seen the one whom he knew. But he acted for our sake, so that he might touch the one whom he saw: if perhaps we should say that his eyes had been deceived, we could not say that his hands had been frustrated.

In the manifestation of the resurrection, there can be uncertainty about sight; there can be no doubt about touch. It is established by the testimony of Truth itself that the Savior returned from the underworld.

### 2. Christ, the Firstborn from the Dead

The Birth of the Resurrection.

Who would not place his hope in Christ? Who would not place his faith in the Lord, so that, believing that he rose from the underworld, he himself might rise from the dead?

The blessed Apostle says: “For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen” (1 Cor. 15:13). Since Christ has risen, the dead too will be raised; since the Lord has risen, his servants too will live again.

He is, as the Apostle says, “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18). Just as among those above he is the firstborn among many brothers, so from the underworld he is the firstborn from the dead.

[Col. 2065]

Someone is called firstborn because he is generated first, before the others who will follow. Christ is therefore called the firstborn from the dead because the birth of the resurrection brought him first from the darkness of the underworld into the light.

It must be called a birth where, through a certain transformation, the soul dies under the laws of Tartarus so that it may be reborn for the restored use of the body. The birth of the resurrection above is a kind of death of the underworld.

### 3. What Death Dies

Death Consumed in Victory.

Thus death itself in a certain way undergoes death, when the multitude of the dead is taken away from it into life. For the blessed Apostle says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death”; and again: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

When death is consumed in victory, it is destroyed by a kind of self-annihilation through its own defeat. It suffers defeat when its power is emptied by all who rise.

Let us consider what it means that he says death has been consumed in victory. Death has plainly been consumed in its own victory: when it subjected Christ to the laws of the underworld, it overwhelmed itself by conquering him.

For in possessing the one whom it thought it had overcome, it was itself defeated by him when he rose. We must therefore place all our faith in the glory of the resurrection and hope in the Lord chiefly for the life to come.

For the blessed Apostle says: “If we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:26, 54, 19). Miserable, then, is the one who hopes in the Lord only in this life. He is plainly miserable, because his hope is quickly taken away when this brief life quickly ends.

His hope becomes perishable when the pleasure of its sweetness slips away in temporal passing. Of such hope the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24).

Let us therefore hope in the Lord for the life to come, which is solid and everlasting, so that we may be not more pitiable than all human beings but better than they, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CLXIII

[Note: Formerly *On Time* 138, and later in Appendix 53.]

### On Easter, V

[Note: The author is uncertain. It contains several statements from Eusebius’s sermons, whether transferred here from the Eusebian sermons or from this sermon into the Eusebian sermons. For no. 1, see Sermon 160 of the Appendix, no. 5.]

### 1. Signs of Christ’s Divinity

Rejoice, dearest brothers, because the price of our redemption has been paid. We are not of little value, for us the one who redeemed us himself became the price.

For Christ the Lord and Savior was born in order to teach; he died in order to heal [Note: Manuscript cb adds, “he rose in order to reward.”].

The cross was deadly for Christ, but life-giving for the Christian. The Savior rose manifest to all by the signs of his divinity. For a star followed him after the womb, and glory followed him after the tomb. The angel who had announced that he would be born guards him upon his return.

The underworld gives back the victor, and heaven receives the triumphant. At his birth he removed error; when slain, he trampled death; he recalled from the underworld the one whom he had created. Upon his cross both our price and his kingdom hung.

Creation returns to the light with the Lord [Note: The same manuscript adds, “which had formerly been darkened by sin.”]. For you deserved to receive light from Light, which you lost when Christ closed his eyes.

Let heaven cast away the darkness that our Savior denied even to the underworld. Let the elements that had mourned rejoice together here, because Christ lost nothing of his majesty and freed the human being whom he had made.

### 2. The Necessity of Christ’s Death

Yet the faithless Jews sealed the tomb with a stone so that Christ would have no way out. But if the world cannot contain him, how can a burial guard him?

He is held there, yet reigns everywhere [Note: The same manuscript reads, “How is he held in the tomb who reigns everywhere?”].

He would have risen with difficulty if, before [Col. 2066] rising, he had not raised others. For how could he be unable to leave the tomb who came forth from an incorrupt womb without injury to virginity? He deceived the guards, sprang from the tomb, and appeared to his disciples through doors that had not been opened.

From there he came out enclosed; here he entered despite exclusion. The mystery of immeasurable majesty made even in death a mystery.

Crucified, he returns from the underworld and triumphs. Put your hand into the Savior’s side, Thomas; touch the wounds that our sins made; examine the place from which blood flowed, so that it might offer us the cup of healing.

Look, Thomas, upon our price; carefully attend to the marks of the nails. In those very wounds recognize the medicine—or treasure—of the human race.

Unless he had been fastened to this wood, the transgression committed through that wood would not have been removed. But he wished to be struck so that sins would not continue to strike us. He handed over the innocent in order to absolve the guilty.

Who could worthily express such great compassion? The innocent is afflicted so that the guilty may be freed; the Son is killed so that the slave may be redeemed [Note: After the words “the Son is killed,” the manuscripts add, “Look, Pharisees.”].

He performs the office of a merciful and mighty king when he displays the scars that he received for the salvation of his people.

### 3. Why Christ Preserved His Scars

Look, Pharisees, upon the empty tomb and recognize the sacrilege of your impiety. We recognize the nails that you drove in, and we worship the one whom you killed. See the one whom you pierced.

The Lord could have repaired the marks of his nails through his resurrection. But they are preserved so that those who committed this sacrilege may see them and be confounded.

O Pharisees, we see that you are impious and faithless [Note: The manuscripts, with one exception, read “foreseeing.”].

Death was given to one so that it might be removed from all. But when Christ the Lord accepted death, he experienced no corruption, just as, when he was born, virginity lost no integrity.

Hurry, disciples, and, having received authority, go throughout all the nations. Let those who are born in the flesh be reborn in the Spirit. Let the water of the washing cleanse whatever transgression has defiled.

Let all nations be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

But we, dearest brothers, who by no preceding merits deserved to be freed from the prison of the underworld and the darkness of eternal night, should strive to live so soberly, chastely, and devoutly that, preserving the garment of Baptism whole and undefiled, without any stain of luxury, we may happily come to the bridal chamber of the eternal Bridegroom and to that heavenly wedding feast, radiant with love and adorned with the pearls of good works.

May he himself assist us, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CLXIV

[Note: Elsewhere *On Time* 150.]

### On Easter, VI

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was left doubtful by the Louvain editors but was rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus. It differs considerably from Augustine, both in manner of expression and in its use and application of Scripture.]

### 1. The Figure of the Legal Lamb Is Fulfilled

The Old Priesthood Is Abolished.

That legal lamb, by whose sacrifice the ancient Hebrew people cast off the yoke of Egyptian slavery, contained in figure, through many sacraments, the more genuine victim of the holy Church. This was proved most clearly by the very reality of events when Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7).

He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). This is the lamb who, as a living victim, was offered to God the Father upon the altar of the cross as a fragrant sacrifice for us, and opened for us the passage from the region of the shadow of death to the promised land.

This, I say, is the one who, both victim and priest, brought the whole shadow of the former priesthood and sacrifice into the clear light, revealing it and bringing an end to figures and enigmas. He inaugurated for the new [Col. 2067] people of the Church a new priesthood and a new sacrifice, so that new wine might be put into new wineskins (Matt. 9:17).

### 2. All Things Are Renewed and Smile: the Earth with Fruits and Flowers, the Sky with a More Joyful Face

The sun is now brighter. The moon is full. And these things are for humanity; how much more, then, ought humanity itself to rejoice!

If a grain of wheat, falling into the earth and dying, renewed all things so wonderfully (John 12:24), how much more did it fertilize everything by rising again in itself with multiplied fruit!

And not only did it provide at this time a greater increase of spiritual growth for rational earth, but it also gave the earthly seeds themselves a more abundant yield. Hence now the whole face of the earth, bursting into shoots, is more cheerful in the varied adornment of its fruits and, together with its risen Lord, raises up again the whole nature of things, which until now had seemed almost dead.

Here is the pleasing beauty of trees and grasses. Through the varied gift of shoots, yet with an equal expression of joy, it festively greets this singular solemnity.

And what shall I say of the sky, which until now had been in a certain sense sorrowful, but at last has a joyful face? For some time a dense darkness of clouds had covered it and disturbed the whole expanse of this air. And behold, suddenly, as though justice were looking down from heaven upon earth (Ps. 84:12), wondrous serenity smiles upon the world, and the desires of heaven and earth come together in a single joy.

Thus they receive with common exultation Christ, God and human being, who came to bring the common peace of both and, dissolving the dividing wall of hostility, made both one (Eph. 2:14).

Now the source of all the stars, that solar splendor, cleanses its brow, greatly wrinkled until now. Like a conspicuous king in the diadem of his head, on the day of his wedding and on the day of the joy of his heart, he bestows more abundant gifts of his light upon the other stars as though they were his companions.

The moon, which from the day of its rising has always been subject to a certain diminution of itself, prepares itself with full light for the joys of Easter.

To summarize everything briefly: just as everything that exists in the created order serves human authority by divine dispensation, so all things share in a single exultation over human salvation.

Since every creature displays its joy for humanity through such great signs, it follows that human beings themselves should not fail to offer testimony to such joy.

### 3. Christ’s Resurrection Prefigured in Adam, Noah, and Jonah

Christ’s resurrection was prefigured in Adam, the first-created human being. Just as Adam, rising after sleep, recognized Eve fashioned from his side (Gen. 2:23), so Christ, rising from death, built the Church from the wound in his side.

Noah likewise, a farmer who, after planting a vineyard, became drunk with wine, fell asleep, and lay uncovered in his tent, then awoke from sleep and imposed a curse of perpetual servitude upon the son who had not concealed his father’s shame—Noah signified Christ.

Christ made his vineyard the Church. Drunk with love of it from the cup of his passion and stripped for a time of the covering of the flesh he had assumed, he rose from the dead, as he himself says in the Song of Songs: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” (Song 5:3).

As for Jonah, the Gospel passage plainly declares how he too expressed in himself the Lord’s death and resurrection (Matt. 12:40).

### 4. The Spiritual Celebration of Easter

Since, therefore, brothers, every creature rejoices in our salvation through a certain service of love, it is our task to draw from this something useful for our manner of life, lest the common joy of all things lose its rightful place in us, upon whom the whole substance of the matter rests as upon its head.

First, then, like the sheep of the Lord’s pasture, let us offer ourselves as a living and holy sacrifice pleasing to God upon the altar of the heart, roasted by the fire of love (Rom. 12:1).

With the unleavened bread of self-restraint, let us already have put to death the members that are upon the earth—that is, fornication, impurity, and the other workshops of vice—and let us prepare for ourselves a place in the ranks of the virtues.

Renouncing dead works, let us bear the finest fruit like good earth, and, following the example of a good [Col. 2068] tree, let us bear fruit in all goodness and righteousness.

And lest the brightness of the sun also be absent from our manner of life, let our light shine before human beings, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

If, then, we act in this way and the final day finds us so living, the resurrection of our bodies itself will one day be our reward. When Christ our life appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory (Col. 3:4, 5), for God lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON CLXV

[Note: Elsewhere *On Time* 153.]

### On Easter, VII

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It had remained doubtful with the Louvain editors but was rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus. It has some affinity with the preceding sermon.]

### 1. The Lord’s Death and Resurrection Prefigured in Various Ways

In Adam and in Noah.

Beloved, divine providence wished the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection to be prefigured several times through various figures of events and prophetic oracles, so that throughout all the passing ages of the world the hope of all the saints might be directed toward that one who is the expectation of all nations.

Thus, the fact that, at the very beginning of the world’s birth, Eve, the mother of all living, was brought forth from the rib of a sleeping man (Gen. 2:22), shows that the Church, the mother of believers, arose from the side of Christ dying upon the cross, just as the act of Adam’s awakening is a figure of the Lord rising from death.

Noah, who in the work of the ark and even in his own name signifies God’s rest among the saints (Gen. 9), most especially represents a figure of our Redeemer in this respect: since he was a farmer, he planted a vineyard and, made drunk by a cup of wine, was stripped naked in his tent.

This event properly refers to the one who became so drunk from the cup of his passion that he was temporarily stripped of the covering of his body; and immediately, awakening in the resurrection, gave a blessing to those who honor his passion in the mystery, but an appropriate curse to those who mocked him.

Of this cup the Psalmist says: “How excellent is my cup, making me drunk!” (Ps. 22:5). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “The cup that the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” (John 18:11).

### 2. In Moses’ Staff and in Jonah

The Mystery of the Time at Which Easter Is Celebrated.

When Moses’ staff was also thrown upon the ground and changed into a serpent, and, when it was seized by the tail, returned again into a staff (Exod. 7), it signified that the power of divine majesty, descending from heaven to earth for our sake, wished to become mortal; but after completing the dispensation of the flesh that he had assumed, it returned to the seat at the Father’s right hand.

Concerning Jonah, whom the fish vomited up unharmed onto dry land after swallowing him, we have the Lord’s own clear statement: just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth (Jonah 2; Matt. 12:40).

There are also many other holy proclamations concerning this solemnity of solemnities, and all of them are supported by the very order of the seasons. That order assigned the Paschal limit to the spring equinox, with only the full moon of the following first month awaited.

Thus, just as the sun, advancing upward from below, now first equals the nights in length, while the moon, through the daily increase of its light, also appears completely full, so the Sun of righteousness, rising from the underworld, illumines with his light the Church that had until then been established in darkness.

### 3. Christ’s Death and Resurrection to Be Imitated

These are the most sacred Paschal joys of this day; these are the solemn observances desired and proclaimed throughout all ages. It is right for us always to venerate them in mind and always, according to our ability, to imitate them in conduct, as the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). He was crucified for us for a time; we, however, must take up the cross daily and follow him (Luke 9:23). He tasted death for an hour; we must always put to death our members that are upon the earth—fornication, uncleanness, and the rest (Colossians 3:5). He rose from the dead; we are commanded to rise from vices, as the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). If, then, we now crucify our flesh for Christ, together with its vices and desires, and if, having been planted together in the likeness of his death (Romans 6:5), we have become conformed to him through the putting to death of our vices, then, when Christ our life appears, we too shall appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4)—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 166

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 142.]*

### On Easter, VIII

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors consider it doubtful; Verlin and Vinding consider it spurious. Neither the style nor the reading of Psalm 117:24 cited here is fitting for Augustine.]*

### The Cost of Human Salvation

The salvation of the human race, dearest brothers, and the world’s restored freedom are required at no small price; rather, it is tempered by Christ’s blood. *[Note: Morel, in* Elem. Crit.*, pp. 181–182, thinks that* comparatur* should be read instead of* temperatur*, and not without reason. M.]* Yet as much joy as the service of this venerable day has brought to believers, so much destruction and mourning has it brought to unbelievers. It brings joy to Christians through faith; it inflicts punishment upon the Jews who despair because of the cross. The insult directed against the Son of God brought them eternal death; for us it advances our everlasting salvation.

What an excess, I ask, of divine compassion is this, or how great a fullness of love is revealed! For this purpose God wished to descend from heaven on account of the ruined human being—not so that he might appear to receive honor in the world, but so that he might be hung upon the cross. And when he wished to rescue the deceived from the snares of death, he did not disdain to undergo death itself. And what kind of death? One more detestable than every other death. The Apostle affirms this, saying: “He humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). Thus, after his death, a victorious resurrection was prepared.

Let us say, brothers: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24). This is the Passover that we celebrate; in this we make our pilgrimage; this past event returns; this is rolled forward into the future.

## SERMON 167

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 154.]*

### On Easter, IX

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors regard it as doubtful, but Verlin and Vinding as spurious. They also reject the author’s unsupported assertion that all the events mentioned here occurred on the Lord’s Day: namely, the crossing of the Red Sea, Christ’s baptism in the Jordan, the changing of water into wine, the multiplication of the five loaves, and so forth. The passages enclosed in brackets belong to a sermon falsely attributed to Jerome, entitled “On the Paschal Vigil, concerning the eating of the lamb,” beginning, “Today, dearest brothers, the people of Israel.” We believe that the excerpts found here were taken from it, since there they fit better with what precedes and follows.]*

### 1. Why the Lamb Was Slain in the Evening

Today the God of mercy and justice rose from the dead by the power of the Father, as Paul says: “Who raised him from the dead” (Galatians 1:1); and the prophet: “Among the dead he is free” (Psalm 87:6). In him we too shall all rise afterward and live.

Because he has provided us with guidance to his kingdom, we too are commanded to prepare the way of the Lord—that is, humility, love of God and neighbor, justice, goodness, integrity, patience, charity, prudence, piety, and innocence. The Lord commanded all these things to us by his own example; he is signified by the lamb.

*[The question therefore arises why this lamb is sacrificed not during the day but in the evening. The reason is clear. For our Lord and Savior suffered at the consummation of the ages, as John says: “My little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).]*

Today the faith of the Church has been confirmed in Christ; in the seed of Abraham all nations are blessed; the Savior of the world has been made known; and he has brought complete joy to the citizens above and to human beings, when, after his Passion, he showed himself alive in accordance with his promise.

### 2. How Many Mysteries Make the Lord’s Day Glorious. The Day of Judgment

The Lord’s Day and the Lord’s resurrection are rightly joined together. This day is venerable: it is the Lord’s Day, the first day, the perfect day, and the day of light, on which the first light appeared (Genesis 1:3); on which the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea on dry feet (Exodus 14); on which manna rained upon the children of Israel in the desert (Exodus 16); and on which the Lord was baptized in the Jordan (Matthew 3). On it water was made wine at Cana of Galilee (John 2); on it the Lord blessed five loaves, with which he satisfied five thousand people (Matthew 14). On it the Lord rose from the dead (Matthew 28); on it the Lord entered the closed houses where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews (John 20:19); on it the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles (Acts 2:4); and on it we hope that our Lord Jesus Christ will come for judgment.

On that day every creature will be restored to a better condition, so that the sun and moon may receive sevenfold light, and holy people may receive eternal life from God on account of the merits of good obedience.

## SERMON 168

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 163.]*

### On Easter, X

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition it is doubtful, but Verlin and Vinding condemn it as spurious. It is composed of two parts: the latter reflects the style of Caesarius, while the former reflects that of Faustus; but the manuscripts do not agree in the latter part. Most of them, after the words in section 2, “Attend, therefore, dearest ones, and see,” introduce a markedly different discussion. On section 3, compare Homily 12 published by Baluze and Caesarius’s Homily 13; on section 4, Caesarius’s Homilies 35 and 31.]*

### 1. What Christ’s Passover Is

Christ’s Passover, beloved brothers, is the kingdom of heaven, the salvation of the world, the life of believers, the setting of hell, the glory of those above, the resurrection of the dead, the testimony of divine compassion, the reward of human redemption, and the destruction of abolished death.

This festival, consecrated by God’s mystery and recognized through the sacrament, announces the power of the Lord’s resurrection through the angels, makes it known through the Apostles, and multiplies good things in the hearts of believers.

This, therefore, is the day, beloved, which the Lord has made (Psalm 117:14), as you have heard: higher than all others, brighter than all, on which the Lord rose; on which he acquired for himself, as you see, a new people through the spirit of regeneration; on which he filled the minds of individuals with joy and exultation.

This, then, is the day of Christ’s resurrection: life for the dead, forgiveness for sinners, glory for the saints. For by the working of his powers it raises people from the depths, lifts them from earthly things, places them in the heights, brings the righteous to perfection, strengthens the doubtful, and condemns unbelievers.

For this reason the Lord rose today: to show us an image of the resurrection that is to come. Therefore today, rising through the life-giving washing, God’s people illuminate our Church with the splendor of snowy whiteness, in the likeness of the resurrection.

### 2. Baptism as an Image of the Future Resurrection. The Thief’s Devotion Is to Be Imitated

We ought to give thanks to our God that, while we celebrate the solemnity of holy Easter, we already behold an image of the resurrection to come. The human race will rise at the consummation of the age after death; now it rises in Baptism. Then God’s people will be raised after sleep; now they are raised after unbelief. Then they will be freed from mortal condition; now they are freed from the blindness of ignorance. Then they will be reborn for eternity; now they are reborn for salvation.

Therefore all who were baptized long ago in Christ but cannot put on a white garment should at least not abandon a white way of life. A sufficiently pure soul may often lie hidden beneath a black garment; and it makes little difference if someone does not have a white garment.

Such was the thief in the Gospel, who is said to have cried out with the crucified Savior: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Attend, therefore, dearest ones, and see what the believer obtains and what he deserves. The thief asks for the Savior’s kingdom on the cross; and while he endures a multitude of punishments, he is brought to eternal rewards.

Imitate his devotion, then; imitate his love for Christ. What the thief asks for while dying, desire through living well. Paradise is opened to his faith, and the certainty of eternal rewards is shown to our hope.

Let us therefore rejoice and exult on this day, on which the rising Lord struck down death and brought salvation.

### 3. The Duty of Sponsors

I therefore admonish you, beloved brothers: whenever the Easter solemnity arrives, let every man and woman who has spiritually received children from the sacred font recognize that they have become sponsors for them before God. For this reason they must always show them the care of true charity.

Let them admonish them to preserve chastity, to keep virginity until marriage, to restrain their tongues from curses and perjury, and not to utter shameful or lustful songs from their mouths. Let them not be proud or envious; let them not harbor anger or hatred in their hearts. Let them not observe omens; let them never hang amulets or demonic signs, either on themselves or on their own people; let them shun enchanters as ministers of the devil.

Let them hold the Catholic faith, hasten frequently to church, and, setting aside loquacity, listen to the divine readings with attentive ears. Let them receive strangers and, according to what was said to them in Baptism, wash the feet of guests.

*[Note: These words, like those of Caesarius below, sermon 257, section 2, where among the things for which we are liable to God’s justice he lists “that, contrary to our promise in Baptism, we neglected to wash the feet of guests,” are illuminated by ancient rites of the Church recently published by our Edmund Martène, book 4, p. 160. There, from the Gothic-Gallican Missal, among the rites of Baptism is listed: “While you wash his feet, say: I wash your feet. As our Lord Jesus Christ did for his disciples, so may you do for guests and strangers, so that you may have eternal life.” Likewise, on p. 169, from another Gallican Missal, after the chrism has been poured, the heading “For washing the feet” follows, and then this formula: “Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ washed the feet of his Apostles. I wash your feet, so that you too may do this for guests and strangers who come to you; if you do this, you will have eternal life.” An old Gallican Missal of the Italian Museum, published in volume 1, agrees with these words. It reads: “Collect for washing the feet,” followed by: “I wash your feet. As our Lord Jesus Christ did for his disciples, so you too shall do for guests and strangers. Our Lord Jesus Christ wiped the feet of his disciples, and I do this for you; you shall do it for strangers, guests, and the poor.” From this one may infer that the author of the sermon on the anointing of the head and the washing of the feet, published in the Appendix to volume 6, was a Gaul. There, in an exhortation to the newly baptized, we read: “When all the sacraments had been completed, we also handed on the commandment to you by example and by word. For we washed the feet of each one of you, urging you to imitate us—or rather, our Lord and Savior himself—so that, just as we washed your feet, so you too ought to wash the feet of your brothers and guests. We teach you not merely to be hospitable, but also, by honoring your guests humbly, whom you have received into your homes, not to be ashamed to fulfill toward them the duty of servants.”]*

Let them themselves also maintain peace, strive to restore those who are at odds to concord, and show priests and parents the honor and love of true charity. If, then, you strive to admonish your sons and daughters concerning all these things and those like them, you will happily reach eternal blessedness together with them.

### 4. Everyone Is Obliged to Build Up His Neighbor

Let no one deceive himself, dearest brothers. No human being lives for himself alone or dies for himself alone.
