Rather, as I have often urged, however many people someone has built up by the example of a holy life, with that many and on behalf of that many he will receive the reward of blessed recompense. And however many people he has given the example of an evil way of life—even if they do not follow him—know that he will have to render an account for that many evils.

Therefore, as I have already urged above, with the Lord’s help we must show our newly baptized people, as far as we can, an example of good conduct, so that we may deserve not to receive punishment for their destruction but rather to attain forgiveness of sins through their edification.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 169

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 159; later, Appendix 55.]*

### On Easter, XI

*[Note: The author is uncertain; the sermon uses words from Augustine, Sermon 247, section 2, to Volusianus, Letter 137.]*

### 1. Christ’s Entry through Closed Doors Is a Miracle

The Gospel reading, dearest brothers, which recently sounded in our ears, contains a great miracle. Although the Lord is everywhere, it contains his beneficent miracle, in which the disciples received the Holy Spirit.

It is a miracle that our Lord Jesus Christ, in true flesh, entered to the disciples through closed doors. Perhaps you ask me for an explanation and demand an argument. “If,” you say, “the flesh that rose was real, how did it enter to the disciples through closed doors? Can anyone’s hearing really accept that something which does not observe the work of nature could enter bodily through a threshold? Give me an explanation,” you say.

### 2. No Explanation or Example Is Given Here. Faith Is Required for Miracles. Thomas’s Dead Faith

O man, if you ask me for an explanation, it will not be miraculous; if an example is sought, it will not be unique. Surely you believe that the Lord Christ walked with firm steps upon the waters of the sea? You certainly believe it. You therefore say to me: “If Christ entered through closed doors, where is the body’s physical limitation?” And I answer: “If he walked upon the sea, where is the body’s weight?”

Let limitation and weight withdraw for a little while. He did these things for whom nothing is impossible. Christ, who was able to bring his flesh out of the tomb, could he not enter to the disciples through closed doors?

When you hear of a miracle, preserve faith; let the mind not inquire into an explanation. This is why the disciple Thomas also wavered and did not believe, although the Lord later strengthened him. His fellow disciples had said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into his side, I will not believe.”

For he knew that Christ had been fastened to the cross with nails; he knew that his side had been struck with a spear. He was seeking these signs, and therefore he did not believe. He sought the hands and the side; and while he was inquisitive about the wound, he had incurred death in faith.

O blessed Apostle, before your eyes Christ was able to raise Lazarus, and he himself could not rise from the tomb? You seek the places of the nails and have forgotten such great miracles of his signs? Before your eyes he gave sight to the blind, healed the paralytics, and cleansed the lepers. Have you lost the memory of the teacher within three days, so that you do not believe in Christ’s power?

Christ’s death in the flesh ought to be your life in faith. You did indeed see the spear striking him, but it did not penetrate the divine power.

### 3. He Revived at Christ’s Touch

Behold, the Lord comes again, lest the disciple perish, and says to Thomas: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing.”

O compassion of the Savior, who does not disdain to show the place of the scar! Thomas answered and said: “My Lord and my God!” Now he is your Lord and your God, because he wished you to see, lest you lose your soul through unbelief.

The Lord rightly speaks to him in this way: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:25–29).

Behold: the disciple trembled; the Church believes what it has not seen. Blessed is our merit, brothers, if it is accepted and preserved in the Catholic Church. Here the reward is received, where the true faith is held and recognized.

Christ established this Church through his resurrection; in it he has placed eternal rewards. Believe, brothers. Let him hope for rest who has not departed from the root. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 170

*[Note: Formerly, among the Vignerian sermons 20.]*

### On Easter, XII

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It contains none of Augustine’s characteristic force, as even Vignier judged, the first to publish it in the Supplement to Augustine’s Works.]*

### 1.

In the garden of delight Mary seeks the Lord; in the necessity of abandonment the grieving Church seeks Christ, so that she may at least find a comforter in paradise, since she has not yet deserved to see the planter in the arid fields.

Where the Lord rises, there the sorrowful Church seeks the pious planter. The Lord rises in the garden of delights, with the plantations of the dead propagated alongside him. That garden of the resurrection is depicted with the lofty cedars of the saints, the clusters of the prophets, the pine groves with their palms, and the fruits of the almond tree, the olive, Abel, Enoch, Elijah, Zechariah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

And in the withering field the Church seeks the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Who would not delight, after the ugliness of abandonment, to enter the paradise of delight through fields clothed with no flowering heads of ears of grain? Who would not delight to behold, after days of drought, trees whose dried bark bears witness to the earth’s mourning; to behold fragrant honey, dewy pomegranates, and the milky and scarlet blossoms of almonds and peaches?

The angels delighted to look upon these things in that little garden house—that is, in that pleasant tomb—where the angels were seated, one at the head and the other at the feet. Outside, throughout the garden, the vines of the risen blessed covered the world.

The angels delighted on that day of resurrection, because it had brought peace to the whole earth. They delighted in the new fragrance of sweetness from the dead, like amomum and cinnamon, where dewy balsams gave off their fragrance and irrigated the dead wounds of Christ.

The rose of the streaming blood delighted them; the lily extended from death delighted them in the flowering field.

There Mary bowed her anxious head, and with the linens of the Lord’s burial, like the broad leaves of plane trees in the streets, the grieving woman wiped her eyes of tears of devotion.

She looked and saw a lake, a spring rising from death, and, as it were, green plants emerging from that lake—plants interwoven by nourishing waters through hollow fleeces.

### 2.

Having contemplated the shroud with the napkin, she did not find the spring, and, though thirsty, was not satisfied; rather, in her more ardent thirst she lamented with greater feeling.

Nor did she plainly receive consolation from the angels, because she desired to see the firstborn of the dead. The angels say to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?”

Would that they might also say to us amid the tears of our distress: “Servants of God, why are you weeping?” There would be for us a renewal of joys at the tomb; there would be for us delight in the field, security upon the sea, and protection in the fortress.

And would that he himself might also question us—he who said to Mary, “Woman, why are you weeping, and what are you seeking?”—and say likewise to us: “Whom are you seeking, and why are you weeping?”

We would say: “Lord, we mourn and seek you, without whom we can do nothing; because in you we live, move, and exist. We seek you. Why have you rejected the living, when you have raised the dead?

“When you rose, Gehenna blossomed with trembling; and the earth withers without fruit. Behold, the rocks have burst forth with plantations of the dead; and the furrows of the earth, in their hardened depths, know nothing of the adornment of crops.

“We seek you, Lord, from whom we have been sought, because our feast days have been turned into mourning, and our songs into lamentation.

“Alleluia, which is the delight of the angels, is sung with the fear of pirates; our harp has become a mournful song amid the tears of the hungry, and the funerals of the dead have been darkened over with gloom.”

### 3.

Let us too say with Mary: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have placed him” (John 20:12).

Tell us, Lord: “Why are you weeping?” For your question is our consolation—just as if a physician were to say to a sick person, “Do not weep.” Does he not thereby give that person assurance of an easy recovery?

Where are your angels? Let them say to us: “Why are you weeping?”

And if we do not say, “They have taken away our Lord,” let us say: “They have taken away our father, our priest, our mediator.” For just as Mary was sorrowful without the Lord, so the Church mourns sadly without her own priest.

But he who said to Mary, “Go, tell my disciples: Let them go before me into Galilee” (Matthew 28:10), will himself say to us: “Announce to my peoples that they should come before me to the church, so that they may quickly see the presence of the father and receive forgiveness in it.”

## SERMON 171

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 162.]*

### On Easter, XIII. On the Resurrection of the Dead

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful; Verlin and Vinding considered it spurious, observing that Augustine would not have written what is said here concerning the two parts of the first death. In the Cluniac Library this same sermon is Abbot Odilo’s Sermon 5, On the Resurrection.]*

### 1. The Certainty of Faith in the Resurrection, Confirmed by the Testimony and Example of Truth

The confidence of Christians in the resurrection of the dead, divinely promised, is absolutely certain. Truth itself promised it; but Truth cannot lie. Otherwise it would not be Truth if it could lie.

The truth promised concerning the resurrection of bodies is therefore true, because Truth does not know how to lie; it must fulfill everything it has promised.

The Lord himself graciously demonstrated this resurrection of bodies in his own body, so that we might know with complete certainty that it will occur in the future. Christ rose, so that a Christian might not doubt that he too will rise. What went before in the Head will follow in the body.

### 2. Two Deaths. Two Parts of the First Death. The Second Death. Christ Assumed the Second Part of the First Death. Two Resurrections

We must know, beloved brothers, that there are two deaths and two resurrections. The first death is spoken of, and the second as well.

The first death, moreover, has two parts: one by which the sinful soul departed from its Creator through guilt; the other by which, when God judged, it was excluded from its body through punishment.

The second death is the everlasting punishment of body and soul.

Through the first death, therefore, the soul of every good and evil person is separated from its body; through the second death, the soul of the evil person alone is tortured forever with its body.

Thus both deaths held every human being bound, because the transgression of nature made everyone liable through the propagation of sin.

But the immortal and righteous Son of God came, and, in order to die for us, assumed mortal flesh from us. Since in that flesh he could have no sin, he endured the punishment of sin without guilt.

Therefore the Son of God accepted for us the second part of the first death—that is, the death of the body alone—through which he removed from us both the dominion of sin and the punishment of eternal retribution.

Christ mercifully accomplishes this in his faithful people: first, in this life, he raises them in soul by granting faith, so that they may believe rightly, and by bestowing charity, so that they may devote themselves willingly to good works. But on the last day he will graciously raise their bodies also, in order to grant them eternal blessedness.

*[Note: In Odilo the passage reads: “For this purpose he will graciously raise them in body.”]*

### 3. How One Passes from the First Resurrection to the Second

Having therefore been raised in soul through faith, beloved brothers, let us live with justice, so that we may also rise in body to eternal joy.

Let us depart from evil works, which mortify the soul even while the body lives, so that in eternal blessings both our soul and our body may deserve to be present.

Let us preserve the gift of the first resurrection, which Christ has granted us through faith, so that, when we have risen bodily, we may deserve to reign without end with Christ the Savior.

Then “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54); then true life and true joy will be given to the faithful. Then God will give his faithful the kingdom of heaven according to the merits of their faith and good works—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit in divine power, and so forth.

## SERMON 172

*[Note: Formerly, On the Season 157; later, Appendix 86.]*

### Sunday within the Octave of Easter, for the Newly Baptized

*[Note: On this very day it is read in many Breviaries under Augustine’s name. The opening, which is by an uncertain author, belongs to this day; but the remainder of the sermon, beginning with the words “we have, he says, a more certain prophetic word,” was copied from Sermon 210, in which Augustine discusses the Lenten fast, with scarcely any alteration except the change of sequence visible here.]*

[Col. 2075]

### 1.

Today’s festival concludes the Easter solemnity; and therefore today the clothing of the newly baptized is changed, yet in such a way that the whiteness removed from the garment is always kept in the heart.

Our first duty in this matter is that, since these are Easter days—that is, days of indulgence and remission—we should celebrate the festival of these holy days in such a way that bodily relaxation does not obscure purity of mind. Rather, abstaining from every kind of luxury, drunkenness, and wantonness, let us devote ourselves to sober relaxation and holy sincerity, so that whatever we do not acquire through bodily abstinence we may seek through purity of mind.

This sermon concerns all whom our care embraces; nevertheless, today, now that the solemnity of the sacraments has ended, we address you, new shoots, holiness regenerated from water and the Spirit, pious germination, new swarm, flower of our honor and fruit of our labor, my joy and crown—all of you who stand firm in the Lord (Philippians 4:1).

I address you in the words of the Apostle: “Behold, the night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and immoralities, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:12–14).

### 2.

“We have,” he says, “a more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19).

Therefore let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding feast (Luke 12:35–36).

Behold, the days are coming in which the Lord says: “A little while”—he says—and so forth. [lacuna] The more abundantly it is poured out through spiritual work, the more the mind that pours it out is suspended from carnal pleasure.

Moses, the administrator of the Law, fasted for forty days; Elijah, the greatest of the prophets, for forty; the Lord himself, bearing witness through the Law and the Prophets, fasted for forty, through whom Baptism is set before them.

For John baptized Christ while professing himself lesser than Christ. Christ, however, baptizes the Christian, who shows himself greater than John—just as with circumcision of the flesh, which Christ also received, but which no Christian now receives. For the sacrament of Christ’s resurrection is much better, and so forth. [lacuna]

Therefore, when the time of his death was already approaching, he said to Peter: “Satan has asked to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have recovered, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32).

And he plainly strengthened us through the Apostle, or when he revealed himself on the mountain together with those two observers of this fast, namely Moses and Elijah.

But because we cannot continue such a lengthy fast, receiving no food, as they did, through so many days and nights, let us at least do as much as we can. Except on those days when, for definite reasons, the custom of the Church forbids fasting, let us frequently impose even daily fasts upon the Lord our God.

Although abstinence from food and drink cannot continue uninterrupted for so many days, nevertheless, because of the errors of human beings—who do not cease, through empty talk, seductions, and depraved customs, to impose upon us troublesome concern on your behalf—I have commended, as far as I could, a time for humbling the soul.

For some people observe Lent more as pleasure-lovers than as religious persons, and so forth. [lacuna]

Consider, brothers, whether one should be called a Christian who is unwilling during these days to end hostilities that he ought never to have practiced.

## SERMON 173

*[Note: Formerly, among the Vignerian sermons 23.]*

### On the Litany, I

*[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. This is the very homily 37 of Caesarius in the Library of the Fathers, and it is also attributed to him in the Portarum manuscript and others. Vignier had published a mutilated and interpolated version in the Supplement to Augustine’s Works. On section 2, see Caesarius at the end of Homily 35 and above, Sermon 142, section 7; on section 3, see the following sermon, section 33, and Sermon 140, section 1; on section 4, see Caesarius at the beginning of Homily 12 and Appendix, Sermon 45, section 4.]*

### 1. Medicinal Days. How One Must Fight the Devil

Behold, beloved brothers, holy and spiritual days are approaching, medicinal for our souls. Therefore whoever wishes to heal the wounds of his sins should not despise salutary medicines.

The person who does not feel sick does not seek a physician on such days. And who is there, beloved brothers, who can rejoice in fighting in the arena of this world in such a way that he cannot receive any wound from the devil?

Who could stand day and night always armed against thousands of demons, so as never to be struck by the devil’s cunning? Who could even think through, not to mention enumerate, the deceptions and ambushes of the ancient enemy, of whom it is written: “Whose names are a thousand, and a thousand are his arts of harming”?

Therefore, dearest brothers, just as he always tries to wound us on every side, so each one of us, with God’s help, must prepare with all his strength against his ambushes.

Because he strives to overthrow us not only through harsh things but also through agreeable ones, and because we often receive the wounds inflicted by him not only when they are bitter but also—what is worse—when they are falsely sweet, we must always have spiritual medicines ready, that is, every good work, insofar as the Lord grants us the ability.

Let us therefore hear the blessed Apostle’s counsel and always fortify ourselves with spiritual weapons against the devil’s ambushes. “Take up,” he says, “the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:16–17).

What evil could the devil inflict upon one who has equipped himself with such weapons? He rises with unbelief; resist him with faith. He fights with pride; fight with humility. He displays lust; preserve chastity. He seizes wickedness; hold fast to justice. He suggests anger; pursue patience. He casts in greed; practice mercy. He casts in gluttony; practice abstinence.

Likewise, in all other matters, let us always strive to set opposing weapons against the devil’s wickedness. Then his devices will never be able to deceive us.

Therefore, so that with God’s help we may accomplish these things and, with divine grace assisting us, overcome the most cunning enemy, we must continually provide ourselves with the weapons of fasting, vigils, and prayers.

## 2. The Whole Church Celebrates Three Days of Litanies

He is a deserter of the heavenly camp who withdraws himself from the Church. Although these observances are shown to be necessary for us at all times, especially on these three days, which the Church regularly celebrates throughout the whole world, let no one withdraw from the holy assembly. Let no one abandon the Church, as though it were the school of the heavenly Physician, because he is occupied with earthly affairs; let no one desert the spiritual camp.

For we know, dearest brothers, that if one who serves an earthly king withdraws from the battle line, compelled by fear when he ought to fight, he will not only fail to receive the glory or rewards prepared for him, but will not escape the danger of the present life either. What, then, is to be thought of the one who deserts the army of an earthly king? Without doubt, the same must be judged of the person who abandons the Church of Christ on these three days.

Therefore, whoever, without some illness or a definite occupation, deserts the people of God on these days should know that in that heavenly kingdom he will receive not a reward but reproach, not glory but disgrace. Indeed, as a fugitive and deserter from the heavenly camp, he will endure eternal shame and a punishment worthy of his deeds. But far be it from us, dearest brothers, to suspect such things of you. Therefore, fearing this rather than believing anything unfavorable about you, I presume to offer this exhortation. Trusting more fully in your devotion, I believe that you will hasten faithfully, like the wisest of bees, to Christ’s hive,

> [Note: [Col. 2077] Thus one manuscript reads: “I believe, like bees.”]

so that you may receive the sweetness of spiritual honey from the divine readings and say with the prophet: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

## 3. How the Days of the Litanies Are to Be Celebrated; What Fruit They Bear

When sins cease, scourges also cease. Since, dearest brothers, the wounds of our sins creep upon us throughout the whole year, let us run faithfully to the Church on these three days and implore God’s mercy with contrite hearts and humbled bodies, so that by this three-day medicine of compunction we may restore all the wounds of our sins to their former health.

Let no one deliberately arrange occupations for himself, and let no one occupy himself with idle conversations, lest he make wounds for himself precisely where he could have prepared medicines. On these three days let no one draw blood or take a potion, unless some exceedingly dangerous illness compels him to do so.

Let us also prepare modest meals according to the discipline of Lent, and let us seek spiritual banquets for our souls by reading, singing psalms, and praying rather than bodily pleasures. Thus, devoting ourselves wholly to God, earnestly imploring his mercy, we may deserve, through God’s mercy, both to be healed of every sickness, freed from all sins, and delivered from the frequent inundation of waters.

For we must firmly believe, dearest brothers, that if our sins ceased, divine mercy would immediately remove the scourges due to us. Thus he himself deigned to promise through the prophet, saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3); and again: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Isa. 45:22).

Let us therefore turn to better things while remedies remain in our power, and let us move the good and merciful Lord, whom we have provoked by sinning, to mercy through good works, so that in accordance with his custom he may deign, in his goodness, both to drive away adversity and to grant us prosperity.

## 4. How the Church Is to Be Attended Profitably

Again and again I ask that those who, as I have already said, hasten with complete devotion to the Church’s hive, as to Christ’s sweetest honeycomb, should prepare within themselves, like the wisest bees, cells from the various flowers of the divine Scriptures, where they may receive holy and heavenly honey.

But those who come late, leave quickly, and are unwilling to wait until the divine mysteries have been completed are not to be counted among Christ’s swarms. For they do not produce spiritual honey through good conduct; rather, through pride and contempt they hinder themselves and overthrow others by the example of their evil behavior.

Therefore, dearest brothers, all who truly love the Lord, who come quickly to the Church and leave late, should persevere in good work. Rejecting idle or worldly conversations as deadly poison, let them strive rather to sing psalms and pray. Despising the bitterness of the world, let them seek in the Church that from which they may receive the sweetness of Christ.

But those who are negligent, who not only come late to the Church but also depart before the mysteries have been completed, and who occupy themselves in the Church itself with idle conversations, neither singing psalms themselves nor allowing others to sing or pray—those who are such should quickly correct themselves, lest they prepare death for themselves in the place where they could have found life.

I give the warning that belongs to me: let the one who despises the herald fear the Judge. The physician’s instruments are indeed harsh,

> [Note: [Col. 2077] The same manuscript reads “instruments.”]

but they make people well. The pleasures of the world seem sweet, but they deceive disastrously.

Hear me, then, brothers, as I entreat you; hear me as I admonish you with fatherly affection, so that God may grant you in this age health of body, abundance of crops, and forgiveness of sins, and in the future permit you to reach eternal rewards happily.

Thus may divine goodness govern our actions and deign to guide our souls, so that when the time of recompense arrives, I, who admonish you with charity, may deserve to obtain forgiveness, and your Charity, through your gracious obedience, may attain the crown; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 174

> [Note: [Col. 2078] Formerly, On Time 173.]

## On the Litany, II

> [Note: [Col. 2078] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars considered it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus regarded it as spurious. Its style is genuinely Caesarius’s, and the following phrases are characteristic of him: “In all the divine Scriptures”; “And although at all times”; “With great roaring or groaning”; “From there they make cruel wounds for themselves, from where they could have had healing medicines”; “I believe,” or “We believe in the mercy of God,” and so forth. For no. 1, see Caesarius, Homilies 6, 7, and 11 in the editions published by Baluzius; for no. 2, see above, Sermon 173 of the Appendix, no. 2; for no. 3, see the preceding sermon, no. 3, and Caesarius, Homilies 10, 12, 29, and others.]

### 1. Eternal Sadness Must Be Avoided for a Short Time

We must know and understand, dearest brothers, that we are celebrating days of compunction and repentance. Therefore it is not fitting for us to dissolve into excessive laughter or into any ill-considered and inappropriate outburst of mirth, fearing what the Lord said in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25); and also what is written elsewhere: “At the end of joy, mourning takes possession” (Prov. 14:13).

Nor should what we seem to do—summoning you more to sadness or lamentation than to joy—appear harsh to anyone. For if you pay careful attention, brothers, the Lord exhorts and admonishes us throughout all the Scriptures to be so watchful in this world that we may be secure in the future, as the Psalmist says: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. 125:5); and in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). For “narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, while broad and spacious is the way that draws toward death” (Matt. 7:13–14).

It is better for us, after a few hardships, to reach eternal blessedness than, after brief joy, to descend into the depths of hell. Therefore we must labor with all our strength to escape the punishment of the rich man clothed in purple and to reach the blessedness of the poor Lazarus (Luke 16).

For what did pride profit that rich man? Here, for a short time, he luxuriated in his pleasures; now, without any end, he feeds the flames of hell with his very marrow. It is better, then, that for a short time we summon you to salutary sadness and afterward deserve to reach eternal joy with you, than that we wish to pour a false sweetness into you for a time and afterward experience perpetual bitterness with you.

### 2. The Practices and Goal of These Days; Peace with One’s Neighbors Must Be Secured Alongside Peaceful Times

Although, dearest brothers, you ought at all times to seek God’s mercy with contrite bodies and compunctious hearts and faithfully ask him for forgiveness of sins, now, because the severe and most serious punishment owed for our sins is impending, we must implore God’s mercy with great roaring or groaning, constant prayers, and more generous almsgiving. May he grant us mercy and the blessing of heavenly waters, deign to restore peace, grant forgiveness of sins, and in his goodness deign to bestow prosperity upon us.

During these days let us strive especially to put an end to idle conversations, and, as far as our strength permits, let us devote ourselves to praying and singing psalms. If we wish to receive peaceful times, let us not neglect to preserve peace with our neighbors. For if you truly want your enemy the devil to be defeated, let your neighbor be reconciled to you quickly.

Let your anger rage against no one, and soon divine indignation will cease against you, according to that promise of the Lord and Savior: “If you forgive people their sins,” he says, “your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14).

### 3. The Church Must Be Frequently Attended

Let no one deliberately seek occupations by which he may withdraw himself from the Church’s assembly. Without doubt, he loves the wounds of his sins who during these three days, by fasting, praying, and singing psalms, does not seek spiritual medicines for himself.

The negligences that we have gathered throughout the whole year abound—indeed, they abound exceedingly. Therefore, at least during these three days, let us strive to do what pertains to the cleansing and purification of the soul.

Do not withdraw yourselves from the Church’s assembly, for we are not wearied by so long a period that we cannot endure it. Just as the one who does not withdraw himself from the Church’s assembly during these six hours is known to provide a great remedy for his soul, so, conversely, those who refuse to be present either through greed or for some other insufficiently necessary occupation make cruel wounds for themselves precisely where they could have had healing medicines, and burden themselves where they could have been relieved.

But I trust in God’s mercy that he will deign to inspire you in such a way that you will not acquire the negligence of sins, but rather, by fasting, praying, singing psalms, and giving alms in compunction, will be able to attain the remedy of forgiveness; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 175

> [Note: [Col. 2079] Formerly, On Time 172.]

## On the Litany, III

> [Note: [Col. 2079] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the judgment of the Louvain scholars it was doubtful; in the opinion of Verlinus and Vindingus it was spurious because of the harshness of its style. It is clear that it was delivered during a time of fasting, but it is uncertain whether this was the period now called the Rogation days, although the sermon occurs in printed editions and manuscripts before the feast of the Ascension.]

### 1. Fasting Especially from Vices

Since it is the season of fasts, dearest brothers, we must discuss fasting with Your Holiness, so that you may know how you should fast. For the fasts of Christians ought to be practiced spiritually rather than carnally.

Therefore let us fast principally from sins, lest our fasts, like the fasts of the Jews, be rejected by the Lord. What sort of thing is it for some impostor to abstain from foods that the Lord created while growing fat on the nourishment of sins?

“This is not the fast I have chosen,” says the Lord. “If you bend,” he says, “your neck like a circle and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, even so I will not call this an acceptable fast. But what then? Untie every bond of wickedness and every stubbornness of evil. Release the afflicted into rest, and dissolve every unjust agreement.”

For it is not enough merely to abstain from sins in fasting unless we add good works as well. “Break your bread for the hungry,” he says, “and bring the poor without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him” (Isa. 58:5–7).

Moreover, our fasts must also include what the Lord commanded in the Gospel: “When you fast,” he says, “do not become gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly” (Matt. 6:16–18).

Therefore, brothers, Your Holiness clearly sees that fasts cannot be accepted otherwise unless one happens to fast lawfully.

### 2. Fasting without Holiness Is Displeasing to God

According to the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, it does not weary me to say the same things to you, and for you it is safest” (Phil. 3:1). The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

> [Note: [Col. 2079] Thus Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain. The Greek text and the Vulgate likewise read this way. In B. it reads, “who brings forth from his storeroom new things and old.” M.]

Therefore, so that Your Holiness may know, brothers, not only new things must be said, but old things must also be repeated. We read that the Holy Spirit, through the prophet Isaiah, rebuked the imperfect in this manner: “I cannot endure your new moons and sabbath and great day,” says the Lord (Isa. 1:13).

The fast approved by the Most High is not merely the interruption of bodily nourishment, but also withdrawal from evil actions. Therefore take care that your mind is not weighed down and oppressed by sins, and that your spirit does not delight in the allurements of vices; then you will have performed fasts worthy of God.

But if long fasts consume your body and you remove food from it while not removing vices and persisting in evil, you are more hateful than pleasing to God. Fasts will then be acceptable to God if the conscience has been cleansed by holy works.

Why do you torment your body with hunger while you flatter it shamefully by sinning? Therefore let the spirit fast principally from evil, and then let the body undertake the fasts that must be practiced. Since fasting is the humbling of the soul, what sense is there in being humbled by food while being increased by sin?

Whoever therefore devoutly imposes fasts upon his body should first renounce vices, suppress the kindling of desires, break the impulses of the mind, conquer lusts, extinguish the torches of burning greed, extend the power of love more broadly through deeds, and generously distribute the expenses of his lavish preparations as food for the poor.

### 3. Fasting Does Not Move God to Grant Requests; What Requests Are Easily Obtained

Therefore let all the detestable sins of the body be trampled underfoot by the strength of the spirit, so that the soul may also be assisted by the holiness of the body. What one desires can then be obtained, if a chaste body and devoted spirit proceed, through careful observance, to fulfill the duties of holiness.

These are the things that move divine goodness and always open access to holiness being obtained through prayers. But if you lay your head down and scatter ashes over it; if, finally, you twist your neck like a circle and pour forth abundant tears to implore God’s mercy, you will accomplish nothing.

You cannot move divine goodness if you have neglected the love owed to your neighbors. For it is written: “This is not the fast I have chosen,” says the Lord. “If you bend your neck like a circle and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, even so I will not call this an acceptable fast. But untie every bond of wickedness and every stubbornness of evil. Release the crushed into rest, and dissolve every unjust agreement. Break your bread for the hungry and bring the poor without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your own household. Then your temporary light will break forth, your garments will quickly arise, your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58:5–9).

These are the things by which a person, even when frequently nourished by food, obtains what he desires, and by which, when fasting, he attains greater rewards of holiness.

> [Note: [Col. 2080] Manuscript N reads: “Then your light will break forth like the morning, and your health will rise more quickly.”]

### 4. The Fasts Acceptable to God

Such fasting delights Christ; indeed, such fasting delights almighty God. A person is not driven to fast by the continual guilt of monstrous sins, nor is he inflamed by an empty desire to attain temporal glory or increase his patrimony. Rather, he is always urged by religious devotion and sincere dedication. When these are accompanied by deeds of complete piety, how much will he accomplish, how much progress will he make?

By acting in this manner he will immediately deserve to feel the Lord present and favorable. Fulfill, then, the duties of compassion, and you have sanctified your fasts. Fill the entrails of the poor, and your soul will grow fat with the gifts of holiness. Clothe the naked, and your sins have been covered. Strive to receive the stranger in your hospitality, so that God may also receive you into the kingdoms of heaven.

# SERMON 176

> [Note: [Col. 2081] Formerly, On Time 176; later, Appendix 58.]

## On the Ascension of the Lord, I

> [Note: [Col. 2081] It is read under Augustine’s name in the Roman Breviary on the octave of the Ascension. The Louvain scholars removed it because it was the second of the Eusebian sermons on this feast. It contains a considerable number of sentences from Faustus’s Book 1, On Free Will, and from his letter to the deacon Gregory. Many of the arguments or words of that book and letter are also found in Eusebius’s first homily on the Nativity of the Lord. Hence our opinion concerning the Eusebian Homilies—that they strongly reflect that semi-Pelagian teacher—is reinforced. For no. 2, see Faustus, Book 1, chapter 1, On Free Will, and his letter to the deacon Gregory, as well as Eusebius’s first homily on the Nativity; for no. 3, see Eusebius’s first homily on the Nativity of the Lord; for no. 4, see Eusebius at the end of his first homily on the Ascension and in his second homily on the Creed.]

[Col. 2081]

### 1. The Lord’s Miracles Were for Our Sake; His Ascension Is the Guarantee of Our Own; Christ’s Two Natures

Everything that the Lord Jesus Christ performed in this world as miracles beneath the frailty of our condition benefits us. By carrying human nature into the realm of the stars, he showed believers that heaven could be opened; and by raising the conqueror of death into the heavens, he showed conquerors where they should follow.

The Lord’s Ascension was therefore a confirmation of the catholic faith, so that we might confidently believe in the future the gift of that miracle whose effect we had already received in the present. Each believer, having now received so much, should learn through the things whose fulfillment he recognizes to hope for what has been promised, and should hold the past and present goodness of his God as a guarantee, as it were, of the future.

A terrestrial body is therefore placed upon the heights of heaven; bones recently enclosed within the narrow confines of a tomb are brought among the companies of angels; mortal nature is poured into the bosom of immortality. Therefore the sacred history of the apostolic reading testifies: “When he had said these things, he was lifted up while they were watching” (Acts 1:9).

When you hear that he was lifted up, recognize the service of the heavenly host. Hence today’s feast reveals to us the mysteries of man and God. In one and the same person, recognize divine power in the one who lifts up, and human substance in the one who is lifted up.

### 2. Eutyches’ Error; From Where Arius’s Error Proceeded

For this reason, the poisons of the Eastern error must be detested in every way—an error that in impious novelty presumes to assert that the Son of God and the son of man are of one nature.

For if one says only that he was man, he denies the glory of the Creator; if one says only that he was God, he denies the mercy of the Redeemer. By this reasoning an Arian cannot easily possess the evangelical truth, where we read that the Son of God is at one time equal and at another lesser.

Whoever, through a deadly persuasion, believes that our Savior is of one nature is forced to say either that only a man was sent from heaven or that only God was crucified. But it is not so. For neither God alone could have experienced death, nor man alone could have overcome it.

Let us therefore recognize in Christ a twofold and twin substance: heavenly from the Father, earthly from his mother. It is easy to explain both in the one and same Redeemer by their own testimonies.

As man he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); but the same one, as God, declared, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). As man he said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38); but as God he spoke confidently: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18). As man he hung upon the cross; but as God he bestowed the heavenly kingdom (Luke 23:43).

The Arians, however, seeing the distinct substances not at all with a clear mind, impiously referred to God what belonged to man, believing that the lesser divinity was speaking when the weakness of man united to God was being displayed. Making no distinction between heavenly and earthly things, and not knowing how to distinguish between God and man, they divided the substance of God. By looking only at the words of the man, they lost God without the light of understanding.

But let us, as we have said, recognize a twofold substance of God and man, yet a single person.

### 3. Valentinus’s Error Is Refuted

That error also must be strongly avoided which impiously asserts that blessed Mary gave birth only to God, on the grounds that our Savior fashioned for himself some heavenly flesh within his mother’s womb and thus passed through the Virgin’s womb as through a foreign body.

But since the divine word says through the prophet, “He will drink from the stream on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7), if he does not possess our body, how is he our head? And when the prophet states elsewhere, “A child is born for us” (Isa. 9:6), he was not born for us if he took nothing from us; if he assumed nothing from what is ours, he bestowed nothing upon us.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if he did not triumph over the devil in our flesh, he exercised himself but did not conquer for us; if he did not rise again in our body, he contributed nothing to our condition by rising.

Whoever says these things does not understand the reason for the flesh that was received and assumed; he confuses the order and empties the benefit. If he did not accomplish the healing in our flesh, then he chose from man only the dishonor of being born.

Let such a dangerous persuasion depart from our minds. What he grasped is from us;

> [Note: [Col. 2082] Thus Faustus in the Letter to Gregory. The printed editions read “what he attached.”]

what he bestowed is from himself. I testify that what fell is mine, so that what rose again may be mine. I testify that what lay within the tomb is mine, so that what ascended into heaven may be mine.

Therefore, in that body of our race, Christ’s death gave us life, his resurrection raised us up, and his ascension consecrated us. In that body of our origin he placed in the heavenly kingdoms the pledge of our condition.

### 4. We Ascend after Christ through Hope and the Subduing of Desires

Let us labor, therefore, dearest brothers, so that just as the Lord on this day ascended to the heights with our body, so we too may ascend after him in hope, as far as we can, and follow him with our hearts.

Let us ascend after him with the same disposition and progress, even through our vices and passions. How through our passions? If each one of us strives to subject them to himself and becomes accustomed to stand above them, he builds from them for himself a step by which he can climb to higher things. They will lift us up if they are beneath us. We make a ladder for ourselves from our vices if we trample those vices themselves underfoot.

For evil does not ascend with the author of goodness; pride does not ascend with the teacher of humility; lust and luxury do not ascend with the Son of the Virgin. I say that vices do not ascend after the parent of virtues, sins after the righteous one, nor can infirmities and diseases follow after the physician.

Therefore, if we wish to enter the kingdom of that Physician, let us first heal our wounds. Let us order and guard within us the condition of both substances, lest the lower part cast the soul—the nobler portion of man—down into Tartarus, but rather that the more glorious nature may acquire with itself in heaven a body sanctified by it, with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 177

> [Note: [Col. 2082] Formerly, On Time 175.]

## On the Ascension of the Lord, II

> [Note: [Col. 2082] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the Roman Breviary and certain others it is read as the Sunday within the octave of the Ascension. The Louvain scholars nevertheless considered it doubtful, while Verlinus and Vindingus regarded it as spurious. It contains some material from the first and second Eusebian sermons on the Ascension, but much more from Augustine’s Sermon 261. For no. 1, compare the preceding sermon, no. 4; for no. 2, see Augustine, Sermons 261 and 351.]

### 1. How We Ascend with Christ

Our Savior, beloved brothers, has ascended into heaven; therefore let us not be troubled on earth. Let our mind be there, and here there will be rest.

For the present, let us ascend with Christ in our hearts; when his promised day arrives, we shall follow him also in body. Yet we must know, brothers, that pride did not ascend with Christ, nor greed, nor luxury; none of our vices ascended with our Physician.

Therefore, if we desire to ascend after the Physician, we must lay aside vices and sins. They all press upon us as though with fetters and strive to bind us in the nets of sins. Therefore, with God’s help, according to what the Psalmist says, “Let us break their bonds” (Ps. 2:3), so that we may confidently say to the Lord: “You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:16–17).

The Lord’s resurrection is our hope; the Lord’s ascension is our glorification.

### 2. “Lift Up Your Hearts” in Two Ways

Today we celebrate the solemnity of the Ascension. If, then, we celebrate the Lord’s Ascension rightly, faithfully, devoutly, holily, and piously, let us ascend with him and lift up our hearts.

But when we ascend, let us not be exalted or presume upon our own merits as though they were our own possessions. We must lift up our hearts to the Lord. For a heart lifted up but not to the Lord is called pride; a heart lifted up to the Lord is called refuge.

See, brothers, a great miracle. God is high: you raise yourself up, and he flees from you; you humble yourself, and he descends to you. Why is this? Because “the exalted one regards the lowly, but knows the proud from afar” (Ps. 137:6). He regards the lowly from nearby, in order to raise them up; the exalted—that is, the proud—he knows from afar, in order to cast them down.

Christ rose again to give us hope, because the human being who dies rises. So that we would not despair by dying or think that our life ended in death, he made us secure. We were troubled about the soul itself, and by rising he gave us confidence concerning the resurrection of the flesh.

### 3. A Heart Cleansed by Faith Draws God to It and Retains Him through Humility; Christ Is Our Way and Our Homeland

Believe, then, so that you may be cleansed. You must first believe, so that afterward through faith you may deserve to see God. Do you wish to see God? Hear him himself: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8).

First, then, think about cleansing the heart. Whatever you see there that displeases God, remove it. God wishes to come to you. Hear him saying: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). See what God promises.

If I, a frail human being of some kind, promised that I would come to your house, you would undoubtedly clean it, throw out what was superfluous, and prepare what was necessary. God wishes to come to your heart, and are you too lazy to clean the house for him?

All vices are hostile to God. Therefore, with his help, cast them out if you wish to receive God. God does not love dwelling with unclean, filthy, and insatiable greed, which unfaithful people wish to serve while desiring to see God.

You, then, cleanse your heart. If you can, work and act so that Christ may cleanse the place where he is to dwell. Ask, entreat, humble yourself. Hear Scripture saying: “God resists the proud” (1 Pet. 5:5). Be humble, so that God may rest in you.

Christ himself is both your way and your homeland: according to his humanity, the way; according to his divinity, the homeland. If you run faithfully, you go through him and will reach him. For in taking the eternal way, he assumed what he was not and did not lose what he was.

Let us therefore implore his mercy, so that he may grant us right faith and an understanding pleasing to him for the practice of good works—he who deigns to grant this, who lives and reigns forever.

# SERMON 178

> [Note: [Col. 2083] Formerly, On Time 177.]

## The Divine and Human Nature in Christ; On the Ascension of the Lord, III

> [Note: [Col. 2083] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars considered it doubtful; in the judgment of Verlinus and Vindingus it is not entirely spurious. Some things here genuinely reflect Augustine, but not everything.]

### 1.

The holy and solemn day of the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ has dawned today; let us exult and rejoice in it.

Christ descended; the lower regions were opened. Christ ascended; the heights shone forth. Christ was in the tomb; let the guards lie. Christ was in hell; let those who were at rest be visited. Christ is in heaven; let all nations believe.

He himself, therefore, must be the author of our discourse, who is the giver of our salvation. For about whom should we speak to you, if not about the one who has just spoken to all of us from the Gospel?

About to ascend to the Father, he said to his disciples: “I have spoken these things to you while I was still with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you. Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it fear. You have heard that I said to you, ‘I am going to my Father,’ because the Father is greater than I.”

He said that he was going to ascend to the Father, and the disciples were saddened because he was leaving them in bodily form. And he said to them: “Because I said to you, ‘I am going to the Father,’ sorrow has filled your heart. If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:25–28).

This is as though he were saying: “For this reason I am withdrawing this form of a servant from your eyes, in which the Father is greater than I, so that, once the form of a servant has been removed from the eyes of the flesh, you may see the Lord spiritually.”

### 2.

Therefore, because of the true form of a servant that he had assumed, he truly said, “The Father is greater than I,” since God is certainly greater than man. But because of the true form of God in which he remains with the Father, he truly said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

He ascended, therefore, to the Father by what he was as man, but remained in the Father by what he was as God, because he came forth to us in the flesh and did not depart from the Father.

The Word that became flesh, so that it might dwell in us (John 1:14), ascended, I say, to the Father, yet promised his presence, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

According to the form of a servant,

> [Note: [Col. 2084] Perhaps “according to the form of God.”]

the apostle John says of him, “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). According to the form of God, the Apostle Paul says of him: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

According to the form of God, he himself says of himself: “I and the Father are one.” According to the form of a servant, he says: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38).

From where comes that confidence, and from where this fear? The former voice proceeds from the property of the substance; the latter from participation in the weakness that was assumed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, understanding these things wisely from the holy Scriptures, let us discern them when we read. But while discerning them, let us ask the Lord himself for understanding, lest we perhaps go astray—to him belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 179

> [Note: [Col. 2084] Formerly, On Time 178.]

## On the Ascension of the Lord, IV

> [Note: [Col. 2084] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars allow doubt concerning it; following Verlinus, Vindingus wishes it rejected, demonstrating that it is the work of an inept poet rather than of a learned orator.]

### 1. The Apostles’ Feelings at Christ’s Ascension

The whole world also sings of the renowned and royal mystery of the Lord’s Ascension, by which Christ raised earth to heaven, and celebrates the triumphs of its Lord with festive rejoicing: for “he raised the needy from the earth and lifted the poor from the dungheap” (Ps. 112:7), and raised him to the Father.

Who, then, can ascend there and pass through the aerial demons, except the one who alone could not have sin? That cross, therefore, did not harm him but benefited him, because Christ conquered for us through it, and could not himself be overcome upon it. Neither tombs nor the underworld subdued the victorious flesh. God expended for humanity what he had decreed, and seized the one whom he desired.

The Apostles, present there, see this. They follow him with fearful hearts, confused minds, and trembling eyes, as he gradually raises himself toward the heights, until serene daylight received the cloud released of its own accord and concealed him from human sight, surrounded by flashing brilliance.

When, therefore, the disciples, struck by so great a light, could no longer see him, and the ruddy radiance eluded their inquisitive eyes in flashing strokes, two angels, sent immediately from among the victors, consoled the Apostles, who had been cast down by fear and grief, with these words: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Thus he will come, they say: manifest, just as now he is gloriously raised above the stars; and the secrets of the heavens receive him, whom they will pour forth again.

### 2. The Affection of the Air, the Heavens, and the Heavenly Hosts

The immense air is sanctified by the divine procession, and that entire flying multitude passes through the breezes as Christ ascends. All heaven trembles; the stars are transformed; immediately that lightning-like army of the heavenly host gathers.

They see their king carrying back the spoils of living flesh and, after conquering the enemy, ascending as a human being into the heights. They recognize in his scars the marks of battle; they adore in his flesh the wounds now healed—where the stain of sin had extinguished nothing, nor had that venom-laden dragon vomited anything through its poisonous violence. For the serpent did not leave its track upon the rock.

The armies applaud; the trumpets sound; gentle melodies, mingling with joyful choirs, pour forth. Behold, at once that splendid heavenly senate departs from its kingdoms. For in the lowest depths of heaven the broad royal palace of God is opened with joyful songs; on every side the barriers of the starry heaven and the secrets of the star-bearing universe are laid open, their structure entirely loosened.

The air, divided into a double citadel, withdrew, and the lofty sides of the broad heavens hung down with their edges cut apart. There the day becomes one, without a heaven; it trembles with bright flashes [Note: [Col. 2085] Perhaps, “it glows.”], and then the joyful services resound among themselves in alternating songs:

“Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

For he was ascending, drenched in the redness of blood and crowned with the victorious laurels of his trophies.

### 3. The Angels’ Wonder

All the heavenly beings saw Christ, beautiful in his wounds, carrying back the spoils taken from the tyrant’s camp. Marveling at the shining standards of divine power, they resound with hymns such as these and lead him onward in joy:

“Who is this King of glory?” they ask.

And they answer: “The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (Ps. 24:7, 10).

This is he who is “white and ruddy, marked by many wounds”; this is he who “had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2): weak in the snare, strong in the spoils; lowly in his little body, armed in battle; hideous in death, beautiful in resurrection; white from the Virgin, ruddy on the cross; darkened in disgrace, radiant in heaven.

Who, brothers, could have known that God was concealed in flesh and majesty dwelt in a body, and that he would wage war in the world in such a way that he would soon raise that very body from the tombs to heaven?

Majesty, therefore, withdrew with the flesh beneath the divine veils. Heaven learned to carry humanity, and the ethereal realms, serving beneath Christ’s feet, lay prostrate.

Behold, the gate that Adam had closed now stands open; the barrier that iniquity had fastened against heaven has been unbarred. If anyone holds fast to Christ and confesses the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of one substance, through him he will enter the gates of heaven without fear. Amen.

## SERMON 180 [Note: [Col. 2085] Previously, On Time 179.]

### On the Ascension of the Lord, V [Note: [Col. 2085] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars consider it doubtful; Verlin and Vinding consider it spurious. The style and manner of speaking are not unlike those of the preceding sermon. It had been wrongly published some years ago under the name of Fulgentius together with the following sermon; compare its section 3.]

### 1. The Joys of Heaven at the Lord’s Ascension

With how many ornaments of joy the palace of heaven shines today! For the angels have at last received what they had long hoped for and have sung their hymn. At the raising of the gates there is light in heaven and splendor at the doors, because Christ has again ascended, coming forth from his bridal chamber (Ps. 19:6), to ascend upon his throne.

Therefore holy David set his instrument at the gates of heaven, singing a new song: for “the one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. 4:10). Striking his instrument with happier plectra, it resounds more joyfully, and he says, seeing the firstborn of the eternal Consul—not adorned with gold and gems, but whitened by the ice of clouds [Col. 2086]:

“He makes the cloud his ascent, he who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 104:3).

For he has already walked upon the asp and basilisk and trampled the lion and dragon (Ps. 91:13)—with the foot of death, with the applause of resurrection.

Wonderful in our eyes, he flashes forth, glorified by the powers of the Ascension. Sitting upon a light cloud, he rains upon the Apostles the inheritance of peace and the testamentary love:

“My peace,” he says, “I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

### 2. The Entreaty of the Mourning Apostles

Invited to this melody of resounding instruments before the royal palace of heaven, the Apostles follow, seeking the grace of blessing. The sons of the bridegroom walk with the Lord, about to receive the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

When he had raised his hands, he blessed them (Luke 24:50). He gave them the precious wedding pledge of his gift—not one fashioned from gold and gems, but a chain woven from the links of love, by which, bound to him, they might follow him to the bride of the Lamb, Jerusalem, their everlasting homeland.

“Lord,” they say, “why do you leave us as you ascend, you who chose us while going before us on the shore? Lord, when shall we receive from afar your words, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and taste the balm dripping and distilling from your lips and throat? Either instruct us where you are ascending, or do not abandon us when you ascend. We have been left exposed and stripped in the open, as though bereft of the shield of your kindness, like young birds deprived of the covering of their mother’s sheltering wings.

“When will you come to us, you who redeemed us? Your death was our sin; let your ascension be our pledge, lest those whom you raised from the groans of the underworld be swallowed up and drowned by excessive grief.”

### 3. Their Consolation

As the Lord ascended, therefore, looking down from the height of the cloud upon the sorrow of his foster-children, he sent forth comforters for their grief—messengers of the one ascending and heralds of the one who would return.

“Men,” they say, “of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

He will come in this way: there will be one ascent, one cloud-bearing litter, one gentle appearance—but glorious for the righteous and fearsome for sinners. His coming will not terrify you, whom his ascension consoles.

He will come in this way, displaying the wounds of the nails unharmed and the bloody necklaces of his openings. When he presents to you, the sons of the bridegroom, the crown of heavenly rule, he will not change the wounds of the cross, because the sign of the Son of Man will shine.

Having therefore received the command of the ascending one (Luke 24:49) and the precious pledge of the Holy Spirit, who was to come from above, the Apostles were in the temple, united in praising the Lord (Acts 1:14), so that the crown of the coming gifts might find them all together in one place, like a crown of fire.

Therefore, brothers, let us always remain united in the temple, and as we walk in the house of the Lord in the harmony of his peace, let us await his coming. In his temple let us all say, “Glory” (Ps. 29:9), so that the fire of grace may also rest upon us. Amen.

## SERMON 181 [Note: [Col. 2086] Previously, On Time 180.]

### On the Ascension of the Lord, VI [Note: [Col. 2086] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars also consider this doubtful; Verlin and Vinding regard it as spurious. In certain manuscripts it is attributed to Fulgentius, but it should be assigned to the same author as the two preceding sermons. Compare the preceding sermon, section 3, concerning section 3 of this sermon.]

### 1. The Apostles’ Feelings at Christ’s Ascension

It is delightful to behold Christ the Lord ascending upon carrying clouds, when, rising from the dead, he began to return to heaven, from which he had come to save the human race.

Who are those who await the ascender? Those who saw him rising, fled from him hanging, and follow the ascending one with their eyes. Fear on the cross, love in the clouds, a delightful sight in the air.

O sweet affection of the one descending! O delightful sight of the one flying upward! He bids farewell and blesses in peace. They commend themselves to him, and he leaves them the grace of blessing. He blesses them with outstretched hands, and clouds prepared for his reception receive him (Luke [Col. 2087] 24:50–51).

He finishes speaking, and now returns to heaven. For suddenly the white ascent of a cloud appeared, prepared in heaven. A cloud appeared, and the one who brings out the clouds from the end of the earth entered it (Ps. 135:7), so that the beauty of the cloud might delight their eyes and the sweetness of the one ascending from heaven sprinkle them with dew, lest only the empty anxiety of those who longed remain.

### 2. The Angels’ Announcement of the Mysteries

Behold, upon the shield of the Acts of the Apostles, the painted lights of the fishermen who were hanging there live. The comforter who ascended as Savior is present.

He immediately sends two heavenly officers, to make his frightened foster-children secure and to turn their tears into joy. For heavenly comforters had to be sent, lest the trembling fishermen remain disconsolate.

When an emperor passes from one city to another and his arrival is announced, only members of his household, officers [Note: [Col. 2087] Cujacius thinks that “protectors” should be substituted.], and courtiers are sent to announce to the provincials the king’s arrival or return. So too, when the Lord ascended, a throng of heavenly officers shone forth, singing, so that, as though they were provincials, they might cause the shepherds’ hearts to breathe again after their fear.

When he also suffers and rises again, household angels are sent to announce from the cloud and from the official chamber of the tomb that the Lord of heaven has risen. And now, when he ascends, two courtiers of the heavenly empire are sent from the choir of the preceding Powers and from the multitude of singers in the aerial army, so that the weeping eyes of the fishermen might find rest; they recite a heavenly hymn.

### 3. What Kind of Christ Will Return

“Fishermen,” they say, “men of Galilee, why do you look at Jesus going into heaven? He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

He departed as one to be desired; he will not come to you as one to be feared. A cloud at his coming, a cloud at his return. He carried wounds; he will bring them back again. He carried back the cross in triumph; the sign of the Son of Man will appear for you in heaven.

He will come in this way: in the same body, in the same cloud, in the same reality; for you in love, for the ungodly in trembling.

Blessed are those to whom it is truly said, “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” Will he come in this way to the eyes of sinners? It will be the same reality, but it will not be the same security.

It will be the day of the fearful judgment, the descent of the angels, and the resurrection of the dead. The angels will ascend, and with a kind of finger of the sounding trumpet they will touch the tombs of the trembling earth, so that they may restore the pledges to the fiery throne of the Judge.

The angels will ascend to the tombs of the prophets, of the Apostles themselves, and of all the saints, and will say to them: “Behold, this is the one who returns again in the same way as he ascended. We said that he would come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven. You who led him away as he departed, receive him as he returns.”

This address is not in the seventy languages. Rather, the clouds are plainly called rain-bearing clouds, so that they may meet in dew and refreshing pleasantness those whose consciences contain no accusation.

Let us therefore ask the Lord our God that, just as today we celebrate the season and day of the Ascension, so we may be found worthy to receive the morning mercy of the one who returns, so that we may say to him: “In the morning I will worship you, Lord; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will contemplate you” (Ps. 5:4–5).

## SERMON 182 [Note: [Col. 2087] Previously, On Time 185.]

### On Pentecost, I [Note: [Col. 2087] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It had remained doubtful according to the Louvain scholars; Verlin and Vinding assert that it is spurious, both because of the difference in style and because the word “gladiators” is improperly used here in section 4: “he draws the sword against the betrayer and the gladiators.” Moreover, we have detected some words of this sermon in the Eusebian Homilies, namely in Homily 1 on the Creed: “I will ask the Father: the Son is the one understood to be asking, the Father is the one indicated as being asked, and the Holy Spirit is the one promised to be sent by the Father.” Some others occur likewise in the Homily on Pentecost. Concerning section 1, compare Eusebius’s words in Homily 1 on the Creed; concerning sections 3 and 4, compare Eusebius’s Homily on Pentecost.]

### 1. The Holy Spirit Is God: Companion of Majesty, Expression of the Trinity, Vicar of the Redeemer

After that singular and remarkable victory by which the public champion both fought for the world and conquered, after he had not only drawn the frailty of our condition from the underworld but also raised it to the heights of his kingdom, on this day, according to his holy word, he gave the Holy Spirit, concerning whom he had already said to his Apostles:

“I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16).

Another, certainly, not lesser; another Paraclete—that is, one of similar glory or nature, and of the same substance—so that the disciples’ faith, prepared by a truthful promise to await so great a gift, might recognize as the true God the one whom it remembered had been promised by the Lord in God’s place.

“And another Paraclete,” he says: understand him as the companion of Majesty, whom you see made equal to Majesty. “I will ask the Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete.”

How well, under the title of promise, he applied the distinction of the Trinity! The Father is the one indicated as being asked; the Son is the one understood to be asking; the Holy Spirit is the one promised to be sent by the Father.

How great and ineffable is the Redeemer’s compassion! He carried humanity to heaven and sent God to earth. How great is the Creator’s care for the restoration of his work!

Behold, again a new medicine is sent from above; behold, again Majesty itself deigns to visit its sick. Behold, again divine things are mingled with human things—that is, the Vicar of the Redeemer—so that the benefits which the Lord Savior began may be completed through the particular power of the Holy Spirit; what he redeemed, let this one sanctify; what he acquired, let this one guard.

Thus the unity of the Godhead is demonstrated through the unity of grace and gift, so that the Holy Spirit, one God in substance, another in person, one in equal mercy, may be worshiped with equal reverence.

### 2. No Longer a Visitor but an Eternal Dweller: Through Substance, Not Operation Alone

The Apostles: rays of the sun and lamps of truth.

Therefore on this day the Holy Spirit descended upon the temples of his Apostles prepared for him, like a rain of sanctification—not now a sudden visitor, but an everlasting comforter and eternal inhabitant.

For just as he had said concerning himself to his Apostles, “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20), so also concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Father will give you the Paraclete, who will be with you forever.”

On this day, therefore, he was present with his faithful not merely through the grace of visitation and operation, but through the very presence of Majesty. Into the vessels there flowed not merely the fragrance of balsam, but the very substance of the sacred ointment, from whose fragrance the breadth of the whole world would be filled, and those who drew near to their teaching would become capable of and sharers in God.

He therefore sat upon each of them like fire, concerning which our Savior testifies, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), and of which it is said, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

He therefore drenched his Apostles with the fountain of living light, so that afterward they might illuminate the whole world like twelve rays of the sun and as many lamps of truth, and, filled with new wine, might fill and water the thirsty hearts of the peoples.

### 3. What the Coming of the Holy Spirit Added to the Apostles’ Perfection

Let us inquire here what, after the Lord’s resurrection or ascension, could still be added to the Apostles’ perfection through participation in the Holy Spirit.

There was indeed faith in them, but the steadfastness of confidence was lacking. They could already preach Christ everywhere, but they could not yet fight for Christ unto death. Indeed, no disciple received the martyr’s crown before the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, the Lord Jesus had already withdrawn from their eyes—the one who, speaking face to face with them in visible preaching, strengthened them and instructed them through miracles of power. While they were with him, they readily believed what they saw: faith was assisted by sight, confirmed by present works, and nourished by signs and powers.

But after the Lord Jesus had been taken from their eyes and withdrawn into heaven, their astonished and trembling minds were not yet sufficient to think, as they ought, about heavenly and eternal things. Nor could their narrow hearts yet bear the greatness of divine meanings, so that they could understand Christ as he was, the Word God with God, just as the Lord himself, while still present in the body, clearly intimated to them:

“I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:12–13).

Do you see that after the departure of the supreme and worshipful Power, the disciples’ hearts were enlarged to sustain the greatness of divine light and the understanding of truth?

It is God, therefore, who can heap grace upon his generosity, increase wisdom, and strengthen steadfastness.

### 4. The Apostles’ Condition before and after the Coming of the Holy Spirit

Before: error. After: wisdom. Thomas’s unbelief. The faith of the others afterward. Peter’s judgment against persecutors. Stephen’s subsequent correction. Those who had previously been fearful later became fearless before every torment.

Let us therefore see how much they lacked in greatness of soul and in perfection before the visitation of the heavenly Comforter.

At first, when they saw him walking upon the swelling backs of the sea, while the unstable path of the waters was made firm beneath his divine footsteps by the serving wave, they were disturbed and said, “It is a ghost,” and out of fear they cried out.

After the infusion of the Holy Spirit, however, they no longer say that it is a ghost, but:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; and again: “There was,” he says, “the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:1, 9).

And the Apostle says, “For he is before all things, and all things hold together through him” (Col. 1:17).

But one of the disciples, Thomas, not yet enriched by the blessing of this gift, sought God in a body already glorified, in a body already heavenly, through the wounds of the flesh. He needed the testimony of nail marks and scars in order to believe in the incorruptible divinity:

“Unless I see,” he says, “the mark of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe” (John 20:25).

But another, already filled with the instruction of the Holy Spirit, confidently exclaims:

“What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to us” (1 John 1:1–2).

And again, elsewhere, the Apostle Paul, enriched by the influx of such majesty, boldly declares:

“Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5:16).

Blessed Peter, when the Lord’s passion was already near, not yet grounded by the divine inspiration of the Paraclete, unwilling to be separated bodily from Christ, drew his sword against the betrayer and the gladiators [Note: [Col. 2089] The words “and the gladiators” are absent from manuscript vd.], and thought that force should be repelled by force.

But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, no longer sought Christ on earth. With heaven opened, he saw the glory of God; nor did he now think of vengeance, but prayed and pleaded for his persecutors:

“Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

Before the coming of the Holy Spirit, at the very time of the Lord’s cross, some of the disciples fled, while others were terrified by the voice of a single maidservant. As fear pierced their trembling hearts, they were compelled to deny their Lord.

But after the illumination and strengthening of the Holy Spirit, tortured in custody and afflicted by blows, they went rejoicing because they were deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for Christ’s name.
