Those who had earlier denied him with an oath, “We do not know this man,” now gloried in punishments on his account. Through the Holy Spirit working in them, they considered what they suffered for Christ’s love to be little.

Those who had previously been frightened by words were now strengthened by penalties and tortures. They confessed Christ the Lord no longer with their voices but with their deaths [Note: [Col. 2089] This should be read, with manuscript vd., “they confess him by their conduct.”], and testified to the greatness of their love by the shedding of their blood.

Meanwhile, warmed and inflamed by the pure wine of the Lord’s love, they exclaimed:

“The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

Thus the blessed Apostles, burning with that fire of faith of which the Lord himself says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49), were thought by the impious crowd to be drunk and full of new wine. They said to one another, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13).

But they were filled with new wine, because they had already been renewed by the Holy Spirit, and what the Lord himself had said was apparent in them: “New wine must be put into new wineskins” (Matt. 9:17).

### 5. Not the Apostles Alone Were Intoxicated with the New Wine of the Holy Spirit

This wine enlivens those who pursue the perfect life; martyrs also burned with it.

Let us not think, however, that only the Apostles then received this new wine. With this must they are inflamed, and with this splendid cup the hearts of the faithful and the souls of converts are intoxicated every day as well.

We frequently see this happen when, out of desire for their salvation, people leave their parents and homeland; they depart, compelled by no one, from their land and kinship, and, dead to this world, seek other parents spiritually, parents of souls.

Freed people come under the yoke; those who shortly before were distinguished and exalted pursue humility, reject pride, desire to become what they had previously despised, and begin to hate what they had been. They are guests of the present and seekers of the future; rejecting the falsehood of temporal things [Note: [Col. 2090] Manuscript vd.: “the happiness of temporal things.”], they sigh for that eternal homeland.

Thus souls intoxicated and wholly transformed by this spiritual must prefer abstinence to pleasures, vigils to sweet sleep, and poverty to riches. They count arduous labor against vices as the most delightful pleasure.

Mean things become sweet to them, and what had previously been precious becomes worthless. They love their enemies and do good to those who hate them. They are not overcome by those who rage against them, are not provoked by insults, and are not broken by injuries. Because of the fervor of the Holy Spirit and because of eternal recompense, they feel none of these things at all.

With this spiritual wine the martyrs burned when, casting aside and flinging behind them all the world’s allurements, they went to sufferings, forgetting their possessions and affections, their estates and marriages, and overcoming the armed tenderness of their little children’s tears.

Their parents cried aloud, threw dust upon their heads, and mothers tore their faces by ripping out their hair. But the martyrs, as though drunk, neither saw nor recognized any of these things. For the Holy Spirit had been infused into their inmost hearts, and they hastened toward pain and punishment as toward consolation and rewards.

### 6. How We Should Invite the Holy Spirit among Us Every Day

We do indeed celebrate the annual day of the Holy Spirit’s coming. But let us act in such a way that every day we invite him to us through chaste deeds and pure hearts.

We ought to be pure and cleansed in our senses and thoughts. We must keep watch over mouth and heart, so that we may always make ourselves and appear worthy of his visitation and illumination, and free from every uncleanness of thought. For, as I said, “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1:3).

Let us strive to be free from every slander and every malice, because “wisdom does not enter a malicious soul, nor will it dwell in a body subjected to sins” [Note: [Col. 2090] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “nor does it dwell in a body subjected to sins.” Manuscript M.] (ibid., 4).

Through anger and pride, the souls of the negligent are stripped of the Holy Spirit’s guardianship and protection. Therefore let us not grieve the Holy Spirit through such passions; rather, let us call him to the throne of our heart through the grace of humility and the gentleness of peace, and make him rejoice through our works and progress.

For he says, “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

If, therefore, we desire to merit the entrance of so great a visitor, let us first cleanse the house of our soul from the unworthy passions of carnal desire, from the abomination of pride, from the stench of boasting, and from the horror of tepidity, concerning which the Lord himself says:

“I wish that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:15–16)—that is, to spit you out from the innermost entrails of the heart.

Let us therefore prepare this house every day for the coming of the sacred King and adorn it with various flowers of commendable conduct. Let us fill it with the pleasant and precious fragrances of chastity; with the incense of faith and compunction; with the balm of benevolence; and with the perfume of charity.

When vices have been cut away and virtues implanted, and the dwelling of the devil within us has been destroyed, let us be changed into a temple of God, so that such a blessed guest, delighted by his bright lodging, may establish in us a lasting and perpetual dwelling.

For this reason he descended to us: so that we might be able to ascend to him. To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON 183 [Note: [Col. 2091] Formerly, On Time 188; later, Appendix 61.]

### On Pentecost, II [Note: [Col. 2091] Compiled from passages of Augustine. For section 1, see Sermon 271.]

### 1. Introduction

Dearest brothers, today we celebrate the annual solemnity of the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Spirit, whom he had previously promised to the disciples.

For he had said, “He cannot come unless I go away” (John 16:7).

On the fortieth day after his resurrection, the solemnity of which we celebrated ten days ago, he ascended into heaven. Not forgetful of his promise, today he sent the Holy Spirit, with whom the first group of one hundred and twenty were filled. They had been gathered together and were faithfully awaiting the Lord’s same promise.

For it is written:

“Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing wind; and divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, which also rested upon each one of them; and they began to speak in all tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:2–4).

That wind cleansed their hearts of the carnal chaff; that fire consumed the hay of their former desire. Thus it pleased God at that time to signify the presence of his Holy Spirit: those who had received him spoke in every tongue.

### 2. Why the Spirit Could Not Come Unless Christ Went Away

Let us first briefly consider why, when he promised the Spirit, he said, “He cannot come unless I go away.”

The Holy Spirit is not separable from the Son of God, nor was he powerless to come while the one from whom he cannot in any way depart was present.

But because the Lord was still showing his weak disciples the form of a servant, in which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—and even carnal people could behold the Lord’s flesh, whereas the form of God, in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, cannot be conceived by spiritual persons—therefore he said, “He cannot come unless I go away.”

It was as if he said: “As long as your carnal affection is occupied with my flesh, your spiritual gaze does not receive my divinity.”

For he had promised that through the gift of the Holy Spirit they would be introduced into all truth, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

The Lord’s bodily form therefore withdrew from their bodily eyes, so that through the Holy Spirit the Lord’s divinity might be conveyed into their hearts.

### 3. The Gift of Tongues as a Sign of the Holy Spirit’s Presence

Charity Gathered the Church. How Every Believer Now Speaks in Tongues.

Let us next consider why, at that time, the sign of the Holy Spirit’s presence was that those who received him spoke in every tongue.

Even now, whenever the Holy Spirit is given, those who receive him do not speak in every tongue, by which evident miracle he demonstrated himself at that time.

Here we must understand, dearest brothers, that this is the Holy Spirit “through whom the love of God has been poured into our hearts” (Rom. 5:5).

Since the love of God was going to gather the Church throughout the whole world, what one person could then do—namely, speak in every tongue upon receiving the Holy Spirit—the unity of the Church itself, gathered by the Holy Spirit, now does in every tongue.

Therefore, if someone says to one of us, “Have you received the Holy Spirit? Why do you not speak in every tongue?” he ought to answer:

“I certainly speak in every tongue, because I am in the body of Christ, that is, in the Church, which speaks in every tongue.”

For what else did God signify then except that, through the presence of the Holy Spirit, his Church would speak in every tongue?

What the Lord had promised was therefore fulfilled:

“No one puts new wine into old wineskins; but new wine is put into new wineskins, so that both may be preserved” (Matt. 9:17).

It was therefore fitting that, when they were heard speaking in every tongue, some said, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13).

For they had become new wineskins, renewed by the grace of holiness, so that, filled with new wine—that is, with the grace of the Holy Spirit—they might burn by speaking in every tongue and, through the languages of all peoples, might foreshadow by that most evident miracle the future catholic Church.

Consequently, heretics are rightly believed not to possess the Holy Spirit, since they are separated from the body that throughout all nations has deserved to resound in every tongue.

### 4. How Those Who Celebrate This Day Spiritually Should Observe It

Therefore, beloved, celebrate this day as members of the unity of Christ’s body.

You do not celebrate in vain if you are what you celebrate, clinging to that Church which the Lord, filling it with the Holy Spirit and causing it to grow throughout the whole world, recognizes as his own, and by which he is recognized as hers, as a bridegroom is recognized by his bride. He does not lose what is his, because no one substitutes what belongs to another.

To you, who are established among all nations—that is, to the Church of Christ, the members of Christ, the body of Christ, the bride of Christ—the Apostle says:

“Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

Observe that where he commanded us to bear with one another, there he placed love; where he mentioned the Spirit of unity, there he showed the bond of peace.

This is the house of God, built from living stones, in which it pleases such a householder to dwell, whose eyes should not be offended by the ruin caused by division.

## SERMON 184 [Note: [Col. 2092] Previously, On Time 184.]

### On Pentecost, III [Note: [Col. 2092] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain scholars, but Verlin and Vinding regard it as spurious and inept. In the Theoderic manuscript the name of Maximus is preferred, while in the Fossat and German manuscripts Leo’s name is preferred; but in both cases falsely.]

1. The Lord promises the Holy Spirit to his Apostles. As our Lord and Savior was about to depart from this world and ascend into heaven, dearest brothers, he promised his Apostles that he would send the Holy Spirit to them when he himself had returned to God the Father. For, as you have just heard, he spoke thus to his disciples, saying: “When the Paraclete has come, whom I shall send you—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

The Savior’s promise has been fulfilled, dearest brothers. The Lord Jesus Christ ascended; the Holy Spirit descended. It remains that both of these things be fulfilled in us: namely, that we possess the Holy Spirit who descended, and that by a good life we follow Christ who ascended. Therefore the Savior sent us the Holy Spirit, just as he himself promised his disciples, saying: “It is advantageous for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (ibid. 16:7).

When he said, “I will send him,” let none of you perhaps suppose that he spoke as though the Spirit were inferior, saying, “I will send him”; or, as the heretics [Note: The Macedonians.] say, that the Holy Spirit, as though subject and serving God, obeys one who commands him. Far be such a suspicion from you. For in the Trinity there is neither anything less nor anything greater; for if anything less is said to exist in God, the divinity is accused of imperfection.

2. One God must be believed in the Trinity. Therefore I beseech you, dearest brothers, to believe with an undivided faith in one God in the Trinity, and in the Trinity in unity, lest the feet of your understanding limp, or your eyes see too little, or your hands become withered. For everyone who does not rightly follow the Catholic faith [Col. 2093] has weak feet; whoever does not see the light of truth suffers the darkness of the eyes; whoever bears no fruit of mercy is dried up by the withering of his hands.

Do this, then; strive for this, lest any part of your members be corrupted by such weakness; lest your appetite recoil within you, or greed displease, or faithlessness languish. Thus, thoroughly cleansed and purified, you may become God’s dwelling place, and the Holy Spirit, who is read to have descended today, may deign always to be in you; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen [Note: In the manuscripts the words “through our Lord,” and so forth, to the end are absent.].

SERMON 185 [Note: Formerly, On Time 183; later, in the Appendix 60.] On Pentecost, IV [Note: In the Theoderician manuscript it is wrongly attributed to Ambrose together with three others which in the other manuscripts are headed with the name of Maximus. These are in fact his three homilies on this feast, two of which are also printed among the Ambrosian Sermons. For section 1 compare Maximus, Homily 3 on Pentecost; for section 2 see Maximus, Homilies 1 and 2 on Pentecost.]

1. The opinion of some concerning the Lord’s Ascension on the day of Pentecost. Why he remained forty days after the resurrection. Dearest brothers, the celebration of your vows should now be familiar to your holiness. For we learn from the annual observance itself what we should care for and how we should care for it. When the solemnity already past returns once more in its cycle, we become more learned as we celebrate the same event repeatedly.

Therefore Pentecost is observed [Note: The printed editions read, “Let us celebrate Pentecost, therefore.” The manuscripts, however, read *curatur*, that is, “is celebrated.” The word is also used in this sense in Maximus’s Homilies 1 and 3 on Pentecost.] today—that is, the fiftieth day from the Lord’s resurrection—not because, as many suppose, the Savior ascended into heaven on this day. For after the resurrection he lived among the Apostles and returned to the right hand of God the Father on the fortieth day, as the evangelist Luke says: “To them also he presented himself alive after his passion, appearing to them for forty days” (Acts 1:3).

Thus, throughout a period of forty days, the Savior displayed his presence among the disciples, so that we might rejoice for as many days in the grace of his resurrection as we had mourned the injuries of his passion, and might be refreshed by his presence for as many days as we had fasted during his absence. Christ therefore did not ascend to heaven today; rather, the Spirit of Christ descended from heaven, as the Lord himself promised, saying: “When I have ascended to the Father, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth; and he himself will teach you all things” (John 16:7).

Great indeed is the grace, and double the joy: that we neither lost Christ when he departed nor failed to possess the Spirit when he came. We retain the former through the merit of faith; we possess the latter through the advance of sanctification.

2. The coming Spirit establishes that Christ reigns. What the Holy Spirit teaches. He is of one substance with Christ.—“When I have gone,” he says, “to the Father, I will send you the Paraclete.” We therefore believe that the Son has reached the Father when we see the Paraclete descend upon the Apostles. We believe, I say, that he reigns in heaven whom we see bestowing gifts on earth, as it is written through the Prophet: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Psalm 67:19).

The victor certainly bestows gifts; the victor distributes gifts. Thus the Savior, victorious after his triumph over the devil, also enriched with blessing those whom he had freed from captivity. He freed us when, by rising again himself, he opened Tartarus to us; he enriched us when, through the Paraclete, he opened the heavenly realms to us for reigning.

Then, as though by certain steps of progress, we learned to return from death to life; now we are taught to ascend from earth to heaven, as it is written: “He himself will teach you all things.” What does the Holy Spirit teach? Certainly, he knows how to teach what is holy. What does the Paraclete teach us? Surely what the Savior said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he himself will teach you all things” (John 16:12–13).

The Paraclete, then, is a good teacher, because he teaches what Christ reserved to be said. For the Holy Spirit teaches what the Lord said he had to say. Clearly he is a good teacher who carries out the Savior’s commands. Therefore he must be of one substance with Christ, whom we see to be of one teaching with Christ.

3. Exhortation. And therefore [Note: This conclusion is absent from the T. manuscript. It is found word for word in the homily which Rabanus Maurus published on the same feast, with whom a little above we read “we shall receive a similar Paraclete . . .” in place of “we shall not receive a similar Paraclete . . .”], dearest brothers, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, so that we may be able to deserve and receive the Holy Spirit.

If we leave this world, we shall receive, like the Apostles, a similar Paraclete—that is, the Spirit of truth whom the Father will send us—for there is no partiality with God the Father. The promises made to the Apostles benefit us if we perform the works, desires, and actions which the Apostles performed.

But if, by fulfilling his commandments, we complete the Lord’s spotless law, which converts souls, we entrust ourselves, with Christ’s grace, as heirs of the Lord and joint heirs with Christ to an eternal inheritance and to dwelling with the Angels. May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

SERMON 186 [Note: Formerly, among Vignier’s Sermons 4, in the first part of the Supplement.] On Pentecost, V [Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It contains nothing belonging to Augustine.]

1. This day is solemn throughout every age. It excels above the other sacraments. Today the ornament of the perpetual gift shone forth, when the holy assembly of the disciples was found worthy to receive the Holy Spirit. About ten days ago we celebrated the devout ascension of the Lord Christ. Today the fiftieth day of the Lord’s resurrection has dawned, on which day the Spirit of God shone forth, aflame with love.

All the Patriarchs and Prophets marked the solemnity of these feast-days with holy reverence; but they celebrated this day with solemnity above all others. In this number of fifty there are many mysteries of holiness: it is called the Year of Remission, offering the servants gifts of freedom.

The blessed Paul hastened to celebrate this day in Jerusalem, knowing that it excelled above all days in wondrous mysteries. On this day, at the time already mentioned, Moses received the Law on Mount Sinai and proclaimed God’s commandments to the people. There God descended upon the mountain; here the Holy Spirit came, revealed in tongues of fire. There were thunderclaps and voices; here Fishermen shone forth with tongues aflame in various languages.

As the divine page was just saying: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled” (Acts 2:1 ff.), and so forth.

2. The Apostles are rightly said to have been filled with new wine. How beautiful, brothers, is the union of charity, which always presents a heart prepared for God! Charity found them; and the overflowing divinity of the Godhead illuminated them. Divine fire came—not burning, but enlightening; not consuming, but shining. It found the receptacles of their hearts clean and freely bestowed the gifts of its graces.

It saw the purest bosom of holy vessels and deigned to pour out new wine. Their vessels began to belch forth wine as it boiled, and to resound in the tongues of all nations. But how could they not have knowledge of the languages of every nation, when they had received within themselves the mystery of the Holy Spirit and the sacrament of the fire of grace?

While many were amazed at so great a mystery, others, mocking, said: “Because they are filled with new wine” (Acts 2:13). They spoke correctly, although unknowingly: for new wine, by boiling, drives out all impurities, so that it may preserve its aroma and conceal its sweetness. New wineskins received new wine, so that they might preserve the wine unharmed and themselves walk in the newness of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning this Holy Spirit the Prophet said: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103:30). Truly the face of the earth was renewed—made new for the better—when the gracious tongue (*lingua eucharis*) sang the praises of heavenly power and a melody resounded of the Godhead.

Concerning this Holy Spirit the same Prophet said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their strength” (Psalm 32:6). He set the heavens aflame, who had made the heavens; he sent divine flame and prepared his instruments for singing.

Therefore, brothers, let us celebrate this day with fear of God, when we were found worthy to receive the Holy Spirit’s pardon.

SERMON 187 [Note: Formerly, among Vignier’s Sermons 25, in the second part of the Supplement.] On Pentecost, VI [Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is not Augustine’s, but belongs to some obscure author, as even Vignier himself judged when he published it in the second volume of the Supplement.]

The written law and the law of grace. He found the Apostles in the upper room and wrote the Law in their minds—he who had written the Law on tablets on the high mountain: on tablets of stone because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, but now in the minds of the Apostles, because there was terror, whereas here there is love.

There he wrote the Law amid flashing brilliance; here he instructed [Col. 2096] apostolic tongues with a cooling fire. From that mountain the peoples fled lest they hear the voice of God speaking terribly; here all the nations from throughout the world do not flee but gather to hear the Holy Spirit speaking through his instruments.

You heard the Parthians, Medes, Indians, and Persians, Cretans and Arabs named (Acts 2:9), along with the others whom the reading of the Acts of the Apostles mentioned. The whole world was there; the fortieth day, the day of the Lord’s Ascension, had gathered them, because the number of the ten commandments embraces the whole authority of the Scriptures throughout the world.

Therefore four times ten makes forty; another ten remains, the ten of eternal life, so that the Fishermen might receive their reward from the pledge of the Holy Spirit. It has been found; what was promised has been fulfilled. The tenth portion of the precious denarius, the pledge of the sacrament, has been given. The grace promised in the fifty days remains, and perfect joy.

Easter has been concluded; the Alleluia is silent, but not in sadness, because we have received the precious pledge of the Holy Spirit, so that we may have his indwelling consolation every day, live with Christ, and through him safely come again to the Easter of the age to come.

[Col. 2095]

CLASS III OF THE APPENDIX. SERMONS ON THE SAINTS. (C, G)*

SERMON 188 [Note: Formerly, On the Saints 13.] On the feast of Saint Vincent [Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the printed books it had been situated among the Sermons of both Leo and Augustine; in nearly all our manuscripts, however, it was assigned to this author. But its style does not permit it to be attributed either to Leo or to Augustine, as Quesnel judged in volume 1, page 384, of the Works of Saint Leo. Indeed, the author himself declares at the beginning of the sermon that he is Spanish by nationality. In particular, by the words “Let those of his own place honor him more, whom foreigners also admire,” he indicates that he is celebrating the martyr Vincent among those who inhabit the place made illustrious and consecrated by his preaching, passion, or bodily presence.]

[Col. 2095]

1. Introduction. Although, dearest brothers, one faith makes the glorious sufferings of all the martyrs—whom places distinct in their regions have been privileged to possess—worthy of veneration by all with undivided honor, nevertheless those who have especially raised up the Church of God by their teaching and aided it by their patronage rightly claim for themselves a particular dignity in this service of veneration.

Among these we rightly celebrate the blessed Levite Vincent, by whose confession and death Christ was preached to unbelievers, as we unmistakably acknowledge through Catholic devotion. Burning with the higher affection of charity, he finally offered himself faithfully to death, so that the strength of faith founded upon Christ, the firmest rock, might be given to his followers for imitation; and so that the seed of apostolic preaching, scattered by him among many, might be preserved through his intercession and, filled with the fruit of perfect completion, finally be stored in the heavenly granaries.

Therefore let those of his own place honor him more, whom foreigners also admire, so that he may show himself more generous toward them in benefits, inasmuch as he recognizes them as more beloved in their joys; and so that at his solemnity there may be a more abundant outpouring of joy, from which the effect of faith has grown.

2. The Levite, minister of the Lord’s blood. Unconquered by torments. Finally, the spirit of this man shone with so great a gift of virtues that, supported by the office of sacred ministry, he who was to follow the Son of God, our Lord, in his passion first ministered Christ’s chalice to believers for salvation.

Happily intoxicated in mind by drinking from it, he approached the madness of the raging enemy who savagely attacked Christ without fear; he endured it with restraint and mocked it with confidence. He knew that he was prepared to resist, but did not presume to be exalted because he would conquer. For because he resisted through the love of him by whose spiritual arms he was fortified, with his help he bravely overcame by unconquerable endurance whatever punishments the furious anger of the persecutor devised against him.

Thus neither the red-hot metal pan, nor the rack, nor the claws and iron hands, nor the terrifying strength of those who beat him, nor the pain of his torn limbs, nor the roar of the furnace and the sprinkling of salt hissing upon his exposed entrails could in any way subject him to Dacian’s command.

But while the swelling of his madness grew so great that, after Vincent had been subdued by such sufferings, he joyfully boasted that he had either conquered or killed him, his hope was frustrated. From the point at which he seemed to appear victorious, he was compelled to blush as the vanquished; for the harsher the punishment with which the Martyr of God was pressed, the more abundantly he exulted in the steadfastness of his confession.

3. The devil’s work in Dacian, Christ’s work in Vincent. Vincent is tortured in secret. Therefore, brothers, it is more pleasing to examine or recall clearly even the final stages of his passion, so that your Holiness may observe where the devil led his own minister by his deceptions, and how Christ preserved his servant to the very end.

Among these things there was truly something remarkable: to the degree that Vincent was externally crushed and confined by various kinds of punishment, to that same degree he was inwardly expanded by his exultant inner self. And to the degree that Dacian was externally puffed up by the arrogance of temporal power, to that same degree, recognizing that he was despised within, he was inwardly choked and tormented by his inner self.

Seeing, therefore, that he was despised, he raged, but could find no one upon whom to inflict vengeance. For he saw that the hands of the executioners, though raging, found more injury in Vincent than in his body; and that the spirit alone remained strong, reproaching their folly precisely by challenging the standard of truth.

Therefore, believing that he would avert the cause of his shame if he removed the person who had despised him, and that Dacian would blush less if the people did not see Vincent, he ordered him to be removed from public view. But even so he was not to be deprived of punishment: the shattered pottery upon which he lay was placed beneath him, so that the sharpness of its points, driven into the crushed mass, might tear the body laid upon it still more, and so that the limbs returned to the tortures which cut them might encounter fragments in their path.

4. He is healed by God and dies on a soft bed. Yet cruel blindness, in its belief that it had conquered, was deceived. For divine goodness, accompanying its beloved one still more fully in his confession, brought new light into the darkness and made the gloomy prison a splendid dwelling.

God’s healing hand tended his mangled limbs and restored the losses of his pierced side with an increase more beautiful than his former health. Struck and astonished by the unfamiliar brilliance of this light, the guards were dumbfounded; indeed, the mind of the pale gatekeeper was frightened by a voice as Angels sang a hymn to God.

The servant ran breathless to the governor, whom the report of the message was to strike more severely than the blow of a sword. Since he could not remain silent about what he had seen because of the magnitude of the event, trembling seized the judge, grief tore him, and fury inflamed him.

And lest Vincent, victorious in his sufferings, obtain the glory of martyrdom, Dacian said: “Let him be brought out of prison at once. Lest, while we persist in punishing a rebel, we appear rather to crown him with victory.” Thus he was brought forth from that dreadful abyss of a prison, more beautiful through heavenly grace and, if he still had to suffer, stronger.

But when Dacian understood that the desire of one reaching toward the summons of the kingdom could be broken by no kind of punishment or death, his envious mind ordered supports for a softer bed to be substituted and Vincent to be comforted with gentler rest—so that, if the executioner were removed for a little while and he quietly breathed out his soul, it might be said that he had not been killed but had died; as though punishment had not destroyed him, when punishment itself had perished together with him.

5. His body is exposed to wild beasts. Meanwhile the heavenly court receives blessed Vincent and grants him the gift of blessed happiness. At his entrance the angelic spirits rejoice, and all the holy fellow citizens rejoice together.

And we give you thanks, Lord Jesus, because the soul worthy of your fellowship, which steadfastly endured punishment, fled deceitful service; and because, content that its persecutor should rage, it disdained that he should spare it.

When the insane judge learned of his holy departure—and Dacian did not know that Christ had conquered in Vincent—he promised himself vengeance by exposing his corpse, though he groaned at the victory achieved through Vincent’s courage. He ordered the executioners to throw it out to be devoured by wild beasts and dogs, so that by such food he might fill the bellies of those whose mind he himself possessed.

6. The raven protects him; the wolf venerates him. But so that, as divine benefits multiplied, a greater grace of victory might be conferred upon Vincent, a raven was sent—an enemy of corpses—to guard the exposed food of his body while remaining unfed.

Here, dearest brothers, here observe the distinct services rendered according to merit. Once, when Elijah was cautiously avoiding the impious hands of Ahab and Jezebel, he was fed in the desert by ravens. But Vincent, the defender of truth, killed by Dacian’s rage, was exposed to wild beasts to be consumed, yet was preserved unharmed by the service of a raven.

Thus, by divine command and through the service of ravens, Elijah obtained food (3 Kings 17); Vincent was granted, through the service of a raven, that he should not be eaten. To show that it had been appointed from heaven as his guardian, the raven disturbed the other birds approaching from a distance with no sluggish attack. Among them it also drove away a huge wolf that was coming nearer, beating it with wings and feathers as though it presumed, with sacrilegious boldness, to touch the treasure entrusted to its care.

But the wolf indicated by a certain expression of its bearing that it had come not so much to inflict injury as to increase the splendor of the miracle. O shameless fury and foolish madness! The raven obeys, the wolf venerates; Dacian persecutes and is not ashamed still, in his ferocity, to wish to destroy one whom tamed bestial savagery was striving to protect.

7. Cast into the sea, he is returned to the shore. Therefore, to conceal the Martyr’s glory, Dacian chose not secrecy but the deep [Col. 2098], believing that the sea, rather than enclosed places, would preserve his glory in hiding—as though the Lord of that element were not the same one by whom the hidden recesses of his prison had earlier shone with heavenly brightness.

Sailors were given the task of sinking the body in the waves, so that the sea might at least contribute to the aid of one whom the land had failed to conquer as a soldier of Christ. After they had sailed across a large part of the strait’s waters, the mighty right hand of God overtook what had been cast among the swallowing waves; and the hand that had brought his spirit into heaven soon returned his body to the tomb.

Thus, dearest brothers, the preacher of truth is neither conquered by the pains of torments nor overcome by the narrowness of a dark prison. Thrown to beasts, he is not torn apart; hidden in the deep, he is not concealed. He is returned to the shore and proclaimed everywhere, so that he who had truly confessed the name of the Godhead might discover that the supports of divine goodness were truly present to him.

The glorious life of his virtues was so adorned by the grace of his precious death that what he taught by living he firmly confirmed by dying. It followed that through death he attained the vision of the one whom he had always borne witness to through the worthy conduct of his life, knowing that from contempt for the present life arises the glory of eternal blessedness; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

SERMON 189 [Note: Formerly, On the Saints 14, and On Various Matters 35.] On the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul [Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It consists of fragments from various sermons. The beginning, “Today a reading from the Acts of the Apostles,” and so forth, belongs to Sermon 278; the words placed here as the conclusion are also taken from its beginning, “The usefulness of the event,” and so forth. The middle, beginning with the words “Striking him and healing him, killing and giving life,” and so forth, belongs to Sermon 279, On the Apostle Paul, formerly number 24 among the Sirmondian sermons. This is the entire structure of the sermon formerly numbered 14 among the Sermons on the Saints, which is read in the Roman Breviary and certain others for the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul. The sermon formerly numbered 35 among the Sermons on Various Matters, although differing from that one in neither its first nor middle part, differed in its final section: after the words “not be troubled when they heard his name,” it immediately added, in place of a conclusion, “O blessed Ananias, you were right to give yourself over to fear,” and so forth, as may be found below at the end of Sermon 204.]

1. Jacob’s prophecy concerning Benjamin is fulfilled in Paul. Today this reading from the Acts of the Apostles was proclaimed, in which Paul the Apostle was made an announcer of Christ from a persecutor of Christians.

For Christ struck down the persecutor in order to make him a teacher of the Church: striking and healing him, killing and giving life. The Lamb killed the wolf, making a lamb out of the wolf [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “the lamb killed by wolves, making lambs out of wolves.”]

For this had been contained in the splendid prophecy, when the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons, touching upon the present and looking toward the future. What occurred in Paul had been foretold. Paul, as he himself testifies, was from the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5).

When Jacob, blessing his sons, came to bless Benjamin, he said of him: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.” What then? Is he always a ravenous wolf? Far from it: “In the morning he will seize the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Genesis 49:27).

This was fulfilled in the Apostle Paul, because it had also been said of him. Now, if you please, let us hear him seizing in the morning and dividing the spoils in the evening.

2. Paul, the wolf seizing in the morning. “Morning” and “evening” are placed as though one were saying, “Earlier” and “later.” Let us therefore understand it this way: “Earlier he will seize; later he will divide the spoils.”

Observe the ravager: “Saul,” it says, “having received letters from the chief priests, was going so that wherever he found Christians [Note: Sirmond, on the basis of manuscripts M and V, reads: “and whenever he found followers of the Way of God.”], he might drag and bring them to the priests” (Acts 9:1–2), undoubtedly for punishment.

He went breathing and panting slaughter; this is the one seizing in the morning. For when Stephen, the first martyr, was stoned in the name of Christ, Saul was conspicuously present. He was so present to those who were stoning him that it was not enough for him merely to stone with his own hands. In order to be in the hands of all those who were stoning him, he himself kept all their garments; he raged more fiercely by helping everyone than by stoning with his own hands (Acts 7:57).

We have heard, “In the morning he will seize”; let us see how he divides the spoils in the evening.

3. In the evening he divides the spoils. Paul as a model for those beginning to believe. Struck down by Christ’s voice from heaven and receiving from above the prohibition against continuing his rage, he fell upon his face; first to be cast down, afterward to be raised; first to be struck, afterward to be healed. For Christ would not afterward live in him unless what had previously lived wrongly in him were killed.

What, then, does he hear when he has been struck down? “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.” And he: “Who are you, Lord?” And the voice from above: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.”

With the limbs still lying on the ground, the head cried out in heaven. He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my faithful ones?” but, “Why are you persecuting me?” And he: “What do you command me to do?”

He is already preparing himself to obey, though previously he raged in persecution. The persecutor is already being formed into a preacher, the wolf into a sheep, the enemy into a soldier. He hears what he must do.

He was indeed made blind so that his heart might shine with an inner light. Exterior light was withdrawn for a time from the persecutor so that it might be restored to the preacher; yet during the time when he saw nothing else, he saw Jesus.

Thus, from his very blindness, the mystery of believers was being formed: whoever believes in Christ must look upon him and count all other things as though they had not been made. Let the creature become worthless, so that the Creator may become sweet in the heart. Let us see, then.

4. Saul’s terrible reputation. He was brought to Ananias, and Ananias means “Sheep.” Behold, the ravenous wolf is brought to follow the sheep, not to seize it.

But lest the sheep fear the wolf as it approached, the Shepherd himself from heaven, who was accomplishing everything, announced to the sheep that the wolf would come, but would not rage. Nevertheless, so terrible was the reputation of that wolf that the sheep could not hear his name without becoming troubled.

For when the Lord Jesus announced to Ananias that Saul had come—already to believe—and that Ananias ought to go to him, Ananias said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints. And now he has received letters from the chief priests, so that wherever he finds followers of your name, he may drag them away.”

But the Lord said to him: “Leave him, for I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:4–16).

A wondrous and great event is taking place: the wolf is forbidden to rage; the wolf is led captive to the sheep. So great had been the reputation of the ravaging wolf that, when his name was heard, even the sheep feared him under the Shepherd’s hand.

The sheep is strengthened, so that it may no longer suppose the wolf to be raging and may not fear one who is himself afraid. Through the Lamb who died for the sheep, the sheep becomes secure regarding the wolf.

5. However much we suffer, what we hope for outweighs it.—“I will show him,” he says, “how much he must suffer for my name.” Where there is terror, there is salvation [Note: Thus in some manuscripts and in the sermon formerly On Various Matters 36. But in the manuscript On the Cultivation, “Where there is error, there is salvation.” In manuscript M: “Where there is terror? Where there is Saul?”]

He who acted against the Shepherd’s name suffers for the Shepherd’s name. O savagery! O mercy! You see him preparing the iron: he is going to cut, not kill; to heal, not destroy.

Christ said: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” But to what end? Hear the one who suffered: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). It is as though he said: Let the world rage, let the world roar, let it denounce with its tongues, flash with its weapons; let it do whatever it can. What will it do in comparison with what we are going to receive?

I weigh what I suffer against what I hope for. This I feel; that I believe. Yet what I believe is greater than what I feel.

Whatever rages against the name of Christ, if it can be endured while one lives, is tolerable; if it cannot be endured while one lives, it makes one depart from here. It does not extinguish the reward or sweetness; it hastens them. And when they come, they will be without end.

The labor has an end; the reward has no end. For a laborer would also fail on the way unless he considered what he was going to receive. When you consider what you are going to receive, everything you suffer will seem worthless to you, and you will not judge it worthy of the reward for which you receive it. You will marvel that so much is given for so little labor.

Christ is our way; look to Christ. He came to suffer, but also to be glorified; to be despised, but also to be exalted; to die, but also to rise again.

6. The usefulness of Paul’s conversion. Thinking on these things, dearest brothers, let us not despair, because even if we are sinners, we have a great physician.

Hear the Physician himself: “I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13).

The usefulness of this event is as follows: the Apostle himself recalls it in his Letters. For he says that he was granted forgiveness for all his sins so that no one who has been entangled in great sins and ensnared in great crimes might despair of himself—as though he would not receive forgiveness if he turned to him who, hanging on the cross, prayed even for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He who had been a persecutor was made a preacher and teacher of the Gentiles. “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Timothy 1:13) [Note: The manuscript On the Cultivation inserts here: “But I received mercy. These were gifts of mercy, not rewards owed for merits. Therefore, when the Lord called him in this way, what merits had preceded? I do not mean merits that preceded him as one to be crowned, but merits that preceded him as one to be condemned. He made the persecutor of the Church a preacher of peace. Behold, brothers: the one to whom punishment was owed is owed a crown. ‘I was,’ he says, ‘a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man.’ You see,” and so forth.]

Do you see the merit of one to whom punishment was owed? Therefore punishment is not repaid to him; instead, he receives mercy in place of punishment. For we are saved from our sins by grace, granted by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

SERMON 190 [Note: Formerly, On the Saints 15, and later, in the Appendix 74.] On the Chair of Saint Peter, I [Note: According to the judgment of the Louvain scholars, this is by an uncertain author, not Augustine, although it is read under his name in the Roman Breviary on this very day. Verlinus and Vindingus also deny that it belongs to Augustine. The preacher says here that he is surprised by the practice of placing food and wine upon the tombs of the dead; Augustine had seen this practice commonly observed in Africa, as is clear from Book 6, chapter 2, of the *Confessions*; *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, chapter 34; *Against Faustus*, Book 20, chapter 21; Letter 22, section 6; and elsewhere. In some manuscripts, after the words “the more honor the priestly office,” there is nothing at all about that practice; instead, the sermon continues with a discussion only of the origin of this feast. Yet this feast seems to have been unknown to Africans in Augustine’s time, and it is not found in the recently published calendar of the Church of Carthage. In the manuscript of Saint Peter of Chartres it is attributed to Saint Clement.]

1. The reason for the feast. The institution of today’s solemnity received from our elders the name “Chair,” because it is reported that on this day Peter, the first of the Apostles, assumed the chair of the episcopate.

Rightly, therefore, the Church celebrates the birthday of that seat which the Apostle assumed for the salvation of the Churches, as the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

The Lord therefore named Peter the foundation of the Church. And for this reason the Church rightly honors this foundation, upon which the height of the ecclesiastical structure rises.

Accordingly, the Psalm that was read says: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the chair of the elders” (Psalm 106:32).

God rightly commanded that he be exalted in the Church, because it is fitting that this foundation be honored, through which one ascends to heaven.

Since, then, the birthday of the chair is celebrated today, the priestly office is honored. The Churches bestow this honor upon themselves, for it is necessary that they possess that much more dignity [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “The Churches grant these things to one another, because the Church necessarily has that much more dignity.”] in proportion as the priestly office possesses greater honor.

## 2. Superstition introduced on this day. Holy souls are already with Christ

Although religious observance has rightly introduced this solemnity into the Churches, I am astonished that among certain unbelievers [Note: [Col. 2101] The manuscript rm has “believers.” Others, with the printed editions, read “unbelievers,” that is, “those without faith,” as they are called in the sermon that follows, no. 1.] such a pernicious error has today grown up that they bring food and wine to the tombs of the dead, as though the souls that have departed from their bodies required bodily food [Note: [Col. 2101] The Council of Tours II, held in the year 567, canon 22, commands the faithful to abstain from the practices condemned here at this feast: “There are also some who offer food to the dead on the feast of the Chair of the lord apostle Peter, and, returning home after the Masses, go back to the errors of the Gentiles”—that is, to the rites which the Pagans observed during the Feralia, which in the ancient Roman Calendar begin on the twentieth day of February and last almost until the end of that month. In those rites the Manes were appeased by placing food at their tombs for them to eat. Hence Varro, book 5 of *On the Latin Language*: “The Feralia,” he says, “are named from *inferiae* and *ferendo*, because at that time they carry food to the tomb, with which they are to perform the parental rite there.”]. Food and refreshment are required only by the flesh; spirit and soul, however, have no need of these things. Someone says that he is preparing something for his loved ones, while he himself devours it; what he gives to his belly he attributes to piety.

Cease, then, brothers, from this pagan error of unbelief. For the holy souls who in this age are either pure through an innocent life or are cleansed by the satisfaction of repentance are received by our Savior, and must be believed to be with him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians I, 23). The souls, therefore, of our brothers and parents take no pleasure in bodily foods; indeed, they can be offended by these rather than delighted, if, while they remain in holy dwellings, you believe them to be on earth.

Cease, then, from these errors, and, as it is written, “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things that are on earth” (Colossians III, 2), so that, rejecting superstitions contrary to our faith, while you do what pleases God, you too may be able to be with Christ forever. May he himself deign to grant this, and so forth.

## SERMON CXCI

[Note: [Col. 2101] This was written in the same style and concerns the same kind of observance, or superstition, that is condemned in the preceding sermon. In the old books it is found immediately after that sermon, and in some manuscripts it is even joined with it into a single work.]

### On the Chair of Saint Peter, II

#### 1. This feast coincides with Lent

Although we rightly honor the solemnity of today’s feast—for while celebrating the Birthday of the Chair, we venerate the episcopate of the apostle Peter—nevertheless, whenever this solemnity falls within the days of Lent, the reverence due to the holy days ought to make it more pleasing to us.

For God has fittingly granted us the Birthday of the Chair at the very beginning of the fasts, so that the day which formerly belonged to excess may now belong to sobriety; what belonged to gluttony may belong to abstinence; what belonged to sin may belong to holiness. And since unbelieving people seem to have been drawn into this superstition under the appearance of piety, I shall show them how they can more usefully help the souls of their dead.

#### 2. In what ways the dead may be helped

Let them pray daily for their loved ones; let them appeal to the Lord in tearful speech; let them beg forgiveness for their errors and remission for their falls; let them feed the hungry and clothe the naked, so that if anything was left undone through the negligence of the dead, it may be supplied by the faith of the living.

Let each person also obtain the prayers of the saints for his loved ones, offer sacrifices, and commend them to the Lord through priestly intercession. If perhaps we are asked by what authority we say this, the answer is that this is not our teaching but that of the Churches; and if it is that of the Churches, it is certainly that of God, because God is the teacher of all the Churches. Thus we shall answer in his words: “These are the things that can help your loved ones; these are the refreshments of those who rest; these are the remedies of the dead.”

[Col. 2102]

#### 3. Food placed on tombs benefits them nothing

But the foods and drinks that are placed upon tombs: if any concern of this superstition pertains to the dead, they can be harmed by these things rather than delighted. If someone were to offer wine to a person whom he knew to be tormented because of excessive drinking and gluttony, this would be an insult rather than kindness, a reproach for his crime rather than an act of charity. So it happens that sinful dead people seem to receive from their loved ones not so much consolations of love as an accumulation of torments for their consciences.

We have said this about sinners. But if the person for whom these things are prepared is holy, they have no relevance to him. Let each one of you do what we said above, so that through prayers, almsgiving, sacrifices, and offerings he may benefit both his dead and himself: that is, if the one for whom he does these things is a sinner, let his sins be relieved; but if he is a saint for whom sacrifices are offered to God, may he deserve to be with the saints forever—through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CXCII

[Note: [Col. 2102] Elsewhere, *On the Saints* 16.]

### On the Chair of Saint Peter, III

[Note: [Col. 2102] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It had remained doubtful among the Louvain editors; Verlin and Vinding reject it as spurious. For it was printed among the sermons of Ambrose and Maximus, with only the beginning altered, and it is ascribed to Ambrose in the Theoderician manuscript, beginning as follows: “We showed in the preceding Sunday that holy Peter profited from his errors during the Savior’s Passion,” and so forth. These words may perhaps designate the homily found in Maximus, no. 3, *On Peter’s Repentance*, which corresponds to the sermon of Ambrose beginning, “We have often said,” and which in an ancient codex written a thousand years ago falsely bears the name of Augustine. The conclusion of this sermon runs as follows: “See, then, how much Peter benefited from his weeping. Before he wept,” and so forth. Compare Ambrose’s *Commentaries on Luke*, chapter 22, sermon 6, *On Various Actions*.]

#### 1. Peter profited from his errors. The dignity and meaning of Peter’s name

You know, dearest brothers, that blessed Peter profited from his errors during the Savior’s Passion and, after denying the Lord, became better in the Lord’s sight. For he became more faithful after he had mourned that he had lost his faith; and therefore he found greater grace than he had lost.

Like a good shepherd he was entrusted with the care of the flock, so that the one who had previously been weak for himself might become a support for all, and the one who had faltered under the test of questioning might establish the others through the steadfastness of faith. Finally, because of the solidity of his devotion, he is called the rock of the Churches, as the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18).

He is called “rock” because he was the first among the nations to lay the foundations of faith, and because, like an immovable stone, he supports the structure and mass of the entire Christian work. Peter, therefore, is called “rock” on account of his devotion; and the Lord is named “rock” on account of his power, as the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Corinthians X, 4). Rightly does he deserve a share in the name who deserves a share in the work.

For in the same house Peter lays the foundation, Peter plants; the Lord gives the growth, the Lord supplies the irrigation. Peter, therefore, profits from his temptations, rejoices through his tears, and grows through his dangers.

#### 2. Peter’s steps upon the waters. He is sustained by faith

This is more wondrous than Israel’s passage through the sea. For here, while the rash traveler walks upon the waves of the sea, he wavers in his step but grows strong in his devotion; his body is endangered, but he does not fall away in faithfulness; his feet sink, but the right hand of Christ sustains him.

Faith sustained the one whom the wave was swallowing; and the love of the Savior strengthened the one whom the storm of the waves was disturbing. Peter walked upon the sea more by love than by his feet (Matthew XIV, 29). He did not see where to plant the footprint of his feet; but he saw where to plant the footprint of love.

While he was in the boat, he regarded the Lord, and, led by love for him, descended into the sea. [Col. 2103] He does not think about the slipping waters or the rushing streams; and while he looks upon Christ, he does not look upon the element. He believes that even amid the waves he can find a solid foothold for faith.

Let the sea be tossed by waves and the ocean be troubled by winds; nevertheless, Peter’s path, which leads to the Lord, is not troubled. Peter therefore walks upon the waters, and beneath his feet the soft wave does not yield.

We read in the Old Testament that the children of Israel walked through the Red Sea by dry paths, and that, for the security of those who walked, lest the wave should slip beneath them, it was changed into a kind of solid surface (Exodus XIV, 29). How much better is it here, where, while Peter walks, the wave is neither changed nor slips away; the water is neither made solid nor retreats! Better, I say, is the place where the same wave that surges also sustains, where the same abyss that swallows also serves.

There, so that the people of Israel might be carried through the sea, nature had lost its course; here Peter is carried upon the waters, and the streams do not lose their course.

#### 3. When faith fails, the path fails. Christ is reached only through dangers

The Apostle, then, a rash traveler, takes up the path of a new journey. Now he climbs the mass of the curved abyss; now he descends into the hollow of the sinking wave; and amid the sea’s billows he does not lack the ascent and descent of the path.

But when he is troubled by the winds and driven about by storms, and begins to fear what he had believed, at once the abyss is withdrawn from him and the wave slips away. For as his faith grows weary, so too the path grows weary.

Then he cries out to the Lord Jesus and begs to be saved. The Savior grasps him by the hand and delivers him, adding: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew XIV, 30, 32). This means: Why are you of such little faith that, having begun to walk upon the sea by believing, you did not cross it by persevering? For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. X, 22).

But while you hesitate and doubt, you have lost the journey upon which you had embarked. Why, I ask, are you of such little faith that you did not arrive with the faith by which you began to come?

Understand, then, that on the sea belief carried you, while unbelief submerged you. Therefore, brothers, holy Peter, while he wavers, while he sinks, while he is in danger, reaches the Lord in this way, showing us that Christ is approached only through dangers.

For many are the devil’s waves in this world, and many the shipwrecks of temptations. We can be delivered from them only if the Savior extends his hand when we cry out. Let us therefore never cease to cry out to the Lord; he will not deny his customary help—Jesus our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 2103] In the Theoderician manuscript the sermon ends with the words “he will not deny.”]

## SERMON CXCIII

[Note: [Col. 2103] Elsewhere, *On Time* 14.]

### On the Annunciation of the Lord, I

[Note: [Col. 2103] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful in the judgment of the Louvain editors and is spurious according to Verlin and Vinding, who criticize the fact that in earlier editions this sermon was imprudently assigned to the Nativity of Christ: “its opening and the whole context,” he says, “reject this,” since it discusses the Incarnation. Nevertheless, in all the manuscripts it held a place among the sermons on the Nativity of the Lord.]

#### 1. The devil deceived by Christ through the very art by which he had deceived humanity. Christ God and man

Dearest brothers, today the day has dawned on which Christ took flesh from the Virgin. He wished to assume the form of humility in order to free our souls from sins.

The transgression of that first man had deceived the whole world, so that there would be no remedy of salvation unless Christ came from heaven. The most horrible dragon rejoiced because he had prepared poison for the new man. But for this purpose Christ descended into the Virgin’s womb: that from it he might receive human limbs, deliver them to the cross, and impose death upon the ancient dragon.

For the devil had used an evil plan: through the serpent he spoke to the woman, while the devil himself remained unrecognized. But here God, the Son of God, reduced him to nothing. He descended from heaven to take a human body, setting before him the snare of death—namely, the appearance of flesh—so that the tempter might approach him as though he were merely a man and might remain completely unaware of the Lord.

He saw the flesh but did not know the majesty of the Lord; he perceived weakness but did not see divinity. The devil remained confounded when the Lord appeared in human form.

Thus he descended from God the Father, from whom he had never departed. He was on earth and did not abandon heaven, as the Lord himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

On earth he spoke to human beings as a human being; and in heaven he confessed himself to be there as God. Divinity is not diminished when weakness is assumed. He received what he had not been, and remained God, as he had been from the beginning. What he became as a human being benefited us and diminished nothing in him.

He emptied himself of the fullness of divinity and assumed the form of humility; yet he remained equal to the Father.

#### 2. Mary’s merit and prerogatives

Such a Virgin is chosen from the whole world: one who would have such merit as to receive the Son of God within herself and, after giving birth, remain entirely a virgin.

“Hail,” he says, “Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women; for behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins” (Luke I, 28–32).

You will preserve the rights of virginity, you will have a son, and you will not lose the name of virgin. For such is that divine power that it makes a mother fruitful and preserves a virgin unharmed.

Therefore you are blessed among women, because you will conceive from the Holy Spirit, where there is no human husband but divine power is recognized. You will nurse your own infant; you will offer the Creator the nourishment of milk, and you will be satisfied with heavenly food.

You will wrap the child in swaddling clothes, and he will bestow upon you immortal clothing. You will place infant limbs in a manger, and he will prepare a heavenly table for you.

You will perform all the duties owed to a child for the sake of nursing, so that you may more willingly attain what he himself promised to his saints.

Why say more? Rejoice, Virgin, in so great a promise. The angelic messenger has departed, and God enters the lodging of your womb—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CXCIV

[Note: [Col. 2104] Elsewhere, *On the Saints* 18.]

### On the Annunciation of the Lord, II

[Note: [Col. 2104] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave it doubtful and say that some attribute it to Fulgentius. Verlin and Vinding reject it entirely as false. And not without reason, although in the Roman Breviary and certain other books it is read under Augustine’s name on the first and second day of the annual solemnity established for celebrating the Nativity of the Mother of God.

Indeed, if it was composed for the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, as it is correctly inscribed in our manuscripts—with the single exception of the Corbie manuscript—the author must be later than Augustine, who several times states in his sermons on the Nativity of John the Baptist that in his own age only the Nativity of John and that of Christ the Lord were customarily celebrated in the Church.

But whatever day of the Blessed Mary the beginning of the sermon is assigned to, certainly the ancient Calendar of the Carthaginian Church does not exhibit any feast of the Virgin herself as customary there at least until Augustine’s death, which is recorded in that calendar.

Moreover, what is said here, very feebly, in no. 2 about the Sabellians—that they imagined Mary did not give birth to Christ after the nine months from conception had elapsed, but happened upon a little child by chance—is neither refuted here nor ever elsewhere refuted or mentioned by Augustine. Indeed, he observes in sermon 52, no. 6, that the Patripassians, who are Sabellians, said that the Father himself was born from a woman.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that in two German manuscripts the sermon bears the name of Jerome, a name of which it seems equally unworthy. For it is the work of some unlearned compiler who has collected here, word for word, several statements from the preceding sermons 119, 120, and 121, as well as from sermon 208, *On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary*.

For no. 1, see sermon 120 from no. 2 through no. 8, except that several additions are inserted here and there. For no. 2, compare sermon 208, *On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary*, no. 4. For no. 3, see sermon 120, no. 7, and sermon 121, no. 4. For the same no. 3 and 4, see sermon 119 in the Appendix, nos. 2–4. For no. 5, see sermon 208, *On the Assumption*, no. 11.]

#### 1. Eve’s losses and Mary’s benefits

The long-desired day of the blessed and ever-venerable Virgin Mary is here for us, dearest friends. Therefore let our land, made illustrious by the solemn day of so great an ever-Virgin, rejoice with the greatest exultation [Note: [Col. 2105] So the printed editions. Two Greek manuscripts add “with solemnity.” The Corbie manuscript, however, has “by conception.” Another Corbie manuscript, together with the Fossat manuscript, has “by departure.” The Michaeline manuscript has “by the Nativity.”]

For she is the flower of the field from whom arose the precious lily of the valleys, through whose childbirth nature is changed and the fault of our first parents is erased.

In her that declaration of Eve’s unhappiness has been cut away, in which it is said, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Genesis III, 16), because this woman gave birth to the Lord in joy.

Eve mourned; this woman rejoiced. Eve carried tears, Mary joy, in her womb, because the former brought forth a sinner, while the latter brought forth the innocent one.

A virgin gave birth because a virgin conceived. She gave birth undefiled because there was no lust in the conception. There is a miracle in both respects: pregnant without corruption, and a virgin giving birth in childbirth.

An angel descended from heaven, sent by God the Father, at the beginning of our redemption, to greet blessed Mary. “Hail,” the angel said to her, “full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

Mary, therefore, was filled with grace, and Eve was emptied of guilt. Eve’s curse is changed into Mary’s blessing: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” The Lord is with you in your heart, with you in your womb, with you in your uterus, with you in your aid.

#### 2. Mary surpasses all praise

Rejoice, blessed Virgin. Christ the King has come from his heaven to your womb; from the Father’s bosom he has deigned to descend into his mother’s womb.

“Blessed,” he says, “are you among women, who have brought forth life for both men and women. The mother of our race brought punishment upon the world; the Mother of our Lord brought salvation to the world.

“Eve was the author of sin; Mary was the author of merit. Eve harmed by killing; Mary benefited by giving life. The former struck; the latter healed. In place of disobedience, obedience is exchanged; in place of faithlessness, faith is offered.”

Mary, therefore, joyfully carries the infant; exulting, she embraces her son; she carries the one by whom she is carried.

Nor, as the Sabellians imagine, did she happen upon a little child by chance; but, after the nine months had elapsed, she gave birth to Christ.

Let Mary now play instruments, and amid rapid measures let the drums of the woman in childbirth resound. Let joyful choirs sing together, and let sweet-sounding songs mingle in alternating melodies.

Listen, then, to how our tambourine player sang. For she says: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from this time onward all generations will call me blessed. For he who is mighty has done great things for me.”

The cause, therefore, of such growing joy was a new miracle. Mary’s new childbirth overcame Eve’s childbirth, and Mary’s song drove away Eve’s lamentation [Note: [Col. 2105] So the cb and m manuscripts read, except that the latter has *errati* in place of *laetitiae*. The printed editions instead read: “The miracle of the new childbirth, therefore, overcame the cause of the spreading error.”]

#### 3. The salvation of the world depends on Mary’s assent. Mary mother and virgin. She was wed to God himself. Jeremiah’s prophecy concerning Mary

Finally, after the foretelling of that blessing, while the Virgin silently struggled with herself in an inward debate over what this greeting might be, the heavenly messenger continued: “Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.”

But she said: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

You have now heard how this will happen; answer with a word. Why are you troubled now? [Note: [Col. 2105] Here too we have followed the cb manuscript, since other books have *quomodo* above, as in sermon 120, no. 7: “Why do you delay life for the world?”]

You have heard how this will happen: the Holy Spirit will come upon you so that you may bring forth a child and not lose your virginity; you will produce a son and remain undefiled after childbirth.

O blessed Mary, the whole world, held captive, begs for your assent. You, Lady [Note: [Col. 2105] Perhaps, “you, Lord,” as above in sermon 120, no. 7], the world has made the pledge of its faith.

Do not delay, [Col. 2106] Virgin. Answer the messenger’s word quickly and receive the Son; give faith and experience the power.

“Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 26–38, 46–49).

Without delay the messenger returns, and Christ enters the bridal chamber of the Virgin. Blessed Mother of God suddenly becomes pregnant, and from that moment onward she is proclaimed blessed throughout all ages.

She conceived at once through belief in the word, ignorant of a man’s embrace. Her womb is filled without being polluted by any human union.

Thus she remains a virgin when she conceives, a virgin when pregnant, a virgin when she gives birth, and a virgin after childbirth. Glorious, therefore, is that virginity and glorious that fruitfulness.

Mary rejoices and happily marvels that she is a mother; she rejoices that she has given birth through the Holy Spirit. She is not frightened because she has given birth unmarried; rather, she marvels with exultation that she has given birth.

Let us too rejoice, brothers, on the day of so great a Virgin [Note: [Col. 2106] Here the printed editions, against the authority of the manuscripts, substituted for “of so great a Virgin”: “of the Annunciation which today took place through the angel at the Virgin’s ears.”], who, while she was betrothed to a carpenter, was wed to the Architect of heaven.

For a Son is promised to her through the visitation of the Holy Spirit. Hearing this, she rejoices and desires to become a mother.

What wonder, then, if he is born without corruption who is conceived through sanctification? For it was not fitting that he who brought salvation to us should deprive his mother of the dignity of integrity.

For he whom earth, sea, and heaven cannot contain is received within the limbs of a tiny body.

This is the novelty foretold in advance by the prophecy of Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth; a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah XXXI, 22).

O woman blessed above women, who knew no man at all and encompassed a man in your womb! Mary encompasses the man by giving faith to the angel, because Eve lost the man by consenting to the serpent.

#### 4. The angel’s words to Mary. Mary’s obedience is commended

The angel greets a young woman who knows nothing of a man’s greeting; the Virgin is terrified by the novelty of the words.

To her the angel, as we quoted above, said: “Do not be afraid, Mary; for you have found favor with the Lord.”

“Do not,” he says, “be terrified at my presence, mother of my Lord. I have come as the minister of your conception” [Note: [Col. 2106] The manuscript m has “messenger.”], not to cause you to lose your virginity; he who is to be born from you himself sent me to you.

For you will conceive and bear a son—not a man of ordinary merit, but the Savior of the whole world.

Recall, Mary, in the book of Isaiah the prophet, the virgin whom you read was to give birth (Isaiah VII, 14), and rejoice and exult, because you have been found worthy to be she.

You are that Virgin prefigured there. Behold, you will conceive in your womb, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit; you will be pregnant and will remain undefiled.

You will indeed bear a son, and you will suffer no loss of virginity. You will become pregnant and will remain an always untouched mother. You will feel the weight of your womb, and you will not lose the modesty of chastity. Your breasts will swell, and your genital organs will remain untouched.

But she said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

O happy obedience, O extraordinary grace! While she humbly gave faith, she embodied within herself the Maker of heaven.

The Lord fulfilled in her what he had long before foretold: “I desire obedience rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hosea VI, 6).

This was true obedience, more pleasing than every sacrifice; this was a will more acceptable than all offerings. From this she deserved the glory that she herself later proclaimed: “Behold,” she says, “from this time onward all generations will call me blessed.”

#### 5. A prayer to the blessed Virgin

O blessed Mary, who could worthily offer you the due pledges of gratitude and praises? By your singular assent you came to the aid of the lost world.

What praises can the weakness of the human race pay you, when through your sole mediation it found the way to restoration?

Receive, then, whatever small and inadequate expressions of gratitude we can offer, however unequal to your merits; and when you have received our vows, excuse our faults by praying.

Admit our prayers into the sanctuary of hearing; bring back to us the antidote of reconciliation. Through you, may what we bring through you be excusable; [Col. 2107] may what we ask with faithful mind be obtainable.

Receive what we offer; give back what we ask; excuse what we fear.

[For you are the sole hope of sinners; through you we hope for forgiveness of our offenses, and in you, most blessed one, lies our expectation of rewards. [Note: [Col. 2107] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the manuscripts and from sermon 208, *On the Assumption*.]]

Holy Mary, help the miserable; aid the fainthearted; comfort those who weep; pray for the people; intercede for the clergy; plead for the devout female sex.

May all who celebrate your commemoration feel your help [Note: [Col. 2107] So the cb manuscript agrees with the printed editions. Others have “your Nativity.” Below, in sermon 208, *On the Assumption*, they have “your name.”].

Stand ready to answer the petitions of those who ask, and return to all the desired result.

Let it be your constant concern to pray for the people of God—you who were found worthy, blessed woman, to bear the price of the world [Note: [Col. 2107] The printed editions have “to bear the Redeemer of the world.” Manuscript m has “to bear the offspring of the world.” One Greek manuscript has “to bring forth blessed offspring for the world.” Another Greek manuscript has “to bring forth a blessed prayer for the world”; with these words the sermon ends in those manuscripts.
