We have followed the cb manuscript, in which the following conclusion is added: “through the Son of God and man, whom you carried in your womb as our Redeemer and Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God in the Trinity, lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”]—who lives and reigns forever and ever.

## SERMON CXCV

[Note: [Col. 2107] Formerly, *On Time* 18; later, in the Appendix 25.]

### On the Annunciation of the Lord, III

[Note: [Col. 2107] In the judgment of the Louvain editors, it is the work of an uneducated man. It is found in very ancient codices: one of them, the Corbie manuscript, designates Ambrose as the author; most of the others designate Augustine, but wrongly.]

#### 1. Mary, the closed gate in the house of the Lord

I would rightly and fully praise the most chaste womb of the Virgin Mary, the closed chamber of the virgin bride’s womb, the sealed upper room of modesty, if I were reaping a harvest that I had not sown, concerning which the Apostle says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians VI, 8).

It is entirely true, it is true that every human being reaps what he has sown. God alone can reap what he has not sown, as the Son of the Virgin himself says in a certain Gospel reading: “I reap where I did not sow, and I gather where I did not scatter” (Luke XIX, 22).

Let him speak—let him alone, the one born from the Virgin, the Son of Mary—let him say to his bride-mother: “I reap where I did not sow, and I gather where I did not scatter.”

Let Mary also speak: “And I gave birth to you as my son, but I did not violate my virginity. I retained the kingdom of virginity, and I gave birth to the king of chastity. I received the Emperor’s Son entering and leaving in the palace of my womb, and from my hands I did not lose the key of royal modesty.

“I became the gate of heaven; I became the door of the Son of God. I became that closed gate which the prophet Ezekiel saw in a divine vision and concerning which he prophesied about me: ‘I saw a gate in the house of the Lord, closed; and the angel said to me, “This gate which you see shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord alone shall enter and leave through it, and it shall remain closed forever”’ (Ezekiel XLIV, 2).”

O wondrous vision of the prophet—but more wondrous still the fulfillment of the prophecy!

What is the closed gate in the house of the Lord except that Mary the Virgin will always remain untouched? And what is “No man shall pass through it” except that Joseph will not know her? And what is “The Lord alone shall enter and leave through it” except that the Holy Spirit will impregnate her and the Lord of angels will be born through her? And what is “It shall remain closed forever” except that Mary will be a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth?

Let Mary therefore say: “I became the gate of heaven; I became the door of the Son of God. I became a closed door for him who after his resurrection entered to his disciples through closed doors; who, born from my womb, left me an untouched mother; who filled my womb with divinity and did not empty my womb of chastity.

“He came forth from my womb, magnificent in his giant stride, and my womb was not emptied of modesty. Neither in conception was I found without modesty, nor in childbirth was I found with pain.”

O wondrous and praiseworthy woman among women, in whom virginity was greeted by an angel, alone made pregnant but not violated, relieved of her burden but not emptied! For the angel greeted her in this way: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace, the Lord is with you!”

Happy navel of chastity, which no marital embrace touched! I contemplate your conception, blessed Virgin, and I am filled with awe; I look upon your childbirth, and I tremble; I adore your Son, and I come back to life.

#### 2. The angelic greeting

Tell me, I beg you: how did you deserve to be called the daughter-in-law of the Lord and the bride of the Son of God? Tell me what I ask, but forgive me as I speak with you. Forgive me, I say, that I, a servant—and would that I were a good servant, rather than also an unprofitable and evil servant, and therefore an evil servant because I do not speak with you as a servant, with trembling—dare to converse with the bride of my Lord.

Forgive me, then, that I dare to speak with the bride of my Lord; and yet tell me how the Son of God could be born through you.

Listen, brothers; listen to Mary speaking with us—absent in the flesh but present in spirit; turning her face away from her interlocutor out of virginal modesty, yet explaining how she was made pregnant by the Creator.

“I was,” Mary says, “in my house, a Jewish girl, born from the seed of King David. I grew to maturity and was betrothed to a husband; and I pleased another, not through the intervention of adultery but through the intervention of the Holy Spirit.

“I was betrothed to a Jewish man, and I pleased God as man. A Jewish man betrothed me, and Christ God loved me.

“My betrothed Joseph did not know that my God had loved me, and he thought that my womb had been made pregnant through adultery.

“For while my betrothed Joseph was unaware, a great bridal attendant (*paranymph*) of Christ came to me—not the first patriarch or an outstanding prophet, but that archangel Gabriel, radiant in face, gleaming in garment, wondrous in gait, terrible in appearance. He visited me and troubled me; he greeted me and made me pregnant; and he said to me: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.’

“‘The Lord is with you,’ he said, but more than with me. ‘The Lord is with you,’ but not as with me. For although the Lord is in me, the Lord created me; but through you he is to be born.

“So it is, Mary: the Lord is with you, so that he may be in your heart and in your womb; so that he may fill your mind and fill your womb; so that he may come forth beautiful from your womb like a bridegroom from his chamber; so that the king may come forth from the innermost part of your womb like a king from his bedroom; so that the prince may come forth from the royal hall, yet without causing your virginity to be violated.”

#### 3. The same subject continued

And she said to him: “How will this happen, that I should become pregnant in a chaste womb while remaining free from a husband, since I know no man at all?

“For I am betrothed to a righteous man. If I do not unite with him, how shall it be that I will give birth? But if it can happen that I both conceive untouched and give birth while remaining closed, explain the manner, and you will find my mind ready.

“For in every way I earnestly desire this of my God: that I may have offspring and not lose my modesty.”

The angel Gabriel explains the manner of conception: that the Savior would come into being through a word.

“O Mary,” he says, “Virgin of God, bride of God, beloved of God, daughter of God, Mother of God, if you ask me how you will conceive as a virgin, give birth as a virgin, and remain a virgin after childbirth—or how the one who made you will come to be in you—listen to me, and do not be troubled within yourself: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’” (Luke I, 34–35).

The power of the Most High will so overshadow you that you will neither suffer the heat of lust nor fail to be the mother of the Creator.

### 4. Joseph Is Troubled

Meanwhile Joseph, the betrothed of Mary, does not know what the angel has done with her. Suddenly, with the familiarity of a household member and the marital license proper to him, Joseph looks upon Mary, his wife: he sees the veins in her throat swelling and her face growing thin; finally, he sees that her steps have become burdened. He understands that Mary’s womb is pregnant. [Note: [Col. 2109] The better manuscripts, after the word “felt,” add “and for a long time with himself,” etc., omitting the intervening words.]

Joseph, a righteous man, is troubled because he feels that Mary—whom he had received from the Lord’s temple and had not yet known—is pregnant, and because the woman whom he had not deserved to possess in the honor of marriage he now finds involved in disgrace. Long agitated and debating with himself, he says:

“Where did this come from? What has happened? I did not know her; I did not touch her. If I did not touch her, I did not violate her; if I did not violate her, I did not make her pregnant. Alas, alas! What has happened? What, do you suppose, has occurred? Through whom has Mary fallen so far? Whom has she found flattering her more than I did? For although I had marital license, I did not disturb the girl’s modesty before the bridal chamber. I was afraid—indeed, very much afraid—because in that Mosaic book of the Law, in a sentence fixed by its wording, it is prescribed that any virgin who has stained her father’s house by adultery is to be subjected to death by stoning; likewise, the man who has not brought the father the garment of her modesty, and who, before witnesses, has denied it and failed to produce the token of her modesty, is himself also to die together with the virgin. Thus Moses wished both kinds of lustful persons to be struck by this sentence, and commanded adulterers to perish together. For thus he says: ‘You shall remove the disgrace from the house of Israel; and everyone who hears will be afraid and will not act wickedly’ (Deut. 22:21–22).

“I was guarding against this sentence of Moses, and I was restraining such wantonness in my own body, especially because I knew beforehand both that I was David’s son and that I had exercised a royal priesthood.” [Note: In some manuscripts: “and I knew beforehand the royal priesthood.” In the printed editions, however: “because I knew that I was David’s son.”]

“But since nothing is extraordinary, nothing new, nothing hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing concealed that will not come into public view, I recall an episode concerning the daughter of King David. Royal audacity drove King David toward Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and marital fear did not deter him. A youthful impulse drove Mary, the daughter of King David, and parental terror did not restrain her.

“What, then, shall I do? What shall I undertake? I am anxious, I groan, I grieve, I hurry about, I seek a solution, and I do not find a complete one. Shall I expose her, or remain silent? I simply do not know what to do. Shall I expose the adultery, or remain silent because of the disgrace? If I expose it, I do not consent to the adultery, but I incur the stain [Note: Older manuscripts read: ‘death.’ Another reading: ‘sacrilege.’] of cruelty, because I know from the book of Moses that she must be stoned. If I remain silent, I consent to evil and place my portion with adulterers. Since, therefore, remaining silent is evil, but exposing the adultery is worse, lest murder be committed through me, I shall quietly dissolve the marriage.”

“Joseph,” as the Gospel says, “resolved to dismiss Mary his wife secretly” (Matt. 1:19). He resolved that she should belong to another, although she already belonged to another [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Some others read: “that she was an adulteress.” The printed editions read: “guilty of adultery.” One manuscript reads: “that there was adultery, although there was already a mystery.”]—not by a rejection of the mind, but by a conception of faith.

### 5. Joseph Is Reassured by the Angel. The Prophecies Concerning Mary Are Explained

But Mary, daughter of that great king David, must not fear, because just as a prophetic utterance brought pardon to David, so the angel of the Savior delivers Mary.

“Come now, chaste Mother of the Lord, in whom there was no male desire but the fulfillment of the Holy Spirit; whom Joseph the Jew did not violate, but whom God almighty alone impregnated; who were not joined to Joseph your betrothed, nor known by any man, but by God almighty alone.

“Invoke, holy Virgin, the Lord your God, David your father—not that David stained by adultery and disgraced by the murder of Uriah the Hittite, but that David, I mean, who fought with strong hand and contended long against the devil.

“Let God arise for your help; let him send his angel from heaven and visit your betrothed in a dream. Let Moses suspend his judgment, lest Joseph claim vengeance for your adultery.”

Thus Joseph prepares his mind for the time when he may dismiss Mary secretly.

### 6. The Same Subject Continued

Behold again that Virgin’s attendant—not a man, but the conspicuous angel Gabriel, the most impartial courier of heaven—at the midnight hour says to Joseph in a vision:

“Joseph,” he says, “son of David, why are you so greatly troubled? Why are you so deeply sorrowful? Why do you sweat while pondering in your sleep? Why do you walk sadly while awake? Why do you entertain an evil suspicion about Mary, when she is to give birth to the Savior for you?

“Remove jealousy from your mind. He who will be born from her is himself the one who impregnated her. For this reason your soul is sad, Joseph: whatever you have read in prophecy, you have not understood in Mary. This is the source of all your sadness: you have not yet known your betrothed, and you feel that she is pregnant, yet you suspect nothing in her except adultery.

“Joseph, son of David, born from a priestly lineage—not merely priestly, but also royal—son of the Prophets and companion of the Scribes: that God who wrote wonders in his Law has himself performed wonders in your wife. What are God’s wonders except those things that are impossible for human beings?

“Have you not, then, read God’s wonders in the Law? And if you have read them, why have you not understood them? The very Law that you read daily was written without a stylus on tablets of stone. Read and understand that bread was brought forth in the wilderness by the earth, although no farmer introduced its seed into the soil. Aaron’s staff also, dry for very many years and without water, came to life again, blossomed in the temple, and produced nuts enclosed beneath its covering.

“Therefore he who wrote the stone tablets without an iron stylus himself impregnated Mary through the Holy Spirit; he who brought forth bread in the wilderness without a sower himself made the Virgin fruitful without violation; and he who caused a staff to sprout without rain himself caused David’s daughter to give birth without seed.

“Finally, Joseph, son of David, son of the Prophets, have you not read what Isaiah, the outstanding among the Prophets, said, and how he wrote: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel’ (Isa. 7:14)?

“What you have therefore read in your books, behold with your own eyes in Mary, so that you may rightly sing the song of your father David: ‘As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God’ (Ps. 47:9).

“Take Mary your wife, therefore, always secure concerning her and troubled about nothing, because what has been conceived in her womb is not from sin but from the Holy Spirit; and he who will be born from her womb will not be called the son of a Jew, but will be called the Son of God.

“Have, therefore, Joseph, together with Mary your wife, a common virginity of the limbs, because from virginal limbs is born the Power of the angels. Let Mary be the bride of Christ, her virginity of the flesh preserved; and let you also be the father of Christ through the care of chastity and the honor of virginity, so that from virginal limbs you may give birth for the Christian ages to the bridegroom of virginity and the husband of chastity, common to every virgin and every married woman, in whom there is no jealousy, because virginity was impregnated by a greeting in Mary.

“Great is the merit of virginity, brothers! Mary’s virginity was impregnated by the angel’s greeting, was greeted by John from the womb, and Mary’s virginity, while giving birth, was praised today by the angels; Mary’s virginity, while nursing, was proclaimed from heaven by the star and honored with gifts by the Magi.

“Rejoice, therefore, Joseph, and rejoice exceedingly in Mary’s virginity, because you alone deserved to possess a virginal marriage. Through the merit of virginity you have been so separated from intercourse with your wife that you are called the father of the Savior, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.”

## SERMON CXCVI

[Note: Formerly, *On the Saints* 20; later, in the Appendix 76.]

### On the Nativity of John the Baptist, I

[Note: On this very day it is read in the Roman Breviary under Augustine’s name; nevertheless, it was rightly rejected as his by the Louvain scholars and by Verlinus and Vindingus. It has very extensive agreement in meaning and wording with various writings of Faustus, namely, with the homily which we stated above, under Sermon 176, to be his; with the first Eusebian homily *On the Nativity of Christ*, where the procession of the Word from the Father is explained in the same manner; with the first of Faustus’s Letters to Felix and the sixth to Ruricius, where two kinds of abstinence are distinguished; with his book *On Free Will*, chapter 9, in several words read here in section 6; and also with the second Eusebian homily *On the Nativity of Saint John*, which we infer to be Faustus’s especially from this statement: “He knew that the grace of the one choosing would not suffice unless the diligence of the one cooperating kept watch,” since Faustus said something similar in Book 1 *On Free Will*. Finally, we observe that the second Eusebian homily *To the Monks* contains a considerable part of this sermon, beginning with the words in section 6: “We know that the human mind, familiarly, in the various enticements of this world,” etc.]

### 1. The Singular Character of This Festival. John as a Type of the Law

After that most sacred day of the Lord’s nativity, we read of the birth of no human being being celebrated except that of blessed John the Baptist. In the case of other saints and chosen servants of God, we know that the day is honored on which, after completing their labors and conquering and triumphing over the world, this present life brought them forth into everlasting ages; in others, the merits completed on the final day are celebrated. In this case, even the first day and the very beginnings of the human being are consecrated. The reason, without doubt, is that through him the Lord wished his coming to be attested, lest people suddenly fail to recognize what they had not expected.

John was a figure of the Old Testament, and in himself he displayed the form of the Law. Therefore John foretold the Savior, just as the Law went before grace. But the fact that, while not yet born, he prophesied from the hidden place of his mother’s womb, and that, already deprived of light, he was a witness to the truth—this must be understood to mean that, hidden beneath the veil and flesh of the letter, the Law proclaimed the Redeemer to the world in the spirit and announced our Lord to us from a certain womb of the Law.

Therefore, because the Jews “went astray from the womb,” that is, from the Law that was pregnant with Christ—“They went astray from the womb; they spoke falsehood” (Ps. 57:4)—he came as a witness, “to bear witness concerning the light” (John 1:8). But the fact that John, while imprisoned, directs his disciples to Christ (Matt. 11:2) signifies that the Law hands them over to the Gospels. The Law, according to John’s type, lay shut up as though in a prison of ignorance, in darkness and concealment, while the understanding of Jewish blindness remained enclosed within the letter.

### 2. The Burning Lamp

Concerning this, the blessed Evangelist declares: “He was the burning lamp” (John 5:35)—that is, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that, while the world was possessed by the night of ignorance, he might show the light of salvation and, as though amid the thickest darkness of sins, display the most splendid sun of righteousness by the ray of his light. Concerning himself he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Matt. 3:3).

Let us see in what wilderness—that is, among the people of the Gentiles. Hearts empty of the fear of God and lacking the Holy Spirit are compared to the desolation of a barren wilderness. This world was deserted by every cultivation of faith and fear of God, and, covered with the thorns of sins, it lay desolate like an untilled field. It had produced no fruitfulness of good works at all and had received no rain of spiritual grace.

Blessed John is sent to plow it, as it were, through prophetic and apostolic preaching: by announcing repentance, he was to make the rough field fruitful and cultivated, fill it with the seeds of the divine word, and prepare it for mature grain—that is, for the grace of regeneration.

### 3. What His Birth Reveals

How great is the glory of this: it is promised to the aged priest Zechariah and the barren Elizabeth by Gabriel—that is, by the very angel through whom the birth of the Lord is announced to Mary. And, as though a certain likeness of the Lord were being sent ahead, a son is born beforehand from a barren woman before the Son of the Virgin, declaring by his birth some still greater miracle.

Posterity is endowed with unexpected offspring, because virginity was to be endowed and enriched by a new birth. John is sent ahead of Jesus Christ like the Old Testament before the New, so that “day may pour forth speech to day” and the obscure depth of the sacraments may be revealed through the clearer mysteries of the new teaching.

Thus a lamp is sent ahead of the sun, a servant before the Lord, a friend before the bridegroom, a herald before the judge, a voice before the Word. Therefore he says of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” Why did blessed John say that he was a voice? Because he was the announcer and preacher of the Word.

[Col. 2112]

### 4. What the Word Is and What the Voice Is

Let us now carefully inquire what difference there is between the word and the voice. The sacred Scriptures define as “word” what we conceive in our mind within the silence of the spirit. They define as “word” the very thought that is still retained within the secret places of the conscience; but the voice is that by which the word is brought forth into the midst.

The voice is the sound that discloses thought; the word is thought itself. For when we conceive a word in the heart, a voice is necessary, as it were a vehicle of the word. Although we transfer the word itself to another through the sound of the mouth, nevertheless it is transferred whole within us—that is, enclosed by the speaker—so that it remains in its own place.

In the same way, the almighty Father, wishing to make himself known to us, took blessed John as the voice through which he might bring forth to us that Wisdom and Word “which in the beginning was God with God” (John 1:1). As he himself testifies: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44:2).

That Word descended to us from its own place in such a way that it remained in the bosom—that is, in the depths—of the Father’s heart, visiting earthly things without abandoning heavenly things.

### 5. John’s Glory Above the Other Prophets. Mediator of the New and Old Testaments

Blessed John the Baptist went before this glory not from far away, as the other Prophets did, but as one near and close at hand. They proclaimed the coming of the king long beforehand. Some said, “He will come at some time”; others, “Behold, he is coming soon.” But John showed that the one whom he had foretold as coming had come, and he fulfilled his prophecy while the very one whom he announced was present.

While still in his mother’s womb, he was filled with the Holy Spirit and anticipated his own birth by prophesying. In likeness to the Lord, he was sanctified before he was born, leaping within the womb and bearing witness to the Savior’s coming through his mother’s mouth.

Truly he was a burning lamp, in whom the singular grace of divine condescension shone forth, so that, through the voice of the holy mother, he might announce that the Redeemer was already at hand, and, through her as through a certain lamp of truth, might show him before he himself had been brought forth into the light.

This is that capable mediator of the New and Old Testaments and worthy herald of the glorious Lamb: he deserved both to announce and to see his Lord at one and the same time, beginning the new and bringing the old to completion at the same age as his own birth.

### 6. Violence Must Be Done for the Sake of the Kingdom of Heaven

The Evangelist testifies concerning this man: “From the days of John,” he says, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. 11:21).

We know that the human mind, easily overcome by the various enticements and desires of this world, flees labor, seeks pleasure, and is scarcely persuaded to exclude from itself the habits of its former life. But when it begins to consider the necessity of the final day and the weight of the future judgment, stirred and goaded either by hope of reward or fear of punishment, it declares voluntary war on its passions. It does violence to its former desires and strives violently to conquer itself.

For it cannot happen without violence that someone passes from abundance and delights to hunger and thirst, to abstinence and the cross; that he destroys through hardship and vigils the flesh previously devoted to sleep and leisure.

I say that it cannot happen without violence that each person exchanges anger for patience, pride for humility; overcomes the abundance of riches and sufficiency through love of poverty; condemns drunkenness by sobriety and lust by chastity; and that a human being is suddenly transformed into a perfect man, becoming in a certain way another person from the former one.

Thus the kingdom of heaven is seized through violence from such things.

### 7. Two Kinds of Abstinence

There are two kinds of abstinence and of the cross: one bodily, the other spiritual.

The first is to refrain from drink and feasts, to restrain the appetite of the stomach from pleasures and the softest delights, and to recall and violently withdraw one’s senses from those things that deceive through touch, taste, and sight.

The second and more precious and exalted kind of abstinence and cross is to govern the movements of the soul and calm its disturbances through the tranquility of moderation; to curb the impulses of anger and pride like a wild beast; to fight daily against one’s vices; to rebuke oneself with a certain censorial austerity of virtue; and, in a certain way, to wage a quarrel with the inner person.

Precious and glorious before God is this cross: to bring evil thoughts under control; to deny one’s own desires, examine them through inward scrutiny, and subject them to the command of the one who governs; to abstain from speech and action by which the soul is wounded as from harmful foods; and to preserve the mind sober through spiritual moderation, keeping it away from things that are contrary.

Whoever does this, breaking through the wall of passion, ascends violently to the kingdoms of heaven.

The soul must therefore do violence to itself, striving with all its strength to seize the palm of victory in its labors, which it sees being taken from it by many hostile enemies. It is necessary, therefore, with the greatest labor, to snatch the palm of salvation from this world; as though surrounded by enemies keeping watch, we must gather the fruits with unceasing vigilance and carry away the prey from the treasure of life, as though snatched from the midst of the fire of this age.

### 8. The Church Seizes the Kingdom from the Synagogue. Christ Is Our Kingdom. Human Beings Seize It from the Apostate Angels

There is another kind of seizure, when we seize what was promised and offered to others.

The Savior had descended above all for this purpose in taking flesh: to justify the people of the Jews. As he himself says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

But the disciples also reproved the unbelieving people of the Synagogue in this way: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Therefore, when the Jews rejected the gifts prepared for them, publicans and sinners from the Gentiles believed; and thus the Church seizes the kingdom from the Synagogue.

For Christ is our kingdom. We seize him when, after he is killed by the Jews, he is buried by us. We seize him while they sleep, as they themselves confess in the Gospel: “Say,” they instruct, “that his disciples came by night and stole him while you were sleeping” (Matt. 28:13).

Let the one who sleeps therefore arise, lest, relaxed through negligence, he lose Christ while his mind sleeps in unbelief and sluggishness.

The kingdom of heaven is seized when he is denied by his own household and worshiped by the Gentiles; when he is sent to some for salvation and found by others; when his own refuse him and strangers receive him; when his own pursue him and his enemies embrace him; when a citizen rejects his inheritance and a foreigner takes possession of it; when a son rejects it and a servant acknowledges it.

The kingdom of heaven also suffers violence in another way, when human beings acquire what the angels lost, when adopted and humble people ascend there from which proud inhabitants fell.

Therefore, since we live among so many envious persons, so many robbers, and invisible ambushers, by what strength shall we seize the kingdoms of heaven? Who can do so, I ask, except by obeying teachers; resisting vices and injustices born from desire; lamenting sins; and redeeming them through fasts and almsgiving?

## SERMON CXCVII

[Note: Formerly, *On the Saints* 21.]

### On the Nativity of John the Baptist

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It remained doubtful among the Louvain scholars and was rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus. It consists of excerpts from the preceding sermon, from two Eusebian sermons on this feast, from the second sermon on the same celebration found among Ambrose’s works, and finally from two sermons numbered 287–289 among the Augustinian sermons. The conclusion is in the Caesarian style.]

### 1. The Birthdays of the Lord Alone and of John Are Celebrated. Whoever Is Born of a Woman Is Inferior to John

Dearest brothers, today we celebrate the natal day of holy John, something that we read was granted to none of the saints. For throughout the whole world, the day of birth of the Lord alone and of blessed John is celebrated and honored.

A barren woman bore the one; a virgin conceived the other. In Elizabeth, barrenness is overcome; in blessed Mary, the ordinary manner of conception is changed. Elizabeth bore a son by knowing a man; Mary believed the angel and conceived. Elizabeth conceived a human being, and Mary also conceived a human being; but Elizabeth conceived only a human being, while Mary conceived God and a human being.

What, then, is the meaning of John? Why was he inserted? Why was he sent ahead?

Great, therefore, is John, whose greatness the Savior himself also attests, saying: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). He surpasses all and rises above everyone; he exceeds the Prophets and transcends the Patriarchs; and whoever is born of a woman is inferior to John.

Someone may perhaps say: “If John is greater among those born of women, he is greater than the Savior.” God forbid. John was born of a woman, whereas Christ was born of a virgin; the one was poured forth from the recesses of a corruptible womb, the other was brought forth from the flower of an undefiled womb.

John’s birth is therefore associated with the Lord’s generation so that the Lord may not appear outside the truth of human condition. If John is compared with human beings, he was sent ahead of God.

Such excellence and such grace were in him that he himself was thought to be the Christ. What, then, did he say concerning Christ? “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16).

What does “we all” mean? It means the Prophets, the Patriarchs, the Apostles—all the saints, both those sent ahead before the Incarnation and those sent by the one who had become incarnate—all of us have received from his fullness. We are vessels; he is the fountain.

### 2. Just as Christ’s Birth, So Also John’s Birth Is Full of Mystery. The Same Is True of Their Passions

If, then, we have understood the mystery, my brothers, John is a human being; Christ is God. Let the human being be humbled, and let God be exalted, according to what John himself said concerning the Lord: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

So that the human being might be humbled, John was born on the day when the days begin to decrease; so that God might be exalted, Christ was born on the day when the days begin to increase.

A great sacrament, dearest brothers! We celebrate John’s nativity, as we do Christ’s, because his birth too is full of mystery. What mystery, if not that of our humility, just as Christ’s birth is full of the mystery of our exaltation?

Let us therefore decrease in the human being, so that we may increase in God; let us be humbled in ourselves, so that we may be exalted in him; let human presumption be humbled, so that divine mercy may increase.

The sacrament of this same truth was also fulfilled in the passions of both. So that the human being might decrease, John’s head is cut off; so that God might be exalted, Christ is suspended on the wood.

### 3. Why John Is Called a Lamp and Sent Ahead of Christ. Why He Is a Voice. He Bore the Type of the Law

If you command it, we wish briefly to explain to the ears of your Charity why the Lord and our Savior called blessed John a lamp and why he wished him to be sent ahead of himself.

He was sent ahead like a voice before the Word, a lamp before the sun, a herald before the judge, a servant before the master, and a friend before the bridegroom.

Because the darkness of sins and the night of unbelief had overwhelmed the whole world, and it could not look upon the sun of righteousness, blessed John was sent ahead like a lamp. The eyes of the heart, oppressed by the disease of iniquity and unable to see the great and true light, were first to become accustomed to seeing a faint brightness in the light of the lamp. Then, little by little, once the cloud of sins had been removed and the moisture of unbelief dried up, when Christ arrived they could be gladdened by that heavenly light rather than tormented by it.

For just as you encourage bleary eyes to see when you show them the slight brightness of a lamp, but torment them more if you thrust a great light upon them, so our Lord and Savior, who is the true light, could not have been endured by the whole world unless he had first sent blessed John ahead like a lamp.

Let John speak and say: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23). He was a voice because he was filled with the Spirit of God’s Word. [Note: The printed editions and Eusebius read: “He was a voice because he was filled with the Spirit of the Word.” Two manuscripts read: “He was a voice because the Word went before; he cried out because he was full of the Holy Spirit.”]

Just as a spoken message is conveyed in a certain way from the speaker to the hearer through the service and vehicle of the voice, so John, sounding forth Christ, was the minister and bearer of the Word.

Blessed John, I say, displayed in himself the type of the Law, which showed Christ from afar through signs and indications; therefore he sent two of his disciples to Christ. These two disciples sent by John to Christ may perhaps be the two peoples, one of whom believed from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles.

John directs them to Christ; the Law sends them to grace, and through faith in the Gospel seeks to establish the truth of the Old Testament.

### 4. Exhortation

Dearest brothers, so that we may celebrate this most holy festival not only with bodily but also with spiritual joy, let us, according to our strength, prepare our minds to give alms and to maintain peace with everyone.

For the love of God and zeal for holy discipline, let us strive with all our strength to prohibit not only ourselves but also our entire household and all who belong to us from every kind of buffoonery and shameful speech. Let us not permit pleasure-seekers to pollute the holy solemnity by bringing forth wanton songs.

Then holy John will be able to obtain for us whatever we ask, if he recognizes that we celebrate his festival peacefully, soberly, chastely, and without any shameful speech.

These things, therefore, dearest brothers, I offer as a father’s concern. For, by God’s favor, I trust so greatly in your devotion that you will preserve not only yourselves but also all who belong to you in complete propriety, chastity, and sobriety.

Therefore, giving thanks to God, I beseech him that he who has granted you faithfully to begin holy things may grant you to preserve a happy perseverance—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CXCVIII

[Note: Formerly, *On the Saints* 36; later, in the Appendix 84.]

### On the Nativity of John the Baptist, III

[Note: It is wrongly attributed to Maximus in the Theoderician collection. It is an Eusebian homily, the first on this feast, but mutilated and interpolated. Whatever does not belong to this homily is enclosed in brackets; these passages appear to belong to Caesarius.]

### 1. John Is Honored with Singular Celebration. He Surpasses Human Merits

Today, beloved brothers, we celebrate the natal day of John, who went before the Lord’s coming—a privilege that we remember was granted to none of the saints. Today, I say, we venerate his natal day with a unique and singular celebration.

Since we cannot rightly exalt him through the service of human speech, let us proclaim him by the oracle of the Lord’s testimony, with Christ declaring that “among those born of women there is none greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11).

He himself says this. Therefore recognize the magnificence of the praise from the dignity of the one praising; and since no one is asserted to be greater than John among those born of women, understand that John escaped the measure of human merits. [Note: Thus in Eusebius. In the manuscripts: “was the measure of human merits.” In the printed editions: “was above the measure of human merits.”]

### 2. He Is a Voice. He Decreases as Christ Increases. He Signified Christ by His Birth and Manner of Life

“I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. 40:3). This means: “I am not the Word who in the beginning was God with God; rather, I am a voice, that is, I am the minister of the Word, so that through me it may reach human hearing and understanding.”

Therefore blessed John the Baptist declares with equal humility: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

“He must increase,” he says, “because throughout the whole world the Gospel of Christ is being spread; but I must decrease, because John’s prophecy is ending. [He must increase, who will be exalted on the cross; but I must decrease, who am to be beheaded.]”

John’s prophecy received its end because the one who was being prophesied had arrived.

John therefore signified the form of the coming Lord by his birth and manner of life. [Note: One manuscript reads: “his birth and manner of life.”]

John was born from an elderly father; Christ was born from a virgin mother in the old age of the world—in that age, I mean, which was barren in faith and works. John came through a barren woman when generation had become hopeless; Christ came through a virgin while nature stood amazed. The one preached salvation; the other bestowed it. The one baptized for repentance; the other regenerated by grace.

### 3. His Freedom in Rebuking. When the Correction of the Wicked May Rightly Be Omitted. A Pious Strategy for Correcting the Wicked

This is the John who publicly condemned the impiety of King Herod, who had seized the wife of his living brother. For the sake of righteousness he lost his life, but he gained glory.

And sometimes, for the sake of human favor or fear of offending, we prefer flattery and sell the truth, [not fearing what is terribly written: “If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:18).

Yet at times teachers of the Church cease rebuking sinners, not through negligence toward those who sin, but because they fear that through the very act of correction they may break out into worse evils. When priests do not preach for this reason, they cannot be held guilty for their silence. For just as good men are sometimes corrected by severe rebuke, so, conversely, all the proud are driven by the gentlest admonition toward still worse abysses.

Indeed, preachers of the Church sometimes do not rebuke sinners, not by choice but by necessity, to such an extent that they sometimes address certain proud people with praise—even undeserved praise—as a spiritual medicine and a strategy of charity. Thus, while they are ashamed that the things said about them might be false, they may be moved toward reforming their lives and doing good works, according to what is written: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who does evil is blessed” (Ps. 10:3, according to the Hebrews).

And because that saying of the wise man is true—“Just as true praise adorns, so false praise chastises”—it is not impossible before God that even those who, invited by human praise, have begun to perform good works may have this transformed by God into love and habit, according to what one of the wise has said: “Once accustomed to doing good, one will be ashamed to become unaccustomed”; and again: “Let us speak good things; speech will pass into affection.”

Nevertheless, blessed John, with complete and perfect freedom, preferred to endure injustice rather than fail to speak what was right.]

Therefore blessed John himself strikes our hearts with a life-giving oracle in evangelical speech, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

If we hold within us the word of truth and an affection for righteousness, there will be in us that way by which Christ enters the human heart.

That is why he says, “I am the voice of one crying.” The voice of a herald speaks of the judge; a cry threatens judgment.

### 4. The Condition of Misery or Happiness Must Sometimes Be Changed

He then announces: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Luke 3:4–5).

This is what the Evangelist recalls in other words: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

[The time will come, dearest brothers, when the proud person who now refuses to humble himself for his own salvation will grieve, without any remedy, that he was proud. The time will come when the humble will be raised to the heavens and the proud plunged into the depths of hell.

The time will come when all the greedy will grieve that they were rich, those who now mock Christ’s poor. The order of human society that exists now will not always remain. Lazarus will not always be tortured by hunger, nor will the rich miser always enjoy an abundance of delicacies.

Rather, soon the one will be lifted by angels from the dung heap into paradise; and the one who refused to give alms, unless repentance comes to his aid, will be dragged from his luxurious banquet into Tartarus. Thus the one who refused to give the poor man a crumb in this world will not deserve to receive a drop in hell; and the one who refused to feed the poor man from his delicacies will feed the flames from his own marrow.]

But we, brothers, must labor as much as we can so that what pride had made swollen and lofty may be leveled by humility and gentleness; what iniquity had distorted may be corrected by the straightness of righteousness; and what malice had embittered may be moderated by the grace of goodness.

May Christ the Lord find us engaged in these pursuits. For he has graciously provided the way by which he may lead us to our homeland, so that he may deign to say concerning us: “I will walk among them and dwell in them, and I will be their God” (Lev. 26:12).

If he walks in us in this world, he will dwell in us there—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

SERMON CXCIX [Note: [Col. 2117] Formerly, *On the Saints* 22; later, in the Appendix 77.] On the Nativity of John the Baptist, IV [Note: [Col. 2117] This is itself a homily of Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, though here it has been abridged not far from the beginning.]

### 1. John is commended through his parents

Those who know how to extract gold from the earth, wherever they discover a rich vein, expend there all their skill and labor. And we, brothers, because we see a heavenly treasure hidden in the holy Zacharias, let us devote to him everything that belongs to our discourse and to your hearing, so that what has been acquired through common labor may be a common gain.

“There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, and his wife was named Elizabeth, from the daughters of Aaron. And they were both,” he says, “righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.”

Blessed, therefore, are those, brothers, whom no fault strikes in this world, whom no crime wounds. Truly blessed are those whom no reproach could ever touch. “Walking,” he says, “in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.”

If their childhood, adolescence, and youth were blameless—when life is most accustomed to be full of reproach—what must their old age have been? If their beginning was such, what must their end have been?

### 2. Elizabeth was barren until the impulse of desire had passed. The praises of John

“And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren” (Luke 1:5–7). He did not say, “They had no children,” but, “They had no child,” because the one who was to be born of such parents would be unique.

Hear the Lord saying, “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

“Because Elizabeth was barren.” Elizabeth was indeed barren in body, but fertile in virtues; slow to bear offspring, but not slow before God; closed not as regards offspring, but by time; not denied children, but preserved for a mystery.

Brothers, the birth of holy Elizabeth was not taken away, but delayed until the time of the flesh, the suffering of the body, the necessity of marriage, the occasion of pleasure, the impulse of desire, and everything that confounds, weighs down, and burdens the human conscience had passed away.

For a long time the house was being cleansed for sacrifice: the dwelling of holiness, the tent of Christ the surveyor, the habitation of the angel, the court of the Holy Spirit, the temple of God. “You are the temple of God,” says the Apostle, “and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Finally, when every complaint of the body had been quieted and they had become altogether blameless, immediately barrenness fled, old age revived, faith conceived, chastity gave birth, and there was born one greater than man [Note: [Col. 2117] In the manuscripts, “greater than men.”], equal to the angels, the trumpet of heaven, the herald of Christ, the Father’s secret, the messenger of the Son, the standard-bearer of the heavenly King, forgiveness for sinners, correction for the Jews, the calling of the Gentiles—and, to speak precisely, the clasp of the Law and grace, which joined the double robe of the high priest to the holy Father upon the body.

Thus the Evangelist describes the virtues of the father and mother, so that the dignity of the offspring might be recognized from the merits of its parents; and so that the one who by his birth surpassed the law of human birth might be shown to be greater than man.

But if John is about to go forth, let him now be born, because the birth of Christ is at hand. Let the new morning star arise, because the radiance of the true sun is already breaking forth. Let the herald give voice, because the judge is present; let the trumpet cry out, because the King has come; and because God is about to go forth, let the angel now precede him.

### 3. How glorious was the angel’s prophecy concerning John. He fulfills it while not yet born

But since what is above man cannot adequately be expressed by man, let an angel now speak of the virtue of the angel who is being born. “The angel,” he says, “said to Zacharias: ‘Do not be afraid, Zacharias, your supplication has been heard, and Elizabeth your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. And you shall have joy and gladness, and many shall rejoice at his birth. For he shall be great before the Lord; he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. And he shall convert many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people’” (Luke 1:13–17).

Here, brothers, human speech is silent; the preacher’s exposition falls quiet when John’s glory is proclaimed by an angelic heralding, his virtue resounds, and praise is joined to praise. Nothing remains for man to add to one to whom God has given everything.

“He shall be filled,” he says, “with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” You see, brothers, how John reached heaven before he touched the earth; received the divine Spirit before the human spirit; received divine gifts before bodily members; and began to live for God before living for himself. Indeed, he lived for God before God lived for him, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

“In the sixth month,” he says, “the child leaped in his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:44), and announced that Christ had come into the Virgin’s womb. What a fervent messenger, who longed to announce before he lived! What an impatient leader, who reached the King before he reached the body; seized his weapons before possessing his limbs; sought the battle line before the light; and, in order to conquer the world, first conquered nature!

For he, though still within the womb, arouses the womb of his mother; and because the body was delayed, by spirit alone he fulfills the office of an evangelist.

What shall I say, brothers? Before John preceded Christ, he preceded himself. The same Holy Spirit fills the hearts of father, mother, and child, so that the song of the Lord’s nativity may resound through a single instrument of holiness.

---

SERMON CC [Note: [Col. 2118] Elsewhere, among the Vignerian sermons 5, in the second part of the Supplement.] On the Nativity of John the Baptist, V [Note: [Col. 2118] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is mutilated and disfigured by many errors, and, in respect of its manner of expression, cannot be compared with the Augustinian sermons.]

### 1.

The Emperor of heaven and earth, who deigned to visit us, was formerly proclaimed in the oracles of the Prophets. From the very beginning of the world, the coming of the Lord and Savior was proclaimed to us. For the Word could not come to earth without the voice of a herald.

The Prophets foretold him, announcing that the Lord Christ would come in the flesh; but holy John, whose Nativity shines forth for celebration today, not only prophesied the Word but also showed him to others. He is rightly called greater than the other Prophets, because he not only proclaimed and pointed him out, but also baptized.

John the Baptist was called greater, yet he is not above the Teacher, nor is the servant above the Lord: “Among those born of women,” he says, “there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11). He says “of women,” for he who was born of the Virgin is the founder, ruler, and lord of the world [lacuna].

### 2.

An angel was sent into the temple to Zacharias and announced that he would receive a son in his old age; the angel was also a messenger to the Virgin Mary. But Mary believed, whereas Zacharias doubted. The one who doubted is condemned to silence; she who believed is honored with praises [lacuna].

O blessed mother, who bore such a son, who went before and announced the Son of God, and also baptized him! Elizabeth was freed from the reproach of barrenness: she bore a son promised from heaven, who, despising the riches of the world, sought the kingdoms of heaven.

So that he might go before the Word in the spirit and power of Elijah, while he was still in the womb he recognized the presence of the Lord’s Mother. He is a faithful witness of the One who was coming, as Scripture says: “As the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb. He himself showed me that you are the mother of my Lord, who have come to me.”

He became my teacher before he was a son; he taught me before I nursed him. He does not yet know how to strike my breasts, and he knows how to instruct my conscience. He has not yet seen heaven and earth, and within my womb he has recognized the God of heaven and earth.

What sort of messenger is this, who recognizes the Lord in hidden places? In hidden places he speaks a mystery; he announces a miracle.

### 3.

“From where,” she says, “is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Matthew 1:11, 44, 43). “From where,” she says, “is this granted to me?” He is God, whereas I am human; he is Lord, whereas I am a servant; he is Creator, whereas I am a creature. He who formed me within the womb has filled the womb of his own mother.

“From where,” she says, “is this granted to me?” I have no merits, yet divine benefits come before me.

There are two mothers of unconquered virtue: a barren woman and a virgin. Two ships laden from heaven: one bears a promise concerning a man, the other carries the Word from God. One sent forth a herald; the other bore the judge. One is illuminated by a lamp, the other by the sun. The virgin bears the bridegroom; the barren woman bears his friend.

For they also appeared as certain signs of holiness at distinct times. John is born as the day declines; the Lord is born as the day increases, so that the flesh may decline and the spirit grow strong.

Therefore, dearest brothers, rejoicing in such great wonders, we ought to believe that he can make [something] from Adam [reading materially uncertain], and render a barren woman fruitful [Note: [Col. 2119] Perhaps: “that we should believe God makes a virgin a mother.”].

He who preserved the mother’s modesty assumed the name of a flower and did not lose his whiteness; he preserved the virgin’s modesty and displayed the light of the mystery.

May he who gave himself for us also grant us prosperity. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

---

SERMON CCI [Note: [Col. 2119] Formerly, *On the Saints* 26; later, in the Appendix 78.] On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, I [Note: [Col. 2119] It also exists among the published sermons attributed to Ambrose, to whom it may perhaps more truly belong than to Augustine.]

### 1. Peter is famous everywhere through miracles, Paul through his Epistles. Peter’s first miracle: the healing of a lame man. The appropriateness of this event. Peter is the rock, Paul the vessel; both are necessary to the Church

It is known to all of you, brothers, and most widely known throughout the world, that today is the Nativity of the most blessed Peter and Paul. Such devotion cannot be hidden from any part of the earth. For when the prophet David says of them, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5), Peter’s wondrous power has indeed spread throughout all the earth, and Paul’s words in his Epistles have penetrated to the ends of the world.

Who has not heard that the blessed Apostle Peter, in his first miracle [Note: [Col. 2119] The Augustinian editions read “the first”; the Ambrosian editions and manuscripts disagree.], restored the strength of his feet to the lame man sitting at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, who had long been weak from his mother’s womb, so that what nature had failed to provide, apostolic grace might restore?

For when that lame man, asking for alms, thought he would receive some money from the Apostles, the Apostle Peter said to him: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

Blessed indeed is the generosity that gave no silver to the petitioner, but gave health! Blessed is the generosity that brought forth no gold from its treasuries, but brought forth healing! Blessed also is that lame man who, while seeking a monetary alms, received the riches of restored health!

For he deserved to receive from the Apostles what he could not have purchased from physicians with any treasures.

Peter therefore performed the first of his wondrous miracles by restoring the steps of the lame man’s feet. We have often said that Peter himself was named “rock” by the Lord, as he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

If, then, Peter is the rock upon which the Church is built, he rightly heals the feet first, so that just as he contains the foundation of faith in the Church, so also he may strengthen the foundations of the limbs in a human being [Col. 2120]. Rightly, I say, he first heals the feet in a Christian, so that he may no longer stand upon the rock of the Church trembling and weak, but may walk strong and steadfast.

Where are the words of the Apostle Paul not read? What place does not inscribe them in its writings, retain them in its heart, and preserve them in its conduct? Paul was named by the Lord a vessel of election.

A good vessel, in which the precious precepts of Christ’s commandments are stored; a good vessel, from whose fullness the substance of life is continually distributed to the peoples—and it is full.

The names of the Apostles are excellent: rock and vessel, necessary to the house of the Savior. For the house is built through the strength of rocks and adorned through the usefulness of vessels. The rock supports the peoples in firmness, lest they fall; the vessel shelters Christians in its keeping, lest they be tempted.

### 2. The appropriateness of their suffering on one day; Peter fastened to a cross; milk flowing from Paul’s neck. How blessed their departure from this world was

No one can be unaware how blessed their departure from this world was. Their first blessedness is that both are known to have suffered on the same day, so that those whom one faith had bound to service might be crowned by one day of martyrdom.

Then, although the actual suffering was different in each case, how full of holy grace it was! Peter underwent death on a cross, like the Savior, and, through the likeness of his devotion to the Lord, was not separated from him even in death: he who imitated him in faith might imitate him also in suffering.

But when Paul’s neck was struck by the persecutor’s sword, it is said that a stream of milk flowed from it rather than blood. In a wondrous manner, the holy Apostle, through the grace of Baptism, appeared in that very slaughter radiant rather than bloodstained.

This event is not astonishing in the case of holy Paul. For what is surprising if the nourisher of the Church abounds in milk? As he himself says to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

This is plainly that land of promise which God promised to our fathers, saying: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:17). He was not speaking of this earthly land, which encloses mud within flowing waters and mixes it with mire, but of that land of Paul and those like Paul, which continually distills what is pure and sweet.

For what Epistle of Paul is not sweeter than honey and whiter than milk? His Epistles, like breasts, nourish the peoples of the Churches unto salvation.

Therefore milk flowed from the Apostle’s neck in place of blood. We read in his Epistle that “flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Paul now possesses the kingdom, therefore, because he is without the blood that is said to impede those who will reign.

Thus Paul, while still placed on earth, was already being transformed into the substance of the heavenly kingdom.

### 3. How the memory of martyrs should be celebrated

Therefore, dearest brothers, whenever we celebrate the memorials of martyrs, we must set aside all the activities of the world and hasten without delay to the house of God; we must render honor to those who won salvation for us by the shedding of their blood, who offered themselves to the Lord as so sacred a sacrifice for our propitiation.

Especially since almighty God says to his saints: “Whoever honors you honors me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Whoever, therefore, honors the martyrs also honors Christ; and whoever despises the saints despises our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God [Note: [Col. 2120] This entire conclusion of Sermon 201 is absent from manuscript t. and does not seem to cohere with what precedes.], forever and ever, etc.

---

SERMON CCII [Note: [Col. 2120] Formerly, *On the Saints* 27; later, in the Appendix 79.] On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, II [Note: [Col. 2120] In the printed editions it also appears among the Ambrosian and Maximian sermons. Among the manuscripts, some assign it to Augustine, others to Ambrose, but many more to Maximus. It is read under his name in the Roman Breviary on the fifth day of July. On section 3, see Hegesippus, book 3, chapter 2.]

### 1. The Apostles are equal to one another, yet Peter and Paul are superior to them. The key of power was entrusted to Peter, that of knowledge to Paul

Although all the blessed Apostles possess equal grace of holiness before the Lord [Col. 2121], nevertheless, I do not know in what manner Peter and Paul seem to surpass the others through a particular excellence of faith in the Savior.

We can confirm this from the judgment of the Lord himself. For he gave Peter, as a good steward, the key of the heavenly kingdom; and to Paul, as a suitable teacher, he entrusted the office of ecclesiastical instruction. Thus those whom the one has taught for salvation, the other may receive into rest; and those whose hearts Paul has opened through the teaching of words, Peter may open the kingdoms of heaven to their souls.

In a certain sense Paul also received from Christ the key of knowledge. For that should be called a key by which hard hearts are unlocked for faith [Note: [Col. 2121] Thus in the published Augustinian and Ambrosian editions and in some manuscripts. In others, and in Maximus, it reads: “the hard hearts of sinners.”], the secrets of minds are opened, and whatever is held closed within is brought into the open through rational disclosure.

It is a key, I say, that opens the conscience to confession of sin and encloses grace within the eternity of the saving mystery.

Both, therefore, received keys from the Lord: this one of knowledge, that one of power. The one dispenses the riches of immortality; the other bestows the treasures of knowledge.

For there are treasures of knowledge, as it is written: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

Thus the blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the Apostles and surpass them through a particular prerogative.

### 2. Peter and Paul are equal in merit. Why they suffered on one day, in one place, under one tyrant. Why in the West

But among the two themselves, it is uncertain which should be preferred to the other. I think they were equal in merit, since they were equal in suffering; and that they lived with a similar devotion of faith, since we see them reaching together the glory of martyrdom.

Let us not think that it happened without reason that they endured the sentence of one tyrant on one day and in one place. They suffered on one day so that they might reach Christ together; in one place, so that Rome might not be lacking to either; under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind them both.

The day, therefore, was appointed for merit; the place, for glory; the persecutor, for virtue.

And in what place did they finally suffer martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the primacy and headship of the nations. Thus, where the head of superstition had been, there the head of holiness might rest; and where the leaders of the Gentiles dwelt, there the leaders of the Churches might die.

We can understand the merit of the most blessed Peter and Paul from this: although the Lord himself illuminated the region of the East through his own Passion, he deigned, lest anything be lacking, to illuminate the western region in his place through the blood of his Apostles.

Although his Passion is sufficient for our salvation, their martyrdom also has been granted to us as an example.

### 3. The cause of their death. The power of prayer. Why Simon Magus was permitted to fly into the heights

On this day, therefore, the blessed Apostles shed their blood. But let us see the reason why they endured these things: namely, that among their other miracles they also struck down the great Simon through their prayers, causing him to fall headlong from the empty air.

When that same Simon claimed to be Christ and asserted that, as a son ascending to the Father, he could rise by flying—and when, suddenly puffed up, he began to fly through magical arts—Peter then fixed his knees and prayed to the Lord, and through holy prayer conquered the magical levitation.

Prayer ascended to the Lord first, before the flight; and a righteous petition arrived before an unrighteous presumption. I say, Peter, while still upon earth, obtained first what lay open before him, before Simon reached the heavenly heights toward which he was striving.

Then Peter, as though bringing down a chained man from the lofty air, brought him down and, hurling him headlong against a rock, broke his legs—and this in mockery of his deed: so that the one who had just attempted to fly could suddenly no longer walk, and the one who had assumed wings might lose the use of his feet.

But lest it perhaps seem strange that this magician should have flown through the air for some time in the presence of the Apostle, Peter’s patience brought this about. He allowed him to ascend higher so that he might fall from a greater height; he wished him to be lifted up on high before everyone’s gaze, so that everyone’s eyes might behold him falling from the heights [Col. 2122].

Such, then, is the elevation of iniquity: it lifts itself high and raises itself to the summit. But holy prayer humbles all arrogance and casts down every vanity.

---

SERMON CCIII [Note: [Col. 2122] Elsewhere, *On the Saints* 29.] On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, III [Note: [Col. 2122] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was considered doubtful by the Louvain scholars and spurious by Verlin and Vinding. If you compare it with the Eusebian homily on this feast, you will easily understand from its wording and manner of expression that both sermons have the same author—unless we are mistaken, Faustus the semi-Pelagian himself. Certainly these words in section 3 belong to a Pelagian: “But in the work of the Apostle’s persecution he foresaw faith; and because he perceived zeal, he honored the devotion.” The words occur in the Ambrosian sermon on Saints Nazarius and Celsus. The conclusion appears to have been attached to the sermon from elsewhere; and it bears no resemblance to Augustine, in whose name it is read in the Roman Breviary on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains. On sections 1, 2, and 3, see Eusebius, homily on this feast.]

### 1. Peter was chosen for the salvation of the Jews, Paul for that of the Gentiles

Today the rejoicing Church celebrates the feast of two founders of the Christian name. These two were chosen for the salvation of two peoples: Peter for the Jews, Paul for the Gentiles.

Peter was chosen to restore in Judea the old and deserted field, and to make fruitful through the healing power of faith and grace the land that, under the shadow of the Law, was barren and hidden from the warmth of the true sun.

Paul, however, was sent to the Gentiles to cut open with the plow of the Lord’s cross the new earth that had previously yielded no crop and had known no cultivator, and to raise up, as an untiring laborer, a new growth of Christ in the uncultivated field.

Peter therefore repairs the vineyard where it had already existed; Paul plants where there was none.

Among the Jews, Peter cultivates at its root the tree that had degenerated from the nobility of its ancient stock; among the Gentiles, Paul grafts foreign branches onto an alien stock.

Among the Jews, Peter cuts away thorns from the vine; among the Gentiles, Paul harvests grapes from the bramble.

Peter rebuilds a house upon ruins; Paul raises one upon new foundations.

Among the Jews, Peter cultivates what had been poorly fruitful; among the Gentiles, Paul makes fruitful what had not yet been cultivated.

Through Peter, the olive tree is restored among the Jews; through Paul, the wild olive is grafted among the Gentiles.

Peter softens hardness among the Jews; Paul illuminates ignorance among the Gentiles.

Peter drives darkness from the eyes that had been corrupted; Paul restored sight to eyes blinded from birth.

In varied and diverse ways innumerable peoples are gathered into the service of one King. Thus the two most powerful leaders assemble two armies: Peter brings back the ancient army from the old, while Paul recruits a new army of Christ from the raw recruits.

### 2. They are merchants and spiritual stewards

The two most splendid merchants therefore travel throughout the whole world, carrying before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel the precious merchandise of faith.

They carry about the spices of righteousness, the incense of divine veneration, the frankincense of remorse, and the balsam of chastity.

They are the salt of spiritual wisdom, of whom it is said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13), so that souls may be seasoned by them and preserved inviolate from the eternal corruption of sin.

Throughout the earth, spiritual stewards distribute the price of salvation and the treasures of holiness. These most devout parents of souls seek those whom they may draw with themselves to heaven: differing in the pursuits of their ministries, but equal in the merits of their works.

### 3. Equal in many respects. Paul is the Jonah of the New Testament

I would call them equal and similar through their various and diverse kinds of virtue. For although Christ lived on earth with Peter, he did not disdain to address Paul from heaven [while Paul was still persecuting]:

“But in the work of the persecutor he foresaw the faith of an Apostle; and because he foresaw zeal, he honored the disposition. And because, under a purpose of pleasing God, he was unknowingly driven into fault, immediately after the admonition he ran devotedly toward grace” [Col. 2123] [Note: [Col. 2123] The material enclosed in quotation marks is omitted by manuscript f.].

Therefore, although Paul did not speak with Christ bodily, what Christ spoke in Paul is no less significant, as Paul himself says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Thus, the one whom he set forth outwardly in his preaching, he carried inwardly in his heart [Note: [Col. 2123] Manuscript f. reads: “And thus indeed (perhaps, ‘whom’) he set [him] before men with a preaching tongue.”].

I do not know, therefore, what holiness was lacking in one from whose breast the Lord, as from his own private temple, uttered saving oracles to the peoples.

Peter presumed, with a power belonging to God alone, to walk upon the waters; while nature stood astonished, he placed his wavering steps upon the swelling backs of the sea, proceeding by the new paths of an unfamiliar journey.

But Paul was no less great, for, as he says of himself, he was “in the deep of the sea night and day” (ibid. 11:25).

Paul was no less great, I say: like the Jonah of the New Testament, he was tossed day and night through the depths of the sea. The waves swallowed him and gave him back, as though unwilling to violate a sacred deposit, as though the water, keeping him safe in its bosom like a servant, preserved him unharmed for the preaching of the peoples [Note: [Col. 2123] Manuscript f. has: “And thus indeed [perhaps: ‘whom’] he proclaimed before men with a tongue preaching.”].

### 4. Peter the destroyer of the synagogue and restorer of the Church

[Note: [Col. 2123] The following material is absent from manuscript f.; instead it supplies the following passage, which fits what precedes more suitably and more fully reflects the sense of the Eusebian homily: “Peter therefore merited the keys of the heavenly kingdom; and while Paul was still in the body, the gates of heaven were opened to him, as he himself says: ‘I know a man in Christ, whether in the body or outside the body, God knows, who was caught up to the third heaven.’ Since this is so, not only the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, but also many with them and through them should be considered to hold those heavenly keys: those who, with Christ inviting and cooperating, open for themselves the door of that age through their pious labors, and who, through the grace of blessed spiritual merits, have the gates of righteousness opened for themselves as they are brought in. Our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever.”]

Here too the blessed Peter is foremost in that school of heavenly disciples, and the first worthy recipient of the words of life from Christ’s mouth. Through the power of the Gospel he sought the lost Jewish people and called the disowned back to their inheritance: interpreter of the Law, defender of grace, destroyer of the synagogue, restorer of the Church.

For this reason alone among the Apostles he deserved to hear: “Amen, I say to you, because you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

He was certainly worthy to be, for the peoples being built into the house of God, a stone for the foundation, a column for support, and a key to the kingdom.

Concerning him the divine word says: “They brought out their sick, so that at least the shadow of Peter as he passed might overshadow them” (Acts 5:15).

If the shadow of his body could then bring help, how much more can the fullness of his power do so now? If a certain breeze from one who was passing by benefited those who entreated him then, how much more does the grace of one who remains benefit them now?

### 5. Praise of Peter’s chains

Rightly, throughout all the Churches of Christ, that iron of penal chains is considered more precious than gold.

If the shadow of one who visited them was so healing, how much more the chain of one who bound them! “So that at least the shadow of Peter as he passed might overshadow them.”

If an empty semblance, a vacant image, could possess within itself the power of salvation, how much more healthfulness did the chains of his Passion, impressed upon his sacred limbs by their iron weight, deserve to draw from his body?

If they were so powerful in providing aid to those who prayed before his martyrdom, how much more effective were they after his triumph?

Blessed are those bonds which, touching the Apostle and martyr, were destined to be changed from handcuffs and fetters into a crown.

Blessed are those chains which, clinging to bones almost stripped bare, seized living relics from flesh already worn away by the sweat of blood; and the touch of his limbs sanctifies the instrument of his torment. As the affliction grows toward punishment, the cause of the punishment advances toward glory.

Blessed are the chains that sent their captive not so much to condemn him as to consecrate him, all the way to Christ’s cross.

Fearing to imitate the Redeemer’s sacrifice upon that cross, he chose to have his head buried in the earth.

O power of innate humility! He fears even to be honored by the manner of his punishment; and he who does not refuse the torments of the Lord’s gallows dreads the likeness of triumph [Col. 2124]!

---

SERMON CCIV [Note: [Col. 2124] Elsewhere, *On the Saints* 25.] On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, IV [Note: [Col. 2124] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars leave it doubtful; Verlin and Vinding reject it as false. It is attributed to Leo in an old Corbie manuscript, and in certain others to Augustine; but it is certainly unworthy of the learning and gravity of these teachers. Its style differs little from that of Sermons 187 and 195 above. It also contains several words from the immediately following sermon.]

### 1. Peter is sought by Paul and is afraid

My little children, hear us and set yourselves free. Run for your own sake, and you will benefit both us and yourselves. Our joy will be shared if we see you put on Christ.

Young men and virgins, the elderly together with the young, let them hasten to grace: our mother does not distinguish between ages in giving birth.

She herself gave birth to Peter; she herself gave birth to all the Apostles; she herself gave birth to Paul, so that a wolf might become a lamb.

Saul was born, grew, and became great. He was baptized by his mother and enlightened by the Father. Then he began to wish to see Peter; and when he earnestly sought to see him, Peter began all the more to fear him.

For Peter heard that Saul was seeking him.

Do not be afraid, blessed Peter, because it is not Saul who seeks you, but Paul, the vessel of election, who desires to see you.

O holy Peter, bless the Father and receive your brother; you now have someone with whom you can defend your mother.

O blessed Peter, you marvel that Saul has been converted. Whatever you are, he too will be such, and you will have one and the same Nativity.

He who made Paul from Saul made Peter from Simon. One honored you both; one will crown you both.

He changed the persecutor, and he changed the fisherman—though he made you first and him later, he nevertheless gave both of you one honor.

Come, holy Paul, come; follow Peter—but follow him as he teaches, not as he flees. He was fleeing when he did not know you.

### 2. Paul’s salvation was won through Stephen’s prayer

For this most blessed Paul, as we heard when the passage from the Acts of the Apostles was read, was struck down by a heavenly voice.
