While he raged toward the sheepfolds with wolfish fury; while he pursued the name of the innocent Lamb, which he hated; while he sought to tear apart or harass the flock, he heard a resounding voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? Why have you raged in vain against my name and killed my martyr?

“Long ago I ought to have destroyed you, but my Stephen prayed for you.”

And he said: “Who are you, Lord?”

And the Lord said to him: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:4–5).

The head cries out from heaven for its members. The body is disturbed, and from heaven Christ thunders: “Saul,” he says, “Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

What is the secret that the roaring heaven bellows, and why does the army of heaven complain against Paul’s savagery, except so that the one who had not believed in the Risen One might at least believe in the One seated in heaven?

For it is said to Ananias: “Approach him and mark him with my sign, for he will suffer many things for my name.”

And he said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints.”

The Lord said to him: “Go, for he is a vessel of election for me” (ibid. 13, 15).

### 3. Paul suffers the evils he had inflicted

O blessed Ananias, you would rightly have trembled in fear if the one under whose command you were serving had not been strong of hand.

For pride is struck down so that holiness may be raised up.

Ananias therefore came, baptized Saul, and made him Paul. He baptized a wolf and made a lamb; and we began to have as a preacher the one whom we had had as a persecutor.

Finally, he began to preach Christ, whom previously he resisted, ready to suffer for him against whom he had previously fought.

Paul suffers what Saul had done.

Saul stoned; Paul was stoned.

Saul scourged Christians; Paul received forty lashes less one five times for Christ.

Saul persecuted the Church of God; Paul was lowered in a basket.

Saul bound; Paul was bound.

And while raging Saul sought to reduce the number of Christians, he himself joined the number of confessors [Col. 2125]. While he inflicted death on others, he himself accepted death for Christ.

While the ravening wolf entered the sheepfold, he suddenly became a sheep himself.

Who, then, would despair because of the magnitude of his crime or the lowliness of his condition?

For the most blessed Peter the fisherman is now worshiped on bended knees by the excellence of emperors; and the multitude of believing Gentiles venerates Paul, the fierce persecutor of believers.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

---

SERMON CCV [Note: [Col. 2125] Elsewhere, *On the Saints* 28.] On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, V [Note: [Col. 2125] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. According to the judgment of the Louvain scholars it is doubtful; according to Verlin and Vinding it is spurious. It was written in no more polished a style than the preceding sermon, with which it agrees in certain sentences and expressions.]

## 1. Peter’s Calling Explained

Today we celebrate with particular devotion the most sacred day of the fisherman and the persecutor, in the coincidence of a twofold festival: the day on which the one escaped the nets of the world, and the day on which the other was changed from a brigand into Christ’s confessor. Behold, he chooses two: one a fisherman, the other a marauder. He calls the one from the shore; to the other he cries from heaven. He summons the one from the sea; he terrifies the other from heaven.

While Peter was loosening his fishing line in the strait, Christ cast his nets through his word. Christ caught, and Peter also caught: Christ caught the disciple, Peter the little fish. And while Peter was encircling the fishy race, he himself fell into the nets.

“Passing by,” it says, “Jesus saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. To them Christ said: ‘Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.’ But they, leaving their nets, followed him” (Matt. 4:18–20).

Peter hung suspended amid the shifting waters of the deep, and among the dark waters of the restless sea he sought by his craft the food he did not possess. He swayed upon the uncertain wave so that he might track his catch. He was carried to and fro by varying movements: he stood while in motion, and moved while remaining steady. He searched through the blind waves of the sea’s offspring and, beneath the dark water, pursued his fugitive prey.

A prison enclosed by water is cast into the deep; a trap, carefully arranged, is extended; a spotted wall rises beneath the waves; a blind enclosure is made for the fish in the sea. And while Peter lies in ambush for the schools of the deep, he himself falls into the nets of the Savior. A predator becomes prey; a fisherman becomes the catch; a pirate becomes a captive.

“Come after me,” he says, “and I will make you become fishers of men.” But they, leaving their nets, followed him.

While Peter seeks to enclose the fish on a hook, Christ casts the hook of the word and catches the fisherman himself. Peter stretched out the empty curtain-net in the sinuous folds of its linen expanse.[^c0074-1] And while he pursues the ever-pregnant offspring of the sea, he makes Christ the Savior, his captor, upon the shore.

He dragged, and was dragged; he exercised violence upon the sea, and suffered capture in his mind.

O pirate of water-born reptiles, you have abandoned this craft and changed from one fish to another. (For Christ is that fish which ascended alive from the river to Tobias: when its liver had been roasted upon the coals of the Passion, the devil was driven away; through the bitterness of its gall the blind man was breathed upon and the world was illuminated.) From fish to Fish, from the net to the Church, from the sea to the font, he has become a captive from a captor.

For he left the tossing salt water and began to walk after the Fish. The likeness of the craft kindles the hearer’s desire, so that the one who formerly cast a catching-net into the sea may now spread the nets of the word throughout the world. Then he brought in fish; now he has entangled human beings in spiritual seines.

[^c0074-1]: Thus the manuscripts r. and gr. read. Manuscript f. has “sinuous folds” and “he calls the cohort.” In the printed editions, as in many other passages of this sermon, the text was corruptly given as: “the bosom of linen, he rolls the empty net into itself.”

## 2. Paul’s Conversion

Paul was small, but great from his smallness. While he was called Saul, he was terrified by the trumpet of a heavenly voice[^c0074-2] and fell, his boldness struck down, so that he might rise and sow teaching throughout the world.

“Saul, Saul,” he says, “why are you persecuting me?”

For Saul was rushing along mounted upon the horses of fury; he exhaled a dreadful poison from the whole breast, and, thirsting for the blood of the saints, was borne through all Judea on the reins of madness, so that he might tear Christ’s members apart on earth.

Through an empty religion he became cruel and an inquisitor of the innocent. He wandered across the fields of a most criminal embankment, so that Judea, which had already raged against the Head, might exercise its cruelty against the Body. Saul had received authority from the chief priests to kill people of our faith and with wicked hand to cut down the field of faith as it was sprouting.

Therefore, while Saul carries a funerary sword against the soldiers of Christ, he receives a lightning weapon from heaven; while he ravages, he is struck; while he persecutes Christ’s holy ones, he is blinded by the violent ray of heavenly light. And he who was being raised up against God by the breath of pride is struck down by the terror of the divine voice:

“Saul,” he says, “Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:2–9).

The Head cries out for the members. The Body is disturbed, and Christ thunders from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

What is the secret meaning of the roaring heavens’ bellow, and why does the heavenly realm complain against Paul’s savagery, except that the man who had not believed in the Risen One might at least believe in the One seated in heaven; and that he who had asserted a lie from the tomb about the dead Lord of the Apostles might receive from heaven testimony to the Living One?

“Saul,” he says, “Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

Then, suddenly struck down to the ground by the divine spear of rebuke, he loses both his savagery and his path; he lays aside his ferocity and encounters blindness of the eyes. He begins to have guides whom previously he had had as followers.[^c0074-3]

[^c0074-2]: The printed editions read “the people’s roar.” The manuscript reads “with the people roaring”; shortly afterward it has “the army complains,” instead of “the province.” We have followed the Floriacensis manuscript.

[^c0074-3]: “Guides” translates *ductores*; “followers” translates *secutores*, preserving the wordplay.

## 3. Rebuke of the Jews

Where were you running, Paul, when you could see? Behold, now wandering, you seek a place; and you who were persecuting Christ run blind toward a hand.

O ravenous wolf Saul, you have eaten; but wait a little, and as you digest, you will yourself be digested.[^c0074-4]

So, Saul, do you believe in God and place your faith in the faithless one? Those hands would not ordinarily be stained with blood, if you did not still see yourself being tormented by them.

Was it not enough for your race that it had crucified Christ? It was not even afraid to stretch out its hands against heaven. It impressed flesh upon the gibbet and stationed guards at the entrance of the tomb.

Now Christ has ascended to the Father, and yet your mother has not been deprived of her ferocity.

O Judea, drunk with the blood of the Prophets, are you not yet satisfied? From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, the rivers of your crime foam; and do they still not satisfy you? You have drunk blood from the beginning of the world, and are you still thirsty? The wave of your crime has not yet dried up in Christ, and now the channel of your crime is thirsty?

Just now you fastened Christ to the gibbet, and so quickly have you grown parched in your desire for blood?

But behold, cruelty is struck down so that holiness may rise: the devil’s soldier falls so that Christ’s standard-bearer may rise.

[^c0074-4]: Manuscript r. reads *digeres* (“you will digest”); manuscript f. has *digereris* (“you will be digested”). Shortly afterward both manuscripts read *adhibes ergo fidem video* (“therefore you place faith, I see”), or rather *Judaeo* (“in the Jew”).

## 4. The Martyrdom of Peter and Paul

Peter casts a little net into the sea; Paul carries the Lord’s standard throughout the world. The one fishes for human beings, and the other marks the Gentiles with Christ’s title.

Both run toward the palm of martyrdom, and both reach the crown—not indeed in the same passage of time, but in the recurrence of the same year.

Peter is hung upside down on the wood for Christ; Paul is beheaded with a dagger for Christ. The one proceeded toward Christ on his own feet and, looking with his eyes toward the heights, led his blessed spirit to heaven; the other bent his neck toward punishment and offered the crown the summit of his head.

The cross kills Peter; the sword sacrifices Paul. Two forms of the Lord’s and Christ’s punishments appear in Christ’s two Apostles. Peter suffers the cross; Paul experiences the dagger of the Lord’s side. The hook of the cross suspends the fisherman; the blade of the persecutor diminishes the persecutor.

Now, in memory of the fisherman, the emperor’s knees are bent. There the gems of the diadem shine, where the benefits of the fisherman gleam.[^c0074-5]

From a fisherman the Lord made him prince of the Apostles; from a persecutor he made him an apostolic confessor. His Passion provided as companions those whom the preaching of faith had made united.

Let us therefore venerate the leaders of the flock, if we wish to enter the folds of the eternal Shepherd.

[^c0074-5]: Manuscript r. reads “where the punishment shines.”

---

# SERMON 206

*Formerly Sermon on the Saints 30; later Appendix 80.*

## On the Feast of Saint Lawrence, I

*The sermon is worthy of being read, in the judgment of the Louvain editors. It appears among the printed Sermons of Ambrose and is attributed to him in the Corbie and Theoderic manuscripts. Compare his Commentaries on Luke and Sermons 86 and 87 of this Appendix, which closely correspond to this sermon. The conclusion beginning with the words “But we, dearly beloved brethren,” and so forth, is taken from Caesarius’s sermon On Martyrs, printed below as Sermon 224.*

## 1. Lawrence Sets the World Ablaze for Martyrdom

### Spiritual Martyrdom

### Lawrence Extinguishes the Power of Fire with Fire

I believe that you know the Passion of the most blessed martyr Lawrence, whose feast we celebrate today, and I have no doubt that Your Belovedness knows how much he endured in persecution. So great was the glory of his martyrdom that by his Passion he illuminated the whole world.

Lawrence truly illuminated the world with the light by which he himself was kindled; and with the flames that he endured he warmed the hearts of all Christians.

Who, following this example, would not wish to burn for Christ with Lawrence, so that he might be crowned by Christ with Lawrence? Who would not wish to endure Lawrence’s fire for an hour, so that he might not suffer the eternal fire of Gehenna?

We are therefore summoned to martyrdom by the example of blessed Lawrence, set aflame for faith, and warmed toward devotion. Even if the persecutor’s flame is lacking for us, the flame of faith is not lacking. We do not burn bodily for Christ, but we burn in affection. The persecutor does not impose fire upon me, but the desire for the Savior supplies me with fire.

We read in the Gospel that the Savior’s fire exists, when the same Lord says: “Do you not know that I have come to cast fire upon the earth? And what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

Kindled by this fire, Amahus and Cleophas said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).[^c0074-6]

Kindled by this fire, therefore, blessed Lawrence does not feel the burning of the flames; and while he burns with desire for Christ, he does not burn under the persecutor’s punishment. In proportion as the ardor of faith burns within him, the flame of punishment grows cold.

Blessed Lawrence suffers a bodily conflagration: on one side he is inflamed by love of Christ, on the other he is tortured by the persecutor’s flame. But the divine ardor of the Savior extinguishes the tyrant’s material fire.

Although his limbs are dissolved into ash, the strength of his faith is not dissolved. He suffers the loss of his body, but gains the profit of salvation.

[^c0074-6]: The printed editions read “those two disciples said.” Manuscript cb. reads “Amahus and Cleophas said,” as does Ambrose’s version of the sermon. Codex t. has “Emahus and Cleophas”; the same form occurs above in Sermon 86. Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke 24, calls the same disciples Amahon and Cleophas.

## 2. He Suffers a Long Punishment

### Not Inferior to the Three Young Men

For, brothers, blessed Lawrence was not destroyed by a swift or simple punishment. The one who is struck by the sword dies once; the one immersed in a furnace of flames is freed in a single assault. But Lawrence is tortured by a long and manifold punishment, so that death is not absent from his suffering, yet is absent from its conclusion.

It is said that the most savage persecutor imposed this punishment upon blessed Lawrence: he was stretched upon a mass of burning coals and extended upon an iron grate, where a slow flame consumed him—not so much killing him quickly by setting him ablaze as torturing him for a long time by burning him. Thus, when the persecutor saw that one side had been burned, he exposed the other side to the flames to be burned.

We read that the most blessed youths Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, shut up by the king in the furnace of fire, walked about in the flames of their punishments and trampled fiery globes under their feet (Dan. 3:24).

Accordingly, blessed Lawrence must be set before them with no lesser glory. They walked amid the flames of their punishments; he reclines in the very fire of his punishment. They trampled the fire beneath the soles of their feet; he extinguishes it by the spreading of his sides.

They, standing in their punishment, prayed to the Lord with hands raised; but he, lying prostrate in his punishment, entreats the Lord with his whole body.

## 3. He Asks to Be Consumed by a Double Fire

Again, therefore, blessed Lawrence is turned onto his back, and his loins are burned by the flames, so that the prophecy of the Psalm might be fulfilled, which speaks in Lawrence’s person: “Prove me, Lord, and test me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 30:2).

He asks to be burned by a double fire. For if he were speaking only of the world’s fire, it would have been enough to offer his loins alone to be burned by the flames. But the heart is burned only by Christ’s flame. Therefore, to demonstrate his devotion, he asks for a twofold fire, so that through the struggle he might show that the love of Christ can accomplish more in him than the tyrant’s punishment.

Let us therefore honor, brothers, blessed Lawrence, who, while conquering the persecutor’s flames by his faith, shows us through the fire of faith how to overcome the fires of Gehenna and not fear the day of judgment because of our love for Christ.

## 4. That We May Imitate the Martyrs

But we, dearly beloved brethren, if we wish to reach fellowship with the holy martyrs, should think about imitating the martyrs. For they ought to be in us, and so forth.[^c0074-7] … so that in the age to come we may gather the fruits of good works with joy and exultation, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[^c0074-7]: The rest is to be repeated from Sermon 224, section 1.

---

# SERMON 207

*Also known as Sermon on the Saints 32.*

## On the Feast of Saint Lawrence, II

*This sermon is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was considered doubtful by the Louvain editors, but Verlin and Vinding judged it spurious. The latter part, beginning with the words in section 3, “The examples of the martyrs ought to be sufficient for us,” is the beginning of Maximus’s homily On Martyrs. The earlier part, since it fits the martyrdom of Lawrence rather poorly, is reasonably thought to have been taken from elsewhere.*

## 1. What We Owe the Martyrs

### Lawrence Is Worthy of Honor for Three Reasons

Although we rightly admire all the blessed martyrs whom antiquity has handed down to us, we ought nevertheless to receive the triumph of blessed Lawrence the martyr with complete devotion.

I ought, therefore, to have greater affection where contemplation compels my belief than where opinion encourages my faith. I ought, I say, to have greater affection where, through things I have seen, I am compelled by devotion to believe even those things I have not seen.

For when I heard of them, some things seemed impossible to me; but I began to believe that they could have happened when I saw similar things had taken place. And therefore the martyrdom of our own time has granted us this grace: that it should confirm our earlier faith.

We ought, then, to receive the blessed man mentioned above with complete devotion: first, because he gave his precious blood for the Lord; next, because he granted us no small privilege before our Lord, showing what faith ought to be in Christians; third, because he was a man of such holy conduct that he found the crown of martyrdom in a time of peace.

## 2. Why He Was Tortured

But when the Gentiles saw blessed Lawrence contending with such holiness for Christ’s name, and reasonably refuting their manifest errors, they, drunk with fury, seized him and wounded him with the most savage slaughter. Then they handed the blessed man’s body over to the flames upon a grate.

Truly blessed was the body that neither the deadly fire of punishment nor tortures changed from the faith of Christ, but holy religion crowned it for the Lord’s rest.

The flame itself received the Martyr for this reason: not so that fire might change him from his faith, but so that it might return him approved to his Lord. In such a conflagration his blessed inward parts were consecrated, not condemned.

What the Apostle says suits this Passion: “He himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15). He was saved in this way, being consumed in the fire of his venerable confession.

This, brothers, is the entire reason for his Passion, on account of which the holy man was handed over to death: that he might encourage the others who were like him. For that exhortation made such progress that, when he departed from the world, his faith spread through every place in that region.

Thus Christ at that time suffered persecutions in his blessed martyr Lawrence; now many Christians rejoice there among the peoples.

## 3. Martyrs Must Have Been Martyrs before Their Martyrdom

### What It Means to Take Up the Cross

The examples of the holy martyrs ought to be sufficient for our progress in salvation. In order to obtain the heavenly crown, they submitted themselves to all the Lord’s commandments and bound themselves to all the Savior’s laws, so that because of their former life they might deserve to attain this glory of martyrdom.

For they fulfilled the Lord’s commandment not only at the time when they endured the punishment of confession. They first had to live according to the Gospel in order to share in Christ’s sufferings.

It is necessary, I say, that the beginnings of those whose end was so excellent should themselves have been good; and that they were not martyrs only when they suffered, but that they were already Christ’s martyrs while they lived.

For *martyr* is Greek; in Latin it is *testis*, “witness.” Therefore, whenever we fulfill Christ’s commandment through good dispositions,[^c0074-8] we bear witness to Christ.

Hence the Lord’s cross is not called only that which is constructed by fastening someone to wood at the time of the Passion; it is also that which is fitted throughout the whole course of life to the virtues of every discipline.

It seems to me that the Savior speaks of this cross when he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:21).

Were all the martyrs who followed the Lord crucified with the Lord?[^c0074-9] Were all the virgins who, according to the Apocalypse, follow the Lamb of God crucified in order to follow him (Rev. 14:4)? Was the Apostle Paul crucified when he said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14)?

He says this so that you may understand that the cross is not the gallows of wood, but the purpose of life and virtue.

The whole life of a Christian, therefore, if he lives according to the Gospel, is a cross and a martyrdom.

[^c0074-8]: Maximus has *actibus*, “through actions.”

[^c0074-9]: “With the Lord” is superfluous and is absent from Maximus.

# SERMON 208

*Formerly Sermon on the Saints 35; later Appendix 83.*

## On the Feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary

*The author is uncertain. He cites Isidore, who is much later than Augustine, from his work On the Life and Death of the Saints. In our manuscript codices the sermon appears without the author’s name. In most of the manuscripts examined by the Louvain editors, however, it is attributed to Fulbert, bishop of Chartres. In the Cassinese and Cluniac codices it is attributed to Ambrose Autpert. Indeed, it would have been easy to fashion Fulbert from Autpert, especially since Fulbert was always known as exceedingly devoted to the worship of the most holy Virgin. There is therefore reason to suspect that not only this Ambrosian booklet On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues, but also several sermons, were mixed among Augustine’s works; perhaps Sermon 195 and others should be attributed to him, since in the manuscripts they bear the name of Ambrose, especially those that do not resemble either Ambrose of Milan or his imitator Maximus of Turin. Here you will find many statements already made above in several sermons on Blessed Mary. For section 3, see Ambrose on Luke 2 and Isidore, On the Life and Death of the Saints, chapter 68; for section 4, above Sermon 120, section 4, and Sermon 194, section 2, and Sermon 121, section 5; for section 5, Sermon 120, section 5, and Sermon 194, section 2; for section 10, Sermon 123, section 2; for section 11, Sermon 194, section 5.*

## 1. This Solemnity Is Preeminent and Now Rightly Received

The very venerable day has arrived for us, dearly beloved brethren—a day surpassing the solemnities of all the saints. The distinguished day has arrived, the glorious day on which the Virgin Mary is believed to have departed from the world.

Therefore, with the greatest exultation, let the whole earth illuminated by the departure of so great a Virgin resound with praises. It would be utterly unworthy for the solemnity of the memory of her through whom we were deemed worthy to receive the Author of life to be among us without the greatest honor.

It must be judged most perverse that, when we celebrate the victories of the holy martyrs, we should not place before theirs the solemnity of her who gave birth to the Prince of martyrs for this world.

On this day the blessed Virgin Mary appropriately cries out to that heavenly Bridegroom: “You have held my right hand; and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72:24).

Today, I say, she also appropriately heard from her Bridegroom, Son, and Lord: “Now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; arise, my beloved, my bride, my dove, and come” (Song 2:11–14).

## 2. What the Church Believes Concerning Mary’s Assumption

We say this, brothers, because, as the Church has now received it into the custom of Christendom, it is handed down that on this day the Virgin Mary was assumed into heaven.

But no Catholic history relates in what manner she passed from here to the heavenly realms. This same Church of God is said not only to reject apocryphal writings but also to be ignorant of these matters.

There are indeed some writings composed without an author’s name concerning her Assumption. As I have said, however, they are avoided so carefully that they are not permitted to be read at all for the confirmation of the event’s truth.

For this reason some people are troubled: neither is her body found on earth, nor is her assumption with the flesh, as it is read in apocryphal writings, found in Catholic history.

They should be told this: if Moses’ body is not found on earth by human beings, although he spoke with God face to face, it is madness to seek the body of her through whom that same God of majesty, incarnate, shone forth on earth.

Nor is it fitting for anyone to be anxious about knowledge of her body when he does not doubt that she has been raised above the Angels and reigns with Christ.

It ought to be sufficient for human knowledge truly to confess her as the Queen of heaven, because she gave birth to the King of angels.

## 3. No Latin Author Wrote of the Manner of Her Death

### The True View Concerning the Assumption

Nor is any Latin writer found to have plainly said anything about her death. For when Ambrose of blessed memory was treating that verse of the Gospel which Simeon spoke to the Lord’s Mother—“And your own soul a sword will pierce” (Luke 2:35)—he said: “Neither history nor Scripture teaches that Mary ended her life by the sword.”

Isidore likewise says: “It is uncertain from this statement whether he meant the sword of the spirit or the sword of persecution.”

But why should I speak about those matters of which I am speaking, when even the one who received her before the Lord’s cross into his own care—that is, John the Evangelist—did not commit anything about this for posterity to retain in his writings?

No one could have narrated it more faithfully, if God had wished it to be revealed, than the man who accepted her to be cared for and who, contrary to custom, did not abandon his mother.

It remains, therefore, that no one should deceitfully present as open what God wished to remain hidden.

The true view concerning her Assumption is proved to be this: in accordance with the Apostle, who says that we do not know whether he was “in the body or outside the body” (2 Cor. 12:2), we should believe that she was assumed above the Angels.

## 4. Mary Is Greater Than All Praise

Leaving these matters aside, let us say something in praise of the most holy Virgin.

But what can we, so insignificant, what can we, so poor in action, say in her praises, when, even if all our limbs were changed into tongues, no one would be sufficient to praise her?

She is higher than heaven, of whom we speak; deeper than the abyss, whom we attempt to praise.

For she carried enclosed in her immaculate womb the God whom no creature can contain.

She alone deserved to be called both mother and bride. She repaired the losses of the first mother; she brought redemption to the lost human race.

The mother of our race brought punishment into the world; the Mother of our Lord brought salvation into the world. Eve was the author of sin; Mary, the author of merit. Eve harmed by killing; Mary benefited by giving life. The one struck; the other healed.

In a wondrous and immeasurable manner she gave birth to the Savior both of all things and of herself.

What virgin was so holy that the Holy Spirit would deign to come to her? What woman was so beautiful that God would choose her as his bride? What woman was so chaste that she could remain a virgin after giving birth?

She is God’s temple, that sealed fountain, and the closed door in the Lord’s house. For, as I have said, the Holy Spirit descended upon her; the power of the Most High overshadowed her.

She is immaculate in intercourse, fruitful in childbirth, a virgin nursing and nourishing the food of Angels and human beings.

Rightly, therefore, the blessed woman is exalted by our singular proclamation, since she offered the world a singular exchange.

Finally, she raised herself so high toward the heights of heaven that she received the Word who in the beginning was with God from the heavenly citadel above.

## 5. Mary Is Most Worthy of All Praise

O blessed Mary, most worthy of all praise! O glorious Mother! O exalted woman who gave birth, whose womb received the Author of heaven and earth!

O happy kisses impressed upon the nursing lips, when, amid the frequent signs of creeping infancy, your true son from you played with you as mother, while the true God from the Father, the Only-Begotten of God, commanded!

For, conceiving your own Creator, you gave birth in time to the One whom you possessed before time as Creator.

O blessed childbirth, joyful to Angels, desired by the saints, necessary for the lost, fitting for the defeated!

After enduring many insults in the flesh he had assumed, at last scourged with lashes, given gall to drink, and fastened to the gibbet, he showed you to be his true mother; and by suffering he revealed himself to be truly human.

But what can I say, poor in understanding, when whatever I say about you is less praise than your dignity deserves?

If I call you heaven, you are higher. If I call you the Mother of the Gentiles, you surpass that title. If I call you the form of God, you are worthy of it. If I call you the Lady of the Angels, you are proved to be so in every respect.

What, then, can I say worthily about you, what can I relate, when the tongue of flesh is not sufficient to recount your virtues?

For now, let the tongue of flesh be silent about those praises that the mind within always utters ardently.

Now I ask that you soothe our ears with the instruments of your teachings. Let holy hands now clap with tambourines, and amid swift movements let the harmony of the woman who gave birth resound.

Let joyful choirs sing together, and let sweet songs mingle in alternating melodies.

## 6. “Magnify” Is Said in Two Ways

Let us listen, brothers; let us listen with devout affection of mind; let us listen to how our Virgin Mary, the tambourine-player, resounds with teachings.

Let us listen, I say, and answer this harmony with our conduct.

When this most blessed woman, already greeted by the angel, filled with the Holy Spirit, and inspired by the fullness of divinity, had come to the house of her kinswoman Elizabeth, after John’s exultation in his mother’s womb and after Elizabeth’s wonder at the arrival of the Lord’s Mother, she sang this hymn of praise to the Lord:

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47).

First, then, we must ask here what it means to magnify the Lord. For the Creator does not become great through a creature.

But we must understand that “to magnify” is used in two ways: either to make great, or to worship as great and to admire as great.

God is magnified by us when he deigns to be magnified by us.

But is he magnified in us in the same way as in Mary, from whom he assumed flesh for us?

The angel said to her: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore, the Holy One who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (ibid. 1:28, 35).

Nevertheless, every holy soul can conceive the Word by believing, give birth to him by proclaiming, and magnify him by loving.

Hence the prophet David says: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. 33:4), as though he were saying: “Sing with me, proclaim with me the greatness of the Lord, and raise high the praises of his name with a great voice.”

Again he says: “Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified” (Ps. 103:1).

And how he is magnified in us, the same prophet says: “Your mercy has been magnified even to the heavens” (Ps. 107:5).

## 7. God Must First Be Magnified for the Gift of Redemption

It should be desired that in each of us our soul magnify the Lord, conceive the Word of God, give birth to and nourish him, and recall the devout exchange of its salvation: how it was saved from iniquity not by any preceding merits of its own, but by God’s gratuitous goodness alone, redeemed by the blood of Christ.

Then let it say: “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

“For God so loved the world,” says the Gospel, “that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

Hence the Apostle also says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:52).

O feeling of wondrous compassion! O immeasurable ardor of charity! Who would not be astonished before such riches of compassion? Who would not tremble before such ineffable charity?

Who could ever have hoped that the One born from God before time would be born in time from a woman, made human for the sake of human beings?

Hence it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:4–5).

Who, I say, could have imagined that the Bearer of the world would be carried in a woman’s hands; that the Bread of Angels would be nourished; that the Power of heaven would become weak; that the Life of all would die?

Let Mary’s soul magnify the Lord in these things; let ours also magnify him.

Let us admire, rejoice, love, praise, worship, and give him thanks, because through the same death of our Redeemer we have been called from darkness to light, from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, from exile to our homeland, from mourning to joy, and from earth to the heavenly kingdom.

## 8. Imbued with This Truth, the Soul Despises Earthly Things

### What Exultation Is Good and What Is Evil

Whatever holy soul is occupied by such incentives desires nothing earthly, nothing transitory, nothing that pleases for a time, nothing that delights for the present.

It counts laughter as mourning and changes joy into sorrow. For it, the world is a prison, but heaven is a dwelling place. It has no exultation in present things, because it desires to rejoice only in the One who is above all.

Therefore, when the glorious Virgin said in the holy Canticle, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced,” she significantly added, “in God my Savior,” as though she were saying:

“My soul, which magnifies the Lord, rejoices not in just anyone, but only in the One whom it magnifies by loving.”

She knew that there was another, blameworthy exultation, since the world is said to rejoice while moving toward mourning. Solomon speaks of such people: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14).

The Apostle likewise does not describe just any joy as existing in the hearts of the saints, but joy in the Holy Spirit.

David, when he said, “Rejoice, you just,” added, “in the Lord” (Ps. 32:1).

When he said to the Lord, “My lips will rejoice when I sing,” he added, “to you” (Ps. 70:23).

No one who rejoices only in present things and does not desire to share in eternal goods rejoices with this exultation.

For such a person exile is believed to be a homeland and death is considered life. His god is his belly, and his adornment lies not in conduct but in clothing.[^c0074-10]

When he is praised, he is puffed up; when he is criticized, he is driven by great goads of anger. He is not humbled among the meek, but is raised up in the bundles of pride and looks down upon others as though from the brow of a high mountain.

[^c0074-10]: Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions have “in conduct” (*in actu*) instead of “in clothing” (*in amictu*).

## 9. What It Means to Rejoice in Jesus

But who can trample all these things so completely that, although the same vices interrupt him, he believes he can never for even a moment be drawn away from this exultation, when Scripture declares: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15)?

Therefore, groaning, O holy soul—whoever you are who rejoice in the Lord—whenever you see that you have been drawn away from this exultation, say:

“Do not cast me away from your face, Lord, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (Ps. 50:13–14).

Here observe more attentively what kind of exultation he requested.

For what is called *Jesus* in Hebrew is called *Salvator*, “Savior,” in Latin.

What is this joy of Jesus, then, except contemplation of him as he will come in his glory?

We must understand that those will then enjoy this brightness who, while placed here, imitate the footsteps of their Redeemer.

We read that the Lord Jesus grieved, wept, grew tired from the journey, endured reproaches and insults, received spittle, scourges, and the cross. Yet we never read that he laughed or prospered in the present world.

From this—from this hope—all the elect rejoice when they begin to be wearied by the world’s adversities and are not deceitfully misled by any of its prosperities, knowing beyond doubt that no other road remains by which they can enter heaven.

Hence the same Lord says to his disciples:

“Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely because of me. Rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:11–12).

But they could not endure these pressures and difficulties, much less rejoice in them, unless they were truly humble before God and human beings.

To them their Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

Again he says: “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4).

## 10. Praise of Humility. Feigned Humility

Hence also this glorious Virgin makes clear that she is called blessed by all generations because God looked upon her humility. For she adds: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48).

O truly blessed humility, which bore God for human beings, brought forth life for mortals, renewed the heavens, purified the world, opened paradise, and freed the souls of human beings from the underworld! O truly, I say, glorious humility of Mary, which became the gate of paradise and was established as the ladder of heaven! Certainly Mary’s humility became a heavenly ladder by which God descended to earth. “Because he has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid; behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.” And what does “he has regarded” mean except “He approved; my humility pleased him”? Hence the Lord said through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the poor and humble person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). David says to the Lord: “Because you have regarded my humility, you have saved my soul from distress” (Ps. 30:8).

Many indeed appear humble in the sight of human beings so that they may be blessed by them; but their humility is not regarded by the Lord, because they falsely, and not truly, glory in humility. For if they were genuinely humble, they would want God, not human beings, to praise them; their spirit would exult not in this world but in God their Savior; they would desire their humility to be seen not by human beings but by God.

The holy Canticle continues: “Because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name” (Luke 1:49). What great things has he done for you, I ask, glorious Virgin, that you should deserve to be called blessed? I think—indeed, I truly believe—that he did this so that you, a creature, might give birth to the Creator; that you, a servant, might bear the Lord; and that through you God might redeem the world, through you enlighten it, and through you restore it to life.

## 11. Prayer to the Blessed Virgin

Thus far, O blessed Virgin, you yourself have faithfully brought forth those things about yourself that should kindle us to the love of God; but what follows you prophesied concerning the human race. My purpose, however, was merely to pass over those things that pertained to the praise of your name. Yet even the things that you yourself related about yourself you were unable to express as your dignity deserves. What praises, then, will the frailty of the human race offer you [Col. 2134], since through your sole mediation it has found the means of recovery?

Receive, therefore, whatever offerings of thanksgiving we can make, however slight and however unequal to your merits; and when you have accepted our vows, excuse our sins by your prayers. Admit our prayers into the sanctuary of your hearing, and bring back to us the grace of reconciliation. Through you may what we offer be excusable; through you may what we ask with faithful hearts be obtainable. Receive what we offer, obtain what we ask, excuse what we fear; for we find no one more worthy than you to appease the Judge’s anger, since you were worthy to be the mother of the Redeemer and Judge.

Come, then, to the aid of the wretched; help the fainthearted; comfort those who weep. Pray for the people, intervene for the clergy, intercede for the choir of monks, entreat on behalf of the devout female sex. May all who devoutly celebrate your name experience your relief.

[Note: [Col. 2134] So the printed editions. But in manuscript cb. with m., “your Nativity.” The Vindocinensis, however, has “your Assumption.”]

May compassion toward the afflicted be yours; may tender affection be shown toward the pilgrims of heaven. And when you behold yourself always rejoicing, we ask that you yourself admit our tears before God and entreat him for us as your own Son.

For we are still afflicted on this earth: we are persecuted, assailed by injuries, subjected to insults; we hunger, thirst, endure sleep, and are kept in prison. But you have been exalted above all the choirs of virgins in the heavenly kingdoms; you follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4). You invite the choirs of virgins, untouched by the enticements of the flesh, through gleaming lilies and blooming roses, to drink from the springs of everlasting life.

In that happiest royal dwelling of the blessed, having obtained the dignity of the first rank, you wander on dewy feet among the delights of paradise and the grassy crocuses, advancing on tender knees, and with fortunate hand you pluck unfading violets. Joined to the highest beings, you sing without end in choirs; associated with Angels and Archangels, with tireless voice you never cease to cry, “Holy!” (Rev. 4:8). You stand adorned with gems and pearls in the chamber of the King of blessedness. A royal throne is placed for you by the Angels in the hall of the eternal King, and the King himself, loving you above all as his true mother and beautiful bride, associates you with himself in an embrace of love.

Nor is it surprising that God, who reigns in heaven, should deign to rejoice with you, since on earth you so often kissed him when he had been born from you as a little human child. Possessing these joys of yours, therefore, turn toward the salvation of our misery.

## 12. How the Blessed Virgin Is to Be Honored

In view of all this, therefore, dearest brothers, let us entrust ourselves with the whole devotion of our minds to the intercessions of the most blessed Virgin, and let us implore her patronage with every effort. As we attend upon her on earth with humble service, may she deign to commend us in heaven by her diligent prayer. For there is no doubt that she who deserved to offer the price for the liberation of captives is able to bestow more powerful assistance than all the saints upon those who have been liberated.

[Note: [Col. 2134] In the manuscripts, “which” instead of “who.”]

But what benefit is it for us to appeal to her with our voices unless we also preserve the examples of her humility? Let us therefore take care, beloved brothers, that we who desire to take part in this day’s festival may appear clothed in the garments of humility and charity. May envy of another’s happiness not torment us; may anger not tear us apart even to the point of division; may greed not exclude Christ from us; may worldly sorrow not consume us; may worldly prosperity not deceitfully ensnare us; may lust not defile us; may impurity not stain us; may self-exaltation not corrupt us; may pride not inflate us.

Then, when the blessed Mother of God sees us adorned with virtues, united in charity, and founded upon humility, taking part in her festival, may she hasten to assist us more fervently before her Son and Lord Jesus Christ, our God and Savior. He glorifies his saints with the crowns of an everlasting kingdom and is the eternal praise and hope of all his elect. To him be glory, power, might, and eternity, now and always, throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCIX

[Note: [Col. 2135] Formerly, *On the Saints* 37; later, in the Appendix, 85.]

## On the Feast of All Saints

[Note: [Col. 2135] It occurs among the published minor works of both Alcuin and Bede. In Bede’s favor is the accepted heading of the readings in Breviaries for this feast, “On All Saints.” In our manuscripts it lacks an author’s name. In certain German manuscripts, however, the name of Walahfrid Strabo is prefixed to it, but without justification, since Rabanus Maurus, somewhat earlier than Walahfrid, in book 3 addressed to Bonosus, chapter 12, excerpts several words from this sermon. Moreover, whoever the author may be, he has formed into one body here excerpts of sayings of the ancients—as Alcuin and Bede commonly do—borrowing some from Augustine and more from Chrysostom, but most from Cyprian: Epistle 9, to the Martyrs; Epistle 77, to Nemesianus and the others condemned to the mines; and Cyprian’s own books *On Work and Almsgiving* and *On Mortality*. For section 1, see Cyprian, Epistle 9, to the Martyrs; for section 3, compare Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, chapter 7; for section 4, Augustine, Sermon 127, chapter 3; for section 5, Cyprian, at the end of *On Work and Almsgiving* and Epistle 77, to Nemesianus; for section 6, Cyprian, at the end of *On Mortality*.]

[Col. 2135]

### 1. The Time of Combat Is Brief; the Prize Is Without End

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of all the saints in one solemn joy: heaven exults in their fellowship; earth rejoices in their patronage; the holy Church is crowned by their triumphs. The more powerful their confession was in suffering, the more resplendent it is in honor; for as the struggle increased, so too did the glory of those who struggled, and the triumph of martyrdom was adorned by a diversity of sufferings. Through more grievous torments, the rewards also became more precious.

While the Catholic mother Church, spread far and wide throughout the whole world, learned from her very Head, Christ Jesus, not to fear the insults of the cross and death, she was strengthened more and more—not in resisting, but in enduring. All those whom a penal prison had enclosed in a noble company were inspired by an equal and similar ardor of virtue to undertake the contest of triumphal glory.

O truly blessed mother Church, whom the honor of divine favor so illuminates, whom the glorious blood of victorious martyrs adorns, whom the white virginity of an inviolable confession clothes! Her flowers lack neither roses nor lilies. Now, dearest brothers, let each person strive toward both kinds of honor, to receive the most splendid crowns of distinction—white ones for virginity or purple ones for suffering. In the heavenly camp, both peace and battle have their flowers, with which Christ’s soldiers are crowned.

### 2. The Same Subject Continued

For God’s ineffable and boundless goodness also provided that the time of labors and struggle should not be prolonged, nor made long or eternal, but brief and, so to speak, momentary. Thus in this short and fleeting life there would be contests and labors, while in the life that is eternal there would be the crown and rewards of merits; labors would quickly come to an end, but the rewards of merits would endure without end. After the darkness of this world they would see the brightest light and receive a blessedness greater than all the bitterness of their sufferings. The Apostle testifies to this when he says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

With what joyful embrace does the heavenly city receive those returning from battle, and how it comes forth to meet those carrying trophies from their conquered enemy! Women come with the triumphant men—women who, together with the world, conquered their sex as well—and virgins of doubled glory, surpassing tender years by their virtues together with boys. The rest of the faithful multitude also enters the royal hall of everlasting life: those who preserved the sincerity of faith in an unshaken and peaceful observance of the heavenly commandments.

Come, then, brothers; let us set out upon the journey of life and return to the heavenly city in which we are enrolled and appointed citizens. We are not guests, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. 2:19), indeed heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Courage will open the gates of this city for us, and confidence will provide a broad entrance.

[Col. 2136]

### 3. Description of the Blessed Life

Let us therefore consider, as far as it is possible to consider, the glorious happiness of that city. For no speech will suffice to comprehend it as it truly is. It is said of it in one passage that “there pain and sorrow and groaning will flee away” (Isa. 53:10).

What life could be more blessed than this? There is no fear of poverty there, no weakness of sickness; no one is injured, no one grows angry, no one envies. No desire burns there, no craving for food, no pursuit of honor, no ambition for power [Note: [Col. 2136] Edition GG adds this note: “In Rabanus, ‘no one pursues honor and ambition for power.’”]. There is no fear of the devil there, no ambushes of demons, no terror of Gehenna nearby, and no death either of body or soul; instead, life is joyful through the gift of immortality.

There will then be no discord anywhere, but everything will be harmonious and fitting, because all the saints will have one accord. Peace and joy will embrace everything; all will be tranquil and quiet. There will be perpetual splendor—not the splendor that exists now, but one so much brighter as it is happier. For that city, as we read, will not need the light of the sun; the almighty Lord will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. There the saints will shine like stars throughout everlasting ages, and like the splendor of the firmament, those who instruct many in righteousness.

Therefore there will be no night there, no darkness, no gathering of clouds, and no harshness of cold or heat. Instead there will be such a tempering of all things as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. 2:9), except by those who are found worthy to enjoy it—those whose names are written in the book of life, who have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb, stand before God’s throne, and serve him day and night.

There is no old age there, nor the misery of old age, since all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s maturity. Beyond all this is the fellowship of the assemblies of Angels and Archangels, of Thrones and Dominions, of Principalities and Powers, and the enjoyment of companionship with all the heavenly and supernal Virtues. There one beholds the ranks of the saints, shining more brightly than the stars: the Patriarchs radiant with faith; the Prophets rejoicing in hope; the Apostles judging the world among the twelve tribes of Israel; the martyrs gleaming with purple crowns of victory; and the choirs of virgins bearing shining garlands.

But no voice is sufficient to speak of the King who sits among them. That beauty, that loveliness, that power, that glory, that magnificence, that majesty escapes every speech and exceeds every human understanding. His glory surpasses that of all the saints; his immeasurable presence is to be gazed upon, and one is to be illumined by the splendor of his majesty.

Even if it were necessary for us to endure torments every day, or to tolerate Gehenna itself for a short time, in order to see Christ coming in glory and to be joined to the number of his saints, would it not be worth enduring everything sorrowful so that we might share in so great a good and so great a glory?

### 4. By What Means Heaven Is Purchased

What will be the glory of the righteous, dearest brothers, and how great the joy of the saints, when every face shines like the sun (Matt. 13:43); when the Lord begins to enroll his people in distinct orders in the kingdom of his Father and restores to each person the rewards promised according to his merits and works; when he grants heavenly things in place of earthly things, eternal things in place of temporal things, great things in place of small things; when he leads the saints into the vision of the Father’s glory and makes them sit among the heavenly beings, so that God may be all in all; when he bestows eternity and immortality upon his lovers, for which he restored them to life through the vivification of his blood; when he brings them back again to paradise and opens the kingdoms of heaven through the faith and truth of his promise?

Let these things cling firmly to our minds; let them be understood with complete faith; let them be loved with our whole heart; let them be acquired through the greatness of unceasing works. The kingdom of heaven is placed within the power of the one who acts, for the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. This matter, O human being—that is, the heavenly kingdom—seeks no price other than yourself. It is worth as much as you are: give yourself, and you will have it.

Why are you troubled about the price [Col. 2137]? Christ gave himself in order to acquire you for God the Father’s kingdom; so you too give yourself, so that you may be his kingdom, and so that sin may not reign in your mortal body, but that the spirit may reign for the acquisition of life. Therefore let everyone who desires the promised rewards throughout the eternal ages joyfully run toward the prize of saving works.

### 5. The Purple Crown of Martyrs and the White Crown of Those Who Live Righteously

Let us therefore, brothers, contend willingly and readily; let us all run in the contest of righteousness while God and Christ look on. Since we have begun to become greater than the age and the world, let us not delay our course through any desire for the age or the world. If the last day finds us unencumbered, swift, and running in this contest of works, the Lord, our rewarder, will never be lacking in granting us our due reward.

He who gave a purple crown in persecution for suffering will himself also give a white crown in peace to those who live according to the merits of righteousness. For neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob were killed; nevertheless, honored for the merits of their faith and righteousness, they deserved to be first among the Patriarchs. Whoever is found faithful, righteous, and worthy of praise is gathered into their banquet.

We must remember that we ought to do not our own will but God’s, because “whoever does his will remains forever, just as he himself remains forever.” Therefore, beloved, let us be ready for every will of God with an undivided mind, firm faith, robust virtue, and perfect charity, bravely preserving the Lord’s commandments. Preserve innocence in simplicity, harmony in charity, moderation in humility, diligence in administration, watchfulness in helping those who labor, mercy in comforting the poor, constancy in defending the truth, and strict judgment in the rigor of discipline, so that nothing belonging to the example of good works may be lacking in us.

### 6. How Greatly the Eternal Life Is to Be Desired

These are the footsteps that all the saints, returning to their homeland, left for us, so that by clinging to their paths we might follow them to joys. Let us count paradise as our homeland together with them. We have already begun to have the Patriarchs as our fathers. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our fathers?

A great number of our loved ones awaits us there; a frequent and abundant crowd of parents, brothers, and children longs for us—already secure in their own safety, yet still concerned for our salvation. What joy there will be, both for them and for us, when we come into their embrace and presence! What heavenly delight awaits those fellow servants who long for our companionship! What supreme and perpetual happiness!

There is the glorious choir of the Apostles; there the distinguished multitude of rejoicing Prophets. There the innumerable people of martyrs are crowned for the victory of their contests; there the most radiant multitude of virgins rejoices; there also the courage of confessors is praised. There the reward is also reckoned for those who, observing the Lord’s commandments, transferred their earthly possessions to the heavenly treasures.

Let us hasten eagerly toward these, dearest brothers, so that we may soon be with them and soon come to Christ, having him as the guide of this journey, the author of salvation, the prince of light, and the giver of joy. He lives and reigns with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCX

[Note: [Col. 2137] Formerly, *On the Saints* 5; later, in the Appendix, 71.]

## On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, the Protomartyr, I

[Note: [Col. 2137] In most manuscripts the name of Maximus is prefixed. Yet several of these same books divide the sermon into two parts and assign to Maximus only the latter, which begins with these words here in section 2: “The reading from the Acts of the Apostles that has been read to us today,” and is also found among the published Sermons attributed to Maximus. However, the final and more important part, beginning approximately here in section 4—“Let us therefore imitate in some respect, dearest brothers”—is understood from other sermons of his to belong to Caesarius [Col. 2138]. For section 5, see Caesarius, homily 9 in the editions published by Baluzius, and below Sermon 225, section 6, as well as above Sermon 115, section 4, and homilies 9 and 10 in the editions published by Baluzius. For section 5 toward the end, see Caesarius, homily 7 in the editions published by Baluzius. For the end of section 6, compare homilies 10, 11, and 25 in the editions published by Baluzius.]

### 1. Stephen Given to the Whole Church as an Example. Stephen’s Utmost Chastity

Yesterday we celebrated the Nativity of the Lord Savior; today, with the greatest devotion, we venerate the suffering of the holy martyr Stephen. Yesterday we were redeemed for the reward; today we are summoned to follow an example. It was therefore fitting that today’s solemnity should be joined to yesterday’s festival, so that the former might raise believers to life, while the latter might lead confessors to the crown.

Blessed Stephen was therefore given to the whole Church for its advancement. Though still a layman, he was deemed worthy of being chosen for the diaconate, and as a Levite he attained the primacy of martyrdom. He was still placed among the common people, but he already excelled in virtues. He was humble in rank, but exalted in faith. He was a disciple in order, but became a teacher by his example. Those whom he followed in the devotion of faith, he surpassed in the speed of martyrdom.

For it is written of him in the Acts of the Apostles that he was appointed by the Apostles for the ministry to widows (Acts 6). In this too—that he was placed in charge of women—he earned testimony to his most sincere chastity. Blessed, therefore, will be, dearest brothers, whoever follows and imitates him; for he will obtain both the palm of chastity and the crown of martyrdom.

### 2. Why He Testified That He Saw the Son of Man, Not the Son of God

The reading from the Acts of the Apostles that was read to us today, dearest brothers, although it contains much that is astonishing in its outward form, contains no less of dignity in its mystery. “Behold,” blessed Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55).

Consider more attentively, dearest brothers: when the blessed Martyr had seen the Lord Jesus Christ standing at the right hand of God the Father, why did he testify that he saw the Son of Man and not rather the Son of God? Surely he would have seemed to confer greater honor upon the Lord if he had said that he saw the Son of God rather than the Son of Man.

But a definite reason required that this should both be displayed in heaven and proclaimed in the world. For the whole scandal of the Jews consisted in this: why should our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to the flesh was the son of man, also be called the Son of God? Therefore divine Scripture fittingly remembered that the Son of Man stood at the right hand of God the Father, so that the one whom the faithless denied in the world might be shown to the Martyr in heaven for the refutation of the Jews’ unbelief, and so that heavenly Truth might give testimony to the one from whom earthly impiety attempted to take away faith.

### 3. If Martyrs Differ Among Themselves, Stephen Is Preeminent

Thus, although according to the Psalm that was read, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15), if there can nevertheless be any distinction among martyrs, the one who is first appears to be preeminent.

For when Saint Stephen had been ordained deacon by the Apostles (Acts 6:5), he preceded the Apostles themselves in blessed and triumphant death. Thus the one who was lower in rank became first in suffering; and the one who was a disciple in position began to be a teacher through martyrdom, fulfilling what the blessed prophet said in the Psalm that was read: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12).

For Stephen was the first to wish to render back to the Lord what he had received from the Lord together with the whole human race. The death that the Savior deigned to suffer for all, he first returned to the Savior.

### 4. Stephen’s Wonderful Charity

After this, sacred Scripture added and said: “Having knelt down, he cried out, saying: Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

Observe, dearest brothers, the disposition of the blessed man; observe his great and admirable charity. He was undergoing persecution, yet he prayed for his persecutors. Amid that downfall of stones, when another person might have forgotten even his dearest friends, he commended his enemies to the Lord.

What was he saying while he was being stoned [Col. 2139]? “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Thus at that moment he grieved more over their sins than over his own wounds; he grieved more over their impiety than over his own death. And rightly so: their impiety contained many things to be mourned, whereas there was nothing in his death that ought to be mourned. Eternal death followed their impiety; everlasting life followed his death.

Let us therefore imitate in some respect, dearest brothers, the faith of so great a teacher and the charity of so distinguished a martyr. Let us love our brothers in the Church with the same disposition with which he then loved his enemies. Yet what is worse, sometimes we not only fail to love our enemies, but do not even preserve unbroken faith with our friends.

### 5. Forgiving Enemies

But someone says: “I cannot love my enemy, whom I endure daily as though he were a most cruel foe.”

O whoever you are, you consider what a human being has done to you, but you do not consider what you have done to God. Since you have committed sins against God that are much more serious, why do you not forgive a human being a small matter, so that God may deign to forgive you much?

Recall what Truth itself promised you in the Gospel, and what kind of guarantee, so to speak, it gave you, or what agreement it made with you: “If you forgive people their sins,” it says, “your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your debts” (Matt. 6:14–15).

You see, brothers, that by God’s grace it has been placed within our power how we will be judged by the Lord. “If you forgive,” he says, “you will be forgiven.”

For I have often said, brothers, and I must say it more frequently: let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself. Whoever hates even one person in this world loses everything he has offered to God in good works, because the Apostle Paul does not lie when he says: “If I give all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”

Blessed John also confirms this when he says: “Everyone who does not love his brother remains in death”; and again: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:14–15). In this passage “brother” must be understood as every human being, for we are all brothers in Christ.

Let no one, then, presume upon virginity without charity; let no one rely upon almsgiving, fasting, or prayers. For as long as he holds enmity in his heart, he will not be able to make the Lord favorable to him through these or any other good works.

But if he wishes to have the Lord favorable to him, let him not disdain to hear good counsel. Let him hear not me but his own Lord: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then, when you come, offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

And we, with inward quarrels and deceitful thoughts turning over in our hearts, presume to approach the altar as though we had a good conscience, not fearing what is written: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

### 6. It Is Difficult, but the Reward Is Great

This is observed because of earthly hope or fear; how much more, then, because of love.

But someone says: “It is a great labor to love one’s enemies and pray for one’s persecutors.”

We do not deny, brothers, that this is indeed no small labor in this age; but the reward will be great in the future. Through love of an enemy you become a friend of God—indeed, not merely a friend but also a son, just as the Lord himself said: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44–45).

If some rich person in this world wished to make you his adopted son, how would you serve him? What indignities inflicted even by his servants, what harsh and sometimes even disgraceful services, and what insults would you endure in order to reach his perishable and fragile inheritance?

What another person endures for the sake of earthly substance, endure for the sake of eternal life. For we are convicted by the clearest reasoning that we can endure injuries for God’s sake, but do not want to.

Indeed, if some powerful person injures us, and even curses us to our face, we dare not answer with anything harsh—not to mention returning the injury. Why? So that we may not suffer even greater things from that powerful person than those we have already endured.

What fear of a human being extorts from us ought to have been demanded from us by love of Christ. If, then, a powerful person rages against us, we keep silent and dare say nothing; but if an equal, or perhaps an inferior, inflicts even a slight insult upon us, we rise like wild beasts, without any patience and without any regard for God. Either we avenge our injury immediately or prepare our minds to return it with greater force.

What is this? When a powerful person inflicts an injury upon us, we accept it patiently; when an inferior does so, we are inflamed with excessive fury. It is because there we feared a human being, while here we do not wish to fear God.

Therefore I ask you, brothers: as far as we are able, with God’s help let us prepare our hearts for patience, strive to act as physicians toward all evil people, and hate not the people themselves but their wickedness. Let us pray for the good, that they may always advance toward better things; and for the evil, that they may quickly flee to the correction of life through the remedy of repentance.

May he himself graciously grant this to you as you pray, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON CCXI

[Note: [Col. 2140] Formerly, *On the Saints* 2; later, in the Appendix, 70.]

## On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, II

[Note: [Col. 2140] It is read under Augustine’s name in the Roman Breviary on the eighth day of Saint Stephen. The Louvain editors nevertheless rejected it and asserted that a good part of it is found in a sermon of Eusebius beginning, “Whenever your charity…” But we searched in vain for a sermon with this opening among the Eusebian sermons. Here, however, sections 2 and 3 contain certain excerpts from Augustine’s Sermon 49, sections 9–11.]

### 1. Stephen’s Crown

After yesterday’s most festive day, on which the birth of our Savior Christ shone forth, today also is illumined by the crown of the blessed martyr Stephen. No part of the world is unaware of that martyr’s merits, for he suffered at the very beginning of the Church, in the very city of Jerusalem. There he served as a deacon, and in the very flower of his youth he dyed the beauty of his age purple with his blood.

His suffering is distinguished and exceedingly wondrous. When it was read a little while ago from the book of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 7), we not only heard it but also awaited it with the eyes of faith.

Christ, therefore, the head of the martyrs, suffered first for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21). Following first in the footsteps of his suffering, the most blessed Stephen, by confessing Christ and being stoned by the Jews, deserved to obtain a crown, as though it had been placed upon him according to his very name. For *Stephanos* in Greek means “crown” in Latin. He already bore the name “crown,” and therefore carried the palm of martyrdom before him in his own name.

When he was being stoned, he not only did not seek to obtain vengeance from his persecutors, but rather asked God to forgive them. For he remembered that the Lord had said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:35); and again: “Do not say, ‘I will avenge myself on my enemies’; but wait for the Lord, and he will be your help” (Prov. 20:22).

God commands us to wait, so that on the day of future recompense we may be avenged together with the holy martyrs. “Blessed are those who wait for the Lord, for they themselves will possess the earth as an inheritance” (Ps. 36:9)—that earth, namely, which has certainly been prepared for the righteous.

### 2. The One Eager for Vengeance Is Restrained

Stephen both rages and loves. But you, O Christian, seek to take revenge upon your adversary, who perhaps has injured you; you burn, rage, pant, and hasten to avenge yourself.

Look upon Christ, the physician of your sickness; look upon the redeemer of your soul. For your sake he hung upon the wood and has not yet been avenged. Yet you wish to be avenged and do not wish to imitate so great and such a teacher? He wished to suffer in order to show you an example of his patience.

Look upon him hanging and preparing medicine for you, in your sickness, from his blood. Look upon him hanging and commanding you from the wood as from a tribunal. Hear him praying: “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

“But Christ could do this,” you say to me; “I cannot. I am a human being, whereas he is the God-man.”

Why, then, is God a human being, if the human being is not corrected? But behold, I speak to you, O human being. It is a great thing for you to imitate your Lord; look upon Stephen, your fellow servant.

Certainly Saint Stephen was a human being, not God. He was plainly a human being; he was what you are. But he could not have done what he did unless the one whom you too entreat had granted it.

Nevertheless, see what he did. He was speaking to the Jews; he raged and he loved. I must demonstrate both: how he raged and how he loved.

Hear him raging: “Stiff-necked”—these are the words of Saint Stephen when he spoke to the Jews—“and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. Which of the prophets did your fathers not kill?” (Acts 7:51–52).

You have heard him raging; hear him also loving. They became angry with him, grew more fiercely inflamed, returned evil for good, ran to the stones, and began to stone God’s servant.

Here let us prove the patience and love of Saint Stephen; here let us behold the victor and triumphant conqueror of the devil. We heard him raging against those who were silent; let us see whether he loves those who rage. He raged against those who were silent; let us see whether he loves those who stone him.

### 3. He prayed standing for himself; kneeling for his enemies

He prayed standing for himself; for his enemies, with knee bent. Behold Stephen being stoned, set before our eyes as though present. Behold the member of Christ; behold the athlete of Christ. Look upon him who first hung upon the wood. He was crucified; this man was stoned. He said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). What does this man say? Let us hear him, if perhaps we can even imitate him.

First, blessed Stephen prayed standing for himself and said: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he bent his knee, and with knee bent he said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And after saying this, he fell asleep (Acts 7:58–59).

O happy sleep, and true rest! Behold what it means to rest: to pray for one’s enemies.

But for a little while, I beg you, holy Stephen, explain this matter to us, which I do not understand: why did you pray standing for yourself, but kneel for your enemies?

Perhaps he would answer what we understand: “I prayed standing for myself because, since I served God rightly, I did not have to labor by praying and entreating for myself. For whoever prays for a righteous person does not labor; therefore he prayed standing for himself.”

When the time came for him to pray for the Jews, for the killers of Christ, for the killers of the saints, and for his own stoners, he considered that their impiety was so great and enormous that it could scarcely be forgiven. He bent his knee and said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, if you cannot imitate the Lord, imitate his fellow servant; imitate holy Stephen; imitate all the holy martyrs. They were human beings; they were your fellow servants; they were born as you were born. They were born as you were, but they were crowned by Christ.

## SERMON CCXII

[Note: [Col. 2141] Formerly, *On the Saints* 3.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, III

[Note: [Col. 2141] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It had remained doubtful among the Louvain editors and was rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus. Its first part differs in nothing from Augustine’s Sermon 319, *On Saint Stephen*. The latter part also, although it seems least appropriate to this feast, reflects the Augustinian style.]

#### 1

The priest’s joy and crown is the people’s salvation. It belongs to the priest to distribute the things of God, and to the people to receive them. May the Lord grant me to say a few beneficial words—the Lord who granted Saint Stephen the ability to say so many courageous ones, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 2141] Repeat the remainder from Augustine’s Sermon 319, sections 1 and 2.]

He saw Christ; he confessed Christ; he was about to die for Christ; he was about to proceed to Christ. The Lord, hanging upon the cross, said for his enemies: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Stephen, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 2141] From the same sermon, sections 4 and 5.]

How could this man not be there where the one whom he followed was, where the one whom he imitated was? He triumphed; he was crowned.

#### 2

The same subject follows. Certainly—[Note: [Col. 2142] Manuscript n. reads: “care” (*cura*).]—our crown is your edification, and our joy is your salvation—both temporal and eternal salvation.
