For we have the promise, as the Apostle said, of the present life and the future life (1 Timothy 4:8). Yet God grants this present salvation both to human beings and to animals; God grants it to both the good and the wicked.

The martyrs, however, despised this temporal salvation for the sake of eternal salvation. Without doubt you rejoice because you see us saved, and we rejoice in Christ over your salvation. But strive so that on that day we may also rejoice over you.

[Note: [Col. 2142] The praised manuscript reads: “so that on that day we shall rejoice with you as well.”]

For what the Apostle said in accordance with his own stewardship—so great and extensive that we can scarcely follow its traces—he was saying to us when he spoke to the people of God whom he was building up: “My joy and crown” (Philippians 4:1).

[Note: [Col. 2142] The same manuscript reads: “This is what he was saying to us, who was building up and saying…”]

Therefore, all who make progress in Christ through our labors are our joy and crown. For it is our task faithfully to distribute, not our own money, but the Lord’s; it is your task to receive it with care and diligence.

I can be a giver, not an exactor; and a giver not as though it were my property, but God’s—by which I too live, since we all belong to one great household and have one master of the house, the Lord. He has a spacious storeroom, from which both we and you can live. Let us only ask him to remove our weariness of food; first let him grant hunger, and then let him offer bread.

From what I live, I speak; what feeds me, I distribute. For with you I am poor. Our common riches are our God; the blessed and eternal life of us all is God.

Therefore, “let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXIII

[Note: [Col. 2142] Formerly, *On Various Matters* 98.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, IV

[Note: [Col. 2142] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It is doubtful to the Louvain editors, false according to Verlinus and Vindingus. In our manuscripts it is nowhere prefaced with Augustine’s name.]

### What the martyrs produce for themselves and for others

If anyone attentively runs through the deeds of the holy martyrs, he will always find in them something at which he may marvel even more. For blessed sufferings bring forth heavenly kingdoms for those who endure them, and display for our imitation the good that has been handed down to us as an inheritance.

What service worthy of such a pious Lord can the servants render, if it is clear that the Lord endured greater things for his servants than the servants endured for the Lord?

Therefore we ought to recount with every expression of reverence with what devotion blessed Stephen the martyr, whose feast we celebrate today, followed the Lord’s example, and with what patience he endured death.

Who would not be seized with immense astonishment and profound admiration at seeing that he received the impacts of stones so sweetly, and the blows of the rebounding rocks so gently, that when his head was battered and his blood flowed, all the members of his body grew numb, drenched in blood?

Then, carrying the trophy of devotion to Christ in his heart, he counted his wounds as medicine. He desired to be removed from this light, so that, at the Lord’s command, he might pass to those radiant dwelling places of eternity, where, in exchange for the departure of a single hour, everlasting joy—destined to perish through no old age—was prepared for him.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is eternal, and he has deigned to crown the martyrs of his kingdom with the glory of eternity.

## SERMON CCXIV

[Note: [Col. 2142] Formerly, *On Various Matters* 99.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, V

[Note: [Col. 2142] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. Verlinus and Vindingus prove that it was wrongly attributed to Augustine from the author’s ignorance: in section 4 he says that, when Christ was saying on the cross, “Truly I say to you, from now on you will see the heavens opened,” and so forth, Caiaphas cried out, “He has blasphemed!” Many other things are displeasing as well, and they do not permit its attribution even to Fulgentius, whose name appears before it in the Corbie manuscript. It may perhaps belong to the same preacher as Sermons 204 and 205 of this Appendix.]

#### 1. The Lord mixes sheep among wolves, and why

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the good, gentle, and merciful shepherd, mixes his sheep among wolves in this world in order to help them from his throne.

Do you wish to see, whoever you are that are a Christian, the Lord Jesus Christ mixing sheep among wolves? In the present Gospel reading he himself cried out, saying: “Behold, I am sending you as sheep among wolves” (Matthew 10:16).

Do you wish again to see the Lord Jesus Christ bringing his sheep out of the wolves’ hands? He himself cries out and says: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11).

The wolf is destroyed when the shepherd is killed; the sheep is redeemed when the shepherd is crucified.

The sheep ought not to fear being mixed among wolves. For this reason they are mixed among wolves—not so that they may be changed into the wolves’ wickedness, but so that the wolves may be converted to the innocence of the sheep.

But if they wish to become lambs, let the sheep not cease to follow the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

#### 2. Stephen, the first sheep. He appears as an angel. Because of the sign of the Trinity. By the keys of faith he opens heaven

Behold how Saint Stephen, the first sheep, by the testimony of faith confounds the wolves as they cry out, and sees the heavens opened with his own eyes.

O first sheep fighting in the midst of wolves, following the Lord though not yet having reached him—and already the friend of angels! How clearly he was a friend intimate with the angels, who amid wolves obeyed as an angel does.

For when the heavens were opened, the confessor’s appearance was transformed. He began to shine as though illuminated by the sun of righteousness, so that he no longer had a human appearance, while the heavens themselves lay open and his enemies themselves bore witness.

For he stood in the midst of wolves, and his face was like the face of an angel standing in the midst of the Jews (Acts 6:15).

What are you doing, O Jews? Do you not fear Christ’s first sheep, his attendant, who bears upon his forehead the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit?

That was the sign shining upon Stephen’s forehead. The heavens saw this sign and were opened; and, as though the sign had been displayed, the gates of heaven were opened in the form of angels.

For Saint Stephen came with the keys of faith; he opened for himself what he had faithfully believed, and gladly beheld. Therefore he did not keep silent about what he saw.

“Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55).

#### 3. There he sees Christ and the angels

But when the heavens had been opened, what remained for him to see except the Lord and Savior himself, who had ascended into heaven?

We all see these heavens, but closed, not opened; shining with stars, not sparkling with angels. But this man was already no longer merely human, but an angel.

As a human being, he does not see the palace of his Lord with its seat closed, but opened. He sees not merely angels but archangels—and indeed he sees them too—but he proclaims the one for whom he was a witness; he extols the one whose servant he is, perfected in the contest.

For how great was the grace granted to Saint Stephen! He saw the army of the heavenly host standing; he saw the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Father.

Behold, he sees God, who was already departing to God; and, by the merit of his confession, he sees the assembly of the heavenly Powers, although he was already about to depart to the region of the dead.

But among the dead he cried out—he who shone among them: “Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

#### 4. As Christ, so Stephen. He is condemned for confessing God. Yet he does not remain silent; but he is not heard

Let friends rejoice if enemies blaspheme. Let the sheep not be silent in bearing witness, even if the wolves cry out in blasphemy.

For they closed their minds and said: “He has blasphemed” (Acts 6:11).

Caiaphas, the high priest, said this as well of the Son of Man who was suffering and enduring everything. For when our Lord Jesus Christ, hanging upon the cross, said, “Truly I say to you, from now on you will see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the Father,” Caiaphas cried out, saying, “He has blasphemed!” (Matthew 26:64–65).

Caiaphas tore his garments; these men closed their minds. Caiaphas did so so that he might remain naked; they did so so that they might persist in their hardness.

O great miracle! The gates of heaven are opened, while the Jews have closed their impious minds. But Saint Stephen did not keep silent, did not falter, and did not yield to those who blasphemed.

He was attentive to the place where he opened the eyes of his heart.

“Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

#### 5. Stephen’s address to the Jews

“But why are you angry with me, Jews, because of such great testimony? Were the heavens opened at my command or by my authority?

“They were opened not to reveal my glory, but to show my shepherd displaying his help in me.

“Consider, then, and see how far I am from heaven, placed with you on earth. Could I have reached heaven and opened its gates? The Lord of angels himself opened his palace to me.

“Therefore, in a certain sense I see; and what I see I do not keep silent about. I did not despise him who hung upon the cross; therefore I see him seated at the right hand of the Father.

“This heavenly testimony has been given to you. But if you do not believe, what have I done to you? ‘The heavens declare the glory of God’ (Psalm 18:1); and should I remain silent about the mercy of my Christ?

“I see Christ seated in his glory, standing for my salvation. He himself is my witness in heaven; shall I not be his witness on earth?

“If I confess him before human beings, he too will confess me before his angels. But if I deny him on earth, he too will deny me in heaven (Luke 12:8–9).

“Yet, for such faithful testimonies, you throw stones, close your minds, and refuse to hear one who speaks to you plainly and openly.”

#### 6. Stephen’s prayer to Christ for himself

“Strike, strike with stones the one who confesses! I have my helper at the Father’s right hand.

“You strike my head; I entrust my spirit to him.

“Lord,” he says, “Jesus, receive my spirit.”

“They curse; you bless. They persecute; you receive the persecuted one.

“It is not without reason, my Jesus, my Lord, that you deign to stand at the right hand of the Father for me, whom I know and believe to be seated at the right hand of the Father.

“You stand for me; you do not fail by standing, and you do not abandon your own when you help them.

“You, my Lord, sent me into the midst of my enemies. You deigned to make me the first martyr after your ascension. If you wish me not to fail you, help me.

“Let the battering of the stones cease; let the strength of my limbs not fail me. For you plead for me, my Lord, while you stand.

“I hear the embassy of your voice. I believe, I receive, I recognize you as asking, giving, and helping for me before the Father, so that my faith may not fail in following you.

“What do you say, my Jesus, my Lord, when you ask the Father for me?

“‘Father, behold this first follower: he has entered a new contest in the world for me. Grant mercy, so that he may reach victory.’

“Let my sheep feel that he is helping it, so that it does not think me a traitor among wolves.

“Behold,” he says, “I see him standing; I presume that he is asking for me.”

And therefore, my Lord, who await my contest, receive my spirit.

[Note: [Col. 2144] The reading is *spectas* (“you look upon”) for *exspectas* (“you await”).]

But since I do not fear the one who is stoning my limbs, receive my spirit into everlasting rest. Among these people I am assigned as a sheep for slaughter; with you let me be placed in the rest of sweetness and peace.

The Jews were stoning; he was groaning. The Jews were striking his head; he was commending his spirit.

#### 7. His prayer for his enemies. What this prayer accomplished

But once he had begun to be secure concerning the spirit he had entrusted, he became an advocate for his enemies.

He did not intercede for his enemies in the same way that he had asked for himself. Here he stood when he saw Christ; here he bent his knees when he prayed for his enemies.

Such advocacy was necessary for enemies so numerous and so wicked. For he knew that the Lord Jesus could not quickly hear him on their behalf—not because of his own merit, but because of their sin.

Therefore, for the great wickedness of the Jews who were stoning him, he bent his knees and poured out tears, saying: “Lord, do not hold this against them as sin.”

See, whoever you are who are a Christian, how this sheep follows the Lamb in everything and imitates the Shepherd.

The Lord Jesus Christ, hanging upon the cross, cried out: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). This man says: “Lord, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:58).

The Lord Jesus Christ cried out for his enemies: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). This man says: “Do not hold this against them as sin” (Acts 7:59).

And clearly, my brothers, the blessed apostle Paul was present among those stoners, the one who raged more fiercely than the rest. If Stephen had then been granted vengeance upon the stoner, how would the Church have had such a teacher?

After saying these things, he gave up his spirit, ascended into heaven, and obtained forgiveness for his enemies. He deserved to rejoice in heaven over the friendship of blessed Paul, who would follow him, because he is the Lord “who makes the barren woman dwell in a house as a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 112:9).

Behold what holy Stephen merited, he who saw the Son of Man standing, whom we know to be seated at the right hand of the Father.

Let us ask him to intercede for us and for our sins, and to rescue us from all our great dangers and birth pangs, through his mercy, not according to our conscience.

For what, or how many, springs of our sin can extinguish its flame? May he himself deign to bury our crimes, so that, just as he briefly entrusted his limbs to a new tomb, so he may bury our sins in the font of forgiveness, that we may always rejoice with you in the holy Church. Amen.

## SERMON CCXV

[Note: [Col. 2145] Formerly, *On the Saints* 1.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, VI

[Note: [Col. 2145] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It lacks Augustine’s name as doubtful in the Louvain collection; they also report that in certain manuscripts it is attributed to Bishop Fulgentius. Vindingus judges that it contains nothing alien to Augustine. To us, however, its manner of expression generally seems humbler than Augustine’s and more concise. What is read here in section 3, beginning with the words in section 4, “For so that Your Holiness may know how powerful prayer was,” and so forth, can be found in Sermon 382 among the Augustinian sermons. For the end of section 4 and section 5, see above Sermon 204, sections 2–3, and Sermon 205, section 3.]

#### 1. The effect of Christ’s birth

Yesterday we celebrated the feast on which the King of martyrs was born into the world; today we celebrate the feast on which the chief of the martyrs departed from the world.

For it was fitting that the Immortal should first take flesh for mortals, and that then a mortal should endure death for the Immortal.

Therefore the Lord was born in order to die for the servant, so that the servant might not fear dying for the Lord.

Christ was born on earth so that Stephen might be born in heaven. The Lord entered the world so that Stephen might enter heaven. The exalted one descended to lowliness so that the lowly might ascend to exalted things.

The Son of God became the son of man so that he might make the sons of human beings sons of God.

Christ performed miracles, and Stephen did too. But Christ performed them without Stephen; could Stephen perform them without Christ?

Stephen lived from Christ as a branch lives from the vine. Do you marvel at fruit hanging from a branch? Look at the branch flowing from the vine.

#### 2. Stephen is stoned for confessing Christ

Come now, holy Stephen, say something to the Jews, so that you may begin to be stoned and may be able to be crowned. Hurl your words, and receive the stones.

Say something about uncircumcised hearts, and you will die by stones. Say something about the one whose name they do not wish to hear.

“Let lying lips be silenced” (Psalm 30:19). Tell them where you see alive the one whom they mocked as he hung crucified. Tell them where you see him, and you will not live here—but you will live better with him.

Tell them that what they did amounts to nothing: the one whom they killed is alive. Tell them that you see standing at the Father’s right hand the one whom they mocked hanging upon the cross.

And he says: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

But they cried out and stopped their ears. They closed their ears and ran toward the stones; they all rushed upon him and stoned Stephen as he called upon the Lord and said: “My soul has clung to you” (Psalm 62:9), because my flesh is being stoned for you.

“Receive my spirit” (Acts 7:55–58), and restore to me your promise.

[Col. 2146]

#### 3. Following Christ’s example, he prays for his enemies

Christ prayed for his crucifiers, and Stephen prayed for his stoners. The Lord Jesus prayed while fastened to the wood; Stephen prayed with his knee bent.

The one who, standing, entrusted his spirit to the Lord prayed for their offense with knee bent.

He prayed to the Lord for his enemies as a friend, saying:

“Behold, I am suffering; I am being stoned. They rage against me and roar against me. But do not hold this sin against them, because I first heard this request from you.

“I, your servant, am suffering; but there is a great difference between you and me. You are Lord; I am servant. You are the Word; I am a hearer of the word. You are Teacher; I am disciple. You are Creator; I am creature. You are God; I am human.

“There is a great difference between the sin of those who are stoning me and that of those who crucified you. When, therefore, you said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,’ you pleaded on behalf of a great sin, and taught me to plead for a lesser one.

“Lord,” he says, “do not hold this sin against them”—as though he were saying: “I suffer in the flesh; let them not perish in mind.”

They were throwing stones; Saint Stephen was pouring out prayers. Great mercy, brothers; great clemency!

Indeed, what he ate at the table of his Lord, such things he himself prepared at his own banquet. For it is written: “When you sit at a great table, know that you must prepare such things” (Sirach 31:12).

Therefore, in prayer he offered the same things that he ate at his Lord’s table.

The Lord Jesus Christ said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Saint Stephen said: “Do not hold this sin against them”; and after saying this, he fell asleep (Acts 7:59).

O sleep of peace! What is more tranquil than that sleep? What is more restful? How was he going to his friends, who loved his enemies in such a way?

#### 4. Saul’s conversion is owed to Stephen’s prayer

For so that Your Holiness may know how powerful the prayer of the holy martyr Stephen was, recall with us that young persecutor named Saul, as we heard when the book of the Acts of the Apostles was read.

When Saint Stephen was being stoned, the garments of all the stoners were being kept by this man, so that he seemed to be stoning with everyone’s hands, since he encouraged them all to stone him.

As he was traveling along the road, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. Falling to the ground, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

He said: “Who are you, Lord?”

And the Lord said to him: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:3–5).

“What have I to do with you, and what have you to do with me? Why do you rise up against me to your own harm, instead of humbling yourself for your own good?

“For the great evils you have committed against me, I ought long ago to have destroyed you. But my servant Stephen prayed for you.

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? But because you rage against my name, I will make you my servant.”

#### 5. Saul’s crime is both forgiven and punished

O Saul, ravenous wolf, you have devoured; wait a little, and you will digest.

I shall speak plainly: the son of perdition was struck down, and the vessel of election was raised up.

For if Saint Stephen had not prayed in this way, the Church would not have Paul today. But Paul was raised up because, with Stephen bent down on earth, his prayer was heard.

Therefore, what Saul did, Paul will suffer; what the persecutor did, the preacher will suffer; what the wolf did, the lamb will suffer. For this is how such a person must be punished.

Let him learn to suffer what he used to do; let him himself feel what he inflicted on others.

The Lord Jesus Christ says to Ananias: “Go to him and mark him with my seal, for he will suffer many things for my name” (Acts 9:15–16).

Ananias went, baptized Saul, and made Paul; he baptized a wolf and made a lamb; he baptized a persecutor and made a preacher.

We began to have as a preacher the one whom Saint Stephen had had as his stoner.

Thus Saint Stephen was heard: through his prayers the sin committed by Saul was wiped away.

Therefore, let us commend ourselves to his prayers. For he will now be heard all the more on behalf of those who venerate him, since he was then heard on behalf of those who stoned him.

## SERMON CCXVI

[Note: [Col. 2147] Formerly, *On Various Matters* 96.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, VII

[Note: [Col. 2147] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. The Louvain editors regard it as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus regard it as false. Nothing here has the flavor of Augustine; indeed, many things are contrary to him, such as the statement concerning Stephen that “the proclamation about the stone that had been rejected—‘This has become the cornerstone’—was fulfilled.” Also the claim that “while still placed in the body here, he deserved to see the Trinity itself.” Finally, the style is impure and less suitable.]

[Col. 2147]

#### 1. Stephen, while dwelling here, saw the Trinity

The magnificent solemnity of the martyrs compels us to offer you the precious seeds of the divine word. Therefore we ask you to prepare your hearts for the heavenly rain, so that, when we cast your seeds, you may bring forth a hundredfold fruit.

Today, then, we celebrate the devout day of the most blessed martyr Stephen—not the day on which he was born into the world, but the day on which through suffering he departed to heaven.

He earned great honor through the divine word, both by displaying the acceptable dignity of the Levitical office and by completing an outstanding martyrdom.

He received a double sanctification of grace in the heavenly kingdoms, because he lived holily before God on earth; his soul did so according to Solomon’s saying (Proverbs 31:21).

We heard the voice of the blessed Apostle: “For I betrothed you,” he says to Christians, “to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

But blessed Stephen merited to love Christ, so that he might merit to see him from earth in heaven, as he says: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55).

O pure heart, which rightly knows God!

Now the Gospel proclamation concerning the stone that had been rejected—“This has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117:22)—has been fulfilled.

And again: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

See what the most blessed Stephen merited after his bodily departure: while he was still here in the body, he merited to see the Trinity itself.

#### 2. Stephen’s remarkable charity toward his stoners

Then the Jews, alienated from the life of the saints, decided to stone blessed Stephen.

The Jews were stoning the man of God; he was praying while looking upon God. He was gazing upon divinity; the Jews were exercising their own savagery.

Stones came upon him like rainstorms, while he prayed on bended knees for the sins of the wicked people.

Blessed Stephen prayed for their sins, while they displayed no mercy toward him.

What are you doing, Saul? Why do you, a martyr, rage against a martyr, when you too will be stoned by the hands of others?

The Jews were stoning; Saul was guarding their garments.

Blessed Stephen was entreating God for their iniquities. From the Lord Christ he received a name from which the triumph of martyrdom might paint a crown.

For through the Greek language he received the name “crown” (*stephanos*), which is interpreted in Latin as “perpetual life.”

Therefore, having turned with me, let us beseech the most blessed martyr of Christ, so that by his merits he may obtain for us a crown in perpetual life, that we may be with him forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXVII

[Note: [Col. 2147] Formerly, *On the Saints* 6.]

### On the Feast of Saint Stephen, VIII

[Note: [Col. 2147] Now placed here for the first time in the Appendix. The Louvain editors leave room for doubt about its authenticity; Verlinus and Vindingus, however, produce arguments for its falsity drawn from the author’s style and character, which it is pointless to enumerate in a matter so evident. As the Louvain editors report, some manuscripts attribute it to Fulgentius; among ours, some attribute it to Maximus, but incorrectly.]

#### 1

Since I see that our discussions are bound together by stylus and wax tablets, and that we are by no means capable of reading them, help me myself, I beg you, by your intercession before this martyr, whom robed Gamaliel revealed, stripped Saul stoned, and Christ wrapped in swaddling clothes enriched and crowned with a precious stone.

This is a day of triumph, most blessed ones; it is the triumphal day of Saint Stephen the martyr.

Condemned to death by those who stoned him, he was hurled outside the city by stones; his body was killed, his head wounded, his limbs battered by stones, and he was crowned with the cornerstone.

This minister was beautiful because the Master was beautiful as well. This Stephen was beautiful everywhere, in heart and body.

Of the beauty of the Master it is sung in the Psalm: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Psalm 44:3).

And we ourselves sing in the Psalm: “In your beauty and your loveliness, set forth, proceed prosperously, and reign” (Psalm 44:5).

Thus Stephen the martyr possessed bodily beauty, the flower of youth, eloquence in speaking, the wisdom of a most holy mind, and the working of divinity.

Great envy had arisen among the Jews on account of the Christian profession.

#### 2

For the Jews saw Stephen, a Jew among Jews, disputing in the metropolitan city of his ancestors against the Jewish sacred rites, against the sacrifices, against the Law, against circumcision, and against the Sabbaths.

They rose up in anger and conceived poisonous thoughts. They said such things to one another:

“What is this? What is happening? What are we doing? What should we do? What should we say? What does this man want for himself—this young, handsome, most eloquent, and wisest man?

“For this man performs great and marvelous signs, and Christ died as a man without cause.

“Come,” they said, “brothers, let us meet together and assemble as one. Let us make a plan and confirm a false testimony.

“We acted against the Lord; let us act against his servant as well. We said against the Lord, ‘It is better that one man should die than that the whole nation perish’ (John 18:14). Let us say against his servant, ‘Let us destroy him from the land of the living, and let his name no longer be remembered’ (Jeremiah 11:19).

“When we made our plan against Jesus, we profited greatly, because we prevailed. We deceived him, gave him over, received him, bound him, handed him over, overcame him, oppressed him, and crucified him.

“We gave money to the lover of greed, money that each of us extracted from the wealth of iniquity. We bound the unconquerable Son of virginity; we handed the Judge over to the judge of equity; we overcame the one who overcomes the empire of vanity; we oppressed the one who oppresses the pride of calamity; we spat upon the face of holiness; and we, blind men, crucified the Son of majesty.

“We killed him, buried him, and sealed his tomb with our ring. But we found it unsealed by an angel.

“We entrusted the sealed tomb to guards to keep watch over it, and we gave money to those who saw the miracle of the resurrection so that they would lie to Pilate. We produced witnesses and, in our confusion, were deprived of the watchful guards.”

#### 3

“But now also,” they said among themselves, “men, what are we doing? What should we do? What should we say, when we killed one Christ and see so many Christians?

“Behold, they say, from the one Christ killed by us there are two hundred of his disciples. From our own number, Nicodemus, our priest, belongs to them; and three thousand and five thousand men have run to their baptism.

“They have baptized many Jewish, Greek, and barbarian nations and placed them over their own shrines.

“Behold, what is worse and more disastrous for us: they have ordained seven deacons. Among them is one called Stephen, a young, handsome, most eloquent, and wisest man above all. He is full of miraculous signs; and if he is full, our people must flock to him, and he must be magnified before all the Jews to our confusion, unless he is stoned by our hands.

“Why, then,” they say, “are we still standing here? Whom are we waiting for? Why do we delay?

“Let us publicly seize this Stephen, the public exposer of our confusion, and bring him before the council. Let us place him in our midst; let us trouble him with a priestly synod; let us crush him with the most false testimony; let us do to the servant what we did to the Master.

“For if we did not hesitate to pierce the Master with a lance, we ought not to hesitate to stone Stephen.”

And all the Jews, men of impiety and always ready for murder, agreed.

They seized Stephen and brought him to their council. They harassed and disturbed him, questioned him, listened, and paid attention.

They heard the wisest man and looked upon the most beautiful.

[Col. 2149]

#### 4

O Jews, always enemies of God, pay close attention—you who judge unjustly. If, then, you truly speak justice, “judge rightly, children of men” (Psalm 57:2).

Pay attention together, high priests, ministers, priests, and people. All of you Jews together, look upon the face of God’s minister; look upon the face of Stephen, if you can.

For Moses, because of your blindness, placed a veil over his own face. But Stephen, for your confusion, announces the mystery of the resurrection before your assembly.

But, O Jews, envious of the prophets and faithless toward the martyrs, we are not at all surprised that in many ways you correspond to your own iniquities.

For you who despise the face of the lawgiver show favor to the accuser. You despised the face of Moses the lawgiver, Jews, and showed favor to the most savage accuser; and you continually add your crime to your disgrace.

Your Moses, when he placed the veil before his holy face, did not wish to see your criminal face. But Stephen, with his face unveiled, gazed into heaven upon the glory of the Son of God. Therefore the Jews saw his face as though it were the face of an angel of God.

5. And now, blessed martyr Stephen, despise the earth, gaze upon heaven; disdain the high priest, look toward the Father. Despise the Jew, the priest, and the people; behold in heaven the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet tell the Jew what it is that you have long been contemplating in heaven.

“Behold,” says Stephen, “I see the heavens opened” (Acts 7:55), “and I myself see Jesus standing at the right hand of the Father—Jesus whom you crucified, whom you mocked as he was dying, whom you placed lying in a sealed tomb.”

What, then, did it profit you, Jews, that you crucified the Son of God and stone the martyr of the Son of God? Behold, you have been twice over shaken down: you have lost your city, and you have lost the very leader of those who stoned him; and your plant has been uprooted from the holy city. For that Davidic curse has been fulfilled in Judaea:

“Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living” (Psalm 51:7).

The Jewish crowds, however, kept silent; in damnable hostility they gnashed their serpent-like teeth at the martyr Stephen, whom they held like a serpent in their hearts. They then cast the holy martyr outside their city, presenting witnesses beforehand and speaking falsehood. They rage, strip themselves, and throw their garments before Saul’s feet; they run with stones, raise their elbows, extend their arms, and hurl rocks. The unjust stone the righteous man as he falls down, prays, and says:

“My Lord Jesus, my revealer, my defender, for whose sake my naked stoner rages against me: hear me, hear me, my Holy One, Son of the Virgin, living Stone, who, in order to hear me, has but one stoner short of a believer [the wording is uncertain]. Look,” he says, “upon me, cleansed by the bath of your fountain, consecrated without stain by your saving grace, stripped for your name, stoned by human hands, yet not separated from Saul by love. And in your mercy do not hold this sin against them forever.”

Thus holy Stephen, dying, slept in eternal peace with Christ Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2149] Formerly, *On the Saints* 9.]

### On the Feast of the Holy Innocents I

[Note: [Col. 2149] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It remained doubtful to the Louvain editors; it was rejected by Verlinus and Vindingus. If the first part of the sermon is removed, everything remaining from the words in section 2, “Therefore the deceiver Herod,” and so forth, belongs to Eusebius’ homily on the Epiphany. Moreover, in the Corbie manuscript the sermon is found in a considerably fuller form, with an added account of the punishments suffered by Herod, the killer of the Innocents.]

### 1. The Magi come from the East

When Christ, therefore, had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in accordance with the testimony of prophecy, during the reign of King Herod, certain men from the eastern regions, belonging to the race of the Magi, came and asked Herod where the king who had recently been born of the Jews was. They affirmed that they had seen his star in the East and that it had also served as their guide on the journey; and they declared that the reason for their great haste was that they wished to adore and venerate the newly born king.

When Herod heard this, he was extraordinarily terrified, fearing and dreading that the security of his imperial position might be endangered. He therefore summoned and called in the teachers of the Law and questioned them about where they expected Christ to be born. When the place of his birth had been identified from the oracles of Micah as Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), the king, by a single command, ordered all nursing infants—not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all its territory—from two years old and under, according to the time he had ascertained from the Magi, to be killed and destroyed (Matthew 2:5, 16), so that somehow he might also extinguish Jesus together with those of his own age. But the child, having been taken away to Egypt after an angel warned his parents beforehand of the king’s plot, forestalled the king’s ambush.

### 2. The blessedness of the Innocents

Therefore King Herod, deceived by the Magi, sends men into Bethlehem and throughout all its territory so that the boys from two years old and under may be killed. The little ones are slain for Christ; innocence dies for righteousness. How blessed is the age that cannot yet speak of Christ and already deserves to be killed for Christ; not yet fit for a wound, and already suited for suffering! How happily born are those for whom eternal life came to meet them at the very threshold of birth! They encounter danger and the end of salvation amid the very beginnings of the light they have received; yet from that very end they immediately receive the beginnings of eternity. They appear immature for death, but happily die for life. Scarcely had they tasted the present life when they immediately passed to the future; they had not yet entered the cradles of infancy, and already they reached the crowns. They are indeed torn from their mothers’ embraces, but are given back to the laps of angels.

### 3. Herod’s error and foolish terror

“Therefore you have accomplished nothing, most savage boldness” [Note: [Col. 2150] In the manuscript, *auctoritatis* (“of authority”). In Eusebius’ homily on the Epiphany, *impietatis* (“of impiety”). In another homily of Eusebius, *On the Seven Brothers*: “Therefore you have accomplished nothing, most savage man; the audacity of impiety can make martyrs, but …”], “you can make martyrs, but you cannot find Christ.”

The unhappy tyrant thought that, at the royal arrival of the Lord and Savior, he would be driven from his royal throne. But it is not so. Christ had not come for this purpose, to seize another’s glory, but to bestow his own. He had not come to snatch away an earthly kingdom, but to confer a heavenly one. He had not come to seize powers and dignities, but to endure insults and injuries. He had not come to prepare that sacred head for a jeweled diadem, but for a crown of thorns. No, I say, he had not come to be established in magnificence above scepters, but to be mocked and crucified.

### 4. Herod’s disturbance and deception

When the Lord was born, Herod was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. What wonder if impiety is disturbed when piety is born? Behold: the armed man fears him lying in a manger; the proud king trembles before the humble one; the man clothed in purple is afraid of one wrapped in swaddling clothes.

He addresses the Magi deceitfully: “Go,” he says, “search carefully for the child; and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and adore him” (ibid., 8). He pretended that he wished to adore the one he was attempting to kill.

But Truth does not fear the snares of falsehood. What blind savagery—to believe that he could discover God by deceit! Behold: the one whose coming earth and heaven proclaimed, who was not hidden from the simplicity of the shepherds, whom the Magi, coming from the farthest region of Ethiopia, were privileged to recognize—the sacrilegious king cannot reach him by his stratagems.

The tyrant’s foolish fury is therefore deceived. Faithlessness cannot find Christ, because God must be sought not through cruelty but through belief. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXIX

[Note: [Col. 2151] Formerly, *On the Saints* 8.]

### On the Feast of the Holy Innocents II

[Note: [Col. 2151] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors and judged spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. It does not sound like Augustine, to whom it is not attributed alone in the manuscripts, but also to Bede and Chrysostom. It is read in the Roman Breviary on the octave of the Innocents. The opening is taken from Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book 1, chapter 2.]

[Col. 2151]

### 1. One God

The Innocents are victims owed to the God who was born. We believe the Jews, because “God was once known in Judaea” (Psalm 75:2); and they deny the very thing on account of which we believe, because they do not know the Father, since they deny the Son.

The common nature of things testifies to one God, because there is one world. Faith signifies one God, because there is one faith of the New and Old Testaments. Grace testifies to one Holy Spirit, because there is one Baptism in the name of the Trinity.

The Prophets proclaim God. The Apostles preach him. The Magi believed in one God, and as suppliants brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to Christ’s cradle. The shepherds glorify God; the Magi bring three gifts. The most cruel Herod sharpens his sword, so that the eternal altars may be filled with the bloody sacrifices of infants.

For where the little ones are sacrificed, the wretched mothers lament. At the Lord’s birth, mourning began—not in heaven, but in the world. Lamentation is imposed upon mothers, exultation upon angels, migration upon infants.

It is God who has been born. Victims are owed to him who came to condemn the world’s wickedness. Lambs must be sacrificed to him who is to be crucified as the Lamb, who takes away the sins of the world.

### 2. The mothers’ mourning

But the mothers, like bleating sheep, howl, because they are losing lambs that bleat without a voice. A great miracle! A cruel spectacle! The sword is drawn, and no cause intervenes; only envy hisses, even though the one who has been born does violence to no one.

Yet we see the mothers, like sheep, mourning over their lambs. “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and much wailing” (Jeremiah 31:15).

They are children not entrusted but created; not laid down but exposed. Nature itself is witness, for it fought against the martyrs when the tyrant hurled the infants about. The mother tore apart the hair of her head, as she lost the adornment of her head. In how many ways she wished to hide the infant—and the little infant himself made his presence public! He did not know how to be silent, because he had not yet learned to be afraid.

Mother and executioner struggled: he dragged, and she held on. The mother cried out to the executioner:

“Why are you separating from me the one whom I gave birth to from myself? The womb gave birth to him; he did not remain there when he lived [Note: [Col. 2151] In manuscripts r. and n.: “The womb gave birth to the name of the stylus” (or *stile*) “joined together.” A little later, where the printed editions have *contorquet* (“twists”), we restore *replentur* (“are filled”) from the manuscripts.]; my breasts are filled with milk in vain. Carefully I carried the one whom I see you hurling with a cruel hand. Just now my womb poured him forth, and you dash him to the ground.”

Another mother cried out when the executioner of the robbers compelled her:

“Kill the mother together with the child; why do you leave me empty? If there is guilt, it is mine; if there is no crime, join us in death and set the mother free.”

Another said:

“What are you looking for? You are looking for one, and you are killing many; yet you cannot reach the one who is himself one.”

Another cried out in reply:

“Come now, come, Savior of the world! How long will you be sought? You fear no one. Let the soldier see you, and let him not kill our infants.”

### 3. How sad Herod’s fate will be on the day of judgment

The mothers’ lamentation mingled with the offering of the little ones as it passed up to heaven. But he who tested the Lamb himself slaughtered the little lambs through Herod. Punishment remains for the author of the deed, and the devil’s judgment for Herod, when the resurrection of these dead begins.

Herod, what do you think you will do when companies of so many infants begin to bring a judicial charge against you? You will find them with a clear tongue and a great voice, of perfect stature, all young men in white robes, shining with the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age (Ephesians 4:13). When they begin to stand before the one whom you had thought to kill, for whom they shed their precious blood, you will see him himself presiding upon a fiery throne, and them surrounding the Lord’s throne, shining with red-white brilliance because of their youthful purity and the blood of their passion.

What will you do? What will you say? You will be silent as the guilty one while so great an army of saints sings:

“Avenged be the blood of your servants, which has been shed” (Revelation 6:10).

“Let the groaning of the prisoners come before your presence” (Psalm 78:11).

With the help of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXX

[Note: [Col. 2152] Formerly *On the Saints* 10; later, in the Appendix 72.]

### On the Feast of the Holy Innocents III

[Note: [Col. 2152] It consists of excerpts from Augustine and Ambrose and of other fragments that have the flavor of Caesarius. It is read in the Roman Breviary on the feast of the Innocents. For section 1, see Ambrose’s sermon *On Saints Nazarius and Celsus*; for section 2, Augustine’s sermon 8, section 8; Appendix sermon 21, section 8; Caesarius’ homily 13; and Augustine’s *Sermons* 48, sections 7 and 8. For section 6, see Caesarius at the end of homily 10.]

### 1. Herod benefited the Innocents more by hatred than he would have by favor. The Innocents, flowers of the martyrs

Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the feast of those infants whom, as the text of the Gospel declares, the most cruel King Herod killed. Therefore let our earth rejoice with the greatest exultation, since it is the fruitful mother of heavenly soldiers and of such great virtues.

Behold: the profane enemy could never have benefited the blessed little ones so greatly by favor as he benefited them by hatred. For, as the most sacred feast of this day reveals, to the extent that wickedness abounded against the blessed little ones, to that same extent the grace of blessing shone forth in them.

Blessed are you, O Bethlehem, land of Judah, which endured the savagery of King Herod in the destruction of the boys, and which at one time deserved to offer God a white-robed people of defenseless infancy.

Yet rightly do we celebrate the feast of those whom the world brought forth more blessedly for eternal life than the birth from their mothers’ wombs brought them forth: for they attained the dignity of perpetual life before they had received the use of this present life.

The precious death of other martyrs earned praise through confession; the death of these pleased God in its completion. For at the beginnings of their newly begun life, the very setting of the sun gave them the beginning of glory, even as it brought the present life to an end.

Herod’s impiety tore them, nursing infants, from their mothers’ breasts. They are rightly called the flowers of the martyrs: springing up amid the deep winter of unbelief, like the first gems bursting forth from the Church, they were cut down by a kind of persecution’s frost.

And therefore it is fitting to offer honors—not grief—to infants killed for Christ; to give the sacraments vows, not tears; because the one who was the cause of their punishment was also the cause of their crown, and the one who was the cause of hatred was also the cause of reward.

While Herod was preparing death for the little ones, Joseph was warned by an angel to transfer Christ our Lord into Egypt (Matthew 2:13), an Egypt filled with idols. After the persecution of the Jews and the consent of the profane people to kill Christ, Christ deigns to pass over to the Gentiles devoted to idols; and, leaving Judaea, he is brought to an ignorant world to be worshiped.

### 2. The one who inflicts injury suffers the greater injury. The thought of death restrains desire. Then no evil is well, and no good is ill

And because, dearly beloved brothers, we know from the divine Scriptures that good and righteous men have always suffered persecution from the wicked, if we consider carefully, we find that those who inflict it suffer greater punishments. For every person who persecutes another in the body is first understood to suffer persecution in his own heart.

Even if he has taken something from the substance of the one whom he persecutes, he inflicts a greater loss upon himself, because no one has unjust gain without just loss. Where there is gain, there is also loss: gain in the strongbox, loss in the conscience. He takes away clothing and loses faith; he acquires money and loses justice.

But people do these things because they do not wish to consider the last day. For if they wished to think continually about the day of their death, they would restrain their minds from every desire and wickedness. But what they now refuse to consider for their salvation, they must later endure without any remedy.

For their final day will come; the day of judgment will come, when they will be permitted neither to repent nor to redeem themselves from eternal death by good works. For the sinner is struck even by this punishment, so that when dying he forgets himself, since while living he forgot God.

The day of judgment will come, when the foundations of the mountains will be shaken and the earth will burn down to the underworld; when the burning heavens will be dissolved; when the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light; when the stars will fall from heaven; when sinners and the impious will be cast into the lake of fire, and the smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

The time will come, dearly beloved brothers, when no good person will suffer evil and no wicked person will enjoy good. I say, the final day will come, when the pious will be distinguished from the impious, the just from the unjust, those who praise God from those who blaspheme God.

It will also come when they will be distinguished [Note: [Col. 2153] So Augustine in *Sermon* 48, section 7. In manuscript B., *discernuntur* (“are distinguished”). M.], so that, as it has been said, no good person will suffer evil and no wicked person will enjoy good.

### 3. Even now it is better for the good than for the wicked. To suffer evil and to be evil

Why, then, is it not so now? Perhaps it is so even now. But what is hidden now will then be manifest.

Read the divine Scripture; enter with me, if you can, into the sanctuary of God. Perhaps there, if I am able, I shall teach you—or rather, learn with me from the one who teaches me—that even now it is not well with the wicked, and that it is better with the good than with the wicked, although the complete happiness of the good has not yet come, nor has the final punishment of the wicked yet arrived.

If you attend carefully to God’s Law, perhaps you will understand with me that it is not well with the wicked. For I ask and inquire of you: Why is it ill with you? You will answer: “Poverty oppresses me; difficulty weighs me down; perhaps it is pain in my limbs, or fear of an enemy.”

Is it ill with you because you suffer evils, while it is well with the one who is evil itself? There is a great difference between suffering evil and being evil. You are not what you suffer: you suffer evil, but you are not evil. He does not suffer this evil, and yet he is evil.

Do not be deceived. It cannot be that it is ill with you, who suffer evil, and well with him, who is evil. When he is evil, do you suppose that he does not suffer evil when he suffers himself? It is ill with you because you suffer another’s evil in your body, and it is well with him who suffers evil itself in his heart? It is ill with you, who perhaps have a bad estate, and well with him who has a bad soul?

Be good, you who possess good things.

### 4. Wealth is good: the means by which things may go well. Good by nature, but bad for the wicked

Wealth is good; gold is good; silver is good; households are good; possessions are good. All these things are good—but they are means by which you may do good, not things that make you good. Possess the good things that make you good.

“What are they?” you ask. “Do judgment and justice.” The things you possess are good; do judgment and justice. Be good yourself among your good things.

Be ashamed before your good things: be good while remaining among good things that will perish. Be ashamed before your good things: do not be evil among them, lest you perish with them.

Thus the Creator of all things and God their governor distributed gold and silver among human beings so that, in themselves and by their nature, they would be good; yet their abundance would not exalt the good, nor their scarcity crush them.

But an evil person is blinded when wealth is offered to him and tormented when it is taken away, because when riches are acquired they give false joy, while when they are lost they leave behind genuine sorrow.

### 5. True and false riches. Desire is always in need

Let us learn to love true riches—that is, chastity and justice, peace and mercy. These are called just riches because they are bestowed upon good and righteous people. They are called true riches because whoever possesses them will not be in need, since, according to the Apostle, “having food and clothing, with these he is content” (1 Timothy 6:8).

But it is unjust to consider these earthly riches riches, since they do not remove poverty. For the more someone loves them and the greater his possessions become, the more fiercely he will burn with the poverty of greed.

How, then, are they riches by which poverty increases? The greater they are for their lovers, the less they bring satisfaction; instead, they inflame the rich person with desire. You suppose that you would need less if you possessed less.

Thus someone rightly said:

> “The love of money grows as the money itself grows.”  
> (Juvenal, *Satire* 14, line 139.)

For as money increases, the madness of desire increases. Indeed, all greedy or covetous people appear to suffer from the disease of dropsy. For just as a dropsical person becomes thirstier the more he drinks, so the greedy or covetous person is not satisfied by acquiring more.

### 6. Conclusion

But we, brothers, remembering that we are foreigners and guests in this world, should reserve for ourselves on this journey of life only what is necessary for food and clothing, and, as much as we can, direct the rest toward eternal blessedness through almsgiving to the poor.

Then, when on the day of judgment the greedy and avaricious deserve to hear, because of the sterility of their good works, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41), may we be able to hear, because of our good works:

“Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me” (ibid., 34, 36).

May the Lord bring you to this blessing under his protection; to him belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXI

[Note: [Col. 2154] Formerly *On the Saints* 11; later, in the Appendix 73.]

### On the Feast of the Holy Innocents IV

[Note: [Col. 2154] By an uncertain author, who borrowed several sentences from the works of Pope Gregory. For section 2, see Gregory, *Moralia*, book 2, chapter 4, and book 25, chapter 9; for section 3, the same author, *Moralia*, book 2, chapter 4.]

And on the words of the Apocalypse, “I saw beneath God’s altar the souls of those who had been slain,” etc., chapter 6, verses 9–11; chapter 7, verses 9–17.

### 1. The Savior is praised in the worship of the martyrs. How fittingly the martyrs are beneath God’s altar. The Innocents intercede more than the others

Whenever, brothers, we celebrate the martyrdoms of the saints, we proclaim the praises of the Savior; and whenever we affirm their sufferings, we preach Christ’s glory. For we do not admire what they suffered, but the one for whom they suffered. Thus it is not punishment that is praised, but faith that is honored.

Let us therefore magnify the martyrs, especially those who, when Christ was born, confessed him at the very beginning—not by speaking but by dying—and preceded the others to the everlasting kingdoms.

Consider, moreover, what place among human beings is deserved by those who deserved a place beneath God’s altar. For Holy Scripture says:

“I saw beneath God’s altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony of Jesus that they held,” and so forth.

“Beneath God’s altar,” he says, “I saw the souls of those who had been slain.”

What can be said more reverently or more honorably than to rest beneath that altar at which sacrifice is celebrated to God, at which victims are offered, and at which the Lord is priest, as it is written:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4)?

The souls of the righteous rightly rest beneath the altar, because the Lord’s body is offered upon the altar. Nor is it without reason that the righteous ask for vengeance there upon their blood, where Christ’s blood is also poured out for sinners.

Accordingly, and as though by a kind of fellowship, burial was decreed for the martyrs in the place where the Lord’s death is celebrated daily, as he himself says:

“Whenever you do this, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26),

so that those who had died because of his death might rest beneath the mystery of his sacrament.

Not without reason, I say, is a tomb established there for those who were slain, in a kind of fellowship, where the members of the Lord’s slaughter are placed, so that those whom the cause of one passion had bound to Christ might also be joined by the sacredness of one place.

We read that many of the righteous are refreshed in Abraham’s bosom and that some rejoice in the delights of paradise. Yet no one deserved more than the martyrs to rest there where Christ is both victim and priest, so that they might receive both the atonement from the offering of the victim and the blessing and service of the priest.

Among all the martyrs, therefore, whom we proclaim to stand beneath God’s altar, those blessed nursing infants also—firstfruits of the martyrs for Christ, confessing not by speaking but by dying—earned crowns. For there is no doubt that those who preceded the others in martyrdom intercede more than the others in martyrdom.

### 2. How the saints ask for vengeance. Now one robe for the saints; later there will be two

“And they cried out,” John says, “with a loud voice: ‘Avenge our blood, O Lord.’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their brothers and fellow servants should be completed.”

A question arises here: why do the saints, who now remain with the Lord, seek vengeance upon their enemies, when the Lord says in the Gospel, “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute and slander you”?

But we must understand that those saints, already standing in the presence of their Creator, see his will. Therefore they receive from him what they know he wishes to do, and they drink from him what they thirst for from him.

They ask for vengeance upon their enemies in two ways, and this for the sake of charity: so that those predestined to eternal life may be converted from evil to good; and so that those whom God foreknows to be condemned may die and cease to sin, thereby suffering a lesser punishment in hell, where each person will endure the magnitude of his punishments according to the quality of his deeds.

They ask vengeance upon the reprobate because they desire the final day of judgment to come and await the resurrection of their bodies.

“And individual white robes were given to them.” By the white robes we should understand the reward of Baptism, the prize of martyrdom, the recompense of eternal things, and the joy of the heavenly homeland.

Before the resurrection, therefore, the saints have individual robes, because they already enjoy eternal blessedness in the soul alone. Later they will receive two, when, having received their bodies, they will be unchangeable in soul and incorruptible in body.

Isaiah speaks of this:

“In their land they shall possess double” (Isaiah 61:7).

### 3. How God speaks to the saints

“And they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed.”

This utterance is divine inspiration. Through it, the power of patience is infused into their minds as they desire the day of judgment, so that they may patiently endure all things while awaiting the number of those who are likewise to be killed for Christ and who will afterward reign with them.

Thus those who desire to receive their bodies rejoice in the number of the brothers who are to be gathered.

God Almighty speaks to the saints in this manner, just as any head of a household who has many sons and, when each returns from the field and asks him to give him food, replies:

“Your meal is indeed prepared, but wait for your brothers, so that when you have all been gathered together, you may all eat and feast together with rejoicing.”

For they too are to be killed, either by open martyrdom or by hidden martyrdom. Thus, after the gift has been given, those who ask for vengeance are told to rest and endure until the number of their fellow servants has been completed.

### 4. Let us follow the footsteps of the martyrs as far as we can

You see, therefore, that the vengeance of the martyrs is delayed on our account. For while we delay, their blood is abundant. But this happens because of our laziness, since we do not live religiously, as has been said, and do not act devoutly, as is fitting.

For if the justice of our good works went before the Lord, the number of the fellow servants who are awaited would already be complete. No one doubts that the martyrs will receive vengeance after judgment, since even before judgment they are honored with heavenly rewards.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, since on today’s feast we venerate the firstfruits of the martyrs, we ought diligently to think about the eternal feast of the martyrs that is in heaven. By following their footsteps as far as we can, let us also strive to become participants in that glorious feast, as the Apostle testifies:

“If we are companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation” (2 Corinthians 1:7).

Let us not grieve so much over their death as rejoice over their just reception of the palm.

Indeed, whenever each of them was driven from this life through torments, Rachel, mourning—that is, the Church—groaned and followed them with mourning and tears. But once expelled from this world, heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, immediately welcomed them into another life with ministers of joy and brought them into the joy of their Lord, where they are to be crowned forever.

### 5. The martyrs’ condition transformed

Therefore John says:

“They stood before the throne in the presence of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands.”

Those who once lay bound by punishments before the throne of earthly judges now stand crowned before God’s throne. They stand in the presence of the Lamb, in no way to be separated from contemplating his glory, from whose love they could not be separated even by punishments here below.

They shine in white robes and hold palms in their hands, because they possess rewards in their deeds. They receive, glorified through the resurrection, the bodies which for the Lord they endured to be burned by fire, torn apart by beasts, consumed by scourges, destroyed by being thrown from heights, scraped by claws, and dispersed through every kind of punishment.

“And they cried out,” he says, “with a loud voice, saying: ‘Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.’”

With a loud voice they sing salvation to God, recalling with great thanksgiving that they overcame the struggles of the tribulations that attacked them not by their own strength but with his help.

### 6. While their robes are thought to be stained, they are whitened. The service of God

Again, describing both their former struggles and their everlasting crowns, he says:

“These are the ones who came out of the great tribulation; they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

The martyrs washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb when they cleansed from every defilement, by the blood poured out for Christ, the limbs that in the eyes of the foolish seemed to be defiled by the squalor of punishments; moreover, they made those limbs worthy of the blessed light of immortality. This is what it means to have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.

“Therefore,” he says, “they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple.”

It is not a burdensome service, but a beloved and desirable one, to attend perpetually upon the praises of God (Psalm 84:11). “Day” and “night” signify not properly the alternation of time but, figuratively, perpetuity.

For night will not exist there, but one day—better than thousands in Christ’s courts. In that place Rachel does not weep for her children; rather, God wipes away every tear from their eyes and gives the voice of joy and eternal salvation in the tents of the righteous. God lives and reigns, and so forth.

## SERMON CCXXII

[Note: [Col. 2156] Formerly *On the Saints* 43.]

### On the Holy Apostles

[Note: [Col. 2156] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was uncertain to the Louvain editors, but Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. Its style is not Augustine’s; moreover, the fact that the sermon was composed for recitation equally on all the feasts of the Apostles indicates an author more recent than Augustine’s age.]

### 1. The Apostles are rams

If the solemnity of all the holy martyrs ought to be pleasing to us, dearly beloved brothers, how much more pleasing should be that of those who followed the present Prince of the martyrs? If that of lambs, how much more that of rams?

All those who later confessed Christ unto death became their children—not by the generation of the flesh, but by imitation of virtue. The peoples of the Gentiles offered these men, concerning whom the Psalm had earlier sung:

“Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 29:1).

When the Lord first urged them to confess his name, he promised them not only that he would crown their victory but also that he would assist them in the contest. Through them he was also admonishing those who would come after, since he was leaving what he said in writing for posterity.

Therefore he addressed them, exhorting them:

“When they bring you before rulers and authorities, do not consider beforehand what you should answer or what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

He forbade premeditation and commanded confession. For he preferred to remove human presumption and give divine grace, so that they might be timid in themselves but bold before the world.

Thus, in another Psalm, the voice of the martyrs says, as though in fear on account of human weakness:

“Rescue me from my enemies, my God, and deliver me from those who rise up against me” (Psalm 59:2).

And shortly afterward, trusting in divine assistance, it says:

“I will keep my strength directed toward you” (ibid., 10).

### 2. They surpass the other faithful

Desiring to show his Apostles as eminent above the other crowds of the faithful, as well as above the ancient righteous and the Prophets, the Lord said to them:

“Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear. For many Prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matthew 13:16–17).

Again, elsewhere:

“Now I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Again, he said in another place:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

Again, elsewhere, when Peter asked what benefit he and his companions would receive from having left everything and followed the Redeemer, he answered:

“Amen, I say to you: you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

### 3. They are the light of the world, the salt of the earth, and the foundations and gates of the Church

These are the light of the world (ibid., V, 14), because through them the Lord first delivered to this world the light of faith and true knowledge, and rescued the nations and peoples from the darkness of errors and sins. These are the salt of the earth, because through them earthborn human beings received the seasoning of the flavor of eternal life, so that they might restrain the wantonness of the flesh and be preserved unharmed from the worms of the corruption of sins and vices. These are the precious stones which John describes in his Apocalypse as placed in the foundation of the heavenly building (Apoc. XXI), because their preaching laid the foundations of the Church. Hence Paul also says: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets” (Eph. II, 19–20). These are the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven, because through them we first entered through the gate of faith and were numbered among the citizens of the saints.

### 4. Their virtues are proposed. The manner of loving friends and enemies

Therefore, dearest brothers, considering what these great leaders of the people have taught us, let us strive to fulfill by our deeds what they commanded. Let us learn from their example to despise the riches of the world, not to love the pleasure of the present age, to desire the heavenly kingdom, and to prefer nothing to Christ, but to obey his commands in all things; to love poverty in present possessions, to possess the riches of virtues, to desire the treasure of wisdom, to seek spiritual delights, to envy no one, but to love all people—to love friends in God and enemies for God’s sake—for this is true and the only love. For carnal and vicious love drags one into destruction and will be reckoned as hatred. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James IV, 4).

### 5. On the manner of loving the Creator and the creature

Therefore, since these leaders of ours were most perfect in the love of God and filled with love for their neighbors, they were able to overcome the assault of the world and subdue the bloodstained age, because they loved nothing in anything except the will of God. So let us also, brothers, love doing God’s will in all things, and let us love our Creator in himself, but the creature in its Maker. Thus we shall have love in the most rightly ordered form, because “God is love” (I John IV, 16), and whoever loves this love loves God.

And if we love in this way, God himself loves us; the holy Apostles, our judges, love us as well and intercede for us, so that at Christ’s universal judgment we may be crowned with them forever. May our judge and Lord himself deign to grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2158] Otherwise, On the Saints 44.]*

### On One Holy Martyr  
*[Note: [Col. 2158] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It remained doubtful to the Louvain scholars; Verlinus and Vindingus rejected it. It is attributed to Augustine in the Roman Breviary. But its style and manner of argument clearly resist that attribution. In an old German manuscript it occupies a place among the Sermons circulated under the name of Ivo of Chartres.]*

### 1. Two things to be considered in the martyr’s contest

Today the anniversary celebration of the triumphant blessed martyr N. returns for us; and just as the Church rejoices with his glorification, so she proposes his footsteps for herself to follow. “For if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him” (Rom. VIII, 17). In his glorious contest we must chiefly consider two things: namely, the hardened cruelty of the torturer and the martyr’s unconquered patience—the torturer’s cruelty, so that we may detest it; the martyr’s patience, so that we may imitate it.

Hear the Psalmist rebuking wickedness: “Do not be jealous of evildoers, for they will quickly wither like grass” (Ps. XXXVI, 1–2). But that patience must be shown toward evildoers, hear the Apostle urging: “You need patience, so that you may receive the promises” (Heb. X, 36). Thus the blessed martyr’s patience was crowned, while the torturer’s uncorrected wickedness was handed over to eternal torments.

### 2. How greatly the hope of eternal glory inflames the martyrs

Attending to this, the glorious athlete of Christ in his contest did not shrink from prison. In imitation of his Head, he endured insults, bore mockery, and did not fear scourges. All the punishments he suffered for Christ before death, he offered to him as sacrifices of himself.

For what he had drunk as the Apostle poured it forth, he held deeply within: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18); and, “This momentary and light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory in heaven” (II Cor. IV, 17).

Therefore, suspended above earthly things by love of this promise and ineffably affected by having tasted in advance the sweetness of heavenly delight, he said with the Psalmist: “What have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion forever” (Ps. LXXII, 25–26).

For he contemplated, as far as human weakness can fix the mind’s eye upon eternity through an enigma, how great are the joys of the heavenly city. Unable to recount them sufficiently, he cried out in wonder: “What have I in heaven?”—as though he were saying: “That beauty, that glory, that exalted state by which, when we have been removed from human disturbance and hidden in the refuge of his face, Jesus Christ our Lord will refashion the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory, surpasses my powers, exceeds the capacity of my eloquence, and transcends the grasp of my understanding.”

In contemplation of this perfect freedom, he avoided no danger and shuddered at no punishment. Even if he could die a thousand times, he did not think that by any means he could sufficiently earn it.

For the sick patiently allow physicians to cut them, burn them, and distress them with various bitter preparations, so that at last they may be restored to temporal health. How much more patiently, then, did the blessed man endure every bitterness of temporal torments, so that he might be crowned with mercy and compassion and at last have his desire satisfied with good things?

### 3. The martyrs’ progress

Thus he wished to be trampled in the winepress, so that, like a ripe grape, he might be crushed into wine and offer his beloved the wine of pomegranates, by which religious minds, made drunk, know how courageously to trample earthly things and to aspire toward eternal realities with eyes turned straight ahead.

He who, in his novitiate, despised worldly riches; who also restrained bodily allurements; who, in the advancement of his service, endured many injuries; reserving nothing for himself in the perfection of his sacrifice, offered himself as a burnt offering, drinking that precious cup which, seated at the great table of sacred reading, he had earlier seen set before him by his inviter. [Col. 2159]

However contemptible his death may appear in the sight of the reprobate, it is nevertheless precious in the eyes of him who is wondrous in his saints. For he himself first called his soldier; he himself justified him; he himself glorified him. He gave him the power to fight, and he also gave him the power to conquer.

### 4. Worldly and Christian warfare

This warfare is very different from worldly warfare, in which those are considered victorious who attain what they wickedly desire, who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things (Prov. II, 14).

But in the Christian contest the punishment is manifest and the victory hidden, according to what the Psalmist cries out in the person of the martyrs: “God, you have rejected us and will not go forth with our armies. Give us help in tribulation, for human salvation is vain. In God we shall perform valorous deeds” (Ps. LIX, 3, 13–14). It is as though they were saying: “Our victory and our glory are within, not outside; despised outwardly, beloved inwardly.”

Hence, when the Church is placed under pressure, she strengthens her weaker members, saying: “Do not consider me because I am dark” (Song I, 5). The Apostle explains this more openly to his hearers in other words: “Do not grow weary because of my tribulations for you” (I Thess. III, 13).

Hence the Truth warns his disciples beforehand, saying: “In the world you will have distress; but do not be afraid, little flock, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33). But how did he conquer the world? He “became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II, 8). And what about death? “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (ibid., 9).

Thus, just as Christ conquered, so let the Christian desire to conquer, so that where Christ is, the Christian too may deserve to be. Hear, O persecutor of Christian warfare, Christ himself praying for his soldiers: “Father, I will that where I am, my minister also may be” (John XVII, 24).

## SERMON CCXXIV  
*[Note: [Col. 2159] Otherwise, On the Saints 46.]*

### On the Martyrs, I  
*[Note: [Col. 2159] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain scholars and false according to Verlinus and Vindingus. It truly does not have Augustine’s style, but that of Caesarius. For no. 1, see Sermon 293 of Augustine and Caesarius near the end of Homily 13; for no. 4, see above, Sermon 69, nos. 1 and 2.]*

### 1. Martyrdom is twofold

The one who imitates the martyrs reaches fellowship with the martyrs. Martyrdom is not completed by the shedding of blood alone, nor does burning in flames alone grant the palm. The crown is reached not only by dying, but also by contempt for the flesh.

Without injury to the holy dead who perished in persecutions, it may be said that afflicting the flesh, overcoming lust, resisting greed, and triumphing over the world constitute a great part of martyrdom.
