If, therefore, dearest brothers, we wish to reach fellowship with the martyrs or priests, let us think about imitating the martyrs. They ought to recognize something of their virtues in us, so that they may deign to intercede for us before the Lord. If we cannot endure the tortures that the holy martyrs endured, let us at least, with their intercession, resist evil desires. And because daily sins are not lacking, daily remedies are not lacking either.

### 2. True joy is not here, where Christ promised nothing but sadness

Let no one believe that he possesses any happiness or any true joy in this age. Blessedness can be prepared here, but it cannot be possessed here. Two times succeed one another in their proper order: a time for weeping and a time for laughing.

Do not deceive yourselves, brothers: this world is not a time for laughter. I know, brothers, that every person desires to rejoice; but not everyone seeks joy where it ought to be sought.

True joy in this world neither was, nor is, nor can be. For the Lord himself warned his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “In the world you will have distress” (John XVI, 33); and again: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John XVI, 20).

Therefore in this life, with labor and sorrow, let us do what is good, with the Lord’s help, so that in the age to come we may gather the fruits of good things with joy and exultation, according to the saying: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5).

### 3. Here we are in exile

We, dearest brothers, were cast into this world through the sin of the first man from the blessed seat of paradise and, as it were, sent into exile. Thus in this age we have no homeland. So the Apostle also says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V, 6).

Let us not, therefore, seek joy in this world, because, as was said above, true joy can be acquired here but cannot be possessed here. Do not seek on the road what is being kept for you in your homeland.

And because, under Christ’s leadership, you must fight against the devil every day, do not seek in battle the reward that is being kept for you in the kingdom. Do not seek in the struggle what is being kept for you in the future, when victory has been perfected. Rather, attend to what the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12); and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21).

### 4. Labor is consoled because we are journeying toward our desired fellow citizens

And the greater the labor, the greater is the reward. Therefore we must act in such a way that we may happily deserve to return to our principal homeland, where our parents—the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles—long to receive or see us; where also our fellow citizens, the Angels, and that heavenly city, Jerusalem, together with the king of that city, Christ, await us with arms of love outstretched, so that, after the devil has been laid low, we may happily return to them full of good works.

For you know, brothers, that all merchants and all who engage in other occupations are meanwhile anxious on the road, so that they may be secure in their homeland; and they have true joy when they deserve to reach their homeland with great profit. So we too, dearest brothers, should prepare our spirit for joy when we shall deserve to reach Christ.

For the present, let us rejoice in hope, intending to have true joy afterward in reality. What is worse, many people, by a perverse ordering, think they rejoice in the pleasure, delights, and luxury of this age. But what they seem to sow in joy, they will necessarily receive with mourning and tears, because the one who spoke in the Gospel does not lie: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI, 25).

So too did that unhappy rich man fare, who was clothed in purple and fine linen. He had joy in the world, but deserved to find flames in hell. Lazarus, who lay at his gate, had sadness on the road, but received true joy in his homeland.

### 5. We must pray that we may be held more firmly by desire for our homeland

But we, dearest brothers, should, as far as we can, implore God’s mercy, so that he may deign to inspire us with such love for eternal life that we may wish to love our homeland more than the road and think more about the future than about the present age.

Thus let us always strive to conduct ourselves in the exile of this world in such a way that we may come to the future judgment with a free and secure conscience, adorned with good works; through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXV  
*[Note: [Col. 2160] Otherwise, On the Saints 47.]*

### On the Martyrs, II  
*[Note: [Col. 2160] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars leave it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus reject it. It contains a certain Augustinian thought, but nevertheless represents Caesarius throughout; for it is by no means foreign to Caesarius’s character and practice to draw upon the sayings of earlier teachers. It is read under Augustine’s name in the Roman Breviary. For no. 1, see Augustine, Sermon 317; for no. 2, Caesarius, Homily 18; for no. 3, his Homily 9, no. 7 in the edition published by Baluzius, and above, Sermon 67, no. 4; for no. 5, Caesarius, Homily 32, above, Sermon 110, nos. 5 and 9, and no. 7 in the edition published by Baluzius; for no. 6, see above, Sermon 210, no. 5.]*

### 1. They truly honor the martyrs who imitate them

Whenever, dearest brothers, we celebrate the solemnities of the holy martyrs, let us expect to obtain temporal benefits from the Lord through their intercession in such a way that, by imitating the martyrs themselves, we may deserve to receive eternal benefits.

For the solemnities of the holy martyrs are truly celebrated by those who follow the examples of those martyrs. The solemnities of the martyrs are exhortations to martyrdom, so that we may not be reluctant to imitate what we delight to celebrate.

But we wish to rejoice with the saints and do not wish to endure with them the tribulation of the world. Whoever is unwilling, insofar as he can, to imitate the holy martyrs will not be able to reach their blessedness.

Thus the Apostle Paul also preaches, saying: “If we are companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation” (II Cor. I, 7). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John XV, 18). The one who does not wish to endure hatred with the Head refuses to be in the body.

### 2. Neither imitation of the martyrs nor of Christ is impossible

But someone says: “Who can follow the footsteps of the blessed martyrs?” I answer him that, with the Lord’s help, we can imitate not only the martyrs but the Lord himself, if we wish.

Hear not me, but the Lord himself crying out to the human race: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). Hear also blessed Peter the Apostle admonishing us: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21). Likewise the Apostle Paul cries out: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. V, 1).

What shall we answer to this, dearest brothers, or what excuse shall we be able to offer? If someone were to say to you that you ought to imitate the wonders performed by the Lord, your excuse could be just, because not everyone has been given the ability to perform wonders and miracles. But to live justly and chastely and to preserve charity toward everyone is easy with God’s help.

The Lord himself does not say, “Learn from me to raise the dead or to walk over the waters with dry feet.” He does not say this. What does he say? “Because I am meek and humble of heart”; and again: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you”; and again: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V, 44–45).

Although there are many other things in which we ought to imitate both God and the blessed martyrs, these two are nevertheless the chief: that we be meek and humble of heart, and that we love our enemies with all our strength.

### 3. Especially in loving enemies. The two feet of charity

Regarding the love of enemies, dearest brothers, no one will ever be able to excuse himself truthfully. Someone may say to me, “I cannot fast; I cannot keep vigil.” Can he possibly say, “I cannot love”? He may say, “I cannot give all my possessions to the poor and serve God in a monastery.” Can he possibly say, “I cannot love”?

If you say that you cannot abstain from wine or meat, we believe you. But if you say that you cannot forgive those who sin against you, we absolutely do not believe you.

And since no excuse remains for us, because we are commanded to fulfill this almsgiving not from the storeroom but from the heart, let us love not only our friends but also our enemies, so that we may deserve to reach the eternal homeland by the road of life.

By these two commandments—loving God and loving our neighbor—as by two spiritual feet, we shall be able to run along the road of true charity and happily reach the eternal homeland. With these feet the Apostle Paul was running when he said: “I therefore run, not as uncertainly” (I Cor. IX, 26).

### 4. The one who loves enemies is a child of God. The one who does not love is a murderer and is in darkness

Whoever loves his enemies will have fulfilled in him what the Lord said: “Love your enemies, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 44–45). Choose now what pleases you. If you love your enemies, you will deserve to be not only a friend but also a child of God. But if you do not wish to love your enemies, you cannot have God as your merciful protector, because it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III, 15); and again: “Whoever does not love remains in death” (ibid., 14); and again: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (ibid. II, 11).

And elsewhere it is written: “The ways of the wicked, who retain injury after doing evil, are toward death.”  
*[Note: [Col. 2162] German manuscript: “they turn it into evil deeds; they are in death.”]*

Are these my words, dearest brothers? They are taken from the holy and canonical Scriptures. Therefore, so that we may be neither murderers nor remain in darkness, let us strive to love not only our friends but also our enemies, so that with a free conscience we may approach the gracious and merciful Lord according to the bond of his warning.

### 5. What is sinned against us is to be forgiven; what is sinned against God is to be punished. The remedy for sins is in us

He himself said: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you your debts.”

Pay close attention, dearest brothers, and know that it is one thing to sin against God and another to sin against a human being. When people sin against us, if we do not grant forgiveness to those who repent, we incur sin. But when someone has sinned against God, if we wish to forgive without great severity, we make ourselves participants in his sins. *[Note: [Col. 2162] Thus the German manuscript and Caesarius, Homily 32; but the printed editions of Am., Er., and Louvain have “discernment.”]*

Therefore the Lord said: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI, 14). I ask you, brothers: what could be said more sweetly or more kindly? He has placed in our power how we shall be judged on the day of judgment.

He did not say, “Go to the East and seek justice; sail as far as the West in order to receive forgiveness.” What does he say? “Forgive your enemy, and you will be forgiven; show mercy, and mercy will be shown to you; give, and it will be given to you.”

He seeks nothing from you outside yourself. God directs you to yourself and to your conscience; for he has placed in you what he requires. You do not need to seek medicines for your wounds far away. If you wish, you can find forgiveness for your sins within, in the storeroom of your heart.

### 6. The one who considers how much he owes God forgives easily

But you say: “My enemy forced me to endure such great evils that I cannot possibly love him.” You consider what a human being has done to you, but you do not consider what you have done to God.

If you carefully examine and investigate your conscience, you have committed many more sins against God, without any comparison, than a human being has committed against you. With what face, then, do you ask God to deign to forgive you much, when you are unwilling to forgive a little?

If you willingly receive these spiritual medicines which we have mentioned above, as you have been accustomed to do with God’s favor, and carefully guard them stored in the treasury of your holy conscience, then, with the Lord’s help, you will not fear the poisons of the devil. Through hatred or anger, wounds to your souls will either never be inflicted upon you, or, if they should perhaps creep in, they will quickly be restored to their former health through charity.

Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXVI  
*[Note: [Col. 2162] Otherwise, On the Saints 49.]*

### On the Martyrs, III  
*[Note: [Col. 2162] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful according to the Louvain scholars and spurious according to Verlinus and Vindingus. There is no need to linger over the matter here.]*

### 1. Christ suffers in the martyrs. Their suffering is a translation to heaven

We ought to be strengthened by the contest of all the martyrs and by the victory of those whose natal day of victorious glory is celebrated, so that our robust faith may be strengthened for the contest and encounter of suffering. We know with certainty that Christ suffers in all things and that they are immediately transferred with rejoicing of body to the kingdom of heaven; and while the nations shudder at death in sickness, these attain an eternal inheritance in death itself.

Through suffering they believe that there is a translation rather than an end. This is the hidden wisdom which, Lord, is not gathered in your elect by persuasion; rather, from your martyrs and from the divine fountain arise virtues by which “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). They triumph in Christ, gaining their sins through their own death, although whoever suffers in him does not die at all.

For death in confession is not death but an inheritance of life. Martyrdom is therefore forgiveness of crimes, the source of virtues, the occasion of righteousness, and imitation of the Lord’s Passion.

O most blessed martyrs! Renouncing the world, they preferred better last things to first things. Their consummation, finally, makes a righteous beginning.

### 2. The devil unwillingly grants crowns to the martyrs

By your divine will, almighty God, the most glorious martyrs of Christ deserved to be witnesses. Meditating upon victory, they confessed Christ amid scourges, prisons, workhouses, and solitude. For confession must always accompany the just.

O renowned souls of the blessed, and glorious victory of the martyrs! Among them most devoted women conquered both the world and their sex. Fighting with the devil, they proved stronger than the men who tortured them; indeed, they gave thanks to the executioner while he raged against them.

For almighty God seeks faith from everyone more than death. But the devil, who hates those who confess, unwillingly grants crowns. He makes martyrs of those whom he kills; and when he strives to conquer God’s servants, he himself is despised while he rages.

Your generosity, therefore, O God, has proposed martyrdoms to us for this purpose: to show that the adversary by whom Adam was overthrown would be steadfastly overthrown by Adam’s children. For you wished not only to rescue humanity from the devil’s power through faith, but also to kill its oppressor through virtue, so that we who rejoice, having died through Christ’s blood, once liberated, may more easily endure martyrdoms in Christ and afterward triumph as crowned.

Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXVII  
*[Note: [Col. 2163] Otherwise, among the Vignerian sermons 18, in the first part of the Supplement.]*

### On the Martyrs, IV  
*[Note: [Col. 2163] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was falsely attributed to Augustine in several Roman manuscripts. Baronius mentioned this same sermon, not yet printed, in his notes on the Martyrology for November 1.]*

### 1. The martyrs’ fields irrigated by streams of blood and tears

It is delightful to see the fields of the martyrs’ and confessors’ crops, where the eyes of Angels look upon them. The ear of the body of the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, flourished.

In the field of the world, the fields of the martyrs began to grow green, irrigated not by flowing waters but by streams of tears. What kinds and how great are these ears of the confessors? Large and small, old and young, virgins and nursing infants, nourished by God’s bloody stream.

But in God’s judgment there are neither greater nor lesser, because the angelic Powers protect them all alike. Now let us see old and young, virgins and nursing infants alike, and confessors.

Look upon Eleazar, a ninety-year-old man, a fighter surpassing the young. Consider those seven young brothers, alike in womb, equal in . . . [Note: [Col. 2163] Perhaps supply: “fortitude.”] grace, united in blood. What ears flowered together as these did? For “behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII, 1)!

Who watered these ears in the field of the tossing world? A suffering and sympathetic mother watered the ears of her testimony with the related spring of her prayers; and the Lord gave the increase, helping both mother and children.

Look also upon the childlike ears of the three martyrs in the furnace of flames. See also the other crops: the infants slain under Herod and the martyrs rejoicing without loss.

Thus the whole world is planted with purpled ears of martyrs. Blessed David walked among these purple fields, crowned with rosy victory. He rejoices, feeds his eyes, and sings with pious voices: “Those who sow in tears,” he says, “shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5).

See the very sowers and likewise the very reapers—but through the angelic Powers. [Col. 2164]

### 2. The martyrs’ relics, like scattered ears of grain

In how many places have these ears been scattered, since the relics of the martyrs are transferred everywhere for the healing of the sick, the illumination of the blind, the solemnity of peoples, and the mercy shown to the needy?

The folds are now loosened, but the perfected crown is not undone. The relics of the martyrs are like ears of grain planted throughout the whole world, [lacuna; surviving fragments: “incimi … the harvest comes … heavenly mo… … of resurrection”] ears gathered into their sheaves. [Note: [Col. 2164] Perhaps: “stored in treasuries until the heavenly harvest comes, that is, the moment of resurrection. Then the ears will be gathered,” etc.] And you will see precious armies, not scattered upon the earth but collected in the everlasting homeland.

In the new heaven and the new earth they will shine like lamps in the hands of the Angels.

Were they not loosened like ears of grain when the wicked judges burned them in a cruel fire? Where are they now? The Lord, who built Jerusalem, gathered them, and gathered the dispersed of Israel.

That field of the army of the dead bears witness. Were not the head and hands, the feet and bones, the joints and sinews, the flesh and skins like ears of grain? The prophet’s cry rang out with a single trumpet; and when the joints had been collected, the ears became one harvest, while heaven and earth marveled—far more clearly through the voices of Angels, as though with sickles of joy (Ezek. XXXVII).

They will be gathered from every place: from earth and sea, from field and deep, from forests and waters, from the jaws of beasts and the bellies of monsters, when sea and earth give back their dead. Bones will be gathered to bones, ears to folds, and a precious harvest will appear in Jerusalem, because these are the ones who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

### 3. They will be united through the resurrection

Regarding this field blessed David cried out: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.” They truly wept when they mourned those who had fallen and helped the weak with tears.

Good are the channels of blood, where the grains do not fall through endless torments. They are stoned and made firm; the grains do not fall, but are better nourished.

See the crop of the body of holy Stephen being stoned, while the grains of its fruit are not shaken at all. The stones struck him and resounded, while he raised his head toward the opened heavens. Where the bread of life shone, there Stephen’s reed blossomed in testimony.

Blood was poured out, but steadfastness was not dissolved; nor was his tongue confounded, because it was found strong upon the foundation of the Gospel.

See the ear of the prophet Isaiah being cut by a sharp saw; yet the ear of his body was not broken apart, because steadfastness held it together in faith.

For when the folds are properly bound by the hands of the reapers, the sheaves are not loosened but are thrown intact onto the cart. So too the bodies of the saints, with their folds intact, are lifted onto the cart of Christ’s flesh. Thus they meet Christ in the clouds and will reign with him in the splendors of the saints, with the same one who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXXVIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2164] It had been published without an author’s name by Holstenius in the book of Rules. But the name of Caesarius is given in an old manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes and in the German manuscript, and the style wholly assigns it to him. You will find the final part of this same sermon, through a scribal error, appended to a certain letter of Caesarius addressed to the Germans and entitled in the Library of the Fathers. For no. 3, see Caesarius, Homily 35.]*

### On the Feast of Virgins, from a Gospel reading

### 1. What is to be understood by the wise virgins and what by the foolish

In the reading that was recited to us, dearest brothers, we heard the Lord say: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matt. XXV, 1).

If we understand this according to the letter alone, it seems exceedingly harsh and severe. Far be it from our thoughts that so small a number should come from the household of any Christian, even a poor one, to eternal life.

And therefore, since it ought by no means to be understood according to the letter, and since the Lord himself said that it was a likeness, let us inquire why five are called foolish and five wise.

The five wise ones signify all the saints who will reign with Christ. Conversely, the five foolish ones seem to represent wicked Christians who boast only in the Christian name, without good works.

They are called five foolish and five wise because there are five senses in all human beings: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. And because through these senses, as through certain doors or windows, either life or death enters our soul, concerning which the Prophet also said, “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. IX, 21), the five virgins who use these senses well are called wise, while the five foolish ones receive death rather than life through these five senses.

## 2. The Five Senses as Five Virgins: Whether They Are Corrupted or Preserve Their Integrity

Let us inquire more carefully how these five senses, like five virgins, either preserve their virginity or become subject to corruption. If a man or woman looks upon a boy or girl, or upon someone else’s male or female slave, and gazes intently with desire, one virgin has been corrupted: for through the eyes—that is, through the windows of the body—the poison of death has entered the heart’s hidden chamber. But if someone, whether religious or lay, willingly listens to people speaking maliciously, to idle talk, or to those uttering wanton or shameful songs, and receives these things with pleasure through a receptive ear, another virgin has been corrupted. If someone is not content with moderate food but seeks sumptuous delicacies, and continually strives to speak evil, the third virgin has been corrupted through an unrighteous taste. If someone also diligently seeks foreign perfumes so that he may please people for the sake of luxury, the fourth virgin has been violated. But if someone wishes, with pleasure and lust, to touch other people’s sons or daughters with his hands, and seeks excessively soft clothing with a sensual mind, then the fifth virgin too has already been corrupted.

In this manner, these five senses, like five virgins, are corrupted in human beings. Conversely, when holy souls restrain these five senses—that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—from every unlawful thing, and release their tongue soberly and chastely for what is lawful and legitimate, they preserve the virginity of the five senses. Therefore the five virgins signify good people, while the other five prefigure those who are evil.

## 3. Virginity Alone Is of No Benefit

And indeed, dearest brothers, what benefit is it to a man or woman, cleric or monk, or consecrated woman, if virginity is preserved in the body while integrity is violated by evil desires of the heart? What benefit is there in displaying chastity in one member while having corruption in all the others? For those virgins who follow the Lamb, if you pay close attention, do not follow the Lamb because they have preserved bodily virginity alone. After saying, “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women,” the text immediately adds, “And no lie was found in their mouth; they are without blemish” (Rev. XIV, 4–5). Therefore, those who glory in bodily virginity alone should pay close attention: if they love falsehood, they will not be able to follow Christ with those holy virgins.

Let no virgin, then, presume upon bodily virginity alone; for if she is disobedient or uncontrolled in speech, let her know that she will be excluded from the chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom. Although a virgin occupies the hundredth rank and a married woman the thirtieth, a chaste and humble married woman is nevertheless better than a proud virgin. The former, serving her husband chastely and humbly, possesses the thirtieth rank; no rank at all will remain for the proud virgin. In both cases what the Psalmist says is fulfilled: “You will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. XVII, 28).

## 4. Every Faithful Person Is a Virgin and Bride of Christ

Because the blessed Apostle called the whole Catholic Church a virgin—not considering only those who are bodily virgins within it, but desiring the minds of all to remain incorrupt—he says: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2). Therefore, not only the souls of consecrated women, but also those of all men and women, if they wish to preserve chastity in the body and virginity in the five senses mentioned above, should have no doubt that they are brides of Christ. Christ must be understood as the Bridegroom not of bodies but of souls.

Therefore, dearest brothers, men and women alike, boys and girls alike, if they preserve virginity until marriage and, by using these five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—properly, do not corrupt their souls, they will happily deserve to enter, with the doors opened, the eternal bridal chamber of the Bridegroom on the day of judgment. But those who corrupt their bodies before marriage through adulterous intercourse and afterward do not cease violating their souls throughout their lives by living wickedly, listening wickedly, and speaking wickedly—unless fruits of repentance worthy of them come to their aid—will cry out in vain with the doors closed, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” and will deserve to hear, “Truly I tell you, I do not know where you are from” (Matt. XXV, 11–12).

If we, brothers—clerics and laypeople, monks and consecrated women, and those living in marriage—faithfully and carefully attend to these things, and, with the Lord’s help, preserve bodily chastity together with integrity of heart, we will not be cast out with the foolish into the outer darkness. Rather, admitted with the wise to the spiritual wedding feast, we will deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid., 21). May he himself deign to grant this.

# SERMON CCXXIX

[Note: [Col. 2166] Elsewhere, *On Time* 252.]

## On the Dedication of a Church or the Consecration of an Altar, I

[Note: [Col. 2166] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is read under Augustine’s name in the Roman Breviary on the feast of the Dedication. To the Louvain editors, however, it seemed doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. In this sermon and the one immediately following it, they attack certain passages which are in fact harmless and blameless if considered according to the meaning and intention of the true author, Caesarius, namely, whom they did not know. For no. 1, see Sermon 8, no. 4, and below, no. 3; for no. 2, Caesarius near the end of Homily 13; for no. 3, Caesarius at the end of Homily 10, and above, Sermon 29, no. 4, and 116, no. 1; for no. 5, Caesarius’s Homily 10 and the end of Homily 15; for no. 6, see above, Sermon 12, no. 4.]

### 1. What Takes Place in Hand-Made Temples Is Spiritually Accomplished in Us

Whenever, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of an altar or temple, if we attend faithfully and carefully and live holily and justly, whatever is done in hand-made temples is wholly fulfilled in us through spiritual edification. For the one who said, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (I Cor. III, 17), did not lie; and again, “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?” (ibid. VI, 15).

Since we have deserved to become God’s temple not through preceding merits but by God’s grace, let us labor as much as we can, with his help, so that our Lord may not find in his temple—that is, in ourselves—anything that offends the eyes of his majesty. Rather, let the dwelling of our heart be emptied of vices and filled with virtues; let it be closed to the devil and opened to Christ. Let us labor in such a way that we may be able to open for ourselves the door of the heavenly kingdom with the keys of good works. For just as evil works close the door of life to us, as though with bars and bolts, so without doubt good works open it.

### 2. Proper Preparation for the Sacred Communion; At Times One Should Withdraw from It

Therefore, dearest brothers, let each person examine his conscience. When someone recognizes that he has been wounded by some crime, let him first strive to cleanse his conscience through prayers, fasts, or almsgiving, and then presume to receive the Eucharist. For if, recognizing his guilt, he himself withdraws from the divine altar, he will soon reach the forgiveness of divine mercy: for just as “whoever exalts himself will be humbled,” so conversely “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 12). Whoever, as I have said, recognizes his guilt and humbly wishes to remove himself from the church’s altar for the correction of his life need have no fear of being completely excommunicated from that eternal and heavenly banquet.

### 3. The Guilt of Those Who Receive It Unworthily; The Punishment of This Guilt

I beg you, brothers, pay close attention. If no one presumes to approach the table of any powerful person wearing torn and filthy garments, how much more should each person who has been struck by the poison of envy or hatred, or filled with the fury of anger, withdraw with reverence and humility from the banquet of the eternal King—that is, from the Lord’s altar—because of what is written: “Go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you come, offer your gift” (ibid. V, 24). Again: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (ibid. XXII, 12).

For the text of the Gospel reading says that a certain man made a wedding feast for his son and entered to see those reclining at table. When he saw there a man who did not have a wedding garment, he said to him, “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” When the man fell silent, he said to the attendants: “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid. XXII, 1–13).

See what sentence the person will deserve to hear who presumes to approach the wedding banquet—that is, the Lord’s altar—while drunk, adulterous, or retaining hatred in his heart. May God turn this away from us, dearest brothers, and grant that we may either never wish to commit such evils, or, if they have been committed, strive without delay to heal them through repentance or reconciliation, and hasten to wash them away through more abundant almsgiving. Otherwise, if we come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge with the wounds of our sins, we may be separated by perpetual excommunication from that eternal Church and that heavenly Jerusalem.

### 4. Temporary and Eternal Excommunication; The Punishments of Eternity

Consider, I beg you, brothers: if someone today were expelled from the assembly of this Church for some crime, in what grief or distress would his soul be? If it is an unbearable grief to be cast out of this holy Church—where the one who is expelled can neither eat nor drink nor speak with other people [Note: [Col. 2167] In the printed editions and also in manuscript *cb*, the particle *non* (“not”), which is found in other manuscripts, is missing. Those excommunicated were in fact excluded from all conversation and meals with the people, as is clear from canon 49 of the Second Council of Arles and canons 38 and 39 of the Council of Auxerre.]—and if he still has hope that he may once again deserve to be recalled to the Church, imagine how great the grief will be if someone, because of his crimes, is separated from that Church which is in heaven, from the assembly of angels and the congregation of all the saints. Nor will this alone suffice as his punishment: besides being cast outside, he will be shut into the outer darkness to be consumed by eternal fire.

Whoever has deserved to be excommunicated from that heavenly Jerusalem will have not only this punishment, that he will be unable to eat or drink, but will also endure the flames of hell without end. There are weeping and gnashing of teeth; there are howling, lamentation, and repentance without any remedy; there is that worm which will not die and the fire which will not be extinguished (Isa. LXVI, 24); there death is sought but not found.

Why is death sought in hell and not found? Because those to whom life is offered in this world disdain to accept it; in hell they will seek death but will not be able to find it. There will be night without day, bitterness without sweetness, darkness without light. Neither riches, nor parents, nor spouses, nor children, nor neighbors will be able to help there. The sinner will find nothing except what he has sent ahead from this world by living chastely and justly and through the generosity of almsgiving.

### 5. The Reward of Those Who Commune Worthily; The Purity Required for This; The Wicked Show That They Do Not Love Their Souls

Considering these things, dearest brothers, let us, with God’s help, strive to approach this altar chaste, sober, and peaceful, so that we may not deserve to be excluded from that eternal altar. Whoever comes to this altar with a chaste body and a pure heart, with a clean and secure conscience, will reach that altar which is in heaven through a blessed migration.

Finally, dearest brothers, what I suggest is neither difficult nor laborious. I am saying what I frequently see you do. Whenever men are about to approach the altar, they wash their hands, and all the women present clean linen cloths on which to receive Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 2168] Thus the printed editions and manuscripts, except manuscript *f*, which here and below has “they put on linen cloths when they receive Christ’s body.”] [Note: [Col. 2168] Concerning this rite, see the Council of Auxerre of the year 578, canon 36: “A woman may not receive the Eucharist with her bare hand”; and canon 42: “Let each woman, when she communicates, receive her Lord’s cloth; but if she does not have one, let her not communicate until the following Sunday.”].

What I say is not difficult, brothers: just as men wash their hands with water, so let them wash their souls through almsgiving. Likewise, just as women present a clean linen cloth on which to receive Christ’s body, so let them present a chaste body and a pure heart, so that they may receive Christ’s sacraments with a good conscience.

I ask you, brothers: is there anyone who would wish to put his garment into a chest full of filth? And if a precious garment is not put into a chest full of filth, with what face is Christ’s Eucharist received into a soul polluted by the filth of sins?

Since we have begun to speak through these very true examples, I will also point out something you know well. I do not think there is anyone who, in his chest where he has stored precious garments, would consent to enclose either a live coal or any kind of spark. Why is this, brothers? Because he fears that the clothes he wears on a festival might be burned.

I ask you, brothers: if someone does not wish to enclose a spark of fire in his chest, why does he not fear kindling in his soul the flame of anger? But why this happens, we understand clearly and plainly. We do not put fire into the chest because we love our clothing; but we do not extinguish the flame of anger because we not only fail to love our soul, we even hate it, according to what is written: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

### 6. Exhortation

Therefore, dearest brothers, thinking more attentively about these examples, let us strive, as much as we can and with God’s help, to guard our inner chests—that is, our consciences—with the greatest care. When the day of judgment comes, in that eternal and blessed Church where the wicked will never be able to dwell and from which the good will never depart, may we not appear to be cast outside into the outer darkness in old rags. Rather, clothed in the stole of immortality, adorned with the jewels of chastity and justice, and dressed in the radiance of almsgiving, may we deserve to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34); and: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid., 21).

May the Lord bring you to that joy under his protection, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCXXX

[Note: [Col. 2168] Elsewhere, *On Time* 255.]

## On the Dedication of a Church or the Consecration of an Altar, II

[Note: [Col. 2168] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain editors, but seemed spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. It is by the same author as the preceding sermon. Compare the other Caesarian sermons. For no. 1, see the preceding Sermon 229, no. 1, and above, Sermon 112, no. 5; for no. 3, see the preceding sermon, no. 1, and above, Sermon 115, no. 3; for no. 5, see above, Sermons 19, no. 2, and 112, no. 3.]

### 1. This Feast Is Celebrated with Joy

As your Holiness knows very well, brothers, today we are celebrating the consecration of an altar; and rightly and deservedly we celebrate with joy the feast on which the stone in which the divine sacrifices are consecrated has been blessed or anointed.

But whenever we celebrate these feasts, dearest brothers, we must pay close attention and labor with all our strength so that what is visibly honored in temples or on altars may be invisibly fulfilled in us. For although the holy temples that we see built of wood and stone are sacred, the temples of our heart and body are nevertheless more precious before God, because the former are made by a bodily human being, while the latter are made by the artisan of the world.

Temples of wood and stone are assembled by human skill; temples of bodies are fashioned by the hand of the heavenly Artisan, as it is written: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII, 73); and again: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. I, 5).

For just as temples are burned, so conversely the person who is filled with the light of charity, if negligent, quickly grows cold in charity and burns with desire. Therefore let neither the one who is evil despair, since he can quickly rise again, nor the one who is good remain negligent or presume upon any part of his virtue, lest his joy be turned into mourning.

### 2. There Is No True Joy for One Whose Heart Is Not Pure and Whose Body Is Not Chaste; Such a Person Is the Devil’s Dwelling

Therefore, beloved brothers, let us strive, with God’s help, to preserve bodily chastity and purity of heart as much as we can. Through these things the fire of charity and compunction is continually kindled and nourished in us.

Whoever preserves neither chastity in the body nor purity in the mind appears to have joy in the body whenever the holy solemnities arrive, but in his heart he celebrates nothing except mourning. For what joy can someone have in whose soul, occupied by many vices, the devil is shown to dwell rather than Christ? What joy can a soul have that is inflamed by the fury of anger, darkened by the blackness of desire, filled with the most bitter gall of pride, struck by the poison of envy, and polluted by the filth of lust?

### 3. God Desires to Dwell in Us

Even if some sins, as commonly happens, creep upon us, let us, dearest brothers, labor as much as we can with God’s help to cleanse what is filthy through fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving; to rebuild what has fallen; and to restore the temple of the living God. Thus, when the Lord comes, he may find in us nothing that offends the eyes of his majesty. For it is written of him: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone rises and opens to me, I will enter and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20). Again: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

How blessed is the soul in which the Father and the Son, when they come, deign not only to dwell or remain but also to dine! We understand clearly what he said, “I will dine with him, and he with me,” because the Apostle Paul shows this when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (I Cor. III, 17). And through the prophet the Lord says: “I will dwell in them,” he says, “and walk among them” (Lev. XXVI, 12).

Since, as you yourselves have seen, brothers, God desires to dwell and walk in us, let us, with his help, strive always to occupy our hearts with good thoughts and continually keep our bodies clean and chaste from every defilement of lust, so that God may delight to dwell in us.

### 4. The Two Altars in Solomon’s Temple; God Requires a Twofold Sacrifice from Us

In the temple built by Solomon we read that two altars had been established, one outside and the other inside. On the one that was outside, the sacrifice of animals was celebrated; on the altar that was inside, incense of fragrant offerings was presented.

Let us therefore see, brothers, whether perhaps two altars have been established in us, namely, of our body and our heart. Indeed, God asks a twofold sacrifice from us: one, that we should be chaste in body; the other, that we should be pure in heart.

Therefore, on the outer altar—that is, in our body—let good works be offered; in the heart, let holy thought emit a fragrant odor. Let us continually perform on the altar of our heart what is pleasing to God.

We celebrate the proper order of the altar’s consecration with joy when we offer the altars of our heart and body clean and pure in the presence of the divine majesty. For I do not know with what face or conscience someone hopes to rejoice at the consecration of an altar when he does not strive to preserve purity on the altar of his heart.

Let us, dearest brothers, strive to act in such a way that we may always deserve to celebrate a twofold feast: and just as we rejoice in the consecration of a temple or altar, so may we deserve to have spiritual joy invisibly in bodily chastity and purity of soul.

### 5. The Two Fires: Charity and Desire

Consider this also, brothers: on that altar which we read was dedicated by Solomon, a daily fire continually burned. May divine mercy complete the same in us! Therefore God must be appeased not only by prayers but also by good works, so that he may always kindle on the altar of our heart his own fire, the one of which he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49).

For there are two fires: that of desire and that of charity. One comes from God, the other from the devil; one devours all evil, the other consumes every good thing.

Let each person examine his conscience. If he sees the fire of desire burning within him, let him hasten, with God’s help, to extinguish it, because nothing good can remain in the person whom the fire of desire has inflamed. Conversely, no evil will remain in the one in whom the fire of charity has burned.

The flame of desire in the hearts of sinners, like an altar of sacrilege, devouring all good things, sends forth a fragrant odor to the devil. But in a holy soul, like a most holy altar, the flame of charity consumes whatever evils come upon it and offers a fragrant odor to God.

### 6. Each Person’s Heart Is Either God’s Altar or the Devil’s; The Priest as Envoy of the Poor

Since each person’s heart is an altar either of God or of the adversary, as I have already said, let each person examine his conscience. If he is consumed by the fire of desire, let him be soothed by the refreshment of almsgiving, because it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. III, 33).

Whoever is consumed by desire should withdraw from himself evil works and strive to practice what is good. Whoever is kindled by the flame of charity should continually increase through good works and nourish within himself the fire that Christ deigns to kindle in him [Note: [Col. 2170] The printed editions close the sermon here. What follows we have copied from the manuscript of Vendôme, as not incompatible with Caesarius.].

Just as the person in whom the fire of desire burns, if he ceases from evil action, quickly blazes up with the fire of charity, so this signifies that if we refresh God in this world through our good works, he will refresh us in the future age with his gifts, according to what is written in the Gospel: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 34); and, “As long as you did these things,” etc.

Therefore, so that we may deserve to be freed from hearing that dreadful word, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (ibid., 41), and may be able to hear that desirable word, “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom,” let us preserve peace of heart and chastity of body in ourselves, and distribute more generous alms to the poor. For the one who said, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (ibid. V, 7), does not lie.

Again and again, dearest brothers, we commend to you the misery of travelers and the poor [Note: [Col. 2170] Perhaps *commendamus* (“we commend”) should be supplied.], hoping [Col. 2171] that this petition may prevail with you on their behalf and that our admonition or preaching may not be in vain.

At Christ’s command we act as the poor’s ambassador before you. If your Charity willingly hears me pleading for the poor, Christ will undoubtedly hear me praying for you. God has placed me among you as a mediator between you and the poor. It seems to me that just as my plea concerning the poverty of travelers is heard by you, so your prayer will be heard by Christ, just as he himself promised, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI, 37–38).

May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCXXXI

[Note: [Col. 2171] Elsewhere, *On Time* 253.]

## On the Dedication of a Church or the Consecration of an Altar, III; And on the Words of 3 Kings, Chapter 10: “And the Queen of Sheba, Having Heard of Solomon’s Fame,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 2171] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus reject it as spurious. It was printed in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* among sermons attributed to Eusebius, but there it is found somewhat longer.]

### 1. Various Figures of the Church

Those rightly celebrate the Church’s feasts who recognize themselves as children of the Church. For she is the mother of all believers: those born for death she regenerates for salvation.

She was indeed called after the Synagogue, but she was promised before the Synagogue. For she was already prefigured in the first human being. Just as Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side, so the Church, redeemed from Christ’s body and wound, grew. Saved within the ark while the flood overflowed, she foreshadowed the benefit of the cross and the mystery of Baptism.

Barren Sarah, despairing in old age yet made fruitful by a single pledge, proclaimed her beforehand: for the Church brought forth one people, that is, a people most beloved by God, when the world was already growing old.

She is that queen of whom it is said to the Lord: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 10)—that is, surrounded by the precious beauty of diverse virtues.

### 2. The Queen of Sheba Represents Her in Many Ways; The Teachings of the Church Handed Down by Christ

She is that queen who came from the regions of Ethiopia to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Yet she came not so much from one region as from all the parts of the world, destined to bring forth kings, just as the Evangelist also recalls: “The queen of the south will come from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.”

The Church came to her Redeemer and Teacher to receive instruction in truth from the folly of error. Concerning her, as we have heard, the history of Kings wrote more fully, saying:

“And the queen entered Jerusalem with a very great retinue and with riches, with camels carrying spices, exceedingly much gold, and precious gems. She came to Solomon and spoke to him all that she had in her heart.”

Therefore, in the figure of this queen, the Church comes from the Gentiles and from the ends of the earth, putting an end to earthly desires and vices, in order to hear Solomon’s wisdom—that is, the wisdom of our true and peaceful Lord Jesus Christ, “who made both one, destroying hostilities between God and man in his flesh” (Eph. II, 14).

After the old and profane superstitions, she came to hear and learn about the enlightenment of faith and future judgment, the immortality of the soul, the hope of resurrection, and glory.

She therefore entered Jerusalem with a great retinue—that is, no longer with only one Jewish people, as previously the Synagogue had only the Hebrews, but with the peoples and nations of the whole world.

She came presenting gifts worthy of Christ: gold and precious gems; and these were carried by camels, that is, by those coming from the Gentile people who had previously been twisted by the foulness of vices, bent beneath the burden of evil deeds, and disfigured by the crookedness of sins.

With these gifts, as it were, this queen enters before Christ the peaceful King, presenting the gold of faith, the precious incense of purity, and the splendors of gems—that is, the marks of character and ornaments of virtues. “And she spoke to him all that she had in her heart”: that is, she opened her heart to him and revealed the hidden things of her conscience in confession and repentance for her former offenses.

### 3. The Church Marvels at Christ’s Wisdom: In the Work of Creation, in the House He Built through the Incarnation, and in the Food of His Table—and What Christ’s Food Is

Let us see what this queen does. “When the queen of Sheba saw,” it says, “all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house he had built, and the food of his table, and the holocausts that he offered in the house of the Lord, she had no longer any spirit.”

What reason was there for such a powerful queen to marvel so greatly at a house, expenses, and royal foods? Therefore, in this passage we must seek out greater meanings.

The Church gathered from the Gentiles saw Christ’s wisdom. That is, after the carnal institutions of the Gentiles and the human and animal teaching of the philosophers, she received an understanding of salvation and life, beheld the wonders of spiritual goods, and recognized the true Maker of heaven and earth and the almighty Creator of the human race. Of his wisdom it is said: “You have established all things by measure and weight and number” (Wis. XI, 21).

She also saw the house he had built—that is, the incarnation of the assumed man, in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.”

She also saw the foods of Solomon’s table—that is, those of which the Lord said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John IV, 34). For Christ’s food is our salvation; he is refreshed by heavenly banquets, by our progress. We are his food when, having been acquired for the Church, we pass into his members and body.

Or, Christ’s food is the heavenly sacraments of his altar, concerning which it is said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 24–25).

She also saw his holocausts, undoubtedly the mysteries of prayers and supplications, and she was astonished when she saw the immeasurable riches of her Lord.

### 4. When the Church Sees the Lord’s Glory, She Will Confess That It Is Greater Than What Was Proclaimed

“And she said to the king: ‘The word is true that I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I myself came and saw with my own eyes and proved that they had not even told me half. Your wisdom and works are greater than the report I heard.’”

When this queen—that is, the Church, or any holy soul—has reached the eternal Jerusalem, the vision of peace, and entered the blessed rest and glory of the heavenly promises, she will see far more and far greater things than were announced to her on this earth through the sacred Scriptures, through the Prophets and Apostles.

For now she sees as in a mirror and in a riddle; then she will see with her own eyes—that is, face to face. Then the blessed and illustrious soul, placed amid the astonishing riches of her Rewarder, will be able to use these words of the queen before God:

“True is the word that I heard in my land concerning your words. Your works are greater than the report I heard.”

And indeed, what God has prepared for those who love him cannot be grasped by faith, reached by hope, or contained by charity; it surpasses desires and prayers. It can be acquired but not valued. The soul will have the fruit of receiving it, but will not experience satiety’s disgust.

May he bring you to these blessings, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 2173]

# Appendix, Class IV: Sermons on Various Subjects (C, G)*

# SERMON CCXXXII

[Note: [Col. 2173] Elsewhere, *On Time* 189.]

## On the Holy Trinity

[Note: [Col. 2173] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, but seemed spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. In the Remigian manuscript it bears Jerome’s name, but it differs very greatly from his style and differs little, or perhaps not at all, from the character of Vigilius of Tapso, whose authorship we have observed for Sermon 113 of this Appendix; in the aforesaid manuscript and in the earlier editions, that sermon is joined immediately to this one.]

### 1. Dangerous Discussion Concerning the Trinity; We Know This about God: That We Do Not Know Him

I hear, brothers, that some people are debating among themselves how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are both three and one. You see from the question how dangerous the discussion is. Clay and a pot made from clay dispute about the Creator and cannot attain an understanding of their own nature; yet they inquisitively seek to know about the mystery of the Trinity what the angels in heaven cannot know.

For what do the angels in heaven say? “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII, 10). Likewise, in Isaiah it is said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with his garments white?” (Isa. LXIII, 1). See what they say: they proclaim his beauty and remain silent about his nature.

Therefore let us too simply say: Do you wish to know God’s nature? Do you wish to know what God is? Know this: that you do not know. Do not be distressed because you do not know; for the angels did not know, and neither did all creatures in the same way.

### 2. By This Knowledge We Surpass Philosophers and Gentiles

But someone says: “How then do I believe what I do not know? How am I a Christian when I do not know how I am a Christian?”

I will speak simply, before bringing forward anything from the Scriptures. O Christian, who seem to yourself to know nothing: if you know this very thing, that you do not know, do you not seem to know more than the others?

A Gentile sees a stone and thinks it is God. Philosophers see the heavens and think they are God. Others see the sun and think it is God. But see how much knowledge you have beyond these people, when you say: “A stone cannot be God; the sun cannot be God, because it moves at another’s command.”

Do you see that, in saying that you know nothing, you know more? The Gentiles, in claiming that they know, do not know, because the things they have learned are false.

At the same time, consider that you are called faithful, not rational. Indeed, after receiving Baptism, this is what we say: “He has become faithful,” or “I have become faithful.”

I believe what I do not know; and for that very reason I know, because I know that I do not know what I do not know.

### 3. The Reckless Assertor Will Be Condemned

He will be condemned, not because he is ignorant of the nature of God, but because he is a reckless assertor. But someone says: “This is not explaining, but evading an explanation. We knew that we knew what we did not know; you were telling us that we knew what we are ignorant of.” Is it not better for me piously to confess ignorance than recklessly to claim knowledge for myself? At the judgment I will not be condemned because I say, “I did not know the nature of my Creator.” But if I say something recklessly, recklessness incurs punishment, whereas ignorance earns pardon.

Let us say something from the Scriptures, following not reasoning but the authority of the Lord our Savior. Christ, about to ascend into heaven, speaks to the Apostles, to whom he preaches as teacher and Lord. No one can speak about his own nature as he can who himself is God. For us, however, it is enough to know about the Trinity what the Lord deigned to explain. What, then, does he say to the Apostles?

“Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the [Col. 2174] Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). I hear three names, yet one name is spoken. For he did not say, “In the names,” but “In the name.” He mentions three names, and yet how does he say “one” in the words, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? The name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one. But “Trinity” is the name spoken in the name of God the Father, in the name of God the Son, and in the name of God the Holy Spirit. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one name of the divinity.

### 4. What Knowledge of the Trinity Is Sufficient for a Christian

The Sabellian is a Jew. The persons are distinguished by their properties, not by their nature.

But you ask me how three are called by one name. I do not know, and I openly profess that I do not know what Christ did not wish to reveal. I know this alone: that I am a Christian because I confess one God in the Trinity.

But if I say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one person, I will be called a Sabellian, and I begin to be not a Christian but a Jew. For the Jew too says that there is one God; and because he does not acknowledge the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he does not hold the mystery of the Trinity. Therefore, if we speak of one God in such a way that we exclude the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit from the mystery of the Trinity, we become Jews.

I freely say—not from myself, but according to the Savior’s teaching—that the scandal is the thought arising in the hearer’s mind: how three are one, and how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not divided in divinity but distinguished in the quality of their persons.

Whenever I use the word “persons,” I ask you not to suppose that I mean human persons. I do not speak of persons in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as though they were human persons. I speak of the person of the Father because he is Father; of the Son because he is Son; and of the Holy Spirit because he is the Holy Spirit. The Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son. They are divided by their properties but united in nature.

Observe that the Apostle Philip once endured this very difficulty when he said to the Lord himself: “Lord, show us the Father.” The Lord answered him: “Philip, have I been with you for so long a time, and you do not know the Father? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:8–9).

What does this mean? Is he himself the Father, and himself the Son? It is impious to say this. Rather, he says: “In seeing the Son, understand the Father.” For one cannot be called “son” unless he has a father. When “father” is said, it is not said unless he has a son.

### 5. What a Christian’s Rivalry Ought to Be

Many things could be said, but let it be enough for the faithful to have heard a little about the mystery of the Trinity.

I ask you: let our contest with one another be about how we may overcome the adversary; how we may fast; how we may mourn our sins; how we may make satisfaction for so great a crime; how we may persist in almsgiving; how our thoughts may not lead us captive into lust; how we may maintain patience against every injury; and how we may not resist a brother who injures us, but conquer him through the humility that we learned from Christ, who, when he suffered, did not threaten (1 Peter 2:23).

Whenever a thought arises and proposes the question, “What is God, and what is the rationale of the Trinity?” it is enough for us to believe that God is, and not recklessly to seek an explanation of the Trinity. Rather, we must always fear the Lord and pray to him, and in this matter offer our knowledge to him alone, so that day and night we may sing praises to him, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON 233

### On Catholic Faith I

*[Note: Formerly, On Time 129. It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In the Leuven edition it is regarded as doubtful, whereas Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. Except for the fourteen later anathemas, which were added here from the Confession of the Catholic Faith of Damasus addressed to Paulinus of Antioch, it is nothing other than the little book of Faith that is entitled in chapter 40 of the canonical code of the Roman Church, “Augustine’s Little Book on the Catholic Faith against All Heresies.” It is also found inserted in the Acts of the First Council of Toledo, held in 400, with some variation in the anathemas. The Master of the Sentences cites it under Augustine’s name in Book 3, distinction 21, perhaps from the Roman canonical code itself. For we have nowhere seen this little book among Augustine’s Sermons and short works in the manuscripts. Certainly these expressions seem less characteristic of Augustine: in section 1, “that this is one Trinity of the divine name”; in the same section, “not an imaginary body, or composed only of form”; also, “and to have experienced all the exercises of the body,” or, as the Roman codex has it, “all the bodily sufferings”; and in section 2, “that this world and all its instruments were not made.” Finally, the word Paraclete is used throughout for “the Holy Spirit.” Estius, in Book 3, distinction 21, paragraph 3, suspects that it was published by a writer inclined toward the Nestorians, whose error certain statements may accommodate, especially the fifth anathema. On section 3, see the Confession of Faith sent by Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch.]*

[Col. 2175]

### 1

We believe in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, maker of visible and invisible things, through whom all things were created in heaven and on earth.

We believe that this one God is one Trinity of the divine name: that the Father is not the Son, but has a Son who is not the Father; that the Son is not the Father, but is the born Son of God [Note: [Col. 2175] In the Roman canonical codex: “but the Son is from his nature.”]; and that the Holy Paraclete is neither the Father nor the Son himself, but proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 2175] This canonical codex does not have “and the Son,” nor, shortly afterward, “and the Son.”].

Therefore the Father is unbegotten; the Son is begotten; the Paraclete is not begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Father is he whose voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17:5). This Son is he who says: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28). The Paraclete is the one of whom the Son says: “Unless I go away to the Father, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7).

This is the Trinity, distinguished in persons [Note: [Col. 2175] Something is missing here and must be supplied from the Roman canonical codex, which adds: “one substance, power, authority, and indivisible majesty”], undifferentiated. Apart from it there is no divine nature—whether of an angel, spirit, or any power—that is believed to be God.

Therefore we believe this Son of God to be God, born from the Father, and to be the beginning, and that the Father sanctified him in the womb of the virgin Mary [Note: [Col. 2175] The Roman canonical codex reads: “born from the Father before every beginning whatsoever, and sanctified the womb of the virgin Mary”], and that from her a true human being was generated without the seed of a man. That is, our Lord Jesus Christ assumed not an imaginary body, nor one composed merely of form, but a solid body.

He hungered, thirsted, suffered, wept, and experienced all the functions of the body [Note: [Col. 2175] In the same codex: “experienced all the bodily sufferings”]. Finally, he was crucified, died, and was buried; on the third day he rose again; afterward he lived among the disciples, to whom he sent the Holy Paraclete when he had ascended into heaven. This one is now called the Son of Man.

We believe in the true resurrection of human flesh. The human soul is not a divine substance or a part of God, but a creature brought low by the divine will [Note: [Col. 2175] It should be read as in the Roman canonical codex: “made by the divine will,” not “fallen from heaven.”].

### 2

If anyone should say and believe that this world and all its instruments were not made by God Almighty, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that God the Father is the same as the Son or the Paraclete, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that God the Son is the same as the Father or the Paraclete, [Col. 2176] let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the Spirit Paraclete is the Father or the Son, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that God the Son suffered, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the man Jesus Christ was a man incapable of suffering, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the God of the ancient Law is one and the God of the Gospels another, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the world was made by another God than the one of whom it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), who alone is the true God, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that human bodies will not rise after death, let him be anathema.

If anyone should say and believe that the human soul is a portion of God or is God’s substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone should regard as authoritative or venerate any Scriptures besides those received by the Catholic Church, let him be anathema.

### 3

If anyone does not say that the Father has always been Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father, that is, from the Father’s substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Word of God is the Son of God, that God is his Father, that he can do all things, knows all things, and is equal to the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that, while the Son of God was established in the flesh and was on earth, he was not in heaven with the Father, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that in the passion of the cross it was God the Son who felt pain, and not the flesh with the soul that he had assumed and the form of a servant that he had taken, as Scripture says (Philippians 2:7), let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that, in the flesh he assumed, he sits at the right hand of the Father, and in that flesh will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, just as the Son is from the divine substance and is true God, let him be anathema.

If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a created work, or was made through the Son, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father made all things through the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, visible and invisible things—let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, equal majesty, power, one glory, dominion, one kingdom, and one will, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that there are three true persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—equal, always living, containing all visible and invisible things, all-powerful, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, and saving all things that are to be saved, let him be anathema.

If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be adored by every creature just as the Son and the Father are, let him be anathema.

If anyone thinks rightly about the Father and the Son but does not hold a right belief about the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic. For all heretics who think wrongly about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the unbelief of the Jews and the Gentiles.

But if anyone permits God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit to be called gods, rather than one God, on account of the one divinity and power that we believe and know to belong to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

If anyone removes either the Son or the Holy Spirit and thinks that only the Father should be called or believed to be God, or that there is one God in that sense, let him be anathema.

---

## SERMON 234

### On Catholic Faith II

*[Note: [Col. 2176] It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Leuven scholars regarded it as doubtful, whereas Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. It comprises two excerpts: one from a short work of Faustus of Riez entitled “A Response on the Reason of Faith to Certain Objections”; the other from Book 6 of Vigilius of Tapsus, On the Trinity. Faustus’s short work, printed at Paris in 1586 by the Nivelle press among the writings of several ancient theologians of Gaul, begins as follows: “What should be answered to those who, when they read in the Gospel, ‘The Father is greater than I,’ understand this to mean that the Son is inferior in divinity and thus blaspheme? Answer: According to the authority of all the Scriptures, there are two births in Christ, one from the Father, knowing no beginning; for we read”—and then immediately follow the words found here—“In the beginning was,” and so on. On section 1, see Eusebius, Homily 1 on the Creed; on sections 6 and 7, see Vigilius of Tapsus, Book 6, On the Trinity; on section 7, see the same author and Faustus in his letter to Gregory.]*

### 1. Christ’s Two Births; Two Substances

“In the beginning [Col. 2177] was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). He who was in the beginning contains every beginning within himself.

But from his mother he received a beginning, as we read through Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23)—that is, majesty concealed in human frailty.

As we read in John the Evangelist: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—among us, that is, in the frailty of our body.

Likewise, concerning the birth from the virgin Mary: “And the gate was shut, and it was not opened” (Ezekiel 44:1). As though asked why it had not been opened, he added: “Because the Lord passed through it” (Ezekiel 44:2). The closed gate means the seal of modesty, the integrity of undefiled flesh. For she was not violated by childbirth who was rather sanctified by conception.

Likewise, concerning Christ’s twofold substance, that of God and man: “And they shall be,” he says, “two in one flesh” (Genesis 2:24)—that is, one Christ, God and man.

The Apostle commanded that this be understood of Christ and the Church, that is, of Christ’s body, when he says: “And they shall be two in one flesh. I speak, however, of Christ and of the Church” (Ephesians 5:32).

He openly explained this to the Romans: “Our fathers, from whom Christ is according to the flesh” (Romans 9:5). He asserted the flesh of a human being; then he consequently asserts the property of God, saying: “Who is God over all, blessed forever.”

The Son’s eminence is declared to be so perfect that nothing greater can be said of the Father. For if he had a beginning, he would not be over all but among all, which, according to the condition of created things, are contained within a beginning.

But Christ, who is equal to the Father, is confined by no law of time or age.

The Apostle also clearly proclaims Christ’s two births and two substances in the Letter to the Philippians, saying: “Although he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). The volumes of the New and Old Testaments are full of these principles.

Likewise the outstanding prophet Job proclaims: “In my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:26). He prophesied this concerning the time when Christ’s divinity would be clothed in the appearance of our flesh.

### 2. Christ Speaks and Acts Some Things as Man, Others as God

Since, as we said earlier, “the Word became flesh,” and it is established that man and God are two in one flesh, at one time he speaks to the Father as man, at another as God; at one time visible through his mother, at another invisible through the Father.

Let the words of the man be heard. He himself says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

Let this poor Son of Man display his riches in the glory of divinity: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). When he says “all things,” he leaves nothing here that he possesses less than the Father. “All things” means the power, substance, and majesty of the one divinity.

Who would not tremble to call him lesser, when he equates himself with the Father in every respect and gives a completely truthful testimony, as the Evangelist declares concerning him: “For this reason the Jews sought to kill him, because he called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18); and in Philippians: “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6)—that is, the equality of divinity that the rebellious angel wished to seize by robbery, Christ possessed by nature?

### 3. As Man, Christ Is Less Than the Father; as God, Equal to the Father

Therefore, when you believe him as he says that he is lesser in the substance of man, believe him also when he professes himself equal in the substance of divinity.

Let the Son of Man speak: “The Father,” he says, “is greater than I” (John 14:28). Let the Son of God speak: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

[Col. 2178]

As man he hungers; as God he satisfies five thousand hungry people with five loaves through the service of his creation.

As man he hangs on the cross; as God he brings the thief from the cross into paradise, with his words proclaimed throughout the world: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

At the time when the Lord’s body was in the tomb, his soul was in the underworld, and his divinity was in paradise, in heaven, and everywhere, embracing all things within itself through the boundlessness of its surpassing majesty.

According to his humanity he is called lesser when he is apprehended, scourged, crucified, dies, and is buried; according to his divinity he is exalted into the heavenly places through the power of the resurrection.

As man, he assumed death; as God, he stood above death. According to this rule, at one time he is poor, at another rich; at one time lesser, at another equal; at one time lord, at another servant.

He is therefore to be believed lesser than the Father when the Creator of the angels is made a little lower than the angels, as we read in the eighth Psalm: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

He is then to be called lesser than the Father when Scripture declares that he assumed the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), when he is also found to be younger than his mother, and when he says of himself in the twenty-first Psalm: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm 21:17–18).

That he is called lesser than the Father according to the flesh and according to humanity is demonstrated by countless testimonies of Scripture.
