### 4. Christ’s Divinity

Concerning his divinity the Apostle says to Titus: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared”; and again: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:11, 13).

It is an enormous sacrilege for him whom Truth itself professes to be the great God to be called lesser through the blasphemies of an unbelieving human being.

The Apostle Thomas too, in the Gospel of John, when after the resurrection he recognized the body of the crucified man by the marks of the nails, confessed, with apostolic and evangelical authority, the God who was hidden within the man, saying: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

If faith is present, the explanation is clear by which Christ is asserted in the sacred books to be now lesser, now equal to the Father. As he himself says of himself: “I am the first and the last” (Revelation 1:8). Recognize without doubt that he who is first cannot have anyone before him.

Likewise: “I am alpha and omega.” Just as no letter precedes the letter alpha, so it is clear that no one is second to the Son of God, because he is God.

### 5. What Should Be Answered to Those Who Call the Holy Spirit a Creature

What shall we answer those who either call the Holy Spirit lesser or, more wickedly, in abrupt impiety declare him to be a minister rather than God?

How can he be called a creature, when he is shown to be the creator of the Lord from Mary, as we read: “Conceived from the Holy Spirit, born from the virgin Mary” (Luke 1:35)?

For Christ was conceived not from the substance of the Holy Spirit but by his power; not by generation but by command and blessing.

And just as he was sent by the Father, so also he was sent by the Holy Spirit for the redemption of our wickedness, the Spirit himself speaking through Isaiah concerning him: “The Father and his Spirit have sent me” (Isaiah 48:16).

If the Holy Spirit is believed to be lesser, how does the Son testify that he was sent by the Holy Spirit just as by the Father?

The Holy Spirit himself spoke in the Apostles; he himself burned forth in the Prophets, as blessed Peter the Apostle says in his Letter: “Prophecy was not brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

And the Savior says to his disciples in Matthew: “It is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 10:20).

Likewise David, full of the Holy Spirit, openly declares who would speak through him, saying: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Psalm 84:9).

### 6. The Catholic Faith, by Professing Which One Attains Blessedness

This, I say, is the way of light, by whose confession the door of salvation is opened. Therefore those who enter upon this profession attain its blessedness.

Blessed is the one who confesses God the Father, the Son, and [Col. 2179] the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone are God.

Blessed is the one who confesses one almighty God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses one supreme God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that the one good God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, is eternal.

Blessed is the one who confesses that the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is undivided.

Blessed is the one who adds or subtracts nothing in confessing the united nature of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that all good things were made by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that there is one equality, in the eternal fullness of divinity, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that, according to the individual names of the Trinity—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—only the distinct individual persons are distinguished.

### 7. Curses on All Who Believe Wrongly

Therefore it was necessary for us to show them that they will eat the fruits of their way, and the curses of all who believe wrongly, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not obey the words of this book, to carry them out in his heart” (Deuteronomy 27:26).

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one eternal substance.

Cursed is the one who confesses that, according to the three persons, there are three divided substances in them.

Cursed is the one who confesses that there are three principles in this eternal unity of their divinity.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the one true God, the Father, the one true God, the Son, and the one true God, the Holy Spirit.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that there is one name in the divinity of the Trinity.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the undivided divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Cursed is the one who, because of the three names of the persons, confesses three gods, three lords, or three spirits.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the three names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished only according to the individual persons.

Cursed is the one who confesses that they are one person.

Cursed is the one who designates the one whom he calls Father as also being the Son.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the Father was born, incarnate, or suffered.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the Son to have been ineffably and truly born from the substance of the Father.

Cursed is the one who confesses that this birth was made, created, or fashioned.

Cursed is the one who says that the true Son of God exists only by will, and not rather by birth.

Cursed is the one who says: “There was a time when the Son did not exist.”

Cursed is the one who does not confess that this birth was from things that did not exist, which the Greeks call *ex ouk ontōn* (ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, “from things that are not”).

Cursed is the one who says that the divinity of the Son of God has a beginning in time, an origin from nothing, and a name resembling adoption from another.

Cursed is the one who does not confess one from one, the Son generated from the Father.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son was born from the Father without suffering.

Cursed is the one who says: “The Father once existed without the Son.”

Cursed is the one who does not confess that, before every principle or beginning, the Son always existed with the Father.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the immortal divinity of the Son of God.

Cursed is the one who says of the eternal Son: “He did not exist before he was born from Mary.”

Cursed is the one who professes that the united divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exists only through the love of concord, and not rather through this very united divinity.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the united divinity exists in these three persons.

Cursed is the one who, against the force and judgment of divine Scripture, presumes that this true God, the Spirit Paraclete, should be confessed as either the Father or the Son [Note: [Col. 2179] In Vigilius: “the Father or the Son, or certainly,” and so forth], or as a created work.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son of God, true God and true man, was recently born from the virgin Mary for our salvation.

Cursed is the one who confesses the Son of God to be merely an isolated man or merely a mere man.

Cursed is the one who assigns to the eternal God the Son, from the assumption of man [Col. 2180], the beginning of his existence only recently.

Cursed is the one who confesses that his divinity suffered.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the incomparable divinity of the Trinity is properly fashioned according to the features of a human being, although we find it written: “For there is no god like you in heaven above or on earth below” (1 Kings 8:23).

---

## SERMON 235

### On Catholic Faith III

*[Note: [Col. 2180] This is almost the same Creed that appears in volume 9 of Jerome’s works under the name of Damasus; in fact, however, it was compiled from the little book of Faith contained in chapter 39 of the canonical code of the Roman Church. The learned Quesnellius maintains that this little book belongs neither to Athanasius, whose works had also included it, nor to Vigilius of Tapsus, to whom Chiffletius wished to attribute it, nor finally to Gregory of Nazianzus, in whose works the same little book is Treatise or Oration 50, but rather to Gregory the Boetian, bishop of Eliberis. For the Oration found in Gregory of Nazianzus 49, cited by Augustine in Letter 148, seems to belong to him; and it is clear that Oration 49 has the same author as the aforesaid Oration 50, since one is an explanation of the other, written by an author asserting his own claim to it. Moreover, here “and the Son,” where the procession of the Holy Spirit is discussed, is an addition and is not found in the Faith-book of the Roman codex.]*

### 1. One God, Not Solitary; the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; the Son Begotten from the Father by Nature, Not by Will

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, and his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, our God and Lord and Savior, and God the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 2180] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have this passage as follows: “And in his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, God and Lord and Savior, and in God the Holy Spirit.” M.].

We do not worship and confess three gods, but one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

We do not mean one God as though he were solitary, nor one who is himself his own father and himself his own son. Rather, we confess the true Father, who begot the true Son: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, almighty from almighty, life from life, perfect from perfect, wholly from wholly, full from full; not created but begotten; not from nothing but from the Father; of one substance with the Father, which in Greek is called *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance”).

But we confess and venerate the Holy Spirit as God, neither unbegotten nor begotten, neither created nor made, but proceeding from the Father and the Son, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, always in the Father and the Son, coeternal and coequal with the Father and the Son, and their co-worker.

Therefore, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we confess one God, because “God” is a name of power, not of personal property. The proper name of the Father is “Father”; the proper name of the Son is “Son”; and the proper name of the Holy Spirit is “Holy Spirit.”

We believe this Trinity to be one God, because what exists from the one Father is of one nature with the Father [Note: [Col. 2180] The printed editions read: “And that God the Father is one, and that from the one Father is the Son, who is of one nature with the Father.” We have followed the manuscript copies], of one substance and of one power.

The Father begot the Son, not by will, not by necessity, but by nature.

### 2. Christ’s Two Natures

At the end of time the Son, through whom all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were made, came from the Father to save us and fulfill the Scriptures. He never ceased to be with the Father. We believe that he was conceived from the Holy Spirit and born from the virgin Mary; that the Word became flesh without being changed, while remaining God; that he was born a man not seemingly but truly; not airy but bodily; not phantasmal but fleshly, possessing bones, blood, sensation, and a soul.

That is, we understand him to be a perfect man, a true man, and true God, so that we do not doubt in any way that he was true God and true man.

[Col. 2181]

For he did not lose what he was, but began to be what he was not, so that he might be perfect in what belongs to him and true in what belongs to us.

For he who was God became man; and he who was born man acts as God; and he who acts as God dies as man; and he who dies as man rises as God.

Having conquered the dominion of death, he rose with the flesh in which he had been born, suffered, and died; he ascended to the Father and sits at his right hand in the glory that he always had and still has.

We believe that we have been cleansed by his death and blood, and that on the last day we shall be raised by him in this flesh in which we now live and which we possess. We shall receive either eternal life as the reward of good merit or punishments of eternal suffering for our sins.

Hold fast to these things; subject your souls to this faith, so that you may receive from Christ the Lord the rewards of the kingdom of heaven. Amen.

---

## SERMON 236

### On Catholic Faith IV

*[Note: [Col. 2181] Formerly, On Time 191. It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Leuven scholars left it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus rejected it. For it is nothing other than a profession of faith addressed by Pelagius to the Apostolic See and contained in volume 9 of Jerome’s works. Here it has been given the form of a sermon by adding a preface and changing the conclusion.]*

### 1. The Attempts of the Arians; the Author’s Prayers for the Church; the Faith of the Fathers

The Arian heretics have indeed often dared many things against the servants of God who preserve the right and Catholic faith. Through adulterous teaching they have attempted to assert their position and to persecute the orthodox.

Now, however, they have risen up against the faith to such an extent that they have polluted many of you and disturbed your ears, so as to tear souls apart.

Yet they conceal the unbelief of their wicked heresy. But they will not be permitted to do this for much longer. For the Lord, who endured death for all of us, is the ruler of his churches.

Therefore, beloved brothers, our prayer must be unceasing: first, that the holy and Catholic Church of the Lord, free from every dissension and heresy, may everywhere preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of charity. To hold, embrace, preserve, and guard this unity through right faith and blameless life is indeed the duty of all who call upon the Lord, but especially of bishops who preside over the churches.

Second, we pray that the rule of the Church, the holy tradition of the fathers, and their judgments may remain firm and solid forever.

Now this is the faith of our fathers.

### 2. Concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

We believe in God the almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible things.

We also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created: true God, the only-begotten, true Son of God, not made or adopted, but begotten, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance”).

He is in every respect equal to God the Father, so that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power. We confess that the one who is begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

But when we say that the Son was begotten from the Father, we do not assign any time to that divine and ineffable generation. Nor do we say that the Father ever began, or the Son. For we cannot otherwise confess the Father to be eternal unless we also confess the Son to be coeternal.

The Father is called Father because of the Son; and he who was always Father always had the Son.

We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in nature, will, power, eternity, and substance.

Source/review notes: Sermons 237–240, including all headings, numbered sections, citations, editorial notes, authorities, and every printed column-anchor occurrence, are retained.

### 3. In nature they are one, but they are distinguished by their properties.

Nor is there any degree at all in the Trinity, nothing that can be called lower or higher. Therefore the whole deity is equal in its perfection, so that—apart from the names indicating the distinct property of the persons—whatever is said of one person may most properly be understood of all three. [Col. 2182]

And just as, refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same substance and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons, marked by the property proper to each: we do not say that the Father is himself the Son, or himself the Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons. Nor does the Father ever exclude the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit; nor, conversely, does the Son or the Holy Spirit take on the name and person of the Father. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always the Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance; they are distinguished by their persons and names.

### 4. On the mystery of the Incarnation. The error of certain persons: Photinus and Apollinaris, and others.

We say that the very Son of God, who possesses eternity without beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages assumed a complete human being of our nature from Mary, ever-virgin, and that the Word became flesh—not by changing the deity, but by assuming humanity. Nor, as certain persons most wickedly suppose, do we say that the Holy Spirit served as the seed; rather, he acted through the power and efficacy of the Creator.

Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, while saying that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely, the deity and the humanity, which consists of soul and body. And just as we condemn Photinus, who confesses in Christ a human being alone and merely human, so we anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than the full human nature, and that the human being assumed in flesh, soul, or understanding was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed. Apart from the single stain of sin—which is not natural—we confess him to have been like us.

We likewise curse the blasphemy of those who, with a novel interpretation, attempt to assert that, from the time when he assumed flesh, everything that belonged to the deity passed over into the human being, and, conversely, that everything belonging to humanity was transferred into God. Thus, by this confusion, both substances—the deity, namely, and the humanity—would seem to have been emptied of themselves, and, having lost their proper state, changed into something else. Although we confess the Son to be both perfect God and human being, we would then be thought to hold neither a true God nor a true human being.

[Note: [Col. 2182] Thus the manuscript. But the printed editions have, rashly, “we believe.” Pelagius, however, in Jerome, has: “Who confess the Son to be imperfect God as well as human being, so that they are thought to hold neither a true God nor a true human being.”]

### 5. Christ truly suffered, but according to his humanity. Faith in the resurrection. The differing rewards of the righteous and punishments of the unrighteous.

We say that the Son of God assumed our passible nature in such a way that God nevertheless remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered, not apparently but truly, everything that Scripture testifies to—hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, death, and other things of this kind—but he suffered according to that which was capable of suffering: that is, not according to the substance that assumed, but according to the substance that was assumed.

For the Son of God himself, according to his deity, is impassible like the Father, invisible like the Father, unchangeable like the Father, incorruptible like the Father. And although the person of the Son—that is, the Word of God—properly assumed a passible human being, nevertheless, through the indwelling of that human being, the deity of the Word suffered nothing according to its own substance, so that the whole Trinity must be confessed to be impassible.

The Son of God therefore died in the same nature of flesh in which he was born and suffered, and in which he also rose again. For the substance of humanity was not emptied of itself, but was glorified to remain forever with the deity. He will come for the judgment of the living and the dead, so that he may reward the righteous and punish sinners.

We believe in the resurrection of the flesh in such a way that we say that we shall be restored [Col. 2183] in the same bodily reality in which we now exist, and that whatever form we shall once have received after the resurrection, we shall retain forever. There is one life for all the saints, but differing rewards according to their labor; and, conversely, there are also punishments for sinners according to the measure of their offenses.

We hold one baptism, which we say must be celebrated in infants with the same sacramental words with which it is celebrated in adults. If a person falls after baptism, we believe that he can be saved, first through reconciliation and then through penance.

### 6. Errors concerning the substance and origin of souls; concerning the commandments of God. The Manichaeans’ and Cataphrygians’ views on marriage; others’ views concerning Christ; Jovinian’s view of merits; the views of Manes and Jovinian concerning free choice.

We accept the New and Old Testament in the number of books handed down by the authority of the holy Catholic Church. We believe that souls are given by God, and we say that they were made by him, anathematizing those who say that the soul, as though it were a part of God, is of the divine substance.

We likewise condemn the error of those who say that souls sinned previously, or lived in heaven, before they were sent into bodies. We also curse the blasphemy of those who say that God has commanded something impossible for human beings, and that the commandments of God can be kept not by individuals but only by everyone collectively; or of those who condemn first marriages with Manes or second marriages with the Cataphrygians.

We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied because of the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the human being he assumed, he could not do everything he wished.

We likewise condemn the error of Jovinian, who says that in the future there will be no distinction among merits, and that we shall then possess the virtues which we neglected to possess here.

We confess free choice in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We say that both those who, with Manes, claim that a human being cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a human being cannot sin, are in error; for each removes freedom of choice. We, however, say that a human being is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we confess ourselves to possess freedom of choice.

This is the faith, beloved brothers, which we have learned in the Catholic Church, which we have always held and do hold, and which we believe can henceforth also be held by your Goodness.

SERMON CCXXXVII [Note: [Col. 2183] Elsewhere, *On Time* 192.]. On the Creed, I: and on the deity and omnipotence of the Father [Note: [Col. 2183] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, spurious to Verlinus and Vindingus. The author is the same as that of this and the two following sermons. Since in the opening he says that he has already shown that the God in whom we believe is the true God, he indicates not the preceding treatise, as Verlinus and Vindingus thought, but some other one unknown to us.].

1. God’s omnipotence is proved from the magnitude of his works. We have shown, most beloved brothers—as your Love surely remembers—that the God in whom you promised to believe and do believe is the true God, and likewise the true Father, and that this same God is omnipotent. For this is shown to be the order of the Creed. Although, indeed, when he is proved to be the true God, he is undoubtedly understood to be omnipotent, nevertheless faith is more advanced when his omnipotence is affirmed, as it is in the holy Scriptures. For great confidence arises in believers when they recognize that he in whom they believe can do all things. Therefore, the works of our omnipotent Lord and God themselves first bear witness to him: he made this whole world from nothing and arranged all its great beauty, as though beautiful forms of things, from no pre-existing material. Of him divine Scripture says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1); and again: “For the sea is his, and he himself made it” (Ps. 94:5). Who, then, would deny him to be omnipotent, when he knows that he has wrought such manifest things?

2. From the ease with which they were made; from the creation of invisible things [Col. 2184]. But one will confess him to be omnipotent much more when one recognizes how easily he wrought these very things. The prophet says in the Psalm: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9). Without any labor, without any difficulty, he founded things by his word. Whatever human reason marvels at, God fashioned not by labor but by command. At his command all things which previously did not exist came into being. When such things proceed from nothing, they proclaim an omnipotent author. Nor were only the things we see created by God; the invisible works of God bear witness to still greater riches of divine power. For all the angelic Powers were created by him. Though they are not seen by us, yet, as we recognize in the divine Scriptures, they serve in God’s army; Thrones, Dominions, and all Virtues and Powers of spiritual substance serve him. “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). Hence, describing the angelic host of so great a king, the prophet says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). [Note: [Col. 2184] The manuscript *rm.* has “ten.”]

3. From the governance of the world; from its dissolution; from the raising of human beings. Certainly, if you have briefly recognized God’s omnipotence from this creation of visible and invisible things, now recognize the same power from his governance as well. When, with the whole world sinning under Noah, he brings on the flood; when he burns Sodom and Gomorrah with a rain of fire; when, after delivering his people from Egyptian slavery, he provides them a dry path in the sea—what else does he do but testify that he is omnipotent, and that he himself made the sea and dried it in the part where he wished? Again, when he fed that same people in the wilderness for forty years with heavenly food, that is, manna, did he not proclaim the ineffable power of his divinity, so as to show that “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3)? And, to pass over God’s countless powers by mentioning a few, God also showed his omnipotence when he raised from the dead his Son, whom according to his humanity he willed to die for our salvation, having loosed the laws of hell; so that in Christ he might show himself to be the one by whom mortal human beings were created, and who also made the dead man immortal. It likewise belongs to the power of omnipotence to dissolve at the end of the ages this world which he once made from nothing. Hence the prophet says: “The heaven shall be rolled up like a book, and all the stars shall fall as leaves from a vine, and as leaves fall from a fig tree” (Isa. 34:4); and the Savior says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). The same omnipotence will raise all who have died and who will die until the end for the day of judgment, as the prophet says: “He will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61:13). Some he will join in the kingdom of heaven to the fellowship of angels; others he will join to the devil in the punishment of Gehenna.

4. Faith in so great a God ought to inspire fear. Believing in this God, most beloved brothers—omnipotent, just, severe, and gracious only to those who here avoided sins by fearing his severity—believing, I say, in this God, “work out your salvation with all fear and trembling,” as the Apostle says (Phil. 2:12). Departing from every sin and from all crimes and vices, hasten to works of righteousness alone. Walk, as the Savior says, “in the light while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). Beware of association and conversation with evil people. Let the hearing of the faithful be prepared only for hearing God’s words, and let the tongue of readers be moved only to speak holy things, so that good works may follow good hearing and good speech. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to accomplish this in us according to the zeal of good will, to whom be honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON CCXXXVIII [Note: [Col. 2185] Elsewhere, *On Time* 193.]. On the Creed, II: or on the Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his deity is without beginning with the Father, but according to his humanity was born for us from the Virgin at a definite beginning [Note: [Col. 2185] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors doubted it; Verlinus and Vindingus rejected it. At the beginning the author seems to indicate the preceding sermon, in which, however, what he later recalls here is not found: “in the preceding treatise we asserted against Arius the perfection of deity in Christ.” Compare Sermons 118 and 236 of the Appendix.].

[Col. 2185]

1. One person, two natures in Christ. Thus far, most beloved brothers, we have spoken of God the Father in whom you believe; and divine Scripture’s authority has shown that he is the true God, the true Father, and omnipotent. Now, according to the order of the Creed, we pass to the Son. After we have said in the Creed, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” there follows, “And in Jesus Christ his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.” Here the attentive hearer should take care to know one and the same person of the Son of God, in accordance with the reality of the humanity he assumed. For when we say that we believe in Christ the Son of God, who was born from the Virgin Mary, we do not say it in such a way as to confess that we have faith in a true human being only, but in the true God who assumed a true human being. For our Lord Jesus Christ is one and the same: both the Word of God, begotten from the Father without beginning, and a true human being, born from the Virgin at the end of the ages.

2. Apollinaris and Arius attack this faith. For in this matter a double heresy strives to attack us with opposite opinions: Apollinaris on one side, Arius on the other. Arius accepts a complete human being in Christ in such a way [Note: [Col. 2185] Augustine speaks differently in his book *On Heresies*, where, concerning not only the Arians, he testifies in chapter 49 “that they suppose Christ assumed flesh alone, without a soul”; and in chapter 55 he declares that the Apollinarians agree with them in this opinion, since they say, he writes, “like the Arians, that Christ God assumed flesh without a soul.”] that he denies that God is perfect, trying to confine the very Word of God within a beginning of time and confessing him to be not Creator but creature. Apollinaris, by contrast, believes the Son of God to be perfect God in such a way that he fears to join a true human being to him, fearing lest the weakness of the assumed human being obscure the dignity of the one assuming. But we Catholics, fortified against both by the authority of the divine Scriptures, defend against Arius the true and perfect divinity of the Word and against Apollinaris the perfect reality of humanity in Christ. Therefore, as in the preceding treatise we asserted the perfection of deity against Arius, so now we demonstrate the perfect human being against Apollinaris.

3. Christ is proved a true human being against Apollinaris; in what sense Christ is said to have been made from seed. The Apostle’s authority is most clear for us when he says: “God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4). First, by saying “made,” he distinguishes the human substance from the divinity of the Word. For the Word of God, through whom all things were made, cannot at all be called made or created, as blessed John says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). “God,” he says, “sent his Son, made from a woman.” Therefore, when he says “made,” he shows that he is not here treating of divinity. But when he adds “from a woman,” he expresses the substance of a true human being, so that the nature of the human being made is that of the one from whom he was made; that is, Christ, who was made from the Virgin, is believed to have the same nature as the Virgin from whom Christ was formed and born. Hence elsewhere the same Apostle says of the Son of God: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). For although a man’s seed did not intervene in the Virgin’s conception, nevertheless, because Christ was formed from flesh that consists of seed, he is said to have been made from seed. Therefore, as Father and Son have one nature according to divinity, so also mother and son have the same nature according to humanity—that [Col. 2186] is, Mary and Christ have the same nature. From both substances, divinity and humanity, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is one and the same: true God and likewise true human being, as the Apostle testifies and says: “From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ages” (Rom. 9:5); and elsewhere: “For there is one God, one mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

4. In Christ God is not changed into a human being, but a human being is joined to God; and he did this and all he did for us. Therefore, from these apostolic statements among others, we prove our Lord Jesus Christ to be one and the same, true God and true human being. Although he possesses equal impassibility and immortality with the Father, nevertheless for our salvation he assumed a passible and mortal human being—not so that divinity might be changed into humanity, but so that humanity might be joined to divinity. According to the reality of this human being, therefore, the Son of God was born from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit for our redemption. For thus the angel speaks to Mary in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; and therefore the Holy One who shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Long ago Isaiah the prophet foretold this marvelous birth: “The Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14), which the Evangelist interprets as “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). For our Lord Jesus Christ also receives this name from the effect of the events: having assumed a human being of our nature, he deigned to be with us; for us he did everything; for us he suffered everything—hunger, thirst, weariness, weeping, pain, and finally death itself. He was scourged and crucified by Pontius Pilate the governor, and died and was buried. For the righteous one was condemned for the unrighteous, and, though without sin, he himself underwent the punishment due to sinners, so that he might both take away the punishment and blot out the sins of those for whom he was punished. He died a brief and temporal death, lest we undergo eternal death.

5. Christ’s resurrection also was for us. But as far as this sequence of events, the weakness of human nature is to be understood in Christ. For he who was passible unto death received the glory of incorruption from the time of death [Note: [Col. 2186] Thus manuscript *rm.* But the printed editions have: “and received the dominion of death itself.”]: indeed, this was already the privilege in Christ’s flesh, that, according to David’s prophecy, though lifeless and buried until the third day, it nevertheless remained incorrupt. Thus we read Christ saying to the Father in the Psalm: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). Hence blessed Peter also says: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by powers and wonders and signs which God performed through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—him, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you killed by fastening him to the hands of the wicked; but God raised him up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:22–24). Jesus Christ died for us; but for us he also rose on the third day. For if his death too was for us, how much more is his life for us? After the resurrection, having received from the Father all authority, he consoles the disciples and says: “Behold, all authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18); and elsewhere: “Going into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16). After this he deigned to remain among the disciples for forty days, and, though immortal, did not disdain fellowship with mortals, in order surely that by teaching he might fill the Apostles with faith and truth, which would also reach us through their testimony.

6. The final judgment. Once the disciples had been strengthened, he was lifted up into heaven and ascended victor to the Father over both sins and death. This we plainly [Col. 2187] read in the Gospel: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19). This language does not signify human limbs in God, but expresses the honor with which the Father received Christ. Therefore, we believe that he will descend for the judgment of the living and the dead, no longer in the weakness that he had [Note: [Col. 2187] Manuscript *rm.*: “which he lacked.”], but in the exaltation that he possesses. For he who came in weakness to redeem will come in power to judge. Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And while they were looking into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, who also said: Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:10–11). Therefore let us be ready for this coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, most beloved brothers, and let us fear lest he find us not such as he wished to find, he who suffered everything for us so that he might find us such that he would inflict not punishments but render eternal rewards. May the Lord and God deign, by his grace, to bring you to these rewards, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON CCXXXIX [Note: [Col. 2187] Elsewhere, *On Time* 194.]. On the Creed, III: or on the Holy Spirit, that he is of the same substance and deity as the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 2187] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. The same preacher continues and completes the exposition of the Creed undertaken in the preceding sermons.].

1. The Holy Spirit is proved to be God by the testimonies of Christ, Peter, and Paul. Most beloved brothers, with God’s help we persevere in completing the order of the Creed, in which the mysteries of our whole faith consist. And, as I think you remember well, we have sufficiently shown, so far as your instruction requires, what we ought to believe concerning God the Father and likewise God the Son. It remains now for us to speak also of the deity of the Holy Spirit. For this is the order of the Creed: after the person of Father and Son, the confession of the Holy Spirit follows. For belief in the Father and Son profits one only when one has also believed in the Holy Spirit with the same veneration of faith. Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ himself established this norm of holy faith, and no one but an impious person doubts the rule of Catholic faith which was dictated by him to whom faith itself is owed. Therefore, after our Lord Jesus Christ had risen from the dead already glorified and was about to ascend to the Father, he left these mysteries of faith to his disciples, that is, the Apostles. For he says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things whatsoever I commanded you” (Matt. 28:19–20). The effect of these very realities dictates that we should believe in the power of three persons in one deity. As the Father, in whose name we are baptized, is God, so also the Holy Spirit, in whose name we are baptized, is God. Certainly blessed Peter the Apostle pronounced this most decisively when he said to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” and a little later: “You have lied not to a human being, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). He most clearly called God the one whom he had called the Holy Spirit. And blessed Paul the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and divisions of operations, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:3–6). Here too the Vessel of Election plainly says that the one whom he had called the Holy Spirit is the same God and Lord, working by his own power what he wills.

2. He is not inferior to the Son, since offense against him is so grave; and he proceeds from the Father. This is the Holy Spirit, against whom it is so sacrilegious to sin that it is forgiven neither here nor in the future judgment. For our Lord Jesus Christ himself says in the Gospel: [Col. 2188] “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the future” (Matt. 12:32). This is the Holy Spirit whom our Lord, as he was about to ascend to the Father, promises to his disciples, saying: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he shall bear testimony concerning me”; and above he says of him: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father shall send in my name, shall teach you all things” (John 15:26; 14:26). Therefore, the Holy Spirit himself, whom the Father sends in my name and who proceeds from the Father, is shown to be of one substance with the Father and the Son.

3. It is advantageous that Christ depart for the Holy Spirit’s coming. Carefully note also that the same Lord again says to his disciples: “It is advantageous for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). The statement “I will send” does not, far from it, indicate that the Holy Spirit is inferior; rather, it simply indicates, without flattery, unity and harmony of will. But note what he said: “It is advantageous for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you.” How is it advantageous for the disciples that Christ ascend from them to the Father, if the one to be sent to the disciples in Christ’s place is inferior? It is advantageous for the disciples that Christ ascend from them because the Holy Spirit, who is promised to come to the disciples, is equal to the Father and the Son. That the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete expresses the characteristic of his operation. For *Paracletus* is a Greek word which in Latin is called *Consolator*, “Comforter.” He is rightly sent to the disciples in Christ’s place, to console them amid all the tribulations which they were to suffer by confessing Christ. Therefore, most beloved brothers, instructed by these testimonies of the divine Scriptures, let us confess with the full perfection of faith that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son. For since we read in the divine Scriptures of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, just as we cannot doubt the deity of the Father and Son, neither can we doubt that of the Holy Spirit.

4. In the Trinity there are three names, three persons, and one deity. But let the polluted impiety of pagan error be far, far from Christian minds, so that by confessing three persons in one deity we may seem to confess three gods. Let this be far from us, I say, and let it be utterly excluded from devout minds. For, as we have shown, in accordance with the authority of holy Scripture, we make in the Trinity a distinction only of names and persons, but confess one indivisible deity: it is one and the same perfect divinity in the Father, in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, we do not speak of three gods when we confess one divinity. For we have not forgotten divine Scripture saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4); and again: “The Lord God is here in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other except him” (Deut. 4:39). We have not forgotten, I say, that God is one, as we have surely learned on Scripture’s testimony. But we are directed to the truth of faith between two errors and two very great heresies, so that we neither make number in deity with the Gentiles nor deny the mystery in the Trinity with the Jews; but, believing that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist in the property of their persons, let us venerate the unity of deity in the Trinity. That is, let us say that the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are one God, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON CCXL [Note: [Col. 2188] Elsewhere, among the Vignerian sermons, 1, in the first part of the Supplement.]. On the Creed IV [Note: [Col. 2188] Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The preacher makes the Apostles authors of the Creed in such a way that he assigns to each a proposition according to his own pleasure. In distributing these propositions, he does not agree with the author of the following sermon, except concerning [Col. 2189] Thomas, Thaddaeus, and Matthias. He teaches that *Christus* in Hebrew means “Anointed”; and finally, in the remaining matters, he agrees least of all with Augustine.].

1. What each Apostle composed concerning the Creed [Col. 2189]. Seven remissions of sins. On the tenth day after the ascension, when the disciples were assembled out of fear of the Jews, the Lord sent the promised Paraclete. At his coming, inflamed like glowing iron and filled with knowledge of all languages, they composed the Creed. Peter said: “I believe in God the Father almighty.” Where he says Father, the Son and the Spirit are understood also; for the substance of each of these three persons is inseparable. He says “almighty,” because, although nothing is impossible for him, he cannot do evil; for if he could, he would not be almighty. “Creator of heaven and earth”: through the Father he signifies all things. Andrew said: “And in Jesus Christ his Son.” Jesus is a proper name and means Savior; Christ is an appellative name, and in Hebrew means Anointed, for prophets and kings were customarily anointed. “Our only Lord”: he says “only” according to nature. Adam and Eve too are sons of God, but by adoption. James said: “Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit”—not because the Spirit was his Father, but because he was conceived in Mary’s faith through the ministry and cooperation of the Holy Spirit. “Born from the Virgin Mary,” who conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin. John said: “Suffered under Pontius Pilate.” He says this so that we may believe in no Christ other than the one who suffered in Pilate’s time; for many antichrists, as he says, will falsely say, “I am Christ” (Matt. 24:24). “Crucified, dead, and buried,” according to the flesh: for this he was born, that he might be crucified; for this crucified, that he might die; for this dead, that he might rise; for this he rose, that he might justify us. Thomas said: “He descended into hell”: that is, in his soul accompanied by divinity, while his body rested in the tomb. “On the third day he rose from the dead,” so that he might show us the example and faith of the resurrection. James said: “He ascended into heaven”: in the very flesh in which he was born and suffered, he rose in that flesh and, victorious, ascended into heaven. “He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.” The Father’s right hand signifies the prosperity of our life; his left hand, however, signifies the punishment of hell. Philip said: “From there he shall come to judge the living and the dead.” In the body in which he ascended, he will come to judgment and separate the righteous from sinners. Bartholomew said: “I believe in the Holy Spirit,” from whom Father and Son can in no way be separated in their work or in the Catholic faith. Matthew said: “The holy Catholic Church”: Catholic, that is, universal, in which alone sins are remitted; having repelled the perversity of all heretics, it extends from the rising of the sun to its setting. “The communion of saints”: because, although the gifts of the Holy Spirit are diverse in individuals in this life, in eternity they will nevertheless be common to all, so that what any saint has had less of in himself, he may share in another’s virtue. Simon said: “The remission of sins.” There are seven remissions of sins: first, baptism; second, penance; third, divine mercy; fourth, pardon through forgiving enemies; fifth, through true charity; sixth, through almsgiving; seventh, through preaching by which the erring are converted. Thaddaeus said: “The resurrection of the flesh”: that is, we shall rise in the very flesh in which we live, changing not sex but frailty. Then the saints who now have single robes, that is, the reward of life, will receive double robes, that is, the recompense of body and soul; but sinners will receive double punishment, so that what body and soul together have deserved in this life they may receive together in the next. Matthias said: “Life everlasting,” which no end will terminate, no vice defile, and no sickness make sorrowful.

2. The faith of the Apostles must be held firmly. Therefore the Apostles, tested like gold by the fire of the Holy Spirit and indignant that they had remained thus far, went out confidently to evangelize every creature, as the Lord had commanded (Mark 16:15), to call the erring back to life, and to baptize believers [Col. 2190]. But let us, dearest brothers, faithfully and firmly hold the faith and Gospel of the Apostles handed down to us through their successors. Let us also keep inviolate the covenant that we made with the Lord in baptism; or, if we fall by sinning, let us strive to rise quickly by repentance, so that we may await securely Christ’s second coming—desirable beyond what can enter the human heart for those who have done good, but exceedingly fearful and terrible for those who have done evil.

# SERMON 241

[Note: Formerly *On Time* 115; later, in Appendix 42.]

## On the Creed, V

[Note: By an uncertain author, who here repeats the Creed as far as the third article, saying that it should “correspond with the mystery of the Trinity.” In this respect he has the writer of the following sermon in agreement with him, but by no means Augustine, who, in his written Sermon 214, *On the Creed*, was restrained by religious scruple from committing the Creed itself to writing even once. The statements of the Creed are not always the same here; indeed, only a few are attributed to the same Apostles as in the preceding sermon.]

### 1. The Creed is a summary: why it is so called; what each Apostle composed from it

The Creed that we are about to hand on to you, dearest brothers, is a summary and perfection of our faith—simple, brief, and complete: its simplicity accommodates the rusticity of its hearers, its brevity their memory, and its fullness their instruction. For what is called *Symbolum* in Greek is called *Collatio* in Latin. It is called a “collection” because the faith of the catholic law, collected into one, is gathered together in the brevity of the Creed, whose text we shall now recite to you, God willing.

Peter said: “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

John said: “Creator of heaven and earth.”

James said: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”

Andrew said: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

Philip said: “Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.”

Thomas said: “Descended into hell; on the third day he rose from the dead.”

Bartholomew said: “Ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.”

Matthew said: “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

James son of Alphaeus said: “And in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church.”

Simon the Zealot: “The communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.”

Judas son of James: “The resurrection of the flesh.”

Matthias completed it: “Everlasting life. Amen.”

### 2. The words of the Creed are the heavenly sacraments of the Lord, preserving grace incorrupt in us

Hear, therefore, dearest brothers, the voice of our Redeemer speaking through the prophet: “Come, children; hear me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12).

He calls “children” those whom he places in the lap of the Church. For she cannot be called a mother unless she has brought forth children. Therefore, dearest ones, recognize that you are being invited to an everlasting reward—you who, with God’s help, have faithfully received the bath of life-giving water, or who desire that, when you have come to the sacred font or to true repentance, the saving and heavenly water may pour over you through the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, dearest ones, let us declare perfectly in our voices the sacrament of this mystery, just as we have conceived it by faith and believe it in our hearts: “I believe in God the Father almighty,” and the rest as above.

Therefore, beloved, these words are not human words but the Lord’s heavenly sacraments. By his mercy, may they remain in your hearts, so that you may receive the Lord’s grace incorrupt and undefiled to the end.

We repeat the Creed again, dearest ones, so that it may correspond with the mystery of the Trinity.

### 3. The distinct property of the Persons, one majesty; faith touches Mary’s virginity, not speech

“I believe in God.”

We must believe, dearest brothers, in God the Father, and likewise in Jesus Christ his Son. The Father cannot be believed without the Son, because although the property of the Persons in them is distinct, their majesty is nevertheless one and undivided. Therefore, just as the Father has always been able to do everything, so also the Son has always been able to do everything.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

Here the sacrament of the body he assumed is indicated: the one whom the Father begot before the ages was conceived at the end of the age by the Virgin Mary, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. And therefore the angel Gabriel says of that mother of the Lord: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

For in order to receive the coming of the Lord’s majesty, it was necessary that divine assistance be present for human weakness. Just as holy Mary gave birth as a virgin, so she conceived as a virgin. How and in what manner these things were accomplished while her virgin integrity remained intact, we can believe rather than explain. Faith has very much freedom in these matters; speech has little.

“Therefore, he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into hell; on the third day he rose from the dead. He ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father.”

He is said to sit at the Father’s right hand, not so that he may be called greater, but so that he may be shown equal.

All these things bear witness to the Lord’s passion, so that we may believe that the Lord Jesus Christ truly suffered and truly died, and likewise truly rose and triumphed. In this Christ the Lord left us an example: just as we do not doubt that he was born, died, rose again, and lives, so we too, just as we know that we were born and have died, should know that after death we shall rise and live forever.

It follows: “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

### 4. Only the holy catholic Church is holy

“And in the Holy Spirit”—so that an equal confession of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit might demonstrate their equal power.

“I believe in the holy catholic Church.”

The Creed rightly calls the Church catholic and holy, because there are many churches of heretics; but what is not catholic cannot be called holy.

It follows: “The communion of saints.”

Since we believe in the holy catholic Church and have communion with the saints—for where there is holy faith, there is also holy communion—you too must believe in the resurrection of the body and the forgiveness of sins.

The whole sacrament of Baptism consists in this: that we believe that the resurrection of bodies and the forgiveness of sins will be granted to us by God.

It remains for you to await daily the coming of the one whose passion you have heard, whose ascension you have heard, and whose judgment you have heard.

# SERMON 242

[Note: Also formerly *On Time* 131.]

## On the Creed, VI: for the Competentes

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition it was doubtful; in the judgment of Verlin and Vinding it is false. It does not sound like Augustine, except in the conclusion, which was taken from Sermon 212. In most other respects it agrees with the Eusebian sermons on the Creed, 1 and 2, perhaps written by Faustus. Compare the criticism of the preceding sermon. In any event, this very sermon was formerly read in the Gallican Church to the *Competentes* at the handing over of the Creed, as is clear from the very ancient Gallican Missal edited by Thomasius; Edmund Martene also inserted it in the first book of his work *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, p. 95. Earlier, on p. 85, he had observed that in the Gallican Church, before the Roman order was adopted there, it had been customary, when the Creed was handed over to the *Competentes*, to repeat it three times.]

### 1. The Creed is brief yet expansive

I ask you, dearest brothers, to listen attentively as we unfold the explanation of the Creed. The teaching of the Creed is the power of the sacrament, the illumination of the soul, and the fullness of believers. In what it teaches or in what is learned from it are found the unity of the Trinity, the Trinity distinguished in Persons, the abundance of the Creator, and the redemption accomplished through the passion.

By it the bond of unbelief is loosed; by it the gate of life is opened; by it the glory of confession is revealed.

The Creed, beloved, is brief in words but great in sacraments: it appears small through the narrowness of its extent, yet contains everything in the compression of its brevity. It is slight, so that it does not burden the memory, but expansive, so that it exceeds the understanding; confirming all by the perfection of believing, the desire to confess, and the confidence of rising again.

Rightly, therefore, you have gathered to hear the Creed with greater attention and in greater numbers, and, in keeping with the season itself, in greater purity.

Whatever was prefigured in the Patriarchs, whatever was announced in the Scriptures, whatever was foretold by the Prophets—whether concerning the unbegotten God, or the only-begotten Son of God from God, or the Holy Spirit, although shown obscurely, or concerning the sacrament of the humanity to be assumed, or concerning the mystery of the Lord’s death and resurrection—all this the Creed briefly contains for confession, in accordance with the prophetic oracle.

Therefore, dearest brothers, holding in memory the collection of faith and the grace and mystery of the profession, let us now come to the sacramental text of this profession of the Creed, which begins in the following manner.

### 2. God wishes his judgments to be believed by us, not investigated

“I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth.

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into hell; on the third day he rose from the dead. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of this flesh, and everlasting life. Amen.”

We must repeat the wording of this Creed, beloved, so that we may more deeply implant in your understanding the things we say.

“I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth.”

It is repeated a third time so that we may proceed in faithful course to comprehend what follows. And because the law of our faith consists in the Trinity, the order of the Creed must be recited a third time, so that the number of repetitions itself may come with the sign of the Trinity.

First of all, beloved, carefully observe what kind of statement occurs at the beginning of the Creed, and consider more attentively with what opening it begins. Thus, at the outset it has: “I believe.”

See that our Lord does not command us to investigate divine judgments, but to believe; nor to demand an explanation, but simply and unwaveringly to offer faith.

“In God the Father.”

Observe that, when it joins the name “Father” to the confession of God, it shows that he did not first begin to be God and afterward become Father. Rather, without any beginning, he is always both God and Father. Since, therefore, he was always Father, he always had a Son to whom he is Father.

It calls him “almighty” because he is almighty, and nothing is impossible for him who created heaven, earth, the sea, human beings, and all animals and reptiles—not by some act of workmanship, but by the command of his word alone.

Therefore, let us not begin to consider how this or that could have happened, since we are commanded to confess him almighty.

“Creator of heaven and earth.”

This says what I stated above: that he perfected everything solely by the power of his word.

### 3. Why Pilate is mentioned

“And in Jesus Christ, his Son.”

Observe that, just as we must believe in the Father, so also we must believe in the Son. And since he is equal to the Father in majesty, we know that we owe him as much honor and service as we owe the Father.

“Jesus Christ.”

Jesus means “Savior”; Christ is so called from *chrism*, “anointing,” because just as ancient kings were anointed with sacred oil by priests, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit.”

She who deserved to bring forth God could not have conceived from any source other than God.

“Born of the Virgin Mary.”

She who was to remain a virgin after giving birth could not have had any other kind of conception.

“He suffered under Pontius Pilate.”

Pilate was the judge at that time, appointed by the emperor in Judea, under whom the Lord suffered. His mention concerns the indication of the time, not the dignity of his person.

“Crucified and buried.”

The cross on which he was crucified in the body we carry on our forehead.

“He was buried.”

Just as he was truly born, so he truly died and was buried.

“On the third day he rose.”

The three-day delay of the burial clearly shows that, while the body lay in the tomb, that soul triumphed over hell.

“He ascended into heaven”—that is, he placed above the heavens, at the right hand of God the Father, the condition of our nature that he had assumed when he was born from a human mother.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

He will come to judgment in the very body in which he ascended into heaven. He judges Christians and pagans, the righteous and sinners, the faithful and the impious.

### 4. Confession of the Trinity is necessary

“And in the Holy Spirit.”

Observe that, just as we must believe in the Father, so also we must believe in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not believe in even one Person of the Trinity will gain nothing from having believed in the other two.

“The holy catholic Church.”

We must understand that we should believe the Church, but not believe in the Church, because the Church is not God; she is the house of God.

It calls her catholic because she is spread throughout the whole world. The churches of various heretics are not called catholic because they are confined to particular places and to their respective provinces. But this Church is spread from the rising of the sun to its setting in the splendor of one faith.

“The communion of saints”—that is, we are to remain bound by fellowship and the communion of hope with those saints who have died in the faith that we have received.

“The forgiveness of sins.”

For after the forgiveness granted to us by the gift of the Redeemer in Baptism, we must maintain the disposition of full faith.

“The resurrection of this flesh.”

Let us believe that the flesh which we carry in this life under mortal conditions will rise immortal and will give an account because of its fellowship with the soul.

“Everlasting life.”

Without any doubt, we confess that we shall obtain everlasting life if you faithfully hold to these sacraments that we expound to you and preserve them through good works.

### 5. Conclusion

“I have rendered to you the brief sermon owed to you concerning the entire Creed,” and so forth.

[Note: The conclusion is Sermon 212 among the Augustinian sermons.]

# SERMON 243

[Note: Also formerly *On Time* 123.]

## On the Creed, VII

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, but Verlin and Vinding considered it false. At the beginning the preacher addresses several people, using the form of address customary and characteristic in spurious sermons, “dearest brothers”; afterward, however, he addresses some one person in the singular. Nor does he imitate Augustine in explaining the Creed.]

### 1. The one who is God is himself our Father

We must observe, dearest brothers, how great God’s compassion is toward the human race. Almighty God, Creator and Maker of angels and human beings, of every visible and invisible creature, wished to be called “Father” by human beings and to regard as children those whom he made from the clay of the earth.

Therefore, if you believe in God, abandon the devil. If you wish to follow God, take care to avoid whatever does not please God.

Rejoice and exult, because you have one and the same being as God and Father. Worship him, love him, and do his will. Give no thought to the worship of idols or to the superstitions of the pagans, because God is almighty and is able to give back everything that he promises you.

### 2. Whence we are to believe in Mary’s virginity before and after childbirth

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.”

Unless you believe and confess with your whole mind, without any hesitation, that he is both the Son of God and the Son of man, confessing the Father will not benefit you.

Believe, therefore, in the only-begotten Son of God from the unbegotten God the Father, life from life, true God from true God, coeternal and coessential, almighty and in every respect equal to the Father; and you will deserve to attain eternal joys with him and with all his saints.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

When you hear that the Holy Spirit was the minister of so great a birth, do not doubt in any way that a virgin could conceive. Why do you not believe that he could be formed in the womb of an undefiled Virgin, when you must believe that he made a human being from the clay of the earth?

Nor should you doubt that Mary remained a virgin after childbirth, because no human speech or understanding can comprehend how this happened. For God the Father willed his Son—equal to himself in every respect and unlike him in nothing—to assume human flesh for the sake of human beings, so that he might grant eternal life and glory to all who believe in him and obey his will; and so that, by assuming flesh and taking on human nature, he might rescue from the devil the human being made in the image of God, deceived through the devil’s envy, and expelled from the eternal kingdom, and restore him to the eternal kingdom through his only Son.

### 3. Whatever weakness there is in Christ is for our sake; whatever glory there is belongs to his own power

“Who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.”

The one who for your sake accepted the corruption of human flesh endured, for your redemption and salvation, the passion of the cross in the humanity he had assumed. For his passion is our life, and his death is our liberation.

“On the third day he rose from the dead.”

If the Lord’s three-day burial troubles you, let his glorious resurrection strengthen you. Whatever weakness you hear of in Christ is the cause of our necessity and our redemption; whatever glory you hear of belongs to his own power.

He died in order to bring us back to life; he rose in order to raise us up to eternal life.

“He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.”

If it seems great and precious to you that the Son of God hung on the cross for you, and sublime that he ascended into heaven, you ought to marvel much more that he died and was buried for you. For he descended for this purpose: to endure, for your salvation, those things that are offensive to human weakness, and to lead you with himself to eternal and heavenly glory.

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

The one who was judged by the wicked and impious to death will himself judge all the good and righteous for glory, and will cast all the impious into punishment.

### 4. Faith in the resurrection is necessary for salvation

“And in the Holy Spirit.”

Just as you believed in God the Father almighty and in his only-begotten Son, so with equal faith and veneration believe that the Holy Spirit is one God, equal to the Father and the Son in all things and unlike them in nothing.

“The holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.”

In it, everyone who has been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit will receive eternal forgiveness of all sins; outside it, all the wicked and impious are assigned to eternal punishments.

“The resurrection of the flesh and everlasting life.”

What you have heard to be accomplished in Christ’s glorious resurrection, believe that the same will certainly be accomplished in you at the future judgment, so that the resurrection of your flesh may restore you forever.

For unless you believe that you will be restored after death, you will not be able to attain the reward of eternal life. But if you believe, you will be joined to eternal joys—through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON 244

[Note: Also formerly *On Time* 195.]

## On the Faith of the Creed and Good Conduct

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors were also permitted to doubt this sermon; Verlin and Vinding wished it to be regarded as spurious. It genuinely resembles Caesarius, not Augustine.]

### 1. The Blessed Virgin persevered without the stain of sin

I ask and admonish you, dearest brothers, that whoever wishes to be saved should learn the right and catholic faith, hold it firmly, and preserve it inviolate.

Thus each person must observe this rule: believe in the Father, believe in the Son, believe in the Holy Spirit. God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—yet not three gods, but one God. As is the Father, so is the Son, and so also is the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, let every believer believe that the Son is equal to the Father according to divinity, but less than the Father according to the humanity of the flesh that he assumed from us; while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

Believe, therefore, dearest ones, in God the Father almighty; believe also in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.

Believe that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, who was a virgin before childbirth and always remained a virgin after childbirth, and persevered without the stain or blemish of sin.

Believe that he suffered under Pontius Pilate for our sins; believe that he was crucified, died, and was buried. Believe that he descended into hell, bound the devil, and liberated the souls of the saints who were being held in custody, leading them with himself to the heavenly homeland.

Believe that on the third day he rose from the dead and showed us an example of resurrection.

Believe that he ascended into heaven with the flesh that he assumed from us.

Believe that he sits at the Father’s right hand; believe that he will come to judge the living and the dead.

Believe in the Holy Spirit; believe in the holy catholic Church; believe in the communion of saints; believe in the resurrection of the flesh; believe in the forgiveness of sins; believe also in everlasting life.

### 2. The humility of many is feigned; what Christ did for us

Therefore, if anyone wishes to be Christ’s disciple, let him keep his commandments and learn humility, as he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Let him pray to God from the heart, because there are many who outwardly appear to humble themselves but inwardly are full of the swelling of pride.

Christ humbled himself for us; he took the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8).

For us, brothers, in order to blot out our sins, he assumed human flesh, was born of a Virgin, placed in a manger, wrapped in cloths, rejected by the Jews, persecuted, seized, and scourged by them, defiled with spittle, crowned with thorns, pierced with nails, pierced with a lance, hung upon the cross, given vinegar mixed with gall to drink, and reckoned among the wicked.

And he endured all these things, dearest brothers, in order to free us from the jaws of hell.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since the Lord endured such great and such terrible things for us, if we wish to come to him, we must follow his footsteps and imitate the examples of the saints.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). And elsewhere he says: “Go, sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

The holy martyrs, dearest brothers, followed Christ’s footsteps and drank the cup of passion that he drank. The Apostle Peter was crucified for Christ’s name; Paul was beheaded; Stephen was stoned; and many others suffered in this way for his name.

### 3. What we in turn must do

Therefore, brothers, crucify and mortify your members that are upon the earth, so that you may please the one who created you.

Let the one who was proud become humble; the one who was unbelieving become faithful; the lustful become chaste; the thief become honest; the drunkard become sober; the sleepy become watchful; the miser become generous; the double-tongued become good-speaking; the slanderer or envious person become pure and kind.

Let the one who once came late to church now run to it more frequently.

Let each person redeem himself through an abundance of almsgiving, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Sirach 3:33).

Give tithes every year from all the produce that you gather to the churches and the poor.

Love fasting; avoid gluttony and drunkenness from wine.

Feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, and visit those who are in prison.

Visit the sick, gather strangers into your homes, wash their feet, dry them with a cloth, kiss them on the mouth, and prepare their beds.

Let no one commit murder, theft, or adultery; let no one swear falsely or give false testimony.

Let him honor father and mother, so that he may live long upon the earth.

Let him love God more than himself and love his neighbor as himself.

Whoever has committed any of the things mentioned above should correct himself quickly, make confession, and perform true penance; then his sins will be forgiven.

If you wish to fulfill these things that I have urged, brothers, you will deserve to obtain the forgiveness of sins and will attain everlasting life, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 245

[Note: Also formerly *On Time* 3.]

## On the Mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation, I

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, false in the judgment of Verlin and Vinding. In the Corbie manuscript it begins as follows: “Our Lord both exhorts and admonishes us, saying, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one. This God cannot be estimated, cannot be diminished, cannot be counted,’ as the prophet David says, ‘Great is the Lord,’” and so forth. Moreover, the sermon is much longer. For after the words “joined them by the interposition of the wood,” there follows, in the same style, a disputation against those “who say that it cannot happen that Christ was born from holy Mary, asserting, since they are unclean, that that part of the body was shameful,” and so forth. Then the preacher attacks those “who say that holy Mary had sons from Joseph after childbirth.” Among other things, in arguing he says: “Holy Mary, heretic, could be a mother; she could not be a woman.” This does not agree well with the teaching of Augustine or with the Apostle’s statement in Galatians 4: “God sent his Son, made from a woman.” We pass over other matters here that are clearly foreign to Augustine.]

### 1. The three Persons of the Trinity are one

We read that holy Moses gave commandments to the people of God, where he said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

He cannot be greater; he cannot be less; he cannot be counted, as the prophet David says: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no number to his wisdom” (Psalm 146:5).

You know these things very well, dearest brothers, who hold the catholic truth firmly in your hearts. Nevertheless, hear briefly what I have undertaken to explain with the Lord’s help.

God the Father is one God; God the Son is one God; the Holy Spirit is one God—not three gods, but one God: three in names, one in the divinity of substance.

### 2. Flesh belongs to Christ alone; this is illustrated by examples of the soul, the sun, and the lyre

But the heretic says to me: “Then, if they are one, were they all incarnate?”
