No. Flesh belongs to Christ alone.

Certainly, soul is one thing and reason another; yet reason is in the soul, and the soul is one. But the soul does one thing and reason another: the soul lives, reason understands; life belongs to the soul, and wisdom belongs to reason. Although they are one, the soul alone receives life and reason alone receives wisdom; nevertheless, neither soul exists without reason nor reason without soul.

So also the Father and the Son, although they are one and there is one God, flesh belongs to Christ alone—just as wisdom belongs to reason alone, although reason does not depart from the soul.

Here is another example. In the sun, heat and brightness are present in a single ray; but heat dries and brightness illuminates. Heat receives one thing and brightness another. Although heat and brightness cannot be separated from one another, brightness receives illumination, not warmth; heat receives warmth, not illumination. They act together in different ways, and yet they are not separated from one another.

So also the Son assumed flesh and did not abandon the Father, nor did he separate himself from the Father. The Son, I say, assumed flesh in the property of his own Person; yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty. There is equality in divinity, but the property of the flesh belongs to the Son alone; the divinity of the Father or the Holy Spirit never departed from him.

Since, therefore, the deity is one and the divinity is one, both the Father and the Holy Spirit filled Christ’s flesh—but by majesty, not by assumption.

Do you wish to know that the Father was with him? The Lord Christ says: “I am not alone; the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

Hear also concerning the Holy Spirit, that he was with him: the Evangelist reports that “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1).

See how Jesus Christ alone assumed flesh, and yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty. If the Father fills heaven and earth, the Holy Spirit also fills them. They could not abandon Christ’s flesh when they remained in the unity of divinity.

Look once more at a lyre. For it to produce a musical melody in sweet sounds, three things appear to be present together: skill, hand, and string. Yet one sound is heard. Skill directs, the hand touches, and the string resounds. Three things work together, but only the string produces the sound that is heard. Neither skill nor hand produces the sound, but they work together with the string.

So neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, yet they work together with the Son. The string alone produces the sound; Christ alone assumed the flesh. The operation consists in three, but just as the production of the sound belongs to the string alone, so the assumption of human flesh belongs to Christ alone.

### 3. The Jew is refuted: the Virgin could give birth

On the other side the Jew says: “A virgin could not give birth, contrary to nature.” And the detestable Manichaean says: “If there was flesh, she could not be a virgin; if a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.”

We must answer both.

I bring forward from the history of the Old Testament a necessary example against the Jew, one that has just sounded in our ears and displays the clearest truth.

The Lord commanded holy Moses to have rods brought from each tribe. Twelve rods were brought, among them also the one belonging to Aaron the priest. Holy Moses placed them in the tabernacle of testimony.

On the following day, Aaron’s rod was suddenly found to have produced flowers and leaves and to have brought forth nuts (Numbers 17:6–8).

It is pleasing to mingle this mystery with your Charity against Jewish unbelief, where the figure of the sacrament is especially present.

Behold, the rod produced what it had not previously possessed: it was not rooted by planting, not dug up by a hoe, not animated by sap, and not fertilized by a seedbed. Yet, when all the laws of nature were absent, the rod produced what could be supplied neither by seed nor by root.

Therefore, could the rod bring forth nuts contrary to nature, but could the virgin not generate the Son of God contrary to the laws of nature?

Let the unbelieving Jew tell me how the dry rod flowered, put forth leaves, and produced nuts; and I will tell him how the virgin conceived and gave birth.

But surely the Jew will be unable to explain either the conception of the rod or the childbirth of the virgin. Let him come to the Church and let it be explained to him, so that he may recognize the true order of natural function.

The virgin completed the periods of childbirth, whereas the rod had no period of budding.

[Variant wording in the supplied text: “The virgin had the periods of childbirth, but the rod produced on another day what nature did not possess.”]

She gave birth after nine months had elapsed; the rod, on another day, germinated what nature had not given it.

The Jew says that nature does not permit a virgin to give birth. But the God who in Numbers displayed a wondrous sign contrary to nature, so that a she-ass might speak (Numbers 22:28), himself wished to do something still more wondrous, so that Christ might be born from a virgin.

### 4. The Virgin’s childbirth is demonstrated against the Manichaean by an analogy

Let that cunning Manichaean hear another sacrament.

A ray of the sun penetrates glass and passes through its solidity with imperceptible subtlety; it appears within just as it is outside. Therefore, brothers, it neither violates the glass when it enters nor shatters it when it leaves, because the glass remains whole both at its entrance and at its departure.

Therefore, if a ray of the sun does not break glass, could the deity, entering or leaving, have violated the Virgin’s integrity?

But why should I linger any longer?

### 5. Aaron’s rod prefigured the Mother of God, and the nuts that grew from it our Savior

Let the Christian hear what the Jew or the Manichaean does not wish to hear, so that the one may advance in faith, redeemed, while the other or the other may fail, hardened.

That rod of which we were speaking, the rod of Aaron, was the Virgin Mary, who conceived and bore for us Christ, the true priest. Of him David sang just now: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” For in the preceding verse he had already said: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion” (Psalm 109:4, 2).

And the prophet Isaiah more clearly designates holy Mary, saying: “A rod will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:1–2).

Therefore, the fact that this rod produced nuts was an image of the Lord’s body.

For a nut has a threefold union of substances in its body: skin, shell, and kernel. In the skin is compared the flesh; in the shell, the bones; in the kernel within, the soul.

The skin of the nut signifies the flesh of the Savior, which bore in itself the harshness or bitterness of the passion. The inner kernel indicates the sweetness of the divinity, which provides nourishment and supplies the function of light.

The shell signifies the wood of the cross, which did not separate what was outside from what was within, but joined earthly and heavenly things through the interposition of the mediator’s wood, as the blessed Apostle says: “For through the blood of his cross he reconciled all things, whether those in heaven or those on earth” (Colossians 1:20).

He lives with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 246

[Note: Formerly *On the Words of the Lord* 58; later, in Appendix 8.]

## On the Mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation, II

[Note: The first part is Augustine’s *Tractate 78 on the Gospel of John*. The latter part, beginning with the words “The Arians object to us,” is by an uncertain author.]

### 1. The Arians object from the statement about Wisdom, “The Lord created me,” etc. The reply: first, this may be understood of the wisdom given to Solomon; second, there are two natures in Christ, united indeed but not confused.

We have received, dearly beloved brothers, the words of the Lord saying to his disciples, “Let not your heart be troubled” (John XIV, 1), etc. [Note: Here the material already found in Treatise 78 on John has been omitted.]

Who would not love Christ in such a way as also to rejoice that his own nature has already become immortal in Christ, and to hope that he himself will one day become this through Christ?

The Arians object to us, asserting that the Son of God is a creature: “What is the meaning of Solomon’s agreement with this, speaking in the person of Christ and saying, ‘The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, in his works; before the age he founded me, at the beginning, before he made the earth, before the springs of waters came forth, before the mountains were established; but before all the hills he begot me’” (Proverbs VIII, 22–25)?

To them we reply as follows. Many highly learned men assert that this was spoken in the person of that wisdom which Solomon received in order to judge and govern the people. But since, with stubborn determination, you demand from us that this be understood as spoken in the person of Christ, we neither resist nor oppose you; strengthened by the help of Truth herself, we follow wherever you lead.

First, as we said above, although we believe Christ to be one person, we nevertheless confess that there are two substances—that is, natures—namely, divinity and humanity, the assuming and the assumed, the creating and the created. Yet these substances are not confused but united, inseparable in one and the same person, while always remaining in their own properties. Therefore what properly belongs to each substance must be assigned to it: weaknesses to the humanity, which was created; signs and miracles to the divinity, which created.

For these two natures have been so united and joined to one another that the same Christ, God and man, sometimes does or speaks things belonging to humanity, and sometimes things belonging to divinity: for example, that he sleeps in the boat and commands the winds and the sea; that he hungers and that he satisfies five thousand men with five loaves and two fish; finally, that he dies and that by divine authority he commands Lazarus, dead for four days, to be recalled from the dead.

### 2. He says that he was created with respect to his human nature, but with respect to his divine nature he existed before every creature.

You should not be surprised, then, if Christ said of his humanity, “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, in his works,” because the statement that follows shows what belongs to his divinity, after the preceding statement has been made. He says:

“Before the age he founded me at the beginning, before he made the earth, and before he made the abysses, before the springs of waters came forth, before the mountains were established; but before all the hills he begot me.”

This is to say: “Although God created me so that I might demonstrate through the Gospel the beginning of his ways and works, yet before the age—that is, before the beginning, before heaven, earth, or times existed—he begot me.” This means that he demonstrated himself to have been begotten by the Father without time and without beginning.

To summarize the whole matter briefly: Christ, the Son of God, God and man, was begotten according to his divinity before the ages, without beginning, ineffably by the Father, as Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8). But at the end of time he was created according to his humanity.

For when the divinity came into the womb of the Virgin Mary, by that same authority by which in paradise he formed Adam from the clay, he fashioned for himself flesh from Mary’s substance. Taking it up for our salvation and uniting it to himself, he was born God and man. Matthew recounts this generation, saying: “Now the generation of Christ was in this manner” (Matthew I, 18), etc.

### 3. They ask, “Was he begotten when he existed, or when he did not exist?” It is shown that he always coexisted with the Father, and how he is distinguished from the Father.

They also habitually construct this poisonous syllogism against us, saying: “If you believe the Son to be coeternal with the Father, tell us, we ask: was he begotten while he existed, or while he did not exist? If while he existed, then there were two unbegotten beings beforehand, and afterward one begot the other; but if, as true reasoning allows, he was begotten while he did not exist, then surely he is later than the Father.”

Regarding this, we need do nothing other than resist the great malice of heretics with apostolic examples, by which worldly wisdom is easily overthrown. When, therefore, they have put the foregoing objections to us, we say:

Just as we know the Father alone to be always and without beginning unbegotten, so we confess the Son to have been always and without beginning begotten from the Father. There is no other cause that distinguishes the persons except that the one is unbegotten and the other begotten—that is, the one is Father and the other Son. The Father is always Father, never Son, because, as we have said, he was not begotten but himself begot. And the Son is always Son, never Father, because he did not beget but was begotten.

### 4. This is illustrated by the example of splendor.

On this subject no one should be summoned into the discussion except the Apostle himself. Foreseeing the malice of Eunomius and Arius, he attempted, through examples drawn from visible things, to explain—so far as the matter itself permitted—the invisible, ineffable, and incomprehensible reality. What does he say about the Son when writing to the Hebrews? “He is,” he says, “the splendor of his glory and the representation of his substance” (Hebrews I, 3).

Let us therefore see why he called the Son “splendor.” For, unless I am mistaken, we speak of splendor only in relation to the sun, the moon, or some other definite light. What, then, does this mean? Are we so insane as to think that the Apostle compared that immeasurable form of divinity to the sun or to fire? Certainly not. Rather, through that example we understand that just as splendor is born from the substance of the sun, so the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father.

Nor is the sun or fire prior to its splendor, although splendor is born from it. From the moment the sun or fire came forth, its splendor appeared together with it; nor can splendor be said to be later than the sun or fire, although, as I have said, it is born from it.

If, then, something is found among created things that is both born and yet is not later than its begetter, why, heretic, do you despair that this can occur with the Creator? Consider another likeness as well. Just as splendor born from the sun fills the whole world, yet is never cut off from or separated from its begetter, so the Son, begotten from the Father, is everywhere and always remains in the Father.

And just as splendor is substantially in the sun, and the sun in the splendor, so substantially the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father. And just as the sun and its splendor have one substance but are not one person—for we neither call the sun “splendor” nor splendor “the sun,” since we know that the sun begot splendor and that splendor was born from the sun—so the Father and the Son, although they are of one essence, are not one person, as we have already fully explained above.

And just as through its splendor the sun warms, illuminates, dries, loosens, whitens, blackens, and accomplishes everything that has been entrusted to it by God, so we read that the Father has accomplished all things through his only-begotten Son.

### 5. They maintain that he was created, not begotten. If this were so, he would be a servant and should not be worshiped. The worship of Christ’s body.

“They say,” they insist, “that the Son was created by the Father, not begotten.”

The brief answer is this: if he was created, then he is certainly also a servant, because everything that is created must serve its Creator. And if the Son is a servant, how, being in the form of God, did he take the form of a servant (Philippians II, 7)? A servant cannot take the form of a servant.

They also say that the Son is not God by nature but a creature. To such questions we must give our customary answer: if the Son is not God by nature but a creature, then he should not be worshiped at all or adored as God, since the Apostle says, “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Romans I, 25); and again, in the Letter to the Galatians: “At that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods” (Galatians IV, 8).

But they will reply to this and say: “What of the fact that you adore his flesh—which you do not deny to be a creature—together with his divinity, and serve it no less than the divinity?”

I adore the Lord’s flesh, or rather the perfect humanity in Christ, for this reason: it was assumed by the divinity and united to the Godhead, so that I may confess not two different beings but one and the same Son of God, God and man.

Finally, if you separate the man from God, as Photinus or Paul of Samosata did, I will never believe in or serve that man. Suppose one of us found a purple robe or a royal diadem lying on the ground. Would he attempt to worship these objects? But once the king had put them on, he would incur the danger of death if he refused to worship them together with the king. So likewise, if anyone refuses to worship in Christ the Lord the humanity—not by itself or naked, but united to his divinity—as the one Son of God, true God and true man, he will suffer the penalty of eternal death.

[Note: Here some manuscripts add: “as do certain of your people, such as Photinus,” etc.]

### SERMON CCXLVII

[Note: Formerly, *On the Saints* 19; later placed in the Appendix as 75.]

## Why Christ Was Born and Suffered

[Note: In an old German manuscript it appears among the sermons of Ivo of Chartres, under whose name it was formerly published.]

### 1. Wisdom could have brought humanity back to himself by power, but preferred to accomplish this gently. This was the reason for assuming humanity, yet it did not diminish him.

The Creator of the world willed, by a secret and wondrous plan, to repair through the mystery of the incarnate Word the fall of that same world, corrupted by original and actual sins. He who by that word was able to create all things from nothing was able also to reform what had been lost. “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm XXXII, 9).

We do not believe that his power was diminished or altered, for with him there is “no change or shadow of alteration” (James I, 17), so that he was no less powerful and wise in restoring than he had been in forming.

The hand of the omnipotent potter, whose every way is mercy and truth (Psalm XXIV, 10), had raised clay taken from the earth to the dignity of rational nature. He therefore willed to restore the ruin of the fragile vessel in such a way that he would neither leave human sin unpunished, because he is just, nor leave it incurable, because he is merciful.

If he had been only just—he whose wisdom “reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things gently” (Wisdom VIII, 1)—he could by his strength have contended against the seducer of the human race and restored the lost sheep to his flock and dominion.

But in that manner he would have seemed merely to display the greatness of his power, rather than to show medicinal mercy to the redeemed. Nor would it have appeared with what love the Creator loved the creature, from whom he sought to be loved through manifold benefits, so that wretched humanity, grace preceding, might obtain by merit what had been undeservedly bestowed upon it despite its evil deserts.

What the wisdom of God could have done wisely and powerfully, he wished to do gently, uniting to himself the weakness of our flesh, which he would first heal in himself, and through this medicinal preparation restore health to the human race. This was not because the matter could not have been accomplished otherwise, so far as the skill and power of the Physician were concerned, but because no more suitable antidote could be provided, so far as the constitution of the sick person was concerned.

“For what is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians I, 25).

This seems to us the particular reason why the Son of God wished to assume humanity and dwell among human beings: so that, by dying, he might overcome the mortality he received from us, and bring our nature, restored above the dignity of its first origin, with himself back to immortality; so that the humility of the flock might follow where the exalted Shepherd had gone before.

Thus the ray of the sun dries the moisture it draws to itself, yet neither diminishes nor alters the power of its heat and radiance. Thus fire converts the material it assumes into itself, but for that reason neither changes nor diminishes its own nature.

Much more powerfully, that fire of which it is said, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy IV, 24), assumed and consumed our mortality and capacity for suffering; and from it the whole body recovered the grace of health.

What a wondrous and incomparable kind of medicine, by which the Physician wished to become sick, and resolved to heal the sick—those for whom he was preparing the remedy of salvation—through his own weakness.

### 2. He added nothing to himself, for he needed nothing of ours.

Here it becomes clear with what incomparable love he loved us: in seeking his deserters, taking hold of the seed of Abraham, bringing back the wanderers, and healing the wounded, he added nothing to himself. He did not thereby become higher; he did not thereby become more blessed.

This entire dispensation served our benefit and our salvation; it contributed nothing to divine power. For even when we were vessels of dishonor, we could not escape the hand of the omnipotent potter. He used vessels of wrath as he wished for the manifestation of his glory. Thus it was said to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Exodus IX, 19).

Did not even the demons, when they were driven by the Lord from possessed bodies, glorify the Lord when they said, “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of the living God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew VIII, 29).

It is therefore clear from these and similar examples that divine power had no need of our restoration. Yet in the same goodness by which he created us, he wished also to reform us; and for this medicine he applied not the strongest remedy he could have used, but the gentlest one he saw to be suitable for the constitution of the sick.

### 3. Christ’s analogy with a skilled physician.

Those skilled in medicine commonly treat the illnesses they undertake to cure sometimes by opposites and sometimes by similars. Our Lord Jesus Christ did this, enriching us by his poverty, lifting us up by his humility, healing us by his weakness, and giving us life by his death.

In medical treatment, dry things are opposed to moist, moist to dry, hot to cold; and weaker opposites are overcome by the stronger opposites that come against them. In a similar way, similars are applied to similars when, according to the size of wounds or swellings, the length or breadth of poultices is proportioned.

Thus scorpion flesh cooked in oil heals scorpion stings. Thus theriac, prepared from a serpent’s flesh, counters serpent bites and expels from the body, when taken as a potion, the poisons introduced through drinking.

Following this likeness, our Physician healed by the death of his flesh the death of our flesh that came from the serpent, and restored it so that, at the appointed time, it might attain the likeness of his immortality.

Here we must observe particularly that the death which came through wood was overcome through wood. The form of the wood itself was fashioned according to the length, breadth, and height of the human body. Just as the whole body had moved when the hands were extended toward what was forbidden, so the body was stretched out in all its members upon the cross, and everything that had been broken by the guilt of the ancestral transgression was made firm again by the kneading of this poultice.

Yet to this medicine, compounded from similars, another medicine made from opposites was also added. Obedience healed what disobedience had corrupted there; and the torment of the cross here restored what the pleasure of the appetite had contaminated there.

### 4. The mystical figure of the cross.

A deeper sacrament is contained in the figure of the cross. The higher it is, the more carefully it must be considered.

In the breadth of the cross is understood love of neighbor—not merely love extending to friends, but also extending to those who are to be loved as enemies. In its length is understood the long and persevering endurance of labors and persecutions, which our pilgrimage, longing for its homeland, must patiently bear, both for love of our neighbors and for the performance of every good work.

In its height, by the same reasoning, is figured the elevation of hope, penetrating to the interior of the veil. There those who here are harassed in many ways by the citizens of Babylon will enjoy the vision of peace, until they are freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

The Lord Jesus signified this breadth of charity on the cross by raising his head toward the east, lowering his feet toward the west, and extending his hands toward the north and south, fulfilling what he had foretold about himself before his passion: “When I have been lifted up from the earth”—that is, when I have been crucified—“I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32), that is, “I will summon the whole world to myself.”

Through this sacrament of the cross, the holy Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite woman by praying, applying his mouth to the child’s mouth and his hands to the child’s hands, and restored him alive to his mother (2 Kings IV, 34).

By the power of this same sacrament, Moses struck the rock twice with his staff in the desert and brought water from the rock for the thirsty people (Numbers XX, 11). The double striking is figuratively understood as the two beams joined together in the cross.

The rock is struck twice when Christ—of whom the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X, 4)—is stretched out upon the two beams of the cross and pierced by the lance. Water flowed from this rock when the blood of redemption and the water of baptism, by which we are transformed into the new man, flowed from Christ’s side.

### 5. Above all, the depth. The mystery of our restoration. God is just in condemning humanity and merciful in redeeming it. He would have been unjust if he had restored the unrepentant.

Among these dimensions of the cross, its depth must also be carefully considered. The mystery of the cross is profound, and in it the intellects of many who were called wise have failed. They dared to criticize what they could not comprehend by human reason: namely, why the Word coeternal with God the Father, containing and filling all things, enclosed himself wholly in the humanity he assumed, and yet did not cease to rule, fill, and contain the whole world.

They did not sufficiently consider that what is possible in the lesser can much more be possible in the greater, since one voice proceeds whole from the mouth of the speaker and reaches whole the ears of many people.

Those who debate this question too scrupulously, and who, like people feeling along a wall before a closed door, grope about in uncertainty, should first hear the Apostle say, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans IX, 20).

Then let them grow gentler and knock with piety, so that the door may be opened to them. They will understand that the Creator was just in condemning and merciful in redeeming, and that what the justice of the Almighty had justly condemned could not be healed without mercy.

From this they will consequently perceive why divine omnipotence humbled itself even to the poverty of captive humanity and the disgrace of the cross—the same omnipotence that had justly condemned guilty humanity in paradise.

When Adam was accused by the Lord of the disobedience he had committed, he did not humbly accuse himself, as his guilt required. Instead, he arrogantly accused the author of his existence, saying, “The woman whom you gave me gave me of the fruit, and I ate” (Genesis III, 12).

By saying this, he thought himself excused and blamed the Creator and maker of the woman who had drawn the man into sin. [Note: Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition have this passage as follows: “By saying this, he thought himself excused, and thus brought the creator and maker of the woman who had drawn the man into sin into culpability.” M.]

If he had humbly accused himself and had not shifted the blame onto his Creator, he would not have been exiled from paradise.

It would have been contrary to divine justice to restore a guilty and unrepentant person to his former state without compelling him by some fitting means to produce the fruit of repentance. Thus, by divine sentence, he was condemned to death; together with all the posterity that would proceed from his loins, he was expelled from paradise and condemned to a painful exile.

Since he could not return to his former state without repentance, he had to be moved and admonished toward repentance, so that voluntary and submissive humility might restore what wrongly exalted iniquity had corrupted.

It was not fitting that one who had fallen voluntarily into punishment should be dragged unwillingly into repentance, lest he should likewise prove ungrateful for his restoration, just as he had been ungrateful for his original creation.

### 6. How he prepared him for this grace.

A medicine was therefore provided that suited the sick person: one that would soften the hardness of the swelling so that, once softened, it might voluntarily pour out its deadly poison. Thus the Psalmist says, “Pour out your hearts before him” (Psalm LXI, 9)—that is, by confession cast out from your consciences everything unclean.

As long as the world delayed doing this, it remained unclean.

To bring this about, our Physician sent his heralds and witnesses before him—lawgivers and prophets—to prepare the hearts of their hearers for repentance and to bear witness to him in the time of grace.

The Physician himself came in the fullness of time and publicly proclaimed the reason for his coming. Having become a teacher of medicine, he said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew III, 2); and again, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI, 16).

Many accepted this prescription of the medicine; many rejected it. For those who rejected it, the hiss of the deadly serpent pleased them more than the persuasion of the redeeming Physician. But the adopted son heard and obeyed the voice of the one who made the promise, although in paradise he had not obeyed the command that threatened death.

When the dispensation of his teaching had been completed, and blindness in Israel still persisted in part, he finally presented himself as physician and made himself the medicine. He presented himself as priest and made himself the sacrifice, so that he might complete what he had come to do and prove with what love he had loved those for whom he offered his body on the altar of the cross.

Therefore, in his Gospel he had foretold: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13).

This is why the Apostle says, “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were enemies, he reconciled us to himself through the death of his Son” (Romans V, 8).

Since it is natural for people who love others to be loved by them, through this humility and charity the hardness of the world was humbled and melted, so that it might recognize the benefit of its restoration, which had not recognized the excellence of its creation.

Thus the Psalmist says, “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII, 13).

But after humanity returned to itself and, through the love of the Redeemer and the instruction of the admonisher, recognized from what great glory it had fallen and in what misery it found itself, it discovered that it greatly needed mercy. And the saying of the Psalmist was fulfilled: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Psalm XV, 4).

### 7. The use and power of the cross.

From that time onward the power of the cross was proclaimed throughout the whole world. It was extended through its parts to the four regions of the world and embraced the entire world in its healing application.

The world could no longer remain wholly ungrateful, having been healed by such great love.

Our Crucified One rose from death and ascended into heaven. He left us the cross as a memorial of his passion; he left the cross for our healing.

By this sign demons are put to flight; by this antidote healings are accomplished. This sign is protection for friends and an obstacle to enemies.

Through the mystery of this cross catechumens are instructed; by the same mystery the font of regeneration is consecrated; through the sign of this cross, baptized people receive the gifts of grace by the laying on of hands.

With the mark of this same cross basilicas are dedicated, altars are consecrated, and the Sacraments of the altar are celebrated with the Lord’s words interposed. Through this same sign priests and levites are advanced to the sacred orders. In general, all ecclesiastical sacraments are accomplished by its power.

Whoever wishes to cross without shipwreck this great and spacious sea, in which are reptiles without number (Psalm CIII, 25), should follow the cross, hold fast to the cross, and not abandon it until he reaches the desired harbor of salvation.

The cross directs our course; it trains us for the contest; it helps us in the struggle; it leads us to victory; it brings us to the crown; it destroys magical arts and reduces all the schemes of demons to nothing.

What the bodily presence of Christ accomplished on earth, the memory of the victorious cross, marked by faithful invocation of Christ’s name, now accomplishes.

It would take too long to explain individually the power of the cross. Whoever bears the cross in the service of Christ will be able to learn by experience more about its power than speech can recount or human thought can comprehend.

### SERMON CCXLVIII

[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 133.]

## On the Lord’s Burial

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave its authenticity doubtful. Verlinus and Vindingus, however, observe that it is a cento, composed partly from the final section of Ambrose’s Sermon 52, *On the Cross*, and entirely from his Sermon 53, *On the Lord’s Tomb*. These two sermons were also published under the name of Maximus. The sentences attributed to Ambrose, who is credited with them in the Theoderic manuscript, contain several passages from his commentaries on Luke. For section 3, see Ambrose on Luke chapter 23; for section 5, the same author on Luke chapter 24.]

### 1. The Lord’s tomb is like a womb; hence he is born from it more gloriously than from his mother.

Let us see, brothers, what happened to the Lord’s body after it was taken down from the cross.

Joseph of Arimathea, a just man, received it, as the Evangelist says, and buried it in his own new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid (John XIX, 38–42).

Blessed, therefore, is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ: when he is born, he is brought forth from a virgin’s womb; when he departs, he is entrusted to the tomb of a just man. Truly blessed is the body that virginity bore and justice guarded.

Joseph’s tomb guarded it incorrupt, just as Mary’s womb preserved it undefiled. For just as it was not touched by pollution there, so it was not harmed by the corruption of death here.

Everywhere holiness is rendered to the blessed body; everywhere there is virginity. A new womb conceived him; a new tomb enclosed him.

The Lord’s womb, therefore, is virgin, and his burial is virgin. Indeed, I would call the burial itself a womb, for the likeness is considerable.

Just as the Lord came forth alive from his mother’s womb, so he rose alive from Joseph’s burial. And just as he was then born from the womb to preach, so now he was reborn from the tomb to evangelize—except that this birth is more glorious than the former.

The former brought forth a mortal body; the latter produced an immortal one. After the former birth there was a descent into the lower regions; after this one there is a return to heaven.

This birth is plainly more sacred than the former. The former held the Lord of the whole world enclosed in the womb for nine months; the latter guarded him only three days in the bosom of the tomb. The former brought forth the hope of all more slowly; the latter raised the salvation of all more quickly.

### 2. Joseph’s likeness to the Lord’s mother.

Perhaps someone may object to the earlier preaching of the Lord’s birth, in which we declared that it is no less glorious that Joseph’s tomb raised the Lord than that the womb of holy Mary brought him forth: “What comparison can there be between a womb and a tomb, when the one brought forth a son from its innermost organs, while the other merely supplied a place for burial?”

But I say that Joseph’s devotion was no less than Mary’s. She conceived the Lord in her womb; he conceived him in his heart. She offered the Savior the secrecy of her limbs; he did not deny him the secrecy of his heart. She wrapped the Lord in cloths when he was born; he wrapped him in linen when he departed. She anointed the blessed body with oil; he honored it with spices.

Their services therefore correspond, and their devotion corresponds. Consequently, their merit must also correspond—except that an angel instructed Mary to perform her service, whereas justice alone persuaded Joseph.

Joseph, therefore, placed the Lord in his own tomb.

### 3. Joseph placed the Lord more truly in the tomb of his heart. The spiritual tomb of Christ.

We read in the prophet, “Their throat is an open tomb” (Psalm V, 11).

If the throat of human beings is an open tomb, then perhaps, according to this likeness, Joseph placed the Lord not so much in an earthly burial as in the monument of his own heart. He received him to be guarded not by the fragile memory of the dead [Note: Manuscripts read “of builders”], but by the holy memory of virtues.

For this is the faithful memory of virtues: containing Christ within itself, it does not permit him to be harmed by the corruption of heretics.

Concerning this memory, the Lord says in the sacraments [Note: Manuscripts read “in the sacred Scriptures”], “Whenever you do this, you will do it in remembrance of me until I come” (1 Corinthians XI, 26).

Whenever we speak of Christ, we entrust him to a holier memory. The prophet therefore rightly says that the throat of human beings is an open tomb.

The open tomb of Christ is the blessed throat of the Evangelists, through which they committed him to the everlasting treasure of letters. It is called an open tomb because whoever wishes to reach the mystery of Christ enters it only through the hidden meaning of evangelical Scripture.

In the secrecy of the written words [Note: Manuscripts read “of the holy writings”; Ambrose has “in the sanctuary”], the Lord has been entrusted, as it were, to a new vessel. Whoever desires to see him will find there both the mystery of his passion and the glory of his resurrection.

The throat of the saints is therefore open. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (2 Corinthians VI, 11), inviting them to enter through the open door of his preaching into the secret mysteries of Christ.

In this memory of the heart, then, Joseph places the Lord, so that he may rest in the seat of justice and that the Son of Man may have a place to lay his head.

### 4. Why the Lord was placed in another man’s tomb.

Let us therefore see why the Savior was placed in another man’s burial and did not have a burial of his own.

He was placed in another’s burial because he was dying for the salvation of others. This death did not happen to him for his own sake; it benefits us. This death was not inflicted upon him for his own sake; it was bestowed upon us.

Why, then, should he have a burial of his own, who did not possess death as his own? Why should he have a tomb on earth, whose dwelling remained in heaven? Why should he have a burial, who for only three days did not so much lie dead in a tomb as rest there as in a bed?

The brevity of the time itself shows that this was sleep rather than death. A tomb is the dwelling place of death. A dwelling place of death was therefore not necessary for Christ, who is life; nor did the One who lives forever need the dwelling place of the dead.

Rightly, however, we place this life in our tomb, so that he may give life to our death and that we may rise from the dead with him.

### 5. Mary Magdalene prophesies without knowing it.

For this reason Mary Magdalene, who sought the Lord in the tomb among the other dead, is reproved and told, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” That is: “Why do you seek in a tomb the one whom you ought to adore in heaven? Why do you seek among the dead the one who has already plainly returned to the living?”

Still not understanding or recognizing him, she answered him, “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him away” (John XX, 15).

For she thought, as Scripture says, that he was the gardener.

Thus the holy and simple woman seeks Christ from Christ and prophesies through the devotion of her mind without knowing it. She says to the Lord concerning himself, “If you have taken him away, tell me.”

She rightly asks, “If you have taken him away.” For the one who brought his body forth from the tomb himself took it away; the one who gathered up his body as it lay sleeping by his breath himself took it away; the one who carried his body, bearing it by the power of his divinity, to the heavens himself took it away.

And therefore the woman wisely asks and seeks, “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him”—that is, “If, taking it from the tomb, you have transferred it to paradise.”

For she had heard him say to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). Or certainly, if you have placed him at the Father’s right hand after bringing him out of the lower regions, as the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians III, 1).

Blessed, therefore, is the person who seeks Christ the Lord in such a way as to believe that he is established both in paradise and in the heavenly places. For whoever seeks him in the lower regions or in a tomb is told, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?”

### SERMON CCXLIX

[Note: Elsewhere, *On Time* 67.]

## On the Last Judgment, I

[Note: It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. To the Louvain editors it was doubtful; to Verlinus and Vindingus it was spurious. For us it is unquestionably a work of Caesarius, not of Augustine. Nor does the name of Bishop Sedatus, under which this sermon appears in an old Ottobeuren Lectionary, seem to designate anyone other than Caesarius. For section 1, see Caesarius, Homily 15 and 26, and above, Appendix Sermon 174, section 1; below, 257, section 4. For section 2, Sermon 10, section 5, and 28, section 4. For section 5, above, Sermon 140, section 4. For section 6, below, Sermon 260, section 2; and above, 173, section 3; and below, 252, section 3.]

### 1. A Priest Must Not Seek to Preach What Is Pleasing; He Must Conduct Himself Like a Physician

I beg you, dearest brothers, and with great humility I admonish you, that none of you be angry with me or perhaps judge me inappropriate and excessive because I strive so frequently to bring before you the dreadful day of judgment, which it is useful to fear. For if there is anyone whom I perhaps displease in this respect, let him consider my danger and hear the Lord terribly threatening the priest through the Prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III, 18); and again: “Cry out,” he says, “do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce their crimes to my people” (Isa. LVIII, 1).

But perhaps someone says: “Why are such harsh things continually preached to us?” Because it is better to endure a little bitterness here and afterward arrive at eternal sweetness than to have false joy here and there endure punishment without end. Hear, brothers, not me but the Lord speaking in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5); and: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI, 25).

And consider this, brothers: whenever ordinary physicians come to those who appear to be sick in body, they cut away everything that seemed pleasurable to them and completely forbid what is sweet. Sometimes they do not even permit them to take anything cold [Note: According to Er., Lugd., and Ven., *frigidam* (“anything cold,” feminine). M.]; at times they force them to drink the most bitter potions and frequently cut their wounds with the harshest instruments. What ordinary physicians do for the health of bodies, therefore, spiritual physicians strive to do for the salvation of souls.

### 2. He Will Have to Give an Account of His Own Salvation and That of the Peoples

Reflecting on these things, dearest brothers, and knowing that I shall have to give an account before the tribunal of the eternal Judge both for my salvation and for yours, I choose to administer to you medicines that are indeed harsh but salutary, so that afterward I may deserve to rejoice with you in perpetual health in the company of the angels.

I do not offer these exhortations because I have found you unwilling to receive our admonitions; but because I must preach more frequently both for your salvation and for mine, I strive to stir your hearts both to fear judgment and to desire the reward, so that, as you have always done with the Lord’s help, you may faithfully prepare the receptacle of your holy hearts for storing the spiritual harvest.

Whenever we preach something difficult to you, we do not say it because we suspect that you do such a thing; rather, we announce again the things you do not do so that we may heal those in which you may perhaps have been caught unawares. For it often happens that, while greater dangers are feared, lesser ones are avoided more quickly. Just as theriac is drunk so that poisons may not prevail against the body, so this is accomplished through austere preaching, by which antidotes for souls are prepared.

### 3. Remembering God’s Benefits Is a Defense against Sins

It is certain, dearest brothers, that if we continually reflect upon all the benefits of our God, which have been bestowed upon us without any preceding merits of ours, our sins either do not rule over us or, if they have perhaps crept in, are quickly corrected through repentance.

Who could even conceive in his mind, let alone express in words, how great are the benefits of our God toward us? He made us when we did not exist; afterward he restored us when we had perished. He accepted death, freed us with his precious blood, descended to the underworld, snatched us from the jaws of eternal death, and even promised us the rewards of heaven.

As we piously and kindly reflect upon all these things, dearest brothers, let us hasten, insofar as we can and with his help, to repay his benefits in kind. Let us not return evil for good; rather, insofar as we can, let us faithfully strive to obey his will, relying upon all our strength so that his commandments may bring us the remedy of following them rather than judgment for transgressing them.

### 4. What Account Will Be Demanded from These People on the Day of Judgment

The sinner imposes upon Christ a cross heavier than the first.

What shall we do, dearest brothers, on that fearful day of judgment, when, with the world trembling and the trumpets of the angels sounding beforehand, the Lord will sit surrounded by the light of the heavenly host upon the throne of his majesty? There, after the human race has been raised from the bosom of the earth and the ancient dust, with the testimony of each person’s conscience standing present, and with the punishments of sinners and the rewards of the righteous set before his eyes, he will begin to demand an account of life. Then, already more just than merciful, in the severity of a judge he will begin to accuse those guilty of having despised mercy, saying:

“I, O human being, made you from clay with my hands. I infused spirit into your earthly limbs. I deigned to bestow upon you our image and likeness. I placed you amid the delights of paradise. Yet, despising the life-giving commandments, you preferred to follow the deceiver rather than God.

“When, expelled from paradise and held by the bonds of death because of sin, you had fallen under condemnation, I entered the virginal womb to be born without diminishing virginity. Exposed in a manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes, I lay there. I endured the humiliations of infancy and the human sufferings by which I might become like you, in order, of course, to make you like me. I received the blows and spittle of those who mocked me; I drank vinegar mixed with gall. Beaten with whips, crowned with thorns, fastened to the cross, pierced by a wound, I surrendered my soul amid torments so that you might be rescued from death.

“Behold the marks of the nails with which I was fastened and hung; behold my side pierced by wounds. I accepted your sufferings in order to give you glory; I accepted your death so that you might live forever. I lay buried in a tomb so that you might reign in heaven.

“Why did you squander what I endured for you? Why, ungrateful one, did you reject the gifts of your redemption? I do not ask you to repay me for my death; give me your life, for which I gave mine. Give me your life, which you continually kill through the wounds of sins.

“Why did you pollute with the filth of lust the dwelling that I had consecrated to myself in you? Why did you stain my body with the disgrace of sensual pleasures? Why have you afflicted me with the heavier cross of your crimes than that on which I once hung? For, in my sight, the cross of your sins, on which I hang unwillingly, is heavier than the one upon which, in pity for you, I ascended in order to kill your death.

“Although I was incapable of suffering, I deigned to suffer for you; but you despised God in a human being, salvation in weakness, return in the way, forgiveness in the judge, life on the cross, and healing in punishments. And because, after all your evils, you were unwilling to flee to the remedies of repentance, you shall not deserve to be delivered from the evil report.”

### 5. The Punishment of the Damned; Repentance Must Be Undertaken While We Are Here

What then will be the gnashing of teeth, when the multitude of the saints has been separated to the king’s right hand and to glory, while the people of sin, plunged into the depths of Tartarus without any hope of mercy or pardon, see themselves shut out by their own darkness from the blessed light of the saints? Descending without end into the bosom of the abyss, with the pit pressing its mouth upon them, they will behold eternal punishments and perpetual death without dying.

In vain will he ask mercy from the poor man whom he despised in this life; in vain will he beg that the tip of Lazarus’s finger be placed upon his burning lips to cool them. How the wretched man will wish, when he sees the glory of the poor, that he had once endured the harsh labors of poverty and borne in that life the evils that die together with life, lest he deserve to reach those eternal punishments!

Therefore, so that we may not deserve to hear such harsh and terrifying things before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, let us, while it is still permitted and while, with God’s help, it lies within our power, examine our consciences. If we recognize that any crimes or mortal sins not yet cleansed by almsgiving and prayers still rule over us, let us hasten, with Christ’s help, to enter the harbor of repentance after overcoming the waves of sin.

And if we recognize that anything in the little boat of our soul has been broken by pride, torn by greed, or loosened by lust amid the many storms of sin, let us hasten to mend or repair it by good works. Let us strive continually to empty the bilge of our vices. For past sins do not harm us if present sins do not please us.

Just as the righteousness of no righteous person is sufficient for him if he does not persevere to the end, so the iniquity of no sinner can harm him if, before he departs from this body, he flees to the remedies of almsgiving or the medicines of repentance.

### 6. Repentance Must Not Be Postponed by Anyone; The Religious Habit

Since we cannot know when or at what hour we shall be snatched from this world, let us hasten, without any delay or hesitation, to flee from the left hand to the right. We must not trust in health or age. One who is always uncertain of his life must not always be slow to seek the remedy of his salvation [Note: Perhaps it should be read as below, Sermon 260, §2: “For he is always slow to seek the remedy of his salvation who …”; or as that manuscript has it: “Let him not always be slow to seek the remedy of his salvation who is uncertain of his life …”].

For the one who made us secure by saying, “On the day when the sinner turns, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion” (Ezek. XVIII, 21–22), also wanted us to be cautious, saying: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclus. V, 8).

If, when we generally call everyone to repentance, someone perhaps thinks within himself: “I am a young man with a wife; how can I cut my hair or assume the religious habit?”—we do not say this, dearest brothers, nor do we preach that young men who appear to be married should change their habit rather than their conduct.

What harm does it do a married man if he wishes to turn his depraved conduct toward good and honorable works, and strives to restore the wounds of his sins to their former health through almsgiving, fasting, and prayers? True conversion is sufficient without changing one’s clothing; religious clothing, however, without good works will not only be unable to provide a remedy but will also incur God’s just judgment.

Let us therefore turn toward better things while the remedies remain in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life through the merits of a life well lived; through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCL

[Note: Otherwise, On the Saints 39.]

### On the Final Judgment, II

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. In the Leuven edition it is uncertain; in the judgment of Verlin and Vinding it is spurious. Its manner of expression seems more similar to Caesarian style than to Augustinian style. On §1, see the following sermon.]

[Col. 2209]

### 1. Pursuits of a Depraved Life; Explanation of the Parable of the Weeds

Let us reconsider, dearest brothers, all the evils we have done, so that, terrified by the threats of the eternal Judge, we may at least at the last strive to do good. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

We must also consider this, dearest brothers: on that day God will repay each person according to his works—good things to the good, evil things to the wicked. He will send the good into eternal life, the wicked into eternal fire. Woe to the person who will have his dwelling with the devil.

Let us consider that this kingdom has an end; the kingdom of God has no end. This laborious, passing, fragile life, full of scandals and envy—what else does it seek except to eat, drink, become drunk, indulge in lust, and engage in slander? Certainly, wherever we wish to remain, there we must hasten.

Brothers, we are pilgrims in this world. Let us turn to the Lord who made us. Brothers, you have heard that the Lord will come to take vengeance and will send sinners into eternal fire, as he says in the Psalm: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Ps. LXVII, 2).

But let us hear what he will say to his own on that day: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV, 34). And the righteous shall reign without end with Christ, as it says: “Let the righteous feast and rejoice in the sight of God” (Ps. LXVII, 4).

“Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, did the weeds appear?” And he said to them: “An enemy has done this.” “First gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to be burned.”

This harvest is the human race, to be gathered for judgment at the consummation of the age. The weeds are sinners; the enemy is the devil, who sowed sins over the seed; the reapers are the angels, who separate the righteous from sinners.

“Bind them into bundles”—that is, rapacious people with rapacious people, adulterers with adulterers, fornicators with fornicators, murderers with murderers, greedy people with greedy people, angry people with angry people, false witnesses with false witnesses, thieves with thieves, mockers with mockers, like with like. These are the bundles to be burned.

“But gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. XIII, 27–30)—that is, send the righteous into paradise.

### 2. Exhortation to Repentance and Good Works; Confession and Penance Imposed by Priests; Almsgiving from Plunder

Brothers, we must be terrified and afraid of such short satisfaction and such long hunger, of such long darkness and such brief light. While we have time, let us turn to the Lord who made us, so that we may not deserve to enter those darknesses but rather the light; for every person whose works he performs is his child.

If we do God’s works, we are God’s children. What we are now doing wrongly, we must quickly correct, and we must not add sins to sins. Hence the Psalmist says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Ps. LXVIII, 28).

Let us seek confession with a pure heart, and complete the penance granted by the priests. Do not store anger in your hearts, because when we carry anger, neither offering nor prayer is received by God.

Give alms; receive strangers into your homes; wash their feet and prepare their beds; comfort those who grieve. Do not despise strangers, because you yourselves are strangers. Do not defraud your brother in business, because God is judge.

Do not oppress the poor, widows, or orphans. Do not make alms out of the plunder of the poor: the one who loses grieves, while the one who acquires rejoices; he gains money and loses his soul. He pays attention to what he acquires and does not pay attention to what he loses.

Brothers, with the Lord’s help, while we have time, let us labor, so that we may repent of our evils through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, prayers, or charity; that we may deserve to reach the heavenly kingdoms, where there is satisfaction without hunger, light without darkness, youth without old age, rest without labor, and joy without end.

May he who created us help us to reach the heavenly kingdoms, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON CCLI

[Note: Otherwise, On the Saints 40.]

### On the Final Judgment, III

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It was uncertain to the Leuven editors, but Verlin and Vinding considered it spurious. It is part of a sermon attributed to Ambrose, 33, *On the Future Judgment*, for the Monday after the First Sunday of Lent. It also occupied a place among the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert*, as number sixty-three. It seems to have the same author as the preceding sermon. See the preceding sermon, §1.]

O dearest brothers, how greatly we must fear that day on which our Lord Jesus Christ, the redeemer of all, has announced that he will come with a flame of fire, which will set his adversaries and those who commit iniquity ablaze!

On that day all the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and exalted majesty (Matt. XXIV, 30). All the ends of the earth will be shaken before him; sinners will perish; heaven will be folded up; the sea will dry up; and the mountains will burn like wax (Ps. XCVI, 5). The earth will burn even to the underworld.

The sun will be turned into darkness, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven to earth, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, namely, the cross of Christ, by whose light the whole world will be darkened.

Then the saints will fly to meet Christ in the air, and so they will always be with the Lord; but sinners will be confounded and will perish. And then judgment will take place.

Then our Lord Jesus Christ will come and send his angels from the four corners of the earth, and they will gather his elect from the summit of the heavens to their farthest boundaries (Matt. XXIV, 29–31). Then the Lord will separate his saints from among sinners and send them into heavenly dwellings; but sinners into the furnace of burning fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Woe to those people who will have their dwelling with the devil. “The smoke of their torments shall rise forever and ever” (Rev. XIV, 11), “where their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI, 24).

There is no voice there except groaning; no rest except fire; no refreshment except flame; no light will ever be seen, only darkness; and they will never come into remembrance before God. Their food is torment, and their dwelling is with the devil, where there is no visitation except darkness.

O human being who desires to possess the kingdom of God, correct what you have done wrongly while you can. While you have time, cry out to almighty God. While opportunity is given, mourn; while permission remains, repent. Hasten while you can; weep while your soul still dwells in the body.

While you still live, obtain a remedy for yourself before the deep snare of punishments swallows you, before hell seizes you—where no pardon is granted, where there is no recourse to confession, and no return to forgiveness.

May the merciful Lord deign to rescue us from that punishment, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLII

[Note: Otherwise, 16 among the Fifty Homilies.]

### An Admonition That God Should Be Praised Not Only with the Tongue but Also in Conduct and Works, Since What Is Conceived in the Heart Is of the Same Kind as What Proceeds in Action; Also Concerning the Purgatorial Punishments and the Pit of Hell

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. The Leuven editors left it uncertain among the Augustinian works; Verlin and Vinding wish it removed, although they do not consider it bad. The latter part, which is also found in Eusebius’s *Homily 3, On the Epiphany*, belongs to Caesarius; the former part belongs to Augustine, extracted from his exposition of Psalm 148, apparently through Caesarius’s own care and effort. The title of the sermon, corresponding to both parts, indeed reflects Caesarius’s character. It is also reported concerning Caesarius that this apostolic man not only fulfilled the ministry of preaching God’s word himself, insofar as he was able, but also arranged for the homilies of Ambrose, Augustine, and himself to be read in church by priests and deacons; indeed, he supplied sermons on various subjects to many provinces within and beyond Gaul. On §1, see the exposition of Psalm 148, §§1–2; and above, Sermon 29, §4, and Sermon 116; see also Caesarius’s Homily 27.]

### 1. We Must Always Do Good Here, Lest We Later Repent in Vain of Having Done Evil

The resurrection and glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, shows us the life that we shall receive when he comes to repay fitting things to those who deserve them, and so forth. [Note: Here repeat the omitted passage from the exposition of Psalm 148, §§1–2.]

And if there is still groaning, temptation, and tribulation, hope in the fact that all these things are passing, and in that day which will come, when we shall praise without weakness. Meanwhile, until that day comes on which we may deserve to praise God together with the angels without any weariness and without any end, let us strive, insofar as we can, to persevere in good works, so that we may reach that unspeakable joy.

Let us look within each day at our consciences. If we recognize that something in the garment of our soul has been ripped through negligence, soiled through lust, burned through anger, torn through envy, or darkened through greed, let us hasten, while it is still in our power and with God’s help, to heal what has been wounded, repair what has been lost, and restore to the brightness of righteousness whatever has been darkened.

Otherwise, if we come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge naked of good works and wrapped in the filthy rags of vices, perhaps that terrifying sentence will be directed against us: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

Therefore, insofar as we can, let us strive to bring forth fruits of righteousness, fearing what the Lord said: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10). This sentence clearly shows that not only will having done evil be damnable, but also having failed to do good.

Let us therefore continually reflect upon what we have said with attentive hearts, lest we repent too late in the presence of the eternal fire, which will question the marrow, bones, and thoughts of our souls. How greatly each person who is then to be punished will wish that he had never desired another man’s wife, that he had never stained the garment of his body, that he had never stained the white garment of Baptism, and that he had never disregarded the counsels and admonitions of priests!

For if priests face great danger when they fail to rebuke the sins of others, how much more dangerous will it be to have been unwilling to correct one’s own sins—not merely failing to amend them, but even defending them and, by defending them, accumulating them?

### 2. Eternal Punishments

Therefore, whatever medicinal satisfaction and salutary conversion could have healed here but failed to do so will there be purified by unquenchable burning.

For the burning pit of hell will be opened; there will be descent, but no ascent. There, stripped of the garment of faith and dead by mortal sin, they will sink forever, to be cast into the outer darkness, where the Eternal will not visit them—wretchedly confined in the outer darkness, to be confined still more wretchedly.

Concerning this pit the Prophet prays and says: “Let not the abyss swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16). He said, “Nor let the pit press its mouth over me,” because, when it has received the wretched sinners without the remedy of repentance, it will be closed above, opened below, and widened into the depths.

No opening, no free breath will be left, as the restraints above press down upon them. They will be thrust down there, bidding farewell to the order of nature. They will no longer be known by God, because they did not wish to know God; they will die to life and live without end for death [Note: Manuscripts read *mortui* (“dead”) instead.]

Blessed are those who, living well now, content with what is necessary for their possessions or their body, generous from what they own, chaste within themselves, and not bloodthirsty toward others [Note: Manuscript codices read *congruentes* (“in agreement” or “fitting”)], redeem themselves from the fiery night of this deep pit.

This punishment awaits those who, having lost Baptism and not restored it through repentance, will perish eternally. To them it is said: “But he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III, 12).

### 3. Purgatorial Punishments; Their Duration and Substance

Those, however, who have done deeds deserving temporal punishments—of whom the Apostle says, “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. III, 15)—will pass through the river of fire, of which the prophetic word speaks: “And a river of fire was flowing before him.”

Through the river of fire they will pass, and through fords made dreadful by seething globes. As great as the substance of the sin has been, so great will be the delay in passing through. As much as the guilt has demanded, so much will a certain rational discipline of flame exact from the human being [Note: Hence it is called “the judging fire”; see above, Sermon 15, §4, at the end.]

As much as foolish iniquity has done, so fiercely will wise punishment rage. And because divine speech, comparing the sinful soul in one place to a bronze pot, says: “Set the pot empty upon the coals, until its bronze becomes hot and all its tin melts away” (Ezek. XXIV, 11), there idle words and wicked or filthy thoughts, there the multitude of light sins that had infected the purity of noble nature, will sweat out; there the tin or lead of various faults that had crept in and obscured the divine image will be consumed.

All these things could have been separated from the soul here through almsgiving and tears by a brief settlement. Behold, this is how the one who gave himself for humanity and, fastened with nails, joined himself to death under the law, will demand an account from the human being [Note: Eusebius has: “and, fastened with nails, fixed the law of death.”]

Since these things are so, dearest brothers, let us understand that no one will be able to escape intolerable punishments and eternal fires unless he has first extinguished within himself the fire of carnal desire and manifold greed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us turn ourselves toward better things while the remedies are in our power. Let us run while we have the light, and let us not neglect the passing opportunities for salvation. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life through the merits of a life well lived.

## SERMON CCLIII

[Note: Otherwise, 12 among the Fifty Homilies.]

### On the Confession of Sins, and on the Devil’s Desire That We, Failing to Confess Our Sins, Should Appear Guilty before the Tribunal of the Eternal Judge; Whereas God, on the Contrary, Wishes Us Humbly to Confess Our Evils in This World, So That We May Deserve to Be Freed from Them in the Future

[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It is uncertain to the Leuven editors, but Verlin and Vinding considered it false. The Leuven editors observe that some think the first part belongs to Eradius or Eraclius, and the second to Augustine. The style from beginning to end is plainly Caesarian. The doctrine, however, is for the most part Augustinian, collected from his sermons on the Psalms. On §2, see Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 91, §3; on §3, see Sermon 68, §4, and Sermon 37, §6; on §5, Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 31, §16, and exposition of Psalm 140, §§10–11.]

### 1. The Commandment of Confession; Why God Gave It; We Must Not Fulfill the Devil’s Designs

Throughout all the divine Scriptures, dearest brothers, we are usefully and salubriously admonished that we must continually and humbly confess our sins not only to God but also to the saints and to those who fear God.

Thus the Holy Spirit admonishes us through the Apostle James, saying: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V, 16). And the Psalmist says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. CXVII, 1); and again: “I said, ‘I shall declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. XXXI, 5).

Just as the wounds of our sins can never be absent from us, so the medicines of confession must not be absent either [Note: Caesarius expresses the necessity of almsgiving in this same way below, Sermon 257, §4].

God does not want us to confess our sins because he himself might not know them; rather, the devil desires to find something that he can bring against us before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, and therefore wants us to be more willing to defend our sins than to accuse them.

Our God, on the contrary, because he is pious and merciful, wants us to confess them in this world, so that we may not later be confounded because of them in the future. If we confess, he spares; if we acknowledge, he forgives.

The first man was not told, “Confess your sin,” because he had not done anything that he could confess; rather, he was told not to sin (Gen. II, 17). He did not obey and sinned.

We were born mortal from the bond of sin; our misery was propagated through the succession of human weakness; and we are told: “Confess your sins.”

Just as that serpent then insisted that the human being should not keep what had been said to him, namely, that he should not sin (Gen. III, 1), so now he insists that the human being should not keep what has been said to him: “Confess your sin.”

Just as then he caused the one who was standing to fall, so now he acts to prevent the one who has fallen from rising. Therefore, against his enchantments and snares, by which he now wishes to hinder our return, let us take up the most salutary commands against him who wishes to prevent our confession of sin, because he knows that we cannot otherwise return, having fallen through pride.

He himself was our guide into pride; now let us follow Christ as our guide into humility.

### 2. The Astrologers Attribute Sin to the Stars; the Manichaeans to the Race of Darkness; Many to the Devil

That serpent tells the human being, through astrologers and Manichaeans, not to confess his sin.

Through the astrologers he speaks as follows: “Does a human being sin? The stars have been positioned in this way; it is necessary that a person commit sin.” Thus, through the astrologers, he says that a star causes a person to sin, whereas the person himself does not sin. In this way he turns blasphemies against God.

For God is the creator of the stars; and while a person does not wish to accuse himself in what he has done, he accuses God, by whom the person was made.

Again, through certain Manichaeans he suggests this: “It is not you who sin; the race of darkness sins. You have no sin.” He says this to the soul and raises it into pride, so that it thinks that it does not sin. This does not remove the sin but doubles it.

Many likewise flee confession of sin by accusing Satan himself and saying that they have done nothing evil. When some people are corrected and are asked, “Why did you do this?” they answer, “Because the devil did it.”

There is nothing that makes the devil rejoice more than when a person says that the devil himself caused him to sin. For when he says, “The devil did this,” he does not accuse himself; and while he disguises his confession of his sins, he does not deserve to receive pardon.

Thus he replies and says, “The devil did this,” as though the devil had truly dragged him along or used force against him. The devil can advise and entice, but he cannot compel at all.

### 3. The Devil Entices but Does Not Compel Us to Sin; It Is within a Person’s Freedom to Consent

Therefore, since, with God’s help, it lies within your power whether you consent to the devil, why do you not deliberate to obey God rather than him?

If the devil alone gave advice and God were silent, you would have something with which you could excuse yourself. But when Christ and your conscience contradict you, and when you hear in church from the divine Scriptures that you must not do evil, why do you choose death and abandon life? Why do you prefer to follow the devil into lust rather than obey Christ, who invites you to eternal life?

I ask you therefore, dearest brothers: why does Satan seduce a person into sin when God has placed it within the person’s power not to consent to Satan?

God is, in a certain sense, on the right, giving commands; Satan is on the left, seducing; and the human being is placed in the middle. Why does he incline his heart toward the devil? Why does he not rather raise it toward God?

The devil does not harm us by compelling but by persuading; he does not extort consent from us but requests it. Let us not assist the devil [Note: Manuscript *rm.* reads: “Let us not consent to the devil”]; and we conquer him.

He indeed gives advice; but, with God’s help, it is ours either to choose or reject what he suggests.

### 4. Excuses in Sins Do Not Remove Them but Rather Their Remedy

Pay attention to something else. When a person says that he has been seduced by Satan, when he says that he was led astray, he confesses in part; but nevertheless he denies that he himself did it, saying: “I did nothing; the devil did it.”

Adam attempted to say the same thing. He wanted to excuse himself by blaming the woman; the woman wanted to excuse herself by blaming the serpent. But the Lord God, who gave human beings free will and had strengthened them against the serpent’s poisons by his command, did not accept these excuses.

The woman had been given for this reason: to be taught by the man, not to teach the man. The will of both had been established in such a way, and free will had been fashioned in such a way, that if the man did not wish to consent to the serpent, the serpent would depart, confounded in his falsehood, while the human being would remain firmly established in the Lord his creator.

These are the evil words we have mentioned, because now the serpent wishes to persuade us to make excuses for sins. Then he caused you to accuse; now he wishes to cause you to excuse yourself.

God stood ready to give pardon to the one who confessed, as though into an open embrace. You make excuses, and you close that embrace; you enclose the sin and exclude the pardon of sin.
