Behold what you have done: not, as I said a little earlier, to remove the sin, but to block the remedy of sin. God was going to heal you through pardon if you confessed; you seek someone whom you can blame instead. But he does not seek someone to punish in your place.

### 5. Confession Is the Beginning of Healing

Say, therefore, with devoted heart what I said shortly before: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me.’”

Why did he add, “I said”? Because of the Manichaeans, who say: “It is not you who sin.”

Cry out: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Ps. XL, 5).

God heals you; only confess your wound. You lie beneath the hands of the physician; patiently implore his help. Whether he applies soothing treatment, cauterizes, or cuts, endure it calmly; pay attention to nothing except being healed.

You will be healed if you show yourself to the physician—not because he does not see if you hide yourself, but because confession itself is the beginning of healing.

### 6. The Severity of One Who Rebukes Is Gentle

“The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5). What does this mean? It is better for me that, when the righteous man sees my sin, he correct me and not spare me; that he say I have sinned and rage against my sin, so that he may free me from sin. He seems to cry out harshly, but inwardly he is gentle in mercy. Therefore he said, “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me.” Thus, when he rebukes, when he cries out, and when the righteous man is severe, he is showing mercy; and all of this proceeds from paternal mercy, not from the severity of an enemy.

Indeed, the more he does not want you to die beneath sin, the more he loves you, because he cuts. For he does not want the other members of your body to waste away through the putrefaction of sin. He brings out the iron instrument; but do not be afraid, do not grow pale: he is a physician. The iron is not brought against you, but against your wound. Thus he says: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.”

### 7. The Flattery of the Adulator Is the Sinner’s Oil

What, then, is the sinner’s oil, if not the flattery of an adulator? If someone severely rebukes another, he seems to rage against his sin; he freely tells him the evil things he has committed; and if that man follows his rebuker’s example, he perhaps becomes angry together with him at his own sin. Why, then, was it said, “Be angry and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, and in your beds, be pricked in conscience” (Ps. 4:5)? Let that man therefore speak the truth; perhaps the other will be corrected.

But let someone else come to him, agree with him, and say, “No, you acted commendably,” since “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the man who does wicked things is blessed” (Ps. 10:3, according to the Hebrew). He squanders himself, and is called happy. He is greedy, and it is said of him that he is preserving his own property. He takes revenge on his enemy, although it was said, “Forgive, and it will be forgiven you” (Luke 6:37), and he is called brave.

Consider the other cases in the same way: see how assenters—that is, flatterers—have deceptive words and names of praise. This is the sinner’s anointing. But let us hear the prophet saying, “My people, those who call you happy lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet” (Isa. 3:12) [Col. 2215].

If, then, one person openly declares another’s sin, while another strokes him with flattery; if a third person sees this and is asked what happened, does he not usually answer in this way: “The first man told him the truth and did not flatter him”? And what of the other? What did he do? “He anointed his head and departed.”

But we, brothers, if we are truly spiritual physicians and think with close attention about the remedy of your souls, must flatter no one—neither ourselves nor you. Let us confess our sins and not excuse them: “You did it; you are guilty; confess, and you will be forgiven.” But if you say, “I did not do it,” wherever you wish to use words to excuse yourself [Note: [Col. 2215] Thus the manuscript Gr., in a second but ancient hand, with whatever word.], your sin remains in you; you are guilty of sin—not only of the sin that you committed, but also of this pride, because you were unwilling to confess it.

From this sin may the Lord deign to deliver us, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON 254

[Note: [Col. 2215] Elsewhere, *On Time* 66.]

### On the Confession of Sins and Penance

[Note: [Col. 2215] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors had doubts about it. Verlinus and Vindingus observe that it was compiled from chapters 12 and 13 of Alcuin’s *On Virtues and Vices*.]

### 1. The Necessity of Confession: How Useful It Is and for Whom

Holy Scripture frequently urges us to flee to the remedies of confession—not because God needs our confession, since everything we think, say, or do is present to him, but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, in repentance, we confess what we have done wickedly through negligence.

Whoever accuses himself of his sins, the devil will not have him to accuse again on the day of judgment—provided that, by confessing and repenting, he wipes away what he has done and does not renew his former deeds.

“Confess your sins to one another,” the apostle James says, “and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Likewise the blessed Apostle says, “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). Solomon also said concerning confession of sins: “He who hides his crimes shall not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13).

It is a great remedy of salvation not to repeat what we have done wickedly and not to reopen the scars of former wounds. As the evangelist John says, “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:9). Likewise the Psalmist says, “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. 31:5).

### 2. The Fruitlessness of the Penance of the Damned; Double Torment; The Penitent’s Double Weeping; The Worthy Fruit of Penance

While he is alive, let the sinner confess what he has done, because confession is not fruitful in hell, nor is there repentance that profits toward salvation. “Behold, now is the time of salvation; behold, now is the acceptable time before God” (2 Cor. 6:2). Now is the time of forgiveness for the penitent; but after death there will be a time of vengeance for those who neglected to confess their crimes.

All the wicked have bitter repentance amid their torments; but their repentance does not profit them toward forgiveness. Rather, their conscience torments them, increasing the punishments they suffer. They could have guarded themselves against the enormity of their torments through confession, but they neglected to do so. Thus they are tormented outside by flames and inside by their own conscience.

How can a physician heal a wound that the sick person is ashamed to show? God desires our confession so that he may have a just reason for forgiving. Whoever conceals his sins and is ashamed to confess them for his own healing will have God, whom he has as witness, again as his avenger.

Let a person judge himself most carefully in this life, so that he may not be judged by God with everlasting condemnation. Every sinner ought to have a double weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through presumption he committed evil. He did not do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

Confession justifies; confession grants pardon for sins [Col. 2216]; all hope of forgiveness rests in confession. Confession is a work of mercy, the sick person’s salvation, and—together with repentance—the one remedy available to our strength.

The Savior himself displayed the power of repentance in the Gospel, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4:17). John the Baptist likewise said, “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8).

The worthy fruit of repentance is to mourn sins that have been committed and not commit the same sins again, as Scripture says, “Do not add sin upon sin” (Sir. 5:5). “Wash yourselves,” the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah, “and be clean” (Isa. 1:16).

Thus the person who both mourns past sins and does not commit them again is washed and clean. But the person who mourns what he has done without abandoning it, and after his tears repeats the very things over which he wept, is washed but not clean.

Concerning those who return to their former offenses after their tears, blessed Peter says terribly: “The dog has returned to its vomit” (2 Pet. 2:22). “Son,” Scripture says, “you have sinned; do not add to it again, but pray that your former sins may be forgiven you” (Sir. 21:1).

### 3. True Penance Is Measured Not by Years but by Contrition of Heart

True repentance is not measured by the number of years, but by the bitterness of the soul. Hence blessed Peter immediately received forgiveness from the Lord, because he wept most bitterly over the guilt of his threefold denial (Matt. 26:75).

Although repentance may last only a short time, if it is performed with the innermost bitterness of the heart, it is not despised by God, the just Judge, who considers the secrets of the heart. For God does not require merely an extended period of time; he weighs the sincerity of the penitent’s disposition.

Whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind, even if he dies with many sins, will live forever through his faith, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25–26).

He was speaking of the death of the soul, which will come upon it because of the sickness of sins. God is merciful by nature. He is ready to save through mercy those whom he does not find it possible to save through justice. He “wills all people to be saved and none to perish” (1 Tim. 2:4). Through the prophet he says, “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. 18:21).

No matter how much of a sinner or wicked person anyone may be, if he turns to repentance, let him not doubt that through God’s mercy he can obtain forgiveness. In this age, God’s mercy comes to the aid of those who repent; but in the future repentance does not profit, and we shall have to give an account of our works. Only in this life is the opportunity for repentance open; after death there is no permission for correction.

---

## SERMON 255

[Note: [Col. 2216] Elsewhere, *On Time* 57.]

### On Penance

[Note: [Col. 2216] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors marked it as a doubtful sermon and Verlinus and Vindingus counted it among the spurious works. Its author’s character and style are in fact very different from Augustine’s and somewhat similar to Caesarius’s.]

### Those Conscious of Crimes Withdraw from Communion; It Would Be Better for Them to Make Themselves Worthy, Through Swift and Laborious Penance; What Should Be Thought about a Penitent at the Point of Death

We often observe, beloved brothers, that some of you avoid ecclesiastical communion; and I understand that this happens because of a consciousness of grave and enormous sins. Therefore I warn you, beloved, that this evil is doubled by an unhealthy decision: those who act in this way both increase the burden of their offenses and lose the gift of eternal salvation. For this is to accumulate guilt and avoid the remedy.

Therefore, beloved brothers, I exhort and admonish you: if anyone among you, conscious of his crimes, thinks himself unworthy of ecclesiastical communion, let him make himself worthy.

You say, “How can anyone make himself worthy?” How else than by abandoning his former errors and seeking penance, so that the person polluted by the filth of his crimes may be cleansed through the satisfaction of *exomologesis*—public confession?

Let him not reserve himself for that moment when, at the end of his life, he seeks penance when he is no longer able to perform it. For this expectation is useless, beloved. It is not enough for the sinner to repent unless he carries out his repentance. The voice of the penitent alone is not sufficient for correcting crimes; in satisfaction for enormous sins, works as well as words are required.

Penance is indeed granted even at the point of death, because it cannot be denied. Nevertheless, we cannot guarantee that the person who asks for it in this way will deserve to be absolved. For how does one who has fallen perform penance? How does a person placed at the very end of life perform penance? How can someone perform penance who can no longer carry out any works of satisfaction on his own behalf?

Therefore the penance requested by a sick person is weak. The penance requested only by a dying person—I fear that it may itself die. And so, beloved, whoever wishes to find God’s mercy should perform penance in this age while he is healthy, so that he may be able to be healthy in the age to come.

---

## SERMON 256

[Note: [Col. 2217] Among the sermons of Caesarius published from the Regius manuscript through the care of the distinguished V. C. Étienne Baluze, this appears second in order. Our manuscripts attribute it to the same Caesarius. For no. 3, see above, Sermon 77, no. 1, and 78, no. 3, and Augustine, Sermon 393; for no. 4, see Eligius, Homily 6.]

### Admonition Showing the Difference between the Penance That Is Continually Practiced with Good Works and That Which Is Received in Illness or at the End of Life

### 1. Does a Dying Person Who Receives Penance Obtain Forgiveness? He Obtains It If He Has Continually Practiced Penance and Good Works

Many of our brothers or sons are concerned about whether every person who, while ill, receives penance and then immediately dies can attain complete forgiveness. As they investigate this matter, they argue among themselves with no little irritation. Some say that a person who receives penance in this way is completely freed; others insist that it profits him very little.

I wish briefly to suggest to Your Charity what seems to us concerning this matter according to the rules of the holy fathers. It may reasonably be believed that there are three ways by which a person may arrive at this sudden penance.

The first and chief way is for a Christian not to commit capital crimes; or, if he happens to commit them, to repent of them in such a way and wipe them away through good works that he does not afterward return to those sins. He should give tithes from all his produce, and from the nine remaining portions use whatever is left over after his necessities to redeem the minor sins that daily creep in. He should hold to that charity which loves not only friends but even enemies themselves.

Whoever faithfully wishes to fulfill these things, even if he does not receive penance at the end—for he has always performed it fruitfully and faithfully—will depart well from this life. If, at the time when he is about to die, he receives penance and makes one portion of his property for himself and Christ together with his children, we believe that he will not only obtain forgiveness of sins but also receive eternal rewards.

### 2. He Also Obtains It Who Lived in Sins, but Under What Condition?

The second form of the penance mentioned above is this: someone may commit not only minor sins but perhaps even capital sins throughout his life, and yet commit those evils without knowing on what hope of penance he is acting [Note: [Col. 2217] Thus the Laon manuscript. But the Regius manuscript reads: “acting ignorantly, as though in the hope of penance.”], nor for that reason abandon his soul to sins or reserve himself for sudden penance. At his departure, with great humility and contrition of heart, amid groaning or sighing, he may ask for that penance and resolve most firmly in his heart that, if he recovers, he will perform fruitful penance with all his heart and all his strength for as long as he lives.

He must restore in full whatever he knows he has wrongfully taken, according to the prophetic command to restore what was seized (Ezek. 33:15); forgive all his enemies wholeheartedly; set aside one portion of his property for Christ and himself together with his children; and, during his illness, order generous alms to be distributed as far as he is able [Col. 2218].

If he wishes faithfully to fulfill these things with a humble and contrite heart, we both can and must believe that the Lord will deign to forgive him all his sins, according to the prophetic saying, “On whatever day the sinner turns, all his iniquities shall be forgotten” (Ezek. 18:21–22), and again, “On whatever day you turn and groan, you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12).

### 3. It Is Difficult to Form a Judgment about One Who Does Not Demonstrate Penance by His Works

The third form of penance seems to some to apply when a person who has always lived wickedly reserves himself for penance at the end of life and sins in the hope that, through this sudden penance, all his accumulated sins will be forgiven. Yet after receiving it, he neither restores even in simple measure what he has wrongly taken, nor forgives his enemies wholeheartedly, nor resolves in his heart that, if he recovers, he will perform penance with great compunction and humility for as long as he lives, nor makes a portion of his property for himself and Christ together with his children for the redemption of his sins.

If he receives penance in this way and departs this life without these remedies that we have mentioned above, though we hesitate to say what will happen to him, the Lord himself spoke most decisively in the Gospel: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will the Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15). He also said, “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:38, 37).

How can forgiveness be given to that sinner who was unwilling to forgive? Or how can it be given to one who did not give? And because the Lord will say to those who did not give alms, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41–42), if the person who did not distribute anything from his own resources is sent into the fire, what will he do with this penitent, who not only gave nothing of his own but was also unwilling to restore even in simple measure the property of others that he had wrongfully taken?

If such a person asks penance from me, and if he is of an age at which penance may or ought to be granted [Note: [Col. 2218] Penance was not granted to people of every age. Hence the Synod of Agde, presided over by Caesarius, canon 15: “Penance should not readily be entrusted to young men, because of the instability of their age.” The Third Council of Orléans, canon 24: “No one should presume to entrust the blessing of penance to young persons. Certainly, in the case of married persons, no one should dare to grant it unless both parties consent and they have reached full age.”], I can give him penance, but I cannot give him complete assurance.

God, however, who knows the consciences of all and will judge each person according to his merit, knows with what faith or intention of mind he sought penance. I fear, however, that perhaps such a penitent did not even possess in his conscience what he failed to show in his works. For although we cannot see the heart, nevertheless, according to the Gospel saying, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16), we see that he utterly failed to fulfill the things written above.

Since this is so, who could prevent us from believing that he did not depart well from this life, when we know that he did not perform good works? Behold, I have explained to Your Charity what I think about sudden penance. If anyone is troubled by some doubt arising from what we have said, we both wish and desire that he ask us for an explanation with complete charity.

### 4. It Is Safer to Perform Penance Continually; The Hour of Death Is Uncertain; What That Continual Penance Consists In

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, leaving aside what is uncertain or doubtful, let us think with the greatest attention and all our strength about that penance which good Christians practice throughout their lives, by which both all capital crimes are condemned and minor sins are continually redeemed. If we practice it with good works for as long as we live, it promises us complete security concerning God’s mercy.

Since everyone wants to receive penance at the end of life, while we see scarcely anyone obtain it as he wishes, why do we not perform penance daily, so that by holding to what is certain we may be freed from uncertain and doubtful things?

How many people who believed that they would receive penance at the end of their lives were overcome by sudden collapse, drowned in a shipwreck, killed by lightning, struck by a hemorrhage, or afflicted by the illness called apoplexy, so that they could not only ask for penance but could not even make the sign of the cross or say the Lord’s Prayer?

Since human frailty is subject to such dangers, it is an exceedingly perilous presumption for us to reserve ourselves for a long period in which to perform penance, when we cannot control even the life of a single day.

Therefore, with fear and trembling, let us hear the Lord speaking through the prophet and warning us with pious exhortation: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Sir. 5:8). The one who said, “On whatever day you groan, you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:12), also said, “Do not delay turning to the Lord.”

With God’s help we can attain this if we continually entreat him to inspire us, in his goodness, to flee all evil swiftly; to practice what is good without weariness; not to covet the property of others; not to commit capital crimes; continually to redeem the minor sins without which we cannot be, through the forgiveness of our enemies and alms to the poor; frequently to devote ourselves according to our strength, with perfect charity, to fasts, vigils, and prayers; to visit the sick; to seek out those confined in prison; to receive strangers; humbly to wash their feet and, as far as our strength permits, to provide them with what they need; to preserve peace ourselves with everyone and also to restore those who are at odds to harmony.

If the day of our departure finds us faithfully occupied with such holy works, as I have already said, even if we do not receive penance at the hour of our death, we shall depart this life securely. By the Lord’s gift we shall be able not only to escape punishment but also to reach eternal life happily. Amen.

---

## SERMON 257

[Note: [Col. 2219] Attributed to Caesarius in the manuscripts and published under his name as the thirteenth sermon in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. For no. 1, see Appendix, Sermon 29, nos. 3 and 1; Sermon 22, no. 6. For no. 2, see Sermon 76, no. 2; Sermon 168, no. 3; Sermon 22, no. 2. For no. 3, see below, Sermon 263, no. 2; 364, no. 5; and 220, no. 2. For no. 4, see Sermon 224, no. 1; Sermon 229, no. 2; and below, Sermon 245, no. 4.]

### Admonition That One Should Resort to the Remedy of Penance without Any Concealment for Capital Crimes

### 1. Presumption and Despair Concerning Forgiveness; Penance Must Not Be Delayed or Ashamed Of

Whenever it happens, dearest brothers, that someone, as human frailty is disposed, falls into any grave sin or even crime, he must neither despair because God is just nor trust with excessive security because he is merciful. Rather, he should fear justice in such a way that he seeks mercy, and trust in mercy in such a way that he nevertheless trembles before justice. For the longer God waits for us to be corrected, the more severely he punishes if we are slow to consider our conversion.

A medicinal poultice or bandage is best applied while wounds are still warm, and a wound is quickly restored to health when it is not allowed to putrefy through prolonged misuse [Note: [Col. 2219] In several books, “burning.”]

But someone says, “When I reach old age, then I will flee to the remedies of penance.” Why should human frailty presume this about itself, when it does not possess even one day of its life in its own power? How many people believed that they would live for a long time, yet sudden death carried them away so that they could not even reach that momentary penance?

We are ashamed to perform penance for a short time, yet we do not fear enduring eternal punishments without end. O unhappy person, you are not ashamed of the wound itself, but you are ashamed of binding the wound! Sin is the wound, and penance is the bandage of the wound. You who do not wish to perform penance are plainly pretending that you need not apply medicines to your wounds. You do not recognize that an uncovered wound is more offensive and produces greater horror than one wrapped in medicines.

### 2. Penance Is Necessary for Everyone; Enumeration of Minor Sins; They Can Be Redeemed Only by God’s Mercy

Consider this also, brothers: even if capital crimes did not creep upon you, the minor sins themselves—which, what is worse, we either do not notice or certainly count as nothing—would, if gathered together, amount to such a mass that I do not know what abundance of good works would be sufficient to outweigh them.

Let us consider, from the time when we began to have understanding, what we owe for oaths, for perjuries, for curses, for slanders, for idle conversations, for hatred, for anger, for envy, for evil desire, for gluttony, for drowsiness, for filthy thoughts, for the desire of the eyes, for sensual pleasure of the ears, for aggravating the poor, for visiting Christ in prison late or with difficulty, for receiving strangers carelessly, for neglecting to wash the feet of guests according to our promise at Baptism, for visiting the sick later than we ought, for failing to restore those who are at odds to harmony with a whole and sincere heart, for wishing to eat while the Church was fasting, for being occupied with idle stories while standing in the church during the reading of the holy lessons, for sometimes thinking about something other than what we ought while singing psalms or praying, and for speaking at banquets not always about holy things but sometimes about luxurious pleasures.

If these things and similar matters, which can scarcely be known or counted, are gathered into one heap from the time when we began to have understanding, even without the addition of capital crimes, by what quantities and kinds of good works could they be redeemed, unless, with divine mercy outweighing them, God’s severity or justice were appeased through humble and contrite repentance, together with more generous alms according to our strength?

Since these things I have mentioned, without which no human being can exist, press heavily upon us, and since perhaps capital crimes and sins also creep upon us, I do not know with what conscience we create for ourselves a dangerous security and neglect to seek the remedy of penance through deadly concealment.

While we are wearied on the sea of this world by innumerable waves, we reserve ourselves for seeking the harbor of penance only after long periods of time. We do not understand that despair arises from the multitude of sins; from despair, the restraints on sin are loosened without any reverence; and what is written is fulfilled: “When the wicked comes to the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

### 3. Whom Late Penance May Benefit; How Unjustly and Dangerously It Is Awaited

But someone says, “When I reach old age, or when I have been given up for dead by some excessive illness, then I will ask for penance.”

We do not say that such penance cannot be beneficial. It is certain that it profits, if each person receives it with great and abundant almsgiving, grants forgiveness to all his enemies, asks pardon from everyone whom he has wronged, and resolves with his whole heart that, if he recovers, he will perform it humbly and faithfully for as long as he lives, with groaning, sighing, and many alms.

Yet, wise man, consider amid all these things whether it is just for you to serve vices and sins throughout your whole life and rise, already half-alive, to acquire life. Would you want your servant to do this to you—to serve your enemies for as long as he was strong and young, and only when he reached old age to wish to return to your service? What you do not wish to suffer from your servant, it is not just for you to do to your Lord.

Nevertheless, we know that many people, while they were healthy, often said that they desired penance with their whole heart. Yet because they did not wish to perform it immediately, they departed from this world without its remedy [Col. 2221]. The sinner is struck even by this punishment: at death he forgets himself, having forgotten God while alive. For the person who did not wish to seek the remedy of his soul when he could do so may later, even if he wishes, be uncertain whether he deserves to receive it.

### 4. Minor and Grave Sins Must Be Redeemed Continually; False Hope and False Despair

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us wisely and profitably consider the time of judgment and the day when we must render an account. Let us mourn our greater crimes and sins with groans and sighs for as long as we live; and let us redeem those minor offenses, whether those we have committed in the past or those we continually commit, through constant prayers and more generous alms.

As daily wounds of sin are never absent, so let the remedies of almsgiving and prayer never be absent. If we discipline ourselves with our own severity, we anticipate the sentence of the future Judge. For God quickly grants forgiveness to the person who does not spare himself on account of his sins; and the person who now suspends himself from communion because of his guilt cannot be removed from that altar which is in heaven, according to the saying, “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Prov. 18:17).

If you acknowledge your iniquity, God forgives. Let no one therefore despair, but let no one hope wrongly. He despairs wrongly who believes that, even if he performs penance for his sins, divine mercy will not forgive him. He hopes wrongly, however, who reserves himself for the remedies of penance after a long time.

Just as it is said to those who despair wrongly, “On whatever day the sinner turns, all his iniquities shall be forgotten” (Ezek. 18:21–22), so it is said to those who hope wrongly, “Do not delay turning to the Lord” (Sir. 5:8).

Let us therefore, dearest brothers—men and women, religious and lay, old and young, boys and girls—consider these things with the greatest attention. Rejecting without any concealment the deadly security, let us strive to apply the remedies of penance to our sins every day, fearing the saying, “Remember that death does not delay” (Sir. 14:12).

If we faithfully do these things, we shall come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge not to receive a sentence of condemnation, but to be rewarded with eternal prizes; and we shall come happily with joy and exultation, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON 258

[Note: [Col. 2221] Elsewhere, *On Time* 58. Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It had remained doubtful among the Augustinian sermons for the Louvain editors; Verlinus and Vindingus wish it to be placed among the spurious works. It is Caesarius’s homily 14 in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and all our manuscripts prefix his name. For no. 1, see Eligius, Homily 15, and above, Sermon 29, no. 4; for no. 4, Caesarius, Homily 35, and above, Sermons 13, no. 5, and 29, no. 4.]

### Hence the Above

### 1. The Fallen Person Should Rise Again Quickly; How Dangerous It Is to Heap Sins upon Sins

I beg you, dearest brothers, that if anyone among you, as human frailty is disposed, has been overcome by the devil’s cunning and entangled in capital crimes, and, in the words of the Apostle, has violated and destroyed God’s temple within himself, he should not despair of God’s mercy. Rather, let him rise quickly from the evil of his iniquity, lest through the habit of sinning he bury himself in those very ruins.

For it is not the person who has sinned, but the person who has persevered in sins, who will be hateful and abominable to God. So that no one may doubt divine forgiveness, the Lord consoles us through the prophet like a most merciful father, saying, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11); and again, “The wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness” (ibid., 12).

Although this mercy is so great, it benefits us only if we do not delay turning to the Lord and do not add crimes to crimes [Col. 2222].

Indeed, even in the wounds and fractures of the body we can recognize the illnesses of souls. If someone’s foot or hand is broken, it is usually restored to its former function with difficulty. But if the limbs themselves are broken a second and third time, and still more frequently, Your Charity can understand with how many pains those wounds must be treated. Even then, after long and numerous treatments, the limbs will scarcely be able to be restored to their former condition.

The same principle should be believed to apply to the fractures or wounds of souls. If someone sins once or twice and, without any concealment, flees to the remedies of penance, he will recover his former health without delay [Note: [Col. 2222] Here Lov., Am., and Er. add, “and perhaps without any disfigurement”; Caesarius, Eligius, and the manuscripts do not have this wording.]

But if he begins to add sins to sins and prefers to allow the wounds of his soul to putrefy by covering or defending them rather than to cure them through confession and the practice of penance, we must fear that what the Apostle said may be fulfilled in him: “Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to the hardness of your heart and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5).

## 2. Let no one, however guilty, despair of God’s mercy, but hasten without delay to obtain it. The example of David

But perhaps someone thinks that he has committed sins so grave that he can no longer merit God’s mercy. Let this thought be far from the minds of all sinners. O man, whoever you are, you attend to the multitude of your sins, but you do not attend to the omnipotence of the heavenly Physician. Since God wishes to show mercy because he is good, and can do so because he is omnipotent, the one who believes that God either does not wish or is unable to show him mercy—and so doubts that he is either good or omnipotent—closes against himself the door of divine mercy.

Therefore, let no one despair of divine mercy, neither after a hundred sins nor after a thousand crimes. Yet let him not despair in such a way that he delays reconciling himself to God; rather, let him hasten to do so without any delay. For if he forms the habit of sinning, it may happen that, even if he wishes to be freed from the devil’s snares, he can no longer escape them.

David, who by God’s gift was deemed worthy to become both king and prophet, was nevertheless so overtaken after receiving such great grace that he not only committed adultery but also perpetrated murder. Yet he did not put this off until his old age, reserving it for the remedies of repentance. Instead, he immediately prostrated himself in sackcloth and covered himself with ashes; and, doing penance with great wailing and groaning (II Kings 11:12), he fulfilled what he himself had said in the Psalms:

> “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7);

and again:

> “I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10).

Because he did not delay doing penance through a deadly presumption of security, he quickly moved God’s mercy toward himself, so that he not only did not lose his kingdom but was also deemed worthy to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 2222] The remaining words of this section are missing from the manuscripts and from the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; nevertheless, they are not inconsistent with Caesarius’s style. See Sermon 249, section 6.].

But perhaps there is someone who says: “I am engaged in military service; I have a wife; how, then, can I do penance?” It is as though, when we urge repentance, we were saying that each person should take greater care to tear out his hair rather than abandon his sins, and tear his garments rather than reform his ways. Whoever attempts by this pretext to deceive himself rather than excuse himself should consider that neither the honor of kingship nor the dignity of royal clothing could prevent King David from doing penance (II Kings 12:13).

## 3. Likewise, the example of Ahab, Manasseh, and the prostitute who washed the Lord’s feet

Ahab too was a sacrilegious king, of whom Scripture says that there had been no one like him who had sold himself to do evil against the Lord (I Kings 21:20). After he had been corrupted by his wife Jezebel [Col. 2223] and had become hateful to God, he desired to seize the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite after having him killed and stoned. Rebuked by Saint Elijah, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth, bowed his head, and did penance.

For this reason the word of God immediately came to Elijah, saying:

> “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself? Because he has humbled himself for my sake,” he said, “I will not bring evil in his days” (I Kings 21:29).

Consider, brothers, that although he was sacrilegious, he did not put off repentance for a long time; rather, he did not delay offering God the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart. Certainly, if he had afterward continued in the humility with which he had begun, God’s mercy would never have departed from him.

Manasseh too, as we read in the Scriptures, was so sacrilegious and impious that it is written of him that he filled all Jerusalem with every kind of iniquity. Nevertheless, after this, when he was led into captivity and thrown into prison, he did penance with great humility and obtained God’s grace, so that afterward he was deemed worthy to be numbered among God’s friends (II Chronicles 33:9, 13).

That prostitute also, who washed the Lord’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair, when she learned that the heavenly Physician had come, thrust herself unbidden into the house where she had not been invited. She who had previously been brazen in pursuing destruction afterward became even more bold in seeking salvation. Therefore she deserved to hear that all her sins had been forgiven (Luke 7:47).

Nor did she put it off until the end of her life to do penance. While she was still able to sin, she wished to abandon her sins, so that it was not inability but her will that kept her from returning to her adulteries.

## 4. Let the one who was not ashamed to commit shameful deeds not be ashamed to do penance

We could still find many others in the divine Scriptures who, after countless crimes, provoked God’s mercy toward themselves by doing penance, and returned not only to their former state but even to a better one. But since it would be lengthy to recount them all, the four whom we have named [Note: [Col. 2223] The manuscripts read: “whom we know.”] are more than sufficient to make us recognize that our God—who forgave David after such a grave sin, spared Ahab the sacrilegious king, counted Manasseh among his friends after he had done penance for countless sins, and completely forgave the prostitute who had drenched the Lord’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair—is ready, if we truly turn to him, not only to forgive our sins but also to grant us eternal blessedness.

Thinking on these things, therefore, dearest brothers, let us labor with all our strength and with God’s help, so that no crimes or capital sins may steal upon us. But if someone has been brought down into this evil by the devil’s cunning, let him obtain a remedy for himself in the day of need before those crimes grow strong through habit, and let him strive with great wailing and groaning to reconcile himself to God.

Let the one who was not ashamed to commit shameful deeds not be ashamed to do penance. Rather, let him quickly strive to restore God’s image in himself through good works, so that he may be acknowledged by the Father among his children. Let him not be excluded from that eternal blessedness and cast out from the wedding feast, bound hand and foot and thrown into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 22:13). Instead, restored to his former health by the remedies of repentance, humility, and compunction, and adorned with the jewels of good works, may he deserve to hear:

> “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid. 25:23).

Amen.

# SERMON CCLIX

[Note: [Col. 2223] In the manuscripts it is attributed to Caesarius, and it is third in order among his homilies published by Stephen Baluzius.]

## An admonition that, since sins are always creeping in, penance should always be done for them, and that no one should, through dangerous dissimulation, reserve repentance until the end of his life rather than undertake it now

### 1. No one should set penance aside here, since we sin daily and tender sins are more easily torn out

I ask you, dearest brothers, to receive this as you are accustomed to do according to our fatherly practice—not only patiently but also willingly—for, with God’s favor, you yourselves know that I strive to impress upon you with great humility and fear what it is fitting for me to say and necessary for you to hear, not for any earthly profit but out of perfect love for you.

Since not only minor sins but also greater crimes strive day and night to creep upon us, let us not reserve ourselves for that repentance which is undertaken at the end. Rather, every day, as long as we live, let us strive to do penance. This practice must be continually exercised not only by laypeople and clergy but also by monks and priests themselves.

Let the bishop who does penance daily pray for me. But whoever, relying on his honor or holiness, pretends that he need not do penance should find someone who ought to plead for him.

Since we cannot pass a single day without sin, what sense is there in gradually piling up minor sins until we make endless whirlpools out of the tiniest drops? From the multitude of sins accumulated over a long time, despair arises, according to what is written:

> “When the wicked has come into the depths of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

You all know that we can tear out tender growth more easily than cut down what has become strong.

### 2. Daily penance is urged through familiar examples

And, to take an example from things we see before our eyes every day, who is found to be so useless or negligent that he does not have his house swept every day? Who is there who continually allows his horses to stand in their own dung?

I ask you, brothers: infer great things from small ones. Do not think it inappropriate that we speak of sweeping a house, for the Lord himself said in the Gospel that when the woman who had lost a drachma swept her house, she immediately deserved to find the drachma she had lost (Luke 15:8).

In the drachma a coin is understood; in the coin the emperor’s image is recognized. Therefore, just as, when a house is swept, the emperor’s image is found on the drachma, so, when the soul is freed from the filth of vices through fruitful repentance, the emperor’s image is recognized in it.

Therefore, as I have already said, dearest brothers, recognize that what I urge is neither difficult nor burdensome. I ask only that, just as we clean our house with brooms so that it may please the eyes of our friends, so, with God’s help, we cleanse our soul from every sin, so that it may not displease the eyes of the angels.

Not only the angels but also the Lord of the angels deigns to come to the house of our soul, just as he himself said:

> “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone rises and opens to me, I will enter him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20);

and:

> “I and my Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

How blessed is that soul which wishes to cleanse the house of its heart from the filth of sins and fill it with holy and righteous works, so that the Lord delights to dwell in it!

Let us not, then, be reluctant to do in our souls what we command to be done in our houses or stables. For just as it is right that we have the stables cleaned every day, lest our horses suffer harm, so it is exceedingly unjust and cruel if we take greater care of animals than of our souls.

### 3. The fruit of that repentance

The sinner cannot dwell within himself; hence he seeks distractions, but by doing so he increases his unrest. From what, then, could he turn it away more truly?

I also urge this upon you; let your holy Charity not receive it with disgust, for I wish to give you an evident comparison drawn from the very matters of which we are speaking.

Just as our houses or stables, if cleaned every day, cause us neither disgust nor labor, so minor sins, if expiated daily, can generate neither despair nor grief [Col. 2225].

But if we wish to be negligent about cleansing them, then, just as stables that are not cleaned for a long time become so rotten, and the dung produces such a horrible stench, that not only can human beings not live there, but even animals cannot stand there, so whoever, through negligence, wishes to accumulate the filth of sins in his soul by evil deeds over a long period, and neglects to correct them daily by good works, will not only be deemed unworthy of God’s visitation, but the sinner himself will be unable to remain within himself.

In short, all negligent people whose hearts are torn by many sins as if by certain beasts and pierced as if by the most poisonous thorns commonly say this to those like themselves:

> “You should know that we are sad and anxious; therefore come, let us distract ourselves—by going to the circus or the theater, by playing at the gaming table, or by exercising ourselves in some kind of hunting” [Note: [Col. 2225] On playing at the gaming table, see above, Sermon 141, section 3; on hunting, Sermon 146, sections 2–3.].

Such people seek consolation from the world outside because they do not deserve to receive the consolation that God gives inwardly in the soul.

When they return to their consciences from their many acts of slander or plunder, and from those wretched spectacles and dangerous hunts, they cannot dwell or rest within themselves at all. Through such activities they have added sorrow rather than removed it, and so they are tossed about by the conflicts of their sins.

Through pride they are torn as if by lions; through envy they are struck as if by the bite of vipers; through anger they are consumed in a cruel fire; through cruelty they are torn apart by the bite of savagery; in plundering they are devoured as if by wolves’ teeth; in lust and drunkenness they roll about as if in the filthiest sewers. Thus, as they return from the most cruel theaters to consciences still more cruel, as if from bad things to worse, they cannot find rest.

How much better it would be if, wearied by the goads of vices, they devoted themselves to the divine Scriptures, where they could find true diversion and complete consolation; if they frequented the shrines of the saints and sought their help against those very sins; if, persisting in fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, they strove to punish rather than nourish or increase their sins.

Then, when the most savage army of vices had been driven from their hearts, they could return with all their heart to true rest, that is, to Christ, and hear him call to them with the most merciful voice:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28).

### 4. Even minor sins must be carefully expiated

Those who humbly and faithfully wish to do these things will be able to pass from a violent storm to tranquility, and from the most savage barbarism of vices to true peace.

But if there are some who trust that they are free from the evils mentioned above, and, because they do not commit capital crimes, glory in their supposed innocence with dangerous complacency, let them fear lest an abundance of minor sins, like an exceedingly harsh infestation of flies or fleas, afflict and torment them so greatly that even they cannot dwell within themselves.

Therefore, just as we fear cruel and deadly beasts that usually kill with one bite, and shudder at tiny creatures that can torment us, so, with God’s help, let us redeem both capital crimes and minor sins—sins without which we cannot be—through daily almsgiving and prayers, especially while we love our enemies with our whole heart.

For if we reserve ourselves until the final period of our life for doing penance or redeeming sins and crimes, we must fear lest unexpected death overtake us and prevent us from reaching that sudden moment of repentance to which, through deadly complacency, we wish to reserve ourselves.

Therefore, let us fear what is written:

> “Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day” (Sirach 5:8).

O man, why do you put it off from day to day, and do you not rather fear that today may be your final day?

These things, then, dearest brothers, which we have urged—if you receive them willingly according to your holy custom, and continually reflect upon them with an attentive and watchful heart—will enable you both to live this life with a good conscience and to arrive happily at eternal blessedness in the age to come, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion for ever, etc.

# SERMON CCLX

[Note: [Col. 2226] This is the seventeenth homily of Caesarius in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and it also bears his name in the manuscripts. On section 1, see below, Sermon 262, section 2; on section 2, above, Sermon 249, section 6, and Eusebius, Homily 3, *On the Epiphany*.]

## An admonition excerpted from the books of the ancient Fathers, that whoever recognizes that he has committed capital crimes should flee without any dissimulation to the remedies of repentance

### 1. Confession as a plank after shipwreck. A dead soul is raised by tears. But not by almsgiving alone

Therefore, dearest brothers, as I have often admonished you, I admonish and solemnly urge you again and again: whoever recognizes that he has been hurled from the shore of continence by the storm of lust into the sea of debauchery, and has suffered shipwreck of chastity, should quickly seize the confession of sins like a plank from a broken ship. Through it he may escape from the abyss and depth of debauchery and reach the harbor of repentance, where he may now cast the anchor of hope in a safer place and restore the salvation he has lost.

For each person ought to cry out over himself as over a dead man and raise great laments over his extinguished soul. And just as a mother usually mourns over her only dead son with her whole heart, so we ought to pour out the entire weight of our grief over our one soul, slain by the sword of crime, if perhaps it may be revived by the fomentations of tears through the warmth of faith.

Above all, as I have often warned, every sinner must take care and see to it that he does not give alms for his crimes in such a way that he does not abandon the crimes themselves, fearing what the Apostle said:

> “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Corinthians 13:3).

### 2. The almsgiving of the sinner

But someone says: “How will he be judged not to have charity who gives so much to the poor?”

I answer him: How does he preserve charity toward others who kills himself, who is cruel toward his own soul? For the Holy Spirit does not lie when he says:

> “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

If, whenever we commit adultery or murder, we kill our souls, what does it profit us that we are kind to others while we are recognized as impious toward ourselves? By giving alms we nourish another person’s flesh, but by committing crimes we slaughter our own soul.

Therefore, as I have often admonished, let us give alms for our greater sins in such a way that we never return to those crimes.

One must not rely on health or age. The person uncertain of his life is always too slow in seeking the remedy of salvation.

Would that the time of repentance were arranged while it lies within our power in the same way that the time already lost would be desired [Note: [Col. 2226] The manuscript reads: “in the way that the lost time is desired?”]!

### 3. Conclusion

Therefore, while we are still granted—though within an uncertain brevity of time—to cleanse stains, wash away guilt, remedy the past, provide for the future, and undo what has been done, let us labor with all our strength so that what we live may be added to life, and so that what we live may contribute not to death but to salvation.

Let our groans be so effective that they search out sins in the bones and pursue crimes into the marrow. Let the pain of healing repentance leave untouched and uncured nothing that might rise against us on the day of judgment, nothing that, after ancient ages, might suddenly appear as a new charge against the evil conscience of the mind.

Let us hasten to offer the Lord an amended life before it is taken away. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life through the merits of life [Col. 2227]. Let us not reserve ourselves for the remedies of repentance until the time of old age.

For the one who said:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion” (Ezekiel 18:21–22),

also said:

> “Do not delay turning to the Lord” (Sirach 5:8).

If that promise made you secure, let this solemn warning make you vigilant. And hear Scripture saying:

> “Remember, son, that death does not delay” (ibid. 14:12);

and:

> “Do not say, ‘The Lord’s mercy is great; he will forgive the multitude of my sins.’ Mercy and wrath belong to him, and his wrath looks upon sinners—that is, upon those who persist in sins” (ibid. 5:6–7).

If we faithfully and diligently attend to these things, and flee without any delay to the remedies of repentance, then, with the help of our Lord who lives and reigns for ever and ever, we can both escape everlasting punishment and arrive happily at eternal rewards.

Amen.

# SERMON CCLXI

[Note: [Col. 2227] Among the Caesarian homilies edited by Stephen Baluzius, this is the first. Our manuscripts also assign it to Caesarius. On section 1, see above, Sermon 68, section 4; on section 2, Sermons 229, section 2, and 257, section 4.]

## An admonition concerning those who seek public penance

### 1. Why public penance is sought. The penitent’s clothing. Supplication

Whenever, dearest brothers, we see one of our brothers or sisters publicly seeking penance, we can and ought, with God’s inspiration, kindle within ourselves a great compunction arising from divine fear.

For who would not congratulate and rejoice, and give God as many thanks as possible, seeing a sinner becoming angry against his own sins and crying out in a public voice, so that he begins to accuse salutarily what he once used to defend with the most shameless face?

He has already begun to join himself to God; therefore he does not wish to be the defender of his sins but their persecutor. And because God hates sins, as soon as a negligent person begins to hate his own sins, he is separated from his crimes and joined to God.

The one who has undertaken public penance could have done it more privately. But, I believe, considering the multitude of his sins, he sees that he alone is not sufficient against such grave evils; therefore he desires to seek the assistance of the entire people.

Just as it commonly happens that someone whose vineyard has been left abandoned through negligence asks his neighbors and friends for help, and, gathering a multitude of people on one day, repairs with the aid of many hands what he could not repair alone, so the one who wishes publicly to seek penance is understood, as it were, to make a collection, so that, assisted by the prayers of the whole people, he may uproot the thorns and thistles of his sins.

Thus, with God’s help, a harvest of good works may arise in him, and the vineyard of his heart, which was accustomed to produce not grapes but thorns, may begin to offer the sweetness of spiritual wine.

This too, dearest brothers, should not be considered idly: the one who undertakes penance is covered with sackcloth [Note: [Col. 2227] On this garment of the penitent, see the Council of Agde, canon 15, and Eligius, Homily 8.].

Since sackcloth is woven from goats’ hair, and goats appear to bear a likeness to sinners, the one who undertakes penance publicly declares that he is not a lamb but a kid, crying out through his actions and saying:

> “See me, all peoples, and pour out over me, a wretched man, all the tears of compassion. Recognize that inwardly I am what I am outwardly.

> “I no longer wish to appear outwardly as righteous while hiding iniquities or plunder within my soul. Now, like that publican, bent down to the ground, I do not dare to raise my eyes to heaven (Luke 18:13), but I humbly offer the wounds of my sins to that heavenly Physician to be healed.

> “Therefore I ask that you all plead for his mercy on my behalf, so that he may deign to cure the rottenness of my sins down to the living flesh and restore me to true health.

> “For I fear that what the Lord said about hypocrites may be fulfilled in me:

> ‘They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves’ (Matthew 7:15).

> “Therefore, as I have already said, I show outwardly the kind of person I recognize myself to be inwardly.

> “Because until now I adorned myself outwardly in costly garments while inwardly in my soul I was covered with the leprosy of sins, I now put on sackcloth and, seeking penance with my whole heart, ask that through your prayers I may deserve to be freed from the paralysis of my sins.

> “Therefore, again and again I beg you: since, with God inspiring you, you know how to weep with those who weep, may your compassion be moved to tears and groans for the forgiveness of my sins. For I believe that your holy prayers can obtain pardon for me from that most merciful Judge.”

### 2. To remain unmoved by this plea is inhuman. Nor does God despise the Church’s prayers for the penitent

I truly tell you, dearest brothers: if there is anyone who does not sympathize with one who seeks penance in this manner and does not strive to plead with God for him with his whole heart, he must be judged exceedingly inhuman and impious.

Since the Lord said:

> “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (ibid. 7:12),

let us hasten to grant others with our whole heart and soul what we wish others to do for us when we resolve to seek public penance.

For what did we wish when we were deemed worthy to reach the remedy of repentance, except that the whole people should strive to implore divine mercy on our behalf?

Therefore, what we desire others to do for us, we too ought to grant to others with perfect charity, because it is written:

> “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16);

and:

> “A brother who helps a brother will be exalted” (Proverbs 18:19).

If we faithfully wish to do these things with perfect charity, we can and must most certainly believe that the ineffable mercy of the Lord will deign to hear us.

Since he himself said:

> “If two or three agree on earth, whatever they ask will be done for them” (Matthew 18:19),

can the kind and merciful Lord, who promises to hear two or three, fail to hear the whole people for the forgiveness of one penitent? Far be it from us even lightly to think such a thing about his ineffable mercy.

We must believe with our whole heart that he hears us when we plead for our penitent brothers with a kind and devout spirit—he who invites us to pray, as he himself said in the Gospel:

> “Ask, and you will receive” (John 16:24).

And attend to this, brothers: the one who seeks penance begs to be excommunicated. Once he has received penance, he is cast outside covered in sackcloth.

He asks to be excommunicated because he judges himself unworthy to receive the Lord’s Eucharist. For this reason he wishes for a time to be separated from this altar, so that he may deserve to reach the altar that is in heaven with a secure conscience.

Therefore, with great reverence, he wishes to remove himself, as guilty and impious, from communion in the body and blood of Christ, so that through this very humility he may at last deserve to approach communion at the most holy altar.

### 3. The penitent must not, however, abstain from good works. Wine and meat are forbidden to him

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, this very person who so faithfully seeks penance with a contrite and compunctious heart must be so confident in the intercession of the whole people that, exercising himself with all his strength in good works and with God’s help, he remains concerned for his salvation.

He must not say in his heart: “Behold, the whole people has pleaded for my iniquities; therefore I can and ought to be secure.”

Far be it from the one who does penance to harbor this thought—not to mention expressing it in speech. Rather, with God’s help, let him rely on the prayers of others to such an extent that he strives to exercise himself in fasting, almsgiving, prayer, humility, charity, and every holy work; visiting the sick, restoring those in disagreement to harmony, receiving strangers, humbly washing the feet of holy pilgrims, and refraining from detraction and slander.

If his weakness permits, he should not drink wine. But if he cannot abstain because of old age or stomach pain, let him hear the Apostle saying:

> “Use a little wine for your stomach” (I Timothy 5:23).

There are some penitents who wish to be reconciled quickly for the sake of eating meat. It is certain that a person does not receive penance with sufficient compunction if, without being compelled by illness, he desires or presumes to eat meat.

Therefore even a penitent who has been reconciled [Note: [Col. 2229] In the Theoderic manuscript: “so that he may already have been reconciled,” etc.], wherever he may find vegetables, legumes, or small fish, whether at his own banquet or another’s, ought not to eat other meat [Note: [Col. 2229] See the Council of Chalon under Charlemagne, canon 35.].

I say this because, what is worse, there are some penitents who eat meat with great greed and sometimes drink strong wine even to drunkenness.

Our little body must be guarded with great caution, lest through drunkenness and gluttony it again urge us to commit such sins, so that what we appear to have done in penance may profit us little or nothing.

Let us therefore labor with all our strength, with God’s help, so that whatever, through God’s mercy, is restored to health from the wounds of our sins may not again be wounded through negligence.

May he himself grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.

Amen.

# SERMON CCLXII

[Note: [Col. 2229] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* this was the first homily of Caesarius, and it is likewise Eusebius’s tenth homily *To the Monks*. It should further be observed that the same sermon bears the name of Saint Faustus in the Ottobeuren Lectionary—by which Faustus of Riez is usually meant—but in the equally old Codex Compendiensis it is attributed to Caesarius. If anyone should maintain that it was first written by Faustus and afterward adopted by Caesarius along with several others, we would not strongly object, especially since in the aforementioned Ottobeuren Lectionary it has a different beginning, namely: “Behold, dearest brothers, the holy days of Lent.” On section 1, see above, Sermon 256, section 4; on section 2, Sermon 174, section 3, and Sermon 260, section 1; on section 3, Sermon 142, section 8; on section 4, Sermon 51, section 4.]

## On Penance

### 1. The effects of penance. It should correspond to offenses. Crimes subject to public penance. The nature of public penance

The divine word says in one place:

> “On the days of your solemn celebrations, afflict your souls” (Leviticus 16:29).

Why did it say this? Because fasts, vigils, and holy afflictions weaken humbled bodies but purify stained hearts; they take strength from the limbs but add brightness to the consciences.

Nevertheless, crimes of pleasure are redeemed through contrition of spirit, and the pleasures of the flesh that once deceived us are punished through the exercises of the hard cross. Thus, by present mortification, the sentence of future death is anticipated; while the author of the fault is humbled, the fault is consumed; and while outward affliction is imposed through voluntary discipline, the offense against the dread Judge is appeased. A small labor pays enormous debts that eternal fire would scarcely consume.

Therefore, as we discuss the matter of our salvation, let us do within ourselves what physicians usually do around us.

If an injury or irritation is felt in the outermost skin of the body, a milder medicinal treatment is applied. But if a wound is hidden in the bones or has penetrated into the depths of the organs, the concealed disease demands a harsher and more forceful medicine.

A similar method must be applied to the illness of the inner person.

If offenses are perhaps slight—for example, if someone has sinned in speech, in some blameworthy intention, with the eye, or with the heart—the stains of words and thoughts must be healed by daily prayer and wiped away by private compunction.

But if someone, examining his conscience, has committed a capital crime—for example, if he has attacked and betrayed his faith through false testimony, or violated the sacred name of Truth through the recklessness of perjury; if he has stained the true garment of baptism and the beautiful silk garment of virginity with the filth of violated chastity; if he has killed the new human being in himself by murdering another person; or if, through augurs, diviners [Col. 2230], and enchanters, he has surrendered himself captive to the devil—such offenses and those like them cannot be thoroughly expiated by common, moderate, or secret satisfaction.

Rather, grave causes require more grave, more severe, and public remedies [Note: [Col. 2230] The Synod of Agde, with Caesarius presiding, decreed concerning those guilty of these crimes—namely, “murderers and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion”—“unless they have cleansed their admitted crimes through the satisfaction of penance” (canon 37). It made the same provision in canon 42 concerning sorcerers and augurs. On perjurers, see the First Council of Mâcon, canon 17.], so that the one who destroyed himself along with the destruction of many may in a similar way redeem himself through the edification of many.

A man deceives himself if, while he feels a disease burning in his marrow, he applies a soft ointment only to the surface of his body.

## 2. Tears Should Be Added for the Death of One’s Only Soul. Why the Soul Is Called “Only.” Nor Should Works of Mercy Be Lacking

These principal evils therefore require abundant wailing and groaning and a fountain of tears. Through tears one must cry out with the prophet: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Psalm 37:9); and, “Every night I will wash my bed” (Psalm 6:7); and again, “I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10). Let no one despise this humility: it was the supreme King who did and said these things.

Thus, just as lamentation is raised over a dead person, so great mourning must be made over a soul that has perished. And just as a mother who has been bereaved commonly laments the loss of her only child with a broken heart, so it is fitting to grieve over one’s only soul—but with hope of restoration. Concerning this “only one,” the prophetic utterance says: “Deliver my soul, O God, from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm 21:21). Why did he say “only one”? Either because it must be loved as an only child, or because it alone, solitary before the heavenly tribunal and with all other consolations removed, will have to render an account.

Thus, I say, it is necessary to pour out the whole weight of sorrow over this only soul, pierced by the sword of sins, if perhaps, made alive by the fountains of tears, it may be roused by the warmth of faith. Compunction must be kindled; prayers must be strengthened by remembrance of the future judgment; and they must be assisted by works of mercy. The prophet’s sentence must be heard—but heard with the ear of obedience—when he says: “Receive my counsel, O king, and redeem your sins by almsgiving” (Daniel 4:24).

The example of that man in the Gospel must also be heard as though it had truly been written for our redemption: “Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor” (Luke 19:8). Concerning them we heard the Lord say, with ineffable condescension and love: “Whoever has done this for one of these least ones has done it for me” (Matthew 25:40). These words commend to us the efficacy of almsgiving by heavenly authority.

## 3. The Poor Can Perform These Things. Why God Permitted the Poor

But perhaps, when we speak of almsgiving, narrow poverty is frightened. It is not so, beloved. Rather, let it remember that small coins were preferred to the treasures of the rich, because our God is pleased not only by the abundance of generosity but also by the goodwill of the giver.

I think, beloved, that our God permitted the poor to exist in this world so that through the poor he might test the faith of the rich, or through the mercy shown to the poor might have mercy on the rich; so that those who possess abundance might not lack the opportunity for good works and redemption; so that a benevolent rich person might be enriched by another’s poverty; and so that every wealthy person might receive great profits from the needy.

By a wondrous and supreme exchange, while temporal generosity grants mercy to the needy, an eternal treasure is repaid in return. Let us therefore direct our actions, and devote whatever we can and whatever strength we possess to exercises of good will and to the pursuit of justice and mercy.

## 4. There Is No Place for Works of Mercy after This Life. The Merits Are the Garments of the Blessed. The Poor Can Enrich Another

Let us run while we have the light of life, before darkness overtakes us (John 12:35), because in that age it will no longer be possible to provide for amendment and redemption [Column 2231], as the divine word says: “For in death there is no one who remembers you” (Psalm 6:6).

Just as there will be no fear there of losing merits, so there will be no forgiveness of sins granted there; no opportunity for practicing good works will then be allowed. Will anyone be able to feed the hungry there, where the need to eat will not exist, where neither the wicked amid the flames of hell nor the righteous amid the delights of paradise will need food and drink? Will anyone be able to clothe the one who is cold there, where all care for covering the body will cease, where there will be that cold of which the prophet says: “Who can stand before his cold?” (Psalm 147:17)?

There the one who lost the wedding garment here will be naked forever; there the wicked will be clothed in the darkness of a stained conscience, while the good will be clothed with the cloak of immortality and blessedness. There garments will be merits, as the Lord says: “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Wisdom 3:7); and the prophet: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131:9); or again: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Psalm 44:10).

Where, then, an eternal light will shine in place of the tunic of the saints’ bodies, there clothing will be transformed into the body, never to be removed throughout the ages; there the garment will become a reward; there that angelic robe will no longer be an outer covering or apparel, but nature itself.

Will the greedy or miserly person be able to do good for another from his abundance there, where he will not find even a drop for himself in the midst of the burning lake? For he will carry nothing with him of what he believed he possessed as his own, as the prophet said: “For when he dies, he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend with him” (Psalm 48:18). He will hear amid unremitting punishments: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matthew 25:42).

Let us understand what condemnation it will be to strip the poor person whom it is the greatest crime not to have fed. To the one who now oppresses the frail and needy without any consideration of the future judgment—to him, I say, as someone has said, a great day will come when he will wish that the poor person had remained untouched by him rather than despoiled, and he will hate that day [Note: Alternatively: “which he hated.”].

It will be an unbearable pain if anyone incurs the causes of death from which he could have gained the joys of life. Therefore, do not despise the needy person who, although poor for himself, can make you rich. Let us eagerly seize from the present age what we can. Our days pass quickly; if only they may pass well.

Let us therefore seize what we can from this world, giving thanks to him who has so ordered both lives that the times of labors and struggles should quickly come to an end, while the joys of honors and rewards should last without end.

## SERMON 263

[Note: [Column 2231] Attributed to Caesarius in the manuscripts, and is his fourth homily among those published by Baluze. On no. 1, see above, Sermon 77, no. 5; on no. 2, Caesarius, Homily 24, and above, Sermon 77, no. 5, and 78, no. 3; on no. 4, Sermon 16, no. 4, and 37, no. 8.]

### An Admonition to Those Who Think That It Suffices for Eternal Life If They Have Done No Evil, Even Though They Refuse to Perform Good Works

### 1. Abstaining from Evil Is Not Enough

There are many, dearest brothers, who think that this alone suffices for them for eternal life: that they have done no evil deeds. Therefore, if there are any who deceive themselves by this false security, let them know most certainly that it does not suffice for any Christian merely not to have done evil, unless, to the extent that he can, he also performs those things which are good. For he who said, “Turn away from evil,” himself said, “and do good” (Psalm 33:15). In the Gospel he solemnly warns us, saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10). He did not say, “which bears bad fruit,” but “which does not bear good fruit.” From this you may recognize what hope one who has done evil can have, when one who has not done good will be cut down and thrown into the fire. Hence the Lord himself says: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21); and: “What profit is it that you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Matthew 7:21).

### 2. Whether One Who Has Not Taken Another’s Property Will Be Secure at Judgment

But someone says: “Although I have not given from my own possessions, neither have I taken another’s property; I shall be able to be secure on the day of judgment.” Attend carefully, and do not deceive yourselves with false security. For what does the Lord say? “When the Son of Man comes in his glory, all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Then he will say to those at his right: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom; for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.’ But to those on the left he will say: ‘Depart from me, cursed ones, into eternal fire; for I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink’” (Matthew 25:31, 42).

Attend carefully to what he said. He does not say, “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom, because you did not take another’s property”; rather, “because you distributed alms from your own possessions.” Likewise, he will not say to those set on the left, “Depart from me, cursed ones, into eternal fire, because you committed fraud”; rather, “because you did not give to the poor from your substance.” I beg you, brothers, consider this sentence carefully, and, as I have warned you, retain it also in memory. If the person who did not give his own substance to the poor is cast into the fire, where, do you suppose, will one be cast who seized another’s goods by whatever frauds? If one who did not clothe the naked is cast into the fire, consider where one will be cast who stripped the clothed.

Therefore, let the person who believes that it suffices for him not to have done evil, even if he has not done good, tell me whether he wants from his servant what he himself does to his Lord. Does he want his servant to do neither good at all nor evil? For we all want our servants not only not to do the evils we forbid, but also to perform the tasks we command. Although your servant is gravely guilty if he secretly steals away your animals, nevertheless the one who chooses to guard those animals negligently will not be without fault. It is not just that we should do to our Lord what we do not wish a servant to do to us. For we neither made our servants nor feed them, as it were, from our own substance; our God created and feeds both us and them. Yet we want servants whom we ourselves did not make to serve us with great diligence. Hence it is right that we acknowledge the lawful Lord, whose lordship we exercise over those subject to us. Brothers, we have said all this so that from our own servants we may recognize that it does not suffice for us not to do evil if we refuse to perform good.

### 3. Whether One May Justly Wish to Be at Death Such as One Was on the Day of Baptism. Illustrated by Examples
