For those who think it sufficient for themselves not to have done evil are also accustomed to say this: “Would that I might deserve to be found on the day of my death such as I came forth from the sacrament of Baptism.” It is indeed good that each person be found cleansed of all evils on the day of judgment; but it is a grave evil if he has made no progress in good works. Only the one who departed from this light immediately after receiving Baptism is sufficiently such as he came forth from the sacrament of Baptism: he had no time in which to exercise himself in good works. But for one who has had both a long time to live and an age capable of doing good, it does not suffice to be inactive in evil if he chooses also to be inactive in good.

I should like the person who wishes to be found at his departure such as he was when he deserved to receive the sacraments of Baptism to tell me—although it is good always to be cleansed from evils, it is a grave evil not to advance in good—if he planted a young vineyard in his field, whether after ten years he would want it to be such as it was on the day it was planted. If he grafted an olive grove, let us see whether it pleases him that after many years it should be such as it was when it was grafted. If a son has been born to him, let him consider whether he wishes him, after five years, to remain in the smallness and age of infancy in which he was born. Since there is no one to whom this would be pleasing concerning his own affairs, just as someone grieves over a vineyard, olive grove, or son if they have had no growth, so let him grieve if he discovers that he himself has made no progress from the time when he was reborn in Christ.

For we ought most certainly to know that, just as we want everything belonging to us—whether in flocks or in any fruits of the fields—to grow and prosper in every good, so without doubt our God both desires and expects this of us. Therefore let the Christian people, as his own special young vine, bear grapes rather than thorns, lest it be said of it as you have often sung in the Canticle: “I planted a vineyard and expected it to bear grapes; but it bore wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2). But because, as the Apostle says, when we were wild olive trees we were grafted into the good olive tree (Romans 11:24), we ought, with God’s help, so to persist in good works that with the prophet we may say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God” (Psalm 51:10).

### 4. Recapitulation

Therefore, through the matters set forth above, I beg you, brothers, that none of you should believe that this alone suffices for him, if he has not committed evil deeds; rather, with all the strength he can, let him so turn away from evil that he does good, and hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “What profit is it that you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46); and: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:16). By God’s favor, you know well what things Christ commanded to be done in the Gospel. “Love,” he says, “your enemies; do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father” (Matthew 5:44–45); and again: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41). On this matter let us hear blessed James also crying out with unreserved voice: “For as the body without the soul is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us do what is good with all our strength. Nor should it suffice us that we are such as we were when we received the sacraments of Baptism. For through Baptism we were emptied of all evils; but by doing good through God’s grace we ought to be filled with every good, lest perhaps, if we rely upon the sacrament of Baptism alone without good works, the unclean spirit which was expelled from us through Christ’s grace should return and, finding us empty of good works, bring with him seven spirits worse than himself, and our last state become worse than the first. Therefore, dearest brothers, if according to your holy custom you willingly receive these things and consider them more attentively, trusting not in faith alone but also in good works, you will be able so to abstain from evil acts that, with Christ’s help, you may continually exercise yourselves in good works. Thus you may deserve happily to hear, with exultation and joy, that blessed and desirable voice: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34), which may he deign to grant, who lives and reigns for ages, etc.

## SERMON 264

[Note: [Column 2233] Attributed to Caesarius in several manuscripts, and is the twelfth of the Homilies published under his name by Stephen Baluze. On no. 3, see Caesarius’s letter to certain Germans; on no. 5, Appendix Sermon 29, no. 3; 257, no. 4; and 279, no. 7.]

### An Exposition of Faith and an Interpretation of Its Name

### 1. Faith’s Praises Are Celebrated by All. Faith Is Named from *fit* [“it is done”]

In all the divine readings, dearest brothers, faith is praised with many encomiums; and not only the divine Scriptures but the whole human race does not cease to praise it. Would that, as it is praised by the tongue, so it were praised by life; as it is preached from the mouth, so it were held in the heart; and as it is promised by the lips, so it were fulfilled in works. So great, indeed, is the power of faith that even those who neglect to keep it presume to praise it. Faith is deservedly praised, for without it no good work is ever begun or completed, according to what is written: “Without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). Of it, in the person of Christ and the Church, it is said: “Come, my near one, from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4:8, according to the Septuagint). Blessed Paul the Apostle also, in that catalogue in which he praised all the ancient saints, commended them one by one, saying: “By faith Abel, by faith Enoch, by faith Noah, by faith Abraham pleased God” (Hebrews 11), etc. Of this the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 17:19); and: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and transplanted,’ and it will be done for you” (Matthew 17:19).

Although the good of faith is proclaimed with such great praises, many nevertheless do not know the meaning proper to its name. For *fides* [faith] takes its name from *fit*, that is, “it is done,” because in it lies the stability of all things, not only divine but also human. Hence, even if someone says in any words, and even with many oaths, that he has faith, if he refuses to fulfill in deeds what he says in words that he believes, it is not faith; for, as I said, faith takes its name from *fit*.

### 2. For Faith to Be Whole, One Must Believe Both What God Promises and What He Threatens. To Be True, It Must Act So as to Avoid the One and Obtain the Other

Let us see what one who wishes to keep faith whole ought to do: undoubtedly this, in which the foundation of the Christian religion is most firmly contained—that with his whole heart he trust as true both what God promises and what he threatens. For then he will be able both to understand the name of faith and to recognize its power more fully, if he sets these two things before his eyes: the reward of eternal life and the punishment of everlasting penalty. Since it does no good to believe one and doubt the other, let each person question his heart with great diligence as to whether he faithfully believes both. If in these two matters he finds that he has true faith, firmly retaining in his heart that the just will receive glory after good works and that the unjust will suffer everlasting punishment after evil works, then, when he has faithfully believed these things, if with his whole mind he strives to do good works by which he may attain the reward and not to do evil so that he may escape punishment, let him rejoice that he holds right faith, give thanks to God, and strive with his help to persevere in the work itself.

Thus, brothers, if you wish to attend carefully to these things, you will be able more fully to recognize both the name of faith and its power. Since faith takes its name from *fit*, as I said above, though you say a thousand times that you have faith [Note: [Column 2234] Perhaps: “a thousand times.”], if you refuse to fulfill in works what you promise in words, it is not faith at all. And if you assert that you believe the reward God promises and the punishment he threatens, yet—as has often already been said—refuse to act so that you may escape everlasting punishment and attain eternal rewards, there is no faith in you at all. Not only does it not help you to call yourself faithful in words, but it also greatly harms you, because it is better for anyone not to promise than to refuse to fulfill what he has promised. The name of faith alone will not be able to save you; rather, as has already been said, you will thereby be guilty in two ways: because you refused to fulfill what you promised in words; and because the Holy Spirit cries out to you through James: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

### 3. Therefore What Was Promised Especially in Baptism Must Be Fulfilled. Let No One Here Be Secure. Faith Is Imperiled Even by an Idle Word

Although everything that a person promises, if he can, ought to be fulfilled in works, we must especially keep, with God’s help, that first and distinguished promise which we make to God when we are reborn in Baptism. For at Baptism we are asked whether we renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works, and we answer freely that we will renounce them. Since infants cannot at all make this profession for themselves, their parents stand as sureties for them. Therefore, if we faithfully keep this primary matter, in which the foundation of the Christian religion consists, it is certain that with God’s help we shall be able to fulfill the rest. But if we neglect to fulfill what we promise God, I do not know whether we can keep the faith that is transacted among human beings. For if we dangerously promise something to any person in authority and neglect to fulfill it, how much more dangerous is it to promise God and not pay what is due?

But we fear a human being because we dread either death or bodily injury; we neglect to render to God what we promise because we wholly do not fear the death of the soul. And where is that Gospel saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body; rather fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28)? Therefore let what is promised to God be done first, so that what is promised to human beings may be fulfilled. Let each consider his conscience, and, if he sees that he has fulfilled what he promised, let him recognize that he has renounced the devil and his pomps not only in words but also in works, and rejoice that he has kept faith whole. Yet let him be secure concerning the past in such a way as to be solicitous about the future, because “not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end, will be saved” (ibid., 22).

But lest anyone perhaps think that faith can be broken only by capital crimes, what difference is there whether a person kills himself by striking himself with a greater or a smaller sword? Whoever says this should note that faith may be imperiled even by an idle word, for which the Lord said an account must be rendered on the day of judgment; and: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ or ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22).

### 4. The Pomps of the Devil

Therefore let each consider, as has already been said, what he promised in the sacrament of Baptism. Since he made a covenant with the Lord, let him see whether he has violated it in any respect. For when he was asked, “Do you renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works?” the priest then offered him the covenant to be subscribed. When he answered, “I renounce,” he subscribed it. Therefore, if, as has already been said above, we do not fulfill what we promised God, I do not know whether we can keep faith with human beings.

For we promised to renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works. What the devil’s pomps are, almost no one fails to know; nevertheless, it is necessary for us to mention some of them. All spectacles—frantic, bloody, or obscene—are pomps of the devil. To be enslaved to gluttony or drunkenness, to subject one’s unhappy soul to lust or luxury, certainly belongs to the devil’s pomp, because in such acts his pleasure is fulfilled. As to adulteries, murders, robberies, or false testimony, what need is there to say that they belong to the devil’s pomp or works, since no human being can be ignorant of this? Likewise, observing auguries, employing enchanters, and seeking out *caragii* [uncertain term] or diviners: all this undoubtedly belongs to the devil’s pomp or works [Note: [Column 2235] See what is to be said on the following sermon.].

And therefore, since few can be found who rejoice that they are free from all these things, let each, as I have said, have recourse to his conscience. While his soul is still contained in this little body, whatever he recognizes in himself either to have been or to be among the evils mentioned above, let him hasten to redeem or amend through penitence and almsgiving, and especially through forgiving his enemies. Thus, with God’s help, let him strive to heal past wounds in such a way that he never afterward presume to admit anything by which he may again be wounded.

### 5. Faith Without Works. There Is No Faith in One Who Despairs or Presumes

Nor should anyone vainly deceive himself by saying: “I believe in God’s mercy that my faith or my Baptism, which I received, will never perish.” You believe well if you have done what you promised. If you kept the covenant you entered with the Lord, be secure: neither your faith nor your Baptism will perish. But if you neglected to fulfill in works what you promised in words, with what face or conscience do you know that your Baptism has not perished, when you have not kept the covenant? Hear the Lord saying: “What profit is it that you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46); and again: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21); and again: “Not all who say to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but those who do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

Attend carefully, because according to the sentences written above it does a person no good to say that he has faith if he neglects to fulfill in works what he promises in words, according to that Scripture: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. It is much better not to vow than, after a vow, not to render what was promised” (Ecclesiastes 5:3–4). And that we may recognize this clearly also in relation to ourselves or our servants, let someone tell me whether it suffices him for his servant all day long to call him lord and never cease to extol him with many praises, while neglecting to perform the tasks he has commanded. Therefore, if words without works do not please us, how much more can faith without works be of no avail before God!

Above all, one must fear lest anyone believe that he will receive God’s mercy in such a way that he does not dread his justice: if he does this, there is no faith. Again, if he so dreads justice that he despairs of mercy, there is no faith. Therefore, because God is not only merciful but also just, let us believe both: fearing justice, let us not despair of mercy; nor let us so love mercy that we neglect justice. Therefore one must neither hope wrongly nor despair wrongly. One hopes wrongly who thinks that he will obtain mercy without penitence and good works; one despairs wrongly if, after good works, he does not believe that he will receive mercy. Hence above all we must consider and fear lest we believe faith can suffice us without good works. Rather, let us fear that saying of the Apostle James: “As the body without the soul is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James 2:26); and: “You believe,” he says, “that God is one? You do well. The demons also believe—and tremble” (ibid., 19). See, brothers, that the Apostle said that one who believes and does not act has the belief of demons. For if one who believes and does not act is called like the demons, it is for you to judge what hope one who does not believe has. The demons believe that God exists and do not do what God commands; this person is proved not to believe because he does not wish to fulfill in works what he seems to promise in words.

### 6. Recapitulation

That you may more fully recognize the works and power of faith, I wish briefly to set this before your Charity. For the whole power of faith seems to consist in two matters. One has often already been stated: that we should most certainly believe true what God promises. The other is that it should be settled among us that what he threatens is not false. For if with all your heart and all your mind you believe that after good works you will receive the promised reward, and likewise without any hesitation believe that, if you do evil works, you will suffer punishment without end, recognize that you retain faith whole—on this condition, however, that you fulfill in works what you believe in your heart, and without any delay turn away from evil and do good. In turning away from evil, you believe that punishment exists; in doing good, you believe that you will attain the reward.

Know, however, that it does you no good if you choose to believe one matter and doubt the other. For turning from evil benefits the one who immediately does good; and doing good benefits the one who wholly turns from evil. I say this because there are many who seem to give alms from robberies and frauds, yet do not wish to cease from those very evils. For you, dearest brothers, as I have said, your not doing evil benefits you only if you perform what you know pleases God. And you will be able faithfully to believe that recompense will be rendered you for your good works when, with God’s help, you have begun wholly to abstain from evil acts. For if you wish to do both good and evil works at once, what profit is it to build on one side and destroy on the other, to strip one person and clothe another?

To such persons the Lord cries in the Gospel: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matthew 12:33); and Solomon: “As a dog is hateful when it returns to its vomit, so is a sinner when he returns to his sin” (Proverbs 26:11); and the prophet: “Woe to the sinner entering upon the earth by two ways” (Ecclesiasticus 2:14); and: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). Therefore, as we have often suggested above, because faith takes its name from *fit*, that is, from what is done, the person who confidently says that he believes is the one who wishes to fulfill in works what he says he believes. As has been said, the whole power of faith is that we believe both what God promises and what he threatens. If we wish perfect faith to remain in us, let us, fearing punishment, not do evil works; and, desiring the reward, let us labor with all our strength to do what is good, so that we may not be compelled to endure eternal punishment with the unbelieving and ungodly, but may be able to attain the everlasting kingdom with the faithful and those who persevere in good works. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON 265

[Note: [Column 2237] Elsewhere, *On the Season*, 215.]

### On the Christian Name Accompanied by Non-Christian Works

[Note: [Column 2237] Now placed for the first time in the Appendix. In the Louvain edition it is doubtful; in the judgment of Verlin and Vinding it is spurious. Its style and subject agree especially well with Caesarius, of whom we read in his Life that “sermons against the evil of drunkenness and lust, against discord and hatred, against anger, sacrilegious persons and haruspices, against the utterly pagan rites of the Kalends, and against augurs, worshippers of trees, worshippers of springs, and various vices” were delivered; these were circulated through various provinces to be read to the people in church. Several items from these discourses were transferred into the treatise *On the Rightness of Catholic Conduct*, in the Appendix to volume six, and into certain other sermons published under the name of Eligius. On no. 1, see Appendix Sermon 233, no. 4; 115, no. 1; and 116, no. 1; on no. 2, below, Sermon 267, no. 5; and above, Sermon 168, no. 3; 21, no. 8; and 220, no. 2; on no. 3, below, Sermon 282, no. 4; Caesarius, Homilies 33 and 34; Sermon 17, no. 3; on no. 4, below, Sermon 277, no. 4; on no. 5, Sermon 129, no. 2; and 130, nos. 1 and 2, with notes; 278, no. 1; 130, no. 288, no. 2; 4; 277, no. 4; and, at the end, Caesarius, Homily 33.]

### 1. The Christian Name Is Not Enough. The Sign of Christ. Who Signs Himself to His Own Destruction. Whom It Benefits

I beg you, dearest brothers, that we consider more attentively why we are Christians and bear Christ’s cross upon our foreheads. For we ought to know that it does not suffice us to have received the Christian name if we do not perform Christian works, as the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “What profit is it that you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” If you call yourself Christ’s soldier, continually sign yourself with Christ’s cross, and do not give alms according to your means, or refuse to have charity, justice, or chastity, the Christian name will be of no profit to you.

Christ’s sign and Christ’s cross are a great thing; therefore something great and precious ought to be sealed with this most precious seal. What profit is it if you make a seal from a golden ring and store rotten chaff inside? What profit is it if we bear Christ’s sign on forehead and mouth, yet store crimes and sins within our souls? One who thinks, speaks, and acts wickedly, if he refuses to amend, does not diminish his sin when he signs himself, but increases it. For many, when they go to theft or adultery, if they strike their foot [against something], sign themselves, yet do not turn themselves back from the evil deed. Wretches that they are, they do not know that they shut demons more within themselves than they exclude.

But the person who, with God’s help, drives vices and sins away from himself and strives both to think and to perform what is good, rightly applies the sign of the cross to his lips, because he strives to do such works as deserve to receive Christ’s sign. And because it is written, “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Corinthians 4:20), and again, “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26), let us turn ourselves to good works, while remedies are in our power, so that we may possess the Christian name not for judgment but for remedy.

## 2. The Duties of a Christian: of the Head of a Household; of a Judge

And so, with God’s help, in order that you may fulfill these things, keep peace yourselves, and bring those who are at odds into harmony. Flee lying; do not make perjury, as it were, an everlasting death. Above all, as has already been said, according to your means give alms to the poor, and offer gifts to be consecrated on the altar. A person of adequate means ought to be ashamed if he receives Communion from another’s offering. Those who can should provide little candles, or oil to be placed in lamps [Note: [Col. 2238] *Cicindile* properly means a glowworm—French *ver luisant*. From this word it was transferred to mean an oil lamp. Caesarius uses the word in this sense in Homilies 21 and 22.]. Hold fast yourselves to the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and teach them to your children. For I do not know with what face someone can call himself a Christian if he neglects to learn the few verses of the Creed or the Lord’s Prayer.

Know that, for the children whom you receive at Baptism, you have become sponsors before God. Therefore always discipline and correct both those born from you and those whom you receive from the font, so that they may live chastely, justly, and soberly. Conduct yourselves in such a way that, if your children wish to imitate you, they may not burn in the fire together with you, but may reach eternal rewards together with you.

Those who hear legal cases should judge justly, and should not accept gifts against the innocent, because gifts blind the hearts of the wise and alter the words of the just; lest, while they acquire money, they lose their souls. No one has unjust profit without just loss. Where there is profit, there is also loss: profit in the chest, loss in the conscience. Let no one get drunk; let no one at his banquet force another to drink more than is proper, lest through drunkenness he destroy both his own soul and the other’s.

## 3. What Should Be Done on the Lord’s Day: in Churches and in Illnesses; the Effect of Extreme Unction

On every Sunday gather at church. If the wretched Jews celebrate the Sabbath with such devotion that they perform no earthly work on it, how much more ought Christians to devote themselves to God alone on the Lord’s Day and gather at church for the salvation of their souls? When you gather at church, pray for your sins. Do not engage in quarrels; do not stir up disputes and scandals. Whoever does these things when coming to church wounds himself there, where he could have been healed by prayer.

While standing in church, do not chatter, but listen patiently to the divine readings. Whoever wishes to chatter in church will have to give an account both for himself and for others, since he neither hears the word of God himself nor permits others to hear it. Also give tithes from your produce to the churches.

Let the one who was proud become humble; let the adulterer become chaste; let the one who used to steal or seize another’s property begin to distribute even from his own substance to the poor. Let the envious become benevolent. Let the one who has inflicted injury promptly ask forgiveness; let the one who has been injured promptly forgive.

Whenever any illness comes upon someone, let the sick person receive the body and blood of Christ, and then anoint his little body, so that what is written may be fulfilled in him: “Is anyone sick? Let him call for the presbyters, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5:14–15).

See, brothers, that whoever in illness has hastened to church will deserve both to receive bodily health and to obtain forgiveness of sins. Since, then, twofold blessings can be found in the church, why do miserable people try to bring upon themselves manifold evils through enchanters, springs, trees, and diabolical amulets, through magical characters, haruspices, diviners, or sorcerers [Note: [Col. 2239] These vices are frequently censured in the sermons that follow. The Council of Agde says that “the Catholic faith is especially harassed” by them, and establishes that those guilty of them “are to be regarded as strangers to the Church.” The Council of Auxerre likewise says in canon 4: “It is not permitted to consult sorcerers or auspices, nor *caragios*, nor lots, which they call those of the saints,” and so forth. Canon 3 adds: “It is not permitted to hold *compensos* in one’s own houses, nor vigils at the festivals of the saints, nor to fulfill vows among hedges, or at sacred trees or springs.” Canon 22 of the Second Council of Tours is also notable on this matter. Perhaps the same practice of tree-worship is meant by what we read in chapter 22 of the *Life of Saint Valerius*: “Near the bank of that river stood a great stump, marked with various images and thrust deeply into the earth with great force; the peasants worshiped it with excessive devotion in the manner of the pagans.” Certainly one of those sacrilegious trees was the one which Saint Martin, as Sulpicius relates in his *Life*, ordered to be cut down. Below, in Sermon 278, section 5, he again attacks these same rites sharply.].

## 4. What Must Be Avoided in Conversation; Bleatings before the Basilicas of the Saints

As we have already said, brothers, admonish your children and all your households continually, so that they may live chastely, justly, and wholesomely. Provoke them to good works not only by words but also by examples. Above all, wherever you are—whether in the house, on a journey, at a banquet, or in an assembly—do not utter shameful or lustful words from your mouths. Rather, continually admonish your neighbors and those close to you to strive always to speak what is good and honorable, lest, by slandering, speaking evil, and leading dances at holy festivals, they utter lustful and shameful songs with the tongue from which they ought to have praised God, and thus appear to inflict wounds upon themselves.

For these wretched and miserable people, who neither fear nor are ashamed to engage in bleatings and dances before the very basilicas of the saints, even if they come to church as Christians, return from church as pagans, because this custom of dancing has remained from pagan observance. Consider now what sort of Christian that person is who comes to church to pray and, neglecting prayer, is not ashamed to utter from his mouth the sacrilegious words of the pagans.

Yet see, dearest brothers, whether it is right that from the mouths of Christians—where the body of Christ enters—a lustful song should issue forth like the devil’s poison. Above all, whatever you wish others to do to you, do that to others; what you do not wish others to do to you, do to no one else. If you wish to fulfill this, you can free your souls from every sin. Even one who does not know letters can hold these two sentences in memory and, with God’s help, can and ought to fulfill them in his deeds.

## 5. Remnants of Pagan Superstitions; Superstition on Thursday

And although I believe that the wretched custom which remained from the profane observance of the pagans has now, through our corrections and by God’s inspiration, been removed from these places, nevertheless, if you still recognize anyone practicing that most filthy disgrace involving the little mule or little deer (*hinnicula* or *cervula*), correct them with such severity that they will repent of having committed the sacrilegious act.

And if, when the moon is obscured, you still know of anyone shouting, admonish them also, declaring to them that they commit a grave sin when they trust that by their shouts they can defend the moon, which is obscured at appointed times by God’s command, against evil influences.

And if you still see anyone making vows at springs or trees, and, as has already been said, seeking sorcerers, diviners, or enchanters, or hanging diabolical amulets and magical characters—or herbs or juices—on themselves or their dependents, rebuke their many sins with the utmost severity and say that whoever does this evil loses the sacrament of Baptism.

And because we have heard that the devil so deceives certain men and women that on Thursday neither the men perform work nor the women engage in wool-working, we call God and his holy angels to witness that whoever wishes to observe this practice, unless he makes amends for such sacrilege through a long and severe penance, will be condemned in the place where the devil will burn.

For these wretched and miserable people, who do no work on Thursday in honor of Jupiter, certainly do not, I suspect, fear or blush to perform those very works on the Lord’s Day. Therefore, whoever you discover to be such, correct with the utmost severity; and, if they refuse to amend, do not permit them to come either to your conversation or to your banquets. If they belong to you, even beat them with rods, so that they may at least fear bodily wounds, since they do not think about the salvation of their souls [Note: [Col. 2240] What is said here about superstition on Thursday is splendidly illustrated and confirmed by canon 15 of the Council of Narbonne of the year 589. The bishops first say: “It has come to our attention that certain people of the Catholic faith cultivate Thursday, which is also called Jupiter’s day, with an execrable rite, and do no work on it.” They then decree: “Whoever, apart from the festivals, dares to keep free and do no work on that day: if he is freeborn, he is to be expelled from the church and placed under penance, satisfying for one year by almsgiving and tears; if he is a male or female slave, after correction by lashes he is to be handed over to his master.” The same council, in canon 4, decrees that those who work on Sunday are to be fined six solidi if freeborn, but, if slaves, punished with one hundred lashes. Since Sedatius, bishop of Béziers, is recorded as a signatory of this synod, this might provide grounds for conjecturing that several preceding sermons do not bear the name of Bishop Sedatius without reason, and that this one too perhaps ought to be attributed to him, unless Caesarius’ distinct manner of speech and other indications make his authorship evident. Yet no equal agreement with this sermon is found in the words of the Council of Narbonne as regards the matters explicitly expressed.].

For we, dearest brothers, mindful of your danger, admonish you with paternal concern. If you willingly listen to us, you will bring us joy, and you yourselves will happily reach the kingdom. May he grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 266

[Note: [Col. 2240] Formerly, *On Time* 216.]

### What Good Christians and Bad Christians Are Like

[Note: [Col. 2240] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave its authenticity doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus reject it as spurious. Among the Ambrosian sermons it appears as number 58, *On the Ascension*, where it is somewhat longer because of an addition near the end; at the beginning it differs by only one or two words, beginning, “Let us praise the Lord, dearest brothers, and let us give thanks,” and so forth. It is certainly by the same author as the preceding sermon, namely Caesarius of Arles. For section 1, see Caesarius, at the beginning of Homily 20, and Appendix Sermon 141, section 4; for section 2, Sermons 116, section 6; 142, section 7; and 277, section 4; for section 3, Sermon 45, section 3; the preceding sermon, section 1; 115, section 1; 116, section 1; and 142, section 7; below, Sermon 295, section 6; and above, Sermon 130, section 2.]

### 1. Why We Are Christians

He whose entire thought is about this life alone is like the beasts. We rejoice, dearest brothers, and give thanks to God, because we have been worthy to find you safe according to our desires. And truly, brothers, a father rightly and deservedly rejoices whenever he finds his children healthy in body and devoted to the fear of God.

And since divine mercy has now granted us a twofold joy, concerning both your salvation and our own, we ought to bring before your Charity what pertains to the progress of your souls. It is necessary, dearest brothers, that with the whole attention of our minds we strive to inquire and understand why we are Christians and why we carry the cross of Christ on our foreheads.

Recognize and understand, brothers, that we have not become Christians merely so that we may be concerned with this life, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people” (1 Corinthians 15:19). For whoever thinks only about this life is like the animals and cattle. What do animals seek except to eat and drink, to indulge in lust, and to sleep? [Col. 2241] Such are those who think more about their flesh than about their soul, who love appetite and lust more than chastity and justice.

You must know, dearest brothers, that we became Christians so that we might always think about the future age and eternal blessedness, and work more for the soul than for the body. Our flesh will be in this world for only a few years; but our soul, if we act well, will reign in heaven without end.

If, however—which God forbid—we practice evil deeds and labor more for the lust of the flesh than for the salvation of the soul, I fear that, when good Christians receive eternal life with the angels, we may, God forbid, be cast headlong into hell.

### 2. Who Is Truly a Christian

It is not enough for us, brothers, that we have received the name Christian if we do not perform Christian works. The name Christian benefits the person who loves chastity, flees drunkenness, detests pride, and rejects envy as the devil’s poison.

That person is truly a Christian who does not steal, does not give false testimony, neither lies nor commits perjury, does not commit adultery, comes frequently to church, does not taste the produce of his fields before first offering something from it to God, gives tithes every year to the poor, shows honor to his priests, loves all people as himself, and hates no one.

Indeed, not only is that person a Christian, but Christ himself dwells in him: he fears fraudulent scales and double measures as the devil’s sword.

That person is a good Christian who, when he comes to church, both brings offerings to be placed on the altar and, according to his means, extends money or a morsel of bread to the poor; who receives travelers into his home; who washes the feet of guests; who not only does not stir up disputes but also reconciles those who are at odds; who shows honor and the love of true charity to his elders and parents; who himself lives chastely and teaches his children or neighbors, both by words and by example, to live chastely and soberly.

That person is a good Christian who, whenever holy solemnities arrive, preserves chastity with his own wife for several days beforehand so that he may receive Communion more securely, and may dare to approach the Lord’s altar with a sincere and secure conscience, chaste in body and pure in heart; who knows the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart, and faithfully teaches his sons and daughters so that they too may know them.

### 3. Who Is Unworthy of the Name Christian

Behold, brothers, you have heard what good Christians are like. Therefore, as far as we can, with God’s help let us labor so that the Christian name may not be false in us, and so that Christ’s sacraments may not suffer injury in us; but let us always both conceive Christian works in our hearts and fulfill them in action.

For what sort of Christian is someone who scarcely ever comes to church, and, when he comes, does not stand to pray for his sins, but either tells stories [Note: [Col. 2241] The older manuscript reads “fables.”] or stirs up disputes and quarrels; and, if he finds the opportunity, drinks to the point of vomiting, then, after getting drunk, rises like a frantic and insane person to bleat in the devil’s fashion, dance, and sing shameful, amorous, or lustful words?

Such a person does not hesitate to steal, is not afraid to commit adultery, gives false testimony, curses, and commits perjury. Whether men or women, those who do such things receive the Christian name and the sacrament of Baptism not for a remedy but for judgment; and unless they do penance, they will perish forever.

Behold, brothers, we have shown you what good Christians and bad Christians are like. Therefore imitate those whom you see to be good; but those whom you recognize as bad, continually discipline, rebuke, and correct, so that you may receive a double reward for your own progress and for their perfection.

Let those who are good—chaste and sober, humble and kind—persevere, with God’s help, in good works. But let those who do evil works correct themselves quickly, before their souls depart from this light. For if they die without penance [Col. 2242], they do not come to life but are cast down into death.

May the merciful Lord deign to free us from that punishment, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 267

[Note: [Col. 2242] Formerly, *On Time* 116.]

### An Exhortation to the Candidates for Baptism

[Note: [Col. 2242] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors regarded it as doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus considered it spurious. Its author is easily recognized by comparison with other sermons of Caesarius. For section 2, see Appendix Sermon 115, section 4; below, Sermons 274, section 2; 265, section 3; 68, section 3; and 266, section 2. For section 4, Sermons 261, section 3; 294, sections 1 and 10; and 10, section 5. For section 5, Sermon 264, section 4.]

### 1. Candidates as Those Who Seek Together; What They Seek

Today, dearest brothers, the sermon of our humility is addressed especially to the Candidates for Baptism. Although our admonition also applies to all baptized believers, and we believe that everyone who is concerned for the salvation of his soul will find in this humble exhortation of ours something by which he may progress, nevertheless we wish to admonish particularly those who now desire the sacraments of Baptism.

First, therefore, let these Candidates recognize why they are called by this name. They are called *Competentes*, “those who seek together,” just as *considentes* means nothing other than “those sitting together,” *colloquentes* means nothing other than “those speaking together,” and *concurrentes* clearly means “those running together.” So *Competentes* can mean nothing other than “those seeking together.”

Behold, they have now learned why they bear the name *Competentes*. But those who seek together must now know what they seek. What, then, do those who desire the sacraments of Baptism seek? What indeed except that those who were vessels of the devil may deserve to become vessels of Christ? All this is fulfilled spiritually in us through the ministries of the angels.

### 2. How They Should Prepare to Obtain This; Let Them Abandon Hatred and Restore What They Possess Unjustly

Therefore I beg and admonish you, all you Candidates, and at once solemnly declare and announce to you: with God’s help, during these days up to Easter carefully search your consciences, lest there be even one person against whom you retain hatred in your heart.

For if the person who is to be baptized keeps anger or hatred in his heart, I do not know whether divine grace will prosper in him. He is going to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). And if what he prays is to take place in him, what remains except that, just as he has forgiven, so divine justice may forgive him, according to what the Lord himself said: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37–38). Thus the person who does not forgive closes the door of divine mercy against himself by saying, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive.”

First, then, let the Candidates pay special attention not to hate anyone. Second, let them examine their consciences, and if, as commonly happens, they have injured anyone, let them promptly ask forgiveness. Third, if through theft, false testimony, some deceit, fraudulent scales, or double measures they have taken anything from anyone, let them restore it—if they cannot, following Zacchaeus’ example, fourfold (Luke 19:8), at least in the same amount.

For I do not know with what face someone can believe that he is able to receive the grace of divine mercy if he refuses to restore another’s property, which he wrongly took.

### 3. Let Them Do Penance for Their Crimes

Perhaps the Candidates must also observe this: if they recognize that, persuaded by the devil, they have committed theft, homicide, or adultery; or if a female Candidate has at some time taken diabolical potions to cause an abortion and killed her children while they were still in the womb, or even after they were born—for this is a very grave sin—let them seek God’s mercy for all these things with groaning and contrition, and let them come to the sacraments of Baptism cleansed through penance.

Above all, all who see that they bear these guilts must observe this: let them preserve chastity both before Baptism and, after Baptism [Col. 2243], let them abstain from sexual pleasure for a considerable time.

### 4. What They Must Avoid, Lest They Be Cast Out of the Church as a Miscarriage

Let them flee the poison of envy, lest they appear to be imitators of the devil, of whom it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his faction imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25).

Let them also strive to avoid pride, through which the devil himself fell, because Christ, whom they desire to follow, was gentle and humble of heart. They must fear greatly what is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Let them not utter lies from their mouths, because it is written: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7); and again: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

Let them abstain not only from perjury but also from swearing, because the one who said it did not lie: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague will not depart from his house” (Sirach 23:12).

Let them take little wine during these days; and when the days of Easter arrive, let them guard themselves with great care from gluttony and drunkenness, lest what has been cleansed or illumined through the sacrament of Baptism be darkened by intemperance if gluttony should creep in.

Therefore, even if someone tries to force them to drink under the guise of an unfriendly friendship, let them flee entirely and never consent at all; but let them take in food and drink what is fitting and beneficial for Christians.

And since Christ, inspiring it, has conceived all the Candidates in the womb of Mother Church, let them practice nothing unjust or dishonorable, lest by acting wrongly they disturb the maternal entrails and the holy mother cast them out as an abortion before the appointed birth. Rather, let all the Candidates be kind, humble, gentle, and sober, so that, coming in due order to the sacrament of saving Baptism, they may be changed from goats into lambs, transferred from the left to the right, and, with those who will be on the right, happily hear that desirable voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

### 5. The Duty of Sponsors; Sponsors and Those Sponsored Enter into a Covenant with Christ

If your Charity carefully considers its customary practice, you can recognize that our admonition, although spoken to the Candidates, can nevertheless apply to all baptized believers.

Therefore, we who were reborn in Christ long ago should provide these who are to be baptized with an example of holy conduct in everything, so that, if they wish to imitate us, they may not be dragged to death along the broad and spacious way, but may deserve to reach life by the narrow and constricted way.

Therefore you ought to admonish them not only by examples but also by words concerning every good work. Especially those who desire, in religious love, to receive sons or daughters should not cease, both before they are baptized and after they have been baptized, to admonish and teach them concerning chastity, humility, sobriety, and peace, and should recognize that they are their sponsors.

For they answer on their behalf that they renounce the devil, his pomp, and his works. Therefore both those who receive and those who are received—that is, both fathers and children—should strive to keep the covenant which they write with Christ in the sacrament of Baptism. Let them never desire anything from the devil’s pomp or from the lustful pleasures of this world.

Thus, with God’s help, both those who receive children, if they live chastely and justly, and those who are received, if they wish to imitate them, may, as we believe, reach eternal rewards together. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 268

[Note: [Col. 2243] Formerly, *On the Words of the Lord* 3; later, Appendix 1.]

## On Keeping God’s Commandments

[Note: [Col. 2243] In very many manuscripts it is attributed to Augustine, but in two better-quality Corbie manuscripts it is attributed to Chrysostom.]

### 1. In Keeping God’s Commandments, Disciple and Teacher Must Agree Equally; Whoever Does Not Keep Them Hates Life

Since it is appropriate for us, in fulfillment of our office, to speak, and fitting for you, in devotion, to listen, what could be so necessary and so pertinent to both sides as that what is religiously spoken and devoutly heard should be maintained by corresponding obedience?

For if it is gain not to be silent about religious matters, and loss to be silent, how much greater gains can arise when the effect of action demonstrates whatever is learned and retained from heavenly teaching? The same obligation binds both speaker and hearer, so that the profession of each may be marked by the testimony of deeds.

Although the office of teacher and learner is different, the obedience owed to the holy laws must nevertheless be equal in both: those separated by office must be joined in deeds; those differing in name must be united in practice; and those whom titles separate from one another must be faithfully and devoutly joined by observance of the commandments.

Thus the activity of each is different, but the necessary result of observance must be equal in both, so that agreement in deeds may correspond in both, even though their names sound differently.

In a teacher it is a grievous matter to speak and not act, to command and not obey. In a learner it is likewise grievous to wish to hear what he does not wish to fulfill: to offer his ears to hearing while turning his will away from action.

But the one who does what he teaches, and the one who fulfills what he commands, is declared by the Lord’s judgment to be greatest in heaven (Matthew 5:19). The person who neglects what he learns, however, and the person who despises what he hears, is guilty of his salvation, because he despised what ought to be observed and did not avoid the dangers.

For the person who does not keep the commands of life loves death; and the person who repeatedly commits sins deserving death with a mind abandoned to despair hates life. Just as life is acquired through observance of the law, so death is found by the disobedient through contempt, as the Lord says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17).

Thus the perfect teacher is free from blame regarding the learner whom he has taught, while the contemptuous disciple will be without excuse: he learned what ought to be done and despised it.

Conversely, the teacher is punished more severely and afflicted by the example of an obedient disciple when he has handed on to others what ought to be done but has not done it himself, so that he could not learn from the disciples whom he taught, nor borrow from them the example of deeds after giving them the mastery of teaching.

Perfection does not consist in knowledge of the laws, since it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 2:13). Nor, I say, is the person religious and holy who knows the law while his deeds cease, since doing is better than teaching without doing. For it is troublesome to teach and not to do.

### 2. God’s Kindness toward Humanity: He Draws People to Himself through Threats and Promises, and Punishes Reluctantly; a Person Merits According to What He Wills

“You are my friends,” he says, “if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

O great goodness of God! Although, according to our condition, we owe him obedience—as servants to a lord, attendants to God, subjects to the powerful, slaves to the redeemer—he promises us the rewards of friendship, so that he may obtain from us the obedience owed by servants. Those whom he sees unwilling to serve of their own accord he can invite through promises of his benefits; and those whose wills he sees estranged from him he can make his own through the generosity of rewards.

Why else does he so often invite through reward or terrify through punishment, except that, by the counsel of his kindness, he may care for the human being formed by him and provide for the one he redeemed? Thus the person who is not frightened by punishment may be invited by reward, and the person whom fear cannot recall from sin may be recalled by the kindness of promises.

For he desires to help even the guilty [Note: [Col. 2244] We have preferred the reading of manuscript *cb* to that of the other manuscripts and printed editions, which have “the unwilling.”]; he longs to show mercy to sinners. If anyone has sinned, let him offer worthy fruits of repentance. He punishes the guilty unwillingly if they despise God’s indulgence in his mercy [Note: [Col. 2244] So the better manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “if they do not despise God’s indulgence in his mercy.”].

He loves to correct sinners, since from the beginning he established human beings for life, not death. The person who despises the counsel of the healing Lord brings destruction upon himself.

“Return to me,” he says, “and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7); and again: “I do not desire the death of the dying; let him only return and live” (Ezekiel 18:32).

The Lord does not wish death to rule over anyone; he does not wish a human being whom he established for life to be led into punishment. Rather, the human being himself makes himself worthy of death if he does not obey the law. The person who despises divine instruction hates life.

For when the Lord showed a human being what he wished and what he did not wish [Note: [Col. 2245] So the *cb* manuscripts. The printed editions read: “when the Lord wished to show the human being,” and so forth. After the words “bring death,” they add: “he invited through reward, terrified through punishment.” In place of this addition, manuscript *g* had: “If you wish to have life, keep the commandments,” with this note written in the margin: “Read thus until you find something better.”]—which bring life to the one who observes them and death to the one who despises them—life cannot arise from contempt, just as death cannot arise from observance.

Thus a person now receives according to what he wills and is judged according to what he has deserved. Everything depends on the human will: from the quality of his life a person acquires for himself the merit he will possess.

Therefore, having carefully considered these matters—namely, from where salvation and from where danger arise—let us hold fast to the benefits of salvation through diligent observance, and, as prudent people, avoid the evils of danger through contempt of the law. Thus, while we hold fast to prosperity and repel adversity, may we be found in the sight of the Lord and be rewarded by him with all the saints forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 269

[Note: [Col. 2245] It appears among the Caesarian Homilies both in manuscripts and in printed editions: in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* after the fortieth homily, but in the book printed under the care of V. C. Baluzius as the tenth homily in order. For section 1, see below Appendix Sermons 270, section 1; 28, section 4; and 273, section 1. For section 2, Sermons 210, section 6; and 271, section 6; 66, section 1; and 210, section 6. For section 3, Sermon 298, section 3. For section 4, Sermons 107, section 2; 112, section 2; 273, section 5; and 107, section 3. For section 5, see Augustine’s Sermon 350, under whose name it is cited in Eligius’ Homily 11.]

## An Exhortation to Hold Fast and Preserve Charity

This admonition also shows that no one can ever excuse himself truthfully by claiming that he cannot possess true charity. We also believe that some sentences from the homily which Saint Augustine wrote concerning charity should be inserted into this sermon, insofar as seemed appropriate to us.

### 1. The Possession of Charity Is Sweet and Its Acquisition Easy; the Holy Spirit Pours It into the Hearts of All Christians; Charity Cannot Coexist with Greed; the Sweetness of Charity

The chief reason why we so frequently impress upon you the good of true charity, dearest brothers, is that it is the Lord’s principal and distinctive commandment, and that nothing can be possessed more sweetly or, with God’s help, fulfilled more easily and successfully.

The matter is enacted in our mind. If the will does not admit some evil into it, iniquity does not know how to find a place. And where greed, the root of all evils, is absent, charity, the root of all good things, cannot be lacking.

The first and singular cause of divine mercy is that, through the Holy Spirit, charity itself is so poured into the hearts of all Christians (Romans 5:5) that, if they wish, they can continually preserve it and be unceasingly satisfied by its sweetness.

And because opposites are accustomed to be healed by opposites, and nothing is so contrary and opposed to charity—the foundation of all good things—as greed, the root of all evils, and because these two can in no way exist together, since sweetness does not accord with bitterness, light with darkness, or life with death, whoever recognizes that the root of greed rules within him should implore God’s help so that he may uproot greed and plant charity.

Whoever faithfully does this will fulfill all God’s commandments with joy and exultation. Whenever any bitterness of the world comes upon him, the sweetness of charity will not permit it to prevail in him. True charity will so reveal to him the sweetness of all heavenly good things that it will make him endure patiently [Col. 2246] the bitterness of earthly things.

The second reason is that the burden of charity is so light that it is accustomed not to weigh one down but to lift one up. Whoever wishes to preserve it, as he received it from Christ, with Christ’s help, will not feel weariness either in running with his feet or in working with his hands, nor will he be able to labor while carrying heavy burdens on his shoulders.

For as long as he exercises himself in difficult works for the love of charity, the sweetness of that love does not allow him to feel the labor. Whatever is heavy to one who does not love is pleasant and light to one who loves.

## 2. His Practices and Works

Let each person therefore maintain good will and love all people as himself; and whatever he wishes others to do to him, let him wish to do to others. Let him pray for the good, that they may be protected by the Lord; for those of middling character, that they may become better; for the wicked, that they may correct themselves quickly. In all sinners, let him hate their vices rather than the people themselves, and, following the example of good physicians, hate the disease, not the sick person.

For whoever hates sinners—or any enemies of his—more than their vices either wishes them to be punished in the present or burned in the eternal fire in the future. Your holy Charity clearly recognizes how execrable and abhorrent this is. Good Christians, however, all desire their enemies to be corrected rather than perish, and because of that ineffable goodness they strive not to curse either them or anyone else, on account of what is written: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Let them never swear, because it is written: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and punishment will not depart from his house” (Ecclus. 23:12). When it says that punishment will not depart from his house, this is to be understood not of his earthly house but of his soul, which is the temple of God.

Let him also strive never to lie, because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and “You will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5:7). Let him strive to maintain justice, because of this saying: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. 105:3). Let him hasten with his whole heart to preserve chastity, because chastity makes people like the angels.

All these things that I have recommended are brief, so that they can be committed to memory, and so pleasant and sweet that, with God’s help, they ought to be fulfilled in deeds.

## 3. No Excuse Is Possible for These Things. All Good Things Are in Charity

Behold, in all these works of true and perfect charity, as has already been said, nothing is done either with the hands or with the feet, so that no one may try to excuse himself on the grounds of impossibility or weakness. Since greed is more bitter than every bitterness, and charity sweeter than every sweetness, why do people willingly bear the harsh and rough yoke of avarice, with such dangers and labors, while they shake Christ’s sweet burden and his gentle yoke from their shoulders?

Against these things that I have recommended to your Charity, no one will be able to offer any kind of plausible excuse by claiming that he cannot accomplish them. He is not told, “Fast more than you can,” or “Keep vigil more than you are able.” Nor is he required to abstain from wine or meat if his bodily weakness does not tolerate this. And if perhaps he is not strong enough to be perfect, he is not compelled to sell all that he has and give it to the poor. And if he cannot be a virgin, he is not pressured into being forbidden to take a wife.

In all these matters that concern the body’s exertion, no Christian is compelled unwillingly. Let the one who can fulfill them give thanks to God; but let the one who cannot fulfill them hold fast to true charity, and in it he will possess everything. For without those good works mentioned above, charity is sufficient in itself; but those good works without charity can be of no benefit at all.

I say all this to you repeatedly, dearest brothers, so that you may more fully recognize that no one can excuse himself by saying that he cannot fulfill God’s commandments. When he tries to excuse himself from those matters in which the body labors, he will be unable to offer any excuse concerning those matters that consist in strength of soul, and especially charity, in which all good things are contained—things that, with God’s help, he can already accomplish.

Therefore, whoever is unwilling to hold true charity finds nothing that he can rightly charge to others; rather, he finds what he must charge to himself.

## 4. Without It There Is No Good

Hold fast, therefore, dearest brothers, to the sweet and salutary bond of charity, without which the rich person is poor, and with which the poor person is rich. If the rich person does not have charity, what does he have? If the poor person has charity, what does he not have?

And since, as blessed John the Evangelist says, “Charity is God” (1 John 4:16), what can be lacking to the poor person if, through charity, he has merited to possess God? Conversely, what benefit will earthly wealth bring the rich person if he has not merited to possess God?

Love and hold fast to charity, therefore, dearest brothers, without which no one will ever see God. Do not flatter yourselves in the absence of charity, even if you have performed the other good works. Rather, fear what is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10).

What is this one thing, if not true and perfect charity? Concerning it the Apostle again said: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying in you: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Gal. 5:14). For the other works are so useless without charity that the Apostle cries out in a clear voice: “If I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Therefore, since true charity is that which loves all people, whoever recognizes that he hates even one person should hasten to vomit out the bitterness of gall, so that he may deserve to receive within himself the sweetness of charity. For without it neither fasts, vigils, prayers, almsgiving, faith, nor virginity can benefit anyone.

And because, admonishing us about charity, the Apostle said, “Rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. 3:17), and charity is the root of all good things, it is most evident that just as any beautiful and pleasant tree, full of flowers and fruits, withers in all its beauty if it does not have a living root, so any Christian who shows that he possesses the other good works as though they were branches, and who presumes upon them without charity, refusing to possess the root of charity itself, will remain barren and without any fruits.

## 5. An Encomium of Charity

True charity endures in adversity, exercises restraint in prosperity, is strong amid harsh sufferings, joyful in good works, most secure in temptation, sweetest among true brothers, most patient among false ones, innocent amid ambushes, grieving amid iniquities, and breathing freely in truth.

It is chaste in Susanna toward her husband, in Anna after her husband, and in Mary apart from a husband; humble in Peter for obeying, free in Paul for reproving, human in Christians for confessing, and divine in Christ for forgiving.

True charity, dearest brothers, is the soul of all the Scriptures, the power of prophecy, the foundation of knowledge, the fruit of faith, the wealth of the poor, and the life of those who are dying.

Hold fast to it faithfully, therefore; love it with your whole heart and the whole strength of your soul; cling to it continually. For the Lord is sweet and sweeter than every sweetness. Fellowship with him has no bitterness, and life with him has no deceit.

If you wish to hold it with an undivided heart, it will enable you in this world to fulfill God’s commandments with joy, and in the future to attain eternal rewards. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 270

*[Note: [Col. 2247] Elsewhere, 8 among the Fifty Homilies.]*

On the love of charity and hatred of greed; and that the kingdom of heaven can be purchased not only with two small coins but also with good will; and on the pressing of grapes and olives.

*[Note: [Col. 2247] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. To the Louvain editors its authenticity was uncertain; Verlino and Vinding considered it spurious. The author imitates or copies Augustine, but intermixes certain things that are foreign to him, such as the statement about charity and greed in section 1, “Unless one has been uprooted from the root, the other cannot be planted”; and the expression in the same place, “Someone therefore tries in vain to cut off the branches”; and in section 5, “so that wine and oil may be stored in the canava.” From other homilies of Caesarius we have learned that these words and phrases belong to Caesarius. For section 1, see Appendix, Sermon 269, section 1; for section 3, Sermon 142, section 2; Augustine, Expositions on the Psalms 49, section 13, and 111, section 3; for section 5, Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 83, section 1, and Caesarius, Homily 32.]*

## 1. Charity and Greed Cannot Exist Together

Blessed Paul the Apostle, dearest brothers, in order to commend to us the sweetness of true and perfect charity, set before us the bitterness of greed. Like a most skilled and spiritual physician, he showed us what we ought to flee and what we ought to seek.

Since greed is the root of all evils and charity is the root of all good things, and since the two cannot exist together, unless one has been uprooted entirely, the other cannot be planted. Someone therefore tries in vain to cut off the branches if he does not strive to uproot the root.

Thus the same Apostle says: “The root of all evils is greed. By desiring it, some have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows; but you, man of God, flee these things.” Let us therefore listen to the counsel of the one in whom Christ the Lord was speaking, and, as far as we can, let us strive to flee the bitterness of avarice if we wish to reach the sweetness of charity.

## 2. What the Rich Person Should Do with His Wealth

### An unjust desire for the increase of one’s patrimony

But when we speak about contempt for riches, some rich person replies to me: “I have learned not to hope in the uncertainty of riches. I do not want to be rich, lest I fall into temptation; but since I already am rich, what am I to do with what I have happened to possess?”

The Apostle continues: “Let them give easily; let them share” (1 Tim. 6:10–11, 18). What does it mean to share? It means to make your property common with the one who has nothing.

If you begin to share, you will no longer be that plunderer and robber who clings to the necessities of the poor as though they were another’s property. Indeed, you have made your property common with those who have nothing, and you provide even more, since you have become a provider for the poor.

You take some care to ensure that food reaches the poor person in safety, and in this way you exercise mercy in advance. For this reason God accords you honor and, as it were, says to you: “First take from the common property what is sufficient for the needs of your household; what remains, give to Christ.”

Prepare yourself to hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that was prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:34–35).

Perhaps you used to despise some poor or needy person. Do not despise Christ, who sits in heaven and is in need on earth. He will come with recompense, eternal life, and eternal fire.

Thinking about this, you can be rich with some hope. But if you still want to become rich, and not only are unwilling to distribute to the needy what lies unused beyond your needs, but also want to increase your patrimony, perhaps you place some hope even in acts of plunder.

Unless perhaps you say: “God knows that I do not want to increase my patrimony through plunder.” How do you want to increase it? “By buying.” Do you seem innocent to yourself because you want to increase it by buying? You are not wicked through robbery, but you are wicked in your desire.

If someone said to you, “Sell your possessions,” you would shudder, tremble, and regard it as a curse. When, therefore, you want to buy, do you not wish that others should sell their possessions? For how will you be able to buy unless someone else has been compelled to sell?

## 3. Less Labor Is Required for Good Than for Evil

### The Price of the Kingdom of Heaven; it is available to everyone; good will is charity

And observe this, brothers: how much the person labors who wishes to strip someone who is clothed, and how little labor is required by the one who wishes to clothe someone who is naked.

If he has something, he brings it out and gives it. If he has nothing, good will before God is sufficient for him. Behold, he does not labor if he has something; but if he has nothing, he possesses what is greatly necessary: he is poor in his chest, but rich in his conscience; poor in his house, but rich in his soul.

Or perhaps you have nothing because you have good will? Hear the angels crying out at the Lord’s birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

For how little the kingdom of heaven costs! At how small a price so great a possession is offered! What you are to possess in heaven is offered on earth; what you are to possess eternally is offered in time.

You cannot say, “I have no means by which I can buy it,” because that possession is so great that I cannot find a price equal to it. Is it not worth as much as you are able to possess—and even what is beyond that?

How much was it worth to Zacchaeus? Half of his patrimony, for he was rich. “Half of my possessions,” he said, “I give to the poor” (Luke 19:8). But because he bought first, perhaps you do not find anything left for you to buy? He bought the kingdom of heaven, and what you may buy remains intact for you.

Do not fear that a fellow possessor will confine you: what charity possesses is spacious enough for everyone.

A certain widow bought the kingdom of heaven with two small coins. She put two coins into the treasury. “Amen, amen, I say to you, no one has put more into the treasury of God than this widow. For they gave from their abundance, but she put in all that she had” (Mark 12:42, 44).

Because the Lord was providing her livelihood, two coins had already remained beyond what she needed for that day’s food. Therefore she put them into the treasury of God and bought the kingdom of heaven for herself.

Behold, what you feared might be expensive, and for which you might not be qualified, is worth two small coins. If the price paid by Zacchaeus frightened you, let the price paid by this widow console you.

I add something further, dearest brothers: it is worth even less. A cup of cold water is cheaper; mere good will is cheaper still. Hear the angels crying out: “On earth peace to people of good will.”

Or did we not rightly say that good will is cheaper? Indeed, it itself is more precious than everything, and the one who has good will possesses everything. For even if Zacchaeus had not had good will, he would have given nothing from half of his possessions.

Good will is what is called charity. And what does the Apostle say? “If I distribute all that I have to the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Therefore, the one who has good will possesses everything. It is sufficient if the other things are absent; but if it alone is absent, whatever else a person may possess is of no benefit. It alone is sufficient if it is present; all the others are useless if charity alone is absent.

If you had treasures in your house that would make you secure, you would rejoice and exult. You have good will in your heart, and you are sad? In your chest you might fear a thief; but having good will in your heart, you fear nothing.

*[Note: [Col. 2249] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “In your heart, whom do you fear? Do not endure yourself as an enemy in your heart while possessing good will,” and so forth.]*

## 4. Whoever Seeks Justice Is Threatened with Suffering from the Wicked

Perhaps someone thinks and says: “If I begin to give my possessions to the poor, and refuse to avenge myself against my adversaries for God’s sake, and strive to be humble and gentle, then I will immediately have to endure the persecutions of wicked people.”

You who fear these things—have you not read that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21)? Have you not heard Scripture say: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1)?

It is true that once you begin to seek God in truth, you will necessarily have to endure the wickedness of proud or evil people. For Christ is not worshiped by them in the way he is preached to them every day. Whatever they want, whatever they ask from God, they want to consume in their luxuries and banquets, in spectacles, amusements, fornications, and drunkenness.

They want to consume the very things in which they desire to abound, and then they think that God is good when he provides them with the means by which they may corrupt themselves.

## 5. Through This the Church Progresses More

### The wicked are winepresses from which grapes and olives are pressed; one must pray for them

But someone says: “Behold, the times are harsh, and they will become harsher.”

Through these harsher circumstances the Church progresses more, and those who have their hearts above make progress. But for those who do not have their hearts above, their hearts are thrown into turmoil on earth, and they tell their hearts to change their place, so that they too may have their hearts above, singing with us: “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:1).

To say, “The times are becoming harsher,” is like someone saying that the times are becoming harsher for the olive when its fruit is being gathered because it is being sent to the press. When it hung on the tree, the times seemed pleasant; but they did not notice that it was full of bitterness.

A harsher time comes, the time of the press; greater pressures come. Through the sins and crimes of the proud, through the avarice and luxury of the wicked, greater pressures are brought upon the human race.

All wicked people and lovers of the world are like winepresses. Just as in winepresses both grapes and olives are pressed so that wine and oil may be stored in the canava,

*[Note: [Col. 2250] Thus Am., Er., and the Greek manuscript. Louvain has *cavea* (“enclosure”); manuscript rm. has *camera* (“chamber”). See above, Appendix, Sermon 141, section 2, with the note.]*

so, through the wickedness of evil people, those who are good and just are physically wearied by many tribulations, so that their souls may deserve to be stored away like oil and wine in eternal blessedness.

Do not therefore despair of God’s mercy or justice whenever you see yourself wearied by wicked people. Consider instead that those who persecute you are reckoned before God as mills and winepresses, while you, like an olive or a sound grape, are compelled for a short time to endure the pressure of wicked people. But afterward disgrace will remain with them without end, while you will pass, through a blessed exchange, into the kingdom.

Then, freed from all evils, you will be able to say with the prophet: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12).

But in order to deserve to reach that blessedness, pray for those who persecute you, because God is powerful enough to turn them toward goodness. May those who now seem to be chaff pass from weeds into wheat and from bitterness into oil; may those who now persecute others through wickedness afterward suffer persecution for the sake of justice; and may those who now cruelly wish to seize what belongs to others begin mercifully to distribute their own possessions to the poor.

If, when you pray, divine mercy grants this according to its custom, then, when God rewards you in eternal blessedness, you will receive a double recompense—not only for your own salvation but also for the salvation of others. May he deign to grant this, God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 271

*[Note: [Col. 2250] Elsewhere, 6 among the Fifty Homilies.]*

On love not only for friends but also for enemies, and that those who are enemies can be brought back to friendship in this way.

*[Note: [Col. 2250] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave its authenticity uncertain; Verlino and Vinding reject it as spurious. It is composed from Augustine’s sayings by the same method, and we believe it to have the same author as the preceding sermon.
