For section 2, see Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 93, section 7; for section 3, Appendix, Sermon 189, section 2; for section 5, Sermons 273, section 3, and above, Sermons 29, section 2; 41, section 1; 140, section 1; 174, section 3; for section 6, Sermon 271, section 6; for section 7, Sermons 4, section 2, and 274, section 2; for section 8, Sermons 275, section 1; 295, section 7; 301, section 1; 273, section 6.]*

## 1. Enemies Must Be Loved. God Loved Us Even When We Were Enemies

Frequently in the Gospel, dearest brothers, we have heard the Lord say: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44).

Why did the Lord say, “Love your enemies,” unless because we were going to have enemies? But someone says: “Who can love enemies?”

Your God first loved you when you were impious, although he was never impious. Even if you are no longer impious, you once were; for no one becomes just except from a sinner, as we have frequently sung: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. 31:1). He did not say, “Blessed are those who have committed no sins,” but, “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.”

For if you seek someone who has committed no sin, you will find no one. How, then, will anyone be blessed? If what he did is forgiven, if what he committed is covered.

If, then, your sin has already been forgiven, the person who pursues you is one who is not yet just. Before you were justified, you too pursued others; you had perished, and you were found. The person who opposes you will also be found and will cease to pursue you.

Do not think that you became such a person through your own merits, because God’s grace made you such. If you consider the matter well, you will see that God is powerful enough to make such a person of one whom you see that you rightly hate.

*[Note: [Col. 2250] The Greek manuscript reads, “the one whom you seem to have seen as unjust toward you”; manuscript rm. reads, “the one whom you seem to have lived toward unjustly.”]*

## 2. How Unjustly the Destruction of the Wicked Is Desired

For you speak to yourself as though you were just: “Great is the patience of God, which allows such a person to live.”

Would that this were the only thing you said! But I fear that you go further and reproach God, saying: “Why has God chosen to spare such people? Why do people commit so many evils and live?”

Let another person say: “O God, why does this man live, when he says so many things and reproaches your justice?” He does not consider what he himself says, but considers what another person does.

The person who displeases you perhaps does not reproach God or pour out such insults against him as you do. Suppose, then, that God were willing, as you wish, to spare no wicked person. What will he do with you, who cannot be without sin? Do you not consider where he will find you?

Pray, therefore, that he may spare not only others but also you.

All the wicked have this as something almost peculiar to them: they do not want God to spare the wicked, and they do not see what they themselves are, even from the very fact that they have this desire.

“But I am just,” you say. If God had not spared you when you were wicked, how would you have arrived at justice? Or perhaps you wanted God to be patient only until you reached justice? God extended the bridge of his mercy so that you could cross; do you want him now to withdraw it so that no one else may cross?

## 3. One Who Is Wicked Today May Be Better Than We Are Tomorrow

Let us therefore love our enemies, dearest brothers. Perhaps a person who is your friend today will commit such sins that he will not be able to be with you in eternal life, for “you do not know what tomorrow may bring” (Prov. 27:1).

Conversely, someone who is your enemy may be converted to repentance in such a way that he deserves to become your fellow citizen in that heavenly Jerusalem—and perhaps even to become greater.

Do not think this difficult. Let us question the Scriptures, and in them we will be able to recognize it more clearly.

The Apostle Paul was formerly a criminal and an enemy of Christians. He robbed, devastated, and raged. He was there when the martyr Stephen was stoned. His own hands were not enough for him; he stoned him with the hands of everyone else. To ensure that the others would not be hindered by their garments but could throw stones with free hands, he guarded everyone’s clothing; and thus he carried out the crime through everyone’s hands.

See how, by one word of the Lord, a man was made a preacher from a persecutor. He surpassed those whom he had hated. For all those Christians whom he had persecuted were not what he himself became. They were not all apostles, as he became.

You see that it can happen that an enemy who exists today may become not merely a friend and brother through grace, but may even surpass others and become better.

## 4. The Fruit of Prayer Is the Death of the Enemy

Man and sinner are two things.

Therefore, my brothers, do you think that all those Christians whom Saul was persecuting did not pray? Surely they did, if they knew Christ, if they were Christians, if they knew that the Lord Jesus himself had died for the ungodly.

For he did not die for believers; he died in order to make believers. I ask you, brothers, pay close attention: if our Lord and Savior gave his death for unbelievers, what must he be reserving for believers?

Consider also this: those whom the Apostle Paul was persecuting knew well the mercy of God, and they knew that Saul the persecutor could become a preacher. Therefore they prayed for him, and they were heard.

He was persecuting, but they conquered. By praying for him, they killed and destroyed him more effectively than he persecuted them.

How? Behold, by one word the persecutor was struck down. He rose no longer as a persecutor but as a preacher. The one who had persecuted, therefore, died. Seek the persecutor, and you will no longer find him, because he has risen.

They therefore killed him by praying more than he killed them by persecuting.

You too, brothers, should pray for your enemies so that God may kill them—that is, so that he may kill their wickedness, which is hostile to you.

For in this way he does not kill what he created, but what they themselves made. “Man” and “sinner” are two names.

In these two names, seek what God has done; seek what the devil has persuaded. Man was made by God; sin was committed by man at the devil’s persuasion.

Which of these two is persecuting you? If you live well, no one persecutes you except the one who is wicked. It is therefore not the man but the sinner who pursues you.

Pray for the man, so that God may destroy the sinner. For when the sinner has died, nothing will oppose you; indeed, the living man who was persecuting you while dead in sins will console you.

## 5. All Our Hope Lies in Forgiving

### The greatest sacrifice offered to God; it is available to everyone; two kinds of almsgiving; spiritual almsgiving is superior

Let it not therefore be burdensome for you, I beseech you by the mercy of our Lord himself, because we have no other hope unless we forgive whatever people have done to harm us.

Let no one deceive us. There is no greater sacrifice that we ought to offer to God than to do whatever good we can even to evil people, who are nevertheless human beings.

God says to you: “I do not grow through you; rather, you grow through me. I desire a sacrifice that benefits a human being; what benefits you reaches me in this way.”

You may say to me: “I have nothing to give to the needy. I cannot fast frequently, and I cannot abstain from wine or meat.”

Can you say to me that you are unable to have charity? It is charity whose possession increases all the more the more generously it is distributed.

Forgive, therefore, what you were holding against another, lest that person hold something against you whom you have nothing to forgive: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

Know, dearest brothers, that there are two kinds of almsgiving: one of the heart and one of money. Almsgiving of the heart is to forgive what you have suffered.

Sometimes you seek to give something to a needy person and do not have it. But to pardon the sinner: however much you wish, it overflows for you.

It may happen that you do not have gold, silver, clothing, grain, wine, or oil to give to the poor. But you can never excuse yourself from loving all people, from wishing for others what you wish for yourself, and from forgiving your enemies.

For if you do not have something to give from your storeroom or granary, you can bring forth from the treasury of your heart something to give.

Since good will alone is sufficient for all people, even if it is the only thing they possess, and since almsgiving of the heart is much greater than almsgiving of the body, who is there who can offer even the shadow of an excuse?

Consider also this, brothers: the almsgiving of charity is sufficient in itself even without earthly possessions. But the almsgiving given bodily is entirely insufficient if it is not offered with a generous heart.

And since, as you yourselves see, dearest brothers, for the forgiveness of all sins, if earthly possessions are absent, charity and love of enemies are fully and abundantly sufficient, no excuse concerning this matter will remain for us on the day of judgment. No one will be able to say that he did not have the means by which to redeem his sins.

## 6. Exhortation

Therefore let us all strive to love everyone with our whole heart, praying that those who are good may become better and persevere in good works, and that those who are wicked may correct themselves quickly.

Let us fear what the Lord threatened when he said: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15).

Rather, with his help let us labor so that this may be fulfilled in us: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

Since, according to the Lord’s previously mentioned saying—“If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins” (ibid. 6:14)—it has been placed in our power how we will be judged on the day of judgment, let us forgive all our enemies, so that with a clear conscience we may say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. 6:12).

May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 272

*[Note: [Col. 2253] Elsewhere, On Time 168.]*

On Loving Enemies I

*[Note: [Col. 2253] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, spurious to Verlino, and to Vinding, who observes that it is the same as Caesarius’s Homily 11 in the Library of the Fathers. For section 1, see Appendix, Sermons 40, section 6, and 66, section 3; for section 2, Sermon 15, section 6, an excerpt from Pelagius’s Letter to Demetrias; for section 4, Sermons 271, section 4, and 269, section 2; for section 5, Sermon 273, section 3, and above, Sermons 29, section 2; 41, section 1; 140, section 1; 174, section 3; for section 6, Sermon 271, section 6; for section 7, Sermons 4, section 2, and 274, section 2; for section 8, Sermons 275, section 1; 295, section 7; 301, section 1; 273, section 6.]*

## 1. In the Scriptures There Are Both Ornaments for the Healthy and Medicines for the Sick

### The chief medicine is love of enemies

In the divine books, dearest brothers, the Holy Spirit has arranged matters so that spiritual ornaments for the healthy and medicines for the sick may never be lacking.

Recognizing this, by the Lord’s gift, I have taken pains to provide a unique and singular remedy for souls, as a spiritual antidote. The first and principal medicine for a sick soul is to retain the sweetness of charity in such a way that it wishes to love not only friends but also enemies with its whole heart, because of what is written: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14).

Therefore, so that you may both retain so splendid a love in your memory and, with God’s help, fulfill it in deeds, we have excerpted a few brief chapters from the Holy Scriptures. If each person receives them not by scrutinizing but by believing, he will receive forgiveness of his sins and, with God’s help, reach the blessedness of eternal life.

## 2. The Saints Joseph, Moses, and Job Practiced This

First, the kindly charity of the ancient saints, even toward enemies, must be considered and imitated with all one’s strength.

Blessed Joseph, in response to the crime of parricide committed by his impious and hostile brothers, repaid them not with the bitterness of hatred but with the sweetness of charity. He kissed each of them and wept over each one. Repaying them not with any evil but with every good, he always loved them with the same affection, both while his natural father was alive and after his death.

*[Note: [Col. 2253] Manuscript t. reads “reproving” instead of “repaying.”]*

Likewise, when the rebellious people had frequently wished not only to despise blessed Moses but even to stone him, mindful of divine charity he pleaded with the Lord for them in such a way that he cried out and said: “If you do not forgive the sin of your people, blot me out of the book that you have written” (Exod. 32:32).

In the Old Testament itself we read: “The paths of those who retain the injury of a wrong lead to death”; and again: “Do not remember,” he says, “the injury done by your neighbor” (Lev. 19:18); and again: “If you see your enemy’s donkey lying in the mud, you shall not pass by until you have first lifted it up” (Exod. 23:5).

Here each of you should carefully consider that if one is not permitted to leave an enemy’s donkey in the mud, how much more must a human being made in the image of God not be hated or neglected?

Blessed Job likewise faithfully retained true and perfect charity even toward his enemies, so that with joy and a clear conscience he said to the Lord: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of my enemy and exulted because evil had found him, or if I said in my heart, ‘Good’” (Job 31:29).

## 3. David Also Practiced This, and the Fruit He Reaped from It

Blessed David, although adorned with many virtues, was nevertheless joined to God by no action more intimately than by love for his enemies (1 Sam. 16). When his enemy cursed him to his face, he preferred to spare him and leave the matter to God’s judgment rather than satisfy his own anger. His love was so far from feigned or false that he even wept for his adversaries and took vengeance on those who had dared to kill them (2 Sam. 1).

Therefore he confidently said in the Psalms what all people ought to say with a sufficiently attentive and trembling mind: “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies; may the enemy pursue my soul, overtake it, trample my life to the ground, and bring my glory down into the dust” (Ps. 7:5–6).

See with what a curse he condemns himself who, disregarding God’s commandments concerning the love of enemies, does not fear to keep hatred in his heart. Hence one must consider with what countenance or conscience a person who repays his enemies evil for evil can bring forth this verse from his mouth.

Through Solomon too the Holy Spirit cries out and says: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, lest God see it, be displeased, and turn his anger away from him” (Prov. 24:17–18). And surely, when he turns it away from that man, he directs it against the one who rejoices at his enemy’s downfall, according to the saying: “He who rejoices at another’s ruin will not go unpunished” (ibid. 17:5). Again, in the same place: “One man stores up anger against another, yet seeks healing from God” (Ecclus. 28:3)! And: “He has no mercy on a man like himself; though he is flesh, he stores up anger, yet seeks propitiation from God! Who will pray for his sins?” (ibid. 4–5).

## 4. In what sense it is said, “You shall hate your enemy”

It is indeed said in the Old Testament, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Lev. 19:18). But whoever wishes to recognize the meaning of divine Scripture with sound understanding should understand this statement in the following way: let him love every human being as his neighbor, and hate the devil as his enemy. This can also be fulfilled in one evil person. For in that one person who is evil, you have both a neighbor and an enemy. Insofar as he is a human being, he is your neighbor; insofar as he is evil, he is not only your enemy but also his own.

Therefore, love in him the flesh and soul—that is, your neighbor, whom God made—and hate the wickedness which, with his consent, the devil has introduced. When you do this with a holy and devout spirit, you act in the place of the heavenly Physician: hating the disease and loving the sick person.

## 5. “You will heap coals of fire upon your enemy’s head”

The literal sense is not always to be followed in Scripture. The Holy Spirit also speaks through Solomon: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Prov. 25:21–22).

In this passage, therefore, we must observe with great care lest, while we fail to understand it correctly, we turn medicines into wounds for ourselves. Some people are accustomed to use this command as though it were intended to satisfy their fury. They say to themselves, “See, I feed my enemy so that he may burn forever.” May God turn such an interpretation away from our minds.

How, then, should this passage be understood? The holy and ancient Fathers, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, have determined its meaning. “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” and so forth; “for by doing this,” he says, “you will heap coals of fire upon his head.”

The head in a human being signifies the rational understanding. When that understanding, withdrawing from the fervor of charity, has become cold—for it is written, “Because lawlessness has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12)—it is necessary that it should judge what is contrary to salvation and become an enemy to the one whom it ought to regard as a friend.

To heal such a madman, therefore, the Holy Spirit exhorts holy men, inflamed with the fire of charity, saying: “You will heap coals of fire upon his head.” For when you frequently do good to your enemy with a devout spirit—however impious and cruel, barbarous and bloodthirsty he may be—at last he becomes ashamed and grieved, and begins to repent of what he has done.

Once he has begun to repent, his rational understanding—that is, his head—begins to be kindled by the fire of charity. He who previously, like a cold and frenzied person, was accustomed to retain anger against you, now set ablaze by the spiritual warmth of your goodness, begins to love you with his whole heart.

This is how the holy Fathers said that this passage of Scripture should be understood. For it would be far from Catholic understanding that anyone should try to do some good to his enemy with the intention that, because of this benefit, he might wish him to be burned in eternal fire. Therefore, we must consider and fear this with great vigilance of faith: that we should not follow the killing letter, but rather love the life-giving Spirit.

[Col. 2255]

## 6. The heavenly Jerusalem has walls of peace, impassable to those who do not keep peace

And this, dearly beloved brothers, we must consider with great trembling: what the Holy Spirit said terrifyingly in the Psalm. When he was calling that heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the gathering of all the saints, which will reign with Christ—to praise the Lord, after saying, “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” he added, “He has established peace as your boundaries” (Ps. 147:12, 14).

Thus, as you yourselves see, that heavenly Jerusalem has walls constructed from peace. Whoever possesses such peace and such charity that he loves everyone, prays for the good that they may become better, and pleads for the wicked that they may quickly correct themselves—that person, from whatever side he wishes to enter, will deserve to find the gates of that heavenly Jerusalem open.

But whoever does not wish to possess such charity as Christ commanded and the Apostle taught will find the gates of Jerusalem closed on every side. And because he did not wish to possess the oil of charity, when the bridegroom’s doors are shut he will hear, together with those foolish virgins, that dreadful voice: “Amen I say to you, I do not know where you are from” (Matt. 25:12).

Just as that heavenly Jerusalem will open its doors to the five virgins who possessed the oil of charity, so that they may enter into the joy of their Lord, so conversely it will close them against those who come without charity, drive them away in eternal separation from itself, and fulfill what is said in the Psalm concerning Jerusalem: “For,” he says, “he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:13).

When the gates have been closed and the bars secured, a friend will never go out and an enemy will never be able to enter; for just as the righteous will never depart from glory, so the sinner will never be able to escape punishment.

## 7. Let nothing separate us from charity

Therefore, if we wish divine mercy to deem us worthy of being delivered from these evils and of entering happily into that heavenly Jerusalem, let us strive with all our strength so that what the Apostle said may be fulfilled in us:

“Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or danger, or the sword?” And again: “For I am sure that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither powers nor height nor depth, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:35, 38–39).

Behold: as you have heard, neither those great and terrifying things nor torments were able to separate the blessed Apostle and the apostolic men from the charity of God. Therefore, it is exceedingly grievous that, although they could not be separated from the charity of God even by tortures, we are sometimes separated from it by idle tales and sometimes, because of the smallest insult or the slander of some wretched person, abandon charity [Note: [Col. 2255] The Theod. manuscript reads, “we sin against charity.”] so completely that we will neither speak with that person nor wish to come to a meal with him—not merely for many days, but perhaps for months and even years.

We do not consider that, while we hate one another, we close the walls of the city of Jerusalem against ourselves in such a way that no entrance remains by which we can enter. And since that city has God as its inhabitant, and the evangelist John says, “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), whoever does not wish to have charity—with what face or conscience will he dare to approach the Lord, who is charity?

## 8. No one can excuse himself for failing to keep charity

All these things, dearly beloved brothers, while I frequently impress upon you with paternal affection, absolve my conscience before God. And because no one will ever be able truthfully to excuse himself by claiming that he cannot keep true peace and true charity, let us entreat God’s mercy with all our strength, so that he may deign to impress upon us and grant us that charity without which no one will ever see God, and so that we may not be separated from his love or sweetness by any tortures, losses, or persecutions.

If you wish, there is no need for us now to weary you longer with a more extended discourse. Therefore, let what has been said for the present suffice for your Charity, so that you may continually ruminate upon [Col. 2256] these things pleasing to God, which you have received, as clean animals ruminate their food, and determine in your hearts how, with God’s help, you may fulfill them.

What follows concerning love of enemies you will hear more suitably, without any bodily weariness, either tomorrow or certainly on the Lord’s Day, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 273

[Note: [Col. 2256] Elsewhere, *On Time* 61.]

## On loving enemies, II

[Note: [Col. 2256] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was regarded as doubtful by the Louvain editors, and as spurious by Verlin and Vinding. Among the Caesarian sermons printed by the care of Étienne Baluze from the Royal manuscript, it appears as the seventh in order. In other ancient books as well that we examined, it bears the name of Caesarius; moreover, in those same manuscripts it is joined immediately to the preceding sermon, at the end of which Caesarius promised that he would speak on the matter treated in this following sermon. For no. 1, see Appendix sermon 62, no. 2; 225, no. 3; and 271, no. 4; 141, no. 2; 269, no. 1; 225, no. 5. For no. 3, sermon 272, no. 4; 62, no. 5. For no. 5, sermon 62, no. 6; 269, no. 4; 107, no. 3. For no. 6, sermon 274; 210, no. 5; 225, no. 5; 272, no. 8; the conclusion of the Council of Orange II, and the conclusion of sermons 28 and 271.]

## 1. Charity is a great remedy for sins. With God’s help it can be possessed by everyone, since it rests upon the good will

I know and believe that your Charity wisely understands that it is not without reason that I so frequently admonish you concerning true and perfect charity. I do this because I know of no medicine so healthful and effective for all the wounds of sins. There is also this: although the remedy of true and perfect charity is so great, no one is found who, with God’s help, cannot possess it.

In other good works, someone may occasionally put forward some sort of excuse; but in the practice of love no one will be able to excuse himself. Someone may say to me, “I cannot fast.” Can he say, “I cannot love”? He may say, “Because of the weakness of my body, I cannot abstain from wine or meat.” Can he say, “I cannot love”? He may say that he cannot preserve virginity, that he cannot sell his possessions and distribute them to the poor. Can he say, “I cannot love my enemies and forgive those who have sinned against me”?

Let no one deceive himself, dearly beloved brothers, for God deceives no one. Although there are many things which, because of human frailty, we cannot physically accomplish, nevertheless, if we truly wish it, with God inspiring us we can possess charity in our hearts without any hesitation.

There are many things which at times we cannot bring forth from the granary, the storeroom [*canava*], or the cellar [Note: [Col. 2256] See above, Appendix sermon 141, no. 2, with note.]; but it is exceedingly shameful and disgraceful if we appear to put forward any excuse from the treasure of our heart. For there neither our feet grow weary from running, nor our eyes from seeing, nor our ears from hearing, nor our hands from working, so that we might attempt to excuse ourselves by such exhaustion.

We are not told, “Go to the East and seek charity; sail to the West and you will find love.” We are commanded to return within, into our hearts, from which anger is accustomed to exclude us, as the prophet says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46:8).

For, as I have already said, what the Lord seeks from us is not found in distant regions: he sends us inward, to our heart. He has placed within us what he seeks, where the whole perfection of charity consists in the goodness or will of the soul. Concerning this will or goodness the angels cried to the shepherds: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

And therefore, since we will have no excuse before the tribunal of Christ, let us strive with all our strength, with God’s help, so that goodness may prevail in our souls over wickedness, patience over anger, kindness over envy, and humility over pride. To sum everything up in a brief sentence: let the sweetness of charity so possess our whole heart that bitterness of hatred can find no place in us.

## 2. It is futile for anyone to say that he cannot love his enemies

But someone says, “There is no way I can love my enemies.” Throughout all the Scriptures God has told you that you can; you, on the contrary, answer that you cannot. Consider now whether God or you ought to be believed [Note: [Col. 2257] The Theod. manuscript reads, “you ought to believe.”].

Therefore, since Truth cannot lie, let human frailty now abandon its empty excuses. The one who is just could not command something impossible, nor will the one who is merciful condemn a person for what he could not avoid.

Why do we argue vainly? No one knows what we are capable of better than the one who gave us the ability itself. So many men, so many women, so many boys, and so many young girls—delicate as they were—endured flames, fires, swords, and wild beasts with composure for Christ. Yet we say that we cannot endure the insults of foolish people; and sometimes, for the very smallest losses inflicted upon us by the wickedness of evil people, we even avenge our injuries, if possible, unto their death!

How, then, and with what conscience, do we desire to have a share with all the saints in eternal blessedness, when we refuse to follow their examples even in the smallest matters?

## 3. They produce a passage of Scripture in support of their position, but it chiefly signifies love of God. God loved those who did not love him, and by this he wishes us to imitate him. Those who torment us are madmen

Some people think that a testimony of divine Scripture supports their anger. They say that it is written, “My soul loves the one who loves me.” While they misunderstand divine authority, they turn medicines into wounds for themselves.

Your Charity should attend to how this statement both ought to and can be understood: “My soul,” it says, “loves the one who loves me.” Although it may also be understood literally of all [Note: [Col. 2257] The manuscript reads, “of all people.”], it ought more certainly to be understood of God, since no one loves us better than he does.

For if only the good are to be loved, what shall we say of our God, concerning whom it is written, “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” [Note: [Col. 2257] Manuscript T adds, “for the world.”] (John 3:16)? What good had the world done that God should love it in this way? Our Lord Christ found all human beings not only evil but also dead in original sin. And yet, even when we were such, he loved us and handed himself over for us.

Thus he loved even those who did not love him, as the Apostle Paul also says: “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). Through his ineffable goodness he gave this example to the entire human race, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

The blessed Apostle Peter likewise commanded the same thing in his Epistle, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

What example of the Lord are we to follow? Is it that we should raise the dead? Is it that we should walk on the sea with our feet? Certainly not; rather, that we should be gentle and humble of heart, and love not only our friends but also our adversaries: “so that you might follow,” he says, “his footsteps.”

The blessed evangelist John also said this: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). How did Christ walk? While hanging upon the cross, he prayed for his enemies, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

For they are madmen, possessed by an opposing spirit, and in order to persecute us they suffer a greater persecution from the devil. Therefore, we ought to pray that they may be freed rather than condemned.

The blessed Stephen acted in this way. He was the first to follow Christ’s footsteps most gloriously. While he was being struck by a hard storm of stones, he stood and prayed for himself; but for his enemies, kneeling, he cried out with all his strength and said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

If, therefore, we think that we cannot imitate our Lord, let us at least imitate our fellow servant. Let us also imitate the blessed James, who likewise, when he was being stoned by the Jews, made supplication on bent knees for his persecutors.

## 4. Love of enemies is not advice but a command

The Lord likewise, in the Gospel, did not give advice but a command that we should love our enemies. Advice is one thing; a command is another.

Advice is given that virginity should be preserved, that one should abstain from wine and meat, and that all possessions should be sold and distributed to the poor. A command, however, is given that justice should be kept, that every person should turn away from evil and do good.

Finally, concerning virginity it is said, “Let the one who can accept it accept it” (Matt. 19:12). But concerning justice it is not said, “Let the one who can do it do it”; rather: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10).

Whoever willingly hears and carries out advice will have greater glory. Whoever does not fulfill a command will not be able to escape punishment unless repentance comes to his aid.

For the Lord commanded: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44). And if you ask what reward you will receive, hear what follows: “so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:45).

Take note: if we do not love our enemies, we cannot be children of God. And with what face do we say in prayer, “Our Father, who art in heaven”? Or with what conscience will we be able to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6:12)?

## 5. Whoever loves only those who love him is no different from pagans and wild beasts. True charity

But someone says, “I hear Scripture saying, ‘My soul loves the one who loves me.’ Do you love your children and parents? A robber loves; a dragon loves; wolves love; bears love. If we do not love those who love us, if we despise our children or parents, we are worse than lions and the wild beasts mentioned above. But if we love only those who love us, we appear to differ in nothing from those beasts.”

The Lord himself said the same thing: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the pagans do this?” (Matt. 5:46–47).

Those, therefore, who love only their friends—as you yourselves see—are still in this respect like tax collectors and Gentiles. In order, then, that we may be superior to both Gentiles and beasts, let us love even our enemies and adversaries. And let us fear what the Lord said in the Gospel:

“Wicked servant, I forgave you the whole debt because you pleaded with me. Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” And what follows? “He handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.” “So,” says the Lord, “my heavenly Father will do to you if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18:32–35).

Again the Lord himself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). And again: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” [Note: [Col. 2258] The words “And again: This is my commandment, that you love one another” are added from the manuscript of the College of Clermont.] (John 15:12).

And again: “Whoever fulfills the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10). What is this one point, except what we said above: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34)? What, I say, is this one point except what the Apostle says: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14)?

But lest someone say that this passage ought not to be understood in this way, let him hear the Apostle again proclaiming this command in a sublime voice: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

This is true and genuine charity, which extends not only to friends but even to enemies themselves. Our Lord is likewise known to possess such great charity toward the human race that he allows his rain to fall and his sun to rise every day not only upon the good but also upon the evil.

[Col. 2259]

## 6. Conclusion

Above all, we must recall and retain with great reverence and fear what the Lord said in the Gospel:

“If you forgive people their sins,” he says, “your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14).

[It has been placed in our power how we shall be judged on the day of judgment. Therefore, I do not know with what face anyone will be able to obtain forgiveness of his sins before the tribunal of Christ if, when God commands it, he refuses to grant pardon to his enemies.]

The Apostle also preaches, saying: “Repaying no one evil for evil. Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:17, 14). And again: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Rom. 12:21). And again: “Not repaying evil for evil or insult for insult, but, on the contrary, blessing” (1 Pet. 3:9).

The blessed evangelist John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper, admonishes us in his Epistle, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that every murderer does not possess abiding eternal life in himself” (1 John 3:15). And again: “Whoever says that he remains in the light and hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).

Here we must understand “brother” to mean every human being. The blessed John himself also says: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

But now [Note: [Col. 2259] The same manuscript reads more aptly, “also.”], if you wish, let these things suffice. There are countless passages in both the New and Old Testaments which appear to confirm the matter of which we are speaking with the strongest testimonies, but it would take too long to impress all of them upon the ears of your Charity now.

But holy souls accept even small things as great, because in truth, for one to whom small things—which are nevertheless great—are of no benefit, more things will be of no benefit either [Note: [Col. 2259] Elsewhere, “few things.”].

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, considering what has often been said, that the whole law is fulfilled in one saying among us—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—love not only your friends but also your enemies [for whoever refuses to fulfill this will gain no benefit from his other good works]. And therefore forgive all your enemies in such a way [Note: [Col. 2259] The words enclosed here and above in brackets are absent from the manuscripts.] that with a secure conscience you may say in prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

May he himself deign to grant this, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 274

[Note: [Col. 2259] This is Caesarius’s ninth homily among those published by Baluze; we also found it inserted as the eighth homily of Eligius in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. For no. 1, see Appendix sermon 308, no. 1; 210, no. 5; and 225, no. 5. For no. 2, sermon 225, no. 6; 267, no. 2. For no. 3, sermon 107, no. 3. For no. 4, sermon 139, no. 2; 309, no. 4. For no. 6, Tractate 18 on John.]

This admonition explains how the pious and merciful Lord has placed in our power the manner in which we shall be judged on the day of judgment; that there is one unique and singular remedy against all sins; and that no one will ever be able truthfully to excuse himself by claiming that he cannot love his enemies.

## 1. God has provided remedies accessible to everyone. The two principal kinds are forms of almsgiving

The pious and merciful Lord, knowing that the human race cannot pass through the present life without any sins, has deigned to provide such remedies that not only the rich but also the poor can apply to the wounds of their sins.

What are these remedies? Those two, certainly, of which the Lord said: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37–38).

“Give, and it will be given to you” refers to the almsgiving offered to the hungry, naked, and captive. “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” refers to the almsgiving by which forgiveness is granted to all enemies.

If any poor person wishes to excuse himself by claiming that he cannot feed the hungry, clothe the naked, or free the captive, he will in no way be able truthfully to say that he cannot forgive his enemies or adversaries. Thus he may confidently say in the Lord’s Prayer the petitions which the skilled heavenly Judge [Note: [Col. 2260] Perhaps, “jurist.”] dictated to us: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). And he may hear without any fear the Gospel sentence: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matt. 6:14–15).

We are treated with sufficient gentleness when it is placed in our power how we shall be judged on the day of judgment. “If you forgive,” he says, “you will be forgiven; if you do not forgive, you will not be forgiven.”

## 2. A person readily forgives his enemy when he remembers what he owes God

Those debts, moreover, cannot be paid in any other way, nor can those who do not pay them offer an excuse. But someone says, “I cannot forgive my enemies.”

If you have no sin for which you need God’s forgiveness, then perhaps you may say that you do not wish to forgive your neighbor. But if you have sinned incomparably more against God than another human being has sinned against you, why, when the Lord commands it, do you not forgive a small debt so that God may deign to forgive you much?

God has not commanded you to fast more than you can, to abstain from wine or meat, to afflict yourself more frequently with vigils, or to sail east or west amid endless labors and dangers. None of these things is imposed upon us. Rather, this is commanded of us: that, considering more attentively the ark of our conscience, we should hate no human being in this world, fulfilling what the Lord himself said: “All things whatsoever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12).

And since there is no one who would not wish to be forgiven for what he has sinned against God or against another human being, why do we not do for others what we wish to be done for us, so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in us: “The whole law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal. 5:14)?

Therefore, we must by no means deceive ourselves with false security, believing that if we refuse to forgive our neighbors, we may nevertheless deserve to receive forgiveness for our sins.

We must consider with great trembling that terrifying and dreadful sentence of our Lord which that cruel servant deserved to hear: “Wicked servant, I forgave you the debt because you pleaded with me; should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” And what followed? “He handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.”

And to impress this even upon the slower of understanding, he added: “So my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. 18:32–35).

Since, without any bodily labor, if we forgive our brothers with our whole heart, we can obtain forgiveness for all our sins, what excuse will we be able to have on the day of judgment if we neglect to fulfill this, which we can accomplish very easily with his help?

Without any doubt, our Lord will fulfill this sentence in us, so that we shall be judged by the judgment with which we have judged, and according to the measure by which we have granted forgiveness to our neighbors, forgiveness will be granted to us (Matt. 7:2). Whoever refuses to fulfill these things closes the door of divine mercy against himself.

## 3. Other works are useless

However many good works someone may have performed, they will all be emptied of their value if true charity is not in him—charity which extends not only to friends but even to enemies themselves. For the blessed Apostle Paul, in whom Christ spoke, does not lie when he says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

And since “the desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10), while charity is the root of all good things, what does it profit a person to have a thousand branches, either with flowers or with the most beautiful and pleasing fruits, if the root in him is not living and true?

For just as, when the root of desire for money is torn out [Note: [Col. 2261] Perhaps, “the root of the tree.”], all the branches immediately wither and perish, so whoever extinguishes the root of charity within himself through hatred and anger will have nothing remaining in him by which he may reach eternal life.

## 4. Almsgiving is useless. Why God wishes almsgiving to be performed

But let the person who keeps the evils mentioned above in his heart and believes that he can redeem those very sins through many alms hear the Lord saying in the Gospel:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

This statement clearly shows that offering a sacrifice or giving alms will profit nothing unless reconciliation with the enemy has first taken place.

The Lord himself also said in the Gospel that God does not wish to hear our prayer if we choose to keep hatred in our heart: “Whoever has my commandments and does them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21); and, “What benefit is there in your saying to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not doing what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

What are these things which the Lord specifically asserts that he has said? Those, certainly, which pertain to peace and concord: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44); and: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

For if we give alms generously but do not forgive our enemies according to Christ’s commands, we offer our possessions to God but subject our soul to the adversary. Consider whether this division can be just and pleasing to God.

For God desires not so much our possessions as ourselves. Since he knows that we love earthly substance greatly, he therefore wishes what we love to be offered to him, so that, according to his command, where our treasure has gone before, our heart may follow there (Matt. 6:21). Then, when the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” we may answer with a secure conscience that we have them with the Lord.

## 5. Recapitulation

Who, then, would not tremble at that statement of the blessed Apostle John, which we have frequently brought forward and ought constantly to impress upon you?

“Whoever hates his brother,” he says, “is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). And again: “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:9). And: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).

And this: “The ways of those who retain the injury of wrongdoing are in death.”

Since, in accordance with what we have stated above, no shadow of any excuse remains for us, let us strive with all our strength, with God’s help, to fulfill what he commanded, so that we may deserve to receive what he promised.

And so that we may not lose the other good works, whatever they may be, which we perform with God’s inspiration, let us faithfully preserve charity, as the mother of all good things, with the Lord’s inspiration.

And so that you may recognize more fully and clearly what we have stated above, I have thought it appropriate to add a brief passage from the work of Saint Augustine pertaining to the matter under discussion [Note: [Col. 2261] It would certainly be better to read, “pertaining.” M.]. By it, it may be proved most clearly that no one can merit God’s mercy if, despising the two commandments of charity, he neglects to forgive his enemies with his whole heart.

## 6. The Mystery of the Number Forty. He Is Weak Who Has Two Fewer. Love of God: Love of Neighbor

The holy bishop Augustine, when treating of that paralytic who had been ill for thirty-eight years, said:

“By the number forty, dearest brothers, the course of our life and our conduct in the divine Scriptures are mystically signified. For this reason, before Easter—which signifies the present life—we observe a fast of forty days, so that we may celebrate Easter, which bears the image of eternal life, with joy. For this reason Moses also fasted for forty days (Exod. 34:28), and Elijah likewise for forty (1 Kings 19:8), and our Lord and Savior consecrated a forty-day fast (Matt. 4:2); and the Israelite people remained in the wilderness for forty years after they had merited liberation from Egypt (Deut. 8:2).

“Thus, as you see, dearest brothers, this number forty seems to signify a figure of all good and holy Christians. That sick man, of whom we read in the Gospel that he lay there, seemed to bear the type of the human race. But because he had been in his sickness for thirty-eight years, he had two fewer than the number forty which we mentioned above. Let us see what those two things were that were lacking from that consecrated number. And what could they be, brothers, except the two commandments of love—namely, love of God and love of neighbor? These two are such that without them the rest are of no benefit. Even if someone possesses good works, virginity, or martyrdom, if he does not possess these two on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40), he lies sick and paralyzed.

“Christ therefore came and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, bestowed these two things upon us, so that we might love God and also love our neighbor. Finally, for the man who had fallen among robbers he gave two denarii (Luke 10:35), and among the Samaritans he spent two days (John 4:40), in order to strengthen them in love of God and neighbor. That widow too, as a type of the Church, put two small coins into the treasury (Luke 21:2), and the Lord sent his disciples out two by two to preach charity [Note: [Col. 2262] Eligius: “and the Lord sent his disciples to preach bipartite charity”] (Luke 10:1).

“For, as we have said, before Christ’s coming the human race did not merit to possess these two things. Pay attention, brothers: the Lord also said two things, which evidently seemed to be lacking in him [Note: [Col. 2262] Perhaps: “which seemed to be lacking in him”]: ‘Rise, take up your pallet’ (John 5:8). Those two things the sick man lacked.

“What does ‘Rise’ mean except ‘Love the Lord’? For everyone who loves God has his heart above. And what does ‘Take up your pallet’ mean except ‘Love your neighbor’? This love of neighbor is signified by carrying the pallet. The Apostle said: ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ’ (Gal. 6:2). Therefore, if your brother has been overtaken by something, let him be carried by you; and if you have been overtaken, let him sustain you. So rise, love God, and take up your pallet. Love your neighbor—that is, carry the burden in which you may rest.

“These two things were necessary for the human race. But people could not possess them entirely by themselves, because ‘the love of God has been poured into our hearts,’ not from ourselves, but ‘through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Rom. 5:5). May he help us, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

## SERMON CCLXXV

[Note: [Col. 2262] Elsewhere, from the Vignerian manuscripts, 38.]

Why holy and just men exercised vengeance upon sinners in this world

[Note: [Col. 2262] In the manuscripts it is attributed to Caesarius, and it is the final item among the Homilies published under his name by Étienne Baluze. For no. 1, see Appendix, sermons 15, no. 3, and 34, no. 1; for nos. 3 and 4, sermon 41, nos. 1–2.]

### 1. Why sins were punished bodily under the Old Law. Moses’ anger without irascibility. He burns with zeal for God and love for the people. The same must be understood of Phinehas.

The judgments of God, dearest brothers, are for the most part hidden, but they are never unjust. Since in the Law we read that certain sinners were punished in the present world by holy men, we must examine with the utmost purity of faith the reason why this was done.

Because in the Old Testament sins seemed to be punished bodily, examples were provided for everyone whenever deserved penalties were inflicted upon certain persons. Yet no individual imposed such punishment upon the people according to his own anger, as he pleased; rather, those set in authority or appointed as judges exercised vengeance with complete justice, so that the others might be afraid.

Thus that blessed Moses, of whom we read that he was gentler than all human beings (Num. 12:3), came down from the mountain and, when he learned that the people had sacrificed to idols, ordered three thousand of the people to be killed (Exod. 32:27)—not to satisfy his anger, but to avenge the injury done to God, and so that the others, seeing this, would never dare to commit such sins.

And so that we may understand with what disposition he ordered this to be done, he returned to the Lord and pleaded, saying: “If you will not forgive your people their sin, blot me out of the book that you have written” (ibid., 32).

Behold true and complete charity. He ordered a few to be killed [Note: [Col. 2263] Manuscript of the College of Clermont: “Behold, with true and complete charity, he ordered a few to be killed”], so that he might save six hundred thousand, excluding women and children. For unless he, moved by zeal for God, had exercised vengeance upon a few, God’s justice would have destroyed them all.

The blessed priest Phinehas likewise killed with his own hand and sword one of the leaders who was lying with a foreign woman. The Lord himself bore witness to the spirit in which he had done this, saying: “Phinehas, moved by zeal for me, has appeased my anger, so that I would not destroy my people” (Num. 25:11). Phinehas did this not from carnal hatred, but from divine zeal and love—not to avenge himself, but to free the people from God’s anger.

### 2. Elijah had the same disposition, both when soldiers were consumed by heavenly fire and when he ordered priests to be killed, acting as one moved by the Holy Spirit.

We recognize that the blessed Elijah also did this. When the most arrogant and sacrilegious king sent a captain of fifty with his soldiers to him, commanding him to come to the king, the blessed Elijah, grieving over the destruction of his people, whom the impious king had persuaded to worship idols, said in the Holy Spirit that fire should descend from heaven and consume them, so that, when these had been struck in body, others might be healed in heart.

But since no spiritual medicine had any effect upon them, the Holy Spirit, through Elijah’s mouth, also ordered another captain of fifty, who likewise had come arrogantly, to be killed together with his men. With what piety the Holy Spirit did this, and with what disposition Elijah acted, is shown by the humility of the third captain of fifty who came (2 Kings 1:9–14). In him we clearly recognize that if human frailty had first humbled itself, divine mercy would immediately have granted pardon.

For we must not suppose that those men had been sent to Elijah in order to kill him, but rather to summon him to the king. Therefore the blessed Elijah did not satisfy his own anger, but rather avenged the injury done to God.

He also exercised this against the priests of the idols on Mount Carmel [Note: [Col. 2263] The same manuscript reads, “on Mount Carmel”], when he ordered them all to be killed (1 Kings 18:40)—namely, so that false religion, extinguished together with its teachers, might make room for true religion in human hearts.

The blessed Elijah must be believed to have carried all this out not by his own power, but by the power of the Holy Spirit. Finally, if you wish to know what Elijah himself was like, consider what happened when the grace of the Holy Spirit briefly withdrew from him in order to test him: he could not endure the threats of a single woman of ill repute, but fled into the wilderness on a journey of forty days.

The man who, when grace supplied him with power through the Holy Spirit, had closed heaven with a word and caused avenging flames to come from above could not endure the words of one little prostitute. I have said this so that we may recognize that all those things were accomplished not so much by Elijah as by the Holy Spirit through Elijah.

Therefore it is impious to believe that the blessed Elijah wished to avenge himself upon those whom he caused to be killed.

### 3. What Elisha’s being mocked represents. Why he sought vengeance.

We must think the same concerning the blessed Elisha. When wanton boys shouted at him, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (2 Kings 2:23), the Holy Spirit who dwelt in him commanded two bears to come up and tear forty-two of the boys apart.

Although this was done mystically and signified the Lord’s Passion, when the mocking Jews cried, “Let him be crucified, let him be crucified” (Matt. 27:23), just as those boys had cried, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead”—that is, “Go up onto the cross at the place of Calvary”—nevertheless, even according to the literal sense, a few were struck so that many might be healed. Since the Jews not only despised the prophets but also mocked them, they were struck by such a punishment so that they might recognize the power of the Holy Spirit.

But because they did not wish to correct themselves, the Holy Spirit himself cries elsewhere through the prophet: “I struck your children, and you did not accept correction” (Jer. 2:30).

If, then, the Holy Spirit accomplished this, it is impious to attribute anything to the blessed Elisha, since in truth a human being alone, without the Holy Spirit, could not possess such power. For if we attribute something to holy Elisha, we presume to dispute, as it were, the just judgment of God.

### 4. The same zeal in Peter.

And lest we think that this happened only in the Old Testament, consider that most blessed and gentle apostle Peter, and see what the Holy Spirit accomplished through him concerning Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:5–10).

This was certainly not done so that the blessed Apostle might avenge himself, for he appeared to have suffered no injury from them. Rather, the Holy Spirit, springing forth through his mouth, cut off at the very root an exceedingly evil example of unbelief.

Considering all these things spiritually and faithfully, therefore, let us suspect nothing sinister in the holy zeal or judgment of the righteous. May our Lord and Savior himself deign to grant us this, he who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLXXVI

[Note: [Col. 2264] The manuscripts place the name of Caesarius before it, and it is his Homily 21 in the Library of the Fathers. For no. 1, see Appendix, sermons 265, no. 2, and 270, no. 3; for no. 2, sermon 69, no. 8, and the following sermon 277, no. 3; for no. 3, sermon 115, no. 4; for no. 4, sermons 277, no. 3, and 308, no. 2; for no. 6, sermons 10, no. 5, and 140, no. 5.]

On love of parents and on tithes

### 1. Parents are owed honor, love, and assistance in poverty. Some despise poor parents, though they may be better than themselves.

We read, dearest brothers, that the Lord, through the prophet, urges us always to show our parents both honor and love, and, if it should happen that they suffer some poverty, to relieve their needs as far as we can.

For he says: “If you see someone naked, cover him, and do not despise the members of your own seed” (Isa. 58:7). By “the household of your own seed,” he wished our parents to be understood.

But someone says: Who hates his parents, so that the Lord would give this warning through the prophet as something of great importance? Without doubt, brothers, the Holy Spirit knew that some people, when they have attained honors or riches acquired from any source, despise their poor parents so greatly that they do not even deem them worthy to see.

If they do this, let them have no doubt that they have committed not merely a sin but a serious crime. Perhaps it happens that a man, through riches and pride, commits great crimes or sins, while his parents, because of their poverty, humility, and simplicity, maintain righteousness. With what face does he disdain to look upon his innocent and just parents, when he himself is a sinner and impious? [Note: [Col. 2264] Manuscript: “the wretched man disdains.”]

If someone is able, then, and has parents who are poor, let him first provide them with what is necessary, and afterward give alms to strangers in need. For if you do not give to other poor people, someone else will; but if you give nothing to your poor parents, it is difficult for anyone else to give to them.

### 2. The proper order of almsgiving. What of our wealth is ours, and what is another’s.

The just and proper order of almsgiving is this: first provide for yourself and your own a sufficient and moderate supply of food and clothing—not splendid or luxurious; then, as I have said, if any of your parents are poor, give as much as you can; then do not allow your male and female slaves [Col. 2265] either to hunger or to suffer cold.

After this, whatever God has given you, as I said, apart from food and clothing, do not store it on earth, where thieves break in and steal, but store it in the heavenly treasury, so that “where your treasure is, there your heart may be also” (Matt. 6:20–21). Then, when the priest cries, “Lift up your hearts,” let us answer confidently and truthfully, “We have them with the Lord.”

Whatever God has bestowed, apart from moderate and reasonable food and clothing, whether from military service, agriculture, or any other source, he has not given specifically to you; rather, he has sent it through you to be distributed to the poor. If you do not wish to give, know that you are taking away another’s property. For, as I said, only that is ours which reasonably suffices for us and our own. Whatever remains, our God has sent to be distributed to the poor.

### 3. Tithes are unjustly withheld, although nine parts are owed by right.

Thus we must not only give tithes; from the nine parts also, whatever remains after taxes have been paid and our expenses met, we must faithfully distribute as though it had been sent to others.

If we do this, what we give is truly ours. But if we do not, neither is what we keep ours, nor are we ourselves our own, though we seem to preserve ourselves.

And yet, brothers, I do not see with what face we fail to offer a tenth to him from whom we received everything. If God should wish to reckon with us and say: “The land that you cultivate—I made it; you yourself who cultivate it, and your servants—I made you; the animals that help you cultivate it—I created them; the heat of the sun—I provide; the rain—I distribute in its seasons; the very seed that you scatter—I grant,” then, if you attend to the reckoning of justice, you ought to reserve a tenth for yourself and give me nine parts.

Nor do I demand this because I need it; I wish to be merciful. I give you an example, so that just as I have shown mercy to you, you may show mercy to the poor.

If, then, brothers, God should wish to make a just reckoning with us, is there anything we could answer? Although God warns us about these things in many passages of the holy Scriptures, he cries out and admonishes us especially through the Apostle, saying:

“Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is greed; desiring it, some have made shipwreck of the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows. But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, and faith” (1 Tim. 6:8–11).

I ask you, brothers: leaving aside the rest of the Scriptures, what Christian is not satisfied with this apostolic sentence? [Note: [Col. 2265] The manuscript reads more suitably: “this apostolic sentence is sufficient for every Christian.”]

I truly say, brothers, that whoever does not rise from the sleep of avarice under such thunder must be regarded not as sleeping but as dead.

### 4. The necessity and manner of fleeing to God’s mercy. Whoever does not give his surplus invades another’s property.

Therefore, brothers, since on account of this carnal weakness we are constantly disturbed and pierced by many sins, like flies swarming around us, let us hasten amid the storms and tempests of this world to the harbor of God’s mercy.

Perhaps someone asks how he may reach this harbor. Let him hear Christ saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7); and again: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Therefore, if we wish to escape from the sea of this world, we must always keep this sentence of the Apostle before our eyes. Let it be enough for us to have food and clothing—not splendid, not luxurious. Whatever more God gives must not be withheld from the needs of the poor, because it is shown to have been sent through us to them.

If we do not give what is superfluous to us, we have invaded another’s property. And however many poor people die of hunger, with our knowledge, they will bring charges against us before the tribunal of Christ.

[Col. 2266]

### 5. Two kinds of almsgiving. Without each other they are of no benefit.

Since there are two kinds of almsgiving—one that we distribute to the poor, and another by which we grant forgiveness to our neighbors or brothers whenever they have sinned against us—let us practice both with God’s help, because one without the other is of no benefit.

If you extend alms to a poor person but do not grant forgiveness to someone who has sinned against you, it benefits you nothing. Conversely, if you forgive those who sin against you but refuse to give the hungry as much as you can, then, as I have said, one virtue cannot benefit you without the other.

Let us, brothers, prepare these two kinds of almsgiving for ourselves as the oars of spiritual wings, so that, freed and released from every earthly desire, we may be able to fly and come happily to our true homeland and to that heavenly Jerusalem on the wings of virtue, like spiritual doves—according to what the Psalmist desires and asks when he says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54:7).

### 6. At times to set aside the business of the world.

It is certain, brothers, that unless each person strives to free the wings of his soul from the glue of sins and from the excessive obstacles and snares of this world, he will never be able to reach true rest.

With God’s help, therefore, brothers, if we cannot remove the obstacles of this world from us completely, let us at least strive to moderate them as far as our strength permits, or to cut away some part of them, so that some intervals of time may remain for us in which we can devote ourselves to reading or prayer.

For if earthly occupation takes away all our time, we must fear that what is written may come upon us: “The obstacles of the world made them wretched.” Let us therefore labor more earnestly, with the Lord’s help, so that in us too, at least in part, what is written of the blessed man may be fulfilled: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

May the Lord, in his mercy, grant this to your holy Charity, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLXXVII

[Note: [Col. 2266] Elsewhere, On Time 219.]

On returning tithes

[Note: [Col. 2266] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors had left the matter doubtful; following Verlinus, Vinding rejected it, chiefly because the tithes whose return is discussed here can be understood, from the exposition on Psalm 103, sermon 3, no. 9, and the exposition on Psalm 146, nos. 16–17, not yet to have been given or assigned to clerics and priests in Augustine’s time. It seems rather to belong to Caesarius than to Augustine. For no. 2 and following, compare Appendix, sermon 276; for no. 3 below, sermon 308, nos. 2 and 6; for no. 4, sermons 266, no. 2; 294, no. 8; 205, no. 6; 265, nos. 4–5.]

### 1. Offering tithes benefits us. Tithes are the tribute of the needy. They must be returned from the fruit of one’s labor.

With Christ favorable, dearest brothers, the days are now near when we must gather the harvest. Therefore, while giving thanks to God who has given it, let us think about offering—or rather, returning—our tithes.

For our God, who has deigned to give everything, deigns to demand a tenth from us, which will undoubtedly benefit not him but us. Thus he himself promised through the prophet, saying:

“Bring every tithe into my storehouses, so that there may be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord, whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and give you fruit in abundance” (Mal. 3:10).

Behold, we have shown how tithes benefit us more than God. For this reason it is written elsewhere: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23:1).

If, then, the earth and its fullness are the Lord’s, we are equally the Lord’s servants and tenants. I do not know how we do not all acknowledge the owner. For he says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood” (Isa. 1:3).

O foolish human beings, what evil does God command, that he does not deserve to be obeyed? For he says: “You shall not delay offering me the firstfruits of your threshing floor and your winepress” (Exod. 22:29). If it is a sin to give late, how much worse is it not to have given at all?

Again he says: “Honor the Lord your God from your just labors, and offer him from the fruits of your righteousness, so that your barns may be filled with grain and your winepresses overflow with wine” (Prov. 3:9–10). You do not provide this without compensation, since you will quickly receive it back with great interest.

Perhaps you ask whom it benefits that God receives what he will return. You ask again whom it benefits that what is given is given to the poor. If you believe, it benefits you; if you doubt, you have lost it.

Tithes are the tribute of needy souls. Therefore return the tribute to the poor; offer libations to the priests. If you do not have tithes from earthly produce, the thing by which the farmer lives, whatever skill sustains you belongs to God; and from the source of your livelihood he demands tithes. From military service, from trade, from craftsmanship, return tithes.

For we pay one thing for the land and another as the price of our life. Therefore pay, human being, because you possess; pay, because you have been granted the privilege of being born. For the Lord says: “Each shall give a ransom for his soul, and there will be among them neither disease nor calamity” (Exod. 30:12).

Behold, in the holy Scriptures you have your Lord’s guarantee, by which he promised you that if you give tithes, you will receive not only abundance of fruits but also bodily health. “Your threshing floors will be filled with grain, and your winepresses will overflow with wine; and there will be among them neither disease nor calamity.”

Since by giving tithes you can merit both earthly and heavenly gifts, why through greed do you defraud yourself of a double blessing?

### 2. God reduces the person who denies the tithe to the tithe alone. It is mercy that he does not demand the nine parts.

Listen, then, ungodly humanity. You know that everything you receive belongs to God, yet you do not lend anything of his own to the Creator of all things? The Lord God is not in need; he does not ask for a reward, but for honor. He does not demand anything of yours that you must repay.

He asks for the firstfruits and the tithes of your possessions, and you refuse? Miser, what would you do if, after taking nine parts for himself, he left you the tenth? This has certainly already happened when your harvest, deprived of the blessing of rain, withered in famine, and your vintage was either struck by hail or shriveled by frost.

What do you say, greedy calculator? Nine parts have been taken back from you because you did not wish to give the tenth. It is true that you did not give it, but God nevertheless exacted it.

For this is the Lord’s most just custom: if you do not give him the tenth, you will be reduced to the tenth. For it is written: “Thus says the Lord: Because the tenth of your field and the firstfruits of the earth are with you. I see you, and you thought to deceive me; within your treasuries and your houses there will be plunder” [Note: [Col. 2267] Clermont manuscript: “not only in your lands but also in your houses there will be plunder”; Vatican manuscript: “The year has been consumed, and you have brought my tithes into your treasuries. For there will be plunder in your houses.”]

You will give to the wicked soldier what you do not wish to give to the priest. “Return to me,” says the Lord Almighty, “so that I may open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out my blessing upon you; and your land’s fruits will not be corrupted, nor will your vine languish in the field, and all nations will call you blessed” (Mal. 3:7, 11–12).

God is always ready to do good, but human wickedness prevents him, because a person wishes everything to be given to him by the Lord God, yet does not wish to offer him anything from what he seems to possess.

What if God were to say: “Surely you are mine, human being, whom I made; the land you cultivate is mine; the seeds you scatter are mine; the animals you exhaust are mine; the showers and rains are mine; the blasts of the winds are mine; the heat of the sun is mine. Since all the elements by which you live are mine, you who merely lend your hands deserved only the tenth?”

But because almighty God feeds us with goodness, he grants a most generous reward to those who labor least: claiming only the tenth for himself, he has granted us everything else.

### 3. Good use must be made of possessions in this life. It is useless to leave this care to others. Whoever does not give tithes invades another’s property. The use of the other nine parts.

Ungrateful defrauder and faithless person, I address you with the divine voice. Behold, the year has now ended; pay the Lord who sends rain his due reward.

Redeem yourself, human being, while you live; redeem yourself while you can; redeem yourself while you have the price in your hands. Redeem yourself, lest bitter death overtake you and you lose both life and the price at once.

You leave this without purpose to your wife, who perhaps will have another husband. Without purpose, woman, you leave it to your husband, who perhaps desires to take another wife without delay. In vain you entrust your care to parents and relatives: no one will faithfully redeem you after your death, because during life you did not wish to redeem yourself.

Now lay down the burden of greed from your shoulders; despise that most cruel mistress. While she presses you under the harshest yoke, she does not permit you to take up Christ’s yoke. For just as the yoke of greed customarily presses down into hell, so Christ’s yoke customarily raises up to heaven.

Tithes are required as a debt, and whoever does not wish to give them has invaded another’s property. And however many poor people have died of hunger in the places where he himself lives because he did not give tithes, he will appear guilty of as many murders before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, because he reserved for his own use what the Lord had assigned to the poor.

Whoever therefore desires either to obtain a reward for himself or to merit forgiveness of sins should return tithes and strive to give alms from the nine parts. Yet he must do so in such a way that whatever remains from those nine parts, apart from moderate food and reasonable clothing, is not reserved for luxury but deposited through almsgiving to the poor in the heavenly treasury.

Whatever God gives us beyond what we need, he has not given specifically to us; he has sent it through us to be distributed to others. If we do not give it, we have invaded another’s property.

### 4. Preparing oneself for the feast of Saint John. On avoiding pagan bathing on that day.

Since we desire to celebrate the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist with joy, as we do the other festivals that come upon us, let everyone, as this most glorious solemnity approaches, observe chastity and honorable conduct for many days beforehand, so that all may celebrate the festival with joy and may merit approaching the Lord’s altar with a free and sincere conscience.

I also beg you, and adjure you by the dreadful day of judgment, to admonish all your neighbors, all your households, and everyone under your authority [Note: [Col. 2268] The following material is published for the first time from the manuscripts], and to correct them with the utmost severity in zeal for God, so that no one at the festival of Saint John may dare to bathe in springs, marshes, or rivers, whether at night or in the morning. For this wretched custom still remains from pagan observance.

Since not only souls but also—what is worse—bodies very often die in that sacrilegious bathing, let those who do not think about the salvation of their souls at least fear for the death of their bodies.

But we trust in God’s mercy that, when you correct them, few or perhaps none will henceforth dare to commit this evil.

Admonish them also of this, brothers: they must not utter from their mouths songs that are filthy and lustful, hostile to chastity and honorable conduct. For it is not right that from the mouth into which Christ’s Eucharist enters there should proceed a lustful or amorous song.
