If you gladly hear these things according to your custom and strive, with Christ’s help, to fulfill them, then in this world you will celebrate the solemnities of the saints with a pure heart and chaste body, and in the world to come you will happily come to share in their company, by the favor of him to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2268] Formerly, On Time 241; later, Appendix 68.]

On Auguries

[Note: [Col. 2268] Boniface, bishop of Mainz, formerly called the Apostle of the Germans, cited it under Augustine’s name in his letter to Pope Zachary. Nevertheless, the Louvain editors rightly relegated it to the Appendix, noting that Lipsius doubted whether its phrasing was Severian’s. It seems to us entirely to belong to Caesarius. For no. 1, see Appendix, sermon 249, no. 2; Caesarius, Homily 15; Appendix, sermons 272, no. 8; 279, no. 4; 265, no. 5; for no. 2, sermons 4, no. 2, and 272, no. 7; for no. 5, Boniface’s letter to Pope Zachary; Appendix, sermons 28, no. 4, and 76, no. 6.]

### 1. The author’s effort to draw the people away from diviners. Those who consult them lose Baptism. Superstitious observances. Pious observances.

You know very well, dearest brothers, that I have often pleaded with you and warned you with paternal concern, and have likewise solemnly charged you, that you ought not in any way to observe those sacrilegious customs of the pagans. Yet, as I have learned from the reports of many, my warning has made little progress among some people.

If I do not tell you, I will have to render a bad account both for myself and for you on the day of judgment, and I will have to endure eternal punishments with you. I acquit myself before God by warning and solemnly charging you again and again: none of you should seek out fortune-tellers, diviners, or casters of lots, nor question them about any matter or illness whatsoever.

Let no one employ enchanters. Whoever does this evil immediately loses the sacrament of Baptism and instantly becomes sacrilegious and pagan; and unless abundant almsgiving and harsh, prolonged penance come to his aid, he will immediately perish eternally.

Likewise, do not observe auguries. When you are on a journey, do not pay attention to birds singing, nor presume to announce diabolical predictions from their song. Let none of you observe on what day he leaves his house or on what day he returns. God made all days, as Scripture says: “The first day was made, and the second day, and the third, likewise the fourth, and the fifth, and the sixth, and the Sabbath” (Gen. 1:1–3); and also: “God made all things very good” (ibid., 31).

Do not consider or observe those not only sacrilegious but also ridiculous sneezes. Whenever you need to hurry anywhere, sign yourselves in the name of Jesus Christ, faithfully reciting the Creed or the Lord’s Prayer, and set out on your journey confidently in God’s help.

### 2. The devil harasses those who despise his deceptions. By this God tests those who truly cling to him.

When, with God inspiring you, you begin to despise or reject all the sacrileges mentioned above, the devil will take this badly, because he sees you withdrawing from his friendship and fellowship and despising the sacrileges by which he deceived you.

He will try to inflict some wickedness upon you, or send you an illness, or take away some animal, either through disease or by causing it to stray. God permits this in order to test you, so that he may discover whether you come faithfully to him, whether you despise the devil’s machinations with your whole heart, and whether his love is worth more to you than the loss of any animal.

But if, once or twice, you endure with courage and complete faith the misfortunes the devil has sent, God will afterward deign to drive the devil away from harassing you, so that he will never be able to deceive you by his cunning.

Negligent and fickle people, who have weak desires and sluggish faith—and who therefore, even if they begin, do not persevere long in the works of God, but, after abstaining from the aforementioned sacrileges and suffering even one of the devil’s misfortunes, immediately regret having turned to the Lord and abandoned the devil’s machinations—return again to observing auguries, like dogs to their vomit.

But you, to whom God has given both wisdom and true faith, despise the devil’s deceptions quickly and wholeheartedly; turn faithfully to God; and patiently and courageously endure whatever the devil wishes to send. Then you will be able to say with blessed Job: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (Job 1:21). Likewise, with the Apostle, say with a firm and undivided heart: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or persecution? Or distress? Or hunger? Or nakedness? Or the sword? Or danger?” (Rom. 8:35).

For good Christians are not separated from Christ even by torments. But the lukewarm and negligent are sometimes separated from him by idle stories; and if they suffer even a slight loss, they are immediately scandalized, presume to murmur against God, and return to wicked and detestable auguries.

### 3. Why diviners often announce the truth, and why danger is often avoided only through them; consulting them is a grave sin

But perhaps someone says: “What are we to do, since the auguries themselves, and the *caragi*, or diviners, often announce true things to us?” Scripture warns and admonishes us about this matter, saying: “Even if they tell you something true, do not believe them. For the Lord your God is testing you, to see whether or not you fear him” (Deut. XIII, 3).

But you say again: “Sometimes, if enchanters are not consulted, many people suffer peril almost to the point of death, whether from a serpent’s bite or from some other illness.” It is true, dearest brothers, that God permits this to the devil—as I have already said—in order to test the Christian: so that, when they are sometimes able to obtain some remedy for that illness through those sacrileges and to recognize something true, they may consequently believe the devil more readily.

But whoever desires to preserve the whole Christian religion must utterly despise all these things with the full strength of his soul, fearing what the Apostle says in rebuke: “You observe days and months and seasons; I fear that I have labored over you in vain” (Gal. IV, 10–11). Behold, the Apostle says that whoever observes auguries will receive his teaching in vain. Therefore, as far as you can, flee the devil’s deceptions.

### 4. The devil can harm no one unless permitted; God permits this for two reasons

Above all, know this, brothers: the devil cannot harm either you yourselves, or those who belong to you, or your animals, or any other possession—not even in small matters—except insofar as he has received power from God. Thus he did not dare to destroy the holy Job’s affairs unless the Lord permitted it.

And, as we read in the Gospel, when the demons were driven out from human beings, they asked that they might at least be permitted to enter the pigs (Matt. VIII, 31). If the demons did not dare to enter pigs unless they received permission from God, who could be so unbelieving as to think that they can harm good Christians unless God, by his own dispensation, permits it?

God permits this for two reasons: either to test us, if we are good, or to correct us, if we are sinners. But whoever patiently endures the Lord’s dispensation and, as I have already said, whenever he has lost something says, “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord,” receives, for this patience pleasing to God, either a crown, if he is righteous, or forgiveness, if he is a sinner.

And pay attention to this, brothers: when the devil had destroyed all the substance of blessed Job, Job did not say, “The Lord gave, the devil has taken away,” but, “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away.” The holy man did not wish to give the devil the glory of having been able to take away something which the Lord had not permitted him to remove.

Since the devil could not harm blessed Job’s sons, servants, camels, or donkeys before the Lord permitted it, why do we think that he can do anything more to Christians than divine power has permitted according to God’s godlike and hidden judgment?

### 5. Believing in diviners, *caragi*, and the like is a mortal sin; remnants of pagan superstitions

Therefore, believing with complete certainty that we can lose nothing except what God permits to be taken from us, let us go with our whole heart to his mercy. Let us faithfully abandon sacrilegious observances and always place our hope in his help.

For whoever believes in the evils mentioned above—that is, in *caragi* and diviners, soothsayers, amulets, and any other auguries—even if he fasts, even if he prays, even if he continually hastens to church, even if he gives generous alms, and even if he torments his little body in every affliction, none of this will benefit him so long as he has not abandoned those sacrileges. For that impious observance of sacrilege overwhelms and destroys all these good works.

Those who wish to perform some good works while retaining these evils can gain nothing from them, because what the Apostle said is true: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V, 6); and also: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (ibid. X, 20–21). The Lord likewise says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24).

For this reason Christians must neither make vows at trees nor pray at a spring, if they wish, through God’s grace, to be freed from eternal punishment. Therefore, whoever has in his field, or in his estate, or near his estate, any trees, altars, or any other vain objects where wretched people customarily make vows: if he does not destroy and cut them down, he will undoubtedly share in the sacrileges committed there.

For what sort of thing is this: when those trees at which vows are made have fallen, no one brings wood from those trees to the fire? And observe the misery—or rather, the folly—of the human race: they show honor to a dead tree and despise the commands of the living God; they do not dare to put the branches of a tree into the fire, yet through sacrilege they cast themselves into hell.

Therefore, whoever has until now not practiced this evil should rejoice, give thanks to God, and strive faithfully to persevere in good works. But whoever has until now surrendered himself to the devil to be held captive in these diabolical matters should repent with his whole heart and flee and despise the sacrileges mentioned above with complete horror, so that God may deign to grant him forgiveness and, for the glory of his name, bring him to eternal blessedness.

### 6. Those who eat food offered to idols kill their soul

Since it has also come to my attention that some people—whether through simplicity, ignorance, or, what is more credible, through gluttony—neither fear nor blush to eat of those sacrileges, sacrifices, or sacrilegious foods that are still carried out according to pagan custom, I charge you before God and his angels, and I declare that you must not go to those diabolical banquets held either at a shrine or springs, or at certain trees.

And if anything is sent to you from there, shudder at it and reject it as though you were seeing the devil himself. Reject it in such a way that you do not even permit anything from that sacrilegious banquet to be brought into your house. This is because of what the Apostle has already said: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, nor partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.”

Since some people are accustomed to say, “I make the sign of the cross over myself, and then I eat,” no one should presume to do this. For the person who crosses himself and eats something from sacrilegious food is like one who makes the sign of the cross over his mouth and drives a sword into his chest. Just as the body is killed by a sword, so the soul is killed by that sacrilegious food.

But we trust in the mercy of the Lord, because he will deign to inspire you to do what is holy, and never permit wickedness to creep upon you through auguries, or through the other sacrilegious observances or divinations of the devil mentioned above. May you place all your hope in the Lord, so that you never return to those wicked evils described above; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CCLXXIX

[Note: [Col. 2271] Elsewhere, in the Vignerian collection, no. 29.]

### On Martyrs or Amulets

[Note: [Col. 2271] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. I am reluctant to demonstrate how falsely Vignier published it under the name of Augustine. In the latter part you will detect the style and sententiae of Caesarius, especially in sections 5 and 6. For section 4, see Appendix Sermons 265, no. 5, and 276, no. 1; for section 5, Sermon 278, no. 1; for section 6, Sermons 28, no. 4; 76, no. 6; 264, no. 2; 13, no. 5; 258, nos. 2 and 4; for section 7, Sermons 257, no. 4; 264, no. 5; 256, no. 4; 260, no. 3; 257, no. 1; 77, no. 6; 13, no. 5; 44, no. 6; 45, no. 3.]

### 1. The various tortures of the martyrs

Through the apostolic reading we have heard that the servants and friends of God, of whom the world was not worthy, endured unworthy yet glorious sufferings through the power of faith, as the divine Word says: “Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were sawn apart, they died by the killing of the sword” (Hebr. XI, 36–37).

We therefore read that some were tortured in prisons, others, as persecution grew stronger, were destroyed by the whirlwind of an impious storm and pelted with hard showers of stones; others were deprived of their heads by the hostile sword consecrated by sacrilegious persons, yet were exalted in the kingdom of the eternal Head.

“He says, ‘They were stoned and sawn apart.’” The dreadful cutter dragged out slow delays with a new sword through their entrails; numerous bites of savage teeth ran through their triumphant viscera. Thus, while faith persevered, the weight of their merits was revealed through the unprecedented novelty of their punishments.

### 2. Why the saints are handed over to the impious; here we can conquer evils, not avoid them; the martyr’s palm can still be won

But perhaps someone thinks to himself and says: “Why are good and holy men handed over into the hands of the impious?”

You ask what this means? It means that “human life upon earth is a trial” (Job VII, 1). Straining in the contest of this world, they are tested so that they may be proved; they are proved so that they may be rewarded.

And therefore, at times, when the devil had asked for the saints to be placed under his power, he obtained this with the Lord’s permission—not in order to harm them in the strength of their souls, but to afflict them in the weakness of their bodies—so that, since they did not succumb and faithfully resisted through fear of the Lord, the trial of injury might become an occasion of glory.

The Lord himself, moreover, was handed over into the hands of sinners, and during the time of his Passion the impious judge addressed him in this way: “Do you not know that I have power to kill you and to release you?” (John XIX, 10). The Lord answered him: “You would have no power unless it had been given you from above” (ibid., 11).

He therefore accepted and conquered the hostile misfortunes of this world in order to instruct and strengthen us, so that we too may understand that we cannot flee the evils of this age, but that with God’s help we can overcome them.

There is therefore a portion belonging to Christ’s faithful together with the holy martyrs, if they patiently and bravely endure, out of fear of God, the things that this world imposes. Therefore the divine Word says to us: “If you are sharers in sufferings, you will also be sharers in consolations” (II Cor. I, 7).

### 3. The persecutor is not lacking even now

But perhaps you say: “There is no persecutor of religion; no persecutor of piety threatens us. How can I share the martyr’s portion without an enemy?”

It is not so, dearest ones; if only faith were present. For although a public tempter is lacking, a hidden tempter is not lacking. If you wish, let us briefly speak of the enemy’s hidden and evil, flattering temptations, and of his snares.

For example, does someone entice you toward fraud, false testimony, or any other unjust profit? Through his mouth the voice of the ancient serpent hisses.

Does an ugly seducer entangle you with dishonorable counsels and flattering blandishments so that you commit the crime of unchastity, and entice you toward the precipices of lust? The enemy is secretly setting snares for you.

### 4. Those who consult diviners sacrifice to the devil and violate Baptism; having renounced Christ, they make a pact with the devil

It often happens, brothers, that a persecutor from the devil’s side comes to someone who is ill and says: “If you had consulted that enchanter, you would already be well; if you had been willing to hang those characters around your neck, you could already have recovered your health.”

If you consent to this persecutor, you have sacrificed to the devil; if you despise him, you have won the glory of martyrdom.

Perhaps another comes and says: “Send to that diviner; send him your belt or band, so that he may measure it and examine it. He himself will tell you what you should do, or whether you can escape.”

Another says: “He knows well how to fumigate; for whoever has had this done for him immediately became better, and every affliction departed from his house.”

Whoever gives in to all these practices has violated the sacrament of Baptism.

The devil also often deceives careless and lukewarm Christians in this matter. If someone has suffered a theft, that most cruel persecutor stirs up one of his friends and says to him: “Come secretly to that place, and I will produce a person who will tell you who stole your silver or your money. But if you wish to discover this, when you come to that place, do not make the sign of the cross.”

Behold to what evils lukewarm Christians are led: while they wish to recover temporal health, they do not fear committing such wicked sacrileges.

Whoever consents to such counselors of the devil should have no doubt that, having renounced Christ, he has made a pact with the devil.

Women also commonly persuade one another that, when their children are ill, they ought to apply some charm inconsistent with the Catholic faith. This deception too comes from the devil’s side.

### 5. More wholesome remedies for evils

How much more right and wholesome it would be for them to hasten to church, receive the body and blood of Christ, and faithfully anoint themselves and their families with blessed oil; and, according to what the Apostle James says, receive not only health of body but also remission of sins.

For the Holy Spirit made this promise through him: “If anyone is sick, let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V, 14–15).

But perhaps someone says: “Why does our bishop admonish us about this matter so frequently?”

For this reason, brothers: although we admonish you so frequently, we nevertheless learn from the reports of many people that these sacrileges are still being committed by some. Therefore I ask you: whoever has not yet done this must never commit it; whoever has done it should hasten, as far as he can, to perform worthy penance.

### 6. What preparation is required for the feasts of the martyrs

But we, dearest ones, whenever we wish to celebrate the solemnities of the saints and martyrs, should strive, as far as we can with God’s help, to prepare and adorn ourselves with good works.

Therefore, whoever examines his conscience and discovers that he is truly chaste, sober, humble, and merciful should rejoice and give thanks to God. With all his strength and with God’s help, he should strive not only to preserve the divine gifts within himself but also to increase them.

But whoever sees that he is careless or drunk, angry, envious, and proud, and perhaps stained with the filth of lust, should quickly have recourse to the medicine of repentance. Before that dark soul departs from its most wretched body, let him acquire a remedy for himself on the day of necessity. Let him give abundant alms and devote himself frequently, with groaning and sighing, vigils, fasts, and prayers, so that before his soul—as I have already said—is snatched from its little body burdened with sins, he may provide himself with the medicines of a contrite and humbled heart, which will profit him forever. For “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L, 19).

Under the hand of the almighty Physician, no sinner should ever despair. For the abundance of mercy is so great that, when people are truly corrected, he not only grants forgiveness of sins but also allows them to reach eternal rewards.

### 7. We must neither despair nor presume falsely

Therefore we must neither despair nor hope wrongly.

He despairs who thinks that God will not forgive those burdened with many crimes, even if they do penance. But he hopes wrongly who believes that, even if he wishes to remain in sins until the end of his life, he can still obtain God’s mercy.

For our God knows how to reward merits, just as he knows how to punish sins. He who said, “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12), also said: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Ecclus. V, 8).

Fear, therefore, O man, the justice whose mercy you seek. For the longer he waits for you to be corrected, the more severely he punishes you if you do not wish to amend yourself quickly.

In this world God dispenses mercy; in the future he exercises justice. Here he pays out the money of his admonition or patience; there he will exact interest. And what is written will be fulfilled: “Then he will repay each person according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27). He did not say, “according to his mercy,” but “according to his works.”

The Apostle Paul also confirms this, saying: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10).

Let us therefore, brothers, with the Lord’s help, act in such a way that whatever he has entrusted to us when we are judged, he may find whole when he judges; and that the solemnities and patronage of the holy martyrs may bring us not judgment but progress.

Let us strive, as far as we can, to act so that, while we celebrate the feasts of those saints in this world, we may deserve to obtain their fellowship in heaven; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CCLXXX

[Note: [Col. 2274] Elsewhere, *De Tempore* 251.]

### On the devout celebration of Sunday and the other feast days

[Note: [Col. 2274] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, and Verlino and Vinding considered it spurious. Certain fragments of Alcuin and Caesarius have been gathered here by an author who had also worked somewhat in Benedict’s Rule; some of its words occur here as well. For section 2, see Alcuin, *On the Divine Office*, chap. 27; for section 3, the Rule of Benedict, chap. 50; for section 4, Caesarius, *Homily* 33, near the beginning; Appendix Sermon 281, no. 1; the Rule of Benedict, chap. 19; for section 5, at the end, Benedict’s prologue to his Rule.]

### 1. By whom and why the rest of feast days and Sunday was established

It must be known, dearest brothers, that our holy fathers established and commanded that Christians should have rest on the solemnities of the saints, and especially on Sundays, and should be free from earthly business, so that they might be more prepared and ready for divine worship, since no troublesome occupation would hold them back from it. At that time they should leave earthly concerns behind, so that they might more easily attend to God’s will.

For this reason the Lord himself says through the prophet: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11).

But those who, entangled in various cares and occupations, despise this sentence of God and do not wish to be free for divine contemplation—I fear that at the future judgment, when they knock at the Lord’s door and ask that it be opened, the Lord will answer them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12); “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Ps. VI, 9).

Those who now neglect to seek God will then be rejected by him. Therefore, my brothers, let it not be burdensome for you to devote yourselves to divine worship on Sundays and on the birthdays of the saints.

### 2. Why Sunday is so called; its many distinctions

The Apostles and apostolic men decreed that Sunday should be kept with religious solemnity because on it our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is therefore called the Lord’s Day, so that on it, abstaining from earthly works and the attractions of the world, we may serve only divine worship. We give this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection that we possess in it.

For just as the Lord Jesus Christ and Savior rose from the dead, so we too hope to rise on the last day.

It is also evident that this day is solemn in the Holy Scriptures. It is the first day of the world; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created; on it Christ also rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the Apostles; and on it manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness.

By these and similar signs the Lord’s Day stands distinguished. Therefore the holy teachers of the Church decreed that all the glory of the Jewish Sabbath should be transferred to it, so that what they celebrated in figure we might celebrate in truth. For our true rest will come when the resurrection has been accomplished and the reward in soul and body has been perfected together.

### 3. How it is to be observed

Let us therefore observe Sunday, brothers, and sanctify it, just as the ancients were commanded concerning the Sabbath, the Lawgiver saying: “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths” (Lev. XXIII, 32).

Let us see to it that our rest is not empty; but from the evening of the Sabbath day until the evening of the Lord’s Day, separated from rural labor and every business, let us devote ourselves solely to divine worship.

In this way too we properly sanctify the Lord’s Sabbath, since the Lord says: “You shall do no work on it” (ibid., 35).

Therefore, whoever is able should come to the evening and nocturnal celebration and pray there in the assembly of the Church to God for his sins. Whoever cannot do this should at least pray in his own house and not neglect to pay his vow to God and render the due service of his devotion.

During the day, no one should separate himself from the sacred celebration of the Mass. No one should remain idly at home while the others go to church, nor occupy himself with hunting and become enslaved to the devil’s service, wandering through fields and woods, raising shouting and laughter from his mouth instead of sighs, and not uttering words of prayer to God from the depths of his heart.

### 4. Various perverse practices condemned: games, jokes, quarrels, and fights

What is even more detestable is that some people come to church but do not enter, do not persist in prayer, and do not wait in silence for the celebration of the holy Masses. When the divine lessons are being read inside, they themselves remain outside, either conducting lawsuits, attacking others with various slanders, or sweating over dice games and useless amusements.

Sometimes, what is worse, certain people become inflamed with excessive anger and quarrel most bitterly, so that they attack one another with weapons or clubs and often commit homicide. This is done especially by those who, full of envy and hatred and led by the devil, go to the church assembly not to help themselves but to harm others.

If such people die there through homicide or are carried off by sudden death, where do they go except into eternal torments with the one whose footsteps they followed?

Do not do these things, my brothers. Do not deceive yourselves. Do not give the devil a place in your assembly. Instead, prepare yourselves as a dwelling for Christ.

Therefore devote yourselves not to stories outside, but inside to psalmody and prayers. Do not talk noisily to one another in church; keep quiet.

There are many people, especially very many women, who chatter and talk so much in church that they neither hear the divine lessons themselves nor permit others to hear them. Is such an assembly, conducted in such a manner, appropriate in the house of God? Is it fitting to stand in this way in the presence of God and his holy angels?

### 5. The powerful force the Mass to be shortened; judgments held on feast days; banquets

What is also very regrettable is that I wish to complain to you about certain people, especially the powerful of this world, who, when they come to church, are not devout in celebrating the praises of God. Instead, they force the priest to shorten the Mass and sing according to their wishes. Because of their gluttony and greed, he is not permitted to follow ecclesiastical custom, so that one brief part of the day is assigned to God’s service and the rest of the daylight, together with the night, to their pleasures.

Do not do these things, my most beloved brothers; do not consent to those who do them. For not only those who commit such acts but also those who consent to their perpetrators perish (Rom. I, 32).

Above all, do not plead or hear cases on feast days, but at another time and with justice. Do not overturn just judgments by accepting gifts, because according to the Lord’s sentence, “With whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. VII, 2).

None of you should get drunk, because a drunk person is very much like a madman. Do not, by drinking to names, erase your names from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 2275] “To names” (*in nominibus*) must be read in this way, as it appears in Rabanus, not “among men” (*in hominibus*). Here a superstition is being noted, as Caesarius explains in Sermon 295, no. 5: “After the banquet had already ended, they began to drink to various names—not only of living men, but also of angels and the other ancient saints.” This custom has not yet been entirely extinguished among the Germans.]

Indeed, many people, what is worse, not only get themselves drunk but also force and urge others to drink more than is appropriate. From this quarrels and homicides often arise among them.

Do you understand, brothers, whose will they are following in this? For the Apostle says: “Drunkards and murderers will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

I beseech you, most beloved fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by his coming kingdom and judgment, that you withdraw yourselves from every person who walks disorderly (II Thess. III, 6), and that you walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called (Eph. IV, 1). Do not neglect your honor or think lightly of the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

You have been called sons of God because the true Son of God has freed you. Strive by good conduct to please so great a Father, so that he may not consign you as utterly wicked servants to everlasting punishment, but lead you as beloved children to the heavenly homeland, so that you may be fellow heirs of his Son Jesus Christ, with whom God lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

---

## SERMON CCLXXXI

[Note: [Col. 2276] This is the homily of Caesarius numbered twelve in the *Library of the Fathers*. The authors of his Life testify how impatiently Caesarius tolerated people leaving the church before the end of the Masses—the subject of this and the following sermon—in Book 1, section 14, in these words:

“After this, one day, looking out from the altar, he saw some people leave the church after the Gospels had been read, who disdained first to hear the blessed man’s word, that is, his preaching. Immediately he ran out and cried to the people: ‘What are you doing, O sons? Where are you being led, overturned by evil persuasion? Stand firm for your souls at the word of admonition, and listen attentively. You will not be permitted to do this on the day of judgment. I warn and cry out and charge you,’” and so forth.

They add that for this reason he very often ordered the doors to be closed after the Gospel. Hence Baronius rightly considers Caesarius, under the year 506, the author of the canons of the synod of Agde, especially canon 47, established concerning this same matter: “We specifically command that secular people remain for the whole Mass on Sunday, so that the people may not presume to leave before the priest’s blessing. If they do so, they are to be publicly put to shame by the bishop.” Shortly afterward the same was decreed in the first Council of Orléans, canon 26, and the third Council of Orléans, canon 29.

For section 1, see Appendix Sermons 285, no. 3; 265, no. 3; and 283, no. 1; for section 2, Sermon 115, no. 1; for section 3, Sermons 249, no. 2, and 300, no. 5; for section 4, Sermons 249, no. 5, and 265, no. 3; for section 5, Sermons 45, no. 4; 259, no. 1; 290, no. 7; 289, no. 9.]

### Admonition urging the whole people to wait faithfully in church until the divine mysteries are celebrated

### 1. Those who chatter in church

I ask you, dearest brothers, and admonish you with paternal affection, that whenever Masses are celebrated, whether on Sunday or on other major feast days, no one leave the church until the divine mysteries are completed.

Although there are many whose faith and devotion cause us joy, there are nevertheless more who think little about the salvation of their souls. As soon as the divine lessons have been read, they immediately go out of the church, even though, while the lessons themselves are being read, some of them are so occupied with idle and worldly stories that they neither hear them themselves nor permit others to hear them.

Such people would be less blameworthy in our eyes if they did not come to church at all, because there they are shown to offend God more seriously, in the very place where they could have earned forgiveness for their sins.

### 2. When the Masses take place; the Lord’s Prayer during the Masses; some hear it unto judgment; how much good is accomplished in the Masses

Therefore I ask you, brothers, to receive the suggestion of our humility not only patiently but willingly.

If you pay careful attention, you will understand that the Masses do not take place when the divine lessons are recited in the church, but when the offerings are presented and the body or blood of the Lord is consecrated.

[Note: [Col. 2276] Amalarius of Trier also writes about his own time, *On the Divine Office*, book 3, chapter 36: “The uneducated crowd commonly asks at what point of the entire Office the Mass begins, so that, if someone should happen not to arrive for the whole service, he may know at which Offices he must be present without hesitation.” He answers them: “It seems to us that the Mass is called by that name from the point at which the priest begins to offer the sacrifice to God, until the final blessing—that is, from the Offertory (*Offerenda*) until ‘Go, the dismissal is made’ (*Ite missa est*).”]

For you can read the lessons—whether prophetic, apostolic, or evangelical—in your own homes, or hear others reading them. But you cannot hear or see the consecration of the Lord’s body or blood anywhere except in the house of God.

Therefore whoever wishes to celebrate the Mass in its entirety, with profit to his soul, must remain in the church with humbled body and contrite heart until the Lord’s Prayer has been said and the blessing has been given to the people.

When most of the people—or rather, what is worse, nearly everyone—leave the church after the lessons have been read, to whom will the priest say, “Lift up your hearts”? Or how can those who depart downward into the streets, in body and heart alike, answer that their hearts are lifted up?

How will they cry out with trembling and joy, “Holy, holy, holy; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”?

Or, when the Lord’s Prayer is said, who is there to cry out humbly and truthfully, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12)?

Even those who remain in the church, if they do not forgive the debts of their debtors, utter the Lord’s Prayer from their mouths more for judgment than for remedy, since they are not shown to fulfill it in their deeds. They say “Deliver us from evil” without cause (ibid., 13), when they themselves do not cease repaying evil for evil.

If even those who remain inside are endangered if they do not wish to fulfill what they promise, what do those people think of themselves whom insatiable greed or love of this world holds so entangled that it does not permit them to stand in the church for even one hour?

It is not enough for them that throughout the entire week they are constantly occupied either by necessity or, what is truer, by greed. Even after the period of one or two hours during which they seem to assemble at church more in body than in heart, they turn their backs on the sacrifices or priests of God and return without delay to embrace the pleasure of this world.

[Note: [Col. 2277] Some manuscripts read “will” (*voluntatem*).]

Not recognizing what they are awaiting or what they are abandoning,

[Note: [Col. 2277] Perhaps “what they are abandoning” (*relinquunt*). M.]

they follow darkness and abandon light; they embrace the shadow and despise the truth; they leave the sweetness of Christ and seek the bitterness of the world, loving vanity and pursuing falsehood.

Truly, whoever hurries out of the church does not know how much good is accomplished in the celebration of the Masses.

### 3. The irreverence of those who leave before the Masses are finished; illness or necessity excuses a person from blame

Yet if one of these people had been invited to dinner by a king or some powerful person, I should like to know whether he would presume to leave before the entire meal had been completed. Even if the person did not hold him back, his appetite would.

Why do we not leave a human banquet until it has been completed? Is it not because we wish to fill our stomachs perhaps beyond what is proper, and because we fear offending the host?

Why do we leave the spiritual and divine banquet so quickly? I fear saying this, lest some people become angry; nevertheless, for the sake of both my danger and yours, I shall say it: we do this because we care neither about food for the soul, nor fear God, nor reverence man.

And because, by God’s favor, not everyone is blameworthy in this respect, but many are found who, with great contrition, do not leave the church until the blessing has been given to the people, and who do not cease praying humbly not only for themselves but also for others, God will repay those to whom he has given such contrition that they persevere in the church.

But those who are negligent he will condemn by a just judgment.

Therefore, brothers, admonish those who are unwilling either to say the Lord’s Prayer or to receive the blessing. Do not cease correcting them, saying and most firmly threatening that it does them no good to hear the divine lessons if they leave before the divine mysteries are completed.

Yet we cannot and must not hold responsible those who are occupied with public necessities or those whom illness prevents from waiting. Let them themselves examine their conscience to determine whether necessity or willingness is holding them back.

## 4. One Must Devote the Entire Sunday to Reading or Prayer

Therefore, again and again I ask and earnestly entreat you that on every Sunday, and especially on the greater feast days, no one should leave the church until the divine mysteries have been completed—except, perhaps, those whom we mentioned above, whom serious illness or public necessity does not allow to remain longer.

I truly say, brothers, it is harsh and almost excessively impious that Christians should show less reverence for Sunday than the Jews appear to observe on the Sabbath. For if those unhappy people observe the Sabbath in such a way that they presume to undertake no earthly work on it, how much more ought those who have been redeemed not with gold or silver but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18) to recognize their price, devote the day of the Resurrection to God, and think more attentively about the salvation of their souls?

Finally, if we neglect to devote the whole Sunday to reading and supplication to God, we sin against God by no means lightly. How great, then, is the evil if we cannot endure standing in the church even for the space of one or two hours while the divine mysteries are celebrated? But what is worse is that the love of this present age so intoxicates us that the shadow of fleeting falsity [Note: [Col. 2278] Perhaps, “of happiness.”] and the pleasure of worldly desires continually drag us toward empty and false joys, which produce genuine sorrows.

## 5. Conclusion

Therefore, again and again I ask [Note: [Col. 2278] Thus the manuscript: “Therefore I ask again.”] that none of you leave the church until the divine mysteries have been fully celebrated. And conduct yourselves in the church in such a way that none of you occupies himself with idle or earthly conversations.

What it is useful for me to say and for you to hear, I humbly admonish and earnestly entreat: whoever despises the herald will experience the judge. But whoever willingly listens to me and strives to fulfill what I have asked, I believe, through God’s mercy, will receive glorious rewards both in this age and in the age to come.

But whoever wishes to despise this will not be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of Christ by saying that he was neither restrained from evil nor urged by continual admonition toward those things that are holy and pleasing to God.

But we trust in God’s mercy that you will not incur judgment for contempt; rather, through your benevolent obedience you will reach the kingdom—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 282

[Note: [Col. 2278] Among the homilies published by Stephen Baluzius under the name of Caesarius, this is the eighth; the manuscripts of our Caesarius likewise assign it to him. On section 2, see Sermon 284 of the Appendix, no. 5; on section 3, Sermon 130, no. 2; 140, no. 2; 89, no. 5; on section 4, Sermon 292, no. 7.]

### An Admonition That the People Should Remain Until the Masses Are Completely Finished

#### 1. He Grieves Bitterly That the End of the Masses Is Not Awaited. He Explains the Cause of His Grief and His Paternal Feeling.

If you wished to recognize and carefully consider, dearest brothers, how great the grief and bitterness in my heart are when I see that you do not wish to remain until the Masses are completely finished, you could have mercy both on yourselves and on me.

For whoever understands what takes place in the church when the divine mysteries are celebrated recognizes how great an evil is committed by those who leave the church before the Masses are completed, without some grave necessity. Therefore, if you wish both to free me from the distress of my soul and to release yourselves from sin, do not despise me as I entreat you. Fear what the Lord said concerning priests: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

For whoever neither fears nor blushes to leave the Church quickly, without waiting for the Masses to be completed, should not doubt that he sins in two ways: [Col. 2279] he abandons the divine mysteries and grieves and despises the priest who is concerned for his welfare.

If our humility invited you to undertake some earthly and laborious work, we believe that your Charity would offer us obedience. But since we urge you not toward earthly things but toward heavenly ones, not toward what benefits the soul temporarily but toward what benefits it forever; since we seek no transient profits but invite you to heavenly treasures, consider in what danger those remain who pretend not to offer us obedience.

I, however, dearest brothers, do not grieve when you leave the church merely because you cause me some bodily loss, but because I desire you to be perfect and recognize that you are sinning so gravely against God.

#### 2. The Excellence of This Mystery. In What Posture and With What Disposition the Blessing Should Be Received.

Therefore, again and again I ask that, since we are—whatever we may be, though unworthy—imitators of the Lord, and since when you assemble in church we do not invite you to an earthly banquet, where human food is served, but to a heavenly and spiritual one, where the bread of angels is set forth, you not disdain or despise the banquet of your Lord, lest he despise you in the blessedness of his kingdom.

You must fear that evangelical sentence by which the Lord himself declared those who had been invited to the wedding but had refused to come unworthy of his banquet, and ordered others to be invited instead (Matthew 22:8–9). It must not be considered casually, but feared, that those who refused to come because of worldly impediments were judged unworthy by the Lord’s own mouth.

Therefore, so that this may not also be said of us, let us, as I have already entreated, show patience for one or two hours, until food for souls is set upon that spiritual table and the spiritual Sacraments are consecrated.

And because, after the Lord’s Prayer has been said, the blessing is given to you not by a human being but through a human being, receive the dew of divine blessing with grateful and devout hearts, with body humbled and heart contrite, so that, according to the Lord’s promise, a spring of water welling up to eternal life may be produced in you.

#### 3. What Keeps Each Person From Remaining in the Church. How Each Should Be Corrected.

Various and diverse occupations make it impossible for everyone to remain in the church. Bodily illness holds some; public necessity holds others; desire binds others and drags them along as though they were captives.

How many, even then, are arguing in the streets or in the courtyards [Note: [Col. 2279] Manuscript T: “corners.”] of the basilicas, or are occupied with business? How many are engaged in slander or idle conversation in the porticoes of the basilicas or in the sacristies [Note: [Col. 2279] The manuscript has, “or in the chapels.”], among whom there is often also no small number of clerics, laymen, or women?

What progress in the divine Scriptures can such people make, when they do not even allow the sound of Scripture itself to reach their ears? In them is fulfilled what is written: “Like the deaf asp that stops up its ears so that it may not hear the voice of the enchanters of Scripture” (Psalm 57:5–6).

Therefore you, to whom God has deigned to grant both his fear and his love, and who assemble in church with great contrition, correct most frequently those who have so far either refused to come here or perhaps have been unable to come. Warn them and give them salutary counsel, so that they may fear what is written: “The impediments of this world have made them wretched.”

We do not say that they ought not to be concerned about their food and clothing; but this is what we ask: that for the space of one or two hours, while the readings are being read or the divine mysteries are being celebrated, they not leave the church, and that they strive to labor at least as much for their souls as they strive to labor for their flesh.

And although they ought to provide much more for the soul than for the flesh, because the soul was made in the image of God, whereas the flesh was formed from the clay of the earth, for the present we nevertheless urge them to strive to provide at least equally for what is necessary: [Col. 2280] let them prepare for the flesh what will suffice for a short time in this world, and for the soul what it needs forever.

#### 4. They Are to Be Instructed in What You Hear in the Sermons. This Obligation Is Demonstrated from Scripture.

Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, that what, with the Lord inspiring you, you willingly receive in these sermons, wherever you may be, you report with great zeal to your neighbors and relatives who either cannot assemble with you at church or, what is worse, perhaps do not even wish to, and to those who come and quickly leave.

For just as I shall be liable if I do not tell you these things, so you must fear that you will have to render an account for them if you do not retain what you have heard in your memory in such a way that you can also make it known to others.

Therefore, with the Lord inspiring you, strive to fulfill what the Apostle says: “If a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1); and what the same Apostle proclaims not only to clerics but also to laymen and women, saying: “Correct the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak” (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

For if you wish to correct one another charitably in any sin, the enemy will scarcely, or never, be able to creep in upon you; or, if he does creep in, the evil that has occurred will quickly be amended and corrected.

And what is written will be fulfilled in you: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” (Proverbs 18:19); and: “Whoever brings back a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20).

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 283

[Note: [Col. 2280] This was the thirty-third homily of Caesarius in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Our manuscripts likewise bear his name. Nevertheless, it must not be left unmentioned that this Sermon 283, as well as Sermon 286 and Caesarius’s Homily 35 in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, which begins, “If you attend carefully,” etc., appeared in a Compendian codex written at least 700 years ago, and in the codex of the Church of Chartres, with the name “Lord Ephrem” at the head. No other explanation for so many differences in the attribution of these sermons of Caesarius occurs except that that excellent bishop himself used to attribute his sermons sometimes to Faustinus, sometimes to Ephrem, now to Augustine and others, according as he had expressed their sayings or opinions in them. On section 1, see Sermon 292 of the Appendix, no. 1; 265, no. 3; 281, no. 1; 173, no. 3; 174, no. 3; on section 3, Sermon 140, no. 1; on section 5, see also the conclusion of Sermon 205.]

### An Admonition to Pray Attentively and to Avoid Idle Conversations

#### 1. He Urges Them to Come Earlier to the Vigils and Not to Chatter Then.

Although, dearest brothers, by God’s favor your way of life gladdens us in many respects, and we frequently rejoice in your progress, there are nevertheless certain matters about which your Charity ought to be admonished. Therefore I ask you to receive our exhortation willingly, as you are accustomed to do.

I rejoice, beloved brothers, and give thanks to God because I see you faithfully hastening to church to hear the divine readings. But if you wish to complete both your progress and our joy, you ought to assemble earlier.

For during such long nights, whoever is not detained by illness and comes to church late does so not without guilt to his soul. I ask you, brothers: if shoemakers, goldsmiths, smiths, and the other craftsmen keep watch earlier so that they can provide what the body needs, ought we not rise before daylight to come to church and deserve to receive the forgiveness of sins?

If merchants customarily keep watch for the profit of money, why should we not keep watch for love of eternal life? Sometimes people entrust themselves to winds and storms and sail from East to West and from West to East, enduring many dangers and at times bearing hunger and thirst most bitterly. Yet they patiently endure all these things for perishable possessions. Why, then, should we be reluctant to keep watch for eternal life?

[Col. 2281] Therefore I ask you both to come earlier and, when you have come, to devote yourselves more to praying or singing psalms than to idle or worldly conversations.

For whoever wishes to chatter after coming to church would have been better off not coming: while he occupies himself with fruitless conversations, he neither sings psalms himself nor allows others to sing or hear the readings. Such a person, even if he comes to church with a small sin, returns home with a greater one, because by chattering he has chosen to wound himself in the very place where, by singing psalms or praying, he could have provided remedies both for himself and for others.

#### 2. How One Should Pray

Above all, dearest brothers, whenever we devote ourselves to prayer, we ought to supplicate God in silence and quiet, because whoever wishes to pray in a loud voice appears to deprive all those standing near him of the fruit of prayer.

Let only cries, sighs, or groans be heard. For our prayer should be like that which the holy Hannah, the mother of blessed Samuel, is reported to have offered. It is written of her that, weeping, she prayed, and only her lips moved, while her voice was not heard at all (1 Samuel 1:11, 13).

Let everyone hear this and imitate it, especially those who pray with such loud and shameless chatter, with such a din of voices, that they do not permit others nearby to pray.

Let us therefore pray, as I have said, with sighing, crying out, or groaning, according to the prophetic word: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Psalm 37:9). Let us pray, I say, not with a ringing voice, but with a conscience crying out to God.

#### 3. Wandering of the Mind in Prayer Greatly Offends God

When we pray, dearest brothers, let us labor as much as we can, with the Lord’s help, so that no foreign thought may creep upon us; lest we have one thing in our hearts and utter another with our mouths; lest, while the tongue asks God for something, the mind, occupied with various matters, depart in its thoughts from prayer and thus acquire sin precisely where it could have found a remedy.

For if you wished to plead some necessary case before a powerful person, and suddenly turned away from him, breaking off the middle of your conversation, and wished to occupy yourself with some jesting or disgraceful talk, what insult do you think you would inflict upon the person with whom you were speaking? How would you stir his anger against you?

If, then, when speaking with a human being, we labor with our whole attention lest, by thinking about something else, we seem to insult the person with whom we are speaking, when speaking with God in prayer and pleading before such great majesty the misery of our sins, are we not ashamed and embarrassed to run here and there with captive thoughts and to draw our wretched minds away from the sight of the divine majesty through many distractions?

Therefore, before anyone falls prostrate in prayer, let him, with God’s help, drive all superfluous thoughts away from the attention of his mind, so that our soul, kindled by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, may consume every vice in the fire of contrition or prayer and scatter far away its wandering and fleeting thoughts, so that only virtues and holy meditations may always find a place in our hearts.

#### 4. What One Thinks About Most Attentively Is in a Sense Worshiped. What Alone Should Be Thought About Then.

If it is exceedingly wrong for things that we may think about at another time to creep upon us in prayer, what shall we say about unlawful thoughts?

[For every person, dearest brothers, makes whatever he thinks about most attentively at the time of prayer into a god for himself; and he will appear to possess and, as it were, worship that thing as God and Lord. This matter, beloved, often causes me unbearable grief and trembling, when, during the very concentration of prayer, the mind is snatched away toward various occupations of the world; and while it seems to be doing one thing, it is discovered in thought to have departed far elsewhere, as though there were something else that we ought to think about more.

When we speak with God, we ought to think of nothing else except that with our whole heart, soul, and mind we should seek the forgiveness of sins and the grace of God.

For example, if someone happens during prayer to think about the marketplace: if he thinks about the marketplace, he worships the marketplace. If he happens to be drawn to set before his eyes the house he is building or repairing, then what he has before his eyes is what he worships. Perhaps he thinks about vineyards or a garden or something else: whatever he has set before the eyes of his heart, that he worships in that prayer.

[Col. 2282] I say nothing about evil, and perhaps even shameful or impure, thoughts [Note: [Col. 2282] The words enclosed in parentheses here were absent from the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.].]

Consider, dearest brothers, I beg you, and see how harsh this captivity is: the tongue seems to speak with God, while the whole attention of the mind is directed toward earth, walls, or stones.

And if it is excessively wrong for those things which we may lawfully think about or see at another time to creep upon us in prayer, consider how great an evil it will be if, while engaged in prayer, we think about those things that are unlawful even at another time—that is, if we place before the eyes of our hearts, as we turn toward prayer, desire, hatred, anger, lust, adultery, or anything similar.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with every inward fiber of our conscience let us beseech the Lord to deign to free us from this deception of demons and grant us the forgiveness of sins.

#### 5. For Whom and What We Should Pray

Therefore, beloved brothers, again and again I ask: if you cannot entirely escape these captivities of the soul, let us at least labor as much as we can, with the Lord’s help, so that we may appear to fall into them less readily. Otherwise, through negligence, while praying and thinking about something else, we may find offense before God precisely where we could have obtained grace.

Let us pray, then, brothers, not only for ourselves but also for all Christians, wherever they may be. Let us beseech God’s mercy not only for our friends but also for our enemies.

And because the blessed Apostle says, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26), let us always ask this both for ourselves and for everyone else: that God may deign to grant us what he knows is suitable for our souls.

Above all, brothers, let us say the Lord’s Prayer in our prayers, because without doubt he willingly hears the prayer which he himself, in his ineffable goodness, instituted.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if, with God inspiring you, you willingly receive these things as you are accustomed to do, you will both give us joy and prepare a kingdom for yourselves, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 284

[Note: [Col. 2282] Elsewhere, no. 5 in the Appendix to the Sirmondian sermons.]

### On a Certain Custom of Singing Psalms on the Day of the Epiphany

[Note: [Col. 2282] In Sirmond’s judgment this sermon is spurious, and he rightly included it in the Appendix after the forty sermons he published under Augustine’s name. For it belongs not to Augustine, to whom it is attributed in the Royal Codex, but to Caesarius. The concern and zeal of this holy bishop for advancing the worship of God through the singing of psalms and hymns and through other sacred rites are attested both by the canons of the Second Council of Vaison, which he himself composed, and by the writers of his Life, who, among other things, mention the following especially relevant passage in Book 1, no. 11: “He wished, and even compelled, laymen and common people to recite psalms and hymns and, with a loud and measured voice, like clerics, to sing some prose pieces and antiphons in Greek, others in Latin.” The title may perhaps indicate that the sermon was delivered on the day of the Epiphany. On section 3, see Sermon 173 of the Appendix, no. 4; 140, no. 2; 28, no. 4; 271, no. 6; and 273, no. 6.]

#### 1. On the New Custom of Singing Psalms

I cannot express in words the joy that the Lord has granted me through your holy and faithful devotion. For many years my spirit had burned with longing for this matter, and with the full attention of my heart I desired that the merciful Lord would inspire this custom of singing psalms in you.

Therefore I bless my Lord and continually give him as many thanks as I can, because he has deigned to fulfill my desire.

For since I desired you to sing psalms as they were sung in other neighboring cities, God prepared your minds in such a way that, with the Lord’s help, you are accomplishing this even better.

What is appropriate for us to do now amid our very joys except to beseech the Lord with all our strength that, just as he has given the beginning, he may also deign to give completion, and that to those to whom he has granted such holy devotion in singing psalms, he may, in his goodness, also grant the happiest perseverance?

And because it is not the one who begins but the one who perseveres who will be saved, [Col. 2283] kindle within yourselves, as far as you can, through continual prayer and contrition of heart, the fire of divine love, lest the flame of charity, which has begun faithfully to burn in you, grow cold through some negligence.

#### 2. Let Conduct Harmonize with the Tongue; Let Devout Affections Correspond to the Voices

Above all, devote yourselves not only to prayers but also to holy thoughts, so that what you sing with your words you may fulfill in your prayers, and so that the Holy Spirit, who sounds forth from your mouths, may also deign to dwell in your hearts.

It is indeed good and highly acceptable to God when the tongue faithfully sings psalms; but it is truly good when life also agrees with the tongue. Let voices and conduct agree together, lest good voices bear witness against evil conduct and your own tongue itself convict you.

For if one thing sounds from the mouth and another appears in action, what the tongue seems to build up, evil conduct begins to destroy.

You, however, brothers, should be occupied not only by the sweetness of the voice but also by the meaning of the reading itself, so that just as the sound of the voice delights the ears, so the power of the reading itself may grow sweet in your hearts, according to what is written: “How sweet are your sayings to my throat, O Lord!” (Psalm 118:103); and again: “The sayings of the Lord are desirable above gold and many precious stones, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 18:11).

For whoever, when singing psalms, attends only to the sweetness of the voice and the arrangement of each sound, and does not attend to what should be understood in them, receives transient food in his ears, but God’s word does not reach his soul. It is as though someone were chewing wax, as it were, and did not taste the sweetness of honey at all.

#### 3. How Their Meaning Should Be Conceived While Singing Psalms

You, however, brothers, as I have already suggested above, attend first of all inwardly to the virtues of the Psalms.

When one of you sings the verse of the Psalm that says, “Let the proud be confounded, because they have unjustly committed iniquity against me” (Psalm 118:78), let him strive to flee pride, so that he may deserve to escape eternal shame.

When we sing, “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Psalm 72:27), let us strive to escape every evil desire.

When we sing that blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Psalm 1:2), let us reject as the devil’s poison superfluous occupations, biting jokes, and idle and lustful conversations; and let us either read the divine reading ourselves more frequently or, if we cannot read it ourselves, strive willingly and frequently to hear those who do read it.

Whenever we sing, “If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies: may the enemy pursue my soul, seize it, trample my life upon the earth, and reduce my glory to dust” (Psalm 7:5–6), when we say these and similar words, let us take care not to appear to pronounce so harsh a curse against ourselves. Let us never repay evil to anyone with evil, so that with a clear conscience we may say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

And because it would take too long to repeat everything we have said about these three or four sins—that is, pride, fornication, or hatred—let us understand the same concerning all the remaining vices.

Whenever sinners are cursed in the Psalms, let us strive to flee sin, lest we ourselves appear to curse ourselves with our own mouths. Whenever the just, merciful, sober, chaste, or humble are praised in the Psalms, let us strive, with God’s help, to be such, so that the blessing directed toward them may, by God’s gift, also be extended to us.

Again and again I ask and entreat you: whenever you sing psalms, think attentively about what should inwardly be understood or observed in those Psalms, so that while your tongue praises the Lord, divine blessing may reach your soul.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 285

[Note: [Col. 2284] Elsewhere, no. 8 among the Vignerian sermons.]

### On the Rite of Singing Psalms, etc.

[Note: [Col. 2284] In the Royal Codex this sermon immediately follows the preceding sermon, with the title “On the same subject,” as its editor Vignerius had already noted. It reflects Caesarius’s style and mind no less than the preceding sermon. On section 1, see Sermon 286 of the Appendix, no. 1; on section 2, Sermon 286, nos. 1 and 5; below, Sermon 288, no. 2; on section 3, Sermon 286, no. 1; 288, no. 2; 303, no. 3; 230, no. 4.]

[Col. 2284]

#### 1. Let the Knees Be Bent for Prayer. This Should Follow the Singing of Psalms.

I entreat you, dearest brothers, and admonish you with paternal affection: whenever prayer is announced, whoever is perhaps unable to bend his knees because of some illness should not delay bending his back or lowering his neck [Note: [Col. 2284] Perhaps something is missing here.].

What does it profit you to sing psalms faithfully if, after you stop singing psalms, you refuse to supplicate God?

Therefore, whenever anyone has ceased singing psalms, let him pray and entreat the Lord with complete humility, so that, with God’s help, he may deserve to fulfill in action what he has uttered with his mouth in words.

To sing psalms, brothers, is like sowing; to pray afterward is to bury or cover the seed again [Note: [Col. 2284] This passage is defective.].

For just as one who sows in a field, if he neglects to cover the seed by plowing, will find birds come and snatch away everything that seemed to have been sown, so whoever has sown the word of God in the field of his heart and scattered it through singing psalms or reading, unless afterward he stores it up in his heart through prayer and, in a sense, buries it, will find birds—that is, the fleeting, empty, and vain thoughts of this world—come and snatch away what had been sown in his heart.

Therefore, once anyone has ceased singing psalms, let him not cease praying if he wishes the harvest of divine mercy to grow in the field of his heart.

#### 2. It Should Not Be Done Standing

I ask you, brothers, whenever prayer is offered at the altar, bow your heads, lest, if you wish to pray standing, what is written about the Pharisee who prayed standing be fulfilled in you. For the Publican, who, bent over, confessed his sins, pleased God more than the Pharisee who, standing, praised his merits.

Observe this also, brothers: lest, while some are praying, others become occupied with idle conversations; lest they make wounds for themselves out of remedies and perish through the very means by which they could have been freed.

Those who do these things will have to render a bad account on the day of judgment both for themselves and for the others whom they impede.

I also admonish and ask you, brothers: whenever it is cried out that you must humble yourselves for the blessing, let it not be burdensome for you to incline your heads, because you humble yourselves not before a human being but before God.

#### 3. He Grieves Those Who Come Late to the Vigils and Neglect the Word of God. The Word of God Is Rain. The Word of God Is Light.

Although, dearest brothers, I rejoice greatly in your fervent devotion, because there are some who come later to the vigils and quickly leave once the word of God has begun to be recited, I ask you to admonish them and urge them, through your holy and salutary counsel, to imitate you.

How much time, my brothers, does it seem that we keep them occupied? You yourselves see that it is scarcely half an hour. Yet, so that we do not delay poor people or any craftsmen in their work, whenever a sermon is to be delivered we arrange for Psalm 50 to be said earlier, so that people may leave the church not late but always at the customary hour.

And I ask you, brothers: if, amid so many occupations and unbearable labors, we do not shrink from running through the various volumes of Scripture and providing you with spiritual remedies with great zeal, why should it be burdensome for any of our people to receive them, when it is not burdensome for us to distribute them?

And because the sermon that is recited will be a remedy for the obedient but a judgment for the negligent, each person will do well if he willingly receives the rain of God’s word in the field of his heart, lest, if he neglects to accept the remedy of salvation, he later have to seek a drop of refreshment amid the flames of hell.

I mean that rain, dearest brothers, which we ought to desire, [Col. 2285] about which Moses says: “Let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2).

For it is certain, beloved brothers, that just as this earthly harvest is when it receives rain either late or only after many months, so is the soul that is unwilling to hear the word of God frequently.

And because the law of God is not only rain but also light, according to what is written, “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet” (Psalm 118:105), let whoever disdains to receive the light of God’s word fear that he may have to endure eternal darkness.

But we trust in God’s mercy that through your holy admonition and your correction, pleasing to God, even the negligent will be stirred to the fervor of your faith, so that we may have double joy over the salvation both of yourselves and of them.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 286

[Note: [Col. 2285] It appears among the Caesarian sermons in the manuscripts and is his thirty-fourth homily in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Two manuscripts bear the name “Lord Ephrem” at the head; on this matter see the above judgment concerning Sermon 283. On section 1, see Sermon 285 of the Appendix, no. 1; on section 5, Sermon 282, no. 2; on section 6, above, Sermon 265, no. 3, and 285, no. 2; on section 7, Sermon 17, no. 1.]

### That the Knees Should Be Bent in Prayer and That Idle Words Should Be Avoided

#### 1. Let the Knees Be Bent for Prayers, or, Because of Illness, Let the Back and Head Be Inclined. The Publican Is Heard When He Observes This; the Pharisee Is Despised When He Neglects It.

I ask and admonish you, dearest brothers, that whenever the clergy pray beside the altar, or prayer is announced by the deacon’s cry, you faithfully incline not only your hearts but also your bodies.

For whenever I frequently and carefully observe, when the deacon cries, “Let us bend our knees,” I see most people standing upright like pillars. Yet when prayer is offered in church, this is wholly neither permitted nor beneficial to Christians. The deacon does not cry out for our sake but for yours.

Therefore, because that voice is directed especially toward you, and most of all toward the negligent, it is just that it be faithfully obeyed by you.

Let that voice therefore be a remedy for the obedient, because for the disobedient it will be a testimony, on account of what is written: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48:10).

But this too must be feared and observed in every way, brothers, which the Apostle said: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Colossians 4:2); and again: “Pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things” (1 Thessalonians 5:17–18).

And the Lord says: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41); and again: “One ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18:1).

Therefore, whoever cannot bend his knees or curve his back because of some illness should at least not be reluctant to incline his head. Let him consider that through this humility the Publican obtained God’s mercy: he did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven, but with his head bowed toward the ground he beat his breast and, like a most severe judge, scourged the sins enclosed within.

Therefore he deserved that the Lord deign to say of him: “This Publican went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

The example of that Pharisee must also be considered and feared, lest, because he prayed standing, he therefore fail to deserve to be heard.

#### 2. He Who Denies That There Is Grave Sin in Him. If a Stain on Clothing Is Feared, How Much More Should One Fear It in the Soul?

But perhaps there are some who refuse to bend their knees because they believe that they do not have grave sins. May God turn this away from Christian minds.

The person who sins more dangerously is the one who does not think that he sins gravely; and he suffers the attack most severely when he does not perceive that he is being attacked.

But someone may say: “Who is there who does not believe himself to be a sinner?” Without doubt, the person who does not believe that he has a grave sin is the one who, prostrate or bent over, does not seek a remedy [Col. 2286] for his soul.

But perhaps someone fears that he may harm his costly garments. Whoever fears that his clothing may be stained by praying should fear even more that, by not praying, his soul may remain filthy.

For our soul ought to be worth more to us than a tunic; and we must greatly fear that, while a clean garment is carefully preserved, the soul may be soiled by many sins and negligences.

### 3. We offer this bodily prostration to God.

The saints performed it in their prayers, and Christ himself did so. Yet I should like to know, concerning those who neither bend their knees nor wish to incline their heads, whether, if they were asking some very necessary favor from a judge or from some powerful person, they would negligently and lukewarmly plead their case while standing upright and holding their heads erect.

We ask an earthly matter from an earthly person, and humbly bow ourselves almost to the ground; yet when we seek from God the remission of sins and eternal rest, we do not deign even to bow our heads. We do not read anything of this kind about the blessed Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 4), or about the other saints, of whom it is written that they frequently prostrated themselves upon the ground and prayed to God with complete contrition.

And of our Lord himself it is written in the Gospel that, falling upon the ground, he prayed in such a way that drops of blood trickled from him (Luke 22:41, 44). What need did Christ have to plead in such a manner? He himself lacked nothing; rather, by his example he was preparing for us the remedies of prayer. Mercy prays, but misery does not; charity prays, but iniquity does not. The Physician prays, prostrate upon the ground, while the sick person does not bow down. Innocence prays, but wickedness does not: he prays who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found; yet the one burdened with many sins does not prostrate himself.

The Judge prays, desiring to spare, while the defendant does not pray to deserve to receive pardon. He who will judge prays, while the one who will be judged pretends not to pray. Therefore, if weakness does not prevent it, let no one be reluctant to humble himself by prostrating himself upon the ground.

### 4. Otherwise one cannot drink from the fountain of grace.

Brothers, we ought to assemble in church as at a living fountain and a spiritual river, so that we may receive that living water of which the Lord said: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink; the one who believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:37–38); and again: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will never thirst; rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

Thus the one who comes faithfully to church runs happily to this fountain. But just as no one can drink from an earthly fountain or bodily stream if he is unwilling to bend down, so no one will be able to draw living water from the living fountain, Christ, and from the river of the Holy Spirit, unless he is willing to bow humbly, in accordance with what is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

### 5. Or to receive the dew of divine blessing.

I likewise admonish you, dearest brothers, that whenever the deacon calls out that you should humble yourselves for the blessing, you faithfully incline both your bodies and your heads; for the blessing is given to you through a human being, but it is not given by a human being.

Do not pay attention if perhaps the one who administers it is negligent; look instead to the Lord who transmits it. For the blessing given to you is understood to be heavenly dew and rain. Thus Moses also says: “Let my speech be expected like rain, and my words like dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2).

And you know very well, brothers, that if rain encounters a mountain standing too steeply upright, it quickly runs down into the valley. Therefore those who humbly incline themselves to receive the blessing, making themselves like valleys, receive the rain of divine blessing; and in them that saying is fulfilled: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Luke 3:5).
