What does “Every valley shall be filled” mean except, “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted”? What does “The mountain and hill shall be humbled” mean except, “The one who exalts himself shall be brought low”?

Yet those same people who, in prayer, pretend not to bend their knees or to incline their heads for the blessing prefer, while standing in church, to chatter rather than to sing psalms.

### 6. In church one should either pray or sing psalms. The twofold guilt of chatterers.

Therefore I beg you, brothers, to receive our admonitions—[Col. 2287] or rather, our prayers—as you are accustomed to do, willingly; and when you come to church, do only what is proper to be done in church: that is, either pray or sing psalms. By praying, you may receive forgiveness of sins; by singing psalms, you may reach spiritual joy.

For the person who occupies himself in church with foolish and inappropriate tales is recognized as administering or offering poison and a sword to other people, since he neither hears the word of God himself nor permits others to hear it. Such a person will have to render an account on the day of judgment both for his own destruction and for that of others.

Just as those who faithfully sing psalms and humbly plead will receive glory both for themselves and for those to whom they have offered an example of life, so those who, on the contrary, have offered examples not of edification but of destruction will suffer punishment both for themselves and for others.

Let the one who pretends not to sing psalms either keep silent and maintain silence, so that, if he does not edify himself, he may at least not destroy others by his bad example; for we must fear what the Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

I ask you, brothers: if it is wrong to occupy oneself with idle talk outside the church, what do you think the sin of chattering in church must be?

### 7. The devil chiefly attacks those who are armed against him. Recapitulation.

For the devil, dearest brothers, is accustomed to attack us most intensely when he discovers that we have prepared ourselves against him with spiritual weapons. And because he cannot drive us bodily away from the assembly of the Church, he strives to occupy us within the church itself with fruitless conversations, so that through empty and vain—and perhaps even biting—exchanges and filthy thoughts he may take away from us the fruit of the divine reading or the remedy of prayer; so that we may appear to stand in church only bodily, while in heart and thought we withdraw far from the sight of the divine majesty.

Therefore, as far as we can, with God’s help let us resist his snares, in accordance with what the blessed apostle Peter says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:8–9); and with what is written: “Submit yourselves to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7).

For this reason, dearest brothers, I ask you, with the Lord’s help, to resist as far as we can these most harsh captivities of the soul. Let us especially flee, as though they were the devil’s poisons, the idle tales that we know to be harmful even outside the church.

And whenever the deacon calls out that you should either bend your knees in prayer or incline your heads for the blessing, do this obediently and faithfully, with true humility, so that by praying your hearts may deserve to be freed from every evil, and by receiving the blessing they may deserve to be filled with spiritual goods—through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 2287] Formerly, 7 among the 50 homilies; later, in the Appendix, 15.]

### On the danger of the priest and on the correction of robbers

[Note: [Col. 2287] This was taken from Augustine’s Sermon 178; it differed hardly at all, except in the preface and conclusion, which for that reason we did not wish to omit here.]

#### 1. The burdens of priests. They are bound to preach. Who are those who contradict?

If you pay careful attention, dearest brothers, you recognize that all the priests of the Lord—not only bishops, but also presbyters and ministers of the churches—are in great danger.

For the Holy Spirit testifies to them, saying: “Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isaiah 58:1); and again: “If you do not announce to the wicked person his wickedness, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18).

The Apostle also says of them: “Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they keep watch as those who will have to render an account for your souls” (Hebrews 13:17).

If, dearest brothers, [Col. 2288] each person will scarcely be able to render an account for himself on the day of judgment, what will become of priests, from whom the souls of all will be required?

Therefore, considering our danger, pray for us, so that we may continually strive to provide spiritual pasture for the flocks entrusted to us in such a way that we may deserve to render a good account for them.

Consider, then, dearest brothers, what it is that I wish to suggest to your Charity—provided that, through your prayers, I may deserve that he who terrifies me should help me. Among his other commands, the blessed Apostle also says that a bishop must be “powerful in sound doctrine, so as to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9).

A great task, but a heavy burden. Nevertheless, I shall hope in God that, with your prayers for us assisting, he will free us from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word. For no cause makes God’s steward more reluctant to rebuke those who contradict than fear of the harsh word.

While we fear the slanders, mockery, and insults of proud people, and while we fear being weighed down by them through earthly possessions, fearing the loss of temporal things, we preach the eternal less than we ought. And while we dread losing something worldly through their wickedness, we neglect to heal the wounds of their sins with spiritual remedies.

Therefore we must fear that we shall be compelled to render a harsh [Note: [Col. 2288] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “we speak harsh things.”] account on the day of judgment both for ourselves and for those to whom, out of love for earthly things, we do not speak.

Let us therefore see what it means to “refute those who contradict.” Those who contradict are not to be understood in only one way. Very few contradict us by speaking; very many do so by living badly, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 2288] What was omitted should be supplied from Augustine’s Sermon 178, §§2–5.]

“I would hear and believe you if you restored to a Christian what you had taken from a Jew.”

#### 2. Another objection.

Perhaps someone also reasons this way and says: “There are many rich Christians who are avaricious or greedy. I have no sin if I take from them and give to the poor; for since they do no good, I shall be able to receive a reward if I give alms.”

In this matter also, let each person spare his own soul, because such a thought is suggested by the devil’s cunning. For even if he gives away everything he has taken, he increases his sins rather than diminishing them.

We have spoken against the single vice of robbery, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 2288] The rest may be found in the aforementioned sermon, §6.]

“Have the means, and there I shall praise your conquered greed.”

Therefore, brothers, if you faithfully and carefully attend to these matters, according to your custom, you will be able both to escape the impiety of avarice or greed and to reach happily the eternal rewards for works of mercy—through our Lord, and so forth.

## SERMON CCLXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2288] Elsewhere, among the Vignerian sermons, 37.]

### A reprimand addressed to those who have wives yet neither blush nor fear to commit adultery, or who have wished to take concubines into an unhappy union either before or after their wives

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. Vignier published it under Augustine’s name, but the subject matter and style protest against this, as do the ancient manuscripts examined by us, which attribute it to Caesarius—namely, the manuscripts of the library of the Church of Laon, the Abbey of Vallis Lucensis, and others. Moreover, in the Royal manuscript 3793 it is entitled “Excerpt from the sayings of the holy Fathers Augustine and John, on Priests.” Concerning §2, see above, Appendix sermons 140, §1; 173, §3; 174, §3; 285, §§2–3; 265, §5; concerning §3, below sermons 289, §3; 309, §4; 289, §6; concerning §5, sermons 309, §4; 289, §§4–5; 301, §4; concerning §6, sermon 292, §3.]

#### 1. Four necessary virtues.

I ask you, brothers, to consider more attentively the cause of our salvation, so that we may escape all those things written concerning the future judgment and may deserve happily to reach that blessedness which has been promised to us.

With all the strength we can summon, and with God’s help, let us strive with complete dedication to preserve charity, justice, mercy, and likewise chastity [Col. 2289], so that by this heavenly and spiritual four-horse chariot we may be carried off to our homeland, the kingdom of paradise.

Let us go there meanwhile in heart; and when the day of judgment comes, let us follow there also in body, so that in us may be fulfilled what the Apostle said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20); and: “When Christ, your life, appears, you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4).

Therefore, let us not love any one of these four virtues less than is proper. For what does it profit you if you appear to possess charity but do not wish to possess justice? Or what can help you if you say that you possess mercy, while by not possessing chastity you hate yourself, in accordance with what is written: “The one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6)?

#### 2. Chastity is rare. Adulterers are many. They are often admonished by the bishop. Yet each person must also correct them. Otherwise he becomes a participant in their sins. Those corrected but not amended are to be reported to the bishop. The state is sometimes punished on account of one criminal.

And because we know that very few wish to preserve chastity, we admonish you more earnestly concerning chastity, in accordance with what is written: “Neither fornicators, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males shall possess the kingdom of God”; and: “Neither adulterers nor drunkards shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

But what is worse, there are many who, although they appear to have wives, nevertheless, at the devil’s persuasion, pretend not to preserve chastity. Inflamed by the fury of lust, they neither fear nor blush to commit adultery with their own or other men’s maidservants, or even with the wives or daughters of strangers, so that they fear neither the Lord nor respect human beings.

Yet it would have been right, brothers, for our frequent admonitions over so many years to benefit such people, so that they would neither make wounds for themselves out of medicines nor kill themselves with what could have given them life. For the priest’s correction will be for glory to the obedient, but for punishment to the disobedient.

And because, as I have already said, they neither reverence the Lord nor fear human beings, you who, inspired by Christ, faithfully preserve both faith and charity, if you learn that some people are committing such sacrilegious sins, correct them once, twice, and three times.

If they refuse to listen to you, neither associate with them nor invite them to your meals, nor eat with them at their tables, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “With such a person, not even to eat” (1 Corinthians 5:11). Let them at least blush when they see themselves rejected by upright people who fear God.

For if what I suggest is not done, whoever knows that his brother or neighbor is committing adultery, and refuses to rebuke him, will be a participant in his sins, in accordance with what is written: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm 50:18); and with what the Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32).

Those who neither rebuke adulterers themselves nor bring these sacrilegious acts to the priests’ attention give us grounds to suspect that they do not rebuke them because they themselves also commit such sins.

For me, it is enough that I cry out with great grief of soul and endless groaning. But you, if you wish to be free from your own sins and from the sins of others, do not spare such people. If they refuse to listen when you admonish them privately and repeatedly, see that the matter comes to the attention of our humility, in accordance with what is said in the Gospel: “Reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother; but if he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church”—that is, bring it to the priest’s attention. “But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:15, 17).

But what is worse, while those who commit so great an evil are not only not rebuked by some people but are even flattered and received with favor, these people nourish sacrileges and crimes and commit them without any fear or shame.

But we must fear what is written concerning Achan, who had stolen a golden rule from Jericho [Col. 2290]: because on account of one man’s sin the wrath of God raged against everyone, and God’s fury did not cease from the people until the one who had done the evil was crushed at the Lord’s command (Joshua 7:2, 11).

#### 3. Men think adultery is permitted to them; it is no more permitted to them than to women.

Since the men of whom we are speaking wish their wives to be chaste, with what conscience do they commit these wicked acts and say that something is permitted to them which is not permitted to them at all—as though God had given one set of commandments to men and another to women?

Let whoever he may be say by what law he is permitted to commit these crimes, when every adultery is punished by both divine and human law.

This evil is not prohibited merely because many people commit it. But the less strictly it is punished by human beings, the more severely it is avenged by divine judgment.

For what sort of thing is it that they burst into such shamelessness as to say that these cruel evils are permitted to men but not to women? They do not consider that men and women alike have been redeemed by Christ’s blood, washed together in the sacred bath, and, approaching the Lord’s altar, receive together the Lord’s body and blood; nor that with God there is no distinction between male and female, and that God is not a respecter of persons.

Therefore what is not permitted to women was likewise never permitted to men, nor can it ever be permitted.

But an unhappy custom has been introduced: if a wife is found with her servant, she is punished; but if a man wallows with many maidservants in the sewer of lust, he is not only not punished but even praised by his companions. Speaking among themselves, they confess with laughter and foolish guffaws which of them has done this more often.

But their laughter will be turned into weeping on the day of judgment, and their jokes will be turned into wounds. This is done by those who neither believe nor fear God’s future judgment.

#### 4. These sins are mortal. At times even intercourse with one’s wife is not without sin.

With a clear conscience I cry out and solemnly declare that whoever has a wife and commits adultery will perish eternally—unless extended repentance and abundant almsgiving come to his aid and he ceases from the sin itself; and if, as sometimes happens, he dies suddenly, he will perish, and the name “Christian” will not benefit him. For he has not merely failed to do what Christ commanded; he has also committed what Christ prohibited.

Since even intercourse with one’s wife, except for the desire to have children, is a sin, what can such people think about themselves, or what hope can they promise themselves, when, although they have marriages, by adultery they prepare for themselves the means by which they will descend into hell? They do not wish to hear the Apostle saying: “The time is short; henceforth let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29); and: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the gentiles who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:4–5).

Consider that those who use their wives, except for the desire to have children, cannot be without sin if they do not give continual alms.

And if this is said concerning legitimate marriage, what do you think will happen on the day of judgment to those who presume to commit public or secret adultery without any consideration of divine fear? Of them it is written: “The Lord will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4); and, as was already said above by the Apostle: “Adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

What does it profit you, unhappy man, whoever you are, that you are called a Christian, if by the sin of adultery you deserve to be excluded from the kingdom of God?

#### 5. Concubinage is extremely common. It is not considered a sin. It is a worse sin than adultery. The custom at Rome concerning those who marry without being virgins.

And this I ask, dearest brothers, and admonish your Charity: whoever is going to take a wife should preserve virginity until marriage. For just as no one wishes to take a defiled bride, so no one ought to corrupt himself before marriage through adulterous intercourse.

But what is worse, there are many who take concubines before they take wives. And because the multitude is so great, the bishop cannot excommunicate everyone [Col. 2291]; rather, with many groans and sighs he tolerates and awaits them, in case the merciful and compassionate Lord should perhaps grant them fruitful repentance, by which they may reach pardon.

And because this evil has become customary, so that it is thought not to be a sin, I profess before God and his angels that whoever takes a concubine, whether before or after taking a wife, commits adultery—and a worse adultery at that, because, although it is in no way permitted publicly, he commits it without any shame, as though by law.

Finally, we recognize from this also that it is no small sin that whatever children these women conceive are born not as free persons but as slaves. Therefore, even after receiving freedom, they are permitted by no law and in no order to receive their father’s inheritance.

Consider also whether it can be without sin when the honor of noble blood is so humbled that slaves are born from the noblest people.

For it is such a grave sin that in the Roman city, if a man wishes to take a wife and knows that he is not a virgin, he must not presume to come at all to receive the nuptial blessing.

Consider also how harsh it is that he is not deemed worthy to receive the blessing with the woman whom he desires to marry.

#### 6. A sermon is like a mirror.

But when we have made these suggestions, I fear that some people may wish to be angry with us rather than with themselves. For our sermon is set before your Charity like a mirror. Therefore, just as a matron, when she looks into a mirror, corrects in herself what she sees to be misshapen rather than breaking the mirror, so each one of you, whenever he recognizes his own disgrace in some preaching, ought to correct himself rather than wish to become angry with the preacher as though he were angry with a mirror.

Likewise, those who receive wounds prefer to heal their injuries rather than despise the medicines. Therefore, so that no one may sin doubly in this matter by becoming angry with spiritual medicines, let each person receive what is said not only patiently but willingly.

For the one who is willing to receive salutary correction is already recognized as turning away from evil in some measure; and the one to whom his evils are displeasing already finds what is good pleasing. Thus, the more he separates himself from vices, the nearer he will come to virtues.

May he himself deign to grant this—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCLXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 2291] Elsewhere, On Time, 243.]

### On chastity

[Note: It is now placed in the Appendix for the first time. It remained among the Augustinian sermons, but with a mark indicating doubt, among the Louvain editors; it was rejected as spurious by Verlinus and Vindingus. It was published by precisely the same author as the preceding sermon. Concerning §1, see Appendix sermon 290, §3; concerning §2, sermon 309, §4; concerning §3, sermons 288, §3, and 309, §4; concerning §4, Augustine’s Sermon 392 and Appendix sermon 288, §5; concerning §5, the preceding sermon, §5; concerning §9, sermons 45, §4, and 281, §5.]

#### 1. Age does not excuse the incontinence of the young.

Whenever, dearest brothers, we commend chastity as is fitting and beneficial, perhaps adolescents and those still in the vigor of youth say: “We are young men; we cannot practice continence.”

To them we can and must reply, lest perhaps they are unable to preserve chastity because they eat more than is proper, drink more wine than they ought, refuse to avoid intimacy with women, and neither fear nor blush to maintain suspicious associations with them.

Let such people hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18); and: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18); and Solomon: “Wine and women make the wise apostatize and rebuke the sensible” (Ecclesiasticus 19:2).

But those who say that they cannot preserve chastity should answer us whether they have wives or not. If they have wives, why do they not heed what the Truth says in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish [Col. 2292] people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matthew 7:12)? Why do they not preserve toward their wives the fidelity they desire to have preserved toward themselves?

Since a man receives his name from virtue, while a woman receives hers from softness—that is, weakness—why does each man wish his wife to be victorious against the most savage beast, lust, when he himself falls defeated at lust’s first assault?

#### 2. The law of justice condemns them if they are married—and even if they are not yet married.

At this point perhaps those who are not yet joined to wives say that they can excuse themselves because they have no marriages to which they must remain faithful, and therefore cannot practice continence.

To those who attempt to offer this false and wretched excuse, the most just answer can and must be given: no one ought more carefully to avoid what is unlawful than the person who rejects what was lawful.

Since it is permitted to take a wife, while committing adultery is never permitted against the authority of all the Scriptures, why, when by God’s grace you do not take what is permitted, do you presume, to God’s offense, to do what is not permitted?

Yet I should like to know whether those who have no wives and, before they are joined in marriage, neither fear nor blush to commit adultery would wish their betrothed, before coming to the wedding, to be violated by some adulterer.

Since no one would accept this patiently, why does each man not preserve toward his betrothed the fidelity he desires her to preserve toward him? Why does he wish to receive a virgin wife when he himself is corrupt? Why does he desire to be joined to a living wife when, through adultery, he is already dead in soul, according to what is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20)?

And consider what the Apostle cries out terrifyingly: “God will judge fornicators” (Hebrews 13:4); and: “Neither adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9); and again: “All adulterers—their body is like an oven” [Note: [Col. 2292] In B., “their hearts are like an oven.” In the Vulgate the first part of this verse reads: “All adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.” M.] (Hosea 7:4).

#### 3. Fornication is thought permitted to men but not to women. Both sexes are bound by the same laws.

Perhaps some people think that it is not permitted for women to fornicate before marriage, but is permitted for men.

These evils, which ought to be punished and are exceedingly grave, are committed by many men without any fear of the Lord; and, what is worse, they are committed for this reason: because so many people have made them customary and regard them as so cheap or trivial that they are no longer even considered among serious crimes.

For in the Catholic faith, whatever is not permitted to women is entirely not permitted to men either. Men and women alike are redeemed at one price, namely, by Christ’s precious blood; they are called to one faith and gathered into one body of the Church; together they receive the sacrament of Baptism; together both approach the altar to receive the body and blood of Christ; and commandments have been given alike to both sexes.

Since this is so, with what face or conscience do men alone believe they may commit with impunity what is not permitted to men and women alike?

But let those who presume to do this know for certain that, unless they quickly amend themselves, and unless fruitful repentance comes to their aid, if they are suddenly snatched from this life, eternal flame will torment them without any remedy.

#### 4. Concubinage. It was never permitted. It is more criminal than adultery.

And what of the fact that many men are not ashamed, before marriage, to take concubines for themselves, whom they dismiss after several years and then afterward take legitimate wives?

They make plans among themselves first to acquire unjust wealth and unlawful profits through many calumnies and robberies, and afterward to take wives more noble or richer than they themselves are, contrary to reason.

See how many evils they bind themselves to, who desire to serve unhappily not only lust but also avarice or greed.

Therefore, before God and the angels I solemnly testify and declare that these evils have always been prohibited [Note: Perhaps “by God” should be supplied here.] and have never been pleasing to him; for especially in Christian times it was never [Col. 2293] permitted, nor will it ever be permitted, to have concubines.

But what is worse, many men do this by the law of the marketplace, not by the law of heaven; not at the command of justice, but under the domination of lust.

Since the Apostle says to married people: “The time is short, and it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29); and: “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (ibid. 7:5), how does the one who commanded married people to preserve chastity permit them to have adulterous concubines?

For this reason I cry out again and again with a free voice: the man who presumes to take a concubine before legitimate marriage commits a worse sin than the one who commits adultery. For the adulterer still wishes to commit so grave an evil secretly; in public he either fears or blushes to commit it. But the man who wishes to have a concubine publicly, with the most shameless face, considers himself permitted to commit an abominable act openly, while the entire people look on.

#### 5. Many admit it, and therefore it is not punished by excommunication. The man who is not a virgin does not deserve the nuptial blessing.

Perhaps those who have not been stained by this sin say: “Why are those who do these things not suspended from communion?”

Such a great crime is not punished by the priests for this reason alone: because many people commit it. For if one, two, four, or five people presumed to commit these evils, they could and ought not only to be suspended from communion but also separated from the conversation and meals of the Christian people, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “With such a person, not even to eat” (ibid., 5:11).

Nevertheless, as has already been said, the multitude of sinners prevents the priests of the Lord from distinguishing among them.

Good priests nevertheless do what they can. With complete charity they strive continually to pray and sigh, pouring forth groans and lamentations, so that, where they cannot exercise severity or ecclesiastical discipline because of the immeasurable multitude, they may nevertheless, by admonishing or praying for them, perhaps at some time call them to repentance.

Therefore I ask and solemnly urge again and again that the man who wishes to take a wife, just as he desires to find her a virgin, should himself also remain a virgin until the wedding. For if he has not done so, he will not deserve to receive the blessing with his betrothed, and what is written in him will be fulfilled: “He did not desire blessing, and it shall be removed far from him” (1 Corinthians 7:29).

Now consider: if the remedy of repentance does not come to his aid, what will become of him, and under what sentence will he necessarily be placed at the future judgment, when already in this world he was not deemed worthy to receive the blessing with his betrothed?

#### 6. Adulterers lack faith.

And consider this, brothers: if those who have no wives and either take concubines or commit adultery are in such great danger, what do those unhappy men think about themselves who, although they perhaps have marriages, commit adultery and, in insane fury or cruel misery, despair of God’s judgment?

They neither fear the punishments of hell nor desire eternal rewards. For if they had faith, they would certainly believe God and fear the coming judgment with trembling.

It is proved that they believe human beings but do not believe God: publicly, where people see them, they fear to commit adultery; secretly, where God sees them, they do not fear it at all.

If they possessed even the smallest spark of faith, just as they do not permit their servants to sin in their presence, so they would not presume to commit adultery in the presence of their Lord.

But concerning such people the Holy Spirit cries out through the prophet: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1).

For it is certain that the person who does in darkness and secrecy, in God’s presence, what he fears to do publicly in the presence of human beings does not believe that God exists. The unhappy man does not know that “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33:17).

### 7. Those whose business keeps them long separated from their wives make excuses for themselves—and thereby condemn themselves

But perhaps someone says: “Here I am, compelled by business or ordered by the king to be separated from my wife for so many months or years. How can I preserve chastity?” To him the most just answer can be given: let him return to his wife. But when I say this to the businessman, he may reply that, if he abandons his business, [Col. 2294] he will have no means of living. The soldier says, “If I leave the army, I incur the king’s anger.” To such men it can truthfully be said: if he fears the king and therefore does not return to his own wife, he ought to fear God, so that he does not touch another man’s wife. For just as the king can kill the man who, without being ordered, leaves the army and returns to his wife, so God can condemn to everlasting punishment the man who, stationed far away, commits adultery.

I ask you, dearest brothers: if, because of the demands of business and the king’s command, each person is sometimes separated from his wife even for a long period, why is chastity not preserved for so long a span of time for the sake of God and his own soul? Does business deserve—and does the king’s command deserve—that one should not know his own wife for so many days, while the love and command of God do not deserve that one should not touch another’s wife? But those who observe these things for the sake of commercial profit and the king’s authority, while pretending not to observe them for God’s sake, should know that, unless repentance comes to their aid, when they begin to stand before Christ’s tribunal they will not be able to escape the evil sentence; rather, it will be said to them: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41).

### 8. The soldiers’ wantonness is restrained

And what of this? Sometimes a very brave man goes forth to battle and perhaps kills no fewer than ten enemies; yet, taking some girl from the spoils of that very victory, when he joins himself to her in adultery, his soul is killed by the sword of sin. See how great an evil it is that someone should be more savage toward himself, killing his own soul through lust, than when he slaughtered the bodies of his adversaries in bodily victory.

It is truly to be mourned and lamented that the man who, as I have already said, overcame ten adversaries should be overcome by one woman; and that he who killed so many enemies in the body should be strangled in the heart by a single girl. It is truly an exceedingly grave evil that a brave man who is not conquered by iron should be overcome by lust; that soft or alluring things should overthrow the one whom hard things do not overcome; and that he who disdains to be a captive or slave to human beings should deserve to become a slave of sin, since it is more disgraceful to serve in the mind than in the body, according to what is written: “For by whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is also made a slave” (2 Peter 2:19).

### 9. Conclusion

Therefore, dearest brothers, if I do not tell you these things, I shall have to render an account for your souls on the day of judgment. But whoever wishes rather to be angry with me than to amend himself will have no way to excuse himself before the tribunal of the eternal Judge on the grounds of ignorance, saying that he was not admonished, not restrained from evil, and not repeatedly urged by correction and admonition toward those things that please God.

But we trust in the Lord’s mercy that he will deign to inspire all who are negligent in such a way that they will be angry with themselves—or rather with their sins—more than with priestly remedies; and that, just as the sick seek bodily health from bodily physicians, so they will desire remedies for their souls from spiritual physicians.

But we are confident that divine mercy will grant this: that they will strive to give us such joy through their amendment that they may happily attain the eternal reward; through our Lord’s granting it, and so forth.

---

## SERMON CCXC

*[Note: [Col. 2294] Elsewhere, On Time 248.]*

### On Continence

*[Note: [Col. 2294] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was doubtful to the Louvain editors, but Verlino and Winding judged it spurious. Its author is uncertain; he was trained in the Benedictine Rule. Its style does not differ greatly from that of the following sermon. On section 2, see Cyprian, On the Discipline and Conduct of Virgins, and the Benedictine Rule, chapter 4.]*

### 1. The precepts and necessity of continence

The divine law admonishes and exhorts us, dearest brothers, to avoid the desire of this world and devote ourselves to salutary continence, lest the enticement of pleasures lead us through various desires and, entangled in the snare of death, deliver us into the precipice and abyss of hell.

Wisdom speaks to a human being and says: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desire [Col. 2295], it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Sirach 18:30–31). For love of this world produces enmity toward God; hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

Knowing this, the Apostle John, his fellow apostle, persuades us and says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone has loved the world, the Father’s love is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of the spirit” (1 John 2:15–16).

His fellow apostle Paul likewise admonishes us and says: “Those who buy should be as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not use it; for the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:30–31).

Therefore the Savior himself also shows in his parable that the riches and pleasures of the age choke the word, so that it bears no fruit (Matthew 13:22). Elsewhere he commanded, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (ibid. 16:24); and again: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses,” he says, “cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Considering these things, therefore, dearest brothers, weigh how necessary continence is for you. Through it you can become worthy of Christ’s discipleship and come with him into the everlasting kingdom.

### 2. What it consists in

Continence and sobriety do not consist solely in bodily integrity; they also consist in one’s dress and adornment, and likewise in one’s life and conduct. Everyone who practices continence ought to abstain from everything unlawful; but he ought to use what is lawful with modesty and sobriety.

It is not fitting for a Christian, to whom the heavenly kingdom has been promised, to yearn after the profits of the world. Rather, he should live worthily for his Lord through continence, so that he may rejoice with him forever.

He ought to love chastity and flee fornication; not devote himself to greed, but be content with food and clothing; not be proud or place his hope in the uncertainty of riches, but think humbly and despise the world’s pomp.

He must not be a vain talker or arrogant, not a liar or injurious, not double-tongued, a whisperer, or a detractor. Rather, he must speak truth from mouth and heart and restrain his tongue from excessive speech, because it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs 10:19).

He should close his eyes against vanity; turn his hearing away from buffoonery and falsehood, indeed from every evil utterance; not love loud and uproarious laughter; not eagerly expose his throat and nose to the allure of sweet foods and pleasant scents, but seek rather the good and sweet fragrance of virtues.

He must carefully guard his hands, feet, and all the members of his body, so that they do not become weapons of iniquity for sin, but rather weapons of power for God, for destroying the spiritual enemy (Romans 6:13).

### 3. Its chief part: guarding the heart

The soldier of Christ must above all preserve his heart with vigilant care, lest boasting lift it up, anger inflame it, envy pierce it, greed attack it, lust burn it, sadness weigh it down, or sluggishness and indolence burden it; and lest—which is more serious than all the rest—heresy tear it apart through presumptuous novelties.

For whoever strives through continence to keep the heart’s hidden places quiet within will certainly guard the body’s members more easily from evil acts without. For it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds” (Proverbs 4:23). Elsewhere also: “Death is placed with you at the entrance of pleasure” [Note: [Col. 2295] You will find this very passage in chapter 7 of the Benedictine Rule, in Bernard’s Sermon 3, On the Nativity of the Lord, and in the Acts of Saint Sebastian, chapter 4.].

And the Savior says in the Gospel: “The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35); and again: “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications” (ibid. 15:19).

Since, therefore, fruits—whether good or evil—come forth from the root of the heart, we must first cleanse the heart, and then discipline our flesh through fasts and vigils for useful labor, lest the lust of the flesh stain the mind. For it is difficult for those who live in pleasures to have a pure heart [Col. 2296].

Hence the Apostle said: “I chastise my body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27); and again: “Those who belong to Christ,” he says, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5:24).

Let us live soberly and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from every iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works (Titus 2:12).

Thus, when he comes in his majesty with thousands of holy angels, may he grant us the rewards of eternal life for our good labors and holy conduct, rather than repay our laziness and the pleasures of the present life with everlasting torment; for it is truly written of him that he repays each person according to his works (Matthew 16:27)—namely, Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

---

## SERMON CCXCI

*[Note: [Col. 2296] Elsewhere, On Time 249.]*

### On Chastity and Purity

*[Note: [Col. 2296] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It had been left doubtful in the Louvain edition; but the judgment of Verlino and Winding rejected it, on the grounds that it contains chapter eighteen of Alcuin’s book On Virtues and Vices.]*

### 1. Praise of chastity. Uncleanness is the devil’s dwelling; by what consideration it may be restrained

Chastity and purity hold a glorious and distinguished place among the other virtues, dearest brothers, because chastity alone enables human minds, once cleansed, to see God. Hence Truth himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). As though he were saying the opposite: “Wretched, then, are those whose hearts are polluted by carnal desire, because they are plunged into eternal punishments.”

Chastity is an angelic life. Chastity joined with humility will earn the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, which the impurity of lust drives away, as Scripture says: “The Holy Spirit will flee a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4).

Our members ought to be dedicated to God, not to fornication. Let a person set the flames of eternal torments against the desire of his flesh. Let the young man become accustomed to chastity, so that he may be worthy of God’s wisdom.

Where there is bodily uncleanness, there is the dwelling of the devil’s spirit, which takes the greatest delight in the defilement of our flesh. Every kind of uncleanness displeases God, especially that which is unnatural.

### 2. What must be avoided by turning away from it

Holy Scripture therefore admonishes us, saying: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you come to the joy of your enemies” (Sirach 18:30–31).

The wisest Solomon likewise offered teachings about avoiding uncleanness, saying: “The lips of a prostitute drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet descend to death, and her steps reach the underworld; they do not walk along the path of life, her steps wander and cannot be traced. Now therefore, my son, hear me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house” (Proverbs 5:3–8).

He said this not only about the uncleanness of prostitutes, but also about every desire of the flesh that urges the soul to consent to its desires. But the judgment of the mind must restrain the impulses of the flesh and bridle its unlawful pleasures.

Again, the one who above forbids cohabitation with women says to young men: “Can a man hide fire in his bosom without his garments burning, or walk on burning coals without scorching the soles of his feet? So also the one who goes in to his neighbor’s wife will not be pure when he touches her” (ibid. 6:27–29).

Likewise the blessed Apostle admonishes us: “It is good,” he says, “for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1), as though danger were immediately present in the touch.

### 3. A return to the praise of chastity

This exceeds no one’s strength. It is entirely necessary for Christ’s ministers. The chaste modesty of the young [Col. 2297] is beautiful, beloved by God, and useful for every good thing.

Whoever has spiritual or bodily children should raise them in chastity for God, not in fornication for the devil. What benefit is it for a person to have, raise, and love a son if he raises him for eternal torments?

Those who live in chastity have an angelic way of life on earth. Chastity unites a human being to heaven and makes him a fellow citizen of the angels.

Whoever has a legitimate wife should use her legitimately at appropriate times, so that, according to the Apostle, he may devote himself to prayer (1 Corinthians 7:5) and deserve to receive from God the blessing of children.

Let no one say that he cannot guard himself from fornication. “God is faithful,” the Apostle says, “who will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out” (ibid. 10:13).

Such a temptation is given to each person—whether in the desire of the flesh, or in worldly ambition, or in any distress of temptation—as he will be able either to overcome with praise or to succumb with shame.

Chastity is necessary for everyone, but especially for the ministers of Christ’s altar, whose life ought to be instruction for others and a constant proclamation of salvation. It is fitting that the Lord should have such ministers, who are corrupted by no contagion of the flesh, but rather shine through the restraint of chastity and radiate examples of complete integrity among the people.

To them the Lord says through the Lawgiver: “Be holy, because I also am holy, the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19:2). For God is light, and there are no darknesses in him; nor can any foulness be joined to him.

Therefore, dearest brothers—whether men or women, clerics or laypeople—let us follow the Apostle’s admonition: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1).

Let us strive to please him who called us to his eternal glory, so that we may be able to reign happily with him forever; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, and so forth.

---

## SERMON CCXCII

*[Note: [Col. 2297] Elsewhere, On Time 244.]*

### On Conjugal Chastity

*[Note: [Col. 2297] An old manuscript of the Church of Carcassonne has this title prefixed: “Homily on chastity to be observed even with wives, and on women’s abortions, and on how one should act when Sunday or the other festivals arrive,” etc.]*

*[Note: [Col. 2297] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain editors and spurious according to Verlino and Winding. It clearly reflects Caesarius, but not purely. On section 1, see Appendix sermons 283, section 1; 210, section 6; 269, section 2; 271, section 6; 224, section 1; on section 2, sermon 267, section 3; on section 3, sermons 266, section 2, and 277, section 4; on section 4, sermons 288, section 1; 68, section 5; 104, section 4; on section 6, sermon 104, section 4, and 229, section 5; on section 8, sermons 45, section 4; 259, section 1; 282, section 4.]*

### 1. True peace and justice. For what the martyrs intercede. Virginity before marriage

You give me great joy, dearest brothers, when on the solemn feasts of the martyrs you gather in such faithful devotion to the church. But if, with God’s help, you wish spiritually to complete both your progress and our joy, preserve peace and charity among yourselves, with the Lord inspiring you, so that you harbor hatred toward no one in your heart.

Pray for the good, so that they may always advance toward better things; pray constantly for the wicked, so that they may quickly correct themselves. And in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to everyone” (Matthew 7:12).

Peace, justice, and mercy are preserved in truth when we not only do no evil to anyone, but also strive to help wherever we can. If, therefore, with Christ’s help, we faithfully do these things, imitating the blessed martyrs in the outstanding and splendid works mentioned above, we shall be able to have a share with them in eternal blessedness.

The holy martyrs then intercede for us without any doubt when they recognize something of their own virtues in us.

Guard chastity above all with God’s help, because it is written: “Neither fornicators nor [Col. 2298] adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9); and also: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4).

Boys and girls who are to be joined in marriage should preserve their virginity until the wedding. For if they are corrupted through adultery before a lawful union, they come to the marriage alive in body, certainly, but are shown to be dead in soul, because it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20).

### 2. No woman should take anything to cause an abortion. How guilty is the woman who does what prevents conception

No woman should take potions [Note: [Col. 2298] Thus here and shortly below, according to manuscript c. [potationes, “drinks”].] to cause an abortion, nor kill children, whether conceived or already born. Whoever does this should know that before Christ’s tribunal she will have to give an account for those whom she has killed [Note: [Col. 2298] Thus according to the same manuscript c. [daturam, “will give”].].

Nor should women take other diabolical potions. Any woman who does something by which she can no longer conceive should recognize that she is guilty of as many homicides as the number of children she could have borne.

As for a freeborn woman who takes deadly potions so that she will not conceive, I would like to know whether she would want her maidservants or female tenants to do this. Therefore, just as each woman wants slaves to be born to her who will serve her, so, however many children she conceives, she should either raise them herself or entrust them to others to raise; lest perhaps she be unwilling to conceive them—or, worse, wish to kill them—when they might have become good Christians.

With what conscience does she want slaves to be born to her from her maidservants, when she herself is unwilling to beget those who could become Christians [Note: [Col. 2298] The text is restored in this form from the same manuscript, c. [“who could have become good Christians, once begotten.”]]?

### 3. Marriage contracts

Whenever you come to church on any solemn feast and wish to receive Christ’s Sacraments [Note: [Col. 2298] Manuscript c.: “wish to receive Christ.”], preserve chastity for several days beforehand, so that you may approach God’s altar with a clear conscience.

Observe this faithfully throughout the whole of Lent and until the conclusion of Easter, so that the Paschal solemnity may find you chaste and pure.

A good Christian not only preserves chastity for several days before receiving Communion; he also does not know his wife except out of desire for children, because a wife is taken not for lust but for the procreation of children.

Indeed, the marriage contracts themselves contain this: “For the purpose,” they say, “of procreating children.” See that they did not say, “For the purpose of lust,” but “For the purpose of procreating children.”

Nevertheless, I would like to know: if the man who uses his wife without restraint were to plow or sow his field in a single year as often as he knows her when overcome by lust [Note: [Col. 2298] Thus according to manuscript c. [“if, whenever he recognized himself as overcome by lust”],], what harvest could he gather?

If, then, those who do not wish to restrain themselves were to plow and sow again the same piece of land [Note: [Col. 2298] Thus according to manuscript c. [“if they were to plow and sow again the same land”],], their own *condamina* [Note: [Col. 2298] This word means “field” in Occitan, apparently derived from *condominium*, “joint estate,” from its being subject to the right of a single lord. It is used in the *Placitum* of Atto, archbishop of Arles, where we read: “And likewise they released to Archbishop Atto the boundary of his *condamina*, which is beside the house, with the reed-bed, as much as the aforesaid *condamina* contains.” This also establishes that the sermon fits Caesarius better than Augustine.], which they had already sown, let us see how they will rejoice in its fruit. For, as you know very well, no land can yield a proper crop if it has been sown frequently in a single year.

What, then, someone does not want on his field, why does he do in his own body?

### 4. Stimuli of incontinence. Remedies. Almsgiving is foremost

But someone will say: “I am a young man; I absolutely cannot restrain myself” [Note: [Col. 2298] If from the same manuscript c.: [“I cannot restrain myself.”]].

Perhaps you do not restrain yourself because you eat more than is appropriate and drink more wine than you ought. Perhaps you also occupy your mind with shameful thoughts and do not fear or blush to speak lustful words yourself—not merely willingly, but frequently—or to listen when others speak them [Col. 2299].

Begin, with God’s help, to restrain the desires of your appetite, and constantly occupy your mind and tongue with chaste thoughts and honorable speech. You will see that, with God’s help, you can preserve chastity.

If bodily weakness does not prevent it, do not be reluctant to fast more frequently and rise earlier for church, so that you can keep your soul clean from lustful stains.

And if, doing this faithfully, you see that you are still wearied by the assaults of the flesh and perhaps are sometimes overcome, apart from the desire for children, into knowing your own wife [Note: [Col. 2299] In the same manuscript c.: “And if, doing these things faithfully, you see yourself immediately overcome,” instead of “to be overcome”], add daily almsgiving according to your means. For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33).

Also apply the great and salutary remedy against all sins: grant full forgiveness to everyone who has sinned against you, so that what is defiled through incontinence may be washed away through fasts, almsgiving, and especially forgiveness of enemies.

### 5. To know one’s wife except from desire for children is a sin

But you say: “To know one’s wife except from desire for children is not a sin.”

It is so much a sin that the repentant prophet cries out: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50:7).

We likewise read in the Old Testament that when the Jewish people were about to approach Mount Sinai, they were told by the Lord’s command: “Sanctify yourselves and be ready for the third day, and do not approach your wives” (Exodus 19:15). And also: “If anyone has been polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall not eat the meat of the sacrifice of salvation, lest his soul perish from the people” (Deuteronomy 13:10).

If, after the pollution that ordinarily happens to us against our will, it is not permitted for us to receive Communion unless contrition and almsgiving first precede it—and, if weakness does not prevent it, fasting as well—who can say that what we do while awake and willing is not a sin?

Finally, when women take husbands, they should not presume to enter the church for thirty days. Men likewise ought to observe this [Note: [Col. 2299] The same manuscript: “Men ought to do this.”] [Note: [Col. 2299] What is asserted here concerning the prohibition against married people entering the church, and what follows below in section 7 concerning those who do not abstain from their wives on Sunday or a solemn feast, is confirmed not only by the authority of the manuscript of the Church of Carcassonne, but also by the customs and discipline of these and earlier times. Pope Gregory, cited by Jonas of Orléans in book 2, chapter 11, of *On the Institution of the Laity*, says in book 12, letter 31, that married couples ought to abstain from entering the church after intercourse. Gregory of Tours, too, in *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book 2, chapter 24, makes almost the same threats against the incontinent as are found here in section 7. Jerome also belongs with these authorities, in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 18, verse 6, cited by Jonas in the aforementioned book *On the Institution of the Laity*, chapter 10.].

### 6. Not a capital sin, but if frequent it makes the soul unclean and disfigures the image of God

But you say: “It is indeed a sin, but it is a small one.”

Nor do we say that it is a capital sin. Yet if it is practiced frequently and is not redeemed through fasts or almsgiving, it makes the soul exceedingly unclean.

Do not despise your sins because they are small; rather, fear because they are many. For raindrops are also tiny [Note: [Col. 2299] The text is restored from the same manuscript, c.: “Do not despise your sins because they are small. For raindrops are also drops.”]; but they fill rivers, drag down masses, and uproot trees together with their roots.

You who say that it is a small sin: I would like to know whether, as often as you commit such a sin, you would want that many small wounds to be made on your body, or that many stains or tears to appear in your clothes.

If, then, you do not tolerate wounds on your body or tears and stains on your clothing, with what conscience do you not fear doing this in your soul? And so [Col. 2300] whoever does this loves his clothing and flesh more than his soul.

Since we have been made inwardly in the image of God, whenever we say or do anything shameful, we soil God’s image.

Consider also whether this is fitting or proper for you. Truly I tell you, dearest brothers: God does not deserve that his image should suffer injury in us through evil desires.

And when no one wishes to come to church wearing a tunic full of filth, I do not know with what conscience someone dares approach the altar with a soul polluted through lust, not fearing what the Apostle said: “Whoever eats the body and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27).

If we are ashamed and afraid to touch the Eucharist with dirty hands, we ought to fear even more receiving that Eucharist within a polluted soul [Note: [Col. 2300] Manuscript c.: “receiving the Eucharist within the soul.”].

And because, as I said, we have been made in our soul according to the image of God, if you made your image on a wooden or stone tablet and some shameless person wished either to break that image with stones or pollute it with filth, I would like to know whether you would not be angered against him.

I ask you: if you would so jealously defend your lifeless image, what sort of injury do you suppose God suffers when his living image in us is soiled through lust [Note: [Col. 2300] The same manuscript c.: “I ask you: if you would so jealously defend a painted image on a lifeless tablet, what sort of injury does God suffer when his image in us is soiled through lust?”]?

Therefore, if we do not spare ourselves for our own sake, let us at least spare ourselves for the sake of the image of God in whose likeness we were made.

### 7. Especially when one must abstain from one’s wife. What punishments those who act otherwise often incur. Some are more incontinent than beasts

Above all, whenever Sunday or another festival arrives, no one should know his wife. And whenever women suffer menstrual bleeding, the same rule must be observed, because the prophet says: “You shall not approach a menstruating woman” (Ezekiel 18:6) [Note: [Col. 2300] Thus according to the same manuscript: “because of which the prophet says.”].

For those who know their wives while they are in their flow, or who refuse to abstain when Sunday or any other solemn feast arrives [Note: [Col. 2300] Thus according to the same manuscript: “or who refuse to abstain when any other solemn feast arrives”], will have children conceived at such times who will be born lepers, epileptics, or perhaps even possessed by demons.

Indeed, lepers generally come not from wise people who preserve chastity both on other days and on feast days, but especially from country people who do not know how to restrain themselves.

And truly, brothers, if animals lacking reason do not mate except at a fixed and proper time, how much more ought human beings, who were made in the image of God, to observe this?

But what is worse, there are some so lustful or so drunken that sometimes they do not even spare their pregnant wives. Therefore, if they do not amend themselves, let them see whether they ought not to be judged worse than animals.

To such men the Apostle cries out, saying: “Let each person know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not have hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:4–5).

And because many do not preserve lawful chastity with their wives, as I said above, let them give abundant alms and forgive all their enemies, so that, as has already been said, what lust has made filthy may be washed away by continual almsgiving.

### 8. With what attitude the author has dealt with these matters

I ask you, brothers, to forgive me, because for the salvation of your souls I seem to be admonishing you about such matters with great fear or trembling [Note: [Col. 2300] Thus the same manuscript c.: “with great fear and with embarrassment.”] and with embarrassment. For it is necessary for me to say these things, and necessary for you to hear them.

Therefore, wherever you are, tell one another everything you have heard from us, and admonish one another with charity.

[Col. 2301] For just as I shall be guilty before Christ’s tribunal [Note: [Col. 2301] Thus according to the same manuscript: “For I shall be guilty.”] if I do not tell you, so you too, if you recognize negligent people among one another and refuse to admonish them, must fear that you will have to render an account for them.

But we trust in God’s mercy that he will inspire you to act in such a way that God will repay us with doubled rewards, not only for your conduct pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 2301] Corrected from manuscript c.: “that he will inspire us to act in such a way that God will repay us not only for our conduct pleasing to God”], but also for the salvation of others, both in this age and in the age to come. Amen [Note: [Col. 2301] In manuscript c. the sermon concludes: “May he himself deign to grant this.”].

---

## SERMON CCXCIII

*[Note: [Col. 2301] Formerly in volume 9, and afterward in volume 10, sermon On Time 250.]*

### On the Careless Familiarity of Foreign Women

*[Note: [Col. 2301] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is doubtful to the Louvain editors and spurious according to Verlino and Winding. It also appeared in volume 9 under the title “On the Good Conduct of Women.” Its style is entirely characteristic of Caesarius, who in fact arranged for canon 10 of the Council of Agde concerning the matter proposed here to be published. On section 1, see below sermon 294, section 3; sermon 224, section 1; Caesarius’s letter to certain Germans; on section 2, see the letter of Caesarius just cited; on section 5, sermons 90, section 6, and 142, section 8; 314, section 3.]*

### 1. Peace has its martyrs. Other vices are conquered by resisting; lust by fleeing. Familiarity with women must be avoided by all

Let no one say, dearest brothers, that in our times there can be no contests of martyrdom. Peace has its martyrs. For, as we have often said, to calm anger, flee lust, preserve justice, despise greed, and humble pride is a great part of martyrdom.

It was not inappropriately said: despise greed, calm anger, flee lust. Desire must be despised, for it obtains unjust profits for us in order to make us its own. We would belong to ourselves if it were not ours.

I say, greed must be despised [Note: [Col. 2301] These words—“which obtains unjust profits for us in order to make us its own”—through “greed” are absent from the manuscripts.], which, like fire, seeks more the more it receives.

Anger, meanwhile, must be calmed, because it harms those who are about to harm before it harms those who deserve harm.

As for our statement that lust must be fled, we have learned it clearly from the Apostle as our teacher. Although he declared that we must resist all vices, he did not say concerning lust, “Resist it”; rather, he said: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18).

Thus, with God’s help, we ought to resist the other vices in the present, but overcome lust by fleeing.

Likewise we read elsewhere in Scripture: “Do not,” he says, “look intently upon the face of a virgin, lest her appearance scandalize you” (Sirach 9:5).

And blessed Joseph, so that he might escape his shameless mistress, left behind the cloak by which he had been seized and fled.

Therefore, seize flight against the assault of lust if you wish to obtain victory. Do not be ashamed to flee if you desire to gain the palm of chastity.

See, brothers, how an unworthy and dishonorable familiarity must be avoided by all Christians, but especially by monks or clerics. For without any doubt, whoever does not wish to avoid familiarity with women quickly slips into ruin.

## 2. Chastity is greatly endangered among them. The hope of continual victory is vain, since victory over so harsh an enemy is rare. Moreover, they provide others with a most pernicious example.

But perhaps some negligent person, less concerned for the salvation of his soul, replies and says: “Look, I associate with women who are not my relatives, and yet I preserve the ornaments of chastity.” This presumption is wretched and exceedingly dangerous. For many, while they thought they were conquering, were themselves conquered.

But someone adds: “I live among women who are not my relatives, and I maintain continence; indeed, I want to have something to conquer.” What does it mean to say, “I want to have something to conquer,” except, “I want to have a means by which I may perish”? “But,” he says, “I want to keep the assault of lust [Col. 2302], as my adversary, continually captive.” Take care lest that very captivity begin to prevail against you, and lest from the place where you thought you would obtain triumph, you incur everlasting disgrace.

Among all the contests of Christians, the battles of chastity alone are the more difficult: there the struggle is daily, and victory rare. Chastity has drawn a heavy enemy, one who is conquered every day and yet feared. Therefore, as has already been said, let no one deceive himself with false security, and let no one dangerously presume upon his own strength; rather, let him hear the Apostle saying, “Flee fornication.”

That most holy David saw a naked woman from a thousand paces away, and immediately committed both murder and adultery. Those who think that, while living among women, they can obtain the triumph of chastity do not realize that they stand guilty before God in two ways: they put themselves in danger and display to others an example of improper familiarity. For however many, imitating their folly, lose the ornaments of chastity through dishonorable familiarity, their souls will be demanded on the day of judgment from those who displayed to them an example of perdition.

## 3. Who are now the persecutors and martyrs of Christ. No familiarity whatsoever with a woman is to be maintained. The cost of a momentary pleasure.

Therefore, dearest brothers, so that the deadly flatteries and the devil’s assistants—those who neither fear nor blush to maintain suspect familiarity—may not deceive us by their example, let us continually implore God’s help, that he may deign to free us from the snare of the hunters. We know that, amid all the evils mentioned above, Christians cannot lack daily martyrdoms.

For just as Christ is chastity, truth, and justice, so the one who lies in wait for these things is a persecutor of Christ. But the one who wishes both to defend them in others and to preserve them in himself will be a martyr. Therefore, whoever loves these things with all the strength of his soul, both in himself and so that others may love them, and demonstrates this by words and example; whoever, wherever truth, justice, or chastity is suffering, willingly comes forward as far as he can and strives to defend it according to his strength—such a person will receive, with God as his rewarder, not one but many crowns.

And so, with God’s help, let us become worthy to obtain these things. Let each person strive to avoid not only familiarity or secret conversation with women who are not his relatives, but also with our own maidservants, or any female neighbors, or daughters, foster-daughters, or servants; for the lower their condition, the easier the fall.

Concerning familiarity with such persons Solomon warns us, saying: “Can anyone carry fire in his bosom without burning his garments? Or can anyone walk upon hot coals without scorching the soles of his feet?” (Prov. VI, 27–28). And again: “The price of a prostitute is scarcely half a loaf, but a woman captures a man’s precious soul” (ibid., 26).

What great iniquity, and what lamentable perversity it is, that someone in lust should sell and hand over to the devil, for the pleasure of a single moment, the soul that Christ redeemed with his blood! Truly, the condition is exceedingly pitiable and deserving of mourning when what gives pleasure quickly passes, while what torments remains without end. The assault of lust passes in a moment, but the disgrace of the unhappy soul remains forever.

## 4. Whether it can easily be repaired. Lust, the hammer of the whole earth.

But someone says: “I am a young man. I do what pleases me now, and afterward I shall do penance.” It is as though he were saying: “I strike myself with a cruel sword, and afterward I shall go to a physician.” He does not know that a wound is received in a single instant, but is scarcely restored to its former health after a long time.

When an adulterer says that he will repent afterward, why does he not fear that a sudden little fever may overtake him and carry him away; that delay may prove fatal and everlasting condemnation follow?

And because we should believe that the following saying of the prophet was spoken concerning the unhappy lust of which we have already spoken—“How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken!” (Jerem. L, 23)—although, after the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, that hammer [Col. 2303] may seem to have been broken throughout all the monasteries and among clerics and even laypeople who preserve chastity, nevertheless, what is worse, there are still far more who are daily shattered by that hammer than those who are freed from its ruin or collision.

Therefore I ask again and again that we consider this more carefully and fear as much as we can what the Lord said in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

## 5. How death enters through the windows.

For this reason, as has already been said, not only familiarity with women who are not one’s relatives but also secret association with one’s own maidservants, and the heedless vulnerability of the eyes, must be restrained, lest what the Lord cries out terrifyingly through the prophet should happen to us: “Death has entered through your windows into your souls” (Jerem. IX, 21).

Through what windows does death enter our souls, unless through the sight of the eyes and the hearing of the ears? If, through your tongue, you order a friend or servant to bring a prostitute to you, then through your mouth the sword of eternal death enters your soul. But if you willingly listen to evil advice, or do not reject someone who slanders, speaks lasciviously, or produces shameful songs, then through the windows of your ears death has entered your soul.

And because the Lord said, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart,” it is understood that a fully formed intention [Note: [Col. 2303] The manuscripts read “ready” (prona).] to carry out the deed is reckoned as the deed itself. Thus, when someone looks at a woman with a lustful mind, through the window of his body he drips the poison of death into the secret place of his heart.

Such a thought, even if some circumstance prevents it from fulfilling its intention, is nevertheless condemned by the Lord for the crime of the act. Thus the woman with whom he wished to commit the evil of lust remains chaste, while he is already held adulterous in his heart.

Therefore let us hear Scripture saying, “With all vigilance keep your heart” (Prov. IV, 23), and again, “Turn my eyes away, lest they behold vanity” (Ps. CXVIII, 37).

For if someone takes hold of burning coals and quickly throws them away, they will harm him nothing; but if he wishes to hold them longer, he cannot cast them off without a wound. So too, the person who fixes his gaze upon something in order to lust, receives the evil of lust into his heart, and allows it to linger in his thoughts: he will not be able to shake those thoughts from himself without a wound to his soul.

Therefore let us continually cry out with the prophet: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. XXIV, 15), through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

# SERMON CCXCIV

[Note: [Col. 2303] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 231.]

### An admonition that the evil of drunkenness must be avoided with all one’s strength

[Note: [Col. 2303] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors left the matter doubtful, whereas Verlinus and Vindingus wished to regard it as spurious. It is actually Caesarius’s fifth homily among those edited by Baluzius; in some of our manuscripts as well it is assigned to Caesarius. For no. 1, see Appendix, sermons 295, no. 1; 286, no. 5; 267, no. 4; for no. 3, sermon 266, no. 3; for no. 6, sermon 286, no. 6; for no. 8, sermons 272, no. 8; 295, no. 6; 277, no. 4; 265, no. 5.]

## 1. Drunkenness is not even considered a sin. The friendship of drunkards is hostile.

Although, with Christ favorable, dearest brothers, I believe that you dread the evil of drunkenness as an abyss of hell, and that you not only do not wish to drink more yourselves but also do not urge or compel others to take more than they should, nevertheless, since it cannot be that there are not some negligent people who do not wish to be sober, you who always provide sober banquets must not take it as an insult to yourselves when we are obliged to rebuke others who are drunk.

For, dearest brothers, although the evil of drunkenness is an exceedingly grave vice and hateful to God, it has become so customary throughout the whole world among many people that those who refuse to learn God’s commandments no longer even consider or believe it to be a sin. Indeed, at their banquets they mock those who are able to drink less, and, through a hostile friendship, are not ashamed to urge people to take [Col. 2304] more drink than they ought.

Whoever compels another person to become drunk by drinking more than is necessary would do less harm if he wounded that person’s body with a sword than if he killed his soul through drunkenness.

## 2. Drunkards are compared with marshes.

Since our bodies are earthly, just as, when rain is excessively heavy and prolonged, the earth becomes so saturated and dissolves into mud that no cultivation can be carried out in it, so our flesh, when it has been made drunk by excessive drinking, can neither receive spiritual cultivation nor produce the necessary fruits of the soul.

Therefore, just as everyone desires to receive sufficient rain in his fields, so that he can both cultivate them and rejoice in an abundance of fruits, so in the field of the body people ought to drink only as much as is appropriate. Otherwise, through excessive drunkenness, the earth of the body itself, turned as it were into a marsh, will produce more worms and snakes of vice than it can bring forth fruits of good works.

For all drunkards are such as marshes appear to be. Your Charity knows what grows in marshes: everything that grows there is recognized as bearing no fruit. Snakes and leeches are born there; frogs and various kinds of worms are born there, creatures more capable of producing horror than of supplying anything useful for food.

The grasses and trees that commonly grow either in the marshes themselves or around their banks seem to possess no usefulness, so much so that they are burned up every year. See, then, that what is born from drunkenness is prepared for fire.

## 3. Their condition is depicted.

All drunkards are, as I have already said, like this: their lunches continue until night, and the morning star sees their dinners; they cannot stand even when they appear to be fasting; their senses are slow, heavy, dull, and in a certain manner already buried.

Finally, while still in the drunken state, they frequently recognize neither themselves nor others; they are unable either to walk or to stand; they cannot speak or hear anything that pertains to reason.

They are often not ashamed to stuff themselves until they vomit, and to drink without measure according to a measureless standard. Larger cups are provided, and contests are held under a fixed rule of drinking [Note: [Col. 2304] Manuscript r reads, “a law is established.” Manuscript I reads, “with a law established.”]; whoever is able to win earns praise from a crime.

From this arise quarrels and brawls; from this their limbs are twisted in various and horrifying dances; from this adultery and sometimes even murder are committed. And whenever they take excessive drink, they become as limp as though stricken with paralysis; since they cannot walk on their own feet, they are carried to bed in a most disgraceful conveyance, in the hands of others.

They suffer dimness of the eyes, dizziness, exhaustion and headache, flushing of the face, trembling of all the limbs, and stupefaction of soul and mind. In such people what is written is fulfilled:

“Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has quarrels? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and seek to drain their cups?” (Prov. XXIII, 29–30).

## 4. They excuse themselves on the grounds of friendship. A guest must not be compelled to drink. Drunkards are prodigal toward their equals, stingy toward the poor. They are worse than animals. They destroy themselves and their possessions.
