But those who wish to be such people try to excuse themselves miserably, saying: “I regard my friend as ungrateful if, whenever I invite him to a banquet, I do not give him as much drink as he himself wishes.”

Do not regard as your friend the person who wishes to make you an enemy of God—one who is an enemy both to you and to himself. If you make both yourself and another person drunk, you will have a human being as your friend and God as your enemy. Therefore consider wisely whether it is just for you to separate yourself from God while joining yourself to a drunkard.

In the end, do not urge him and do not compel him; leave it in his power to drink as much as he wishes, so that if he wants to make himself drunk, he may perish alone and not both of you perish [Note: [Col. 2304] The manuscripts read, “and not both of you sin.”].

O the unhappiness of the human race! How many are found who compel drunkards and debauched people to drink more than they ought, while at the door they neglect to give even a single cup to poor people who ask for it [Col. 2305]. They do not consider that what they seem to force upon the debauched ought to be received by Christ in the poor, who said: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

But such people, when they have buried others in excessive drinking, say to a poor person asking for alms: “Go, go farther on; God will give to you.” And indeed, when the man has gone away, God will give to him. What, then, does “Go farther on, and God will give to you” mean, except, “Go to the man who has God, because he will give to you”? Thus, by his own mouth, he confesses that God is not with him, inspiring him to distribute anything to the poor.

I ask you, dearest brothers, to pay careful attention and see that when horses or other animals are led to water, once they have satisfied their thirst, even if they are kept beside the water for a long time, they neither want nor are able to drink. Let drunkards consider whether they should not be judged worse than animals. For while animals do not wish to drink more than they need, drunkards take twice or three times as much drink as they ought.

And what they could have used for a reasonable refreshment over three or four days, they strive to waste in a single day with great sin, rather than to spend it properly. Would that they wasted only the drink and did not also perish themselves!

## 5. The evils of drunkenness are demonstrated by examples and the words of Scripture.

How much evil drunkenness contains was clearly shown even in Lot and his daughters. For, after becoming drunk with wine, he unknowingly lay with his own daughters (Gen. XIX, 33, 35).

Pharaoh, too, after becoming drunk, had the chief baker hanged on a cross (ibid. XL, 20, 22).

The Jewish people, of whom it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6), after taking more wine than they ought, requested that idols be made for them. In honor of those idols they began to lead choral dances and, in the manner of the frenzied, to twist their limbs in various dances.

Herod, too, when he had been inflamed by excessive wine, ordered the holy John the Baptist to be killed for the sake of a single girl’s dancing (Matt. XIV).

The Holy Spirit also testifies through Solomon what further evil is born from drunkenness, saying: “Wine and women make wise men apostatize, and they rebuke the sensible” (Eccli. XIX, 2). And again: “Do not look upon wine when it becomes red, when its color shines in the glass. For it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and pour out poison like a basilisk. Your eyes will see strange women, and your heart will speak perverse things” (Prov. XXIII, 31–33).

The Apostle Paul also warns us against the evil of drunkenness, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. V, 18).

Again and again we clearly demonstrate from the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures what evil drunkenness contains to those who love it.

It is written in Solomon: “He who loves wine and rich foods will not become wealthy” (Prov. XXI, 17). And again: “Do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest they drink and forget the judgments of God and alter the cause of the sons of the poor” (ibid. XXXI, 4–5).

It also says there: “A drunken laborer will not become rich” (Eccli. XIX, 1). And again: “If you drink wine moderately, you will be sober” (ibid. XXXI, 32).

It likewise says there: “Wine was created for gladness, not for drunkenness, from the beginning. Wine drunk moderately is the joy of soul and heart; wine drunk in abundance is the weakness of soul and body. It causes irritation, anger, and many falls. Much wine drunk is bitterness of soul, the fury of drunkenness, an offense to the imprudent, diminishing strength and producing wounds” (ibid., 35–40).

## 6. Drunkards have no share in the kingdom of God.

When we offer these admonitions, perhaps drunkards become angry with us and grumble. And although there are certainly some who become angry, nevertheless, with God’s favor, many will gladly hear this salutary counsel and, through God’s mercy, be freed from so grave a sin.

Let those themselves who become angry at anyone speaking against their dove and friend, drunkenness, hear us openly: whoever does not do penance for drunkenness itself, but remains in that drunkenness [Col. 2306] until his death, will certainly perish forever. For the Holy Spirit does not lie when he says through the Apostle: “Nor will drunkards possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

Therefore, whoever is a drunkard does better to become angry not with us but with himself, and, with God’s help, to hurry with all possible speed to shake himself from the mud of filth, or from the sewer of drunkenness, while there is still time for repentance. With all the strength of his soul, let him plead with the Lord and say with the prophet: “Deliver me from the mire, that I may not stick fast” (Ps. LXVIII, 15); and again: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16).

For drunkenness is like a well of hell. Whoever it receives, unless worthy repentance comes to his aid and amendment follows, it claims so forcefully for itself that it completely prevents those same people from returning from the dark well of hell to the light of chastity or sobriety.

## 7. By what method they may give up drunkenness.

Above all, we must understand and know that people do not become drunkards in a single day. Rather, little by little, when the most cruel enemies—more enemies than friends—urge and compel them, they add one or two cups each day to their customary drinking.

But once they have made this a habit, the very heat of drunkenness takes possession of them and compels them always to thirst.

Whoever desires to be freed from this evil should return to the light of sobriety by gradually reducing his drink, just as he reached the darkness of drunkenness by adding drink at intervals. For if he withdraws all at once whatever he had been taking in excess, then, when he begins to burn with extreme thirst, he cries out with great bitterness that he would rather die than have his habit of drinking and becoming drunk taken away from him. He does not consider that it would have been more bearable for him to die in the flesh than to kill his soul through drunkenness.

Therefore, so that he may neither suffer excessive burning thirst nor remain enslaved to so grave a sin, he should, as has already been said, withdraw something from the excess of his drinking at intervals of days, until he returns to a reasonable habit of drinking.

Whoever wishes to reduce it gradually in this way, as we have instructed, will be freed from drunkenness and will not suffer that intolerable burning thirst.

## 8. Clerics are not exempt from this vice. Pagan superstition.

Dearest brothers, while I offer these admonitions, I clear my conscience before God. Whoever disdains to listen to me, and is himself inclined to drinking or wishes to urge or compel his guests to drink, will be guilty before God’s judgment both for himself and for them.

And because—what is worse—some clerics also, who ought to prohibit this practice, themselves compel certain people to drink more than is appropriate, let them now begin to correct themselves and rebuke others. Thus, when they come before Christ’s tribunal, they will not incur punishment either for their own drunkenness or for that of others. Rather, by correcting themselves and not ceasing to rebuke others, may they deserve to reach eternal reward.

Above all, I ask this of you, and I adjure you by the fearful day of judgment: whenever you provide banquets for one another, reject from your banquets, as the devil’s poison, that shameful custom by which three people, willingly or unwillingly, used to drink an excessive measure without measure. For this unhappy custom still remains from the observance of the pagans.

Whoever permits this to be done at his own banquet or at another’s should have no doubt that he has sacrificed to the devil. Through that drinking not only is the soul killed, but the body also is weakened.

But I believe that, through God’s mercy, he will deign to inspire you in such a way that this evil, so lamentable and even shameful, will become so abhorrent to you that you will never permit it to occur. Instead, what would have perished in that drunkenness may be used to refresh the poor, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCXCV

[Note: [Col. 2307] Elsewhere, *On Time*, 232.]

### An admonition against the evil of drunkenness

[Note: [Col. 2307] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. Concerning this sermon, which the Louvain editors likewise left doubtful, Vindingus, following Verlinus, reached the same conclusion as regarding the preceding sermon. He reasonably wishes the following passage from these two sermons to belong to one of them: in the Testament of Count Evrard, written in the age of Louis the Pious, in the year of Christ 837, it is expressly stated (*Spicilegium*, vol. 12, p. 494): “We wish Judith to have one missal and one book that begins with a sermon of St. Augustine on Drunkenness.” It has been observed above, in connection with Sermon 278, that certain Caesarian sermons were formerly cited under Augustine’s name. Baluzius restored this sermon to Caesarius on the authority of the Royal manuscript, to which several of our manuscripts also agree, and placed it sixth among the fourteen recently published sermons. For no. 1, see Appendix, Sermon 294, nos. 1 and 3; Augustine, Sermon 9, no. 12; for no. 2, Sermon 291, no. 1; for no. 3, Sermons 257, no. 3; 263, no. 2; and 264, no. 5; for no. 4, Sermon 277, no. 4; for no. 5, Sermon 294, no. 8; for no. 6, Sermons 69, no. 8; 281, no. 3; 130, no. 2; 266, no. 3; and 285, no. 3; for no. 7, Sermon 272, no. 8.]

[Col. 2307]

## 1. Drunkards are like shipwrecked vessels. They mock the sober as though they were not men.

I have frequently admonished your Charity, dearest brothers, with paternal affection, that you ought to avoid or flee the evil of drunkenness as an abyss of hell.

And although our rebuke has benefited many, there are still many who neither fear God nor respect those who are honorable or sober. They drink so much that at times they must empty their entrails, filled with excessive drink, through vomiting. Like shattered, shipwrecked vessels, they are so battered by the dreadful waves of drunkenness that they do not even recognize where they are, and are wholly unable to say or hear anything pertaining to reason.

But what is this? When those unhappy drunkards stuff themselves with excessive wine, they ridicule and reproach those who wish to drink reasonably only as much as is sufficient, saying to them: “Be ashamed, and let it be a disgrace to you that you cannot drink as much as we do.” They say that such people are not men.

And observe the misery of drunkards. They call themselves men, though they lie in the sewer of drunkenness; and they say that those are not men who stand honorably and soberly. They lie prostrate, and are men; others stand upright, and are not men? The conqueror of drunkenness is reproached, while the one conquered by drunkenness is praised. The sober person, who can govern both himself and others, is mocked; but the drunkard, who can recognize neither himself nor others, is not mocked—indeed, he is not even mourned.

## 2. They claim, by way of excuse, that they were compelled. Yet they should have resisted even unto death. What martyrdom is, and how it is now endured.

Drunkards nevertheless customarily excuse themselves by saying: “A powerful person compelled me to drink more, and in the presence of a king I could do nothing else.”

We put this forward as an excuse for excuses in sins; what we do not wish to fulfill, we say we were unable to fulfill. Unwillingness is our fault, but inability is alleged.

Even if matters came to this point, so that you were told, “Either you will drink or you will die,” it would be better for your sober flesh to be killed than for your soul to die through drunkenness.

But this excuse is falsely advanced. For those very kings and other powerful people, because—by God’s favor—they are Christians and prudent, sober, and fearful of God with all their hearts, if they see you determined, for fear of God, not to consent to becoming drunk, may appear angry for the moment, but afterward they receive you with great admiration, saying: “How much we pressed him, with how many threats and terrors we harassed him—and yet we could never separate him from sobriety!”

For God too, seeing that you do not wish to become drunk for love of him, will himself grant you the favor even of those who seemed to encourage and compel you to drink more.

Let no one say, dearest brothers, that in these times there are no martyrs. Martyrs are made every day. For *martyr* means “witness.” Whoever, therefore, bears witness for the truth and judges all matters with justice—whatever he suffers for the testimony of truth or justice—God will count all of it to him as martyrdom.

Thus, the person [Col. 2308] who resists drunkenness, if he wishes to persevere with God’s help and suffers some tribulations for this very reason, will have all these things counted by God toward the glory of martyrdom.

## 3. Drunkards are convicted of injustice toward God.

I would like to know, dearest brothers, whether any master who has several servants would ever want even one of them to become a drunkard. Without doubt, no one has ever wanted or would want this.

With what face, then, and with what conscience does a person who does not want to have a drunken servant wish to become drunk himself?

Look: you have a servant from God’s gifts, and God has you as his servant. Just as you wish your servant to serve you, so you ought to serve your Lord.

Tell me, I ask you: does it seem just to you that you should have a sober servant, while God should have you as a drunkard? Thus you judge yourself worthy to be served by a sober servant, while you consider God unworthy to be served by you soberly.

Therefore, dearest brothers, pay careful attention and consider that it is not just for us to do to God what we do not want done to us.

Perhaps you will say: “How do I do to God what I do not want done to me?” Listen to how. You are displeased to have a drunken servant, yet you do not wish to serve God soberly.

## 4. They scarcely consider drunkenness a sin. They will be punished with eternal punishment. Nor is it committed with impunity in the present life. Clerics of the higher orders are also subject to this vice.

People become drunk so readily, dearest brothers, because they think drunkenness is either a small sin or no sin at all.

But for this ignorance priests above all will have to render an account on the day of judgment if they have continually refused to preach to the peoples entrusted to them what evils, and how great, arise from drunkenness.

Whoever therefore believes drunkenness to be a small sin, if he does not amend himself and do penance for that drunkenness, will be tormented without remedy by eternal punishment together with adulterers and murderers, according to what you yourselves know the blessed Apostle preached:

“Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor adulterers, nor drunkards will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9–10).

Observe that he joins drunkards with fornicators, those who serve idols, those who lie with males, and adulterers.

And again: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. V, 18).

Therefore let each person decide and determine within himself that drunkenness is a grave sin. Then drunkenness will either never or only with difficulty be able to conquer him.

For people will not only be tormented because of drunkenness in the world to come; even in the present life they are frequently afflicted by many illnesses through drunkenness. Let those who do not think about the salvation of their souls at least fear bodily sickness, and dread the flushing and dimness of their eyes, dizziness of the head, and trembling of their limbs, if they do not fear the punishments of hell.

We say this not only to laypeople but also to clerics. For, what is worse, there are many clerics, even of the higher orders, who, although they ought continually to preach the good of sobriety to others, not only fail to do so but are also not ashamed or afraid to make both themselves and others drunk.

Let all who are such acknowledge and grieve, because if they refuse to amend themselves, they will necessarily have to endure eternal punishments both for themselves and for others.

## 5. Drinking bouts after banquets under various names. Irritants of thirst. Only two places exist after this life.

What is this, moreover? Once the banquet has ended and thirst has been satisfied, when they can no longer drink more and ought not to do so, they begin to drink under various names as though they were newcomers, as though they had arrived only at that moment—not only in the names of living people but also of angels and the other ancient saints. They think they are showing them the greatest honor if they bury themselves in excessive drunkenness under their names.

They do not know that no one is recognized as inflicting so grave an insult upon the holy angels or holy human beings as the person who, by drinking in their names, is proved to kill his own soul through drunkenness.

There are some who, for this sole purpose [Col. 2309], order salty foods to be prepared for themselves, so that through the saltiness they may overwhelm themselves with excessive drunkenness.

If pagans who do not know God do this, it is neither astonishing nor especially grievous, because they place no hope in God and preserve the ancient custom of their parents.

But why do Christians—whom God has led from darkness into light and called from death to life, to whom all the Scriptures cry out to flee drunkenness and love sobriety—imitate the most shameful drunkenness of those from whose unbelief they have merited to be freed through God’s grace?

Therefore I ask you, and I adjure you by the fearful day of judgment, that, with the Lord’s help, you flee the evil of drunkenness as far as you can, and that you begin to be truly ashamed that, until now, you have wished to show yourselves like the Gentiles and pagans in the shamefulness of drunkenness.

Since, by God’s favor, you differ from them in faith, you must not at all be like them in drunkenness. For even if Christians avoid the other sins, drunkenness alone, if it is frequent and amendment and repentance do not come to their aid, plunges them into the depths of hell, according to what has already been said: “Nor will drunkards possess the kingdom of God.”

But someone says: “I do not want the kingdom of God; I desire only to obtain eternal rest.”

Let no one deceive himself, brothers. There are two places, and there is no third. Whoever does not merit to reign with Christ will without any doubt perish with the devil [Note: [Col. 2309] Caesarius revolved this constantly in his mind day and night, so that it is said to have burst from him even in sleep in these words: “There are two things; there is nothing in between. One goes either into hell or into heaven.” *Life of Caesarius*, book 2, no. 4.]

## 6. Drunkards are to be corrected.

In the end, the person who, by giving his friend too much to drink, becomes his enemy in soul, is proved both to weaken his body and to kill his soul.

It would have been better if, from what he compelled him to take in one day beyond what was appropriate, he had invited that same friend to his banquet over two or three days, and if, instead of weakening him by excessive drinking on one day, he had refreshed him on the other days with sufficient drink. In this way he would neither waste the drink nor deceive his friend.

Or, certainly, what is better, whatever the appetite would have wasted through excessive drinking should be given as alms to the poor. Thus the flesh would be refreshed by drinking reasonably, and through mercy shown to the poor redemption of the soul would be prepared.

We have not offered this correction for the sake of those who are honorable and sober, for, with God’s favor, we know many who prepare frugal and sober banquets.

Therefore, you who, for love of God, drink only what is appropriate, take care that what drunkards waste on earth may be stored up by you in heaven through almsgiving.

It is not enough for you to be honorable and sober yourselves. As far as you can, rebuke and correct drunkards so that, in your presence, they may never again be permitted to drink more than is appropriate. Thus, while you yourselves love sobriety and, through your admonition, recall others from the destruction of drunkenness, you will prepare for yourselves double rewards in eternal blessedness—not only for your own salvation but also for that of others.

[Note: [Col. 2309] What follows is lacking in the manuscripts.]

7. The Custom and Extravagance of Certain Country People

And how mournful and shameful it is, dearest brothers, that some country people are said, whenever they have wine or have prepared other drinks for themselves, to invite their neighbors or close associates to drink as though to a wedding feast, keeping them there for four or five days and burying them in excessive drunkenness. They do not return to their homes from that lamentable drinking until they have entirely consumed all the drink possessed by the man who invited them. Thus, what could have reasonably sustained him and his whole family for two or three months, they consume in four or five days in a drinking bout that ought to be lamented and blushed for.

Brothers, dearest to me, while I humbly and with great charity admonish you about these matters out of paternal concern, I clear my conscience before God. Whoever willingly hears me and faithfully wishes to fulfill what has been preached to him will receive an eternal reward; but whoever despises it should fear lest he be compelled to endure eternal punishment without end. Yet we trust in the mercy of God that, by God’s grace, all drunkards will return from the evil of drunkenness to the good of sobriety, so that they may bring joy to us and themselves happily deserve to attain the eternal reward. Amen.

## SERMON CCXCVI

[Note: [Col. 2310] Elsewhere, among the Vignerian sermons, 39.]

An admonition showing that, from the beginning of the world, all the Scriptures have blessed the humble and cursed those who persevere in pride.

[Note: [Col. 2310] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The authority of several of our manuscripts, apart from that Royal codex from which it was published by Baluze among the fourteen Caesarian sermons as the eleventh, attributes it to Caesarius. For number 3, see Sermon 68 of the Appendix, section 4; for number 4, Sermon 17, section 2; for number 5, Caesarius, Homily 18, and Sermon 269 of the Appendix, section 1; for number 6, Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 128, section 9.]

### 1. The Scriptures everywhere bless the poor and curse sinners

In the Holy Scriptures, dearest brothers, the poor are blessed without ceasing, while sinners appear to be cursed. First, then, just as you yourselves frequently recognize through reading and singing the psalms, I will present to your Charity in a few statements how the divine Scriptures bless the poor; afterward I will indicate what they say about sinners.

Of the poor it is said: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33:7); and again: “Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131:15); and again: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); and again: “To you the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 10:14, according to the Hebrew); and again: “For the Lord has heard the poor” (Ps. 68:34).

Of sinners, however, it is said: “Let sinners be turned into hell—all the nations” (Ps. 9:18); and again: “For sinners shall perish” (Ps. 36:20); and again: “Break the arm of the sinner and the evil man” (Ps. 10:15, according to the Hebrew); and this: “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine mingled with mixture; all the sinners of the earth shall drink from it” (Ps. 74:9); and again: “I will break all the horns of sinners” (ibid., 11).

Statements of this kind are found abundantly throughout all the Scriptures: the poor are highly praised, while, conversely, harsh sentences are directed against sinners.

### 2. With what intention the Scriptures pronounce curses

But since these things are so, someone may perhaps think within himself and say: How are we commanded in the divine Scriptures, “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14); and, “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10); and, “Bless those who persecute you” (Rom. 12:14)? How, then, do the divine Scriptures themselves, which prohibit this for us, curse so often?

These curses, dearest brothers, are uttered not with the intention of wishing something upon sinners, but with the intention of foretelling it. They do not wish these things to come upon sinners; but because they will undoubtedly come, these curses are shown to be prophecies. Therefore, all who recognize that they are sinners and desire through the sacred Scriptures to be blessed rather than cursed should hasten to the remedy of repentance, lest, if sudden death overtakes them while they persist in their sins, all the curses read in the Holy Scriptures from the beginning of the world come upon them in such a way that they are not permitted to be freed from everlasting punishment.

### 3. The proud are signified by sinners, and the humble by the poor

And yet, brothers, when the poor are blessed in the divine Scriptures and sinners are cursed, anyone who carefully attends to the meaning of Holy Scripture understands that this is not said of all sinners, nor of all poor people in rags. For among the sinners whom the divine Scriptures appear to curse, not all sinners are meant, but only the proud—those who not only do evil, but are also not ashamed to defend their very evils with the most shameless expression.

[Col. 2311] These are the ones of whom it is written: “Let the proud be confounded, because they have unjustly committed iniquity against me” (Ps. 118:78); and: “You,” he says, “will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:28); and: “The proud were acting unjustly to the utmost” (Ps. 118:51); and: “God resists the proud” (Jas. 4:6). There are innumerable testimonies of this kind by which the arrogance of the proud is marked.

Therefore, whenever you hear sinners cursed in the Scriptures, understand—as I have already said—that the proud are meant, that is, those who defend their sins. And whenever you hear the poor highly praised, do not take this as referring to all poor people, but only to good Christians who are meek and humble in heart. Of them it is written: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

### 4. Poverty helps many not at all; wealth harms certain rich people not at all. Poverty is worthless if proud; if humble, it should be heaped with blessings

For many poor people are angry, greedy, proud, and lustful. Their lack of possessions benefits them nothing, since they are wealthy in vices and evil habits. And many rich people are humble and gentle. Of them it is said: “Blessed is the man who has not gone after gold, nor hoped in treasures of money” (Ecclus. 31:8); and: “He has distributed; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9).

What does it profit a poor person not to possess wealth if he has the desire to possess it, when the Apostle condemns not the one who has wealth but the one who desires it, saying: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9)? Or what does it profit him to lack possessions if he burns with greed? What, I ask, does it profit a poor man that he is poor if he chooses to be proud rather than humble? Or how does abundant wealth harm a rich man if perfect humility is found in him—if he wishes, with all his heart and soul, not to use his wealth for luxury but to distribute alms and preserve humility and gentleness?

Finally, as I have already said, all the Scriptures praise the humble poor and condemn the proud rich. They promise an eternal reward to the poor, while threatening the proud rich with everlasting punishment, according to this: “Repay recompense to the proud” (Ps. 93:2); and: “God will destroy the memory of the proud” (Ps. 33:17); and: “Pride is hateful before God” (Ecclus. 10:7).

Through pride the angels fell from heaven to earth, became devils in hell, and those who are proud are like them.

[Note: [Col. 2311] The Royal Manuscript does not contain this passage: “Through pride the angels fell … are like them.”]

But if there is someone who boasts of his religious life or of whatever good works he has without humility, let him pay careful attention and tremble, because pride cast the archangel himself down from heaven. And if it cast down one so great and so exalted, do you, who are earth and ashes, hope that you can climb into heaven with pride?

Therefore, let each person examine his conscience. If he recognizes that the evil of pride rules within him, let him hasten to the remedy of humility; for if he wishes to persist in pride until the end of his life, he must endure the punishments of hell with the devil, whose imitator he is, according to this: “Those who trust in pride fall there” (Prov. 11:28).

But those who have fewer possessions and are poor, if they wish the blessing of all the Scriptures to look upon them, should hold to true humility and hear the Lord saying to them: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Let them fear what is written: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before the Lord.”

From what I have set forth above, recognize clearly that poverty helps poor people not at all if they refuse to be humble; and that wealth harms rich people nothing if they strive to maintain humility, mercy, and justice.

### 5. Two cities made up of the humble and the proud

And because two divisions of humanity, as it were two peoples—the humble and the proud—have been constructed from the beginning of the world in two cities, one of which is called Jerusalem, interpreted as “Vision of peace,” and the other Babylon, interpreted as “Confusion,” Christ builds one and the devil the other, all who persist in pride belong to Babylon, while those who persevere in humility belong to Jerusalem.

All the saints and all the Scriptures have blessed, and continually bless, those who are humble, according to this: “Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart” (Ps. 124:4); and they have cursed, and continually curse, those who are proud.

Therefore, as I have already said, let each person return to his conscience. If he recognizes that the root of pride rules within him, then, while he is still permitted to do so and the time for doing good remains in his power, let him uproot pride with all possible speed, with God’s help, and plant humility, knowing with complete certainty that no good works he may perform can benefit him so long as he remains in the swelling of pride.

Nor should he be content merely to remove its branches through a false and pretended humility. Let him strive to tear the root from his heart if he wishes to please the one who deigns to look upon the heart. Whoever refuses to do this will be subject to the curses of all the Scriptures, and this will be fulfilled in him: “The just Lord will cut off the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128:4); and: “He will rain snares of fire upon sinners” (Ps. 10:7).

### 6. Whose necks God will cut off: the proud are stiff-necked

When sinners hear this statement, they tremble and say: If the just Lord will cut off the necks of all sinners, how will we, who are sinners, be able to escape?

Far be it that anyone should despair of the Lord’s mercy. Divine mercy quickly receives us if repentance and amendment follow. Yet in this passage he intended proud sinners to be understood, because they both defend their sin and are praised by people like themselves, who say to them, “You acted well and wisely.” You rejoice in answering and defending yourself in this way because you seem to have defeated another person, but you do not grieve because you have been defeated by the vice of pride. How much better it would have been for you to follow Christ in humility than to be trampled under the feet of the devil through pride.

“The Lord,” he says, “will cut off the necks of sinners.” That this ought and can be understood not of all sinners, but only of the proud, recognize from the part of the body that is struck. He did not say, “The just Lord will cut off the hands or feet of sinners,” but “the necks of sinners.” Why is this? Because all the proud are stiff-necked. Therefore understand that only the proud are to be struck by this blow.

Those who are humble should give thanks to God and remain humble until the end of their lives, so that the blessing of the angels, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the Scriptures—which is given to all who persevere in humility—may come upon them. With these blessings may they attain eternal rewards, and may this be fulfilled in them: “The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the just” (Prov. 10:6).

But those who recognize that the tyranny of pride rules within them should, as we have already said above, reject the arrogant exaltation by which they had destroyed within themselves the temples of the Lord, and hasten to establish in themselves the foundation of true humility. Thus, through humility, they may deserve to rise to glory, having fallen through pride into ruin.

### 7. Neither greed exists without pride, nor love without humility

But while we are speaking about the accursed evil of pride and the good of humility that must be sought, someone may perhaps think within himself and say: Why does he speak in this sermon only about these two, and say nothing about love, the foundation of good things, or greed, the root of all evils?

We sometimes do this, dearest brothers, because those two cannot exist without these other two. For neither has greed ever been able to exist, nor will it ever be able to exist, without pride; nor has love ever been able to exist, nor will it ever be able to exist, without humility.

Thus, whoever praises humility also preaches with it the love from which humility is born. Conversely, whoever condemns pride also condemns greed, without which pride cannot exist.

[Col. 2313] Just as love and humility are like two wings by which humble souls are lifted to heaven—and if one is lacking, the other can accomplish nothing—so, conversely, greed and pride are shown to be like two fetters. With these fetters the unhappy souls of the proud, while they raise themselves up through arrogance, descend by God’s just judgment into the depths of hell.

Therefore, whenever in the divine Scriptures or in any preaching you hear praises of humility, recognize there also the praises of love. Conversely, understand that condemnation of pride includes the execration of greed. And because pride is born from greed, while humility is generated from love, they are so joined to one another that neither mother can exist without her daughter.

Whoever, then, desires to be freed from the evil of pride should first strive to extinguish within himself the greed from which it is born. Conversely, whoever desires continually to obtain true humility should faithfully preserve love, its mother.

Therefore, with all our strength let us implore God’s mercy to free us from the evil of pride and greed and, in his mercy, to grant us the good of humility and love. Let us not imitate the devil, the prince of pride, and descend into hell; but, following Christ, the teacher of humility, may we deserve to ascend into heaven.

May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCXCVII

[Note: [Col. 2313] Elsewhere, On the Season, 213.]

On Humility and the Fear of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 2313] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It was considered doubtful by the Louvain scholars and spurious by Verlinus and Windingus. It is compiled from chapters 10 and 15 of Alcuin’s work *On Virtues and Vices*; and in its conclusion it repeats certain matters from chapter 7 of the Rule of Benedict in almost the same words.]

### 1. God demands humility from his own. By this virtue heaven is climbed. Without it there is neither the grace of the Holy Spirit nor the light of truth; nothing is good. What avails before God

The prophet and psalmist David, who, as Scripture testifies, was chosen according to God’s heart and fulfilled all his wishes, himself shows us in a certain passage what our Creator seeks and loves in these matters, saying: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the humble in heaven and on earth?” (Ps. 112:5–6).

If, then, the Most High Lord, whose excellence and greatness have no end, considers and approves humility in every creature of his—in both those established in the heights and those established in the depths, namely, in angels and human beings—how necessary it is for us always to strive for humility and preserve it in everything, so that we may thus please our Creator.

How great is the virtue of true humility can easily be recognized from the Lord’s words. To condemn the pride of the Pharisees, he said: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

By the steps of humility one climbs to the heights of heaven, because the exalted God is reached not through pride but through humility. Of him it is said: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Hence it is also said in the Psalms: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble; but he knows the proud from afar” (Ps. 137:6). “The exalted” means the proud. He regards the humble in order to raise them up; he knows the exalted—that is, the proud—in order to cast them down.

Let us learn humility, by which we can draw near to God, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

Through pride the wondrous company of angels fell from heaven; through the humility of God, the frailty of human nature ascended into heaven. Humility is an honorable practice among human beings, as Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace; but where there is humility, there is wisdom” (Prov. 11:2).

Again, another Wise Man says: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3:20). Again, God says through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Whoever is not humble and quiet cannot have the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelling in him. God became humble for the sake of our salvation; let proud humanity be ashamed. To the extent that the heart is bent downward through humility, it advances upward in glory. For whoever is humble will be exalted in glory.

The first step of humility is to hear the word of truth humbly, retain it in memory, and willingly put it into practice. Truth flees a mind that it does not find humble. The humbler a person is about himself, the greater he will be in God’s sight. But the prouder he appears among human beings, the more cast down he will be before God.

Whoever performs good works without humility carries dust into the wind. Scripture also says: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10:9)—when what appears to be gathered through fasts or almsgiving is scattered by the wind of pride.

Do not, O human being, glory in your virtues, because you will have another judge, not yourself. In his sight, strive to humble yourself in your heart, so that he may exalt you at the time of his judgment and reward.

Descend in order to ascend; humble yourself in order to be exalted, lest, having been exalted, you be humbled. Whoever is contemptible in his own eyes is beautiful before God; and those who displease themselves please God. Be small, therefore, in your own eyes, so that you may be great in the eyes of God. You will be that much more precious to God the more despicable you are in your own eyes.

When you are in the highest honor, let your humility be greatest. Praise belongs to honor; virtue belongs to humility.

### 2. There is no humility without fear of God. One fear belongs to sons, another to servants. The fear of God drives out sins—and therefore also the fear of hell

But no one can possess this virtue of true humility without the fear of God, because neither of these can exist without the other. What the fear of God accomplishes, brothers, listen.

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). It is a great safeguard against sin always to fear God’s presence. Whoever perfectly fears God carefully guards himself from sins. “It will be well with the one who fears God at the end” (Ecclus. 1:13), and his reward endures for ever.

If someone is ashamed to sin in the presence of a human being, how much more ought he to be ashamed to commit iniquity in the presence of God, who considers not only deeds but also hearts?

Those who fear God with holy fear seek what is pleasing to him. One fear belongs to sons, another to servants. Servants fear their masters because of punishments; sons fear because of love for their father. If we are children of God, let us fear him through the sweetness of love, not through the bitterness of fear.

A wise person fears God in all his works, knowing that he can never escape his presence, as the psalmist says to God: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 138:7). Again: “For neither from east nor from west …” (Ps. 74:7); that is, no place is open to one fleeing from God.

Whoever fears the Lord will receive his instruction, and whoever watches over his commandments will find everlasting blessing (Ecclus. 32:18). Blessed is the soul of the one who fears God (ibid. 34:17), and it remains safe from diabolical temptation.

“Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14), and to whom it has been granted always to keep the fear of God before his eyes. Whoever fears the Lord turns away from the evil path and directs his ways toward the path of the virtues.

The fear of God repels sins and adds virtues. Fear makes a person cautious and concerned lest he sin. Where the fear of God is absent, there life is dissolute. Whoever does not fear God in prosperity should fear him at least in adversity; let him flee to the one who chastises and heals.

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly desires his commandments” (Ps. 111:1). The fear of God drives out the fear of hell, because it makes a person avoid sin and increase works of justice. After this he will attain that fear which is called holy and endures for ever and ever (Ps. 18:10), because it exists in love.

### 3. From this come peace and every good

Therefore, brothers, let us fear God in such a way that we love him, because perfect love casts out servile fear (1 John 4:18). In this way we can possess an abundance of security and a fullness of every good.

Hence the prophet says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing. The rich have been poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good” (Ps. 33:10–11).

Therefore, beloved, I beseech you always to keep the fear of God before the eyes of your minds and entirely to flee forgetfulness of God’s commandments. Diligently consider how those who fear God and obey his commandments go to eternal life, while those who despise him and reject his commandments go to eternal punishment.

Hold true humility inwardly in your hearts, and manifest it in your conduct before your neighbors without pretense, so that they too, instructed by your good examples, may glorify God and strive with you to receive an eternal reward in heaven.

By the favor of our Lord, and so forth.

## SERMON CCXCVIII

[Note: [Col. 2315] Elsewhere, On the Season, 111.]

On Temporal Adversity

[Note: [Col. 2315] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain scholars regarded it as doubtful; Verlinus and Windingus considered it spurious. Baronius, however, judging it genuine, referred it to the time of the Vandal siege and inserted it whole in his Annals under the year 430 as the latest of all Augustine’s sermons. But its thoroughly Caesarian manner of speaking requires that it be assigned elsewhere; and there seems no doubt that it concerns the period of the siege of Arles by the Frankish army against the Goths. We have descriptions of the calamities of that time in the first book of the Life of Caesarius, section 15 and following, and also in Cassiodorus, Variorum, book 3, letters 32 and 40, from which Baronius gave certain excerpts under the year 508. For number 1, see Augustine, Sermon 311, section 14; for number 3, Sermon 29 of the Appendix, section 2; Sermon 17, section 3; Sermon 244, section 3; Sermon 269, section 3; and Sermon 274, section 2.]

### 1. Calamities must be attributed to our sins. What they produce in the good and the wicked. The world’s hope is bitter

Whenever, dearest brothers, some adversities come upon us—whenever hostility, drought, or pestilence is inflicted upon us by God’s just judgment—we must attribute this not to his injustice but to our sins, because, as the Apostle says, “God is not unjust, who inflicts wrath” (Rom. 3:5).

The world has been shaken by the evil morals and outcries of many. So that everyone may understand this, I will explain it more plainly to your Charity. The good and the wicked are like two vessels that are full, one containing rot and the other precious spices. When they are winnowed with the same fan, the vessel containing the spices gives off a desirable fragrance, while the other gives off an intolerable stench.

So the good and the wicked are disturbed together indiscriminately, but separated by God’s profound judgment. Whenever some tribulation comes upon the world, those who are good, like holy vessels, give thanks to God, who deigns to chastise them. But those who are proud, lustful, and greedy blaspheme and murmur against God, saying: “O God, what great evil are we doing that we should suffer such things?”

Thus it often happens that these unhappy people, bound by love of this life, can retain neither this life nor avoid losing the eternal one, from which pain and groaning will flee. Worse still, they cannot escape the present evils, and their crimes cause them to arrive at those that are eternal.

I say this not in mockery, but with groaning and grief. Behold, in the person who refuses to correct himself in a proud and rebellious spirit, this is fulfilled: “Let the one who is filthy become filthier still; but let the just person act more justly, and the holy person become holier” (Rev. 22:11).

The hope of the good is not placed in this world. “Hope that is seen,” says the Apostle, “is not hope” (Rom. 8:24), because even the worldly hope that is visible is truly bitter. The world offers a bitter drink to those who love it.

O unhappy human race! The world is bitter, yet it is loved. Imagine how it would be loved if it were sweet!

### 2. A description of dreadful devastation

Truth addresses you, lovers of the world: Where is what you loved? [Col. 2316] Where is what you regarded as so important? Where is what you refused to abandon? Where are all those regions, where are so many splendid cities?

These things are said with mourning rather than mockery. They would be judged with deep emotion if they were merely heard. But when dreadful calamity and siege have struck our eyes, and pestilence now afflicts us, scarcely have those who seemed to remain been able to attend to the burial of the bodies of the dead.

Considering also those evils inflicted by God’s just judgment, when entire provinces were led into captivity, we endured seeing mothers of families carried away and pregnant women cut open. Nurses had infants torn from their hands and thrown into the streets, and they were permitted neither to keep their children alive nor to bury them when dead.

[Note: [Col. 2316] Perhaps, “they were permitted.”]

Great torture and grief, fear and horror, pressed upon the heart at once as tormentors, especially when barbarian power wickedly demanded such things of women who knew themselves to have been mistresses of many slaves and suddenly, without any price being paid, mourned themselves as barbarian handmaids.

Thus was fulfilled in us what was said through the prophet David: “You sold your people for no price, and there was no multitude in their exchanges” (Ps. 43:13). Hard servitude was exacted from delicate and noble women by the barbarians without any human compassion.

The din of this outcry presses upon our ears as we hear and see such things. Are human bodies made of iron, even if an iron servant [or: iron spirit/sense] is found in some people?

[Note: [Col. 2316] In B. a marginal note reads perhaps “spirit.” Morel, in *Eem. Critic.*, p. 155, judges that *sensus* should be read here instead of *servus*: more correctly, M.]

Who, hearing and seeing these things, would not grieve? Therefore, with the prophet we can say: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for those slain of the daughter of my people?” (Jer. 9:1).

We speak to Christians not only of the death of bodies but also of souls. We know that many, during this visitation, were taken from this life without the sacrament of Baptism itself and left among the vessels of wrath.

What grief could be more fitting, what lamentation more exalted, than when the wrath of the Almighty burned so fiercely that he even rejected his own tabernacle in which he had dwelt among human beings? And he who did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all (Rom. 8:32), did not even take account of the price of such blood, sparing no church, no clergy, no consecrated virgin, no city?

### 3. The yoke of Christ is easy. Many prefer to it the yoke of greed

We, dearest brothers, whom the Lord deigns to spare not because of our merits but to reserve still for repentance, must consider with great fear the examples presented to us by these events.

Therefore, may their death advance our salvation; may their tribulation be our correction; let us make medicines for our wounds from the wounds of others. Let us always fear what the Lord said in the Gospel: “Do you think that these Galileans were greater sinners than all the others because they suffered such things? I tell you, no; but unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way” (Luke 13:2, 5).

Therefore, let the one who used to be lustful become chaste; the proud, humble; the envious, kind; and the one who used to seize other people’s property through fraud or slander should begin to give more generous alms from his own possessions.

Our Lord does not demand anything excessively difficult of us, dearest brothers. He did not say to us, “Fast more than you can, and keep vigil beyond what your strength can endure.” He does not say to us, “Abstain from wine or meat.” Such things are not demanded of us. Rather, he deigns to command what all people can fulfill, with his grace, without great labor.

But, worst of all, many people are willing to bear the very hard and bitter yoke of greed with great labor, while they refuse to place upon their shoulders Christ’s sweet yoke and his light burden. They prefer to collapse beneath a heavy load with many sins rather than take up Christ’s yoke, which can [Col. 2317] lift them into heaven.

But you, brothers, reflecting wisely and faithfully with us, break from your necks the hard and harsh yoke of greed, and place Christ’s sweetest yoke upon your shoulders. According to the Apostle, lift your manner of life toward heaven (Phil. 3:20), so that, when Christ, your life, appears, you too may appear with him in glory (Col. 3:4).

He himself will grant this, and so forth.

## SERMON CCXCIX

[Note: [Col. 2317] It bears the name of Caesarius in the manuscripts and is his twenty-sixth homily in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. For number 3, see Sermon 141, sections 4 and 5; for number 4, see the *Life of Caesarius*, book 1, section 30.]

On Hungering and Thirsting for the Word of God

### 1. What it means to hunger for righteousness. The people’s right to demand the word of God from the priest

Among the other beatitudes that our Lord and Savior deigned to enumerate in the Gospel, he also added this, saying: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

Happy are those to whom God deigns to grant this excellent hunger and desirable thirst. But how does one hunger for righteousness, brothers? You hunger for righteousness if you are willing to hear the word of God patiently and willingly. For of such food it is said: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Ecclus. 24:29).

Although doing is better than knowing, knowing must nevertheless come before doing; for the one who desires to fulfill something must first learn it. Finally, hear Scripture saying: “Everyone who has not learned righteousness upon the earth will not practice truth.” And again: “Zeal will seize an unlearned people, and fire will consume the adversaries.” In this passage it is called “adversarial fire” because it is understood to belong not to Christ’s side but to the devil’s.

And again: “Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon [or judge] the earth” (Wis. 1:1).

[Note: [Col. 2317] Manuscript *t.* reads “you who judge.”]

It is therefore evident that the one who desires to learn righteousness is the one who hungers for righteousness. We must first learn, so that afterward we may deserve to fulfill it.

Therefore, so that this beatitude may be fulfilled in you by God’s grace, if, as we believe, you truly hunger and thirst for righteousness, whenever the word of God has been preached to you later than usual, do not wait for us to offer it to you without your asking. Rather, you yourselves should faithfully and thirstily demand it from us, as something rightfully owed to you.

## 2. The Obligation of Priests to Deliver It; God’s Word as Money to Be Doubled

For if we always wished to offer it freely, and you, whenever we were slow, did not wish to demand it, we might perhaps be judged importunate by those who do not know our danger. But whoever knows well how heavy a burden threatens the necks of priests understands that, however constantly we preach the word of God, we nevertheless render less than we ought.

For the Holy Spirit testifies to priests through the prophet: “Cry out, do not cease”; he does not say, “Cry out after many days,” but “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their sins” (Isaiah 58:1). And again: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18). And the Apostle says: “Remember me, because for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears” (Acts 20:31).

If the Apostle preached the word of God day and night in order to absolve himself before God, what will become of us, who scarcely provide spiritual pastures for the flock entrusted to us even after many days? And for this reason the same Apostle solemnly charges Timothy, saying: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his coming and his kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:1). And as though he were asked why he prefaced his words with so fearsome an adjuration, he continued: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, beseech, rebuke” (ibid., 2).

What does “in season and out of season” mean except “in season for those who are willing, out of season for those who are unwilling”? The word of God must be offered to those willing to hear it; to those who find it wearisome, it must be pressed upon them—lest perhaps, standing against us before the tribunal of Christ, they say that they were not admonished by us, and the blood of their souls be required from our hands.

Therefore we must weigh this with great trembling, lest that terrifying sentence also be directed against us which the servant deserved to hear who refused to double the talent he had received: “Wicked and lazy servant,” he said, “why did you not give my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might have recovered it with interest?” (Matthew 25:26–27). And what follows? May God avert this from us: “Throw the useless servant,” he says, “into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 30).

Why, he says, did you not give my money to the money-changers? Beloved, by “money” nothing else is understood except that which is preached in the Church. The money-changers who ought to receive the money are none other than the Christian peoples. For just as it will be a grave sin for us not to have placed the Lord’s money upon the table of your hearts, so, conversely, a considerable danger threatens each one of you if he is unwilling to double by good works what he has received in words.

## 3. It Is Food for the Soul

Since, then, you have recognized both our danger and your own, whenever it happens that the word of God is administered to you more slowly, take this amiss just as you would if the substance of your daily nourishment were withdrawn from your body. For hunger of the body ought not to be greater among us than hunger of the soul. Indeed, the more we know the soul to be nobler, the greater concern we ought to have for its nourishment.

If our flesh is refreshed twice a day, why should anyone consider it troublesome or absurd if the soul is fed with the word of God only after seven days? For just as the flesh is refreshed by this earthly food, so the soul is nourished by the word of God. Therefore, whenever it is offered to you more slowly, rouse our sluggishness by your holy persistence, and demand what is rightfully owed to you.

## 4. Priests Should Prepare the Milk of God’s Word Like Cows; the People Should Eagerly Seek It Like Calves. Caesarius Welcomes Being Troubled in This Matter

Priests in the Church seem to bear the likeness of cows, while the Christian peoples present the type of calves. For just as cows run through fields and meadows and go around vineyards and olive groves, so that, after feeding on grasses and leaves, they may prepare nourishment in the form of milk for their calves, so priests, by reading constantly in the various mountains of the sacred Scriptures, ought to pluck flowers from which they can provide spiritual milk to their children, so that they may share in the lot of the Apostle Paul, who said: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

Not inappropriately, dearest brothers, priests seem to bear the likeness of cows. For just as a cow has two udders from which it feeds its calf, so priests ought to nourish the Christian people from two breasts, namely, the Old and the New Testament.

Consider, nevertheless, brothers, and see that these physical cows not only come themselves to their calves, but their calves also run to meet them and so frequently strike their mothers’ udders with their heads that sometimes, if the calves are larger, they seem to lift their mothers’ bodies from the ground. Yet the cows willingly endure this very injury, because they desire to see the growth of their calves.

Good priests also ought faithfully to desire and wish this: that their children should trouble them with continual questions for the sake of their souls’ salvation; so that, while divine grace is granted to the children who knock, an eternal reward may be prepared for the priests who reveal the secrets of the sacred Scriptures.

I say this so that this likeness may be preserved both in us and in you. We desire to endure from you this welcome disturbance, provided that we may deserve to see your souls advance in the love of Christ. Therefore, just as it is advantageous for us to gather the flowers of the Scriptures and prepare spiritual food, so it is necessary for you to seek it with great eagerness. For just as calves customarily trouble their mothers’ udders with great force so that they may draw from within them the food they need, so Christian peoples ought to provoke their priests, as the breasts of the holy Church, by continual questioning, so that they may acquire food for their salvation and provide the nourishment necessary for their souls.

Otherwise, if priests should wish to offer it slowly, and peoples, occupied by excessive entanglements with this world, should disdain to inquire, what is written may be fulfilled: “I will send a famine upon the land,” he says, “not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

Nevertheless, we trust in God’s mercy that he will grant both us zeal for reading and preaching and you a desire to hear, so that before the tribunal of the eternal Judge we may be able to give a good account of our preaching, and you may be able to attain eternal rewards for your gracious obedience and perseverance in good works—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 300

*[Note: [Col. 2319] Elsewhere, 26 among the Fifty Homilies.]*

### How God’s Word Should Be Received

*[Note: [Col. 2319] In the manuscripts the title is: “An admonition that silence be maintained in church.” In the printed editions: “On permission and prohibition concerning sitting in church when readings are being read or the word of God is preached.”]*

*[Note: [Col. 2319] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition its authenticity is uncertain; Verlin and Vinding judged it spurious. Its style and subject matter are scarcely Augustinian, but are thoroughly Caesarian. For no. 1, see Sermon 265 of the Appendix, no. 3; for no. 4, Sermons 285, no. 3, and 301, no. 5; for no. 5, Sermons 249, no. 2; 281, no. 3; 282, no. 4.]*

## 1. His Fatherly Concern for the Weak; He Rebukes Women Lying on the Ground as Though in Beds

Some days ago, out of fatherly concern, I gave advice and, in a certain sense, pleaded on behalf of those who either have pain in their feet or suffer from some bodily infirmity: when lengthy Passions, or at least some longer readings, are being read, those who cannot stand should sit humbly and quietly and, with attentive ears, listen to what is being read.

Now, however, some of our daughters think that this should be done either by all women or at least by many who are physically healthy. For whenever the word of God begins to be recited, they want to lie on the ground as though in their own little beds. And would that they merely lay there and received the word of God with a thirsty heart in silence! But they occupy themselves with such idle conversations that they neither hear what is preached themselves nor allow others to hear it.

Therefore I beg you, venerable daughters, and admonish you with fatherly concern: whenever readings are being read or the word of God is being preached, let no woman throw herself upon the ground—unless perhaps an exceedingly serious illness compels her to do so; and even then, she should not lie down but rather sit, and receive with eager heart and attentive ears what is preached.

## 2. The Word of God Is in No Way Less Than the Body of Christ; It Must Not Be Received with Less Reverence

I ask you, brothers and sisters—tell me: what seems to you to be greater, the word of God or the body of Christ? If you wish to answer truthfully, you must certainly say that the word of God is not less than the body of Christ.

And therefore, with whatever concern we observe, when the body of Christ is administered to us, that nothing of it should fall from our hands upon the ground, with the same concern let us observe that the word of God which is distributed to us should not perish from our heart while we think or speak of something else. For the one who has heard the word of God carelessly will be no less guilty than the one who through negligence has allowed the body of Christ to fall upon the ground.

## 3. The Preacher as Distributor of Spiritual Gems

I would nevertheless like to know whether, from the hour when the word of God began to be preached, if we always wished to distribute the most precious gems, earrings, or golden rings, our daughters would be willing to stand or receive them. Without any doubt, they would receive what was offered to them with great eagerness. But because we neither can nor ought to offer bodily ornaments, we are therefore not heard gladly.

Yet it is not right that those who administer spiritual things should be judged superfluous. Whoever gladly hears the word of God should not doubt that he has received earrings for his soul, sent from the homeland of paradise. Whoever is admonished to give something to the poor, while he stretches out his hand for almsgiving, will receive bracelets sent by Christ.

For just as the flesh is adorned for a short time with earthly ornaments, so that it may please bodily eyes either for its own ruin or for the ruin of others who wrongly desire it, so the holy soul is adorned with divine sayings as with spiritual and eternal pearls of good works, so that, happily adorned, it may arrive at the company and wedding feast of that heavenly Bridegroom. Thus it will not be said to it as it is written in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew 22:12). Let it not, stripped of the ornaments of good works and naked, deserve to hear: “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 13). Rather, in return for the adornment of good works, let this desirable voice be directed to it: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

## 4. Like a Mother Eager to Adorn Her Daughter; What Reward She Seeks for Her Labor

I ask you, daughters, listen carefully to what is said by us. If a mother wished to adorn her daughter with her own hands, and the daughter, despising the ornaments she received, repeatedly bent toward the ground and moved restlessly here and there so that her mother could not adorn her according to her wishes, would she not justly be rebuked or beaten?

Think of me, then, as the mother of your souls, and as wishing to arrange you in such a way that no stain or wrinkle might appear in you before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. Desiring to provide your souls not only with ornaments but also with remedies, I strive to sew what has been torn, mend what has been ripped, heal what has been wounded, wash what is dirty, restore what has been lost, and adorn what is whole with spiritual pearls.

If I am not wearied, why should anyone wish to receive these things with disgust? Since earthly and temporal bodily ornaments, if no one is found willing to give them, are purchased at a very high price, how much more is it right that the eternal ornaments of souls—sought by us with no small labor and offered to your spirits without any price—should be received by you with perfect love?

For, while procuring pearls for you from the homeland of paradise, we wish to receive no other reward in this world than to see you listen patiently and gladly to what is commended to you, and, with God’s help, fulfill it in works according to your strength.

## 5. Conclusion

Dearest brothers and venerable daughters, we do not say these things because we have discovered that you do not gladly receive the word of God. By God’s favor, our soul rejoices and exults in your obedience more than can be thought or expressed. But because we wish you always to ascend toward better things, with fatherly concern we presume to admonish you even about those things which we know you already practice perfectly.

And because not all the men and women wished to gather today for the vigils, I ask you, sons and daughters, to report with complete faithfulness what has been said to you to those who were absent, so that you may receive a reward not only for your own correction but also for the correction of others.

# SERMON 301

*[Note: [Col. 2320] Elsewhere, 36 among the Vignerian sermons.]*

### An Admonition That Preaching, Even When Harsh, Should Not Only Not Be Rejected for the Soul’s Salvation but Should Be Sought with Ardent Desire

*[Note: [Col. 2320] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. In some manuscripts and in Vignerius’s Supplement it is wrongly attributed to Augustine. It is Caesarius’s in the Library of the Fathers, homily 15; and it certainly contains many Caesarian turns of expression, which are interwoven with his other genuine sermons and with the speech he delivered in the case of the bishop Contumeliosus. For no. 1, see Sermons 249 of the Appendix, no. 1, and 295, no. 7; for no. 2, see the same Sermon 295, no. 4, and Sermon 68, no. 3; for no. 3, Sermons 34, no. 6, and 22, no. 4; for no. 5, Sermon 249, no. [sic].]*

## 1. A Priest Must Not Be Negligent; Let Him Fear the Punishments of Eli; Phinehas Is Praised for His Severity

Whenever, dearest brothers, for both your salvation and mine it is necessary for me to preach something hard or harsh, you ought to receive it calmly and patiently, considering my danger; for harsh preaching provides medicine for the sick and fashions ornaments for the healthy.

It is no light matter that the Holy Spirit threatens the priests of the Lord through the prophet. “If,” he says, “you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18). And again: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their sins” (Isaiah 58:1). There is also that exceedingly fearful word spoken in the Gospel to the negligent priest: “Wicked servant, why did you not give my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might have recovered it with interest?” And what follows? “Throw the useless servant,” he says, “into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 25:26–27, 30).

See what sentence the negligent priest will endure if he is unwilling to preach the word of God constantly. Therefore, dearest brothers, whenever I humbly suggest something harsh to you for the salvation of your souls, I absolve my conscience before God. For I fear, and I am exceedingly terrified, by the example of the priest Eli. When he heard that his sons were committing adulteries, he neglected either to beat them or to suspend them from communion, but only admonished them lightly, saying: “Sons, it is not good what I hear about you. If a man sins against a man, the priest will pray for him; but if the priest himself has offended, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:23–25).

Yet, although he said this, because he did not restrain them with great severity, he himself later fell backward from his seat, died with his neck broken, and his name was erased from the book of life; in one day thirty thousand of the people were killed, his two sons were slain, and the Ark of the Covenant was captured by the enemies (ibid., 4).

See how grave an evil was brought about through the negligence of the priest, who was unwilling to fear what was said above: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand.” This exceedingly terrifying sentence causes me intolerable fear, and therefore compels me to be importunate with you and to cry out frequently.

And since you have heard how grievous a wound the negligent priest suffered, look at what Phinehas the priest, who maintained holy severity, deserved to hear from the Lord. When he had struck down and killed two adulterers at one blow, he deserved to hear the Lord say: “Phinehas the priest, moved by my zeal, has turned away my anger, so that I would not destroy the people” (Numbers 25:11). Therefore it is written in that very Psalm: “Phinehas stood up and interceded, and the plague ceased; and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation forever” (Psalm 105:30–31).

## 2. When Rebuked, Sinners Reply That They Are Not Alone; How Foolish This Is

But when sinners are chastised for their crimes, what is worse is that not all receive it humbly and obediently. Rather, there are many who do not blush to respond with the most shameless face, saying: “Was I the only one who did this? Did this one and that one not commit similar or worse things? Do not clerics of even higher rank do such things?” *[Note: [Col. 2321] Thus from the manuscript of the College of Clermont, with the added particle “not”: “Did this one and that one not commit similar or worse things? Do clerics of even higher rank not do such things?”]*

Unhappy man! Is a crowd of sinners a consolation to you? *[Note: [Col. 2321] The same manuscript reads: “a crowd of wretched people.”]* Will each sinner therefore be tormented any less if countless multitudes of sinners begin to suffer eternal punishment together with him?

How much better it would be for each person, fleeing the evils of his sins, to cry out in humble confession: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you’” (Psalm 41:5); and: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 51:5). He should rather follow, as a remedy for his soul, the examples of those who, after many sins, were converted to a good life, instead of proposing for imitation those whose brief joy is followed by punishment without end.

## 3. They Add That the Fortunes of the Wicked Are Not Less Prosperous; Why This Happens; The Necessity of Affliction

Criminals or negligent people who despair of God’s justice also commonly say, with profane presumption, that many who commit such crimes, or perhaps worse ones, suffer no evil in this world, but remain healthy and wealthy in complete prosperity.

O unhappy and deeply lamentable presumption! Do the proud and impious who commit capital crimes therefore seem blessed to you because they suffer no evil in this world? Hear Scripture speaking about such people: “They are not in the troubles of men, and they will not be scourged with men; therefore pride has possessed them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity has come forth as though from fatness” (Psalm 73:5–7).

For this reason they are by no means scourged in this world: because, on account of the enormity of their crimes, they are being reserved for eternal punishment. They could not be chastised for a short time, since they will have to be tormented without end.

For our Lord and God, who in his justice refrains from chastising these people, does not cease to exercise his children through various tribulations, according to what is written: “The Lord scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6); and: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

If he scourges every son whom he receives, then the one whom he does not scourge he does not receive; and if he disciplines everyone whom he loves, then the one whom he does not discipline he does not love. And that this is so does not result from God’s power *[Note: [Col. 2322] Manuscript rm. reads: “it operates through injustice.”]*, but from the wickedness of those who deserve to endure it, according to what is written: “Let the filthy still be filthy, and let the righteous still practice righteousness” (Revelation 22:11).

## 4. We Must Provide Here for Remedies That Will Last Forever

Let the person who thinks he sins less in comparison with worse people consider these things more carefully and attentively. While this sinful soul is still contained in this fragile little body, let him provide for himself remedies that will last forever. Otherwise, if he takes delight in being clothed for a short time in purple and fine linen and in serving pleasure or luxury amid riches and delicacies, it will later be necessary for him, amid the flames of hell and without any remedy remaining, to ask for a drop of refreshment. *[Note: [Col. 2322] Thus from the manuscript of the College of Clermont: “to serve luxury unfaithfully.”]*

But when the luxurious hear these things, like madmen who have lost their sound judgment, they customarily laugh at and mock those who preach such matters to them with great labor. Let them laugh as much as they wish; on our behalf we have the Lord responding: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5). And they have the Lord saying to them: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep; woe to you who are filled, for you shall hunger” (Luke 6:25).

Let the proud mock us, then. Nevertheless, for their salvation, though we are less worthy, let us plead for God’s mercy day and night with groaning and lamentation, trusting in his ineffable compassion: that he may soon deign to discipline them as his children, so that through that very discipline they may be recalled from the precipice of every sin and, practicing worthy repentance, deserve to receive eternal rewards with the saints. This can happen truly only when the sinner flees without any delay to the remedies of repentance. *[Note: [Col. 2322] The manuscripts read “nevertheless” instead of “only.”]*

## 5. Priests Are Spiritual Physicians; In What Respect They Excel Physicians of the Body
