You, dearest brothers, recognizing how heavy a burden threatens the necks of priests, from whom the souls of all will be required, as we have already suggested above, and seeing what evils the negligent priest Eli suffered and what glory Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, received when the Lord rewarded him, receive according to your custom what is preached to you, even if at times it seems bitter and harsh.

For you yourselves know well that physicians do not always offer sweet potions to the sick, but frequently bitter and harsh ones; sometimes they even cut certain limbs with surgical instruments and burn them with cauteries. Those who are ill endure all this patiently, because after brief tribulation they desire to recover lasting health.

Therefore we too, who, although less worthy, nevertheless seem to be spiritual physicians of some sort, must not always administer things agreeable and gentle, but at times things harsh or hard, to those who appear to be sick in soul. For just as bad humors are expelled by a very bitter potion, so the worst habits are diminished by harsh correction.

For what of this, dearest brothers? When physicians of the body neglect to visit the sick, they are begged with great humility, rewards and gifts are promised them, and yet it is uncertain whether their medicines will accomplish anything. But we, who have no despair whatsoever concerning spiritual medicine and seek neither earthly reward nor any temporal profit—must we therefore be treated with distaste because we offer ourselves freely and desire to find nothing in the sick except repentance *[Note: [Col. 2323] Some manuscripts read “patience.”]* and correction?

For it is uncertain whether a bodily physician can restore the sick person; but if spiritual medicine is gladly received, the soul is raised up without any doubt, even if it has been wounded by many sins, even if it is dead.

Why, then, when bodily health is sought at such great expense and with many pains, and the health of souls is given without any expense, is it not gladly received by some? Why is this, dearest brothers? Because there are many who take greater care of their flesh than of their soul.

Yet they ought always to devote greater concern to the soul, in which the image of God exists. For when the flesh, which is now loved so much, begins to be devoured by worms in the grave, the soul is presented to God by the angels in heaven. There, if it has been good, it is crowned; but if evil, it is thrown into darkness.

Concerning those darknesses, let us pray more attentively that God may deign to free us, he who lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 302

*[Note: [Col. 2323] Elsewhere, On the Seasons, 112.]*

### On the Pursuit of Wisdom, Reading, and Meditation on God’s Law

*[Note: [Col. 2323] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors doubted its authenticity, but Vinding, following Verlin, rejected it, observing that it had been copied from Alcuin’s book On the Virtues and Vices, chapters 1 and 5.]*

## 1. Nothing Is Better Than Knowledge of God; True Knowledge; Perfect Wisdom; Blessed Life

It is necessary, dearest brothers, that with a pure heart and chaste body you love to learn divine wisdom and desire to understand it, because this knowledge is granted to those who faithfully seek it *[Note: [Col. 2323] Erasmus reads: “to those who seek it faithfully.”]* and meditate upon it diligently. *[Note: [Col. 2323] “It would be better to read ‘is granted’ instead of ‘grants.’ M.”]*

There is nothing better than knowledge of God, because nothing is more blessed, and it is itself true blessedness. Therefore the Savior also says to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

Hear, then, how this wisdom is attained. First of all, a person must seek to know what true knowledge and true wisdom are, because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19).

True knowledge is to withdraw from the service of the devil, which consists in sins; and perfect wisdom is to worship God according to the truth of his commandments. For blessed life is acquired in these two things, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 34:15).

Nor is it sufficient for anyone not to do evil unless he also does good; nor is it sufficient to do good unless he also refrains from evil. Therefore everyone who is wise in this way will undoubtedly be blessed forever.

Blessed life is knowledge of divinity; knowledge of divinity is the strength for good works; and the strength of good works is the fruit of eternal blessedness.

## 2. How Many Benefits Sacred Reading of the Scriptures Confers; Its Distinction from Prayer

We still possess the good consolation of reading the divine Scriptures, because the reading of the sacred Scriptures is no small foreknowledge of divine blessedness. In them, as in a certain mirror, a person can consider himself: what he is and toward what he is tending.

Constant reading purifies everything *[Note: [Col. 2324] Alcuin reads: “the soul.”]*; it instills fear of Gehenna and stirs the heart of the reader toward heavenly joys. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and read. For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

The reading of the sacred Scriptures confers a twofold gift: both because it educates the understanding of the mind and because, drawing a person away from the vanities of the world, it leads him to the love of God.

The labor of reading is honorable and greatly contributes to the cleansing of the soul. For just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nurtured and fed by divine utterances, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 119:103).

But the one who turns the divine Scriptures into works is supremely blessed. All the holy Scriptures were plainly written for our salvation, so that we might advance through them in the recognition of truth.

A blind person stumbles more often than one who sees; so one who is ignorant of God’s law sins more often through ignorance than one who knows it. Just as a blind person scarcely travels the right road without a guide, so a person scarcely travels the right path without a teacher.

## 3. What Must Be Done After Sacred Reading

And therefore, dearest brothers, whoever among you can read and understand sacred readings should devote himself to them, so that he may frequently make use of meditation upon them. But those who cannot grasp the meaning of sacred speech from reading should listen more attentively to the interpreter, so that at least they may receive edification from it.

When, then, dearest ones, you have been instructed by heavenly teaching about what must be done and what must be avoided, let there be no delay in doing what you understand inwardly through comprehension. For, as the blessed Apostle Paul says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law” (Romans 2:13).

And Truth itself says: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten severely” (Luke 12:47). It is also written elsewhere: “For one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17).

Therefore strive with every diligence to know the will of God. Once you have come to know his will, contend with the greatest effort to do it by fulfilling his commandments, and earnestly ask that, persevering in this, you may attain his promises.

May he deign to help us in this—he who in his goodness called us, who by his grace freed us, and who promised the heavenly kingdom to those who fight the good fight—Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON 303

*[Note: [Col. 2324] It is Caesarius’s homily 20 in the Library of the Fathers. For no. 1, see Sermons 69, no. 1; 107, no. 1; 112, no. 1; and 266, no. 1 of the Appendix; for no. 2, Sermon 90, no. 6; Sermon 294, no. [sic], and 1; Sermon 295, no. 1; Sermon 141, nos. 4 and 5; Sermon 299, no. 3.]*

### An Admonition to Encourage the People to Take Care to Hear the Divine Readings, etc.

## 1. No One Is Excused from Sacred Reading; Not on Account of Lack of Time

We give thanks to God, dearest brothers, because he has deigned to present us to your holy Charity, even amid many occupations. For divine clemency knows that even if we were able to visit you only twice or three times in each year, we still could not satisfy our desires.

What father is there who does not desire to see his children frequently, especially faithful and good children? May God grant you, as you pray, that you may be able to find some good also in us, whom you have received with such love; and may we always see in you something over which we can rejoice more fully.

Since, then, we rejoice as much as is fitting over the presence of your Charity, let us speak about our common salvation as much as the Lord grants.

Whenever we say something concerning the soul’s welfare, dearest brothers, let no one attempt to excuse himself by saying: “I have no time to read, and therefore I cannot either recognize or fulfill God’s commandments.” Let none of you say: “I do not know letters; therefore whatever I fail to fulfill of God’s commandments will not be counted against me.”

This is an empty and useless excuse, dearest brothers. First, although someone who does not know letters cannot read the divine reading himself, he can nevertheless gladly listen to someone reading. And whoever knows letters—can it be that he does not find books in which he can read the divine Scripture?

Let us remove from ourselves empty stories and biting jokes; let us reject, as far as we can, idle and lustful conversations. Then let us see whether no time remains for us in which we can devote ourselves to divine reading.

Let us flee sumptuous lunches, which occupy us until evening. Let us despise dinners, which sometimes drag us even into vices until midnight, during which our flesh is weakened by drunkenness and our soul is wounded, or perhaps even killed, by shameful speech and buffoonery. Let us flee these evil occupations, which weaken both soul and body; and we shall see that time remains for us in which we can think about something concerning the soul’s salvation.

## 2. Not on Account of Inability to Read; God’s Word Is the Light and Food of the Soul

When the nights are longer, who could sleep so much that he could not either read the divine reading himself or listen to others reading for even three hours? Those are unable to read the divine reading who, as has already been said, strive to remain drunk until midnight.

But if we wish to please God and think more attentively about the salvation of our soul, we ought to love sobriety and flee drunkenness far away as though it were a pit of hell.

Attend, I beg you, brothers: I am saying what you do not fail to know. We know some merchants who, although they do not know letters, hire literate mercenaries for themselves; and although they themselves do not know letters, they acquire enormous profits while others write out their accounts. *[Note: [Col. 2325] The manuscript of the College of Clermont reads: “and although they themselves do not know letters.”]*

And if those who do not know letters hire literate mercenaries for themselves in order to acquire earthly money, you—whoever you are and do not know letters—why do you not also, with payment and a fee, ask someone to reread the divine Scriptures to you, so that from them you may acquire eternal rewards?

Certainly, brothers, the one who earnestly seeks this believes that it can benefit him forever. But whoever neither wishes to read the divine reading himself nor gladly listen to someone reading does not believe at all that he can acquire any good from it.

Therefore, brothers, I ask and admonish you: whoever among you knows letters should reread the divine Scripture frequently; those who do not know them should listen with attentive ears when others read.

For the light of the soul and eternal food is nothing other than the word of God, without which the soul can neither see nor live. For just as our flesh dies if it does not receive food, so our soul is extinguished if it does not receive the word of God.

### 3. The rustic can both hear and retain this, although he learns shameful songs

But someone says: “I am an uneducated countryman, constantly occupied with earthly work; I can neither read nor hear divine Scripture.” How many countrymen, and how many countrywomen, memorize devilish, amorous, and shameful songs and sing them aloud? They are able to retain and learn what the devil teaches, yet unable to retain what Christ reveals? How much more quickly and profitably could any countryman or countrywoman learn the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, and some antiphons, as well as Psalms 50 or 90, learn and retain them, and recite them frequently [Col. 2326]—through which they could both unite their soul to God and free it from the devil?

For just as shameful songs send people into the devil’s darkness, so holy songs reveal the light of Christ. Let no one therefore say: “I cannot retain anything of what is read in church.” Without doubt, if you are willing, you can. Begin to be willing, and immediately you will be able. And so that no one may be able to excuse himself from good works, with God’s permission I wish to offer you some sort of instruction.

### 4. Matters concerning agriculture

The care of our soul, dearly beloved brothers, is especially like the cultivation of the earth. For just as, in cultivated soil, some things are uprooted and others torn out by the roots so that good things may be sown, so it must also happen in our soul. Let evils be eradicated and good things planted; let harmful things be uprooted and useful things grafted in. Let pride be torn out and humility planted; let greed be cast away and mercy retained; let lust be despised and chastity loved.

For just as you cannot plant good things in your land unless you have cast out the bad, so you cannot plant the holy shoots of the virtues in your soul unless you have uprooted the thorns and briars of vices. Tell me, I beg you, whoever you are who a little while ago said that because you did not know how to read, you therefore could not fulfill God’s commandments: tell me, who taught you how to prune your vineyard, or when to plant a young vine? Who showed you this? You either saw it, heard it, or asked the best cultivators how you ought to tend your vineyard. How then are you so concerned about your vineyard? Why are you not equally concerned about your soul?

### 5. God’s estate and man’s estate: the care to be given to each

Pay attention, I beg you, brothers: there are two kinds of fields. One field belongs to God, the other to man. You have your estate, and God has his. Your estate is your land; God’s estate is your soul. Is it just for you to cultivate your estate while leaving God’s estate deserted? If you cultivate your land, cultivate your soul as well. You want to arrange your estate properly, yet leave God’s estate deserted? Is this just, brothers? Does God deserve this from us—that we neglect the soul which he loves so greatly?

How do you look upon your cultivated estate and rejoice? Why do you not look upon your deserted soul and mourn? From the field of our estate we shall live in this world for only a few days; therefore, in that place—that is, in our soul—we ought always to devote greater care. God has deigned to entrust our soul to us as his estate, so that we must cultivate it with every effort.

Let us therefore labor with all our strength, with God’s help, so that when God wishes to come to his field—that is, to our soul—he may find it wholly cultivated, wholly arranged, wholly ordered; may find a harvest, not thorns; wine, not vinegar; wheat rather than weeds. If he finds everything pleasing in his sight, he will repay us with eternal rewards. But if he sees everything deserted and filled with thorns, he will consign us, together with those thorns of our works, to eternal fire.

### 6. God’s emulation concerning the cultivation of the soul, and the origin of tribulations

God demands nothing difficult in this matter. This is why, brothers, we frequently endure tribulations and hardships: God in a certain way repays us in kind. We do not wish to love the soul which he loves, and he allows the estate which we love to be abandoned and perish. For in order that our land might remain deserted by enemies for a long time, our soul had remained deserted through many vices and crimes.

Because we did not love the soul which God loves, we lost everything that we loved in this world. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let us at least in this way learn to love the soul more than the flesh, and to love eternal things rather than things that pass away. Whatever we labor for on behalf of the flesh will all perish [Note: [Col. 2326] Manuscripts: “will perish.”]; this alone cannot perish: whatever each person has stored up in heaven for the salvation of his soul.

Let no one therefore excuse himself and say that he does not know how to read and therefore cannot fulfill God’s commandments. God does not require anything great from us, nothing difficult or harsh. Eternal justice cries out to you in your conscience:

“As you govern your field, govern your heart as well; as you cultivate your estate, cultivate your soul as well; as you remove useless shoots from your vine, so remove evil affections from your soul. You cut away from your vine what is bad; cut away from your soul what is wicked.

“As one who refuses to prune his vine for a year produces more abundantly in that year but afterward remains barren and without fruit, so one who does not remove evil thoughts and desires from his soul seems to produce fruit from thefts and frauds during the year of life in which he lives in this world, but afterward will remain barren forever.

“And because he did not produce legitimate fruit, like luxuriant and fruitless branches, eternal flame will torture him without mercy, as the Lord himself said: ‘But he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire’ (Matthew 3:12).

“As in your vine you cut off all the superfluous shoots, leaving two or three that are legitimate [Note: [Col. 2327] Thus the manuscript; Portarum has ‘branches.’], so in your soul you must cut away with the sword of the Holy Spirit and the sickle of the cross every desire that looks wickedly upon and most evilly covets what belongs to others, preserving only that by which justice or mercy is discerned.”

### 7. In cultivating the soul, the same principles should be observed as in agriculture. Threefold fruit and three professions: good virgins, widows, and married people

For when land is cultivated, dearly beloved brothers, you know what practice is followed. First the thorns are uprooted and the stones removed; afterward the earth itself is plowed, harrowed, and worked a third time; then, with a fourth or fifth furrow, it is sown in proper order.

Let this therefore be done in our soul, dearly beloved brothers. First let the thorns—that is, evil thoughts—be eradicated. Then let the stones be removed, that is, let every form of malice or hardness be cleansed away. Next let our heart be plowed and tilled with the Gospel plow and the share of the cross; let it be broken by repentance, softened by almsgiving, and prepared for the Lord’s seed by charity, so that the purified and well-cultivated soil of our heart may receive the seed of God’s word with joy and yield not only a thirtieth-fold fruit, but also a sixtieth- and hundredfold one.

For there are three professions in the holy Catholic Church: there are virgins, there are widows, and there are married people. Virgins produce a hundredfold, widows a sixtyfold, and married people a thirtyfold. One indeed produces more [Note: [Col. 2327] Thus from the manuscript of the College of Clermont. [“One indeed has more.”], another less; but all are stored in the heavenly granary and happily enjoy eternal blessedness.

Virgins, therefore, contemplating Mary; widows, Anna; and married women, Susanna, should imitate their chastity in this age, so that they may deserve to be joined to them forever. Good virgins—those who wish to be virgins not only in body but also in heart and tongue—are joined to holy Mary and the rest of the army of virgins.

Good widows—neither pleasure-loving, nor talkative, nor inquisitive, nor envious, nor proud, but serving God through fasts, almsgiving, and prayers, as blessed Anna did—are joined with that same holy Anna to many thousands of widows [Note: [Col. 2327] The Portarum manuscript has “quarrelsome.”].

Married people, however, who preserve fidelity to one another and know no one outside their marriage, who know one another only for the desire for children, who give alms continually, and who observe God’s commandments as far as they can, will deservedly be happily joined to holy Job, holy Sarah, or holy Susanna, together with the holy Patriarchs and Prophets.

### 8. How what has been heard in the sermon should be repeated to one another

I beg you, dearly beloved brothers, always recall and always retain what we recommend to you for the salvation of your soul. Do not receive it as something passing. Our sermon ought to strike roots in your hearts, so that at the time of recompense it may happily produce the fruit of eternal life [Col. 2328].

Whoever can retain everything we say should give thanks to God and always share with others what he remembers. Whoever cannot retain everything should at least remember some part. And if one person cannot retain it all, retain three or four statements each. While one person explains to another what he has heard, by recounting everything to one another you will be able not only to retain it by heart but also, with Christ’s help, to fulfill it in good works.

Let one say to another: “I heard my bishop speaking about chastity.” Another may say: “I remember that he also preached about almsgiving.” Another may say: “I remember that he said we should cultivate our soul as we cultivate our land.” Another may report: “I remember my bishop saying that whoever knows how to read should diligently read divine Scripture, while whoever does not know should seek out and ask someone who can reread God’s commandments to him, so that with God’s help he may fulfill what he has read.”

Another may also say: “I heard my bishop saying that, just as merchants who do not know letters hire literate wage-earners in order to acquire money, so Christians ought to seek and ask for someone—and, if necessary, even pay him—to reread divine Scripture to them; so that, just as the merchant acquires money while another reads, they may acquire eternal life.”

If you do these things and admonish one another, you will be able to live faithfully in this world and afterward attain the blessedness of eternal life. For if, immediately after leaving the church, you forget everything you heard from the bishop, you came to church without fruit and return home empty, without fruit.

But may this never happen to you, brothers. Rather, may what is written be fulfilled in you: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times” (Psalm 105:3); and this also: “But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him, and his righteousness upon children’s children, for those who keep his commandments and remember them in order to do them” (Psalm 102:17–18).

May the Lord, in his goodness, lead you to this mercy—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCCIV

[Note: [Col. 2328] Elsewhere, *On the Season*, 203.]

## On Mercy and Forgiveness

[Note: [Col. 2328] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors had left it doubtful among the Augustinian works; later others observed that it was composed from chapters 7 and 8 of Alcuin’s *On Virtues and Vices*.]

### 1. Mercy is utterly necessary for man; it is obtained by showing it to others. Mercy and discipline must not be separated in a judge. Mercy must first be practiced toward oneself

Among all the things human frailty needs, mercy is especially necessary, because the more fragile corrupted nature is, the greater is its need for the provident gift of kindness. And therefore, brothers, since our life cannot endure without it, let us learn how first to call forth divine clemency upon ourselves, so that he may deign to assist our misery according to the multitude of his mercies. In this way, during the course of the present life, we may avoid the loss of our salvation and in the future escape everlasting destruction.

To obtain this, dearly beloved, as holy Scripture shows us, the chief good is mercy. Concerning it the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). A sinner cannot hope for mercy from God if he does not show mercy to those who sin against him. Therefore let a man forgive a temporal debt, so that he may deserve to receive an eternal good.

If we desire our souls to be cleansed from the filth of sins, let us not deny mercy to those who sin against us, so that on the day of recompense we may be helped by works of mercy to obtain God’s mercy. How does one expect or hope for mercy from God who is cruel toward his fellow servants? If anyone desires God to have mercy on him, let him likewise have mercy on his debtors. Certainly, the one who knows how to forgive others may expect forgiveness [Col. 2329].

In the Gospel the Lord strengthened us most effectively by his example for the work of mercy, saying: “Be merciful, therefore, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36), who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Every act of mercy makes room for each person according to the merit of his works. Whoever shows mercy offers God a sacrifice that is most acceptable.

There ought to be both mercy and discipline in a judge, because one cannot rightly exist without the other. If there is mercy alone, it will give those subject to judgment security in sinning; if discipline alone is always present, the mind of the offender is turned toward despair, and the judge will not deserve mercy from God.

But a person must begin this mercy with himself. How can one be merciful toward others who is cruel toward himself? He is cruel toward himself who prepares everlasting flames for himself through his sins. He is truly merciful who begins with himself and carefully guards himself so that he will not be punished with the devil; and who then grants to others what he sees to be good for himself.

### 2. Forgiveness wins mercy by being shown to others

Through forgiveness the Lord taught us how we can obtain mercy from him, when he says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). Again: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:14–15).

This true teaching also clearly proclaims great mercy toward us [Note: [Col. 2329] Alcuin: “But this promise of the Lord clearly proclaims great mercy toward us.”] to those who can understand it correctly. Therefore God judges us according to our own judgment, and in a certain sense it lies in our power how we shall be judged by God the Judge. If we judge mercifully those who offend against us, God judges mercifully concerning us who sin against him.

Let us therefore attend to his example, as the Teacher of the Gentiles admonishes us: “Forgive one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; as God in Christ forgave you, so also do you” (Colossians 3:13). That is, just as God forgave us our sins in Christ, so we too should forgive those who sin against us.

The same apostle says elsewhere: “Returning evil for evil to no one” (Romans 12:17); and in another place: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). We must know with absolute certainty that each person will receive from God the kind of forgiveness that he himself has granted to his neighbor.

Then our prayer for our sins will quickly reach the ears of almighty God, if the prayers of those who offend us are acceptable in our ears. Whoever knows how to pardon sinners mercifully will certainly receive the clemency of divine goodness. Hence it is written: “He who is inclined to mercy is blessed by the Lord” (Proverbs 22:9). For we are forgiven in the same way that we forgive those who have harmed us by any kind of malice.

### 3. Many kinds of mercy

There are therefore many kinds of mercy. When we practice them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. But there is nothing greater than forgiving from the heart whatever another person has sinned against us.

Not only does the person who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to travelers, and other things of this kind give alms; the person who grants pardon to one who sins also gives alms. And the person who corrects with a blow someone over whom he has authority, or restrains him by some discipline, yet forgives from the heart the sin of the person who has been harmed or offended by him [Note: [Col. 2329] It would more suitably be read, “by whom,” instead of “by whom he has been harmed.” M.], or prays that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in rebuking and imposing some corrective punishment—because he shows mercy.

Therefore, brothers, I beseech you above all to practice mercy and to help your neighbors in whatever ways you can. Be ready also to forgive your neighbors their offenses, so that for this you may obtain forgiveness of your sins from the almighty Judge and deserve to possess eternal life with all the saints in the heavenly kingdom; through the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCCV

[Note: [Col. 2330] It was the twenty-second homily in the Library of the Fathers of Caesarius. For no. 1, see Appendix Sermon 107, section 3; 78, section 5; and 142, section 3; for no. 2, Sermon 308, section 1; 78, section 6; 225, section 4; 265, section 2; and 270, section 3; for no. 3, Sermon 78, section 6.]

## On Divine and Human Mercy: Why God Allowed the Poor to Exist in This World, So That the Rich Might Have a Means of Redeeming Their Sins

### 1. One comes to heavenly mercy through earthly mercy. Divine and human mercy

A moment ago, brothers, when the Gospel was being read, we heard our Lord and Savior say: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). The name “mercy” is sweet, dearly beloved brothers; and if the name is sweet, how much more the reality itself?

Although all people wish to have mercy—and what is worse, not all act accordingly—and although all wish to receive mercy, there are few who wish to give it. O man, with what face do you wish to ask for what you pretend not to give? Therefore, the person who desires to receive mercy in heaven must give it in this world.

And so, dearly beloved brothers, because we all desire mercy, let us make it our patron in this age, so that it may itself free us in the future. There is mercy in heaven, and one reaches it through earthly acts of mercy. For Scripture says: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven” (Psalm 35:6).

There is therefore both earthly and heavenly mercy, that is, human and divine. What is human mercy? It is surely this: that you look upon the hardships of the poor. What is divine mercy? Without doubt, it is that which grants you forgiveness of sins. Whatever human mercy gives along the way, divine mercy returns in our homeland.

For God is both nourished and hungry in all the poor, as he himself said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). Therefore God, who deigns to give from heaven, wishes to receive on earth.

What kind of people are we, who wish to receive when God gives, but do not wish to give when he asks? For when the poor person is hungry, Christ is in need, as he himself said: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25:42). Do not therefore despise the misery of the poor if you wish confidently to hope for forgiveness of your sins.

Christ is hungry now, brothers. He deigns to hunger and thirst in all the poor; and what he receives on earth, he returns in heaven. I ask you, brothers: what do you want or seek when you come to church? What indeed, except mercy? Give earthly mercy, therefore, and you will receive heavenly mercy.

The poor person asks you, and you ask God; he asks for a morsel, you ask for eternal life. Give the beggar what you deserve to receive from Christ. Hear him say: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:38). I do not know with what face you wish to receive what you do not wish to give.

Therefore, when you come to church, give alms to the poor according to your means, whatever they may be. Whoever can should bring money; whoever cannot should offer wine. If he does not have even that, let him offer a morsel to the hungry; if he does not have a whole one, at least some portion, so that he may fulfill what the Lord exhorted through the prophet: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58:7). He did not say, “Give all of it,” lest you perhaps be poor and unable to have more.

### 2. Almsgiving benefits us. Why God allowed the poor to exist

And if we pay careful attention, brothers, the very fact that Christ hungers in the poor benefits us. For this reason God allowed the poor to exist in this world: so that every person might have a means of redeeming his sins. If there were no poor person, no one would give alms and no one would receive forgiveness.

God could have made all people rich, but through the misery of the poor he wished to help us, so that the poor through patience and the rich through almsgiving might be able to merit God’s grace. The poverty of the poor serves our interests [Col. 2331].

Indeed, if you understand wisely and carefully weigh the balance of your heart, what you receive for the poor is incomparably greater than what you give to the poor. Consider and see: a coin, and a kingdom. What comparison is there, brother? You give a coin and receive a kingdom from Christ; you give a morsel and receive eternal life from Christ; you give clothing and receive forgiveness of sins from Christ.

Let us not therefore despise the poor, brothers. Rather, let us desire them and hasten voluntarily to offer ourselves to them, because the misery of the poor is medicine for the rich, as the Lord himself said: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41); and again: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12:33).

And through the prophet the Holy Spirit cries out: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33); and again: “Store up almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will deliver you [Note: [Col. 2331] The Portarum manuscript has, “it will plead for you.” Here the manuscript of Clermont agrees with the Portarum manuscript.] from every evil” (Sirach 29:15).

Let us therefore practice mercy, brothers, and with Christ’s help hold fast to the pledge he has given. I mean the one mentioned above, where he says: “Give, and it shall be given to you”; and again: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

Let each person, according to his means, take care not to come to church empty-handed. The person who wishes to receive ought to offer something. Whoever can should clothe the poor person in a new garment; whoever cannot should at least give him an old one.

Whoever does not consider himself capable of these things should offer a morsel, receive a stranger, prepare a bed, or wash someone’s feet, so that he may deserve to hear Christ say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food; I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:34–35).

No one, dearly beloved brothers, will be able to excuse himself from giving alms, since Christ promised that he would repay even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42).

### 3. Two kinds of almsgiving

And because, as I have often admonished you, there are two kinds of almsgiving—one good, the other better—one consisting in offering a morsel to the poor, the other in promptly forgiving a brother who has sinned against you, let us hasten, with the Lord’s help, to fulfill both kinds of almsgiving, so that we may attain eternal forgiveness and Christ’s true mercy.

For he himself said: “If you forgive, your Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:14–15). And elsewhere the Holy Spirit cries out: “Does a man preserve anger against another man and seek healing from God? He does not show mercy to a man like himself, yet he asks mercy from God” (Sirach 28:3–4).

For blessed John says [Note: [Col. 2331] The manuscript of the College of Clermont more suitably reads: “Blessed John also says.”]: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15); and again: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, so that we may escape eternal evils and attain everlasting goods, let us strive, as far as we can and as long as we live, both to possess and to extend to others the two kinds of almsgiving I have mentioned, so that on the day of judgment we may confidently say: “Give, Lord, because we have given; we did what you commanded; fulfill what you promised.”

May he deign to grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCCVI

[Note: [Col. 2331] Elsewhere, *On the Season*, 227.]

## On Almsgiving

[Note: [Col. 2331] Placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors had left it doubtful; Vinding, following Verlinus, rejects it, observing, among other things alien to Augustine, that the preacher makes these words be spoken to that rich man concerning whom Luke 16 speaks: “Scripture cried out to you, and you did not listen; the prophet did not keep silent, the apostle preached, the Gospel thundered,” and so forth. No one fails to see how absurd this is. It perhaps contains some material taken from Caesarius and Faustus. For no. 1, see Appendix Sermon 142, section 3; for no. 3, Sermon 307, section 2; for no. 5, Sermon 276, section 5, and 78, section 2.]

### 1. Those who may be excused from giving alms

Concerning the giving of alms, dearly beloved brothers, I admonished your Charity and presumed to offer counsel. Although, by God’s inspiration, our admonition has benefited many, I nevertheless fear that there are some who either give less than they can or perhaps give nothing at all.

But someone says: “I am poor; therefore I cannot give alms.” So that no one might excuse himself on the grounds of poverty, our Lord and Savior promised that he would repay even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42).

You say, then, “I am poor.” If you have nothing more in your possessions than is sufficient for you in reasonable or modest food and clothing, good will alone can be sufficient for you. But I beg you, carefully examine your conscience, lest perhaps you sometimes lose through drunkenness what you could have given as alms; lest perhaps through gluttony you strive to consume on earth what you ought to have stored up in heaven through almsgiving; lest perhaps, while preparing delicacies and purchasing ornaments for luxury, you have nothing that you can distribute to the poor as a remedy for your soul; and while our expensive clothes are usually devoured by moths, the poor do not even deserve to receive cheap garments.

If, therefore, all these obstacles do not burden our soul, and we possess only what can suffice for ourselves or our families, we will not appear guilty if we do not distribute alms to the poor. But if, as has already been said, luxury frequently devours what mercy could have stored up in heaven, let us correct ourselves while there is time, and strive with all our strength to fulfill what up to now we have either not done or have done less than we ought.

### 2. The necessity and efficacy of almsgiving

And therefore, Christian soul, which hears and reads with me, help yourself by the counsel of the most holy Daniel. For he says: “Accept my advice and redeem your sins with almsgiving” (Daniel 4:24). If you do not willingly listen to this counsel, you will knock at heaven’s door without purpose.

O soul, dwelling within fleshly and fragile walls, watch, pray, ask, seek, knock. Watch, I say, by asking; pray by seeking; knock by working. To you who watch and ask, the Lord replies: “Behold, I am here.”

If you pass through fire, your Lord is with you, and the flame will not burn you; for as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Sirach 3:33). If, therefore, you open your hands to the poor, Christ will open his doors to you, so that you may enter as an inhabitant of paradise.

If you think that the end of the world is delayed, consider at least your own end. Behold, the world gradually fails; all the good things that existed are being taken away, and evils that did not exist are approaching. Every day what God’s word foretold is being fulfilled, and even so man does not change.

Accept counsel, therefore, while your price is in your hands. Give to yourself from what is yours while it is yours, because what you hold is fragile, while what you are awaiting belongs to others. Consider what price your Lord paid for you: he shed his blood. He held you dear, since he purchased you at so dear a price.

### 3. The fortunes of the rich man and the poor Lazarus reversed

Flee, brother, the example of the rich man dressed in purple, whose dogs the poor Lazarus fed with his wounds, while he did not receive the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table. But after no long interval of time, their fortunes were reversed. The poor man purchased blessedness through his poverty, and the rich man punishment through his wealth.

The poor man is lifted by angels into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man is led into the depths of hell. From there the rich man saw the poor man—indeed, now poor, he saw the rich man. He who had denied a crumb desired a drop.

Let the rich, who do not wish to redeem themselves by their possessions, consider these things, lest they suffer the same. That man was rich, about whom we are now speaking; there are also rich people here, to whom we are now speaking. They share one name; let them beware lest they share one condition.

Thus the fortunes of the rich man dressed in purple and Lazarus covered with sores were reversed. The rich man lost what he possessed; the poor man began to possess what he had not possessed. That rich man had left behind storehouses full in this world; in hell, burning, he asked for a drop and could not obtain it.

### 4. The rich man is tortured especially in his tongue. He speaks on his own behalf before God. He falls because of the guilt of hardness

Pay attention, brothers. The rich man’s entire body is consumed by the flames of Gehenna, but his tongue alone is tortured more severely. Without doubt, he feels greater heat in his tongue because by speaking proudly he had despised the poor man. The very tongue that had refused to say that alms should be given to the poor man is burned more severely by the flames of Gehenna.

For he cried out and said: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (Luke 16:24). O rich man, with what face do you ask for a drop, when you refused to offer a crumb? You would now rightly demand it if you had given one.

O goods of the world, evils in hell! Fires came to serve the rich man, and savage torturers to attend him. He suffers harsh ministers of Tartarus. He is tormented and cries out:

“O just and upright judge, either let these punishments be measured according to my sins, or, in proportion to the years in which I possessed good things, let me receive evils—or at least double or quadruple! Why do you command me to be held in the flame for so many thousands of years? I am bound by the chains of my sins, so that I cannot flee. I am pierced moment by moment, so that I may suffer. The fire rages against me and shows no mercy; it torments and preserves me. Nor is all that is being punished the whole of my misery, since what spares me is itself cruel.”

After those lamentable words, he could doubtless have been answered:

“What shall I do for you? You did not give alms, which could have extinguished the punishments of your sins. Scripture cried out to you, and you did not listen; the prophet did not keep silent, the apostle preached, the Gospel thundered. The punishment of the wicked was announced and the reward of the just promised. Believing that you possessed the shadows and mists of this age, you rejected the divine commandments as empty fables.

“Let the poor intercede for you, and I will grant whatever you ask. But by a just judgment I repay you in kind: ‘Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy’ (James 2:13). My justice cannot grant you anything except what your deeds deserve. You cry out in vain, dead and placed under another’s power, because at the time when you could have acted, when you saw me in the poor, you were blind.”

### 5. The reward of almsgiving is set before us

My brothers, formed by God’s hand and purchased with me at a great price, hear the counsel of our Lord God. Fulfill the desire of your bishop, so that with him you may receive an inheritance in the kingdom of your Father.

You were made a friend from a servant; despise what you were born as, and establish an exchange with Christ. Why should he not receive a portion of your possessions who prepared eternal rewards for you? Why should he not receive even a tenth who bestowed everything?

In exchange for an earthly inheritance God offers heaven. For he says: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom, because I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:34–35).

Then, if you now give alms generously and faithfully, you will be able to say joyfully: “Lord, when did we see you hungry and minister to you?” (Matthew 25:37). What is this, brothers? The faithful debtor appears, and the creditors excuse themselves?

Then the Father, the Lord and friend with whom you made a heavenly transaction, will answer you: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). Did I not receive earthly things? I will return heavenly things; I will give an eternal reward and a kingdom at my right hand—not because you did not sin, but because you redeemed your sins through almsgiving.

I beg you, brothers, let these words be received in your souls and so benefit those who are on pilgrimage, that before the tribunal of the eternal Judge forgiveness may be granted to me for my kindly admonition and eternal glory to you for your generosity in almsgiving; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON CCCVII

[Note: [Col. 2334] It is attributed to Caesarius in an old manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portarum, and in the Library of the Fathers it is his twenty-fourth homily. For no. 2, see Appendix Sermon 206, section 3; for no. 3, Sermons 142, section 6; 77, sections 1 and 5; 78, section 5; and 263, section 2.]

## On the Comparison of the Elm and the Vine, or, What the Rich and the Poor Confer on One Another

[Col. 2334]

## 1. The elm represents the rich; the vine, the poor servants of God. What they contribute to one another

We read, dearest brothers, in a certain book about a comparison proposed to us between an elm and a vine; whoever considers it carefully will find no small edification for his soul. For the elm tree and the vine seem to be quite well matched. The elm tree, although pleasant and stretching upward, is nevertheless shown to bear no fruit. The vine, on the other hand, although small and lowly, is known to be full of fruit; yet unless some kind of wood raises it up high, its fruit rots and perishes on the ground. But if the elm extends its branches and raises up the vine, it both adorns itself and frees the vine from decay.

Let us therefore consider carefully why this comparison has been made. The elm tree signifies a rich man in this world. For just as that tree is lofty, pleasant, and luxuriant, yet empty of fruit, so also any rich man of this age, although elevated by honors and seemingly pleasant and agreeable because of his many possessions, will nevertheless remain empty of the fruits of eternal life if he does not humbly stretch out toward the vine—that is, toward Christ’s poor—the arms of his almsgiving, like most compassionate branches.

The vine, however, signifies the servants of God: abbots, monks, or spiritual clerics devoted to God and constantly occupied with teaching, as well as any others like them who, having despised the world, serve God day and night. Through this service they are believed to possess abundant fruits in eternal blessedness. Thus the rich of this world abound in this age, and Christ’s poor in heaven.

What, then, [Note: [Col. 2334] Alternatively, “what must be done?”] must happen so that neither the elm tree remains without fruit nor the vine rots on the ground? This must be done: just as the elm extends its branches and raises up or supports the vine, so the rich man of this age should stretch out his branches—that is, his hands full of the fruits of his field—and support Christ’s poor. If he does this in this world, without doubt Christ’s poor themselves will repay him many times over in the future.

## 2. The punishment of the stingy rich. How greed deprives him of grace

Nor should a rich man disdain, or consider it an injury to himself, that he has been compared to a tree, if he hears the Lord saying: “A good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits.” Rather, let him fear what follows: “Every tree,” he says, “that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7:18–19). Let him therefore extend his hands toward almsgiving, so that he may escape the eternal flames.

Let all the rich, then, fear the example of that fruitless and barren tree, namely, the man who was clothed in purple and fine linen. He was a pleasant and lofty tree in the world; but because he did not extend the branches of mercy toward Lazarus, he deserved to receive flames in hell, and he begged a drop from the one to whom he had denied a crumb (Luke 16:24).

Let the rich who do not wish to redeem themselves from their possessions while those possessions are still theirs consider these things, so that they may not do such things and suffer such things. The rich man of whom we speak is dead; there are also certain rich men to whom we now speak. They share one name; let them beware lest they share one condition.

Since this is so, if those who are rich have dry and contracted hands when it comes to giving alms, and refuse to provide the necessities of the body to whatever servants of God are devoted to vigils, reading, or prayer, they become like a barren elm that refuses to support the vine. And when a rich man gives nothing to Christ’s poor, they are compelled [Note: [Col. 2334] Perhaps, “it is necessary that.”] to devote themselves more than usual to earthly work. While they are occupied with worldly [Col. 2335] activities, they apply themselves less to prayer, reading, fasting, and vigils; and it is necessary that their fruits, like those of the vine, lie upon the ground and be diminished in part. They suffice only for themselves and give nothing to the rich.

For blessed the apostle Paul, when admonishing the rich of this world to support Christ’s poor, was speaking, as it were, of the vine to the tree; that is, he was speaking on behalf of Christ’s poor to the rich: “Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also be a supply for your need” (2 Corinthians 8:14). So that everyone may understand this, we ought to explain it more clearly.

## 3. The exchange between the rich and the poor. Members of the household of faith

The rich of this world abound in money in this age; Christ’s poor abound in eternal life in heaven. Let the rich therefore distribute money in this world, so that they may receive eternal life in heaven.

The rich of this world store grain, wine, and oil in abundance in their granaries or storerooms; Christ’s poor, by praying, keeping vigils, and fasting, store spiritual treasures in heaven. Let the rich of this world therefore make whatever servants of God they can participants in their earthly wealth, so that those servants may make the rich their co-heirs in the heavenly treasure.

The rich of this world, when they bind themselves too closely to earthly affairs, cannot keep vigil, read, pray, or fast as much as they ought. Hence it is to be feared that they may offer less for their sins, or not store as much as is fitting in the heavenly treasury. Christ’s poor abound in these fruits by devoting themselves continually to God. Let the rich therefore not be sluggish in distributing earthly goods if they desire to possess heavenly ones.

For Christ, who lavishly bestows his gifts upon all human beings, deigns to suffer need, hunger, and cold in his poor. Let no one hesitate to give to the poor, because the poor man’s hand is Christ’s treasury: what it receives on earth, it stores in heaven. Thus the Lord himself said: “When you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Let us hear the Apostle saying: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Corinthians 9:6); and shortly afterward: “Let us do what is good toward all, but especially toward the members of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10).

Who are the members of the household of faith, brothers, except clerics, good monks, and whatever other servants of God flee the hindrances of this world, devote themselves to God, and apply themselves to readings and prayers? Certainly, we must give to all who ask, according to our ability. But to the servants of God, who are ashamed to ask from us, we must offer even when they do not ask.

Let us therefore strive to act in this way, dearest brothers, so that we may be safe from hearing the evil pronouncement. What will that evil pronouncement be? “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25:41–42).

I beg you, brothers, do not hear this carelessly or negligently. Rather, with all your strength, and with God’s help, strive so that you neither seize what belongs to others nor distribute too sparingly from your own possessions to Christ’s poor. With contrite hearts, continually thinking and saying to one another: “If the one who did not give his own is sent into the fire, where, do you suppose, must the one be sent who took what belonged to another?”

Therefore, because of greed, let that dreadful and terrifying voice not be directed against us: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire.” Rather, because of our almsgiving, may we deserve to hear that desirable voice: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25:34–35). May the voice of the Lord who sends us also be happily directed toward us: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:23). Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

---

# SERMON CCCVIII

[Note: [Col. 2335] In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* this homily is Caesarius’s ninth, and it is likewise headed under his name in our manuscripts. For no. 1, [Col. 2336] see Appendix, Sermon 284, no. 1; 305, no. 2; for no. 2, Sermon 225, no. 3; 271, no. 5; 276, no. 4; 277, no. 3; for no. 3, Sermon 271, no. 5; for no. 4, Sermon 78, no. 6; 305, no. 3; for no. 5, Sermon 270, no. 3; for no. 6, Sermon 276, no. 2; 277, no. 3.]

## An admonition showing three kinds of almsgiving by which sins can be redeemed without labor

### 1. God has provided easy remedies for sins. Therefore [Col. 2336] some are in need and others abound. The former are healed by patience, the latter by mercy

The pious and merciful Lord, dearest brothers, deigns to provide in many ways occasions or opportunities by which we can redeem our sins without great labor or difficulty. For those whom he sees lacking the strength to fast on account of their sins, or unable to abstain from meat or wine, he instructs to sell even their possessions and distribute them to the poor.

He provides for the poverty of the poor and grants richer fruits, so that, while the wealthy give their surplus to the poor, they may obtain forgiveness of sins. What could be so pious and appropriate [Note: Perhaps, “delicate.”], what could be so easy and readily available, dearest brothers, as to strive to redeem your sins by giving alms from what God has deigned to give you beyond what you need?

God does not command you to distribute what is necessary for you or your family. Concerning such things the Apostle also says: “Not that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you” (2 Corinthians 8:13). He does not need you to spend your surplus on himself; rather, he wishes to preserve it for you in eternal blessedness.

He also willed that there be poor people so that the rich would have a means of redeeming their sins. God could have made all human beings rich, but he wished to provide the rich with an opportunity for mercy. The few rich do not gather more than they need because of their own merit, nor do the many poor fail to gather even what is necessary for them by their own fault. As I have already said, this is an arrangement of divine mercy: while the poor patiently endure need, they receive forgiveness of sins; likewise, while the rich mercifully distribute their surplus, they both redeem themselves from sins and attain eternal rewards.

### 2. There is no excuse for failing to distribute surplus goods. Nor should sons be enriched by them, since what we possess is not our own

Consider, dearest brothers, and see that no excuse can remain for us by which we might say that we were unable to redeem our sins. Perhaps you can say that you cannot afflict your flesh with fasts and vigils, or abstain from wine or meat. But can you say that you cannot distribute to the poor, for your sins, what God has given you beyond what you need?

But perhaps you answer and say: “From what God has given me beyond what I need, I wish to buy silver for my sons or daughters and acquire the most precious ornaments.” To this I reply: You buy ornaments, but you do not redeem your sins.

And because not only are tithes not ours but assigned to the Church, but whatever more than we need we receive from God must be distributed to the poor, if we reserve for our desires or vanities what has been assigned to them, let us understand that many poor people in the places where we live may have died of hunger or nakedness, and that on the day of judgment we shall have to render an account for their souls.

### 3. The second kind of almsgiving: forgiving enemies. This is easy for everyone

There is still another kind of almsgiving by which we can redeem our sins without any labor. If someone is so poor that he possesses neither gold nor grain nor wine or oil from which to give bodily alms—since it is impossible for anyone not to suffer injury from some people—let him forgive all his enemies with his whole heart, leaving no sin that gnaws at his conscience, and let him say confidently in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

Then what Christ deigned to promise in the Gospel will be fulfilled in him: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (ibid., 14); and also: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” [Col. 2337] (Luke 6:37–38).

See, dearest brothers, that just as in the other kind of almsgiving about which we spoke earlier, so also in this almsgiving no one can find an excuse for himself or offer any reason why he cannot fulfill it. This almsgiving, by which we grant forgiveness to those who sin against us, is brought forth not from the storeroom, granary, or little field [Note: The Claromontanus manuscript reads “or from a little purse”; read “from a purse.”], but from the treasury of the heart, concerning which the Lord himself said: “The good man brings good things forth from the good treasury of his heart” (Matthew 12:35).

Many poor people can excuse themselves regarding the things mentioned above—gold, silver, grain, wine, and oil. But with what face or conscience can anyone say that he cannot possess that almsgiving which is brought forth from the heart?

### 4. Let no one say that he cannot possess the almsgiving brought forth from the heart

And therefore, since we have no excuse by which we can defend ourselves, let the one to whom God has given more than he needs hasten to redeem his sins from his surplus. But the one who cannot redeem captives or feed or clothe the poor should preserve hatred toward no one in his heart; he should not only refrain from returning evil for evil to his enemies, but should also love them and never cease to pray for them.

Confident in the promise and mercy of his Lord, he will be able to say before Christ’s tribunal with a clear conscience: “Give, Lord, because I have given; forgive, because I have forgiven.” Yet this condition must be observed: once he has begun to redeem his sins through such almsgiving, since he will never lack small sins to redeem daily, he must not commit capital crimes, in accordance with what is written: “If one who is washed from a corpse again touches a corpse, what benefit is there in his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:30); and: “As a dog becomes hateful when it returns to its vomit, so a sinner is hateful when he returns to his sin” (Proverbs 26:11).

### 5. The third kind of almsgiving. Good will is charity

But while we seem to be explaining these two kinds of almsgiving, someone may say: “Look, I possess neither earthly property that I can distribute to the poor, nor do I suffer injury from anyone whom I could forgive and thereby redeem my sins. What shall I do, since I possess neither of these things and cannot abstain from wine or meat by fasting?”

To one who says this I could reply that what he is attempting to assert is false, because no human being is found in this world who never suffers injury from others. Nevertheless, let us grant that matters are as he asserts [Note: Morel considers that one should read, “let us grant that matters are as he asserts.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 303 M.]. Let us grant this only so that we may show him that there is still a third kind of almsgiving, one that excludes every excuse so completely that no one can ever find anything to bring against it.

You have said that you neither gather grain in abundance from which you can give food or clothing to the poor, nor suffer injury that you ought to forgive your enemies; and for this reason you doubt that you possess any means by which you can redeem your sins. Receive, then, and faithfully hold fast the distinguished and chief third kind of almsgiving.

Let there be good will in you. Love all people as yourself. Pray for everyone, and desire for them what you desire for yourself. Then the angels proclaim to you: “Peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

And because good will itself is charity, if you wish to possess it, what is written will be fulfilled in you: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Recognize, then, that every excuse or objection of yours has been removed. You cannot say that you are unable to have good will, because it may happen that you do not want to have it; but you will never be able to prove that you cannot have it.

### 6. What and when should be set aside for almsgiving

Therefore, with the Lord’s help, let us strive to receive and preserve faithfully—not carelessly—[Col. 2338] the many and splendid benefits and remedies of our Lord and Savior, so that we may deserve not only to receive forgiveness of sins but also to attain eternal rewards.

Of the two kinds of almsgiving set forth second and third, one is that we forgive those who sin against us, pray for our enemies, and love them with our whole heart; the other is that through good will and true charity, which covers a multitude of sins, we strive to make God favorable toward us. This admonition is so clear that it needs no interpreter at all.

As for the almsgiving we placed first, by which, from what God gives us beyond what we need, we can redeem our sins and, with the Lord’s inspiration, prepare eternal rewards for ourselves: if you are willing to hear my advice, you will be able, with God’s help, to fulfill it with joy and gladness.

Whenever you gather your harvests or your grape harvests, calculate the expenses of yourself and everyone dependent upon you, and also what you will pay into the treasury. Whatever you recognize to remain for you, since it was not given to you as your private possession but, as has already been said, was sent through you to be distributed to the poor, set aside either all of it or as much as God inspires your heart to set aside. Let it remain with you as though you had already offered it into God’s hand.

If, as we believe, you faithfully wish to do this, then when captives and poor people come, your spirit will not merely fail to become irritated or saddened; it will also be made joyful and glad. For you will hasten with the greatest eagerness to spend what you have assigned, for the love of God, to the needs of the poor. In you will be fulfilled what is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7); and: “Whoever gives to the poor will never be in need” (Proverbs 28:27); and: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33); as well as what the Lord said in the Gospel: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

May he himself deign to grant this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

---

# SERMON CCCIX

[Note: [Col. 2338] A substantial part of this sermon is found in the eighth homily of Eligius. But its style and the authority of the ancient books prove that it all belongs to Caesarius. In the *Bibliotheca Patrum* it is his sixteenth homily. For no. 1, see Appendix, Sermon 53, no. 2; 137, no. 2; 274, no. 4; 53, no. 2; Augustine, Sermon 9, no. 18; for no. 3, Sermon 257, no. 3; 297, no. 7; 274, no. 4; for no. 4, Sermon 289, no. [uncertain]; 288, nos. 3 and 6; 289, nos. 3 and 9; 45, no. 3.]

## An admonition to those who frequently give alms in this way, yet practice robbery and commit adultery

### 1. Almsgiving alone is not sufficient to erase crimes. It is empty if sins are not avoided

I beg you, dearest brothers, consider this carefully and, as far as you can, tremble and beware lest that cruel enemy of the human race creep upon you in the way he usually deceives the heedless and negligent through wicked cunning.

For he instills a false security in certain murderers, robbers, and adulterers, so that, although they commit crimes every day, they believe that they redeem them through daily almsgiving. They suppose that God accepts money and forgives sins in the manner of corrupt judges.

He certainly accepts money and delights in almsgiving, but on this condition: whenever a sinner offers his money to God, he must offer his soul as well. For I ask you, brothers, what justice is it for a criminal to offer his money to God through almsgiving while handing his soul over to the devil through lust? To offer God the image of the emperor on his money, while handing over to the devil the image of God in himself?

The Lord does not command this in the Gospel. For when he says, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21), what else does he seem to say except that, just as you render Caesar’s image to Caesar on a coin, so you should render God’s image in yourselves to God?

However generously someone may give alms, if he does not avoid [Col. 2339] capital crimes, I fear—indeed, I greatly fear—that, deceiving himself with false security, he may both lose his money and fail to redeem his sins. Let no one therefore suppose that daily almsgiving consumes daily adulteries.

### 2. Changing one’s life or merely enduring it. What almsgiving accomplishes if life is not changed

For it is one thing to change one’s life and another to endure one’s life. To endure one’s life [Note: [Col. 2339] The manuscript of the Claromont College and the Colbert manuscript read here and above, “to color one’s life.”] is to redeem through daily almsgiving the small sins without which we cannot be; to change one’s life is to abstain from capital crimes.

As I said above, a more generous almsgiving frees the soul when the criminal has already abandoned deadly sins [Note: [Col. 2339] Manuscript T reads: “A more generous almsgiving will be beneficial—perhaps, will be of benefit—if, together with the money offered, he has offered his soul to God. But if …”].

But if, as has already been said, he gives his possessions to God while offering his soul to the enemy, what is written is fulfilled in him: “If one who is washed from a corpse again touches a corpse, what benefit is there in his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:30). And what the apostle Peter cries out is fulfilled: “If, after escaping the defilements of the world, they are again filled with them and overcome, their latter state has become worse than their former” (2 Peter 2:20).

Consider, brothers, that blessed Peter declares this to sinners: if, after beginning to redeem their sins, they return again to the mire of crimes, their latter state will become worse than their former. What the same apostle Peter adds will happen to them: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (ibid., 22).

Solomon also admonishes this matter even more terribly and clearly, saying: “As a dog is hateful when it returns to its vomit, so a sinner is hateful when he returns to his sin” (Proverbs 26:11).

The Lord himself also confirms this in the Gospel: “Look, you have become well; do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). Solomon again bears witness and cries out: “My son, if you have sinned, do not add to it again; but pray that your former sins may be forgiven you” (Ecclesiasticus 21:1).

It is clear that he said this not about the small sins without which we cannot be, but about capital crimes. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Afterward it returns and finds its house from which it came out cleansed; and it brings with it seven spirits more wicked than itself, and the final condition of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:43–45).

This happens to those who try to redeem capital crimes through almsgiving but are again defiled through lust [Note: The manuscript of the Claromont College reads: “and again return to the same crimes; just as …”]. Just as almsgiving cleanses, so lust defiles.

For if someone frequently washes his robe and then again and again plunges it into mud, I do not know with what face he would dare to put it on for any festival—especially since the Apostle cries out concerning Christ: “He prepared for himself a Church without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

If no one can enter eternal life with spot or wrinkle, with what conscience does someone oppressed by capital crimes presume that he will enter it, unless he cleanses himself by correcting his ways and giving alms?

### 3. If one changes, almsgiving is greatly beneficial

Pay careful attention also to what I am saying, dearest brothers, lest someone misunderstand it and think that I am saying almsgiving cannot benefit sinners. Far be this from us, brothers. We believe not merely that it benefits, but that it benefits greatly—yet on this condition: whoever distributes alms for his sins must cease committing capital crimes. He must give alms at the Lord’s command in such a way that he refuses to serve sin.

I wish to offer your Charity a comparison concerning this matter. I ask you, brothers: does any one [Col. 2340] of us want his servant to repay him wages for his work while nevertheless continually serving his enemies and never withdrawing from their company? Certainly, I do not know whether anyone could endure this.

What, therefore, you do not wish to suffer from your servant, it is not right for you to do to your Lord. And therefore, as we have often said, when we distribute money to the poor, let us offer our souls to God [Note: [Col. 2340] After the words “let us offer our souls,” the same manuscript adds, in an old second hand: “so that where our treasure is, there our heart may also be. For why does God ask money from us? Clearly because he knows that we love it greatly and think about it continually, and that our heart is where our money is.” These words do not seem superfluous or foreign to Caesarius.], where our heart also is.

For this reason God exhorts us to store up treasure in heaven through almsgiving to the poor, so that our heart may follow where we send our treasure ahead (Matthew 6:20–21). Then, when the priest says, “Lift up your hearts,” we may answer with a clear conscience that we have them with the Lord.

### 4. Incontinence is reproved. What men commonly think permissible for men but not for women

But someone says: “I am young, and therefore I cannot conquer pleasure or overcome lust.”

If you cannot remain continent, hear the Apostle saying: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9). Since it is permitted to take a wife, but not to keep concubines or commit adultery, why do you wish to practice what is not permitted and refuse to have what is permitted? No one ought to avoid what is unlawful more than the one who rejects what was lawful.

I speak truly, brothers: according to the Lord, this was never permitted to anyone, is not permitted, and never will be permitted. But what is worse is that these sins have become so customary, and so many commit them, that they are now believed to be practiced almost as though they were lawful.

If there is no man who wants his betrothed to have sexual relations adulterously before the wedding, but all men wish to receive virgins as wives, with what face or conscience are they not ashamed to have concubines before marriage? With what face does a man wish to find an untouched wife when he himself is corrupted?

For if, according to divine Scripture, “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:20), how does anyone wish to receive a living spouse when he himself is dead?

But, as I have already said, this evil and very wicked custom is committed by so many without any fear of God that it is not even believed to be a sin. Perhaps someone thinks that this is permitted to men but not to women, since, as I have already said, the multitude of sinners has established that it is permitted to men.

But in the Christian people, whatever is not permitted to women has never been, and never will be, permitted to men either. Therefore, whoever recognizes that he has done this, I beg not to become angry with me but rather with himself, and to strive to think more about his correction than about our reproach or persecution, so that when the day of judgment comes, even if he does not deserve to receive a crown, he may at least obtain forgiveness of his sins. Amen.

---

# SERMON CCCX

[Note: [Col. 2340] Elsewhere, 47 among the 50 Homilies.]

## On almsgiving

[Note: [Col. 2340] This sermon is placed here for the first time in the Appendix. It was considered doubtful by the Louvain scholars, but Verlinus and Windingus judged it spurious. Its spuriousness is certainly quite evident from its style.]

### 1. The efficacy of almsgiving—provided that it is not made from another’s property. Those who give from robberies are brought before the judgment

Brothers, almsgiving is a remedy for sins, a medicine. For “almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit a person to go into darkness” (Tobit 4:11). It comes to a person’s aid on the day of judgment, so that he need not fear the eternal flames, as James says in his Epistle: “Mercy triumphs over judgment; and judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

But such must be the mercy, brothers, that is accepted rather than rejected; that cleanses sins rather than burdens the soul; that comes from good and just labor and from one’s own resources, not from the poverty of the poor.

Brothers, God does not [Col. 2341] want a person to cease from mercy, nor does God gladly look upon anyone who gives from fraud. As the prophet Solomon says: “Honor the Lord your God from your just labors” (Proverbs 3:9). He commanded that gifts be given from just labors; but he prohibited giving from unjust robberies.

But when God begins to judge, those who live by fraud and make alms from the spoils of the miserable will say: “Lord, we have kept your commands and in your name have shown mercy; we have fed the poor, clothed the naked, and received strangers in hospitality.”

God will say to them: “You mention what you gave; why do you not mention what you stole? You remember those whom you fed; why do you not remember those whom you killed? Those whom you clothed rejoice, while those whom you stripped lament. Those whom you received as guests you retain, but you have forgotten how many you expelled from their own dwellings. I—I—commanded mercy to be shown; I did not command frauds and robberies to be practiced.

“One person is filled with bread, whom you satisfied with your robberies, and he blesses God [Note: [Col. 2341] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and the Lord will bless.”], not you, but God. The poor man whom you killed groaned in his misery as he died, and the one who saw what you had done to him heard his groan.

“You acquire from evil and rejoice; you rob and celebrate. The poor man begs, and you are saddened. You prepare a meal and invite such people to your meal as will repay you. You adorn your banquet so that nothing is lacking and feast with your friends, but you do not hear the poor man begging before your door.

“You are filled with various good things and show no mercy to the needy. Stuffed with many dishes and drowsy from much wine, you disregard the poor man who begs.

“You have forgotten the prophet’s saying: ‘Whoever turns his ear away from the poor will himself call upon the Lord, and he will not hear him’ (Proverbs 21:13). Incline your ear; hear the voice of the needy and of the one perishing from hunger, so that God may also hear your voice when you are in distress.
