“Give from what Christ has deigned to give you. He himself made you rich; therefore, return to him what is his. He himself says that he receives what is given to the poor; he declares that what has been sown in the heart of the poor has been given to him. Thus he says in the Gospel: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings’ (Luke 16:9).

“Look, Christian: you have an eternal dwelling if you give food to the poor. Whatever you give, you send there and store up for yourself in the future—not something by which you may be filled carnally, but something by which you may be glorified spiritually; not something by which you fill your stomach, but something by which you extinguish flames. For it is written: ‘Almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit a person to go into darkness.’”

### 2. Mercy averts God’s anger. All things are God’s gifts. Why he gives more to some and less to others

For mercy, brothers, averts God’s anger, redeems from sins, and extinguishes future fires, as the prophet Solomon says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving resists sins” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33).

Give, then, to the needy; share with the one who has nothing; help the one perishing from hunger. It is cruel that, from what you possess, you do not give to one whom you know possesses nothing. It is grievous that, from your abundance, you do not support the poverty of the needy.

For this reason we are continually scourged in our harvests: because we do not do good to those in need. Truly, if you consider it, human being, where do losses and accusations come from except from this—from your sterility? You do not give the needy what you can give, what does not burden you; then one accusation comes, and you lose even what you do not possess.

You walk with a full stomach and do not consider the poor man’s empty stomach. You are well supplied with God’s good things, lack nothing, and wear respectable clothing; yet you do not clothe the naked person trembling with cold.

If God were to say to you: “I made you yourself; the fact that you live is mine, and what you possess I gave you—and you are ungrateful. I take away what I gave, I deny what I bestowed, I abandon you whom I made; live without me, if you can. I gave you more so that you would have something to give the poor. I did not give to the poor for this reason—that I had no means by which to give to both—but I wished to test you through the poor.

“I am the one who made both rich and poor; I appointed you as steward of my goods. Show mercy, because you will lose nothing and will not offend me, who gave to you. Give—why do you hesitate? For if you give, I will give more. Why do you claim for yourself alone what I gave to both [Col. 2342]? Why do you alone eat what I created for both? Do you assign this as the result of your own labor, or do you think it belongs to you? I take away my help; let your own labor remain. I take away my mercy, and then your misery will appear.”

### 3. The Prudence of the Greedy Is Empty

Divine providence fails no one. What we possess is not our own. What will you say to this, wretched man? You are wretched, because you do not see the wretched person; you alone make use of beasts, cattle, animals, birds, and serpents. Food is common to all, yet you deny a human being sustenance? But, I suppose, you do not give so that you may not run out by giving, so that you may not be exhausted by distributing. While you consider these things, do you not consider the end of your life? Even if money does not run out, life nevertheless ends; and when you do not expect it, the end comes to you.

That is what the rich man failed to consider, the one who was tormented amid abundance and, as it were, was asking about his poverty. “What shall I do,” he said, “how shall I find a place to gather my harvest?” And he heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:17, 20).

O the vanity of this rich man! He does not know whether he will live, yet he thinks about his harvest; destined to die at night, he plans to build. Behold, Christian, you too have heard what you should fear. Show mercy. Why do you hesitate? The one who appointed you his steward does not abandon you. For his is the voice in the Gospel rebuking the unbelieving and saying: “Consider the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap, and they have no storehouses; yet your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26).

If you say that whatever you possess is yours, then, if you can, station guards in your house against thieves, dig pits, hide your wealth, make purses and chests for yourself in which to store it; hold it against God’s will, possess it, live—if you can. Therefore, brothers, let us show mercy, let us feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and receive strangers into our homes. Therefore, while doing good, let us not grow weary, and in due time we shall reap eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCCXI  
*[Note: [Col. 2342] Elsewhere, 39 among the Fifty Homilies.]*

### On Almsgiving  
*[Note: [Col. 2342] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. It is among those that remained doubtful to the Louvain editors and were later rejected by the judgment of Verlinus and Vindingus.]*

#### 1. Almsgiving purchases piety before the judgment. The blessed worker.

No disaster will befall at the judgment the person who has purchased piety through almsgiving. Blessed is the worker and cultivator of almsgiving, because from his granary he has purchased heaven; by giving bread to the hungry, he has pressed down the fire of his sins. The prophet offers such a person this testimony, and the Holy Spirit is his advocate in the case.

Such a worker lives blessedly and now dies securely, accompanied by an immortal inheritance. He makes the Lord his debtor in the granary where he feeds another; by giving, he himself receives. With a little bread he has purchased heavenly life, making himself an heir. On the day of judgment no disaster can befall the person who has purchased piety through almsgiving.

The prophet offers him this testimony: “Save him and give him life, O Lord” (Psalm 40:3). O the prophet’s twofold benefit! He both saves him and commends him so that he may be saved, because he himself has saved; he gives him life so that he may be given life, because he himself has given life on earth to the one asking for it.

Blessed is this person, as long as he thus hastens toward heaven.  
*[Note: [Col. 2342] Manuscripts: “Blessed is this lord who thus hastens toward heaven.”]*

But so that the benefit of life may never be empty in him, let him hurry toward the great reward and leave behind in this world the testimony that says: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (ibid., 2).

Isaiah also says, and thus bears witness:

> “Release,” he says, “every bond of injustice. Release the strangulations of helpless dealings; send the battered into rest, and scatter every unjust exaction. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own flesh. Then your timely light will break forth, and your clothing will quickly arise;  
> *[Note: [Col. 2342] Erasmus: “and your healing will arise more quickly.” Louvain: “and your healings will quickly arise.” M.]*  
> and righteousness will go before you, [Col. 2343] and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and the Lord will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isaiah 58:6–9).

#### 2. Perfect mercy does not wait for someone to ask.

This is how God acts toward us. This is how Christ also acted. Therefore, dearest brothers, mercy is perfect when one comes to the hungry before a beggar ever asks. For piety that is wrested by prayers is not perfect.

But if the beggar is silent, pallor speaks in his face, almost exhausted—  
*[Note: [Col. 2343] Manuscript rm.: “weary from punishment”; Greek: “weary from hunger.”]*  
weary and crushed, noticed by no one—  
*[Note: [Col. 2343] Both manuscripts: “weary and looked upon from heaven.”]*  
Hasten to help with compassion, lest you hear him asking, lest you claim for yourself what is owed to the Lord.

Imitate your God, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Behold, rain will come to you before you ask; abundance will descend during the night while you sleep; while you are still in bed, at his command the day keeps watch, the elements stand guard, and fruits are poured forth without your knowing. Heaven casts forth and earth gives birth. While we are unaware, we receive so many storehouses of harvest and eat such vast riches before we ask.

And for you, human being, is that very bread so small—and do you sell it for prayers? Four thousand people did not ask Jesus in the desert for seven loaves and a few fish, so that countless multitudes might dine at a meal where the measure of food would have surpassed even the interest on a loan. When these were being distributed, he said: “Gather up the fragments, so that nothing may be lost” (John 6:12), because everything he himself had made was holy. Seven baskets were filled with pieces; so many thousands were satisfied; nothing was diminished, and their food increased as nourishment was distributed. So too does almsgiving increase when it is distributed to the needy.

#### 3. Almsgiving does what God does. It is a second baptism. It frees from Gehenna. It must be distributed here and now.

Almsgiving is a great work, dearest brothers: it enables a person to do what God has done. For he has left these few hungry people on earth, while with one vessel he feeds the vault of heaven, so that we too may distribute.

But if there had been abundance everywhere, mercy would have perished. God has given us a second baptism. For who is without sin? “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33).

In our granaries we have an abundance that can extinguish our flames through the offering of a single loaf. Mercy stands before the gates of Gehenna and permits no one to be sent into prison. Whoever has shown mercy will receive mercy; and if someone has not shown mercy, mercy will not be shown to him.

Give bread when you can, because no one whom you could feed will hunger in hell. After death you will have no grain, nor will you ever find a beggar there, because it will not then be the time for mercy.

The distinction between the good and the evil will remain in their deeds, when Christ the Lord, our king and judge, separates the sheep from the goats and places them apart on the right and the left. He says that he himself was hungry and thirsty, and asserts that he endured the other things in his least ones.

Therefore, give to everyone, beloved brothers; give especially to those of the household of faith. Give to everyone, lest the person to whom you do not give be Christ himself, and lest the person to whom you give be Christ himself.

## SERMON CCCXII  
*[Note: [Col. 2343] Elsewhere, On Time 76.]*

### On Almsgiving  
*[Note: [Col. 2343] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors leave it doubtful; Verlinus and Vindingus reject it as spurious. It is tedious to adduce proofs in a matter so certain.]*

#### 1. Almsgiving is urged in view of divine judgment. Its reward. Wealth has been entrusted to the poor.

If a person knows the ancient origin of humanity, understands the dignity accumulated in himself, or carefully weighs the appointed judgment with anxious fear, he will discover what the first progenitor lost, what the mercy of Christ later bestowed, and what it has destined for the future judgment. Thus, carefully considering these beginnings, he should review the past, hold fast to the present, and fear the future with anxious dread.

“Shut up almsgiving,” says Wisdom, “in the bosom of the poor, [Col. 2344] and it will pray for you” (Sirach 29:15). For the wounds of sins are easily healed in the person who has healed the needs of the poor; and he will receive mercy who does not deny his neighbor the duties of compassion.

Finally, the person who is commanded to give should rejoice that he was not born under the lot of needing. It is sufficient for the giver’s glory that, by giving, another’s misery makes him rich in the poor person; that mercy lends at interest to God; that he feeds Christ in the poor; and that through another’s poverty he receives forgiveness of sins.

It is the voice of the rebuking Lord: “If you have not been faithful in another’s wealth, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12). A person ought to present himself to the poor in the way he would wish another to present himself to him, if he himself had been poor.

But it is a great loss if you are unwilling to win God’s favor through God’s gift, or if, when the Lord has given it to you for the purpose of distributing it, you do not preserve what he has entrusted. For the Lord has always entrusted his own possessions to you for temporary distribution; he has commanded you to give from what belongs to him to the poor.

Why do you despise the commands of the giver? Why do you abandon the agreement? Why do you not hear the Lord commanding you to give? A person who is unwilling to distribute the money he has received for profit can easily lose the money he received.

#### 2. So that we may show ourselves to be God’s children. Money should be safely stored. Perhaps it would be preserved for an ungrateful heir.

“Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father has had mercy on you” (Matthew 18:33). Let actions reveal the likeness of the father in the offspring. Let likeness of conduct indicate likeness of origin. Let conduct confirm the name, so that the name may reveal the lineage.

Let the son preserve what the father has bestowed, so that the father may also display to the son the promised rewards. The inheritance you possess is yours if you put it to work; if you let it lie idle, it belongs to another. Money that is merely preserved serves chance; money preserved through mercy acquires a future reward.

Why are you afraid to entrust to Christ what you will scarcely be able to preserve from thieves? “The one who gives to the poor,” he says, “will not be in need” (Proverbs 28:27). You allot your estate to your heir [reading *Dividis*, “you divide,” for the printed *Davidis*, which is corrupt here]; and is Christ unworthy to take something of what is yours with you, to carry something of what is yours with you into the future ages?

Why do you preserve something for an heir when you do not know whether he will use it? Why do you heap up property that perhaps you will leave to an ungrateful person? Perhaps you will give him whatever you withdraw from his portion for the sake of mercy.

Therefore, first do what is commanded, so that you may be able to receive what is promised. The person who is unwilling to lend to the Lord cannot receive interest. “The one who gives to the poor,” he says, “lends to God” (ibid. 19:17). For the person who is unwilling to observe the heavenly commandments cannot receive the divine promises.

## SERMON CCCXIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2344] Ancient codices attribute this to Caesarius, and it is his tenth homily in the Library of the Fathers. For no. 1, see his Homily 34, no. 3; for no. 3, compare Appendix Sermon 293, no. 5; for no. 4, Sermons 229, no. 5, and 283, no. 3; for no. 5, Sermons 104, no. 7; 89, no. 3; 22, no. 6; 29, no. 4; 69, no. 8; 116, no. 2.]*

### An Admonition by Which We Are Taught to Flee Shameful Thoughts and Continually Keep Holy Thoughts in Our Hearts

#### 1. Holy thought protects; unholy thought destroys. When thought concerning food and clothing is holy. Whoever breaks the habit of evil thoughts.

In the Holy Scriptures, dearest brothers, we read that holy thought protects those who are concerned for the salvation of their souls. Thus the divine word says: “Holy thought will guard you” (Proverbs 2:11).

If holy thought protects, that which is not holy not only fails to protect but also destroys. But someone may say: Who can think always about God and eternal blessedness, since all people necessarily have to be concerned with food, clothing, and the ordering of their household?

God does not command that there should be no concern for the present life, since he gives this command through his Apostle: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10); and the same Apostle said of himself: “Working night and day, so that we might not burden any of you” [Col. 2345] (ibid., 8).

If avarice and greed, which usually serve luxury, are not joined to this thought by which one reasonably thinks about food and clothing—for God specifically commanded these things—then whatever is done and whatever is thought is rightly believed to be holy.

The only requirement is that these occupations not be so excessive that they prevent us from being free for God, in accordance with what is written: “The cares of the world have made them wretched.” And because the body’s necessity is satisfied by little, while greed is never satisfied even if it acquires the whole world, let us reject the impious thoughts born from the poisonous root of greed, and love only those by which we attain the eternal reward.

Thus what was said earlier may be fulfilled in us: “Holy thought will guard you.” And because two kinds of thoughts, good and evil, continually try to insert themselves into our hearts, let us hasten, with God’s help, to receive with our whole heart and soul those that are holy, so that we may exclude lustful and wicked thoughts.

But perhaps someone says: Evil habits and shameful thoughts have become so fixed in my heart that I cannot drive them away from me by any means. It is known to everyone that love is conquered by love. Let us therefore begin to love good thoughts, and God will immediately deign to free us from those that are evil.

Let chastity occupy the place that lustful and filthy thought held in the heart; let mercy restore the place that avarice ravaged; let humility rebuild the place that pride destroyed; let the sweetness of charity and kindness heal the place that malice or envy had struck with viperous poison.

#### 2. Lustful thoughts are no more to be admitted than spittle on clothing, dogs, pigs, or dung in temples, or a prostitute’s kiss in public.

That we ought not to receive lustful thoughts in our hearts can be demonstrated by obvious examples. Consider, I ask you, how, if someone were to throw phlegm or spittle onto our clothing, it would cause us such horror that we would neither wish to look at it with our eyes nor even touch it with our fingertips.

And if spittle, which is cast forth without sin, causes us horror on our clothing, what kind of horror do you think the lustful thoughts that the devil injects cause God in our souls?

And if we recoil so greatly from spittle or phlegm, which we receive unwillingly, how much more ought we, with God’s help, to reject quickly the filthy thoughts that we willingly permit to remain in our hearts?

Consider also that if someone were to bring pigs or dogs into a temple of God made of wood and stone, or throw mud there, or scatter dung, our spirit would be so offended that we would want the person through whose negligence it happened to be scourged.

And since these things are so, what should we think about ourselves if, in our souls—which are the living temples of God—we receive things much worse than dung, namely lustful or malicious thoughts, and thereby inflict injuries upon God, who deigns to dwell in us?

Therefore, although we ought to do much more, let us at least strive to guard our souls from the filth of sins in the same way that we do not wish either God’s temple or our clothing to be stained by any dirt.

And tell me this, I ask: if, in a public gathering, some notorious prostitute tried to embrace or kiss you with outstretched hands, would you receive it patiently or willingly? Would you not rather push her away with your hands and spit in her face, fearing that anyone who saw it might judge that she had done this out of habit?

It is certain that not only honorable or chaste people refuse to permit this to happen to them; even those who secretly serve lust recoil from a prostitute’s embrace in a public gathering, fearing human reproaches in public more than God’s presence in secret.

If, then, no one wishes to be kissed publicly by prostitutes because of human judgment, why do we permit the most filthy prostitutes in the secrecy of our conscience—that is, lustful and impious thoughts—not only to enter frequently but also to remain there for considerable periods?

*[Col. 2346]*

#### 3. They are also compared with burning coals and with sewers.

There is another comparison that we must consider wisely. Pay attention to this, brothers: if someone takes a live coal, however large, in his hand and immediately throws it away, he can do so without suffering a burn or pain. But if he holds it even for the space of an hour, he cannot throw it away without injury.

Why, then, do we observe this concerning live coals in the body but do not fear it concerning evil thoughts in the heart?

There is another example by which we can prove what we have said. Tell me, I ask: is there anyone who would want to stand over a privy or a sewer full of worms and fan its decay?

Now compare the stench of a sewer with lustful thoughts, and see which is capable of exhaling the greater stench. If you judge rightly and fairly, lustful thoughts produce an incomparably heavier stench than sewers, because the former are the stench of souls, while the latter are the stench of bodies.

Without doubt, just as the soul is better than the body, so filthy thoughts produce a greater stench in the soul than a privy or sewer does in the flesh.

Therefore, just as we do not wish our bodies to remain long in a place full of stench, so let us not permit lustful and filthy thoughts to remain even for a moment in our souls or our senses.

#### 4. The thoughts that chiefly assail us. Sacred reading as a remedy against them. Many love clothing more than the soul.

Because anger, greed, and lust, above all other thoughts, continually try to creep into our hearts, if we wish to repel them with Christ’s help, let us strive to occupy our minds with holy thoughts.

For we have much in the Holy Scriptures by which our Lord both promises us the rewards of the saints and threatens the punishments of sinners, mercifully warning us so that the righteous may persevere in good and the impious be recalled from evil.

If we frequently read these things ourselves, or willingly wish to hear others reading them, evil thoughts will never be able to creep upon us.

Since these things are so, dearest brothers, we can and must think with great shame that, although we do not wish even some spark of fire to enter the chest where our clothes are kept, nevertheless, through wicked thoughts, we not only permit the flames of anger to enter the chest of our conscience but also provoke and kindle them into a greater fire through false suspicions.

And what excuse will we be able to have before God, when we love our clothing more than our soul?

What is required of us is neither burdensome, difficult, nor impossible, dearest brothers. Although we ought to guard our souls incomparably more carefully than our clothing, the person who at least guards his soul so that it is not stained by evil and shameful thoughts makes no small progress, just as he guards his clothing so that it is not destroyed by moths or mice.

I ask you, brothers: what evil has our soul, made in the image of God, deserved from us, that we should be unwilling to devote to it as much care as we appear to devote to our clothing?

And since human eyes see our bodies, while the eyes of angels look upon our souls, I do not know with what conscience we adorn and arrange our flesh with precious things—flesh that after a few days or years will be devoured by worms in the grave—while we do not adorn our souls with good works, though they will have to be presented to God and the angels in heaven.

#### 5. Conclusion

Therefore, changing our priorities for the better, let us provide our bodies with moderate and sufficient food and clothing, so that we may store everything better that we can possess for our souls in eternal blessedness through almsgiving to the poor.

Otherwise, if we think more about the flesh than about the soul, when we come to that wedding feast not adorned with good works but rather wrapped in the filthy rags of vices, it may be said to us: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew 22:12).

May God turn away from us what follows: “Bind his hands and feet,” he says, [Col. 2347] “and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 13).

Behold the sentence that the person will deserve to hear who adorns his flesh through vanity and luxury and neglects to adorn his soul with good works for the sake of eternal life.

But we trust in God’s mercy that he will deign to inspire us so that, with his help, we may guard our hearts unharmed from evil thoughts and preserve our bodies clean in complete chastity and sobriety.

Thus, when we are found worthy to come before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, may we not deserve to receive punishment for evil deeds, but attain eternal rewards for good works—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCCXIV  
*[Note: [Col. 2347] Manuscripts from the Carthusian monastery of Portes and the Colbertinus attribute this to Caesarius, and it is his twenty-third homily in the Library of the Fathers. For no. 1, see Appendix Sermon 16, no. 4; for no. 3, Sermons 256, no. 4; 22, no. 6; 29, no. 4; 2, no. 4; and 313, no. 1.]*

### On the Delivered Demoniac

#### 1. Why neither the demoniac nor the demon should be feared. Everyone feeds either Christ or the devil. His actions reveal which one is his guest. As many vices as a person has, so many demons does he have.

Last Sunday, dearest brothers, while Mass was being celebrated, that frenzied demoniac generated no small fear in the whole congregation. It is certain, dearest brothers, that scarcely anyone can see an unfortunate person so tormented by the devil without becoming frightened and afraid.

And yet, dearest brothers, if you wish, with God’s help we can show you how you can avoid fearing a demoniac. You will never fear the demon who is in another person’s flesh if you do not have him in your own soul.

Indeed, holy and perfect men not only do not fear demoniacs; they are feared with great trembling by demoniacs and even by the demons themselves.

But if we fear a demon in another person’s body in this way, how greatly ought we to fear nourishing him in our own hearts through evil deeds?

Every human being, dearest brothers, feeds either Christ or the devil at the banquet of his heart. If he wishes to pursue justice, peace, chastity, mercy, and charity, he undoubtedly feeds and refreshes Christ within himself, according to what is written: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter him and dine with him” (Revelation 3:20).

Behold, it has been proved to you how and with what food a holy soul feeds and refreshes Christ.

Conversely, whoever wishes to love pride, malice, envy, lust, and other things like them should not doubt that he refreshes the devil and prepares for him such evils as desirable delicacies.

Each person can learn from his actions what kind of guest he deserves to receive in his heart. It is certain that whatever banquet you prepare, such guests you will deserve to have.

Many fear a demon in another person’s body but pretend not to fear him in their own heart.

Everyone who loves pride is full of the devil. If, together with pride, he also wishes to have envy, he will be subject to two demons. If, together with envy, he also commits adultery, he is possessed by three demons. If, along with these evils, he wishes to love falsehood, he is subdued and oppressed by an entire team of demons.

For as many vices as a person has, so many demons does he have.

Indeed, in the Gospel, when the unclean spirit had gone out from the person who, through God’s grace, had deserved to be freed from one demon of idolatry, because he did not wish to admit virtues into the place of vices, that unclean spirit returned and brought with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself (Luke 11:24). And what is written was fulfilled in him: “By whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” [Col. 2348] (2 Peter 2:19); and again: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

#### 2. The proud person is not without a demon, nor the envious, adulterer, or liar.

But perhaps someone says: How can it happen that a person who has sinned through lust in his flesh has the devil in his soul?

We, beloved brothers, prove what we have said by the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures.

That the proud person is full of a demon, hear Scripture saying: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God”; and again: “The beginning of every pride is to apostatize from God” (Sirach 10:14).

What is “to apostatize” except to depart from God? And surely whoever is separated from God is joined to the devil.

That the envious person cannot be without a demon, Scripture says: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his side imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25).

That the person who fornicates is also possessed by the devil, canonical Scripture likewise bears witness. Thus the prophet says: “You have been deceived by the spirit of fornication” (Hosea 4:12).

That every liar also cannot be without an evil spirit, Scripture bears witness: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:7); and again: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

In the Book of Kings we also read that an evil spirit said to the Lord: “I will deceive Ahab.” The Lord said to him: “By what means will you deceive him?” And he replied: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of his prophets.” The Lord said: “You will deceive him, and you will prevail” (1 Kings 22:21–22).

We ought to believe similarly concerning the other capital sins and crimes: no one commits them except at the devil’s instigation.

#### 3. So that medicine may quickly heal sins.

What then, brothers? Since we recognize that we are burdened with many sins and crimes, should we despair? Far be this from the Christian people.

We must not despair, but neither must we persist in those sins with hostile complacency. The one who said, “When you turn and groan, you will be saved” (Ezekiel 33:12), also said: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Sirach 5:8).

A poultice or bandage is best applied while wounds are still hot; and a wound is quickly healed if it is not permitted to fester for a long time.

Therefore, whenever one of us receives a wound from any sin, before it festers and reeks through long habit, let him flee with all speed to the remedies of repentance.

If sin is permitted to dominate for a long time, it is known to exhale a most dreadful stench to all holy people and to all who fear God.

Therefore, with God’s help, we must labor so that, once all sins have been cleansed away or put to death, virtues may enter into possession of the places occupied by vices: let humility occupy the place held by pride; let almsgiving take possession of the place ravaged by avarice; let chastity cleanse and take possession of the place defiled by lust; let goodwill possess the place held by envy; and where falsehood appeared to be, let truth rule.

If we strive to do these things, brothers, with Christ’s help, then not only will we not fear demons in the bodies of others, but by God’s grace we will also drive them from our own hearts—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON CCCXV  
*[Note: [Col. 2348] Elsewhere, 35 among the Fifty Homilies.]*

### On the Foretelling of the Times of Christians and on the Church’s Not Being Free from Temptations  
*[Note: [Col. 2348] It is placed here in the Appendix for the first time. The Louvain editors considered it doubtful, while Verlinus and Vindingus judged it spurious. It has been stitched together from various scraps of Augustine, Faustus, and others. For no. 1, see Appendix Sermon 58, no. 1; for no. 3, Sermon 238, no. 2; Faustus, Letter 1 to Felix and Letter 6 to Ruricius; Appendix Sermon 228, no. 1; for no. 4, Sermon 76, no. 1.]*

#### 1. The Church’s vengeance upon its adversaries. What should be considered in the persecutor.

Throughout all the divine Scriptures, dearest brothers, the times of Christians were foretold. This was because it was destined to happen that the kings of the earth, who [Col. 2349] persecuted Christians because of idols, would destroy idols because of Christ, and every power would be subjected to the yoke of Christ, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “I have avenged myself upon them” (Psalm 117:10).

What does “I have avenged myself upon them” mean? I have taken vengeance on them. The body of Christ speaks: “I have avenged myself upon my enemies.”

How did he avenge himself? By killing error in them and raising up faith. Whatever it was that in all the evil and perverse people persecuted Christians has been destroyed.

When a person persecutes you, do not pay attention to the form that God made or to the soul that God breathed into him. It is not what God made that persecutes you, but the wickedness that the person made.

Everything God made praises God. You have heard this in the blessings, and you hear it at every solemnity when they are read: how all things praise God—the heavenly and earthly things, angels, human beings, the lights of heaven, the trees of the earth, rivers, and seas. Whatever God created, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, praises God.

Have you ever heard that avarice praises God? Have you ever heard that drunkenness praises God? Have you ever heard that lust praises God? Have you ever heard that heresy praises God?

Why do none of these praise God? Because they were not created by God.

The tree preserved what it had been created as; the human being destroyed the uprightness in which he had been made.  
*[Note: [Col. 2349] German manuscript: “what was set upright.” Remigius: “what was right.”]*

For if he preserved in himself the good that God created in him—that is, God’s image—he would always praise God, not only with his tongue but also with his life.

Therefore our times too were foretold; but in our times future schisms were foretold. Just as that Church fought against the devil, so this one also fights.

#### 2. The devil first attacked the Church as a lion, now as a dragon. How he is conquered. The necessity of Christ’s death. He underwent it willingly.

Does the struggle against the devil cease? The devil is called both a lion and a dragon: a lion because of his assault, a dragon because of his ambushes. The lion grows angry openly; the dragon lies in wait secretly.

The earlier Church fought against the lion; now it fights against the dragon. But just as the lion was conquered, so the dragon is conquered.

What strength does the lion have against that Lion of whom it is written, “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5)? And what strength does the dragon have against the death of the Lord, who hanged the serpent upon the wood?

For he triumphed over the death that the devil had offered to humanity through his schemes. When Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness upon the wood, the people who were being bitten by the serpent looked at the serpent and were healed. So now, whoever has been bitten by Satan’s cunning should look toward Christ hanging upon the wood; for there death was killed.

The Lord always lives, but in order to kill death he was clothed in death. Death could not die except in life. Bitterness does not die except in sweetness; cold does not die except in heat. Death was not dead except in life.

What is life? Our Christ. But life was clothed in death. He was crucified, killed, and died, and he rose again, so that the Apostle might say of him: “We know that Christ, having risen from the dead, does not die again, and death will no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9).

But since death first ruled, it ruled over one who wished it to. The lion’s attendant puffed himself up against him. Then the judge by whom he was being judged raised his neck and said: “Do you not answer me?” (John 19:10).

The lion’s roar rages; the serpent’s neck swells. But hear the response of the Lamb, who knows how to kill the lion; hear that death ruled over him willingly.

For when he heard these words from him, he replied: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (ibid., 11).

Who gave this power from above? God. Who is God? The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, so that human beings might have power over God, the human being received power from God to judge God: God hidden, and a human being manifest.

### 3. The Devil as a Lion When He Harasses, as a Dragon When He Flatters

Against flattery vigilance is necessary. Therefore, so that with God’s help we may be able to conquer both the lion and the dragon mentioned above, let us keep before our eyes, with great fear and trembling [Col. 2350], what the apostle Peter said: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8); and also what the Apostle warns us about the dragon, urging us to beware of him with every possible care: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 11:2–3).

Whenever some public tribulation arises for you, understand it as the lion’s rage and savagery. Whenever evil desires solicit you toward avarice or lust through cunning seduction, recognize the dragon’s flatteries. If, therefore, you desire faithfully to preserve the right faith, be strong in adversity against the lion’s savagery. But if you wish to preserve the soul’s virginity intact, guard against the dragon’s flatteries as far as you can, lest, if you are heedless, you allow the five senses within you—like five virgins—to be corrupted by the serpent.

For whatever delights the sight, whatever sweetens the taste, whatever flatters the hearing, whatever entices the sense of smell, and whatever softens through touch—in all these things, if we are heedless, we allow the virginity of the soul to be corrupted by creeping evil desires. Thus what was spoken through the prophet is fulfilled in us: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. 9:21). For through these five senses, as through certain doors, either death or life enters our soul.

### 4. Praise and Blame Should Be Valued Little

Let us therefore, with the Lord’s help, belong among those five wise virgins who, as we read in the Gospel, carried oil in their lamps. And as far as we can, let us be careful not to be found among those foolish virgins who, boasting merely of the integrity of their bodies, lost the virginity of their souls through the corruption of the five senses. They did not carry oil with them; and they were told, “Go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.”

For in this passage oil means flattery and human praise: all flatterers sell oil. Those foolish virgins, then, were so called because they sought praise outwardly and did not possess it within, in their consciences. That is why they did not carry oil with them: they wished to have praise on another person’s tongue, not in their own consciences.

Yet what did they reply to those foolish virgins? “Perhaps there will not be enough for us” (Matt. 25:4, 9), just as the Apostle said: “Indeed, I do not even judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3). If, then, our conscience trembles under the examination of God’s judgment, and although it appears right to itself fears that the standard of justice [Note: [Col. 2350] The manuscript reads: “wickedness.”] may emerge from its treasury—and that what seemed straight may be found crooked—how much less ought we to concern ourselves, dearly beloved, with the judgments of others about us, whether bad or good?

We ought not to rejoice greatly when we are praised, nor be saddened when we are blamed. False praise cannot crown us, and false blame cannot condemn us. As long as we live here, we cannot judge ourselves, not merely concerning what we shall be tomorrow, but even concerning what we are today. How much less, then, ought we to be disturbed by the judgments of others than by our own conscience, which bears witness to us? For our glory ought to be our conscience.

### 5. What Has Been Heard Must Be Ruminated

Therefore, brothers, let your Charity attend for a little while, so that I may say what I wish to say—though not as I wish, but as the Lord grants and wills—something especially necessary amid the daily temptations of the Catholic Church. For she lives amid temptations, grows amid temptations, endures amid temptations, and reaches her goal amid temptations. But when she has arrived, rest will succeed labor: temptation will depart, while blessing remains.

But I ask you, brothers, not to listen without purpose. Hold on to these things, ruminate on them, feed on them; let what has just been entrusted to your memory not depart from your mouths. Human memory is like the stomach of an animal. You know that in the Law animals that do not ruminate are called unclean, while those that ruminate are clean. And whatever has a divided hoof pertains to discerning truth from falsehood. The divided hoof signifies discerning what is right and what is left.

[Col. 2351] Ruminating pertains to those who afterward reflect on what they have heard and retained. For just now we are eating, and what we hear is cast into our memory as into a stomach. But what does an animal do when it ruminates? It brings back to its mouth what had been thrown into the manger and stored in its stomach, and rests in that very sweetness.

I have said this so that I might urge you not to be like unclean animals. An unclean animal receives its food into its stomach, but afterward does not ruminate, and all the sweetness passes away. What has been stored does you no good if its sweetness does not return to your mouth.

Hear this stated explicitly and clearly in another saying: what was spoken obscurely and mystically in the passage about ruminating animals is explained elsewhere in plain terms, so that we may understand its meaning: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a fool swallows it” (Prov. 21:20).

## SERMON 316

*[Note: Elsewhere, On Various Matters 38.]*

### On Saint Lawrence

*[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. There is nothing in it deserving criticism, except that, Vinding says, its style indicates that it is not Augustine’s.]*

#### 1. The Saints Are Kindled by Hope for Endurance

When we celebrate the anniversaries of the holy martyrs and admire them in their praises, we ought to live in such a way as to imitate them in everything. For when we love the martyrs, we choose for ourselves the means by which we may please the Lord.

Look at the most blessed martyr Lawrence, whose anniversary we celebrate today in the Church. He chose such a cause for his confession that he deserved to receive the martyr’s crown from Christ. What great constancy the martyrs possessed, what good faith the saints displayed, who willingly endured many torments for Christ’s name and yet, by despising those same torments, overcame the devil in their persecutors!

Of them Solomon says: “Although in the sight of men they suffered torments, their hope is full of immortality” (Wis. 3:4). The saints therefore possessed great hope, believing that in the resurrection they could receive what they hoped for while enduring temporal suffering.

And what did they hope for when they endured such things? What they endured can be stated very easily; for who could explain what they hoped for? Hear the apostle Paul: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

#### 2. They Are Made White by the Lamb’s Blood

They therefore possessed great hope of resurrection, and for that reason endured the torments of suffering. They hoped for great splendor and glorious rest; they hoped for the heavenly Jerusalem; they hoped for paradise. And to the place from which Adam had been expelled because of his transgression, the saints returned bearing victorious trophies, after overthrowing the one who had deceived Adam.

The saints washed their robes in the blood of their suffering and made them white in the blood of the Redeemer. For it is well known, brothers, that if blood touches anyone’s clothing, it is stained. But the blood of the spotless Lamb knows how to make white; it does not know how to stain.

Thus blessed Lawrence, adorned in dress, appearance, and holiness, possessed a conscience white before his suffering, and through his suffering whitened the robe of his body and mind still more. O holy Lawrence, white in mind and white also in bodily clothing, I cannot praise your merit adequately, because I perceive the greatness of your purpose.

You conceived a great plan and conducted a heavenly undertaking. Receiving the treasures of the Church, you distributed them to poor Christians, and you deserved to receive heavenly treasures. For thus the Lord admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: “Sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

You fulfilled the Lord’s command, and he gave you the reward of his kingdom. How shall I honor you? With what praise shall I commend you? Placed in the very battle of confession, while you were still under the custody of Hippolytus, you constantly displayed the Lord’s power: you made the sign of Christ’s cross over the eyes of the blind, you gave sight to the blind, and you wondrously converted Hippolytus, your custodian, to faith in Christ.

*[Col. 2352]*

#### 3. Lawrence Is Compared with Stephen

Whom shall I compare to you? Whom shall I make equal to your honor? I shall find you someone like you, and in a certain way your predecessor both in honor and in confession: in honor, the first deacon of Christ; in confession, blessed Stephen.

After Christ’s ascension, Stephen was the first of the seven deacons ordained by the Apostles, and he was crowned in martyrdom before the Apostles. Attend, brothers, to the equal conduct and confession of these two leaders of the victorious army of martyrs.

Stephen was being stoned, and he prayed; Lawrence was being roasted, and he rejoiced with a cheerful face. Stephen prayed for Saul, his stoner; and Lawrence made Hippolytus, his custodian, a Christian.

These archdeacons performed great wonders: upon those from whom they suffered punishments, they bestowed divine benefits. For they did what they heard the Lord Christ himself doing in his passion: he prayed for his enemies on the cross, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

The Lord also taught them this very thing when he said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (John 12:26). They deserved to be with Christ because, confessing Christ with great constancy, they conquered the Antichrist.

Therefore, brothers, let us confess the Lord Jesus Christ with the full attention of our minds; let us fear and love him with all our strength, so that with all the saints we may deserve to reach the rewards of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## SERMON 317

*[Note: Elsewhere, 17 among the Vignerian sermons, Supplement, part 1.]*

### On the Anniversary of the Martyrs of Massa Candida

*[Note: Now placed in the Appendix for the first time. This does not sound like Augustine, because of the affected elegance—whatever its quality—of the discourse; and the sermon seems to be composed in excessively elaborate language, especially in the passage “Not the old man, already broken by declining years, with his throat withering,” and so forth. Furthermore, the martyrdom of Massa Candida, celebrated by Augustine and the Africans, was completed not by the sword, as stated here, but by fire in a lime kiln. The Martyrologies and Prudentius in *Peristephanon* 13 report that the group consisted of a definite number of men, not people gathered from every age and sex, after Pontius in the Acts of Saint Cyprian. Nevertheless, two Roman manuscripts attribute this sermon to Augustine, and Baronius cites it under Augustine’s name in the notes to the *Martyrologium*, August 24 and November 1.]*

### Why Massa Candida Was So Called; From Whom It Was Gathered

Dearest brothers, we are celebrating the anniversary of the martyrs whose multitude made them a mass and whose splendor made them white. It was called a mass because of their number, and white because of their merit. For what else should *Massa Candida* be understood to mean except a multitude made white by martyrdom?

Just now, when the Apocalypse was being read, we heard that the blessed disciple and apostle who used to recline upon Christ’s breast saw crowds of martyrs shining in white garments and triumphing with green palms; and what he saw happily, he faithfully reported to us.

For he says, as we have just heard: “I saw, and behold, a multitude that no one could number, from every people, tribe, and language; all clothed in white garments, with palms in their hands” (Rev. 7:9). The white garment signifies innocence; the palms, victory.

And one of the elders said to John: “Who are these, and from where have they come?” (ibid., 13). John replied: “Lord, you know.” But the elder had asked in order to teach him: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation, and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (ibid., 14).

What kind of blood is this, brothers? This blood washes; it does not stain. It has redness, certainly, but nevertheless it cannot stain whiteness. This is a wondrous thing, dearest brothers, for it is the blood of the one of whom his bride says in the Song of Songs: “My brother is white and red” (Song 5:10).

If he is white, why is he red? If no blemish of sin darkened Christ’s innocence, why did he shed blood? If he is white, why is he red? If that white one did not darken himself with any night of iniquity, why did he, though spotless, ascend the cross?

You ask why? Hear the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains [Col. 2353] alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24–25).

Look at the mass, and understand the reason for the seed. This mass, brothers, as you have heard, was gathered from every people, tribe, and language, from both sexes and every age. Not the old man, already broken by declining years, with his withering throat, withdrew his trembling neck; not the old woman, worn out by sex and age, escaped the right hand of the bloodstained executioner; youth was not recalled from the crown by the sweetness of this life; the bloodstained executioner did not shrink from the throbbing limbs of dying little children.

But if perhaps some infants, clinging to their mothers’ breasts, were able to evade the sword of their pursuer, crushed beneath the collapse of corpses, they died amid their mothers’ sweet embraces. The one who redeemed every age crowned them all in that contest.

What a spectacle there was then, dearest brothers—how bloodstained the age, through which it appeared pitiable and horrifying to those who looked upon it [Note: Morel thinks this passage should be restored as follows: “What a spectacle there was then, dearest brothers! How bloodstained and harsh! How pitiable and horrifying it appeared to those who looked upon it!” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 359. Perhaps, however, only the latter part should be corrected by punctuation in this way: “How bloodstained the age! Through it [or: exceedingly] it appeared pitiable and horrifying to those who looked upon it, but …” (M.)]—but “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his [Col. 2354] saints” (Ps. 115:15).

Would you like to know how precious it is? Recall how we read in the apostolic Epistle: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them” (Heb. 11:16).

O if only we could see how great the joy was in that heavenly city when, while there was such sorrow on earth over their slaughter, these martyrs advanced toward heaven in a single company and the citizens of that blessed city—that is, thousands of angels—came out to meet them!

O if only we could see these martyrs leaving their bodies, as though treading upon the roofs of houses made of clay!

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, bring joy in heaven to the holy angels. The holy martyrs too ought to rejoice over us, because they do not cease to pray for us. But when do they rejoice over us? When we imitate those whom we venerate. For they wish their solemnities to be celebrated by our assemblies in such a way that we gladden their piety through our conduct.

26–31 **SERMON III.** On Hagar and Ishmael.—How heretics and schismatics are represented by Hagar and Ishmael.

32 **SERMON IV.** On Jacob and Esau.—1. Spiritual understanding is given by the Holy Spirit. 2. Peter, thinking carnally, was weak. His strength, and that of all the martyrs, came from the Holy Spirit. 3. Esau represents the carnal, Jacob the spiritual. 4. The blessed life of the angels comes from the vision of God. 5. God is not bodily, nor of a kind that our thought can fashion. 6. What should be thought when God is mentioned. A brief treatment of the Manichaean error. 7. What sort of light God, who is light, should be conceived to be. 8. What kind of happiness is to be hoped for in the future age. The two Testaments. 9. The difference and harmony of the Old and New Testaments. This world is a wilderness for the Christian. 10. Our figures are found in what happened to the Israelite people. 11. What Isaac and Rebekah signified in Jacob’s blessing. All the saints belong to the Church. 12. The carnal are, in their allotted portion, Esau. 13. The blessing of the younger under the appearance of the elder. 14. The sins of others must be patiently borne. 15. How Jacob was without deceit and yet with deceit. 16–17. What it means to have goatskins. 18. The two goats: the two peoples. 19. Why the peoples are called goats. 20. Others’ sins must be borne in such a way that they are corrected. Charity. 21. Isaac understood the figure in Jacob’s deception. 22. Deception that was not deception. 23. What the deception in Jacob signifies. Jacob is defended against lying. 24. Jacob’s blessing. 25. One thing signified in many ways. 26. The Church as a field. 27. Esau’s blessing. 28–29. Jacob’s supplanting. 30. In the blessing, what is proper and what is common to Jacob and Esau. 31. Scripture and the sacraments are common to good and wicked persons. 32. All nations are subjected to spiritual things. 33. Why the nations are not subjected to carnal persons [Col. 2354]. 34. Against schismatics. 35. The blessing obtained by force. 36. Epilogue concerning the struggle against the devil, to be undertaken on the example of the martyrs. The anniversary of Vincent the martyr. 37. The martyrs are to be imitated.

33–52 **SERMON V.** On Jacob’s wrestling with the angel.—1. The good are to be imitated, but the wicked are to be tolerated until the separation is made at the last judgment. 2. Debts must be forgiven to enemies. An enemy must be loved in such a way that he is nevertheless corrected. 3. We must wrestle so as to pursue Christ’s charity and patience by imitation. 4. Jacob and Esau as figures of the Christian and Jewish peoples. 5. The Jews are servants of Christians. 6. Jacob’s wrestling with the angel. 7. What the angel’s refusal to be held signifies.

52–58 **SERMON VI.** On the Lord who appeared to Moses in the bush.—1. How God appeared to Moses. 2. God appeared to Moses through an angel. 3. Why God’s appearance took place in a bush. 4. The name of God. 5. Another name of God. 6. The signs given to Moses. 7. What the rod signifies; what the serpent signifies. 8. What Moses’ hand and bosom signify; what the water signifies.

59–62 **SERMON VII.** On the reading from Exodus, concerning the bush in which there was flame and which was not consumed.—1. What should be observed in the appearance from the bush. 2. What the bush, with the flame clinging to it but not burning it, signifies. 3. The opinion of some that the one speaking to Moses was Christ. 4. In that opinion, the Arian argument must be avoided. 5. The opinion of others that an angel, not Christ, appeared to Moses.

62–66 **SERMON VIII.** On the ten plagues and the ten commandments.

67 **SERMON IX.** On the ten strings.

75 **SERMON X.** On Solomon’s judgment between two prostitute women.—1. The narration of the event. 2. The two women disputing before Solomon over the child: the Synagogue and the Church. The life of the sacraments is Christ. 3. The Jews falsely claiming that Christian grace is owed to them. 4. Hypocrisy must be opposed in such a way that the danger of schism is avoided. 5. Another meaning of the two women. 6. Simulators in the Church come after good workers. 7. The fraud of simulators against good workers. 8. One’s personal honor must be disregarded so that the unity of the Church may be preserved.

91–96 **SERMON XI.** On Elijah and the widow of Sarepta.—1. Works of piety to be practiced in the present time. 2. Why Elijah is sent to be fed by a poor widow. How God’s command is to be understood. 3. The reward of good works is not to be expected in this present time.

99 **SERMON XII.** On what is written in Job 1:6, “And behold, the angels came into the presence of God, and the devil among them,” etc., and on what is said in the Gospel, Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”: against the Manichaeans.—1. The Manichaeans’ slander against the book of Job. 2. Adimantus’s slanderous objection based on the Apostle. The rulers of this age. The world: sinners. The devil as prince of sin [Col. 2355]. 3. How the devil came into God’s presence. 4. The various ways in which God speaks to us. 5. The devil could hear God’s voice. 6. What it means that the devil came into God’s presence. 7. How the devil was among the angels. 8. The Manichaeans refuted from their own doctrine. 9. The Manichaeans do not deny that Christ was seen by the devil. Angels appear through a true assumed body. 10. How Christ appeared to the devil. 11. The Manichaeans are pressed by the fact that the sun, which they consider a god, is seen by the wicked. 12. Why Christ was born of a woman. The Son of God was not changed through the incarnation.

100–105 **SERMON XIII.** On Psalm 2:10, “Be instructed, all you who judge the earth.”—1. What it means to judge the earth. 2. Those who presume on their own strength perish from the right way. Trust must be placed in the Lord. Improper humility. 3. A good will is aroused by God. 4. Address to judges. The adulterous woman. 5. She receives mercy. 6. Paul’s words concerning authority. 7. A judge must first pronounce judgment on himself, then on others. 8. He must pursue sins, not the sinner. 9. Discipline and correction must not be neglected. Striking is pious; sparing is cruel.

107–111 **SERMON XIV.** On Psalm 9:14, “The poor man is left to you; you will be the helper of the orphan.”—1. Who the true poor person is. 2. Pride must be avoided by the rich. 3. The poor must not exalt themselves over Lazarus’s lot. 4. The poor and the rich share the same lot of blessedness if both are humble. Abraham’s bosom. 5. The true poor person is scarcely found among the poor. 6. Riches are full of dangers and destined to perish. 7. The poor person who is rich in desires is worse. 8. Again the poor person is compared with the rich. 9. The true poor person. Christ is poor and rich. Christ’s poverty. 10. Who is the orphan.

111–116 **SERMON XV.** On Psalm 25:8, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory.”—1. The beauty of God’s house. The living Church. 2. Number and what is beyond number. Vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor. 3. It belongs to the wicked to use good things badly; to God, on the contrary, to use the wicked well. Adulterous and fornicating souls. 4. Why evil exists in the world. 5. The abundance of evil for the purification of the good. 6. Evil persons inside and outside must be tolerated. 7. Steadfastness in bearing evils within. 8. Hard commands, but great promises. 9. The wicked are numerous so that the good may be exercised. Dregs and oil.

116–120 **SERMON XVI.** On Psalm 33:13, “Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days?”—1. The present life is not truly life. 2. The good life must be pursued here. What it means to redeem the time. 3. What life is proposed in the psalm. 4. The good days promised in the psalm are not those of this age but of eternity. Speaking deceit. 5. With what ardor peace and eternal life must be sought.

121–124 **SERMON XVII.** On Psalm 49:3, “God manifest shall come, our God, and shall not keep silence,” etc.—1. The final judgment. 2. The office imposed on those in authority. The vow of a pious shepherd. 3. Sins become cheap through habit and are no longer felt. Drunkenness. Excommunication. 4. God sees and hates sinners, even if he is now silent. 5. God’s judgment against sinners. The time for repentance. 6. Medicine must not be postponed until after sin. 7. The brevity of life. A human being is more fragile than glass.

124–128 **SERMON XVIII.** On the same verse of Psalm 49, “God manifest shall come,” etc.—1. One coming of Christ is hidden, the other manifest. God’s commandments become a subject of ridicule to some. The perverse judgment of carnal people. 2. Why God now judges some things but not all. 3. The treasury of works, whether good or evil. 4. Each person’s own treasury remains with him. The poor as bearers of burdens for the rich. 5. Unfruitful repentance.

128–131 **SERMON XIX.** On Psalm 50:5, “For I acknowledge my iniquity,” and Psalm 72:1, “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart!”—1. God must be asked not to turn his face away from us, but from our sins. 2. It belongs to the penitent both to acknowledge and to punish his own sins. 3. God is to be appeased by the sacrifice of a contrite heart. 4. A person ought to be displeased by what displeases God, and conversely. Happiness must not be sought here. Acclamation of the hearers. The scandal caused by the happiness of the wicked. 5. What happiness and reward are to be expected from God. 6. We are warned to live well amid daily dangers.

132–136 **SERMON XX.** On Psalm 50:12, “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” and Psalm 40:5, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me,” etc.—1. A sinner cannot rise from sin by himself without grace. 2. Confession of sin is necessary to obtain forgiveness. Sin must be punished either by the sinner himself or by God. Excusing sin is wicked and is suggested by the devil [Col. 2356]. 3. Both despair and the hope of remaining unpenitent cause impenitence and destruction. 4. Conversion must not be delayed. A person wants everything of his own to be good except his life. 5. Presbyters as ministers of the word of God.

137–141 **SERMON XXI.** On Psalm 63:11, “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord.”—1. The joy of the devout in God, even in this life. 2. We now draw near to God through humility and charity. 3. Sin itself is not loved; rather, the disordered love of a creature is sin. 4. Against those who prefer a creature to God. 5. Faith is loved by everyone, even if perhaps this is not apparent. 6. Faith is honored in a servant. 7. Faith owed to God by servants purchased with his blood. 8. Joy in God and in the eternal goods he has given. The upright in heart is the person who praises the Father’s scourge. 9. The delight of the devout in God when earthly possessions are lost. 10. When the use of gold is bad and when it is good.

142–148 **SERMON XXII.** On Psalm 67:3, “As smoke fails, so may they fail,” etc.—1. The prophet’s use of the figure of wishing signifies the certainty of his vision. 2. In the prophet’s figure of wishing, the approval of the divine decree is to be understood. 3. The ways in which God urges people to repentance. God’s scourge is our warning. Unfruitful and fruitful repentance. 4. Faith in the future judgment is strengthened by so many other prophecies that have been fulfilled. The martyrs’ blood is seed. 5. God is both just and merciful. 6. When the accused changes, the judge changes. 7. Let the sinner perish, so that the human being may not perish. 8. Those who defend their sins fail like smoke. 9. How great God’s mercy is toward humanity. 10. Two parents lead to life, and two to death.

148–154 **SERMON XXIII.** On Psalm 72:24, “You have held me by the hand of my right hand,” and on the vision of God.—1. The office of teachers is dangerous; the condition of hearers is safer. 2. All are fellow disciples under Christ the teacher. The duty of hearers toward teachers. 3. Holy Scripture is adapted to the weakness of little ones. 4. Who are carnal hearers and who are spiritual. 5. Understanding belongs only to one who thinks truly. To be mistaken about God is dangerous; to lie about him is destructive. 6. Carnal thought concerning God. 7. The heart of the faithful is not too narrow to be God’s temple. Fear has narrowness; love has breadth. 8. The enlargement of the heart through charity, which is also called a pledge and earnest. How an earnest and a pledge differ. 9. Charity is more properly called an earnest than a pledge. 10. The fountain of charity is the highest good. 11. The good things proper to the devout. 12. The distinction between human beings and the sons of men. 13. Charity is loved, yet is not perceived. 14. How God appeared here to Moses. 15. God appeared without changing himself, in the form he chose. 16. God will be seen by his children as he is. 17. The peacemakers are children of God. 18. God will be seen only by the peacemakers.

155–162 **SERMON XXIV.** On Psalm 82:2, “God, who is like you?”—1. He congratulates the faithful who are inflamed with zeal for God against idols. 2. The piety of Christians toward pagans. 3. No human being should be compared with the true God, much less the idol of Hercules, whose inscription is refuted. 4. How God is asked not to be silent or grow mild. 5. The zeal of certain faithful persons against idols. 6. He congratulates the citizens because they do not want the Roman gods, overthrown at Rome, to stand at Carthage. 7. God is gentle when angry.

162–166 **SERMON XXV.** On Psalm 93:12, “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord,” etc.—1. The Gospel is the law of the New Testament. The promises of the Old Law must be understood spiritually. 2. The servitude of the Old Law when God is worshiped for the sake of earthly things. Lift up your heart. 3. The evil days began with the beginning of sin. 4. The origin of the evil days. 5. The evil days benefit the devout by helping them find the good days. 6. Under what condition the good days are offered. 7. What kind of peace is commanded to be pursued. Lift up your heart. 8. Christ is to be clothed and received in the poor.

167–170 **SERMON XXVI.** On the words of Psalm 94, “Come, let us adore and fall down before him; let us weep before the Lord who made us,” etc.; on the Apostle’s words to the Galatians, chapter 2, “For if righteousness comes through the law,” etc., and chapter 3, “For if a law had been given that could give life”; and to the Romans, chapter 9, “O human being, who are you,” etc., and chapter 11, “O the depth!” etc. Against the heresy of the Pelagians.—1. A human being was created by God and, when he calls upon him, is not abandoned by God. 2. The Pelagian error: that they were made human beings by God, but righteous by themselves. 3. What free will is worth without God. 4. We are what we are by God as author. The grace of creation. God’s election. 5. If we are faithful, we are so by God’s grace. 6. Grace. 7. The grace of Christ the Mediator. The Mediator. 8. The emerging Pelagian heresy is to be rejected with horror, although it pretends to admit God’s grace. 9. The necessity of Christ’s grace, beyond nature and the law, must be acknowledged. For what purpose was the law given. 10. The Manichaean [Col. 2357] heresy concerning the author of the Old Law. 11. The insufficiency of the law once given; the necessity of grace represented in Elisha. 12. The grace of Christians. 13. The mass of perdition, from which we have been chosen. Election from the mass of perdition is inscrutable. 14. Grace excludes every preceding merit. 15. We must claim nothing for ourselves.

171–178 **SERMON XXVII.** On the title and opening verses of Psalm 95, and on the Apostle’s words in Romans 9, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,” etc. Against the Pelagians.—1. The house of God that is now being built. 2. The captivity from which we are freed through Christ. 3. There is no injustice in God, who has mercy on whom he wills. 4. Why God has mercy on whom he wills is beyond human comprehension. 5. How all things were made known here to the Apostles. 6. The equity of God, who has mercy on whom he wills, is to be believed now until it is seen afterward. The sign of the cross. 7. God’s judgments in the mystery of grace are not to be investigated by reasoning but pursued with wonder.

178–181 **SERMON XXVIII.** On Psalm 104:3, “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.”—1. The heart should rejoice in God. 2. God is light, fragrance, and food to the heart. 3. The light of the eyes, as food, nourishes many without diminishing itself. 4. The sound and meaning of a voice reach many without division. 5. On understanding.

182–184 **SERMON XXIX.** On Psalm 117:1, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.”—1. God alone is good from himself; all other good comes from him. 2. There are two kinds of confession: that of praise and that of repentance. 3. Confession of sins is necessary for salvation. 4. Both confessions, of praise and of sin, are owed to God. 5. The wicked person wants everything to be good except himself. 6. Sin must be punished either by God or by the repentant person.

185–187 **SERMON XXX.** On the words of Psalm 118, “Direct my steps,” etc., and of the Apostle, Romans 7, “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” etc. Against the Pelagians.—1. The dominion of iniquity over human beings before grace. 2. Human captivity through sin. 3. The adversary of grace is refuted by the experience of one’s own weakness. 4. The struggle of flesh and spirit. 5. The false defender of nature is ungrateful to the physician. 6. What must be done in the struggle of flesh and spirit. 7. The adversary of grace is under the yoke of iniquity. 8. The Church’s prayer overcomes the enemy of grace. 9. Christ the teacher of humility. 10. Why Christ’s yoke is easy. The Pelagian argument.

187–192 **SERMON XXXI.** On Psalm 125:5–6, “Those who sow in tears,” etc.—1. Sowing in tears belongs to all Christians. 2. The suffering and reward of the martyrs foretold in the psalm. 3. Certain weaker Christians sow in tears. 4. How all sow in tears. Every righteous person weeps more abundantly here. 5. The prayers of the righteous with groaning. 6. The tears of the devout are compared with the weeping of the wicked.

192–195 **SERMON XXXII.** On Psalm 143, concerning Goliath and David and contempt for the world.—1. Remedies in the divine Scriptures. 2. The title of the psalm. 3. The description of Goliath and David. 4. David’s confidence in God. 5. What mystery David’s five stones contain. 6. A rule for understanding the allegories of Scripture. 7. What the stones taken from the stream and placed in the shepherd’s pouch signify. 8. The Jewish people did not fulfill the law because they feared rather than loved. 9. A person must not presume on his own strength. 10. What belongs properly to a human being is nothing except sin and falsehood. 11. The devil’s two doors for tempting: desire and fear. 12. Christ finds everyone guilty. 13. What the sign of the cross on the forehead signifies. 14. The temptation of desire. 15. The temptation of fear. 16. Evil truly harms nothing that is good, but benefits it. 17. The wicked person is a sharp razor. 18. Happiness must not be placed in temporal things. 19. The happiness of the wicked is a stumbling block to some. A person who asks for what is superfluous is not heard by God in his favor. 20. The misuse of riches. 21. How desire for temporal things is unjust toward one’s neighbor. 22. The good and the wicked think differently about earthly happiness. 23. The fruit of God’s word is required even from one who does not listen. 24. Worldly happiness; even what appears lawful must be despised. 25. Whoever highly values the happiness of this age is an alien. 26. Goliath’s pride arising from earthly happiness. 27. Against those who rejoice in earthly happiness. 28. Who the blessed people are.

196–206 **SERMON XXXIII.** On Psalm 143:9, “God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.”—1. The new song is sung through charity. 2. The law is fulfilled through charity. 3. The three commandments that concern God. The spiritual Sabbath. The Sabbath of Sabbaths [Col. 2358]. 4. The seven commandments that concern one’s neighbor. 5. Whose it is to sing the new song. The Donatists do not sing it.

207–209 **SERMON XXXIV.** On these words of Psalm 149:1–2, “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the saints,” etc. On the new song and the new life.—1. Whose it is to sing the new song. 2. Charity is from God. 3. We love God from God. The idols of the heart. 4. The lowest form of love. 5. When God is loved, he is continually possessed. 6. The Lord must be sung both with the mouth and by one’s conduct. 7. The price by which charity must be acquired. 8. How much one’s neighbor must be loved. 9. Prayer after the sermon.

209–212 **SERMON XXXV.** On what is written in Solomon’s Proverbs, “If you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors; but if you become wicked, you alone will bear the evil,” chapter 9, verse 12, according to the Septuagint.

213 **SERMON XXXVI.** On what is written in the same book, chapter 13, verses 7–8: “There are those who pretend to be rich, possessing nothing; and there are those who humble themselves, though they are rich. The redemption of a person’s soul is his riches; but the poor person does not endure threats.”—1. Explanation of the words of Scripture. 2. The disease of riches: pride. 3. The rich who are not of this world. Christ’s poverty and riches. 4. All good believers are inwardly rich. What our winter and summer are. 5. The rich of this world are not despised by Christ. The emptiness and danger of riches. 6. What riches can be useful for. 7. Rich in inner riches. 8. Inner riches, faith, are to be preferred to gold. 9. Riches are to be spent in almsgiving for the salvation of the soul. 10. Poverty of spirit before the fear of threats that causes the spirit to fail. 11. True riches are to be sought from God.

215–219 **SERMON XXXVII.** On the reading from Solomon’s Proverbs beginning where it says, “Who will find a strong woman?” etc., and ending, “And let her husband be praised in the gates,” chapter 31, verses 10–31.—1. What is said about the strong woman in that chapter of Proverbs is referred to the Church. 2. The Church cannot remain hidden. 3. The woman described above by Augustine is more precious than precious stones. 4. “The heart of her husband trusts in her.” 5. “For she works good and not evil for her husband” at all times. 6. “Finding wool and flax, she worked with her hands for useful purposes.” 7. “She rises in the night and gives food to her household and tasks to her maidservants.” 8–9. “Considering a field, she bought it.” 10. “She girded her loins firmly and strengthened her arms.” 11. “Her lamp will not be extinguished throughout the night.” 12. “She stretches out her hands to useful things.” 13. “She also applied her arms to the distaff.” 14. “She opened her hands to the poor.” 15. “She is not anxious about the affairs of the household when her husband is staying elsewhere.” 16. “All in her household are clothed.” 17. “She made double garments for her husband.” 18. “She made garments for herself from fine linen and purple.” 19. “Her husband becomes conspicuous in the gates.” 20. “She made linen garments and sold them.” 21. “But sashes for the Canaanites.” 22. “She is clothed with strength and beauty.” 23. “She opened her mouth attentively. She ordered the arrangement of her words.” 24. The strict conduct of her household. 25. “Her children rose up and became rich.” 26. “And her husband praised her.” 27–28. “Many daughters have displayed strength.” 29. False favor and vain beauty. 30. The business of the blessed is nothing other than praising God.

221–235 **SERMON XXXVIII.** On the words of Ecclesiasticus 2:1–5, “My child, when you approach the service of God,” etc., and on Psalm 38:7, “Although a person walks in an image,” etc. On continence and endurance.—1. The two virtues of this life. 2. Good and evil are common to the good and the wicked. The scandal caused by the happiness of the wicked. 3. Faith is necessary here. The time of faith and the time of sight. 4. The time of faith is laborious. 5. Faith is the first commandment. As a human life grows, it diminishes. 6. People labor for their desires but do not want to labor for God’s promises. 7. The fear of death is continual distress to the rich person. 8. Riches are placed in safety when they are distributed. Almsgiving is a pious loan to God. 9. Riches must be sent ahead to heaven. 10. Faith in the heart, like Christ sleeping in the boat, must be awakened. 11. The world abandons its lovers.

235–241 **SERMON XXXIX.** On Ecclesiasticus 5:8–9, “Do not delay turning to God, nor postpone from day to day,” and on the Apostle’s words, 1 Timothy 6:7–19, “We brought nothing into this world,” etc.—1. Conversion must not be delayed. 2. Contempt for the world. 3. How dangerous the desire for riches is. 4. The worm of riches: pride. 5. The use of riches in good works. 6. In what measure and for what purpose almsgiving must be done [Col. 2359].

241–243 **SERMON XL.** On the same passage of Ecclesiasticus 5:8, “Do not delay turning to God,” etc. Against those who postpone conversion from day to day, some of whom perish through false hope and others through despair.—1. What it means to wait for the Lord. 2. Those who delay conversion through hope and those who delay it through despair. 3. Most delay through false hope. 4–5. Repentance must not be postponed until tomorrow. 6. The sick person must be aroused even unwillingly. 7. There is no security except from God.
