244–246 **SERMON XLI.** On Ecclesiasticus 22:28, “Maintain faith with your neighbor in his poverty, so that you may also enjoy his goods.”—1. Faith must be kept with a friend in his poverty. 2. With what hope faith should be kept with a poor friend. 3. Not in hope of his future temporal prosperity. 4. The story of Lazarus and the rich man demonstrates the same point. The rich person who despised the poor here must not hope for the poor man’s companionship in eternal happiness. 5. The rich person who despises the poor is wretched when life ends. 6. Friendship with the poor is acquired through almsgiving. Mammon of iniquity. 7. Faith in Christ the poor man.

247–251 **SERMON XLII.** On Isaiah 1:11, “What do I want with the multitude of your sacrifices?” and Psalm 139:1, “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil person.”—1. Almsgiving to the poor is the Christian’s sacrifice. Two kinds of almsgiving. 2. The measure and reward of almsgiving. What a maritime loan is. 3. The evil person.

252–253 **SERMON XLIII.** On Isaiah 7:9, “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”—1. Faith is necessary. 2. Faith is a great gift of God. 3. God’s benefits toward humanity. Understanding and reason are different. 4. Whether one must first believe what will later be understood. 5. Prophetic speech is more effective for strengthening faith. 6. Why fishermen and uneducated persons were chosen as Apostles. 7. Faith precedes understanding. 8. Faith grows through understanding. 9. How one must both believe what is to be understood and understand what is to be believed.

254–257 **SERMON XLIV.** On Isaiah 53:2–9.—This passage is understood as referring to Christ.

258 **SERMON XLV.** On what is written in Isaiah 57:13, “But those who are devoted to me shall possess the land and inhabit my holy mountain,” and on the Apostle’s words, “Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God,” 2 Corinthians 7:1.—1. Whatever happens opportunely without human effort is to be attributed to divine mercy. 2. Desires do not end but increase if present things are despised for the sake of earthly promises. 3. Obscure passages of Scripture are illuminated by other clear passages. 4. The land of the living promised to us. 5. The mountain is Christ and the Church. 6. How Christ and the Church are a mountain. 7. What kind of mountain Christ is; against the Donatists. 8. Purity of flesh and spirit is commanded. 9. Holiness is perfected in the fear of God. 10. The future transformation of the flesh. Human flesh is to be transformed into an angelic body.

262–269 **SERMON XLVI.** On the shepherds in Ezekiel 34:1–16, beginning with the words, “And it happened,” and ending, “And I will feed them with judgment.” Against the Donatists.—1. On shepherds who feed not the sheep but themselves. 2. Christians exist for their own sake; those in authority exist for the sake of others. 3. Shepherds who feed themselves rather than the sheep. 4. Shepherds are given the power to receive milk. 5. They should take the milk in such a way as to benefit the sheep; nor, if they do not receive the milk, should they neglect the sheep. 6. What it means to cover oneself with wool. Wool means honor. 7. Paul does not spare the vices of those by whom honor is shown to him. 8. Shepherds must not spare vices for the sake of gathering a multitude. 9. On those who slaughter fat sheep. 10. The weak sheep: from where it is to be strengthened. 11. Those who promise earthly happiness build on sand. 12. How the weak person is to be strengthened. 13. The difference between the weak and the sick person. Christian firmness. 14. Shepherds are obliged to bring back wandering sheep. The Donatists’ foolish objection. 15. Wandering sheep are not neglected without danger to the healthy. 16. The misery of wandering sheep. 17. The evil mountains and hills on which the sheep wander. The good mountains. 18. They wander over the whole face of the earth. 19. How sheep are safe from evil shepherds. 20. How the destruction of the sheep is charged to the shepherd. 21. How God brings back sheep from evil shepherds. A wandering sheep is not safe when it follows a wandering shepherd. 22. An evil shepherd is to be heard not in what he speaks from himself but in what he speaks from God. 23. God himself takes responsibility for the sheep. 24. The mountains of Israel, where the good pastures are. 25. The sheep’s hope is in God alone. 26. The sheep’s health and rest come from God [Col. 2360]. 27. Feeding with judgment. 28. The partridge gathering without judgment: the devil. 29. The partridge as a contentious bird; against the Donatists. 30. There is one good shepherd because all the good are one in him. 31. The Donatists exclude Catholics from their communion. 32. The Donatists’ voice is not the shepherd’s voice. 33. Nor is it the shepherd’s voice when they speak about the handers-over (*traditores*), nor when they say that the Church will perish. 34. The shepherd’s voice and his flock are not hidden. 35. A passage from the Song of Songs vainly produced by the Donatists. The Song of Songs contains enigmas. 36. A passage from the Song is contrary to the Donatists. 37. If “midday” is understood in the cited passage, it works against the Donatists. Going out is characteristic of heretics. 38. A passage from Habakkuk wrongly used by the Donatists. 39. The testimony of Habakkuk does not fit the Donatists. 40. The more accurate interpretation of the prophet Habakkuk. 41. The Donatists interpret the deed of Simon of Cyrene in their own favor.

270–294 **SERMON XLVII.** On the sheep in Ezekiel 34:17–31, beginning with the words, “And you are my sheep,” and ending, “And I am your God, says the Lord God.” Against the Donatists.—1. We are sheep of God’s pasture and of his hands. 2. The shepherd’s voice must be heard with trembling. 3. The security of God’s flock. 4. The shepherd’s voice must be heard in the present time. 5. We must not abuse God’s patience. 6. The weeds must not be uprooted before the harvest, nor the goats separated before judgment. 7. The good await God’s judgment securely; the wicked await it trembling. 8. The conscience must quickly be cleansed. 10. Envious and bitter teachers. 11. A good conscience is not sufficient if one’s conduct before others is negligent. 12. To what extent one should strive to please people. 13. When conscience is sufficient. 14. Care for good conduct. 15. Only God can now distinguish the sheep and goats. 16. The proud founders of the Donatist schism. 17. The Donatists cannot excuse their separation. 18. The Donatist schism does not please any prudent person wishing to profess Christianity. 19. The sheep are saved when they hear the shepherd’s voice. 20. The prophecy concerning Christ the shepherd, teaching that he is one with God. 21. The unity of the Godhead and the distribution of the persons. How Christ is the Mediator. 22. The covenant of peace. The covenants of schismatics invalidated by imperial laws. The Donatists boast that they preserved the Scriptures from the fire. 23. Dwelling and rest in the wilderness of conscience. 24. The rain of blessing. 25. Fruit-bearing trees in the field, allegorically. 26. Against the Donatists. 27. Those who hear the shepherd are snatched from the teeth of wolves. 28. The planting of peace. 29. Who are God’s sheep. 30. God belongs to all and is not divided among all his own, but is possessed whole and entire.

295–315 **SERMON XLVIII.** On the words of the prophet Micah 6:6–8, “What worthy offering shall I make to the Lord?” and on Psalm 72, “How good is the God of Israel,” etc.—1. The preacher of the word works upon the ears; God works in the heart. 2. We ourselves are the sacrifice to God. To practice judgment and justice. Perverse judgment is not judgment. 3. Those are not upright in heart who are scandalized by the happiness of the wicked. 4. How close they come to falling. 5. The governance of things belongs to God. 6. This is what the psalmist undertook to know. 7. How, and for how long, God permits the wicked to prosper and the good to suffer. 8. The wicked are not truly well, nor are the good truly ill. It is evil to suffer evil. The good things by which one acts well, and which make one good.

316–319 **SERMON XLIX.** On the same passage of Micah, concerning the justice that was commanded to be practiced, and on Matthew 20, concerning those hired for the vineyard.—1. Reference to the preceding sermon. 2. Those hired for the vineyard. The work assigned. Justice. To believe is the work of God and that very same justice. Faith in deed and word. 3. Now there is darkness, afterward light. The faithful are the days. 4. A friend and an enemy are scarcely distinguishable now. 5. Holy Scripture is a mirror. 6. How a friend of both should conduct himself when two people are in disagreement. 7. Justice. Anger is a speck; hatred is a beam. A murderer is one who hates his brother. 8. The remission of debts. 9. The example of Christ. 10. Stephen’s charity toward those who stoned him. 11. He kneels and prays for his enemies.

320–325 **SERMON L.** On what is written in the prophet Haggai 2:9, “The gold is mine and the silver is mine.” Against the Manichaeans.—1. The Manichaeans’ slander against the ancient Scriptures. 2. Gold and silver are not human property but God’s. 3. God not only created these things but administers them according to his will, giving them to some for support and testing, and to others for punishment. 4. Gold properly belongs to the person who uses it well, and therefore is more truly God’s. 5. Why gold is given to the good and the wicked. 6. Gold cannot rightly be condemned. Mammon of iniquity. Some riches are true, others false [Col. 2361]. 7. The pious use of riches. It is madness to transfer the crime of those who use things badly to the things themselves. 8. Gold unjustly accused by the Manichaeans. The desire for gold is condemned, while its proper use is commended by the Lord. 9. The Manichaeans as slanderers of the prophets. 10. Haggai’s passage vindicated. 11. Gold and silver allegorically. 12. Peace promised after the resurrection. 13. Contempt for gold commended in the prophetic writings.

326–332 **SERMON LI.** On the agreement of Matthew and Luke in the genealogies of the Lord.—1. The question proposed on Christ’s birthday is to be treated. The day of spectacles. 2. Christian spectacles. Carnal and spiritual people view the death of the martyrs differently. 3. Why Christ wished to be born of a woman. Through a woman came poison; through a woman, salvation. 4. The faith of the Gospel received throughout the whole world. 5. It may safely be believed that there is no discrepancy between the Gospels even before they are understood. The usefulness of secrecy. Veils hung in a house. 6. Pious faith in the Scriptures. Augustine, at times approaching the divine Scriptures without a pious mind, is deceived. 7. How Christ is the son of Abraham and David. 8. The genealogies from Abraham to Christ. 9.

Christ’s conception from the Holy Spirit. Joseph’s sincere justice, not harshness. 10. Interpretation of the name Jesus. 11. The usefulness of heretics. The usefulness of the traitor Judas. 12. In Matthew, three sets of fourteen generations are found, with Jechoniah counted twice. 13. Why Jechoniah is counted twice. 14. The transition of the Gospel to the Gentiles signified in the Babylonian exile. 15. Christ, the cornerstone between Jews and Gentiles, foreshadowed in Jechoniah. 16. Why Christ’s genealogy is traced through Joseph. Joseph the true husband of Mary. 17. How Mary called Joseph Christ’s father. Christ does not deny that he is Joseph’s son. 18. Mary’s modesty and humility, to be imitated by women. Mary called both virgin and woman. The Creed. 19. Christ does not deny Joseph as his father. The obedience of the boy Jesus, to be imitated by boys. 20. Christ both son and Lord of David. 21. Marriage is constituted not by carnal intercourse but by conjugal love. Married couples abstaining by mutual agreement. 22. Carnal intercourse only for the sake of procreation. Marriage contracts. The origin of adultery. When sexual intercourse within marriage is a venial sin. 23. The human race is sustained by two supports. 24. In regard to the necessities of life, some are led by desire, others by reason. 25. The patriarchs were permitted to have many wives solely for the purpose of procreating children. 26. The dignity of virginity began with the mother of the Lord. How Joseph was truly Christ’s father. Adoption of children. Natural children and children born in wedlock. 27. It is rightly admitted that Joseph had two fathers, in order to reconcile Matthew and Luke. 28. Adoption in Holy Scripture. How intercourse with slave women among the ancients occurred without adultery. 29. Children, in a particular sense, among the Jews. The generations of the Lord counted in different ways by the Evangelists without falsehood. 30. Why they are counted through Joseph, not through Mary. 31. Why Matthew counts downward, whereas Luke counts upward. 32. On the number forty in the generations of the Lord. The significance of the number forty. 33. Why Luke counts seventy-seven generations. 34. The significance of the number seventy-seven. 35. How the Scriptures are to be read.

**332–354 SERMON LII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 3, verses 13–17: “Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him,” etc.; and on the Trinity.—1. God the Trinity is commended in Christ’s baptism. 2. The difficulty concerning the inseparable Trinity. 3. The necessity of divine assistance for resolving the knot of the difficulty. 4. The works of the Father and the Son are inseparable. 5. The Father both made and governs all things through the Son. 6. The difficulty whether the Son’s birth and passion are also the Father’s. The heresy of the Patripassians. 7. The knot of the difficulty. 8. Birth from a virgin belongs to the Son alone, but was accomplished by the Father and the Son. 9. The Son’s birth was accomplished by the Father. Paul, learned in divine law. 10. The Apostle’s passage in which Christ is said to have been born of a woman. 11. The Son’s birth was also accomplished by the Son. 12. The Son’s passion likewise by the Father and the Son. 13. The same is proved concerning Christ’s resurrection. 14. Repetition of the doctrine explained. 15. God must not be conceived as a body located in space. 16. God is incomprehensible. 17. God’s likeness is to be sought in us. 18. Our soul was made in the image of God. 19. The likeness of the Trinity in the human being. 20. Memory, understanding, and will are shown to be separable, yet operate inseparably. 21. Through these three, the mystery of the Trinity is illuminated. 22. What pertains among them to the Father, what to the Son and the Holy Spirit, is left for consideration. [Col. 2362] 23. From this it is sufficiently understood that the persons of the Trinity can be demonstrated separately and operate inseparably.

**354–364 SERMON LIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc., but especially on what is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Chapter 5, verses 3–8.—1. Everyone wishes to be blessed. Who is poor in spirit? 2. Who is meek? 3. Those who mourn. 4. Those who hunger. 5. The merciful. 6. The pure in heart. 7. What are God’s face, hands, and feet? 8. Rewards corresponding to works in the beatitudes. 9. How the vision of God is specially promised to the pure in heart. 10. The heart is purified by faith in order to see God. 11. The faith of Christians must be distinguished from the faith of demons. Hope and love as companions of faith. 12. God must not be conceived as a body. 13. A passage from Isaiah apparently contrary to this. 14. The cited passage examined. Heaven: the saints. Earth: the earthly. “Lift up your hearts.” 15. Breadth, length, height, and depth. 16. The four dimensions of the cross.

**364–371 SERMON LIV.** On what is written in Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 5, verse 16: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”; and conversely, chapter 6, verse 1: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them.”—1. Commands apparently contrary to one another. 2. The Apostle fulfills both commands. 3. The two commands reconciled. 4. Who truly fulfilled both commands.

**372–374 SERMON LV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 5, verse 22: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna,” etc.—1. Useful fear. 2. The necessity of divine assistance for mastering the tongue. 3. God, the master of the tongue. 4. The scourge of God the master must be endured. 5. To what hope we are mastered here. 6. God our refuge.

**375–377 SERMON LVI.** On Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 6, verses 7–13, concerning the Lord’s Prayer, for the Competentes.—1. The Creed and the prayer are delivered to Christians. 2. Two things must be avoided by the one who invokes God. 3. We should not wish evil upon evildoers, but pray that they may become good. 4. Excessive talk in prayer must be avoided. What our prayer is for. The form of desires in the Lord’s Prayer. 5. The first petition. 6. The second petition. 7. The third petition. 8. On the same petition. 9. The fourth petition. 10. Daily bread as the word of God. The Eucharist. 11. The fifth petition. 12. Cleansing from daily sins. Small sins must not be despised, because they are numerous. 13. The agreement to forgive debts. 14. He urges love of enemies. 15. Loving enemies is the work of few, yet it must be performed by all. 16. At least when an enemy asks, forgiveness should be granted. 17. Discipline without hatred. One who refuses forgiveness to an enemy harms not him but himself. 18. The sixth petition. 19. Three petitions concern eternal life, and three the necessities of this present life.

**377–386 SERMON LVII.** Again on Matthew, chapter 6, verses 9–13, concerning the Lord’s Prayer, for the Competentes.—1. First the Creed, then the prayer, is to be delivered. 2. The Son of God willed us to be his brothers. 3. What should be asked of the Father. 4. The first petition. 5. The second petition. 6. The third petition. 7. The fourth petition. 8. The fifth petition. 9. The sixth petition. 10. Deliverance from evil. 11. A great temptation, a terrible temptation: the desire for revenge. 12. The commendation of love toward enemies. Daily debts. 13. An exhortation.

**386–393 SERMON LVIII.** Likewise on Matthew, chapter 6, verses 9–13, concerning the Lord’s Prayer, for the Competentes.—1. The Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. 2. One Father of all. 3. The first and second petitions. 4. The third petition. 5. The fourth petition. 6–7. The fifth petition. 8. Against anger and hatred. 9. Desire must be resisted. 10. Small sins must not be despised. 11. Deliverance from evil. 12. The distinction among the petitions. 13. The Creed must be committed to memory.

**393–399 SERMON LIX.** Likewise on Matthew, chapter 6, verses 9–13, concerning the Lord’s Prayer, for the Competentes.—1. The Creed as the rule of faith. 2. One Father of all. 3. The first petition. 4. The second petition. 5. The third petition. 6. The fourth petition. 7. The fifth petition. 8. The sixth petition.

**400–402 SERMON LX.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 6, verses 19–21: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth,” etc.; an exhortation to give alms.—1. In the tribulation of this world, Christ’s counsel must be accepted. 2. Life here is laborious. 3. The one who hoards is troubled in various ways. He does not know for whom he is gathering. 4. Perhaps he is storing up for a thief. 5. Counsel must be sought from Christ. 6. Treasure must be stored in heaven. 7. Wealth must be transferred from earth to heaven. 8. Our carriers are the poor. [Col. 2363] 9. At the judgment, only works of mercy are mentioned. 10. Why the judgment speaks only of almsgiving. 11. God willed to be in need in the poor. 12. Fruitless repentance profits nothing.

**400–408 SERMON LXI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 7, verses 7–11: “Ask, and it will be given to you,” etc.; an exhortation to give alms. 2. A human being does not become good from evil except through God. He refutes the Pelagians. 3. The twofold good. 4. Money must be distributed in order to obtain righteousness. God’s beggar. Through comparisons God urges us to ask. 5. The widow before the judge. 6. A friend before a friend. 7. Whom, from whom, and what we should ask. 8. Who these beggars of ours are, and from whom and what they ask here. 9. Rich and poor are equal in birth and death. 10. It is one thing to be rich, another to wish to become rich. The worm of riches: pride. 11. The use of riches for acquiring eternal life. 12. Let the rich use their surplus so as to give the poor what they need. 13. He presses the giving of alms.

**409–414 SERMON LXII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 8, verses 8–12: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof,” etc.; and also on the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians 8:10–12: “For if anyone sees someone who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s shrine,” etc.—1. The centurion’s humility. 2. The proud man rejected from Christ’s discipleship. 3. The centurion’s faith in humility. 4. The Gentiles signified in the centurion. 5. The woman touching Christ’s fringe while the crowd presses him. 6. What was foretold in the Gospel is now fulfilled. 7. Those who dine with pagans in an idol’s shrine are reproved. 8. Those reclining in an idol’s shrine through fear of some greater person. Observance toward every superior must be properly ordered. 9. Causing a brother to stumble is a sin against Christ. 10. The foolish excuse of those reclining in an idol’s shrine. 11. Pressing upon and touching Christ’s body. 12. Whether a prelate is good or bad, he cannot harm the godly. 13. The properly ordered observance of authorities. 14. The deceit of a powerful evil person compared to a razor. 15. The security of the godly under God’s protection. 16. Eternal life as the reward of labor. 17. Idols must not be broken unless legitimate authority gives permission. 18. The unjust complaints of idolaters.

**414–423 SERMON LXIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 8, verses 23–27: “And when he had entered the boat,” etc.—1. Those who sail in the world. 2. Christ must be awakened amid the storms of anger. 3. When Christ commands, tranquility comes.

**424 SERMON LXIV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 10, verse 16: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves,” etc.—1. Wolves made into sheep. 2. From where the Christian has confidence among wolves. 3. How the serpent’s cleverness is to be imitated. 4. The dove’s simplicity is to be imitated.

**425–426 SERMON LXV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 10, verse 28: “Do not fear those who kill the body,” etc.—1. One fear must be driven out by another. 2. A human being should fear nothing from another human being. 3. Why the persecutor does not terrify God’s martyr. 4. The soul is immortal in its own manner. 5. How the soul can die. God is the soul’s life. 6. By what signs the death of both body and soul is recognized. 7. The death of the soul is more to be mourned and feared than the death of the body. 8. What the eternal death of body and soul is.

**426–430 SERMON LXVI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 11, verses 2–11: “When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, sending two of his disciples, he said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” etc.—1. John’s testimony concerning Christ. 2. Christ’s testimony concerning John. 3. The difficulty whether John doubted about Christ. 4. The difficulty resolved. 5. Care for the poor.

**430–433 SERMON LXVII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 11, verse 25: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise,” etc.—1. There are two kinds of confession: that of the sinner and that of the one who praises. What it means to beat one’s breast. 2. The sinner’s confession itself is also praise of God. The raising of Lazarus as a figure of the sinner rising again. 3. How the Church’s loosing of sinners benefits them. 4. Praising God. Accusing ourselves. 5. Our invisible enemies. 6. From where protection against our enemies comes. 7. Grace shines forth most brightly in Christ, and in the thief. 8. Faith denied to the proud. 9. John was not the light but a lamp. 10. Prayer to the Lord.

**433–437 SERMON LXVIII.** Likewise on the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 11, verse 25: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” etc.—1. The wise and prudent, from whom the mysteries have been hidden. 2. However great one’s knowledge, it profits nothing if the knowledge of God is absent. 3. The truth must not be held down in unrighteousness. 4. Why the wise of this world are without excuse. [Col. 2364] 5. To glorify God and to give thanks are the same thing. 6. The mysteries are hidden from the proud but revealed to the little ones.

**438–440 SERMON LXIX.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 11, verses 28–29: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,” etc. 1.—1. From where this labor comes. 2. Humility as the foundation of the spiritual building. 3. The vision of God promised to us who see him. 4. The sinner must flee to God.

**440–442 SERMON LXX.** Again on the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 11, verses 28–30: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” etc. The yoke of Christ apparently hard.—2. How Christ’s yoke becomes easy. 3. Through love, all difficult things become mild.

**442–444 SERMON LXXI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 12, verse 32: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” Or, on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.—1. A preliminary observation for the question to be treated. From their own words the Pharisees are warned to depart from the kingdom of the devil. 2. The expulsion of the devil through Christ’s power. 3. Liberation from the devil through grace. The distinction made from the mass of perdition. 4. Christ’s kingdom remains undivided even when heresies and schisms arise. 5. The difficulty of the question to be treated. 6. What sin against the Holy Spirit is like among pagans. It is not irremissible for Jews and heretics. 7. The opinion of some concerning sin against the Holy Spirit in the baptized is rejected. 8. The most difficult question of all. 9. Not every blasphemy against the Spirit is irremissible. 10. There is a definite blasphemy that is irremissible. 11. John’s passage concerning a specific sin of the Jews. 12. It is the Holy Spirit who is spoken of here. 13. The other Evangelists agree with Matthew on this matter. 14. The difficulty in Mark’s words. 15. Two kinds of temptation. 16. Salvation promised to the believer and the baptized. 17. A particular manner of eating Christ’s flesh belonging to the godly. 18. He undertakes the solution of the question. God is Trinity. 19. The forgiveness of sins is given through the Holy Spirit. Fire: tribulation. Fire: the Holy Spirit. 20. Impenitence is sin against the Holy Spirit. 21. No one is to be despaired of in the present life. 22. An objection is answered. 23. Every other blasphemy, once the sin against the Holy Spirit is excluded, is forgiven; why. 24. The blasphemy against the Son is not therefore forgiven more easily than that against the Spirit because the Son is lesser insofar as he is human. 25. The forgiveness of sins belongs to the whole Trinity. 26–27. The power and operation of the Trinity are indivisible. 28. Sins are not forgiven outside the Church. 29. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. 30. The Holy Spirit is not possessed outside the Church. 31. Carnal and natural human beings, infants in Christ. 32. Pretended Catholics, heretics, and schismatics do not possess the Holy Spirit. 33. Forgiveness of sins does not occur outside the Church. 34. Luke persuades us that impenitence is to be understood by the name “irremissible blasphemy.” 35. The same is suggested by the other two Evangelists. 36. To resist the unity of the Church with an impenitent heart is irremissible blasphemy. 37. Congregations outside the Church do not possess the Holy Spirit, through whom the forgiveness of sins takes place. The irremissible sin. Refuge against irremissible blasphemy. 38. The humility of the expositor.

**445–466 SERMON LXXII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 12, verse 33: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good,” etc.—1. A bad person cannot have good works. 2. We were all found to be bad. 3. God’s patience toward us. 4. The two roots: love and cupidity. 5. A human being wishes to possess every good thing except himself. 6. What true good is. 7. Why the world is scourged so severely.

**467–468 SERMON LXXIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, where the Lord explains the parable of the sower, chapter 13, verses 24–30, 36–43.—1. The wicked among the good. 2. One thing has many names, and two things sometimes receive one name in the figures of Scripture. 3. An exhortation to bad Christians to change. 4. An exhortation to good Christians to tolerate the wicked.

**470–471 SERMON LXXIV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 13, verse 52: “Therefore every scribe instructed for the kingdom of God,” etc.—1. Who the scribes were among the Jews. 2. Scribes not instructed for the kingdom of God. 3. How evil officials may speak good things, and how they are to be heard by their subjects. 4. A cluster of grapes among thorns. 5. The ancient Scriptures annulled through Christ.

**472–474 SERMON LXXV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 14, verses 24–33: “But the boat was being battered by the waves in the middle of the sea,” etc.—1. A higher meaning lies hidden in the event. 2. What the crossing of the sea in the boat signifies. 3. Christ’s prayer on the mountain. 4. The ship battered by the storm. 5. The storm in the Lord’s absence. 6. Looking back. 7. The fourth watch of the night. The faith of the cross. 8. The disciples’ error signifies the error of heretics. [Col. 2365] 9. Another error likewise signified. 10. Peter walking upon the sea.

**472–476 SERMON LXXVI.** Again on Matthew, chapter 14, verses 24–33, concerning the Lord walking upon the waters of the sea and Peter wavering.—1. The sea: the world; Peter: a type of the Church. 2. The Church is built not upon human beings but upon Christ. 3. Peter first blessed, and soon afterward called Satan. 4. In Peter, the steadfast and the weak are signified. 5. A human being is weak in himself, powerful in the Lord. 6. Recognition of one’s own weakness is necessary for obtaining grace. 7. Paul, acknowledging his weakness, is perfected. 8. Peter is powerful not in himself but in the Lord. 9. In the adversity or prosperity of the world, cupidity is a storm.

**479–482 SERMON LXXVII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 15, verses 24–28: “Jesus went out from Gennesaret and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon, and behold, a Canaanite woman,” etc.—1. The Canaanite woman as an example of humility. 2. How Christ was sent only to the Israelites. The question resolved. 3. Saul changed into Paul. The reason for Saul’s name being changed to Paul. 4. The Jews converted after hearing Peter. The sheep to whom Christ was sent. 5. Christ was not sent to the Gentiles, but he sent others. 6. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue and the woman with the hemorrhage. 7. Although the event narrated about them truly occurred, it is nevertheless a figure. 8. What is signified by them. 9. The Canaanite woman’s persistence in asking. 10. Why the Gentiles are called dogs. 11. Humility commended in the Canaanite woman. The great remedy against pride: God as man. 12. After the Jews were rejected because of their pride, the Gentiles were substituted in their place because of their humility. Great faith, like a mustard seed. 13. Carnal things are not to be expected in the kingdom of heaven. Wealth here is evidence of need. The health of this life is a prolonged illness. 14. The necessity of dying begins at birth itself. True health is immortality. 15. Why the natural branches are cut off and the wild olive is grafted in.

**483–489 SERMON LXXVIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 17, verses 1–8: “After six days Jesus took Peter, and James, and his brother John,” etc.—1. The kingdom of Christ. 2. The allegory of the Lord’s transfiguration. Christ’s garments. 3. Peter’s wish. 4. The voice from the cloud. The disciples’ prostration. 5. The disciples’ rising. Jesus alone is seen by those who have risen. God himself is the reward promised to us. 6. Out of love, the salvation of others must be cared for.

**490–492 SERMON LXXIX.** Again on the words of Matthew’s Gospel, where Jesus manifested himself on the mountain to three disciples. Chapter 17, verses 1–8.

**493 SERMON LXXX.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 17, verses 18–20: “Why were we unable to cast it out?” etc.; concerning prayer.—1. The apostles’ unbelief. 2. Although God knows our poverty, he must nevertheless be entreated. 3. God must be entreated to heal us from our vices. 4. Two kinds of sick people. Christ finds all the sick. 5. By what remedy the sick are healed through Christ. A heavenly bargain. Christ’s prayer for his crucifiers. 6. Prayer amid the dangers of this life. 7. How temporal and eternal benefits are to be requested. 8. From where bad times come, and how they are to be endured.

**493–498 SERMON LXXXI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, where we are warned to beware of the world’s scandals, chapter 18, verses 7–9.—1. How we are fortified against scandals. 2. The meek in tribulation, fortified against scandal. 3. Who the meek are. The good world and the evil world. 4. Scandal from the eye, the hand, and the foot. 5. Falsehood forbidden by divine law. 6. Let human beings act not as human beings but as children of God. 7. The pagans’ scandal arising from the tribulations of the world. 8. The foretold tribulations of the failing world. 9. The pagans’ complaints against the Christian religion arising from devastation.

**499–505 SERMON LXXXII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 18, verses 15–18: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone,” etc.; and on Solomon’s words: “He who winks with deceit causes sorrow among men, but he who rebukes openly makes peace.” Proverbs, chapter 10, verse 10, according to the Septuagint.—1. A preliminary observation. The speck: anger; the beam: hatred. 2. The sin of the angry person; the cruelty of one who hates. 3. Hatred harms the one who hates more seriously than the other person. 4. In what spirit a brother should be rebuked. Sin against a human being must not be despised. 5. The remedy for this sin. 6–7. What the person who has suffered an injury ought to do. 8. The Gospel reconciled with Solomon. 9. Rebuke must sometimes be private and sometimes public. 10. When it should be private and when public. 11. The manner of rebuke, and why it is done privately. Sins of the flesh are deadly. 12. Life must quickly be corrected. 13. Sins of the flesh must not be despised. 14. Correction must not be postponed. The raven’s voice. Human beings wish to possess everything good except life. 15. The pastor’s burden must not be cast off.

**506–513 SERMON LXXXIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 18, verses 21–22: “How often will my brother sin against me?” etc.—1. On forgiving injuries. 2. Every human being is God’s debtor and has a brother as debtor. Two works of mercy. We are God’s beggars. 3. How often a brother must be forgiven. 4. All debts must be forgiven. 5. A notable figure concerning this matter. 6. Another figure concerning the same. The Decalogue. 7. All sins are signified by the number seventy-seven. Forgiven sins are reinstated when one refuses to forgive. 8. Forgiveness must be granted in such a way that discipline is not neglected.

**514–518 SERMON LXXXIV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 19, verse 17: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.”—1. How greatly eternal life is to be loved is understood from the love of this present life. 2. The days of this life are evil. The true and blessed life is eternal.

**519 SERMON LXXXV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 19, verses 17–25: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” etc.—1. Observance of the commandments for deserving life. The Gospel, Christ’s mouth. 2. The rich are saved with difficulty. What the poor must guard against. 3. What the Apostle wishes to command the rich. The worm of riches: pride. 4. What must be done concerning riches. Let the rich give readily. 5. How much is to be distributed among the poor. 6. The poor are bound to restrain their desires. 7. Conclusion.

**520–523 SERMON LXXXVI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 19, verse 21: “Go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor,” etc.—1. Treasure must be stored in heaven. “Lift up your hearts.” 2. The one asking for the counsel of salvation, yet unwilling to hear it. God himself preserves what is given to the poor. 3. God received it in the poor. Pious interest and unjust interest. 4. God himself arranges that creditors receive what is theirs. 5. What he returns in exchange for earthly things. 6. Two mistresses issuing contrary commands: avarice and luxury. 7. Christ frees us from their yoke. 8. The foolish counsel of avarice. 9. Another foolish counsel. 10. God’s counsel, commanding what avarice commands. 11. The false piety of the avaricious toward their children. A deceased son must have his share conveyed to him. 12. What was being preserved for the living is owed to the dead. 13. Christ must be counted among one’s children in the division of an inheritance. 14. The excuse of avarice removed. 15. Against luxury, Christ counsels the same thing as luxury. The foolish rich man. 16. Another rich man, given to luxury. 17. God’s counsel concerning giving alms must now be embraced.

**523–530 SERMON LXXXVII.** On what is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who sent laborers into his vineyard.” Matthew, chapter 20, verses 4–16.—1. We cultivate God, and God cultivates us. 2. How God cultivates us. 3. The vineyard planted by God. 4. Laborers hired to cultivate the vineyard. 5. What it means that the last were paid first. Those called at the first hour, the third, and so on. 6. The denarius as eternal life. 7. Another interpretation of those called at the first hour, the third, and so on. 8. Concerning those who delay coming after being called to the vineyard. 9. How the householder went out to call people to his vineyard. The Church speaks in the languages of all nations. 10. Despair and perverse hope destroy souls. 11. Perverse hope by which conversion is postponed. God has promised no one tomorrow. 12. Christ teaches that the friendship of the powerful, when it obstructs salvation, is to be despised. 13. Christ the physician must be obeyed, while the powerful who oppose him are disregarded. 14. The frenzied and the lethargic. 15. Conclusion.

**530–538 SERMON LXXXVIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel concerning the two blind men sitting beside the road and crying out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” Chapter 20, verses 30–34.—1. Christ, our physician. Through bodily miracles he built up faith. 2. The Church’s later faith without miracles is more praiseworthy. Why he preserved the scars on his body. 3. Christ now performs greater miracles. 4. The eye of the mind, by which God is seen, is cleansed through faith. 5. Our entire work now consists in healing the eye of the heart. 6. Zeal for cleansing the eye of the heart. 7. By Christ’s example we are invited to drink the cup. 8. Why Christ honored his cross here. 9. What the healing of the two blind men signifies. What it means that Jesus was passing by. 10. The two blind men: the two peoples. Christ the cornerstone. 11. Jesus, while passing by, is called upon and heals. 12. What it means to cry out to Christ. 13. The crowd forbidding them to cry out. 14. How the eyes are healed. What it means that Jesus stood still. 15–16. The interior light compared with visible light. 17. One must cry out amid crowds that forbid crying out. [Col. 2367] 18. Through perseverance, opponents are overcome. 19. The good and the evil are mingled in the Church. The evil person does not stain the good person in two ways. 20. Correction must not be undertaken in a proud spirit. 21. Unity must never be abandoned. The separation of the Donatists is rejected from the parable of the weeds. 22. The Donatists’ fiction concerning the diminution of the wheat. 23. A passage misunderstood by schismatics concerning separation. 24. The prophets reproved the people’s vices but did not withdraw from the people. 25. One must withdraw from the wicked in heart, not in body.

**539–553 SERMON LXXXIX.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 21, verses 19–22, where Jesus causes a tree to wither; and on the passage in Luke, chapter 24, verse 28, where he pretended that he was going farther.—1. What the cursing of the fig tree admonishes us about. 2. The mountain cast into the sea by the apostles. 3. The cursing of the tree foreshadowed something future. 4. A rule for interpreting the Scriptures. 5. The event as a figure. 6–7. An event that truly occurred and was nevertheless a figure.

**553–558 SERMON XC.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 22, verses 1–14, where the wedding feast of the king’s son is described. Against the Donatists, concerning love.—1. The Lord’s banquet is twofold: one here, belonging to the faithful; the other in heaven, belonging to the blessed. 2. All the righteous in this life are both evil and good. 3. The wicked excluded from the banquet; who are to be understood. 4. The exclusion of one signifies the exclusion of many. 5. What the wedding garment is. 6. The wedding garment is love. Other good things are of no benefit without love. Love and cupidity in the human being. 7. One’s neighbor is every human being. 8. Not every faith is praised. 9. Love must extend to enemies. What prayer against enemies is unlawful and what is lawful. 10. Love must be extended so that it draws everyone to God.

**559–566 SERMON XCI.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, where the Lord asked the Jews whose son they said Christ was. Chapter 22, verses 42–46.—1–2. It is proved against the Jews that Christ is the Messiah. 3. The mystery of the incarnate Word is disclosed to the worthy. To love God without ulterior motive is piety. 4. The devil, a slanderous adversary. Why he spreads evil reports about the good. 5. Why, after the question about Christ, the discussion turns to morals. Ecclesiastical offices. 6. From where the mind capable of understanding the mysteries comes. 7. No one ascends into heaven except the one who clings to Christ. 8. Christ and the Church are one human being. 9. We reach the vision of God through faith and good works.

**567–571 SERMON XCII.** On the same words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 22, verses 42–46.—1. The question about Christ put to the Jews. 2. Christ does not deny that he is David’s son. 3. Christ is God and human being.

**572–573 SERMON XCIII.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, chapter 25, verses 1–13: “The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” etc.—1. Who the ten virgins in the Gospel parable are to be understood as representing. 2. The ten virgins: every soul belonging to the Church of God. 3. Neither virginity nor good works alone are sufficient. 4. Every Christian soul is a virgin. 5. In addition to continence and good works, love is required. The oil is love. 6. What it means to go out to meet the bridegroom. The virgins’ sleep. 7. Why the dead are called sleepers. 8. The cry at midnight. 9. The virgins’ resurrection. Oil in the vessels. 10. Carrying oil with oneself. Another’s oil. 11. The foolish virgins are mocked by the wise. 12. Those buying and selling oil. 13. The humility of the prudent virgins. 14–15. Why the door is not opened to those who knock. 16–17. How the five prudent virgins are to be imitated.

**573–579 SERMON XCIV.** On the words of Matthew’s Gospel, where the lazy servant who refused to put out the talent he had received is condemned. Chapter 25, verses 24–30.—From where the bishop is named. The office of the episcopate is imposed upon every head of a household.

**580 SERMON XCV.** On the words of Mark’s Gospel, where the miracle of the seven loaves is recounted. Chapter 8, verses 1–9.—1. Banquets in the Holy Scriptures. 2. The allegorical meaning of the miracle of the seven loaves. 3. The mysteries in those who were satisfied with the seven loaves. 4. What kind of person the one who invited them to the banquet was. 5. The one reclining without a wedding garment rejected. 6. One person cast out signifies many. 7. The wedding garment is love.

**581–583 SERMON XCVI.** On the words of Mark’s Gospel, chapter 8, verse 34: “If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself,” etc.; and on the words of 1 John 2:15: “Whoever loves the world does not have the Father’s love in him.”—1. Through love, the commandments become easy. 2. Self-love, the first destruction of the human being. 3. Where Christ is to be followed and by what way. 4. The cross must be endured and the world despised. 5. How the world is evil, though made by the good God. 6. The good world made from the evil. 7. The world persecuting the world. [Col. 2368] 8. The twofold world in Scripture: the redeemed and the condemned. 9. Everyone is commanded to deny himself. 10. The various degrees of those following Christ, and what it means in them to look back.

**584–588 SERMON XCVII.** On the words of Mark’s Gospel, chapter 13, verse 32: “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.”—1. Preparation for the last day. 2. Mortality ought to benefit a human being by producing humility. 3. Only death is certain here. 4. The world conquered for us through Christ.

**589–590 SERMON XCVIII.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel, chapter 7, verses 11–15; and on the three dead whom the Lord raised.—1. The Lord’s miracles in bodies and in souls. 2. Two kinds of dead people. 3. The three dead raised by the Lord. Christ’s miracles were performed for the sake of their significance. A fitting comparison. 4. The raising of the three dead. 5. Three kinds of sinners, signified by those three dead. Evil habit. 6. Four stages of progress in sins. 7. One must rise quickly from sin.

**591–595 SERMON XCIX.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel, chapter 7, verses 36–50: “And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city,” etc. On the forgiveness of sins, against the Donatists.—1. The sinful woman at the feet of the reclining Lord. 2. The proud thought of the Pharisee. 3. The Lord rebukes the Pharisee’s thought. 4. A difficult question arising from the Lord’s words. 5. The matter clarified by examples. 6. The question resolved. He wishes the sins we have avoided to be counted among the debts forgiven. 7. Next, concerning the forgiveness of sins: sins cannot be forgiven by a human being. 8. The error and arrogance of the Donatists. 9. The Donatists’ argument. The Holy Spirit forgives sins through the Church. 10. Sins are forgiven by God both through a human being and apart from a human being. The Holy Spirit was given through the ministry of human beings. 11. The Spirit given without human ministry. The example of the eunuch of Queen Candace. 12. Another example in the centurion Cornelius. 13. Cleansing in baptism comes not from the merits of the ministers but from God’s grace.

**595–602 SERMON C.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel, where three men are discussed: one said, “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go,” and was rejected; another was afraid and was encouraged; a third delayed and was reproved. Chapter 9, verses 57–62.—1. Why the one who professes that he will follow Christ is rejected. 2. Another called by Christ. He wishes to delay out of carnal affection but is pressed to act. How parents are to be honored. The dead burying their dead. The proper ordering of love. 3. The third is reproved for looking back toward his own people. Election according to grace. 4. The elect owe everything to God’s grace.

**602–604 SERMON CI.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful,” etc. Chapter 10, verses 2–6.—1. The harvest among the Jews, the sowing among the Gentiles. Paul as one of little stature. 2. Two harvests, of the Jews and of the Gentiles. 3. The seed of the Gospel transmitted to the Gentiles. 4. What benefit comes from explaining the pastor’s duties to the people. 5. The instructions established for preachers are not to be understood carnally. 6. The command not to carry a purse. 7. On not putting on sandals.

8. That no greeting be given to anyone on the way. The first, obvious exposition. 9. A second, more hidden meaning. Preaching the Gospel when opportunity arises. 10. How preachers seeking their own interests are to be heard. 11. Preachers commanded to bring peace.

**605–610 SERMON CII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

1. The reverence owed to pastors. 2. What kind of death is truly good or evil. 3. The contrary lot of the rich man and Lazarus after death. 4. Why death should be considered evil. 5. An exhortation to good works.

**611–612 SERMON CIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “And a certain woman named Martha received him into her house,” etc. (Luke 10:16).

1. Unity is commended. 2. Christ deigns to offer himself to be fed. 3. Both Martha’s and Mary’s service are good, yet Mary’s is better. 4. The one thing necessary. 5. Martha’s service is good; Mary’s portion is better. 6. Martha’s service tends toward Mary’s rest.

**613–615 SERMON CIV.** Again on the passage of Luke’s Gospel concerning Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42).

1. Martha’s and Mary’s services are compared. 2. Martha’s service was not reproved by Christ. 3. Mary’s better portion. 4. The two lives figured in Martha and Mary.

**616–617 SERMON CV.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Which of you will have a friend and will go to him at midnight,” etc. (Luke 11:5–13).

1. Christ urges us to ask God by means of comparisons. 2. A friend coming from a journey is to be received. 3. Another friend is approached at midnight to give three loaves [Col. 2369]. 4. The three loaves given. 5. Faith, hope, and charity, gifts of God. 6. The same three things signified again: the bread, charity; the fish, faith. 7. The egg, hope. 8. How disasters and devastations are useful to Christians. 9. A city and kingdom in heaven await them eternally. 10. Eternity flatteringly promised to an earthly kingdom. 11. Steadfastness in bearing adversities. “Lift up your hearts.” The Gospel hen. 12. The devastation of Rome falsely attributed to the Christian religion, or to the destruction of idolatry. 13. The Roman disaster did not consequently result from the overthrow of the idols.

**618–624 SERMON CVI.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the dish,” etc. (Luke 11:39–42).

1. The Pharisees’ outward cleanliness. 2. Whether almsgiving can cleanse without faith. 3. The Pharisees’ almsgiving is insufficient. 4. The true almsgiving that is commanded.

**625–626 SERMON CVII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “I tell you, beware of all greed” (Luke 12:13–21).

1. The command to beware of every form of greed. 2. The occasion on which Christ gave it. 3. What Christ teaches by refusing to be the divider of an inheritance. The Donatists are censured. 4. He is condemned for greed who even eagerly hoards what is his own. 5. The foolish rich man who proposes to store up rather than distribute. 6. One must care for the soul, not that it possess goods, but that it itself be good. 7. Those who inwardly bear Christ’s sign on their forehead are secure among the wicked. 8. Every form of greed must be cut off, lest one sin. 9. Again concerning the danger of the greedy person, or of one who eagerly hoards what is his own. 10. Greed for life itself must also be avoided.

**627–631 SERMON CVIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like…” (Luke 12:35–36), and on the words of Psalm 33:12–15, “Who is the man who desires life,” etc.

1. Awaiting the Lord’s coming. Why we have become Christians. 2. Three things commended in the Gospel. 3. Good days are sought here in vain. 4–5. Where life and good days are to be sought. 6. What must be done to obtain good days. Life and good days. 7. The tongue must be restrained.

**632–635 SERMON CIX.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “You know how to interpret the face of the sky and of the earth,” etc., and on these words: “When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be freed from him,” etc. (Luke 12:56–59).

1. The time of mercy must be used for repentance. We are more fragile than glass. 2. Who is the adversary with whom we are commanded to agree. 3. Our adversary is the word of God. 4. A person’s years diminish rather than increase.

**636–638 SERMON CX.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel concerning the fig tree that bore no fruit for three years, and concerning the woman who had been ill for eighteen years (Luke 13:6–17); also on the words of Psalm 9:20, “Arise, O Lord; let man not prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight.”

1. What the barren fig tree of three years signifies. 2. The woman ill for eighteen years. A person is good not from himself but from God’s grace. 3. The prophet’s prayer that man may not prevail. 4. The certainty of the coming judgment, confirmed by the fulfillment of so many other prophecies. God is a debtor, not on the basis of what he has received, but of what he has promised. 5. The promised kingdom of God.

**638–641 SERMON CXI.** On the words of Luke’s Gospel, where the kingdom of God is said to be like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour; and on what is written there, “Lord, are those who are saved few?” (Luke 13:21–24).

1. The three measures of flour. Few are saved. Those who are to be saved are many in themselves, but few in comparison with others. 2. Reproof and exhortation to almsgiving.

**641–642 SERMON CXII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “A certain man prepared a great dinner,” etc. (Luke 14:16–24).

1. The Jews were invited to the dinner; we were led and compelled. 2. The three excuses of those unwilling to come. 3. The five yoke of oxen: curiosity concerning the five senses. 4. An impediment to faith. The dinner consecrated by the Lord’s hands. 5. Curiosity of the senses is of no use for salvation. 6. The wife, the pleasure of the flesh. 7. The other senses are signified by the name of the eyes. 8. No one should delay coming to the dinner.

**643–647 SERMON CXIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” etc. (Luke 16:9).

1. Who are the friends who will receive their benefactors into heaven, and who are Christ’s least ones. 2. The mammon of iniquity. Almsgiving must be made not from plunder but from honest labor. 3. Zacchaeus is to be imitated. 4. To whom riches are called the mammon of iniquity. 5. Which riches are true and which false. 6. True riches. We worship God, and God tends us.

**648–651 SERMON CXIV.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him,” etc. (Luke 17:3–4). On the remission of sins [Col. 2370].

1. Whenever a brother sins against us and repents, he must be forgiven. 2. Forgiveness must be granted to a brother so that it may be received from God. 3. Debts must be remitted according to God’s example. 4. Let the sinner forgive the one who sins. 5. Forgiveness is requested from God in prayer with the condition that we grant forgiveness to others.

**652–654 SERMON CXV.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “We ought always to pray and not lose heart,” etc. On the two men who went up into the temple to pray, and on the little children presented to Christ.

1. Faith is the source of prayer. 2. Faith belongs not to the proud but to the humble. 3. Against the Pelagians. 4. Christ’s Baptism is necessary for little children.

**655–657 SERMON CXVI.** On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, “Jesus stood in the midst of them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you,’” etc. (Luke 24:36–47).

1. The Manichaean heresy. 2. The disciples’ doubt. 3. How faith in Christ’s resurrection was made convincing. 4. Against the Manichaeans. 5. Christ inspires faith. 6. The Church is promised for all nations. 7. Saul transformed into a preacher of the Gospel.

**657–660 SERMON CXVII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John 1:1–13, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” etc. Against the Arians.

1. How the Word of God is to be understood, and at what price it is to be acquired. 2. The human being himself is the price of the Word. 3. The Word of God is a certain form that was not formed. A form without time or place. 4. It is no smaller in part than in the whole. 5. In divine matters, devout ignorance is better than presumptuous knowledge. God is incomprehensible to the eye of the heart. Through knowledge of God a person becomes blessed. God does not increase through our knowledge. 6. The Word is asserted to be coeternal with the Father against the Arians. 7. It is difficult to convey divine things to carnal people. 8. Comparisons are to be employed to refute the Arians. 9. Yet our faith in the Word does not rest on comparisons. 10. Comparisons drawn from creatures for the birth of the Son of God are imperfect. Coeval and coeternal. 11. Among coeval things there is a certain likeness of the Word coeternal with God. Fire and light are coeval. 12. Another coeval pair: the image and the thing from which it arises. 13. There is inequality in the comparisons offered. 14. The coeternity and equality of the Son of God are established from the two kinds of comparisons brought together. 15. The eye of the heart must be cleansed so that God may be seen. 16. Through the incarnation the Word was made, as it were, milk, so that we might receive him. 17. Humility is to be learned from the incarnate Word.

**661–671 SERMON CXVIII.** On the same words of John’s Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1:1–3).

1. The eternal Word of God, begotten, not made. 2. By a comparison it is shown that the Son is coeternal with God the Father.

**671 SERMON CXIX.** On the same words of John, “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1:1–14).

1. The eternal Word with God. 2. The Word of God was not made. 3. The Word of God is incomprehensible. 4. The Word became flesh. 5. The mystery of the incarnation is commended. 6. The incarnation is the work of the almighty Word. 7. The incarnation of the Word is explained by a comparison.

**673–675 SERMON CXX.** On the same words of John, “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1:1–3).

1. The incomprehensible Word of God revealed in the Gospel. 2. The Word of God is wholly everywhere. 3. The excellence of the divine Word is to be understood from the properties of the human word. The recently baptized in white garments.

**676–677 SERMON CXXI.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “The world was made through him,” etc. (John 1:10–14).

1. There are two worlds. 2. The evil world. 3. Who are the children of Abraham. 4. There are two births. 5. On the same subject.

**678–680 SERMON CXXII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you,” etc. (John 1:48–51).

1. Nathanael under the fig tree; the human race under sin. 2. Jacob’s dream was a figure. 3. The twofold name and Jacob’s struggle. 4. Why Abraham does not retain his first name together with his later one, whereas Jacob does the opposite. 5. The vision of God promised to Israel when he believes at the end. 6. Christ is both here and above.

**680–683 SERMON CXXIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding,” etc. (John 2:1–11).

1. Christ’s humility is the remedy for our pride. 2. Why Christ, when hungry, did not make bread from a stone, as he made wine from water at the wedding. 3. Christ, humble, is the way to the homeland. 4. Christ is both above and below. 5. Every human being is poor and God’s beggar.

**684–686 SERMON CXXIV.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “Now there is in Jerusalem a pool called the Sheep Pool,” etc. (John 5:2–4).

1. The healing of the sick at the pool was figurative. 2. This whole life is tribulation. Fear and pain are torturers of the soul. 3. The meaning of the Sheep Pool [Col. 2371]. Christ’s humility must not be rejected because of pride. 4. Christ assumed mortality in order to give immortality. The brevity of this life.

**686–688 SERMON CXXV.** Again on John 5: concerning the five porticoes where a multitude of sick people lay; and concerning the pool of Siloam (John 9).

1. The same things are not repeated pointlessly by an expositor of Scripture. 2. The five porticoes signified the Law of Moses. The Law’s inability to heal. Why the Law was given. 3. What is signified by one sick man healed when the water was stirred. 4. God’s rest on the seventh day. The six ages of the world. How God rested and yet always works. 5. God’s providence in the ordering of evils. 6. The Jews’ disturbance arose from two causes. The sick man was healed by descending into the pool. Only one was healed. 7. The illness of thirty years. The perfection of righteousness signified by the number forty. Love of the world is incompatible with love of God. 8. From what possession of temporal things is recognized as innocent. 9. The number forty in the fasts of Moses, Elijah, and Christ. Lent before Easter. The fifty days after Easter. 10. The Law is not fulfilled without charity. 11. Temporal things must be abandoned in one’s mind. Temptation generally does not make a sinner, but reveals him.

**686–697 SERMON CXXVI.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “The Son can do nothing from himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

1. Faith must precede understanding. 2. It is perverse to refuse to believe anything except what one sees. 3. From visible creatures we must rise to the invisible Creator. 4. Christ performed unusual miracles so that he might also be recognized as the maker of the ordinary things that had become commonplace. 5. The miracle of Christ’s birth from a virgin. 6. The miracle of Christ’s birth moves us to believe in God. 7. How the Son does what he sees the Father doing must be explained. 8. The Arians’ error concerning the Lord’s words. 9. He refutes the Arians and rejects their carnal understanding. Whatever the Father did, he did only through the Son. 10. The Father does not do one set of works and the Son another; the Trinity performs the same works. 11. The Trinity of persons and the unity of divinity. 12. The meaning of Christ’s words must be sought by those already imbued with right faith. 13. The difficulty of understanding these words arises because the seeing of the Word itself is not understood. 14. In Christ, the form of a servant was shown to mortals, while the form of God was reserved for the blessed. 15. Seeing the Word is not something other than the Word. Charity makes people capable of receiving divine things. The meaning of the passage under discussion.

**698–705 SERMON CXXVII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live,” etc. (John 5:24–29); also on the words of the Apostle, “What eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Corinthians 2:9).

1. The hope of Christians concerns things that are not seen. A fitting comparison. 2. How greatly we should love the eternal life promised to us. 3. What eternal life is, and at what price it must be acquired. The price of eternal life. Eternal life cannot be expressed in human words. 4. The Son is eternally begotten by the Father. 5. The eternal generation of the Son of God cannot be explained. 6. God is the food of the blessed mind. 7. The resurrection of the soul through faith. 8. The resurrection of the body is for some good and for others evil. 9. The cause and reason for the incarnation of the Son of God. How he died. 10. Christ the judge in the form of a servant. 11. To see God is supreme happiness. 12. The form of a servant will be seen by all; the form of God only by the godly. 13. After the resurrection, eternal life in the vision of God. 14. The resurrection of the flesh is to come. 15. The raising of the dead by God is no less credible than creation.

**705–713 SERMON CXXVIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “If I bear witness concerning myself,” etc. (John 5:31–35); and on the words of the Apostle, “Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires,” etc. (Galatians 5:14–17).

1. How true Christ’s testimony is, even when he testifies concerning himself. 2. Why John’s testimony was sought. 3. In the martyrs Christ himself bears witness to himself. 4. Charity comes from the Holy Spirit. 5. The struggle between soul and flesh. The soul must be subjected to God, and the flesh to the soul. 6. The Apostle concerning the struggle of flesh and spirit. 7. The Apostle misunderstood. It is the pastor’s duty to explain difficult passages of Scripture. 8. The inward struggle must be conducted so that the spirit is not conquered by the flesh. 9. To fight against the desires of the flesh is the work of the Holy Spirit in us. He acts well who is moved by the good. 10. How the saints here do not do what they wish. 11. A person wishes not to have desires, yet does not do what he wishes. 12. We must fight so that sin does not reign. 13. What it means to fulfill desires [Col. 2372]. 13. The three dead whom Christ raised signify three degrees of sinners.

**713–720 SERMON CXXIX.** On the words of the Gospel according to John 5:39–47, “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life,” etc., against the Donatists.

1. An exposition of the Gospel reading. 2. Christ’s words to the disciples also apply equally to us. 3. The Jews’ unbelief. 4. Christ’s words against the Jews apply to the Church’s words against the Donatists. 5. Testimonies of the Old Testament concerning Christ and the Church. 6. The testimony of the New Testament for Christ and the Church. 7. The Donatists imitate the crime of Antichrist. 8. What the doctrine of the Catholics and of the Donatists is. 9. The Donatists believe neither Moses nor Christ, even after his resurrection. The Donatists do injury to Christ.

**720–724 SERMON CXXX.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, where the miracle of the five loaves and two fish is recounted (John 6:5–14).

1. The meaning of the miracle. 2. Christ became bread through the incarnation. Christ the merchant. How he is our Redeemer. 3. Christ is to be loved. From what God has done, what he promised becomes credible. 4. What Christ has accomplished is more wonderful than what he promised. 5. Christians’ security under Christ’s protection.

**725–728 SERMON CXXXI.** On the words of the Gospel according to John 6:54–66, “Unless you eat the flesh,” etc., and on the words of the Apostle and of the Psalms, against the Pelagians.

1. The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. 2. Faith is God’s gift. The gentle force of grace. 3. Neither faith nor a good life is to be claimed as arising from one’s own powers. 4. Grace is necessary for the justified person to walk in the right way. 5. If one who walks in the right way attributes this to himself, he perishes from the right way. 6. Against the Pelagians. The remission of sins in Baptism. Illness after Baptism. 7. Four benefits of grace: remission of sins, healing of illness, redemption from every corruption and desire. 8. The final benefit of grace, the crown of righteousness. 9. The righteousness of God, unknown to the Jews and Pelagians. Grace hidden in the Old Testament, revealed in the New. 10. Councils against the Pelagians.

**729–734 SERMON CXXXII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh,” etc. (John 6:56–57).

1. The catechumens are invited to the grace of regeneration. 2. Married believers, already eating Christ’s body, are admonished to preserve chastity. 3. Those bound by a vow of continence. 4. Each person must preserve his own degree.

**734–736 SERMON CXXXIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, where Jesus said that he would not go up to the feast, and yet went up (John 7:2–10).

1. An exposition of the Gospel reading. 2. Christ did not lie in that passage. 3. To lie is worse than to be deceived. 4. How being deceived and lying differ. 5. Christ can neither be deceived nor lie. 6. Christ is vindicated from lying by the very truth of the Gospel. 7. A solution to the question. 8. Another solution.

**737–742 SERMON CXXXIV.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples,” etc. (John 8:31–34).

1. Christ is the teacher of all. 2. The reward of remaining in Christ’s word. “To be freed” is said in two ways. 3. The slavery of sin. 4. No one but Christ frees from the slavery and death of sin. The likeness of sinful flesh in Christ. 5. Sins and sacrifices for sins. 6. Conclusion.

**742–745 SERMON CXXXV.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “I came to do the works of him who sent me.” Against the Arians. And on the statement of the man who had been blind from birth and was given sight: “We know that God does not hear sinners” (John 9).

1. The blindness of all human beings from birth. 2. A passage maliciously appropriated by the Arians. 3. The works of the Father and the Son are the same. 4. The Son of God is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father. 5. Just as the Son does the works of the Father, so the Father does the works of the Son. 6. The prayers even of sinners are heard. 7. No one here is without sin. 8. The Apostles were also subject to sin after Christ’s resurrection.

**746–749 SERMON CXXXVI.** On the same Gospel reading from John, concerning the giving of sight to the man blind from birth (John 9).

1. The illumination of the man born blind. 2. The blind man’s error in thinking that sinners are not heard. 3. The blindness of the Jews, who maliciously accused Christ of breaking the Sabbath. 4. How the blindness of the Jews was increased by Christ’s coming. 5. Paul’s testimony concerning the Law’s inability and the blindness of the Jews. 6. What Elisha, sending his staff ahead and then coming himself to raise the dead man, prefigures.

**750–753 SERMON CXXXVII.** On John 10:1–16, concerning the shepherd, the hired man, and the thief [Col. 2373].

1. The health of the members lies in unity and charity. 2. The unity of Christ and his members. 3. Christ is the door. Peter, weak and unknown even to himself. 4. What is required of Peter. 5. Three persons coming to the sheepfold: the shepherd, the thief, and the hired man. The shepherd is to be loved, the hired man tolerated, and the thief avoided. 6. Christ’s statement concerning the Pharisees also applies to wicked pastors in the Church. The Church is one, from Jews and Gentiles. 7. Wicked clerics strive to pervert the Gospel while drawing laypeople into sin by their example. 8. A perverse interpretation of the Gospel. 9. Wicked pastors exist in the Church, like the Pharisees. Who is a shepherd, who a hired man, and who chaste. A chaste wife. 10. God must be sought chastely. 11. How hired men are useful. Shepherds are few, hired men many. 12. The hired man who flees. The Donatists are wolves and thieves. 13. How “grapes from thorns” is to be understood. 14. Hired men flee while favoring the wicked. Augustine is not a hired man. 15. What account the shepherd must give concerning the sheep.

**750–762 SERMON CXXXVIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “I am the good shepherd,” etc. (John 10:11–16).

1. Why the good shepherd is commended in the singular. 2. Martyrdom without charity profits nothing. 3. How great a good charity is. 4. Peter and others exist as good shepherds. 5. Yet Christ is the one good shepherd. 6. The bride’s affection for Christ. 7. How the bride’s words are to be understood. “Companions,” as though “fellow table-companions.” 8. The bridegroom’s reply. 9. The bride’s words wrongly appropriated by the Donatists. 10. The Donatists are refuted.

**763–768 SERMON CXXXIX.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

1. How Christ is God the Father’s only-begotten Son. 2. The Son of God and the Father are of one substance. 3. The Arians’ objection. 4. What blasphemy it is to say that the Son of God is of another substance. 5. By insulting the Son, the Arians falsely honor the Father.

**769–772 SERMON CXL.** On the words of the Gospel according to John 12:44–50, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me.” Against a certain statement of Maximin, an Arian bishop who, together with Count Segisvult, was established in Africa and blasphemed.

1. Faith in Christ. 2. Christ’s two births. 3. Why Christ is called the true Son of God. 4. No one except Christ would dare say that he is one with the Father. 5. The equality of the Son with the Father. 6. The Word of God as the Father’s command.

**773–775 SERMON CXLI.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

1. The truth was discovered by the philosophers of this age, but not the way. 2. From where they discovered truth. 3. The foolishness of those who worship idols. 4. Christ became the way.

**776–777 SERMON CXLII.** On the same words of John’s Gospel, “I am the way,” etc. (John 14:6).

1. Christ is the safe way. 2. Christ is the humble way. To commit fornication against the Lord. 3. The sinner is reproved so that he may be healthfully ashamed. 4. Hatred of sin together with love for the sinner. 5. The swelling of pride must be healed by the medicine of humility. Christ is both the way and the door. 6. Christ the physician first drank the potion for the sick person. 7. Christ does not ask us to perform miracles, but to learn to be humble. 8. Charity without self-inflation. 9. Without charity, the other gifts of God are of no benefit. 10. Perfection and charity are attained through imitation of Christ.

**778–784 SERMON CXLIII.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away,” etc. (John 16:7–11).

1. Faith in Christ is necessary for justification. 2. Why the sin of unbelief in Christ alone is reproved. 3. The great gift of the Holy Spirit after Christ’s ascension. 4. The righteousness of faith from the Holy Spirit after Christ’s departure. 5. The world’s unbelief is without excuse.

**784–787 SERMON CXLIV.** On the same words of John’s Gospel, “He will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment” (John 16:8–11).

1. Why the sin of unbelief alone is reproved. The Holy Spirit is called the grace of God. 2. “To believe Christ” and “to believe in Christ” differ. 3. The righteousness concerning which the world is convicted. 4. Why the righteousness consists in Christ’s going to the Father. 5. Christ alone ascended into heaven. 6. How Christ’s righteousness is ours.

**787–790 SERMON CXLV.** On the words of the Gospel according to John 16:24, “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” And on the words of Luke 10:17–20, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

1. How the passage in John is reconciled with Luke’s words. 2. The sweetness of God is hidden from those who fear and revealed to those who hope. 3. Fear under the Law, hope under grace. 4. Charity comes not from us but from God. 5. Presumption is removed by the Law, captivity by grace. 6. The disciples, still under the Law, were not yet free from desires. Those who ask God for temporal things ask for nothing.

**790–794 SERMON CXLVI.** On the words of the Gospel according to John, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” etc. (John 21:15–17).

1. The duty of the shepherd and of the sheep. God himself is our inheritance. 2. The recently baptized are commanded to beware of wicked Christians and schismatics.

**796 SERMON CXLVII.** On the same words of the Gospel according to John, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” etc. (John 21:15–19).

1. Peter’s presumption and denial. 2. Peter’s true love for Christ. The unity of all shepherds represented in Peter. 3. Peter abandoned by Christ and afterward strengthened.

**797–798 SERMON CXLVIII.** On the words of the Acts of the Apostles, “Was it not yours while it remained, and after it was sold was it not in your power?” (Acts 5:4), delivered to the twenty holy martyrs on the Sunday of the octave of Easter.

1. Ananias and Sapphira did not receive a harsher correction: temporal death. 2. Vows must be paid to God.

**799 SERMON CXLIX.** In which questions proposed from the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10, and from the Gospel are resolved; or, concerning four questions: first, concerning Peter’s vision; second, concerning the words of the Gospel, “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works,” etc., and shortly afterward, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them,” etc.; third, concerning the words of the Gospel, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing”; fourth, concerning love of the enemy (Matthew 6:1–4 and 5:43–48).

1. The questions to be resolved: the first question, concerning Peter’s vision. 2. Voracity was not commanded to Peter. 3. The Jews’ abstinence from unclean animals was figurative. 4. The animals forbidden to the Jews are signs: the split hoof and rumination. 5. Why the commandments of Jewish observances are read to Christians. 6. Peter’s vision was figurative. The vessel. The four corners. 7. Peter represents the person of the Church. 8. The reception of the nations within the Church. 9. The linen cloth. 10. The threefold lowering. 11. The second question, from the Gospel. 12. Discord resulting from an erroneous interpretation of the passages. The virgins who brought no oil. 13. Passages that appear contrary are reconciled. 14. The legitimate meaning of both passages is drawn from Christ’s own words. 15. The third question, concerning the Gospel passage that the left hand should not know the work of the right. 16. The fourth question, concerning love and hatred of the enemy. 17. We must pray for those who persecute us. 18. Under the name of neighbor, even an enemy is commanded to be loved. 19. The Apostle’s passage about heaping coals upon the enemy’s head is explained.

**800–807 SERMON CL.** On the words of the Acts of the Apostles, “Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers were discussing with him,” etc. (Acts 17:18–34).
