1. Paul preaching among the Athenians. 2. The faith of Christians. 3. The Epicureans and Stoics debating with the Apostle. 4. Everyone desires the blessed life. 5. The Epicurean and Stoic opinion concerning the blessed life. 6. The Epicurean opinion rejected by the Apostle. What the Epicureans think about the soul. Some Christians are Epicurean in their conduct. 7. Fasting with prayer and almsgiving. 8. The Stoic opinion is not approved by the Apostle. 9. The Epicurean and Stoic opinions concerning happiness must be rejected. 10. Christ is both blessedness and the way to blessedness.

**807–813 SERMON CLI.** On the words of the Apostle, “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do,” etc. (Romans 7:15–25).

1. The Apostle’s passage is dangerous for those who misunderstand it. 2. The life of the righteous here is war, not yet triumph. 3. The destruction of desire must be our prayer. The madness of the Manichaeans. 4. How desire and evil habit must be resisted. 5. Desire is innate in us and arose from the first sin. Original sin from desire. Christ was conceived without sin so that he might undo sin. 6. The Apostle’s struggle against desire is set before us so that we may not despair. 7. What it means to do but not complete either good or evil. 8. By Christ’s grace desire will eventually be destroyed. What the faithful must do now.

**814–819 SERMON CLII.** On the following words of the Apostle, Romans 7 and 8:1–4, up to “God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” etc.

1. There is no difficulty in obscure meanings when the Spirit gives assistance. 2. On the same subject. 3. The evil of desire remains without guilt in the baptized. 4. The error of the Manichaeans must be avoided. 5. Three laws: the law of sin, the law of faith, and the law of works. 6. The Law of Moses is defended against the Manichaeans. 7. The three laws. 8. Christ’s flesh alone is not sinful flesh. 9. How sin was condemned in Christ concerning sin. 10. The opinion of certain people concerning the Apostle’s passage [Col. 2375]. 11. The Apostle’s more accurate interpretation. How Christ was made sin.

**819–825 SERMON CLIII.** On the words of the Apostle, Romans 7:5–13, “When we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that are through the Law were at work in our members, so as to bear fruit for death,” etc. Explicitly against the Manichaeans, and implicitly against the Pelagians.

1. How difficult this passage of the Apostle is to explain. 2. The Manichaeans abuse this passage. 3. The Manichaeans’ slander is refuted from what follows. 4. In the same passage the Apostle himself condemns the detractors of the Law. 5. The Law that forbids desiring evil is not evil. 6. The evil of desire was unknown before the Law. 7. Through the Law desire was increased, not conquered. 8. The person who presumes on himself is conquered. 9. We must trust not in ourselves but in God. 10. Delight in God’s Law and delight in desire. 11. The proud person is killed by his own sword. 12. The Apostle is again and again an unmistakable praiser of the Law. 13. On the same subject. 14. Sin derived from the first human being.

**825–832 SERMON CLIV.** On the words of the Apostle, Romans 7, “We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” etc. Against the Pelagians, who say that a person can be without sin in this life.

1. For what purpose the Law was given. 2. Whether the Apostle is speaking here about himself. 3. The Apostle himself was not without desire. 4. The Apostle speaks of his own imperfection. 5. The Apostle confesses the weakness of his soul. 6. A poultice for swelling was given to the Apostle. 7. Every holy person in this life is both carnal and spiritual. 8. Who is wholly carnal, and who is partly or wholly spiritual. 9. The same person is simultaneously carnal and spiritual. 10. Agreeing with the Law. 11. Ignorance of sin. 12. The saints are not permitted to fulfill the Law completely in this life. 13. On the same subject. 14–15. Likewise on the same subject. 16. In the resurrection only the righteous will be freed from the body of death. 17. The bodies of the saints will be immortal after the resurrection.

**832–840 SERMON CLV.** On the words of the Apostle, Romans 8:1–11, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,” etc. Against the Pelagians.

1. Why desire is called sin. How sin loses its reign. 2. How there is here no condemnation in the saints. 3. No one is freed from the law of sin except by grace. 4. What the law of sin and death is. Why the Law of Moses was given. 5. The harmony of the old and new Laws. 6. The difference between those same Laws. 7. The Law’s weakness comes from the flesh. Christ in the likeness of sinful flesh. 8. Christ was made sin. 9. To walk according to the flesh and according to the Spirit. How the righteousness of the Law is now fulfilled in us. 10. The wisdom of the flesh and of the Spirit. 11. The error of the Manichaeans. 12. Not to be in the flesh. 13. To be not in the flesh but in the Spirit. 14. What is to be hoped for concerning the flesh. 15. The restoration and immortality of the flesh promised to the godly.

**840–848 SERMON CLVI.** On the words of the Apostle, Romans 8:12–17, “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh,” etc. Against the Pelagians.

1. In Scripture some things are closed and others open. 2. Why the Law was given. The necessity of medicinal grace. 3. Using the Law lawfully. The Law as a pedagogue. 4. The usefulness of the Law. 5. The necessity of the Mediator. What faith is worthy of praise. 6. To live according to the flesh is evil. Let the soul live according to God, and the flesh according to the soul. 7. The Epicureans live according to the flesh, and the Stoics according to the soul. 8. The soul living according to itself is carnal. 9. Our task in this life is the mortification of the flesh. 10. Presumption on oneself must be avoided in the mortification of the flesh. 11. We are both moved toward the good and ourselves act. 12. Nothing good is possible without God’s help. What kind of freedom exists without grace. 13. Grace is necessary not merely so that one may do something more easily, but so that one may do it at all. 14. The old and new Law. The spirit of slavery and of freedom. 15. “Abba” and “Father,” because there are two peoples in Christ. 16. The Spirit is a pledge more properly than a guarantee. 17. The inheritance of the children of God.

**849–858 SERMON CLVII.** On the words of the Apostle, “We were saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8:24–25).

1. The Christians’ hope concerns eternal things. The deceptive world is believed rather than God. 2. Patience and gentleness are necessary. 3. In our head we see what we hope for. 4. Even now we are not without joy. The fleeting pleasures of sins. 5. The vanity of temporal things. 6. The certainty of our hope.

**659–661 SERMON CLVIII.** On the words of the Apostle, Romans 8:30–31, “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified,” etc., “If God is for us, who is against us?” Against the Pelagians.

1. No one can harm those who are predestined. 2. God has become our debtor because of his promises. 3. We have been called and predestined freely. 4. Whether we have already been justified. 5. There is a certain justification truly through faith. 6. Justifying faith is distinguished from the faith of demons through hope and charity: hope; charity. 7. The gratuitous worship of God, who alone satisfies the soul. 8. Hope in this pilgrimage.
consolation. 9. God will be all things to the blessed in all things. Charity alone always remains.

**862–867 SERMON CLIX.** On the same words of the Apostle, Romans 8:30–31, or on justification; also on the words of James 2–4, “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials,” etc.—1. Justification here is imperfect in us. 2. Love of righteousness admits several degrees. The first degree. Lawful and unlawful pleasures of the senses. 3. The mind’s delight in righteousness and faith. 4. Righteousness is to be loved above all lawful pleasures. 5. The delight of righteousness is to be preferred to other delights. 6. Righteousness is to be pursued with delight arising from love. 7. For the sake of righteousness, not only pleasure but also pain must be endured. 8. The martyrs are perfect lovers of righteousness. 9. Whatever righteousness we possess is from God.

**867–872 SERMON CLX.** On the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 1:31, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord”; and on the verse of Psalm 70:2, “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.”—1. Let man boast in the Lord, not in his own righteousness. 2. The Jews were blinded by their opinion of their own righteousness. 3. To know Christ crucified is great wisdom. Pride prevents a person from believing in Christ. 4. The humility of the cross is the way to exaltation. 5. The sons of Zebedee, desiring exaltation, are called to the way. 6. The circumcision of the Old Testament and the cross of the New are signs. 7. Let boasting be in Christ’s cross, not in our own righteousness.

**872–877 SERMON CLXI.** On the words of the Apostle, “Do not err: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males . . . shall possess the kingdom of God. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” etc., 1 Corinthians 6:9, 10, 15, 19.—1. Fornication must be fled. 2. The fornicator commits an offense against the Holy Spirit. 3. Fornication excludes one from the kingdom of God. 4. There are two dwelling places: in the fire or in the kingdom. How greatly the body is feared. 5. The death of the soul is to be feared more than that of the body. 6. Whence come the life of the soul and the life of the body. God is the soul’s life. 7. Empty fear and useful fear. 8. Fear of punishment, when it does not prevent evil, is not yet praiseworthy. What fear of Gehenna is useful for. 9. Charity drives out one fear and introduces another. 10. The power of impure love. 11. Love makes sacred virgins. Women’s adornments. 12. The love of sacred virgins.

**877–884 SERMON CLXII.** On the words of the Apostle, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body,” 1 Corinthians 6:9–20.—1. A difficult question arising from the Apostle’s words. 2. The difficulty resolved. Why fornication alone is said to be a sin against one’s own body. 3. General fornication, by which one does not cleave to God. The Apostle’s interpretation is twofold.

**885–888 SERMON CLXIII.** On the words of the Apostle, “Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” Galatians 5:16–21.—1. The dedication of a temple previously profane. 2. In us, as in a profane temple, some things must be cast down and others consecrated. 3. Building takes place through faith; dedication through resurrection. 4. The new song. Christ, God’s salvation, desired by the ancients. 5. Christ’s preaching. 6. The struggle of flesh and spirit. 7. Victory after the resurrection. Why victory is delayed. 8. The remedy for exaltation in Paul. 9. Victory is to be obtained through humility. 10. Law without grace. 11. The necessity of divine assistance. 12. God’s assistance must be invoked.

**889–895 SERMON CLXIV.** On the words of the Apostle, Galatians 6:2–5, “Bear one another’s burdens”; and on these words, “Each one will bear his own burden.” Against the Donatists.—1. The law of Christ is fulfilled by those who bear one another’s burdens. 2. Burdens must be distinguished. 3. Two kinds of burdens. 4. Each person’s own burdens are sins. Christ, the preacher to the world. 5. The burden of avarice; the burden of sloth. 6. In place of the burdens of desire, the burdens of charity must be taken up. 7. What Christ the teacher wishes to be learned from him. Christ’s burden is light. 8. Each person bears the burden of his own desire or charity. 9. Burdens that are to be shared. Poverty is a burden. Wealth is a burden. 10. The Donatists persisted in schism after the Conference. 11. One who tolerates the wicked does not thereby share in their sins. 12. Caecilianus was condemned in his absence although innocent. The emperors’ laws against the Donatists. Caecilianus acquitted three times. Primianus. 13. The Donatists condemned by their own judgment. 14. What keeps the Donatists in error [Col. 2377]. 15. Patience must be shown toward them.

**895–902 SERMON CLXV.** On the words of the Apostle, Ephesians 3:13–18, “I ask that you not lose heart over my tribulations for you, which are your glory,” etc.; and on grace and free will, against the Pelagians.—1. Hope must be placed in God, not in the powers of free will. The cooperation of grace and free will. 2. God is asked for the very thing that is required of man. 3. The mystery of the cross in its four dimensions. 4. The breadth, length, and height of the cross. 5. The depth of the cross. 6. Whence arose the error that souls sinned before the body. 7. Death comes only from sin. The death of infants comes from the sin of the first man. 8. Infants who die in the womb. 9. Grace comes to the aid of infants and adults. The mystery of grace is inscrutable.

**902–907 SERMON CLXVI.** A sermon on the words of the Apostle, Ephesians 4:25, “Putting away falsehood, speak the truth”; and on Psalm 115, “Every man is a liar.”—1. Falsehood is forbidden to man. 2. People are reproached for being human. In the old man there is falsehood; in the new, truth. 3. How the things that belong to God become ours. 4. You have been called not to be merely human, but a son of God.

**907–909 SERMON CLXVII.** On the words of the Apostle, “See carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil,” Ephesians 5:15–16.—1. Whence the evil days arise. 2. The righteous here are never without persecution. 3. Redeeming the time. 4. A Punic proverb agrees with Christ’s command.

**909–910 SERMON CLXVIII.** On the words of the Apostle, Ephesians 6:23, “Peace to the brothers, and charity with faith.” Or, on the grace of God according to the confession and teaching of the “Vessel of Election,” since faith is a gift of God’s mercy.—1. He who made the promise makes us children of Abraham’s faith. 2. The faith of Christians differs from the faith of demons. The faith of God’s children is accompanied by charity. Faith is the beginning of salvation. True peace. 3. All good things, including faith itself, are from God. Complete faith. 4. Grace was given to an unbeliever and cruel persecutor. 5. Both faith and prayer arise from God’s grace. The Pelagian objection. 6. Prayer made for Saul, an unbeliever, proves that faith is God’s gift. 7. Paul—that is, “the little one”—a preacher of the grace bestowed on him. 8. Prayer is offered for unbelievers, that they may believe.

**SERMON CLXIX.** On the words of the Apostle, Philippians 3:3–16, “For we are the circumcision, who serve God by the Spirit,” etc. Against the Pelagians.—1. What it means to serve God by the Spirit. 2. How we are circumcision and righteousness. Our righteousness comes from God’s gift. 3. Spiritual circumcision consists in those who glory in Christ. Why circumcision took place on the eighth day. The Lord’s Day. 4. Trusting in the flesh. 5. What cause Paul had for boasting in the flesh. 6. Walking blamelessly in the law. 7. Why righteousness in the law removes one from Christ. 8. He begins to resolve the question. 9. Saul the persecutor of the Church, because he established his own righteousness. 10. Paul rejects his own righteousness in order to possess righteousness from God. 11. True righteousness is not ours except through grace. 12. It is a great thing to know the power of Christ’s resurrection. Our resurrection is more wondrous. 13. Our justification comes from grace, but not without our will. 14. Sharing in Christ’s sufferings through charity. 15. Charity and the enlargement of the heart by the Holy Spirit. 16. The Apostle professes himself imperfect. 17. The duties of Martha and Mary. 18. One must always make progress on the way to God.

**915–926 SERMON CLXX.** On the same words of the Apostle, Philippians 3:6–16, “According to the righteousness that is from the law, being blameless,” etc.; and on the words of Psalm 142:1–2, “Hear me in your righteousness,” etc.; and finally on the Gospel reading from John 6:39, “The will of my Father is that everything he has given me should not perish,” etc.—1. Righteousness from the law seems a loss to the Apostle. 2. The Apostle’s statement must be understood in such a way as to avoid the Manichaean error concerning the Old Law. For what purpose the law was given. Original sin. 3. There was no sin in Christ. 4. The world, sinners, and lovers of the world. Christ alone is innocent. Original sin. 5. Blameless conduct according to the law. 6. Human righteousness is nothing unless it comes from God. 7. How little the righteousness of this life is to be valued when compared with future righteousness. 8. Present righteousness must be despised in the desire for perfect righteousness. 9. Perfect righteousness and happiness will come when God is seen. 10. Christ is our day. We must strive toward heaven with our whole desire. 11. Christ is our way.

**926–932 SERMON CLXXI.** On the words of the Apostle, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” etc., Philippians 4:4–6.—1. Let joy be in the Lord, not in the world. The Lord is near to us. 2. The Samaritan who aided the wounded man is Christ. 3. Through the Incarnation, God became near to man. 4. Joy in the world. 5. Impunity is God’s greatest vengeance.

**933–935 SERMON CLXXII.** On the words of the Apostle, 1 Thessalonians 4:12, “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope.” And on works of mercy by which the dead are helped.—1. What sort of grief for the dead is forbidden. 2. Prayers, sacrifice, and alms for the departed. 3. Mourning and duties to be rendered to the dead.

**935–937 SERMON CLXXIII.** On the same words of the Apostle, 1 Thessalonians 4:[Col. 2378] 12–17.—1. What should be considered in the services for the dead. 2. Faith in the resurrection, consolation in the death of loved ones. 3. Consolation in mourning for the dead.

**937–939 SERMON CLXXIV.** On the words of the Apostle, 1 Timothy 1:15, “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, because Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners,” etc.; and on the Gospel reading from Luke 19:1–10, concerning Zacchaeus. Against the Pelagians.—1. Christ’s coming into the world is to be understood with reference to the flesh. The necessity of the Incarnation. 2. Sin was the cause of the Incarnation. The weakness of free will is seen in Adam. The gift of grace is manifested in Christ. 3. The deed of Zacchaeus understood allegorically: the sycamore signifies Christ’s cross. The cross on the forehead. 4. The necessity of prevenient grace. 5. Receiving Jesus into the heart. 6. Those who think themselves healthy rave against the physician. The physician’s blood becomes medicine for his killer. 7. Original sin is proved. Christ is Jesus even for infants. The baptism and communion of infants. 8. The reason Christ came. The meaning of the name Jesus. Infants need a Savior. Let the faith of those answering on their behalf at Baptism be sound. 9. All infants are to be regarded as orphans. Infants require regeneration. Objection against original sin. The ancient rule of faith: to baptize infants.

**939–944 SERMON CLXXV.** On the same words of the Apostle, “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance,” etc., 1 Timothy 1:15–16.—1. The reason for Christ’s Incarnation. 2. The Jews’ illness is more dangerous. The Jews rave against the physician. 3. Christ prepares medicine from his own blood for his killers. 4. The conversion of Christ’s killers. 5. Christ loves sinners so that they may not remain sinners forever. 6. How Paul was the first of sinners. 7. First of sinners because he was worse than all. 8. Paul’s conversion. 9. The physician Christ’s skill commended in Paul’s cure.

**945–949 SERMON CLXXVI.** On three readings: 1 Timothy 1:15–16, “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance,” etc.; Psalm 94:6, 2, “Come, let us worship and fall down before him,” etc.; and the Gospel of Luke 17:12–19, concerning the ten lepers cleansed by the Lord. Against the Pelagians.—1. Readings and singing in the Church. 2. Thanksgiving owed by all to the physician. Original sin in infants. Bishops as guardians of orphans. 3. How Paul was the first of sinners. 4. In Paul’s healing, hope of salvation is brought to the despairing. 5. Our salvation is from God, not from ourselves. The benefits of grace. Twofold confession. 6. The varied and inconsistent doctrine that is the leprosy of the mind.

**949–953 SERMON CLXXVII.** On the words of the Apostle, “We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away,” etc., 1 Timothy 6:7–19.—1. Avarice is condemned in words by everyone, but not in deeds. 2. The teaching given to Christians concerning what must be avoided in avarice. 3. The necessities of this life’s journey are to be possessed without desire. 4. Inner riches are to be pursued. 5. The foolish excuse of those who wish to store up riches here. Lift up your heart. 6. The insatiability of the desire for riches. 7. Riches, if possessed without desire, are not to be condemned. The poor person must beware of desire for riches; the rich person must beware of pride. 8. Hope must not be placed in riches. Enjoyment and use. 9. God alone is sufficient for man. The crime and punishment of avarice. 10. Riches are to be spent on pious works. True life is purchased with riches. 11. The moth of evil thought that turns one away from giving alms.

**953–959 SERMON CLXXVIII.** On the words of the Apostle, Titus 1:9, “So that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict.” Against robbers of other people’s property.—1. The burden of bishops. 2. The miser who hoards his own possessions is condemned. 3. The rich man is punished because he is without mercy. 4. Alms from a robber are not acceptable to God. 5. It is not lawful to seize the property of pagans. 6. He rebukes robbers. 7. Found property must be restored. 8. An outstanding example concerning the restoration of alms. 9. On the same subject. 10. Servile fear does not prevent wickedness of heart. 11. How pure love of righteousness is proved.

**960–965 SERMON CLXXIX.** On the words of the Apostle James, “Let each of you be swift to hear, slow to speak”; and on those words in the same passage, “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only,” chapter 1:19, 22.—1. What must be said concerning the duties of both hearers and preachers of God’s word. 2. Hearing God’s word is safer than preaching it. 3. The duties of Mary and Martha. Martha’s portion is good. The goodness of hospitality. 4. Mary’s portion is better, because it is not taken away. Martha’s work is taken away, not its reward. 5. How Mary’s portion does not pass away. 6. Being nourished by truth: Mary’s portion, which does not pass away. Delight in the light of truth. 7. We must be doers of the word both inwardly and outwardly. 8. Hearers of the word build, some on rock and others on sand. 9. Not hearing is evil, as though one were not building. 10. A negligent hearer must not use the preacher’s faults as an excuse.

**966–971 SERMON CLXXX.** On the words of the Apostle James, “Above all, do not swear,” chapter 5:12.—1. An admonition to beware of swearing. 2. Although swearing is employed by God, it must nevertheless be avoided by man. In how many ways perjury occurs. 3. The danger of perjury in swearing. It is permissible to swear truly; not to swear is safer. 5. Swearing employed by the Apostle. 6. Various forms of swearing. [Col. 2379] 7. What it means to swear. 8. Perjury is deadly to the soul. 9. Why it is said that one must abstain from swearing above all. 10. Augustine was at times subject to the habit of swearing. Under what condition an oath should be used. 11. How one sins who demands an oath from another. 12. The habit of swearing must be resisted with greater effort. 13. To swear falsely by idols is perjury. 14. How the habit of swearing is uprooted.

**972–979 SERMON CLXXXI.** On the words of the First Epistle of John, chapter 1:8–9, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Against the Pelagians.—1. No one lives here without sin. 2. The Pelagian error that the righteous can be found here without sin. 3. They are refuted by their own profession concerning themselves. Heretics are outside the Church. 4. The Pelagians’ deceptive humility. 5. A lie in the guise of humility is sin. 6. It is clear from the Lord’s Prayer that the Church here is not without sin. 7. Here the whole Church asks that its sins be forgiven. Here the Church works toward being without spot or wrinkle in heaven. 8. Remedies for sins, without which one cannot live. A Christian of good faith and good hope does not commit deadly sins. The condition under which our daily sins are forgiven.

**979–983 SERMON CLXXXII.** On the words of the First Epistle of John, chapter 4:1–3, “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” etc., against the Manichaeans.—1. One must not believe every spirit. 2. He is not from God who denies that Christ came in the flesh. 3. The Manichaeans’ ambush in this very passage of John. The error concerning two natures. 4. The Manichaean error that the soul is a part of God is refuted. 5. Man cannot be light for himself. Evil comes not from nature but from nature’s defect. 6. Man’s two evils: error and weakness. 7. Another question concerning the same passage of John is deferred to the following sermon.

**984–987 SERMON CLXXXIII.** Again, on the words of the First Epistle of John, chapter 4:2, “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God.”—1. The question to be discussed. 2. Heretics agree in denying that Christ came in the flesh. 3. How the Arian denies that Christ came in the flesh. 4–5. On the same subject. 6. The Eunomian. 7. The Sabellian. 8. Photinus. 9. The Donatist. 10–11. On the same subject. 12. The Pelagian. 13. It is common to heretics and evil Catholics to deny Christ’s Incarnation. 14. Both right faith and good conduct are from God. 15. By believing and by living well, we must confess that Christ came in the flesh.

**988–994 CLASS TWO.—SERMONS FOR THE LITURGICAL YEAR**

**995–996 SERMON CLXXXIV.** On the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, I.—1. The mystery of the Incarnation hidden from the wise of the world. 2. Christ’s Nativity is a cause of joy for all. 3. Christ’s birth is twofold. Things to be marveled at in God as an infant.

**995–997 SERMON CLXXXV.** On the Nativity of the Lord, II.—1. Through the Incarnation of the Word, Truth has arisen from the earth. 2. Through Christ’s Incarnation, righteousness has been brought to us. 3. God’s glory in the gratuitous justification of human beings.

**997–998 SERMON CLXXXVI.** On the Nativity of the Lord, III.—1. Christ was born from a virgin’s giving birth. Through the Incarnation, God did not cease to be God. 2. Without any alteration of the Word, he became the same Son of God and son of man. The rule of faith, the Creed. 3. Through the Incarnation, the Son of God is the same person as the Son of man.

**999–1000 SERMON CLXXXVII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, IV.—1. The wondrous harmony in the infant Christ of attributes that appear contradictory. 2. The Word did not depart from the Father by coming in the flesh; this is shown by an analogy. 3. The Word was not changed by the Incarnation. 4. The incarnate Word is God and man.

**1001–1002 SERMON CLXXXVIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, V.—1. The Word of God cannot be explained by man. 2. The eternal Word was born in time for our sake. 3. The infant Word, teacher of humility. 4. Mary bore Christ without loss of virginity.

**1003–1004 SERMON CLXXXIX.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VI.—1. Christ is day from Day. 2. Christ’s wondrous birth from a virgin. 3. The benefit of regeneration through Christ’s human birth. 4. Christ’s birth is twofold.

**1005–1006 SERMON CXC.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VII.—1. Christ chose the day on which he would be born for the sake of the mystery. 2. Christ’s births are two. Why he wished to be born from a woman. 3. Christ became an infant in a manger for our sake. 4. Christ’s Nativity is to be celebrated.

**1007–1008 SERMON CXCI.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VIII.—1. The Word became incarnate in order to bear what was unworthy for the unworthy. 2. Christ was born with his mother’s virginity unharmed. 3. The Church is both virgin and mother in mind. 4. Mary’s virginity is to be imitated.

**1009–1011 SERMON CXCII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, IX.—1. How wondrous is the Incarnation of the Son of God for the sake of human beings. 2. Christ’s Nativity is a cause of joy for virgins, widows, and married women. The Church is mother and virgin. 3. Truth from the earth, righteousness from heaven. Why Christ was born on the shortest day of the year.

**1009–1013 SERMON CXCIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, X.

**1013 SERMON CXCIV.** On the Nativity of the Lord, XI.—1. Christ’s Nativity is twofold. The birthdays of Christ and John. 2. The Word is the food of angels in heaven and of human beings in the manger. 3. After this life we shall be satisfied by the vision of the Word [Col. 2380]. 4. Conclusion.

**1015–1017 SERMON CXCV.** On the Nativity of the Lord, XII.—1. Christ’s births are two, and both are indescribable. 2. Christ is the son of a virgin and the bridegroom of a virgin. 3. Why Christ came in the flesh.

**1017–1018 SERMON CXCVI.** On the Nativity of the Lord, XIII.—1. Christ’s births are two. The Son, eternally begotten by the Father without beginning. 2. Three ways of life—married, widowed, and virginal—bear witness to Christ. 3. God became an infant for our sake. 4. The superstitious solemnity of the Kalends of January.

**1019–1020 SERMON CXCVII.** On the Kalends of January, I, against the Pagans.

**1021 SERMON CXCVIII.** On the Kalends of January, II.—1. The solemnity of the Kalends of January. 2. Our separation from the Gentiles by Christian faith, hope, and charity. 3. Christians are distinguished from pagans by pious works. False gods delight in the evil conduct of their worshipers.

**1024–1025 SERMON CXCIX.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, I.—1. Christ soon joins Jews and Gentiles in himself. 2. The faith of the Magi, and the Jews’ unbelief in contrast. 3. The error concerning astral fates.

**1026–1027 SERMON CC.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, II.—1. The solemnity of Christ’s manifestation. 2. Herod’s terror. 3. The Jews’ blindness amid the very illumination of the Magi. The Scriptures were preserved among the Jews for the faith of the Gentiles. 4. The Gentiles are joined to Christ through charity with the Jews.

**1028–1030 SERMON CCI.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, III.—1. Christ’s manifestation to the Gentiles. The star is the language of heaven. 2. In Pilate and the Magi, the Gentiles to be gathered from East and West are signified. 3. The Jews are guardians of the Scriptures for the salvation of the Gentiles.

**1031–1032 SERMON CCII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, IV.—1. Epiphany means Christ’s manifestation. 2. In the Magi, the first fruits of the Gentiles are offered. 3. The Jews display Christ through their rites and Scriptures. 4. The former life must not be resumed after repentance.

**1033–1035 SERMON CCIII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, V.—1. The feast of the Epiphany was rightly instituted. 2. Among the Jews, grace came first; among the Gentiles, humility is greater. 3. The salvation of all the Gentiles prefigured.

**1035–1036 SERMON CCIV.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, VI.—1. Epiphany, Christ’s manifestation. 2. Christ is the cornerstone joining Jews and Gentiles. 3. Of the Jews, some were rejected and others chosen. Jacob both blessed and lame.

**1037–1038 SERMON CCV.** In Lent, I.—1. During Lent, the cross of bodily discipline must be taken up. A Christian must hang upon the cross continually. The cross is the whole of our life. 2. Pious works must be practiced more fervently during Lent. 3. Above all, one must fast from quarrels.

**1039–1041 SERMON CCVI.** In Lent, II.—1. The season of Lent ought to burn with works of piety and humility. 2. Prayer must be supported by fasting and almsgiving. Two kinds of almsgiving. God is fed in the poor. No one is poor with respect to the other kind of almsgiving. 3. Fasts acceptable to God.

**1041–1042 SERMON CCVII.** In Lent, III.—1. Alms should be distributed especially at this time. 2. What sort of fasting and abstinence is required. Pleasures must be reduced, not exchanged. 3. The prayer of one who fasts must be free from desire and hatred. How prayer makes alms.

**1042–1044 SERMON CCVIII.** In Lent, IV.—1. What Lenten abstinence should be. Luxuries must be restricted, not exchanged. 2. Works of almsgiving must be increased. One kind of almsgiving is to spare one’s enemies.

**1044–1045 SERMON CCIX.** In Lent, V.—1. Hostilities must be ended through the observance of Lent. Three vices by which hostility lives. 2. Prayers must be supported by alms. 3. What sort of abstinence must be undertaken.

**1046–1047 SERMON CCX.** In Lent, VI.—1. During Lent, the season of the year and the number of days must be considered. 2. The question: Why is fasting undertaken at that time before the celebration of Baptism? The answer. 3. The baptism of John must be distinguished from Christ’s Baptism. Why Christ accepted the sacraments of the Old Law. When temptation is brought upon us, we must fast. 4. Why the Lenten fast occurs before Easter. When the bridegroom is taken away, the children must mourn. 5. Why we must groan and fast in this life. 6. Fasting before the solemnity of Christ’s Passion is especially appropriate. 7. The present days are days of labor and sorrow. 8. Why fasting was instituted with the number forty. 9. During Lent, abstinence and pious works ought to be practiced more fervently. 10. Those who observe Lent luxuriously. 11. Abstinence from fine wine. 12. Works of mercy toward the poor. The other kind of mercy consists in forgiving.

**1047–1053 SERMON CCXI.** In Lent, VII.—1. Complaints must be ended during Lent. The agreement to forgive so that we may be forgiven. Anger is one thing, hatred another. 2. The one who hates is in darkness and prison. We must forgive so that we may be able to say the Lord’s Prayer. 4. The person to whom forgiveness is denied by a brother when he asks it is secure before God. Concerning those who are ashamed to ask forgiveness from a human being. From some people forgiveness must be requested only silently and with gentle words. 5. How one should forgive from the heart someone unwilling to ask forgiveness. [Col. 2381] 6. Offenses are to be forgiven following Christ’s example.

**1054–1057 SERMON CCXII.** At the presentation of the Creed, I.—1. Why it is called the Creed. 2. Why the Creed must be kept in memory.

**1058–1060 SERMON CCXIII.** At the presentation of the Creed, II.—1. What the Creed is. How God is omnipotent. 2. Christ, the only Son of God. How he became incarnate. Christ is our one Savior. 3. How Christ, the Son of God, died and was buried. 4. God’s right hand is eternal happiness. 5. Our Savior, our judge, and our advocate. 6. Concerning the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit must be understood in such a way that he is not believed to be less than the Son or less than the Father. 7. What the holy catholic Church is. A harlot found and made a virgin. Like Mary, it both gives birth and is a virgin. 8. Forgiveness of sins in Baptism and the Lord’s Prayer. Daily Baptism. 9. What sort of resurrection of the flesh has been promised.

**1060–1065 SERMON CCXIV.** At the presentation of the Creed, III.—1. Why the Creed of faith was instituted. 2. We must believe in God Almighty, the creator of all things. 3. The Almighty is not overcome although the wicked do many things against his will. 4. The Almighty cannot do only what he does not will. 5. Christ, the only Son of God. 6. Christ’s birth from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. 7. Christ, the Son of God, crucified, dead, and buried. 8. Christ’s resurrection and ascension. His sitting at the Father’s right hand. 9. Christ will come as judge in visible form. 10. The Holy Spirit, God proceeding from the Father. The mystery of the Trinity. 11. The holy catholic Church, the pillar and foundation of truth. Forgiveness of sins. 12. The resurrection of the flesh. Conclusion.

**1065–1072 SERMON CCXV.** At the giving back of the Creed.—1. The Creed of faith must always be revolved in the mind. 2. What must be believed concerning God. 3. Concerning Christ. His eternal and temporal birth, both indescribable. He was born in the flesh without injury to his mother’s virginity. Mary conceived through believing, without a man. Christ was born in the flesh for our sake. 5. He died for us. The cross must not be a cause of shame. 6. Faith in Christ’s resurrection. This faith distinguishes Christians. 7. Christ’s sitting at the Father’s right hand. 8. Concerning the Holy Spirit, forgiveness of sins, etc. 9. One must live in the catholic Church.

**1072–1076 SERMON CCXVI.** To the Competentes.—1. Who the Competentes are. 2. He urges them to renounce the world. 3. Let them think of purchasing the kingdom of heaven. 4. Having turned to God, let them strive toward eternal life. 5. Here let them mourn from desire for eternal life and put their members to death. 6. What contest has been declared for them. Exorcism in the name of Christ, with adjuration. Curses against the devil. The expulsion of the devil. 7. Let them cooperate with Christ and the Church in spiritual rebirth. 8. The grace of the new regeneration. 9. Spiritual ages. 10. Pride must be avoided and vigilance exercised. 11. How great is God’s mercy, and how one must flee to it.

**1076–1082 SERMON CCXVII.** On Christ’s prayer, “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be where I am,” John 17:24.—1. Christ prays and gives what he prays for. 2. The good place to which we must migrate from this evil place. 3. By doing good in the evil place, one reaches the good place. The days of Lent; the days of the fifty-day period after Easter.

**1083–1084 SERMON CCXVIII.** On the Lord’s Passion on Good Friday.—1. The mysteries of the Lord’s Passion are to be explained. 2. What it signifies that Christ carried his cross. 3. The place of Calvary. 4. The robbers on the right and left. 5. The title above the cross. 6. Why it was written in three languages. 7. The Jews’ action before Pilate concerning changing the title. 8. The garments divided into four parts. 9. The seamless tunic entrusted to the lot. 10. His mother entrusted by the dying Christ. 11. Vinegar given on a sponge. 12. The final voice and inclination of the head. 13. The robbers’ legs were broken, but not Christ’s. 14. Blood and water from the wound in his side. 15. Joseph and Nicodemus burying him.

**1084–1087 SERMON CCXIX.** At the vigils of Easter, I.—The sacred vigils. How they are to be celebrated.

**1087 SERMON CCXX.** At the vigils of Easter, II.—Who died for us. The solemnity of Easter.

**1089 SERMON CCXXI.** At the vigils of Easter, III.—In Genesis, days are counted from light; now they are counted from night. The same place.

**SERMON CCXXII.** At the vigils of Easter, IV.—We must keep vigil against the devil. The rulers of the world are the devil and his angels. In what heavenly places they dwell. The devil cast out from the hearts of the devout.

**1090 SERMON CCXXIII.** At the vigils of Easter, V.—1. The day; the baptized faithful. He urges them to imitate the good and tolerate the wicked. 2. The mixture of good and wicked in the Church.

**1092 SERMON CCXXIV.** On Easter Day, I, to the people and to the infants—that is, those baptized on that day.—1. The grace conferred on the baptized. 2. The devil makes the sins of the flesh seem light, although they are serious and deadly. 3. The incontinent are rebuked and excommunicated. Any concubine other than one’s wife is a prostitute. 4. Correction of conduct must not be postponed.

**1093–1095 SERMON CCXXV.** On Easter Day, II, to the infants.—1. What Christ was before the Incarnation. 2. Christ’s Incarnation is the work of the whole Trinity. The purpose of virginity in Mary. 3. How through the Incarnation the Word did not depart from the Father [Col. 2382]. 4. Drunkenness must be avoided. Holy drunkenness.

**1095–1098 SERMON CCXXVI.** On Easter Day, III, to the people and to the infants.

**1098 SERMON CCXXVII.** On Easter Day, IV, to the infants, concerning the sacraments.

**1100 SERMON CCXXVIII.** On Easter Day, V, to the people and to the infants.—1. Days assigned to the sacraments of infants. Let the other faithful provide the infants with examples of uprightness. 2. He urges the infants to imitate the good. 3. The sermon owed to the infants, concerning the sacrament of the altar.

**1101–1102 SERMON CCXXIX.** On the sacraments of the faithful, Easter Monday.

**1103 SERMON CCXXX.** During the Easter season, I.—On the verse of Psalm 117:24, “This is the day that the Lord has made.” The same place.

**SERMON CCXXXI.** During the Easter season, II, on Christ’s resurrection according to Mark.—1. The disciples were rightly rebuked for not believing. 2. What is the mystery of Christ’s Passion and resurrection? Sin is the parent of death. 3. A good life embraces death and resurrection. 4. What does it mean to live well? To seek the blessed life on earth is a lie. 5. Where the blessed life must be sought.

**1104–1106 SERMON CCXXXII.** During the Easter season, III, on Christ’s resurrection according to Luke.—1. The resurrection is customarily recited according to the four Evangelists. The Passion only according to Matthew. 2. The disciples’ unbelief when they heard of Christ’s resurrection. 3. The disciples adopt others’ opinions about Christ. Peter’s confession concerning Christ. 4. Peter soon forms a merely human conception of Christ. 5. Neither death was owed to Christ nor life to us. 6. How great the robber’s faith was, while the disciples wavered. 7. The Lord is recognized in the breaking of bread. 8. To penitents.

**1107–1111 SERMON CCXXXIII.** During the Easter season, IV, on Christ’s resurrection according to Mark.—1. Faith in the resurrection is proper to Christians. 2. The salvation promised to believers must be distinguished from temporal salvation. Christ is the fountain of life. 4. Christ found no true salvation here. Christ was born mortal in order to remove death. 5. Death died in Christ.

**1112–1114 SERMON CCXXXIV.** During the Easter season, V, on Christ’s resurrection according to Luke.—1. The four Gospels must be read. The four Evangelists are necessary. 2. The disciples doubting about Christ were defeated by the robber. 3. Faith distinguishes Christians from pagans and Jews.

**1115–1116 SERMON CCXXXV.** During the Easter season, VI, on the same Gospel reading from Luke 24:13–31.—1. The Evangelists vary while preserving the truth of their narrative. 2. Christ with the disciples on the road. 3. Why Christ wished to be recognized in the breaking of bread. The reward of hospitality. 4. Christ withdrew bodily so that faith might be built up.

**1117–1119 SERMON CCXXXVI.** During the Easter season, VII, on the same Gospel reading from Luke 24:13–31.—1. Christ died for one reason and rose for another. 2. Hope was taken from the disciples by Christ’s death. 3. The merit of hospitality.

**1120–1121 SERMON CCXXXVII.** During the Easter season, VIII, on the final Gospel reading from Luke 24:37–39, with a refutation of the Manichaeans.—1. The Manichaeans are like the disciples who thought they were seeing Christ’s spirit, not his flesh. Those who deny Christ’s flesh empty the entire mystery of our redemption. 2. It is not a better view of Christ to say that he was a spirit without flesh. 3. The Manichaean error is condemned in the disciples’ rebuke. The disciples are rebuked for thinking they were seeing a spirit. 4. What must be believed concerning Christ. The Word of God assumed the whole human being in the Incarnation.

**1122–1124 SERMON CCXXXVIII.** During the Easter season, IX, on the same Gospel reading from Luke 24:38–47.—1. The true Christ and the true Church are recognized from the passage in Luke. 2. Against the Manichaeans and Priscillianists. 3. Against the Donatists: the Church is spread throughout the whole world.

**1125–1126 SERMON CCXXXIX.** During the Easter season, X, on Christ’s resurrection according to Mark and Luke.—1. The resurrection is customarily recited according to the four Evangelists. 2. Christ is recognized in the breaking of bread. To be a guest…

Why Christ willed it. 3. Elijah is sent to the widow to be fed, so that a benefit may be conferred upon the one who feeds him. 4. One who helps a poor person should not exalt himself over him. 5. Lending at interest to God. 6. Why Christ became needy. 7. Christ is needy in the poor.

1125–1129 **SERMON CCXL.** During the Paschal season, XI, on the resurrection of the bodies, against the pagans.—1. The Evangelists’ variation in the account of the resurrection is without contradiction. Defense of the faith is necessary for those who waver. 2. The resurrection is proved against unbelievers from God’s omnipotence. 3. The flesh will rise without defect. Sin is the cause of every calamity. 4. Philosophers’ opinions concerning the condition of the soul after death. 5. The wisdom of the world is foolishness to God. The resurrection is promised to the pious who believe in the Mediator.

1130–1132 **SERMON CCXLI.** During the Paschal season, XII, on the resurrection of the bodies, against the pagans.—1. The resurrection is the faith of Christians. [Col. 2383] God is known by philosophers from the works of the world. 2. The beauty of creatures is a confession of the Creator. How the philosophers proceeded from knowledge of the human being to knowledge of God. 3. After knowing God, the philosophers became idolaters. 4. What the philosophers thought concerning the state of souls after death. 5. Virgil does not approve the doctrine of the souls’ return to bodies. Souls cannot be blessed in that belief. 6. The hope here is happier than in that supposed happiness. 7. Porphyry’s view that every body must be fled. Refuted. 8. He is refuted again from Plato’s words.

1133–1138 **SERMON CCXLII.** During the Paschal season, XIII, on the resurrection of the bodies, against the pagans.—1. The faith in the resurrection, plainly proved, is rashly attacked by human beings. 2. Against the resurrection of the flesh they object: “If there will be no corruption, why will it be eaten?” 3. “If the defects of the flesh will not rise, why are there scars in Christ?” 4. What the resurrection of infants will be like. 5. How will an earthly body be in heaven? 6. Christ’s body in heaven. 7. By God’s will what otherwise cannot happen comes to pass. 8. The order of bodies according to differences of weight. An earthly body contrary to the order of weights upon water. 9. Lead upon water. 10. The faster movement of certain heavier bodies. 11. Why bodies are called spiritual after the resurrection. 12. The promise of the resurrection is confirmed by so many other promises of God already fulfilled.

1138–1143 **SERMON CCXLIII.** During the Paschal season, XIV, on the Lord’s resurrection according to John, on the words in chapter XX, verse 17, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father”; and on the use of the limbs after the resurrection.—1. The difficulty in the Lord’s words, in which he does not wish Mary to touch him before the ascension. 2. What it means to touch Christ. 3. The difficulty concerning the use of the limbs after the resurrection. 4. The limbs of the body will exist either for use or for appearance. The harmony of the limbs. 5. Neither the inner organs nor the hearts themselves will be hidden after the resurrection. 6. Some limbs will be for use, others for beauty. 7. In the bodies of the blessed there will be beauty complete in every respect. 8. What the activity of the blessed will be. Lent before Easter and the fifty days after Easter. Alleluia. In the future life the praise of God will be without cessation and without weariness.

1143–1147 **SERMON CCXLIV.** During the Paschal season, XV, on the same reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XX, verses 1–18.—1. Neither Mary Magdalene nor the apostles believed the resurrection of Christ. Peter’s faith was swallowed up by the Lord’s suffering. 2. Christ is recognized by Mary Magdalene. The difficulty in the Lord’s words to Magdalene. 3. What the disciples’ faith in Christ was like before the resurrection. What must be believed concerning Christ. To touch Christ is to believe in him. What kind of touch of faith Christ requires. 4. The Arians and Photinians do not touch Christ with right faith.

1147–1150 **SERMON CCXLV.** During the Paschal season, XVI, on the same reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XX, verses 1–18.—1. The apostles did not believe that Christ had risen. 2. The difficulty in Christ’s words to Magdalene. 3. “Do not touch me,” that is, “do not believe that I am merely human.” 4. The meaning of the Lord’s words.

1151–1153 **SERMON CCXLVI.** During the Paschal season, XVII, on the same reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XX, verses 1–18.—1. Variation among the Evangelists without falsehood. 2. The disciples believe that the Lord’s body has been taken away. 3. Christ’s appearance to Magdalene. 4. How Christ’s words to Magdalene are to be understood. To touch by faith. 5. Why Christ says distinctly, “My Father and your Father,” and so forth. 6. Conclusion.

1153–1156 **SERMON CCXLVII.** During the Paschal season, XVIII, on another reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XX, verses 19–31.—1. The resurrection as recounted from the four Gospels. 2. The miracle of Christ’s entering to the disciples through closed doors is supported by other miracles. 3. It is confirmed by the Lord’s saying about the camel, which, when God brings it about, can enter through the eye of a needle.

1156–1158 **SERMON CCXLVIII.** During the Paschal season, XIX, on the reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XXI, verses 1–14; and on the two catches of fish, one before the Passion and the other after the resurrection.—1. The catch at the Sea of Tiberias is not without a mystery. In the two catches the figure of the present and future Church is represented. 2. The first catch. 3. The second catch. 4. What mystery the number of the fish contains. No one fulfills the commandments unless aided by grace.

1158–1160 **SERMON CCXLIX.** During the Paschal season, XX, on the same reading and on the two catches of fish.—1. The twofold catch made at the Lord’s command. 2. The two catches foreshadow the condition of the present and future Church. 3. That God’s commandments are fulfilled only through grace is understood from the number of fish caught.

1161–1172 **SERMON CCL.** During the Paschal season, XX, on the same subject.—1. Why the lowly were chosen first by Christ. 2. The difference and mystery of the two catches. In the first catch, the good and the wicked who are to be gathered are signified. Danger arising from the prosperity of the wicked. Schisms. 3. The other catch. The number of fish is stated only in this one. The law is worthless without grace. The division of the Ten Commandments. God’s help is necessary for fulfilling the law.

1163–1165 [Col. 2384] **SERMON CCLI.** During the Paschal season, XXII, likewise on the same subject.—1. The two catches made at the Lord’s command. 2. In the other catch the number of the elect is signified: the net was cast to the right because only the good are to be gathered. “The number” refers to the elect; “beyond the number” refers to the reprobate. 3. The shore signifies the end of the age. The net was not torn because there will be no heresies. Who is great and who is least in the kingdom of heaven. 4. The great person in the kingdom of heaven. 5. What the number of one hundred and fifty-three fish signifies. The Holy Spirit commended through the number seven. Our sanctification is complete. 6. The law is not fulfilled without God’s help. The law is fulfilled not through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness. 7. The word of God is our adversary.

1167–1171 **SERMON CCLII.** During the Paschal season, XXIII, again on the same reading.—1. The catch made at the Lord’s command is not without a mystery. The other catch took place before the Passion. 2. The difference between the two catches. The nets are the word of God; the sea is the world. 3. The two boats are the two peoples. The danger of sinking because of the multitude. The boat of the Jews is endangered. 4. The boat of the Gentiles. The torn nets are heresies and schisms. 5. On the Lord’s threshing floor some chaff is always mixed with the grain. The winds blow the chaff back to the threshing floor. 6. Those who seek carnal things, whether inside or outside, are chaff. Chaff can become grain. 7. It is signified that after the resurrection the Church will have only the good. 8. What the one hundred and fifty-three fish signify. 9. The fifty days and the Alleluia after Easter according to ancient tradition. 10. The mystery of the numbers fifty and forty. The number forty signifies this present time. 11. When forty has been rightly completed, ten is added. The number fifty signifies the future Church. 12. Forty days before and fifty after Easter. Carnal observance of festivals. Perfect blessedness.

1171–1178 **SERMON CCLIII.** During the Paschal season, XXIV, on the final reading from the Gospel of John, chapter XXI, verses 15–25.—1. Peter is questioned three times about his love because of his threefold denial. 2. Christ asks that love be shown to him in the person of his sheep. 3. Peter, formerly weak concerning himself, is now, through Christ’s grace, mature for suffering. 4. The question concerning the Lord’s words: how he wishes John to remain until he comes. 5. Those words of the Lord can be understood in two ways: first, with reference to the Passion that John would not undergo; second, with reference to the Gospel of John, which cannot be properly understood except in future blessedness.

1179–1181 **SERMON CCLIV.** During the Paschal season, XXV.—1. A time of sadness precedes a time of joy. 2. What sadness should be. Repentance that must not be repented of. 3. Manure applied to a fruitless tree as a figure of repentance. 4. Sadness over the affairs of the world is harmful. What must be mourned here. 5. What the two periods, Lent and the fifty-day season, signify. What the Alleluia signifies. 6. God is a debtor because he has promised, not because he has received. We are unable to repay anything to God. 7. A human being has nothing of his own except falsehood. 8. God must be praised now and always.

1182–1185 **SERMON CCLV.** During the Paschal season, XXVI, on the Alleluia.—1. The Alleluia, the consolation of the pious here, will be the sole activity of the blessed. 2. The differing duties of Mary and Martha. 3. God’s benefits bestowed upon all, both good and wicked. Health comes from God. 4. God reserves something for the good. How human beings and the sons of men differ. 5. The enjoyment of praising God promised to the pious, which is not given to the wicked. 6. The two lives represented in Martha and Mary. The one necessary thing—the enjoyment of God—will take the place of all good things for the blessed. 7. Carnal thought concerning future blessedness. Carnal joy arises from sickness of mind. Our true health is immortality. Earthly riches are evidence not of capacity but of weakness.

1186–1189 **SERMON CCLVI.** During the Paschal season, XXVII, again on the Alleluia.—1. God must be praised by life and by tongue. 2. The error of certain people who say that the flesh does not belong to the human being. 3. How the Alleluia is to be sung here amid the dangers of temptations.

1190–1192 **SERMON CCLVII.** During the Paschal season, XXVIII, on the verse of Psalm 115:11, “Every human being is a liar.”—1. God must be praised with the heart. 2. A human being is false from what is his own; he must flee to God in order to be truthful. 3. Peter, false from himself, became truthful through God’s gift.

1193–1194 **SERMON CCLVIII.** During the Paschal season, XXIX, on the verse of Psalm 117:24, “This is the day that the Lord has made.”—1. The day made by the Lord is Christ’s Church from Jews and Gentiles. 2. The baptized are made a day from darkness. 3. Thomas was made a day.

1194–1196 **SERMON CCLIX.** On the Sunday of the Easter octave.—1. Christians’ attention must be directed toward the future life. 2. The mystery of the eighth and seventh days. The kingdom of Christ and of the saints on earth after the separation of the wicked. The Sabbath-rest of the saints on earth. 3. He commends works of mercy. 4. Works of mercy must surpass our offenses. Twofold mercy. 5. Almsgiving must be practiced with humility and cheerfulness. 6. Holidays.

1196–1201 **SERMON CCLX.** On the same day.—1. The octave of infants. False believers. Continence must be observed according to each person’s station. Whoever fails to fulfill a vow of continence is condemned.

1201 **SERMON CCLXI.** On the fortieth day, the Ascension of the Lord, I.—1. The Lord’s Ascension must be celebrated in such a way that we ascend with him. “Lift up your heart”: when does this express piety, and when pride? 2. Christ is always God. Vanity seeks knowledge of God through disputation; piety seeks it through believing. 3. Paul’s modesty in the knowledge of God. 4. The heart must be cleansed so that God may be seen. 5. God wishes to dwell in a clean heart. A person serves greed, not God. 6. Darkness is constituted by desires and evil works. 7. God, having become human, remains always God. God and human being are one person in Christ. 8. Both commandments of love toward Christ are fulfilled. 9. Good works must be practiced frequently. Apart from crimes, there are other, lesser sins. 10. Daily remedies. Lesser sins overwhelm by their multitude. 11. Conclusion.

1202–1207 **SERMON CCLXII.** On the Ascension of the Lord, II.—1. The solemnity of Saint Leontius. 2. On the same subject. 3. The faith and celebration of the Ascension throughout the whole world. 4. The prophecy of Christ’s Ascension. 5. The Church is Christ’s glory.

1207–1208 **SERMON CCLXIII.** On the Ascension of the Lord, III.—1. Christ’s glorification and victory were completed through the resurrection and Ascension. Christ is both lion and lamb. The devil is a lion. The devil’s trap. 2. Christ’s Ascension is the pledge of our ascension. 3. Christ ascended with his body. 4. Why Christ fasted for forty days and spent an equal number of days with the disciples after the resurrection.

1209–1211 **SERMON CCLXIV.** On the Ascension of the Lord, IV.—1. The mystery of Christ’s Ascension must be discussed. 2. Through the resurrection Christ remains with the disciples so that they may be strengthened in faith. He ascended into heaven so that they would not remain attached to the flesh. 3. The Son of God is equal to the Father by nature, but through mercy he was weakened even to death. 4. Christ wishes to depart so that, in the absence of his flesh, his divinity may be contemplated. The Son of God is not diminished in himself by the Incarnation. 5. Christ spends forty days with the disciples after the resurrection to signify that faith in the Incarnation is always necessary here. 6. The future resurrection of the flesh. 7. The mystery of the Trinity.

1212–1218 **SERMON CCLXV.** On the Ascension of the Lord, V.—1. The truth of the resurrection is confirmed by Christ’s spending forty days with the disciples. 2. Christ’s coming for judgment is foretold. 3. The disciples inquire about the time of Christ’s future coming. 4. Christ’s answer. 5. Christ is a good teacher, teaching what it is useful to know. 6. The one Church, spread everywhere, is preached against schismatics. 7. Christ’s final words are despised by schismatics. The seamless tunic of Christ. 8. Christ’s two glorifications. The Holy Spirit was given twice. 9. The Holy Spirit was given twice so that the two commandments of love might be commended. 10. Love is the gift of the Holy Spirit. 11. Love is not possessed outside the Church. 12. How often the unity of the Church was commended after Christ’s glorification.

1218–1224 **SERMON CCLXVI.** At the vigil of Pentecost, on the verse of Psalm 140:5, “The righteous will correct me,” and so forth. Against the Donatists.—2. The coming of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. The unity of the Catholic Church signified by the gift of tongues. 3. The gift of the Holy Spirit comes not from a human minister but from God. The Donatists’ error: that the Holy Spirit is not given except through holy ministers. 4. The Holy Spirit has sometimes been given without human ministry. 5. The deacon Philip was someone other than the apostle. The Holy Spirit was given to Cornelius without the laying on of hands and before Baptism. 7. From these points he refutes the Donatists. 8. One who rebukes must be loved; a flatterer must be avoided.

1225–1229 **SERMON CCLXVII.** On Pentecost, I.—1. The solemnity of the Holy Spirit’s coming. 2. The gift of tongues. 3. Why the gift of tongues is no longer granted. 4. The Holy Spirit, like the soul of the body of the Church, is not possessed outside it.

1229–1231 **SERMON CCLXVIII.** On Pentecost, II.—1. Through the gift of tongues the Holy Spirit commends the unity of the Catholic Church. 2. The Holy Spirit is not possessed outside the Church. 3. Unity is commended in the creation of things and in Christ’s birth. 4. Christ commends the unity of the Catholic Church to the apostles.

1229–1233 **SERMON CCLXIX.** On Pentecost, III.—1. The coming of the Holy Spirit with the gift of tongues foretells the unity of the Church among all nations. Against the Donatists. 2. Although schismatics possess Baptism, they do not possess the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is given through the sacraments and without the sacraments. 3. Schismatics are “soulish” and do not possess the Holy Spirit. The Donatists lack love. 4. By their deeds they cannot say, “The Lord Jesus.”

1234–1236 **SERMON CCLXX.** On Pentecost, IV.—1. Why the Holy Spirit was sent on the fiftieth day after Easter. 2. Why the Holy Spirit could not come unless Christ departed. Christ’s humanity, to which the disciples clung with human affection, had to be taken from their eyes. The rock upon which the Church was built is Christ himself. 3. Why the Holy Spirit came on the tenth day after the fortieth day, the Ascension. The mystery of the number forty. The mystery of the number ten. The Holy Spirit came on the tenth day to signify that the law is fulfilled through grace. How the law without grace is the letter that kills. The Holy Spirit was sent so that the law might be fulfilled. 4. The law is fulfilled by love [Col. 2386], not by fear of punishment. One fear is chaste, another servile. Love comes from the Holy Spirit. 5. The Holy Spirit is commended through the number seven. The sanctification and rest of the seventh day. 6. The law through the number ten and the Holy Spirit through the number seven are commended in the number fifty. 7. On the two catches of fish and the one hundred and fifty-three fish caught after the resurrection.

1237–1243 **SERMON CCLXXI.** On Pentecost, V.

1245 **SERMON CCLXXII.** The final sermon on Pentecost, to the infants, on the sacrament.

1246 **THIRD CLASS.—SERMONS ON THE SAINTS.**

1247–1248 **SERMON CCLXXIII.** On the feast of the martyrs Fructuosus, bishop, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons.—1. The death of the soul, not of the body, is to be feared. God is the life of the soul. 2. The solemnities of the martyrs are held for the exhortation of the faithful. Saint Fructuosus’ reply. 3. The deacon Eulogius’ reply. Martyrs are to be honored, but God is to be worshiped. The worship rendered by pagans to dead human beings. 4. The temple and sacrifice are owed to the one true God. 5. Aromatic spices, saints, and martyrs. 6. Blessed Agnes. The gods of the pagans are not to be compared with martyrs. 7. Temples and sacrifices are offered not to the martyrs but to God alone. The martyrs are mentioned in a better place at the altar. 8. The saints shudder at having the worship owed to God offered to themselves. 9. On the days of the martyrs we must think about following in their footsteps. The martyrs are to be praised and loved; the God of the martyrs is to be worshiped.

1247–1252 **SERMON CCLXXIV.** On the feast of the martyr Vincentius, I.—Vincentius conquered everywhere. Redeemed by Christ’s blood, he does not perish. Patience is God’s gift. Complete victory over all the enemy’s devices.

1252 **SERMON CCLXXV.** On the feast of the martyr Vincentius, II.—1. Vincentius’ courage amid punishments came from Christ’s help. It is the cause, not the punishment, that distinguishes martyrs. 2. In Vincentius’ torments the devil was tortured more than Vincentius. 3. The martyr’s lifeless body was not deprived of divine protection. Honor was divinely conferred upon the relics of the saints.

1254–1255 **SERMON CCXXVI.** On the feast of the martyr Vincentius, III.—1. The martyr’s courage comes from Christ. 2. The world’s two battle lines against Christ’s soldiers are flatteries and terrors. 3. Vincentius was not ravaged by his torments as much as Dacianus was. 4. Vincentius’ glory after the Passion, even in this world.

1255–1257 **SERMON CCLXXVII.** On the feast of the martyr Vincentius, IV, in which discussion is given of the spiritual body after the resurrection and whether God can be seen by the eyes of such a body.—1. Vincentius’ unconquered corpse. The relics of the saints are given for the consolation of the faithful. The bodies of the saints are given to churches as memorials for prayers, not for the glory of the martyrs. 2. By not sparing his body, the martyr takes care of it. Judgment in place of eternal punishment. 3. The martyrs did not despise the body but took good care of it. 4. The body’s glory after the resurrection. The body’s health: the concord of the things of which it consists. 5. Health is to feel nothing unpleasant or burdensome. 6. Dacianus raging against a dead body. To live in the body and feel none of its burden is to be healthy. The body’s burden always remains in this life. 7. Something must be sought in this body from which the swiftness of the future spiritual body may be understood. 8. The spiritual body must be discussed by way of occasion. 9. The speed of heavenly bodies. 10. The speed of the eye’s rays. 11. The resurrection compared with the speed of the ray emitted from the eye. 12. From the ease of the future resurrection the ease of the spiritual body is to be understood. This will be more marvelous than the speed of the eye’s ray. 13. Will God be seen through the spiritual body? God cannot be seen in a place in the manner of a body. 14. Whether through a spiritual body a substance that is not seen in a place can be seen remains unknown. 15. What is already certain concerning the spiritual body and the invisible nature of God. 16. Whether the vision of God is promised to the flesh. God’s salvation. Christ will be seen through the flesh by every flesh. 17. Simeon saw God’s salvation here with his eyes. Christ will be visible at the future judgment. 18. What must be held concerning the proposed difficulty, concerning God, and concerning the future spiritual body.

1257–1267 **SERMON CCLXXVIII.** For the solemnity of the conversion of Saint Paul, I, on the apostle Paul’s calling and on the commendation of the Lord’s Prayer.—1. Paul changed from a persecutor into a preacher of Christ. In Paul an example of God’s grace was given so that no sinner might despair. 2. Falling ill and recovering are not equally within a human being’s control. From the free will of the human being comes the seed of death. Who is properly a physician. 3. By observing the physician’s instructions, the sick person becomes healthy only little by little. 4. Along with the physician’s instructions, the pain of incision must also be endured. 5. How Christ the physician gradually heals us. 6. The antidote against all sins. Two commandments are set against two kinds of sin. 7. One sins against God who corrupts his temple in himself. 8. Those who corrupt themselves are not innocent. Who is innocent. 9. The proper use of permitted things is difficult to maintain. Immoderate use of one’s wife, unless it is for the purpose of producing children. 10. God himself is offended by the immoderate use of permitted things. A remedy against sins of this kind of immoderation. 11. Once that remedy is despised, no hope of salvation remains. 12. Serious sins that require more intense labor of repentance [Col. 2387]. Lesser sins overwhelm by their multitude unless they are forgiven by God. 13. Bailing out [the bilge], by forgiving the debts owed us by our debtors. 14. Hatred must quickly be put aside lest it corrupt the heart.

1268–1274 **SERMON CCLXXIX.** For the solemnity of the conversion of the apostle Paul, II.—1. In Paul’s transformation Jacob’s prophecy concerning Benjamin is fulfilled. 2. Paul is brought captive to Ananias as a wolf is brought to a sheep. 3. Christ is gentle and humble: when does he neither keep silent nor relent? 4. Toward Paul he displays both: he neither remains silent nor grows gentle. 5. Why he was called Saul. Paul means “small” and “humble.” 6. God exalts the humble. 7. We must not be ashamed of Christ crucified. 8. Why we must not be ashamed of Christ’s death. Christ assumed our two evils in order to give us his two goods. 9. Temporal death, not eternal death, is not to be feared.

1275–1280 **SERMON CCLXXX.** On the feast of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas, I.—1. Perpetua and Felicitas attained the reward of perpetual blessedness through their distinguished martyrdom. 2. The glory of the martyrs. 3. Why the martyrs receive the greatest rewards. Love of this laborious life. 4. The martyrs despised both death and sufferings for Christ. 5. The martyrs’ blessedness is one thing before and another after the resurrection. 6. With what disposition the solemnities of the martyrs are to be celebrated. The martyrs pity us and pray for us.

1280–1283 **SERMON CCLXXXI.** On the feast of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas, II.—1. In Perpetua and Felicitas, Christ is unconquered. 2. Perpetua’s victory over the devil. 3. Felicitas’ childbirth and martyrdom.

1284 **SERMON CCLXXXII.** On the feast of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas, III.—1. On the names of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas. 2. Women victorious over the enemy. 3. Why the names of their fellow martyrs are not celebrated equally.

1285 **SERMON CCLXXXIII.** On the feast of the Massilitan martyrs.—1. God’s grace must be preached at the festivals of the martyrs. Pleasure and pain, two incitements to sin. 2. Patience and continence are gifts of God. 3. We have not received the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God. 4. True and false patience. Against the Donatists.

1286–1287 **SERMON CCLXXXIV.** On the feast of the martyrs Marianus and James.—1. The martyrs’ patience is God’s gift. 2. The martyrs were tempted by the flatteries of their carnal parents. Marianus’ mother, Maria, rejoices in her son’s Passion. 3. The martyrs’ courage comes not from themselves but from God. 4. By God’s grace the heart is turned from many things to one. Through love of the one delight, the martyrs conquer the world’s flatteries and bitterness. 5. The Church commends itself to the martyrs’ prayers. The martyrs’ complete victory. The Lord’s threefold temptation concerning enticements. Another kind of temptation in torments. 6. An example of patience was given in the Lord and in our fellow servants, the martyrs.

1288–1292 **SERMON CCLXXXV.** On the feast of the martyrs Castus and Aemilius.—1. The solemnities of the martyrs must be celebrated in such a way that it delights us to imitate them. 2. It is not punishment but cause that makes a martyr. The faith of the thief on the cross changed the cause of the sufferer. Three crosses. The cross of Christ, the tribunal of the Judge. 3. The gifts of grace are bestowed from the depth of God’s judgment. Peter, presumptuous, is briefly abandoned so that this may be shown to him. God hates the presumptuous. 4. In their torments, how Castus and Aemilius were first defeated and then became victors. 5. The martyrs are our advocates, yet Christ alone is our advocate. 6. Outside the Church, not Christ’s sheep but goats are fed by schismatics. The Donatists’ claim. 7. The martyrs must be honored in the unity of the Church.

1293–1297 **SERMON CCLXXXVI.** On the feast of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius.—1. “Martyrs” in Greek, “witnesses” in Latin. Not everyone who believes in Christ is Christ’s witness unto death. Three degrees among believers. 2. Before the Lord’s death, Peter was weaker than the martyrs and than certain women. Peter dies by denying life. 3. The martyrs affirm Christ more by dying than by living. Their death is precious. 4. The discovery of Protasius and Gervasius was made illustrious by miracles. 5. Through the martyrs, health is not granted to everyone, but immortality is granted to their imitators. The sick person is not heard according to his will but according to his health. 6. More was granted to the martyrs and the Maccabees than to the three youths rescued from the fire. 7. Booklets about the martyrs’ miracles are read in the church. Martyrdom in bed.

1297–1300 **SERMON CCLXXXVII.** On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, I.—1. The Church celebrates the birthdays only of Christ and John. 2. Christ has a birthday here as a human being, not as God. 3. Both births, Christ’s and John’s, are marvelous, although there is such a great difference between them. 4. What the difference between Christ and John on their birthdays and in their Passion signified.

1301–1302 **SERMON CCLXXXVIII.** On the feast of John the Baptist, II, on the voice and the Word.—1. The celebration of Saint John’s birth. 2. John, more than a prophet, commends Christ by making himself of no account. 3. What distinction there is between the voice and the Word. 4. The ministry of the voice is needed so that the Word may be conveyed to the listener’s mind. 5. The ministry of the voice diminishes as the mind advances toward the Word.

1302–1306 **SERMON CCLXXXIX.** On the feast of John the Baptist, III.—1. John was not born so marvelously and made so great without reason. [Col. 2388] 2. John is merely human; Christ is God and human being. 3. John was such an excellent human being that Christ was thought to be John. John’s testimony concerning himself and concerning Christ. 4. John avoids the proud appropriation of Christ’s name. 5. John, the greatest human forerunner, so that Christ may be recognized as more than human. 6. Not John alone but also the apostles are lamps. The lampstand of the lamp is Christ’s cross.

1308–1311 **SERMON CCXC.** On the feast of John the Baptist, IV.—1. John’s testimony concerning Christ and Christ’s testimony concerning John. 2. Why Christ’s and John’s birthdays, but not those of others, are celebrated. 3. John was such a great human being that, by humbling himself before Christ, he showed Christ to be more than human. 4. Zacharias and Mary used nearly the same words, but their unbelief was not the same. 5. Zacharias asks in despair; Mary inquires. How great God’s grace is in the Incarnation of the Word. 6. The rich—that is, the proud—must be emptied, and the hungry—that is, the humble—must be filled. The Pharisee is rich; the tax collector is poor. 7. The Lord’s judgment concerning the Pharisee and the tax collector. He rebukes the Pelagians, who are even prouder than the Pharisee.

1312–1315 **SERMON CCXCI.** On the feast of John the Baptist, V.—1. John’s birth is marvelous because of Christ. 2. From John’s greatness Christ’s majesty is to be understood. 3. An angel was sent to Zacharias and to Mary. How Zacharias’ prayer was heard. 4. Mary is blessed among women. 5. Zacharias and Mary ask similarly, but their dispositions differ. The resolve of virginity. 6. Mary became the mother of the Son of God through grace.

1316–1319 **SERMON CCXCII.** On the feast of John the Baptist, VI, in which he argues against the Donatists.—1. Why John’s birth, but not that of others, is celebrated. 2. Why John was such a great human being, not among the Lord’s disciples but having disciples together with the Lord. The Donatists’ proud claims. 3. Christ was baptized and became incarnate in order to teach the way of humility. 4. Why he wished to be baptized by John. 5. The Donatists wrongly transfer the Gospel passage about the tree and its fruit to the minister of Baptism. 6. The Donatists are shown to boast on behalf of Christ. 7. How the Gospel passage about the tree and its fruit is to be understood. 8. He rebukes the Donatists from the words of John and of the Apostle.

1319–1326 **SERMON CCXCIII.** On John’s birth, VII.—1. Comparison of John and Christ in their births. 2. John is in a certain sense the boundary between the Old and New Testaments. Therefore he is born of old people and leaps in the womb. Zacharias’ mouth is first closed and then opened. 3. John is the voice; Christ is the Word. The voice was thought to be the Word. 4. Why so great a grace was given to the human being who was sent to bear witness to Christ. 5. Christ is God hidden in the flesh. 6. For God hidden in the flesh, the testimony of a human being was necessary—one greater than whom there would be no other—so that John, having disciples as Christ did, might become a more credible witness of Christ. 7. At Christ’s wedding John is the friend of the bridegroom. Christ is Mediator insofar as he is human. 8. The Mediator’s grace is necessary for all, so that they may be reconciled to God. 9. All are in Adam, and all are in Christ. 10. Infants themselves also need a liberator. 11. Christ is also Jesus, that is, Savior, for little children. 12. John was born with sin and therefore needed a Savior.

1327–1335 **SERMON CCXCIV.** On the feast of the martyr Guddentis, on the Baptism of infants, against the Pelagians.—1. The occasion of the sermon. 2. The Pelagians grant that infants should be baptized, but not for eternal life; rather, they say, for the kingdom of heaven. 3. Eternal life is not something other than the kingdom of heaven. Between the right hand belonging to the kingdom of God and the left hand of the condemned there is no intermediate place. 4. Exclusion from the kingdom of God is joined to the punishment of eternal fire. 5. The Pelagian distinction between eternal life and the kingdom of God is wholly arbitrary. 6. Once original sin is denied, the Pelagians cannot overcome the one who does not wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of God. 7. In the question of unbaptized infants, one must take refuge in divine authority. 8. The Lord’s judgment excluding the unbaptized from the kingdom of God, as the Pelagians themselves admit. 9.
