The Pelagians are defeated by the same Gospel reading. 10. Christ alone ascended into heaven. Christ’s members with the head are one Christ. 11. How we become Christ’s members. Faith in Christ is necessary for salvation. 12. Children wounded by another’s deed are helped by another’s faith. 13. The bronze serpent raised up is a figure of Christ crucified in the likeness of sinful flesh. 14. Whoever does not believe in Christ is condemned. Judgment for condemnation. Infants are called believers. Original sin. 15. The Pelagians’ escape when pressed by the Apostle’s words concerning original sin. What is signified there is not the first example of sinning but the sin of origin. 16. The Pelagians’ objection against original sin. Why is a just person not born from one who has been baptized? 17. Another quibble of theirs is dismissed. Christ benefits unbelievers nothing. Christ benefits baptized infants. Baptized infants truly believe through the faith of others. Infants believe through the faith of their parents. 18. The Apostle is wrongly cited against original sin. There are many modes of sanctification. 19. Cyprian’s authority in favor of original sin. 20. To what extent the enemies of truth are to be tolerated patiently.

1335–1348 **SERMON CCXCV.** On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, I.—1. The rock upon which the Church was built is Christ himself. [Col. 2389] 2. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter as representing the Church. They were given to one because of the unity of the Church. Christ first raises up, and then the Church looses. 3. The strength and weakness of the Church are represented in Peter. 4. Christ entrusted the sheep to Peter, who signifies the unity of the Church. Why Peter was questioned three times about his love. 5. Against the Donatists, dividers of the Lord’s flock. 6. Paul changed from a persecutor into a preacher of Christ. 7. Paul and Peter suffered for Christ. 8. The days of the martyrs are celebrated so that it may delight us to imitate them.

1348–1352 **SERMON CCXCVI.** On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, II.—1. In his weakness Peter promises more than he can do. 2. Peter’s weakness when he feared the Lord’s death. 3. Once Peter is already loving, Christ entrusts the sheep to him. 4. The suitable shepherd is the one who is able to give his life for the sheep. 5. The same command was given to the other shepherds of the Church as to Peter. The intention of martyrdom makes a martyr. 6. Temporal tribulations must be endured for future glory. The devastation of Rome in Christian times. 7. What answer should be given to a pagan who taunts Christians because Rome was burned in Christian times. A Christian is called not to earthly things but to heavenly things. 8. It belongs to Christians to suffer temporal evils and hope for eternal goods. Tribulations were foretold by Christ. 9. Whether tribulations are greater in Christian times, and why. We are commanded to store up treasure in heaven, not on earth. 10. We must not murmur against God in adversity. The great prosperity of the wicked is God’s great anger. 11. Love for God becomes apparent when God’s gains are loved. 12. Those who return from heresy, even after relapse, must be received kindly.

1352–1358 **SERMON CCXCVII.** On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, III.—1. Peter’s presumption. Fear comes from human weakness; love from divine grace. 2. Peter is foretold as suffering what he will not wish. 3. The bitterness of death endured by the martyrs. Their crown is thereby more glorious. Thorns trampled beneath Peter’s feet. 4. Whose love of life is praised. 5. The crown is rightly returned to Paul because undeserved grace came first. 6. Our merits are God’s gifts. We conquer through him who loved us. 7. It belongs to God to preserve his gifts in us. 8. Life is to be loved, but…
good things. People want everything good except their own soul. 9. Blessed life is not to be sought here. We do not make the evil days. For a human being, evil comes only from another human being. A person freed from his own evil cannot be harmed by anyone. 10. Paul freed from his own evil. 11. The wicked do not harm a person freed from his own evil. How the feasts of the saints are to be celebrated.

**1359–1364 SERMON CCXCVIII. On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, IV.**—1. The nativity of Peter and Paul should be celebrated with greater attendance. 2. Peter and Paul are to be loved above all. 3. Paul’s joy as his passion approached. Through narrow straits one passes to a place of spaciousness. 4. The crown would not be owed as a debt unless grace had first been given as an unearned gift. 5. Victory is granted to the combatant through Christ. Human merits are God’s gifts.

**1365–1367 SERMON CCXCIX. On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, V, in which the heresy of the Pelagians is refuted.**—1. Peter was the first of the apostles, Paul the last. 2. On the same subject. 3. The Apostle’s words concerning his approaching passion. Through God’s grace we are made both debtors and repayers. The virtue of the martyrs comes from God. Paul, strengthened by revelation concerning his future passion and victory. 4. The crown of righteousness is promised not only to martyrs but to all who preserve the faith. Desire for the coming of Christ the future judge. 5. The crown owed to those who preserve the faith. 6. Christ Jesus the Savior; Paul the foremost sinner, because he surpassed the other persecutors in cruelty. Salvation was given back to him in place of the punishment he deserved. In Paul’s healing Christ the physician commended the power of his art. 7. Peter, now healed, is told beforehand of his passion, just as, when he was weak, his denial had been foretold. 8. How Peter would suffer unwillingly. Death is the punishment of sin. 9. It is shown that Paul too was unwilling to die. 10. Against the Pelagians, it is proved that death comes from sin. 11. The Pelagian error that death belongs to nature, not to sin; the example of Enoch and Elijah gives it no support. 12. He commands that the Pelagians, whose numbers are increasing, be avoided.

**1367–1376 SERMON CCC. On the Solemnity of the Maccabean Martyrs, I.**—1. Some Christians existed before Christ. 2. The Maccabees were Christians not merely in name but in reality. 3. The passion of the Maccabees is rightly celebrated in the Church. The mystery of Christ was veiled in the Old Testament. The key of the Old Testament is the cross. 4. The prophecies were fulfilled in Christ’s passion, and everything belonging to the cross was revealed in mystery. 5. Other martyrs confessed Christ revealed in the Gospel; the Maccabees confessed him veiled in the Law. 6. A solemnity was rightly instituted for the Maccabees. A basilica was erected in their memory at Antioch. Let mothers learn from the mother of the Maccabees to love their sons. 7. She urges the remaining son to martyrdom.

**1376–1380 SERMON CCCI. On the Solemnity of the Holy Maccabees, II.**—1. How strong the mother of the Maccabees was during the passion of her sons. 2. God was present not only to the three youths but also to the Maccabees. Why the three youths were delivered from the fires, while the Maccabees were consumed. 3. Against those who think that happiness exists in this life and doubt the life to come. 4. Here the wicked are placed in their proper position for beneficial purposes. 5. The handing over of Christ both by Judas and by God. 6. The wicked man’s place here among the just, not in the life to come. 7. The godly should not be disturbed by the worldly happiness of the wicked. 8. What heavenly happiness is prepared for the godly. The world’s happiness for the godly is not honor but a burden. 9. The brevity of life.

**1380–1385 SERMON CCCII. On the Solemnity of the Martyr Laurence, I.**—1. Why God grants temporal benefits through the prayers of the martyrs. An apt comparison. 2. The two lives: the present life, full of troubles and yet passionately loved. Eternal life should be loved in the same way as this temporal life. 3. We are Christians not for the sake of temporal things but for the sake of eternal life. What the cross of Christ on the forehead is meant to remind us of. 4. Temporal life is greatly loved; eternal life is not loved in the same way. 5. A person provides necessities in order to live here longer or more miserably; he does not provide superfluities in order to reign with Christ forever. 6. This life is loved inordinately. 7. Eternal life is God; the present life is vapor. 8. What Laurence produces when the persecutor demands the Church’s wealth. 9. The martyrs are to be imitated. 10. It is not lawful to rage against the wicked. 11. Each person must restrain his own subjects from harming the wicked. 12. How one who does good deserves praise when he has the power to do otherwise. 13. It is not lawful for just anyone to kill the wicked. 14. The Lord’s judgment concerning merciful people. 15. Soldiers are prevented from being good not by military service but by wickedness. What was commanded to tax collectors, and what was commanded to everyone. 16. The merchant is exposed to fraud and perjury; only the wicked rage against the wicked. 17. A pious bishop is compelled to deal with secular authorities. 18. A wicked person who has died is to be mourned twice over. 19. Everyone must prevent civil disturbances according to his ability. 20. God’s anger arises from the sins of the people. 21. The people must not take upon themselves what belongs to the authorities, nor rage disorderly against the wicked.

**1385–1393 SERMON CCCIII. On the Nativity of the Martyr Laurence, III.**—1. Laurence, the archdeacon, was ordered to produce the Church’s wealth. 2. The reward prepared for those who follow Christ.

**1393–1394 SERMON CCCIV. On the Solemnity of the Martyr Laurence, III.**—1. The deacon’s duty is to minister the blood of Christ. The mystery of the Lord’s Supper: since we receive his blood, we should give our life for him. 2. We must all follow Christ. 3. The ways in which Christ may be followed apart from martyrdom. His humility is to be imitated. Vengeance is not to be sought, following Christ’s example. Present things are to be despised. 4. True and unconquerable virtue is charity.

**1395–1397 SERMON CCCV. On the Solemnity of the Martyr Laurence, IV.**—1. The grain multiplied through death. 2. The soul is not to be loved here. As death approached, Christ was troubled because he transforms us into himself. 3. Christ died by his power and rose by his power. 4. He was troubled as death approached so that we might not despair.

**1397–1399 SERMON CCCVI. On the Nativity of the Martyrs of Massa Candida.**—1. The glory of the martyrs is hidden from the foolish. Wickedness serves as punishment. 2. Punishment does not harm if the cause is good. Massa Candida. 3. Everyone equally desires the blessed life, although in different conditions of life. 4. What the blessed life is. Everyone wants to live and to be healthy. 5. Life amid sufferings is not properly life. Only what is blessed should be counted as life. 6. The same point is demonstrated from another passage of Scripture. Blessed life exists only if it is eternal. 7. True life is eternal and blessed. Certainty of eternity is necessary for the blessed life. 8. False suspicions, which are here the origin of evils, are far from the happiness of God’s kingdom. 9. For life to be blessed, truth and knowledge of friends without fear of deception must be present. 10. Christ is the way to life and truth. The martyrs followed the difficult way after Christ and made it smooth for us.

**1400–1405 SERMON CCCVII. On the Beheading of John the Baptist, I.**—1. On what occasion John the Baptist was killed. 2. Every oath is prohibited because of the danger of a false oath. 3. Oaths are used by God. 4. Nevertheless, they are rightly prohibited for us. 5. Augustine overcame the custom of swearing oaths.

**1406–1407 SERMON CCCVIII. On the Same Solemnity, II.**—1. Herod was caught between committing perjury and a bloody crime. 2. A rash oath must not be fulfilled by committing murder. David’s perjury was a great sin, although less than murder. 3. A person who swears after being challenged by another does not sin in the same way as the other person. 4. The one who compels a person whom he believes will swear falsely is worse than a murderer. 5. Tutlymenus was scourged by divine correction because of this sin.

**1408–1409 SERMON CCCIX. On the Nativity of the Martyr Cyprian, I.**—1. Cyprian’s passion is commemorated. 2. His exile. His return from exile. 3. His arrest by two officials. 4. Cyprian’s pastoral concern. 5. How he should provide for himself. 6. Cyprian’s words. The sentence pronounced against Cyprian.

**1410–1412 SERMON CCCX. On the Nativity of the Martyr Cyprian, II.**—1. Cyprian’s nativity is celebrated throughout all Africa. 2. The Church of Carthage was ennobled by Cyprian’s episcopate and martyrdom. Cyprian’s table near Carthage. 3. Cyprian’s precious death. 4. Cyprian is renowned throughout the world both for his passion and for his writings.

**1412–1413 SERMON CCCXI. On the Nativity of the Martyr Cyprian, III.**—1. The solemnities of the martyrs are to be celebrated by imitating their virtues. The errors of the flattering world and the terrors of the raging world are overcome by wisdom and patience. 2. The apostles died while confessing what they themselves had seen concerning the Lord. 3. The martyrs teach contempt for the world by their example. 4. Love of earthly things is a snare for the soul. 5. Profane songs and dances were driven from the church where Cyprian was buried. 6. Our song must harmonize with our conduct, as with a dance. 7. Those who dance harmonize with the spiritual song by a change of life. 8. Evil times are made only by wicked people. 9. From gold a good person produces many good things, a wicked person many wicked things. 10. The good are not absent from the midst of the wicked in the Church. Massa Candida. Cyprian is the chosen grain. 11. Things that may be used for good or evil. Some good things belong particularly to the good; others are common to the good and the wicked. 12. To whom, including the wicked, God gives temporal goods. 13. They are given even to the wicked so that the good may despise them and seek better things. What sort of good wealth is. 14. The world, having become bitter, does not cease to be loved; what if it were sweet? 15. Treasure is to be stored in heaven. Lift up your hearts.

**1418–1419 SERMON CCCXII. On the Nativity of the Martyr Cyprian, IV.**—1. A martyr is to be praised not in himself but in the Lord. 2. What Cyprian was before his conversion to the faith. 3. Converted by God’s grace, he became the true Cyprian. 4. From a courtroom advocate he became a preacher of Christ. 5. How evident the martyrs’ victory over demons now is. 6. Cyprian surpassed the martyrs in teaching and example. The place of his burial. The benefits of grace bestowed upon Cyprian. How greatly Cyprian loved the unity of the Church.

**1420–1422 SERMON CCCXIII. On the Nativity of the Martyr Cyprian, V.**—1. No tongue is equal to Cyprian’s praises. 2. The praises of the martyrs redound to God. 3. The martyrs are armed by God and are helped by the same God who armed them. 4. How the armed God is to be understood. 5. The great sword of God is Cyprian’s soul. An altar erected over Cyprian’s body.

**1423–1424 SERMON CCCXIV. On the Nativity of the Martyr Stephen, I.**—1–2. Stephen is to be imitated, especially in love of enemies.

**1425 SERMON CCCXV. On the Solemnity of the Martyr Stephen, II.**—1. Stephen’s deeds are contained in the canonical book. The book of the Acts of the Apostles is customarily read from Easter Sunday onward. 2. Stephen’s passion resembles Christ’s passion. The great power of truth. 3. Why Stephen, when brought before the council, does not remain silent as Christ did. To preach from the housetops. 4. Through Christ the Jewish people were freed in certain respects. 5. Stephen was fierce in speech toward the Jews but gentle in heart. 6. Stephen stands praying for himself because he is asking for what is owed. A human being is evil from himself but good through God’s gift. 7. Saul was the more savage persecutor in Stephen’s killing. Saul was called Paul from Saul, meaning “moderate” or “small.” Stephen prays on bended knee for his enemies because he is asking for what is not owed. 8. Christ, teaching from the chair of the cross, sets forth the rule of piety. Stephen is his disciple and imitator. 9. Gentleness toward enemies. Anger is a scorpion. Anger is an enemy; apart from it, the other enemies do very little harm. 10. How greatly anger, our enemy, harms us. Anger cannot be killed, but it can be restrained.

**1426–1431 SERMON CCCXVI. On the Solemnity of the Martyr Stephen, III.**—1. Stephen was the first among the deacons. Stephen performed wonders, but through the name of Christ. 2. The Jews were harsh toward Stephen. 3. As he died, Stephen imitated the Lord by commending his spirit and praying for his killers. 4. Saul was a wolf who, through Stephen’s prayer, was changed into a sheep. 5. A picture depicting Stephen’s stoning and Saul’s conversion.

**1431–1434 SERMON CCCXVII. On Stephen the Martyr, IV.**—1. Stephen’s relics were brought to Africa and became renowned everywhere because of God’s benefits. The command to love enemies carries a great reward. An example is given from the heavenly Father. 2. Another example is found in Christ. 3. An example is also found in Stephen. The Gospel is both an instrument and a testament. 4. A lamp is lit for weak eyes in the examples of the saints. Love of enemies is God’s gift. 5. The rebuke of one who loves is sometimes harsh. Stephen’s love for his killers.

**1435–1437 SERMON CCCXVIII. On the Martyr Stephen, V.**—1. The relics of the martyr Stephen were placed in a sacred site. The discovery of the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius. An altar was erected to God over Stephen’s relics. 2. The martyrs conquered not only the pleasures of the age but, what is more difficult, tortures. The struggle extends even to bloodshed. 3. A certain form of martyrdom occurs in daily temptations.

**1437–1439 SERMON CCCXIX. On Stephen the Martyr, VI.**—1. How prudent Stephen’s address to the Jews was. Stephen performs miracles as a servant, in Christ’s name. 2. He commends his spirit to Christ. 3. Where Christ received his spirit. 4. Why he prays on bended knee for those who stoned him. 5. Stephen, in his passion, imitates Christ in his suffering. 6. The discovery of his body. His prayers obtain many things, though not everything. 7. Stephen is our fellow servant, not to be worshiped as God.

**1440–1442 SERMON CCCXX. On a Man Healed through the Prayers of Saint Stephen; in which Bishop Augustine excuses himself for having been unable to preach.**

**1442 SERMON CCCXXI. In which he promised a booklet about the healed man.**

**1443 SERMON CCCXXII. In which he presented the promised booklet about the healed man.** *Ibid.* [Col. 2392]

**SERMON CCCXXIII. Delivered after the booklet concerning Saint Stephen.**—1. How greatly the curses of parents against their children are to be feared. 2. Health was not obtained for two brothers at Ancona so that it might be granted to them at Hippo. On what occasion a memorial of Stephen was built near Ancona before the discovery of his body. 3. On the miracles performed at Uzalis. 4. The people’s cry that arose after the healing of a girl.

**1445–1446 SERMON CCCXXIV. In which Augustine completes part of the sermon immediately preceding, interrupted by a miracle.**—A miracle performed at Uzalis. Life was restored to a little child who had died before baptism so that he might receive the sacraments.

**1446 SERMON CCCXXV. On the Nativity of Twenty Martyrs.** In the martyrs, not the punishment but the cause is considered. He attacks the false martyrs of the Donatists.

**1447–1448 SERMON CCCXXVI. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. The martyrs ran swiftly toward happiness. 2. The persecutor’s questions and the martyrs’ answers.

**1449–1450 SERMON CCCXXVII. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. It is not punishment but cause that distinguishes the martyrs from criminals. The crucified shared one punishment with the Lord but had different causes.

**1450–1451 SERMON CCCXXVIII. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. Christ suffered first and gave the martyrs the strength to suffer. 2. How can the martyrs be truthful if every human being is a liar? *Martyr* in Greek means “witness” in Latin. 3. The martyrs are truthful because God’s Spirit spoke in them. 4. To suffer for the truth belongs to the martyrs; even the wicked suffer for falsehood. A good cause of suffering must be chosen. 5. The certainty of the future judgment. Each person will rise with his own cause. The punishments of the condemned will be harsher after the resurrection. 6. The martyrs’ blessedness and glory will be greater after the resurrection.

**1451–1454 SERMON CCCXXIX. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. The precious death of the martyrs was purchased at the price of Christ’s death. 2. The martyrs were victorious not from themselves but through God’s grace.

**1454–1455 SERMON CCCXXX. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. Opening of the sermon. 2. How a disciple of Christ must deny himself. 3. This love is perverse; more truly, it is contempt for oneself. Love of money even to contempt for the soul. 4. Peter’s fear when he heard of Christ’s future passion. What it means to deny oneself.

**1456–1458 SERMON CCCXXXI. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. “To love and lose one’s soul” is understood in two ways. 2. It is not punishment but cause that makes a martyr. Those who died for Christ provided not for Christ but for themselves. 3. God’s gifts are common to the good and the wicked. What is proper is reserved for the good. 4. God himself will be the reward of the good. 5. The avaricious are martyrs of gold.

**1459–1461 SERMON CCCXXXII. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. Why the martyrs are friends of Christ. We are commanded to love one another for the sake of God’s kingdom. 2. How greatly we are commanded to love one another. 3. Charity is God’s gift. 4. Fornicators will not enter the heavenly city.

**1461–1462 SERMON CCCXXXIII. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. Security is given to the martyrs. 2. The reward owed to Paul. Grace was first given to him in place of the punishment he deserved. 3. Paul’s transformation. Jacob’s prophecy was fulfilled in Paul. 4. After God’s grace, Paul rendered good works. 5. Good works are God’s gifts. Paul’s own contributions were nothing but evils. 6. Against those who presume upon free will, it is proved that we possess nothing good unless it comes from God. The spirit of this world makes people proud. 7. Thanks must be given to God.

**1463–1467 SERMON CCCXXXIV. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. The martyrs’ security under God’s protection. 2. From where our confidence and certainty concerning God’s protection arise. Christ’s death is the pledge of the life given to us. 3. Christ himself will be our possession.

**1467–1469 SERMON CCCXXXV. On the Nativity of the Martyrs.**—1. The voices of the holy martyrs. The martyrs conquered pleasures and pains. 2. The martyrs are distinguished not by punishment but by charity. The avaricious person is, as it were, a martyr of gold.

**1470 SERMON CCCXXXVI. On the Dedication of a Church, I.**—1. The building and dedication of God’s house in us. 2. God is to be loved for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. 3. Christ’s passion foretold in the psalm of dedication. 4. Christ’s blood is our price. 5. The prophecy concerning Christ the head applied to us, his members. 6. The dedication of a new church.

**1471–1475 SERMON CCCXXXVII. On the Dedication of a Church, II.**—1. The construction of a church is a good work, to be evaluated according to the faith and charity of the one who performs it. The construction of the heavenly Church. 2. Building takes place in labor, dedication in joy. 3. The desire to dwell in God’s house. God’s house consists of its inhabitants themselves. 4. Our foundation is above, not below. 5. An eternal dwelling is to be prepared through good works.

**1475–1477 SERMON CCCXXXVIII. On the Dedication of a Church, III.**—1. Good works done openly have a double usefulness. 2. The lamp on the lampstand. 3. The Lord’s two commandments, apparently opposed, are reconciled. 4. We are forbidden to seek our own praise in a good work.

**1475–1479 SERMON CCCXXXIX. On the Day of His Ordination, I.**—1. The weight of the episcopal burden. Augustine’s attitude toward human praise. 2. How great a concern for the salvation of others is imposed upon a bishop. 3. He urges his people to relieve him by living well themselves. 4. The Gospel makes him afraid, lest, having laid down the episcopal burden, he choose a more secure life. It belongs to a servant to distribute; it belongs to the Lord to demand an account. 5. He urges them to change their lives for the better. People care about everything except having a good life. 6. Conclusion.

**1480–1482 SERMON CCCXL. On the Day of His Ordination, II.**—1. The episcopal burden. He needs Christ’s help in order to carry it. God’s gratuitous love does not remove hope of reward. 2. The bishop must pray for the faithful, and the faithful for the bishop.

**1482–1484 CLASS FOUR.—SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS.**

**1493–1494 SERMON CCCXLI.**—1. The three ways in which Christ is understood in Scripture. 2. The first way in which Christ is proclaimed as God. A comparison drawn from the Word. 3. Another way in which Christ is commended as God and human being. 4. Christ commended in both ways by the Apostle. 5. He commands that the Arian heresy be avoided. Virginity means integrity of mind and faith. The serpent seducing through a promise of knowledge. 6. It now does in the Church what it once did in paradise. Against the Arians: how the Father is greater than the Son. The Son is equal to the Father in the form of God and lesser in the form of a servant. 7. Before the incarnation the Son of God was in no way lesser than the Father. 8. The Son cannot be called equal in one respect and lesser in another. In God power is not one thing, wisdom another, and the remaining virtues something else. 9. Justice and similar qualities are said of God not properly but because nothing better can be said. 10. The Son of God cannot be called equal in one respect and unequal in another. 11. Christ is understood in a third way as head and body. 12. Christ is expressed in Scripture in three ways. Christ and the Church are one Christ. 13. Christ’s bride should act so as to be without stain or wrinkle.

**1495–1500 SERMON CCCXLII. On the Evening Sacrifice, in which the Beginning of the Gospel of John is Explained.**—1. The sign of the cross. The sacrifice of the cross. 2. John was sent before Christ as a lamp before the light. 3. “The world” is understood in two ways. 4. How Christ was not received by his own. The Jews were cut off because of pride; the Gentiles were grafted into the olive because of humility. The centurion’s humility and faith. 5. Power was given so that we might become children of God.

**1501–1504 SERMON CCCXLIII. On Susanna and Joseph, with an Exhortation to Chastity.**—1. Susanna is an example of conjugal chastity. Chastity is God’s gift. Susanna was divinely freed from false witnesses. 2. Since Susanna was delivered, this did not make her happiness greater. 3. Mary was freed from Joseph’s false suspicion. 4. The chastity of virgins and married people has an unequal reward, but both possess an eternal reward. Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light for those who love him. 5. Susanna is an example for women. One must act not only so that one’s life is good but also so that one’s reputation remains unstained. 6. Joseph is an example of chastity for men. 7. Even the impure themselves love chastity in others. 8. In temptation, one must resist through love of chastity, following the example of Susanna and Joseph. 9. Pleasures and annoyances must be despised for the sake of chastity. 10. How rich Job was on the dung heap.

**1505–1511 SERMON CCCXLIV. On the Love of God and the Love of the World.**—1. The struggle between love of God and love of the world. 2. God is to be loved above parents. 3. Human affection must be overcome by Christ’s example. In Christ, human will recoiled from death. 4. There are two deaths, the first and the second. The first death must necessarily be undergone by all; the other is prepared only for the wicked. A person ransoms himself from temporal death with money; from eternal death, with righteousness. Christ’s blood was poured out for our redemption. 5. How greatly eternal life should be loved, since temporal life is loved so greatly. Against those who lose eternal life through love of temporal life. 6. To lose one’s soul so that one may find the soul. 7. Which soul we are commanded to lose, and for whose sake.

**1512–1516 SERMON CCCXLV. On Contempt for the World.**—1. The present life is to be despised in hope of the future life. For the rich, this life is a sleep. 2. Perishing life is redeemed at the price of all good things; at what price eternal life must be purchased. 3. Lest wealth perish here, it should be sent ahead to heaven. 4. Christ receives what is distributed to the poor. A person’s heart is with his treasure. 5–6. The true riches of the kingdom of heaven. Earthly riches bring nothing except anxiety. It is not enough to distribute what is yours unless you also follow Christ.

**1517–1521 SERMON CCCXLVI. On Our Pilgrimage in This Life, through Faith.**—1. This life is more truly death than life. True life is only eternal. 2. In this life we make our pilgrimage through faith.

**1522–1523 SERMON CCXLVII. On the Fear of God, I.**—1. How frequently the fear of God is commended in Scripture. 2. The steps from fear to wisdom. 3. Seven steps from Isaiah are compared with the eight beatitudes of the Gospel.

**1324–1325 SERMON CCCXLVIII. On the Fear of God, II.**—1. True courage is compared with the fear of God. Fear must be expelled by charity, not by vanity. 2. It must be examined through what love freedom from fear is attained. 3. Epicureans and Stoics desire to be free from fear, but perversely. 4. In a Christian, one kind of fear must gradually be expelled, while another remains.

**1526–1529 SERMON CCCXLIX. On Charity and the Blind Man Who Was Given Sight, I.**—1. One charity is divine, another human. Human charity is either lawful or unlawful. 2. On lawful human charity. 3. On unlawful love. The members of Christ. 4. Divine charity does not tolerate the unlawful love of a prostitute. 5. Because of love for the inner light, one should cry out through a good life, following the example of the blind man. The world’s contradiction. 6. Christ’s passing by. 7. Parents are to be loved, but Christ more.

**SERMON CCCL. On Charity, II.**—1. Praise of charity. Through it divine teaching is understood without error and preserved without labor. The new commandment makes a new human being. 2. Through charity the whole teaching of Scripture is possessed. 3. He continues his praise of charity.

**1533–1535 SERMON CCCLI. On the Usefulness of Doing Penance, I.**—1. How necessary the humility of penance is. The exalted God is approached through humility. For what purpose the Law was given. 2. Three kinds of penance. The first penance, before baptism. 3. The second penance, which belongs to everyone here and is perpetual. We ought to repent of this life because it is subject to corruption and temptations. 4. The humility of penance is necessary even for those who have been justified. However righteous people may be, there is always reason not for boasting but for repentance. Why dispensers of God’s word and sacraments have reason for penance. 5. The daily sins of laypeople. When the use of marriage is blameless. 6. Because of the weakness of the flesh, we all contract daily sins. The Christian soul’s struggle. 7. The third, harsher kind of penance for deadly sins. The penitent’s tears are blood. 8. Against those who promise themselves salvation apart from the kingdom of heaven. The final sentence sends one either into the kingdom or into fire. 9. Those who relapse after baptism must embrace penance. 10. Against those who take from others an example for neglecting penance. They are not excluded from communion unless they have confessed voluntarily or have been lawfully convicted. 11. Against those who, following bad examples, despise penance. Bad superiors are not to be imitated. An elegant comparison. 12. No sinner should despair, but should flee to penance. A change of life and satisfaction for sins committed.

**1535–1548 SERMON CCCLII. On the Usefulness of Doing Penance, II.**—1. The occasion for the sermon arose from the reading. 2. Three kinds of penance. The first belongs to those preparing for baptism. Penance was commanded to the Jews before baptism. 3. Our figures in the events that happened to the Israelites. The rock, a figure of Christ. The crossing of the Red Sea, baptism. The manna, a figure of Christ’s heavenly bread. How the Israelites took the same spiritual food and drink as we do. The rock struck with a rod. 4. Moses’ doubt as a figure. 5. What Moses’ death on the mountain foreshadowed. 6. He invites them to baptism. Moses’ hands against Amalek, now raised and now lowered. 7. The second penance, which belongs to everyone and is daily. Medicine and covenant in the Lord’s Prayer concerning the forgiveness of debts. One must forgive one’s brother. 8. The third kind, a sorrowful penance for deadly sins. The soul is suffocated by despair of forgiveness. 9. Against pagans who taunt Christians by claiming that permission to do penance grants a license to sin.

**1549–1559 SERMON CCCLIII. On the Day of the Octave of the Infants, Whom He Exhorts with the Words of the Apostle Peter, “Therefore, Having Put Away All Malice,” etc.**—1. He exhorts the baptized. Innocence of conduct must be retained. Humility must be pursued. 2. Innocence must be preserved above all toward God. In the Israelites, a figure of Christian life was given to the baptized.

**1560–1561 SERMON CCCLIV. Addressed to Those Practicing Continence, in which He First Strengthens Them against Slanderers and Envious People and Then Commands Them to Beware of Pride.**—2. The members of Christ suffer not only enemies outside but also certain enemies within. 3. Continence occupies a more excellent place in Christ’s body. Their continence is attacked by the envious so that it may be tested. The wicked are necessary for the good. 4. In Christ’s body, not only those practicing continence but also married people have a place. Humble married people are better than proud celibates. 5. Pride is the mother of envy. Agnes, a virgin, and Crispina, a married woman, both martyrs. The celibate should consider what he lacks, not what he has. 6. Charity must be pursued so that inflation may be avoided. What pride is and why it produces envy. Should knowledge be avoided lest it inflate? 7. The Apostle was given a thorn in the flesh so that he would not become proud. We should wish to be heard not according to our desire but for our health. How eternal things and temporal things are to be requested. 8. Against proud celibates. 9. Celibates must beware of pride above all. How much better a humble married person is than a proud celibate. A proud celibate has no place in the kingdom of God.

**1563–1567 SERMON CCCLV. On the Life and Conduct of His Clergy, I.**—1. Care must be taken that not only one’s conscience but also one’s reputation is good. 2. Common life, whose example is found especially among the first Christians. Augustine established a monastery first in a garden and later in the bishop’s residence. Salvation is found in a lowly place, danger in a high one. Common life in the monastery. By the rule of that life, no one is permitted to possess anything privately. 3. The presbyter Januarius retained private property contrary to the monastery’s rule. He made a will. Augustine does not wish to accept his inheritance for the Church. A dispute among Januarius’s sons concerning his inheritance. 4. Augustine does not accept anyone’s inheritance when his sons have been disinherited. 5. Why he did not accept Boniface’s inheritance. 6. He commands his clergy that if any of them possess private property, they should soon give it up. If anyone wishes to leave their community, he proposes not to remove his clerical office. Pretending to pursue holiness is worse than falling away from one’s purpose. The clerical office is more a burden than an honor. 7. He promises a subsequent sermon.

**1568–1573 SERMON CCCLVI. On the Life and Conduct of His Clergy, II.**—1. The manner of life of the cenobites is described in the Acts of the Apostles. 2. Why Augustine thought he should address the people concerning the life of his clergy. 3. All Augustine’s clergy were found steadfast in their commitment to poverty. The deacon Valens. The subdeacon Patricius. 4. The deacon Faustus. 5. The blind deacon Severus. 6. The deacon of Hippo. 7. The deacon Eraclius. 8. The subdeacons. 9. On the presbyters. 10. The presbyter Leporius. 11. The dispute among Januarius’s sons ended voluntarily. 12. The slanders of detractors should be refuted without quarrelling. 13. He wishes what the faithful offer to his clergy to be used in common. Augustine’s modesty. 14. He decrees that anyone who violates the commitment to poverty is to be removed from the list of clergy. 15. The presbyter Barnabas.

**1574–1580 SERMON CCCLVII. On the Praise of Peace.**—1. Praise of peace. 2. To possess peace is to possess what one loves. 3. Schismatics are to be recalled peacefully to peace. 4. Gentleness must be shown to heretics who quarrel and abuse others. Against heretics one must act not through disputes but rather through prayers before God. 5. Pious works for obtaining the peace of the Church: a solemn fast after Pentecost. Hospitality toward those who come to Carthage for the conference.

**1582–1585 SERMON CCCLVIII. On Peace and Charity.**—1. Catholic bishops’ concern to establish peace. Whoever refuses to be conquered by truth is conquered by error. 2. Testimonies in favor of the unity of the Catholic Church. How the contention of Catholics is a matter of love, not litigation. 3. Testimony in favor of the Catholic Church. 4. Charity is the broad commandment by which peace is restored. 5. In what spirit Catholics come to the conference. 6. He asks that no member of the people rush into the place of assembly.

**1586–1589 SERMON CCCLIX. On What Is Written in Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 25, Verse 2, “The Concord of Brothers and the Love of Neighbors,” etc. On Dispute and Concord with the Donatists.**—1. Three excellent things. Why concord is rare. 2. Love of earthly possessions is the cause of discord. 3. Why the Lord, when asked to command a brother to divide an inheritance, refused to do so. 4. Concord among brothers in the heavenly inheritance. Who should be considered quarrelsome. 5. The Catholics’ purpose and desire for the peace of the Church. 6. They wished judgment concerning Caecilianus to be held without prejudice to the Church’s cause. 7. Many were converted from the Donatist schism to the Church. 8. The foolish excuse of certain obstinate people. The madness and fury of others. 9. Concord among brothers in Christ.

**1590–1597 SERMON CCCLX. At the Vigil of Maximianus, on a Donatist Who Returned to the Church.**

**1598 SERMON CCCLXI. On the Resurrection of the Dead, I.**—1. Introduction. 2. Our hope and faith are the resurrection of the dead. Our charity. Two questions concerning the future resurrection. 3. In one, the unbeliever errs; in the other, the carnal Christian. The Christian must be guided by the weight of authority. 4. He undertakes to prove that the resurrection will take place. 5. Against those who decide to live here as though nothing remained after death. 6. The faith in resurrection is mocked by unbelievers. Funeral commemorations. Against those who object that no one has returned from the dead. 7. Our faith in the heart, like Christ asleep in the boat, must be awakened so that the storm may be calmed. 8. The future resurrection is sufficiently confirmed by Christ’s rising. The whole world bears witness to our faith. Everything gives testimony to the resurrection. 9. An example of resurrection in the seed. 10. An example of our resurrection in Christ. Every creature speaks of resurrection. The awakening of animals. The new moons. The leaves of trees. 11. How certain things are renewed from the earth. 12. The objection that the body turns to ashes. The custom of the Egyptians. *Gabbarae* [uncertain reading]. 13. Against evil conversations, faith strengthened by Christ. 14. Against those who say that only Christ was able to rise. The members’ union with Christ the head. An apt comparison. 15. Christ is deceitfully praised by unbelievers so that we may not hope for a similar resurrection. 16. That the hope of resurrection was rightly brought to us through Christ’s resurrection. The source of Christ’s mortality. How Christ became mediator. How sins were in Christ. Mortality is the punishment of sin. 17. Mortality in Christ was real, not arising from merit but from mercy. Christ’s resurrection was according to the flesh that had previously been mortal. If they confess him to be just, he did not deceive us when promising resurrection. 18. From where the future resurrection was proved above. 19. We are admonished by Noah’s example to await the final judgment. 20. Nineveh was overthrown according to the prophecy, but through repentance. 21. Those who now refuse to be converted while Christ is building the Church deserve greater rebuke than those who refused when Noah was building the ark.

**1599–1611 SERMON CCCLXII. On the Resurrection of the Dead, II.**—1. What the resurrection of the righteous will be like must be explained. 2. On the same subject. 3. By the name of vessels, the hidden dwelling places of the blessed are signified. The hiddenness of God’s face. 4. Through faith we sigh for our homeland. 5. The Church teaches what it has believed, not what it knows. 6. A Christian may not doubt the resurrection. 7. The question: what will the bodies be like? The rule of faith, the creed. An apt comparison. 8. The building of the heavenly Jerusalem has a foundation [Col.

[2396] above. Christ is both our foundation and our head. 9. We must act so as to be built up in Christ. Christ is the foundation if he holds the first place in the heart. How greatly the fire of Gehenna is to be feared. 10. We should hope for a resurrection like the one that preceded us in Christ. The angels truly ate at Abraham’s house. 11. A human being eats out of necessity, an angel by power. 12. After the resurrection there will be the power to eat, as in Christ, but not the necessity. 13. The question: how can flesh and blood not possess the kingdom of God? 14. The question is solved. The Apostle’s first interpretation. 15. The Apostle’s more accurate meaning. 16. How Christ, as a human being, is heavenly from heaven. 17. At the resurrection what preceded in Christ must be accomplished in us. “Flesh and blood” in the sense of corruption. 18. How will our body be in heaven if corruption will not be there? The works of the flesh will not be the same after the resurrection. The error of the Jews and Sadducees concerning the resurrection. Resurrection to the life of angels. 19. Resurrection to life without corruption. The transformation of the flesh for the better belongs specifically to the good. 20. The swiftness of the resurrection. What an atom is. An atom in the body. An atom in time. The blink of an eye. 21. What the transformation of the saints at the resurrection will be like. “Flesh and blood” are properly names for corruption and mortality. 22. The error of certain people concerning the truth of the resurrection. 23. The resurrection is twofold, in spirit and in body. What sort of bodies the wicked will rise with. 24. Testimonies from the Apostle concerning the twofold resurrection. 25. Both resurrections in the Gospel. The resurrection according to the spirit, which now takes place through faith. 26. The resurrection according to the flesh, which is to come. 27. What the body will be like, and what the life of the saints will be like after the resurrection. 28. Their life will be like that of the angels, free from works of corruption and need. The perpetual Sabbath. Why works of mercy will not exist there. 29. What the activity of the blessed will be after the resurrection. “Amen” and “Alleluia” will be our entire activity, without weariness. 30. The rest and reclining of the blessed in contemplation and praise of the truth. 31. The life of those who devote themselves delightfully and supremely to the vision of God. Prayer after the sermon.

**1611–1633 SERMON CCCLXIII. On the Song of Exodus, chapter XV, verses 1–21.**—1. In considering the Holy Scriptures, the authority of those same Scriptures should not govern us. 2. The crossing of the Red Sea as a figure of Baptism. 3. The journey through the wilderness as a figure of our pilgrimage in this life, in which we overcome our adversaries with Christ’s help. 4. What is signified by Miriam singing with a tambourine in her hand.

**1634–1638 CLASS FIVE.—DOUBTFUL SERMONS.**

**1639–1640 SERMON CCCLXIV. On Samson, Judges, chapters XIII–XVI.**—1. Samson’s strength came from the Spirit of God. 2. Christ prefigured in Samson. Samson’s wife. His riddle. 3. The companion who took Samson’s wife as a figure of heretics. The foxes dragging fire behind them in their tails. 4. His approach to the prostitute. The gates of the city, carried away to the mountain when he had risen from sleep. 5. Strength in the hair. Samson’s blinding and death.

**1639–1642 SERMON CCCLXV. On verse 7 of Psalm XV, “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding,” etc.**—1. God must be praised with the heart and with love. Praise without love is neither true nor acceptable to God. 2. Against heretics who boast that they possess good understanding, by which God is blessed, by nature. 3. They are refuted again by Solomon’s words. 4. Good understanding comes from the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is a gift purchased for us by Christ’s passion. 5. Finally, they are convicted by experience of their own weakness and lust.

**1643–1645 SERMON CCCLXVI. On Psalm XXII, “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.”**—1. The psalm contains the mystery of the restoration of humanity. 2. The figure of fallen humanity in the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho. 3. The security of the sheep brought back by Christ to the fold. The pastures of the Christian soul. 4. Conversion comes from God’s grace, not from merits. Which are the paths of righteousness. 5. The shadow of death is the way of sin. 6. The rod signifies discipline, the staff assistance. The table prepared through Christ. 7. Prevenient and subsequent grace. 8. What is the end of grace and of the Christian profession.

**1646–1650 SERMON CCCLXVII. On the words of the Gospel according to Luke, chapter XVI, verses 19–31, concerning the rich man and Lazarus.**—1. A comparison of the rich man with poor Lazarus. Insatiable greed. 2. Why the rich man was condemned. 3. An exhortation to almsgiving.

**1650–1651 SERMON CCCLXVIII. On the words of the Gospel according to John, chapter XII, verse 25, “Whoever loves his life will lose it,” and on the words of the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter V, verse 29, “No one has ever hated his own flesh.”**—1. If someone loves his life, how does he lose it? 2. A certain perverse love, and a certain proper hatred of the soul. 3. The manner of loving one’s soul. Two kinds of love. 4. The beginnings of love. 5. The true and honorable love by which it is acquired, and the order in which it is acquired.

**1652–1654 SERMON CCCLXIX. On the Nativity of the Lord, I.**—1. Christ has two births: one before every day, the other in time. Christ’s Nativity illuminated by divine testimonies. 2. Christ’s eternal birth. 3. Christ’s temporal birth.

**1655–1656 SERMON CCCLXX. On the Nativity of the Lord, II.**—1. Four kinds of the birth or formation of a human being. 2. Every rank of the faithful bears witness to the Savior, who was born for all. 3. How great was the desire for the Christ who was to be born among the ancient saints. 4. Children, old men [Col. 2397], and married people bear witness to Christ.

**1657–1659 SERMON CCCLXXI. On the Nativity of the Lord, III.**—1. Christ’s two births. 2. In the Incarnation, God made visible is presented for humanity to follow. 3. How could God and humanity be mingled? The mingling of soul and body is more difficult. 4. Humanity’s dignity arises from God’s condescension toward it.

**1659–1661 SERMON CCCLXXII. On the Nativity of the Lord, IV.**—1. Christ’s birth is twofold. 2. Jews and Gentiles are invited to Christ’s wedding. We are nourished by Christ’s flesh and blood. Christ is the bridegroom and the giant, beautiful and strong. 3. How Christ ran his course.

**1661–1662 SERMON CCCLXXIII. On the Epiphany of the Lord, I.**—1. Christ manifested to the Magi. 2. On the same subject. 3. Herod’s fear and his cruelty in the slaughter of the infants. The Innocents were granted the crown of martyrs. 4. The unhappy Jews are very like the craftsmen of Noah’s ark and like milestones. 5. The spiritual spectacle in this feast.

**1663–1665 SERMON CCCLXXIV. On the Epiphany of the Lord, II.**—1. The Magi were led to Christ by a star and by the revelation of angels. 2. Christ was pointed out by the Jews themselves to the Gentiles. 3. Sacrifice is owed to God alone.

**1666–1667 SERMON CCCLXXV. On the Epiphany of the Lord, III.**—Christ was first manifested to the Jews and afterward to the Gentiles. Infants were made martyrs. The two walls meeting at the corner.

**1668 SERMON CCCLXXVI. On the Sunday within the Octave of Easter.**—1. The great miracle of entering through closed doors. 2. The octave of the infants. The old and new human being. 3. He exhorts the baptized not to imitate bad Christians. The wicked are mingled with the good in the Church. 4. Those who lead others into sin must be avoided. Illicit remedies of incantations. Almsgiving.

**1669–1671 SERMON CCCLXXVII. On the Ascension of the Lord.**—1. The Word of God cannot be praised by us worthily. How he rejoiced to run his course. Why it is said twice in the Psalm, “Lift up the gates,” etc.

**1671–1672 SERMON CCCLXXVIII. On the Day of Pentecost.**—Charity is the effect of the presence of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the pledge of eternal life. The difference between a pledge and a security. The pledge of eternal life is given so that we may desire it.

**1673 SERMON CCCLXXIX. On the Nativity of John the Baptist, I.**—John was so great a human being that he proclaimed Christ as God. Why so many prophets were sent before Christ.

**1674 SERMON CCCLXXX. On the Nativity of John the Baptist, II.**—1. John preceded Christ, who was born in time. Christ’s two births. Pride is swelling. The reason for the Incarnation was that God might provide humanity with an example. 2. On the same subject. 3. From John’s words, the Arians’ slander: “For the Word was in the beginning,” and was not made. 4. The Arians’ quibble that Genesis likewise says, “The earth was.” 5. Objection: Christ is said to have been made insofar as he is the Word. Christ was made before John—that is, he was placed before him and preferred to him. 6. The subsequent words of John agree with the interpretation given. 7. John the Baptist was not the light, in comparison with Christ, the true light. Yet John was light through participation in wisdom. 8. The difference between the Passion and the Nativity. Christ increases; John decreases.

**1675–1682 SERMON CCCLXXXI. On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul.**

**1683 SERMON CCCLXXXII. On Saint Stephen.**—1. The commandment concerning love of enemies. 2. Christ’s example in praying for his executioners. Christ prays for us, prays in us, and is prayed to by us. 3. Stephen’s example in praying for his executioners. 4. Through Stephen’s prayer, grace and salvation were obtained for Saul. 5. How unjust it is to wish evil upon one’s enemies.

**1684–1686 SERMON CCCLXXXIII. On the anniversary of episcopal ordination.**—1. He leads himself to inquire how he should bear the episcopal burden. 2. He forgives his debtors. 3. He wishes to reconcile himself with those whom he may perhaps have offended.

**1687–1688 SERMON CCCLXXXIV. On the Trinity, or on the Old and New Scriptures against the Arians.**—1. What God is. 2. The Trinity is one God. The error of the Arians. In the sun there are three inseparable things. In fire also there are three inseparable things. 3. Testimonies of the Scriptures concerning the divine Trinity. Praise of the Catholic faith.

**1689–1690 SERMON CCCLXXXV. On human love for another human being.**—1. One kind of human love is proper, another perverse. 2. The degrees of lawful love. 3. One kind of friendship arises from custom, another from reason. 4. The gratuitous love of friendship. 5. God must be loved freely. 6. To love the creature while abandoning the Creator is adultery. 7. How empty the salvation of this life is. 8. True salvation is eternal life. A friend must be loved for eternal salvation. Perfect charity. 9. Conclusion.

**1690–1695 SERMON CCCLXXXVI. On the Love of Enemies.**—1. Charity must extend even to enemies. The prayers were handed down by Christ himself, the judge. We must forgive in order to be forgiven. He is secure before God to whom pardon is denied by a brother when he asks for it. We must pray for one who does not ask forgiveness. 2. Christ’s example in praying for those who insulted and killed him. Stephen’s example.

**1695–1697 [Col. 2398] SERMON CCCLXXXVII. On the Correction of One’s Neighbor.**—1. The duty of correction has been imposed on priests. The word of God is our adversary. 2. Correction must be applied to one’s neighbor not out of hatred. 3. Conclusion.

**1697–1699 SERMON CCCLXXXVIII. On Giving Alms, I.**—1. At the last judgment, mention is made only of almsgiving. 2. Almsgiving does not help with more serious sins unless one’s conduct is changed. No one here is without sin.

**1700 SERMON CCCXXXIX. On Giving Alms, II.**—1. Heavenly bread and earthly bread. The advice to give earthly bread in order to obtain heavenly bread. 2. The one who gives to the poor must not exalt himself. By receiving, the poor person does more for the rich man than the rich man does for him by distributing alms. 3. Christ’s advice concerning the distribution of riches, so that they may not perish here.

**1701–1705 SERMON CCCXC. On Giving Alms, III.**—1. Among holy people, almsgiving accompanies fasting. The advice to send riches ahead into heaven. 2. By distributing riches into heaven, they are lifted up. Almsgiving is a loan at interest with God.

**1705–1706 SERMON CCCXI. To Young Men.**—1. No age is free from temptation—not even childhood. 2. Nor old age. 3. Youth is attacked more forcefully. 4. The words of those who live in luxury. Cruelty follows softness. 5. Young men must not be captivated by sensible things. Let them turn to the love of wisdom. 6. These words also apply to younger women. They must not display themselves in the churches.

**1706–1709 SERMON CCCXCII. To Married People.**—1. The bent woman as a symbol of the human race. 2. It is not permissible to keep concubines, to marry married women, or to marry women repudiated by their husbands. 3. Those who have fallen from their resolve of chastity must embrace repentance. Public penance. The penance of Theodosius. 4. How Christian women should be jealous of their husbands. 5. The husband is the head of the woman. Let him lead toward the good, and let her follow. 6. Penitents must be changed. Catechumens should imitate the good among the Church.

**1709–1712 SERMON CCCXCIII. On Penitents.**—1. Repentance is not genuine unless one’s life is changed. How uncertain repentance is at the point of death.

**1713 SERMON CCCXCIV. On the Feast of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.**

**1715 SERMON CCCXCV. On the Ascension of the Lord, VI.**

**1716 SERMON CCCXCVI. At the Installation of a Bishop.**

**1717 SERMON OF THE HOLY PRESBYTER HERACLIUS, DISCIPLE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, DELIVERED IN HIS PRESENCE.**

**1717–1718 FRAGMENTS OF SOME SERMONS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE.**

**1719–1736 APPENDIX TO VOLUME FIVE OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, CONTAINING SPURIOUS SERMONS, NOW ARRANGED FOR THE FIRST TIME IN FOUR CLASSES.**

**1735–1736 CLASS ONE.—ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT.**

**Ibid. SERMON ONE. On the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. Genesis II, 16–17.**—1. The foolish questions concerning the tree of paradise are resolved. 2. Death did not come about through the tree. 3. The tree was not evil. Evil things are not evil by nature, but by misuse. 4–5. Sin must be attributed to Adam alone, not to the tree or to God. 6. Why God, knowing that Adam would sin, did not recall him from sin. 7. Death resulted from contempt for the divine command. Scripture must be received with what reverence. 8. Whether God ought to have permitted sin. 9. Adam was not therefore evil because he was the father of a murderer.

**1735–1740 SERMON II. On the Calling of Abraham, “Go forth from your land,” etc. Genesis XII, 1.**—1. What it means to go forth from one’s land. 2. To go forth from our kindred. 3. To go forth from the house of one’s father. 4. Recapitulation of the matters stated above.

**1741–1742 SERMON III. On Blessed Abraham.**—1. Abraham was justified by faith. 2. Abraham receives three angels as guests. 3. Hospitality is not without reward.

**1743–1744 SERMON IV. On the Three-Year-Old Cow, Ram, or Goat, and Also the Turtledove and Pigeon. Genesis XV, 9–17.**—1. The carnal and the spiritual are signified in Abraham’s sacrifice. 2. In the Catholic Church, the carnal are set against one another. 3. A figure of the final judgment.

**1745–1746 SERMON V. On the Three Men Who Appeared to Blessed Abraham. Genesis XVIII.**—1. In reading Scripture, attention must not be given only to the letter. 2. Lot was far inferior to Abraham. 3. Praise of hospitality. 4. Abraham knew the mystery of the Trinity. The washing of the feet. 5. On the same subject. 6. How God’s descent is to be understood. 7. How God does not know sinners.

**1747–1749 SERMON VI. On the Sacrifice of Isaac, I.**—1. Introduction. 2. The mystery of the Trinity. 3. The ram and Isaac as figures of Christ. 4. The children of Abraham are a figure of the Jews. 5. Adam was buried at the place of Calvary. 6. The sacrament of Baptism must not be sought carelessly or too late.

**1749–1751 SERMON VII. On the Sacrifice of Isaac, II.**

**1751 SERMON VIII. On Abraham’s Servant Who Was Sent to Rebekah.**—1. The oath by Abraham’s thigh. 2. Rebekah meets Abraham’s servant, who, after obtaining the consent of her parents, her brother, and herself, takes her as a wife for his master Isaac. 3. Abraham and his servant, and what they signify. Rebekah betrothed to Isaac as a figure of the Church. 4. Isaac coming into the field as a figure of Christ who was to come into the world. 5. The Synagogue foreshadowed by Sarah, the Church by Rebekah.

**1753–1754 SERMON IX. On Saint Rebekah.**—1. Those who rarely attend church or neglect to hear the word of God are rebuked. 2. An exhortation to pray. 3. Spiritual betrothal. 4. The word of God both feeds and is fed. 5. The Lord’s day is every day for Christians.

**1755–1757 SERMON X. On Rebekah’s Conception. Genesis XXV.**—1. The learned should accommodate themselves to the ignorance of the simple. 2. Isaac is a figure of Christ, Rebekah of the Church. Jacob and Esau in Rebekah’s womb signify the good and the evil in the womb of the Church. 3. The greater people are the Jews; the lesser, the Gentiles. 4. The greater people are the wicked; the lesser, the good. 5. The virtues to be cultivated during Lent.

**1758–1760 SERMON XI. On Blessed Jacob, I.**—1. The mysteries of Christ are foreshadowed in Jacob. 2. Jacob carries a staff; Christ, the wood of the cross. 3. What the ladder seen by Jacob signifies. 4. The Lord leaning upon the ladder signified Christ. 5. Preachers are the ascending and descending angels. 6. Recapitulation of the matters stated above.

**1760–1762 SERMON XII. On Blessed Jacob, II.**—1. Jacob as a type of the Savior. The marriages of the Patriarchs at wells. 2. Leah and Rachel, the Synagogue and the Church. 3. Jacob returning rich as a figure of Christ. 4. Laban as a type of the devil. 5. Jacob’s wrestling signifies the Jews persecuting Christ. 6. Jacob carrying a staff as an image of Christ bearing the cross.

**1762–1764 SERMON XIII. On Blessed Joseph, I.**—1. Jacob bore the type of God the Father; Joseph, that of Christ. Joseph’s brothers signify the Jews and sinners. 2. The translations do not agree concerning the price for which Joseph was sold. 3. Through the poison of envy, death entered the world. 4. Joseph’s dream was fulfilled only in Christ. 5. In Joseph only Egypt increased; in Christ, the whole world. Who is the one who repays good with evil?

**1765–1766 SERMON XIV. On Blessed Joseph, II.**—1. Envy spares not even one’s own brothers. 2. The fault lies in the one who looks wrongly, not in the one who does not wish to be seen wrongly. 3. Immodest love is not love. 4. It is not flesh but chastity that should be loved. 5. Joseph’s kindness. 6. Envy is compared with rust and vipers. 7. Whoever is envious should vomit out the poisons of his bitterness.

**1767–1770 SERMON XV. On Blessed Joseph, III.**—1. Why Joseph did not immediately make his situation known to his father. 2. By God’s hidden judgment he did not send word to his father. 3. Why, by retaining Simeon and Benjamin, he increased his father’s grief. 4. God’s friends are not without minor sins, which are consumed by the fire of tribulation. 5. From Joseph’s example we learn that the one who asks help no more from God than from a human being is chastised. 6. Why Joseph dealt so harshly with his brothers. 7. Brotherly correction; we must forgive others in the manner in which we wish God to forgive us. 8. Concerning the poor who hasten to their work. He reserves speaking further about Joseph for the following day.

**1770–1772 SERMON XVI. On What Is Written, “Joseph died, and the children of Israel increased,” etc. Exodus I, 6.**—1. When Joseph died, the Israelites multiplied; when Christ died, Christians multiplied. 2. The people of Israel in Egypt, and the soul in the flesh, under two kings. 3. The things that were written were written for our instruction. 4. It is not enough for the heart to be emptied of evil unless it is also filled with good.

**1773–1774 SERMON XVII. On the Struggle between the Egyptians and the Israelites.**—2. The devil persecutes no one except the good. God has the good as his ministers; the devil has the wicked as his. 3. Let us strive to heal opposites with opposites and, after destroying vices, to build virtues.

**1775–1776 SERMON XVIII. On Moses, I.**—1. Christ is prefigured in Moses; the Church in Pharaoh’s daughter. 2. The Church is again represented in Moses’ Ethiopian wife. 3. The Synagogue in the bush. 4. Good words come from God, evil words from the devil. 5. Moses’ staff, the mystery of the cross. 6. Moses’ hands. 7. Moses is forbidden to take his wife with him into Egypt.

**1776–1778 SERMON XIX. On Moses, II.**—1. The flame signifies the Holy Spirit; the bush signifies the Jews. 2. Two fires, that of charity and that of desire. 3. Moses and Joshua are commanded to remove the strap of their sandal. 4. Why that command was given to both. What is signified by the holy land. 5. The Apostles took the wife of their deceased brother. 6. Whatever the preacher declares, hearers should examine it more attentively.

**1778–1780 SERMON XX. On the Ten Plagues of Egypt. Exodus VII–XII.**—1. Moses is understood as the Law. The staff is Christ’s cross. 2. The plagues of Egypt: blood; frogs; flies; the death of animals; ulcers and blisters; thunder; locusts; darkness; the death of the firstborn. 3. Recapitulation of the matters stated above.

**1781–1782 SERMON XXI. On the Ten Plagues and the Ten Commandments, Exodus VII–XII, and chapter XX, verses 3–17.**—1. The plagues are wounds; the commandments are medicines. 2. The water is turned into blood because the understanding of the wicked is darkened. 3. The frogs are philosophers or heretics. 4. The spiritual Sabbath. Gnats are the restless and turbulent. 5. Cynomia (the dog-fly): the despiser of parents. 6. The adulterer is changed into an animal. 7. Good ardor and evil ardor. 8. Unjust profit. Hunger of soul and body. 9. The locust signifies the slanderer. 10. When the marital act is not without sin. 11 [Col. 2400]. Those who covet another’s inheritance. Faith is the firstborn of the heart. 12. Exhortation.

**1783–1786 SERMON XXII. On What Is Written, “The Lord Hardened Pharaoh’s Heart.” Exodus IX, 12.**—1. On Pharaoh’s hardening. 2. Hardness of heart arises from despair. God hardens through patience, not through power. 3. Another objection on the same subject. 4. Hardening follows from the absence of grace. 5. Why God does not mercifully scourge everyone. In what sense he is said to harden. 6. As often as we have sinned, let us hasten to apply the medicine of almsgiving or repentance to the wounds of the soul.

**1786–1788 SERMON XXIII. On Pharaoh’s Cruelty and Drowning. Exodus I, V, XIV.**—1. Pharaoh’s cruelty toward the Hebrews. 2. On the same subject. 3. The mystical meaning of Moses’ name. 4. He orders the male children of the Hebrews to be thrown into the river. 5. The just striking down of Egypt’s firstborn. 6. God wonderfully provides for his own.

**1789–1790 SERMON XXIV. On the Three-Day Journey. Exodus VIII.**—1. The crossing of the Red Sea as a figure of Baptism. The threefold immersion. 2. The cry of the saints without a voice. 3. The mystery of the cross in the staff. Who extinguishes the spiritual Egyptian? 4. What the three-day journey signifies. 5. On the same subject.

**1791–1793 SERMON XXV. On the Bitter Water and the Manna. Exodus XV–XVI.**—1. The bitter water is the letter of the Law. 2. The wood by which the bitter Law becomes sweet is wisdom. 3. Manna began to be given on the Lord’s day. How it is to be eaten. 4. What it means to gather twice as much on the sixth day. Worms in the manna. 5. To the sinner the word of God becomes a worm. 6. The word of God tastes differently to each person according to his desire. 7. Let us devote ourselves diligently to divine reading.

**1793–1795 SERMON XXVI. On Raphidim, the Rock That Was Struck, and Amalek. Exodus XVII.**—1. What it means to come from the wilderness of Sin to Raphidim. 2. The many kinds of thirst. 3. Christ is the struck rock that brought forth springs. Who declares war on the devil. 4. The first mention of the sacred name Jesus in Scripture. 5. Moses raised his hands; he did not stretch them out. What it means to raise the hands. Victory is won by prayer.

**1795–1797 SERMON XXVII. On the Children of Israel.**

**1797 SERMON XXVIII. On the Spies and the Cluster of Grapes.**—1. The two men carrying the grape cluster signify the two Testaments and the two commandments. Christ is in the midst of the two Testaments. 2. Mary is the promised land. 3. The two men carrying the grape cluster signify the Jewish and Christian peoples. Christ is salvation to the believer, but a burden to the unbeliever. 4. Christ’s burden lifts rather than weighs down. Everyone is subject either to Christ’s yoke or to that of the world.

**1799–1800 SERMON XXIX. On How the Older People Died in the Wilderness and the Younger Entered the Promised Land.**—1. The older Israelite people signify the Jews, the younger the Gentiles. God’s justice and mercy toward the Israelites. 2. God’s sentence against sinners is not unchangeable. Conversion must not be postponed. 3. The example of God’s severity in punishing the Israelites should move us to repentance. An argument for eternal punishments. 4. The wounds of sinners are more easily healed while they are still fresh.

**1801–1803 SERMON XXX. On the Censers.**—1. The censers signify the Scriptures. The bronze censers signify the sayings of heretics. The usefulness of heresies. The ambition of clerics is cut away. 2. Aaron as a type of Christ the mediator. What the destroying angel feared. 3. Who will be living and who dead on the day of judgment.

**1803–1805 SERMON XXXI. On Aaron’s Staff.**—1. The staff belongs to rulers. 2. A comparison of the nut with the Law in allegory. 3. God’s generosity. 4. A figure of the resurrection and its four prerogatives. 5. Four stages of spiritual life are foreshadowed. 6. The one Christ is both flower and staff, different for different people.

**1805–1807 SERMON XXXII. On the Bronze Serpent and Moses’ Staff.**—1. The bronze serpent is a figure of the Incarnation. Death came from the bite. The devil acted against Adam as though justly, but against Christ unjustly. Christ paid Adam’s debt. 2. Why the serpent was bronze, not gold or silver. 3. Let all who have been struck by the devil look faithfully toward Christ. 4. The mysteries of the cross in Moses’ staff.

**1807–1809 SERMON XXXIII. On Balaam and Balak.**—1. Exposition of the reading. 2. Balaam was a magician rather than a prophet. 3. Balaam and Balak, and what they signify. 4. Conclusion.

**1809–1810 SERMON XXXIV. How, by the Just Judgment of God, the Children of Israel Received the Promised Land after Expelling the Canaanites.**—2. The first reason: unjust possession. The second reason: serious guilt. 3. The promised land signifies human beings before sin. 4. It is recovered only through Jesus, and after crossing the Jordan—that is, after Baptism. 5. On the same subject. 6. Adversity must be endured with equanimity.

**1811–1812 SERMON XXXV. On What Jesus Commanded the People Concerning Their Preparation to Cross the Jordan, and on the Destruction of the Walls of Jericho.**—1. Moses is a figure of the Law. Jesus is a figure of the true Jesus. Faith in the Trinity is necessary for Baptism. 2. The two spies signify the two commandments. 3. The stones in the Jordan signify the patriarchs; those placed in the camp, the Apostles. 4. A figure of the Jews and Gentiles. 5. Jericho is a type of the world. The priestly trumpet. The sound of the trumpet is for terror, not pleasure. 6. By the trumpets the walls of Jericho fall [Col. 2401]; by preaching, iniquity falls.

**1813–1815 SERMON XXXVI. On Gideon.**—1. A foreshadowing of predestination. 2. A figure of our redemption. Christ is the rock in relation to the flesh. 3. The abolition of the ancient sacrifices revealed. Christ is the kid, the sheep, and the calf. The mystery of the cross. 4. Dew first on the fleece, then on the threshing floor: faith first in Judea, afterward among the Gentiles. 5. What the fleece on the threshing floor signifies. 6. Recapitulation.

**1816–1817 SERMON XXXVII. On David and His Father Jesse, and on Goliath.**—1. The same thing can be a figure of different things. Jesse is a type of God the Father. 2. David is a figure of Christ. 3. The brother rebuking David signifies the Jews or the devil, envying Christ’s coming. 4. The lion and bear killed by David signify the devil stripped of his spoils by Christ. 5. Before Christ there was neither the will nor the strength to fight. After Christ’s coming, the devil was bound. 6. He cannot bite except one who is willing. 7. David with a staff against Goliath. Christ with the cross against the devil. Goliath was struck by his own sword; the devil by his own iniquity. Our members are the devil’s weapons or Christ’s temples. 8. The spiritual Goliath struck on the forehead.

**1818–1821 SERMON XXXVIII. On the Plague upon the People Because of David and on the Building of the Altar on the Threshing Floor of Araunah the Jebusite.**—1. A figure of the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles. 2. On the same subject.

**1821–1822 SERMON XXXIX. On Solomon’s Judgment between Two Prostitutes, against the Arian Heresy.**—1. The Catholic Church and the Arian heresy are represented by the two prostitutes. The Son’s equality is demonstrated from the omnipotence and goodness of the Father. 2. The inheritance left by Christ’s testament. 3. God’s division. Among the Arians. 4. Unity in the Lord must be preserved.

**1822–1823 SERMON XL. On Elijah.**—1. Elijah is a type of the Savior. The Gentiles are represented by the ravens. The Church is black and beautiful. 2. God speaks to everyone who does good. The widow who received Elijah is a figure of the Church. 3. Spiritual death is necessary for the believer. 4. A figure of the resurrection of the Gentiles. This is accomplished by the whole Trinity. 5. A figure of the grace to be bestowed through Christ’s coming. Christ preached for three years and six months. 6. Recapitulation.

**1823–1825 SERMON XLI. On Elisha, I.**—1. From what do the Manichaeans blaspheme the Old Testament? The prophets were despised in Elisha’s age. The striking of the children was more an act of mercy than of cruelty. An example of this severity from the New Testament. 2. The madness of the Jews in the Lord’s Passion. Their punishment through Titus and Vespasian is foreshadowed. How many Jews were then killed, and how many taken captive. 3. Warned by the misfortune of the Jews, let us labor to serve the Lord, holding to the right faith and preserving intact charity.

**1826–1827 SERMON XLII. On Elisha, II.**—1. Christ is presented in Elisha. The poor widow represents the Church. She was released from debts by oil; the Church from sins by charity. 2. The empty vessels are the Gentiles. 3. Self-love is poor and needy. Charity is rich and overflowing for all. It grows by being distributed. 4. The vessels of charity, human beings, are filled when they are loved. 5. What one should do with the door closed or open. 6. The woman of Shunem, passing from infertility to fruitfulness, is a type of the Church. 7. What the command in Scripture not to return a greeting forbids. Like Elisha’s servant, Moses also could not restore life. 8. Elisha bent over the child; Christ, humbling himself, raised the world from death.

**1827–1830 SERMON XLIII. On Naaman the Syrian.**

**1830 SERMON XLIV. On Elisha and His Servant Gehazi.**—1. Elisha represented the Lord; Gehazi, Judas or the Jews. The greedy are lepers. 2. Naaman is the people of the Gentiles, assenting to the girl’s prophecy. 3. The Jews were struck with leprosy when the Gentiles were freed from it. 4. A figure of the calling of the Gentiles to faith through Baptism. 5. Those who are baptized begin to be born. 6. The Lord’s great gifts should bring us not judgment but progress.

**1831–1834 SERMON XLV. On Elisha and the Axe That Fell into the Pool.**—1. A figure of the fall of the human race. 2. A figure of its restoration. Relapse must be avoided. 3. Whoever sins destroys the temple of God. 4. Conclusion.

**1834–1836 SERMON XLVI. On the Famine of Samaria.**

**1836 SERMON XLVII. On Blessed Tobit.**

**1838 SERMON XLVIII. On Judith, I.**

**1839 SERMON XLIX. On Judith, II.**

**1840 SERMON L. On Blessed Job, I.**

**1841 SERMON LI. On Blessed Job, II.**—1. Job was victorious in prosperity and adversity. The treasure of the righteous is faith. 2. A rich person can be good, and a poor person blessed. How greatly contempt for the poor must be avoided. 3. It is not the dignity of nobles that is to be blamed, but their arrogance. How dear a human being is to God. 4. God’s favor toward the poor.

**1842–1843 SERMON LII. On Blessed Job, III, and on the Words of Psalm XCVII, verses 5–6, “Sing to the Lord with the lyre,” etc.**—1. Who sings with the psaltery and lyre? Job is a drawn-out trumpet; Job afflicted for the purification of lesser sins. 2. Afflicted Job was better than Adam in his integrity. 3. The devil is the hammer of the whole earth. 4. The just and the unjust are hammered by the devil.

**1844–1845 SERMON LIII. On the Words of Psalm XLIX, verses 20 and 23, “You sat and spoke against your brother with slander,” etc.**—1. Almsgiving without [Col. 2402] devotion to righteousness. 2. On the same subject. 3. Good things should be set before oneself behind one’s back, and evil things before one’s face. 4. The wicked do not praise God, nor do the proud among the righteous. 5. Exhortation.

**1846–1848 SERMON LIV. On What the Prophet Says in Psalm LXXXIII, verses 3–4, “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.”**—1. Complete love of God excludes love of the world. Let heart and flesh rejoice in God. 2. Christ, the turtledove and the sparrow. The voice of the turtledove is the teaching of chastity. Christ’s house is the Church. The young birds are Christians.

**1848–1849 SERMON LV. On What Is Written in Psalm CXVIII, verse 66, “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.”**—1. What should be prayed for. Discipline is necessary for goodness, and knowledge for both. 2. Peter displayed these virtues in himself. 3. Paul likewise. 4. John the Baptist likewise. 5. Peroration.

**1849–1850 SERMON LVI. On the Words of Psalm CXXXV, “Give thanks to the Lord,” etc., and also of Proverbs, chapter III, verses 11–12, “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God,” etc.**—1. The necessity of confession. God’s readiness to forgive. 2. God’s scourges are benefits and remedies. We should grieve over our insensibility. 3. Sinners are afflicted so that they may amend; the righteous, so that they may be tested and make progress. 4. The soldier of Christ must always keep watch. He must be even more watchful in peace.

**1851–1852 SERMON LVII. On the Strong Woman and on the Church, in Proverbs, chapter XXXI, verses 10–31.**—1. The word of God must be cherished with fervor of heart. 2. The Catholic Church cannot remain hidden.

**1853 SERMON LVIII. On the Same Passage of Proverbs, chapter XXXI, verses 10–31.**—1. The Church is represented in many ways. 2. What the wool and linen signify. 3. What the distaff and spindle signify. 4. Christ must be praised both in two ways and simply. 5. Those who give alms should hasten to draw from the distaff to the spindle, and transfer from the left hand to the right.

**1854–1855 SERMON LIX. On the Three Boys Cast into the Fiery Furnace.**—1. The tyrant’s cruelty toward the three boys. 2. The three boys unharmed in the furnace. 3. The tyrant recognizes the miracle.

**1855–1856 SERMON LX. On Susanna.**—1. The righteous are victorious amid the world’s ambushes when God delivers them. 2. Susanna’s danger and deliverance.

**1857 SERMON LXI. On Peace, on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter V, verse 9, “Blessed are the peacemakers,” etc.**—1. The fruit of peace. Harmony among brothers. 2. Whoever does not preserve peace despises Christ. 3. Peace is God’s work; discord, the devil’s.

**1858–1859 SERMON LXII. On the Words of the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter V, verses 43–48, and chapter VI, verses 1–6, “But I say to you, Love your enemies,” etc.**—1. How an enemy is to be loved. Who is one’s neighbor? 2. God’s commandments are not impossible. No one can excuse himself from love. 3. There is nothing in Scripture opposed to the commandment concerning love of enemies. For whom one must not pray. The sin unto death. 4. What the saints pray for when they ask vengeance.
