How the reign of sin is to be overthrown. 5. Who are the children of God. 6. Who are the Publicans and Gentiles. Enemies must be loved more than friends. 7. On the same subject. 8. The commandments are observed in two ways. 9. The hypocrite. No one is without the stain of hypocrisy. 10. What the left hand and the right hand signify. Another explanation of the right and left hands. 11. The room. The door. What the wings of prayer are.

**1859–1864 SERMON LXIII. On the Words of the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter VI, verses 1–6, “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” etc.**—1. Almsgiving in public, yet in secret. 2. Public fasting. What the right hand and left hand signify. 3. Public prayers. Why they are made with the door closed. Where temporal things should be requested.

**1864–1865 SERMON LXIV. On the Words of the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter VI, verses 1–18, “When you fast,” etc., and on the Lord’s Prayer.**—1. Two things must especially be considered by a human being. The fall must be mourned. 2. The medicinal grace of the Redeemer is necessary. Christ taught by word and example. A compendium of all the things that may be requested. Three things are requested for eternal life, four for temporal life. 4. Christians are distinguished from Jews in one respect, and in that same respect are not distinguished from one another. An arousal of charity. Confidence in obtaining what is requested. Why we turn toward the east when praying. 5. The beatitudes are enumerated. The fear of God. 6. Piety. 7. Knowledge. 8. Fortitude. 9. Counsel. 10. Understanding. 11. Wisdom. 12.

Three remedies for sins. Threefold manner of sinning.

**1866–1869 SERMON LXV.** Again on Matthew, chapter VI, vv. 9–13, concerning the Lord’s Prayer.

1. By the words “Our Father,” we profess God’s goodness and grace.  
2. Those who have received grace ought to give thanks. What the words “Thy kingdom come” signify. We must always regard God’s will, not our own.  
3. The eradication of greed, and the remembrance of death in the word “today.”  
4. One must forgive one’s brother, so that the Father may forgive one.  
5. Why God tests.  
6. The substance of the Lord’s Prayer.

**1870–1871 SERMON LXVI.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter VII, vv. 1–5, “Judge not, that you be not judged,” etc.

1. Manifest evils are to be judged, but not things that are unknown or doubtful. It is better to suspect good concerning evils than evil concerning good. Manifest evils may and ought to be judged, but with charity.  
2. Sudden anger is a splinter; anger that has grown old is a beam. Anger disturbs the eye of the heart; hatred blinds it.  
3. Recapitulation. Rash judgment [Col. 2403] is no small sin.

**1871–1873 SERMON LXVII.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter VII, vv. 13–14, “Enter through the narrow gate,” etc.; and on the two ways, the narrow and the broad.

1. Free will.  
2. Christ presides over the narrow way, the devil over the broad. Neither way is to be discerned by the eyes of the flesh, but by those of the heart.  
3. Christ is both the way of pilgrims and the homeland of angels.  
4. The benefit of redemption.  
5. The two feet with which one runs on Christ’s way: the twofold charity.  
5. Humility must accompany charity.

**1873–1875 SERMON LXVIII.** On the same words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter VII, vv. 13–14, “Broad and spacious is the way,” etc.

1. The two hells. After his fall, Adam was between paradise and the lower hell.  
2. The broad way leads to the lower hell; the narrow way leads to paradise.  
3. Who proceed along the broad way, and who along the narrow. The journey on either way is brief, whether its labor or its joy.  
4. Let the sick person who desires health attach himself to the physician, not to the disease.  
5. Exhortation to almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

**1875–1876 SERMON LXIX.** On the same passage of Matthew, chapter VII, vv. 13–14; on the pilgrimage of Christians and on the two ways, one to heaven and the other to hell.

1. Those who are separated in body are united in love.  
2. There are two cities: the world and heaven. In this age, let the person who wishes to be a citizen of heaven live as a pilgrim. The homeland, city, citizens, parents, and king of Christians.  
3. The joy of the saints at our good life, and their sorrow at our evil life.  
4. Christ watches over and helps those who contend for him. The different promises of Christ and the devil.  
5. Freedom to choose the right-hand or the left-hand way. The sweetness of the broad way is brief and false, but its punishment is long; the narrow way is the opposite.  
6. We must labor so that by good works we may acquire joy for ourselves in heaven.  
7. Perfect charity.  
8. Exhortation to almsgiving.

**1877–1879 SERMON LXX.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XI, vv. 25–30, “I confess to you, Father,” etc.

**1879 SERMON LXXI.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XIII, vv. 24–30, “While the men were sleeping, the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat,” etc.; and on other passages; an exhortation to good works.

1. The enemy is called a man figuratively.  
2. Who the weeds in the Church are. The love of Christ above all things.  
3. Whoever desires the things that belong to God must abandon his own.  
4. What is given to the poor is not lost.  
5. Gold is in the earth, from the earth, and is earth.  
6. Why God calls one person and does not call another.  
7. Good things must be provided here. There is no hope of mercy except for the merciful. Whoever has no need of an enemy becomes his own enemy. One must pray for him before he prays. What praise of God ought to be like.  
8. Here there ought to be not security but solicitude. The body is a prison.  
9. In the resurrection the whole person will be spiritual.  
10. The land of the living and the land of the dying.

**1880–1883 SERMON LXXII.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XIV, vv. 23–32, where the Lord walked upon the waters and Peter faltered.

1. Explanation of the text.  
2. The little boat is the Church; the sea, the world; the mast, the cross. Persecution enlarged the Church and enriched the world.  
3. The Christian must be both secure and watchful. Flatterers are hidden reefs; detractors are sea-dogs. They cannot bite the person who clings to the cross.  
4. Vigilance.  
5. The death and resurrection of faith.

**1884–1886 SERMON LXXIII.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XVII, v. 20, “This kind is cast out by nothing except prayer and fasting.”

1. The effect of fasting.  
2. Prayer, the refreshment of fasting. What prayer itself is.

**1886–1887 SERMON LXXIV.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXII, vv. 2–14, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son”; and on the adulterous clothing of men and women.

1. The master of the household is God.  
2. The many reprobate are one.  
3. Immodest bodily dress among men and among women. Adulterous clothing is injurious to the Creator.  
4. It is condemned by the Fathers. The devil’s work is the alteration of nature.  
5. Who bears God in the body.

**1887–1889 SERMON LXXV.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXIV, v. 19, “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing,” etc.

1. What Scripture promises here.  
2. Those who are pregnant and nursing.  
3. The words “Woe to those who are pregnant” are not to be understood literally. Every person conceives: one conceives Christ, another the devil.  
4. Lift up your heart.  
5. The certainty of the promises in Scripture.

**1889–1891 SERMON LXXVI.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXV, vv. 1–13, “The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” etc.

1. The sleep of the virgins is death. Midnight is the day of judgment.  
2. Oil is mercy or charity. The obligation to give abundant alms.  
3. Why the wise virgins were afraid. The poor as merchants. Oil in vessels means good works in the conscience. Flatterers are sellers of oil.  
4. The practices of virgins, lest virginity be vain.  
5. Everywhere there are helpers of Christ and of the devil. Who the devil’s ministers are in monasteries.  
6. Who truly belong to Christ.

**1892–1894 SERMON LXXVII.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXV, vv. 31–43, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc.

1. Sacred reading is to be used frequently.  
2. Heaven, not Gehenna, has been predestined for us.  
3. The necessity of giving alms.  
4. Sterility alone is guilty of condemnation. Who will not come to judgment.  
5. What torments await robbers, and what torments await those who do evil.  
6. Faith without works profits a Christian nothing.

**1895–1896 [Col. 2404] SERMON LXXVIII.** Again on Matthew, chapter XXV, vv. 34–43, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc.; an exhortation to give alms.

1. The force of this reading.  
2. The basis of salvation or condemnation.  
3. How greatly evildoers will be punished.  
4. Exhortation to good works.  
5. Praise of almsgiving.  
6. One must give with a cheerful spirit. Whoever gives gains.

**1897–1898 SERMON LXXIX.** On the words of the Gospel of Matthew, chapter XXVI, vv. 31–35, 69–75, “You will all be scandalized,” etc.; on Peter’s fall.

1. The human being without God’s grace. Why God abandoned Peter for a time.  
2. Peter was sterner by nature.  
3. Peter’s fall and repentance.  
4. Peter’s fall was permitted for our sake.

**1899–1900 SERMON LXXX.** On Matthew, chapter XXVII, vv. 3–10: on Judas the betrayer, and on the field purchased from the price of Christ’s sale for the burial of strangers.

1. Judas was the most severe judge of himself.  
2. God’s providence in the use of the price of Christ. The potter’s field is the world.  
3. The potter is the Lord of the world.  
4. Strangers are devoted Christians. Christ is their burial place.

**1901–1902 SERMON LXXXI.** On the words of the Gospel of Mark, chapter VIII, vv. 1–9, “When there was a great crowd with Jesus, and they had nothing to eat,” etc.

1. Christ’s divinity and humanity shine forth in many ways. The error of Eutyches is refuted.  
2. The crowds signify the nations. The food of which they were deprived was the Law of Moses.  
3. The Apostles were unbelieving until the mysteries were revealed.  
4. A comparison of the two multiplications of the loaves. The first represents the Jews, the second the nations.  
5. Exhortation.

**1902–1904 SERMON LXXXII.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter III, vv. 12–14, “The tax collectors also came to John,” etc.

1. No condition excuses the sinner. Pay and wages. The first military service of the Christian.  
2. Just taxes. Public robbers.  
3. The name of those serving in the army extends to many others.  
4. Clerics are soldiers. Their belt. Their pay. A cleric who is not a cleric.

**1904–1905 SERMON LXXXIII.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter VII, vv. 36–50, “A woman who was a sinner in the city came.”

1. Everyone must undertake repentance. From whom fasting is especially required.  
2. The sinful woman is the Church.  
3. The mouth, hands, shoulders, and feet of Christ.

**1906–1907 SERMON LXXXIV.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XI, vv. 1–4, “Lord, teach us to pray,” etc., with an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.

1. God is Christ’s special Father, and our Father in common. Heaven is where guilt is absent.  
2. The kingdom of God is grace.  
3. The consecration of Christ’s body. Communion is rare among the Greeks. Daily communion is recommended.  
4. We must forgive others so that God may forgive us. Whoever entrusts himself to God in temptations does not fear the devil.

**1907–1909 SERMON LXXXV.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XI, “Which of you will have a friend,” etc.; and on John, chapter XVI, “Until now you have asked nothing,” etc.

1. Incentives to pray to God. God is pious and rich. Access is easy. The angels are ready to announce to the Lord who has knocked at the door. Prayer should be urgent and persistent.  
2. The mystery of the Trinity.  
3. Sometimes one must knock with persistence, so that the master of the household may open.  
4. The guest at night is grace amid ignorance. The guest from heaven is a good thought. Christ.

**1909–1911 SERMON LXXXVI.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XII, vv. 16–21, “The property of a certain rich man produced an abundant harvest,” etc.

1. The blindness of the greedy man.  
2. The greedy man does not love his children. The care of children must be entrusted to God.  
3. Tithes and alms are to be given generously. Excusing oneself from almsgiving on account of one’s children.  
4. Lawful interest. Debtors should not be pressed excessively.

**1911–1912 SERMON LXXXVII.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XIII, vv. 18–19, “To what is the kingdom of heaven like,” etc.

1. The mustard seed is great in power. Christian faith is small in appearance but great in power.  
2. Laurence, the mustard seed.

**1915–1916 SERMON LXXXVIII.** Again on the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XII, vv. 18–19, “To what is the kingdom like,” etc.

1. Christian faith is the kingdom of God. Mustard is its symbol of vigor.  
2. Christ is humble, a mustard seed.

**1914–1915 SERMON LXXXIX.** On the words of the Gospel of Luke, chapter XVII, v. 21, “The kingdom of God is within you”; and on the Apostle’s words to the Romans, chapter XIV, v. 17, “The kingdom of God is not food,” etc.

1. Introduction.  
2. Perfect justice.  
3. Justice derives its name from the administering of law between two opposing parties. The law of the soul and the law of the flesh. A person cannot be just toward others who is not just toward himself.  
4. True peace. Many are displeased with God. Peace is perfect if one is at peace with God.  
5. True joy is the kingdom of heaven, and Christ is this joy. It is the fruit of justice and peace.

**1915–1917 SERMON XC.** On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter II, vv. 1–10, “On the third day there was a wedding,” etc.

1. What this wedding signifies; what the six water jars signify; what the three measures signify.  
2. The mystery of the restoration of humanity. Christ gave the Church her pledge and dowry.  
3. A symbol of regeneration.  
4. Wine is sacred Scripture. Water becoming wine signifies grace succeeding the Law.  
5. The greatest miracle is the conversion of the sinner.  
6. Gifts pleasing to God.

**1918–1919 SERMON XCI.** Again on John, chapter II, vv. 1–10, concerning the six water jars changed into wine at the wedding in Cana of Galilee.

1. [Col. 2405] The six jars are the six ages of the world. The six ages of human beings. These jars are filled with the mysteries of Christ.  
2. Christ in Adam.  
3. In Noah.  
4. In Abraham.  
5. David represented Christ in many respects.  
6. Prophecy concerning Christ in Daniel.  
7. On the calling of the nations in John. The stones are the nations. To those who do not understand Christ, the Law is water; to others, wine.  
8. The disciples were unbelieving after Christ’s death.  
9. The two or three measures. The mystery of the Trinity and the precepts of charity.  
10. How fervor of spirit is to be cultivated.

**1920–1922 SERMON XCII.** Likewise on John, chapter II, vv. 1–10, concerning the wedding at Cana of Galilee.

1. Why Christ came to the wedding. Why he said, “My hour has not yet come.”  
2. The mind of one who faithfully confesses God is not deceived.  
3. The Church calls Christ to the wedding. She desires wine from him. What held Christ back.  
4. The Church teaches obedience to the teacher. The best wine comes only after the inferior has been exhausted. The best wine is Christ’s blood.

**1922–1923 SERMON XCIII.** On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter IV, vv. 5–13, “Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar,” etc.; and on not delaying baptism.

1. Christ became the lawful heir of Jacob.  
2. Christ grows weary on account of our weakness. He rests in the faithful.  
3. Why Christ, the fountain, sat above the well.  
4. Those who delay baptism do not know God’s gift.

**1924–1925 SERMON XCIV.** On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter V, vv. 20–30, “As the Father raises the dead,” etc.; and also chapter VI, vv. 37–40, “Everything that the Father gives me,” etc.

1. One judgment is judgment of discernment, another judgment of condemnation.  
2. The humble person given to Christ cannot perish. There are two resurrections.

**1925–1926 SERMON XCV.** On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter XI, vv. 1–44, “Lazarus our friend is sleeping, but I am going to awaken him from sleep,” etc.

1. Christ’s divinity is demonstrated in the raising of Lazarus. The Apostles did not raise the dead by their own power.  
2. Why Christ rejoices and weeps over Lazarus’s death. The power of Christ’s tears.  
3. Christ was both absent from and present at Lazarus’s death.  
4. Why God asks about things he does not fail to know. Adam is saved through confession of guilt; Cain is condemned through denial. God leaves to human beings what belongs to human power.  
6. The power of Christ’s voice. Another miracle: Lazarus walks with his feet bound.

**1927–1928 SERMON XCVI.** Again in the Gospel of John, chapter XI, vv. 1–14, on the raising of Lazarus.

**1929 SERMON XCVII.** On the words of the Gospel of John, chapter XIV, v. 27, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.”

What peace is. What it does. What kind it is. How great its loss. Discord is the crime of obstinacy.

**1931 SERMON. The same, more fully.** In the same place. **SERMON XCVIII.** On the same words of the Gospel of John, chapter XIV, v. 27.

1. Peace is Christ’s inheritance.  
2. The peacemaker is a son of God.  
3. The priest’s office. Without received peace there is neither prayer nor offering.  
4. Peace and unity are often commended in Scripture.  
5. Diminution of charity is a defect of faith.  
6. Watchfulness.

**1932–1934 SERMON XCIX.** On the words of Acts, chapter III, vv. 1–8, “Peter and John were going up to the temple,” etc.

1. Praise of evangelical poverty.  
2. The worthlessness of gold. Why it is hidden away in such a manner.  
3. It is the use of gold, not its nature, that is condemned.  
4. It is possessed at one’s peril and renounced to good effect.  
5. The poor person’s riches.  
6. The speed of the resurrection.  
7. The flesh is good by nature and is from God. Every vice lies in the will.

**1934–1936 SERMON C.** On the words of Acts, chapter IV, vv. 32–35, “No one said that any of the things he possessed was his own.”

1. The fervent charity of the first believers. The brotherhood of charity is greater than that of blood.  
2. Charity is now growing cold. A truly rich person is scarcely found anymore.  
3. Illiberal almsgiving. Ananias is guilty of fraud and sacrilege.

**1937–1938 SERMON CI.** On the words of Acts, chapter X, vv. 1–28; “Peter went up into the upper room at about the sixth hour, and, being hungry, wished to taste [food],” etc.

1. Whom the clean and unclean animals signify. Who belong to the Church. Why the Church reads the Jewish precepts. Christian food. The vessel shown to Peter is the Church.  
2. The animals are the nations. Peter bears the figure of the Church.  
3. The killing and eating of the nations.  
4. The linen cloth is a symbol of incorruption. It was lowered from heaven three times, signifying the mystery of the Trinity. The four corners signify the four parts of the world.  
5. Recapitulation.

**1939–1941 SERMON CII.** On the Apostle’s words, Romans, chapter VII, v. 15, “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, this I do.”

1. Care must be taken lest the Apostle’s passage be misunderstood.  
2. What is the good that the Apostle could not accomplish? The merit of contemplation. When good things are compared with a greater good, they cease to appear good.  
3. From where created things are “very good.” Why, nevertheless, they are vanity.  
4. Human goodness is evil in comparison with the divine.  
5. The Law is good in itself, but not good in comparison with the Gospel. Scripture justifies those who sin less by comparison with the ungodly.

**1941–1943 SERMON CIII.** On the Apostle’s words, Romans, chapter VII, v. 24, “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person,” etc.

1. Even the saints do not lack reasons for continual groaning. The struggle of the inner and outer person.  
2. The law of sin. It is universal. [Col. 2406]  
3. Adam sold freedom. Hence his descendants are born as slaves.  
4. Yet the Lord did not thereby lose his right. But to free a person against his will would be both unjust and evil.  
5. Our iniquity is the cause of our sale and an obstacle to redemption.  
6. The power of the law of sin.

**1943–1945 SERMON CIV.** On the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians, chapter III, vv. 11–15, “No one can lay another foundation,” etc.

1. Only lesser sins are purged by fire.  
2. Capital sins.  
3. Lesser sins. No one is free from them. They do not kill the soul, but defile it.  
4. They are purged either by good works, by fire, or by punishments inflicted by God here. The benefit of punishments inflicted by God.  
5. What sort of punishment the fire of purgatory is.  
6. By what works lesser sins are redeemed.  
7. By what means capital sins are erased. Public penance.  
8. Recapitulation. The threefold lot of human beings at judgment.  
9. With God’s help we must strive to avoid greater sins, and to redeem lesser sins through love of enemies and generosity in almsgiving.

**1946–1949 SERMON CV.** On the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians, chapter XII, v. 26, “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it,” etc.

1. The mutual love of the members teaches love of one’s neighbors.  
2. The envious person is a corruption that must be cut away. Through charity, the virtues of others become our own.  
3. An example of charity in Christ.  
4. Those who rejoice in another’s tribulation are dead members.  
5. Whoever does not suffer with the suffering person is outside the Church.

**1949–1951 SERMON CVI.** On the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians, chapter XIII, vv. 4, 7, 8, “Charity endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, bears all things.”

1. Introduction.  
2. The four virtues of charity. They do not exist apart from one another. No saint exists without them.  
3. The first virtue of charity: to endure all things.  
4. What must be provided for one who desires this.  
5. The second virtue of charity: to believe all things. It shines forth in Abraham when he abandons everything. He does not doubt concerning his son.  
6. He sacrifices his son and becomes God’s friend. What a friend does.  
7. Isaac as a type of suffering Christ.  
8. What God expects from a follower of charity who believes all things.  
9. The third virtue: to hope all things.  
10. The fourth: to endure all things.  
12. How the Jews, conquered through Christ’s death, serve Christ.  
13. The powers of charity.  
14. Imitation of Christ’s patience.

**1952–1956 SERMON CVII.** Again on the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians, chapter XIII, v. 1, “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing,” etc. On love of God and neighbor, of friends and enemies.

1. Charity makes those separated in body be together.  
2. Charity teaches the proper use of riches. Charity is oil. Charity is a good organizer.  
3. True charity embraces enemies. Charity is the root of good works.  
4. Charity is always sweet.

**1957–1958 SERMON CVIII.** On the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians, chapter XIII, v. 13, “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity.”

1. Faith is necessary for a Christian. Its effect. What it ought to be like.  
2. Firm hope. Concerning forgiveness of any sins, provided one ceases from sinning; and concerning God’s consolation in distress.  
3. Charity is greater than hope and faith. It is the reward of the saints.  
4. It holds the chief place among God’s commandments.  
5. One’s neighbor is every Christian.

**1959–1960 SERMON CIX.** On the Apostle’s words, 2 Corinthians, chapter V, v. 10, “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.” On the certainty of the future resurrection.

1. The joy of Christians in hope. The chief distinction between Christians and pagans. What kind of people we shall rise as.  
2. The resurrection is demonstrated by God’s omnipotence and truth.  
3. Likewise from creation, and from the revivification of seeds.  
4. Created things testify to the future resurrection.  
5. Christ’s resurrection is the pledge of ours.

**1961–1962 SERMON CX.** On the same words of the Apostle, 2 Corinthians, chapter V, v. 10.

1. God is merciful here, but just in the future.  
2. To set the final judgment before oneself.  
3. To forestall unfruitful repentance with fruitful repentance.  
4. The condition of the blessed.

**1963–1964 SERMON CXI.** On the Apostle’s words, Ephesians, chapter V, vv. 15–16, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

1. Malice and misery make the days evil.  
2. Regeneration frees one from misery, and how it does so. The reward of Christian service is not in this life. The Christian’s attitude toward temporal and eternal goods.  
3. The present times are not more unhappy than earlier times.  
4. Persecution of the godly in a time of peace. The danger of false brothers.  
5. To redeem the time.  
6. A Punic proverb. To avoid lawsuits.  
7. What follows concerning lawsuits.

**1964–1967 SERMON CXII.** On the Apostle’s words, 1 Timothy, chapter I, v. 5, “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

1. Charity is something brief and great. Charity is sweet.  
2. It makes one rich.  
3. Two roots are planted in human hearts. From one nothing evil emerges; from the other nothing good comes forth.  
4. The hearts of the faithful are heaven. The hearts of the covetous are earth.  
5. The wicked must beware of despair, and the just of presumption. Repentance must not be delayed.

**1967–1969 SERMON CXIII.** On the Apostle’s words, Hebrews, chapter I, v. 3, “For he is the brightness of eternal light and the image of the invisible God.”

1. One must not judge what sort or how great God is. What God is.  
2. The Son’s different names. The reasons for each.  
3. The equality of the Son with the Father.

**1969–1971 [Col. 2407] SERMON CXIV.** On the Apostle’s words, Hebrews, chapter XII, v. 1, “Since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses,” etc.

1. There is a great contest in the arena.  
2. The saints are clouds. For the saints there is already rest and patience.  
3. Stephen’s wisdom.  
4. We must run, and therefore lay aside the burden of sin. Sin is agile.  
5. Patience is a thing of God.  
6. Praise of Stephen the protomartyr.

**1971–1972 APPENDIX, CLASS II.** —ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT.

**1973–1974 SERMON CXV.** On the coming of the Lord, I.

1. What must be done before celebrating the Nativity of the Lord. We must labor so that Christ’s body may be received worthily.  
2. The conscience must be cleansed.  
3. The soul must be adorned with good works. Repentance must immediately follow guilt.  
4. Vices must be avoided before solemn celebrations, especially hatred.  
5. Exhortation.

**1973–1975 SERMON CXVI.** On the Advent of the Lord, II.

1. Let the Nativity of the Lord not find us unprepared.  
2. It is Christ’s wedding day. At Christ’s wedding, who is the bride, and what is the food?  
3. What must be done before the solemn celebrations.  
4. The poor must be invited to the banquet.  
5. Friends should also be invited, but more rarely, and to modest banquets.  
6. Recapitulation.

**1975–1976 SERMON CXVII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, I.

1. The grace of this day.  
2. What makes repentance certain. True, or voluntary, repentance.  
3. The vanity of passing pleasure. The true happiness of this life.  
4. A vow must be made to God who is born. Vows turned in different directions. The best vow.  
5. How each person should vow concerning his own vice: the irascible person, the immodest person, the envious person, the murderer, the detractor, the harsh person, the proud person, the drunkard.  
6. The fruit of such vows. Guardian angels offer our vows to God.  
7. The fruit of remembering Christ incarnate.  
8. What virgins must care for or avoid.  
9. What married people must do. Widows. Women.  
10. What penitents must do. To mourn intelligently.  
11. An address to the poor.  
12. To slaves.

**1977–1980 SERMON CXVIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, II.

1. The Son of God does not change when he becomes human.  
2. Christ’s birth is real, but not ordinary. Yet through it he did not condemn marriage.  
3. God with us.  
4. The twofold cause of the Incarnation: restoration and instruction.

**1981–1982 SERMON CXIX.** On the Nativity of the Lord, III.

1. The proud person is restored through the humble God. The procreation of the first human is renewed.  
2. The work of the Holy Spirit declares Christ’s holiness and divinity.  
3. Prophecy concerning the virgin birth.  
4. The angels’ address to Mary.  
5. The grace of the Word’s self-emptying.

**1982–1984 SERMON CXX.** On the Nativity of the Lord, IV.

1. Through a woman sin arose; through a woman it is uprooted.  
2. The miracles of the virgin birth.  
3. Gabriel’s words are examined. The sublimity of Mary’s faith.  
4. Eve’s curse is erased through Mary. The woman is also a virgin.  
5. Mary’s song of exultation.  
6. God is the author of offspring.  
7. The salvation of the world depended upon Mary’s consent. Mary’s faith opens heaven.  
8. Christ’s betrothal to humanity and to the Church.

**1984–1986 SERMON CXXI.** On the Nativity of the Lord, V.

1. Bearing witness to the Savior.  
2. The excellence of the virgin birth. Virginity bears in the mind the one whom Mary bore in her womb.  
3. The wondrous birth. It becomes the consolation of the world.  
4. The Lord’s power shines forth from the order of his birth and from various testimonies concerning him.  
5. The blessed Virgin as a type of the Church.

**1987–1989 SERMON CXXII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VI.

1. The benefits of Christ at his birth.  
2. The manner of his birth proves him God and human.  
3. The possibility of this manner. Three wondrous kinds of birth.  
4. Christ’s humility is revealed through signs of power. The virtues commended on this day.

**1989–1990 SERMON CXXIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VII.

1. Christ’s wondrous birth. A virgin before and after childbirth.  
2. Mary is the window and ladder of heaven, the restorer of women. Mary’s good things counter Eve’s evils.  
3. Mary assumed every condition of women.

**1990–1991 SERMON CXXIV.** On the Nativity of the Lord, VIII.

1. Christ is born for me, not for himself.  
2. Virginity is never naked.  
3. The mysteries of the one born in the flesh, who had no place in the inn and was wrapped in swaddling clothes, are explained.

**1992 SERMON CXXV.**

1. Why God assumed humanity from a Virgin.  
2. Christ’s generation prefigured in Adam.  
3. Why Christ was born from a woman. Why his resurrection is announced by women.  
4. The necessity of chastity for one who wishes to be a Christian.

**1993 SERMON CXXVI.** On the Nativity of the Lord, X.

1. Christ’s two generations are compared with one another. Christ’s mother is always a virgin, who is always a bride. Both generations are incomparable.  
2. The prerogative of Christ’s birthday. Christ’s resurrection day is the same as the day of his conception.  
3. The mystery of the lengthening day at Christ’s Nativity.  
4. Christ’s power shines forth in his self-emptying.

**1994–1995 SERMON CXXVII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, XI.

There are two births of the Lord. Pride is not greatness but swelling. The necessity of humility. Christ is the only-begotten and firstborn.

**1996 SERMON CXXVIII.** On the Nativity of the Lord, XII.

1. The remedy of our restoration. Christ alone was born without sin.  
2. Christ yesterday and today.  
3. Simeon’s desire.  
4. Testimonies to Christ’s birth.  
5. Christ is beautiful everywhere.  
6. What Christ purchased from us, and what he returned.  
7. The figure of the Law: Elisha’s staff. The foundation of Christian faith.  
8. Christ’s divine generation.  
9. Whoever meditates on this must raise his mind above [Col. 2408] all created things. A person is as far from God as he is unlike him.

**1997–2000 SERMON CXXIX.** On the Kalends of January, I.

1. Who Janus was. The origin of idolatry. Why Janus has two faces. The superstition of the January Kalends.  
2. Those who make a little deer. Men dressing as women.  
3. Other superstitions. New Year’s gifts.  
4. A fast was formerly proclaimed on the January Kalends. Masked people are not to be looked upon.

**2001–2003 SERMON CXXX.** On the Kalends of January, II.

1. The sources of all sins are pride and error. Error. How it passes into pride. The madness of the masked. How the devil rules over them.  
2. Such people must be restrained.  
3. New Year’s gifts. Fasting on the January Kalends.  
4. The empty honor offered to the planets. Why the days are named after the planets. Their first naming. Such a designation is to be taken up again.

**2003–2004 SERMON CXXXI.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, I.

1. The unique star. It did not indicate Christ but stirred people to seek him.  
2. Then another revelation made him manifest.  
3. The star appeared for two years.  
4. What is signified by the two-year appearance. The two commandments of love. Christ’s two advents. The two generations of humanity.  
5. The joining together of Jews and nations.  
6. The mystical gifts of the Magi.

**2005–2007 SERMON CXXXII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, II.

1. Today the Jews have been joined to the nations.  
2. The star appeared two years earlier. What led the Magi to worship.  
3. Herod’s detestable cruelty, but even more remarkable the Jews’ stupidity.

**2007–2008 SERMON CXXXIII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, III.

1. The reason and meaning of the solemn celebration.  
2. The necessity of the Incarnation.  
3. Let no one here be secure.  
4. Signs of God’s indwelling in us. Charity is the mother of all virtues.

**2008–2009 SERMON CXXXIV.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, IV.

1. The differing tradition concerning the celebration of the Epiphany.  
2. John’s baptism did not erase sins. Christ’s humility.  
3. John’s testimony concerning Christ.  
4. The manifestation of the Trinity. Christ’s power.

**2010–2011 SERMON CXXXV.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, V.

1. The water was enriched more than Mary.  
2. Christ’s second birth.  
3. God the Father, the craftsman.  
4. When Christ is baptized, he cleanses the waters.

**2011–2012 SERMON CXXXVI.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, VI.

1. Christ’s fourfold manifestation on this day. The mysteries of our salvation are contained in each.  
2. All waters were blessed in Christ’s baptism.  
3. The gravity of sin must be weighed from its remedy. Sin must be avoided with what great care.  
4. Faith in the Trinity and the Incarnation is contained in the Magi’s gifts. How the Magi are to be imitated.  
6. From where the Magi possessed such devotion. Their mystical gifts. Gifts pleasing to God.

**2013–2015 SERMON CXXXVII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, VII.

1. Christ first became known in his baptism.  
2. A brief exposition of Psalm 28. The fruitfulness of the Church, previously deserted.

**2015–2016 SERMON CXXXVIII.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, VIII.

1. Human beings are made equal to angels.  
2. John is a lamp.  
3. When John baptized the Lord, the mystery of the Trinity is inferred.

**2017 SERMON CXXXIX.** On the Epiphany of the Lord, IX.

1. On the word “Epiphany.”  
2. How we imitate the Magi.  
3. The gifts of the Magi.

**2018 SERMON CXL.** On Lent, I.

1. Lent is healthful for body and soul.  
2. The devout practices of Lent.  
3. Good works are followed by sweetness, evil works by bitterness.  
4. Food for the soul must be provided for the whole year during Lent. Losses must be repaired.  
5. Worldly occupations must at least be moderated. Either we laugh at the world, or the world itself laughs at us.

**2019–2020 SERMON CXLI.** On Lent, II.

1. The days of Lent signify the present life; the days of Easter signify the future life.  
2. Lent is the time of spiritual harvest and vintage. What food is for the flesh, the word of God is for the soul. The wine cellar.  
3. Occupations must be exchanged. The game of tables.  
4. Lunches should be distributed to the poor. The foods of dinner should be neither luxurious nor excessive. The flesh should be treated as a servant, the soul as mistress.  
5. Divine readings in church, at home, and during meals.

**2020–2022 SERMON CXLII.** On Lent, III.

1. Whoever cannot fast should give more abundant alms.  
2. Almsgiving is better than fasting.  
3. No one is easily excused from it.  
4. Christ must be received in the poor, so that he himself may receive us into our homeland.  
5. Those who accumulate riches are rebuked.  
6. Fasting must not be without almsgiving. Meals should be distributed to the poor.  
7. Chastity must be maintained throughout Lent.  
8. The poor fulfill the commandment of almsgiving by good will.

**2022–2024 SERMON CXLIII.** On Lent, IV.

1. Lent was celebrated according to the examples of the saints: Moses, Elijah, and Christ himself.  
2. At that time virtue is easier.  
3. The principal fast is from vices.  
4. The poor should be refreshed from frugality.

**2025–2026 SERMON CXLIV.** On Lent, V.

1. The usefulness of fasting is shown by the examples of Moses and Adam.  
2. Likewise by Elijah.  
3. Likewise by Daniel, John the Baptist, and the Gospel itself. The difference between fasting and being full.  
4. From what one must abstain, and why. Fasts must not stand alone.

**2026–2027 SERMON CXLV.** On Lent, VI.

1. The length of Lent [Col. 2409] must not become wearisome.  
2. The number forty is mystical. The Flood as an effect of mercy.  
3. The Flood is like our baptism, and likewise like Lent.  
4. The Church is a three-chambered ark. Noah preaches the destruction of the world.

**2027–2028 SERMON CXLVI.** On Lent, VII.

1. Fasting is useless for those who do not depart from iniquity.  
2. Even those who do not devote themselves to pious exercises, but to hunting.  
3. The wickedness of masters toward slaves. A slave who yesterday was a brother is treated as inferior to dogs.  
4. Fasting acceptable to God.  
5. Meals should be distributed to the poor. Fasting without almsgiving is a kind of commerce.

**2029–2030 SERMON CXLVII.** On Lent, VIII.

1. Lent was consecrated by Christ and must be observed as necessary.  
2. The reason for its institution. Satiety is prodigal of chastity. A comparison of the first and second Adam.  
3. Why Christ fasted in the desert. How dangerous the presence of a woman is.  
4. A certain desert is a body that is fasting and chaste.

**2031–2032 SERMON CXLVIII.** On Lent, IX.

One must constantly devote oneself to one’s renewal. The undivided separation of God and humanity. Why God gives commandments.

2. This life is full of dangers. The dangers of the just: the tongues of detractors, and scandal arising from the prosperity of the wicked. The stars have no power.  
3. Repentance is necessary for everyone.  
4. How dangerously the person who desires vengeance prays. Mercy is ready for the merciful.

**2033–2034 SERMON CXLIX.** On the Lord’s Supper. On what is written in the Gospel of John, chapter XIII, vv. 4–8, “He rises from supper and lays aside his garments,” etc.

1. The washing of feet is to be offered to pilgrims according to the Lord’s example.  
2. The mysteries instituted on the day of the Lord’s Supper.  
3. One must presume upon nothing except God’s help. Peter’s presumption.  
4. The conscience must be cleansed from sins.  
5. One must persevere in pious works.

**2034–2036 SERMON CL.** On the Passion of the Lord, I.

1. Judas did not see Jesus, although Jesus had not been changed.  
3. Peter’s fall. His weeping as well.  
3. The price of Christ’s sale.  
4. Signs appeared at Jesus’ death.

**2036–2038 SERMON CLI.** On the Passion of the Lord, II.

1. Why Christ was sorrowful.  
2. Why Peter struck the ear. Why he grew cold. Whom he denied.  
3. Peter’s weeping.  
4. Christ on the cross is a worm and a beetle.  
5. Why Joseph secretly asked for Jesus’ body.

**2038–2040 SERMON CLII.** On the Passion of the Lord, III; and on Susanna.

1. Why Christ remained silent when accused.  
2.

Susanna defended by her chastity. She merits a virgin judge. 3. Daniel’s and Pilate’s judgment is the same. Pilate’s wickedness. 2040–2041

**SERMON CLIII.** The whole world redeemed. 2. How dear the human being is to God, how much he is worth, and how much he owes. The mystery of the scarlet cloak, the crown of thorns, the thirst on the cross, the torn veil, and the opened tombs. 2. The mystery of Judas refunding the price of the Christ who had been sold. 2042

**SERMON CLIV.** On the Passion of the Lord, V; and on the blessed Thief.—1. Christ’s purpose in the mysteries of his flesh. 2. God’s immeasurable condescension toward humanity. Christ’s death reveals the human being; his resurrection reveals God. The absolution of the Thief becomes the world’s hope and consolation. The hope of salvation rests on two things. 3. The Thief obtains salvation by his merit, believing in Christ while Christ is being abandoned. 4. Confessing God while suffering. 5. The faith of his prayer. The Thief as martyr. 6. The reward promised to him. 7. Christ’s divinity on the cross is attested by his judgment concerning the thieves, his wondrous patience, and the whole of creation. How great is human hardness. 8. How much a human being is worth and ought to be. How guilty one is when committing sin. Forgetfulness of the future judgment is a great punishment for sin. 9. Let the Thief’s example not become an occasion for a more careless life, since few possess the Thief’s faith and many have been deceived by this empty hope. 10. To postpone the time of salvation is most dangerous, most foolish, and hateful to God. The Thief did not postpone the work of salvation. 2043–2046

**SERMON CLV.** On the Passion of the Lord, VI; or, On the Cross and the Thief.—1. The cross, now glorious, is the cause of innumerable gifts. 2. The feast of the cross instituted by Paul. The cross, the altar, Christ, the priest, and the victim. 3. Why he was sacrificed under the open sky, not in the temple. The cross consecrated every place as a temple. 4. The cross opened paradise. 5. The Thief’s entrance into heaven greatly commends the Lord. 6. The Thief’s merit. The Thief as teacher. 7. Thief and Thief. The Thief’s charity and preaching. 8. The Thief’s confession and its fruit. 9. The cross, the insignia of the kingdom. Therefore Christ carried it into heaven. 10. He will bring it back at his second coming. Christ’s second coming will not be hidden, and why. The sun, moon, and stars will be darkened by the brightness of the cross. The angels will tremble at the final judgment, and why. 11. Why the cross will appear at the judgment. 12. Christ’s prayer on the cross for his enemies. The effect of that prayer. 13. Imitation of Christ. It is not impossible. Stephen, an apostle. 2047–2052

**SERMON CLVI.** On the Passion of the Lord, VII.—1. The benefit of our redemption. What God demands in return for it. 2. God’s method of coming to the aid of the earth and satisfying justice. 3. Hence the devil was outwitted and overthrown. 4. Hence paradise was reopened. Conversion is never too late. The Thief’s faith. From what source, and why, this change occurred. 5. The Thief’s words are to be taken upon our own lips. 2053–2054

**SERMON CLVII.** At the vigil of Easter, I, on the words of Genesis, chapter I, verses 1–6: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” etc.—1. Opening of the sermon. 2. The created light: as much as a mortal eye could contain. The invisible earth becomes visible. 3. The Spirit over the waters—not God, but a thing belonging to God. It is the seedbed of the enlivened creation. Two spirits: God’s and the world’s. 4. Allegorical exposition of the invisible earth, the division of the waters, the earth bringing forth vegetation, the sun, moon, stars, and fish. 2055–2056

**SERMON CLVIII.** At the vigil of Easter, II.—1. Joseph asks Pilate for Jesus’ body. 2. Peter knew of Christ’s resurrection before the crucifixion. 3. The angel rebukes Mary. 2056–2057

**SERMON CLIX.** On Easter, I.—1. This day is brighter than the others, the mother of all days. 2. The whole grace of the Sabbath has been transferred to this day. The crown of the righteous is Christ, by whom they are also adorned. 3. Today heaven’s gate has been opened. The Church’s gate is the gate of paradise. 2058–2059

**SERMON CLX.** On Easter, II.—1. How Christ acted freely. In what manner he is the death of death and the bite of hell. 2. The voices of Tartarus at Christ’s coming. 3. Tartarus’ address to its own ruler. 4. The righteous’ entreaty to Christ. 5. They turn their torments back upon their tormentors. 2059–2061

**SERMON CLXI.** On Easter, III.—1. The effects of Christ’s descent into hell. 2. Humanity could have been freed without the incarnation of the Word, but it was not fitting. 3. Christ, born of the Virgin, could have entered through closed doors. 4. In Thomas there was not the feeling of one who doubts, but of one who inquires. His inquiry becomes instruction for the whole world. Why Christ showed his scars. 5. We shall rise again with the same bodies. Therefore death is compared with sleep, and resurrection with a grain of wheat. 2063

**SERMON CLXII.** On Easter, IV.—1. Thomas’s concern strengthened everyone’s faith. Thomas, being faithful, did not doubt. 2. Christ, the firstborn from the dead, is the birth of the resurrection. 3. What death may die. How death was consumed in victory. 2064–2065

**SERMON CLXIII.** On Easter, V.—1. Signs of Christ’s divinity. 2. The necessity of Christ’s death. 3. Why Christ preserved his scars. 2065–2066

**SERMON CLXIV.** On Easter, VI.—1. The figure of the legal lamb is fulfilled. The old priesthood is abolished. 2. Everything is renewed and smiles: the earth with fruits and flowers, the sky with a happier face. The sun is now brighter. The moon is full. And all this is on humanity’s account: how much more ought humanity itself to rejoice. 3. Christ’s resurrection prefigured in Adam, Noah, and Jonah. 4. Spiritual celebration of Easter. 2066–2067

**SERMON CLXV.** On Easter, VII.—1. The Lord’s death and resurrection prefigured in various ways—in Adam and Noah. 2. In Moses’ staff and in Jonah. The mystery of the time at which Easter is celebrated. 3. Christ’s death and resurrection are to be imitated. 2068

**SERMON CLXVI.** On Easter, VIII.—An assessment of human salvation. 2069

**SERMON CLXVII.** On Easter, IX.—1. Why the lamb was sacrificed in the evening. How many mysteries make the Lord’s day glorious. The day of judgment. 2069–2070

**SERMON CLXVIII.** On Easter, X.—1. What Christ’s Passover is. 2. Baptism, an image of the future resurrection. The Thief’s devotion is to be imitated. 3. The duty of sponsors. 4. Everyone is obliged to edify his neighbor. 2070–2071

**SERMON CLXIX.** On Easter, XI.—1. Christ’s entrance through closed doors is a miracle. 2. No explanation or example is available for this. Miracles require faith. Thomas’s faith was dead. 3. It came back to life through Christ’s touch. 2072

**SERMON CLXX.** On Easter, XII. 2073

**SERMON CLXXI.** On Easter, XIII, on the resurrection of the dead.—1. The certainty of belief in the resurrection, confirmed by the testimony and example of truth. 2. Two deaths. Two parts of the first death. The second death. Christ assumed the second part of the first death. A twofold resurrection. 3. How one passes from the first to the second. 2074

**SERMON CLXXII.** Sunday in the Octave of Easter, for the newly baptized. 2075

**SERMON CLXXIII.** On the Litany.—1. Days of healing. 2. The whole Church celebrates the three days of the Litanies. Whoever withdraws from the Church is a deserter from the heavenly camp. 3. How the days of the Litanies should be celebrated. What benefit comes from them. When sins cease, punishments also cease. 4. How the Church may be worshiped fruitfully. 2077

**SERMON CLXXIV.** On the Litany, II.—1. Eternal sorrow is to be avoided by brief sorrow. 2. The practices and purpose of these days. The peace of the times is to be secured through peace with one’s neighbors. 3. The Church is to be frequented. 2078–2079

**SERMON CLXXV.** On the Litany, III.—1. One should fast especially from vices. 2. Fasting without holiness is displeasing to God. 3. Nor does it move God to grant requests. 4. Which fasts are acceptable to God. 2079–2080

**SERMON CLXXVI.** On the Ascension of the Lord, I.—1. The Lord’s miracles were performed for our sake. His ascension is the guarantee of ours. 2. Eutyches’ error. The origin of Arius’ error. 3. Valentinus’ error is refuted. 4. One ascends after Christ through hope and the extinguishing of desires. 2081–2082

**SERMON CLXXVII.** On the Ascension of the Lord, II.—1. How one ascends with Christ. 2. “Lift up your heart” in two senses. 3. A heart cleansed by faith draws God to itself; humility keeps him there. Christ is our way and our homeland. 2082–2083

**SERMON CLXXVIII.** On the Ascension of the Lord, III.—In Christ, the divine and human nature. 2083

**SERMON CLXXIX.** On the Ascension of the Lord, IV.—1. The apostles’ state of mind at Christ’s ascension. 2. The feeling of the air, heaven, and heavenly beings. 3. The angels’ amazement. 2084–2085

**SERMON CLXXX.** On the Ascension of the Lord, V.—1. The joys of heaven at the Lord’s ascension. 2. The entreaty of the grieving apostles. 3. Their consolation. 2085–2086

**SERMON CLXXXI.** On the Ascension of the Lord, VI.—1. The apostles’ feelings at Christ’s ascension. 2. Angels as messengers of the mysteries. 3. What kind of person Christ will be when he returns. 2086–2087

**SERMON CLXXXII.** On Pentecost, I.—1. The Holy Spirit is God, companion of the divine majesty, expression of the Trinity, and the Redeemer’s vicar. 2. He is no longer a visitor but an eternal inhabitant—not merely through operation but through substance. The apostles are rays of the sun and lamps of truth. 3. What the coming of the Holy Spirit added to the apostles’ perfection. 4. The apostles’ condition before and after the coming of the Holy Spirit: before, error; afterward, wisdom. Thomas’s unbelief. The faith of the others afterward. Peter’s judgment against his persecutors. Stephen later corrects him. Those who were timid before subsequently become fearless in every torment. 5. It was not only the apostles who were intoxicated with the new wine of the Holy Spirit; those pursuing a perfect life burned with this fervor, and the martyrs burned as well. 6. How the Holy Spirit should be invited each day. 2087–2090

**SERMON CLXXXIII.** On Pentecost, II.—1. Opening. 2. Why the Spirit could not come unless Christ departed. 3. The gift of tongues, a sign of the Holy Spirit’s presence. Charity gathered the Church together. How every believer may now speak in tongues. 4. Those who celebrate this day spiritually. 2091–2092

**SERMON CLXXXIV.** On Pentecost, III.—1. The Lord promises the Holy Spirit to his apostles. 2. One God in the Trinity is to be believed. 2092

**SERMON CLXXXV.** On Pentecost, IV.—1. Some people’s opinion that the Lord ascended on the day of Pentecost. Why he remained here for forty days after the resurrection. 2. The arriving Spirit establishes Christ as reigning. He is of one substance with Christ. 3. Exhortation. 2093–2094

**SERMON CLXXXVI.** On Pentecost, V.—1. This day has been solemn throughout every age. It stands out above the other sacraments. 2. The apostles are blessed, full of new wine. 2094

**SERMON CLXXXVII.** On Pentecost, VI.—1. The written law and the law of grace. 2095

**APPENDIX, CLASS III.—SERMONS ON THE SAINTS.** 2095–2096

**SERMON CLXXXVIII.** On the feast of Saint Vincent.—1. Opening. 2. The Levite, minister of the Lord’s blood, unconquered by torments. 3. The devil’s work in Dacian, Christ’s work in Vincent. Vincent is tortured secretly. 4. He is healed by God and dies on a soft bed. 5. His body is exposed to wild beasts. 6. The raven, the turtle-dove, and the wolf honor him. 2095–2097

**SERMON CLXXXIX.** On the feast of the conversion of Saint Paul.—2. Paul, a wolf that seizes in the morning. 3. In the evening he distributes food. Paul, a model for those beginning to believe. 4. Saul’s terrible reputation. 5. However much we suffer, what we hope for outweighs it. 6. The usefulness of Paul’s conversion. 2098–2100

**SERMON CXC.** On the Chair of Saint Peter, I.—1. The reason for the feast. 2. The superstition introduced on this day. Holy souls are already with Christ. 2100–2101

**SERMON CXCI.** On the Chair of Saint Peter, II.—1. This feast coincides with Lent. 2. The ways in which assistance may be given to the dead. 2101

**SERMON CXCII.** On the Chair of Saint Peter, III.—1. Peter made progress through his errors. The dignity and meaning of Peter’s name. 2. Peter’s steps upon the waters. He is supported by faith. This is more wondrous than Israel’s crossing of the sea. 3. When faith fails, the path fails. One comes to Christ only through dangers. 2102–2103

**SERMON CXCIII.** On the Annunciation of the Lord, I.—1. The devil was deceived by the very art by which he had deceived humanity; Christ is God and human being. 2. Mary’s merit and privileges. 2103–2104

**SERMON CXCIV.** On the Annunciation of the Lord, II.—1. Eve’s losses and Mary’s benefits. 2. Mary surpasses all praise. 3. The salvation of the world depends on Mary’s consent. Mary is mother and virgin. She was wedded to God himself. Jeremiah’s prophecy concerning Mary. 4. The angel’s words to Mary. Mary’s obedience is commended. 5. Prayer to the blessed Virgin. 2104–2106

**SERMON CXCV.** On the Annunciation of the Lord, III.—1. Mary, the closed gate in the house of the Lord. 2. The angelic greeting. 3. Continuation on the same subject. 4. Joseph is troubled. 5–6. Joseph is reassured through the angel. Prophecies concerning Mary are explained. 2107–2109

**SERMON CXCVI.** On the Nativity of John the Baptist, I.—1. The distinctive character of this feast. John as a type of the law. 2. A burning lamp. 3. What his birth reveals. 4. What the Word is, and what the voice is. 5. John’s glory above that of the other prophets. He is the mediator of the New and Old Testaments. 6. Force must be exerted for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. 7. Two kinds of abstinence. 8. The Church seizes the kingdom from the Synagogue. Christ is our kingdom. Human beings also seize it from the apostate angels. 2110–2113 [Col. 2412]

**SERMON CXCVII.** On the Nativity of John the Baptist, II.—1. Only the Lord’s and John’s births are celebrated. Whoever is born of a woman is inferior to John. 2. Just as Christ’s birth, so John’s birth is full of mystery. The same is true of the passion of each. 3. Why John is called a lamp and sent before Christ. Why he is a voice. He bore the type of the law. 4. Exhortation. 2113–2115

**SERMON CXCVIII.** On the Nativity of John the Baptist, III.—1. John is honored with a unique celebration. 2. He is a voice. As Christ increases, John decreases. He marked Christ by his birth and manner of life. 3. His freedom in reproving. When correction of the wicked is omitted without fault. A pious method for correcting the wicked. 4. A state of misery or happiness can sometimes be changed. 2115–2116

**SERMON CXCIX.** On the Nativity of John the Baptist, IV.—John is commended to his parents. 2. Elizabeth was barren until the sense of desire had passed away. John’s praises. 3. The angel’s illustrious prophecy concerning John. He fulfills it while not yet born. 2117

**SERMON CC.** On the Nativity of John the Baptist, V. 2118

**SERMON CCI.** On the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, I.—1. Peter is famous everywhere through miracles, Paul through his Epistles. Peter’s first miracle was the healing of a lame man. The appropriateness of this event. Peter, the rock; Paul, the vessel: how necessary both are to the Church. 2. How fitting it is that they suffered on the same day: Peter being fastened to the cross, and milk flowing from Paul’s neck. 3. How the memory of martyrs should be celebrated. 2119–2120

**SERMON CCII.** On the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, II.—1. The apostles are equal to one another, yet all are inferior to Peter and Paul. The keys of power were entrusted to Peter, those of knowledge to Paul. 2. Peter and Paul are equal in merit. Why they suffered on one day, in one place, under one tyrant. Why in the West. 3. The cause of their death. Why Simon Magus was permitted to fly into the heights. 2119–2121

**SERMON CCIII.** On the Nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul, III.—1. Peter was chosen for the salvation of the Jews, Paul for that of the Gentiles. 2. They are merchants and spiritual stewards. 3. Equal in many respects. Paul is the Jonah of the New Testament. 4. Peter the destroyer of the Synagogue, the restorer of the Church. 5. Praise of Peter’s chains. 2122–2123

**SERMON CCIV.** On the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, IV.—1. Peter is sought by Paul and is afraid. 2. Stephen’s prayer earned Paul’s salvation. 3. Paul suffers the evils he had inflicted. 2124

**SERMON CCV.** On the Nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul, V.—1. Peter’s calling is explained. 2. Paul’s conversion. 3. Rebuke of the Jews. 4. The martyrdom of Peter and Paul. 2125–2126

**SERMON CCVI.** On the Nativity of Saint Laurence, I.—1. Laurence sets the world aflame for martyrdom. 2. He endures prolonged punishment. He is not inferior to the three youths. 3. He asks to be burned in a double fire. 4. We are to imitate the martyrs. 2127–2128

**SERMON CCVII.** On the Nativity of Saint Laurence, II.—1. What we owe the martyrs. Laurence deserves honor for three reasons. 2. Why he is tortured. 3. Martyrs must have been martyrs before their martyrdom. What it means to take up the cross. 2128–2129

**SERMON CCVIII.** On the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary.—1. This solemnity is especially important and now rightly received. 2. What the Church believes concerning Mary’s assumption. 3. None of the Latins has written about the manner of her death. The true view of the assumption. 4. Mary is greater than all praise. 5. Mary is most worthy of all praise. 6. “To magnify” is used in two ways. 7. Above all, God is to be magnified for the gift of redemption. 8. Instructed by this truth, one despises earthly things. What rejoicing is good and what is evil. 9. What it means to rejoice in Jesus. 10. The commendation of humility. Feigned humility. 11. Prayer to the blessed Virgin. 12. How the blessed Virgin is to be honored. 2129–2134

**SERMON CCIX.** On the feast of All Saints.—1. The time of struggle is brief, the prize without end. 2. Continuation on the same subject. 4. Description of the blessed life. 4. By what means heaven is purchased. 5. The martyrs’ purple crown; that of those who live justly, white. 6. How greatly eternal life is to be desired. 2135–2137

**SERMON CCX.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, I.—1. Stephen is given to the whole Church as an example. Stephen’s most sincere chastity. 2. Why he testified that he saw the Son of Man, not the Son of God. 3. If martyrs differ among themselves, Stephen is preeminent. 4. Stephen’s wondrous charity. 5. Forgiving enemies. 6. It is difficult, but it also has an immense reward. This is observed for the sake of earthly hope or out of fear; how much more should it be observed through love! 2137–2139

**SERMON CCXI.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, II.—1. Stephen as crown. 2. He is restrained when eager for vengeance. Stephen both rages and loves. 3. He prayed standing for himself; for his enemies, on his knees. 2140–2141

**SERMON CCXII.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, III.—1. The priest’s joy and crown is the salvation of the people. It is the priest’s task to distribute God’s things, and the people’s to receive them. 2. Continuation on the same subject. 2141–2142

**SERMON CCXIII.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, IV.—What martyrs produce for themselves and for others. 2142

**SERMON CCXIV.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, V.—1. The Lord mixes wolves among the sheep, and why. 2. Stephen is the first sheep. He obeys like an angel. Because of the seal of the Trinity. By the keys of whose faith he opens heaven. 3. There he sees Christ and the angels. 4. As Christ, so Stephen. He is condemned for confessing God. Yet even then he does not keep silent, but he is not heard. 5. Stephen’s address to the Jews. 6. Stephen’s prayer to Christ for himself. 7. The same man’s prayer for his enemies. What this prayer accomplished. 2142–2144

**SERMON CCXV.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, VI.—1. The effects of Christ’s birth. 2. Stephen is stoned because of his confession of Christ. 3. Christ prays for his enemies as an example. 4. Saul’s conversion is owed to Stephen’s prayer. 5. Saul’s crime is both forgiven and avenged. 2145–2146

**SERMON CCXVI.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, VII.—1. While living here, Stephen saw the Trinity. Stephen’s wondrous charity toward those who stoned him. 2147

**SERMON CCXVII.** On the Nativity of Saint Stephen, VIII. Same place.

**SERMON CCXVIII.** On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents, I.—1. The Magi come from the East. 2. The blessedness of the Innocents. 3. Herod’s foolish error and terror. 4. His disturbance and deception. 2149–2150

**SERMON CCXIX.** On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents, II.—1. There is one God. The Innocents are owed as victims to the God who was born. 2. The mothers’ mourning. 3. How grievous Herod’s lot will be on the day of judgment. 2151

**SERMON CCXX.** On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents, III.—1. Herod benefited the Innocents more through hatred than he would have benefited them through service. The Innocents are flowers of the martyrs. 2. The one who inflicts injury suffers the greater injury himself. The thought of death restrains desire. Then no evil will befall the good, and no good the wicked. 3. But even now it is better to be good than wicked. To suffer evil and to be evil. 4. Wealth is good when used well; good by nature, but bad for the wicked. 5. True and false riches. Desire is always in need. 6. Conclusion. 2151–2154

**SERMON CCXXI.** On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents, IV.—1. In honoring the martyrs, the Savior is praised. How fittingly the martyrs are beneath God’s altar. The Innocents intercede more than the others. 2. How the saints ask for vengeance. The saints now have one robe; later they will have two. 3. How God speaks to the saints. 4. Let us follow the martyrs’ footsteps as far as we can. 5. The martyrs’ condition has changed. 2155–2156

**SERMON CCXXII.** On the holy apostles.—1. The apostles are rams. 2. They surpass the other faithful. 4. Their virtues are set forth. The manner of loving friends and enemies. 5. The manner of loving the Creator and the creature. 2156–2157

**SERMON CCXXIII.** On one holy martyr.—1. Two things must be considered in the martyrs’ struggle. 2. How greatly the hope of eternal glory inflames the martyrs. 3. The martyrs’ progress. 4. Worldly and Christian military service. 2158–2159

**SERMON CCXXIV.** On the Martyrs, I.—1. Martyrdom is twofold. Whoever imitates the martyrs reaches fellowship with the martyrs. 4. The labor is made bearable by the fact that we are making our way toward fellow citizens whom we long for. And the greater the labor, the greater the reward. 2159–2160

**SERMON CCXXV.** On the Martyrs, II.—1. Those truly honor the martyrs who imitate them. 2. Neither imitation of the martyrs nor of Christ is impossible. 3. Especially in loving one’s enemies. The two feet of charity. 4. Whoever loves his enemies is a child of God. Whoever does not love is a murderer and is in darkness. 5. What is sinned against us is to be forgiven; what is sinned against God is to be punished. The remedy for sins lies within us. 6. One forgives easily when one considers how much one owes God. 2160–2162

**SERMON CCXXVI.** On the Martyrs, III.—1. Christ suffers in the martyrs. Their passion is a transfer to heaven. 2. The devil, unwillingly, grants the martyrs crowns. 2162–2163

**SERMON CCXXVII.** On the Martyrs, IV.—1. The martyrs’ fields are watered by a river of blood and tears. 2. The martyrs’ relics, like scattered ears of grain. 3. They will be reunited through the resurrection. 2163–2164

**SERMON CCXXVIII.** At the festival of Virgins, on the Gospel reading.—1. What is to be understood by the wise virgins and by the foolish. 2. The five senses are like five virgins: they may be corrupted or preserve their integrity. 3. Virginity alone is of no benefit. 4. Every faithful person is a virgin and the bride of Christ. 2164–2166

**SERMON CCXXIX.** On the Dedication of the Church, or the Consecration of the Altar, I.—1. What is accomplished in handmade temples is completed spiritually in us. 2. Due preparation for the sacred assembly. At times it is fitting to withdraw from it. 3. The crime of those who receive it unworthily. The punishment for this crime. 4. Temporary and eternal excommunication. Eternal punishments. 5. The reward of those who communicate worthily. The purity required for this. The wicked demonstrate that they do not love their soul. 6. Exhortation. 2166–2168

**SERMON CCXXX.** On the Dedication of the Church, or the Consecration of the Altar, II.—1. This feast is celebrated with joy. 2. Joy is not genuine for one whose heart is not pure and whose body is not chaste. 3. God desires to dwell in us. 4. The two altars in Solomon’s temple. God demands a twofold sacrifice from us. 5. Two fires: charity and desire. 6. Everyone’s heart is either God’s altar or the devil’s. The priest is the ambassador of the poor. 2168–2170

**SERMON CCXXXI.** On the Dedication of the Church, or the Consecration of the Altar, III; and on the words of 1 Kings, chapter X: “And the queen of Sheba, having heard Solomon’s fame,” etc.—1. The Church’s various figures. 2. The queen of Sheba represents it in many ways. The doctrines of the Church handed down by Christ. 3. The Church marvels at Christ’s wisdom: in the work of creation; in the house he built through the incarnation; in the food of his table—and what Christ’s food is. 4. When the Church sees the glory of the Lord, it will confess in words that he is greater. 2171–2172

**APPENDIX, CLASS IV.—SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS.** 2173–2174

**SERMON CCXXXII.** On the Holy Trinity.—1. Disputation concerning the Trinity is dangerous. This we know about God: that we do not know him. 2. By this knowledge we surpass philosophers and pagans. 3. The one who will be condemned is not the person ignorant of God’s nature, but the rash assertor. 4. What knowledge of the Trinity is sufficient for a Christian. A Jew is a Sabellian. The persons are distinguished by their properties, not by their nature. 5. What a Christian’s emulation should be. Same place.

**SERMON CCXXXIII.** On the Catholic Faith, I. 2175

**SERMON CCXXXIV.** On the Catholic Faith, II.—1. Christ’s two births. Two substances. 2. Christ speaks and acts some things as a human being, others as God. 3. As human being, Christ is less than the Father; as God, equal to the Father. 4. Christ’s divinity. 5. What should be answered to those who call the Holy Spirit a creature. 6. The Catholic faith: whoever professes it attains blessedness. 7. Curses upon all who believe wrongly. 2176–2179

**SERMON CCXXXV.** On the Catholic Faith, III.—1. One God, not solitary. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son. The Son is begotten from the Father by nature, not by will. 2. Christ’s two natures. 2180

**SERMON CCXXXVI.** On the Catholic Faith, IV.—1. The efforts of the Arians. The author’s prayers for the Church. The faith of the Fathers. 2. On the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 3. They are one in nature but distinguished by their properties. 4. On the mystery of the Incarnation. The error of Photinus and Apollinaris, and of others. 5. Christ truly suffered, but according to his humanity. Faith in the resurrection. The different rewards of the righteous and punishments of the unrighteous. 6. Errors concerning the substance and origin of souls; concerning God’s commandments; the Manichaeans’ and Cataphrygians’ views of marriage; others’ views of Christ; Jovinian’s views of merit; Manes’ and Jovinian’s views of free will. 2181–2183

**SERMON CCXXXVII.** On the Creed, I; and on the divinity and omnipotence of the Father.—1. God’s omnipotence is demonstrated by the greatness of his works. 2. By the ease with which they were made; by the creation of invisible things; and by their dissolution. 3. By the raising of human beings. 4. Faith in so great a God ought to inspire fear. 2183–2184

**SERMON CCXXXVIII.** On the Creed, II; or, On the Lord Jesus Christ, who without beginning is with the Father according to his divinity, but according to his humanity was born of the Virgin for us at a definite beginning.—1. In Christ there is one person, two natures. 2. Apollinaris and Arius oppose this faith. 3. Christ is proved to be truly human against Apollinaris. In what sense Christ is said to have been made from seed. 4. In Christ God is not changed into a human being; rather, the human being is joined to God. This, and everything he did, was for us. 5. Christ’s resurrection also was for us. 6. The final judgment. 2185–2186

**SERMON CCXXXIX.** On the Creed, III; or, On the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son.—1. The Holy Spirit is proved to be God by the testimonies of Christ, Peter, and Paul. 2. He is not inferior to the Son, whose offense is so serious. He also proceeds from the Father. 3. Because of his coming, Christ’s departure is advantageous. 4. In the Trinity there are three names, three persons, and one divinity. 2187–2188

**SERMON CCXL.** On the Creed, IV.—1. What each apostle composed concerning the Creed. 2. The apostles’ faith must be held firmly. 2188–2189

**SERMON CCXLI.** On the Creed, V.—1. The Creed of faith is a summary. Why it was so called. What each apostle contributed to it. 2. The words of the Creed are the Lord’s heavenly mysteries, which preserve grace incorrupt in us. 3. The distinct property of the persons, one majesty. Faith touches upon Mary’s virginity, not speech. 4. Only the Catholic Church is holy. 2190–2191

**SERMON CCXLII.** On the Creed, VI; for the Candidates for Baptism.—1. The Creed is brief and expansive. 2. God requires us to believe his judgments, not discuss them. 3. Why mention is made of Pilate. 4. Confession of the Trinity is necessary. 2191–2193

**SERMON CCXLIII.** On the Creed, VII.—1. The very one who is God is our Father. 2. How Mary’s virginity before and after childbirth is to be believed. 3. Whatever weakness there is in Christ is for our sake; whatever glory there is belongs to his own power. 4. Faith in the resurrection is necessary for salvation. 2193–2194

**SERMON CCXLIV.** On Faith in the Creed and on Good Morals.—1. The blessed Virgin remained without the stain of sin. 2. The humility of many is feigned. What Christ did for us. 3. What we in turn ought to do. 2194–2195

**SERMON CCXLV.** On the Mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation, I.—1. The three persons of the Trinity are one. 2. Yet flesh belongs only to Christ. This is illustrated by examples of the soul, the sun, and the lyre. 3. The Jew is refuted: a virgin could give birth. 4. The Virgin’s birth is demonstrated against the Manichaean by an analogy. 5. Aaron’s staff prefigured the Mother of God; and the nuts that sprang from it [prefigured] our Savior. 2196–2197 [Col. 2415]

**SERMON CCXLVI.** On the Mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation, II.—1. The Arians object with the statement concerning Wisdom, “The Lord created me,” etc. The reply: first, this may be understood of the wisdom given to Solomon; second, there are two natures in Christ, united but not confused. 2. He says that he was created with respect to his human nature, but with respect to his divine nature he existed before every creature. 3. They ask, “Was he begotten while he existed, or while he did not exist?” It is explained that he always coexists with the Father, and in what respect he is distinguished from the Father. 4. This is illustrated by the example of radiance. 5. They reply that he was created, not begotten. If that were so, he would be a servant and should not be worshiped. The worship of Christ’s body. 2198–2200

**SERMON CCXLVII.** Why Christ was born and suffered.—1. Wisdom could have brought humanity back to itself by power. It preferred to accomplish this gently. This was the reason for assuming humanity, and yet it was not thereby diminished. 2. Nor did he add anything to himself, for he needs nothing of ours. 3. The analogy between Christ and a skilled physician. 4. The mystical figure of the cross. 5. Especially its depth. In the mystery of our restoration, God is just in condemning humanity and merciful in redeeming it. He would have been unjust if he had restored the unrepentant. 6. How he prepared humanity for this grace. 7. The use and power of the cross. 2200–2203

**SERMON CCXLVIII.** On the Burial of the Lord.—1. The Lord’s tomb is like a womb. From it he is born more gloriously than from his mother. 2. The analogy between Joseph and the Lord’s mother. 3. Joseph places the Lord more truly in the monument of his heart. Christ’s spiritual tomb. 4. Why the Lord was buried in another’s tomb. 5. Mary Magdalene prophesies unknowingly. 2204–2205

**SERMON CCXLIX.** On the Final Judgment, I.—1. The priest must not seek to preach what pleases people. He should act like a physician. 2. He will have to give an account of his own salvation and that of the peoples. 3. Remembering God’s benefits is a defense against sins. 4. What account of these must be given again on the day of judgment. The sinner lays upon Christ a cross more grievous than the first. 5. The punishment of the condemned. Repentance must be undertaken while we are here. 6. It must not be postponed by anyone. The religious habit. 2206–2208

**SERMON CCL.** On the Final Judgment, II.—1. The pursuits of a corrupted life. 2. Exhortation to repentance and good works. Confession and repentance imposed by priests. Alms from stolen goods. 2209

**SERMON CCLI.** On the Final Judgment, III.—Eternal punishments. 2210

**SERMON CCLII.** An admonition that God should be praised not only with the tongue but also in morals and works, since what is thought in the heart is what proceeds in action; and on purgatorial punishments and the pit of hell.—1. One must always do good here, lest one later repent in vain of having done evil. 2. Eternal punishments. 3. Purgatorial punishments. 2210–2212

**SERMON CCLIII.** On the Confession of Sins, and that the devil desires us not to confess our sins at all, so that we may appear guilty before the tribunal of the eternal Judge; whereas God wants us humbly to confess our evils in this age, so that we may deserve to be freed from them in the future.—1. The commandment of confession. Why God gave this command. Let us not fulfill the devil’s efforts. 2. The mathematicians refer sin to the stars; the Manichaeans, to a nation of darkness; many, to the devil. 3. The devil persuades but does not compel one to sin. It is free for a human being to consent. 4. Excuses for sins. They do not remove sins but their remedy. 5. Confession is the beginning of health. 6. The severity of the one who reproves is gentle. 7. The flatterer’s caress is the sinner’s oil. 2212–2214

**SERMON CCLIV.** On the Confession of Sins and Repentance.—1. The necessity of confession. How useful it is, and for whom. 2. The repentance of the condemned is fruitless. A double torment. The repentant person’s tears should be twofold. 3. True repentance is measured not by years but by contrition of heart. 2215–2216

**SERMON CCLV.** On Repentance.—Those conscious of crimes withdraw from communion. It would be better for them to make themselves worthy of it—through swift and laborious repentance, that is. What should be thought concerning a penitent person at the point of death. 2216

**SERMON CCLVI.** An admonition showing the difference between the repentance that is always practiced together with good works and that which is undertaken in illness or at the end of life.—1. Does a dying person who has accepted repentance obtain forgiveness? The one who has continually exercised himself in repentance and good works does obtain it. 2. The one who has lived in sins also obtains it—but under what condition? 3. It should be judged harshly in the case of one who has not demonstrated repentance through works. 4. It is safer to practice repentance continually, since the hour of death is uncertain. What that continual repentance consists in. 2217–2218

**SERMON CCLVII.** An admonition that those conscious of capital crimes should, without any concealment, have recourse to the remedy of repentance.—1. Presumption and despair concerning forgiveness. Repentance must not be postponed or regarded with shame. 2. Repentance is necessary for everyone. An enumeration of minor sins. They can be redeemed only by God’s mercy. 3. Whom late repentance benefits. How unjustly and dangerously it is awaited. 4. Both minor and grave sins should be redeemed immediately. A false hope and a false despair. 2219–2221

**SERMON CCLVIII.** As above.—1. So that the fallen person may rise quickly. How dangerous it is to heap sins upon sins. 2. So that no one, however guilty, may despair of God’s mercy, but may hasten without delay to reconcile himself to it. The example of David. 3. Likewise the example of Ahab, Manasseh, and the prostitute who washed the Lord’s feet. 4. Let the person who was not ashamed to commit things requiring repentance not be ashamed to repent. 2221–2223

**SERMON CCLIX.** An admonition that, since sins are always creeping in, repentance should always be practiced for them, and no one should, through dangerous pretense, reserve repentance for the end of life rather than practice it.—1. No one here should abandon repentance, since we sin daily and tender sins are more easily torn away. 2. Daily repentance is recommended through familiar examples. 3. The fruit of that repentance. A sinner cannot dwell within himself; therefore he seeks distractions, but by this increases his restlessness. From what source he could more truly turn it away. 4. Even minor sins must be carefully expiated. 2223–2225

**SERMON CCLX.** An admonition excerpted from the books of the ancient Fathers, that whoever recognizes that he has committed capital crimes should, without any concealment, have recourse to the remedy of repentance.—1. Confession
[a plank after shipwreck.] The dead soul is raised to life by tears, but not by almsgiving alone. 2. The almsgiving of the sinner. 3. Conclusion.

**2226 — SERMON CCLXI.** An admonition concerning those who ask for public penance.—1. Why public penance is sought. The penitent’s clothing. Supplication. 2. It is inhuman not to be moved by this prayer. Nor does God despise the Church’s prayers for the penitent. 3. Nevertheless, the penitent must not therefore abstain from good works. Wine and meat are forbidden to him.
