**2227–2228 — SERMON CCLXII.** Concerning penance.—1. The effects of penance. It should correspond to the offenses. Crimes subject to public penance. The rationale of public penance. 2. Tears must be added on account of the destruction of one’s only soul. Why the soul is “one.” Nor should works of mercy be lacking. 3. The poor too can accomplish these things. Why God has permitted there to be poor. 4. After life there is no opportunity for works of mercy. The merits of the blessed’ clothing. A poor person can enrich another.

**2229–2230 — SERMON CCLXIII.** An admonition to those who think that it is sufficient for them for eternal life if they have done no evil, even if they have been unwilling to fulfill good works.—1. Abstaining from evil is not sufficient. 2. Whether the person who has taken nothing belonging to another will be secure at the judgment. 3. Whether one may rightly wish to be on the day of death as he was on the day of Baptism. Illustrated by examples. 4. Recapitulation.

**2231–2233 — SERMON CCLXIV.** An exposition of faith and an interpretation of its name.—1. The praises of faith are celebrated by everyone. Faith is called *fides* from *fiat* (“let it be done”). 2. For faith to be whole, one must believe both what God promises and what he threatens. For it to be true, one must do what ensures that the one is avoided and the other obtained. 3. Therefore, especially those things promised in Baptism must be fulfilled. Let no one here be secure. Faith is also endangered by idle speech. 4. The pomp of the devil. 5. Faith without works. The despairing person and the presumptuous person do not have faith. 6. Recapitulation.

**2233–2236 — SERMON CCLXV.** Concerning the Christian name accompanied by un-Christian works.—1. The Christian name is not sufficient. The sign of Christ. Who marks himself with it to his own destruction. Whom he presides over. 2. The Christian’s duty: that of a head of household; that of a judge. 3. What should be done on the Lord’s Day: in the churches; in illnesses. The effect of extreme unction. 4. What must be avoided in conversations. Dances before the basilicas of the saints. 5. Remnants of pagan superstitions. Superstition concerning Thursday.

**2237–2239 — SERMON CCLXVI.** Who are good Christians and who are bad. 2. Who is truly a Christian. 3. Who is unworthy of the Christian name.

**2240–2241 — SERMON CCLXVII.** An exhortation to the candidates for Baptism.—1. *Competentes*, “those seeking together,” as though they were asking together. What they ask for. 2. How those who prepare themselves to obtain it should act. Let them lay aside hatred. Let them restore what they possess unjustly. 3. Let them do penance for their offenses. 4. What they must avoid, lest they be cast out of the Church through abortion. 5. The office of sponsors. Both sponsors and those sponsored enter into a covenant with Christ.

**2242–2243 — SERMON CCLXVIII.** Concerning the observance of God’s commandments.—1. In observing God’s commandments, disciple and teacher must alike agree. Whoever does not observe them abhors life. 2. God’s kindness toward the human being, whom he draws to himself by threats and promises and whom he punishes unwillingly. A person merits according to what he wills.

**2243–2244 — SERMON CCLXIX.** An exhortation to hold fast to and preserve charity. This admonition also shows that no one will ever truly be able to excuse himself by saying that he cannot possess true charity. We believe that some statements from Saint Augustine’s homily, which he wrote concerning charity, should also be inserted into this sermon, insofar as it seemed useful to us.—1. Possessing charity is sweet, and acquiring it is easy, since the Holy Spirit pours it into the hearts of all Christians. Charity cannot coexist with covetousness. The sweetness of charity. 2. Its pursuits and works. 3. There is no excuse for these things. 4. Praise of charity.

**2245–2247 — SERMON CLCXX.** Concerning love of charity and hatred of covetousness; and that the kingdom of heaven can be purchased not only with two small coins but also with a good will; and concerning the pressing of grapes and olives.—1. Charity and covetousness cannot exist together. 2. What the rich person should do with his wealth. An increase of patrimony is desired unjustly. 3. There is less labor for good than for evil. The price of the kingdom of heaven. It is available to everyone. A good will is charity. 4. Whoever desires justice must expect to suffer from the wicked. 5. He thereby makes greater progress. The wicked are the winepresses from which the grape and the olive are pressed. We should pray for them.

**2247–2249 — SERMON CCLXXI.** Concerning love not only of friends but also of enemies, and that those who are enemies can be brought back into friendship.—1. Enemies must be loved. For God loved us even when we were enemies. 2. How unjustly the destruction of the wicked is desired. 3. The person who is wicked today may perhaps be better toward us tomorrow. 4. The fruit of prayer is the death of the enemy. The human being and the sinner are two different things. 5. All our hope lies in forgiving. The greatest sacrifice is offered to God. It is available to everyone. There are two kinds of almsgiving. Spiritual almsgiving is superior. 6. Exhortation.

**2250–2252 — SERMON CCLXXII.** Concerning the love of enemies.—1. In Scripture there are both ornaments for the healthy and medicines for the sick. The chief medicine is love of enemies. 2. The saints practiced this: Joseph, Moses, and Job. 3. David also practiced it, and what fruit he gained from it. 4. In what sense it is said, “You will hate your enemy.” 5. And also, “You will heap burning coals upon the head of your enemy.” The literal sense is not always to be followed in Scripture. 6. The heavenly Jerusalem has walls made of peace, impassable to those who do not keep peace. 7. Let nothing separate us from charity. 8. No one can excuse himself by saying that he does not possess charity.

**2253–2255 — SERMON CCLXXIII.** Concerning the love of enemies, II.—1. Charity is a great remedy for sins. With God’s help it can be possessed by everyone, since it rests upon a good will. 2. It is useless for anyone to say that he cannot love his enemies. 3. They produce a passage of Scripture in their own favor, but above all the love of God is indicated. God loved those who did not love him, and in this he wishes us to imitate him. Those who harass us are mad. 4. Love of enemies is not advice but a commandment. 5. Whoever loves only those who love him is no different from pagans and beasts. 6. Conclusion.

**2256–2258 — SERMON CCLXXIV.** This admonition explains how the pious and merciful Lord has placed in our power the manner in which we shall be judged on the day of judgment, and that there is one unique and singular remedy against all sins, and that no one will ever truly be able to excuse himself by saying that he cannot love his enemies.—1. God has provided easy remedies for everyone. The principal ones are the two kinds of almsgiving. 2. A person easily forgives an enemy when he remembers what he owes God. Moreover, those debts cannot be repaid in any other way, nor can those who do not repay them offer an excuse. 3. All their other works are useless. 4. Useless almsgiving. Why God wishes almsgiving to be given. 5. Recapitulation. 6. The mystery of the number forty. Whoever lacks the two is sick. Love of God; love of neighbor.

**2259–2261 — SERMON CCLXXV.** Why holy and just men took vengeance upon sinners in this world.—1. Why sins were punished bodily in the Old Law. Moses’ anger without irascibility. He burns with zeal for God and love of the people. The same should be understood of Phinehas. 2. Elijah’s disposition was no different, both when the soldiers were consumed by heavenly fire and when he ordered the priests to be killed, since he acted through the Holy Spirit. 3. What the mocking of Elisha represents. Why he asked for vengeance. 4. The same zeal in Peter.

**2262–2264 — SERMON CCLXXVI.** Concerning love of parents and tithes.—1. Parents are owed honor, love, and assistance in poverty. Some despise poor parents who may perhaps be better than they are. 2. The proper order of almsgiving. Of our resources: what belongs to us and what belongs to another. 3. Tithes are unjustly withheld, although by right nine parts ought to be owed. 4. The necessity and manner of fleeing to God’s mercy. Whoever does not give his surplus seizes what belongs to another. 5. Two kinds of almsgiving. 6. Sometimes worldly business must be set aside.

**2264–2266 — SERMON CCLXXVII.** Concerning the payment of tithes.—1. The offering of tithes benefits us. Tithes are the taxes of the needy. They must be paid from the fruit of one’s labor. 2. God reduces the person who refuses a tenth to the tenth alone. It is a kindness that he does not demand the nine parts. 3. Good use must be made here of good things. It is useless to reserve this concern for others. Whoever does not give tithes invades what belongs to another. The use of the other nine parts. 4. To prepare for Saint John’s Day. On that day pagan baths must be avoided.

**2266–2268 — SERMON CCLXXVIII.** Concerning augury.—1. The author’s struggle to draw the people away from diviners. 2. The devil attacks those who despise his deceptions. By this means God tests those who truly cling to him. 3. Why diviners often announce true things. Why danger is often not avoided except through them. To consult them is a grave sin. 4. Yet the devil cannot harm anyone unless permitted. God permits this for two reasons. 5. To believe diviners, *caragi*, and others is a mortal sin. Remnants of pagan superstitions. 6. Those who eat sacrificial food kill their souls.

**2268–2271 — SERMON CCLXXIX.** Concerning martyrs or amulets.—1. The various punishments of the martyrs. 2. Why the saints are handed over to the impious. Here we can conquer evils, not avoid them. The palm of martyrdom can even now be acquired. 3. Nor is a persecutor now lacking. 4. Those who consult diviners sacrifice to the devil and violate Baptism; having renounced Christ, they enter into a covenant with the devil. 5. More healthful remedies for evils. 6. What preparation is required for the festivals of the martyrs. 7. Neither despair nor hope wrongly.

**2271–2273 — SERMON CCLXXX.** Concerning the devout celebration of Sunday and the other feast days.—1. By whom and why leisure on feast days and Sunday was established. 2. Why it is called the Lord’s Day. It is distinguished by many features. 3. How it should be observed. 4. Various corrupt practices are censured: games, jokes, quarrels, and disputes. 5. The powerful force the Mass to be shortened. Judgments held on feast days. Banquets.

**2274–2275 — SERMON CCLXXXI.** 1. An admonition urging all the people faithfully to remain in the church until the divine mysteries have been celebrated. 2. When Masses are held. The Lord’s Prayer at Masses. Some hear it for judgment. How much good is accomplished at Masses. 3. The irreverence of those who leave before they are finished. Illness or necessity excuses one from guilt. 4. The whole of Sunday should be devoted to reading or prayer. 5. Conclusion.

**2276–2278 — SERMON CCLXXXII.** An admonition that the people should remain for the entire Mass.—2. The excellence of this mystery. With what posture and disposition the blessing should be received. 3. What keeps each person from remaining in the church. How they should be corrected by each individual. 4. And instructed through what they hear in sermons. This obligation is demonstrated from Scripture.

**2278–2280 — SERMON CCLXXXIII.** An admonition that one should pray attentively, and concerning idle speeches.—1. He urges people to come earlier to the vigils and not chatter then. 2. How one should pray. 3. Wandering of the mind in prayer greatly offends God. 4. For that is, as it were, worshiped which is considered with greater attention. What alone should then be contemplated. If it is altogether difficult for things that we may think about at another time to steal upon us in prayer, what of illicit thoughts? 5. For whom and for what we should pray.

**2280–2282 — SERMON CCLXXXIV.** Concerning a certain custom of singing psalms on the day of Epiphany.—1. Concerning the new custom of singing psalms. 2. Let the morals harmonize with the tongue; let pious dispositions accord with the voices. 3. How these dispositions should be formed while singing psalms.

**2282–2283 — SERMON CCLXXXV.** Concerning the rite of singing psalms, etc.—1. Let the knees be bent for prayer. This should follow the singing of the Psalms. 2. Let it not be done while standing. 3. He grieves over those who come late to the vigils and neglect the word of God. The word of God is rain and light.

**2284 — SERMON CCLXXXVI.** That the knees should be bent in prayer, and concerning the avoidance of idle words.—1. Let the knees be bent for prayers, or, because of bodily weakness, let the back and head be inclined. The tax collector, observing this, is heard; the Pharisee, neglecting it, is despised. 2. Whoever denies that there is serious sin in himself. If there is a stain on clothing, how much more should one fear a stain in the soul. 3. We display this bodily lowering to a human being. The saints displayed it in their prayers, and Christ himself did so. 4. Otherwise one cannot drink from the fountain of grace. 5. Nor receive the dew of divine blessing. 6. In church one should either pray or sing psalms. 7. The devil attacks most fiercely those who are armed against him.

**2285–2287 — SERMON CCLXXXVII.** Concerning the danger of the priest and the correction of plunderers.—1. The burdens of priests. They are bound to preach. Who are those who contradict them. 2. Another objection.

**2287–2288 — SERMON CCLXXXVIII.** A chastisement of those who have wives and commit adultery, neither being ashamed nor afraid; or who, before or after marriage, have wished to take concubines into an unhappy union.—1. Four necessary virtues. 2. Chastity is rare. Adulterers are many. They are often admonished by the bishop. But they must also be corrected by each individual. Otherwise he becomes a participant in their sins. Those who are corrected but not reformed should be reported to the bishop. Because of one criminal person, the commonwealth is sometimes punished. 3. Men think adultery is permitted to them; it is no more permitted to them than to women. 4. These are mortal sins. Sometimes even having intercourse with one’s wife is not without sin. 5. Concubinage is very common. It is not considered a sin. It is a sin worse than adultery. 6. The sermon is like a mirror.

**2288–2291 — SERMON CCLXXXIX.** Concerning chastity.—1. Age does not excuse the lack of self-control of the young. 2. The law of justice condemns it if they are married—and even if they are not yet married. 3. Fornication is thought to be permitted to men, but not to women. Both sexes are bound by the same laws. 4. Concubinage. It was never permitted. It is more criminal than adultery. 5. It is practiced by many, and therefore is not punished by excommunication. Whoever is not a virgin does not deserve the nuptial blessing. 6. Adulterers lack fidelity. 7. Those whose occupations separate them from their wives for a long time offer excuses. By this they condemn themselves. 8. The wantonness of soldiers is restrained. 9. Conclusion.

**2291–2294 — SERMON CCXC.** Concerning continence.—1. The commandments and necessity of continence. 2. What it consists in. 3. Its principal part: guarding the heart.

**2294–2295 — SERMON CCXCI.** Concerning chastity and purity.—1. The praise of chastity. By what consideration the habitation of the devil, impurity, should be restrained. 2. What must be avoided by turning away from it. 3. A return to the praise of chastity. It exceeds no one’s strength. It is necessary for the ministers of Christ.

**2296 — SERMON CCXCII.** Concerning marital chastity.—1. True peace and justice, for which the martyrs should intercede. Virginity before marriage. 2. Let no woman take anything to cause an abortion. How guilty is the woman who does what prevents her from conceiving. 3. Marriage contracts. 4. Stimuli to incontinence. Remedies. The chief remedy is almsgiving. 5. To have intercourse with one’s wife except for the desire for children is a sin. 6. It is not indeed a capital sin; nevertheless, if frequent, it makes the soul impure and disfigures the image of God. 7. When one should especially abstain from one’s wife. What punishments those who act otherwise generally suffer. Some are less continent than beasts. 8. With what disposition the author has addressed these matters.

**2297–2300 — SERMON CCXCIII.** Concerning careless familiarity with foreign women.—1. Peace possesses martyrs. Other vices are conquered by resistance; lust by flight. Familiarity with women must be avoided by everyone. 2. Among such associations chastity is greatly endangered. The hope of perpetual victory is held out in vain when victory over so harsh an enemy is rare. Such conduct also provides others with a very bad example. 3. Who are Christ’s persecutors and martyrs now. There must be absolutely no familiarity with a woman. How great the loss caused by momentary pleasure is. 4. Whether the damage can easily be repaired. Lust, the hammer of the whole earth. 5. How death enters through the windows.

**2301–2303 — SERMON CCXCIV.** An admonition that the evil of drunkenness must be avoided with all one’s strength.—1. Drunkenness is not even considered a sin. The friendship of drunkards is hostile. 2. Drunkards are compared with marshes. 3. They are depicted. 4. They make excuses concerning friendship. A guest must not be forced to drink. Drunkards are extravagant toward those like themselves, stingy toward the poor, and worse than animals. They lose both themselves and their possessions. 5. The evils of drunkenness are demonstrated by examples and words of Scripture. 6. Drunkards have no share in the kingdom of God. 7. How they may become unaccustomed to drunkenness. 8. Clerics are not immune from this vice. Pagan superstition.

**2303–2306 — SERMON CCXCV.** An admonition against the evil of drunkenness.—1. Drunkards are like shipwrecked vessels. They mock sober people as though they were not men. 2. By way of excuse they say that they were compelled. Yet they should have resisted even unto death. What martyrdom is, and how it is undergone now. 3. Drunkards are convicted of injustice toward God. 4. They scarcely consider drunkenness a sin. They will be punished with eternal punishment. Nor is it committed with impunity in the present life. Clerics, even those of higher rank, are subject to this vice. 5. Drinking bouts after banquets under various names. There are only two places after this life. 6. Drunkards must be chastised. 7. The custom of certain country people.

**2307–2309 — SERMON CCXCVI.** An admonition showing that from the beginning of the world all Scripture has blessed the humble and cursed those who persist in pride.—1. Scripture everywhere blesses the poor and curses sinners. 2. With what disposition one is to curse in Scripture. 3. The proud are signified by sinners, the humble by the poor. 4. Poverty benefits many people not at all. Wealth harms certain rich people not at all. Poverty is useless if it is proud. If it is humble, it is to be heaped with blessings. 5. Two cities formed from the humble and the proud. 6. Whose necks God will break. 7. Neither covetousness exists without pride nor charity without humility.

**2312 — SERMON CCXCVII.** Concerning humility and fear of the Lord.—1. God demands humility from his own. By this virtue heaven is ascended. Without it there is neither the grace of the Holy Spirit nor the light of truth—no good thing. What it achieves before God. Humility does not exist without the fear of God. There is one fear belonging to sons and another belonging to servants. The fear of God drives out sins, and thus also the fear of hell. 3. From this come peace and every good thing.

**2313–2314 — SERMON CCXCVIII.** Concerning temporal adversity.—1. Calamities must be attributed to our sins. What they produce in the good and the wicked. Worldly hope is bitter. 2. A description of shameful devastation. 3. Christ’s yoke is easy. Many prefer to it the yoke of greed.

**2315–2316 — SERMON CCXCIX.** Concerning hungering and thirsting for the word of God.—1. What it means to hunger for justice. The people have the right to demand the word of God from the priest. 2. The priests’ obligation to deliver it. The word of God is money to be doubled. 3. It is food for the soul. 4. Priests should prepare the milk of God’s word like cows. The people, like calves, should earnestly seek it. Caesarius likes to be importuned about this matter.

**2317–2318 — SERMON CCC.** How the word of God should be received.—1. His fatherly concern for the weak. He reproves women lying on the ground as though on beds. 2. The word of God is nothing less than the body of Christ. 3. The preacher is a distributor of spiritual gems. 4. And like a mother eager to adorn her daughter. What payment he should demand for his labor. 5. Conclusion.

**2319–2320 — SERMON CCCI.** An admonition that harsh preaching for the salvation of the soul should not only not be rejected, but should be sought with ardent desire.—1. Let the priest not be more lax. Let him fear the punishments of Eli. Phinehas is praised for his severity. 2. Corrected sinners reply that they are not alone. 3. They add that the affairs of the wicked are no less prosperous. Why this happens. The necessity of affliction. 4. We must provide here for remedies that will endure forever. 5. Priests are spiritual physicians: in what respect they surpass physicians of bodies.

**2320–2322 — SERMON CCCII.** Concerning the pursuit of wisdom, reading, and meditation on God’s law.—1. Nothing is better than knowledge of God. True knowledge. Perfect wisdom. Blessed life. 2. How many good things reading Scripture confers. The difference between this and prayer. 3. What should be done after the sacred readings.

**2323–2324 — SERMON CCCIII.** An admonition to the people that they should strive to hear the divine readings, etc.—1. No one is excused from sacred reading—not for lack of time. 2. Nor for inability to read. The word of God is the light and food of the soul. 3. A peasant can both hear and retain it. He learns obscene songs. 4. So too the things that pertain to agriculture. 5. God’s farm and the human farm: what care should be given to each. 6. God’s rivalry concerning the cultivation of the soul, and the origin of tribulations. God demands nothing difficult in this. 7. In cultivating the soul, let what is observed in agriculture be observed. Threefold fruit and three professions: good virgins, widows, married women. 8. How what has been heard should be repeated to one another in confession.

**2324–2327 — SERMON CCCIV.** Concerning mercy and forgiveness.—1. Mercy is entirely necessary for a human being. By showing it to others, one earns it. In a judge, mercy and discipline must not be separated. Mercy must first be practiced toward oneself. 2. It is secured by forgiving others. 3. There are many kinds of compassion.

**2328–2329 — SERMON CCCV.** Concerning divine and human mercy; why God has permitted the poor to exist in this world, so that the rich would have a means by which to redeem their sins.—1. Through earthly mercy one comes to heavenly mercy. Divine and human mercy. 2. Almsgiving benefits us. Why God has permitted the poor. 3. Two kinds of almsgiving.

**2330–2331 — SERMON CCCVI.** Concerning almsgiving.—1. Who may be excused from giving a donation. 2. The necessity and efficacy of almsgiving. 3. The changed fortunes of the rich man and the poor Lazarus. 4. The rich man is tormented more in his tongue. He speaks to God on his own behalf. Because of the guilt of hardness, he falls into condemnation. 5. The reward of almsgiving is offered.

**2331–2333 — SERMON CCCVII.** Concerning the likeness of the elm and the vine, or what the rich and the poor contribute to one another.—1. The elm represents the rich; the vine, the poor servants of God. What they contribute to one another. 2. What punishments await the stingy rich person. Of what grace his grasping deprives him. 3. The commerce between the rich and the poor.

**2334–2335 — SERMON CCCVIII.** An admonition showing three kinds of almsgiving by which sins can be redeemed without labor.—1. God has provided easy remedies for sins. Therefore some are in need and others abound, so that the former may be healed by patience and the latter by mercy. 2. There is no excuse for distributing one’s surplus. Nor should children be enriched from it, since these things are not ours. 3. The second kind of almsgiving is forgiving enemies. This is easy for everyone. 4. Let no one say that he cannot give the almsgiving that proceeds from the heart. 5. The third kind of almsgiving. A good will is charity. 6. What and when things are to be set aside for giving.

**2335–2337 — SERMON CCCIX.** An admonition to those who give alms frequently in this manner and yet commit robberies and adulteries.—2. To change one’s life or endure. What almsgiving accomplishes if one’s life is not changed. 3. If it is changed, it is greatly beneficial. 4. Incontinence is reproved. It is thought to be permitted to men but not to women.

**2338–2340 — SERMON CCCX.** Concerning almsgiving.—1. The efficacy of almsgiving—provided it is not given from what belongs to another. Those who give alms from robberies are brought before judgment. 2. Mercy turns away God’s anger. Everything is God’s gift. Why he gave more to some and less to others. 3. The foresight of the greedy is futile. No one lacks what is divine, etc.

**2340–2342 — SERMON CCCXI.** Concerning almsgiving.—1. At the judgment, no destruction will befall the person who has acquired mercy through almsgiving. 2. Perfect mercy is not to wait for someone to ask. God acts this way toward us. Christ also acted this way. 3. Almsgiving does what God does. It is a second Baptism. It frees from hell. It must be distributed here and now.

**2342–2343 — SERMON CCCXII.** Concerning almsgiving.—1. Almsgiving is urged in view of divine judgment, because of the reward it receives. Wealth has been entrusted to the poor. 2. By this we show ourselves to be God’s children. Let money be safely kept. What would otherwise fall to an ungrateful person.

**2343–2344 — SERMON CCCXIII.** An admonition teaching that we must flee shameful thoughts and continually keep holy thoughts in the heart.—1. Holy thought guards; unholy thought destroys. When is thought concerning food and clothing holy? How one may become unaccustomed to the practice of evil thoughts. 2. Thoughts of lust are no more to be admitted than spittle on clothing, dogs, pigs, or dung in temples, or a prostitute’s kiss in public. 4. Which thoughts especially trouble us. Sacred reading is a remedy against them. Many love clothing more than the soul. Conclusion.

**2344–2346 — SERMON CCCXIV.** Concerning a demoniac who was delivered.—1. Why neither the demoniac nor the demon should be feared. Each person feeds either Christ or the devil. By his actions it is revealed what sort of guest he is. As many vices as a person has, so many demons he has. 2. The proud person is not without a demon, nor the envious, adulterer, or liar. 3. How medicine may quickly heal sins.

**2347–2348 — SERMON CCCXV.** Concerning the times foretold for Christians, and that the Church is not free from temptations.—1. The Church’s vengeance upon its adversaries. What must be considered in a persecutor. 2. The devil first attacked the Church as a lion, then as a dragon when he flatters. Concerning flatteries. 4. Praise and blame should be considered of little importance. 5. What has been heard should be pondered repeatedly.

**2348–2351 — SERMON CCCXVI.** Concerning Saint Lawrence.—1. The saints, inflamed by hope, were stirred to endurance. 2. They are made white by the Lamb’s blood. 3. Lawrence is compared with Stephen.

**2351–2352 — SERMON CCCXVII.** On the feast of the martyrs of Massa Candida.—Whence Massa Candida (“White Mass”) received its name. From whom it was gathered. In the same place.

[Col. 2421]

## [NOTE]

At the end of volume XI of the Benedictine edition, besides quite a few additions pertaining to the present volume V—which we have interwoven in their proper natural place in the course of the volume—there occur, in addition, several notes which it will not be out of place to place here before the eyes of readers.

1. Thus, at column 1579, note 2, after the words “I do not want you to have such a *byrrhus*,” which it does not contain, add:

> “And in the *Expositions on Psalm 130*, no. 10: ‘If your garment is torn, you do not say, “He tore my *byrrhus*,” but, “He tore me.” If your garment, which is not you but your garment, could and deserved to be called “you,” etc.’ Messianus, etc.”

2. Column 1866, note (b), in place of these words concerning Sermon 64 of the Appendix—“but has the preface and conclusion borrowed from elsewhere”—the following should be substituted:

> “It was restored to Ivo of Chartres and published among his works at Paris in the year 1647.”

3. Column 1895, Sermon 77, no. 1, line 7, instead of *attendite*, etc., read, with the old Colbertine manuscript:

> “*Contendite*, and frequently read this divine reading in your homes, and hear it willingly and obediently in church. As, etc.”

And shortly afterward in the same place, instead of *sceleratis* (“the wicked”), read with the same manuscript *sterilibus* (“the barren”); and again below, no. 2, lines 6–7, in place of the words *nobis praedestinatum est* (“was predestined for us”), the aforesaid manuscript has only *propter nos* (“for us”).

4. Column 2011, note (b), after the words “there was need,” add:

> “Although what was said above may suitably be interpreted in this way: namely, that in these passages Christ is said to be reborn or consecrated not for himself but for us, especially since it is taught there more than once that the waters or John contributed nothing to Christ, but, on the contrary, that through Christ much was contributed to the waters and to John.”

5. In column 2055, in place of note (b), which concerns Sermon 163, the Reverend Fathers advise that the following be substituted:

> “Except for the conclusion, beginning with the words ‘but we, most beloved, who [fragmentary: *qui nullis*],’ etc., which unmistakably breathes the spirit of Caesarius, the rest [of the aforesaid sermon] has the flavor of Eusebius or Faustus. Here, indeed, in no. 3, it is suggested that Christ’s death was necessary for our restoration; whereas in the preceding Sermon 161, no. 2, Faustus teaches that Christ could have struck down the enemy of the human race by majesty alone, without the humility of the Incarnation and without the contest of the Passion. But the preceding words can be interpreted as referring to a necessity of fittingness or even of justice—the causes of which kind of necessity Eusebius the commonly circulated author explains in Homily 6 on Easter, although there he grants that God could absolutely have freed humanity by a mere nod of his majesty.”

6. Column 2087, in the final note, which concerns Sermon 182, after the word *mittendus*, supply:

> “We have discovered those same words, as well as the preceding ones in the same no. 1—‘another Paraclete, that is, of similar glory or nature, and of the same substance,’ etc.—in book 1 *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 9. Although this work is commonly attributed to the deacon Paschasius, many now reasonably restore it to Faustus of Riez, as we proved in the new edition of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, p. 1200, note (g).”

7. Finally, column 2291, at the end of no. 5, the Maurist Fathers note:

> “What is stated here concerning the Roman custom of denying the nuptial blessing to those who have not been virgins is confirmed by these words of Innocent I’s letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 10: ‘Nor can a corrupted man be blessed with his bride.’ See Jonah of Orléans, *On Lay Instruction*, book 2, at the beginning of chapter 2.”

M.
